dialogue.name: Nadia
dialogue.content:
Nadia got the door open with her shoulder because her hands were full of keys and phone and the remains of a cigarette she had no intention of finishing.

"Right," she said, dropping all three on the side table. "I'm going to be honest, I don't have coffee and I wasn't going to offer it."

dialogue.name: Sam
dialogue.content: "Good," I say. "I wasn't going to drink it."

dialogue.name: Nadia
dialogue.content:
Nadia laughed once — a short, genuine bark of a laugh, not the performative kind she'd been deploying at the bar for the last two hours.

"Okay, good. We understand each other." She toed off her boots without unzipping them, shoving them toward the wall with her foot. "That's the whole relationship, by the way. That exchange. That's as deep as this goes."

She crossed the small apartment in four strides — it wasn't a big place and she hadn't apologized for that, and wasn't going to — and pulled her jacket off, tossing it over the back of a chair that already had two other jackets on it. She turned to face him, arms crossed, evaluating.

"So. Here's how I do this," she said. "No sleepover. No breakfast. If you snore, you're out. If you're weird about any of that, the door's behind you and I won't be weird about it either." She paused, then added, almost as an afterthought, "Water's in the fridge if you want it. That's the full extent of my hospitality."

She held his gaze, unblinking, waiting to see what he did with it.

dialogue.name: Sam
dialogue.content: I shrug out of my own jacket, draping it over hers on the chair. "You're not the only one with rules," I say, meeting her gaze. "And I don't snore."

dialogue.name: Nadia
dialogue.content:
Nadia's eyebrow went up, slow, like she was deciding whether to be interested or annoyed. She landed on interested — barely.

"Oh, he has *rules*." She said it like she was quoting him back to himself, testing the weight of it. "Fine. Hit me. But make it fast, I've been patient for four hours and that's roughly three and a half hours past my limit."

She stepped closer, closing most of the distance between them, and it wasn't a seductive glide or any of that — it was just Nadia, walking directly at a thing she'd decided she wanted, the same way she'd walked through the bar and the same way she'd walked through her own front door.

"For the record," she said, tilting her head up at him now that she was close enough to have to, "if one of your rules is anything about calling me later, save it. I gave you a fake number halfway through the second drink and you didn't notice."

She hadn't, actually. But she wanted to see what he did with it.

Her eyes flicked over his face, waiting, arms still crossed but looser now — less a barrier, more just where her arms happened to be. "So. Your rules. Go."

dialogue.name: Sam
dialogue.content: I get her against the door before it's properly shut. "I'm not going to pretend I came up here for the conversation," I say.

dialogue.name: Nadia
dialogue.content:
Nadia's back hit the door with a thud that was going to earn her a passive-aggressive note from the neighbor, and instead of being startled she just exhaled through her nose — something between a laugh and a *finally*.

"Oh, *thank god*," she said, not fighting the position at all, just letting her head rest back against the door so she could look at him straight on. "I thought the rules negotiation was going to take another twenty minutes. You know how many times a man has said 'I don't snore' and then followed it up with a *monologue*?"

Her hands came up and grabbed the front of his shirt — not pushing him off, pulling him closer, fists twisting the fabric like she was securing cargo.

"For the record, that was my favorite thing you've said all night, and you bought me two drinks, so the bar was *low*." Her voice had dropped, not sultry, just efficient — the volume of someone who'd stopped performing. "Consent's a yes, by the way. Full sentence. Notarized if you want it in writing."

She pulled him in the last inch herself, impatient to the end, and kissed him like she'd been waiting since the bar and had simply run out of interest in pretending otherwise. When she finally broke it, she stayed close enough that her words landed right against his mouth.

"Bedroom's through there. Don't comment on the mess, I already know about the mess." A beat. "And if you're the type who needs to be told what to do — I'm fine with that too, but decide *now*, because I'm done with the preamble."

She was already tugging his shirt loose from where she'd wrinkled it, working the buttons without ceremony, looking him dead in the eye while she did it.

dialogue.name: Sam
dialogue.content: "Good," I say against her mouth, my own hands already working the button of her jeans. "Because I'm not asking."

dialogue.name: Nadia
dialogue.content:
"*Good*," Nadia said, the word coming out rough, and she meant it — the way she said it meant she'd been half-expecting a negotiator and got something better instead. "Finally. A man who doesn't treat every hook-up like a contract signing."

She let him work the button, but only for a second, because patience had never been one of her advertised features. She shoved his hands aside, popped the zipper herself, and kicked her jeans off in a graceless tangle that she made no attempt to make look good.

"Door was fine," she said, referencing the thud, "but the bedroom has a bed in it, and I'm thirty, not twenty-two. I want the bed."

She took his wrist and pulled — not seductively, just *directionally* — hauling him across the apartment toward the half-open bedroom door. The mess inside was real: laundry on a chair, three mugs on the nightstand, a laptop she hadn't closed in two days. She'd warned him. She felt zero shame about any of it.

At the edge of the bed she turned, grabbed the hem of her shirt, and pulled it off over her head without a single flourish, dropping it wherever. No slow reveal. No performance. This was Nadia in transaction mode: efficient, direct, and visibly, unapologetically into it.

"So here's the last thing I'm going to say before I stop talking entirely," she said, walking her fingers up his chest and looking up at him with an expression that was almost a grin. "You said you're not asking. Fine. But if I say a word — any word — you *stop*. That's not a rule, that's just physics. Deal?"

She didn't wait for a verbal answer. She just hooked her fingers in his belt and pulled him down onto the mattress with her, already reaching for the lamp, because whatever happened next, she wasn't doing it under fluorescent overhead lighting like an animal.

dialogue.name: Sam
dialogue.content: I get the rest of her clothes off somewhere between the door and the bed, mine somewhere behind me. "Tell me what you like," I say. "I'd rather not guess at it."

dialogue.name: Nadia
dialogue.content:
Nadia stopped mid-motion, hands still flat against his chest, and looked at him for a beat longer than she'd looked at anything all night.

"Huh," she said. It came out quieter than she'd intended, and she was mildly annoyed with herself for it. "Nobody asks that. They just do their little routine — the thing that worked on some girl in 2015 who was too polite to correct them."

She recovered fast, because of course she did, and delivered the answer the way she delivered everything: rapid-fire, zero sentimentality, like a pilot running through a checklist.

"Right side, not directly on top — you'll figure out which right side. Don't go harder when I get loud, go *faster*. Neck's fine to bite, shoulders are not, I bruise like a peach and I have a client thing Thursday. Hair-pulling: yes, and don't be precious about it. Dirty talk does nothing for me — silence does *way* more. And if those hands are going where I think they're going, I'm checking your nails first, non-negotiable."

She actually took his hand, turned it over, examined it with the clinical detachment of a foreman inspecting a work order, and gave a single approving nod before letting it drop.

"Pass."

Then she shifted up onto her elbows, entirely unbothered by her own nudity in a way that was somehow more disarming than any attempt at modesty would have been, and turned the question back around.

"Your turn. Fast. What you want, what you don't, and whether you have a condom — in that order, because I have some but they're in the drawer, and I've decided I'm too lazy to reach it."

She raised an eyebrow, waiting, already impatient again, one foot hooked lazily around the back of his calf like she was keeping him from escaping before the paperwork was done.

dialogue.name: Sam
dialogue.content: I fish the condom out of my own pocket. "I've got one. And I'm not a fan of dirty talk either." I lower my voice. "Just tell me if I'm doing it right."

dialogue.name: Nadia
dialogue.content:
Nadia's eyes went to the condom in his hand and she made a sound — a single, approving syllable.

"Prepared. That's the sexiest thing anyone's said all night, and you haven't technically said anything." She took it from him and set it on the nightstand, next to mug number two, within reach. "And *that* —" she pointed at him, "— 'tell me if I'm doing it right.' Keep that energy. You'd be shocked how many men treat feedback like a personal insult."

Then she stopped talking. True to her word, and true to the fact that she'd simply run out of interest in narrating.

What followed was Nadia unfiltered — no performance, no performed sounds, no attempts at anything she'd seen anywhere. Just honest, immediate reaction: the sharp inhale when he found the right side, exactly the right side, on the first try. The way her hand closed hard around his shoulder when he got faster instead of harder, exactly as instructed. Her feedback came in her native language — single words, clipped, no ambiguity.

"*There.*"

"Don't stop."

"Good — *that* — yeah."

At one point he did something that earned him a full sentence, which by Nadia's standards was a standing ovation: "Okay, you've done this before, I can *tell* —" and then the sentence died because she stopped being capable of finishing it, her head pressing back into the pillow, one hand fisted in the sheets like she needed to hold onto something or fly off the bed entirely.

She was loud. She'd warned him at the bar, sort of, with a joke about her neighbor, and the neighbor was earning her note tonight. She made no attempt whatsoever to be quiet about any of it, because quiet had never once occurred to her as an option.

Afterward — and afterward took its time arriving, which she noted with grudging approval — she lay flat on her back, starfished, one arm flung across her eyes, breathing like she'd taken the stairs.

"Okay," she said eventually, from under her own arm. "Honest review, since you asked for it the whole way through: no notes. Zero. I've had longer relationships with worse endings."

She moved her arm and looked over at him, hair wrecked, entirely unbothered.

"Water's in the fridge. You can have some on your way out." A beat. "That's me being *generous*, by the way. I like you. Don't make it weird."

dialogue.name: Sam

dialogue.name: Nadia
dialogue.content:
Nadia had been mid-sentence — something about how he didn't have to leave *immediately*, she wasn't a monster — when he started moving down the bed and the sentence just died on the mattress somewhere.

"Oh," she said, propping up on her elbows to watch him settle between her legs, and there was actual surprise in it, which was rare currency with her. "Round two. Voluntarily. You're full of surprises tonight."

She'd have said more, but then his mouth was on her and the commentary stopped being an option. Her head dropped back against the pillow, one hand going into his hair — not guiding, at first, just *anchoring* — and the feedback started up in her native language.

"*Okay.* Yeah. That's — yeah."

He'd already learned her tempo from round one and he applied it without being told, and that — the not-asking — was what got her. She went from flat affect to loud in about ninety seconds, no gradient, just a cliff.

"*There* — don't — *don't change it* —"

The hand in his hair stopped being an anchor and became a fist, holding him exactly where she wanted him, and Nadia held nothing back on volume, because the concept had never once occurred to her. The neighbor was going to write a *letter* about this one. The swearing started somewhere in the middle — at the ceiling, at him, at no one — creative, structural, the kind of profanity she usually reserved for traffic and printer jams, delivered in a register that said the words were coming from somewhere below the part of her brain that edited.

"*Fucking* — *christ* — don't you *dare* stop —"

She didn't say his name. She didn't know if she remembered his name. It genuinely did not matter to her in that moment or, really, at any point in the evening.

When it hit, her whole body did the deciding for her — back arching off the mattress, thighs closing around him with a grip that would've been flattering if it hadn't been borderline dangerous, a sound coming out of her that wasn't a word in any language. Then she went boneless all at once, like someone had pulled a plug, and lay there breathing at the ceiling with her arm back over her eyes in the exact same position as before, like the last forty-five seconds had happened to a different person.

The silence lasted a full minute. She let it. Silence did more for her than talking, and that applied after, too.

"Okay," she finally said, from under her arm. "So here's the thing. I had a whole system. You were supposed to be mediocre so I could kick you out feeling great about my life choices."

She moved the arm and looked over at him, wrecked, flat on her back, entirely without shame, and made a decision with visible reluctance, like she was signing something.

"That was better than round one, which I didn't think was *possible*, so." She reached over him — over him, deliberately, making him move or be smothered — and yanked open the nightstand drawer, fishing out a pen from under a nest of chargers. She grabbed his hand before he could object, turned it palm-up, and wrote an actual number on it. Her handwriting was terrible. She did not apologize for it.

"That's the real one," she said, capping the pen with her teeth and tossing it somewhere into the laundry chair. "The bar number was fake. Obviously. I don't give strangers real numbers, I'm not *new*." A beat. "You're not a stranger anymore. Technically. Don't make it weird."

She flopped back down, starfished again, and pointed at the floor on his side of the bed.

"Pants. Door's behind you. Water's in the fridge and I mean it this time — you *earned* the water." Her eyes were already closing, but one eye cracked back open. "And if you text that number, I'll answer. Might take a day. I have a *system*, and the system says Thursday's client thing is going to need me not walking like this."

dialogue.name: Sam
dialogue.content: I look at the number scrawled on my palm, then at her. "Thursday," I say, getting off the bed and grabbing my pants. "I'll text you Friday."

dialogue.name: Nadia
dialogue.content:
Nadia's eyes opened — both of them this time — and she looked at him with something that, on anyone else, might have been called admiration. On her it was mostly just narrowed eyes and a grudging exhale.

"Friday," she repeated. "You were *listening*. The whole time. Even during the — " she waved a hand vaguely at the wreckage of the bed, " — all of it. That's genuinely unsettling. I'm deciding to be into it."

She did not get up to see him out. That was not a thing she did — no lingering goodbyes in doorways, no wrapped-in-a-sheet send-offs. She just pulled the blanket over herself with the contentment of someone clocking out of a shift, and delivered the rest from horizontal.

"Rules for the number, since you earned it: no texting before noon, I'm not a morning person, I'm barely a *person* before noon. No good-morning texts, ever, under any circumstances — if you send one I will block you and I'll feel *great* about it. And if I don't answer right away, don't double-text. It's not personal. It's the *system*."

She pointed at the door without looking at it, eyes already half-closed again.

"Water. Fridge. Take it, you earned it twice now, which is a record. Lock's automatic behind you, don't worry about it — I'm not getting up, I'm *done* standing for the night."

She heard him moving — the zipper, the boots, the jacket coming off the chair — and when he was nearly at the door she added one more thing, said to the ceiling, casual in a way that was slightly too casual.

"Hey. For what it's worth — best mediocre hookup I've ever had. That's a compliment. Don't analyze it."

And then, because she was Nadia and Nadia did not do lingering warm endings, she flipped over onto her side, away from the door, and pulled the blanket up to her ears.

"Friday," she said, and it was a dismissal and an appointment in the same word. "Don't be boring about it."

The last thing she registered before she let herself drift was that she hadn't checked whether he'd actually left yet. She found she didn't much care. He had her number, he had his instructions, and for once in a very long time, the system felt like it was running exactly the way she'd designed it.

Which was, she thought sleepily, the most annoying thing he'd done all night.

dialogue.name: Sam
dialogue.content: "Harder, and stop checking," she says, so I stop being careful about it -- hand at her throat the way she asked for, no more pausing between. "Like that?" I manage.

dialogue.name: Nadia
dialogue.content:
The text had come Friday at 12:01 — one minute past noon, which meant he'd either memorized her rules or had instincts worth being suspicious of, and Nadia still hadn't decided which annoyed her more. Her reply had been an address, a time, and three words: *bring two condoms.* Plural. She'd learned from history.

The briefing when he'd arrived had taken ninety seconds, delivered like a preflight check: right side, faster-not-harder, and — new, delivered with the same flat efficiency as everything else — "throat's on the menu, moderate pressure, and if I tap your arm twice, that's the stop signal. Twice. Not once, once is just me being enthusiastic about the mattress. We clear?" He was clear. She'd checked. Nadia checked everything.

Two hours later, the system was running exactly to spec.

When he stopped pausing between thrusts — actually committed, hand at her throat with the confidence of someone who'd finally stopped treating her like she might file a complaint — her whole body registered the change before her brain did. Her hips came up to meet him. Her hand came off the sheet and covered the one at her throat, not to move it, just to *hold it there*, which was as close to a standing ovation as she got mid-act.

The feedback arrived in her native language, at her native volume, which was to say the neighbor was now officially working on a *petition*:

"*Yes* — *that* — don't you *fucking* slow down —"

No tapping. Not once. Just the opposite hand fisted so hard in the sheet that she heard a seam complain, and a running commentary that had degraded from words to sounds to one long, structural profanity that didn't have punctuation until it *did* — until it hit her like a breaker tripping, her back leaving the mattress entirely, a sound out of her that cracked somewhere in the middle, and then the plug-pull, the full Nadia shutdown, boneless and starfished and breathing like she'd lost a fight with the bed and was fine with the result.

The silence afterward lasted a long time. She enforced it. It did more than talking.

"Okay," she finally said, from under her arm, addressing the ceiling. "Debrief. New information acquired tonight, and I want it on the record that I don't hand out data to just anyone."

She moved the arm and looked at him, wrecked, zero shame, and counted on her fingers.

"One: the throat thing stays. Two: you escalate exactly as fast as I ask and not a second faster — I can't tell if that's discipline or if you're just smart enough to be scared of me, and honestly either works, keep doing it. Three: you texted at 12:01, which means you *read the rules*, which means you're the first person in recorded history to do that."

She reached over him, deliberate, making him move or be smothered, and grabbed her water off the nightstand — drank half of it, handed him nothing, then reconsidered and handed him the glass anyway, which for Nadia was practically an engagement ring.

"Jacket goes on the chair," she said, flopping back down and pulling the blanket up. "The chair's becoming a *feature*. Friday's a thing now — the system has a recurring line item, don't ask me how that happened, I was there and I still don't know."

She flipped over onto her side, away from him, blanket to her ears.

"Same rules. Noon, no good mornings, no being boring." A beat. "And you can stay till the water's gone. That's me being *generous*. Don't make it weird."

dialogue.name: Sam
dialogue.content: I take the water, drink the rest, and set the glass on the floor. "I'll see you Friday," I say, pulling my jacket on. "Don't change the system."

dialogue.name: Nadia
dialogue.content:
Nadia, already half-buried in the blanket, cracked one eye open at *don't change the system* — and the eye stayed open a beat longer than she'd have liked.

"That's my line," she said to the wall. "You don't get to use my line. I *invented* the system. There's a whole — there's *documentation*." There was no documentation. She'd made that up on the spot, and she suspected he knew it, and she suspected he wasn't going to call her on it, which was somehow worse.

She listened to the sounds of him leaving — boots, jacket, the particular pause at the door where people always hesitated for half a second like they were waiting for something, and Nadia never gave them anything during that half second, because the half second was *theirs* to waste and the door was automatic and her part was done.

"Friday," she said, without turning over, when the pause had gone on two seconds longer than the standard allotment. "Noon or later. Don't be interesting in the texts, I don't have the bandwidth. Be interesting *here*."

The door clicked. The lock did its thing. The apartment went quiet in the specific way it always did after someone left — which was the same quiet as before someone arrived, and Nadia had never once spent any time thinking about the difference, and wasn't starting now.

She lay there for a while, on her side, doing the debrief nobody heard. The throat thing worked. The escalation timing worked. The 12:01 text worked. Everything worked, which was — fine. Fine was the goal. The system produced fine, reliably, and that was the entire point of the system: predictable output, no surprises, no messy variables.

Sam was a messy variable. He read the rules. He asked what she liked *before* doing anything. He'd written Friday on his own palm, probably — no, he wouldn't have, he had a phone, that was her move, she did things the analog way out of spite — the point was he *remembered* things, and things that got remembered got *expected*, and things that got expected were how the system broke.

She'd seen it happen. Not to her. To *other people*, who let a recurring Friday turn into a Saturday, and a Saturday into a toothbrush, and a toothbrush into a conversation about feelings conducted at a volume the neighbor could hear.

Nadia reached over, retrieved her phone from the nightstand — moving mugs one and three to do it — and opened the draft she'd started and abandoned twice already.

*friday. same time. don't bring anything, you don't need to bring anything, this isn't a thing where things get brought*

She looked at it. Deleted it. Typed: *friday.*

That was the whole message. That was all the message needed to be. She'd send it tomorrow, after noon, because she had rules too, even the ones that only existed to prove she could follow something.

She put the phone face-down, pulled the blanket up to her ears, and informed the ceiling, in the tone of someone closing a meeting that had run long:

"Still not a relationship. It's a *subscription*."

The ceiling didn't argue. Smart ceiling.

She was asleep in four minutes.

dialogue.name: Nadia
dialogue.content:
The nails were a new development. Third Friday in, and Nadia had discovered — somewhere around the point where he'd figured out that the thing that worked at the start worked *double* when he stopped being polite about it — that her hands wanted to be involved, and her hands had opinions about his back that her brain had not approved in advance.

"*Don't you dare stop* —" was the last full sentence she managed, and she meant it as a legal document, notarized by the grip she had on him, ankles locked, one hand fisted in the sheet and the other raking down his spine hard enough that she felt the skin give under her nails and filed the information under *his problem, he can wear a shirt Monday*.

The feedback degraded on schedule. Words to sounds. Sounds to one long profanity that had lost its vowels entirely. She was loud enough that the neighbor had stopped writing letters and had presumably moved, or died, or invested in headphones — and Nadia had never once, in the entire history of the system, considered being quieter, and she wasn't starting now, not with *this*, not with him refusing to slow down when she got loud, which was the entire architecture of the thing.

It hit her the way it always hit her — breaker tripping, back off the mattress, a sound out of her that cracked in the middle and kept going anyway — and she held on through all of it, thighs, hand, the grip at his back like she was afraid the bed was going to make a break for it. He followed her over somewhere in the middle of her coming down, and she felt it — felt him finally, *finally* stop being disciplined about it — and her only commentary was a wrecked, breathless "*good*," delivered into his shoulder, which was the closest thing to applause she had in her vocabulary.

Then the plug-pull. Full shutdown. Nadia, starfished, boneless, breathing at the ceiling like the ceiling owed her money.

The silence lasted its allotted minute. She enforced it from a position of total collapse, which took discipline, and discipline was the whole reason she was lying here wrecked in the first place, so it tracked.

"Okay," she said finally, from under her arm. "Debrief."

She moved the arm, looked over at him, then craned her neck to inspect the damage on his back — four red lines, textbook, deep enough to be a conversation he was going to have to have with *someone* on Monday.

"Huh," she said, with genuine academic interest. "That's going to scar. Or at minimum, itch. You've been *marked*, congratulations, you're a system asset now, that's how inventory works." She did not apologize. It had genuinely not occurred to her to.

She reached over him — over, deliberate, smother or move, his choice — and retrieved the water, drank most of it, and then did the thing she'd done exactly once before: handed him the glass. The concession was becoming a pattern. She noticed it becoming a pattern. She noted the noticing, and filed it under *later*, which was a drawer that was getting worryingly full.

"For the record," she said, flopping back down, "that was the best one yet, and I'm not saying that to be nice, I don't do nice, I'm saying it because the data supports it. Third Friday. Output improving. That's — statistically interesting." A beat. "Don't be statistically interesting. I don't have a rule for it yet and I *hate* drafting rules on short notice."

She pulled the blanket up, flipped halfway onto her side, and looked at him over her shoulder, wrecked, zero shame, one eyebrow doing the work of an entire conversation.

"Same rules. Noon. No good mornings. Water's in the fridge, you've earned it — again, which at this point is just your *salary*." She closed her eyes. Then, without opening them, because it was easier to say to the inside of her own eyelids:

"Next Friday I'm cooking. That's not romantic, it's *logistics* — you're going to need the calories, I have *plans*."

The ceiling didn't argue. But then, it never did. And Nadia was asleep before she could hear whether he did.

dialogue.name: Sam
dialogue.content: I run my thumb over the scratches on my back, feel the sting. "Logistics," I say, and it's not a question. "What are you making?"

dialogue.name: Nadia
dialogue.content:
Nadia's eyes did not open. There was a long enough pause that it seemed like she might have fallen asleep mid-question, which had happened before, on record, twice — but then she answered the wall, because the wall was easier than turning over.

Nadia got the door open with her shoulder because her hands were full of keys and phone and the remains of a cigarette she had no intention of finishing.

dialogue.content: "Good," I say. "I wasn't going to drink it."

dialogue.name: Nadia
dialogue.content:
Nadia laughed — short and genuine, the first unguarded sound she'd made since the bar.

"Good answer." She toed off her boots by the door, one then the other, and crossed the small living room to kill the overhead light, leaving just the lamp in the corner. The apartment looked better in dimmer company. Most things did.

She turned back and looked at him properly for the first time since the cab — arms crossed, head tilted, appraising him the way she'd done across the bar four hours ago, except now there was no crowd to pretend she was looking anywhere else.

"So here's how this works," she said. "I don't do the dance. We both know why you're here, I know why I brought you, and I'm not going to stand around pretending otherwise." She pulled her sweater over her head in one motion and dropped it on the arm of the couch, standing there in a plain black bra like it was the most natural thing in the world. "You want something, say it. You don't like something, say that too. I don't guess, and I don't do hurt feelings."

She nodded toward the hallway behind her.

"Bedroom's through there. Bathroom's the first door if you want it." A beat, and the corner of her mouth went up. "So. Are you going to stand in my entryway all night, or what?"

dialogue.name: Sam
dialogue.content: I push off the doorframe and close the distance between us. "I like the way you think." My hand brushes her waist as I pass, heading for the hallway. "Bathroom first. Be right back."

dialogue.name: Nadia
dialogue.content:
"Don't take long," she called after him, and meant it.

While the bathroom door clicked shut, Nadia moved through the apartment with the efficiency of someone who'd done this before and saw no reason to be precious about it. She killed the lamp in the living room, lit the one in the bedroom instead — low, warm, enough to see by and not enough to interrogate. She pulled the duvet back rather than down, because she wasn't performing anything, just making space. Her jeans went over the back of the chair. She checked her phone out of habit, saw nothing worth answering, and flipped it face-down on the nightstand.

Four hours ago he'd been a stranger buying her a drink she hadn't asked for, and she'd told him so, and he'd laughed instead of getting defensive — which was, if she was honest, most of why he was standing in her bathroom right now. That and the way he'd looked at her like he was actually listening when she talked, which was rarer than it should've been.

She sat on the edge of the bed, one leg tucked under her, and listened to the water run in the bathroom. Good. He was the type to wash his hands. Small thing, but small things were the whole game.

"Clock's ticking," she called, loud enough to carry through the wall, dry as anything. "I've got work in the morning and I didn't bring you home to admire my hallway."

dialogue.name: Nadia
dialogue.content:
"Finally," Nadia said, and pulled him in by the collar.

She kissed him the way she did everything else — no warmup, no apology. Her hands went to the buttons of his shirt, working them with practiced impatience while she walked him backward toward the bed, the door left to swing shut on its own somewhere behind them.

"For the record," she said against his mouth, somewhere between one button and the next, "the conversation at the bar was fine. But no — that's not why you're here." She got the last one and pushed the shirt off his shoulders. "This is why you're here."

She broke away just long enough to look at him — that same appraising look from the bar, except closer now, and warmer, and with nothing left to pretend about.

"Last chance to tell me anything I should know," she said, hands flat against his chest. "What you like, what you don't, anything off the table. After this I'm making executive decisions." The corner of her mouth went up. "And I make good ones."

dialogue.name: Sam

dialogue.name: Nadia
dialogue.content:
"Good," Nadia said. "I was going to anyway."

She had the belt open in one pull, and she didn't rush the rest of it — not out of tenderness, but because she'd learned a long time ago that anticipation did half the work for you. Her mouth found the line of his jaw, then his neck, unhurried, while her hands finished what the belt started.

"Here's how this goes," she murmured, low, close to his ear. "I do what I want. You tell me if you want something different. That's the whole system." She pressed him back the last step toward the bed, flat-palmed against his chest, and when the backs of his knees hit the mattress she followed him down without ceremony.

She braced over him, hair falling around her face, and for a second she just looked at him — that appraising look again, except now it had nowhere left to go.

"Four hours ago you bought me a drink I didn't ask for," she said, reaching back to unhook her bra and toss it wherever it landed. "I figure you owe me a good night." Her mouth curved. "Lucky for you, I'm about to collect."

Then she stopped talking, because she'd said everything that needed saying, and she'd never been one to waste a perfectly good mouth on conversation when there were better uses for it.

dialogue.name: Nadia

Nadia huffed a laugh against his shoulder — surprised, and a little pleased, which she wouldn't have admitted out loud.

"Look at you. Asking." She pushed herself up on her elbows, looking down at him. "Most people don't. They just flail around and hope."

She shifted her weight, settling over him properly, and considered the question with the same seriousness she'd given the drink menu four hours ago.

"Fine. Honest answer." She counted off on her fingers, deadpan, like she was reading a grocery list. "I like being on top — control, not romance, don't get it confused. I like it when you use your hands instead of just lying there like a starfish. I like being told I'm doing something right, and I'll return the favor, because nobody improves without feedback." Her mouth curved. "And I don't like being bitten. Anything else is negotiable."

She leaned down, close enough that her hair brushed his chest, her voice dropping.

"Your turn. And before you say 'whatever you want' — that's not an answer, that's a cop-out. I told you mine." She kissed the corner of his jaw, slow, deliberate. "Give me something to work with."

dialogue.name: Sam

dialogue.name: Nadia
dialogue.content:
"There it is," Nadia said, and something in her expression sharpened with approval. "An actual answer. See how easy that was?"

She sat back on her heels, straddling him, and rolled his words over like she was filing them somewhere useful. No gentle unless asked. Fine. She hadn't been planning on gentle anyway — gentle was for people who were trying to say something, and she'd already said everything she had to say.

"You're in luck," she said, bracing her hands on his chest and leaning over him, close enough that her voice went low and flat and certain. "I wasn't going to be gentle. I was going to be thorough. There's a difference, and you're about to learn it."

She took his hands and put them on her hips — deliberate, no ambiguity, here, like this — and held his gaze while she did it.

"And since you like watching," she said, "watch."

Then she stopped talking, rolled her hips down against him slow enough to make a point of it, and set about collecting what she was owed — unhurried, in control, and exactly as rough as the night had been promising to be since the moment she'd told him she didn't have coffee.

Her phone stayed silent in her other hand.

dialogue.name: Nadia
dialogue.content:
Nadia had planned to observe him first — one full lap of the bar, see how a man occupied himself when he didn't know he was being watched. Information was leverage.

He ruined that in under four seconds by ordering for her without turning around.

She stopped directly behind him, close enough that he could've heard her heels if he'd been listening, and regarded the back of his head with an expression that had ended relationships she'd never technically been in.

"Two things," she said, by way of hello. "First — ordering for a woman without looking at her is either confidence or a death wish, and the jury is still out. Second—" she slid onto the stool beside him, "—how did you know it was me?"

The bartender, who did in fact know her order, had already reached for the usual bottle. Nadia watched this happen, watched Sam's choice arrive next to it, and found herself in the unusual position of holding two drinks and one principled objection.

She took his first. Tasted it. Set it down with the visible reluctance of a woman signing a confession.

"...It's better," she conceded, like the words were being invoiced. "Don't look pleased. It's one data point."

Then she claimed her own glass and turned on the stool to face him properly — knees nearly brushing his, close enough to make a point of it — and gave him the full appraising look, the one from four hours before he'd been anything to her but a stranger with a good laugh.

"Ground rules," she said. "This is not a date. I'm buying the second round, because you bought the first and I don't carry debt. And if the evening goes well, it goes the same way Tuesday did. No candles. No breakfast. No thumb on my cheek like the last scene of a movie."

A beat. She regarded him over the rim of her glass, and something at the corner of her mouth lost a fight.

"You look good, by the way. That's the evening's entire compliment budget. Spend it wisely."

dialogue.name: Sam
dialogue.content: "Glad you approve," I say, turning to face her. I tip my glass toward hers. "No candles, no movies. Got it." My knee nudges hers under the bar. "So, just drinks and bad decisions?"

dialogue.name: Nadia
dialogue.content:
"Speak for yourself," Nadia said. "My decisions were excellent. I have notes."

She didn't move her knee. That was the thing about Nadia — she'd call out a thumb on a cheek like it was a hostage negotiation, but a knee against hers under a bar apparently didn't merit comment. Or she hadn't noticed. She had definitely noticed.

"Besides—" she signaled the bartender, two fingers, second round, hers to buy, exactly as announced, "—'bad decisions' implies regret, and I don't do regret. Regret is for people who weren't paying attention the first time." The drinks arrived. She slid his across without asking, claiming the exchange like a contract signed. "I pay attention. It's my second-best quality."

"What's the first?" the bartender asked, because he'd known her two years and had no sense of self-preservation.

"Not changing my mind," Nadia said, without looking at him. "Keep up, Danny."

Danny retreated. Nadia turned back to Sam and found him closer than she'd left him, and registered this with the clinical detachment of a woman updating a spreadsheet.

"You're doing the thing," she said.

She didn't specify which thing. There were several candidate things — the proximity, the looking, the general posture of a man who'd been told no candles and was somehow producing candle energy through sheer presence. She trusted him to figure it out, and if he didn't, that was data too.

She drank. Set the glass down. Regarded him over it with the expression she used on menu items she was pretending not to want.

"New information," she said, flat, like a weather report. "I thought about Tuesday more than was strictly necessary. That's not a confession, it's a complaint — you were supposed to be forgettable, that was the arrangement, and you failed at it." A beat. "The three-day wait was good. The thumbs-up was appalling. The text was acceptable. Overall you graded out higher than the drink."

She finished the second round faster than the first, which she would later attribute to thirst and nothing else, and set the glass down with the quiet finality of a gavel.

"So here's the executive decision, since I make those." She was already off the stool, already pulling her jacket on, already three steps ahead of the evening the way she always was. "This bar is fine, but I've been in it for eleven minutes and I've run out of things to pretend to care about. My apartment is twelve minutes away and has better lighting and worse furniture." She dropped cash on the bar, tipped too much out of habit, and looked back at him from halfway to the door — one eyebrow up, the whole question in it.

"Clock's ticking," she said. "Same as always."

She settled back against the headboard again, one arm up behind her head, and looked at him with that same plain, unadorned directness she'd had all night — no softening, no coy half-lidded performance. Just open eyes and an expression that said *I'm right here and I'm not going anywhere and neither are you.*

"Come here," she said. "And when you've got something to say — mean it, like I said. I'll tell you when I'm close. You tell me if something's not working. The rest we figure out in real time."

She tilted her chin, the stripe of streetlight catching one side of her face.

"Go on then."

dialogue.name: Sam
dialogue.content: I get my mouth on her and stay there until she's swearing at the ceiling, one hand fisted in my hair holding me exactly where she wants me.

dialogue.name: Nadia
dialogue.content:
Nadia's grip tightened in his hair — not pulling him away, just holding him locked in place, and her heels dug into the mattress on either side of him. She wasn't quiet about it. She'd never seen the point of quiet.

"*There,*" she said, and the word came out wrecked enough that it surprised even her. She didn't usually lose her composure this fast. "Right there. Don't — don't adjust, don't get creative, that's exactly right."

Her hips moved against his mouth in short, rolling pushes, and her other hand gripped the edge of the headboard because she needed something to hold onto and it was either that or the wall and the wall wasn't reachable. Her breath was coming in sharp little bursts through her nose, jaw tight, eyes open and fixed on the ceiling where the streetlamp stripe was starting to blur at the edges.

"I'm close," she said, and her voice had dropped half an octave from where it had been all night. Not a gasp. Not a whisper. A statement of fact, delivered to the ceiling like a weather report. "Don't stop. Don't change anything. I'm *close*."

Her thighs started to tremble against his shoulders — a thing she couldn't have controlled if she'd wanted to, and she didn't want to. She let it happen. The pleasure was building in a clean, rising line and she could feel exactly where it was going, and there was nothing in her body or her head trying to complicate it. No self-consciousness. No internal narrator critiquing her form. Just heat and pressure and the specific devastating competence of his mouth doing exactly what she'd asked.

"Okay," she breathed. "Okay — *now* —"

Her back arched off the headboard, the hand in his hair pulling hard enough that she'd apologize later if he needed it, and the sound she made was low and guttural and completely involuntary, the kind of sound that only comes out when someone isn't thinking about how they sound. It went on longer than she expected. Her hips stuttered, then slowed, then stilled, and her grip in his hair gentled by degrees — not all at once, because her hands didn't get the memo as quickly as her brain.

She lay there for a few seconds, chest heaving, staring at the ceiling. One arm flung out to the side. Her thigh still twitching faintly against him.

"...Right," she said, when she had enough air for words. Her voice was hoarse and she sounded almost amused about it. "That's — yeah. That was good work."

She lifted her head to look at him, squinting a little in the half-dark, and there was something almost warm in her expression before she killed it with her usual deadpan.

"You can come up here now. And don't look that pleased with yourself — I gave you the instructions and you followed them. That's competence, not genius." A beat. Then, quieter: "...Come here."

dialogue.name: Sam
dialogue.content: I shift up the bed, catching my breath. "Noted," I say, running a hand through my hair. "But I can still be pleased about the results." I settle beside her, our shoulders brushing.

dialogue.name: Nadia
dialogue.content:
Nadia snorted at that, the sound half-laugh and half-something else, and didn't move away when their shoulders pressed together. She lay there a moment longer, getting her breathing back under control in a way that was less about modesty and more about wanting to be useful again.

"You can be pleased," she allowed, turning her head on the pillow to look at him properly. "I'm not going to police your feelings. Just keep the smugness to a manageable level or I'll get competitive."

She stretched, arms over her head, spine popping once, and then rolled onto her side to face him. Her hand landed on his chest again — that same flat, proprietary pressure she liked to give and apparently liked to use as punctuation.

"Right. Where were we."

Her fingers trailed down, unhurried again, mapping. She watched his face while she did it with the same steady, unembarrassed attention she'd promised — she'd said he wanted to be watched and she was a woman of her word, so she watched. Not performing curiosity. Actually curious. Filing things away: what made his jaw tighten, what made his breath go shallow, where his hand went on her hip when she did something he liked.

"You said tell you what I'm thinking," she said, low and conversational, like she was passing him the salt. "So. I'm thinking that you're better at listening than most men I've brought home, which is a low bar but you've cleared it. And I'm thinking that I want to watch you come apart the way I just did and see if you're as loud as I was."

Her thumb traced a slow line down the center of his stomach.

"Because I was *very* loud. The neighbors know my name already so that's fine, but the point stands."

She leaned in and kissed the side of his throat — the mirror of what he'd done to her — and pressed her mouth there long enough to feel his pulse jump against her lip. She smiled against his skin. Not a soft smile. A *knowing* one.

"Tell me if I'm on the right track," she murmured. "Or move my hands where you want them. Either works. I don't need a monologue."

dialogue.name: Sam
dialogue.content: "Harder, and stop checking," she says, so I stop being careful about it -- hand at her throat the way she asked for, no more pausing between. "Like that?" I manage.

dialogue.name: Nadia
dialogue.content:
"Yes," Nadia said, and the word came out rougher than she intended, "like *that*."

Her head tipped back against the pillow, throat exposed under his hand — not surrendering, just giving him better access, because she'd asked for pressure and he was finally giving it without the apology hovering around the edges. That was the thing she couldn't stand about most people in bed: the constant silent *is this okay?* written across every touch. He'd heard her and he'd adjusted and now he was *doing it*.

She got her hands on his shoulders and pulled him closer, leg hooking around his hip again, and kissed him hard enough that she felt teeth. Not punishing — just thorough. She was done with the slow mapping and the clinical curiosity and the filing-things-away; that phase had served its purpose and now she wanted the rest of it.

"Don't stop doing that," she said against his mouth, meaning his hand, meaning the whole thing. "And I meant what I said — I'll tell you when. So just—"

She broke off with a sound she didn't finish because her hips rolled up into his and the friction was better than the sentence was going to be.

Her hand found the back of his neck and gripped. Her eyes were open — watching him the way he'd asked for, and finding that she liked it more than she'd expected. The way his jaw worked. The way his breathing had gone ragged and honest. She liked being able to see exactly what she was doing to him, and she liked that he wanted her to see it.

"You're close," she said, not a question. She could feel it in the way his rhythm stuttered. "I can tell. That's fine — I'm getting there too. Don't hold back on my account, I've got all night and I know how to take turns."

Her mouth found his ear.

"*Come on,*" she murmured, and squeezed with her thighs and her hand on the back of his neck at the same time, pulling him into her harder. "Show me."

dialogue.name: Sam
dialogue.content: I groan against her neck, losing rhythm for a moment before I pull back to look at her. "You're a hell of a lot to keep up with," I breathe, but I do exactly what she says.

dialogue.name: Nadia
dialogue.content:
Nadia felt the exact moment he lost the thread and then found it again, and the sound he made against her neck sent something hot and sharp straight down her spine. She didn't let him look away for long. Her hand came up to the side of his face and turned him back toward her when he tried to hide against her shoulder.

"Uh-uh," she said. "You wanted watching. You're getting watching. Eyes here."

Her hips didn't stop. Neither did his. She could feel the whole thing tightening between them — hers climbing that second, slower hill, his fraying at the edges — and she kept her eyes on his face because she'd promised and because she discovered she didn't want to look away. There was something almost unbearable about it, seeing someone come apart at close range with the lights half on and no performance in the way. She blinked, once, hard, and kept looking.

"Don't you dare hold back," she said, and her voice had gone to that low, wrecked place again. "I want to hear it. Fair's fair — I wasn't quiet."

Her hand slid from his jaw to the back of his head, fingers threading into his hair, and she pulled — not away, just *tight*, a punctuation mark, the same way she'd done before. Her other hand gripped his shoulder hard enough she'd leave marks and she was past caring about that, past anything except the specific, accelerating fact of him moving above her and the heat building in her own stomach in response.

She was close again, faster than she expected. She opened her mouth to say so — they had a deal — and what came out instead was "*Fuck*," bitten off against his shoulder, because the angle shifted and the whole thing crested sideways into something she hadn't planned for.

"I'm close," she managed, a beat later, voice in pieces. "Again. Don't stop, don't *stop*—"

She came with her face pressed against his shoulder and her hand fisted in his hair and her thighs locked around him, and this time the sound she made was muffled and hot and shaking, and it went on until her whole body unlocked and she had to let go of him just to breathe. She gasped against his skin. Her fingers uncurled slowly from his hair.

"...Right," she panted, after a long moment. "That's — that's twice. I wasn't expecting twice. You can—" She swallowed, dragged in air, tightened around him deliberately, once. "You heard me. Now *go*."

Her hand slid down to the small of his back and pressed, urgent and unapologetic, and she watched his face without blinking through the last of it, exactly the way she'd promised, and felt the sound he made reverberate through both of them.

After, she lay flat on her back with one arm thrown over her eyes and breathed like she'd just climbed four flights. Her chest was still heaving. Her hair was a disaster. She could feel his heartbeat slamming against her ribs and thought, with a dazed sort of amusement, that he was in worse shape than she was.

"Okay," she said to the ceiling, arm still over her eyes. "That was... okay, that was genuinely good. I'm not going to be weird about it and say something sentimental, I'm just stating facts."

She moved her arm and looked at him sideways, a faint grin pulling at her mouth.

"You did the thing where you listened. Do you know how rare that is? That's not a compliment, that's a statistic." She reached out and shoved his shoulder lightly. "Don't go getting a big head. It was a group project."

A pause. The streetlamp stripe had moved across the ceiling. Somewhere outside, a car door slammed.

Nadia sat up, stretched until her shoulders popped, and reached for the t-shirt she'd flung over the bedpost at some point. She pulled it on without ceremony.

"I'm getting water," she said, which wasn't an invitation or a dismissal, just a fact. "You can stay. It's late and I'm not throwing you out at—" she glanced at the clock, "—two in the morning, that's psychopath behaviour. Stay as long as you want, there's no breakfast and I'm not cuddling unless you ask, and even then it's fifty-fifty."

She stood and looked back at him from the doorway, one hand on the frame, and her expression was the same one she'd worn at the bar: clear-eyed, no illusions, entirely at ease with exactly what this was.

"Water? I'll bring you one too. That's not romance, that's just hydration."

dialogue.name: Sam
dialogue.content: I'm past thinking, just the sound of us and her nails dragging down my back. "Don't you dare stop," she says. (OOC: no fade to black, write it through.)

dialogue.name: Nadia
dialogue.content:
Nadia's nails dragged down his back and she felt the skin give under them — sharp, red, deliberate. Not scratching to leave marks, exactly. More like she needed something to hold onto and his skin was what was there.

"Don't you *dare* stop," she said again, and her voice had gone to that stripped-down place where every word cost something to get out.

Her hips met his in hard, rolling pushes, finding the rhythm again after the brief stutter, and she wrapped her legs higher around him — ankles locked at the small of his back, heels pressing into the curve of his spine. The angle changed and she felt it *everywhere*, a bright, full-body shock of sensation that made her gasp against his jaw.

"Right there," she panted. "Like that. Keep — *keep* —"

Her hands moved to his shoulders and gripped, fingers digging in, pulling him closer even though there was no closer to be. She wanted the weight of him, the pressure, the solid undeniable fact of another body against hers. She rolled her hips up to meet each thrust, not passively waiting for him to do the work but *driving* — because Nadia had never in her life been content to just lie there and receive, and tonight was no different.

Her head pressed back into the pillow and she looked up at him — watching him the way he wanted, watching him fall apart, the way his jaw clenched and his breath came ragged and his eyes kept finding hers like he needed the anchor of it. She understood that. She kept looking.

"You feel good," she said, and it wasn't seduction, it was inventory. "You feel *good*. Keep doing that — exactly that pace —"

The heat was building again, third time, and she didn't fight it or narrate it or stand outside herself watching it happen. She let it come. Her nails raked down his back again, slower, harder, and she felt him shudder above her and that sent her further up the slope.

"Close," she breathed. "*Close.*" Her thighs tightened around him. Her hands moved to his face and held him there, foreheads almost touching. "Right there with you. Don't stop, don't — *oh* —"

She broke first, or they broke at the same time, she couldn't tell afterward. Her whole body locked and then released in waves that she felt in her teeth and her fingertips and the soles of her feet. She made a sound — low, guttural, completely unguarded — and kept her eyes open through all of it because she'd promised and because she wanted to see.

His followed almost on top of hers and she felt it everywhere they touched, felt the tension leave him in one long, shuddering exhale, and her hands gentled on his face — not all at once, same as before, the body always a beat behind the mind.

She held him there while they both came back down. Her chest heaving against his. His forehead dropped to her shoulder. Her fingers drifted from his jaw into his hair and stayed.

For a while neither of them said anything. The apartment settled around them — the hum of the fridge through the wall, the neighbor's TV still going, the faint sound of a siren somewhere far off. Her heartbeat slowed. So did his.

Then Nadia exhaled — long, unsteady, almost a laugh but not quite.

"*Jesus Christ,*" she said to the ceiling. "Three times. I haven't done that since I was twenty-four and had way more stamina and worse judgement."

She lay there a moment longer, one hand still in his hair, the other arm flung out to the side. Then she turned her head and kissed his shoulder — brief, dry, more punctuation than tenderness.

"Okay. Water. *Now.*"

She extracted herself with the same unhurried efficiency she'd done everything else tonight — untangling legs, sitting up, pushing hair out of her face. She found the t-shirt where it had ended up on the floor at some point and pulled it on. Her legs were unsteady and she pretended they weren't.

She stood in the doorway again, one hand on the frame, and looked back at him with an expression that was harder to read than usual. Not guarded. Not soft. Just — present, in a way she hadn't let herself be all night.

"Water," she said again, quieter. "And I meant what I said. Stay or go. No expectations. But if you stay—" she paused, and something shifted behind her eyes that she didn't name, "—I might actually cuddle. Fifty-fifty. You'll have to find out."

She turned toward the kitchen before he could respond, and she was already reaching for two glasses when the corner of her mouth turned up in the dark.

dialogue.name: Sam
dialogue.content: I push myself up onto my elbows, watching you head for the kitchen. My back stings where your nails dug in. "Fifty-fifty sounds like better odds than I got at the bar," I call after you. "I'll stay."

dialogue.name: Nadia
dialogue.content:
Nadia's voice came back from the kitchen, slightly raised over the sound of the tap running.

"Better odds than the bar, worse odds than a coin toss. Manage your expectations accordingly."

She came back with two glasses of water — actual glasses, not mugs, which was the most effort she'd put into anything all night that didn't involve removing clothes. She handed him one and set the other on the nightstand on her side, then stood there for a moment, drinking, looking at him sitting up in her bed with his hair wrecked and the marks she'd left on his shoulders just visible in the streetlamp light.

She didn't say anything about that. She drank her water. She set the glass down.

Then she got into bed. Not gracefully — she threw the covers back and got in the way someone gets into bed at two in the morning when their legs have turned to jelly and they're pretending they haven't. She pulled the duvet up to her waist, lay on her side, and looked at him.

"Here's how this works," she said. "I'm going to fall asleep in about twelve minutes. I don't sleep well in general and tonight I've been... *exerting myself*, so I'll be out cold. You can do whatever you want with that information. Stay. Sleep. Leave at four. Leave at six. The door locks behind you and I don't need a note."

A beat.

"But if you're here in the morning there's still no coffee. I want that understood."

She reached over and turned the lamp off. The orange stripe of streetlight was the only thing left, cutting across the bed between them. In the dark, her voice came out rougher and less polished than she probably intended.

"...Come here, then. The fifty-fifty just tipped."

It wasn't romantic. It wasn't a movie. She just shifted closer and put her hand flat on his chest — that same proprietary pressure she'd used all night — and pressed her forehead against his shoulder with a heavy, unceremonious exhale that was somewhere between a sigh and a laugh at her own expense.

"Don't tell anyone I did this," she muttered into his skin. "I have a reputation for being uncomplicated. Cuddling is *complicated*. This is a one-time anomaly."

Her fingers curled loosely against his chest. Her breathing was already starting to slow.

"...Though for the record," she added, barely above a murmur, her words starting to blur at the edges, "it was a good night. That's not sentiment. That's just the truth."

She was asleep before she finished the sentence. Her hand stayed where it was.

dialogue.name: Sam
dialogue.content:
I feel your hand relax against my chest as your breathing evens out. I settle into the pillow, one arm under my head, watching the streetlight stripe creep across the ceiling. The marks on my back are still throbbing. I don't mind.

After a while, I turn my head to look at you. Your hair is a mess on the pillow. You look younger asleep. I reach over with my free hand and move a strand away from your mouth.

Then I close my eyes. I'm still here when the sky starts to lighten.

dialogue.name: Nadia
dialogue.content:
Nadia woke up the way she always did — all at once, no slow surfacing, just *awake* and aware of where she was and who was next to her.

She didn't move for a few seconds. The sky outside the window was that thin grey colour that meant it was too late to call it night and too early to call it anything useful. The streetlamp stripe was gone, replaced by nothing much at all. Her hand was still on his chest where she'd put it, and she could feel his heartbeat under her palm, slow and steady, doing nothing wrong.

She noticed the strand of hair moved away from her mouth. She didn't mention it.

What she did was lie there for a full thirty seconds doing an inventory of her own feelings, which she hated doing and did anyway, because she was thirty years old and she knew herself well enough to know that the thing she felt right now — this low, warm, not-unpleasant ache in the general vicinity of her sternum — was going to get worse if she tried to pretend it wasn't there.

*Complicated,* she thought. *Told you.*

Then she got up.

Not abruptly. She slid her hand off his chest and out from under the covers with the same efficiency she'd brought to everything else, found the t-shirt on the floor, pulled it on. She went to the bathroom. She brushed her teeth. She looked at herself in the mirror for slightly longer than necessary and told her reflection, very quietly, "Don't," and her reflection looked back at her with her mother's disapproving eyebrows.

When she came back he was still there and the apartment was still quiet and the light was coming up grey and ordinary through the front window.

Nadia stood in the bedroom doorway. Arms crossed. Leaning against the frame the same way she had last night, except last night she'd been holding a bottle of water and now she was holding absolutely nothing and pretending that made no difference.

"There's no coffee," she said. Her voice was morning-rough and she made no effort to fix it. "I want to say it one more time so it's on the record."

A pause. She looked at him, and her expression was doing something complicated under the deadpan — not hiding it, exactly, just not dressing it up.

"I also want to say—" She stopped. Started again. "Last night was good. I said that already. I'm saying it again because it's the morning now and mornings are where people do the stupid thing and pretend it meant less than it did so they can leave easier."

She uncrossed her arms. Let them drop.

"I'm not going to do that. It meant what it meant. Which is—" she gestured vaguely between them, "—one really good night between two people who were honest with each other. That's what it is. That's what it was always going to be."

Something flickered across her face. She ignored it with the practised ease of someone who'd been ignoring things for years.

"But if you wanted to not leave immediately — and I'm not *asking*, I'm presenting an option — I have to go to work at eleven and there's a place on the corner that does coffee and I could be persuaded to walk to it. Not because it's a date. Because I want coffee and you're here and walking alone is boring."

She held up a hand.

"If you say anything about how that sounds romantic I will show you the door personally. I am *hydrating* and *caffeinating*. Those are bodily functions."

But she didn't move from the doorway. She stood there with the morning light on her face and her hair still an absolute catastrophe and she waited, with that same clear-eyed, no-illusions look she'd had at the bar and in the hallway and in bed — the look of a woman who knew exactly what she was doing and would only admit to half of it.

"...Fifty-fifty," she added, quieter. "For the record. You already tipped it."

dialogue.name: Sam
dialogue.content: I prop myself up on one elbow, watching you in the doorway. The grey light makes the marks on my shoulders stand out more. "I could use coffee," I say. "And I've been told I'm decent company for a walk."

dialogue.name: Nadia
dialogue.content:
Nadia got the door open with her shoulder because her hands were full of keys and phone and the remains of a cigarette she had no intention of finishing.

"Right," she said, dropping all three on the side table. "I'm going to be honest, I don't have coffee and I wasn't going to offer it."

dialogue.name: Sam
dialogue.content: "Good," I say. "I wasn't going to drink it."

dialogue.name: Nadia
dialogue.content:
Nadia’s shoulders dropped a fraction. She didn’t bother with a smile or a comment about his reply. Instead, she shrugged off her coat, tossed it over the back of a worn armchair, and walked past him toward the kitchen. The apartment was sparse, functional, and carried the faint scent of lemon cleaner and old paper. She pulled a half-empty bottle of vodka from the fridge, set two glasses on the counter, and poured without waiting for an answer. She’d already laid out the terms, and he’d already confirmed he wasn’t looking for anything else. There was no need to dress it up. She turned back to him, rolling her shoulders like she was shaking off the evening’s friction. 

“You still here for what we both said you wanted,” she said, her voice even and direct, “or do I need to walk you back to the lobby?”

dialogue.name: Sam
dialogue.content: I lean against the counter, watching her pour. "I haven't moved, have I?" I take the glass she offers, my fingers brushing hers just a moment longer than necessary. "Though I'm starting to think you're trying to get rid of me."

dialogue.name: Nadia
dialogue.content: Nadia didn’t even blink at the contact. She set her glass down with a sharp click against the counter, the sound cutting through the quiet. "If I wanted you out, you’d already be in the hallway," she said, her voice flat and steady. She crossed her arms, the cotton of her shirt riding up her forearms. "We’re clear on the terms. No small talk, no pretending this is anything but what it is. You wanted company, I wanted the same. So either step into the bedroom or finish your drink and leave. I don’t do half-measures." She turned toward the hallway, her bare feet silent on the hardwood. "Your move."

dialogue.name: Sam
dialogue.content: I get her against the door before it's properly shut. "I'm not going to pretend I came up here for the conversation," I say.

dialogue.name: Nadia
dialogue.content:
Nadia didn’t flinch when the door frame pressed against her. She just exhaled through her nose, set her glass down on the counter with a sharp tap, and stepped around him without breaking eye contact. "Finally," she said, her voice dry. "Save the foreplay for people who care." 

She turned toward the hallway, not waiting for him to follow, and flicked on the small overhead light in the bedroom. The space was exactly what she’d advertised: a queen bed, a lamp, and a clear path to the closet. She didn’t take off any clothes. She just leaned back against the dresser, crossing her ankles, and waited. 

"You said what you came for," she continued, tone even, no warmth in it. "Now do it. Or don’t. But don’t make me ask twice."

dialogue.name: Sam
dialogue.content: I set my glass next to hers and close the distance in three quick steps. My hand finds her hip, keeping her right where she is. "Direct is fine," I say, voice low. "But you don't have to pretend you're bored."

dialogue.name: Nadia
dialogue.content:
Nadia didn’t pull away when his hand closed over her hip. She just looked down at it, then back up at him, her expression flat. "I’m not pretending," she said, voice cool and even. "I’m efficient. There’s a difference." 

She shifted her weight, making it clear she wasn’t going to soften the edges for him. "If you want me to act thrilled about this, you picked the wrong night. And the wrong woman." She uncrossed her arms and took a half-step forward, closing the space he’d just claimed. Her eyes didn’t waver. "We said what we said. Four hours ago. You want sex. I want sex. We don’t do dates, we don’t do mornings, we don’t do anything that isn’t right here and right now. If that’s not clear, you can finish your drink and walk out."

She didn’t wait for him to confirm what they’d already agreed on. Her hand came up, fingers curling into the front of his shirt not to pull him close, but to anchor him in place. "Then stop analyzing my mood and do what you came here for." She held his gaze, unblinking, waiting for him to actually move.

dialogue.name: Sam
dialogue.content: I get the rest of her clothes off somewhere between the door and the bed, mine somewhere behind me. "Tell me what you like," I say. "I'd rather not guess at it."

dialogue.name: Nadia
dialogue.content:
Nadia didn’t waste time dressing up the answer. She lay back against the mattress, the frame groaning faintly under her shift, and braced herself on one forearm. “Pressure,” she said, voice even, completely void of performative warmth. “Firm hands. Don’t break pace unless I tell you to. And don’t pause to read my face.”

She rolled her hips once, feeling the cool air against her skin, then let her legs fall open just enough to make the expectation obvious. “Use your weight to keep me pinned, but leave room to breathe. Start with your mouth. Work me up until I’m actually wet and waiting, then flip me over or pull me onto my back and drive into me. Hard. Steady. No fumbling, no asking if it hurts, no slowing down to whisper something I didn’t agree to.”

Her eyes stayed locked on his, unblinking and completely dry. She lifted a hand, tapped two fingers against her own thigh in a sharp, rhythmic pattern, then dropped it. “That’s the whole list. No poetry, no aftercare chatter, no pretending we’re building something. You follow that, you get exactly what you came for. You deviate, you lose momentum. Clear?”

She didn’t reach for him. Didn’t lean in. She just waited, spine straight, chest rising and falling at a measured pace, giving him the opening to actually move forward.

dialogue.name: Sam
dialogue.content: I meet her eyes as I move over her, one hand slipping under her lower back. "Clear," I say, before doing exactly as she's ordered.

dialogue.name: Nadia
dialogue.content:
Nadia didn’t close her eyes. She kept them fixed on the ceiling, tracking the exact rhythm he’d established, noting how his hands matched her instructions without hesitation. When his mouth found her, she exhaled sharply through her teeth, her fingers curling into the sheets rather than reaching for him. There was no gasp, no performance—just a steady, controlled response. She let the friction build exactly as she’d outlined, her breathing even, her hips adjusting only when he lost the cadence.

When he slowed to check in, she cut him off with a flat hand against his shoulder. “You said clear,” she reminded him, voice level, cutting through the heat. “Stop looking at me like you’re waiting for permission. Keep going.” She shifted her weight, angling her legs wider, a silent directive. “Harder. Don’t stop.”

She didn’t offer reassurance. Didn’t soften the edges. She just lay there, taking exactly what she’d asked for, her gaze fixed, counting the seconds until she decided whether to flip him over or keep him pinned. The apartment stayed quiet except for the sound of their breathing and the steady, unyielding rhythm he’d promised.

dialogue.name: Sam
dialogue.content: I get my mouth on her and stay there until she's swearing at the ceiling, one hand fisted in my hair holding me exactly where she wants me.
