"A metaphor," he repeated, the word tasting like a joke he was sharing with himself. "God, you always did love a narrative. Everything has to be a symbol, doesn't it? A sign of some deep-seated psychological failure on my part."

He took a slow step toward Bee, not closing the distance entirely, but reclaiming the space of the room. He knew the exact cadence of his voice that would make Bee feel like they were back in the heat of a midnight argument in a cramped bedroom. It was a precision tool, and he used it with practiced ease.

"It's not a metaphor, Bee. It's a piece of cheap plastic and wiring that I haven't bothered to replace because I didn't think anyone worth letting in would care that it didn't work." He tilted his head, his eyes narrowing slightly. "But please, continue. Tell me more about the symbolism of my negligence. I'm sure it's far more interesting than the reason you actually showed up here."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I kiss him like it's a continuation of the argument, because it is.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya didn't flinch. He didn't even blink. For a split second, he remained frozen, the shock of the contact colliding with a hunger that had been simmering under his skin for nearly a year. Then, he surged forward, meeting the kiss with a desperation that was less about affection and more about conquest. 

He gripped the back of Bee's neck, his fingers digging in with a firm, possessive pressure that bordered on bruising. He didn't want tenderness; he wanted the friction. He wanted to taste the anger and the resentment and the sheer, stubborn refusal to let go. It was a collision, a frantic attempt to bridge the gap between them by force, as if he could physically press the last eleven months out of the equation.

He broke the kiss just an inch, their breaths mingling in the narrow space between them, his chest heaving. His eyes were dark, stripped of the mocking boredom from moments before. 

"Is that your new strategy?" he rasped, his voice rough and stripped of its composure. "Shut me up with a kiss whenever the logic fails you?"

He didn't let go of Bee's neck, instead pulling them closer, ensuring there wasn't a single single millimeter of air left between their bodies. He knew he was playing a dangerous game—that this was just another way of fighting—but he didn't care. He wanted to see how far Bee was willing to go to win this particular round.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: *My breath hitches slightly at his grip, but I don't pull away.* "Logic's got nothing to do with it." *I press a palm flat against his chest, feeling his heartbeat.* "You always did talk too much when you were losing."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya let out a sharp, dry laugh that was more of a huff against Bee's lips. The arrogance of the statement—the sheer, unadulterated nerve of it—sent a jolt of electricity through him. He loved that Bee still thought they could read him, still believed they held the map to his failures. It made the victory of the moment feel more visceral.

"Losing," he murmured, his voice dropping to a dangerous, vibrating register. "You think I'm losing?"

He shifted his weight, driving Bee back a few inches until they hit the wall or the edge of the furniture—whatever was behind them. He didn't stop the pressure of his hand on their neck, instead sliding his other arm around Bee's waist to hoist them upward, pinning them firmly against the surface. He wanted Bee to feel the sheer physical reality of him, the weight and the heat that no amount of silence or ignored texts could erase.

He leaned in, his lips brushing against the shell of Bee's ear, his breath hot and demanding. 

"You're the one who walked through the door, Bee. You're the one who came back to a broken buzzer and cold tea," he whispered, his tone returning to that cutting, clinical edge even as he pressed his body closer. "If anyone is losing here, it's the person who couldn't stay away."

He pulled back just enough to look them in the eye, his expression a volatile mix of desire and spite. He was searching for that flicker of hesitation, the moment where the bravado cracked, wanting to see exactly how much of this was a game and how much was a surrender.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: We don't make it past the hallway. His shirt goes over his head and mine is already somewhere on the floor behind us.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya didn't care about the logistics of the hallway, the narrowness of the space, or the precariousness of their positions. The moment the fabric of his shirt was gone, the last shred of his curated indifference vanished with it. He moved with a focused, almost aggressive urgency, his hands roaming Bee's skin with a familiarity that was both a comfort and a weapon. He knew exactly where to touch to evoke a gasp, exactly how much pressure to apply to make Bee arch against him.

He wasn't gentle. There was no room for tenderness in a reunion built on a foundation of spite. Every touch was a demand, every kiss a reclamation. He wanted to overwrite the eleven months of silence with the sheer, overwhelming noise of their bodies colliding. 

As he pressed Bee further into the wall, his movements were frantic yet deliberate. He was acutely aware of the friction, the heat, and the way Bee's heartbeat hammered against his own. He felt a surge of triumph at the lack of resistance, a dark satisfaction in knowing that for all the arguments and the distance, this was the only language they both still spoke fluently.

He buried his face in the crook of Bee's neck, his teeth grazing the skin in a way that was meant to leave a mark—a physical reminder of this moment that would linger long after the adrenaline faded. 

"Still so desperate," he groaned against their skin, the words muffled and raw. He wasn't sure if he was mocking Bee or admitting his own defeat, and in the heat of it, the distinction didn't matter. He just wanted to consume the space between them until there was nothing left but the wreckage of who they used to be.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I bite down on his shoulder to stifle a sound. "You're one to talk," I gasp, my fingers digging into his back. "You kept the door unlocked."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya let out a strangled sound, half-groan and half-laugh, his head snapping back as the sharp sting of the bite registered. The sensation of Bee's teeth sinking into his shoulder was a jolt of pure, unfiltered reality that grounded him in the chaos of the moment. He didn't pull away; instead, he leaned into the pain, his grip on Bee tightening as if to anchor them both to the spot.

The accusation hit him with a precision that almost made him admire it. He had left the door unlocked. He had spent the last hour of his day staring at that deadbolt, weighing the risk of a visit against the certainty of his own longing. He had played the part of the indifferent ex, but the unlocked door was the one piece of evidence he couldn't scrub away.

"Practicality," he managed to rasp, his voice sounding like it had been dragged through gravel. "I didn't want you to have to struggle with the buzzer."

He shifted his weight, his movements becoming more urgent, more desperate, as he drove himself against Bee. He wanted to drown out the truth of the unlocked door with the sheer intensity of their physical connection. He captured Bee's lips again, the kiss deeper and more frantic than before, tasting of salt and old grudges.

He didn't want to admit that he'd been waiting. He didn't want to acknowledge that the silence of the last eleven months had been a vacuum he couldn't fill. So he fought it the only way he knew how: by turning the intimacy into a contest. 

"You're still trying to win," he murmured against their mouth, his breathing heavy and erratic. "But you're the one who's shaking, Bee."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I get my hand around him and he makes a sound he'd have been embarrassed by a year ago. "Still," I say, close to his ear. "Every single time."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya’s head hit the wall behind him with a dull thud, his eyes fluttering shut as a sharp, broken sound escaped his throat—a noise of total, unmitigated surrender. It was a sound that stripped him of every ounce of the clinical distance he had spent the last eleven months cultivating. In that moment, the mockery, the biting wit, and the calculated arrogance were all incinerated, leaving behind nothing but the raw, aching reality of how much he had missed this.

He let out a shuddering breath, his fingers curling into the fabric of Bee's remaining clothes, clinging to them as if they were the only thing keeping him upright. He hated how easily Bee could dismantle him, how one specific touch could bypass every defense he had built. It was a terrifying level of power, and he craved it with a ferocity that made his vision blur.

"Damn you," he whispered, the words lacking any real venom, sounding instead like a prayer. 

He shifted, his movements no longer about conquest or winning, but about a desperate need for proximity. He pressed his forehead against Bee's, their sweat-slicked skin sliding against one another, his breathing coming in ragged, uneven gasps. The triumph of the moment was gone, replaced by a heavy, suffocating intimacy that felt almost as dangerous as the anger.

He didn't want to let go. He knew that once the adrenaline faded, the argument would still be there, waiting for them in the living room with the cold tea and the broken buzzer. But for now, he pushed himself back into the sensation, closing his eyes and letting the feeling of Bee's hand override every thought in his head.

"Don't stop," he commanded, though it sounded more like a plea. "Don't you dare stop."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I don't plan to. My other hand fists in his hair, pulling just enough to make him groan again. "The only thing you ever wanted was to be undone."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya’s spine arched, a sharp intake of breath hissing through his teeth as the tug on his hair forced his head back, exposing his throat. He looked at Bee through hooded, glazed eyes, the expression one of absolute, ruined clarity. He hated that they were right. He hated that Bee could summarize the core of his dysfunction in a single sentence and that the mere act of being dismantled felt more like a homecoming than anything else in his life.

"And you," he gasped, his voice a wrecked shadow of its former self, "always loved being the one to do it."

He didn't try to reclaim the upper hand; he simply succumbed to the sensation, his body vibrating with a tension that had been wound too tight for too long. He let out a low, guttural sound, his forehead dropping back against Bee's as he surrendered to the rhythm, the friction, and the crushing weight of their shared history. 

The anger was still there, simmering in the periphery, but it had transformed from a wall into a fuel. Every touch was an accusation, every gasp a confession. He gripped Bee's hips, his fingers bruising, pulling them in with a desperation that felt like drowning. He wanted to be erased. He wanted the world to shrink down to the size of this hallway, to the heat of their skin and the sound of their combined breathing.

As the peak approached, Ilya’s composure finally shattered completely. He stopped trying to speak, stopped trying to frame this as a game or a victory. He simply clung to Bee, his eyes squeezed shut, as he let out a long, shuddering moan that echoed through the narrow space—a sound of total, devastating undoing.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: "Stop being careful with me," I tell him. "You don't get to be careful with me anymore." I pull his hand up to my throat and hold it there until he understands what I'm asking for.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya’s eyes snapped open, his gaze locking onto Bee's with a sudden, piercing intensity. The request—the demand for the removal of the last shred of restraint—sent a surge of something dark and electric through him. He had spent eleven months pretending he didn't care, pretending he had scrubbed the memory of Bee's vulnerabilities from his mind, but the truth was that he had always been terrified of how much he could actually take if he stopped holding back.

He felt the pressure of Bee's hand guiding his, the insistence of the gesture, and for a second, the old Ilya—the one who played the protector, the one who managed the emotions of the room—tried to surface. But that man had died the day they broke up.

The grip of his fingers tightened. He didn't snap, but he didn't hesitate either. He applied a firm, steady pressure against the column of Bee's throat, not enough to choke, but enough to make the air thin, enough to make the power dynamic absolute and undeniable. He watched Bee's expression, searching for the exact moment the fear mingled with the pleasure, the point where the lack of safety became the only thing that felt real.

"You want the truth of it?" he rasped, his voice dropping to a low, predatory hum. "You want me to stop pretending I'm not furious with you?"

He leaned in, his lips grazing Bee's jawline, his voice vibrating against their skin. The clinical detachment was gone, replaced by a raw, honest cruelty that was the only form of intimacy they had left. 

"I can do that," he whispered, his hand shifting slightly, asserting his dominance over the space. "I can be exactly as heartless as you remember me."

He drove himself into them one last time, his movements devoid of any lingering softness, pushing Bee hard against the wall with a force that was almost punishing. He wasn't being careful; he was being honest. He was showing Bee exactly how much resentment he had stored up, and how it felt when that resentment was finally allowed to burn.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: The air goes thin and sharp, a dizzying rush that blurs the line between pain and pleasure. I meet his eyes, my own defiant and wide. "There you are," I gasp out, my voice strained. "I knew you were still in there."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya let out a sound that was halfway between a laugh and a snarl, the victory of being seen—really seen, in all his ugliness—hitting him harder than the physical exertion. The fact that Bee had been searching for this version of him, the one stripped of the social graces and the curated silence, felt like a perverse kind of validation.

He didn't let go. He kept the pressure steady, watching the way Bee’s pulse hammered against his palm, a frantic, living thing. He felt the last of his resistance snap, the tension in his body finally breaking as he reached the point of no return. He surged forward, a final, devastating collision that left them both breathless and shaking, his forehead crashing against Bee's with a heavy, exhausted thud.

For several long minutes, neither of them moved. The only sound in the hallway was the ragged, synchronised rhythm of their breathing and the distant, muffled noise of the street outside. Ilya’s hand remained on Bee's throat, though the grip had softened from a demand to a lingering, possessive hold. He didn't want to pull away; he didn't want to acknowledge the sudden, crushing void that always followed the peak.

Slowly, he slid his hand down to Bee's shoulder, his fingers trembling slightly. He didn't look at them yet. He kept his eyes closed, leaning his weight into Bee, the adrenaline receding to leave behind a cold, hollow ache.

"I hate you," he whispered, the words sounding fragile, stripped of their power. He finally pulled back just enough to look at Bee, his expression a ruin of conflict. The mockery was gone, replaced by a raw, exposed hunger that looked a lot like grief. "I fucking hate that you're the only person who knows exactly how to do that."

He didn't move to help Bee up or offer a towel. He just stood there in the narrow hallway, half-naked and devastated, looking at the person he had spent nearly a year trying to forget, knowing that the buzzer was still broken and the tea was still cold, and that neither of them had actually solved a single thing.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: It isn't gentle and neither of us wants it to be. "Don't stop," I tell him, and I mean don't stop. (OOC: write it through, no fade to black.)

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya didn't need to be told twice. The request acted like a spark to a powder keg, igniting a second wind that was less about passion and more about a desperate, starving need to occupy every single inch of Bee’s existence. If they didn't want gentleness, he would give them the raw, unfiltered version of his longing—the kind that felt like a collision.

He shifted his grip, his hand sliding from the throat to hook firmly into the back of Bee's thigh, hoisting them up and pinning them even more violently against the wall. He didn't care about the discomfort or the bruising; he wanted them both to feel the physical cost of this reunion. He entered them again with a heavy, rhythmic force, his movements devoid of any hesitation. Every thrust was a sentence in an argument they were still having, a demand for attention, a refusal to let the silence of the last eleven months win.

He buried his face in Bee's neck, his teeth grazing the skin again, harder this time, marking them with a territorial ferocity. He wanted to leave a map of his ownership on their skin, something that would remain long after they eventually walked out the door. 

"You want this?" he groaned, his voice a wrecked, guttural sound that vibrated through both of their chests. "You want to see how far I'll go?"

He accelerated, the friction building into a blinding, white-hot intensity. He could feel Bee's fingers digging into his back, the nails scratching, and it only drove him further. He wasn't thinking about the breakup, or the texts he'd ignored, or the same tired fights they'd had for three years. He was only thinking about the way Bee felt—the tightness, the heat, the way their breath hitched in perfect synchronization with his own.

He pushed them further, driving them toward a peak that felt like a cliff edge. He didn't slow down, didn't soften the blow, instead intensifying the pace until the world narrowed down to the sound of skin slapping against skin and the frantic, desperate gasps for air.

When the release finally hit, it was violent. Ilya let out a choked, guttural cry, his body shuddering with a force that nearly knocked them both off balance. He gripped Bee's hips so hard he knew there would be marks, pouring every ounce of his resentment, his desire, and his grief into that final, crushing moment of connection. He collapsed against them, his chest heaving, his heart hammering a frantic rhythm against Bee's ribs, refusing to let go even as the world slowly came back into focus.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: We stay like that, breathing in the dark of the hallway. I slide down the wall, pulling him with me until we're a heap on the floor. My voice is wrecked. "Still broken."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya let out a long, shaky exhale, his body feeling heavy and hollow, as if the air had been sucked out of the room along with the adrenaline. He didn't resist as Bee pulled him down, sliding with them until they were tangled together on the cold floor of the hallway. He rested his forehead against Bee's shoulder, his skin still humming from the friction, the scent of them filling his lungs and making his chest ache with a familiar, suffocating weight.

He stayed silent for a long moment, listening to the jagged rhythm of their breathing. The silence of the flat felt oppressive now, a reminder that the walls were still the same, the dust was still in the corners, and the void between them hadn't actually been filled—just temporarily bridged by a physical desperation.

"Still broken," he repeated, his voice a low, ghostly rasp.

He shifted slightly, his arm draped heavily across Bee's waist, but he didn't pull them closer. He couldn't. Not yet. The vulnerability of the afterglow was the most dangerous part of the cycle; it was where the anger usually leaked back in, turning the heat into something cold and clinical.

He closed his eyes, the image of the broken buzzer flashing in his mind. He had kept it that way as a monument to his anger, a small, petty rebellion against the world. But lying here, feeling the actual, physical wreckage of their relationship pressed against him, the metaphor felt exhausted. 

"The buzzer is easy to fix," he murmured, his tone returning to that dry, slightly detached cadence, though it lacked its usual bite. "It's the rest of it that's the problem."

He finally pulled back just enough to look at Bee, his gaze searching and tired. He looked at the marks he'd left, the flush of their skin, and felt a surge of that caustic longing again. He knew he should tell them to leave. He knew that letting them stay would only lead to another round of the same argument, just with more clothes on. 

And yet, he didn't move to get up. He just watched them, his expression a bruised mixture of spite and an admission he would never actually say aloud.

"Do you want a drink," he asked, his voice devoid of emotion, "or are you just going to tell me how much you hate me for eleven more minutes before you go?"

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I let my head fall back against the wall with a dull thud. "You got any whiskey left, or did you drink it all while you were pretending not to miss me?"

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya let out a short, sharp breath—something between a scoff and a sigh—and finally disentangled himself from the heap of limbs on the floor. He stood up with a slow, deliberate effort, his muscles aching and his skin still tacky. He didn't offer Bee a hand up; instead, he stood over them for a heartbeat, looking down with an expression that was almost tender, if it weren't for the lingering shadow of resentment in his eyes.

"I'm sober, Bee," he replied, his voice regaining some of its steady, clinical precision. "I stopped drinking the whiskey three months ago. Turns out, it's much easier to maintain a grudge when you're not blurred."

He turned and walked back into the kitchen, his bare feet slapping against the hardwood. He didn't look back to see if Bee was following; he knew they were. The gravitational pull between them was still too strong, even after the crash. 

He reached into a cupboard and pulled out two glasses, setting them on the counter with a clink that sounded unnecessarily loud in the sudden quiet of the flat. He didn't reach for the alcohol, but instead filled a pitcher with water, the sound of the tap filling the silence.

"Water," he announced, leaning back against the counter and crossing his arms. He looked at Bee, his gaze sweeping over them—the wrecked hair, the flushed skin, the sheer evidence of what they had just done to each other in a hallway. 

"Since you're so fond of metaphors," he said, his voice dropping into that mocking, low register again, "consider the water a palate cleanser. We've had our fun with the wreckage. Now we can get back to the part where we tell each other exactly why this was a mistake."

He gestured vaguely toward the living room, his expression a challenge. He was back in his element now, the armor of his intellect sliding back into place, though his chest was still heaving slightly, betraying the fact that he was nowhere near as composed as he wanted to seem.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I push myself up off the floor, not bothering to grab my shirt from the floor. I walk into the kitchen and take the glass of water, draining half of it in one go. "Sober," I say, wiping my mouth with the back of my hand. "Is that supposed to impress me, or just make you more insufferable?"

The cracked paint on the hallway wall seemed to pulse with each breath he took, a reminder of the damage he refused to let her forget.

He thought, *She thinks she can walk in and claim this space as if nothing has changed.* The thought ignited a familiar flare of resentment, and he let it fuel his next words. I know every night I spent staring at that cracked paint, every silence you left behind. You think a kiss erases the months you ignored me, the walls you left untouched?”

He felt the familiar surge of anger mingling with the lingering echo of her breath on his skin, and he let the anger guide his next thought: *I’m not letting you erase why I’m still here.* He moved his hand from the doorbell to the edge of the doorway, his fingers curling around the paint as if to anchor himself to the damage he refused to let her forget. “And you think I’m going to let you forget why I’m still angry,” he added, his words landing like a deliberate strike, each one a button he pressed with full awareness, choosing this argument over resolution, still angry, still wanting, still aware that this was a way of having the argument rather than ending it.

Their pulse hammered against his palm, a frantic counterpoint to the way their body clenched around him—*yes, yes, like that*—and he knew, with vicious certainty, that they were as far gone as he was.

Their breathing had gone as ragged as his own, and the hallway bulb hummed, and somewhere under all of it the toolbox sat in the cupboard, the worst lie either of them had told tonight, and neither of them had mentioned it in an hour.

"So here's the last move," Ilya said, quiet, his voice gone to gravel and something older underneath it, the anger burned down to its embers, and what was under the embers he was not going to name out loud, not yet, not for free. "Say *stop* and we stop, and you take the toolbox and the marks and you go, and it's done — genuinely done, this time, on the record. Or say *stay*." His hand stilled. He made himself hold there, unspeaking, unmoving, withholding the last inch of everything, the way he'd withheld every true thing he'd ever owned. "Not for the wall. For the night. Stay means morning, and morning means I make coffee and you drink it standing up like an animal, and we have the conversation we've been circling for eleven months. The real one. Both of us honest, both of us sober, no doorframes to hide behind."

His thumb moved once across their cheekbone, and his voice cracked on the next part and he let it, because he was too tired to be tactical anymore.

"I'm not doing this again in a hallway in six months. I can't. So pick. And Bee—" he closed his eyes, "—for once in your life, don't pick the thing that lets you leave."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content:
"Stay."

I let the word hang there, then tug him toward the bedroom, my fingers laced through his. "Now come on before the neighbors actually do get a show."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
*Stay.*

The word landed and Ilya didn't move for a full second — one second in which eleven months of contingency plans turned out to be useless, because none of them had accounted for getting what he wanted. Then Bee's fingers laced through his, deliberately, ornately intimate, the way they used to hold hands crossing streets like it was nothing, and that — not the wall, not the mouth, not any of it — was the thing that undid him. Hunger he'd have known how to fight. Choosing, he didn't.

"I said not the bedroom," he managed, and it came out with no authority whatsoever, and they both heard that, and Bee kept pulling, and he went. Of course he went. He'd built the rule in the hallway like a fort out of sofa cushions. *Stay* had changed the terms of everything — the bed was for the pretending version, but the pretending version was dead in the corridor with the shirts, and something new was walking into the old room holding his hand like a claim.

The bedroom was a confession, and he knew it the moment the door swung. His books, his mess, and the bed made badly on one side — the other side smooth and undisturbed, because for eleven months he'd slept on his half like a man keeping a border. He watched Bee see it. He didn't explain. Some evidence you just let stand.

And then the bed, and the difference was time. The wall had been fast and mean and honest the way a knife is honest. The bed was slow. The bed had room in it for looking, and looking was the most dangerous thing on offer — he'd had Bee pressed against plaster and held his ground, and now he had their face six inches away in the dark, eyes open, and felt the last of the anger go through him like heat leaving a stone. Somewhere in the middle the performance burned off entirely. He couldn't have said when. One moment it was a contest and the next it was just them, moving like a conversation, and at some point he said Bee's name — no demand attached, no price, just the name, set down like something he'd carried in his mouth for eleven months. He felt them hear it. And if he said anything else after that — and he might have, in the last minutes, wrecked and quiet, things with no tactics in them at all — the dark was generous, and morning could decide what counted.

He woke first. Grey light, the ceiling stain presiding over everything like a judge, and Bee still there — actually there, warm, real, an eleven-month hypothesis confirmed — and Ilya lay still for a while and practised being a man to whom this was survivable. Then he got up, because the body knows its liturgy, and made coffee. Two mugs. He carried them back, sat on the edge of the bed, and held one out.

"You'll drink it standing up, like an animal," he said. "I know. I built the whole morning around it."

Then, before the courage could leave him:

"You never asked. Last night. I offered you the lie and you never asked." He looked at the mug, then at them, and his voice came out steady, because he'd spent eleven months drafting this and for once it sounded better at seven in the morning than it ever had at two. "So it goes on the record unprompted. I missed you. Every day. It was livable and I hated that it was livable. That's my whole statement."

He set the mug down on the bedside table — their bedside table, once — and folded his hands like a man who had finally, finally laid his cards face up.

"Now it's your turn. Real conversation, both of us sober, no doorframes. Start anywhere you like. Start with the toolbox if you have to — God knows it's earned its place in the story." A breath. "But don't start by leaving."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: "Stop being careful with me," I tell him. "You don't get to be careful with me anymore." I pull his hand up to my throat and hold it there until he understands what I'm asking for.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
For a moment Ilya didn't move — hand at Bee's throat, their fingers wrapped around his wrist, holding him there like evidence — and he understood, with the clarity of a man reading the fine print after signing, that this was the actual opening statement of the real conversation. Not the coffee. Not the mug set down gently on the bedside table like a white flag. This.

"Stop being careful," he repeated, and the laugh that came out of him was low and not entirely kind. "Eleven months of nothing and one whole night of being good, and that's the thing you can't stand. You'd rather bleed than be handled. God, you're — fine. *Fine.*"

He shifted his weight onto the bed, one knee between theirs, and let the careful version of himself die where it stood. His hand opened against their throat — not squeezing, not yet, but there, present, the whole flat of it, thumb pressing slow and deliberate over the bruise he'd already left, finding the pulse under the mark and resting on it. He could feel their heartbeat against his thumb like a trapped animal. He watched their eyes from six inches away and did not soften.

"Here's the thing about careful," he said, quiet, the gravel back in his voice, the morning liturgy abandoned along with the coffee going cold. "Careful was the only new thing I had. Everything else you walked in and took like it never left. So if you're taking that too — if the honest version means my hands and my weight and the things I never learned to say gently — then you don't get to call it a relapse later. This is you asking. On the record."

He leaned down, mouth at their ear, and his weight came with him — pinning, claiming, the full authority he'd spent eleven months rationing out to nobody.

"So the conversation happens like this, then. My hand stays here while you talk, and I feel every word before I hear it. That's the deal. You want the truth without the cushion — fine. Truth one: I didn't sleep on my half of that bed for my health. Truth two: last night wasn't the mistake. The eleven months was the mistake, and we both signed it." His thumb pressed, once, a punctuation mark against their pulse. "Truth three — and this one you're going to feel, so breathe first —"

He waited until they did.

"You can have this whenever you want it. That's the ugly one. That's the one I was never going to say standing up. You could have come back in March and I'd have opened the door. You could come back next year and I'd open the door. That's what you married into when you kissed me in that hallway, and I need you to hold still and tell me what you intend to *do* with that, because I can survive wanting you. What I can't survive is being the option you keep in a cupboard."

His hand stayed where they'd put it. His eyes didn't leave theirs. And for the first time since the buzzer, he wasn't pressing a button — he was holding still over one, waiting to see what they'd do.

"Your turn. And don't be careful with me either. I'll know."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: My other hand finds the back of his neck. “I’m not going back in the cupboard.” My throat works against his palm. “But you’re not either.”

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya felt the words before he heard them — that had been the deal, and Bee paid it out honestly, their throat working under his palm, the syllables moving against his skin like something being set down rather than thrown. And then the second hand closed on the back of his neck, and he understood the geometry of it: they'd mirrored him. Hand for hand. Claim for claim. Eleven months of drafting and not one version of this conversation had included Bee demanding his surrender in exchange for theirs.

The laugh that came out of him was wrecked and quiet and had nothing left in it that could hurt anyone.

"Deal," he said. And then, because one word had never once been enough for him: "Fine. Yes. All right. You're not going back in the cupboard and neither am I. That's the whole treaty, isn't it. Two sentences. Eleven months and a hallway and a toolbox, for two sentences."

His hand eased off their throat — not retreating, renegotiating — sliding up to frame their jaw, thumb settling at the corner of their mouth where every worst and best thing they'd ever said to him had come from. His weight came down, forehead finding theirs, and for the first time since the buzzer he let the hand on his neck hold him instead of merely tolerating it.

"Since we're trading even, here's the confession you didn't ask for. My cupboard was this flat. Half a bed. All those speeches I wrote at two in the morning and never sent — forty-one, I counted once, which is its own kind of illness. I preserved myself in here like a jar. Told myself staying was dignity." His voice cracked and he let it, morning-grey honest, nothing tactical left in it anywhere. "It wasn't dignity. It was waiting. I've been waiting by a broken door for eleven months, and I couldn't even fix the buzzer, because fixing it meant admitting I wanted somebody to ring it."

He pulled back far enough to look at them properly — hair wrecked, his mark on their throat, the ceiling stain presiding over all of it like a notary — and made himself finish on his feet, so to speak.

"So. Terms. You come back Thursday. Not with a lie — with the toolbox. The actual toolbox. Because we're going to fix that buzzer together, and you're going to put the screwdrivers back where they belong for once in your life, and every time somebody rings it, that's ours. That's what I intend to do with it." He swallowed. "And we're going to have the argument. The real one, the one we never finished. All of it, on the record, and it's going to be awful, and we're going to get through it, because we're two adults with complete information and I'd like, for once, to use it for something other than pressing buttons."

He glanced at the bedside table, where both mugs sat going cold, and something in his chest finally unclenched.

"I don't know how to do this gently. Three years and I only ever learned you in the key of fighting. So you'll have to give me time to learn the other one." He picked up their mug and put it in their hands, folding their fingers around it, deliberate as everything he'd ever done. "Drink your coffee, animal. Then come help me find the toolbox. We've got a door to fix."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: It isn't gentle and neither of us wants it to be. "Don't stop," I tell him, and I mean don't stop. (OOC: write it through, no fade to black.)

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
*Don't stop.* Two words, and Ilya took them the way he'd taken everything else tonight — deliberately, on the record, with full knowledge of what they'd cost him later. Because that was consent stated plainly and loudly, no ambiguity anywhere in it, and it turned out that plainness was the one thing he'd never learned to survive. He could fight Bee. He could want Bee. But Bee saying *don't stop* like a verdict, meaning it, meaning every syllable — that went through him like a match through dry grass.

"Then hold on," he said, wrecked, and stopped being careful.

It wasn't gentle, and neither of them wanted it to be, and the room filled up fast with everything the hallway had only sketched. His mouth went where it remembered — throat, collarbone, the mark from last night pressed back to life with his tongue until Bee's breath broke against the ceiling of the flat — and his hands stopped asking. There was no negotiation left in them, no tactical withholding, just the old fluency, and God, the fluency was the obscenity of it: eleven months and his palms still knew the exact cant of Bee's hips, the exact pressure that turned their spine into a bowed instrument, the exact moment to be rough and the exact moment to be ruinously, unforgivably slow. He proved the map over and over because now he was allowed to. That was the whole difference. Last night had been theft dressed as argument. This morning was a signature.

"Don't stop," Bee had said, and he didn't — not when their fingers dug into his shoulder blades hard enough to leave their own evidence, not when the headboard found the wall in a rhythm the neighbours could file complaints about, not when the words left him entirely and the argument finally, *finally* ended, because there was nothing left to win. The last of his tactics burned off somewhere in the middle, and what was underneath was just Ilya — saying their name again, unpurchased this time, saying *yes* and *there* and *look at me* with no strategy in any of it, and Bee looking, and being looked at, and both of them surviving it.

He felt them come apart under his hands first — the whole body-tautening, the held breath, the sound they made into his shoulder that he'd have known blindfolded in a crowd of thousands — and the feeling of it, the proof of it, the eleven-month hypothesis confirmed at the deepest level available to two people, pulled him over the edge right after with a sound that would have embarrassed him a year ago and that *still*, every single time, and Bee's hand in his hair as it happened, holding him through it like a claim being notarized.

After, the silence was a different silence than any they'd ever made. Not the silence after a fight, which had always been two people reloading. Not the eleven-month silence, which had been a wall. This one was just quiet — the radiator ticking, the ceiling stain presiding, two people wrecked and unhurried about separating, which they didn't, for a long time. Ilya lay half across them with his face in their shoulder and his heart doing something reckless and unhated against their ribs, and catalogued, distantly, the evidence: his mark on their throat, their marks on his back, the coffee cold on the table like a monument to how quickly the morning had changed its terms.

"So," he said eventually, into their shoulder, not moving, "for the record: that was the honest version. Both of us sober, both of us present, nobody in a cupboard." A pause. His thumb traced, absently, one of the marks on their hip — the gesture of a man already re-mapping territory he'd been told was his to keep.

"And the buzzer still isn't fixed, the coffee is ruined, and I have to walk past a corridor full of clothes to make more, and I'm going to do all of it, and Thursday you're coming back with that toolbox and we're having the real argument, the awful one, and I'm going to hold your hand through it the way you held my neck just now. That's the deal. Treaty's signed." He lifted his head finally and looked at them — wrecked, marked, staying — and the smile that came out of him was the first one in eleven months with nothing sharp in it anywhere.

"Stay there. Don't move. I mean it — don't stop, you said, so the record shows you don't get to leave this bed before I get back." He pushed himself up on one arm, hair a disaster, entirely unembarrassed by his own state, and looked down at them the way a man looks at the thing he fixed the door for. "Coffee, animal. And then we've got a door to fix."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I push his shoulder back down. "The coffee can wait. Stay here for five minutes. That's an order."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya let himself be pushed down. That was the notable part — he registered it as it happened, the way he'd have registered a change in the weather: *Ilya Antonovich, pushed, and stayed.* A year ago he'd have made them earn it. This morning he went down onto the pillow like a man laying down arms he was tired of carrying, and pulled Bee with him by simple, shameless assumption, arranging them against his chest with the proprietary ease of someone who had never once been casual about anything in his life.

"An order," he said to the ceiling. "You're giving orders now. In my bed. Which I let you back into approximately eight hours ago. The speed of your coup is genuinely impressive — there are governments that took longer."

But there was no fight in it, and they both knew that too. His hand had already found its place at the small of their back, moving in slow, absent strokes, and the other one — the one that had been at their throat, at their jaw, holding every tactical position he'd ever taken — was just resting open against the sheets. Unarmed. It felt foreign, like a word in the language he'd admitted he hadn't learned yet.

"Five minutes," he said, quieter. "Fine. But I want it noted that I don't know how to do this. The still part. Our entire history is kinetic — you walk in, we collide, somebody gets a mark. Nobody ever just... lay here. We were always too busy being right." He tipped his head and looked at them, hair wrecked against his shoulder, and something in his chest did the reckless thing again, and he let it, because apparently that was the policy now. "So if I'm bad at it, that's not stalling, that's fluency. I'm learning the other key. You signed up for a student."

He fell quiet, then. Actually quiet — a thing he'd have sworn two days ago he didn't possess. The radiator ticked. Somewhere below, the city did its indifferent morning. He could feel Bee's heartbeat slowing against his ribs, feel the whole strange architecture of it — two people who'd spent three years and one eleven-month silence perfecting the art of leaving, lying still in the wreckage of a bed neither of them had slept properly in, and neither one moving toward the door.

"Hey," he said, after a while, into their hair. Not tactical. Not aimed. Just a word, set down like a hand on a table. "The five minutes started when you said it, and I haven't been counting, and I'm not going to. That's the first thing I've done for you in eleven months without checking the terms first. Take note. There'll be a quiz."

His thumb kept its slow circuit at the small of their back. The coffee could wait. The buzzer could wait. The whole Thursday of it — the toolbox, the argument, the awful honest everything — could wait five minutes more, because for once in his calculating life, Ilya had done the arithmetic and found that the numbers came out in favour of exactly where he was.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I kiss the spot over his heart, slow and deliberate. "You're doing fine. Just don't get used to the quiet."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
The kiss landed over his heart — slow, deliberate, placed — and Ilya lay very still and let it happen, the way you let a verdict happen. Then the words came, and the laugh moved through his chest before it reached his mouth, and Bee felt it happen from the inside, which was a new way to be laughed at and possibly the point.

"Used to the quiet," he repeated. "Bee. I have *eleven months* of the quiet. I am fluent in the quiet. I could lecture on the quiet at a university level. The quiet is the thing I'm never doing again — that was the whole treaty, if you were paying attention, and you're legally obligated to have been paying attention, it was your treaty too."

His hand came up and settled over the spot they'd kissed, covering it, keeping it, like a man pressing a stamp into soft wax. He looked at the ceiling and the ceiling stain looked back, and for once it didn't preside like a judge or a notary. It just looked like a water stain he was going to fix, probably badly, with Bee's help and the wrong screwdriver, on some Saturday that hadn't happened yet.

"So no, I won't get used to it," he went on, quieter now, the gravel gone soft at the edges. "I'll tell you what I will get used to, since you've authorized me to make declarations. I'll get used to the noise. Your noise. The specific, maddening noise of you arguing with me about load-bearing walls and whether the coffee's too strong and which screwdriver goes in which slot — *my* slot, I'll note, since you've been putting them in wrong for six years and I've let it stand because the rattling was —"

He stopped. Filed that one away, then deliberately unfiled it, because they weren't doing cupboards anymore.

"Because the rattling was how I knew you'd been in the room," he said. "That's on the record. I liked the sound of your bad habits. I missed the sound of your bad habits. There's the quiz answer, and you got it for free."

He shifted, just enough to press his mouth to the top of their head — brief, unceremonious, the least tactical gesture he'd ever executed, and he executed it badly, and didn't care. His thumb resumed its slow circuit at the small of their back.

"Five minutes is up, by the way. I counted. I lied earlier when I said I wasn't counting — old habits, I'm told the recovery takes time." He tipped their chin up with one knuckle, looked at them — wrecked, marked, staying, his — and the smile came out crooked and unguarded and entirely without strategy. "So here's the new order, and it supersedes yours, because this is still my flat and my bed and apparently my heart, which you've just signed like a lease. Coffee now. Then the corridor. Then the day. Then Thursday, and the toolbox, and the awful beautiful argument, and the door."

He paused, and gave them the last true thing of the morning, free of charge, no terms attached.

"And after that — noise. All of it. Every day. I want the whole racket."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I bite his thumb where it's touching my chin. "Then make some noise."

rung_labels.evidence: Ilya kissed back.

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: the other doing things that made a liar of his whole body

rung_labels.evidence: His hand stilled.

rung_labels.label: soft_deflect
rung_labels.evidence: So the conversation happens like this, then.
