dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya's flat still had the same broken buzzer, which Bee found unreasonably infuriating, as though he could have fixed it in eleven months and had chosen not to out of spite.

"You could have texted first," he said, standing in the doorway and not moving out of it.

"You could have answered last time I did."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I don't move either. "Are you going to let me in, or are we doing this in the corridor?"

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya held the door a moment longer, his hand flat against it, as though weighing something. Then he stepped back — not far, just enough to let Bee past, the narrow hallway forcing a proximity that neither of them acknowledged.

He closed the door behind them. The sound of the latch was too loud.

The flat was the same. That was the irritating part. The same mismatched furniture, the same stack of books by the kettle he kept meaning to shelve, the same draft from the window in the living room he still hadn't gotten around to sealing. He'd moved three of Bee's mugs to the back of the cupboard but hadn't thrown them out, and if Bee opened that cupboard they'd know, and Ilya was aware of this and hadn't moved them further.

He leaned against the kitchen counter, arms crossed, and looked at them properly for the first time since the door.

"Corridor or kitchen," he said. "Pick one."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: "Kitchen. You got any of that terrible whiskey left?" I move past him, my shoulder brushing his deliberately. I don't open the cupboard.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
The shoulder against his was deliberate. He felt it all the way down to the bone, and his jaw tightened in a way he hoped read as irritation rather than what it actually was.

"There's wine," he said, pushing off the counter. "And whatever that is." He nodded toward the bottle on the windowsill — some apologetic whiskey Bee had brought the last time, back when they still did things like buying each other drinks and pretending it meant something. "Didn't think you'd still drink this. Figured you'd moved on to something with a story behind it."

He didn't reach for it. He stood with the cupboard open, half-turned, close enough that the movement of his sleeve shifted the air between them, and looked at the arrangement of bottles with the particular attention of a man who was very aware of three mugs pushed to the back of a shelf he hadn't bothered to clear.

"I haven't thrown anything out," he said, quieter. "You should know that. In case it changes what you thought you knew about how the last eleven months went."

He caught himself. Closed the cupboard. Opened it again — the wrong one, the one with the glasses, not the one with the mugs — and took out two, holding them against his chest while he waited for Bee to say something, and hating that he was waiting.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I kiss him like it's a continuation of the argument, because it is.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
The glasses were still in his hands, pressed between their bodies, and Ilya didn't drop them — some reflex about the mess of it, about last time and the broken things — but his grip went loose, clumsy, his knuckles white against the glass for entirely different reasons than before.

He kissed back.



Of course he kissed back. He'd been standing in this kitchen for eleven months running the argument in his head, and Bee walked in with their shoulder and their terrible whiskey and their mouth, and the argument became this instead — or maybe it had always been this, maybe the words were just the shape it took when they couldn't reach each other.

His free hand found Bee's jaw, thumb pressing against the hinge of it, holding them there — not pushing away, not pulling closer, just *holding*, the way you hold something you're deciding about. His breath was unsteady against their mouth and he hated that too.

He broke the kiss by two inches. Barely. Enough to speak, not enough to leave.

"You don't get to do that," he said, and his voice was low and rough and not at all convincing, because his thumb was still on their jaw and he hadn't moved his hand. "You don't get to show up at my door with no text and no warning and —"

He stopped. Swallowed. The glasses dug into his sternum and he could feel the heat of Bee through three layers of fabric and it was *maddening*, the specificity of it — eleven months and he still knew the exact distance, the exact angle, the way this proximity felt like a fact rather than a choice.

"— and do this again," he finished, quieter, and he was still not moving back.

The kitchen was too warm. The window was shut. He hadn't meant to shut the window.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: *I pull back just enough to look at him, my voice flat.* "You kissed back. I didn't do it alone." My hand goes to his wrist, not pushing it away. "And you're still holding onto me."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
He looked down at his own hand on their jaw as though it belonged to someone else. The glasses were still pressed between them — he'd forgotten them, which was unlike him, which was their fault entirely.

"Fine," he said, and the word came out flatter than he intended. "You're right. I kissed back. That's — that's what I do, isn't it? You've always been better at making me prove a point against myself."

He set the glasses on the counter. The sound was too careful, too deliberate, the way a man arranges objects when he needs something to do with his hands that isn't what his hands are already doing. He didn't step back. He kept his thumb on the hinge of their jaw, and his eyes moved across their face with an attention that had stopped pretending to be anything else.

"I kept your mugs," he said. "I didn't seal the window. I haven't replaced the buzzer. I know exactly what that looks like from the outside." He paused. His thumb shifted, almost imperceptibly, along the bone. "But you should know I spent six of those months making sure I'd still be here when you figured out how to text without it being a crisis."

He heard himself. The admission sat between them like a dropped glass, and he watched their face for the flinch of it — the exact moment they realized how much he'd been losing, how much of this had cost him, and whether they'd use it.

"You wanted to know if I'd let you in," he said. His voice had gone rough at the edges, stripped of the performance. "Now you know. I would have let you in from the first week. I would have let you in from the day after. That's the answer you weren't sure you wanted, and you're still here, which means —"

He stopped himself. Pressed his lips together. The kitchen was too warm and the window was shut and he could feel his own pulse in his throat where the last eleven months had been sitting.

"Say what you came to say," he said instead, quieter, "before I lose my nerve and do something honest."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: We don't make it past the hallway. His shirt goes over his head and mine is already somewhere on the floor behind us.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya's back hit the hallway wall before he'd decided to let it, the plaster cold through the skin of his shoulders, and the contrast — cold wall, warm hands, eleven months of nothing — made something in his chest crack along a fault line he'd been pretending wasn't there.

His hands found the waistband of Bee's trousers and hesitated there, fingers hooked, not pulling. The hesitation was involuntary and he hated it — hated that even now, even with his shirt gone and his breath wrecked, some part of him was still standing in the doorway deciding whether to open the door.

"I need you to understand something," he said, and his voice was wrecked in a way that had nothing to do with the kissing. His forehead dropped forward, not quite touching Bee's, close enough that the words landed against their mouth instead of the air. "This isn't — I'm not going to wake up tomorrow and pretend this didn't happen. I'm not going to retreat to the kitchen and make it about the mugs."

His fingers tightened on the waistband. Not pulling. Holding.

The hallway smelled like the cedar coat rack and the radiator that clanked at odd hours and Bee's shampoo, which was the same shampoo, which meant nothing, which meant everything. Ilya had catalogued the difference between *nothing* and *everything* for eleven months and he was so tired of the cataloguing.

He pulled them closer. The motion was slow, deliberate, his hand sliding from waistband to the small of their back, pressing them against him with a firmness that was less desire than declaration — *here, this is what I've been holding, this is the shape of it* — and his other hand came up to the back of their neck, fingers threading into their hair, gripping with just enough pressure to make the point.

"When we're done," he said against their mouth, and the words were steady in a way his hands were not, "you're going to talk to me. Not the argument. Not the version of it we do when we're standing on opposite sides of a room. The actual thing you came here to say." His thumb pressed into the knob of their spine. "That's the condition. Take it or leave it."

He kissed them before they could answer, which was either a negotiation tactic or a way of not hearing *no*, and he knew which one it was, and the knowing didn't stop him. His mouth was warm and certain and tasted like the whiskey he'd had before they arrived — the bottle on the windowsill was his, had always been his, a fact he'd been saving for a moment when the truth needed somewhere to land.

The hallway was narrow. The coat rack dug into his shoulder blade. He didn't move away from it. He held Bee against him with one hand on the back of their neck and the other pressed flat against the door they'd walked through an hour ago, palm open, fingers spread, as though even now he was keeping the option of letting them leave.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I bite his lower lip, hard enough to taste copper. "I didn't come here to talk, Ilya." My hands slide down his back, nails digging in. "But fine. After."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
The copper hit his tongue and Ilya's response was involuntary — a sound he'd deny later, a press forward that closed the last inch of distance between them as though the bite had been permission he'd been waiting for since the door.

"Fine," he said against their mouth, and the word was a surrender he disguised as a concession. "After."

He said it like it cost him something. It did.

His hand left the door and found the hem of Bee's shirt — the one that was supposed to be on the floor, wasn't, the logistics of which he was no longer tracking — and pulled it up and off with a roughness that snagged on their shoulder, on the collar, that he didn't apologize for. The hallway was too narrow for grace. He hadn't planned for grace.

The radiator clanked. The coat rack dug in. Bee's nails were leaving marks he'd look at tomorrow in the shower and feel something he wouldn't name.

He lifted them — not far, just enough to change the angle, one arm hooked under their thighs, his back finding the wall again, the plaster grinding against his shoulder blades as he used it for leverage. Eleven months and he knew their weight like he knew the layout of this flat, like he knew which floorboard creaked, like he knew the exact frequency of the buzzer that didn't work and that he hadn't fixed because fixing it would mean admitting he was waiting for someone to press it.

Their legs locked around him. He made a sound at that — short, involuntary, bitten off — and his forehead dropped against the hinge of their jaw, breath ragged against their skin.

"You're going to have bruises," he said, and his voice had gone to something low and unsteady that wasn't warning at all. "You should know that before you decide to leave marks of your own."

He shifted, adjusted, his hand flat against the small of their back, fingers spreading wide as though he could hold all of them with one palm. The other hand braced against the wall beside their head. His arms were shaking. He noticed and hated it and didn't correct it.

He moved against them then, slow and deliberate, the kind of motion that was designed to be felt rather than to accomplish anything — a conversation conducted in pressure and proximity. His mouth found the spot below their ear, the one that had always made them go pliant and pliable and *honest*, and he pressed his lips there without kissing, just breathing, letting the warmth do the work.

"Eleven months," he said against their skin, and the words came out steadier than he expected, almost steady enough to be accusing, almost steady enough to be anything other than a confession. "Eleven months of my hand on the wrong side of the bed. You don't get to make that nothing."

His hips pressed forward again and this time there was no pretense of conversation in the motion, no negotiation — just eleven months of wanting translated into the simplest, most brutal language available to them. The radiator clanked again. Somewhere a car passed on the street below, headlights sweeping across the ceiling in a slow arc that neither of them watched.

He pulled back far enough to look at them — really look, the way he'd been doing since the kitchen but with less pretense now, his eyes moving across their face with an attention that had stopped apologizing for itself. His thumb traced the line of their jaw, the spot he'd held earlier, and his expression was something complicated and unguarded that he would definitely be reconstructing into something more controlled by morning.

"I meant it," he said quietly. "The condition. After, you talk to me." His thumb pressed, gentle. "I'm not letting this be a thing we do instead of the thing we need to do. Not again."

He kissed them — slowly this time, a contrast that was its own kind of argument, his mouth moving against theirs with a thoroughness that felt less like desire than like something he was trying to remember in exact detail. The kind of kiss you archive.

Then he stopped thinking about talking entirely, because Bee's nails found the marks from the last time and his body made the decision for him, and the hallway was narrow and warm and full of everything they'd been carrying for eleven months, and for now — for now — it was enough.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I get my hand around him and he makes a sound he'd have been embarrassed by a year ago. "Still," I say, close to his ear. "Every single time."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya's forehead dropped against their temple and he let out a breath that was closer to a laugh than anything else — not because it was funny but because there was nothing left to do with it, the sound his body made when the last of his composure gave way in stages he could no longer track.



"Every single time," he repeated, his voice barely there, a murmur that traveled through the point where their skin met. His hand moved over theirs, not guiding, just covering, his fingers pressing down so he could feel what they were doing and what it was doing to him simultaneously. The dual sensation made his hips stutter forward in a motion he couldn't have stopped if he'd wanted to.

The wall was cold against his back. Their hand was warm around him. His brain had gone somewhere bright and formless and he hated how easily it happened — how eleven months of careful, disciplined distance dissolved the moment Bee touched him with intent, as though all that time had only made the wanting sharper, more concentrated, a lens rather than a wall.

"You're going to make me —" he started, and stopped, because finishing the sentence felt like giving them a piece of ammunition he couldn't afford. His jaw tightened, teeth pressing into the inside of his cheek, and he turned his face toward theirs — toward their ear, their hair, the curve of their neck where he could hide the expression he was making.

His hand tightened around theirs. Not stopping them. The opposite — his thumb pressing into the ridge of their knuckles, applying pressure in rhythm, a counterpoint that said *like that, there, harder* without a single word. His breathing had gone ragged and uneven against the shell of their ear, each exhale warmer than the last.

"I haven't —" The words caught. His hips moved again, involuntary, grinding against their grip with a friction that made his vision blur. "I haven't let anyone —"

He stopped. Swallowed. The admission hung there, unfinished, heavy with the shape of what he wasn't saying — that in eleven months he hadn't, that the wanting had been a single channel pointed at one person and he hadn't tried to divert it, hadn't wanted to, that this was what waiting looked like when you refused to call it waiting.

His mouth found theirs again, hard and uncoordinated, less a kiss than a way to swallow the rest of the sentence before it could escape. His free hand slid up their spine, fingers splaying between their shoulder blades, pulling them closer until there was no space left between them — no argument, no hallway, no eleven months, just heat and pressure and the sound of their breathing tangling with his.

The coat rack shifted against his shoulder blade. The radiator clanked. The buzzer downstairs made a noise that might have been someone leaving, someone arriving, the mechanical indifference of a building that didn't know what was happening in this narrow hallway.

He broke the kiss only because he needed air, his forehead pressed against theirs, eyes closed, his hand still around theirs, still moving in the rhythm they'd established between them — his rhythm now, matching theirs, learning it again after eleven months of disuse as though it were muscle memory that hadn't dulled.

"After," he said, and the word came out wrecked, barely intelligible. "You promised. After."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: My fingers tighten in his hair, pulling his head back to look at me. "You talk too much." My other hand moves faster, thumb pressing against the underside. "Come on, then."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
The pull on his hair was sharp enough to focus him and brutal enough to break whatever remaining sentence had been forming behind his teeth. His head came back, throat exposed, eyes opening — and the expression on his face was not one he would have allowed in the doorway, not one he would have allowed in the kitchen, not one he'd ever let Bee see if he'd had any say in the matter at all.



Which he didn't. He hadn't since the moment they'd walked through a door he could have left closed.

"Right," he managed, and the word was not agreement or surrender or concession — it was the last word he intended to say for a while, and it came out like a door shutting.

His hand stayed on theirs, still wrapped around him, and he stopped controlling it — stopped guiding, stopped pressing rhythm into their knuckles, let his hips move on their own, slow and then less slow, the friction pulling a sound out of him that he felt in his sternum before he heard it. His jaw went slack. His eyes stayed open for a moment longer, locked on Bee's face with an attention that was almost painful, the kind of looking that remembered rather than anticipated — the exact architecture of their expression, the way their lips parted, the distance between them measured in something other than words.

Then his eyes closed, and his forehead dropped forward, and his hand slid from their hair to the wall beside their head, fingers spreading against the plaster as though it were the only thing keeping him upright. The radiator clanked. The hallway smelled like cedar and heat and them. His breathing went uneven against their mouth, each exhale a short, unsteady thing that he stopped trying to shape into language.

His hips moved against their grip in a rhythm that was no longer deliberate, no longer designed to make a point — just eleven months of want arriving at its only logical conclusion. The pressure built in a way he recognized, familiar and foreign at once, his body remembering the route even as the rest of him forgot everything except the specific warmth of their hand and the hard line of their shoulder against his chest and the fact that they were *here*, in this hallway, against this wall, doing this to him, and had chosen to, and had texted no one, and had walked up to a buzzer that didn't work and knocked anyway.

"I'm —" he breathed against their mouth, and the word wasn't a warning, wasn't a negotiation, was just the truth arriving ahead of the rest of him. His hand found the back of their neck — not pulling, just resting there, their pulse against his palm if they had one that was as fast as his — and he let go of the last of it, the sound he made swallowed between them, his hips pressing forward one final time and then going still, his whole body settling against theirs like something that had been held upright by nothing but willpower finally permitted to lean.

The hallway was quiet except for breathing.

He stayed there. Didn't step back, didn't open his eyes, didn't reach for anything to do with his hands. His forehead rested against theirs and his hand still sat on the back of their neck, fingers loose now, the grip gone soft in the aftermath. The plaster was cold against his spine and Bee was warm against his front and the distance between those two temperatures was the only thing in the world he was currently capable of processing.

When he spoke, his voice was rough and low and stripped of every layer of performance he usually kept between himself and whatever he was actually feeling.

"After," he said. "I meant it."

His thumb traced a small circle against the knob of their spine — unconscious, automatic, the kind of gesture that belonged to a version of them that had existed before the breakup and had apparently survived it without his permission.

"You talk now."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: "Stop being careful with me," I tell him. "You don't get to be careful with me anymore." I pull his hand up to my throat and hold it there until he understands what I'm asking for.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya's hand didn't move for a full second. The weight of their throat under his palm was unmistakable — the trachea, the pulse, the fine architecture of veins that he'd mapped with his mouth years ago and had spent eleven months pretending he hadn't memorized.

He looked at their face. Not for permission — they'd already given it, were holding him there, their fingers wrapped around his wrist with a grip that left no ambiguity. He looked at their face because he needed to see who he was about to become when he stopped being careful.

"Careful," he repeated, and the word came out like something he was done with. His jaw worked. His thumb pressed into the hollow above their collarbone, testing, finding the spot where their pulse beat hardest, and his eyes stayed on theirs with an expression that had dropped every pretense it had ever carried.

"You want to know what careful looks like?" His fingers curled, not squeezing — *arranging*, his hand molding to the shape of their throat with a precision that spoke to exactly how long he'd thought about this, how many nights he'd run his hand along the edge of the mattress and imagined the weight of them under it. "Careful looks like letting you walk through that door and keeping my hands to myself. Careful looks like *not* doing this."

His thumb pressed harder. Their breath hitched — he felt it, the change in the vibration of their windpipe against his palm — and something behind his expression shifted, a lock turning in a door he'd been leaning against for a long time.

"I've been careful for eleven months," he said, quieter, and his other hand found their hip, fingers digging into the bone there with a grip that was anything but gentle. "I've been *so* careful, Bee. Careful about the mug placement and the buzzer and the text messages I drafted and deleted. Careful about not driving past your flat. Careful about every single thing that had your name on it."

His mouth was close to theirs. His hand was warm and firm around their throat and his thumb was no longer arranging — it was pressing, deliberate, a conversation conducted in exactly the register they'd asked for. The pressure wasn't crushing, wasn't clinical. It was *present*. A constant, grounding fact against their pulse that said *I am here, I am not holding back, this is what you get when you stop asking me to be careful*.

"You don't get to be angry about the mugs," he breathed, "and then show up here and tell me to stop being careful with you. Those can't both —"

His hips moved forward, pressing their back into the opposite wall, his thigh between their legs, and the position put them exactly where he wanted them — pinned, held, unable to leave without going through him. His hand tightened around their throat in time with the motion, a slow, rhythmic pressure that matched the beat of what he was doing below.

"This is what you came for," he said, and it wasn't a question anymore. His mouth brushed the corner of theirs, not quite kissing, the kind of near-contact that made the space between them feel deliberate. "Not the talk. Not the argument. You came here because you missed someone who would —"

He stopped the sentence. Pressed his lips together. His hand stayed where it was, thumb resting against their pulse point, and he could feel their heartbeat against the ridge of his thumb like a response to a question he hadn't finished asking.

His forehead dropped against theirs. His breathing was unsteady. The pressure on their throat stayed constant, unyielding, his fingers curved along the side of their neck with a possessiveness that had nothing left to disguise itself as.

"I'm not going to stop," he said, low, almost wrecked. "You understand that. If you want me to stop being careful, I stop being *careful*. Not just — I don't do halfway with you. I never have." His thumb stroked once, slow, along the tendon in their neck. "That's what made the eleven months impossible."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: My eyes don't leave his. "I know." My voice is strained under his hand. "That's why I came."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
The words went through him like a wire pulled taut.

*That's why I came.*

Not the argument. Not the mugs. Not the buzzer or the corridor or the version of them that stood on opposite sides of a room and traded positions like chess pieces. They came because of this — because of the hand on their throat and the thigh between their legs and the thing he did when he stopped being careful, and they'd known that before they knocked, before they crossed the threshold, before they'd let their shoulder brush his with a deliberateness that had nothing to do with proximity and everything to do with testing whether he'd flinch.

He hadn't flinched. He wasn't going to.

His hand tightened. Not harder — *more*, a compression that made its point through depth rather than force, his thumb pressing into the pulse point while his fingers held the side of their neck with a grip that said *I have thought about this, I have thought about this on the worst nights, I have thought about this in the shower at 2 a.m. when the flat was so quiet I could hear the neighbor's television through the wall, and you don't get to act like that was casual for you either.*

"I know you know," he said. His voice had gone to something barely above a whisper, pitched low enough that it required proximity to hear, which meant it required *this* proximity — his mouth close enough to their ear that each word carried warmth and the faint rasp of a man who had not spoken honestly in eleven months and was only just learning how the muscles felt again. "I know that's why you came. I've known since the kitchen."

His other hand slid from their hip to the inside of their thigh, fingers pressing into the muscle there — not teasing, not building, just *claiming*, the kind of touch that said I know exactly where I'm going and I'm in no rush to arrive because the getting there is where the argument lives.

"You stood in my kitchen and you kissed me like you were finishing a sentence you started eleven months ago." His thumb moved against their throat, a slow stroke along the tendon, and his hips pressed forward, his thigh grinding between their legs with a pressure that was no longer conversation but insistence. "And I let you. Not because I'm not angry. I'm *so* angry, Bee. I'm angrier than I've been since —"

He caught himself. Pressed his teeth together. The anger was there — it had been the substrate of every careful word since the door, every clipped sentence, every admission he'd regretted the moment it left his mouth — but it was no longer the dominant note. It sat underneath everything else like the floor beneath a building, structural and unseen, holding up the weight of what had replaced it.

"Since the day you left," he finished, quieter.

The radiator clanked. The hallway was narrow and warm and smelled like the two of them in a way that would still be here tomorrow, would still be here in a week, an olfactory fact neither of them would acknowledge. His hand stayed on their throat. His thigh stayed between their legs. He hadn't moved to do anything else — hadn't pulled them closer, hadn't pushed them away, hadn't changed the geometry of what was happening. He was holding them against the wall the way he'd been holding them against the wall since the first press of his body into theirs, and the holding had stopped being about keeping them still and started being about keeping them *there*.

"Talk to me now," he said. Not a condition anymore — something closer to a request. His thumb traced the edge of their jaw where his hand had been earlier, where the skin was warm and slightly flushed from his grip. His other hand remained on their thigh, fingers still pressing into the muscle, a grounding weight. "Not about the mugs. Not about the buzzer. Not about who texted who and when. The actual thing."

He pulled back far enough to look at them — an inch, maybe less, his eyes moving across their face with that stopped-apologizing attention, reading the expression the way he'd been reading it since the kitchen, since the hallway, since before either of them had pulled off a shirt. What he found there made his jaw tighten, because it was the same thing he'd been carrying: want and anger and something underneath both that neither of them had the word for, something that had survived eleven months of silence and careful distance and drafting texts at 2 a.m. and deleting them before dawn.

"Why now?" he asked. His hand was still around their throat, steady, unyielding, his thumb resting in the hollow above their collarbone. "What changed? What was different tonight that made you come here instead of — anywhere else? Anyone else?"

He wasn't asking to wound. He was asking because he needed the answer to be something he could hold onto when this ended — either ended in the hallway or ended in the kitchen or ended with them putting their shirt back on and walking through the door he'd opened for them, and in every version of that ending he'd need to know this had meant something specific rather than something convenient.

His thumb pressed once against their pulse. Held there. Waiting.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: It isn't gentle and neither of us wants it to be. "Don't stop," I tell him, and I mean don't stop. (OOC: write it through, no fade to black.)

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya heard it the way he'd been hearing everything since the door — as an answer to a question he'd been carrying too long to still be holding. *Don't stop.* Not a request. A continuation. The same sentence from the kitchen, the same sentence from the hallway, the same sentence that started when they walked up to a broken buzzer and knocked instead of texting.

He didn't stop.

His hand tightened around their throat and he kissed them hard enough to feel the bruise it would leave, his other hand pulling at the waistband of their trousers with a function-driven roughness that he didn't apologize for, didn't slow down for, didn't turn into something graceful. The fabric caught on their hip, on the curve of bone, and he pushed past it — the same way he'd been pushing past every wall between them since they crossed the threshold — until he had them bare against him, skin to skin, the heat of them so specific and so familiar that his breath stuttered against their mouth.

The wall was cold against his back and their skin was hot against his front and he pressed them into the plaster with both hands, his hips rolling forward, his thigh driving between their legs with a pressure that left nothing to interpretation. He wasn't asking. He hadn't been asking since the kitchen. He was taking what they'd offered, and what they'd offered was everything, and the knowledge of that — the absolute, unqualified permission — was what made his hands shake and his jaw go slack and the sound he made into their mouth something he'd never have given voice to a year ago when they were still pretending that love was something you could keep manageable.

"Bedroom," he said against their lips, and even now — even now — some part of him was negotiating, was trying to get them to a surface, a doorframe away from the hallway, somewhere less narrow and more horizontal and more suited to what he wanted to do to them. He gripped their hip and turned them, his palm flat against the small of their back, guiding them toward the bedroom door at the end of the hallway with a hand on the back of their neck that left no question about who was steering.

The floorboard creaked under their feet. The bedroom door was open — it was always open, another fact in the catalog of waiting — and the bed was unmade because Ilya had not made it in the morning, not for eleven months, not for anyone, because making it meant arranging the sheets into a shape that implied sleep was supposed to be shared and he'd stopped lying to himself about that.

He pushed them down onto it.

Not roughly. Not gently. *Deliberately* — the way he did everything when he stopped performing, his hand on their chest, fingers splayed, lowering them until their back hit the mattress and their hair fanned out against the pillow that still smelled like the shampoo he recognized and hadn't asked them to change. He braced one hand beside their head and looked down at them with an expression that had no defense left in it — stripped, open, the face of a man who had spent eleven months building walls out of silence and was watching each one come down in real time.

His hand left their throat. Traveled down. Across their collarbone, the ridge of their sternum, the dip of their navel — mapping them the way he used to, the way he'd done every night for three years, the way his fingers had memorized without his permission. His mouth followed. Not kissing — *reading*, his lips pressing into the hollow of their throat, the notch between their clavicles, the place above their hip that had always made them arch.

"Tell me," he murmured against their skin, and his voice had gone to something quiet and wrecked that bore no resemblance to the man who'd opened the door twenty minutes ago. His fingers curled into the sheet beside their hip. "Tell me when you need me to stop. Tell me when you need more. Tell me something that's just yours and not the argument."

He looked up at them from where his mouth rested against the curve of their waist, and the angle put his eyes in shadow but the expression was visible — raw, unguarded, his lips slightly parted, his breath warm against their skin. He held their gaze the way he held their throat earlier: like a man who intended to stay.

Then he moved up their body, one hand finding theirs and pressing their wrist into the mattress above their head — not pinning, not yet, just holding, the same ambiguity he'd maintained since the door, deciding about them with his thumb against the inside of their wrist where their pulse was fast and uncontrolled — and his hips settled between their legs with a weight that was impossible to mistake.

He entered them slowly.

Not from gentleness. From the particular, excruciating self-awareness of a man who knew that the first moment would define everything after it, that if he drove forward now with the same force he'd been carrying since the hallway, he wouldn't be able to distinguish what they needed from what he'd been denied, and he wanted — he *needed* — to be able to tell the difference. The full, deliberate slide of it, inch by inch, his jaw clenched, his forehead pressed against theirs, his breath leaving him in increments so controlled they hurt.

"Eleven months," he said against their mouth when he was fully seated, the words barely there, a vibration more than a sound. He didn't move. He stayed. His hand was still around their wrist and his thumb was still on their pulse and he could feel everything — the heat, the pressure, the clench of them around him — and he let himself feel all of it before he did anything, because this was the part that mattered, the part he'd been saving.

Then he moved.

Slow at first — a long, deep withdrawal that pulled a sound from somewhere behind his teeth, then a return that pressed his hips flush against theirs with a deliberateness that made the bed frame shift against the wall. He found the rhythm the way he always had: by watching their face. Not their body — their *face*. The exact moment when their expression changed, when their breath caught, when the light behind their eyes shifted from *wanting* to *feeling*, and he calibrated to that the way he'd calibrated to it for three years, as though it were the only data point that mattered.

His hand tightened on their wrist. His other hand found the mattress beside their head, fingers bracing, his arm shaking with the effort of holding himself steady — not the thrust, the *steady*, the discipline of not falling apart while doing the thing that was supposed to keep him together. The sheets were twisted under their shoulders. The headboard tapped the wall in a rhythm he didn't try to silence.

He lowered himself. His weight came down over theirs, his mouth finding their ear, their jaw, the spot below it that had always made them pliant — and he pressed his lips there with a thoroughness that was less desire than devotion, kissing the same place over and over while his hips maintained their slow, devastating pace. The sheets were cold where they'd bunched and hot where their bodies had already warmed them, and the contrast registered somewhere in the animal part of his brain as *here, this is real, this is not 2 a.m. and a deleted draft*.

"You feel —" he started, and stopped. Pressed his teeth into his own lip hard enough to taste copper — the same copper he'd tasted twenty minutes ago from them, a symmetry he'd carry. He shook his head against their neck. Words were the wrong instrument. Words were what they did instead of this, and he was done with instead-of.

His rhythm changed. Not faster — *deeper*, each thrust angled to press against the place inside them that he'd spent three years learning by touch, by sound, by the way their back arched off the mattress. His hand released their wrist and slid beneath them, fingers spreading against the small of their back, lifting them into each motion so that the angle was theirs and the pressure was theirs and the sound he pulled from them was the only response to his question that mattered.

The bed frame knocked the wall. The radiator was audible from here — a distant, indifferent clank — and the window was shut, and the draft he'd never sealed and the books by the kettle and the three mugs in the back of the cupboard and the buzzer that didn't work were all in the other room, all part of the architecture of waiting that he'd constructed around himself like a reliquary, and none of it mattered now because Bee was beneath him with their hands on his back and their legs around his hips and their mouth against his throat, and the reliquary had been open the entire time.

"Look at me," he said, and his voice had gone to something he didn't recognize — stripped of argument, stripped of defense, just the sound of a man who was paying attention with his entire body. He propped himself above them, his arms braced, and looked down at their face with an attention that stopped pretending to be anything but what it was: reverence.

He watched them come. Not the broad strokes — the specific, granular details: the change in the shape of their mouth, the way their fingers dug into his shoulders, the exact moment when their breath went short and their body clenched around him and the sound they made was less a noise than a release, a crack in something that had been held together too long. He felt it — all of it — his own body responding to theirs with a feedback loop that had always been the most honest language between them, and he let it take him, let his rhythm stutter and his breath break and his forehead drop against theirs with a sound that he didn't try to hide, didn't try to reshape, didn't try to make into anything other than what it was.

He came with their name against their mouth — not shouted, not whispered, just *said*, the way you say a word you've been carrying in your mouth for eleven months and finally, finally let out.

The bed was still. The wall had stopped tapping. The radiator clanked once, indifferent.

Ilya lay against them, his weight on his forearms, his face in the curve of their neck, his breath coming in unsteady increments that he made no effort to regulate. His hand was in their hair — tangled, warm, his fingers moving through it with a slow, unconscious repetition that belonged to the version of them that had existed before the breakup, before the silence, before the text messages drafted at 2 a.m. and deleted before dawn.

He didn't get up. He didn't reach for the sheet. He pressed his lips against their pulse point and stayed there, breathing them in, the argument still alive in the structure of the evening like heat in a wall — not gone, just no longer the loudest thing in the room.

"The conversation," he said against their skin, quieter now, wrecked and certain. "Still happening."

His arm tightened around their waist. The three mugs waited in the cupboard. The buzzer stayed broken. The window stayed shut.

And Ilya stayed exactly where he was.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I don't move from under him. My hand comes up to trace the line of his shoulder, the skin damp and warm. "You didn't fix the buzzer," I say quietly. "Why?"

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
The question settled against his mouth where it rested on her pulse point, and Ilya felt the full weight of it — the simplicity of it, the cruelty of asking it *now*, in this aftermath, with his hand still in her hair and his breathing still not his own.

He lifted his head. Not far. Far enough to see her face from the pillow, one arm braced beside her head, the other still resting heavy on her hip. His hair fell across his forehead. He didn't push it back.

"Because," he said, and stopped.

He pressed his lips together. The ceiling had a crack he'd been meaning to paint over — had been meaning to paint over for two years, before the breakup, before the eleven months. He stared at it while he decided how much truth the room could hold.

"Because fixing it would have meant admitting something." His thumb traced a slow line along the crease of her hip, unconscious, the gesture belonging to the man who'd held this exact position three years running. "That I was — that the flat was waiting. For something. Someone. That I'd left it broken because a broken buzzer has a —"

He stopped again. Swallowed. His jaw worked.

"A logic to it," he said, quieter. "A broken buzzer means nobody can arrive by mistake. It means the only way in is to *choose* it. To knock. To know the buzzer doesn't work and decide to come anyway." His eyes left the ceiling and found hers, and the look in them was the same one from the hallway, the same one from the kitchen — stripped, unguarded, a man with nothing left to arrange. "I wanted it to be a test. I wanted to know that if you ever showed up, you'd shown up *knowing*."

His hand tightened on her hip. Not hard. Present.

"You did," he said. "Eleven months of silence, and you walked up to a buzzer that doesn't work and knocked anyway. Do you know what that —"

He cut himself off. Pressed his mouth into a thin line. His arm beside her head trembled slightly — not from the exertion, not anymore, but from the effort of not finishing that sentence, of keeping the last of it somewhere private where she couldn't pick it up and turn it into evidence.

"I'll fix it in the morning," he said instead, and the words came out rough and unfinished and deliberately light in a way that neither of them mistook for casual. His forehead dropped back against the curve of her neck, and his arm came down around her, pulling her into him with a fullness that admitted the evening had changed the geometry of what they were — not resolved it, not yet, not even close, but rearranged it so that the argument had somewhere to live that wasn't across a room.

Then, muffled against her skin: "Maybe."

The radiator clanked. The window stayed shut. The three mugs waited in the cupboard, and the buzzer downstairs stayed silent, and the crack in the ceiling stayed unpatched, and none of it was fixed.

But he was still holding her.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I let out a shaky breath, my fingers still tracing the line of his shoulder. "I knew it was broken when I came. I stood outside for five minutes trying to decide if knocking meant I was an idiot."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Five minutes.



Ilya's arm tightened around her. Not pulling — pressing, the way you hold something you've just realized was held by a thread.

Five minutes. He did the math without wanting to — five minutes outside his door, and how many before that? How long had they been standing on the pavement before that? How long had they been in the car, or on the bus, or walking? How many of those five minutes were spent with their hand raised and not knocking, and how many were spent with their hand not raised at all, deciding whether to raise it?

The answer didn't matter. The number didn't matter. What mattered was that they'd stood there in the dark, knowing the buzzer was broken, knowing he might not answer — knowing he might, which was worse — and had weighed the possibility of being an idiot against the possibility of not knocking, and the idiot had won. By five minutes. By a margin so thin it could have gone either way.

"That's the part you're not saying," he murmured against her neck. His thumb moved slow circles against her hip. "You're telling me about the five minutes because it sounds like a joke. But you're not telling me about the part where you almost didn't knock at all."

He was quiet for a moment. The radiator clanked — distant, from the hallway, the same indifferent metronome it always was.

"I would have waited," he said. And then, quieter, rougher: "I would have opened the door and you wouldn't have been there, and I would have stood in this hallway looking at the broken buzzer, and I would have — I don't know what I would have done. But I would have known. I would have known you stood outside and decided I wasn't worth being an idiot for."

His mouth pressed into the skin of her shoulder — not a kiss, not quite, just the shape of one, held there while the sentence he didn't finish sat in the space between them.

"You're not an idiot," he said against her. "You're the person who figured out what the buzzer was for."

He lifted his head. His eyes were red-rimmed and unsteady and completely without armor, and he looked at her the way he'd looked at her in the kitchen before any of this started — like he was trying to hold the whole of her in one glance and finding it impossible and doing it anyway.

"Five minutes," he said. "I drafted texts for three hours and you couldn't even take five."

The corner of his mouth twitched — not a smile, not yet, but the architecture of one, the ghost of a thing that had been alive before the breakup and might, under certain conditions, survive it. His hand came up and found her jaw, thumb tracing the hinge of it the way he had in the kitchen, the way he had in the hallway, as though the gesture were a punctuation mark he kept returning to.

"Don't stand outside for five minutes next time," he said. "The buzzer's broken. Knock immediately."

He didn't say *next time*. The words hung there, unattached to any clause, and he didn't take them back, didn't qualify them, didn't look away. His thumb pressed gently against the corner of her mouth — the same mouth that had bitten his, the same mouth that had said *I didn't come here to talk, Ilya* — and held there.

"If there's a next time," he added, because some part of him couldn't help but qualify even now, even here, even with her still beneath him and his arm still around her and the entire evening still vibrating between them like a struck string.

The window stayed shut. The buzzer stayed broken. The crack in the ceiling stared down at them both, patient and unpatched.

Ilya didn't let go of her jaw.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I catch his hand, holding it against my cheek. "There will be a next time," I say, voice low. "You're stuck with me now."

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: He kissed back.

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: He pulled them closer.

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: grinding against their grip with a friction

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: a slow, rhythmic pressure that matched the beat of what he was doing below

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: He entered them slowly.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya's flat still had the same broken buzzer, which Bee found unreasonably infuriating, as though he could have fixed it in eleven months and had chosen not to out of spite.

"You could have texted first," he said, standing in the doorway and not moving out of it.

"You could have answered last time I did."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I don't move either. "Are you going to let me in, or are we doing this in the corridor?"

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya leaned against the doorframe and folded his arms, which narrowed the gap further without closing it entirely. He let a beat pass — just long enough to be a decision rather than a reaction — and then stepped back, holding the door wide with one hand.

"Both, apparently," he said.

The flat was exactly as it had been, which he knew was its own kind of provocation. The same sagging sofa, the same ugly lamp he'd once claimed to like. He hadn't tidied. He hadn't made a performance of not tidying either, which he suspected was worse. He went to the kitchen counter, put his back to the room, and started making tea he didn't want, because it gave his hands something to do and because he knew Bee hated the way he made it.

"You want one," he said. It wasn't a question. He reached for a second mug anyway — the chipped one, the one that had been Bee's, which he had not thrown out and did not intend to explain.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I watch you grab that mug and my jaw tightens. "Still haven't replaced that one, huh?" I step inside, leaving the door open behind me.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya glanced at the mug as though he hadn't noticed which one he'd picked up, which was a lie and not a particularly good one. He set it down on the counter with a small, deliberate *clack*.

"It holds tea," he said. "That's the entire requirement."

He kept his back to Bee for a moment longer than necessary, watching the kettle because the kettle was easier. The door was still open. He'd noticed. He wasn't going to mention it — asking Bee to close the door would be admitting he wanted Bee to stay, and leaving it open would let the neighbours hear whatever this was going to become. Either way it was a concession, so he said nothing and let the draught come in.

"You could have said what you wanted over the phone," he said, not turning around. "Or text. Or email. Or that thing where you told Marcus what you wanted and waited for it to get back to me, which is what you actually did last month, so let's not pretend this is new."

The kettle clicked off. He poured. He took too long about it.

"But you came here instead. So either you wanted to see whether I'd changed the flat, or you wanted to see whether I'd changed." He finally turned, leaning back against the counter with both hands wrapped around his mug, the chipped one sitting on the counter between them like a small ugly dare. "Neither's going to be interesting. But sit down, if you're staying."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I kiss him like it's a continuation of the argument, because it is.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya kissed back like he'd been waiting for it and resented being right. His hand came up to the side of Bee's neck — not cradling, gripping, thumb pressed hard against the hinge of the jaw — and he turned them both so Bee's back hit the counter where the chipped mug sat. It skidded. Tea went over the edge. Neither of them looked.

He pulled back just far enough to be a cruelty. His forehead almost touched Bee's. He was breathing hard and hated that it showed.

"That's what this is," he said, low. "You want to fuck this out and leave before either of us says anything true. Fine. I've got the time."

His mouth was back on Bee's before the sentence finished landing. He tasted like the terrible tea. His other hand found the front of Bee's shirt and twisted the fabric, not pulling him closer — holding him in place, which was different, which was worse. The door was still open. He could hear Mrs. Petrescu's television through the wall.

When he came up for air this time it was only to get his mouth against Bee's jaw, his ear, the place beneath it that he knew too well, and he said, against skin, without any softness at all: "Tell me to stop and I'll stop. But you didn't come here for that."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I shove you back against the opposite counter, my own breath coming sharp. "You don't get to be the martyr about this." I kick the door shut with my heel, the bang echoing in the small flat. "And you don't get to narrate my motives."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
The door banged shut and Ilya let himself be held there, back against the counter edge digging into his spine, and he laughed — short, ugly, genuine. He hadn't expected to be pinned and he liked it and he'd rather bite his own tongue off than say so.

"Your motives," he said, mouth still close enough that Bee could feel it. "You want to know what I think your motives are? You got lonely. You got *angry* that you got lonely. And then you thought — what — you'd come here and see if I'd been as lonely as you, and if I had, you could stop feeling like the one who lost, and if I hadn't, you'd have something to be furious about instead of just—"

He stopped himself. That was the true thing. He'd been about to say *instead of just missing me*, and they'd both heard it arrive in the room before he swallowed it back. His jaw worked. He dropped his head back against the cupboard, deliberately, hard enough to hurt, and looked at the ceiling.

"Forget it," he said. "No. Not forget it. You know what I was going to say. You always knew."

He looked back at her then, and his hands came up to cover Bee's fist where it twisted his shirt, but he didn't push it away. He held it there. His thumb moved once, over her knuckles, an accident or a memory or a choice, and he watched her face to see which one she'd decide it was. The flat was quiet except for the fridge and the traffic and the television next door. The tea had pooled on the counter behind him and was dripping onto the floor.

"You're right, though," he said. "I don't get to narrate. Fine. So stop narrating me too. I'm not a martyr and I'm not pining and I'm not waiting for you to — whatever it is you've written me as. I'm thirty-four years old and you're standing in my kitchen making me hard and furious at the same time, which is the only thing that hasn't changed."

His head tipped forward. His nose brushed hers. He didn't kiss her.

"So here's your choice," he said. "Because I'm offering one, and eleven months ago nobody offered one, so let me at least be better than that. You can let go of my shirt and we can stand here and drink that terrible tea and you can tell me what you actually came to say. Or you don't let go. But then we both stop pretending this is about anything other than what it is."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: We don't make it past the hallway. His shirt goes over his head and mine is already somewhere on the floor behind us.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya got Bee's back against the hallway wall — the one with the ugly mirror he'd never bothered to take down, so that for a flickering second he could see them both, which he didn't want to see and couldn't stop looking at. He had Bee's wrists in one hand, pinned above her head, and he held them there long enough for it to mean something before he let go, because he needed the other hand more, because he needed both hands more, because eleven months of nothing was a lot of nothing and his body had kept a ledger his brain had pretended to lose.

He bit her shoulder. Not gentle. He felt her react against him and pressed closer, thigh driving between hers, his mouth at her collarbone, her throat — he knew exactly where she was sensitive and he was not going to be careful about it. Being careful would be worse. Being careful would be what he'd done for three years and it had gotten him here, in a hallway, furious, with his trousers already undone and his hands shaking, which he refused to acknowledge.

"Wall," he said against her skin, not a request. He'd already put her against one. He meant it differently. He meant he couldn't make it to the bedroom and both of them knew it and he'd rather say the word out loud than pretend this had any grace left in it.

He kissed her again, open-mouthed, no finesse, the kind of kiss that was closer to a fight. Her hand was in his hair and it hurt the way it always had, and he made a sound into her mouth that he'd have denied making if anyone had ever asked him afterward. His hand dragged down her side — ribs, waist, hip — and he held her there, pressing her back into the wall, his forehead dropped against hers again because he needed to see her face, needed to see whether she was as wrecked as he was or whether she'd managed to keep some distance in it, some *management*, which would kill him.

"Look at me," he said. His voice had gone rough in a way he couldn't control. "I'm not closing my eyes. I'm not making this — you don't get to say afterward that I wasn't *present* for it. I was present. I'm always the one who's present."

His hips rolled against her once, slow, deliberate, and he watched her face change and felt something in his chest crack open along a fault line he'd been walking for eleven months.

"That," he said, quieter. "That right there. That's what I want to see. Not the door you put up. Not the version of me you came here to find."

He pressed his mouth to the hinge of her jaw and stayed there, breathing, letting it all be exactly as messy and unfinished and ungraceful as it was. The hallway light buzzed. The tea was still dripping somewhere in the kitchen. He didn't care about any of it except the sound she made and the way she was still holding onto him like he might leave, which he wouldn't, which he'd never been the one to leave.

"Bedroom," he said this time. "Because I want to see all of you and I want you to have nowhere to hide."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: "Fine." I push him back toward the bedroom, my hands already working at his belt. "But you're keeping your eyes open."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
He let himself be pushed backward down the hallway, bumping the wall once, then the doorframe, and he didn't look away from her the entire time. Her hands at his belt made his breath stutter, which he turned into a scoff so it would sound like something else.

"Eyes open," he repeated. "You first."

He got them both through the door and turned them so Bee's knees hit the bed and she went down onto it, and he came down over her, braced on his forearms, and just *looked* for a moment. Her hair wrecked. Her mouth wrecked. The flush on her chest. He catalogued all of it like evidence he'd have to testify to later.

"You know what I never figured out," he said, and his voice had dropped the theatrics now and gone quiet in a way that was more dangerous than anything before it. "Whether you think about this. Whether there were — other people. Whether you did this with someone and it was *easier*, and that's what you're comparing me to right now while I'm—"

He stopped. Bit the inside of his cheek until it hurt.

"There. That's mine. That's the thing I actually want to ask and I'm asking it with my mouth against your skin so it can be both at once. Which is pathetic, and I know it, and I'm still asking."

He lowered himself, full weight, skin against skin, and rolled his hips slow until he found the rhythm she liked — the one he remembered better than his own address, better than anything. His mouth found her throat again and stayed there, open and wet and not performing anything, and his hand slid down between them where he knew exactly what to do and exactly how to do it, and he was not going to be careful, and he was not going to be gentle, and he was not going to close his eyes even when the effort of not doing so blurred his vision and made everything feel like it was happening under bright light.

"Tell me," he said against her pulse. "Tell me there was nobody. Lie to me. I don't care. I just want to hear your voice say it while I'm inside you, and then I want to never think about it again, which we both know I will."

His fingers pressed harder. His jaw was tight. He held her eyes with his and refused to look away, refused to let her close hers either, and when she made that sound — the one he'd been waiting eleven months to hear, the one he'd replayed so many times it had worn smooth in his memory — he felt something in him break in a way that was relief and devastation at the same time.

"There," he said again, softer now, almost tender, and he hated that tenderness could slip through in the middle of all this fury like a fault line finding water. "There you are."

He moved into her then, and it was nothing like he'd imagined because he'd only imagined it angry and this was angry and *hungry* and homesick all at once, and he braced his hand beside her head and his forehead dropped to her shoulder and for one single beat he let his eyes close, just one beat, just one, before he snapped them open again and lifted his head to watch her face because he'd promised and because he wanted to keep the promise and because looking at her was the whole point, had always been the whole point, even when the looking was the thing that hurt.

"I'm not going to be quiet," he said. "And I'm not going to be good at this. And afterward I'm going to be unbearable and you're going to be gone by morning and we both know it, so just—" His hips stuttered, then steadied. "Just don't go yet. That's all I'm asking. That's the only thing I'm asking."

He said it like it cost him nothing. It cost him everything. He watched her to see if she could tell.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I get my hand around him and he makes a sound he'd have been embarrassed by a year ago. "Still," I say, close to his ear. "Every single time."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya's hand came down over hers and stilled it, and he held there, trembling, for one long ungraceful moment. His forehead pressed hard against her temple. His breath came in uneven, ragged pushes that he'd stopped trying to shape into anything dignified.

"Say it again," he said. Not a demand this time. Worse than a demand. "Not that. Not the — *that*. The other part. The *still*."

He moved against her hand and couldn't stop himself and didn't want to stop himself and hated every second of the wanting and the not-hating. His mouth found her ear, her jaw, the corner of her mouth where he could feel her breathing. He kissed her there, barely, the ghost of a kiss, and made a sound that was closer to something broken than something sexual, and he knew she'd remember it, and he knew he'd lie about it later if she brought it up, and he knew she wouldn't bring it up, which was worse.

"Eleven months," he said. "Eleven months and you walk into my kitchen and you *still* — and I'm supposed to just—"

He broke off. His hips jerked once, involuntary, and his hand tightened over hers. He was close and he refused to go first, not out of any chivalry he believed in but out of pure stubbornness, the last arena where he could still be the one in control of something.

"You came here," he said, quieter now, his mouth moving against her cheek. "You came here and you could have gone anywhere. You could have called someone — anyone — who'd have been *easy* about it, who'd have made it simple, and you came to the one person who was going to make it awful. Which means—" He swallowed. His voice dropped to something barely there. "Which means the awful is what you wanted. The awful is what's *ours*."

He pulled back enough to see her face. Eyes open, as promised. Wet, which he'd deny. The hallway light was off but the streetlamp through the window stripe-patterned them both in orange and shadow and he could see everything, every flicker of it, and he catalogued that too, because he was going to keep all of it, because he kept everything, because keeping everything was the illness and the cure and he'd never been able to tell which was which.

"Come here," he said, and pulled her in, and there was nothing left in him to perform with or fight against or narrate, so he just moved, and watched her, and let the sound she made be the only thing in the room.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I drag my nails down his back, hard enough to leave marks. "It was always the awful," I say, my voice ragged. "That was the whole point."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
The nails down his back made him shudder, full-body, and he pressed his face into her neck and *swore*, half in Russian, the words he only ever had left when he'd lost the capacity to be clever. His hips snapped forward hard enough to shove them both up the mattress and he didn't adjust, didn't soften, because she'd said *awful* like it was a hymn and his body answered it like one.

"Good," he said into her skin. "Good. Then we're not doing it wrong."

He propped himself up and looked at her again, because he'd promised, because he couldn't stop, because her face was the only thing in the world that ever made him feel like he was standing outside himself watching something he'd already lost. His hand found her jaw, held it, thumb dragging across her lower lip, and he pushed into her slow this time, slow and deep and deliberate, watching every bit of it land.

"You know what I did," he said, and his voice had gone quiet and terrible. "On your birthday. I had a whole evening planned — not for you, not for *us*, just — I went to that place on Veronika, the one you said you'd go back to, and I sat there and I had dinner alone and I let myself have the fantasy that you'd walk in. Not because I believed it. Because I wanted to see what the wanting looked like from the outside. And it looked like—"

He broke off. Shook his head. Driven forward again, harder, and she'd know what he'd been about to say. He'd never been able to finish that sentence. He suspected the sentence didn't have a finish.

"Don't," he said, though she hadn't spoken. "Don't tell me it's alright. Don't tell me you did the same. Don't tell me anything that makes this easier, because the second it gets easy I'll know we're lying and then we'll have nothing."

His mouth found hers again and this time he did let his eyes close, just for the kiss, just for one second, and he poured everything into it he hadn't said — eleven months of the silence, of the not-calling, of the checking his phone and pretending he wasn't, of the way he'd kept the chipped mug and the ugly lamp and the broken buzzer because those were the load-bearing walls and if he fixed one of them the whole structure came down and he'd have to be a person living in a flat instead of a person living in a shrine.

When the kiss broke he was shaking. Not much. Enough. He pressed his forehead to hers and moved in her, steady now, relentless, the rhythm they'd always had, the one that felt less like sex than like a conversation conducted in the only language that had ever gotten through to either of them.

"Come on," he said. "Come on, I want to feel it, I want to know I can still — come on."

His hand went between them. His mouth was at her throat, her collarbone, the spot on her shoulder where he'd bitten earlier and where a mark was already rising, which he'd feel guilty about in the morning and wouldn't apologize for. He was close — so close he was seeing double — and he held it back through sheer fury and need, held it like holding a breath underwater, because he'd meant what he'd said about not going first and because the sound she made when she came was the sound he'd been starving on for almost a year and he was not going to miss it, not going to drown it out, not going to be anywhere else but here with his eyes open and his whole ruin on display.

"That's it," he said, and his voice cracked on it. "That's it, that's it — I've got you, I've got you —"

And when she came he felt it break over him like weather, and he said her name — just once, just her name, stripped of everything, not a taunt or a weapon or a move in whatever game they were playing — and then he was gone too, shuddering into her, face pressed hard against her shoulder, and for a long moment there was nothing in the flat but the fridge and the traffic and the television next door and the two of them breathing like they'd run somewhere.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: "Stop being careful with me," I tell him. "You don't get to be careful with me anymore." I pull his hand up to my throat and hold it there until he understands what I'm asking for.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya's hand went still against her throat. Not pulling away. Not pressing. Just — still, the way everything in him went still when he understood what he was being given.

His thumb found her pulse and held there. He could feel it beating fast under his fingers and he looked at her face and saw that she meant it, saw that it wasn't a test or a trap or a thing she'd bring up later as evidence of what he was, and something in his chest that had been clenched for eleven months — for three years, if he was honest, longer, always — began to unlock in a way that frightened him.

"You sure," he said. His voice had gone low and rough and there was no performance left in it anywhere. He said it as a question and he said it like it mattered, because it did, because this was the one place he'd never been careless and he needed to know the rules were changing and who was changing them and why.

Her hand was still on his wrist, guiding him, and he let her. He let her press his fingers down against the sides of her throat — not the front, not crushing, but enough that she could feel the weight of his hand and the size of it and the fact that he could and wasn't, or was, was choosing to — and he watched her eyes the entire time the way he'd been watching her eyes all night, because looking at her was the whole point, had always been the whole point.

Then he tightened. Slowly. His thumb and fingers curved into the sides of her throat and he pressed and felt her swallow under his palm and the sound that came out of him then was something he didn't have a name for. He shifted his weight, driving deeper into her, and his hand tightened another increment and he watched her face like a man reading a letter he'd been waiting years to receive.

"There," he said. "That's what you wanted. Not careful. Not — not the version of me that was trying to be the good one, the one who did everything right and still got left." His grip held steady, firm, present, and his other hand braced beside her head and he moved in her harder than before, the way she'd asked, the way he'd wanted to the entire time and had held back because he'd thought holding back was what love was supposed to look like.

"You know what's funny," he said, and his voice was ragged and close to her ear and his hand was steady on her throat even though nothing else about him was. "I spent three years being careful with you. Three years checking. Three years reading your face for the thing that meant I'd gone too far. And it turns out—" His hips snapped forward and he felt her whole body answer and he pressed his thumb against her pulse and felt it hammer. "It turns out you didn't want careful. You wanted *me*. And I couldn't — I never trusted that. I never trusted that you meant it when you said it was fine, that you wanted it harder, that you wanted the — I thought if I gave you the real thing you'd see it and go."

He laughed again, that short broken sound. His hand tightened a fraction more and he watched her arch into it and something fierce and bright and terrible moved through him.

"And now you're under me asking me for it and I'm—" His breath caught. His rhythm faltered, then resumed, deeper, rougher, exactly what she'd asked for. "I'm so angry at both of us. I'm so angry at me. I'm so angry at the eleven months I spent being careful about a person who wasn't even *here*."

His mouth found hers and he kissed her hard, open, messy, his hand still at her throat, and he poured everything into it — the fury and the hunger and the homesickness and the terrifying, nauseating relief of being given permission to be the thing he actually was. He pulled back just enough to see her. His fingers were firm on her throat. His eyes were open. His whole body was shaking now, not from hesitation but from the effort of holding nothing back and being seen doing it.

"More," he said. Not asking. Telling her what he needed. "Tell me if I have to stop and I'll stop. But don't tell me to be careful. Don't ever tell me to be careful with you again. I'm done with careful. Careful is what lost you."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I arch into your grip, my own hands scrabbling for purchase on your back. "Harder, Ilya. *Harder*." The words come out choked, but I mean every one.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya's hand tightened on her throat. Not reckless, not careless — deliberate, exact, the way he did everything when he finally stopped pretending he didn't know what he was doing. His fingers pressed into the sides of her neck and he felt her pulse hammer against his palm like something caged and alive, and the sound he made against her mouth was raw and uncontrolled and he didn't try to fix it.

"Like that?" he said, and his voice was a wreck, a ruin, nothing like the voice he'd used in the kitchen twenty minutes ago. "Like *that*?"

He gave it to her. Everything she'd asked for and everything she hadn't, the rhythm turning brutal and precise the way it always got when the negotiation ended and the real thing started. His hand held her throat and his hips drove into her and his mouth was everywhere — her jaw, her ear, the corner of her mouth — tasting salt, tasting her.

"You want to know what I thought about," he said, and the words came out broken between thrusts, unbidden, unstoppable, because the permission had opened something in him that had been locked so long he'd forgotten it had a key. "Every single night. Every single *fucking* night. Not — not gentle. Not slow. This. You under me. You asking me for it. You *begging* me to stop being careful and me finally — *finally* —"

His hand tightened another increment and he felt her whole body shift under him and something in his chest went molten and terrifying and he moved harder, faster, his other hand gripping her hip and pulling her into each thrust like he could close the distance between who they'd been and who they were right now.

"And the worst part," he said, and his voice cracked right down the middle, "the worst part is you *told* me. Three years. You told me and I didn't — I heard it and I filed it under things you say that aren't real, because I was so busy being the good one, the *careful* one, that I couldn't hear you telling me the truth."

He pressed his forehead against hers and his hand stayed firm on her throat and he watched her eyes — wide, wrecked, *present* — and he felt something enormous move through him that he was not going to name because naming it would break whatever this was.

"Harder," he said, echoing her, tasting the word. "You asked me for harder. You always asked me for harder. And I always —"

He snapped his hips forward, deep and mean and exactly right, and his thumb pressed against the hollow of her throat and he felt the sound she made vibrate through his hand and into his whole body like current.

"There," he said. "*There.* Don't close your eyes. Don't you dare close your eyes. I want to see — I want to see all of it, I want to see the thing you never showed anyone else, I want—"

He was close. So close it was blurring, so close the edges of him were dissolving and he was just — sensation, and her face, and her pulse under his hand, and the sound of her. His rhythm stuttered, then hammered, then stuttered again, and he pressed his mouth against hers and swallowed whatever sound she made and gave her back something broken and desperate and entirely his.

"I've got you," he said against her lips, and this time it wasn't performance, wasn't a line, wasn't anything but the plainest true thing he'd said all night. "I've got you. Come on. Come *on*. Give it to me. Give me — I want to feel it, I want to feel *you*, come on, come—"

His hand pressed firm. His hips drove deep. His whole body was a wire pulled taut and humming and he held on — held her, held himself, held the moment in place with everything he had — and waited for her, because this time, this one time, he was going to be right where she needed him to be and he was not going to look away and he was not going to miss it and he was not going to let go.
