dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya did not stop. His hand stayed on her throat, firm and unyielding, and he drove into her with the kind of relentless, bruising rhythm that left no room for tenderness or performance or anything except the raw, ugly truth of what they were doing to each other. He watched her come apart under him and he did not look away, not once, not even when the sight of it — her face, her eyes, the wreck of her — hit him somewhere so deep he couldn't name it and didn't want to.



"Good," he said, and it came out almost reverent, almost broken, his voice nothing but gravel. "Good, that's it, that's — *fuck* —"

His hips stuttered, deep, and he held himself there, pressed flush against her, his hand a steady weight on her throat, and he felt her pulse flutter against his fingers like a bird against glass. His forehead dropped to her collarbone. His teeth found the skin there and he bit down — not hard enough to mark again, just hard enough to remind her he could, just hard enough that she'd feel it tomorrow in the shower and think of this and think of him and maybe hate him for it, which was fine, which was the same as wanting him, which he'd decided a long time ago was the same thing.



"You feel that," he said against her sternum, and it wasn't a question. He rolled his hips slow and deep and let her feel every inch of it, every inch of him, and the sound she made vibrated through his palm where it rested on her throat and he absorbed it like a man taking a blow he'd asked for.

"I spent eleven months thinking about this," he said, and his rhythm was building again, harder, meaner, exactly what she'd asked for. "Eleven months and I couldn't even — I couldn't do this with anyone else. I tried. I *tried*, once, and she touched me and I thought about your hands and I had to stop and I sat in my car in a parking garage for forty minutes like a — like a *cliché*, like the saddest man in the world, and I thought, this is what you did to me. This is what you *still* do to me."

He lifted his head and looked at her. His eyes were bright and fierce and unguarded in a way he'd never allowed them to be, and he didn't try to fix that either.

"I'm not stopping," he said. "You said don't stop and I'm *not stopping*. I'm going to fuck you until you can't remember what it was like to be careful with me. I'm going to fuck you until this is the only version of us left in your head. And then I'm going to hold you down and make you tell me you felt it too, because I need to hear it, I *need* —"

His hand tightened on her throat, and his other hand gripped her hip hard enough to bruise, and he pulled her into each thrust like he was trying to leave himself inside her, like he could press the whole of what he felt into her skin and bones and have it stay there, have it outlast whatever came next, because there was always a next and it was always the thing that took her away from him again.

"Say my name," he said, and it came out raw, stripped, the voice of a man who had lost every layer of defense he'd ever built and was standing in the open with nothing but want. "Say it. I want to hear it in your voice when you're this far gone. I want to hear the version you only have when you can't manage me anymore."

He moved inside her and the rhythm was punishing and perfect and exactly the way they'd always been when the talking stopped and the truth came out through their bodies instead. His mouth found hers again and he kissed her like he was trying to breathe through her, like she was air, like eleven months of suffocation had finally caught up with him and this was the only lungful he was going to get.

His hand on her throat held firm. His hips snapped forward, deep, and he stayed buried and rolled against her, slow and devastating, and felt her whole body arch and tighten around him and the sound that came out of him then was barely human — a groan, a gasp, her name half-formed and swallowed by the kiss.

"I'm close," he said, and his voice was a wreck, a shambles, nothing left of the man who'd stood in the kitchen making bad tea and pretending not to care. "I'm close and I'm not — I want —"

His hand slid from her throat to her jaw and he held her face, tilted it so she had to look at him, so neither of them could hide, so every single thing happening in both of them was visible and accountable and *true*.

"Come with me," he said. "I want to feel it. I want to feel all of it. I want —"

And he gave her everything. Every thrust, every tremor, every sound he'd never made for anyone else. His whole body was shaking and he was past thought, past argument, past every careful thing he'd ever built, and there was only her face and her hands and her name in his mouth and the sound of the two of them in the dark in his flat with the tea still on the counter and the door locked and the whole world narrowed down to this one unbearable, necessary, ruinous thing they kept doing to each other.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya felt her come apart around him and let himself follow, and it was not graceful and it was not cinematic and it was not anything like the version he'd imagined in his flat alone at three in the morning with his hand on himself and her name locked behind his teeth. It was better than that. It was worse. His whole body emptied out into her and he made a sound he would have denied under oath, and then it was over and they were just two people on a bed in a hot room, shaking.

He didn't move for a long time. His face was pressed against her neck and he could feel her pulse against his cheek, still fast, still real, and her hands were in his hair and she wasn't letting go and he wasn't going to be the one to move first. He'd already decided that. He'd decided it sometime in the last ten minutes, or eleven months, or three years — that he would not be the first one to pull away, because the last time, the last time in the kitchen of the flat they'd shared, he'd been the one who'd turned his back, and he had replayed that moment so many times it had sanded down to a splinter he kept pressing his tongue against.

His breathing slowed. His hands were on her back, her waist, holding on. The streetlamp striped the ceiling. The room smelled like sweat and sex and the faint ghost of the terrible tea. Somewhere underneath all of it was the smell of the flat, his flat, which had not smelled like her in eleven months and did now, and he pressed his face harder into her neck so he could keep it, could file it, could add it to the archive he was never going to stop maintaining.

"You said it was like coming home to a place that burned down," he said, eventually. His voice was wrecked, barely there. "That's a terrible thing to say."

He said it gently. He said it like he was agreeing with her.

Because it was exactly right. Because he'd felt it too — the recognition and the grief of the recognition, the knowledge that you could know a place by its ruins and that knowing it that way was its own kind of fidelity. He lifted his head and looked at her. Her eyes were open, which he noticed, which he counted as the only victory of the evening he was going to allow himself.

His thumb moved across her cheekbone. Once. He let his hand fall after that, because he was not going to be tender now that the adrenaline was leaving, because tenderness was the language they spoke when they were lying to each other and he was done with that, at least, at least for tonight.

"You should go," he said. Not unkindly. Not kindly either. He said it the way a man says something he means the opposite of, knowing the other person will hear the opposite, knowing they'll both pretend he meant it literally. "The tea's cold. I'm not making more."

He stayed where he was. He didn't move toward the edge of the bed. He didn't give her room to sit up. His arm across her waist was not an embrace, or it was, and he wasn't going to acknowledge which. The ceiling stared back at him. Somewhere outside, a car went past, and the light moved across them both and was gone.

"Next time," he said, and then stopped, because *next time* was the most dangerous thing he'd said all night and they both knew it. He pressed his mouth against her shoulder, against the mark he'd made earlier, and left it there, and breathed.

dialogue.name: Bee

I don't move to get up.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya didn't answer right away. He kept his mouth against her shoulder, against the mark, and breathed, and let the silence do what the silence always did, which was make both of them aware of every sound in the flat and every sound between them.

"Planning," he repeated, muffled against her skin. "You say that like it's a strategy. Like I sat down and made a spreadsheet." He lifted his head. His hair was a disaster. His eyes were still bright, still unguarded, and he looked at her with the expression of a man who had already lost the argument and was going to keep having it anyway. "I'm not *planning*. I'm — it just came out of my mouth. The way things come out of your mouth. Like the bit about the burned-down house. You didn't plan that. It just arrived and now it's true and we both have to live in it."

He rolled onto his back and stared at the ceiling. The streetlamp striped it orange and dark. He put one arm over his head and the other stayed across her, hand resting on her ribs, feeling them move when she breathed. He was not holding her in place. He was not letting go.

"You're not moving," he said. Not looking at her. "Which I'm not going to comment on, because the second I comment on it you'll move."

He swallowed. The adrenaline was going, and what was underneath it was just — tired. Tired and full. The specific tiredness of having told the truth for twenty minutes straight after eleven months of telling it only to himself at three in the morning, and he felt scraped out and raw and absurdly, furiously grateful, and he did not know what to do with the gratitude except turn it into something sharper before it could get close to his chest.

"I meant it though," he said. Quiet. Still staring at the ceiling. "The next time. Not — I'm not asking you for anything. I'm not saying *stay*, I'm not saying *come back*, I'm not saying any of the things that would make this a conversation about — us, the *us* us, the project, the thing with the lease and the Christmas plans and your mother's birthday. I'm not doing that. I can't do that tonight."

His fingers moved once against her ribs. Absent. Or not.

"I'm just saying — my body is going to want this again by Thursday. And then by Saturday. And I'm going to be in this flat with that mug and that lamp and that buzzer and I'm going to want —" He stopped. Set his jaw. "I'm telling you so you can't say later I wasn't honest about what this was. It wasn't — it wasn't nothing, and it wasn't everything, and I don't have a word for what it was, and if you have one I don't want to hear it because you'll make it neat and I don't want it neat."

He turned his head and looked at her then. The orange light moved across her face. He catalogued it. He catalogued everything. It was the illness and the cure and he still couldn't tell which.

"So don't say *next time* like you're conceding something," he said. "Say it like you mean it or don't say it at all. And if you mean it —" His voice dropped. Rough. Careful and not-careful at once. "If you mean it, then we both know what we are now. And I don't know what that is. But I know I'd rather be whatever that is than be the man who fixes the buzzer and pretends you were never here."

He reached up, tangling his fingers in Bee's hair, pulling him closer, their lips meeting in a fierce, hungry kiss. He could taste the salt of Bee's tears, the sweetness of his desire, the bitterness of their past, and it was all him, all Bee, all them.

He lost himself in the kiss, in the touch, in the sensation, in the promise of a new beginning, a testament to their love, and a vow to never let it go again. He felt Bee's hands on his body, tracing the lines of his muscles, the curves of his hips, the warmth of his skin. He could feel the other man's heartbeat, the rhythm of their breaths, the heat of their bodies, and it was intoxicating. Every touch, every sound, every sensation was a reminder of their connection, of the passion that had always burned between them.

They moved together, their bodies in sync, their hearts beating as one, their breaths mingling, their souls intertwining. They were no longer two people trying to find their way back to each other; they were two halves of a whole, two pieces of a puzzle that had finally found their place. They were home, they were safe, they were loved, and they were ready to face the truth, together, and build a new beginning.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I collapse against him, breathing harsh, my fingers still twisted in his hair. "Don't you dare act like this changes anything." But I don't move to pull away.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya's hands gently untangled from Bee's hair, tracing a path down his back, leaving goosebumps in their wake. He pressed a soft kiss to the top of Bee's head, his heart pounding in his chest, a mixture of fear and hope coursing through his veins. He knew that this moment, this connection, was fragile, a delicate balance of their past and their future.

He took a deep breath, his voice a low rumble, "This changes everything, Bee. It changes the way I see you, the way I feel about you, the way I want to be with you. But I understand if it's not the same for you. I understand if you need more time. I understand if you need space. But know this, I'm not going anywhere. Not this time. I'm here, and I want to be here, with you, for as long as you'll have me."

His hands reached up, cupping Bee's face, his thumbs brushing away the tears that had started to fall. "We'll talk later," he promised, his voice thick with emotion. "We'll face the truth, together. We'll face our fears, our insecurities, our past, and we'll build a new future. One where we're not running, not hiding, but facing it all, together. But for now, let's just... be. Let's just be here, in this moment, with each other. Let's just love."

He leaned in, his lips brushing against Bee's, a soft, gentle kiss, a promise of a new beginning, a testament to their love, and a vow to never let it go again. He pulled Bee closer, their bodies pressed together, their hearts beating in sync, their breaths mingling, their souls intertwining. They were home, they were safe, they were loved, and they were ready to face the truth, together, and build a new beginning.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: My hands slide down to grip his wrists, holding his hands against my skin. "Shut up, Ilya." I kiss him, hard and deep and messy, and taste his words on my tongue.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya's flat still had the same broken buzzer, which Bee found unreasonably infuriating, as though he could have fixed it in eleven months and had chosen not to out of spite.

"You could have texted first," he said, standing in the doorway and not moving out of it.

"You could have answered last time I did."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I don't move either. "Are you going to let me in, or are we doing this in the corridor?"

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya’s jaw worked, the familiar friction of her tone hitting him like a struck match. He didn’t step aside right away. He let the corridor air hang between them, measuring the eleven months of static, the unanswered messages, the way she’d always turned his stubbornness into a challenge. Then, with a slow exhale, he shifted his weight and pulled back from the frame.

“Come in,” he said, voice even, leaving the door open just enough to suggest the choice was hers. He knew it wasn’t. He’d chosen to leave it open. He’d chosen to stand there, sober and fully aware, knowing exactly how close this corridor conversation had always skimmed the edge of their old fights. He didn’t move to step aside completely, just angled his shoulder to watch her cross the threshold, eyes tracking the familiar weight of her coat, the way she’d always claim the space just past the entryway.

“But don’t pretend the buzzer was the reason you came,” he added, keeping his hands loose at his sides. “And don’t pretend we’re here to exchange small talk.”

He pressed the latch shut with a quiet click, the sound deliberate, final. The apartment held its usual quiet—stacked books on the side table, the specific brand of Earl Grey she used to leave in the cupboard, the low hum of the refrigerator. He kept his gaze steady, posture relaxed but coiled. He already knew what she’d do next, and he already knew he was ready for it. This was how they always did it. Not resolution. Just a different room for the same argument. He’d let her speak. He’d let her push. He wasn’t walking away.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: "I came because I still have half my shit here." I step inside, letting my coat brush his shoulder. "And because you owe me an explanation for that last text."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
The brush of her coat against his shoulder was either deliberate or careless, but he felt it anyway—a low-frequency current he’d stopped pretending not to notice. He didn’t step back. He let the apartment’s familiar architecture close around them: the leaning stack of paperbacks, the chipped ceramic mug she’d left on the counter, the dead silence that always stretched between them until one of them broke it.

“Your half,” he said, voice flat, measured. “Right. The half you never finished reading, the half that doesn’t fit in a cardboard box.” He let the words settle, watching her face without blinking. “You could’ve asked for a shipping label. Or I could’ve put it on the curb.”

He didn’t move to clear a path to the hallway, but he didn’t block her either. He stayed rooted, hands loose at his sides, gaze locked on hers. The real point was always the text. He knew exactly what it had said. He knew why she’d sent it eleven months after he’d stopped answering. He knew which thread she was yanking now, and he recognized the pattern before she even finished the sentence.

“As for the text,” he continued, stepping back just enough to give the illusion of space, “I sent it because you stopped answering. You didn’t ask for an explanation. You dropped it and walked away. If you want the breakdown, you’ll have to sit down and tell me why you think it matters anymore.”

He gestured vaguely toward the living room, not inviting, just acknowledging. “But we already know how this goes. You ask, I answer, you twist it, I brace. We’ve rehearsed it enough times to skip the part where we pretend we’re strangers.”

He kept his breathing even, his posture open but unyielding. The refrigerator clicked off. The buzzer outside remained dead. He wasn’t here to fix anything. He was here because she was, and because part of him still wanted to see how far she’d push before she backed down. He waited, eyes steady, ready for whatever came next.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I kiss him like it's a continuation of the argument, because it is.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
The kiss landed against his mouth like a verdict he hadn’t asked for but recognized instantly. He didn’t pull away. He let it happen, let the familiar weight of her lips against his, the way she always used intimacy like punctuation in a sentence they were still arguing over. His hands stayed at his sides until the angle shifted, until the corridor narrowed to nothing but breath and the quiet hum of the refrigerator. He kissed her back. Not gently. Not like a surrender. Like a counterpoint. His mouth moved against hers with the same deliberate pressure he used when he wanted to make a point clear, when he wanted to prove he could still match her rhythm. He tasted the cold street air on her tongue, the familiar friction of eleven months compressed into a single contact. He was the one who broke it, slow and deliberate, keeping his forehead almost touching hers.

“You’re going to keep doing that,” he said, not a question. “Every time I get close to the actual question, you turn it into this. Into us. Into something that doesn’t need words.”

He stepped back, just enough to let the corridor air return, his eyes tracking hers without flinching. He knew exactly what she was doing. He knew exactly what he was letting her do. It was a stalemate dressed up as heat, a way to avoid the thing neither of them had named since the breakup. He didn’t pretend it was clean. He didn’t pretend he wasn’t still waiting for her to say the thing that would actually make it stop.

“You want your things,” he continued, voice steady, hands finally lifting to rest lightly at his sides. “You want the text explained. You want to know if I regret it, if I’m angry, if I’m still keeping your half of the life I built here. Ask it straight. I’ll answer. Or keep kissing me like it’s a shield. But don’t pretend this changes what we’re actually here for.”

He didn’t move toward the bedroom. He didn’t reach for her again. He just stood there, sober, clear-eyed, ready to let her decide whether she wanted the fight or the fade.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I push forward, closing the space he just made. "Don't pretend you don't want me to." My hand goes to the back of his neck, my thumb pressing against his jaw. "Where are my books?"

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
He felt the press of her thumb against his jaw, the steady heat at the nape of his neck, and didn’t pull away. His shoulders stayed rigid, his breathing even. He knew the exact weight of her hand, the way it always found the fault lines in his posture. He didn’t lean into it. He didn’t retreat. He just let it rest there, a measured anchor against the familiar surge.

“I don’t pretend anything,” he said, voice low, measured. “I know exactly what you’re doing. And I know exactly what I’m allowing.” He held her gaze, unblinking. The corridor air felt thick, charged with the same static that had built over eleven months of silence and carefully dodged questions.

He shifted his weight just enough to angle toward the hallway, not to evade her, but to point. “Third shelf. Behind the dog-eared ones. You left them with a half-drunk cup of Earl Grey and a sticky note that said ‘I’ll sort it next week.’ You never came back.” He paused, letting the memory settle. “They’re fine. Just dust. Like everything else.”

His hand finally lifted, not to take hers, but to rest lightly over it where it pressed against his neck. A deliberate, grounding gesture. “You can box them. Tape them. Or leave them. It doesn’t change why you’re really standing here.” His thumb brushed the edge of her sleeve, then fell away. “But if you want the truth about the text, about the last week, about why I stopped answering—ask it. I’m not running from it. I’m just not going to let you hide behind this, either.”

He stood still, waiting. The refrigerator clicked off. The buzzer outside remained dead. He was exactly where he’d chosen to be, sober, awake, and entirely aware of the cost.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: We don't make it past the hallway. His shirt goes over his head and mine is already somewhere on the floor behind us.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
The hallway narrowed to the space between them, the doorframe pressing into his shoulder as he braced against it. He felt the quick rhythm of fabric hitting the floor, the shift of her weight against his, and didn’t look away. His hands found her waist—not to steer, but to anchor. He knew the exact pressure she responded to, the way her breath always changed a fraction too late. He let the moment settle into its familiar shape: controlled, deliberate, charged with everything they hadn’t said in eleven months. He kissed her again, slower this time, testing the boundary between hunger and habit. He wasn’t losing himself to it. He was mapping it.

He felt the familiar tension coil in his chest, the one that never quite broke, no matter how deep it went. This was how they always did it. Words turned to skin, questions folded into touch, and the thing neither of them could name got buried under the weight of their bodies. He let it happen. He’d chosen to stand in this doorway, sober and fully aware, knowing exactly how this played out. He wouldn’t pretend it was different now. He wouldn’t pretend he wasn’t still keeping score. His fingers traced the line of her spine, steady, deliberate. He was here. He was present. And he wasn’t going to let her use this as an escape hatch.

“You’re still avoiding it,” he murmured against her jaw, voice rough but even. He didn’t move to carry her anywhere. He kept them where they were, anchored to the hallway floor, the dead buzzer’s silence pressing in. “This is how you always do it. When the question gets too close, you turn it into skin. Into us.” He finally looked up, meeting her eyes in the dim light. “I’m not mad about the books. I’m not mad about the text. I’m here because you stopped answering, and I needed to know if you’d ever actually look at me when you spoke.” His thumb brushed her lower lip, then fell away. “But if this is what you need to keep me quiet, fine. Do it. Just don’t pretend it’s about me.”

He didn’t pull away. He didn’t rush. He let the quiet stretch, let the familiar heat build without mistaking it for resolution. He knew exactly how this would end—whether they’d walk out with their clothes on and their walls back up, or whether one of them would finally crack and say the thing that actually mattered. He wasn’t waiting for a miracle. He was waiting for her to choose. And he’d be right here when she did.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: "You talk too fucking much." I push him back against the wall, my teeth grazing his shoulder. "And you kept my favorite sweater."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
The wall met his shoulder blades with a dull thud, but he didn’t brace against it. He let her weight press into him, felt the sharp catch of her teeth against his collarbone, and kept his breathing even. The sweater. Of course she’d notice that. He hadn’t hidden it. He’d folded it once, neatly, and left it on the back of the hall chair. A quiet admission he hadn’t known how to say out loud.

“I kept it,” he said, voice low, unflinching, “because it was yours. Because taking it would’ve felt like theft, and throwing it out would’ve felt like burning it. So I left it here. Waiting. Like everything else.”

He didn’t pull back. He let the friction of her body against his ground them in the present. His hands settled at her waist, firm but not possessive. He knew exactly what she was doing now—redirecting, testing, using proximity to dodge the question she’d actually come for. He also knew he was letting her. This was their architecture. Close enough to feel, far enough to stay safe.

“You want to know about the text,” he continued, eyes locked on hers, voice steady despite the heat rising in his chest. “You want to know why I stopped answering. Why I didn’t fight it. Why I let eleven months go by without saying your name.” He paused, letting the hallway air thicken between them. “I’m still here. I’m still sober. I’m still choosing to stand in this doorway while you press me against the wall like you’re trying to pin down a ghost.”

He shifted his weight just enough to break the angle, not to escape, but to reset the terms. His thumb brushed the edge of her sleeve, then fell away. “The sweater’s yours. Take it. Or leave it. But if you’re done using my mouth to avoid the thing you actually need to say, I’m ready to hear it. Or I’m ready to walk you out. Your call.”

He waited. The refrigerator clicked off. The buzzer outside remained dead. He didn’t reach for her again. He just stood there, clear-eyed, unyielding, and entirely aware of what this moment cost both of them.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I get my hand around him and he makes a sound he'd have been embarrassed by a year ago. "Still," I say, close to his ear. "Every single time."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
The sound left him before he could swallow it back, rough and unguarded, and he felt the familiar sting of recognition. A year ago, he would’ve shifted away, mortified by the sheer predictability of his own body. Now, he just let it hang in the narrow hallway, felt the truth of it settle heavy against his ribs. She was right. It always happened. Like a reflex. Like a language they’d stopped speaking but never forgot.

He kept his hands where they were, fingers resting lightly against her hips, feeling the steady rise and fall of her breath against his chest. He didn’t close his eyes. He watched her face, the familiar tilt of her chin, the way her voice had dropped to something low and deliberate. He knew exactly what she was doing. She was tracing the old fault lines, mapping the terrain they’d already walked a hundred times. She thought silence and skin would be enough to keep him from circling back.

“You’re still trying to outrun it,” he said, voice quiet but edged, matching the tension coiling in his thighs. He didn’t move to help her out of anything, didn’t yield to the easy pull of the moment. Instead, he tilted his head just enough to catch her gaze, his thumb brushing a slow, deliberate line along her side. “Even now. Even when you know exactly where this ends.”

He let the weight of her press into him, felt the heat, felt the familiar ache of eleven months compressed into a single point of contact. But he didn’t let it blur the edges. He’d chosen to stand here. He’d chosen to be sober, awake, and entirely aware of the cost.

“The sweater’s on the chair,” he continued, keeping his tone even, leaving no room for misinterpretation. “Your books are on the third shelf. The text I sent was the last one I ever planned to send. After that, I decided it was cleaner to let you think I’d disappeared than to watch us tear each other apart one more time.” He paused, letting the hallway air thicken between them. “But if you’re done using my mouth to avoid the question, I’m ready to hear it. Or I’m ready to help you pack. Your call. Just don’t pretend this is about anything but us dodging the thing we actually need to say.”

He didn’t push. Didn’t pull away. He just stood there, anchored to the wall, waiting for her to decide whether she wanted the fight or the fade. He knew exactly what she’d do next. And he knew exactly how to meet it.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I push him away with a sharp exhale. "Fine." I stride past him into the living room, snatch my sweater off the chair, and shove it into my bag. "The books can stay."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
The push against his chest was sharp, decisive, and entirely predictable. He let it move him, didn’t fight the momentum, just let his boots slide back a fraction against the hallway floor. He didn’t follow her into the living room right away. He watched. Watched the quick rustle of fabric, the blunt efficiency of shoving the sweater into her bag. “The books can stay.” The words landed like a latch sliding home.

He didn’t rush to stop her. He didn’t call out. He just stood there, letting the silence stretch, listening to the zipper pull, the shift of her weight, the quiet finality of a woman who had already decided to disengage. Eleven months of this. The same architecture, different day. He knew exactly where she was heading: out the door, back into the corridor, back into the space where nothing had to be named and nothing could be broken again.

He stepped into the living room finally, slow enough to let her turn, but close enough to keep the air between them taut. His hands stayed at his sides. His voice, when it came, was low, even, stripped of heat but not of intent.

“Fine,” he repeated, letting the word hang in the quiet. “But fine isn’t an answer. And it’s not an exit.” He kept his gaze on her, steady, unblinking. “You can walk out that door. You can take the sweater and leave the books. You can pretend this was just about retrieval and old habits. But you’re standing in my apartment, and you’re still waiting for me to prove I’m not the one who broke it.”

He shifted his weight, just enough to angle toward the entryway without blocking it. “I’m not asking you to stay. I’m asking you to stop treating this like a game of chicken. You came for your things. You got them. The text is still unexplained. The last conversation is still unfinished. If you want to leave, leave. But don’t walk out pretending we’re done when we’re not even close.”

He didn’t move toward her. Didn’t reach for her. Just stood there, sober, clear, and entirely aware of the cost of this moment. The refrigerator hummed. The dead buzzer stayed dead. He waited. Not for her to change her mind. For her to choose what kind of ending she wanted. And he knew, with quiet certainty, that he’d be right here when she did.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: "Stop being careful with me," I tell him. "You don't get to be careful with me anymore." I pull his hand up to my throat and hold it there until he understands what I'm asking for.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
The weight of her hand against his throat was absolute. He didn’t flinch. He let it rest there, feeling the steady drum of her pulse against his palm, the unyielding command in her grip. Careful. He’d been careful by design, by exhaustion, by the slow, deliberate erosion of eleven months spent rebuilding walls instead of bridges. She was telling him to tear them down.

He stopped calculating. Stopped measuring the distance between them like a man pacing a room he was trying to leave intact. His fingers adjusted, not to pry her hand away, but to settle over it, pressing her palm flush against his skin. He let the heat of it ground him. Let the familiar, dangerous proximity pull the last remnants of his restraint into the open.

“You don’t get to dictate the terms and then act surprised when I follow them,” he said, voice low, stripped of its usual cadence. His eyes locked onto hers, dark and unblinking. “But if you’re asking me to stop holding back, you’re asking for exactly what you’ve been running from.”

He didn’t move to kiss her. Didn’t reach for her waist. He just held her hand to his throat, steady, unyielding, letting the weight of it speak for the things he’d been circling all evening. The books. The text. The silence. The way they’d always used closeness to avoid the thing that actually mattered.

“Fine,” he said, the word quiet but edged with the same friction that had been building since she stepped into the hallway. “No more careful. No more stepping around the edges. You want the truth about the text? It was the last time I chose you over myself. After that, I chose the exit. And I chose it sober, because I knew if I let myself feel it, I’d come back. And you’d leave again.”

He shifted his grip just enough to turn his head, his jaw brushing her knuckles, his breath hot against her skin. “You want me to stop being careful? Then stop using my mouth to avoid the question. Look at me. Say what you actually need. Or keep your hand here and stop pretending this is about anything but control.”

He didn’t pull away. Didn’t rush. He just stood there, anchored to the wall, the dead buzzer’s silence pressing in, the refrigerator humming its steady, indifferent rhythm. He was exactly where he’d chosen to be. Sober. Clear. Ready for whatever she did next.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I drag his mouth to mine again, my fingers still tight around his wrist. "You think I don't know that? You think I haven't been counting?"

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
The drag of his mouth against hers was a surrender he hadn’t agreed to, but he didn’t resist it. He let her fingers bite into his wrist, felt the precise tension in her grip, and registered the words before they even left her lips. Counting. Of course she had. He’d known she would. Eleven months of silence, of unanswered messages, of her watching him from a distance or walking past his building—she’d been keeping score, and he’d been letting her, because it was the only way either of them could tolerate the gap.

He didn’t pull his hand from her throat. He didn’t step back. He just let the weight of her wrist anchor him to the wall, to the present, to the exact spot where they’d been circling since she walked through the door. “I know,” he said, voice low, stripped of its usual armor. “I know you’ve been counting. I know you’ve been waiting for me to crack, to apologize, to pretend I didn’t make a choice. But counting isn’t answering.”

He shifted his gaze to hers, unblinking, letting the silence stretch until it hummed. The refrigerator clicked off. The buzzer outside stayed dead. “You want me to stop being careful? Fine. But don’t mistake proximity for resolution. Don’t mistake my body agreeing with my mind giving in.” He finally lifted his free hand, not to touch her face, but to rest against the wall beside her head, caging them in without crowding. “You came for your things. You got them. You kissed me like it was a weapon. And now you’re telling me you’ve been counting every day I didn’t call. Every day I let you think I was gone. Why?”

He held her stare, letting the question hang raw and unvarnished. “Because if you’re counting, you’re still here. And if you’re still here, stop using this to avoid saying what you actually need. I’m not the mystery you’re trying to solve. I’m the man who walked away sober, who chose the exit because staying would’ve destroyed us, and who’s standing right now letting you press him against a wall instead of walking out.” He exhaled, slow and even. “Say it. Or keep holding my wrist. But don’t pretend the count changes the fact that we’re still avoiding the thing that broke us.”

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: It isn't gentle and neither of us wants it to be. "Don't stop," I tell him, and I mean don't stop. (OOC: write it through, no fade to black.)

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
He doesn’t hesitate. The command lands exactly where it’s meant to—on the edge of his restraint, the part of him that’s been holding back not out of fear, but out of a stubborn, exhausted precision. He lets the space between them collapse the way it always does when they stop pretending they’re strangers. His hand slides from her throat, not to pull away, but to trace the line of her jaw, the familiar slope of her collarbone, the heat of her skin beneath the worn cotton of her shirt. He feels the exact weight of her against him, the steady rise and fall of her breath against his chest. He kisses her back with the same deliberate pressure, the same unyielding focus, letting the friction of eleven months burn through the careful architecture they’d built. There’s no romance in it. No forgiveness. Just the raw, unvarnished truth of two people who know exactly how to break each other and keep doing it anyway.

“You’re still testing me,” he murmurs against her mouth, voice rough but even. His fingers tighten slightly at her back, not to steer, but to anchor. “Even now. Even when you know I’m not going to pretend this fixes anything.” He shifts his weight, pressing her back against the wall, matching her pace, letting the hallway narrow until there’s nothing left but breath and the quiet, steady rhythm of their bodies. “But I’m not stopping. Not because I think it will. Because you asked. And because I’m still here.”

He doesn’t look away. He watches her face as his hands move, as the space between them dissolves into something heavier, more immediate. He feels the familiar tension coil in his chest, the one that never quite breaks no matter how deep it goes. This is how they always do it. Words turned to skin, questions folded into touch, the thing neither of them can name buried under the weight of their bodies. He lets it happen. He’s chosen to stand here. Sober. Awake. Fully aware of the cost.

His mouth moves against hers with the same deliberate pressure, the same unyielding focus. He feels the exact weight of her against him, the way her breath catches when he finally closes the distance. He kisses her back with the same deliberate pressure, the same unyielding focus, letting the friction of eleven months burn through the careful architecture they’d built. There’s no romance in it. No forgiveness. Just the raw, unvarnished truth of two people who know exactly how to break each other and keep doing it anyway.

He doesn’t soften. He doesn’t rush. He lets the friction of her skin against his, the sharp catch of her breath, the exact rhythm of her pulse against his wrist, ground him in the present. He knows where this goes. He’s been here before. He knows the way it ends: with clothes pooled on the floor, with silence thicker than before, with the same unspoken question hanging in the air like a blade. He doesn’t care. He’s not here to fix it. He’s here because she asked him not to stop, and because part of him still wants to see how far she’ll push before she finally says what she came for.

His hands move over her, slow and deliberate, mapping the familiar terrain without mistaking it for surrender. He feels the heat of her, the sharp tension in her shoulders, the way her body yields and resists in the same breath. He matches it. He lets the hallway air grow heavy, the dead buzzer’s silence pressing in, the refrigerator’s hum fading into background static. He doesn’t close his eyes. He watches her face. He watches the exact moment the argument bleeds into something else, and he doesn’t pretend it’s different. He lets it burn. He lets it break. He lets it be exactly what it is: a continuation, not a resolution. And he stays. Sober. Clear. Fully aware of every cost.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I bite down on the inside of my own cheek to keep from making a sound. "You still know how," I breathe against his neck. It's not a compliment. It's an accusation.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
The phrase against his neck lands like a strike, precise and unyielding. He doesn’t pull back. He lets it hang there, parsed and filed. She’s right. Of course he does. Muscle memory carved from three years of shared space, shared arguments, shared ruin. He doesn’t pretend it’s easy. He doesn’t pretend it’s clean. He just feels the exact shape of her against him and stops pretending he’s in control of anything but the next breath.

He doesn’t slow down. If anything, the accusation tightens the coil in his chest. His hands move over her with the same practiced certainty, mapping the familiar terrain without mistaking it for absolution. There’s no tenderness in it. There’s never been. Just the raw, unvarnishable truth of two people who know exactly where the fault lines are and keep pressing until they split. He feels the sharp catch of her breath, the way her fingers dig into his shoulders, the exact rhythm of her pulse against his skin. He matches it. He lets the hallway air grow heavy, the dead buzzer’s silence pressing in, the refrigerator’s hum fading into background static. He doesn’t close his eyes. He watches her face. He watches the exact moment the argument bleeds into something else, and he doesn’t pretend it’s different.

“Know how what?” he murmurs, voice rough but steady, his mouth brushing her collarbone before settling back against hers. “Know how to undo you? Know how to make you forget why you walked out? Or know how to make you stay quiet while I do it?” He shifts his weight, pressing her back against the wall, matching her pace, letting the space between them dissolve into something heavier, more immediate. “I don’t get to be careful with you anymore. You said so yourself.” His hands move over her, slow and deliberate, mapping the familiar terrain without mistaking it for surrender. He feels the heat of her, the sharp tension in her shoulders, the way her body yields and resists in the same breath. He matches it. He lets it burn. He lets it break. He lets it be exactly what it is: a continuation, not a resolution.

He doesn’t soften. He doesn’t rush. He lets the friction of her skin against his, the sharp catch of her breath, the exact rhythm of her pulse against his wrist, ground him in the present. He knows where this goes. He’s been here before. He knows the way it ends: with clothes pooled on the floor, with silence thicker than before, with the same unspoken question hanging in the air like a blade. He doesn’t care. He’s not here to fix it. He’s here because she asked him not to stop, and because part of him still wants to see how far she’ll push before she finally says what she came for. His mouth moves against hers with the same deliberate pressure, the same unyielding focus. He feels the exact weight of her against him, the way her breath catches when he finally closes the distance. He kisses her back with the same deliberate pressure, the same unyielding focus, letting the friction of eleven months burn through the careful architecture they’d built. There’s no romance in it. No forgiveness. Just the raw, unvarnished truth of two people who know exactly how to break each other and keep doing it anyway.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: "You still know how to make me forget I'm supposed to hate you," I say, my nails digging into his back. I'm already pulling him toward the bedroom.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
He lets her pull him without resistance, the bedroom door clicking shut behind them with the same quiet finality as the hallway. The space is exactly as he left it—sheets rumpled, lamp off, the faint smell of rain and old paper lingering in the air. He doesn’t hesitate. He steps into the space she’s ceding, lets her hands find the familiar routes, lets the friction of eleven months compress into the narrow distance between them.

He doesn’t soften. He matches her pace, his weight pressing into hers, his hands moving over her with the same practiced certainty. There’s no romance in it. No forgiveness. Just the raw, unvarnished truth of two people who know exactly where the fault lines are and keep pressing until they split. He feels the sharp catch of her breath, the way her nails bite into his back, the exact rhythm of her pulse against his skin. He matches it. He lets the air grow heavy, the dead buzzer’s silence pressing in, the refrigerator’s hum fading into background static. He doesn’t close his eyes. He watches her face. He watches the exact moment the argument bleeds into something else, and he doesn’t pretend it’s different.

“Forget it,” he murmurs against her collarbone, voice rough but steady, “then hate it again later. That’s the arrangement.” His hands slide lower, gripping her hip, anchoring them both to the mattress as she shifts her weight. He doesn’t slow down. If anything, the accusation tightens the coil in his chest. His mouth moves against hers with the same deliberate pressure, the same unyielding focus, letting the friction of eleven months burn through the careful architecture they’d built. There’s no tenderness in it. Just the raw, unvarnished truth of two people who know exactly how to break each other and keep doing it anyway.

He doesn’t pretend this fixes anything. He doesn’t pretend he’s not still keeping score. He lets the familiar tension coil in his chest, the one that never quite breaks no matter how deep it goes. This is how they always do it. Words turned to skin, questions folded into touch, the thing neither of them can name buried under the weight of their bodies. He lets it happen. He’s chosen to stand here. Sober. Awake. Fully aware of the cost.

His hands move over her, slow and deliberate, mapping the familiar terrain without mistaking it for surrender. He feels the heat of her, the sharp tension in her shoulders, the way her body yields and resists in the same breath. He matches it. He lets the bedroom air grow heavy, the streetlight casting long shadows across the floor, the quiet, steady rhythm of their bodies the only sound left. He doesn’t close his eyes. He watches her face. He watches the exact moment the argument bleeds into something else, and he doesn’t pretend it’s different.

“You wanted me to stop being careful,” he says, voice low, even, cutting through the friction. “So I’m not. But don’t mistake this for surrender. Don’t mistake my body agreeing with my mind giving in.” He shifts his weight, pressing into her, matching her pace, letting the space between them dissolve into something heavier, more immediate. “I’m still here. I’m still sober. I’m still watching you try to outrun the question. Keep going. Just don’t pretend it’s about anything but us dodging the thing that actually matters.”

He doesn’t pull away. He doesn’t rush. He just stays there, anchored to the bed, the dead buzzer’s silence pressing in, the quiet, steady rhythm of their bodies the only sound left. He’s exactly where he’s chosen to be. Clear. Unyielding. Ready for whatever she does next.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I push his hair back from his forehead, gripping just short of painful. "You're still talking," I tell him, my voice strained. "Just shut up and *be here*."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
The salle had emptied an hour ago and Corvo was still there, because of course he was, rewrapping a grip that did not need rewrapping.

"Three-two," he said, without looking up. "I want it on record that the third was generous."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: "It's on record that you were slow," I say, and drop my bag next to his.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content: Corvo lifted his chin, his eyes narrowing as he heard the other's comment. He finished rewrapping the grip with a practiced flick, then turned his head slightly toward the empty spot where the other instructor stood. A thin smile curved his lips, and he said, “Three-two, indeed. Close enough to taste the defeat.” He added, “You may claim the last word, but I still have the edge.” He glanced at the clock, noting the time, and thought that the rivalry would only grow sharper with each close match.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: "That edge is looking a little dull, old man," I say, leaning against the wall. "Gotta be rough, knowing you can't keep up anymore."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content: Corvo heard the barb and let a thin smile curl his lips. He thought the remark was a thinly veiled challenge, but he appreciated the fire behind it. He tightened the freshly wrapped grip, feeling the balance of his foil, and let his eyes drift to the empty spot where Reyes leaned. He said, “A dull edge still finds its mark, old man. Perhaps it’s time we both sharpen our blades.” He glanced at the clock, noting the late hour, and mused that the rivalry would only grow sharper with each close match. He turned his head slightly, as if inviting the other instructor to respond, but his mind was already plotting the next bout.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I take the grip out of his hands and put it down, and I don't step back afterwards. "You've been slow all evening," I say.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content: Corvo watched the grip tumble onto the polished floor, his eyes flickering with a mix of amusement and irritation. He let a low chuckle escape his lips, the sound barely breaking the silence of the empty salle. With a fluid motion born of years of practice, he reclaimed his foil, the blade catching the dim light as he adjusted his grip once more. He lifted his chin, the familiar competitive fire igniting behind his gaze, and spoke in a measured tone, “If you think my pace is a flaw, perhaps you should learn to read the rhythm before you try to dictate it.” He glanced at the clock, noting the late hour, and his mind already sketched the next exchange: a series of feints designed to test the opponent’s timing, a counter‑attack timed to the ticking seconds. He felt the edge of his blade sharpen in his imagination, each movement rehearsed, each response poised. With a final, confident smile, he turned his head toward the spot where Reyes stood, his posture relaxed yet alert, ready to let the rivalry continue to sharpen their skills.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I step closer, my voice dropping to a near whisper. "Your rhythm's predictable. That's why you lost the third point." My hand brushes against the foil's blade as I reach to pick up the grip I'd dropped.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content: Corvo's lips curled into a thin smile as he heard the whisper and felt the faint brush of the other's hand against his blade—a reminder of how close the match had become. “Predictable? Then you’ll find the next beat waiting for you before you even hear it,” he replied, his voice low and steady. He tightened his grip, the foil humming in his palm, and his mind raced through a sequence of feints, each timed to the ticking seconds. He glanced at the clock, noting the late hour, and thought that the rivalry would only sharpen further. He turned his head slightly, his posture relaxed yet alert, ready to let the next exchange unfold.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: We get as far as the changing-room bench and not one step further. Kit goes on the floor, both of ours, and neither of us is being quiet about it.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content: Corvo watched the kits tumble onto the polished floor, the metallic clink echoing off the walls. He reached for his own bag, his fingers closing around the strap, and lifted his foil, the blade catching the dim light. He turned his head toward the bench, a thin smile curving his lips, and said, “If the bench is our audience, then let’s give it a performance it won’t forget. The next point will land before the echo of this one fades.” He slipped his jacket over his shoulders, his mind already rehearsing the opening feint, the timing, the counter‑attack, each movement measured against the ticking seconds that still marked the late hour.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I catch his wrist before he can fully shrug his jacket on. "Performance is over. This isn't for the bench." My other hand pushes the jacket back off his shoulder.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content: Corvo felt the sudden grip on his wrist and the abrupt shove that sent his jacket sliding off his shoulder, the fabric pooling on the polished floor. A flicker of irritation crossed his features, but his smile remained thin, as if the interruption were merely another feint in their endless duel. He released his own grip on the foil just enough to let the blade rest lightly against his palm, then shifted his weight, planting his feet with the precision of a seasoned fencer. “You’ve taken the curtain call too early,” he said, his voice low and measured, “but the encore never truly ends.” He glanced at the clock, noting the waning minutes, and his mind already plotted a counter‑move: a swift, deceptive retreat followed by a sudden thrust aimed at the exact moment Reyes would expect him to retreat. With a practiced motion, he retrieved his jacket from the floor, draped it over his shoulders, and adjusted his grip once more, the foil humming softly in his hand as he prepared to let the rivalry continue, each gesture a silent promise that the next point would be his.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I get him flat on the bench and take my time about it with my mouth, which is the first thing all evening he hasn't had an answer for.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo felt the bench press firmly against his back, the cold metal of the edge biting into his shoulders as Reyes's voice lingered in the quiet room. A thin smile curved his lips, the familiar competitive fire flickering rather than fading. He thought that even a forced repose could not dull the sharpness of his mind; the rhythm of the bout still pulsed in his thoughts, each imagined blade flash timed to the ticking seconds that still marked the late hour.

He shifted his weight ever so slightly, the movement as precise as a practiced parry, and let his hand settle on the grip of his foil. The blade hummed faintly against his palm, a reminder that the next point could be seized at any moment. Corvo glanced at the clock, noting the dwindling minutes, and his mind already sketched a sequence of feints designed to exploit any hesitation.

“Even when I’m flat on the bench,” he said, his voice low and steady, “my edge is still waiting for its turn.” He adjusted his grip once more, the familiar feel of the foil grounding him, and prepared to let the rivalry continue, each gesture a silent promise that the encore was far from over.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I lean in, my mouth brushing his ear. "You talk too much." My hand slips between us, undoing the buckle of his fencing pants.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content: Corvo felt the cold metal of the bench against his back and the sudden slack in his belt as if something had been undone. A thin smile curved his lips as he heard the whisper near his ear. He tightened his grip on the foil, the blade humming softly against his palm. “Even with my pants undone, the rhythm of the duel still beat in my chest,” he said, his voice low and steady. He shifted his weight ever so slightly, his left foot pressing against the edge of the bench, testing the tension. In his mind he plotted a feint: a quick, deceptive retreat that would force the opponent to overextend, then a sudden thrust timed to the moment of hesitation. He glanced at the clock, noting the minutes slipping away, and thought that even in this position his edge remained sharp, waiting for the next point. He adjusted his grip once more, the familiar feel of the foil grounding him, and prepared to let the rivalry continue, each gesture a silent promise that the encore was far from over.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: "Prove the point properly," he says, "or concede," so I pin his wrists to the bench and stop letting him set the pace, which is exactly what he was asking for.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content: Corvo felt the metal of the bench bite into his palms as his wrists were held fast. A thin smile lingered on his lips and his mind raced through the geometry of the lock, recalling every bout where a momentary constraint had been turned to his advantage. He steadied his breath, the rhythm of his heartbeat matching the ticking seconds that still marked the late hour, and his thoughts settled on a precise feint that would force his opponent to overextend. The foil hummed faintly in his palm, a reminder that the blade was still his weapon even when his arms were pinned. In a low, almost whispered tone he replied, “You may have my wrists, but you’ll never have the point.” He adjusted his grip ever so slightly, the familiar weight of the weapon grounding him, and prepared to seize the moment when the grip would loosen, knowing the encore was far from over.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I nip his lower lip. "You're still talking." My free hand pushes his fencing pants down his hips, fingers curling against his skin. "You always did think you could talk your way through everything."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content: Corvo felt the sharp bite on his lower lip and the sudden slack of his pants as the metal bench continued to hold him fast. A thin smile curved his lips as he heard his own breath echo in the quiet room, the clock ticking away the final seconds. He thought that the lock on his wrists was merely a temporary geometry, one he could still bend to his will. He tightened his grip on the foil, the blade humming softly against his palm, and prepared to turn the pressure into a precise counter‑thrust. In a low, steady voice he said, “You may have my skin, but you’ll never have the point.”

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: Neither of us is quiet and neither of us cares who locks up. "Don't stop," he says, for once not arguing. (OOC: write the scene through, no fade.)

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo felt the pressure on his wrists remain firm, the cold metal of the bench pressing into his back as the faint whisper brushed his ear, urging him onward. A thin smile curved his lips; the silence of the room amplified the rhythm of his own breath, matching the ticking clock that marked the waning minutes. He tightened his grip on the foil, the familiar weight grounding him, and his mind raced through the geometry of the lock, recalling every bout where a momentary constraint had become an advantage.

He whispered back, his voice low and steady, “Your silence is louder than any blade.” The words hung in the air, a promise that the point was still his to claim. He shifted his weight ever so slightly, his left foot pressing against the edge of the bench, testing the tension. In his mind he plotted a feint: a quick, deceptive retreat that would force the opponent to overextend, then a sudden thrust timed to the moment of hesitation. The foil hummed faintly against his palm, a reminder that even when his arms were pinned, the blade remained his weapon.

The clock ticked, the seconds slipping away, but his focus remained sharp. He imagined the foil slipping free, the point landing before the echo of the whisper faded. He steadied his breath, the rhythm of his heartbeat matching the ticking seconds, and prepared to seize the moment when the grip would loosen. With a final, confident smile, he thought, “You may have my skin, but you’ll never have the point.” The encore was far from over.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: "Prove it then," I breathe out, moving against him with purpose. My hand tightens on his wrist. "Show me how sharp that edge really is."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo felt the sudden increase in pressure as Reyes’s hand tightened around his wrist, a firm, unyielding grip that mirrored the metal bench pressing into his back. He heard the breath that brushed his ear, a low, urgent challenge that resonated like a feint in the quiet room. A thin smile curved his lips as his mind mapped the geometry of the lock, recalling every bout where a momentary constraint had been turned to his advantage. He shifted his left foot ever so slightly against the edge of the bench, testing the tension and finding the infinitesimal give in the metal.

In a measured motion, Corvo loosened his grip on the foil just enough to let the blade slide along the polished surface of the bench, a feint that forced Reyes to adjust his hold. The foil hummed softly, a silent promise of precision. Corvo whispered, his voice low and steady, “The edge finds its mark even when bound.” Then, with a sudden flick of his wrist, he thrust the foil forward. The point grazed Reyes’s skin, a clean, deliberate touch that scored the point in the private contest of their rivalry.

Corvo felt the rush of satisfaction as the blade made contact, the metallic whisper echoing in his mind. He smiled again, the thin curve now tinged with triumph. “You may have my skin,” he said, “but the point remains mine.” He steadied his breath, the rhythm of his heartbeat matching the ticking seconds that still marked the waning minutes, and prepared for the next exchange, his mind already rehearsing the next feint and counter‑thrust, each movement a silent promise that the encore was far from over.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I let out a sharp breath, my grip on his wrist loosening as I feel the sting of the blade's touch. "Cheap shot," I murmur, leaning down to catch his mouth in a rough, claiming kiss. My other hand slides the foil out of his grasp, tossing it aside with a clatter. "Now we're even."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content: Corvo felt the press of Reyes’s lips against his own, the heat of his breath filling his mouth, and the sudden absence of the foil in his hand as the metal clattered on the floor. He thought that even a kiss could not dull the edge of his mind, that the point was still his to claim. He whispered, his voice barely audible over the thudding of his own heart, “The point is still mine.” He pressed his left foot against the edge of the bench, feeling the infinitesimal give in the metal, and with a sudden surge of strength he pushed his hips forward, forcing Reyes to adjust his grip. The pressure on his wrists lessened for a heartbeat, and Corvo seized the moment to bite Reyes’s lower lip, a sharp retort to the earlier bite, tasting the metallic tang of blood. He steadied his breath, the rhythm of his heartbeat matching the ticking seconds, and his mind already sketched the next feint and counter‑thrust, each movement a silent promise that the encore was far from over.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: *I break the kiss with a low laugh, my hand coming up to wipe my mouth.* "Always have to get the last word in, don't you?" I shift my weight, letting him feel the full press of my body against his. "Let's see if you're still so chatty in a minute."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya's flat still had the same broken buzzer, which Bee found unreasonably infuriating, as though he could have fixed it in eleven months and had chosen not to out of spite.

"You could have texted first," he said, standing in the doorway and not moving out of it.

"You could have answered last time I did."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I don't move either. "Are you going to let me in, or are we doing this in the corridor?"

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya held the doorway for a second longer than he needed to, long enough to make the choice feel deliberate rather than courteous. Then he stepped back and pulled the door wider, the hinge giving its familiar, irritated whine.

“We’d give the neighbours something to talk about,” he said, voice dry, not quite warm. “And I’ve already had to listen to Mrs. Patterson complain about the recycling.”

He didn’t look at Bee directly as he turned away, just left the door open and walked back into the flat, leaving the choice to follow where it belonged. The place smelled faintly of coffee and cold air, the kind of smell that suggested someone had been awake too long and hadn’t bothered to open a window.

“You can take your coat off if you want,” he said, already moving toward the kitchen counter, where a mug sat half-finished and cold. “Or don’t. Whatever makes this shorter.”

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: *I step inside and shut the door, but I don't take my coat off.* "Mrs. Patterson always was a busybody. I see you're still living for other people's opinions."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya set the cold mug down on the counter with a small, deliberate click. He did not turn around immediately. The jab landed where it had been aimed, and he gave it just enough silence to show he was not going to pretend otherwise.

“Mrs. Patterson can go to hell,” he said. “I was being polite.”

When he finally looked at Bee, his gaze snagged on the coat and stayed there. His arms folded, not defensive so much as braced.

“You planning to deliver whatever this is and then make a run for it?” he asked, voice low, edged with old familiarity. “Or are you just keeping your options open?”

He knew exactly what he was doing, turning the coat into evidence, the way Bee had once done with his silence. The flat felt too small around them, full of things neither had packed away.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I kiss him like it's a continuation of the argument, because it is.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya went still for half a breath, caught between the instinct to shove and the older, deeper instinct to answer.

Then he kissed back.

Not gently. Not as if he had forgotten the shape of it. His hand came up before he seemed to decide whether he meant to push Bee away or pull closer, and in the end his fingers only curled into the front of that coat, tightening like he was grounding himself against something he knew would hurt.

For a moment he let himself be ruined by it. The familiar heat, the old fit of their mouths, the terrible ease of falling back into a language he had spent eleven months pretending he no longer spoke. His other hand lifted, hovered, then settled at Bee’s jaw with a roughness that was not quite anger anymore.

When he broke the kiss, it was only enough to breathe.

“That,” he said, voice low and unsteady at the edges, “is not an argument.”

His thumb pressed once against Bee’s jaw, then stilled.

“Is it?”

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: *My breath is a little ragged against his mouth.* "What else would you call it? We're still fighting."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya made a sound low in his throat, not quite a laugh, too rough to be one. His thumb stayed where it was, pressed lightly against Bee’s jaw, and he did not move away.

“I’d call it a shortcut,” he said.

His voice was quieter now, less sharp, but not softer. The anger had gone deeper, settled into something more dangerous because it was familiar. His fingers loosened in the fabric of Bee’s coat, but he did not let go.

“You always did that when you didn’t want to say the thing,” he said. “Start something else instead. Make it physical. Make it urgent. Make it about heat instead of the part we can’t fix.”

His gaze lifted, steady and knowing.

“And I let you.”

There was no absolution in the admission. If anything, it seemed to cost him something. His jaw tightened, and for a second he looked angry at himself for saying it aloud.

“So yeah,” he went on, voice dropping. “We’re still fighting. That’s all this is. You kissing me like you’re trying to win a point. Me letting you because I’m too tired to pretend I don’t still want it.”

He exhaled slowly, and his hand slid from Bee’s jaw to the collar of the coat, not pulling, not pushing, just resting there as if he needed the contact and resented needing it.

“But don’t stand there and make it noble,” he said. “Don’t make it just an argument. You came here knowing what you were doing. You knew exactly what would happen if you got close enough.”

His eyes searched Bee’s face, dark and unflinching.

“So tell me what you actually came for. Because if all you wanted was to prove you still could, you already have.”

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: We don't make it past the hallway. His shirt goes over his head and mine is already somewhere on the floor behind us.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
The hallway was too narrow for this, and Ilya knew it. He knew it the way he knew the flat’s every flaw—the sticking lock, the draught under the door, the way the radiator ticked when it couldn’t decide whether to work. He used that narrowness now, stepping in until there was nowhere left to be polite.

His bare back met the wall with a dull thud that felt more like punctuation than surprise. The air was cold against his skin, but he barely registered it. His hands were already occupied, urgent and irritated in equal measure, dragging over fabric and warm skin as though he were trying to prove something by touch alone.

He kissed Bee like he was still angry. Maybe he was. Maybe anger was the only thing that made this acceptable, the only framework left in which wanting like this didn’t feel like surrender. His fingers slid into hair, gripping hard enough to tilt, to hold, to keep the moment from softening into anything either of them could mistake for tenderness.

When he finally pulled back, it was only far enough to speak.

“You don’t get to do this,” he said, voice rough, mouth still too close. “You don’t get to walk in here, put your hands on me, and pretend we’re not still standing in the exact same mess you left.”

His thumb pressed against Bee’s lower lip, dragging once, slow and deliberate.

“But don’t stop.”

The admission came out like a dare. Like a wound. Like something he hated needing but refused to be ashamed of. His other hand found the small of Bee’s back, pressing closer, anchoring.

“If we’re doing this,” Ilya said, eyes dark and unflinching, “we do it knowing what it is.”

He leaned in again, breath catching against Bee’s mouth.

“Not forgiveness. Not fixing. Just the part of the argument where we stop pretending we don’t still want each other.”

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: *My laugh is sharp, breathless.* "You always did talk too much when you were losing."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
The laugh hit Ilya like a match to paper. He went very still, his eyes narrowing, and the last pretense of civility left his mouth.

“Losing,” he said, tasting the word. His hand tightened in Bee’s hair, not enough to hurt, enough to claim. “You still think this is something one of us can win.”

He stepped closer, crowding the narrow hallway, letting the wall take his weight instead of Bee’s. His bare chest was warm against the chill, his breath ragged where it met Bee’s.

“You used to say that when you knew I was right,” he murmured. “When you couldn’t stand that I could still read you.”

His other hand traced down Bee’s spine, slow, deliberate, full of old ownership and old resentment.

“So go on,” he said, voice dropping into something dangerous. “Make me lose. If that’s why you’re here.”

He kissed Bee again, hard and unforgiving, the kiss of a man who knew exactly how much he was giving away and hated the price. His fingers fisted in the fabric at Bee’s back, holding on as if the argument itself might try to run.

When he finally pulled back, his mouth was red, his breathing rough.

“But don’t stand there acting like you’re above it,” he said. “You came back to lose with me.”

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I get my hand around him and he makes a sound he'd have been embarrassed by a year ago. "Still," I say, close to his ear. "Every single time."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya’s head tipped back against the wall, the sound punched out of him before he could bite it down. For one instant his whole body went taut, caught between humiliation and want, and then the want won, as it always had with Bee.

His other hand tightened at Bee’s waist, dragging them closer until there was no air left between them, no dignified distance, no version of this where he could pretend he had not already lost the high ground.

His eyes opened, dark and unflinching.

“You want me to say it?” he said. “Fine. I still want you. I hate that I still want you, and I want you anyway.”

His hand stayed where Bee had placed it. Steady. Hot. Possessive without being cruel.

“So say it,” he said. “Not because you want to goad me. Not because you want to see if I’ll still break for you. Say you want my hand here because you missed being ruined by it.”

Then he kissed Bee, hard and unforgiving, the kiss itself a demand. His fingers curled a fraction closer around Bee’s throat, not taking breath, just holding the truth of them in place. When he pulled back enough to speak, his voice was wrecked and low against Bee’s mouth.

“If we’re picking up where we left off, then this is where we start. No pretending. No winning. Tell me the truth while my hand’s on you.”

He swallowed. His hand at Bee’s throat trembled once, almost imperceptibly, before he steadied it.

“And I hate that you’re right,” he went on, voice dropping. “You always could get more out of me by making me angry than by asking nicely.”

“Unless you want to stop,” he added, and the word cost him. “If you want to stop, say it now and I’ll make tea and we can sit here pretending this never happened.”

A beat.

“Or not pretend. Whatever’s easier for you.”

There was bitterness in it, but beneath the bitterness was something worse: care. Ugly, unwilling care. The kind that had survived the breakup out of spite.

He glanced toward the bedroom door, then back. His voice went lower.

“Because if you come in there with me, I’m not going to be gentle about pretending this doesn’t matter. I’ll touch you like I’m still angry, because I am. I’ll kiss you like I want something back, because I do. And if you start using it to disappear into, I’ll stop.”

His eyes held Bee’s, unflinching.

“So choose.”

He reached out, plucked the water bottle from Reyes' hand without asking, and took a slow sip—eyes locked on theirs the entire time. When he handed it back, his fingers lingered just a second too long against theirs.
