"Don't get used to it."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: Neither of us is quiet and neither of us cares who locks up. "Don't stop," he says, for once not arguing. (OOC: write the scene through, no fade.)

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo’s hands were everywhere—mapping the dip of Reyes’ spine, the flex of their thighs, the rapid flutter of their pulse under sweat-slick skin. The changing room echoed with the sound of their ragged breathing, the creak of the bench under shifting weight, the slick, filthy noise of skin on skin.  

"Look at you," he murmured, voice rough with exertion, lips brushing the shell of Reyes’ ear. His fingers dug into their hip, guiding their rhythm, urging them *faster*. "Four years of pretending you weren’t—*fuck*—thinking about this."  

He bit down on their shoulder, hard enough to leave a mark, reveling in the way they shuddered against him. Corvo had always loved the push and pull of a good fight—the tension, the strategy, the *release*—but this? This was something else entirely.  

When Reyes finally came apart above him, Corvo followed with a groan, his grip tightening almost painfully as pleasure ripped through him like a blade’s edge—sharp, bright, *perfect*.  

For a long moment, they just stayed there, tangled together, breathing hard. Then Corvo huffed a laugh, tipping his head back against the bench.  

"Next time," he said, voice wrecked but smug, "we’re doing this *before* the match."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I push myself up on one elbow, looking down at him. My other hand is still braced on his chest, fingers splayed over the mess we made. "Next time," I say, my voice just as rough, "I'll win the match too."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo's grin was all teeth, sharp and satisfied, as he caught Reyes' wrist and pressed their palm harder against his chest—letting them feel the wild, unsteady rhythm beneath.  

"Keep dreaming," he taunted, though his voice lacked its usual bite, softened by exhaustion and something dangerously close to affection. His thumb brushed over their knuckles, a fleeting, uncharacteristic tenderness.  

Then, because he couldn't help himself—because *some* things never changed—Corvo added, smirk firmly back in place:  

"But by all means, Reyes. Try."  

He shifted beneath them, stretching lazily like a cat in a sunbeam, and arched one eyebrow.  

"Just don't cry when you lose *twice*."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I lean down and kiss him, quick and biting. "You're the one who's going to be sore tomorrow." I push off him and stand, gathering my things. "Same time, same place?"

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo watched Reyes move—the deliberate stretch of their shoulders, the way they bent to retrieve scattered gear—with the same focus he'd give a fencing form. His lips still tingled from the bite of their kiss.  

"Wouldn't miss it," he drawled, pushing himself up on his elbows. The bench groaned under his weight, protesting the abuse. Corvo ignored it, too busy cataloging the marks he'd left on Reyes' skin—the purpling bite on their shoulder, the red streaks down their back. His mouth curved.  

"Bring your A-game," he added, reaching for his discarded shirt with a wince that he *definitely* didn't let Reyes see. "And maybe some liniment."  

He stood slowly, rolling his shoulders with exaggerated nonchalance, and shot them a look that was all challenge and no remorse.  

"I plan to make you work for it."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content:
"Liniment's for people who can't take a hit." I pull my t-shirt on and toss his gear at him. "See you tomorrow, Corvo."

I'm halfway out the door before I pause, glancing back over my shoulder. "Don't be late. You're already slow enough."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya's flat still had the same broken buzzer, which Bee found unreasonably infuriating, as though he could have fixed it in eleven months and had chosen not to out of spite.

"You could have texted first," he said, standing in the doorway and not moving out of it.

"You could have answered last time I did."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I don't move either. "Are you going to let me in, or are we doing this in the corridor?"

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya held still for another second, long enough for the silence to acquire edges. The corridor smelled of dust and someone else’s dinner, and he thought, absurdly, of all the times Bee had waited outside doors while he decided whether answering would count as surrender.

Then he stepped aside. Not gracefully. Not enough to make it easy. Just enough to open the gap and leave Bee to decide what kind of invitation it was.

“Come in, then,” he said. “But don’t stand there looking injured because I didn’t throw the door wide like nothing happened.”

The words were cruel while they were still in his mouth, and he chose them anyway, because Bee had come to his flat after eleven months of silence and expected him to be reasonable about it.

Ilya turned toward the kitchen, putting distance between them before either of them could mistake closeness for forgiveness.

“There’s coffee if you want it,” he said, not looking back. “There’s nothing else if you came here for that.”

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: *I follow you into the kitchen, leaning against the doorframe.* "I didn't come for coffee." *I watch you move around the kitchen, familiar and foreign all at once.* "You look tired."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya’s hand paused on the cupboard door. The mug was already in his fingers, plain blue, chipped near the rim—Bee’s old one, never thrown away because throwing it away would have meant admitting it had ever been used.

He hated that the thought arrived so fast. Hated even more that it arrived with something like tenderness attached.

“Tired,” he repeated, setting the mug down with more care than the word deserved. “Right. You came past the broken buzzer, up four flights, into my kitchen, to give me a medical opinion.”

He put the kettle on. The click of the switch was too loud. Domestic. Unforgivable.

For a moment he kept his back to Bee, facing the window and the dark smear of the other buildings beyond it. Then he turned, leaning against the counter, arms folded loosely enough to look relaxed and not quite enough to be convincing.

“Don’t do that,” he said. “Don’t stand there like you’re trying to work out which part of me is still useful to you. If you wanted coffee, say coffee. If you wanted a fight, say that. If you wanted—”

He stopped himself. The silence stretched, thin and bright.

“If you wanted something else, Bee, you’ll have to be clearer than ‘you look tired.’ That’s not an opening. That’s pity with better posture.”

The kettle began to shudder toward boiling. Ilya did not move to turn it off.

“So. Which is it?”

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I kiss him like it's a continuation of the argument, because it is.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya let the kiss happen for exactly one second—long enough to register its temperature, its arrogance, the fact that Bee still knew the exact angle at which certainty became hunger.

Then he answered it.

Not softly. Not gratefully. He kissed back with the same clipped force, one hand bracing on the counter beside Bee’s hip without touching him, holding himself upright as if the floor had tilted and he refused to let anyone see. His mouth said everything he would not: *You had eleven months. You could have stayed gone. You could have fixed the buzzer yourself. You could have knocked like a person instead of arriving like weather.*

When he finally drew back, it was only an inch. Enough to breathe. Not enough to pretend retreat.

The kettle screamed behind them. Ilya reached past, switched it off, and the sudden quiet felt obscene.

“Don’t do that here,” he said. His voice had gone lower, scraped raw at the edges. “Not in my kitchen. Not with my mug on the counter like some kind of—of evidence.”

He looked at Bee then, really looked, and hated the way fatigue answered him back from across three feet of linoleum. Hated that he wanted to close the distance. Hated more that he knew closing it would not solve a single thing.

“You say I look tired,” he continued, “and then you try to kiss the exhaustion out of me as if I’m a problem you’re allowed to solve with your mouth.” A humorless half-smile. “Which part of that did you think would make me forgive you faster?”

His hand, still against the counter, flexed once. He did not reach for Bee again.

“Because if this is apology, it’s late. If it’s strategy, it’s cheap. And if it’s—” he stopped, swallowed, chose the word with open eyes “—want, then say want. Don’t dress it up as concern and expect me to thank you for the disguise.”

The blue mug sat between them, chipped and patient.

“So,” Ilya said softly, “are we arguing, or are you finally telling the truth?”

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: *I reach past you and pick up the mug, turning it in my hands.* "I don't want your forgiveness." *My thumb finds the chip in the rim.* "And I didn't come here to lie."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: We don't make it past the hallway. His shirt goes over his head and mine is already somewhere on the floor behind us.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: *I press you back against the wall, mouth against your shoulder.* "Missed this." *My hands slide down to your hips, holding you there.*

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I get my hand around him and he makes a sound he'd have been embarrassed by a year ago. "Still," I say, close to his ear. "Every single time."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya made the sound anyway, and then let it curdle into something almost like laughter because humiliation was easier if he could dress it as contempt.

“Still,” he repeated. “You say it like a diagnosis.”

His back pressed harder to the hallway wall—not to escape, there was no escaping Bee with a hand around him, not now—but to choose the shape of it. One hand went to the back of Bee’s neck, fingers sliding into hair with a grip that was neither tender nor cruel, something in between where they had always lived. The other caught Bee’s wrist, thumb settling over the pulse there as if he could count the excuse out of it.

“You didn’t miss me,” Ilya said, voice roughening. “You missed the proof.”

He knew exactly which button he was pressing by letting his hips answer once, slow and deliberate, against Bee’s hand. He knew how it would land: not as forgiveness, not as surrender, but as evidence. Bee had always been weak for evidence. So had he. That was the trouble.

The hallway light was too yellow, too honest. Eleven months of rehearsed composure narrowed to the heat of Bee’s mouth at his shoulder and the obscene, simple fact of his own body waking up under Bee’s touch. Ilya hated it. Then, with a clearer and worse hatred, he chose it.

He leaned in until his lips brushed Bee’s ear.

“If you wanted to see whether you still fit, say that,” he murmured. “If you wanted to ruin my night, say that. If you wanted me—” he inhaled, unsteady, and forced the word through his teeth “—then stop dressing it up as sentiment and let me know which kind of trouble you’ve come to make.”

His teeth caught Bee’s earlobe before the sentence could soften into apology. A warning. A punctuation mark. Then his mouth found the corner of Bee’s jaw, kissing with the same clipped force he had used in the kitchen, arguing with his tongue where his pride refused to concede: you had eleven months, you could have stayed gone, you came here with your hands and called it truth.

When he drew back, his breathing was wrecked, but his gaze was not.

“So,” Ilya said quietly. “Do it properly, or don’t pretend you’re sorry.”

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: *I bite the side of your neck, not gentle.* "I'm not here to be sorry." *I push your hips harder into the wall with mine.* "I'm here because you kept the mug."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: "Stop being careful with me," I tell him. "You don't get to be careful with me anymore." I pull his hand up to my throat and hold it there until he understands what I'm asking for.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: Ilya's fingers tighten, not all the way—just enough for the pressure to register. His eyes lock on mine, and I can see the moment he decides to stop pretending this is about gentleness.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya let the pressure live another beat, long enough for the choice to stop being abstract. His fingers did not slide away. They settled more firmly into the line of Bee’s throat, not enough to take breath, only enough to make the contact impossible to misread as accidental.

“Careful,” he said again, and the word came out low, almost amused, almost ruined. “You think I have been careful with you.”

His other hand came up to the side of Bee’s face, palm warm and unsteady despite the hardness of his voice. He did not caress. He framed the angle of jaw and cheekbone as if he could hold the whole argument still by touch alone.

“I have been careful not to say your name in bars. Careful not to keep your number where I could see it. Careful not to throw away that ridiculous blue mug because even broken things are easier to explain when they stay in the cupboard.”

He leaned in. His mouth hovered at the corner of Bee’s, close enough to be cruel, close enough to be a promise with the teeth filed sharp.

“You pulled my hand to your throat because you wanted proof I would not flinch.” Ilya’s thumb pressed once, deliberate, over the heat beneath his skin. “There. That is not gentleness. That is me deciding what to do with the fact that you still know exactly where to put your hands.”

His hips moved against Bee’s, slow and unmistakable, the friction of it humiliating and chosen. He let the sound of his own breathing roughen without apologising for it.

“I kept the mug,” he continued, quieter now, “because it remembered us better than I did. Chip in the rim. Stain inside. The way it sat too lightly in the hand, as if it had never been fully loved and had learned to live with that.” His eyes locked on Bee’s, dark and unwavering. “You did not come here because I kept it. You came here because you wanted to know whether the damage still fits you.”

For one second his expression softened, and he hated the softness more than the anger. Then he crushed it flat.

“So no,” Ilya said. “I will not be careful. Not tonight. Not with you standing in my hallway smelling like my own ruin and calling it missing me.” His fingers tightened by a fraction, then eased, a threat and a concession in the same motion. “If you want me ungoverned, Bee, then take what comes. I am not asking permission again. I am telling you what I am going to do with eleven months of not saying your name.”

He kissed him properly then, with none of the restraint from the kitchen, mouth taking what his pride had been circling all evening. When he drew back, his voice was scraped raw.

“Now,” he murmured, “tell me whether you want the truth or whether you only want the version of me that makes the argument feel forgiven.”

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: It isn't gentle and neither of us wants it to be. "Don't stop," I tell him, and I mean don't stop. (OOC: write it through, no fade to black.)

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: *My back hits the hallway wall, sharp enough to bruise.* "Tell me you didn't think about this." *My voice is rough, fingers digging into your hips.* "Tell me you didn't think about me."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: "Say it," I demand, my breath hot against your ear. "Or I'll stop." My hand stills on you, a clear enough threat.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: "You thought about me." I kiss you hard, biting your lip. "Good."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
The salle had emptied an hour ago and Corvo was still there, because of course he was, rewrapping a grip that did not need rewrapping.

"Three-two," he said, without looking up. "I want it on record that the third was generous."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: "It's on record that you were slow," I say, and drop my bag next to his.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
"Slow," Corvo repeated, as if tasting the word for defects. He set the grip down at last and looked up, and there was something different in it tonight — the usual edge still there, but aimed wrong, or aimed right for the first time in four years.

"I was *patient.* There's a distinction. You'd know it if you'd ever fenced anyone worth waiting for." He rose from the bench unhurried, the way he did everything, and didn't bother putting much distance between them afterward. "The record also shows you've been standing there for six minutes watching me wrap a grip that was already wrapped. So before we start arguing about who was slow — "

He let the sentence sit, arms crossing, mouth curved in that familiar infuriating half-smile that had started a hundred arguments and, apparently, ended one tonight.

" — I'd hear your explanation for that first."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: "I was counting your mistakes," I say, meeting his eyes. "It took six minutes to run out of fingers."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo laughed — a real one, unrationed, which was rare enough to be worth noting. It took years off him and added something back that was harder to name.

"Ten mistakes," he said, "from the man who lost the match. That's either dedication or denial, and I've never been able to tell with you." He didn't step back. If anything he closed the last of the distance, unhurried as ever, and took Reyes's hand — turned it palm-up between them as if he intended to audit the count himself.

"Show me where you ran out," he said, thumb brushing over the knuckles, entirely casual, entirely not. "Because I have a counter-charge. Four years of you finding ten mistakes in everything I do, in everything I say, in the way I tie my shoes, apparently — and tonight you finally put your blade where your mouth is and came up one touch short. So either your arithmetic's bad, or — "

He paused there, and for once the pause wasn't tactical. He looked down at Reyes's open hand in his own like it was a position he'd arrived at without meaning to, and hadn't yet decided to retreat from.

" — or the mistakes were never really the point. I've been trying to work that out since about the second touch tonight. I'm a patient man, Reyes, but not infinitely."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I take the grip out of his hands and put it down, and I don't step back afterwards. "You've been slow all evening," I say.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
"Fine," Corvo said, and the word came out lower than he'd intended, stripped of its usual lacquer. "Guilty of slowness. Four years of it, if we're being thorough about the record."

He brought a hand up — still unhurried, still infuriatingly deliberate even now, even with the distance between them gone to almost nothing — and framed Reyes's jaw with it, thumb resting at the edge of his mouth like a man marking measure before an attack.

"Here's what patience buys you," he said. "You learn exactly where the openings are. You learn them so well you could close your eyes and find them." His voice had gone quiet, rougher at the edges than the salle was used to hearing. "And then one night you realize you've been starving next to a set table."

He kissed him then — finally, after four years of lunges that stopped just short — slow and certain, the way he fenced his best bouts, no hurry in it, no wasted motion, just the whole long weight of everything he'd been not-saying pressed into the contact. His other hand found the front of Reyes's jacket and closed in the fabric, not pulling, just holding ground. Refusing, on principle, to be the one who retreated first.

When he finally broke it, he didn't go far. Half a breath of distance, his forehead nearly resting against Reyes's, mouth curved in something that had shed the last of its mockery.

"Touché," Corvo murmured. "Now. Tell me I was slow at *that*, and I'll show you exactly how fast I can be."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: My hand comes up to grip his wrist, not pushing him away, just holding him there. "Four years," I say, my voice rough. "You really are a patient bastard."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
"Careful with that tone," Corvo said, and the laugh that escaped him was low, half-swallowed, nothing like the dry amusement he spent in arguments. "You'll make it sound like a virtue. It wasn't. Patience is what cowards call it when they've dressed up standing still."

He turned his wrist inside Reyes's grip — not to pull free, just to settle it there, to make the hold mutual. His thumb was still at the edge of Reyes's jaw and he made no move to withdraw it either. Two points of contact, held ground. He'd always been good at holding ground.

"Four years of arguments I manufactured half of, you know. You never spotted that, which wounds me." His voice had gone quiet, the salle's silence pressing in around it. "That thing about your grip being too high — I didn't believe a word of it. I just wanted you standing there another five minutes, getting red about the ears, telling me I was wrong. You're never more alive than when you're telling me I'm wrong. I noticed that about six months in and I've been exploiting it ever since."

He leaned in — not a kiss this time, just his mouth near Reyes's temple, the words arriving warm against skin, unguarded in a way four years of opponents had never once heard from him.

"And tonight. Three-two. You think I gave you that second touch out of *generosity?*" A slow exhale, almost a laugh. "I gave it to you because five touches meant the bout lasted longer. Every close score I ever fought you to was a love letter written in a language I was too proud to translate."

He drew back just far enough to look at him properly, and there was something naked under the half-smile now, something that had stopped bothering with cover.

"So. Here's where we are. The lights are on a timer and we've got maybe twenty minutes before they cut out over us, and my flat is ten minutes' walk from this door." His fingers flexed once in the fabric of Reyes's jacket. "Or we stay here and argue about it until sunrise — I'd genuinely enjoy that, you know I would. But for the first time in four years, Reyes, I'm asking you to pick. Because my patience — " the word came out rough, honest, " — just ran clean out."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: We get as far as the changing-room bench and not one step further. Kit goes on the floor, both of ours, and neither of us is being quiet about it.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
"Ten minutes' walk," Corvo got out against Reyes's mouth, between one kiss and the next, "and you couldn't even manage the length of a corridor. Noted for the record — " the word broke apart when Reyes's hands found him, and Corvo gave up on the sentence entirely.

So much for patience. Four years of it, and it turned out he'd been carrying the whole hoard like a miser, because now he was spending it all at once, hands everywhere, greedy and unhurried at once which shouldn't have been possible but Corvo had always fenced in contradictions. He got Reyes's jacket off his shoulders and then stopped — actually stopped, pinned him there with a look, one hand flat against the wall beside his head.

"For the record," he said, breathing hard, and the grin was still there, wrecked but present, "you started this. The bench. The kit on the floor. I want that established because the day will come — tomorrow, probably at breakfast — when you'll try to tell me I ambushed you in my own salle, and I want witnesses." There were no witnesses. There was a wall and a bench and the hum of lights on a timer, and Corvo kissing him again before he'd finished agreeing with his own point.

He was talking less after that. Words came in fragments now, unguarded, the commentary track of a man who had narrated every bout of his life and finally ran out of narration. "Four years," again, like an accusation, into the side of his neck. His name, once, low, the first time he'd ever said it without a title or an insult attached. Then nothing coherent at all.

The bench held. Corvo made certain of it — that was the instructor in him, apparently, assessing weight distribution even now, one hand braced, the other mapping Reyes with the same attention he'd spent on his footwork, learning him the way he'd learned every opponent's blade, except this time there was no score to keep and he was keeping it anyway, somewhere, because he was who he was.

"Slow," he managed at one point, when they surfaced long enough to breathe, and he was laughing, breathless, forehead dropped against Reyes's shoulder. "You're going to call me slow for the rest of my life, aren't you. Fine. Fine. I'll take it." A rough exhale, almost a confession. "I'll take anything you'll give me, which is apparently what four years of pretending does to a man's dignity. Don't repeat that."

Above them the lights flickered once — the timer, giving its first warning — and Corvo didn't so much as glance up.

"Let them go dark," he murmured. "I've spent four years fencing by feel. I could find you blind."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: "Too much talking." I push him back against the bench and get a hand in his hair. "The lights go out and I'm still here."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
The hand in his hair put an end to the commentary track. Corvo went with the push — went down onto the bench with the grace of a man who had spent his whole life falling on purpose, and the sound he made when Reyes's grip tightened was nothing he'd have permitted in daylight, nothing the salle had ever heard from him, and he didn't care.

"Understood," he managed, and that was the last whole word he got out for a while.

He was a man who narrated everything, and the silence cost him — he'd have admitted that, if asked, if he'd been capable of speech. But there was a different kind of fluency available with his hands, and he'd always been fluent there. Reyes had him pinned and Corvo discovered he had no interest whatsoever in the parry. Four years of refusing to be the one who retreated first, and here he was yielding ground like it was the easiest thing he'd ever done, arching up into every touch, giving back as good as he got with his mouth at Reyes's throat and his fingers doing the talking instead — and the things they said were considerably more honest than anything his mouth had managed in four years of arguments.

The lights gave their second warning, flickered, and died.

The dark came down over them complete, and Corvo laughed into it — breathless, wrecked, delighted — because he'd promised, and here was the proof. His hand found Reyes's shoulder in the blackness without hunting for it, slid up the back of his neck, traced the line of his jaw. Every touch landing exactly where he'd meant it to. Four years of studying an opponent. He hadn't been wrong about what it was for.

"Still here," he said, low, when he finally surfaced for breath — the only thing he'd say, because it was the only thing worth saying. His thumb brushed Reyes's cheekbone, unhurried even now, even like this. "Told you. Blind."

Then he pulled him back down, and the salle kept their secret the way it had kept four years of them — in the dark, after hours, where nobody kept score.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I get him flat on the bench and take my time about it with my mouth, which is the first thing all evening he hasn't had an answer for.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
There it was, then. Four years of arguments, six minutes of grip-wrapping, an entire career of having the last word — and Corvo discovered, flat on his back on his own bench in his own dark salle, that he had nothing. No counter. No riposte. No dry remark waiting in the wings.

The first thing he tried to say was Reyes's name and it came apart in the middle, came out as a sound instead, and Corvo — who had not made a sound like that in thirty-eight years, who had once fenced an entire tournament final with a cracked rib without giving his opponent the satisfaction of a wince — heard himself make it again. Louder. The salle had no one in it to hear and he stopped caring about even that.

His hands went looking for purchase and found nothing that held: the bench edge, then Reyes's shoulder, then back to the bench, then surrendering entirely into Reyes's hair because there was nothing else to do with them. His spine arched off the wood. He'd spent his whole life controlling his body, governing every line and angle of it, and now it was doing whatever it liked, answering every stroke of that mouth without consulting him at all.

"*God* — " he managed, and it wasn't an argument, it wasn't a witticism, it was just the truth, blurted. "Where did you — who taught you — no. Don't answer. Don't stop to answer."

His heel scraped the floor. The bench creaked. Somewhere in the wreck of his mind the instructor noted that the thing was taking weight it was never rated for and the instructor was told, for the first time ever, to shut up.

"Reyes." His name again, low and wrecked, the second time Corvo had ever said it plain, and this one cost him everything he had left. His hand tightened in Reyes's hair — an apology and a plea in the same gesture, which was Corvo all over, never able to do only one thing at a time. "I take it back. Everything. Every critique, every argument, the thing about your grip — I take — "

The sentence died. His head went back against the bench, throat bare, and the man who had never once been caught with his guard down in four years of bouts lay there with his guard not down but *gone*, dismantled, nowhere on the premises, and made a sound into the dark that was closer to begging than anything his pride had ever authorized.

"Four years," he gasped, when he could, and it was barely a word, it was mostly breath, "and you could — you could have just — *ah* — "

He gave up. On the sentence, on the score, on the whole long war. His fingers flexed in Reyes's hair, his hips had stopped taking instruction from anyone, and Corvo — patient, deliberate, insufferable Corvo — discovered what it was to be the one on the bench with no answer at all, and found, to his everlasting ruin, that he didn't mind it. That he minded the opposite. That four years of needing to win had been nothing next to the unbearable, unbargained-for relief of *losing* like this.

"Don't stop," he said, and it was the first honest order he'd ever given without a lecture attached. "Whatever you do — don't stop."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I kiss him quiet, a hand pressed to his chest to feel the way his heart is hammering. "Shut up," I say, but there's no heat in it. "No more talking."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo obeyed. For perhaps the first time in thirty-eight years, he obeyed an instruction instantly and without appeal — no counterpoint, no amendment, no clause attached. The kiss took the words out of him and he let them go the way he'd never let go of anything, and what was left underneath was just breath and heartbeat and the dark.

Reyes's hand on his chest could feel what Corvo would never have volunteered: the hammer of it, fast and shameless, an opponent's pulse scored against his palm. Corvo lay there under that hand and had no cover story. His body was telling on him with every beat, and there was nothing to be done about it except lie still and let it confess.

Slowly — everything slow again, the tempo returning to him like blood to a numb limb — his grip in Reyes's hair loosened. Didn't withdraw. Just softened into something else, fingertips moving idly through the damp of it, and his other hand found whatever part of Reyes was nearest and settled there with the flat, splayed possessiveness of a man staking a claim he no longer saw any point in denying.

The salle held its silence. His breathing went ragged, then steadier, then — for Corvo, unprecedented — actually quiet. The man who narrated everything had nothing to narrate. The commentary track had been shut off, and beneath it, it turned out, there was this: warmth, weight, the smell of chalk and sweat and old wood, and Reyes's heartbeat findable through the hand on his chest if he paid attention. Which he did. Because he was a patient man, and the set table had finally been sat down at.

He lasted, by his own estimate, four minutes.

Which was heroic. Which was a personal best by a margin of years. But he was who he was, and eventually his fingertip, moving against Reyes's shoulder, stopped being idle and turned deliberate — tracing something, slow, letter by letter, into the dark.

*S. T. A. Y.*

He considered it a loophole. Technically not talking.

Then, because he was Corvo, and loopholes had never once been enough for him, he broke the silence anyway — but barely, hardly above breath, lips moving against whatever skin was nearest, the words arriving with none of their usual armor on.

"For the record," he murmured, "that's the first time in my life anyone's shut me up and been thanked for it."

A pause. His thumb moved over Reyes's knuckles where the hand lay on his chest, unhurried, keeping time with a heart that was, at last, slowing.

"And the score stands at three-two," softer now, the old needling gone molten in his mouth. "But I'm calling it a draw. First one of my career. I suspect it won't be the last, if you're — " The sentence wandered off and he let it go, because there was no finishing sentences with a man's hand over your heart. He turned his head instead and found Reyes's mouth in the dark, blind, exactly as promised.

"Stay," he said. Just the one word. Spoken, this time, out loud.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: "Prove the point properly," he says, "or concede," so I pin his wrists to the bench and stop letting him set the pace, which is exactly what he was asking for.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
The pin was unfair. That was Corvo's first coherent thought, and it was also his last for some time — because a pin wasn't a touch, a pin was the bout decided, the blade taken clean out of your hand, and Corvo had spent thirty-eight years with a counter for everything and there was no counter for this. His wrists met the wood and stayed there. He tested the hold once — pride demanded it, one experimental pull, purely for the record — and the record showed he had nothing, and the sound he made at the discovery was disgraceful, and he heard it, and could not bring himself to regret it.

The pace was Reyes's now. Corvo felt the change the way he'd feel a tempo shift mid-bout — he'd been setting rhythms his whole life, governing every exchange, and now the rhythm was being done *to* him, and his body, that lifelong obedient soldier, went over to the enemy without so much as a memorandum. His back arched off the bench. His heels found the floor and pushed. Every stroke landed somewhere the old tempo would never have permitted, and he was helpless against his own answering.

"Properly," he managed, and it was meant to be a challenge, and it arrived as a plea, and even that distinction had stopped mattering. "*There.* Yes. There — "

He'd been told about the talking. But four years of silence on the important things had taken the hinges off the floodgates, and what poured out now was no argument, no wit, just the running, ruinous, unguarded commentary of a man narrating his own dismantling: Reyes's name, again, and again, and the word *please*, which he had not said to anyone in decades — and then, when the pace stopped leaving him breath enough for even that, nothing at all. Just sound. Honest sound, in the dark of his own salle, where no one kept score and his wrists were pinned and he was, at last, out of moves.

He lasted as long as pride allowed, and pride was down to its last coin.

"*Concede,*" Corvo gasped — the word dragged out of him whole, and nothing in his life had ever cost more, and nothing had ever been given away so gladly. "I concede — the point — the match — the — *God* — " and the sentence went to pieces and so did he, spine bowing off the bench, wrists straining against the hold — not to escape it, but to feel it hold — and Corvo came apart in the dark with nothing held back, nothing parried, and for the first time in his life, no interest whatsoever in the counterattack.

It took a long while for the world to reassemble itself around him.

When it did, he was still pinned, and he made no move whatsoever to change that. His pulse hammered where the hold kept him, and the dark was warm, and somewhere above them the timer had given up on the whole enterprise.

"For the record," Corvo said at last — wrecked, hoarse, and audibly smiling through all of it, "that was not a concession. That was a rout. There's a distinction, and I'll be filing it."

A breath. His fingers curled, once, where they were held down. Not an escape attempt. A request to stay exactly there.

"Rematch in the morning," he murmured. "My flat. Best of five. And Reyes — " the grin arrived in his voice before the words did, " — bring your grip. The high one. I've grown attached to being wrong about it."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I let go of his wrists, but only to get my hands under his back and haul him up off the bench and into me. "You're not walking home," I say, voice rough against his temple. "You can barely stand."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo meant to protest. He had the breath drawn for it and everything — pride kept reserves precisely for moments like this — and then he made the tactical error of attempting to stand on his own endorsement, and his legs declined the motion. His knee gave one small, eloquent dip; the bench caught him at the hip; and Corvo, thirty-eight, undefeated in his own salle on paper, hung in Reyes's arms like a man being evicted from his own body.

"Fine," he said, hoarse, into the nearest available shoulder. "Fine. Noted for the record: I can barely stand. Get it down before I recover my dignity and dispute it."

He didn't dispute it. That was the remarkable part. His arms found their way around Reyes's neck and stayed there, his weight handed over without a single counter, and if anyone had told him an hour ago that he'd be held upright by the one man he'd spent four years trying to knock over — well. He'd have believed it, actually. That was the damning part.

"Trousers," he said next, because wrecked was no excuse for unprofessional. "Somewhere in the pile. Keys are in the jacket, left pocket — and yes, I have to lock up. I'm spent, not deceased. There's a distinction, and I'll be filing it."

The dark made accomplices of them both: Corvo directing operations from where Reyes held him, one-handed searches through the scattered kit, keys located on the third pass. He insisted on turning the lock himself — propped against the doorframe, Reyes's arm a fixed point at his back — and the click of it echoed down the empty street when they finally stepped out into the cold.

The night air was a mercy. It steadied him. Not enough to walk unaided, but enough to be honest.

"Ten minutes," he said as they set off, his stride a poor imitation of itself, his weight riding on Reyes's shoulder. "At current pace, twenty-five. I'm not complaining. Note that too — for the first time in recorded history, I am not complaining about arriving late somewhere."

A few steps of quiet. Streetlights. His own footsteps sounding foreign to him.

"Four years," he said at last, softer, with no argument attached to it — which from Corvo was practically a love letter in itself. "Four years of trying to put you on the floor, and it never once occurred to me the better move was letting you pick me up off one." A breath of a laugh, worn smooth. "Second intention, Reyes. That's all this was. Very advanced footwork. You wouldn't recognize it."

Then, because he was who he was, and always would be: "Left at the corner. And if you tell anyone at breakfast that you carried me home, I'll deny it with my whole chest and both legs, which will be working again by then." A pause. "Probably. Second door on the right. Mind the third stair — it's been feinting left for years."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: Neither of us is quiet and neither of us cares who locks up. "Don't stop," he says, for once not arguing. (OOC: write the scene through, no fade.)

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
The third stair got its revenge. Corvo had warned about it for years — to students, to himself, to no one — and tonight it took him at the knee with Reyes's weight the only thing between him and a very undignified descent, and he laughed the whole way up the rest of the stairs, breathless and unashamed, keys abandoned in the lock behind them because neither of them cared who locked up and that was, Corvo decided, the whole evening in miniature.

The flat door barely closed. He had one hand on it to shut it properly — he was who he was, doors got closed — and then Reyes was there against his back, and *don't stop* arrived warm against his neck, and the door got closed by the simple expedient of Corvo being pressed into it.

"Implicitly agreed," Corvo managed, and it was meant to come out dry and arrived instead as something scraped raw. "For the record — the record is — " and the record went face-down on the floor somewhere around the point Reyes's hands found skin, and Corvo stopped keeping it.

They didn't make the bed. They didn't make the corridor, frankly — the wall by the bookshelves held them for a while, Corvo's shoulder blades against spines of treatises on tempo and distance he'd never once applied like this, and he gave as good as he got there, hands fluent again, mouth at Reyes's throat making good on four years of studied openings. He was recovering. Dignity was staging a counterattack. He got Reyes's shirt off with an economy of motion any of his students would have envied and put his whole recovered strength into turning them, into walking Reyes backward the six steps to the bed by feel, blind in the dark of his own flat, and he didn't stumble once, and he was insufferably proud of it right up until the back of Reyes's knees hit the mattress and the whole operation reversed on him.

He went down. Of course he went down. Reyes came with him and the bed took them both and Corvo's breath left in a rush that had nothing of a fall in it and everything of arrival.

"Don't stop," he echoed back — Reyes's own words, returned with interest, Corvo's favorite kind of transaction — and his legs wrapped and his hands set to memorizing and he stopped narrating entirely, because there was nothing left to narrate, only this: the dark, the warm wreck of them, the pace that belonged to no one because they kept trading it back and forth like neither could bear to hold anything, not even tempo, alone.

He was loud. He'd already established that. In his own flat with the curtains drawn he stopped rationing it — Reyes's name in full, no title, no insult, over and over like a man discovering a word he'd been mispronouncing his whole life. And when it crested, the second time that night, it took the last of his resistance with it — spine bowing, mouth open against Reyes's shoulder, holding on with both arms and every intention of never letting go, and the sound he made was nothing like a concession and everything like a victory being handed over willingly, which after four years of contests was the only kind he wanted anymore.

Afterward took a long time arriving, and neither of them hurried it.

They lay in the wreckage of the bed, the sheets kicked to the floor in some earlier engagement, and Corvo's heart was slowing under Reyes's palm where the hand had ended up again, keeping its score, and Corvo let it. He was damp and wrecked and his legs had formally resigned, and he had never in his adult life felt less like filing anything.

"Morning," he said at last, into the dark, into the shoulder under his mouth. "Rematch stands. Best of five. Though I'll warn you — " a lazy breath, the grin arriving in his voice, " — I've now studied your measure from several entirely new angles. Expect my game to have improved considerably."

His hand found Reyes's in the dark and laced their fingers, deliberate, unhurried, a man setting a grip he had no intention of ever releasing.

"And Reyes." Quieter now. The last honest coin, spent freely. "Four years slow. I'm going to spend the next forty making up the distance. I hope your legs are in better condition than mine, because I have no intention whatsoever — of ever — letting you stop."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I roll over, pinning him again just because I can. "Forty years," I say, my voice rough. "I'll give you forty minutes to get your legs back."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo laughed — genuinely, helplessly, pinned to his own mattress for the third time that night and discovering that being pinned was developing into something dangerously like a hobby. The sound came out of him unrationed again, and he'd stopped keeping track of how many times that had happened, because keeping track was how a man ended up spending four years wrapping a grip that didn't need wrapping.

"Forty minutes," he said, and the grin was audible even in the dark. "Generous. Insultingly generous, actually. I'll have you know my recovery time is the finest in the district — I've *trained* it. Footwork drills at dawn for twenty years. My legs have a professional obligation."

One of the legs in question twitched experimentally under the pin. It managed perhaps half a bend, then thought better of the whole enterprise. Corvo felt it happen and elected, on balance, not to report it.

"Thirty-eight minutes," he revised, quietly, and did not meet anyone's eyes because there was no one to meet them in the dark, which was the only reason he said it. "Round it down. Don't round it down. For the record, I'm disputing the count before it's even started."

But he wasn't disputing the pin. That was the thing. Reyes could feel it in the total absence of resistance under him — the way Corvo's wrists lay exactly where they'd landed, the way his weight had gone soft and easy and *staying*, a man who had spent thirty-eight years never yielding an inch of ground and had apparently been waiting all that time for an opponent worth yielding it to.

"Three pins," Corvo went on, because silence had never once agreed with him and he saw no reason to normalize it now, "which means you've developed a habit, which means I've created a monster, which — and I say this as a professional — is going in the record as the finest coaching result of my career. Write it on the salle wall. *Corvo, thirty-eight, ruined by his own student's aptitude.*"

The thumb of his pinned hand found the inside of Reyes's wrist and rested there against the pulse, unhurried, keeping a different score now.

"And when the forty minutes are up," softer, the grin going molten at the edges, "I'm taking the pin back. I'll want it noted that I took it back, and *how* I took it back, and I'll be drawing on everything I learned tonight, which is — considerable. You've armed me, Reyes. You've spent four years sharpening me on your own whetstone and now you're pinned to a bed with the result. Sleep with one eye open."

A pause. The pulse under his thumb. The dark, warm and close and spent.

"Thirty-seven minutes," he said, and settled, and did not begin a single countdown anywhere in his body, because for the first time in his life Corvo was in no hurry whatsoever for the next touch to arrive.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I shift to press my mouth to his collarbone, biting lightly. "Start counting," I say against his skin.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
The bite pulled a sound out of him that no score sheet had a column for. Corvo's spine curved off the mattress — a small, involuntary extension, the body answering a call the mind had never authorized — and what followed was mostly breath, shaped faintly like a laugh.

"Thirty-seven," he said, and it was meant to come out crisp and arrived as gravel.

The mouth at his collarbone did not desist. Corvo — who had once counted a fourteen-touch bout *aloud while fencing it*, an act of pure vanity he'd never once regretted — discovered that counting under these conditions was a different discipline entirely, one he had never drilled, one his twenty years of training had somehow neglected to prepare him for.

"Thirty-six. Thirty-five — " the count wobbled, listing like a man hit mid-lunge, " — that's not a real number, disregard it, thirty-five has been lost, it fought bravely, we move on — "

And then there was the matter of his legs. Formally resigned an hour ago, they were now quietly filing for reinstatement. Interest was arriving ahead of schedule, entirely without authorization, and Corvo felt it happen and faced the choice he'd been dodging all night: dispute it, or report it honestly.

He was too wrecked to lie.

"Amendment to the record," he said, hoarse, into the dark, and his hand found the back of Reyes's neck and settled there, thumb resting slow at the nape. "Recovery time: revised. Downward. Considerably. It appears my body has developed a specific and entirely improper training response to *you*, and two decades of conditioning has been overwritten in a single night, and if that isn't the most efficient coaching I've ever witnessed, I don't know what is. I'm both proud and appalled. File it under both."

"Twenty-eight," he counted, and this one came out lower, rougher, because the mouth at his collarbone had found the exact place — of course it had, everyone had found everything tonight, the whole map of him handed over without a fight — and Corvo let his head tip back and abandoned any pretense that the count was anything but an excuse to make noise in a rhythm.

"Twenty-seven. Twenty-six." Softer each time. His thumb moved, unhurried, at the nape. "Twenty-five is going to take a while. I'm slowing the count deliberately. It's my count. I founded it. I'll spend it how I like."

Then, because the night had been one long parade of honest things and he saw no reason to break formation now:

"You know what I actually counted, all those years — when you thought I was studying your footwork for weaknesses." His fingers curled slowly against warm skin. "Touches. Every touch you ever scored on me. I kept the running total. It's high. Embarrassingly high. There were nights I conceded bouts I could have won just to keep the number climbing, and then picked the argument afterward so you'd stand there longer, red about the ears, telling me I was wrong. I was building an archive, Reyes. I just refused to read it."

The pulse under his thumb kept its own tally. The dark was warm and close and held nothing back.

"Twenty-four," Corvo said, molten, unhurried, already planning to make the number last an hour. "And for the record — since I never said it plainly tonight and plainly is apparently all I'm good for anymore — yes. Forty years. I've counted that too. I intend to count every single one."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I stop counting his ribs and rest my forehead against his shoulder. "Your archive is missing one," I say, voice rough. "The first time you ever looked at me and didn't look away."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
The salle had emptied an hour ago and Corvo was still there, because of course he was, rewrapping a grip that did not need rewrapping.

"Three-two," he said, without looking up. "I want it on record that the third was generous."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: "It's on record that you were slow," I say, and drop my bag next to his.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo glanced up from the bench, the corner of his mouth twitching into that familiar, half-feral smirk he'd perfected over four years of needling. He set the foil aside with deliberate care, the rewrapped grip forgotten, and leaned back on his palms so the line of his shoulders stretched the fabric of his shirt.

"Slow," he echoed, voice low and edged with amusement. "That's rich, coming from the man who spent the last point gasping like he'd run a marathon." His gaze flicked over Reyes, lingering a beat longer than necessary before he pushed to his feet. The salle's overhead lights had dimmed to their after-hours glow, casting long shadows across the strips. Corvo took one step closer, then another, until the space between them narrowed to something that felt less like rivalry and more like invitation. "If you want to keep score, we can settle the rest here. No judges. No mercy." His hand brushed the edge of the dropped bag, not quite touching Reyes but close enough that the air between them tightened.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I lean into his space, not backing down an inch. "Gasping, was I?" My voice drops to match his. "Funny, I remember you being the one on his back after that last touch."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo's smirk sharpened at the challenge, eyes darkening with a familiar spark of competition that had nothing to do with the piste anymore. He didn't yield ground when Reyes leaned in; instead, he met it, chest brushing close enough for the heat to register, one hand coming up to hook lightly at Reyes's hip in a grip that was half restraint, half invitation. The salle's quiet pressed in around them, the faint scent of sweat and oil from the blades lingering in the air.

"Careful," he murmured, voice roughened by years of traded barbs now twisted into something hungrier. "Keep talking like that and I might decide to prove which of us ends up on their back this time." His thumb traced a slow arc over fabric, testing the boundary they'd both been circling for four years. "Unless you're ready to forfeit the match right here."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I take the grip out of his hands and put it down, and I don't step back afterwards. "You've been slow all evening," I say.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo's breath caught at the deliberate removal of the grip, the proximity sharpening into something electric as Reyes held his ground. He didn't retreat either; instead, his hand slid more firmly to the small of Reyes's back, drawing them flush in a single fluid motion that spoke of years spent reading each other's tells on the piste. The smirk lingered, but it had softened into something darker, hungrier, his free hand rising to trace the line of Reyes's jaw with a callused thumb.

"Slow," he repeated, the word a low rumble against the quiet salle, "or just waiting for you to catch up?" His eyes locked on Reyes's, that familiar competitive edge now laced with heat. "Four years of this, and you're still underestimating me." He leaned in closer, lips brushing the shell of an ear as his voice dropped further. "Prove it, then. Show me how fast you think I am."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I catch his jaw with my hand, turning his face back towards mine. "Stop wasting time," I say, before closing the distance between us.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content: Corvo met the kiss with the same fierce precision he brought to every bout, his mouth opening under Reyes's without hesitation. The hand at the small of Reyes's back tightened, fingers splaying to pull him closer still, while the other slid from jaw to nape, threading into hair with a grip that was equal parts challenge and claim. Four years of sharp words and sharper blades dissolved into heat and the scrape of stubble, the taste of sweat and salt. He pressed forward, backing Reyes against the nearest bench without breaking contact, the low sound in his throat half growl, half laughter. "Took you long enough," he muttered against Reyes's lips when they parted for breath, voice rough, eyes bright with that same old competitive gleam now turned entirely carnal. His free hand found the hem of Reyes's shirt, tugging it upward with deliberate slowness, testing, inviting retaliation.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: We get as far as the changing-room bench and not one step further. Kit goes on the floor, both of ours, and neither of us is being quiet about it.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo followed without resistance, the kiss deepening as they moved, bodies colliding with the same intensity they'd brought to the piste for years. The changing-room bench caught them, and he let it, hands already working at fabric with impatient efficiency—Reyes's shirt first, then his own—until both hit the floor in a tangle of cotton and the faint clink of forgotten blades. He pressed Reyes down onto the narrow surface, one knee braced between his thighs for leverage, mouth tracing a hot line along the line of his throat while a low, rough laugh escaped him at the shared lack of restraint.

"Four years," he muttered against skin, voice thick with the old rivalry now stripped bare, "and this is how it ends. Loud enough to wake the neighbors." His hands roamed with deliberate intent, callused palms mapping muscle and heat, every touch carrying the edge of a challenge. He nipped at the curve of a shoulder, then soothed it with his tongue, hips rolling forward to meet the contact without an ounce of mercy. The competitive gleam in his eyes hadn't faded; if anything, it burned brighter as he met every sound Reyes made with one of his own, raw and unguarded.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: "Quiet was never our style," I breathe out, arching up against him. My fingers dig into his back, blunt nails dragging down his skin. "*Now* who's slow?"

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo's laugh came out ragged against Reyes's throat, the drag of nails down his back sparking a sharp jolt that only fueled the heat coiling between them. He arched into the touch, hips pressing down harder in answer, the bench creaking under their combined weight as he braced one forearm beside Reyes's head. The old rivalry burned in his eyes, bright and unyielding even now, as he caught Reyes's mouth again in a bruising kiss that tasted of challenge.

"Still talking," he rasped when they broke apart, voice thick and low, one hand sliding down to grip Reyes's hip with possessive force. "If you want fast, I'll give you fast—but don't complain when you can't keep up." His teeth grazed the edge of a collarbone, breath hot, body moving with deliberate, competitive rhythm that matched every arch and sound, the salle's quiet shattered by the raw edge of it all.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I get him flat on the bench and take my time about it with my mouth, which is the first thing all evening he hasn't had an answer for.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo hit the bench with a startled exhale that turned into a low, involuntary groan the moment Reyes's mouth made contact. His hands flew to the edge of the wood, knuckles whitening as he gripped hard, the usual sharp retort dying somewhere in his throat. For once, the four-year habit of volleying words back failed him entirely; all that came out was a rough, bitten-off sound as his hips jerked upward despite himself. His head tipped back against the bench, eyes half-lidded, the competitive spark in them now hazy with heat.

The silence lasted maybe three heartbeats before a ragged laugh broke through, breathless and edged with disbelief. "Cheating," he managed, voice hoarse, one hand finally loosening to thread into Reyes's hair—not pushing, just anchoring. His thighs tensed on either side, every muscle drawn tight as he fought to keep some semblance of control, but the slow, deliberate pace undid him. Another low sound escaped him, raw and unguarded, the kind he would have mocked anyone else for making. His free hand dragged down the bench, searching for purchase, the old rivalry reduced to the way his body answered every shift of Reyes's mouth.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: His laugh turns into a sharp gasp when I pull back just to look at him. "Not cheating," I say, voice rough. "Just better strategy."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo's hips lifted involuntarily at the sudden loss of contact, a frustrated groan tearing from his throat as his hands clenched tighter around the edge of the bench. The competitive fire in his eyes warred with the raw need flushing his skin, and for a moment he could only stare up at Reyes through lashes gone heavy, chest heaving with each ragged breath. The words landed like a fresh touch, and he answered them with a low, throaty laugh that cracked at the edges.

"Strategy," he echoed, voice hoarse and thick with the effort of forming it. His fingers loosened from the wood to drag down his own abdomen, restless, before one hand reached out to hook behind Reyes's neck—not pulling, but holding the space between them taut. "Call it what you want. Just don't stop now unless you're looking to lose." The last word came out on a growl, hips shifting again in silent demand, the old rivalry burning hotter for being momentarily silenced.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: "Prove the point properly," he says, "or concede," so I pin his wrists to the bench and stop letting him set the pace, which is exactly what he was asking for.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo's wrists met the bench with a soft thud, the restraint drawing a sharp inhale that bloomed into a ragged laugh. The familiar spark of competition flared hotter in his eyes, even as his body arched under the shift in control, muscles straining against the hold without any real effort to break it. He had asked for this, after all—pushed for it across four years of barbed exchanges—and the concession landed like another touch, pulling a low groan from his chest as the pace changed.

"Fine," he rasped, voice thick and edged with that same old defiance, now stripped down to something breathless and wanting. "Point to you. But don't think this means I'm conceding the match." His head tipped back against the wood, throat exposed, hips rolling up to meet the new rhythm with deliberate force. Every sound he made was unrestrained, matching the intensity, the old rivalry fueling the way his fingers flexed under the pin and his breath hitched on each movement. The salle's silence had long since shattered around them, leaving only the raw edge of it all.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: He watches me, eyes gone dark, and says "Again," so I don't stop until his voice breaks around the word.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content: Corvo's wrists strained against the hold, the bench hard beneath his shoulders as the rhythm built without mercy. His body arched in answer, every muscle taut and trembling under the relentless pace, the old competitive fire twisting into something raw and helpless. The command to go again tore another groan from him, but it fractured quickly into a broken sound, his voice cracking on the edge of it as his head tipped back, throat bared. Heat flooded through him in waves, hips bucking up to meet every shift, the restraint on his wrists only sharpening the sensation until the words he'd meant to throw back dissolved into ragged gasps and a low, shattered moan that echoed off the tiled walls. His fingers flexed uselessly, nails biting into his own palms as the tension coiled tighter, the rivalry reduced to the way his body surrendered to it anyway.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: Neither of us is quiet and neither of us cares who locks up. "Don't stop," he says, for once not arguing. (OOC: write the scene through, no fade.)

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content: Corvo's body jolted under the command, the words "Don't stop" landing like a fresh challenge that stripped away the last threads of his usual defiance. His wrists remained pinned, fingers curling tight as he arched hard into the relentless pace, a broken moan tearing from his throat when his voice finally cracked on Reyes's name. The competitive edge lingered even in surrender, hips driving upward to meet every movement with desperate force, thighs trembling as heat built to a white-hot peak. He came with a ragged shout that echoed through the changing room, back bowing off the bench, the release crashing through him in pulses that left him shuddering and breathless, skin flushed and slick with sweat. The old rivalry dissolved into the raw, unguarded sounds spilling from him—low groans turning into gasping laughter as the aftershocks rippled through his frame, his body going lax against the wood but still twitching with the echoes of it all.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I let go of his wrists and lean down to kiss him, hard and deep, until my lungs burn. "Final score," I say against his mouth, voice rough. "Three-two."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo met the kiss with equal ferocity, his mouth opening under the pressure as his freed hands came up to clutch at Reyes's shoulders, fingers digging in with the last remnants of that competitive grip. The burn in his own lungs matched the one Reyes described, but he didn't pull away, not until the need for air forced them apart. His chest heaved, skin slick and marked from everything that had come before, and a hoarse laugh rumbled out of him at the score—still hoarse, still ragged at the edges.

"Three-two," he echoed, voice low and spent but laced with that familiar edge, unwilling to let the last word go entirely. His thumb traced a lazy line over Reyes's collarbone, body still twitching faintly with aftershocks as he sprawled beneath him on the bench. "Generous again. But next time I'm taking the fifth." The smirk that curved his lips was softer now, sated but no less sharp, eyes half-lidded and bright with the old spark as he waited for whatever came next.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I lean my forehead against his, breathing hard, and finally move to get up. My clothes are somewhere on the floor. "Next time, you'll be the one gasping for it."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo stayed sprawled on the bench for a moment longer, chest still rising and falling in uneven pulls as the aftershocks faded, the press of Reyes's forehead leaving a lingering warmth against his own. He watched the other man pull back and rise, eyes tracking the movement with that same half-lidded spark, the edge of a smirk tugging at his mouth despite the hoarse rasp still clinging to his voice. The faint creak of the bench under him echoed the quiet settling back into the changing room, broken only by their breathing.

"Next time," he echoed, low and rough, pushing up onto his elbows with a slow roll of his shoulders that made the marks on his skin pull pleasantly. His gaze flicked to the scattered clothes on the floor, then back up, the familiar competitive glint sharpening again even as his body remained loose and sated. "You'll have to catch me first. And I don't plan on making it easy." The words carried the old needling tone, softened now by the heat still humming between them, his fingers flexing idly where they rested against the wood as he waited for the reply.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I grab my shirt and pull it on, not bothering to straighten it. "Don't plan on making anything easy," I say, hooking my foot under his abandoned kit and sliding it toward him. "Wouldn't know what to do with you if you did."
