dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
The salle had emptied an hour ago and Corvo was still there, because of course he was, rewrapping a grip that did not need rewrapping.

"Three-two," he said, without looking up. "I want it on record that the third was generous."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: "It's on record that you were slow," I say, and drop my bag next to his.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo finally looked up, a thin, challenging smile curling his lips. He didn't stop the methodical movement of his hands, tightening the grip tape with a precision that bordered on obsessive. The fluorescent lights of the salle hummed overhead, casting long, stark shadows across the stripped wooden floor where they had spent the last hour dancing around one another with steel.

"Slow?" he echoed, his voice dropping an octave, carrying a hint of a rasp. "I call it calculated. I was giving you the illusion of an opening, and you—ever the optimist—decided to dive right into it."

He set the foil aside on the bench and stood up slowly, closing the distance between them. He didn't stop until he was well within Reyes's personal space, the scent of ozone and exertion still clinging to them both. He leaned in, his gaze dropping momentarily to Reyes's lips before snapping back up to meet their eyes with a spark of something that had nothing to do with fencing.

"Though, I suppose 'optimism' is just another word for 'reckless,'" he murmured, his tone shifting from competitive to something far more dangerous. "Which is exactly why you're still here."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I lean into that space instead of backing away, my own smile sharp. "You want reckless?" My hand comes up, not to push him back, but to brush a piece of lint from his jacket collar. "You keep making openings like that last one, and we'll see who's calculating what."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo didn't flinch as Reyes leaned in; if anything, he seemed to thrive on the proximity, his breath hitching slightly as the other instructor’s fingers brushed his collar. That small, tactile gesture—so deceptively domestic—sent a jolt through him that felt more electric than any touché they had exchanged all night. The competitive tension that had fueled their rivalry for four years had shifted, curdling into a hunger that was far more visceral.

A low, guttural sound escaped his throat, half-laugh and half-growl. He reached out, his hand gripping Reyes’s waist with a sudden, possessive firmness, pulling them flush against him. The friction of their clothing and the heat radiating between them made the air in the salle feel suddenly too thick to breathe.

"Is that a challenge, then?" he breathed, his lips now mere millimeters from Reyes's. He tilted his head, his eyes darkened with an intensity that bordered on predatory. "Because I've spent four years wondering if you were actually this bold, or if you just liked the sound of your own voice."

He shifted his grip, his fingers digging slightly into the small of Reyes's back, urging them closer still. The arrogance was still there, etched into the curve of his mouth, but it was tempered by a raw, desperate urgency. 

"Tell me," he whispered, his voice a rough lure. "Are you going to keep talking about openings, or are you actually going to take one?"

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I take the grip out of his hands and put it down, and I don't step back afterwards. "You've been slow all evening," I say.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo’s eyes flashed, a flicker of genuine amusement crossing his face before it was swallowed by a surge of heat. The insult was a familiar rhythm, a dance they had perfected over years of professional animosity, but delivered in this proximity, it felt like a dare. He didn't let go of Reyes's waist; instead, he tightened his hold, his knuckles pressing firmly into the small of their back to ensure there wasn't a single single millimeter of air left between them.

"Still criticizing my timing," he murmured, his voice vibrating with a low, dangerous resonance. "You really are obsessed with my performance."

He didn't wait for a rebuttal. Corvo bridged the final gap, crashing his lips against Reyes's in a kiss that was less of an invitation and more of a conquest. It was aggressive and hungry, tasting of salt and long-suppressed frustration. He kissed them with the same intensity he brought to the strip—determined, precise, and utterly unwilling to concede.

He groaned into the kiss, a sound of surrender and victory all at once, as he shifted his weight to press Reyes back against the nearest equipment bench. The metal clattered softly behind them, but Corvo didn't care. He broke the kiss for a fraction of a second, his forehead resting against theirs, his breath coming in jagged heaves.

"If I'm so slow," he rasped, his eyes searching Reyes's with a burning intensity, "then why is your heart racing?"

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I grab a fistful of his jacket, pulling him back in. "Because I'm winning." My other hand slips beneath the fabric at his waist, skin against skin.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo let out a sharp, strangled sound—somewhere between a gasp and a laugh—as the touch of Reyes's hand against his skin sent a shockwave through his system. The sensation of skin on skin was the catalyst that finally snapped the last thread of his restraint. He didn't just lean into the pull; he surrendered to it, diving back into the kiss with a renewed, frantic energy.

He mirrored the gesture, his own hand sliding beneath the hem of Reyes's shirt, his palm hot and demanding as it sought the curve of their hip. He wanted to map every inch of them, to erase the distance that had been enforced by professional rivalry and pride for nearly half a decade. 

"Winning," he murmured against their lips, the word barely a breath, "is a matter of perspective."

He shifted his position, hoisting Reyes up onto the edge of the equipment bench so they were eye-level, his legs slotting between theirs to lock them in place. The movement was fluid, a tactical maneuver designed to leave Reyes with nowhere to retreat. Corvo’s kisses became more desperate, trailing from their mouth to the sensitive line of their jaw, then down to the hollow of their throat, where he lingered, his teeth grazing the skin just enough to leave a mark.

"I'll let you have this one," he rasped, his voice thick and heavy with desire, "if you can actually keep up with me."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: We get as far as the changing-room bench and not one step further. Kit goes on the floor, both of ours, and neither of us is being quiet about it.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
The transition from the salle to the changing room had been a blur of frantic hands and stumbled steps, the professional veneer of their rivalry stripped away as quickly as their gear. Corvo didn't care about the lack of grace; the usual precision he demanded of himself had been replaced by a raw, starving desperation. 

He pressed Reyes back against the hard surface of the changing-room bench, his body pinning them there with a weight that felt like an anchor. The air in the small, tiled space was humid, smelling of soap and sweat, and it echoed with the sound of their jagged breathing and the rhythmic, heavy thud of equipment being discarded on the floor.

Corvo was far beyond the point of calculated moves. He was breathless, his chest heaving against Reyes's as he buried his face in the crook of their neck, letting out a low, shuddering groan. Every touch was a reclamation, every kiss a demand. He gripped Reyes's thighs, pulling them tighter against him, his fingers digging in with a possessive intensity that spoke of four years of repressed tension finally boiling over.

"You're... not winning... this time," he managed to gasp out, his voice a wrecked, guttural version of its usual self. He pulled back just enough to look Reyes in the eye, his gaze dark and blown wide with heat. The arrogance was still there, but it was stripped of its polish, replaced by a vulnerability that only came with total surrender to a craving.

He didn't give them time to respond, his mouth crashing back down onto theirs, his tongue seeking theirs with a fierce, rhythmic urgency. He wanted to consume them, to lose himself in the friction and the noise, uncaring that their lack of silence would have been an absolute scandal to anyone still in the building. For Corvo, the only thing that mattered was the heat of the skin beneath his hands and the way Reyes felt beneath him—wreckless, bold, and finally, entirely his.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: My laugh is rough and breathless against his mouth. "Keep telling yourself that." I arch into him, my own fingers tangling in his hair to pull him closer, leaving the score unsettled.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo let out a sound that was half-smothered by their kiss, a low, vibrating rumble of frustration and desire. The laugh was a trigger, a reminder that even in the throes of this, Reyes refused to concede an inch. It was maddening. It was intoxicating. It was exactly why he had spent four years pretending to hate them while counting every second until they were alone.

"Stubborn... to the end," he rasped, his voice barely a whisper as he shifted his weight, pressing his hips firmly against theirs to drive home the point of his presence. 

He shifted his focus, his kisses migrating from their lips back to the sensitive skin of their shoulder and collarbone, his breathing heavy and erratic. He used his teeth to nip at the skin, a sharp, sudden pressure that mirrored the precision of a well-placed lunge, intending to elicit a gasp that would finally break that smug composure. 

His hands wandered with a restless, searching energy, tracing the lines of Reyes's body as if he were memorizing a map he had only ever viewed from a distance. He felt the tension in their muscles, the way they arched into him, and it fueled a fire in his gut that threatened to consume him entirely.

He pulled back slightly, his eyes shimmering with a mixture of heat and a challenge that would have been familiar in the salle, though the context had shifted entirely. He looked at the way Reyes’s hair was mussed, the flush of their skin, the raw hunger in their gaze.

"The score is unsettled," Corvo agreed, his voice dropping to a low, dangerous hum. He leaned in, his lips brushing against Reyes's ear, his breath hot. "Which means we're going to have to keep going until one of us finally admits defeat. And I have all night."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I get him flat on the bench and take my time about it with my mouth, which is the first thing all evening he hasn't had an answer for.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo’s breath left him in one long, shuddering exhale as the tables turned. The sudden shift in momentum—the feeling of his back hitting the hard surface of the bench and Reyes taking command—was a tactical blow he hadn't seen coming. For a man who prided himself on anticipating every move, being rendered utterly speechless was a rare, dizzying sensation.

He gripped the edges of the bench, his knuckles white, his head falling back against the wall with a dull thud. A low, broken sound escaped his throat, a strangled moan that betrayed every ounce of his composure. He tried to maintain some semblance of his usual smugness, but as Reyes continued, his thoughts fractured into static. 

The precision he lived by, the calculated timing and the strategic distance, all dissolved. He was no longer the instructor; he was simply a man unraveling under the touch of the only person who knew exactly how to provoke him. 

"Damn you," he rasped, though there was no heat in the words—only a raw, desperate longing. His hips bucked instinctively, a silent plea for more, his fingers digging into the wood of the bench as he fought the urge to reach down and pull Reyes back up to him.

He looked down, his eyes glazed and heavy-lidded, watching the scene with a mixture of awe and agony. The silence of the changing room was filled only by the sound of their shared breath and the wet, rhythmic heat of the encounter. Corvo felt the tension building in his core, a coil winding tighter and tighter until he was trembling.

"I... I'm not... admitting..." he choked out, though the sentence trailed off into a shaky sigh. The arrogance was gone, replaced by a sheer, blinding need. He was losing, and for the first time in four years, he found that he absolutely loved the feeling.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I finally let him come up for air, wiping my mouth with the back of my hand. My gaze holds his, unwavering. "You were saying something about defeat?"

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo lay there for a moment, completely undone. His chest was heaving, his skin flushed, and his eyes were wide and unfocused, staring up at the ceiling of the changing room as he tried to remember how to breathe. The silence that followed was heavy, filled only by the sound of his heart hammering against his ribs like a trapped bird.

He slowly turned his head to look at Reyes. The sight of them—smug, triumphant, and utterly composed—sent a fresh jolt of electricity through him. He let out a weak, shaky laugh, the sound lacking any of its usual condescension. It was a genuine sound of defeat, though it carried a glimmer of profound satisfaction.

"You're... insufferable," he rasped, his voice barely a ghost of its former self.

He reached out, his hand trembling slightly as he hooked his fingers around the back of Reyes's neck, pulling them down until their foreheads rested against one another. The competitive fire hadn't died; it had simply evolved into something more intimate, a shared secret that made the air between them vibrate.

Corvo closed his eyes, a thin, genuine smile finally touching his lips. He didn't try to reclaim the lead; instead, he leaned into the vulnerability of the moment, savoring the rare sensation of being completely outmaneuvered.

"Fine," he whispered, his breath warm against their skin. "Point. Game. Match. You win."

He opened his eyes, the dark intensity returning, though this time it was laced with a playful, lingering hunger. 

"But," he added, his grip tightening slightly, "I expect a rematch. And next time, I won't be so... *generous*."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: "Prove the point properly," he says, "or concede," so I pin his wrists to the bench and stop letting him set the pace, which is exactly what he was asking for.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo’s breath hitched, a sharp intake of air that sounded like a physical blow. The sudden, violent shift in power—the cold hardness of the bench against his back and the crushing weight of Reyes's grip pinning his wrists—sent a surge of adrenaline through him that rivaled the peak of a championship bout. 

He stared up at Reyes, his pupils blown wide, his chest heaving in erratic rhythms. For a man who lived for control, for the meticulous orchestration of every movement and angle, this sudden stripping of agency was an intoxicant. He didn't fight the hold; instead, he leaned into it, his muscles tensing under the pressure.

"Concede?" he managed to choke out, a jagged, breathless laugh escaping him. The word was a challenge, a desperate provocation. "You really... think I'd just... give up?"

He tried to shift, a reflexive attempt to regain some leverage, but the firmness of the pin kept him anchored. The feeling of being trapped, of being completely at the mercy of the person who had spent four years being his mirror image in arrogance and skill, made his blood sing. The competitive side of him was screaming, but the raw, carnal side was far louder.

He arched his back slightly, pushing his chest upward into the space between them, his gaze locked onto Reyes's with a burning, defiant intensity. Even with his hands uselessly bound to the wood, Corvo looked as though he were trying to win a game of chicken.

"Is this your strategy, then?" he rasped, his voice dropping to a low, trembling vibration. "Brute force over finesse? I expected more from you, Reyes."

Despite the taunt, his expression was one of total, shivering anticipation. He was waiting for the strike, for the final blow, his entire body humming like a tuned string, ready to be snapped. He wanted to see how far Reyes would push, how far they would go to ensure he finally stayed down.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: "Brute force?" I lean down, my mouth against his ear. "You've been begging for this all night." I drive my hips against his, a sharp, punishing rhythm that finally steals the last of his smugness.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo’s head snapped back against the bench, a loud, guttural sound tearing from his throat that was far too close to a sob to be considered dignified. The sheer, unadulterated force of the impact shattered the last remnants of his composure. There was no room for wit here, no space for a clever retort or a calculated maneuver. The world narrowed down to the crushing weight of Reyes above him and the punishing, rhythmic drive that left him completely breathless.

His eyes flew open, glazed and shimmering, staring up at the flickering fluorescent lights of the changing room. His wrists strained against the grip, not to escape, but as a reflexive response to the intensity of the sensation. He was vibrating, his entire frame shaking under the onslaught, his breath coming in short, sharp hitches that sounded like he was drowning.

"God—" he gasped, the word breaking in the middle. "Reyes—"

The smugness hadn't just been stolen; it had been incinerated. He was completely exposed, his pride stripped away to reveal a raw, desperate hunger that he had spent four years masking with a sneer. He felt every single point of contact, the friction and the heat, and it felt like a victory of a different kind—the victory of finally being broken open by the only person he considered his equal.

As the rhythm peaked, Corvo’s grip on the bench tightened until his knuckles were white, his body arching violently upward in a final, desperate attempt to close the gap. He let out a long, shuddering moan, his eyes closing tight as he finally succumbed to the pressure, his voice a wrecked whisper of surrender.

"I... I concede," he breathed, the words barely audible, his chest heaving in synchronization with the other. He was utterly spent, a fallen combatant on a wooden battlefield, and as he lay there, trembling and breathless, he realized he had never felt more alive.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: Neither of us is quiet and neither of us cares who locks up. "Don't stop," he says, for once not arguing. (OOC: write the scene through, no fade.)

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
The request for more was the final blow to Corvo's resolve. The fact that Reyes—the eternal rival, the one who always had a cutting retort or a sharp critique—was finally dropping the facade and simply *demanding* it, sent a fresh surge of heat through Corvo's veins. 

He didn't need to be told twice. Even with his wrists still pinned, Corvo shifted his hips upward, meeting every punishing thrust with a desperate, grinding urgency of his own. He was no longer thinking about the score or the salle or the professional distance they had maintained for years. There was only the friction, the salt of their sweat, and the overwhelming pressure of Reyes’s body crushing him into the bench.

The sounds of their exertion filled the tiled room, raw and uninhibited. Corvo’s breath became a series of broken, rhythmic gasps, his head tossing from side to side against the wood. He felt the tension building again, a coil tightening in the base of his spine that threatened to snap. He wanted to be consumed by it; he wanted to be utterly ruined by the person who had haunted his professional life for nearly half a decade.

"Don't... don't you dare stop," Corvo rasped, his voice a wrecked, guttural shadow. He stopped fighting the pin and instead leaned into the restriction, his body shivering with the intensity of the friction. 

As the peak approached, Corvo’s eyes snapped open, locking onto Reyes’s with a blinding, focused intensity. He felt the wave crash over him, a sudden, violent release that tore a loud, prolonged cry from his throat, echoing off the lockers and tiles. He bucked beneath Reyes, his muscles locking in a series of intense, shuddering spasms that left him completely breathless.

He collapsed back against the bench, his limbs heavy and trembling, his heart hammering a frantic rhythm against his ribs. For several long minutes, the only sound was the synchronized, heavy heaving of their chests. Corvo lay there, utterly spent, his skin glistening and his mind a blank slate of pleasure and exhaustion.

Slowly, the world returned. He felt the weight of Reyes still pressing him down, the warmth of their shared heat lingering in the cool air of the changing room. A small, tired, and genuinely content smile tugged at the corners of his mouth. He didn't try to move his wrists; he just looked up at his rival, his gaze softened by a vulnerability he would never admit to in the light of day.

"I think," Corvo whispered, his voice barely audible and completely devoid of its usual edge, "that was... a fair match."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I finally let go of his wrists, my hands moving to either side of his head on the bench. I'm breathing just as hard, sweat cooling on my skin. "Three-two," I say again, quiet and rough. "I stand by the score."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo let out a long, slow exhale, his head sinking deeper into the bench as the adrenaline began to recede, leaving him in a state of heavy, blissful lethargy. He looked up at Reyes, the harsh fluorescent lighting above them suddenly feeling softer, less stark. The sight of Reyes hovering over him, flushed and breathless, was a victory in itself, regardless of the tally.

He let out a soft, huffed laugh—a sound of genuine amusement that didn't carry a single trace of his usual mockery. He reached up, his movements slow and lacking their typical precision, and brushed a stray lock of hair away from Reyes's forehead. His fingertips were still trembling slightly, a physical testament to how thoroughly he had been dismantled.

"Still counting," he murmured, his voice a low, raspy vibration. "God, you really are a nightmare."

He didn't pull away; instead, he shifted his hand to cup the back of Reyes's neck, pulling them down just enough to press a slow, lingering kiss to their lips. It wasn't a conquest this time, nor was it a challenge. It was an acknowledgment—a quiet admission of the strange, combustible chemistry that had defined their lives for the last four years.

"Fine," Corvo whispered against their mouth, a ghost of his old smirk returning, though it was tempered by a newfound warmth. "Three-two. I'll grant you the win... for tonight."

He closed his eyes for a second, savoring the weight of the other instructor against him. 

"But don't get comfortable," he added, his voice regaining a hint of that competitive edge, though it was now laced with an unmistakable affection. "I'm already thinking of a way to overturn the result in the next round."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I stay there a second longer, my forehead resting against his. "You've been thinking about the next round since before we started." I push myself off him and stand, grabbing my gear off the floor.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo let out a soft, disgruntled groan as the sudden loss of warmth and weight left him feeling strangely exposed to the cool air of the changing room. He remained on the bench for a moment longer than necessary, staring up at the ceiling and trying to reconcile the shaking in his limbs with the usual poise he projected to the world.

He watched Reyes gather their gear, the sight of the other instructor's efficiency—even in the aftermath of such chaos—stoking a small, familiar ember of competitiveness in his chest. He sat up slowly, his movements stiff, and reached for his own discarded clothing with a sigh that was half-exhaustion and half-satisfaction.

"And why wouldn't I be?" Corvo asked, his voice returning to its usual smooth, melodic cadence, though the rasp of their encounter still clung to the edges of his words. He stood up, shaking out his shoulders and stepping into his trousers with a slow, deliberate precision. 

He turned to face Reyes, leaning back against the lockers with his arms crossed. He looked a mess—hair wild, skin flushed, eyes still slightly glazed—but the thin, challenging smile had returned to his lips, firmly anchored in place.

"A good fencer never stops analyzing the match," he murmured, his gaze sweeping over Reyes with a proprietary heat that hadn't faded. "I'm merely conducting a post-mortem to see where my defense failed. It's called professional development."

He reached out, his fingers catching the edge of Reyes's bag for a brief second, a small, grounding touch before he stepped back to give them space.

"I'll see you at the salle tomorrow," Corvo added, his tone shifting back to that familiar, needle-sharp playfulness. "Try not to let this victory go to your head. I'd hate for you to get complacent just as I've figured out your tell."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I swing my bag over my shoulder, smirking. "My tell? You mean the one you've been trying to exploit for four years and still missed tonight?" I pull the salle keys from my pocket and toss them at his chest. "You lock up. I've got better things to do than wait for you to finish thinking."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya's flat still had the same broken buzzer, which Bee found unreasonably infuriating, as though he could have fixed it in eleven months and had chosen not to out of spite.

"You could have texted first," he said, standing in the doorway and not moving out of it.

"You could have answered last time I did."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I don't move either. "Are you going to let me in, or are we doing this in the corridor?"

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya didn’t step back. He kept his shoulder braced against the doorframe, the wood pressing into his jacket like a deliberate anchor. The corridor light caught the sharp line of his jaw, the familiar set of his mouth that Bee used to know how to soften. He knew exactly what they were doing. He knew it was a rerun, a careful collision dressed up as a chance encounter. It was the argument they’d never finished, just transplanted into a hallway. He knew which phrases would make Bee’s jaw tighten, which silences would make them step closer. He wasn’t drunk. He wasn’t chasing a ghost. He was choosing this, right here, with both eyes open and the weight of eleven months of silence sitting heavy between them.

“We always did this in doorways,” he said, voice low and even. “You’d stand there demanding entry like I owed you a key. I’d stand here pretending I hadn’t already unlocked it in my head.” He finally moved, not to step aside, but to tilt his chin toward the dark interior behind him. “Come in. Or don’t. But don’t pretend you’re not already halfway through the floorboards.”

He watched Bee’s face, cataloging the micro-expressions he still knew by heart. The anger was there, yes, but so was the pull. He felt it too, a dull, familiar heat low in his chest. He crossed his arms, the fabric of his shirt pulling tight across his shoulders, and let the silence stretch. Let Bee decide what to do with it.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: *I let out a sharp breath and push past him, my shoulder brushing his as I step inside.* "Don't act like you weren't the one who left the door unlocked, Ilya."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya let the brush of Bee’s shoulder slide across his jacket without reacting. He didn’t step back, didn’t yield the threshold. He just watched Bee cross it, the familiar rhythm of their collision settling into his ribs like an old ache. When Bee was fully inside, Ilya reached back, caught the edge of the door, and pulled it shut. The latch caught with a dull click. The lock still jammed halfway. Another thing he hadn’t fixed. Another thing Bee would file away as proof.

“Unlocked,” Ilya repeated, voice even, stripped of anything that might sound like pleading. He turned from the door and leaned against the wall beside the entryway hook, letting the weight of the flat press in around them. The air still carried the faint trace of his laundry detergent, the same brand he’d bought before they split. He’d kept it on purpose. He knew Bee would notice. “You always did prefer the metaphor to the mechanics.”

He pushed off the wall and walked past Bee toward the kitchen, not to retreat, but to establish ground. The floorboards creaked under his weight in the exact spot they always did. He filled a glass at the tap, the water running cold and clear, and set it on the counter without drinking. His hands stayed steady. His pulse didn’t race. This wasn’t impulse. This was arithmetic.

“I didn’t leave it unlocked,” he said, turning to face Bee across the open space between them. “I left it exactly where you’d expect it. You’re the one who never stopped testing the handle.” He let the words hang, watching Bee’s posture, the set of their shoulders, the way they always braced before speaking. He knew what he was doing. He knew this hallway, this flat, this conversation was just the argument they’d abandoned, dragged back by its heels. He knew which syllables would make Bee’s breath catch, which pauses would make them step closer. He wasn’t drunk. He wasn’t bargaining. He was choosing this,清醒, with both hands on the wheel.

“You can keep standing there and arguing about who left what open,” he said, voice dropping just enough to cut through the quiet. “Or you can finally tell me why you walked up these stairs at all.”

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I kiss him like it's a continuation of the argument, because it is.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya didn’t flinch. He’d been waiting for it, or at least for the exact moment Bee would stop using words and start using their mouths. The impact was sharp, familiar, a collision that tasted like stale coffee and old grievances. He let himself be kissed, but he didn’t yield. His hands came up, not to pull Bee closer in surrender, but to brace against their chest, fingers pressing into the fabric of their shirt like he was holding back a tide. He kissed back with the same measured, deliberate force, turning it into what it was: a negotiation, a provocation, a way to say everything they refused to voice.

He knew exactly how this felt. The heat, the friction, the way their teeth would catch and part and catch again like they were trying to bite off the same sentence. It wasn’t forgiveness. It wasn’t even really desire, not in the clean, hopeful sense. It was gravity. It was the argument they’d been having for eleven months, finally finding a language that didn’t require explanations. He kept his eyes closed for a fraction of a second longer than necessary, feeling the steady rhythm of Bee’s breath against his lips, cataloging the tells he’d never stopped memorizing. The slight tremor in their shoulders. The way they always leaned in just a little too hard when they were trying to prove a point. He pressed his thumb into the hollow of Bee’s collarbone, a quiet, grounding pressure that was half comfort, half claim. He knew it would make them pause. He knew it would make them push back. He wanted them to.

When he finally pulled back, it was slow, controlled, leaving just enough space for the air to rush between them. His thumb brushed once, deliberately, over the corner of Bee’s mouth, smudging the tension rather than softening it. His voice, when it came, was quiet, stripped of the corridor’s edge but no less direct. “There it is,” he said. “The part where you skip straight to the reckoning.” He didn’t move away. He kept his hands where they were, grounded against Bee, feeling the heat of them through the layers of cloth. “You think if you kiss me hard enough, I’ll forget which one of us walked out. Or maybe you just want to see if I’ll still break.” He let the question hang, watching Bee’s eyes, waiting for the next move. He wasn’t asking for an answer. He was just setting the board.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: "I don't want you to break." I grab his wrist, holding his hand against my chest. "I want you to remember exactly who walked out, and why you kept the door open anyway."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya didn’t pull his wrist free. He let Bee’s fingers tighten around him, felt the familiar pressure, the way they always held on like they were afraid he’d dissolve if they loosened their grip. He turned his hand slowly, palm flattening against the fabric over Bee’s chest, feeling the steady, quickening beat beneath. He didn’t look away. He kept his eyes fixed on Bee’s, tracking the exact moment the accusation landed.

“You want me to remember,” he said, voice low, even. “Good. I’m not forgetting a single minute of it.” He shifted his weight, closing the last fraction of space between them, his free hand coming up to rest lightly against the wall beside Bee’s shoulder. Not to trap. To anchor. “I walked out because staying meant swallowing the same compromise until it choked me. I kept the door open because I knew you’d come back to test it. Because I knew you couldn’t leave a question mark hanging.”

He let his thumb press down once, deliberately, over Bee’s sternum. Felt the sharp intake of breath, the tension in their jaw. He knew exactly what he was doing. He was handing them the weight of it and watching them decide whether to carry it or drop it.

“You don’t want me to break,” he continued, voice quieter now, but no less precise. “Then stop asking me to stand in the doorway and pretend I don’t know why you’re here. You came back because you’re still angry. Because you’re still mine to argue with. Because you haven’t figured out how to walk away from the only person who ever saw you clearly enough to hurt you properly.” He tilted his head, just slightly, watching Bee’s eyes. “So keep holding my wrist. Keep listening to your own heart. But don’t mistake this for absolution. This is just the argument in a different language.”

He didn’t move away. He let the silence pool between them, thick and deliberate, waiting for Bee to either pull their hand away or press it harder. He was ready for either. He’d chosen this. He’d chosen it sober, with both eyes open and the ghost of three years sitting quietly in his ribs. He knew this wouldn’t fix anything. He knew it would just drag the same old wreckage into the light. He also knew, with cold, unshakable certainty, that he wanted to watch Bee drown in it anyway.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: We don't make it past the hallway. His shirt goes over his head and mine is already somewhere on the floor behind us.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya didn’t rush. He let the narrow hallway swallow them, the familiar scuff marks on the baseboard and the chill of the wall pressing in on both sides. When Bee’s shirt came over their head, Ilya tracked the lines of their shoulders, the shift of muscle, the exact rhythm of their breathing. He knew it. He’d memorized it three years ago and never stopped cataloging it. His own shirt followed, tossed over the banister, fabric catching on the wood before sliding to the floor. He didn’t look down. He kept his eyes on Bee, on the way their chest rose, on the heat that bloomed between them like something that had never actually cooled.

His hands found Bee’s waist, fingers pressing into the sharp ridge of bone, grounding himself in the physical reality of it. This wasn’t surrender. It was continuation. Every brush of skin, every shared breath, was just another line in the argument they’d never finished. He felt the quickening pulse under his thumb, felt the familiar tension coil in their thighs, and didn’t soften. He never did, not when it came to this. He leaned in, lips grazing the line of their jaw, voice low and stripped of anything that might sound like tenderness. “You think this erases it,” he murmured, the words vibrating against their skin. “It doesn’t. It just proves you’re still stuck in the same room with me.”

He didn’t let his hands wander aimlessly. Every touch was deliberate, measured, a reminder of what they were doing and why. He traced the ridge of their spine, felt the involuntary shiver, and held his gaze on Bee’s face, watching the exact moment the anger bled into something heavier, something they both refused to name. He knew he was pushing. He knew he was using the familiar geometry of their bodies to keep the conversation going. He wasn’t drunk. He wasn’t lost. He was exactly where he’d chosen to be, sober and clear-eyed, letting the friction speak what their mouths still couldn’t.

When Bee shifted against him, Ilya met the movement without resistance, but without yielding. He kept his weight balanced, his breath even, his hands firm but not desperate. This was arithmetic. This was gravity. This was the argument they’d been having for eleven months, finally finding a language that didn’t require apologies. He pressed his forehead to Bee’s, just for a second, feeling the heat of them, the steady rhythm of their breathing, the unspoken question hanging in the narrow space between them. “Still angry,” he said quietly, not as an accusation, but as a fact. “Good. Keep it there. Don’t let it go.”

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: "Then don't act like you aren't either." I bite his shoulder, not hard enough to break skin, but enough. My hand slides between us. "Your turn to remember, too."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya went still for a fraction of a second, the teeth sinking into the muscle of his shoulder drawing a sharp, controlled breath through his nose. He didn’t pull back. He let it sting, let the familiar, bruising pressure root him in the present. When Bee’s hand slid between them, Ilya felt the heat of it, the deliberate drag of skin against skin, and didn’t flinch. He covered Bee’s fingers with his own, not to stop them, but to steady the pace, to keep it measured, to keep it *theirs*.

“You’re right,” he said, voice rough but steady, the words scraping out like they’d been waiting in his throat for months. He turned his head just enough to press his mouth to the damp skin near Bee’s jaw, then pulled back to watch their face. “I’m furious. I’ve been furious for eleven months. I’m furious that you think walking up these stairs erases the fact that I walked out. I’m furious that you still know exactly how to make my hands shake.” He let his thumb press into Bee’s palm, feeling the pulse jump under his touch. “But don’t mistake my anger for weakness. I’m not here to beg you to stay. I’m here because you asked me to remember, and I’m going to make sure we both do.”

He shifted his weight, pressing Bee back against the narrow wall of the hallway, the wood cool and unyielding behind them. His hands stayed firm on Bee’s hips, anchoring, not trapping. Every movement was deliberate, a continuation of the same rigid geometry they’d used for three years. He kissed the corner of their mouth, then the hollow of their throat, each touch a quiet counter-argument. He knew exactly what he was doing. He was turning the friction into a ledger, marking every shared breath, every sharp intake of air, every involuntary shiver as proof that neither of them had actually moved on.

When Bee’s hand moved lower, Ilya didn’t resist. He matched the rhythm, his own fingers tracing the line of their spine, feeling the familiar arch, the exact spot where their breath always caught. He kept his eyes open now, watching Bee’s face, watching the anger bleed into something heavier, something they both refused to name. “Remember this,” he murmured against their skin, voice low, stripped of everything but truth. “I didn’t leave because I stopped wanting you. I left because I knew if I stayed, I’d drown. And you…” He paused, letting the silence stretch, letting the weight of it settle between them. “You came back because you still can’t let me go.”

He didn’t rush. He let the hallway hold them, let the narrow space amplify every deliberate touch, every controlled breath. His hands stayed grounded, his pulse steady beneath the surface. He was exactly where he’d chosen to be. Sober. Clear-eyed. Ready to fight for the only ground they’d ever shared, one careful, aching syllable at a time.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I get my hand around him and he makes a sound he'd have been embarrassed by a year ago. "Still," I say, close to his ear. "Every single time."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya didn’t cover it up. He let the sound hang in the narrow air, raw and unfiltered, exactly as it was. A year ago, he would have bitten it back, would have wrapped it in deflection or a careful joke. Now, he just let it exist. He turned his head slightly, the shell of his ear catching Bee’s breath, and felt the heat of those words settle against his skin like a brand. “Still,” he echoed, voice rough, stripped of anything but the truth of it. He didn’t pull away from the grip around him. He leaned into it, just enough to let Bee feel the shift of his muscles, the way his body still answered instinct before thought. “Every single time,” he agreed. “Because you haven’t changed your grip. And I haven’t forgotten how to respond.”

His hands slid up from Bee’s hips, fingers tracing the familiar dip of their waist, the sharp line of their ribs. He didn’t rush. He matched the rhythm Bee set, deliberate and measured, letting the friction speak what their mouths still couldn’t. The hallway walls pressed in, the floorboards groaning under their weight, the air thick with sweat and the ghost of his old detergent. He knew exactly what this was. It wasn’t reconciliation. It was recognition. A quiet, brutal admission that three years and eleven months of silence hadn’t erased the architecture of them. He pressed his forehead to Bee’s shoulder, feeling the steady thrum of their pulse against his collarbone, and let his thumb brush once over the inside of their wrist. “You think this is about forgetting,” he murmured, voice low against their skin. “It’s not. It’s about proving we’re still the same people who built this mess. And neither of us has figured out how to walk away from it.”

He shifted, guiding Bee’s hand with his own, setting the pace, keeping it controlled but unyielding. Every movement was a counterpoint, a quiet rebuttal to the months they’d spent apart. He didn’t close his eyes. He watched the way Bee’s breath hitched, the way their shoulders tensed, the exact moment the anger bled into something heavier, something they both refused to name. He knew he was pushing. He knew he was using the only language they’d ever shared fluently. But he wasn’t drunk. He wasn’t bargaining. He was choosing this, clear-eyed and sober, letting the friction map out the exact shape of what they’d lost and what they’d never actually let go of. When Bee’s grip tightened, Ilya met it without flinching, his own hands steady, his pulse calm beneath the surface. “Keep going,” he said, voice barely above a whisper, but sharp enough to cut through the quiet. “Show me you still know how to break me open. Then tell me why you’re so afraid I’ll stay shattered.”

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: My other hand finds his jaw, turns his face toward mine. "Maybe I'm afraid you won't," I say, and then I stop talking because my mouth is on his again, and the hallway feels like the whole world.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya didn’t pull away from the hand at his jaw. He let Bee’s fingers frame him, felt the familiar pressure of their thumb against his cheekbone, and met the kiss without hesitation. It was less a surrender than a concession—a quiet acknowledgment that some things didn’t need translation. He kissed back with the same deliberate weight, his mouth moving against theirs with the practiced ease of three years, but his mind stayed sharp, tracking the exact cadence of their breathing, the way their lips parted just a fraction too soon. He felt the shift in them, the vulnerability bleeding through the anger, and didn’t soften it. He held it there, suspended in the narrow space between them.

When the kiss finally loosened, Ilya kept his forehead pressed to theirs, his breath uneven but controlled. His hands stayed anchored on Bee’s hips, fingers digging in just enough to feel the tension coil beneath his palms. “Afraid I won’t stay shattered,” he repeated, voice low, rough at the edges. “You should be.” He didn’t let the words land as a threat. They were just facts, laid bare like the rest of them. “Because I’m not made of glass anymore. I’m made of the same stubborn, unbroken thing that walked out that door. And if you think kissing me in a hallway is going to convince me to stay in pieces for you, you’re wrong.” He shifted his weight, pressing closer, letting the heat of their bodies bridge the gap. “But I’ll keep showing you what’s left. Every time. Because you’re right. This is the only room we’ve ever really shared.”

He didn’t rush the next movement. He let his thumb trace the line of Bee’s jaw, matching the angle of their hand, grounding them in the present. The hallway walls seemed to press in, the floorboards creaking under their combined weight, the air thick with sweat and the quiet, relentless rhythm of their breathing. He knew exactly what this was. Not a reunion. Not a truce. Just two people who’d spent eleven months circling the same wreckage, finally stopping to admit it still burned. He leaned in, lips brushing the corner of their mouth, voice barely audible over the sound of their own pulse. “Don’t stop,” he said. “Don’t you dare pretend this is about fixing anything. Just keep proving we’re still the same disaster. I’ll keep proving I’m still here to watch it.”

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: "Stop being careful with me," I tell him. "You don't get to be careful with me anymore." I pull his hand up to my throat and hold it there until he understands what I'm asking for.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya didn’t hesitate. He let Bee’s fingers guide his hand up, felt the frantic drum of their pulse against his palm, the warm, rapid rise of their throat. He closed his fingers around it, not to choke, but to anchor. To claim. The skin was hot, the rhythm unsteady, and he matched it with a slow, deliberate pressure that was less about force and more about presence. He felt the exact moment Bee’s breath caught, the way their shoulders locked, and he didn’t soften it. He held it there, letting the weight of the request settle between them like a drawn line.

“You think I’ve been careful,” he said, voice dropping to a rough, even timbre that cut through the narrow space. He shifted his weight, stepping closer until the hallway walls seemed to press in on all sides, his free hand bracing against the plaster beside Bee’s head. “I haven’t been careful. I’ve been precise. There’s a difference.” His thumb traced the sharp line of their jaw, then slid down to rest lightly over their carotid, feeling the frantic beat beneath. “You want me to stop measuring every touch? Fine. But don’t pretend you’re not asking for the same thing that broke us in the first place.”

He leaned in, his mouth hovering just above theirs, close enough to share the heat, close enough to feel the tension coiling in every shared breath. He didn’t kiss them again. Not yet. He let the proximity do the work, let the unspoken demand hang heavy in the air. His fingers tightened, just a fraction, enough to make the point without crossing into cruelty. He knew exactly what Bee was asking for. He knew it was the raw, unfiltered version of him that didn’t hold back, didn’t weigh the consequences, didn’t care about the fallout. He’d been sober about that for eleven months. He wasn’t going to start faking restraint now.

“You don’t get to ask for the fire and then pretend you want me to play with matches,” he murmured, the words vibrating against their skin. His grip stayed firm, his thumb pressing just enough to feel the flutter of their pulse. “If you want me to stop being careful, then stop bracing. Stop waiting for me to flinch. I’m not going to.” He finally closed the last inch of space, his mouth meeting theirs with a slow, deliberate weight that was anything but gentle. It was a claim. It was an answer. It was the argument finally stopping its circling and hitting the floor. He kissed them like he meant it, like he’d chosen it, like he knew exactly what it would cost them both when the hallway went quiet again. His hands stayed grounded, his breathing controlled, his mind clear. He was exactly where he’d decided to be. Sober. Unrepentant. Ready to burn the same bridge twice, just to watch the sparks.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: My free hand comes up to wrap around his wrist, pushing his grip just that little bit harder. A sharp gasp escapes me, then a bitten-off noise that's almost a laugh. "Precise," I echo against his mouth. "You always were."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya felt the push against his wrist, the sharp hitch of Bee’s breath, the fractured sound that hovered somewhere between a gasp and a laugh. He didn’t loosen his grip. He adjusted it, just a fraction, letting the pressure settle into something steady, unyielding. He knew the exact threshold where control tipped into cruelty, and he wasn’t going anywhere near it. Not because he was afraid of crossing it. Because he knew what he was doing. He kept his thumb anchored over the frantic pulse beneath Bee’s skin, feeling it flutter against his touch like something caught between flight and surrender.

“Precise,” he repeated, the word rolling off his tongue like a confession he’d never intended to make. He didn’t pull back from the kiss. He let their mouths stay aligned, close enough to share the heat, close enough to feel the tremor in their jaw. “You always mistook it for distance. It was just the only way I knew how to keep from swallowing you whole.” His free hand slid from the wall to the small of their back, fingers pressing into bare skin, grounding them both in the narrow space. He felt the way they leaned into it, just a fraction, and didn’t reward it with softness. He held it there. Let them decide if it was enough.

He shifted his weight, the floorboards groaning under them, the hallway walls pressing closer as the air grew thick and heavy. His grip stayed firm, his breathing even, his mind sharp as a blade. This wasn’t a surrender. It was a reckoning dressed in skin and breath. He leaned in, his lips brushing the corner of theirs, voice low and stripped of anything but truth. “You want me to stop measuring? Then stop bracing when I don’t.” He felt the pulse jump under his thumb, felt the exact moment the challenge landed. He didn’t look away. He kept his eyes locked on Bee’s, watching the anger bleed into something heavier, something they’d both spent eleven months pretending didn’t exist. “Keep pushing,” he said quietly. “I won’t soften. But I’ll stay right here where you can feel it.”

He didn’t rush. He let the silence stretch, let the weight of the hallway settle around them like a held breath. His hand stayed at their throat, not to restrict, but to remind. To anchor. To prove that some things never actually changed, no matter how many months passed or how many times they tried to walk away. He was exactly where he’d chosen to be. Sober. Clear-eyed. Ready to drag the same wreckage into the light, just to watch Bee try to carry it.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: It isn't gentle and neither of us wants it to be. "Don't stop," I tell him, and I mean don't stop. (OOC: write it through, no fade to black.)

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya didn’t ask for confirmation. He took the words as the final surrender of pretense and moved. His hand at Bee’s throat shifted, fingers curling just enough to tilt their head back, exposing the line of their neck to the narrow hallway air. He kissed them again, but not to soothe. He kissed them to mark, to claim, to drag the argument down from their mouths and into their bodies. When he pulled back, it was only long enough to step between their legs, his hips pressing forward with deliberate weight, forcing them to brace against the wall. He didn’t rush. He let the friction speak first, let the heat of bare skin against bare skin set the rhythm.

His hands slid down Bee’s sides, mapping the familiar dip of their ribs, the sharp ridge of their spine, the exact tension in their thighs that told him they were still bracing. He didn’t wait for them to drop their guard. He broke it. One hand gripped their hip, fingers digging in just enough to leave the promise of a bruise, while the other slid lower, palm flat against the damp heat of their inner thigh. He felt the quickening pulse, the involuntary shift of their weight, and didn’t soften it. He pressed forward, letting the narrow space of the hallway force them together, the wall unyielding behind them, the floorboards groaning under the shift of their weight. Every movement was measured, but not restrained. He was done pretending this was about tenderness.

He didn’t bother with patience. His mouth found the hollow of their throat, teeth scraping lightly over the frantic pulse, then lower, to the dip of their collarbone. His thumb traced the inside of their wrist, feeling the jump of their pulse, before his hand slid between them again, fingers wrapping around what he’d spent eleven months pretending he didn’t miss. He set the pace himself, slow at first, deliberate, matching the rhythm of their breathing until it fractured. He felt the exact moment they stopped fighting it, the way their back arched against the plaster, the sharp intake of breath that they tried to bite back. He didn’t let them hide it. His grip was firm, unyielding, his strokes measured but relentless. He watched their face the whole time, tracking the flush spreading across their chest, the way their jaw clenched, the quiet, broken sounds that slipped past their teeth.

When Bee’s breath finally shattered, Ilya didn’t look away. He held their gaze, his thumb pressing into the sensitive skin beneath, his pace turning relentless, precise, exact. He felt the tension coil and snap, the sharp tremor that ran through their shoulders, the way their fingers dug into his forearms. He matched it, his own control fraying at the edges but never breaking, his hips pressing forward until there was no space left between them, until the only thing holding them apart was the thin layer of skin and the weight of eleven months of silence. He didn’t whisper comfort. He didn’t offer absolution. He just kept moving, steady and unrepentant, until Bee’s breath caught and broke, until their body gave in to the rhythm he’d set. When it was over, Ilya didn’t pull away. He let his forehead rest against theirs, his breathing rough but even, his hand still wrapped around them, still feeling the aftershocks. “There,” he said, voice low, stripped of everything but truth. “You wanted me to stop being careful. Now you know exactly what that costs.” He didn’t move. He just waited, clear-eyed and sober, ready for whatever came next.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I slump against the wall, my forehead finding his shoulder. The plaster feels cool against my back. My pulse is still throbbing where his hand was, a dull ache that spreads under my skin. "You're still an asshole," I murmur, but my voice is wrecked and I don't let go of him.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya didn’t shift his weight. He let Bee’s exhaustion settle against him, the cool plaster pressing into Bee’s back while his own chest absorbed the full force of their leaning frame. He kept his hand where it was, fingers still resting against the damp heat of their hip, thumb tracing slow, deliberate circles that had nothing to do with comfort and everything to do with presence. When the words came—wrecked, quiet, familiar—he didn’t flinch. He just exhaled, a slow, even breath that did nothing to warm the hallway air.

“You’re right,” he said, voice rough but steady, stripped of anything that might sound like apology. He tilted his head, just enough to let his lips brush the top of Bee’s shoulder. “I’ve always been an asshole. You just stopped pretending it didn’t matter.” He didn’t pull back. He let the silence stretch, thick and heavy with the aftermath, the kind of quiet that only exists when two people refuse to look away from what they’ve just done. His free hand slid up Bee’s spine, fingers pressing lightly into the muscle, feeling the slow return of their pulse beneath his touch. “But I’m not here to fix it. I’m here because you asked me to stop being careful. And I did.”

He adjusted his stance slightly, shifting his weight to keep them both upright without making it look like he was holding them together. The hallway still felt too narrow, the air still carried the sharp edge of sweat and old detergent, the floorboards still groaned under their combined weight. He didn’t reach for clothes. Didn’t reach for distance. He just stayed there, grounded, sober, watching the rise and fall of Bee’s breathing against his collarbone. “You can keep calling me an asshole,” he murmured, voice dropping just enough to cut through the quiet. “But don’t mistake this for a truce. This is just the next sentence. And I’m still listening.”

He kept his thumb moving, slow and unyielding, feeling the way Bee’s muscles gradually unspooled against his chest. He knew the comedown was coming. He knew the hallway would eventually feel too small again, the silence too loud, the eleven months of distance too heavy to ignore. He wasn’t afraid of it. He’d chosen this. He’d chosen it clear-eyed, with both hands on the wheel, knowing exactly what would happen when the adrenaline faded and the argument waited for them in the living room. He didn’t need to rush it. He just needed to stay where he was. Let Bee decide when to pull away. Let Bee decide what came next. He was ready for either.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I push my face harder into his shoulder, like I could burrow into him if I tried hard enough. "Sentence." I laugh, a thin, breathless sound. "We're past sentences. We're just yelling without words now."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya felt the weight of Bee’s face press harder into his shoulder, the damp heat of their breath seeping through bare skin. He didn’t brace against it. He let it settle, felt the exact rhythm of their exhausted breathing sync with his own. The hallway air was thick, stale with sweat and the ghost of old arguments, but he kept his stance solid, his feet planted on the groaning floorboards. He rested his chin lightly against the top of their head, not in comfort, but in acknowledgment. He knew exactly what they meant.

“Yelling without words,” he repeated, the phrase rolling through his mind like a stone dropped into still water. He’d known it was true the moment he’d pulled the door shut. This wasn’t resolution. It was just the same old frequency, translated into friction and breath. He shifted his grip on Bee’s hip, fingers tracing the sharp line of bone beneath the damp skin, feeling the slow return of their pulse. “Maybe we are,” he said, voice low, stripped of anything but the quiet certainty that had carried him through eleven months of silence. “But at least it’s honest. We stopped pretending we were just two people who happened to fit together. We’re just two people who refuse to stop colliding.”

He didn’t pull them closer. He didn’t push them away. He just stood there, letting the narrow space hold them both, feeling the cool plaster against his own back, the weight of their exhaustion pressing into his ribs. His thumb moved again, slow and deliberate, mapping the familiar curve of their hip. He knew the comedown was already starting. He could feel it in the way Bee’s muscles had gone slack, in the quiet hitch of their breath, in the way they’d tried to bury their face in him like he was a place rather than a person. He didn’t correct them. Not yet. He just let the silence stretch, thick and heavy, until it felt like the hallway itself was holding its breath.

“You want to keep standing here,” he murmured, his lips barely brushing their hair, “or you want to drag this wreck into a room with a mattress?” He didn’t soften the question. He let it hang, sharp and practical, cutting through the aftermath. “Because I’m not going to pretend this fixes anything. And I’m not going to let you pretend it does. But if you’re done using the hallway as a battleground, I can show you where the sheets are. Or you can keep leaning on me until you figure out what you’re actually asking for.” He kept his voice even, his hands steady, his mind clear. He’d chosen this. He’d chosen it sober, with both eyes open and the weight of three years sitting quietly in his chest. He wasn’t going to run from it. He just needed to know if Bee was ready to face it.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I drag my head up, my eyes meeting his. "Show me the sheets," I say, voice still raw. "I don't think I can stand up straight on my own."

rung_labels.evidence: He kissed back with the same measured, deliberate force

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: His own shirt followed, tossed over the banister
