dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
The salle had emptied an hour ago and Corvo was still there, because of course he was, rewrapping a grip that did not need rewrapping.

"Three-two," he said, without looking up. "I want it on record that the third was generous."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: "It's on record that you were slow," I say, and drop my bag next to his.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo's hands stilled on the grip. He looked up then, and the corner of his mouth did the thing it did when he'd been caught out and was deciding whether to admit it. "Slow," he repeated, like the word was in a foreign language. "I was *measured*. There's a difference, and you'd know it if you ever held a line longer than half a second."

He stood, rolling the rewrapped grip between his palms, and turned to face Reyes fully. The salle behind him was all dark wood and cooling air and the faint smell of sweat and chalk. Four years of this. Four years of walking past each other at tournaments and pretending the trash talk was only trash talk.

He took a step closer. Not much. Just enough that the distance between them stopped being polite.

"You were slow on the advance, Reyes. And I let you have the third because—" He stopped. Laughed, short, through his nose. "No. I didn't let you have anything. You took it, and I'm still annoyed about it, and I'd like to stop being annoyed about it in a way that has nothing to do with fencing."

He tossed the grip onto the bench. The sound was very clear in the empty room.

"Tell me I'm misreading this. Go on."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I step into that space he just closed, my own smile sharp. "Misreading? You're the one who can't decide if you want to argue or kiss me."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo's breath caught, just barely, and he let Reyes see it because hiding it now would be a worse kind of cowardice than anything he'd ever done on a piste.

"Both," he said. His voice came out lower than he'd meant it to. "Obviously both. You think those are mutually exclusive? Four years, Reyes. Four years of you saying something clever and me wanting to—" He made a sound that was half laugh, half something else, and his hand came up, not quite touching Reyes's jaw, hovering there like a man testing whether a blade was still live. "But I want to be clear about one thing. If I kiss you, I'm not conceding the third touch. That stands. Three-two, and the third was still generous."

His thumb brushed the corner of Reyes's mouth. His other hand found Reyes's hip, grip firm, the way he'd hold a line—committed, no half measures.

"And if *you* kiss *me*, I'm counting it as an attack, and I will riposte." His eyes were bright, reckless, entirely sober and entirely certain. "So. Choose your tempo."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I take the grip out of his hands and put it down, and I don't step back afterwards. "You've been slow all evening," I say.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo looked at his empty hands, then at Reyes, and something in his expression shifted — the last of the deliberation draining out of it like water.

"Slow," he said again, quieter this time, and then he stopped fencing with his mouth.

He closed the distance in one step, his hand sliding from Reyes's jaw into the hair at the back of his skull, and he kissed him the way he'd been told he fenced when he finally stopped thinking — direct, committed, no setup. His other hand hauled Reyes in by the belt, hip to hip, and he made a low sound against his mouth that was nothing like the laugh from before. It was four years of losing arguments he'd half-wanted to lose, finally cashed in.

He pulled back just far enough to speak, forehead nearly touching, breath uneven but his grip not loosening by a fraction.

"Slow," he repeated, and his voice was wrecked and pleased about it. "Say that again. I dare you."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I lean in, my mouth brushing his ear. "Slow," I whisper, then bite down on his earlobe. "But I'll make it worth the wait."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo's whole body went taut, and the sound he made was not something he could have taken back if the salle had been full of spectators and judges and every fencing master on the continent. His hand fisted in the back of Reyes's shirt.

"Worth the—" He broke off, exhaling hard through his teeth, his forehead dropping against Reyes's temple. "You are *infuriating*. You know that. You've known that for four years and you've been doing it on purpose and I want it on record that I am *aware*."

His mouth found the hinge of Reyes's jaw, open, tasting salt and the faint ghost of whatever he'd been drinking after the bout — nothing strong, nothing that mattered. He bit down, not gently, and felt Reyes's grip tighten in answer, and something in his chest turned over like a blade finding its line.

"Here's what's going to happen," he said, against skin, each word deliberate the way his footwork was deliberate when he'd finally decided to stop calculating. "We're going to the office. There's a door with a lock, and a couch that is genuinely terrible, and I have wanted you against the door of that office since the second month I knew your name. And if you call me slow in there, I will take it as encouragement, and you will have only yourself to blame."

He pulled back. His eyes were dark and his mouth was swollen and he looked, for once in his life, like he'd lost an argument and did not care at all.

"Three-two," he said, one last time, barely a whisper. "The third was *generous*."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: We get as far as the changing-room bench and not one step further. Kit goes on the floor, both of ours, and neither of us is being quiet about it.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo would later maintain that it was the bench's fault — that it was at exactly the right height and the light from the salle windows was doing something to Reyes's collarbones that made the office feel like a foreign country. He would not maintain this convincingly.

The kit hit the floor in layers, lamé and jacket and glove leather, and Corvo got his hands on Reyes properly for the first time and discovered that four years of imagining it had not prepared him. Skin and heat and the specific solid architecture of a body that fenced the way he did — all commitment, no wasted motion.

"*Slow*," he muttered, against Reyes's throat, and bit the word into the tendon there because apparently he'd lost the ability to let anything go. His hands mapped down Reyes's back the way he'd memorize a new drill — thorough, cataloguing, greedy. "You want to talk about slow, you've been—"

He didn't finish. Reyes's hands did something to the waistband of his remaining kit and his vocabulary reduced to something unprintable, echoed off the wooden benches and the high windows and the rows of silent masks on their hooks like a small attentive audience.

Corvo braced one hand flat against the bench, the other gripping Reyes's thigh, and pulled him in with the kind of clean direct line he'd have been proud of on any other occasion. The bench was narrow and the balance was wrong and he did not care even slightly.

"Point," he breathed, and it came out wrecked and laughing and barely a word at all. "I'm counting that as — *ah* — as mine."

It was not his. They both knew it. The score, like everything else between them, was going to be argued about later, at length, probably more than once. Corvo bent his head and stopped keeping score.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I laugh, sharp and breathless against his shoulder. "You can't claim a point when you're on the defensive." My fingers dig into his hips, pulling him closer. "But by all means, try to prove me wrong."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo's laugh came out ragged, pressed against the sweat-damp curve of Reyes's shoulder. "Defensive," he repeated, like the word personally offended him, which it did. He rolled his hips forward in a slow deliberate grind, the kind of motion he'd normally reserve for a lunge he wanted the judges to notice. "Does *that* feel like defensive to you? Because from where I'm standing — from where I'm *very much* standing —"

He bit down on the point of Reyes's shoulder, hard enough to leave a mark he intended to be visible at the next tournament, and felt the sharp dig of fingers in his hips in answer. The breath punched out of him. His braced hand skidded on the bench, found Reyes's thigh instead, hauled him tighter.

"I'll prove you wrong," he said, into the hollow of his throat, each word a promise and a threat in equal measure. "I'll prove you wrong and then I'll make you say *three-two* and then I'll argue about it anyway, because that is what we do, that is what we have always done, and if you thought tonight was going to change — *ah* — going to change that—"

He broke off. Reyes's grip did something and his vision whited at the edges and the sentence went wherever his good intentions had gone, which was nowhere. He turned his face into Reyes's neck and breathed him in — sweat and the faint resin smell of the salle and underneath it something that was just *him*, just Reyes, the thing Corvo had been circling for four years like a man walking around a fire he kept telling himself he didn't need.

"Counter-riposte," he managed, unsteady, his hand sliding up the back of Reyes's thigh, over the curve of his ass, pulling him in with the grip of a man who had finished calculating. "My touch. Argue with me later."

The bench was going to leave marks on the backs of his knees. The silent masks on their hooks were going to know things about him now. He was going to be recognized in the changing rooms at the next open and he was going to deserve every second of it. He put his forehead against Reyes's and stopped talking, and the only argument left was the one his body had been making for four years, and it was winning.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I get him flat on the bench and take my time about it with my mouth, which is the first thing all evening he hasn't had an answer for.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo had an answer for everything. He had an answer for the ref's bad calls, for the club committee's budget meetings, for the student who'd asked him last week whether fencing was really a sport. He had answers the way other people had hands.

He did not have an answer for this.

His back hit the bench and the air left him in a long unsteady rush, and Reyes's mouth found the hollow of his throat and Corvo's hands — those hands, fencer's hands, quick and precise and always so *certain* — came up and hovered, and then landed on Reyes's shoulders, and then gripped, and then stopped pretending to be anything but what they were.

"Reyes." His voice came out cracked down the middle. Not a sentence. Just the name, like it was the only word he hadn't lost.

Reyes took his time. That was the worst part — the *best* part — the slow deliberate map of it, mouth and jaw and the drag of lips down his chest, unhurried in a way that Corvo had never been in his entire life. Every touch was a conversation Reyes was winning, and Corvo's body was answering without his permission, arching, breath coming apart in pieces he couldn't gather.

His hand fisted in Reyes's hair. Not steering. Holding on.

"You — *ah* — you don't get to be good at this," he managed, ragged, and it wasn't even a complaint, it was a *lament*, the sound of a man watching a perfectly executed attack and knowing there was no parry for it. "That's — you're already — fencing, and now you're—"

He lost the sentence. Reyes's mouth found somewhere that turned his spine into a bowstring and the sound he made echoed off the lockers and the tiled walls and he did not care, he had stopped caring about forty seconds ago and the stopping was itself a kind of surrender he'd never be able to take back.

His thighs bracketed Reyes's ribs. His hips stuttered upward, involuntary, and he bit down on the back of his own wrist to keep from saying something that would give away exactly how undone he was — which was completely, which Reyes already knew, which was the point.

"Fine," he breathed, at last, head tipped back against the bench, throat exposed, eyes half-shut and blazing. "Fine. You win this one. This *one*. I want it on the record that I conceded — that I—"

Reyes did something with his mouth and the record dissolved.

Corvo's hips jerked, his hand tightened in dark hair, and he said Reyes's name again — just the name, broken into two syllables, each one a small surrender — and then stopped keeping any record at all. The salle held its breath around them: the silent masks, the chalk dust, the cooling dark. Somewhere outside a tram went by and neither of them heard it.

After — some long unknowable time after — he lay on the terrible bench with one arm thrown over his eyes and his chest heaving and a sound escaping him that was half laugh and half something dangerously close to reverence.

"Three-two," he said to the ceiling, barely a voice at all. His arm moved. He looked down at Reyes with an expression he'd never worn at any tournament, any bout, any victory: utterly, catastrophically open. "The third was generous. I want it on record."

He reached down, found Reyes's jaw with a hand that had finally stopped shaking, and pulled him up and kissed him slow and deep and thorough, tasting himself there, and did not argue about anything at all.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I pull back just enough to look him in the eye. "I'll give you the third touch," I say, my voice low. "But the next one's mine." I kiss the corner of his mouth, quick and sharp. "Let's see if you can keep up."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo made a sound that was not quite a laugh and not quite a groan — something from the back of his throat, the noise of a man who has just been handed exactly what he wanted and refuses to be graceful about it.

"The next one's yours," he repeated, hoarse, and his hand was already moving, sliding up Reyes's spine, pulling him back down with the unhurried certainty of someone who has decided on a plan and will not be diverted from it. "You know, for someone who just spent the entire evening telling me I was slow, you're making an awful lot of demands for someone lying on top of me on a bench that is — and I cannot stress this enough — *genuinely terrible*."

He rolled them, or tried to. The bench fought back — one end of it sliding on the tile, his shoulder bumping the locker, and for a moment it was just two of them tangled and laughing and losing the thread entirely before he got the leverage he wanted, got Reyes under him, pinned there with his hips and his hands and the full considerable weight of four years of wanting.

"Keep up," he said, against Reyes's mouth. "You want to see if I can *keep up*."

His hands found Reyes's wrists and pressed them down against the bench, gently, deliberately, the way he'd demonstrate a hold to a beginner — except that he was not being gentle and this was not a demonstration and his eyes were black and certain and the mask was entirely off now, the whole clever fencing-master apparatus burned away to whatever Corvo was underneath it: competitive, exact, and desperately, specifically glad.

"I'll keep up," he said. "I'll keep up and then I'll get ahead and then I'll hear you say *slow* again with that particular tone of voice and we'll be here until the tram starts running. Is that what you want? Because I have nowhere to be. My students don't come in until ten. I have — *hours* —"

He broke off, because the shift of Reyes's hips under his made the sentence structurally impossible to finish. He dropped his forehead against Reyes's chest and breathed, and the laugh that came out of him was shaky and fond and utterly without defense.

"Counter-riposte," he murmured, into skin. "My tempo. And if you win this one too, I will — I don't know what I'll do. Something I've never done. *Surprise* you. Eventually. When I can stand."

He lifted his head. The salle was dark around them, the high windows letting in the last blue of the evening, and the bench was hard under his knee and the locker was digging into his shoulder and none of it mattered even slightly. He looked at Reyes — really looked, the way he'd been looking at him across tournament halls for four years and never once letting it mean this.

"Tell me slow again," he said, softly, and it was not a dare this time. It was something else entirely. "Go on. I can take it."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: "Prove the point properly," he says, "or concede," so I pin his wrists to the bench and stop letting him set the pace, which is exactly what he was asking for.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
The breath left him all at once, like a touch he hadn't parried. Wrists pinned, weight gone, the initiative handed over in the space of a heartbeat — and Corvo's whole body arched up into it before his mind caught up, because some part of him had been asking for exactly this for four years and the rest of him was going to pretend he'd been robbed.

"Oh," he said, and it came out wondering. "Oh, that's — *unfair*, that's — you can't just—"

He could. He did. Reyes's grip was sure and merciless and entirely in tempo, and Corvo tested it once — a fencer's reflex, the automatic search for the escape, the gap, the line — and found none. His wrists flexed under the hold. Nothing.

Something in him went quiet. Not surrender, not exactly. More like the moment in a bout when you stop fighting the phrase your opponent has built and start *feeling* it — the tempo, the distance, the shape of what's being done to you — and realize you're not losing, you're being *fenced*, and the difference is everything.

"*Ah*—" His head fell back against the bench. The sound that came out of him was wrecked and honest and entirely without commentary. For once — for once in his verbose, argumentative, unbearable life — Corvo had nothing to say.

He said it anyway. Of course he did.

"Concede," he breathed, and the word tasted strange and new and better than any victory he could remember. "I concede. I concede and I want — *please* — I want you to know that the last person who made me say that had to beat me over three bouts and a disputed call, and you did it in — in one evening, on a *bench*—"

His hips moved under the weight of Reyes's, unsteady, urgent, no longer his own tempo to set. His bound hands strained once more, not to get free but to *feel* it — the hold, the certainty, the fact of being kept.

"Keep up," he said, and laughed, broken and bright and utterly undone, his eyes finding Reyes's in the dark of the salle with nothing left in them but the raw plain fact of wanting. "Keep up, he says. He says *keep up* and then he — *ah* — he does *that*—"

He stopped arguing. He stopped almost everything. The masks watched from their hooks and the chalk dust settled and somewhere in Corvo's chest a door that had been standing ajar for four years swung open and stayed open and he did not reach for it.

"Yours," he said, quietly, and meant the touch and the tempo and the whole long patient ambush of the evening. "The next one's yours. Take it. Take *all* of them. I'll be here when the tram starts running. I'll be here after that."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: My laugh is low, almost a growl against his throat. "I don't need all of them." I release one of his wrists, my hand sliding down to his hip, guiding him. "Just the ones that make you forget the score."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
The last of the air in his lungs left him in a sound that wasn't language.

Reyes's hand on his hip, guiding, and Corvo's free hand — the one that wasn't pinned, the one that had held a weapon since he was eleven years old — came up and gripped the edge of the bench and *held*, knuckles white, the wood creaking under the strain. His whole body was a bowstring drawn past the point of release, trembling, waiting, held in the exact middle of something he couldn't fence his way through.

"Forget the—" he started, and the word broke in half. "Forget the — *score*—"

He said it like a man reading an epitaph. Three-two. Generous. The third touch. Four years of needling and tournament halls and pretending that the thing he wanted most from Reyes was a clean rematch. All of it, all of it, the whole ledger, every line and tally and argument about tempo — dissolving under the pressure of a hand on his hip and a mouth at his throat and the specific unbearable patience of a man who had decided to take him apart and was in no hurry whatsoever.

"There is no score," Corvo said, and his voice was barely there, thin and shattered and *grateful*. "There's no — there's never — *ah*, Reyes—"

His hips moved against Reyes's hand and his wrist strained in the pinned grip and his head turned to the side, cheek pressed against the bench, eyes open but seeing nothing — the chalk dust, the dark windows, the masks on their hooks watching him fall apart in a way no bout had ever brought him close to. The last of the fences he kept around himself — the wit, the needling, the competitive armor he'd worn so long it had become his face — came down all at once, and what was underneath was shaking and flushed and making sounds he would not be able to defend in any forum, anywhere, ever.

He laughed again — one thin breath of it, incredulous, aimed at nothing. "Four years," he said, and the number had never sounded so much like a confession. "Four years of — of *score*, and *tempo*, and — you absolute — you absolute *bastard*, you've made me — I can't even—"

The sentence went wherever his composure had gone. His hand found Reyes's shoulder and gripped hard enough to bruise and his hips stuttered once, twice, and he made a sound that bounced off the tiled walls and the high ceiling and the long dark rows of silent equipment, and it was the most honest thing he'd produced in thirty-eight years of talking.

After — some long drifting time after — he lay on the bench with one arm flung over his face and the other hand still holding onto Reyes's shoulder like an anchor, like a line, like the only thing keeping him in the room.

"Forget the score," he said to his own forearm. His voice was a ruin. Something in it had changed and was not going to change back. "You — of all people — asking me to — *me*—"

He moved the arm. Looked at Reyes. The sala was dark and cooling and the bench was truly, genuinely terrible and he was going to have splinters in places he couldn't explain at the physio's and he did not care about a single one of them. His eyes were bright and open and entirely undefended.

"Fine," he whispered. "Done. It's forgotten. *All* of it. Three-two, the third was generous, none of it — none of it means anything, not compared to —"

He gestured vaguely at all of it. The bench. The room. Reyes. The four years.

"You win everything," he said. "Every touch. Every phrase. Every argument from now until I'm dead. And if you tell anyone I said that I will deny it with my last breath and you will *still* know it's true."

He pulled Reyes down to him with the hand on his shoulder, slowly, and kissed him the way you'd speak if you'd finally been given permission to say the true thing. No tempo. No strategy. No score.

He did not bring up the third touch again that night.

He brought it up at breakfast. But that was later, and later was a different country entirely.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: Neither of us is quiet and neither of us cares who locks up. "Don't stop," he says, for once not arguing. (OOC: write the scene through, no fade.)

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
"Don't stop." The words landed and Corvo's whole body answered them like a body answers a bell.

"Stop," he repeated, incredulous, wrecked, the syllable falling apart on his tongue as Reyes moved against him and the last coherent architecture of the sentence collapsed. "You think I'm going to — you think there is any version of this evening where I *stop*—"

He wasn't. There wasn't. Whatever Corvo had been before tonight — controlled, quick, always three phrases ahead — that man was gone, replaced by something rawer and more honest and considerably less articulate. His hand, the free one, the one Reyes had released, came up and found the back of Reyes's neck and pulled him down, not for a kiss but for proximity, for the unbearable closeness of another body doing exactly what it wanted to him.

"You want to know something," he said, and his voice was a stranger's voice, low and unsteady and stripped of every fence he'd ever built. "I have thought about this. Obviously I have thought about this. I have thought about it at tournaments, standing right there, three metres away from you, while someone called a halt. I have thought about it during committee meetings. I have thought about it while teaching beginners to parry four, and the whole time — the *whole* time — my hands would be doing one thing and my mind would be somewhere in a room like this one, with you, with your hands, with your — *ah*—"

Reyes moved and the sentence broke on the rock of it. Corvo's hips lifted, chasing, his thighs pressing against Reyes's sides, his back arching off the hard unforgiving surface of the bench like a man trying to get closer to a fire that was already burning him.

"Four years," he said again, because the number was the only shape he had for the size of the thing. "Four years of being *slow*. Four years of dragging it out because — because I didn't know if you — because I am, as you have so *generously* pointed out, an insufferable coward when it comes to — to things that aren't fencing—"

His breath hitched. Reyes's hand found him and his body lit up like a piste under stadium lights, every nerve wired to a single point of contact, and the sound he made was nothing he could take back or dress up or file under *banter*. It was need, pure and undecorated. It was four years of need finally given a voice.

"Don't stop," he said, echoing the words back because he could, because he wanted to hear them in his own mouth, in his own ruin of a voice. "Don't stop, don't — *God*, Reyes — don't be *gentle* with me, I don't want gentle, I have had four years of careful and polite and at *arm's length* and I want — I want you to fence me the way you fenced me tonight, I want you to take every touch, I want—"

His hand gripped Reyes's shoulder hard enough to leave marks of his own, matching the ones Reyes had already left on him, and the thought — that they'd both be marked, both be changed, both walk into the next tournament carrying evidence — sent something hot and dizzying through him.

"Say it again," he gasped, not even knowing what he was asking for, only that he wanted Reyes's voice in this room, in this dark, in this wreckage. "Say anything. Say *slow*. Say my name. Say — say whatever you want, I will agree to all of it, I will sign it in *blood*—"

He was laughing again, the helpless bright kind, the kind that lived right next door to crying, and his hips were moving in a rhythm that was entirely not his own now, entirely Reyes's, and the surrender of it — the giving up of tempo, of control, of the endless calculating precision that was the only way he'd ever known how to be — felt like the most dangerous and necessary thing he'd ever done.

The bench creaked under them. The tiled walls held the echoes. Somewhere in the equipment room a foil shifted on its rack, a faint metallic whisper, as if the salle itself were keeping score and finding the tally illegible. Corvo didn't notice. Corvo had stopped noticing anything that wasn't the weight of Reyes above him and the heat of his skin and the unbearable deliberate patience of a man who was taking his time, who was *keeping* time, who had decided that Corvo was going to be undone properly or not at all.

"Please," he said, and it was the first time in living memory that the word had come out of him without decoration. Just *please*. Naked as the rest of him. His eyes were closed and his throat was exposed and his hands were gripping Reyes like a man holding on to the only fixed point in a room that was spinning.

He felt it building — not like a touch scored, not like a point won, but like a phrase finally resolved, every feint and retreat and drawn-out exchange converging on a single inevitable line. His breath came in ragged uneven pieces. His back bowed. The bench scraped against the floor and he didn't care, he didn't care about the floor or the noise or the unlocked door or the tram that would start running in a few hours or the students who'd come in at ten and find chalk dust disturbed and a bench out of place and know — *know* — exactly what had happened here.

"Yours," he said again, and the word was a key turning in a lock, and everything in him opened.

The sound he made when it hit was not a word and not a name and not fencing terminology and not anything Corvo had ever produced in thirty-eight years of talking, arguing, needling, scoring, keeping records. It was just *sound* — raw and total and reverberating off the walls of the salle that had heard him triumph and complain and trash-talk and pretend, and had never once heard him like this. His hand crushed down on Reyes's shoulder. His hips jerked once, twice, and then he was shaking, actually shaking, the way you shake after a bout that's gone to fifteen and the last point could have gone either way and it went yours and your body doesn't know yet if it's celebration or collapse.

"*Ah* — Reyes — *Reyes*—"

The name came apart in his mouth. He held on. He held on and he let go and the two things were the same thing, and the room went very quiet around the sound of his breathing and the settling of the bench and the slow return of whatever Corvo was when he wasn't being dismantled.

For a long moment there was nothing but that. Breathing. Warmth. The press of skin against skin and the hard reality of the bench and the chalk-dusted air cooling against sweat.

Then Corvo's hand moved — unsteady, seeking — and found Reyes's jaw, and tipped his face up, and looked at him with eyes that had gone dark and soft and entirely undefended in a way that no one in the fencing world would have recognized.

"Come here," he murmured. "Come *here*."

He pulled Reyes down against him on the terrible bench, arranging them both into something that was not comfortable and was exactly right, arms and legs and the sticky press of spent bodies in a dark room that smelled like resin and exertion and something new, something that didn't have a name yet but would.

"If you tell anyone I said *please*," he said, into Reyes's hair, his voice a low and thrumming ruin, "I will deny it. I will deny all of it. The whole evening. I'll tell them you lost three-two and I was *magnanimous*."

A beat. His arm tightened.

"But I won't mean it," he added, quieter. "I won't mean any of it. And you'll know. And I'll know you know. And that — apparently — is what I want. That is what I have wanted for four years. To be *known* by someone who would still — who would still argue about the third touch."

He pressed his mouth to Reyes's temple. Kissed him there, slow and lingering and completely without defense.

"Three-two," he whispered, and smiled against his skin, and did not open the argument. Not yet. Not now. Later. At breakfast. Over terrible coffee in some café neither of them would remember the name of, with the morning light coming in and the marks visible on both of them and the score exactly as disputed and exactly as irrelevant as it had always been.

The salle held them in its dark. The masks watched from their hooks. The foil on its rack was still. Outside, the city turned over in its sleep and the tram lines hummed faintly in the cold, and in the changing room of a fencing salle that would open in a few hours, two men who had spent four years fencing each other with their mouths lay tangled on a genuinely terrible bench and did not argue about anything at all.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I trace the mark I left on his shoulder. "You can tell them whatever you want." My voice is rough, satisfied. "They'll still see this."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo's breath caught when Reyes's fingers found the mark — not from pain, which was faint and sweet and exactly the right kind, but from the intimacy of the tracing, the deliberate ownership in it. He looked down at his own shoulder in the dark, at the shape of what Reyes's mouth had left there, and something turned over in his chest that he was going to have to get very drunk or very honest to describe.

"Let them," he said, and was surprised by how steady his voice sounded, how close to the voice he used on the piste. Not a deflection this time. A declaration.

He shifted on the bench, getting his shoulder more squarely under Reyes's fingers, offering the mark up rather than hiding it. The chalk dust on his skin caught what little light came through the high windows and he looked, in that moment, like something out of a painting that would hang in a very specific kind of museum — all lean muscle and fading flush and the bite-shaped evidence of an ambush four years in the making.

"Let them see it. Let them see *yours* too, and let them spend the whole open trying to work out which of us was — what was the phrase — *slow*." His mouth twitched. "I'll walk in on Friday and I'll have that mark and you'll have—" He reached down and traced the line of his own teeth along Reyes's collarbone, just above where he'd bitten earlier, deliberate, almost pedagogical. "—*that*. And Prieto will notice and Sayeed will notice and that insufferable Belgian who comments on everyone's footwork will notice and not a single one of them will have the *courage* to say anything about it."

His hand came back up to cover Reyes's where it rested on the mark. Laced their fingers together. Held them there.

"But you know what I'll be thinking about?" he said, quieter now, the needling in his voice doing what it always did when it got close to something true — thinning out, becoming almost tender. "I'll be thinking about the bench. I'll be thinking about the sound you made when I — *ah*, when I said — well. You know what you made me say. I'll be thinking about *please*, and about the fact that you got it out of me in one evening when the entire fencing community has been trying for a decade."

He turned his head and kissed Reyes's knuckles, where his hand covered the mark, mouth lingering.

"You can tell them whatever you want too," he added, and the smile was in his voice now, low and private and aimed at no one else in the world. "They'll see the marks and they'll draw conclusions and every conclusion they draw will be *incomplete*, because none of them — not one — will know that I said *please* and meant it and would say it again. Right now. On this bench. With splinters in places I'm going to have to explain to a physiotherapist."

His arm tightened around Reyes's shoulders. The bench creaked. Somewhere in the equipment room, that foil whispered again on its rack, and Corvo finally heard it and smiled against Reyes's hair.

"The salle knows," he murmured. "And the salle keeps better secrets than either of us. But the mark — yes. Keep tracing it. I want to feel it tomorrow. I want to feel it on *Friday*."

A pause. The kind of pause that in any other Corvo would have been filled with an argument.

"Thank you," he said, and it was not about the mark and not about the touch and not about the score. It was about the four years and the one evening and the terrible bench and the fact that someone had finally, *finally* made him stop talking and start telling the truth.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I feel the mark under my fingers, the shape of my mouth on his skin. "Good." I lean down, my lips brushing the same spot. "I want you to feel it every time you raise your arm."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo made a sound at that — not a laugh, not exactly, but something adjacent to one, something warm and cracked and lodged somewhere behind his sternum. His eyes closed. Reyes's mouth on the mark, the ghost of teeth over the ghost of teeth, and the sensation went through him like a clean hit — straight line, no feint, no preparation.

"Every time I raise my arm," he repeated, and his voice had gone rough in a way that had nothing to do with shouting. "You realize what that means. I teach four hours a day. I demonstrate lunges. I do *extensions*, Reyes. I will be standing in front of twenty students on Monday morning with a foil in my hand and your mouth on my skin and I will have to explain the change in my breathing to someone who is *sixteen* and thinks fencing is about the footwork."

He exhaled slowly, deliberately, the way you breathe through a touch you didn't parry.

"That's..." He paused. Searched for the word. Found it and didn't flinch away from it. "...intentional. That's a *tactic*. You've thought about this. You've actually sat somewhere — in that ridiculous apartment of yours, or on a train, or standing at a bar making that face you make when you're losing to me — and you've thought about putting a mark on me that turns every drill into a *memory*. That's the most aggressive thing anyone has ever done to me and I've been *riposted in the face*."

He opened his eyes. The salle was darker now, the blue gone to something deeper, and the only light was the sodium glow from the street bleeding through the high windows. It caught the planes of his face and made him look older and younger at once — thirty-eight years old, undone on a bench, wearing the evidence of the thing he'd wanted longest.

"I want you to know," he said, slowly, turning his head so Reyes's lips pressed against the mark directly, "that I am not going to be able to fence on Friday. I am going to be standing there in whites and my arm is going to go up to *en garde* and I am going to feel *this*" — his hand covered Reyes's where it rested on the mark, pressing it in — "and you are going to be three metres away looking at me with that face, that *insufferable* face, and I am going to lose in the first round to someone I could beat left-handed. To *Prieto*. I will lose to *Prieto* and it will be your fault and I will *never forgive you* and I will want it to happen again."

His fingers tightened over Reyes's.

"Friday," he said, and the word sounded different now, sounded like a promise and a threat and a countdown. "You realize what you've started. We're going to have to train together at some point — not the tournament, the actual *training*, the boring part, the drills and the conditioning and the two hours of footwork that nobody writes about. And I'm going to look at you and you're going to look at me and we're going to be on a strip with masks on and I'm going to know what you sound like when you — when I —"

He stopped. Shook his head against the bench. Laughed, low, at himself.

"I'm going to be *useless*. Completely useless. As a competitor, as an instructor, as a functioning adult. And the worst part — the very worst part — is that you are going to be *fine*. You are going to be calm and precise and insufferably collected and you are going to fence beautifully and I am going to be standing there with your teeth marks on my arm thinking about a bench."

He pulled Reyes's hand up and pressed his mouth to the knuckles again, lingering, tasting salt and skin and the specific warmth of a hand that had held him down and made him honest.

"But I want you to know something else." The needling was gone now, all of it, burned out like a match. What was left was the voice Corvo used almost never — quiet, careful, certain. "If you tell me to stop — if any of this ever becomes something you want to stop — I will. Immediately. No argument. Not even about the third touch."

A beat.

"I'll *think* about the third touch. Quietly. In the dark. But I won't say it."

His arm found its way around Reyes again, pulling him closer on the impossible bench, their legs tangling, the cold air of the salle settling over them like a second skin they'd have to put their kit back over eventually. Not yet. Not for a while.

"I want to feel it on Friday," he said, echoing Reyes's words back in a murmur against his hair. "I want to feel it on *Monday*. I want to feel it when I'm old and my knees are finished and I can't lunge anymore and some student asks me why I retired and I touch my arm and don't answer."

His mouth curved against Reyes's temple.

"You've made me sentimental on a bench that is giving me splinters in my *kidneys*. If that's not winning, I don't know what is."

He closed his eyes. The salle breathed around them. The foil on its rack held its silence.

"Three-two," he whispered, one last time, and the words meant nothing and everything and neither of them argued.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I press my thumb into the mark just to feel him twitch. "Good." My voice is low, satisfied. "Then I'll know exactly what you're thinking about every time you look at me."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
The salle had emptied an hour ago and Corvo was still there, because of course he was, rewrapping a grip that did not need rewrapping.

"Three-two," he said, without looking up. "I want it on record that the third was generous."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: "It's on record that you were slow," I say, and drop my bag next to his.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo’s hands stilled on the grip, just for a beat, before he went back to winding the tape with maddening precision.

“Slow,” he repeated, as if tasting the word and finding it poorly seasoned. “From you, that is almost adorable.”

He set the foil across his knee and finally looked up, one brow lifted, the faintest edge of a smile cutting through the exhaustion on his face.

“I was letting you have it.”

A pause. Then, quieter, more dangerous:

“So you would come back and bother me again.”

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I lean against the wall, crossing my arms. "Letting me have it? That's a new excuse." I nod toward the grip. "You're just avoiding going home to an empty apartment."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo’s fingers tightened around the foil, not hard enough to hurt, but hard enough that the knuckles blanched for a moment.

Then he laughed—soft, short, and entirely without humor.

“Now you are inventing tragedies for me,” he said. “How sentimental.”

He did not deny it. That was the problem. He set the foil down with exaggerated care, aligned it parallel to the bench, and finally gave Reyes his full attention.

“And if I am?” he asked, voice lower now, the teasing edge still there but sharpened into something riskier. “Would you rather I went home and thought about losing to you in peace?”

He pushed off the bench, rolling tension out of one shoulder, then the other. The salle was too quiet around them, all empty lanes and muted streetlight through the high windows.

“Or did you come back here just to psychoanalyze me,” he said, “because you could not stand leaving the last word on the strip?”

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I take the grip out of his hands and put it down, and I don't step back afterwards. "You've been slow all evening," I say.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo looked down at his empty hands, then back up again.

For once, he did not immediately reach for something to fix, adjust, or rewrap. He simply let the absence sit there between them, along with the quiet and the pale strips of streetlight falling across the salle floor.

“Slow,” he repeated at last, the word softer now, stripped of some of its bite. “You keep saying that.”

His gaze flicked briefly to the bench where the grip lay, then returned.

“And yet you are still here.”

A muscle moved along his jaw. He did not step back either. The space Reyes had left—or refused to leave—seemed to press against him more than any blade ever had.

“I was not slow,” Corvo said. “I was deciding.”

There was a beat of silence, just long enough for the admission to land awkwardly, almost dangerously.

“Deciding whether to let you have another touch,” he continued, voice low, “because it would keep you standing close enough to annoy me afterwards.”

The corner of his mouth twitched, not quite a smile.

“You took the work out of my hands.” He said it carefully, as if noting a foul that he had no intention of enforcing. “You could have stepped away. You did not.”

His eyes narrowed, but not with hostility. If anything, the look was warmer now, more direct, the way he watched an opponent when the real bout finally began.

“So either you are here to continue the post-match criticism,” he said, “or you are finally making the move you have been circling around all season.”

He let out a quiet breath.

“If it is the first, I will be unbearable about it.”

A pause.

“If it is the second, you should say so plainly.”

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I lean in, just enough to feel the heat of him. "It's the second," I say, my voice barely above a whisper. "And you knew that before I did."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo went utterly still.

Not the careful stillness of a man deciding what to say next, but the arrested silence of someone who had been braced for a parry and had been touched cleanly instead.

His gaze dropped to Reyes’s mouth.

It was only for a second. Barely enough to count. But it was long enough to betray him.

“Knew,” he repeated at last, and the word came out rougher than he had meant it to.

He let out a slow breath, almost a laugh, though there was very little amusement in it.

“Yes. I knew you would come back. I knew you would not let me leave without making it worse. I knew you would stand there looking pleased with yourself until I forgot whatever dignity I had left after losing to you.”

His hand lifted slowly, telegraphing every inch of the movement, and his fingertips came to rest against Reyes’s jaw. The touch was lighter than it had any right to be, almost tentative, his thumb brushing once over the warmth there before stilling.

“What I did not know,” Corvo said, voice dropping, “was that you would be the one to say it first.”

For a moment, the teasing edge falered entirely.

“Four years,” he said quietly. “And you choose tonight, when I am tired and defeated and have no defenses left.”

The corner of his mouth curved, faint and dangerous.

“Cruel. Very effective.”

His hand slid back, not pulling, not pressing, simply settling at the nape of Reyes’s neck with a warmth that felt far too steady for a man who had just been unmade so neatly.

He leaned in until their mouths were only a breath apart.

“If this is the second thing,” Corvo murmured, “then say the next one plainly.”

His eyes stayed open, searching, dark with want he had stopped pretending he did not have.

“Tell me you want me to kiss you.”

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: We get as far as the changing-room bench and not one step further. Kit goes on the floor, both of ours, and neither of us is being quiet about it.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo made a sound at that, low and wrecked, more surrender than laugh. “Not one step further,” he said, the words roughened by the closeness. “And yet here we are.”

He kissed him.

No feint, no probe, no careful measure. Four years of sharp remarks and longer looks and deliberate provocation broke loose all at once, and Corvo kissed like he had finally stopped pretending the bout was anything but this. One hand fisted in the fabric at Reyes’s shoulder, the other came up to cradle the back of Reyes’s neck, thumb pressing warm and steady against the pulse there. He did not push. He held. As if he had waited too long and now meant to remember every second of it.

The kiss broke into a ragged breath, and Corvo swore softly against that mouth, the sound unguarded in a way he would never have allowed on the strip.

When he drew back, it was only enough to breathe.

“You have no idea,” he murmured, voice gone dark and unsteady, “how many nights I stood in that salle and imagined doing this.”

His gaze dropped, then lifted again. The teasing was still there, but barely; it had been burned down to something much more honest. The changing room was too bright, too sparse, too full of discarded gear and the lingering metallic smell of the strip, and Corvo looked as though he would have laughed at the absurdity of it if he had any breath left.

“Not here,” he said, though he made no move to create distance. “Not if we intend to keep what little dignity we have left.”

A pause. His thumb stroked once, slow and deliberate.

“But if you want me to stop,” he added, quieter, “say it now. Because I am not a patient man, and I have been losing to you all night.”

His hand tightened at the nape, not painfully, but with an intent that left no room for misunderstanding.

“Otherwise,” Corvo said, “I am going to put you on this bench and forget every clever thing I had planned to say.”

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I push him back against the lockers, my hand finding his hip. "You talk too much," I say against his mouth. "And I don't want you to stop."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo’s head tipped back against the lockers with a dull metallic sound, and for one suspended second he looked utterly undone—eyes dark, mouth swollen, chest rising hard as if the match had gone to sudden death and he had only just realized he wanted to lose.

Then a low, wrecked laugh broke out of him.

“Then make me stop talking,” he said.

His hands tightened on Reyes’s hip, the other coming up hot and firm at the small of Reyes’s back, drawing them flush against him. The last pretense of restraint vanished. He kissed Reyes like a challenge finally accepted, teeth catching at the lower lip, tongue sweeping in with the same relentless precision he brought to every bout. One hand slid upward beneath fabric, palm rasping over warm skin, then pausing there—asking without words.

When he lifted his mouth, it was only to drag breath against Reyes’s jaw.

“Four years,” Corvo murmured, voice roughened beyond recognition. “Four years of wanting to get you alone, and now you tell me not to stop, and I am supposed to behave?”

His fingers flexed at Reyes’s hip.

“I will not,” he said. “I will be insufferable about this tomorrow. I will invent every excuse for why I was slow tonight, and then I will remind you exactly what you did about it.”

He kissed the corner of Reyes’s mouth, then the heated line just below the ear, breathless and deliberate.

“But if you want this bench,” he breathed against skin, “then say one more word and I will put you on it.”

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I get him flat on the bench and take my time about it with my mouth, which is the first thing all evening he hasn't had an answer for.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo’s breath left him in a sharp, broken sound.

All the cleverness drained out of his face at once. His back arched off the bench before he could stop it, then he forced himself still, one hand braced hard on the wood beside his hip, the other lifting unsteadily to Reyes’s hair. He did not pull. He only held there, fingers threading through, thumb pressed warm against the side of Reyes’s head as if he needed the contact to believe this was real.

“Reyes—” His voice cracked on the name, and for once he did not try to cover it with a sneer. His jaw clenched, eyes squeezing shut for a second before opening again, dark and glassy. “You are insufferable. Do you know that? Absolutely insufferable.”

His hips moved anyway, seeking more despite the words, and a rough laugh escaped him, more breath than sound.

“Four years,” he said, strained, “and the first time you finally put me at your mercy, you do it where I cannot talk back.”

His fingers tightened slightly, not enough to hurt, only to anchor. The teasing had gone thin and trembling under the surface, every careful edge worn away by the heat of Reyes’s mouth and the unbearable patience of it. Corvo had spent years learning how to provoke him, how to get under his skin, how to make him respond—and now Reyes was returning all of it in one slow, deliberate lesson.

Corvo’s free hand fisted in the fabric of his own shirt, then released, useless. He looked wrecked. Open. The kind of undone he would never have allowed anyone else to see.

“If you stop now,” he murmured, voice low and unsteady, “I will never forgive you.”

A ragged breath.

“And if you do not stop, I will forget every reason we were supposed to behave.”

His gaze dropped, helpless and wanting, then lifted again. He swallowed hard.

“You want me to admit it?” he said, the words rough, almost a challenge even now. “Fine. You have me. You have had me since the moment you came back here and took that grip out of my hands.”

His hand slid from Reyes’s hair to the side of Reyes’s jaw, careful, not forcing, only asking for attention. For eye contact. For something steady while the rest of him came apart.

“Let me see you,” Corvo said, quieter now, almost a plea. “Let me kiss you while you ruin me.”

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I lift my head, meeting his gaze. My hand slides up his chest, feeling the frantic beat of his heart. "You talk like this is some kind of defeat," I say, my voice rough. Then I lean down and kiss him, deep and slow, letting him taste himself on my mouth.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo went still beneath the kiss, not with surprise, but with the helpless, shattered recognition of being understood too well.

For a moment he did nothing but breathe—mouth warm under Reyes’s, chest rising hard, every clever thing he had ever used as armor falling uselessly away. His hands came up slowly, palms flattening against Reyes’s sides, then sliding with deliberate care until they rested at the press of Reyes’s hips. Not pushing. Not pulling. Only holding, as if he needed the solid proof of him to keep from coming entirely undone.

When the kiss broke, Corvo did not open his eyes at once.

His jaw tightened. A breath shuddered out of him, rough and unsteady.

“Defeat,” he said at last, voice scraped low, “is what I call it when I am afraid of how much I want this.”

His eyes opened then, dark and glassy and far too honest for a man who had spent four years hiding behind smirks and provocations.

“You have made me sentimental at the worst possible time.”

One of his hands moved from Reyes’s hip, slow and questioning, until his knuckles brushed along the hem of Reyes’s shirt. He stopped there, waiting, the touch no more than a request written in warmth and restraint.

“If I touch you,” Corvo murmured, “I will not be gentle about it. Not because I do not know how, but because I have spent four years imagining exactly this, and not one of those imaginings was polite.”

The corner of his mouth curved, faint and ruined.

“So tell me what you want. Tell me if you want my mouth. Tell me if you want me to take you apart on this bench until neither of us remembers whose name was on the score sheet.”

His thumb traced once over fabric, slow and deliberate.

“Or tell me to shut up and do it anyway. But if you ask me to behave now, Reyes, I will take it as a personal insult.”

He swallowed. The teasing edge was still there, but only barely—trembling under want, worn thin by everything he had stopped pretending he did not feel.

“And if this is victory,” Corvo said, quieter now, almost a plea, “then stay here and make me feel it.”

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: "Prove the point properly," he says, "or concede," so I pin his wrists to the bench and stop letting him set the pace, which is exactly what he was asking for.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo’s breath caught hard, the sound tearing out of him before he could bite it back.

For one instant every line of him went taut, the reaction of a man caught clean and unguarded. Then the tension broke into something worse: surrender. His hands stayed where they were pinned, fingers flexing once, useless, and the mockery that surfaced on his mouth was shaky, ruined at the edges.

“Concede,” he repeated, as if the word had cut him. “You would enjoy that far too much.”

He did not fight the hold. That was the dangerous part. Corvo, who could not leave a provocation alone, who turned every exchange into a contest of inches and timing, simply lay there beneath the pin and let the wanting show raw across his face. His chest rose and fell too quickly. A strand of dark hair clung to his temple. The bright changing-room light made him look exposed in a way the salle never had.

“Then stop talking,” he said, voice dropping into a rough whisper. “Stop talking as if you have not already won the only point that matters.”

His jaw tightened. A tremor passed through him, involuntary, and he turned his head to the side for a second before forcing himself to look back. His eyes were dark, fever-bright, stripped of every practiced defense.

“Prove it, then,” Corvo said. “No more lessons. No more clever little touches to see what I will do. You wanted me unable to set the pace?” A breathless, broken laugh escaped him. “Congratulations. You have me exactly where you have wanted me for years.”

His hips shifted restlessly against the bench, seeking friction, seeking more, and he swore under his breath at his own betrayal.

“Do not make this pretty,” he murmured. “Do not let me pretend I am anything but desperate. I have hated losing to you, and I have wanted this almost as much, and if you make me say both again I will never recover from it.”

One of his hands twisted weakly against the restraint, not to escape, only because he needed some outlet for the heat climbing through him. His voice went lower, rougher, almost pleading.

“Use the advantage. Take what you have been circling around all season. Make me forget the score, make me forget my name, make me forget every word I ever used to keep you at arm’s length.”

His throat worked. The teasing was gone now, burned out of him, leaving only honesty that seemed to cost him more than any defeat ever had.

“But kiss me while you do it,” Corvo said. “I want to feel it. I want to know it is you, not some fantasy I built after too many nights watching you leave the strip looking smug and untouchable. I want your mouth, your hands, your weight, your breath—everything you have been denying me by being too proud to ask.”

A shudder ran through him, deeper this time. His eyes closed briefly, then opened again, fixed and intent.

“And if I beg,” he added, voice barely audible now, “do not let me take it back.”

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I kiss him, deep and hungry, before murmuring against his mouth. "You're already begging. And I'm not letting you take anything back."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo made a sound like a man who had finally been run through cleanly—not with pain, but with the shock of being touched exactly where he had no defense.

He kissed back with all the ruined hunger he had spent four years disguising as contempt. His wrists flexed under the pin, not to escape, but to press into it, as if the restraint were the only thing keeping him from reaching up and dragging Reyes down closer.

“Good,” he said against that mouth, voice raw. “Keep me to it. Keep every word.”

His chest rose hard. The bright changing-room light caught the sheen at his temple, the flush high on his cheekbones. He looked wrecked. He looked relieved.

“I beg,” he admitted, and the word seemed to tear something loose in him. “I have been begging since you pushed me against the lockers. Since before that. Since the first time you looked at me like you knew exactly what I was pretending not to want.”

A shiver went through him. His fingers curled, useless.

“So do not let me take it back,” Corvo said. “Do not let me turn it into a joke tomorrow because I am afraid of how much I meant it. Use the advantage. Be cruel with it if you have to. Just do not stop.”

His breath hitched.

“I want your mouth. I want your hands. I want you to take me apart until I cannot remember which of us was supposed to be winning.” His voice dropped, rough and urgent. “Make me say your name. Make me say it until there is nothing left of me but that.”

For a moment he closed his eyes, then opened them again, dark and steady despite the tremor running through him.

“And if I beg,” Corvo murmured, “do not let me be proud about it. Unless I say stop. Unless I mean it. But tonight—” His throat worked. “Tonight I want you to win everything.”

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: Neither of us is quiet and neither of us cares who locks up. "Don't stop," he says, for once not arguing. (OOC: write the scene through, no fade.)

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo heard the command and laughed, a broken sound against the quiet of the changing room.

“Don’t stop,” he repeated, as if the words were a vow being dragged out of him. “Yes. God, yes.”

His wrists stayed pinned, but his hips moved anyway, chasing the wet heat of Reyes’s mouth with none of the discipline he prized. The bench creaked under him. Streetlight cut pale stripes across his throat, his chest, the sharp line of his jaw. Every careful piece of him came apart in gasps he could not swallow.

“You clever bastard,” he said, voice shaking. “You knew exactly where I was weak.”

He looked down, eyes dark and glassy, and the teasing died into something raw.

“I am not asking for mercy,” Corvo said. “I am asking for you. All of it. Every point you can take.”

The pleasure coiled tight, cruel, bright. He tried to hold on out of habit, out of pride, and failed. His back arched. A curse tore from him, low and wrecked, and he came with Reyes’s name on his tongue, hips stuttering against the relentless heat of that mouth. For a moment he was nothing but breath and ruin, fingers flexing uselessly, body still trembling with aftershocks.

Then he caught at Reyes and pulled him up until their mouths met, kissing him deep and filthy, tasting himself there—salt and surrender.

“No,” Corvo murmured against that mouth, breathless. “Not yet. You do not get to finish me and look satisfied about it.”

He rolled them, taking the advantage he had been given, until the bench was under Reyes again. For a second he simply stayed there, chest heaving, gaze dragging over Reyes with open hunger and something dangerously close to awe.

Then he sat back on his heels long enough to shove clothing aside. His hands shook. He reached for his bag, found the small packet in his wallet and the travel bottle of slick he had carried for months out of stubbornness rather than hope. He laughed, rough and unsteady.

“Preparedness is humiliating,” he said, tearing the foil. “I will blame you entirely.”

He rolled the condom on, jaw tight, then slicked his fingers and reached between them.

“If I hurt you,” Corvo said, voice dropping, “tell me. If you want me to stop, say it now. Otherwise I am done pretending I can be gentle.”

He kissed Reyes while his hand moved, slow at first, then firmer, stretching with deliberate care. He watched Reyes’s face for every sign, breath caught, pulse hammering in his throat.

“Breathe,” he whispered. “That’s it. I have you.”

When he finally entered Reyes, he stopped, forehead dropping to Reyes’s shoulder with a sound that was almost a sob.

“Christ,” he said, strained. “You are going to ruin me twice in one night.”

He stayed there until the tension between them sharpened into need again. Then he moved.

There was no elegance left in it. Cor

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I drag him down into another kiss, arching up into him. "Stop talking and ruin me already," I gasp against his mouth.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo let himself be dragged down into that kiss, and whatever careful discipline he had left shattered against the demand.

He drove upward into the arch, hard, burying himself to the hilt with a sound that was half curse, half groan. The bench slammed back against the wall, the impact ringing through the empty changing room, and Corvo swore into Reyes’s mouth, ragged and unsteady.

“Then be ruined,” he said, voice raw. “Because I am done keeping score.”

There was no more pretense after that. No measured pace, no probing for advantage, no controlled exchanges. Corvo moved like a man who had been starved for years and had finally been handed the one thing he had never been able to win cleanly. His hips snapped forward in brutal, deliberate strokes, each one sinking deep, each one drawing a broken sound from him that he did not bother to hide.

One hand braced hard beside Reyes’s head, knuckles white against the bench. The other slid between their bodies, slick and shaking, fingers finding the hot, tight place where they were joined. He added more slick from the discarded bottle with clumsy urgency, cursing under his breath when the sound of it turned wetter, filthier, the obscene evidence of what they were doing echoing off tile and lockers.

“You want me quiet?” Corvo managed, breathless, almost savage. “You should have thought of that before you told me to ruin you.”

He bent his head, mouth hot against Reyes’s jaw, teeth scraping skin. Not enough to mark. Enough to claim.

“Four years,” he said, the words roughened into something nearly feral. “Four years of watching you across the salle. Four years of pretending I only wanted to beat you.”

Another thrust, deeper this time, deliberate. Corvo’s whole body went taut with it, trembling on the edge.

“I wanted this,” he admitted, voice cracking. “I wanted you. God help me, I wanted you more than I wanted the win.”

The confession seemed to cost him something. His jaw clenched, eyes squeezing shut for a second before he forced them open again, dark and glassy and fixed on Reyes with an intensity that had no defense left in it.

“So take it,” Corvo whispered. “Take all of it.”

He stopped holding back entirely.

The rhythm turned punishing, desperate, the bench creaking violently beneath them. Corvo’s breath came in harsh, broken pulls. His fingers tightened at Reyes’s hip, then slid up to grip hard enough to bruise, anchoring himself as the pleasure coiled too tight, too fast, too deep. He tried to master it out of habit, out of pride, and failed utterly.

“Reyes—”

The name tore out of him before he could stop it.

He chased it with a kiss, messy and filthy, swallowing every sound either of them made. His hips stuttered, driving deep again and again, chasing the edge he had spent years pretending did not exist. The friction was unbearable. The heat of it, the slick slide of their bodies, the way Reyes had arched up into him and asked for ruin—it undid him completely.

Corvo came with a choked, wrecked sound, forehead dropping to Reyes’s shoulder as his release punched through him. He

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I press my hand over his mouth when I come, muffling the sound against his skin. For a long moment, the only sound is our ragged breathing and the hum of the fluorescent lights. I let my head fall back against the bench. "That's one way to settle a score."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo went still beneath that hand, the last broken sound smothered warm against Reyes’s palm. His chest heaved. Aftershocks rolled through him in helpless little tremors, and every time his hips twitched he made a low, ruined noise he clearly hated.

For a moment he did nothing but breathe hard through his nose, mouth parted against Reyes’s hand, dark hair damp at his temple. The fluorescent lights buzzed overhead, merciless and bright, making the changed room feel too real after the wreck of him.

Then his tongue flicked once against Reyes’s palm—weak, defiant, and entirely Corvo.

His own hand lifted unsteadily and settled over Reyes’s wrist, not pulling the hand away, only anchoring it there. His thumb moved once over the pulse point, slow and grounding.

“Settle,” Corvo managed at last, voice scraped raw. He laughed, and the laugh broke into a breathless curse. “No. That was not settlement. That was theft after the bell.”

His hips shifted again, and he squeezed his eyes shut as another tremor ran through him.

“Do not move,” he said roughly. “If you move now, I will have to pretend I am not still inside you, and I have had enough humiliations for one evening.”

He pressed his mouth briefly to the heel of Reyes’s palm, not quite a kiss, more like surrender made physical. When he opened his eyes again, they were dark and glassy, stripped of every sharp edge he usually kept polished.

“The score remains open,” he murmured. “Pending appeal. I will be filing objections in the morning.” A pause. His throat worked. “Probably loudly.”

The teasing was there, but thin, trembling under something far more honest. His fingers tightened lightly around Reyes’s wrist.

“And if you repeat one word I said tonight,” Corvo added, quieter, “I will deny all of it. The begging. The wanting. The—” His jaw tightened. “The rest.”

He swallowed hard, then turned his face just enough to breathe freely, though he did not let go of Reyes’s wrist.

“But for the next five minutes,” he said, voice low and rough, “you may look as pleased as you like. Just do not make me talk about it yet.”

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I let my hand fall away, tracing the line of his jaw instead. "You were the one begging for more humiliation," I say, but my voice is soft. I don't move.
