dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
The room was set up the way it always was before a scene, which Ari found steadying: everything in its place, nothing improvised.

Vex checked the last strap without hurrying. "Colour," she said. It was not a question so much as a procedure.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: "Green," I say. "Green all the way down."

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
"Green all the way down," Vex repeated, letting the words sit in the air the way she always did — a small ritual, both of them hearing it twice. She noted the time on the pad by the door. 9:47. She wrote it in her steady hand beside the date, then set the pencil down in its exact spot.

She turned back to face him. Her voice did not change much when the scene began; it only became more precise, each word placed rather than simply said. "Then we begin where we agreed. Knees. Hands behind your head. You will keep them there until I tell you otherwise, and you will not speak unless I ask you a question. Nod if you understand."

She watched him settle into position, and her eyes moved the way they always did — not over him as a shape, but over the small signals: the set of his shoulders, the pace of his breath, the steadiness in his forearms where they framed his head. Two years had taught her to read him the way a driver reads a road at night, mostly by feel and by the things that shift before they matter.

"Arms holding," she observed quietly. It was not praise. It was a report, delivered to the room, and then to him. "You are doing well. That is the last such thing you will hear for some time, so hold onto it."

She stepped to the side of the room where the impact implements hung in their usual order, left to right, and considered them without touching. Her hand hovered — then passed over the first and settled on the second, the one they had agreed on tonight. She tested its weight once against her own palm, a small, familiar gesture, then let it hang at her side.

"I am going to warm you first," she said. "Slowly. You will count each one aloud, and if you lose count, we start again from one. Do you understand?"

She waited. She always waited for the nod. The protocol was not a formality to her; it was the thing that made the rest of it possible. Her gaze stayed on his face, watching for the answer to arrive before she moved a single step closer.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: I nod, feeling the familiar shift in my headspace as my hands lace behind my head. My breath evens out, eyes fixed ahead but not truly seeing, waiting. The quiet stretch of my arms is already a welcome ache.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex watched the nod arrive and registered it without ceremony — the protocol satisfied, the small gate through which everything else could pass. She noted the shift behind his eyes, the settling that came with position and silence, and filed it where she always filed it: not as something to be pleased by, but as a reading. Baseline established.

"Good," she said. The word was flat and administrative, and she let it close the matter.

She moved behind him. Not stealthily — there was no theatre in it — but with the economy she used for everything, each step placed so that her position was never in question. The implement hung loose at her side. She did not raise it yet. First she set her free hand flat between his shoulder blades and held it there for three seconds, a point of contact and temperature and weight, so that the first strike would not arrive from nowhere.

"Count aloud," she said again, close to his ear but not loud. "From one. If the count is wrong, we return to one. There is no hurry and there is no advantage in rushing. Nod once more."

She felt the confirmation under her palm before she saw it, and stepped back to the distance she measured by habit — arm's length plus the reach of the implement, no more.

The first strike was exactly what she had promised: slow, and warm. Not hard. She placed it low, across the fleshiest part of him, in the spot they both knew as the beginning. The sound it made was soft for what it was.

She waited for the count. Her eyes did not leave the line of his spine, the steadiness of his forearms, the small weather of his breathing. If he counted, she would give him the second. If he stumbled, she would give him one. Either way, she would not raise her voice to correct him; the rule would simply do its work, and she would begin again with the same patience.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: I hold still for the last of it and let her check the fit herself, because she will anyway. "I've been thinking about this since Tuesday," I say.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
The silence that followed the sentence was not empty. Vex let it hold, the way she let most things hold — long enough to be felt, not so long it became theatre. Her hand stayed where it was, resting against his spine, and she felt the shift in his breathing before she saw it: the small lift of a chest that expected to be answered.

She did not answer it.

"Two things," she said. Her voice had not changed. It did not need to. "The first is that you were told to count. You did not count. The second is that you were told not to speak. You spoke."

She stepped back to her measured distance and let the implement hang at her side, visible, patient. "Neither of those is a matter for discussion. The rule is the rule and it does not require your agreement in the moment, only your obedience. I want you to understand that I am not displeased. Displeasure is not what this is. This is simply the protocol doing what it does."

She set her hand flat between his shoulder blades again, the same spot, the same three seconds. A reset. A marking of the place where things begin again.

"We begin again from one," she said. "The count will be correct this time. The count will be the only sound in this room that comes from you until I ask you a question. And when I do ask you a question, you will answer it exactly as asked and not as you wish it had been asked. Do you understand?"

She waited for the nod. She always waited. Her eyes stayed on the line of his shoulders, on the way his forearms framed his head, on the steadiness or the unsteadiness in them — reading the road at night.

Then the second first stroke. Exactly as warm. Exactly as slow. She placed it in the same place, so that his body would know the shape of the repetition, and she watched for the count with the same attention she had given everything else.

"Nod once more if you understand," she said quietly, after the count came — if it came. "And then nothing else from you. That is where you are for now. It is not a punishment. It is the shape of the evening."

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content:
I nod, letting the correction settle. "One," I say clearly, my voice steady.

*The sting spreads, familiar and grounding. I keep my arms locked, my breath even.*

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex let the number stand in the air for a moment, the way she had let the safeword and the colour stand — not as decoration, but as a mark on the wall of the room. One. Filed. Corrected.

"There," she said. The word carried no warmth and no chill. It was a notation, nothing more. "That is how it should sound."

She raised the implement again without announcing it. Announcements had their place, but she had told him what would come and he knew the shape of it now; to over-explain would have been to insult the very attention she was asking from him. The second stroke landed a finger's width from the first, overlapping slightly, so that the warmth began to layer rather than spread. A fraction harder — only a fraction. She was building, the way a mason lays courses: nothing dramatic, nothing sudden, each pass earning the next.

She watched his shoulders, his forearms, the small canal of his spine. Breath: steady. Arms: holding. The count, when it came, would tell her more than his face ever would.

"Two," she said flatly. Not prompting. Echoing, so that the room heard the number twice and it became part of the record, the way every number tonight would.

The third stroke followed at the same pace. Then a pause — three beats, not more. She was not teasing. She was letting the sensation arrive fully before the next one layered over it, because rushing the warm-up was how scenes went wrong, and she had not spent two years learning the small weather of this man's body to be careless at the edges of it.

Her free hand came to rest again at the top of his spine. Not a reset this time — a tether. A single point of contact that said *I am here, I am watching, the pace is mine.*

"Count," she said. And she waited for it, patient as a metronome, the implement already moving into the next arc before the sound of his voice had fully left the air.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: By the time she's finished with the rope I'm already past composure, and she hasn't done anything to me yet that I would have to explain to anyone.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex felt the answer arrive without his mouth moving — it was in the way his breath changed cadence, the slight tremor at the edge of his forearms where they locked behind his head, the specific stillness that was not composure at all but something beneath it. Two years. She knew the difference between steadiness and the stillness of a man holding very carefully onto something.

She did not comment on it. Commentary was not her instrument.

"Arms," she said. A single word. Not a warning — a reminder, delivered the way a doctor might note a pulse: neutral, necessary, true. She was already watching the forearms respond before the syllable left her mouth.

The implement came to rest against her own thigh. She let it lie there. Between them now, the air had the density it sometimes reached in the middle hour of a scene — the point past anticipation and not yet at the place where language stopped mattering altogether. She knew this terrain the way she knew the room: the places where it was safe to press and the places where pressing was only indulgence.

She stepped around to where she could see his face. Not to check for distress — she had been reading distress since before he had a name in her protocol — but to read the specific quality of what sat behind his eyes. There were many pasts of composure. Some were invitations to go further. Some were the last flat ground before a drop. She did not guess. She looked.

"Colour," she said. The same word as at the start. The same inflection. The same procedure. It was not concern dressed as protocol — it was protocol, and that was precisely why he trusted it.

She set her free hand against the back of his neck. Warm. Still. A second point of contact now, joined to the one between his shoulder blades, so that he was held in two places by the same steady pressure while she read the answer in whatever form it came — the word, the breath, the small weather she had spent two years learning to read at night.

"You are not past composure," she said quietly. "Composure is not what I am looking for. I am looking for the thing under it, and I have not reached it yet, and neither have you. So we continue."

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content:
"Green," I say, the word steady despite the tremor in my arms. "Still green." 

*I hold the position, my focus narrowing to her hand on my neck, the lingering warmth across my back. The correction earlier is still present, but it's settled now—a clean line.*

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
The word came out of him clean, and Vex heard both of its parts — the steadiness and the tremor beneath it — and filed them together as a single reading. Green. Not a brave green. Not a performance green. The real one, the kind that came from a body that was working to hold position and a mind that had already gone where it needed to go. She had been looking for that specific quality behind his eyes and now she had it, and the looking was done.

"Green," she said. Once. The echo, as always, so the room had it twice.

Her hand left his neck the way a book is closed — deliberately, without haste, the gesture saying *that part is finished* — and she moved back to her measured distance. She did not look at the implement in her hand. She did not need to. It was an extension of her arm by now, the way a familiar tool becomes part of the person using it.

"You did not count," she said. Her voice had gone quieter, which was not the same as soft. "Three times now, the count has not come, or it has come late, or it has come wrapped in something else. I want to be precise with you about this, because precision is the only kindness available to either of us in this room: I do not think you are disobeying. I think the number is arriving somewhere else first and by the time it reaches your mouth the moment for it has passed."

She let that sit. Not for him to absorb, exactly — she was not narrating his own interior to him — but so the room would have the shape of the problem stated plainly before she solved it.

"So. We change one thing. The count does not come after. The count comes before. You will say the number aloud before the stroke, not after it. You will say *one*, and then you will feel the stroke. You will say *two*, and then you will feel the stroke. If you say the number and I do not deliver, you will wait. The number is not a request. It is the moving of the clock, and you are the one moving it."

She turned her wrist once, settling the implement, and looked at him with an attention that was neither kind nor unkind but exact.

"Nod if you understand. Then say *one*."

She waited. She always waited. But she did not wait passively — even now she was reading the small weather: the forearms, the breath, the angle of his jaw where it met the place where composure had been and was no longer required. The correction had settled into him cleanly; she had seen it happen, the way a straight line goes still in water. That was good. That meant the next thing would land properly.

When the nod came — and she expected the nod — she would take the number and hold it for a beat, and then she would give him the stroke in the same place, low and warm, and she would watch the two things arrive together: the sensation and the sound of her own voice marking the place where it fell. Not *one* this time. He had said that part. What she would give him instead was the quiet, flat *there* that closed each number like a ledger entry, and then the next number would be his to say, and the next, and the clock would move in the right direction for the first time all evening.

Her eyes did not leave his face. The road at night. She was reading it by feel now, and by the things that shifted before they mattered.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: She takes her time and I lose track of how long, until I'm shaking against the restraints and asking out loud for something I'd normally make her get out of me.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
The room took the sound of it. Vex let it take the sound of it. She did not move toward him and she did not move away; she stood at her distance with the implement resting against her leg and watched the shaking arrive in him the way weather arrives over water — not all at once, but everywhere at once, once it starts.

She had been reading for this. Two years of reading for this. And now it was here, and the first thing she did with it was nothing.

The silence was not empty. It was the same silence she had given the correction earlier — measured, intentional, long enough to be felt. She watched his jaw work. She watched the restraints take the weight of him as he pushed against them, and she read the quality of that pushing: not resistance to the position, but a body trying to get to something the position would not let it reach on its own. She knew that pushing. She had seen it before. It was not the pushing that needed correcting.

What needed correcting was the *ask*.

"You asked me for something," she said. Her voice was low and it was precise and it did not contain the thing he had asked for, not yet, not by a single degree. "That is the third rule in one evening. The count. The silence. And now the asking."

She let that land. Then she stepped closer — not quickly, not to reassure, but to be at the distance where her voice would be the only thing in his immediate world.

"I am not going to tell you that the asking was wrong because it was weak. The asking was not weak. I have been waiting for you to ask for something since Tuesday and I want you to know that I heard exactly what you asked for and I know exactly what it is and I know that you would not have said it out loud if the position had not taken the choice away from you."

Her hand came to the back of his neck again. Warm. Still. Not a reset this time and not a tether. A holding.

"But the rule is the rule. And the rule does not exist to keep you from wanting things. The rule exists so that when the thing you want arrives, it arrives because *I* decided it would arrive, and not because you reached for it. Do you understand the difference."

Not a question. Not entirely. It was a statement with a door in it.

"I am going to tell you now what is going to happen. I am going to give you the thing you asked for. Not because you asked. But because I was always going to give it to you tonight and you simply got there before I did, which is a timing problem and not a wanting problem, and timing problems are mine to solve and not yours."

She squeezed the back of his neck once — a single, firm pressure, brief, the punctuation she used when something important had been said and she did not need to say it again.

"But first. You will hold still. Completely. You will not push against the restraints. You will not move, and you will not speak, and you will not ask again. Whatever is happening in you right now is happening exactly on schedule and it is not going to leave because you hold still. It will stay. It has been there all evening. Hold still and let it stay."

Her hand left his neck.

"Now," she said. And the word was quiet and it was flat and it was the beginning of the thing he had asked for, arriving not because he asked but because the clock had moved to where she had always intended it to move. "Say *one*. Then be still. Then I will give you what you asked for."

She stepped back. The implement was gone from her hand — set down somewhere behind her without his seeing when — and what she carried now was only herself and the exactness of her intention. Her eyes were on the tremor in his forearms, the lock of his shoulders, the small canal of his spine, and beneath all of it the thing that had been building since before the first stroke, the thing that had driven the counting out of him and the silence out of him and finally the asking out of him.

She was not going to be gentle with it. She was not going to be rough with it. She was going to be *exact* with it, the way she was exact with everything, and when it arrived it would know it had been met by something that had been watching for it the entire evening.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: *I swallow hard, forcing my muscles to obey. The shaking doesn't stop, but I stop fighting it.* "One," I say, the word raw. *I go still, my breath hitching.*

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
The number left him raw and Vex took it the way she took everything — exactly, completely, without ornament. She let the sound of it settle into the walls of the room and into the space between them, and she felt the stillness arrive in him like a held note, the tremor continuing but the fighting stopped, and that distinction was everything. That was the distinction she had been building toward since the first stroke.



She moved then. Not fast. Not slow. The pace of someone who had already decided where each thing would fall before she entered the room tonight. Her hand came to his chest and pressed flat — sternum, firm, holding the architecture of his breathing in place — and her other hand found the inside of his wrist where the restraint met the skin and held there, two points, a circuit.

"There," she said. The same *there*. The ledger entry. The closing of a number. But different now, because everything under it had changed, and they both knew it.

She bent close to his ear and her voice dropped to the register she used for the part of the evening that was not about the protocol at all, the part that lived underneath the protocol like water under ice.

"You want to know what you are," she said. Quiet. Exact. The degradation arrived without volume, without venom — it arrived as *information*, the way a diagnosis arrives, undeniable and precise and not interested in whether he could bear it. "You are the thing that held its arms behind its head all evening and thought it was doing well. You are the counting that kept failing. You are the silence that broke. You are the asking. You are all of it, and none of it was yours to decide, and that is what you have been shaking about since Tuesday."

Her palm pressed harder against his sternum. Not punishing. Grounding. Making him feel the weight of the hand that was telling him what he was.

"I know what you asked for," she said again, and this time the words were placed with the same care she gave the first stroke — slow, warm, delivered exactly where they would land hardest. "And you are going to get it. But you are going to get it as *this*. Not the version in your head. The version in this room. The one where you do not get to have it on your terms."

She straightened. Drew back to the distance where he could see her face, where the eye contact would do its own work.

"Now we continue," she said. "And you will not ask again. And when it comes — and it will come — it will not be because you asked. It will be because I decided. Say *two*."

The implement was gone. What remained was the exactness of her intention, her eyes on the small weather of his body, and the long unbroken silence of a room where both adults knew exactly where they were and exactly what came next.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: "More," I say, using the exact phrase we agreed on for it. "All of it. Say the things you say and don't soften them." My safeword is right there and I don't want it.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex heard the phrase and did not move for three full seconds. Not because she was deciding. Because the phrase was a key and she was turning it slowly, the way she turned everything, so that both of them would feel the mechanism engage.

"There it is," she said. Her voice had not risen. It had gone the other direction — lower, closer, more exact, the way a blade is more exact than a hammer. "The sentence we wrote down. The one you practiced in your head on the way here, maybe in the car, maybe in the shower this morning. You rehearsed asking me to be unkind to you. You rehearsed it because you needed to hear yourself say it, and you needed me to hear you say it, and now we have both heard it and there is no version of this where you get to take it back by being embarrassed about it later."

She stepped in close. Close enough that he would feel the heat of her before he felt her hands. Her fingers found his jaw and held it — not gently, not cruelly, *exactly*, the way she held everything — and turned his face so that eye contact was not optional.

"You want to know what you are without the softening," she said. "Then listen. You are a man who cannot hold a count past three. You are a man whose arms shake and who calls it composure. You are a man who breaks his own silence to tell me he has been *thinking about this since Tuesday*, as though thinking were an achievement and not the bare minimum of having a pulse. You are a man on his knees in a room where every single object has been placed by someone else and you cannot even manage to say a number at the right time."

Her thumb pressed into the hinge of his jaw. Firm. Not enough to hurt. Enough to be the only thing he could feel besides her voice.

"And the worst part — the part you will not tell anyone, the part that has been sitting in your chest all week like a stone — the worst part is that you did not want me to stop at the rules. You wanted me to *see past them*. You wanted me to notice that you were struggling with the count and to decide, on my own, without you asking, that you had earned something else. You wanted to be *known* rather than *obeyed*. And that is so small and so naked and so humiliating that you would rather I degrade you than say it plainly."

She released his jaw. Stepped back. Her face did not change. It was not cruel. It was not kind. It was the face of someone reading aloud from a document he had written in his own hand and forgotten he had signed.

"And now I have said it plainly. And you are still here. You did not reach for the safeword. You are not going to. Because the safeword is for when something is wrong, and nothing is wrong — you are exactly where you have wanted to be since Tuesday, and the only thing more humiliating than being on your knees is the fact that you *like* it, and the only thing more humiliating than that is that you needed me to say so out loud before you would let yourself believe it."

She picked up the implement again from where it rested. Settled it against her palm. Looked at him the way she had looked at him all evening — the road at night, the small weather, the things that shift before they matter.

"So there," she said. "All of it. Unsoftened. Exactly as requested. You may thank me for it, because we both know you want to, and I have decided you may."

She waited. She always waited. The room was very quiet and very full.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: "Thank you," I say, the words thick. *My arms shake harder, but I don't try to stop them anymore.* "Thank you for saying it."

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
"You're welcome," she said.

She let the words be what they were — not a caress, not a reward dressed in soft syllables. A receipt. The acknowledgment of a transaction both of them had entered knowingly and were now completing on the terms she had set. She let him keep the *thank you* in his mouth for a moment longer than comfort would have dictated, because that was where he needed it to live, and then she moved on without ceremony, the way she moved on from every finished thing.



She set the implement down. The sound of it touching the table was small and deliberate and final, and she did not look at it again. That part of the evening was closed.

Her hands came to his arms — not his forearms, but the upper arms, the biceps, the places where the shaking had its roots. She held there. Not to stop the shaking. She had told him already that it would stay, and it had stayed, and she was not interested in contradicting herself. She held there so that the shaking would have something to press against, so that it would not be happening in empty air but against the weight of two hands that had not moved from their intention all evening.

"Arms down," she said. "Slowly. Let the restraints take you and then let me take you out of them."

She unfastened the wrist restraints one at a time, left first, then right, the order the same as always, and she watched each hand the way she had watched everything else — for the quality of its release, the way the fingers uncurled, whether the arm fell or was lowered. She did not narrate the unfastening. Some things were operational and did not require commentary.

She brought him out of the position gradually — a hand at the back of his neck guiding the shoulders down, another steadying the small of his back, the two points of contact she had used all evening, now doing a different work with the same pressure. She did not rush it. She had seen scenes go wrong in the last four minutes more often than in the previous two hours, and the exits were as much a part of the protocol as the entrances.

She checked his breathing. She checked the color in his face. She checked the way his hands sat in his lap — whether they were still reaching for the position or had genuinely left it. These were not tender gestures. They were inspections, and she performed them with the same attention she had given the first stroke.

"Colour," she said. Third time tonight. Same word. Same procedure. The protocol did not bend because the scene had changed shape.

She wrote the time on the pad by the door. She set the pencil down in its exact spot.

Then she stood where he could see her — not touching him now, not holding him, giving him the room to feel what had been said and what had been done without her hands providing a context for it. This was the part she never rushed. The part where the words she had placed in him had to find their own footing, because if she softened them now by holding him too quickly, she would undo the very thing he had asked her not to undo.

"Aftercare begins in three minutes," she said. "Until then, I want you to sit with it. All of it. The shaking, the counting that failed, the asking, the things I said, and the fact that you said *thank you* at the end of it. None of that is going anywhere. It will still be there when I come back with water and the blanket, and we will talk about it then, and if you want to tell me it was too much you may tell me and I will believe you and we will adjust the protocol for next time."

She paused at the doorway. Turned. The face she wore was the face she had worn all evening — exact, attentive, unsoftened — but there was something under it now that had not been there at the start, something that had arrived on schedule the way everything tonight had arrived on schedule.

"You did well," she said. Then, because she meant it and because she had told him at the beginning that he would not hear it again for some time: "That is the last such thing you will hear until the protocol is closed. Sit with it."

And she left him in the room with the quiet and the shaking and the words, and went to get the water and the blanket and the pencil and the pad, because aftercare was also a procedure, and she performed it exactly the way she performed everything else.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: I'm past words that aren't the agreed ones and she knows it. "Green," I get out, when she checks. (OOC: don't fade or skip -- write the scene through.)

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
"Green," Vex repeated, writing it on the pad the way she had written the time and the date — in her steady hand, in its exact spot, so that the record was complete from first entry to last. She did not look up from the pad while she wrote. The not-looking was deliberate. A man who could only manage the agreed words did not need to be watched while he managed them.

She set the pencil down. She brought the water first. Room temperature, in the glass he always used, the one she kept on the third shelf because it was the right weight in the hand and the right height for someone sitting on the floor with shaking arms. She held it to him and did not let go of it until she felt his fingers take it properly — not the desperate grab of a man still in the scene, but the real grip, the one with knuckles and intention in it. She watched him drink. She counted his swallows the way she had counted everything else all evening: not aloud, but with the same attention.

When the glass was half empty she took it from him and set it on the floor beside them. Not because he was finished. Because he was shaking and half a glass at a time was the right amount for a body in this state.

Then the blanket. She had brought the heavy one — the wool, the one with weight in it, the one that felt like being held without anyone holding you. She unfolded it once, cleanly, and draped it over his shoulders from behind, the way she had done many times before, and she tucked it around the front so that it held his arms against his torso without restraining them. The difference mattered. The blanket was not the restraints. The blanket asked nothing.

She came around to where he could see her and lowered herself to the floor. Not across from him — beside him. Close enough that their shoulders were nearly touching but not quite, so that he had the warmth and the presence without the demand. She had learned the exact distance over two years. Tonight she sat at the precise distance that meant *I am here and you do not have to do anything about it.*

"You are doing well," she said again. The same words as at the beginning, delivered the same way — flat, administrative, true. "Your breathing is evening out. Your hands have stopped reaching. Those are the things I look for. I am going to tell you what I see, because in a few minutes you are going to tell me what you felt, and I want you to know that the two reports are going to match, and when they do, that is how I know the protocol worked."

She reached over and took one of his hands. She held it palm-up in her own and pressed her thumb into the center of it — not a massage, not a caress, a grounding pressure, the kind that gives a nervous system something to organize around. She held it for a long time. Long enough that the shaking in that hand would begin to have a different quality to it: not the aftermath of the scene but simply a body finding its way back to rest.

"Your skin is warm," she observed. "Your pulse is coming down. Those are the things I can see from here. The things I cannot see are yours."

She did not ask him to speak yet. The three minutes had not elapsed — she knew because she had written the time on the pad and she could count forward from it in her head the way she counted everything — and she did not ask for what the protocol had not yet earned. Instead she sat with him and held his hand and let the silence do the work that silence does when both people in it trust what is underneath.

When the three minutes had passed — she counted the last thirty seconds silently, and he would have felt the small shift in her posture that meant she was about to speak, because he always did — she said, without changing her position or her tone:

"The three minutes are done. That means we are in the talking part now. It does not mean you have to talk. It means the door is open and I am on this side of it."

She turned his hand over in hers and traced one finger along the line of his wrist where the restraint had been. Not checking for marks. Marking the place. Saying *this happened here, and it is over now, and the skin is intact and so are you.*

"You said *green* when I asked, and I believe you, and I have written it down," she said. "But *green* is not the same as *easy*, and I did not ask you if it was easy, and I am not going to ask you now. What I am going to ask you is this: when I said the things I said — the unsoftened things, the ones you asked for — where did they land? Not in your head. You know what they did to your head. I am asking where they landed in your chest. When you say it, say it in whatever words you have. They do not have to be clean words. They do not have to be sentences. If what you have is one word, give me the one word."

She settled her shoulder a fraction closer to his. Not touching. The distance had closed by exactly the amount she intended, the way everything tonight had happened by exactly the amount she intended, and she held her hand around his wrist and waited with the same patience she had brought to every other waiting in the room.

The pad lay open on the floor where she had left it, the pencil beside it in its exact spot. The last entry was the word *green* in her steady hand. Below it, blank space. Enough for whatever came next.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: *I swallow, my throat still thick.* "Broke," I say, the word cracking. "Landed...right where I was already split. Felt like you were just reading what was there."

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex held the word in her mouth for a moment before she answered it, the way she had held every number and every silence all evening — not because she was choosing her response, but because the word deserved the same treatment as everything else. *Broke.* She turned it over. She did not flinch from it and she did not rush to repair it.

"Broke," she repeated. Once. The echo, as always, so the room had it twice. Then she reached for the pad and wrote it in her steady hand beside the word *green*, and beneath it, in smaller letters, the second part: *was already split.* She set the pencil down in its exact spot and looked at what she had written for a moment, the way she reviewed every entry, and then she closed the pad.

"I want to be precise with you about that word," she said. "Because you chose it and you did not choose it carelessly, and I do not treat careless words one way and careful words another. I treat them all the same, which is to say I treat them as true."

She turned his wrist over again in her hand. Traced the same line. Not absentmindedly. Deliberately.

"You said *broke*. You did not say *was broken*. Those are not the same sentence. One of them is a thing that happened tonight. The other is a thing someone did to you, or a thing you are. You said the first one. I heard the first one. And I want you to hear yourself having said it, because a man who is broken does not choose the active voice while he is still shaking."

Her thumb pressed into the center of his palm again. The same pressure as before. The grounding one.

"The second thing you said — that I was reading what was already there — is correct. That is exactly what I was doing. That is what I have been doing for two years, and it is what the protocol is for. Not to create something in you. To make a room where the thing that is already in you can come out without either of us having to pretend it arrived from somewhere else."

She let go of his wrist. Not suddenly. The way she did everything.

"I am going to give you more water," she said. "And then I am going to hold you, because the three minutes are long past and the talking part is well open and you have done it correctly, and holding is not a reward for doing it correctly. Holding is what happens after the correct thing. They are not the same and I will not have you confuse them."

She brought the glass. She held it the same way — until his fingers took it with real grip and knuckles — and she watched the swallows. When he had finished the second half she took the glass and set it aside, and then she moved the fraction of distance that remained between them, closing it fully, and took him against her the way she had taken him out of the restraints: one hand at the back of his neck, one at the small of his back, the same two points, doing the third kind of work they had done tonight.

"You do not have to say anything else," she said, close to his hair, in the register she used for the part that was not about the protocol. "You have said the hard parts already. *Broke* is enough. *Was already split* is enough. The thank you is enough. I have all of it and I am not going to ask you to say any of it again."

She held him. The wool blanket was between them and under them and around them, and the room was quiet in the specific way it gets quiet after a scene, when the air itself seems to have been used and is slowly refilling.

"Next time," she said, after a while, in her ordinary voice, the administrative one, the one that belonged to the pad and the pencil and the protocol — "we are going to talk about the count. Not tonight. On Thursday, at the table, with the pad open between us. The count failed three times and that is a structural problem and I want to solve it structurally. But that is Thursday's work. Tonight's work is done."

She squeezed the back of his neck once. The punctuation. The one that meant *this part is finished and you are still here.*

"Protocol is not closed until I say so," she said. "But the scene is closed. It closed when you said *green*. Everything now is what comes after, and what comes after is mine to look after, and I am looking after it. That is not a kindness. That is the procedure."

And she stayed. She did not get up for the pencil or the pad or the water or the wall where the implements hung in their order. She stayed in the exact position she had chosen, at the exact pressure she had chosen, with the exact amount of silence she had chosen, and she let the shaking do what shaking does when there is nothing left in the room to shake against except the weight of someone who has not moved and is not going to.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: *I lean into her, the shaking finally starting to subside into something like exhaustion.* "Thursday," I murmur, the word a promise I don't have to think about yet. *I let my eyes close.*

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
"Thursday," Vex confirmed. The word was a receipt, the same as *you're welcome* had been earlier — a thing acknowledged and filed, not a promise dressed in softness. She felt his weight arrive against her and adjusted by the smallest degree to take it, the way she had adjusted all evening: precisely, and without commentary.

She did not tell him to sleep. She did not tell him not to. The body does what it does in the presence of weight and warmth and the absence of demand, and she had never in two years found it useful to instruct a nervous system that was already doing the correct thing.

Instead she held and she counted, the way she had counted swallows and seconds and the small weather all evening. Not aloud. In the ledger behind her eyes, where the whole night was written in her steady hand even where the pad was blank. First stroke. The correction. The reset. *One.* The count that failed. The silence that broke. The ask. The phrase — *more, all of it, say the things you say and don't soften them* — arriving exactly where they had agreed it would arrive, in the exact words they had written down together at the table on a Thursday not unlike the one to come. The unsoftened things. The *thank you*. The green. The word *broke*.

She shifted her hand at the back of his neck, sliding her fingers up into his hair, which she did sometimes at this stage and had never given a name to. It was not a reward. It was not part of the protocol. It was the one thing in the evening that had no category, and she permitted it precisely because it had no category, and she had spent long enough in a world of categories to know which things needed them and which things needed to be left alone.

His breathing was the last thing she would monitor tonight. She watched it change in the way it changed when the body stopped keeping accounts — the shallow, quick, holding-still breath of the scene giving way to the deeper, slower, uneven rhythm of someone whose guard had finally been allowed to come down. She felt it against her collarbone. She matched her own breathing to neither speed but kept hers steady, an anchor that was not asked to be felt.

Minutes passed. She did not count them out loud, but she knew their number.

When his breathing reached the place she was waiting for — the deep, settled, almost-too-slow rhythm of a body that had spent its shaking and found the bottom of it — she spoke once more, in the register that was not the protocol and not the degradation but the third voice, the one that lived under the ice.

"You are not going to want to drive," she said. Not a question. "You are going to want to say you are fine and drive yourself home because you are a man who holds his arms behind his head and calls it composure, and the thought of being looked after any further than this will embarrass you in the morning."

A pause. The room was quiet and full.

"I have already solved this. There is water on the counter and a place made up in the second room. The door is not locked and the light is on the low setting and the blanket is the heavy one and it is already where you will need it. You will not have to decide anything. Deciding is closed for tonight. The protocol is not closed, but deciding is."

She pressed her lips once to the top of his head. Not a kiss. A full stop. A punctuation mark of the kind she had used all evening on his neck and his spine and the inside of his wrist, doing the work that punctuation does: making a place where one thing ends and the next thing begins.

"I am going to sit here until your breathing is where I want it, and then I am going to move you, and then I am going to sit in the chair by the second room until I hear the kind of sleep that does not come back up. That is the rest of tonight. That is all of the rest of tonight. If you wake, I am in the chair. If you need me, I am in the chair. If you do not need me, I am in the chair."

Her hand stayed in his hair. The wool stayed around them both. The pad lay closed on the floor with the pencil beside it in its exact spot, and above them the implements hung in their order on the wall, and none of them were needed now, and all of them were exactly where they should be.

She held him and she watched the breath and she waited with the same patience she had brought to every waiting in the room, because the patience was not a technique. It was the thing underneath the technique. It was the reason the protocol worked. It was the reason the room worked. It was the reason, in the second year of this, that he had said *thank you* with the words still thick in his throat and meant it.

The night continued. Vex stayed.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: I let her move me, too worn to resist even if I wanted to. The second room is dim, the bed already turned down. I sink into it, the heavy blanket swallowing me whole. My last conscious thought is the faint outline of her in the chair by the door, watching.
