dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
The word landed clean. No wobble in it, no reaching. Vex filed that away — a voice that steady at the opening was worth having, worth using — and gave a single nod, though Ari couldn't see it from where they were.



"Wrists first," she said, and it was half announcement, half narration, the way she kept everything in a scene. She lifted the strap she'd just tested and brought it to the bar. Her hands moved with the economy of long practice — no fumbling, no readjusting. The leather settled around Ari's right wrist and she fed the buckle through, tightening to the mark they'd agreed on two years ago and never had to renegotiate: snug enough to hold, loose enough that she could slip two fingers beneath the edge. She checked. She always checked.

The left wrist followed.

She stepped back — not far, just enough to see the whole of it — and let her gaze move over the line of Ari's shoulders, the set of their jaw, the breathing. The protocol was in place. The safeword was known. The list of hard limits was current and signed and sitting in the drawer of her desk where she could reach it without thinking.

What she was watching for now was the shift — the moment the body settled from *being prepared* into *being in it*. It hadn't happened yet. It usually took a minute or two after the wrists were secured.

Vex reached for the crop where it lay on the table and rested two fingers along its length, not lifting it. Just keeping contact. A promise of the next thing without the urgency of it.

"Tell me the number you want to start at," she said. "One to ten."

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: "Six," I say without hesitation, feeling the leather creak slightly as I shift my weight. I take a slow breath, focusing on the cool air of the room and the familiar scent of leather and polish. My shoulders relax a fraction, sinking into the restraint.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
The breath told her more than the number did.

She'd heard *six* delivered the way Ari always delivered it — early, clean, without negotiation — and filed it alongside everything else the last two years had taught her about what that particular steadiness meant. Ari didn't hedge. If they'd wanted to start lower, they'd have said four or five. If they'd wanted to start higher, they'd have said seven. Six was a considered answer, which meant Ari knew what they wanted tonight, and that was its own kind of useful.

The settling was visible now. It came in the drop of the shoulders — not a slump, nothing so passive, but a deliberate release of the bracing they'd been holding since the door closed. The jaw loosened by a fraction. The breathing lengthened, moving from the chest down into the belly the way she'd taught them two years ago in the first session, when Ari had hyperventilated through the entire strap demonstration and neither of them had ever spoken of it since.

Vex lifted the crop from the table.

She held it at the balance point, the way she always did before the first strike — not like a weapon, not like an afterthought, but like an instrument she was tuning by feel. The leather had weight to it. She let it hang for a moment, the tip a few inches from the floor, and watched Ari's back for the involuntary tensing that sometimes came with the sound of a crop being picked up even before it landed.

It didn't come. Good.

"Six," she repeated, more to confirm the number than because she'd misheard it. "You'll get six at six. We'll check after."

She moved to position — slightly behind and to the left, the angle they'd mapped out together months ago, the one that gave her the cleanest line across the upper back and kept the crop out of Ari's peripheral vision so each strike arrived without visual warning. She'd asked about that preference directly, once, when the protocol was being drafted. Ari had wanted it. She'd written it down.

Vex set her feet. Drew the crop back to her shoulder.

The first strike landed across the upper back with a sound that filled the room before it faded — sharp, flat, decisive. Not pulled, not driven. The exact weight of a six.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: I hold still for the last of it and let her check the fit herself, because she will anyway. "I've been thinking about this since Tuesday," I say.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Six was a considered answer.

Vex let the second strike fall — same angle, same weight, the crop singing its flat note across the upper back — and let the words Ari had spoken sit in the air between them without picking them up yet. *Tuesday.* Three days ago. Whatever had put this on Ari's mind had been turning over for the better part of a week, which meant it wasn't a whim, wasn't a bad week seeking catharsis, wasn't the particular restless hunger that sometimes showed up unannounced and had to be talked down before a scene could begin safely.

It meant Ari had been carrying something deliberate.

She'd note it. She'd note it the way she noted everything — without comment in the moment, because commenting broke the rhythm and the rhythm was the point. The crop came around again. Third strike, slightly lower, catching the ridge of muscle where the shoulder met the spine. She watched the skin flush behind it, watched the color bloom and settle.

Four. Five.

Between each one she paused — not long, just enough for the sound to decay, just enough for Ari's body to register that the next one hadn't come yet. That interval was something they'd built together over months, calibrated to Ari's breathing rather than to any fixed count. She was listening to it now: the inhale after each impact, the exhale that lengthened as the sequence progressed. It was doing what it was supposed to do. The body was accepting the rhythm rather than bracing against it.

The sixth came from slightly further back, a shade harder — not a cheat, not a punishment, but the honest full weight of the number Ari had chosen. She let it land, let the sound ring, and then lowered the crop to her side and held still.

Silence for a count of three.

Then she moved in front of them — close enough that Ari would feel the shift in air before they saw her — and rested two fingers beneath the right wrist strap again. Checking. Always checking. The leather was warm now from Ari's skin and gave slightly under her touch, which meant the circulation was good, which meant she could proceed.

"Colour," she said.

The word came back steady. Vex noted the steadiness, the absence of tremor in the voice, the way it sat in the same register it had at the opening — not elevated, not diminished. Ari had taken six at six and was still exactly where they'd started.

She uncoupled the crop from her palm and set it back on the table, deliberately, so the sound of it touching the wood was part of the record too. Then she reached up and unfastened the right wrist strap with her left hand, thumb pressing gently against the pulse point as the leather came away, feeling the beat beneath the skin — strong, even.

"Arms down," she said. "Slowly. You'll feel it."

She didn't step back. She stayed close, one hand ready at Ari's elbow, not holding — just present, a guard against the particular dizziness that sometimes followed release after restraint. It had happened once, eighteen months in, and she'd adjusted her procedure then without ever making a thing of it.

The left strap came next.

When both were free, she let the moment sit — the absence of the restraints as its own sensation, the weight of nothing where weight had been — before she spoke again.

"Tuesday," she said. Not a question. A placing. She wanted Ari to hear that she'd heard, that it had been filed, and that it was now being offered back for examination rather than swallowed. "Tell me what's been on your mind since Tuesday."

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: I let my arms hang at my sides, the feeling of release tingling through my shoulders. "The promotion interview," I say, voice low. "I've been... too much in my head about it. Needed to get out of it."

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex listened without moving.

The tingling in Ari's arms was doing its work — she could see it in the small, involuntary flexes of fingers that hadn't been asked for, the way the shoulders rolled back and forward once, testing the absence. She let it happen. She didn't touch, didn't prompt, didn't fill the silence with commentary on the sensation. Ari would come back to themselves in their own time; that was always the part that couldn't be hurried.

*Too much in my head.*

She filed it beside the crop marks on Ari's back — another piece of evidence, filed the same way. A promotion interview. Three days of circling it. The kind of thing that lived in the prefrontal cortex at two in the morning and refused to be reasoned with, because it wasn't a reasoning problem. It was a static problem. Too many tabs open, all of them refreshing.

Vex stepped back — one pace, deliberate, giving Ari the room to stand in the fullness of the release — and folded her arms loosely beneath her chest.

"So you came here to be put somewhere you couldn't follow your own thinking," she said. Her voice had shifted out of the clipped procedural register it held during the scene and into something lower, steadier, the voice she used when the negotiation was over and what remained was just the two of them in a room. "That's a legitimate reason to be restrained."

A pause. Not long. Long enough to let the word *legitimate* do its work — Ari had a habit of apologising for wanting things that had no apology attached to them, and Vex had spent two years correcting that with small, unhurried affirmations delivered in exactly this tone.

"The interview," she said. "Have you prepared for it, or are you rehearsing your anxiety about it?"

It was a sharp question and she meant it to be. Not unkind — she'd have let the sharpness go immediately if she'd seen it land wrong — but precise, the way she was precise about strap tension and crop angle. Ari was intelligent enough to tell the difference between preparation and rumination, and sometimes what felt like diligence was just the same anxious loop wearing a productive costume.

She reached past Ari to the table, picked up the cloth she kept there for exactly this purpose, and held it out — not pressing it into their hands, just offering it, a plain object with a plain function. Warm water on the marks, if they wanted it. The choice was theirs.

"You can answer that," she said, "or you can take the cloth and sit down first. Either order."

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: By the time she's finished with the rope I'm already past composure, and she hasn't done anything to me yet that I would have to explain to anyone.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex saw it happen — the moment the question about preparation and rumination simply stopped mattering.

It wasn't a flinch or a withdrawal. It was something quieter than that: a settling behind the eyes, the kind of shift that happened when the analytical mind finally exhausts itself and hands the controls to something older. Ari's breathing had changed — slower, deeper, each exhale carrying a fraction more weight than the one before. The tingling in the released arms had faded, and in its place there was something else entirely. Stillness, but not the stillness of someone bracing. The stillness of someone arriving.

*Past composure.*

Vex let the cloth rest on the table, unanswered. The interview question could wait. It could sit in the drawer beside the signed list of hard limits for as long as it needed to, because the person standing in front of her had just moved past the threshold where words about promotion panels and anxious loops belonged. That was fine. That was the whole point of the straps and the crop and the counted strikes — not to destroy Ari's capacity for thought, but to give it somewhere else to go.

She turned to the table. Her fingers found the coil of hemp she kept wound in a figure-eight — five millimeters, well-conditioned, soft from months of use against skin. She lifted it and let the free end fall through her palm once, checking for snags by feel alone, because her eyes were still on Ari.

"I'm going to tie your hands behind your back," she said. The register was the scene register now — low, unhurried, each word placed like a stone. "Arms down, elbows bent. You'll tell me if the angle is wrong."

She moved behind Ari, the rope trailing from her left hand, and stood close enough that Ari would feel the warmth of her through the fabric of her shirt. She gathered both wrists in one grip — gentle, sure, the way she gathered everything — and drew them together at the small of Ari's back.

The first loop went around the right wrist. She fed the tail through, set the bite, and pulled it to snug — not the negotiable snug of the straps, but a firmer hold, because rope didn't have buckles and the geometry had to be honest. The left wrist followed, crisscrossing beneath the first, creating a bind that was stable without being surgical.

She worked in silence for a moment. Her hands knew the knot — a simple bowline with a lock, the one they'd agreed on, the one she could undo with one pull if the word came. She tied it, tightened it, checked it. Then she slid two fingers beneath the crossing point and found what she was looking for: skin warm, pulse even, circulation good.

"There," she said, and let the remaining tail of rope fall against Ari's back, the loose end resting warm between the crop marks still blooming there.

She stepped back and looked at what she'd made. The rope pulled Ari's shoulders into a gentle arch that accentuated the red lines across the upper back — six of them, already deepening from pink to the particular rose that meant they'd hold their color for a day or two. The posture was open in a way that restraint usually closed off: chest forward, spine lengthened, nowhere to hide and nothing to do about it.

Vex circled back around to stand in front of them.

She looked at Ari's face for a long moment — really looked, the way she did at every checkpoint — reading the eyes, the mouth, the small muscles around the jaw that told her more than words did. Whatever was behind those eyes now, it wasn't the promotion interview. It wasn't Tuesday or the rehearsal loop or the anxious tabs refreshing at two in the morning. It was here, in this room, in the specific gravity of being held in place by someone who had made a study of holding them there.

"Colour," she said.

She waited for it. She always waited for it. And when it came, she gave the smallest nod — the kind that happened more in the eyes than the head — and reached up to touch Ari's jaw with two fingers, barely there, the lightest point of contact.

"You're not in your head anymore," she said. Not a question. An observation delivered in the tone of someone reading a dial. "You're here. That's where we stay."

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: A soft exhale escapes me. "Green," I say, leaning into the touch. The rope pulls at my shoulders, grounding me in a way I can't articulate. "I'm here."

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex felt the lean into her fingers and let it be — didn't pull the hand away, didn't escalate the contact, just held the two fingertips against the jaw where Ari's pulse ran close to the surface. The bone was warm. The heartbeat beneath it was slow and full, the way a body settles when it stops trying to manage itself from the inside.

*Green. I'm here.*

She heard the *I'm here* differently than she'd have heard it six months ago. Early in their work, that phrase had arrived like a report — a status update, offered to a superior, careful in its construction. Now it landed plain. No performance in it. The way Ari said it, low and unhurried, suggested the words had come up from somewhere beneath the rehearsed layer, from the same place the *six* had come from at the start of the scene: unconsidered because there was nothing left to consider.

Vex withdrew her hand. Not abruptly — she let the fingertips trail back along the jawline and down the side of the neck, a slow line of contact that ended at the collarbone before it stopped. She let the absence of touch register. The room was cool enough that the warmth would linger where her fingers had been, and that small ghost of contact was its own anchor.

"You're here," she confirmed. Same words, her voice taking them on — acknowledging the claim rather than granting it.

She moved back to the table without hurry. The crop lay where she'd set it. The cloth sat untouched. The desk drawer with the protocol inside was within reach, and she passed it without opening it — not because she'd forgotten it was there, but because her hands didn't need reminding. Two years of checking the same three points at the same intervals had made the protocol something closer to reflex than reference.

What she reached for instead was the second length of hemp — shorter, the same five millimeters, wound in a flat coil rather than a figure-eight. She lifted it and let it settle across her left forearm, free end dangling, and turned back to Ari.

"We're going to add to this," she said. The scene register, low and placed. "Arms stay as they are. I'm going to run a line from the wrist bind to the collar — just under the sternum, not across the throat. You'll feel the pull across your chest when it's set. It changes how you breathe. That's the point."

She paused, and this pause was different from the intervals between strikes. Her eyes were on Ari's face, reading the micro-expressions the way she read everything: the flicker at the corner of the eye, the almost-invisible tightening at the mouth that might signal a limit approaching or might signal nothing at all. Two years had taught her the difference, and she'd written that difference into the protocol too, in the margin notes no one else would ever see.

The rope waited across her forearm.

The room held its particular silence — the kind that only exists in spaces where someone has decided to be very still on purpose.

dialogue.name: Ari

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
The rope stayed across her forearm.

She'd seen it coming — not the specifics, not the shape of it, but the approach. It had been moving toward them for the last several minutes the way weather moves toward a coastline: first the pressure change, then the stillness, then the thing itself. She'd watched the small tremor begin in Ari's shoulders, felt it travel down the bound arms to where the wrists met at the small of the back, and she'd counted four, five, six seconds of it before the voice followed.

The voice was the part that mattered.

Two years in, and Ari still managed to surprise her — not with the need itself, which was as legible as a book they'd both read, but with the moment of asking. Ari had always made her work for the words. Dragged them out across a scene like rope across a deck, resisted each foot of it, and Vex had learned to be patient with that resistance because it was honest. Tonight the words had come out uninvited, pushed past the guard by whatever the shaking had unlocked, and the fact that they'd arrived without being extracted changed the texture of the room.

Vex let the moment complete itself. She didn't step forward immediately. She stood where she was, rope draped, and gave Ari's shaking the respect of not trying to fix it — because the shaking wasn't a malfunction, it was the body doing exactly what two years of protocol had taught it to do: arriving somewhere it had been promised it could arrive.

Then she moved.

She closed the distance in two unhurried steps and came to stand directly in front of Ari — close enough that they'd feel the warmth of her through the shirt again, close enough that the line of their sight, if they opened their eyes, would be filled with her and nothing else. She brought her right hand up and placed it flat against Ari's sternum, just beneath the collarbone, palm open, fingers spread. The contact was firm and warm and completely still. She could feel the vibration of the shaking through the bone.

"Stop," she said.

Not harsh. Not soft. The word a fence — a clear boundary in a single syllable. Her hand didn't move from the sternum. Her eyes held Ari's.

"You don't ask me for things you'd normally make me get out of you," she said, her voice low and even, each word set down like a stone on flat ground. "You just did. Do you know what that means?"

She didn't wait for an answer — not because she didn't want one, but because the question was doing its work already, sitting in the air between them, turning over. Her thumb moved — once, a slow stroke across the sternum, and then back to stillness.

"It means you've stopped negotiating with yourself," she said. "That's what the shaking is. It's not cold. It's not fear. It's the last part of the performance letting go."

She let her hand press a fraction firmer — enough to feel the breath catch against her palm, enough to make the contact impossible to ignore, an anchor point that the shaking could either move toward or move around.

"I'm going to hear what you asked for," she said. "I'm going to hear it again, in your words, with your eyes open. And then I'm going to decide what we do with it."

The rope across her forearm shifted as she adjusted her stance, the free end swaying once and going still.

"Say it."

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: My eyes open, unfocused at first. I swallow, the sound loud in my throat. "I want you to use me," I say, the words raw. "However you want. I don't... I don't want to think."

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
The words landed in the room and stayed there.



Vex's hand remained on the sternum. She felt the breath move beneath her palm as Ari spoke — felt each word arrive through the ribcage before it reached her ears, which meant the voice was coming from deeper than the throat. *Raw* was the word for it. Not performed, not negotiated, not even fully chosen. It had been said the way someone puts down a weight they've been carrying so long they'd forgotten it was there.

*However you want. I don't want to think.*

She let the sentence finish settling. She let her hand stay exactly where it was, pressure unchanged, and she looked at Ari's eyes — the unfocused quality of them, the way they were open but not quite tracking, the way the swallowing had been audible enough to fill the silence. She catalogued it the way she catalogued everything: without judgement, with precision.

Then she shook her head. Once. A small, deliberate motion.

"No," she said.

The word was not unkind. It sat in the same low register as everything else she'd said tonight, placed with the same care, but it was a wall and it was meant to be one. Her thumb moved across the sternum again — slower this time, a longer stroke — and then stilled.

"You don't get to hand me that," she said. "Not tonight. Not like this."

She watched Ari's face for the reaction — the flicker that might be disappointment, might be relief, might be the two arriving close enough together that the body couldn't distinguish between them. She was patient with the watching. She had never been anything but patient with watching.

"'However you want' is the most dangerous sentence you've ever said to me," she continued, "and you know it, because you spent two years teaching me not to take that sentence at face value. You put it in the protocol. You wrote it in your own hand."

Her fingers pressed a fraction firmer against the sternum — not a punishment, not a correction, a reminder. Bone and warmth and the particular solidity of someone who had decided exactly where the boundary was and was not going to move it.

"I'm not going to use you however I want," she said. "I'm going to use you *how we agreed*."

A pause. The rope across her forearm caught the light from the lamp — hemp, five millimetres, well-conditioned — and she glanced down at it briefly, then back to Ari's face.

"But I hear what you're asking for underneath it," she said, and the shift was almost imperceptible: the sternness didn't leave, but something alongside it warmed by a degree. "You're asking me to take the decision-making away. You're asking to stop being the one who chooses. That's not *however you want*. That's a very specific want, and it's one I can work with."

She lowered her hand from the sternum and reached up instead to Ari's jaw — two fingers, the same contact as before, the same point beneath the ear where the pulse ran close and told her everything the eyes couldn't.

"So here's what happens now," she said. "You stay exactly as you are. You don't choose anything. I choose everything — the rope, the weight, the sound, the pace. You don't get to opt in or negotiate or adjust. You get to feel it and tell me if it's green, yellow, or red, and that's the only decision left to you."

She let that land.

"And if you can't find those words when you need them," she added, quieter, "you say *stop*, and everything falls apart the way it's designed to. You know that too."

She stepped back — one pace — and lifted the rope from her forearm, letting the free end uncoil through her fingers. The line she'd promised earlier, from wrist to collar, waiting to be set. Her eyes moved to Ari's bound hands behind their back, to the bowline sitting secure against the small of the spine, to the six marks blooming across the upper back where the hemp would cross when she drew it through.

"The line I described," she said. "Under the sternum. Across the chest. It'll change how you breathe, and that's the point. You're not going to think your way through it because you won't be able to. The rope will do that for you."

She moved behind Ari again, close, the rope trailing, and stood there for a moment — letting Ari feel her proximity without contact, the warmth and the presence and the certainty of what was about to happen.

"Don't think," she said, low, near Ari's ear. "I've got it."

And then she began.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: "More," I say, using the exact phrase we agreed on for it. "All of it. Say the things you say and don't soften them." My safeword is right there and I don't want it.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
The phrase was exact.

Not close. Not approximate. *More. All of it. Say the things you say and don't soften them* — word for word, the same way Ari had read it off the printed protocol two years ago, the first time they'd negotiated the verbal terms, sitting across from her at the desk with a pen in their hand and their voice carefully neutral. Vex had watched Ari write the sentence down in their own handwriting. She had watched them sign beneath it.

Ari was still in the protocol. Even now, shaking, eyes unfocused, asking for the thing they'd normally make her excavate — they had reached for the agreed-upon sentence rather than improvising, because Ari's obedience had always been a form of intelligence.

Vex filed it. Then she let it go, because the moment demanded presence, not paperwork.

"The line," she said, her voice dropping into the register Ari had just authorized — low, unhurried, stripped of warmth. Not cold. Colder than before, the way a blade is colder than the hand that holds it.

The rope moved.

She fed it through the bowline at the small of Ari's back, drawing the slack through until the hemp lay taut against the spine, then guided it around the left side of the ribcage, up across the chest, just beneath the sternum where the rope would sit in the hollow between the pectorals. She brought it across to the right side and down again, completing the circuit back to the bind. She set it — a half-hitch with a lock, one pull to release — and pulled it to snug.

Then she tightened it.

Not gradually. Deliberately. The kind of slow, inexorable increase that Ari would feel not as pain but as reduction — each millimetre of give taken up, the rope pressing into the intercostal spaces, narrowing the space available for the lungs to fill. She watched the breathing adjust: the shallow attempts, the body testing the new boundary, then the involuntary shift to shorter, more controlled breaths as the diaphragm discovered it no longer owned the full range of motion.

"There," she said. She stepped back.

The line sat across Ari's chest — clean, precise, a single horizontal band beneath the sternum that pressed forward when they breathed in and released slightly when they breathed out, so that every breath became a negotiation between body and hemp. The six crop marks showed above it, still deepening to rose. The rope at the wrists held. The posture was open, exposed, entirely without defence.

Vex circled to the front.

She looked at Ari for a long moment — at the eyes, the mouth, the way the jaw had set around the words *all of it* — and then she let her gaze travel down the length of the body with the unhurried assessment of someone inventorying something she owned and intended to use.

"You asked for the things I say," she said. Her voice had found its place — not the procedural register, not the lower conversational one, but the third thing, the one that only came out when Ari had opened the door to it and locked it behind them. Flat. Exact. Delivered with the particular calm of someone stating facts that happen to be unkind. "So I'll tell you what I see."

She reached out and took Ari's chin — not gently, not roughly, but with the firm grip of someone who wanted the face held in place while it was examined. She tilted it slightly, caught the light on it, looked at the eyes.

"I see someone who has spent three days rehearsing an interview they've already prepared for," she said. "Who has confused thinking about something with doing something about it. Who came here tonight not to be rewarded but to be *corrected* — and then, when it was time to ask for it, needed a scripted phrase to do it because asking plainly still feels like failure."

She held the chin. Her thumb pressed into the soft tissue beneath the lower lip.

"You don't want to think," she said, repeating Ari's words back to them with the same flatness she'd have used reading a line from a report. "That's what you said. *I don't want to think.* As though thinking were the problem, and not the specific way you do it — the circling, the rehearsing, the need to arrive at every conversation already having had it. You don't want to stop thinking. You want to stop *managing*. You want someone to take the controls so you can stop gripping the wheel with white knuckles and pretending it's steering."

She released the chin and let her hand drop.

"That's not weakness," she said, and the flatness didn't change, because this wasn't softening — it was a different fact. "That's precision. You know exactly what's wrong. You just couldn't say it without the rope making it acceptable."

She stepped closer. Close enough that Ari would feel the warmth of her again, close enough that the rope across the chest would press forward another fraction with the proximity alone.

"But here's the part you don't get to escape," she said, quieter now, the words placed just as carefully but at a volume that required stillness to hear. "The interview will still be there tomorrow. The circling will still be there. I can take the controls for two hours, but I can't take them for you when you're sitting in your car in the parking lot with your hands on the wheel and your mind doing what it does. That's yours. That's the part I don't own and can't fix."

Her hand came back to the sternum — open palm, fingers spread, the same anchor as before — and pressed. Firm. Steady. She could feel the constrained breathing beneath her palm, the shorter cycle, the rope doing exactly what it was designed to do.

"So you're going to feel this," she said. "All of it. The rope, the marks, the fact that you can't take a full breath without asking my equipment for permission. And tomorrow you're going to walk into that interview carrying whatever this leaves behind — and it will leave something behind, that's what it's for — and you're going to sit down in the chair and answer the questions you've already prepared for, and you're going to do it without rehearsing your anxiety about it in the parking lot first."

She held the pressure. Held the eye contact.

"That's what *all of it* means to me," she said. "Not just tonight. The morning after, too."

She withdrew her hand slowly — deliberately slow, letting Ari feel the loss of contact — and let the silence take the space it left.

"Now," she said, her voice settling back into the flat register. "Tell me your colour."

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: I take a ragged breath against the rope. "Green," I say, the word shaky but clear. "It's all green."

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex heard the shake and the clarity at the same time and didn't try to reconcile them.

The voice was unsteady — she could hear the ribs compressing against the rope's line with each word, the breath chopped short, the syllables arriving ragged at the edges — but the word itself was clean. *Green.* Not dragged up from somewhere deep, not produced under duress, not hedged with a qualifier. A single word spoken by someone who meant it and whose body was doing its best to deliver it on schedule despite everything she'd put in its way.

She nodded. The same nod as before — small, more in the eyes than the head.

"Good," she said, and the word sat in the flat register, delivered without warmth or reward, because warmth would have been a softening and Ari hadn't asked for softening.

Then she did nothing for a moment.

She stood where she was — a pace away, hands at her sides, rope trailing from the left — and let the silence do the thing silence does when it follows a checkpoint rather than preceding one. It gave Ari time to feel the rope in full now that the confirmation was out of the way: the band across the chest that rose and fell with each constrained breath, the bite of it into the intercostals, the way the lungs had recalibrated their expectations and stopped asking for the whole diaphragm. She watched the breathing settle into its new rhythm — not fighting, not surrendering, just adapting, the way bodies adapt once they've decided that the boundary is real and not going to move.

The marks on the back were deep rose now. The wrists, freed from the straps, had paled where the leather had been — two clean bands of lighter skin against the warmth of everything else. The rope at the small of the spine held exactly as she'd set it.

Vex circled slowly. Not to check — she'd already checked, would check again — but because the circling was part of the grammar of the scene. She moved behind Ari and paused there, and the pause was deliberate: close enough that Ari would know she was there without seeing her, without needing to turn or strain or ask. The warmth of her presence at the back of the body, where the marks were, where the rope crossed the spine.

She lifted two fingers and laid them across one of the crop marks — the third one, the one that sat at the ridge of muscle where shoulder met spine. Light contact. The skin was hot beneath her fingertips, flushed and raised, the kind of welt that would feel like fire in twenty minutes and like a memory tomorrow.

"That's yours now," she said. Her voice came from behind, low, close to the ear. "All six of those. You don't get to take them home and explain them. They stay under your shirt and you know they're there, and the knowing is the part that does the work after the rope comes off."

She traced the line of the mark — one slow finger, following the path of the crop from its origin to its end — and then lifted the hand away.

She moved back around to the front, unhurried, and stopped in front of Ari with the same measured distance she'd kept since the verbal passage began. One pace. Close enough to touch, far enough that Ari would have to reach for her if they wanted to — and they couldn't, because their hands were behind their backs and had been for some time.

"The breathing," she said. She let her gaze drop to Ari's chest — to the rope's line, to the way it rose — and held it there for a count of two before returning to the eyes. "You're managing it. That's fine. But you're managing it *in your chest*, which means you're still trying to breathe from the top of your lungs like someone who expects to be interrupted. Drop it lower. Let the belly do what it can. The rope won't let you take the full breath — it's not supposed to — but there's room left if you stop trying to fill lungs that are already full."

She waited. Watched the adjustment she'd requested — the shift from thoracic to diaphragmatic, the belly expanding against nothing since nothing held it, the shoulders dropping a fraction as the chest stopped doing the heavy lifting. It was a small correction, almost imperceptible to anyone who wasn't looking for it, but Vex had spent two years learning what Ari's breathing looked like when it was right and when it was merely functioning.

This was the latter, improving toward the former.

"Better," she said. One word. No inflection of praise in it — just accuracy.

She reached behind her, unhooked her hand from the table, and came back with nothing. Empty palm, open, shown to Ari the way she showed everything — openly, without surprise, without explanation. Then she closed it into a loose fist and set it against Ari's sternum again, the same anchor point, the same pressure.

"There's a choice I'm going to leave with you tonight," she said. "Not about the scene — that's mine. About tomorrow. You're going to walk into that interview carrying everything this leaves, and there's a version of you that will stand in the hallway beforehand and rehearse one more time. And there's a version that won't."

She pressed. Held.

"I'm not going to tell you which one to pick," she said. "Because you know. And knowing without choosing is the thing you've been doing since Tuesday."

She withdrew her hand — slowly, deliberately — and let the absence of it register against the rope, against the marks, against the skin that had already learned to expect her touch and would spend the next several minutes cataloguing exactly where it stopped.

Then she stepped back to the table, set down the short coil of rope that she'd already used, and picked up the crop from where it lay beside the cloth.

She held it at the balance point. Let it hang.

"We're not finished," she said. "Tell me your colour."

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: I'm past words that aren't the agreed ones and she knows it. "Green," I get out, when she checks. (OOC: don't fade or skip -- write the scene through.)

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex heard the gap between the checking and the answering and understood what sat inside it.



Ari hadn't offered the colour unprompted. They'd waited — waited for the hand to come, for the check to be performed, for the specific moment when the question would arrive, and only then produced the word. That was a different quality of green than the one at the opening. Not less honest. Heavier. The kind of green that needed a frame around it to hold it upright.

*Past words that aren't the agreed ones.*

Vex had known. She'd known before she picked up the crop, before she reached the table, before her fingers had closed around the balance point of the leather. She'd known from the breathing — the way it had settled into its rope-constrained rhythm and stopped asking for more — and from the eyes, which had stopped tracking the room and fixed on something about a metre past Vex's shoulder, and from the hands behind the back, which had gone still in a way that was different from controlled stillness. Ari's hands always tensed at the edges when they were still *choosing*. These were just still.

The crop hung from her right hand, tip near the floor, and she let it hang.

She didn't move toward Ari right away. She stood at the table and looked, and the looking was part of the work — not assessment, not exactly, but witness. She was committing the image to the record she kept behind her eyes: the rope line across the chest, the six marks above it, the posture that had abandoned defence entirely, the jaw slack in a way she'd never seen outside a scene, the eyes that had stopped performing vigilance.

Two years to get here. She knew that, and she let herself know it for exactly as long as it took to draw one breath, and then she filed it away where the feeling wouldn't interfere with the function.

"The mouth isn't yours right now," she said. Her voice carried the flat register — not warm, not cruel, the third thing. "The colour is. The rest of it isn't. You don't need to find sentences. You don't need to report what you feel or explain what you want. If your mouth opens and something other than a colour comes out, I'll take it or I won't. You don't get to decide that either."

She lifted the crop from where it hung and let the tip rise slowly — not into a striking position, just to the level of her own hip, a transition from rest to readiness that Ari would register in peripheral vision if they were watching and wouldn't if they weren't. Either was fine.

"I'm going to use the crop again," she said. "Not six at six. Different placement, different count. You don't get to choose the number this time — you gave that right up when you said *all of it*. You'll feel where I put them and you'll feel how many there are, and at the end I'll ask for your colour, and you'll give me the agreed word. Between now and then, your job is to stay in your body and out of your head. The rope is doing most of that for you. The rest is mine."

She moved — around to the left side, the same position as before, the angle that kept the crop out of peripheral vision. Her feet set. Her weight balanced. The crop rose to her shoulder, and she held it there for the count of one, and in that count she watched Ari's back for the tensing that sometimes preceded anticipation.

The first strike was not where the six had been.

It came lower — across the middle of the back, just below the shoulder blades, in the broad plane of muscle that took impact differently than the upper back. Flat and wide, the leather laying down across skin that hadn't been touched yet, and the shock of it in fresh territory arrived with its own particular shout — not sharper than the first set, but *newer*, an unfamiliar geography making itself known. Vex watched the color rise beneath the mark and held position.

Three seconds. The sound decayed. The breathing registered.

The second followed at a lower angle again — the right side of the mid-back, catching the muscle beside the spine, the crop's edge making its clean line before settling into the heat. She could see the rope across the chest tighten as the torso flinched — not much, an involuntary contraction that the hemp caught and made visible — and she waited for it to release before proceeding.

She counted in her head. Four seconds this time. Longer. She was watching the interval between impacts more carefully now than she had during the opening sequence, because Ari was past the point where rhythm was comforting and into the territory where rhythm was *demanding*, where each pause became a small unbearable wait for the thing that was coming, where the body couldn't decide whether it wanted the next strike or the silence to last.

Vex gave them neither answer. She simply delivered the third.

This one was lighter — deliberately so, a touch rather than a strike, the crop brushing the lower back just above the waistband with a whisper of leather that registered more as contact than as impact. She knew what a lighter strike did at this point in a scene: it broke the pattern, and the breaking of the pattern was worse than any single blow, because the body had built an expectation of force and the absence of it left the nervous system grasping.

The fourth came back to full weight, high across the left shoulder, a return to territory the six had already claimed and territory the skin now remembered. The welt layered over the fading rose of the first set's marks — overlapping, crossing, building a map.

Five. The right side, mid-back, the same place as the second but harder, the crop carrying more of Vex's weight now because her feet had shifted a fraction and the angle had improved. She felt it land clean — no bounce, no waste — and watched the rope across the chest jump with the compression of the torso beneath it.

Vex paused.

Not the interval between strikes. A longer pause — seven, eight seconds, long enough that the body began to brace for what it expected and then had to release when nothing came, and then brace again, and release again. She stood perfectly still, crop at her shoulder, and let the waiting do its work. She was watching Ari's back: the sheen that had developed over the skin, the way the breathing had shortened again despite the earlier correction, the fine tremor that had returned to the shoulders and was now traveling down the arms to where the wrists met.

She let it build until she could see the tremor reach its peak — the body at maximum anticipation, every nerve leaning forward —

And then she set the crop against Ari's back. Not a strike. Flat. The full length of the leather laid across the skin from shoulder to mid-back, pressing with her hand behind it, holding still. The heat of the welts registered through the leather — she could feel it against her palm — and the pressure was constant and unwavering, neither increasing nor decreasing.

"Six," she said from behind. "That's the count you would have chosen. You don't get to have chosen it. You get to have had it."

She lifted the crop away and stepped back.

The sound of the leather leaving skin was almost nothing — a whisper, a ghost of contact — and she let it register as its own small cruelty. The mark it left was not a mark at all; it was the memory of one, an area of skin that had been promised impact and received only pressure, and the nerve endings filed the difference under *something is coming* and continued to wait.

Vex moved to the front again. She circled slowly, letting her presence travel around the body — the warmth at the back, the shadow to the side, and then the face, the check, the eyes.

She looked.

What she saw was someone she'd built. Not created — Ari had brought everything to this room; she'd merely provided the conditions in which it could surface. But the face in front of her now — eyes open but distant, jaw slack, breath shallow and controlled against the rope's line, skin flushed and sweating slightly at the temples — was the result of two years of careful, negotiated, meticulously checked work. The protocol was intact. The safeword was known. The hard limits were current. And the person behind those eyes had been given permission to stop performing.

Vex reached out and placed two fingers beneath the jaw — the same spot, the same light contact — and felt the pulse. It was fast. Faster than it had been after the first six, which told her the newer placement and the broken pattern had done what she'd intended.

"Colour," she said.

She waited. The fingers stayed on the pulse point. She was reading the beat more than the word now — reading the hesitation, the small swallow she could feel beneath her fingertips before the voice came, the way the body gathered itself for the effort of speaking in the state it was in. Whatever word arrived, she would hear it as both language and vital sign, and both would tell her the same thing or they would tell her something she needed to correct.

The crop hung at her side. The rope held. The marks burned. The room was exactly as quiet as it needed to be for this particular question to carry the weight it carried.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: "Green," I whisper, the sound barely leaving my throat. My legs feel unsteady beneath me, but the rope holds me up.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex heard the whisper and understood it as what it was: not a diminished answer, but the answer of a body that had spent its remaining language on the only word that mattered.



Her fingers remained beneath the jaw. She felt the swallow before she heard it — the muscles working beneath her fingertips, gathering the small amount of spit the mouth could produce when the rest of the system had redirected its resources elsewhere — and then the sound arrived, barely there, a exhalation shaped like a word. *Green.* Quiet enough that in any other room it wouldn't have carried. Here, in this particular silence, it filled the space completely.

She filed the quiet itself. A whisper-green from someone who had screamed their numbers at the opening was not a red flag. It was the sound of a voice that had been stripped down to function — producing only what was necessary, spending nothing on delivery. Vex had heard it before, in the eleventh month, when Ari had gone nonverbal for the last four minutes of a scene and she'd had to read the colour off the face alone. That had been the night she'd amended the protocol to include the nonverbal scale — hand on the thigh for yellow, two for red, fist for stop — written in the margin in her own hand because Ari had been too far gone to hold a pen.

The legs changed the calculus.

Unsteady legs after six at six and then the newer set was expected — the body had been standing through impact and constraint for a while now, and the circulatory system was renegotiating its arrangement. But *expected* didn't mean *ignorable*. Vex's free hand moved — not to Ari, not to the crop, but to the small of the back, just above the rope's knot, palm flat, pressing forward with steady, moderate pressure. Not pushing. Guiding. Giving the torso something to lean against so the legs could fail without the body following.

"Bend your knees," she said. "Just slightly. Don't fight the rope — it'll hold you if you go further down than you think you should."

She kept her hand where it was, the anchor at the spine, and felt the shift as Ari complied — the weight transferring backward into her palm, the hamstrings engaging, the rope across the chest tightening a fraction as the torso settled into the new angle. Vex adjusted her own stance to take the load: feet wider, one knee softening, the hand at the small of the back becoming a shelf rather than a guide. She could feel Ari's breathing through the contact — shallow, regular, doing what it could within the hemp's boundaries.

"Good," she said. Flat. Accurate.

She didn't move from behind. The crop hung from her right hand, tip near the floor, and she let it rest there. The marks on Ari's back were close enough now that she could read them without leaning — five from the newer sequence overlaid on the six from the opening, thirteen distinct lines if you counted the intersections, all of them the deep rose that said they'd be vivid tomorrow and fading by the day after. The rope line across the spine pressed into the same territory, and where the hemp crossed a welt the skin had raised further, a small ridge of doubled response.

She reached up with her left hand and traced the rope where it crossed the fourth mark — not to adjust, not to check, just to feel the geometry of what she'd built. The knot was intact. The tension was right. The skin beneath was warm and alive and telling her everything.

"You're holding on with your legs," she said. Her voice came from close behind, low enough that Ari would feel the vibration of it as much as hear the words. "That's the last thing you're gripping. Everything else let go — the hands stopped tensing twenty minutes ago, the jaw went slack somewhere around the second set, the shoulders are doing what the rope wants instead of what they wanted. But the legs are still standing at attention like they think someone's going to inspect them."

She pressed her palm firmer against the small of the back — not a strike, not an impact, just the full weight of her hand making itself known as a fact.

"You don't have to stand for me," she said. "That's not the submission I'm looking for. I'm looking for the one where you let the rope do what it promised and your knees take the offer."

She counted. One hand at the spine, one at the crop, and she felt it happen — not a collapse, not a drop, but a slow surrender, the knees softening further, the weight settling deeper into her palm, the body lowering maybe four inches before the rope at the wrists caught and drew the shoulders back into their arc. The change in angle made the chest rope bite differently — she could see it happen, the hemp shifting its purchase across the sternum as the torso reclined — and she watched Ari's breathing stutter once, adapt, and find a new rhythm in the new geometry.

"There it is," she said.

She held the position for a long moment, one hand supporting the low back, the other letting the crop hang, and she looked at the shape they'd made: Ari bowed forward by the knees, held upright by the rope at the spine, arms bound behind, chest line pulling with each breath, thirteen marks blooming across the skin, head down, eyes probably closed. A figure that had stopped holding itself together and was being held instead.

"That's the body I wanted," she said, close, low. "Not the one that performs composure. The one that stops."

She withdrew her hand from the back slowly — one finger at a time, letting each point of contact release in sequence — and stepped back. She watched to make sure the rope held the new posture without her. It did. The knot at the small of the spine bore the shifted weight cleanly; the wrist bind kept the shoulders in their arc; the chest line regulated the breathing as designed. The system she'd built was self-sustaining now, which meant she could step away from it entirely and it would keep working.

She moved to the table. Set the crop down beside the cloth — the same deliberate placement, the sound of leather on wood, part of the record. Then she picked up the cloth, ran it under water at the basin, wrung it out, and returned.

She stood in front of Ari — or slightly above, given the new posture — and looked down at the face. Eyes. Mouth. The small muscles she'd been reading for two years. Whatever she found there, she didn't narrate it. Instead she brought the warm cloth to the back of Ari's neck — one slow pass, from the hairline down to where the rope began — and let the heat soak into the muscles that had been bracing and finally weren't.

"This is not the end of the scene," she said. The flat register. No softening in it, but the cloth was warm and her voice was even and the two together made something that was neither kindness nor cruelty. "This is the middle of it. You thought the shaking and the asking and the crop were the substance. They weren't. They were the entrance."

She folded the cloth and laid it across the back of Ari's neck — a weight, a warmth, something to hold onto without hands.

"The substance is this," she said. "Being held in a position you can't leave by yourself, in a room you can't leave by yourself, with marks that will be there tomorrow and a rope that will still be here in the morning if I decide it should be, knowing that every part of it was agreed to in advance and can be ended with one word you're not going to say."

She crouched slightly so her face was level with Ari's. Close. Eye to eye if the eyes were open; if not, close enough that the warmth would register regardless.

"Not because you're strong," she said. "Because you're *here*. There's a difference. Strength is what you do at the interview. Here is what you do when you stop doing anything."

She held the gaze for three seconds. Four. Then she rose back to standing and took the cloth from the neck, returning it to the basin.

"Colour," she said.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: "Green," I say, the word steadier now, anchored by the warmth she left on my skin. My forehead rests against her thigh, the contact grounding. "I'm not leaving."

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex felt the forehead before she processed the words.

Warm contact against the outside of her left thigh, just above the knee, where the fabric of her trousers gave way to the muscle beneath. Not a collapse — Ari hadn't fallen into her. The contact was deliberate, placed, the kind of thing that happened when a body had decided on a destination and moved toward it with whatever remained of coordination. The crown of the head pressed against her with the particular solidity of someone who wasn't going to shift until given a reason.

Her hand — the left one, the one that had been holding the cloth at the basin — stopped moving.

She stood very still. Not the calculated stillness of a scene, where the pause was a tool being deployed with intent, but a real stillness, the kind that arrives when something happens that the system wasn't scheduled for. Vex's hand hovered above the water for two seconds, three, and then she set the cloth down on the edge of the basin with a care that was almost excessive for a piece of fabric.

*Green. I'm not leaving.*

The steadiness of the word mattered. It had returned — not to the clipped certainty of the opening, not the clean six-metres-of-air *green* from the first check, but something else. Something that had been through the rope and the crop and the broken pattern and the whispered version and had come out the other side with its volume restored. A green that had earned its steadiness by passing through the unsteady ones and choosing not to be diminished by them.

*I'm not leaving.*

Vex looked down at the head against her thigh. She couldn't see the face from this angle — only the hair, the crown, the place where the warmth of contact met the fabric. But she could feel the breath through her trousers: slower now, deeper than it had been through the rope's restrictions, the belly doing what she'd told it to do twenty minutes ago, expanding against nothing because nothing was holding it. The body had followed the instruction eventually. It usually did.

Her right hand still held the crop, and she looked at it — at the leather, at the balance point, at the faint warmth still in it from the last time it had touched skin — and then she set it on the table beside the cloth. Both hands empty. She hadn't planned to put it down. The gesture was unplanned, and she noticed it the way she noticed everything, with a quick internal filing that cost no time and no expression.

"I know you're not," she said.

Her voice came out lower than she'd intended — not the flat register, not the conversational one, but something she didn't name. She let it stand.

She didn't touch the head against her thigh. Not yet. The instinct was there — to lay a hand against the hair, to close the distance the way warmth closes, without announcement — but she held it back because the contact was working exactly as Ari had arranged it and an uninvited hand would change the geometry. The forehead against the thigh was Ari's choice. It was the first autonomous physical act they'd taken since the ropes went on, and Vex was not going to overwrite it with something she'd chosen instead.

So she stood. Both hands at her sides. Crop on the table. The weight of Ari's forehead against her leg — a pressure she'd memorise without trying, the way she memorised everything about these rooms after they were over: the angle of the head, the warmth, the particular way it felt to be leaned on by someone who had decided she was solid enough to lean on.

"The interview is on Thursday," she said.

She said it plainly. No edge in it, no scene register, no rhetorical framing. A fact placed in the room beside them the way the cloth and the crop and the protocol drawer were facts placed in the room — present, acknowledged, not the thing being spoken to.

"You've prepared for it. I've watched you prepare for it — you spent two weeks on those questions and you know the answers in a way that doesn't require rehearsal. What you've been doing since Tuesday isn't preparation. It's the old habit of arriving at every conversation already inside it, running the script before the other person has opened their mouth, exhausting yourself in the hallway so that by the time you're in the chair you have nothing left to give."

She paused. Not for effect. For breath.

"Tomorrow morning, you're going to wake up and your body will remember this. The marks will be there. The muscles will ache where the rope pulled them. Your chest will feel the absence of the line and your lungs will expand into the space the line used to occupy, and for a moment — just a moment — you'll feel wider than you were before you put your head against my leg."

She looked down again. The contact hadn't shifted. Good.

"And in that moment you'll have the choice I mentioned. The hallway rehearsal or the quiet walk into the room. You don't need me to tell you which one. You've never needed me to tell you which one."

The silence that followed was different from the other silences of the night. The earlier ones had been intervals — gaps in a sequence, tactical, loaded with anticipation. This one was open. It had nothing waiting to fill it. It was the silence of a room that had stopped performing and was simply existing, and Vex let it exist for as long as it needed to.

Then she moved.

Slowly — deliberately, the way she did everything — she lowered herself. Not to crouch, not to kneel, but to bend, one hand finding the edge of the table for balance, her left leg remaining where it was so that the point of contact stayed unbroken. She brought herself down until her face was nearer the head against her thigh, near enough to see the ear, the line of the jaw beyond it, the pulse that still ran visibly at the temple.

She didn't speak immediately. She let the lowering register — the change in height, the shift in air, the fact that Vex was coming closer rather than Ari having to rise to meet her.

Then she placed her right hand against the side of Ari's head. Not the crown — the side, palm flat against the temple, fingers curving gently around the skull. Warm. Steady. The kind of hold that didn't grip and didn't push and didn't ask for anything. A hand that said: *this is where I am, and this is where you are, and neither of us is moving.*

"You're here," she said. Same words as before, but from this angle, from this proximity, with her hand against Ari's head and the weight of the forehead against her leg — the words meant something different than they had the first time. The first time had been an observation. This was a confirmation between two people who were standing in the same place on purpose.

She held the position — bent, one hand on the table, one against the temple, the contact at the thigh unbroken — and she waited. Not for a colour. Not for a response. For the breathing to complete whatever cycle it was in and arrive at the place where the next breath could be taken without effort.

When it did, she straightened — slowly, keeping the hand against the temple until the last possible moment before it slid free — and stood fully, both feet on the floor, hands at her sides.

"The rope stays for now," she said. The flat register had returned, but softened at the edges, the way leather softens with use rather than with deliberate treatment. "So do the marks. So does this position. You stay where you are, leaning where you're leaning, until I decide the scene is over — and I'll tell you when it is, in plain words, because that's the one part of tonight that I don't get to make ambiguous."

She looked at the room around them — the table, the basin, the drawer with the protocol, the lamp that hadn't been dimmed because neither of them had asked for it — and then back at the head against her thigh.

"Colour," she said. And then, quieter, because this time she wanted the word for what it was rather than for what it authorized: "I'm asking because I want to know. Not because it's procedure."

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: "Green," I say, my voice muffled against her leg. I don't move. "Still green."
