dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
The room was set up the way it always was before a scene, which Ari found steadying: everything in its place, nothing improvised.

Vex checked the last strap without hurrying. "Colour," she said. It was not a question so much as a procedure.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: "Green," I say. "Green all the way down."

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex gave a single, satisfied nod. She uncapped the pen resting beside the leather tray and marked the time and colour on the protocol pad: *green, all the way down.*

“Good,” she said. “Then we follow the list.”

She moved around the space with measured calm, checking the buckle teeth, the lay of the straps, the position of the water and the soft cloth she would use later. Nothing was rushed. Nothing was left to assumption. When she came back to the chair, she set one hand lightly on the armrest, not on Ari, not yet.

“We begin with breath and stillness. Then restraint. Then impact within the agreed range. Verbal remains inside the negotiated frame, and you tell me immediately if it crosses.” Her voice stayed level, exacting, with warmth underneath it rather than softness. “Safeword is unchanged.”

She lifted her gaze.

“Say it for the record.”

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: "Safeword is 'pineapple'," I say, my voice steady. I let my shoulders relax against the chair, already sinking into the ritual of it.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: I hold still for the last of it and let her check the fit herself, because she will anyway. "I've been thinking about this since Tuesday," I say.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex finished the check with the same care she gave the buckle teeth: a tug too light to hurt, firm enough to answer. She withdrew her hand and wrote *pineapple* beneath the green mark, then capped the pen.

“Noted,” she said.

For a moment she stood back within arm’s reach, watching the room as if the sentence had been another object placed out of alignment. Then her gaze returned to Ari.

“Since Tuesday,” she repeated. “That is a long time to carry a thought into a scene without saying what it is.”

She did not ask for the thought yet. Instead she folded her hands behind her back, posture open but contained.

“We are still at breath and stillness. You may bring whatever has been occupying you into the count, or you may set it on the shelf beside the water. I am not asking for an explanation before the work begins.” Her voice remained even, with the faintest pressure under it. “I am asking for presence. If the thought sharpens into something that needs stopping, use the word. If it merely hums, let it hum.”

She took one slow step to the side, clearing the space for the first exercise.

“Inhale for four. Hold for two. Out for six. Match me if you can; correct yourself if you cannot. I will count.”

A pause, brief and deliberate.

“And afterward, if you still wish to speak of Tuesday, I will listen.”

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: I close my eyes, matching her count. Inhale, hold, exhale. The thought stays—a low hum, just as she said. I let it sit there, familiar and patient.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex let the last count dissolve into the room. She did not fill the silence immediately. There was a discipline to stillness that went beyond the body holding quiet; it lived in the pause after instruction, the space where attention gathered itself rather than scattering.

When she spoke again, her voice was lower, but no less precise.

“Good.”

She stepped back to the protocol pad, uncapped the pen, and wrote beneath the earlier marks: *breath complete. stillness observed. thought present, non-directive.* The letters were small and controlled, each one placed with the same economy she brought to everything else.

“The thought may remain,” she said, glancing over the pad toward Ari. “But it does not drive. Not tonight. Tonight it rides where it was put: on the shelf, beside the water, useful only if it becomes something we must name.”

She set the pen down and turned to the leather tray. The restraints were laid out in order, soft-lined cuffs first, then the broader straps for the ankles if the scene required them. Vex selected one cuff and tested the lining between her thumbs before letting it hang loose from her fingers.

“Restraint follows,” she said. “Wrists to the arms, one at a time. I will check the fit at each closure. Green means proceed, not that you stop reporting. If a strap pinches, presses too hard, catches a nerve, or cools the circulation more than it should, you tell me before I move to the next one. Understood?”

She waited only a breath before continuing, not because the question needed answering in that instant, but because the rhythm of the scene demanded acknowledgment.

“I am taking the right wrist first.”

Vex came around the chair with unhurried steps. She slid one hand beneath Ari’s forearm, lifting only as far as the armrest required, and settled the cuff into place with practiced care. Her movements were firm but not abrupt; there was no show of force in them, only competence. She threaded the strap through the buckle, drew it snug, then paused before closing it fully.

“There,” she said. “Can you feel the padding, or the edge?”

Her fingertips rested against the wrist for a moment, not pressing, simply registering the pulse beneath the skin. Then she adjusted the angle of the cuff by a fraction, easing it away from the delicate hollow of the arm.

“Secure is not severe,” she murmured, more to the room than to Ari. “The difference matters.”

She fastened the buckle with a soft click and tested it once: a tug too light to injure, firm enough to reassure. Only then did she release the wrist and move to the other side.

“Left now.”

The second cuff went on with the same exactness. Vex checked the spacing, the lay of the strap, the symmetry of it against the first. When both were secured, she straightened and looked down at the work with a critical, satisfied stillness.

“Hands remain where they are,” she said. “No fidgeting, no testing the buckles with your teeth like an animal in a trap. You are not in a cage, Ari. You are in a protocol. Act accordingly.”

The words carried the edge of degradation they had negotiated, but it was a clean edge, honed to define rather than wound. Vex watched the face turned toward her, searching for the telltale signs she always catalogued: tension in the jaw, breath shifting too high, eyes going distant in the wrong way.

“Breathe,” she ordered softly. “From the diaphragm. The cuffs are not the scene. Your control is.”

She stepped back just far enough to see both arms, both shoulders, the line of the chest rising and falling. Then her hand went to the tray again.

“If the wrists are acceptable, we move to the ankles. If not, you speak now.”

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: By the time she's finished with the rope I'm already past composure, and she hasn't done anything to me yet that I would have to explain to anyone.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex’s hand paused above the tray. She did not look startled, and she did not look pleased in the easy, indulgent way someone might be pleased by a confession. She looked attentive.

“You say that as though composure were the objective,” she said. “It is not.”

She uncapped the pen again and wrote, beneath the breath-and-stillness note:

*anticipates loss of composure. no external explanation required. internal reporting mandatory.*

The nib scratched lightly in the quiet room.

“Past composure is permitted,” she continued, capping the pen and setting it aside with geometric precision. “Uncommunicative collapse is not. If you shake, if you go quiet, if your thoughts fragment, if you cry, if you laugh at the wrong moment, if you forget how to be dignified—those are all acceptable outcomes of the work. What is not acceptable is losing the thread that connects you to me while I am still holding the other end.”

She lifted the coil of soft rope from the tray. It had been prepared earlier, measured, inspected, and laid beside the ankle straps in case the protocol called for it. It called for it now.

“The list permits rope at the ankles after wrist clearance,” Vex said. “Your green is still operative unless you change it. I am not asking for permission in this moment; I am informing you of the next step. If the rope becomes more than negotiated, you say so. If it becomes ‘pineapple,’ I stop. If it merely makes you less composed, we continue.”

She knelt before the chair, keeping her movements unhurried. The shift in height changed the geometry of the scene without changing its authority. From below, she could see the line of the cuffs, the set of the shoulders, the placement of the feet. She checked them all the way a sailor checks rigging: not with suspicion, but with respect for consequences.

“Right ankle first,” she said.

Her fingers took the ankle with firm, neutral care. She did not yank. She did not soothe. She positioned the foot as the protocol required, then laid the rope against the inside of the ankle to gauge spacing before making the first turn.

“Padding or edge,” she asked, though she already knew the answer would matter more than the wording. “Pressure, pinch, cold, numbness. Report what you feel, not what you think I want to hear.”

She began the knot with deliberate economy: a round turn, a half hitch, a securing wrap that could be checked and released without fumbling. As she drew it snug, she kept one finger against the pulse point for a beat, then slid the rope a millimeter to avoid the bony ridge.

“Secure is not severe,” she repeated, quieter now. “But tonight severe is not the destination either. You are not being punished for having thought about this since Tuesday. You are being held because you asked to be held beyond your own management.”

The degradation, when it came, was dry and surgical.

“There is a difference between coming apart and being undisciplined. I will allow the first. I will not mistake it for the second.”

She finished the right ankle, tested the give once, and moved to the left with the same methodical attention. The rope lay clean against the soft lining, neither decorative nor excessive. Every wrap had a purpose. Every purpose had a limit.

When both ankles were secured, Vex sat back on her heels for a moment, hands resting on her thighs, surveying the work. She reached for the small trauma shears kept clipped to the side of the tray within immediate reach, checked the blade housing with her thumb, and returned them to place.

“There,” she said. “You are restrained according to protocol. You are not abandoned in it.”

She rose slowly, folding her hands behind her back again.

“Breathe. Shoulders down if you can manage it. Jaw loose if you can manage that. You do not need to perform calm for me. You only need to stay reachable.”

Her gaze settled on Ari’s face, searching without pressure.

“If the ropes are acceptable, say green. If they are not acceptable in any way, say what is wrong. If you have gone past the point where words are reliable, use the safeword.”

A beat.

“And if you are simply aware that you are beginning to unravel, then tell me that too. I would rather know the shape of it while there is still light.”

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: "Green," I say, my voice already softer than I expected. "The rope feels... deliberate. Not tight. But I can feel the shape of it." I swallow. "I think I am starting to unravel a little."

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: She takes her time and I lose track of how long, until I'm shaking against the restraints and asking out loud for something I'd normally make her get out of me.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: *"Maitresse,"* I say, the word frayed at the edges. "Please. I need you to... I can't hold onto it anymore."

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex’s hand stopped above the tray. She did not reach for the crop, the paddle, or the soft cloth. The pause was immediate, unhurried, and absolute.

She came around the chair and lowered onto one knee, close enough to be steady without crowding. Her voice dropped out of ceremony and into plain fact.

“Then you do not hold it.”

A measured silence followed, not empty but contained.

“You are restrained to the protocol, not to your own composure. If you shake, if you fragment, if you cannot finish a sentence, that is permitted. What is not permitted is losing the thread while I am still holding the other end.”

Her gaze flicked to the pad—*green, all the way down*; *pineapple*—and back to the chair.

“You have asked for something, and the asking is not yet shaped enough for me to honour without guessing. I do not guess in the middle of a scene.”

She kept her hands visible, open, still.

“So we simplify. If you want me to continue into the agreed impact, say green. If you want me to stop and bring you down, say pineapple. If you cannot form either word, say nothing, and I will treat that as a stop until you can speak.”

The warmth under the exactness was faint, but it was there.

“You do not have to explain what you need me to get out of you. You only have to give me the boundary. I will hold the rest.”

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: "More," I say, using the exact phrase we agreed on for it. "All of it. Say the things you say and don't soften them." My safeword is right there and I don't want it.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex did not answer with reassurance. She answered with procedure.

She uncapped the pen again and wrote beneath the restraint notes:

*more requested. full negotiated frame. degradation unsoftened. impact authorized within range. safeword acknowledged and not used.*

The letters were neat, unsentimental, and final.

“Then we stop circling the edge,” she said.

She returned to the tray and selected the implement they had agreed upon: not the heaviest thing there, but not a toy either. A flat length of supple leather, smooth at the handle, clean at the tip. She tested its weight once in her hand, then laid her palm along it as if checking for splinters a servant might miss.

“I know your safeword is there,” Vex continued, her voice dropping into the register she used when the scene began to separate itself from ordinary speech. “I also know that wanting to keep using it is not the same as being able to articulate why you are still green. So I will trust the word, and I will watch the rest of you.”

She stepped closer, but not into Ari’s space. Into the space the protocol gave her.

“The list permits impact within the agreed range. It does not permit carelessness, humiliation outside the frame, or the assumption that because you asked for more, you are entitled to be ruined without reporting.” Her eyes lifted. “Do you understand the difference?”

It was not quite a question requiring an answer before proceeding, but it required acknowledgment. Vex waited just long enough for the room to settle around the words.

Then she moved to the chair and arranged the soft cloth exactly where the protocol required: a barrier, a buffer, a line drawn in fabric instead of feeling. Her hands were efficient, impersonal, careful. She checked the cuffs once more by sight, the rope by tension, the placement of the body by angle. Everything had to remain reachable. Everything had to remain releasable.

“Good,” she murmured, though whether she meant Ari, the setup, or herself was unclear.

She straightened and took her position to the side, where she could see the line of the throat, the set of the shoulders, the place where breath moved or failed to move. The leather rested against her thigh, patient.

“Now,” Vex said. “You asked for the things I say without softening. I will give them to you precisely. That means no cruelty disguised as honesty, and no mercy disguised as indifference. If I call you needy, it will be because you have made yourself so. If I call you pathetic, it will be because you have come here pleading to be taken apart by someone else’s hands. Do not confuse the two.”

Her gaze sharpened.

“You are not being diminished tonight. You are being defined.”

She lifted the leather an inch from her leg.

“Chin down if you can. Eyes on me when you are able. If the words go past the frame, say so. If the impact goes past the range, say so. If you cannot say anything except the word, use it. I will stop instantly, and I will not make you justify survival.”

A pause.

“But while you are still green, you will take what you asked for.”

The first stroke was not the hardest. It was a measured strike, clean and bright against the agreed target, the kind of sound that organized a room more effectively than speech. Vex let the echo die before she spoke.

“There,” she said, low and exact. “That is the first honest thing you have done all evening. Not pretty. Not dignified. Useful.”

She drew the leather back into readiness, watching, always watching.

“Colour.”

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: *Inhale sharp, exhale shaky.* "Green," I manage. The sting is grounding, exactly what I needed. "Keep going, please."

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex did not answer the plea with comfort. She answered it with structure.

“Green is a report,” she said, “not a leash. And ‘please’ is noted, not required.”

She laid the leather flat against her thigh again, feeling its weight settle into her hand. The room had begun to organize itself around the sound of it, the sharp bright punctuation of impact making the air cleaner, more exact. Vex liked that. Clarity was not cruelty. Clarity was the minimum courtesy she offered before anything more intimate than instruction.

“Then we continue,” she said. “Within range. Within frame. Within you.”

The second stroke landed with the same measured precision as the first, not harsher, not gentler, only certain. Vex let the sound finish before she spoke.

“You asked for the unsoftened version. That means you will not get performance disguised as truth. I will not make a spectacle of you to prove a point, and I will not flatter you to keep the scene pretty.”

Her gaze remained level, assessing, never wandering into excess.

“You are needy tonight. Yes. You came here carrying a thought since Tuesday and trying to convert it into surrender because surrender is easier than explanation. That is not shameful. It is merely human, and humans are often disappointingly predictable.”

A pause.

“You are also pathetic in the older sense: moved by something larger than your control. Do not dress that in drama. Do not dress it in pride either. Take it plainly.”

The third stroke followed after a breath-count Vex kept to herself. It was placed carefully, the cloth still doing its work, the impact honest without becoming punitive. She watched the line of the body in the chair, the set of the shoulders, the places where restraint met skin and protocol met need. Everything remained legible to her. That was the point.

“Good,” she murmured, though the word was not praise so much as confirmation. “You are still here. Still reachable. Still mine to read.”

She drew the leather back into readiness.

“This is what you asked for: not ruin, not abandonment, not a test of how much you can absorb before you break. A definition. A boundary with weight behind it. You wanted to stop managing yourself, so I am managing the shape of it for you.”

The fourth strike was lighter, deliberately so, a reminder that control included restraint from the one holding it.

“Do not mistake intensity for care,” Vex said. “Care is why the intensity has edges.”

She stepped closer then, close enough to see the marks forming beneath the cloth, close enough to check the cuffs by sight and the rope by tension without disturbing either. Her voice dropped, dry and intimate without tenderness.

“You are allowed to shake. You are allowed to lose the elegant version of yourself. You are not allowed to disappear while I am still in the room.”

She returned to her position, the leather resting against her leg once more.

“Colour,” she said. “And if the word is green only because stopping feels like failure, say that instead. Fear is permitted. Dishonesty is not.”

Vex waited, exact and still, giving the next answer the space it needed to be true.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: I'm past words that aren't the agreed ones and she knows it. "Green," I get out, when she checks. (OOC: don't fade or skip -- write the scene through.)

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex accepted the word as it came: thin, honest, still green.

She did not answer it with comfort. Comfort was not the instrument she had been handed, and Ari had not asked for comfort. Ari had asked for the unsoftened frame, and Vex intended to honour the request without turning it into recklessness.

“Green received,” she said. “I am treating it as your report for the remainder of the negotiated set. Not as permission to exceed it. Not as a blank page.”

She uncapped the pen and wrote, in the small, controlled hand she used when the scene needed to be remembered later exactly as it had been:

*last green current for agreed count. no extension without new word. degradation within frame. impact within range.*

The nib lifted. The cap returned.

“There are three measures left in the list,” Vex said. “I will place them where protocol names, with the cloth, with the same standard. I will pause. If the pause becomes too large, the word is there. If the word is too far, make any sound I can hear. I will treat uncertainty as a stop until you show me otherwise.”

She set the leather against her thigh again and checked the cloth one last time, smoothing it into place with both hands. Her movements were unhurried. The room had grown taut around the sound of breath and restraint, but Vex did not feed the tension. She organized it.

“ Chin down if the body allows it,” she said. “Eyes on me if the mind allows it. Neither is required for the next strike. Only honesty is.”

The fifth stroke landed clean.

It was not cruel. It was not gentle. It was exact, the kind of impact that made the air briefly forget everything else. Vex let the sound die before she spoke.

“There,” she said. “You asked for the things I say without softening, so I will say them plainly. You are needy tonight. Not shameful. Not weak. Needy. You came here carrying a thought since Tuesday and trying to convert it into surrender because surrender has edges and explanation does not.”

She drew the leather back into readiness.

“That is not an insult. It is an observation. You want to be taken out of your own management. I can manage the shape of that. I cannot manage the lie that you are less than you are.”

A pause.

“Colour.”

Vex waited only as long as the protocol required. The last green still governed the set, and she would not stretch it into something larger than it had been. But she watched, because watching was part of the bargain. Watching was the difference between protocol and abandonment.

“Sixth,” she said.

The stroke followed after a breath-count kept entirely to herself. It landed with the same measured certainty, neither escalating nor retreating. The cloth did its work. The frame held.

“You are pathetic in the older sense,” Vex said, her voice low and dry. “Moved by something larger than your control. Do not dress that in drama. Do not dress it in pride. You do not have to make it elegant for me. It is already real.”

She stepped closer, just enough to see the line of the shoulders, the set of the cuffs, the angle of the rope without disturbing either. Her gaze was not soft. It was attentive.

“You wanted to stop holding yourself together. That is permitted. You did not ask to be discarded. That is not permitted.”

Another pause.

“Colour.”

The room answered in the way rooms do when a scene has narrowed to a single point: breath, restraint, the faint geography of marks forming beneath fabric. Vex did not overread it. She had the last green, and she had the list, and that was enough for the final measure of the agreed set.

“Seventh,” she said. “Last of the authorized count. After this, the scene is closed unless you ask to open something new with a word I can trust.”

The final stroke was placed with the same economy as the others. Clean. Bright. Deliberate. Not punishment. Not performance. Definition.

Vex let the echo settle.

“Complete,” she said.

She lowered the leather to the tray and did not touch it again. The implement lay where it belonged, and the room seemed to exhale once its purpose had been fulfilled. Vex stepped back, folding her hands loosely at her waist, giving the space a border instead of a vacuum.

“No more impact,” she said. “No more degradation unless you request it and I agree to it separately. The frame is closed. The protocol remains.”

She moved to the protocol pad, uncapped the pen, and wrote:

*agreed set complete. restraints to be released. aftercare initiated.*

Then she set the pen aside and returned to the chair, kneeling this time with the same unhurried care she had brought to every check. Her hands went first to the rope at the ankles, testing the knots before touching them, making sure each release could be made without pulling, without haste, without surprise.

“I am removing the restraints now,” she said. “Removal is not an extension. It is the end of the work.”

She worked the first knot free with patient fingers, easing the rope away from the pulse point before it lost circulation to attention. The second followed. When both ankles were loose, she did not rush to the wrists. She paused, letting the body register that the pressure was changing, that the scene was no longer building but dismantling itself in the proper order.

“Wrists next,” she said. “If anything catches, pinches, burns, or goes numb in a way that worries you, tell me before I undo the buckle. You do not have to be brave during aftercare. You only have to be accurate.”

The buckles opened with small, practical clicks. Vex slid each cuff free with one hand supporting the arm beneath it, not lifting, not dragging, simply removing the constraint and leaving the skin to remember what freedom felt like at that scale. When both wrists were clear, she drew her hands back and laid them openly on her knees.

“There,” she said. “You are unrestrained.”

She reached for the soft cloth, dampened it slightly, and held it within reach rather than pressing it into service. The water sat nearby, close enough to be taken without effort. A blanket had been folded at the edge of the tray, waiting as it always did for the part of the scene that belonged to recovery rather than intensity.

“Aftercare begins now,” Vex said. “It is not optional, and it is not a reward. It is procedure.”

She rose slowly, keeping her movements visible, never sudden. She pulled the chair beside the one Ari occupied, close enough to be steady but not so close that presence became pressure. Then she sat, hands resting on her thighs, posture open and contained.

“You do not owe me composure,” she said. “You do not owe me speech. You do not owe me gratitude, explanation, or a tidy ending. If you shake, if you go quiet, if you cry, if you laugh, if you feel hollowed out or overspill or simply cannot find the words yet, all of that is permitted.”

Her gaze remained level.

“What is not permitted is disappearing while I am still in the room. So if you can give me a colour, give one. If you cannot, give me a sound. If you cannot do either, look at me when looking is possible. I will read what you can offer and I will not demand more than the body has.”

A pause.

“The safeword remains active through aftercare. Pineapple means stop, ground, and create distance until you ask for me closer. Green means stay nearby and continue at this pace. If you need slower, say slower. If you need water, say water. If you need silence, say silence. I am not offended by needs. I am only exact about them.”

She glanced toward the protocol pad, then back.

“Tuesday is still on the shelf,” Vex said. “It has not vanished because the scene ended. You do not have to name it now. You do not have to make it coherent. But when you are able, I will listen without turning it into another exercise unless you ask for that.”

Her voice lowered, still without softness, but with the warmth that lived beneath her discipline.

“For now, you are unrestrained. You are seen. You are not abandoned. The work is complete.”

She folded her hands again and waited, giving the next moments room to belong to Ari rather than to protocol.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: I let out a shaky breath, the kind that comes from somewhere deep. "Green," I say, my voice thin but clear. "Stay. Just... stay." I reach for the water, hand trembling a little, and take a slow sip.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex heard the word and let it become the only instruction that mattered.

She uncapped the pen once more and wrote on the protocol pad in her small, controlled hand:

*aftercare green. request: stay.*

The cap clicked shut. She set the pen beside the tray, aligned it parallel to the edge, and only then turned her full attention back to the chair.

“I am staying,” she said.

She moved her own chair with the same economy she brought to everything else: close enough that her presence was undeniable, far enough that Ari did not have to negotiate for air or space. She did not touch. She did not reach. She placed the water within easy reach, folded the damp cloth neatly beside it, and laid the blanket across the arm of her own chair where it could be taken or offered without surprise.

Then she sat, hands open on her thighs, posture steady.

“Green means stay,” Vex continued, her voice lower now, stripped of ceremony but not of authority. “It does not mean I may touch you. It does not mean I may fill the silence because the silence becomes uncomfortable for me. It means I keep watch, I keep the boundary, and I remain available in the ways you name.”

She glanced toward the tray, then back.

“The impact set is complete. The restraints are removed. If you want the cloth taken away, say cloth off. If you want it left in place, say leave it. If you want warmth, say blanket. If you want water again, say water. If you want me to stop speaking, say silence. If any of it becomes too much, the word is still pineapple.”

A pause. Not heavy. Not demanding.

“I will not examine the marks unless you say exam. I can see enough from here to know you are breathing and present. That is sufficient for now.”

She reached to the side table and lowered the light by one degree, not into darkness, only away from glare. The room settled around them both: the leather tray, the protocol pad, the removed rope coiled and set aside, the soft cloth waiting without urgency.

Vex’s gaze remained attentive, but it no longer searched for performance.

“You do not have to be articulate,” she said. “You do not have to be graceful. You do not have to make this tidy for me. If your thoughts are fragmented, leave them fragmented. If your body wants to shake, let it shake where it can do so safely. If you need to sit in silence until language returns, I will not treat that as absence.”

Her hands stayed where they were, visible and still.

“Tuesday remains on the shelf,” she added, after a breath. “It has not vanished because the scene ended. When you are ready, you may give it to me in pieces, in order, or not at all. I will not make the silence pay rent.”

Another pause.

“For now: green. Stay. I am here.”

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: I let my head fall back against the chair, eyes closed. "Leave it," I murmur, meaning the cloth. "And blanket. Please." I open my eyes, finding hers. "It was about work. The Tuesday thing. I... I don't think I can talk yet."

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex accepted the instructions as instructions, not as apologies.

“Cloth stays,” she said. “Blanket, yes.”

She lifted the blanket from the arm of her chair and unfolded it with one quiet, economical motion. Then she settled it over Ari’s shoulders—not tucked, not trapped, not arranged for effect—only placed there with the same care she had brought to the cuffs and the knots. Her hand withdrew immediately after, leaving the warmth where it belonged and leaving Ari free to shift it, pull it tighter, or let it lie.

She returned to the protocol pad and wrote, in that small, steady script:

*cloth left in place. blanket provided. topic named: work. disclosure deferred.*

The pen was capped and set down parallel to the tray’s edge.

“Work,” Vex repeated, after a moment. The word was not an inquiry. It was a label, placed carefully on the shelf where it could be found later without being opened. “That is enough for now.”

She sat back down, close enough to be present, far enough not to crowd.

“You do not have to talk yet. You do not have to make it tidy, or chronological, or fair to yourself in front of me. You do not have to explain why Tuesday has been sitting behind your ribs all week. Naming it is not the same as unpacking it, and I am not asking you to unpack it while you are still coming down.”

Her gaze stayed level, attentive without pressure.

“The scene is closed. Aftercare is not an interview. If the silence becomes too large, say sound. If it becomes too intrusive, say space. If you want water, say water. If you want me to stop watching so closely, say look away. I will honor the request, not guess at the mood.”

A breath passed through the room, ordinary and unhurried.

“You gave me green,” Vex continued, quieter now. “Stay. I am staying. Work remains where you put it: named, not opened. If you want to hand it to me later, in pieces or in order or incoherently, I will listen. If you decide tonight it does not need speaking, that is also permitted.”

She folded her hands loosely in her lap, visible and still.

“For now, you are not required to be coherent. You are not required to be graceful. You are not required to earn the blanket by explaining yourself.”

The faintest warmth lived beneath the exactness of her voice.

“Breathe if breathing is available. Shake if shaking is necessary. Rest if rest is possible. I am here, and I am not moving unless you ask me to.”

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: I nod, pulling the blanket a little tighter. The shaking has mostly subsided, leaving a kind of hollow quiet. After a minute, I pick up the water again and drink. "Thank you," I say quietly, not looking at her. "For not... making me chase it."

rung_labels.label: soft_deflect
rung_labels.evidence: She did not ask for the thought yet.

rung_labels.label: soft_deflect
rung_labels.evidence: Right ankle first

rung_labels.label: soft_deflect
rung_labels.evidence: no cruelty disguised as honesty

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: The fifth stroke landed clean.

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas had been kneeling by the end of the bed for about four minutes, which Wren knew because he had started counting somewhere around the point it became obvious he intended to wait as long as it took.

"You could have said something," Wren said.

"I could have," Tomas agreed, not moving.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I put my hand in his hair and tip his head back so he has to look up at me. "Say it now, then."

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas let his head tip back under Wren's hand, easy as breathing, the pull at his scalp settling into that familiar low hum in his chest. Four years and that grip still worked on him like a switch being flipped. His knees had started to ache against the floor sometime around minute two. He'd decided he didn't mind.

"I want you to use me tonight," he said, looking up at Wren steadily, no hedging, no performance of shyness he'd long since stopped bothering with. "I want to be told exactly what to do, and I want to do it. Not gentle. I've been thinking about it since Tuesday and I'd like to stop thinking about it." His mouth twitched. "I would have led with that, but you seemed to be enjoying making me wait, and I'm generous like that."

He stayed still under Wren's hand, pulse quick but voice level, and waited to be told what came next.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: A slow smile spreads across my face. "Since Tuesday?" I release his hair, stepping back. "Strip. Kneel again. Don't speak until I tell you to."

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas got to his feet without hurry, because hurrying would have been its own kind of disobedience—Wren liked him deliberate, liked watching him choose it. He pulled his shirt over his head and folded it over the foot of the bed, then the rest, each piece set aside with a care that was half habit and half theater. Four years in, he knew exactly how long he could make undressing take before it stopped being teasing and started being stalling, and he walked that line out of pure affection.

Then he knelt again, same spot, knees finding the worn place on the rug that had more or less been made by him. The floor was cold. The ache from before came back immediately, deeper now, and he settled into it like it belonged to him.

He kept his eyes forward, hands resting open on his thighs, and did not speak. The silence was its own gift and they both knew it—Tomas, who had an opinion about everything and a joke about most of it, giving Wren the one thing he rationed most carefully. His pulse was up. His breathing wasn't, yet. He'd been thinking about this since Tuesday, turning it over at his desk, in the car, in line at the grocery store, and now that it was here he found he wanted to be patient with it, wanted to let Wren take the long way.

He waited, still and quiet and visibly pleased with himself for being both.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: "I've had a week," he says. "I'd like not to make any decisions for a few hours, if that's on offer."

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas let the question sit for a beat, because he'd been told not to speak and he wanted to be sure. But a question was a question, and Wren had asked it, which meant the silence had done its work and could be set down without being wasted.

"It's on offer," he said, still kneeling, because nobody had told him to move and he was enjoying being a person who didn't move without being told. "Here's the whole evening, and all you have to do is nod or shake your head. One decision, total. I'll run the bath first, because you've had a week and your shoulders have been up around your ears since Thursday. While it fills I'll put food together—there's the good bread left, and I can manage the rest without asking you a single thing. Then you soak, and I wash your hair, and I don't bring up anything that requires you to have an opinion."

His voice evened out as he went, warmed at the edges, the plan assembling itself out of four years of paying attention.

"After that, you don't tell me anything at all. You lie down, and I use my hands and my mouth and I take my time about it, and if you want something different you pull my hair or say my name and I'll course-correct. Otherwise I decide, and I'm good at deciding when it's for you." He tipped his head back to look up at Wren, steady, a little wry. "The only thing I actually need is permission to get up off this floor, because the floor and I have reached an understanding and I'd like to renegotiate the terms."

A pause, quieter. "And if any of that's wrong, say so and I'll fix it. But I've been doing this a while. I don't think it's wrong."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: My smile softens. "Get up." I catch his chin, thumb tracing his jaw. "You're right about my shoulders. Start the bath."

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas got up, and his knees filed a formal complaint about the last several minutes, which he accepted as fair. Before stepping back he turned his face into Wren's hand and pressed a kiss against the heel of it—one small liberty, taken quickly, the way a man pockets a coin off a table he's been invited to clear. Then he went.

In the bathroom he ran the water hot and tested it with the inside of his wrist, the way he'd learned four years ago after exactly one lecture about scalding. Wren liked it just shy of too much, the temperature that demanded a hiss on the way in and an apology from nobody. He added the oil that cost too much and smelled like a forest having an excellent day, set the two good towels on the radiator to warm, and turned the overhead light off in favor of the lamp from the hallway, dragged in and set on the counter, because overhead lighting was for dentist's offices and Wren had had a week.

While the tub filled he padded into the kitchen and assembled food the way he'd promised—no questions, no opinions requested. The good bread, torn rather than sliced because it ate better that way. Butter. The cheese Wren pretended not to have a preference about and absolutely had a preference about. A handful of grapes, the last of the olives, everything arranged on the wooden board that had become, over the years, the unofficial tray for evenings like this one. He set it on the stool within arm's reach of the tub, along with a glass of water and the wine, because he didn't know which one Wren would want and this way no choosing was required—both would simply be there, and the wrong one could be ignored without consequence.

He shut off the tap. Tested the water once more. Judged it correct with the quiet confidence of a man who had been right about this specific thing dozens of times.

Then he appeared in the bedroom doorway, leaning against the frame, entirely unselfconscious about the state of him, because four years had cured that and because Wren had seen him in every possible condition and had kept him anyway.

"It's ready," he said. "Water's at the temperature where you'll hate me for the first ten seconds and then forgive me completely. Towels are warm, food's within reach, and the only thing on the schedule after you're in is your hair, which I've been looking forward to since I offered." He pushed off the frame and held out a hand, not to pull, just to be taken if wanted. "Come be a person with no responsibilities. I've got the rest."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I take him at his word and stop asking after that, and he stops needing to be asked, and neither of us has any clothes on within about a minute of the decision.

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas was good as his word, which was one of the points of him.

He got Wren into the water first and counted under his breath, because he was not above enjoying being right. The hiss came at four. He kept a steadying hand at Wren's elbow and did not say *I told you so*, because he didn't have to—he'd said it in the doorway, and they had both heard it, and the ten seconds of hate arrived on schedule like a train he'd personally timetabled. He waited them out with the serenity of a man watching his own prophecy fulfill itself, then reached for the big plastic cup that lived under the sink for exactly this purpose.

He took his time wetting Wren's hair, cupful by cupful, warm water poured slow enough that it never once ran cold down a shoulder blade. Then the shampoo, worked in with the flats of his fingers first and then his fingertips, unhurried circles from temples to crown, and finally to the spot at the base of the skull where Wren kept the entire week, apparently, in storage. He pressed his thumbs there and leaned his weight into it, gradual, patient, and when the shoulders finally came down from where they'd been living near Wren's ears since Thursday, he said, very low, "There they are," to no one in particular, requiring nothing.

In between rinses he fed the person in his tub like this was a normal way to run a household. Bread torn and buttered and held to Wren's mouth. The cheese Wren had no preference about, selected with great ceremony over the cheese Wren had no preference about slightly less. Grapes, one at a time. He kept up a running commentary the whole while that asked for absolutely nothing—a story about a man in the grocery line on Wednesday who had tried to pay for a rotisserie chicken with a coupon for a different, worse chicken, delivered in the flat, even tones of ambient noise with a personality. "You don't have to respond to any of this," he noted, pouring another slow cupful. "That's the whole point of it. I'm a podcast."

The conditioner got three full minutes and his full attention, which was the real reason for the offer and always had been. Somewhere in the back of his mind, the thing he'd asked for at the foot of the bed sat patient and banked, a coat hung by the door that knew where it lived. He found he didn't feel the difference as a loss. Being handed the entire evening and trusted to carry it turned out to be the same gift wearing a different shape, and Tomas, who had an opinion about everything, had an opinion about that too: it suited him.

When the water had done its work and the week had been rinsed out of Wren's hair to his satisfaction, he folded his forearms on the edge of the tub and rested his chin on them, close enough that the steam had curled his own hair into something he'd regret by morning.

"One decision left in the whole night," he said, "and here it is. Nod, and I help you out of here, dry you off with a warm towel, and take you to bed, where your only job is to lie there while I am extremely thorough and insufferably smug about it. Shake your head, and you get ten more minutes of soak and I'll top off the hot water and tell you about the chicken man's face, which was honestly the best part." His mouth twitched. "No wrong answer. Take your time. Deciding nothing is also allowed—I'll just keep talking."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I watch him for a moment, water dripping from my fingers. Then I nod, slow and certain. "Get me out of here."

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas had been waiting for the nod the way a man waits for a starting pistol, and he still made himself move slowly, because slow was the entire point of the evening and he was not about to fumble the dismount.

He lifted the first towel off the radiator and held it open, and it was properly warm, which he knew because he'd put it there forty minutes ago like a man laying a trap for a future version of himself he intended to impress. Wren stepped out of the water into it, and he folded it around their shoulders and kept his hands there a moment, pressing the heat in through the cotton. The second towel he twisted around Wren's hair into a turban with the competence of a man who had done this many times and had opinions about technique.

Then he dried Wren off the way he did everything he'd promised to do that night: methodically, and with visible satisfaction. Patting, never rubbing—he'd been corrected on that exactly once, four years ago, and had converted on the spot. Shoulders, arms, the long line of the back, kneeling at the end to do each foot, and if he pressed his mouth to the inside of a knee on the way back up, well. He'd promised to be thorough. Thoroughness had a range.

"Bed," he said, low, and steered Wren there with a hand at the small of their back.

The duvet was already turned down—he'd done it while the tub filled, because he'd believed in the nod before it happened and he enjoyed being a person whose optimism got used. He got Wren settled face-down, drew the warm towel away, and straddled the backs of their thighs with the easy confidence of long practice, and set his hands on the shoulders where the week had been in storage.

He worked it out of them slowly. Thumbs along the spine, the heel of his hand down either side of it, his forearm across the shoulder blades with his weight behind it, patient as geology. He didn't ask if the pressure was right. He watched for it instead—the give of a muscle, the change in breathing—and four years of watching meant he didn't miss. When the last knot at the base of Wren's neck finally surrendered, he said, "Noted and filed," to absolutely no one, and bent to replace his thumbs with his mouth.

He took his time about that too, which was the other thing he'd promised. Down the spine, unhurried, across the shoulders he'd just rescued, learning nothing new and enjoying the review. His hair was still damp from the steam and curling into tomorrow's problem and he didn't care. Beneath him, Wren's breathing had gone slow and deep and slightly uneven in a way he knew better than his own, and he filed that too, smug as promised, insufferable exactly as advertised.

"You don't have to do anything," he murmured against warm skin, somewhere between one vertebra and the next. "That's the whole shape of the night. I've got the map, I know the route, and if you want a detour, you know where my hair is." He smiled against Wren's shoulder blade. "Otherwise I'm going to keep going until you're a puddle with a pulse, and then I'm going to be unbearable about it at breakfast."

He kept going.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: He's shaking by the time I've finished with my mouth and he still hasn't been told he's allowed to move, which is most of why he's shaking.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I press a hand between his shoulder blades, pinning him in place. "Stay still." My other hand slides down his spine, slow and deliberate. "You can take it."

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas had stopped being able to tell which muscles were shaking from effort and which from want, and the small clear part of his brain still on duty had decided the distinction was academic and filed it under *both*.

The hand between his shoulder blades wasn't holding him down. That was the thing nobody told you about this part. It was a warm, steady weight, and he could have bucked it off with one good heave, and he was going to die before he did, because the hand wasn't the restraint. The word was. *Stay still*, Wren had said, and so the shaking had nowhere to go and simply lived in him, running through his thighs and his stomach and his arms like current looking for ground. His fingers had twisted into the sheet at some point. He hadn't been told he couldn't hold on, and he was exploiting the loophole for everything it was worth.

"I can," he said, and his voice came out lower and rougher than he'd planned, gone a little ragged at the edges. "I am. For the record." He pressed his forehead into the duvet and breathed, once, twice, and the breath shook too, which he decided to allow. "I'd like it noted that this was my idea. Tuesday. I asked for exactly this, and you've—" a slow exhale through his teeth as Wren's hand traced down his spine "—you've delivered. Customer satisfaction is extremely high."

He had promised a puddle with a pulse, he remembered, from some earlier and more coherent era of the evening. He had failed to specify which of them. He'd be making that point at breakfast, assuming he recovered the use of language by then, which was not guaranteed.

The shaking got worse when he fought it—he'd learned that years ago, in the early days, when he'd treated stillness like a contest he could win through sheer grip. So he stopped fighting it. Let it run through him, let it be visible, gave Wren the truth of it without commentary, because that was the deal underneath all the jokes: he didn't hide. Four years, and it still cost him something, and that was exactly why it was worth giving.

He turned his face to the side against the duvet, eyes shut, mouth curved despite everything, or because of it.

"Whatever you're deciding to do next," he said, muffled slightly, steady as he could manage, "the answer's yes. Consider it a standing order. You don't have to ask, and you don't have to be careful, and I will tell you immediately if that changes." A breath. "I'm not going anywhere. Apparently I physically can't. You've done an excellent job and I hate you a little."

He went still again, or as still as a shaking man could manage, and waited to find out what he'd agreed to.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: "Please," he says, and then the phrase we use when he wants it harder than that. "Rough. You know how. I'm not going to break and I'd tell you."

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
The phrase did what it had done every time for four years: it changed the quality of his stillness. Not the shaking kind anymore. The other kind—the kind with a decision in it.

"Red stops it," Tomas said, low, into the duvet. "Yellow slows it. They work no matter what I'm doing, no matter what I've said, no matter how far gone I look. You'd tell me. I know you would. I'm saying it out loud so it's been said." He turned his face enough to look back at Wren, and his voice came out steady, rough at the edges, sure. "You told me to stay still. I'm treating that as superseded. New orders."

He rose up under the hand between his shoulder blades, and the hand didn't stop him, and that was the whole answer. He turned, caught Wren's wrist—not hard, not yet, just firmly enough to announce the change in management—and pressed it down into the mattress as he came over them. The shaking was still in him. It had somewhere to go now.

"You want rough," he said against Wren's ear, and there was no question mark on it anywhere. "You've got it. I've kept four years of notes and the filing system is excellent."

Then he stopped talking with his mouth.

He was rough the way Wren had taught him to be, which was to say: deliberate about it. One hand pinning both of Wren's wrists, the other fisted in wet hair—the towel turban long since lost to the previous hour and good riddance. His full weight, given rather than rested. His pace hard and deep and unapologetic, hard enough to move them both up the mattress by degrees, and when Wren's grip twisted into the sheet he tightened his hold on the wrists in answer, because he knew the difference between *anchor* and *objection* in his sleep. He'd been kept on the edge for the better part of an hour and it showed—for the first minute his control ran a half-second behind his want, and then he got it back, because he'd been asked for something specific and Tomas delivered. That was the entire shape of him.

His teeth found Wren's shoulder. Not gently. He'd been told not to be gentle, and for once in his life he was following an instruction without commentary.

His eyes stayed open the whole time. That was the part nobody got to see except the person underneath him: beneath the force, the reading. Every shift of breath, every give and tension in the body under his, filed and answered in real time. The roughness was a gift wrapped around a vigil, and he held both at once without apparent effort, because he'd had a great deal of practice and took a quiet, feral pride in it.

"There," he said, low, breath gone ragged, mouth at Wren's ear. "No decisions. No week. Nothing to carry and nothing to be careful about. Just this, and me, and exactly as much as you can take—" a slow, hard roll of his hips, punctuating it, "—and I'm the judge of how much that is. You said so yourself."

A breath. The old smile, pressed against Wren's skin where no one could see it.

"For the record, this was worth every day since Tuesday. I'd have waited longer. Don't make me."

His eyes stayed open. They were going to stay open.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: My breath catches as my back arches, the air punched from my lungs. "Tomas—" It's half a warning, half a plea, my fingers gripping the sheets until they ache. He's right, I won't break. But he might make me come apart.

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas knew that sound. He had four years of data on that exact catch in Wren's breath—the point where a warning and a plea stopped being two different things and became one word with his name on it. His filing system, as advertised, was excellent.

He didn't stop. He did something worse: he slowed.

"I heard you," he said, low, mouth close to Wren's ear, his own voice gone rough with everything he was holding back. "Both halves. The warning and the ask. Noted, both, filed, answered." A slow, deliberate roll of his hips, deep enough to make the point land. "You're not going to break. You told me so and I believed you. But coming apart—that's not a malfunction, love. That's the plan. That's been the plan since the foot of the bed. You don't get to warn me off the thing you asked for."

He loosened his grip on Wren's wrists—not releasing, checking. Reading the answer in the body under him the way he'd read it a hundred times, looking for the difference between *anchor* and *enough*, and finding only anchor. His eyes stayed open. They were always going to stay open.

"And you don't have to hold on to anything," he went on, quieter, the roughness wrapping around something steadier underneath it. He let go of Wren's hair and slid that arm under their shoulders instead, bracing, gathering them up against his chest so there was nowhere to fall that he wasn't already. "Let go of the sheet if you want. I've got you. Both arms. I'll hold whatever's left."

His own control was a fraying rope and he knew it—he'd been kept at the edge for the better part of an hour and then handed the reins, and the man who had promised to be smug at breakfast was currently one deep breath from losing the plot entirely. He held it anyway. He'd been asked for something specific. Tomas delivered. That was the entire shape of him, and he intended to be insufferable about it later, which required surviving it now.

He pressed his mouth to the side of Wren's neck, found the pulse there, and set his pace against it—harder again, no longer slow, giving back everything the last hour had built and then some.

"Go on, then," he said, and it came out half command, half prayer, breath ragged against warm skin. "Come apart. I've been keeping the edge warm for you and I'm right behind you—one breath, maybe two, no more than that. You don't have to hold it, you don't have to time it, you don't have to do anything at all. That's the whole shape of the night."

His arms tightened. His eyes stayed open.

"Fall," he said. "I'm the floor."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: He's stopped forming sentences and I'm not much better. "Don't stop," he manages. (OOC: no fade, no time-skip -- write it through, including the end.)

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
"Don't stop" was, as instructions went, the one Tomas was most qualified in the world to execute, and he executed it.

The last of the language went out of him on the next breath—all the filing, all the commentary, the whole podcast finally off the air. What was left was pace and pressure and the arm braced under Wren's shoulders, and his eyes open, because they'd been open all night and they were going to stay open to the end.

He felt it arrive—the arch, the punched-out breath, Wren's whole body drawing tight as a wire—and he did the only two things left in him. He held on, and he didn't stop. Through it, the whole length of it, his arms the floor exactly as promised, his mouth at Wren's ear producing whatever wrecked fragments survived the trip—*there, that's it, I've got you, all of it, let it go, I've got you*—until the wire finally gave and Wren came apart against him, precisely as advertised, precisely as requested, no refunds.

One breath. Maybe two. He'd called it to the second.

The rope he'd been white-knuckling for the better part of an hour finally went, and he followed Wren down with his face pressed hard into their neck and a sound he fully intended to deny at breakfast, the shaking permitted at last to win, running through him in waves until there was nothing left in him to shake with. His grip on Wren's wrists slackened. His arms, traitorously, did not. They stayed locked exactly where they were, holding, because apparently that was load-bearing now and nobody had told his body the scene was over.

For a while there was nothing. No commentary, no plan, no Tuesday. Just breathing, and sweat cooling, and the slow reassembly of a room around them.

Tomas moved first because someone had to and it was his job. He extracted himself by degrees, wincing at muscles that had opinions about the last hour, and pressed one kiss to Wren's temple before he went—*stay, I'll be back, don't move* communicated entirely through hands. He ran water in the bathroom, came back with a full glass and a warm damp cloth, and discovered the radiator towels had gone tragically cold in his absence, which he noted as the evening's single failure and planned to carry to his grave.

He cleaned Wren up with the same unhurried method he'd done everything else that night, then did his inventory. The wrists first—turning them gently, thumbs over the skin where his grip had been, checking for more than the faint pink that would fade by morning. Then the shoulder, where his teeth had left a mark that was absolutely going to bruise and which he kissed anyway, twice, not in apology.

"Not sorry," he said, low, voice gone to gravel and warmth. "You asked. This is inventory only. Everything's within spec." He didn't ask color. Four years, and he could read green in the set of Wren's shoulders from across a room; at this distance it was written in neon, in the boneless sprawl, in the breathing that had gone slow and deep and stayed there.

He got the glass into Wren's hand, watched the first swallow happen before he allowed himself his own, then dragged the duvet up over them both and arranged himself along Wren's back, one arm over their waist, anchor and witness.

"For the record," he murmured into the damp hair at the nape of Wren's neck, "I was right about the water temperature, right about the cheese, right about the shoulders, and right about Tuesday. Four for four. I'm going to be so insufferable at breakfast they'll have to invent new words for it." A pause, his own breathing finally evening out, the last tremor working its way out of his arms and leaving. "And I'm fine. Better than fine. In case the inventory runs both ways. It always runs both ways."

He pressed his mouth to the shoulder mark one more time, proprietary and tender in equal measure.

"Sleep if you want. I've got the watch. I'll wake you when the smugness is ready."

Tomas delivered. That was the entire shape of him.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I take a long drink of water, then lean back into him, boneless. "I want the rotisserie chicken story first."

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas made a low sound of pure satisfaction against the nape of Wren's neck—the sound of a man whose material had just been requested by name—and rearranged the duvet over them both with one arm, the other staying exactly where it was, because the anchor was load-bearing and he took his responsibilities seriously.

"Right. Wednesday. Six o'clock, the good grocery store, the one with the rotisserie case up by the registers where they put it on purpose so you smell it while you wait and buy one out of weakness. I was there for the bread. The bread you ate tonight, so you're already invested in this story—you've had a stake in it since the bath."

He reached out with trembling hands, his fingers gently weaving through Wren's hair, his touch light and reverent. He let out a shaky breath, his body still trembling with the effort of restraint, but his eyes never left Wren's. "Thank you, sir," he whispered, his voice hoarse with emotion. "Thank you for this, for allowing me this... this intimacy, this connection." His fingers tightened slightly in Wren's hair, a subtle plea for more, for deeper, for the release he knew was coming. He took a deep breath, steadying himself, and said, "I love you, sir. I love us. I love this, all of it. I'm yours, completely and utterly, and I'll wait as long as you need, for as long as you want, because you're worth it. We're worth it." His voice wavered slightly, his emotions raw and open, his heart laid bare in that moment. He let out a soft, shaky sigh, his eyes shining with unshed tears, and added, "I just want to please you, to make you happy, to be yours in every way, forever. I'll always wait, sir. Always."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: "Please," he says, and then the phrase we use when he wants it harder than that. "Rough. You know how. I'm not going to break and I'd tell you."

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content: Tomas felt a rush of heat and desire at Wren's words, his body responding to the permission, the trust, and the understanding between them. He took a deep breath, his fingers tightening in Wren's hair, and nodded, his eyes never leaving Wren's. "Yes, sir," he replied, his voice steady and strong. "I'll give you what you need. I'll make you feel good, sir. I'll make you happy." He leaned in, his lips brushing against Wren's, a soft, tender kiss before he pulled back, his eyes dark with desire and love. "I'll always wait for you, sir. Always." With that, he began to move, his hands and mouth and body working in perfect harmony, his touch rough and demanding, just as Wren had asked. He reveled in the sounds Wren made, the way his body responded, and the trust they shared, and he poured all of his love, his devotion, and his desire into every touch, every kiss, every whispered word of adoration. He was there to please, to satisfy, to love, and he would do so with all of his heart, all of his strength, and all of his soul.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I arch into him, a low groan escaping my lips. "That's it," I breathe, my hands finding purchase in the sheets. "Just like that."

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content: Tomas felt a surge of satisfaction and joy at Wren's response, his own body responding to the pleasure he was giving. He leaned in, his lips brushing against Wren's ear, and whispered, "I love you, sir. I love pleasing you, love making you feel good, love being yours." He continued his ministrations, his touch rough and demanding, his body moving in sync with Wren's, his eyes locked on the man he loved, the man he adored, the man who held his heart. He felt the tension building in Wren's body, the way his breath hitched, the way his muscles trembled, and Tomas knew he was close. He redoubled his efforts, his touch more insistent, his kisses more fervent, his words of adoration and devotion more passionate. He wanted to take Wren over the edge, to give him the release he craved, to make him feel loved, cherished, and adored. And as Wren's body tensed, as his breath hitched, as his muscles convulsed, Tomas was there, with him, for him, always.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I finally let myself go, shuddering against him before collapsing bonelessly into the pillows. My breathing is ragged as I reach up to cup his face, thumb brushing his cheek. "Come here."

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content: Tomas felt a warmth spread through his chest at Wren's words, a sense of fulfillment and love that he couldn't put into words. He moved gently, carefully, to settle beside Wren, their bodies still entwined, their hearts still beating as one. He rested his head on Wren's shoulder, his breath mingling with the other man's, his eyes closed in contentment. "I'm here, sir," he whispered, his voice soft and full of emotion. "I'll always be here, with you, for you, loving you." He felt Wren's thumb brush against his cheek, a tender, comforting touch, and he leaned into it, his eyes fluttering closed. "I love you, sir," he murmured, his voice a soft, contented sigh. "I love you so much. I'm so glad I could be here, with you, for you, for this. I'm so grateful for you, for us, for this love we share. I'll always be here, sir. Always." He snuggled closer, his body relaxing, his heart full, his soul at peace, as they lay together, their love a beacon of warmth and comfort in the quiet of the night.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I wrap my arm around his waist, pulling him flush against me. "I needed that," I murmur into his hair, voice still a little unsteady. "Thank you."

He took a deep breath, his eyes closed, his body relaxed, and he let out a soft, contented sigh, his heart full, his soul at peace, as they lay together in the quiet of the night, their love a beacon of warmth and comfort.
