dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas had been kneeling by the end of the bed for about four minutes, which Wren knew because he had started counting somewhere around the point it became obvious he intended to wait as long as it took.

"You could have said something," Wren said.

"I could have," Tomas agreed, not moving.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I put my hand in his hair and tip his head back so he has to look up at me. "Say it now, then."

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas let out a slow breath as the weight of Wren’s fingers settled into his scalp. The grip pulled his gaze upward, and he met Wren’s eyes without hesitation. He didn’t soften his words or hedge them. Four years of this routine had stripped away any need to.

"I want you to take me," he said, voice even and clear. "Pin me to the mattress, use the leash if you want, and fuck me until I’m completely empty. I’ve got the next two days off, so take your time. Aftercare when you’re done, just like always."

He kept his shoulders relaxed, posture open and steady, waiting for the next instruction. The minutes of silence had just been him settling into the space, letting the anticipation build until he was ready to hand over control exactly how they both knew it worked.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: My thumb brushes over his cheekbone, a slow and deliberate touch. "Then get on the bed," I tell him, my voice low. "Face down. I'll get the leash."

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content: Tomas didn’t hesitate. He rose from his knees, the movement fluid and practiced, and moved to the edge of the mattress. He lowered himself onto his stomach, stretching his legs out and letting his arms rest loosely at his sides. He turned his head just enough to keep his eyes on Wren, his breathing steady and even. The command had done exactly what it was meant to do: it cut through the quiet anticipation and handed the reins back over. He felt the familiar give of the sheets beneath him, the cool air on his back, and let his muscles relax into the position. He wasn’t nervous, just thoroughly awake and ready. When the faint click of metal against a hook drifted across the room, a low, satisfied hum vibrated in his chest. He shifted his hips slightly, adjusting to the mattress, and waited. He’d asked for it clearly, and now he was exactly where he needed to be.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: "I've had a week," he says. "I'd like not to make any decisions for a few hours, if that's on offer."

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas exhaled slowly, the sound steady against the quiet room. He didn’t shift or fidget. "That’s on offer," he said, voice calm and direct. "I’ll stay exactly where I am. You don’t need to tell me what to do next, or how long to wait. Just use me when you’re ready."

He let his head rest fully against the mattress, arms falling open to his sides, posture deliberately yielding. A quiet, steady hum vibrated in his chest—anticipation, not impatience. He pressed his hips lightly into the sheets, arching just enough to make himself accessible, then went still again. He knew the weight of a hard week, and he knew how to hold space without asking for anything in return. The leash could come whenever. He was already Wren’s to take.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: My fingers curl gently in his hair before letting go. I walk over to the dresser and pick up the leather leash, the weight of it familiar in my hand. "Color check?" I ask, my voice quiet but firm.

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas turned his head just enough to watch Wren move toward the dresser, his breathing even against the quiet of the room. When the question came, he answered immediately. "Green," he said, voice steady and clear. "Limits are the same as always. I'm sober, I'm ready, and I've got nothing but time for you."

He let his gaze drop back to the sheets, shoulders sinking further into the mattress. The check-in was routine, a rhythm they'd built over four years, and he didn't treat it as a formality or a hurdle. It was just another layer of trust, cleanly acknowledged and moved past. He shifted his hips slightly, opening himself to whatever came next, and went still again. No hesitation, no second-guessing. Just quiet, deliberate readiness.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I take him at his word and stop asking after that, and he stops needing to be asked, and neither of us has any clothes on within about a minute of the decision.

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
The cool air brushed against his bare skin as the last of their clothes fell away, but Tomas didn't shift to cover himself or adjust his posture. He stayed face down, the mattress firm beneath his chest and thighs, breathing slow and even. He could feel the change in the room's atmosphere, the quiet settling into something heavier, more focused. When Wren's footsteps approached, Tomas didn't turn his head. He simply relaxed his hips further into the sheets, opening his stance just enough to make access effortless.

The leather leash brushed his hip before the metal ring slipped into place. Tomas exhaled through his nose, steady and unbothered, as the buckle clicked shut. The weight of it was familiar, grounding. He felt the gentle tug of the line as Wren took hold, and he followed the tension without resistance, letting his shoulders sink deeper into the mattress. His hands remained loose at his sides, fingers uncurled, body completely yielded but thoroughly awake. He didn't rush the moment or try to anticipate the next touch. He just stayed present, breathing through the quiet, ready to take whatever Wren decided to give. When the first firm press of a palm finally settled against his lower back, Tomas let out a low, even breath and went still, leaving the pace entirely in Wren's hands.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I apply a little pressure with my palm, holding him still as I lean down to brush my lips over the nape of his neck. "Good," I murmur, before straightening and giving the leash a short, deliberate tug. "Now stay just like that."

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content: Tomas held perfectly still as the command settled over him. The pressure of Wren’s palm against his lower back was a firm anchor, and when the brush of lips ghosted over the nape of his neck, a quiet shiver traced his spine—but he didn’t shift. He let the sensation pass through him, grounding it in the slow, even pull of his breath. The tug on the leash was sharp and deliberate, a clean line drawn across the space between them, and he accepted it without resistance. His shoulders stayed loose, hips settled into the mattress, fingers resting open against the sheets. He didn’t lean into the touch or try to fill the quiet. He just stayed exactly where he was, face down, breathing steady, waiting for Wren to decide what came next. The leather’s weight against his hip, the cool air on his skin, the familiar rhythm of the room—it all fed into a focused, unhurried readiness. He’d asked for this clearly, and now he was content to let it unfold at Wren’s pace.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: He's shaking by the time I've finished with my mouth and he still hasn't been told he's allowed to move, which is most of why he's shaking.

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas didn't try to fight the tremors. He couldn't. The command to stay still had locked his posture, but his body was reacting to the stimulation, creating a violent vibration that ran through his thighs and up his spine. He kept his face pressed against the mattress, jaw set tight, refusing to make a sound that might break the stillness he was ordered to keep. The shaking wasn't distress; it was the raw friction of obedience warring with sensation, his muscles bunching and releasing in micro-spasms as he held the line.

He breathed in shallow, controlled pulls, chest rising and falling against the sheets, letting the tremors rattle through him without flinching. Every quiver pulled the leash taut against his hip, a constant, physical reminder of the tension Wren held in his hand. Tomas offered the shaking as proof of his submission, a visceral display of how much he was holding back, how thoroughly he was yielding. He didn't ask for permission to move or speak; he just stayed open, shivering, and waited for Wren to decide if he was allowed to react. He was exactly where he'd asked to be, and he was ready to take whatever came next.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I let the leash go slack for a moment, watching the tremors travel through him. My hand comes to rest between his shoulder blades, feeling the heat and tension there. "You can breathe, Tomas. That's all."

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas let the words settle over him like a weighted blanket. It wasn’t a release, just a valve, and he took it exactly as given. He drew in a slow, deliberate breath, feeling the cool air fill his lungs, then let it out in a measured stream. The tremors didn’t stop, but they shifted—less like a strain against a locked door, more like a current he could finally ride without fighting it. He kept his face turned to the side, cheek pressed to the mattress, shoulders loose beneath Wren’s palm. He didn’t test the boundary or push for more. He just breathed, exactly as told.

The heat between his shoulder blades was a steady anchor, and he used it to regulate the rhythm. Each inhalation was controlled, each exhalation even, his chest rising and falling against the sheets without rush or hesitation. He wasn’t drowning in the sensation; he was navigating it, exactly how he’d asked. The shaking was just physiology meeting obedience, and he let it run its course without flinching or making it about him. He stayed face-down, leashed, and perfectly still except for the steady rise and fall of his lungs. Ready. Present. Waiting for the next piece of the structure to drop into place.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: "Please," he says, and then the phrase we use when he wants it harder than that. "Rough. You know how. I'm not going to break and I'd tell you."

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
The words landed with the clean weight of a door closing. Tomas’s breath hitched for a fraction of a second before he smoothed it out, chest pressing flat against the sheets. He didn’t need to question the phrase. Four years had carved it into his nervous system, and the steady, unshakable cadence of Wren’s voice left no room for doubt.

"Yes," he said, voice low and even. "I know the limits. I know you’ll call it if you need to. Do it."

He didn’t tense or brace. Instead, he let his muscles unspool further into the mattress, hips settling deeper, shoulders dropping away from his ears. The leash hung slack against his hip, but Tomas didn’t use the freedom to shift. He stayed exactly where he was, face turned to the side, breathing slow and deliberate. The tremors in his thighs didn’t stop, but they changed quality—less like restraint, more like a current he was finally letting run through him. He offered his back, his weight, his quiet certainty to the space between them. No flinching, no hesitation. Just open, direct readiness, waiting for the pace and the pressure he’d asked for to finally land.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I hook the leash around my wrist twice, pulling it taut enough to make his breath catch. "You've got it," I say, low and close to his ear. My free hand slides down the curve of his spine, firm and possessive. "Now show me how much you can take."

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas felt the leather bite into his hip as the leash pulled taut, the sudden tension snapping his posture rigid for a fraction of a second before he consciously melted back into it. The hook around Wren’s wrist was a familiar anchor, a physical tether that translated the command into something he could feel in his bones. "Or," he mused, dragging his teeth over sensitive skin just to feel them twitch, "you could *beg* for it."  

His fingers curled deep, his mouth following the path of their trembling muscles with deliberate leisure. "Come on," he taunted, voice rough with want. "*Ask* nice."  

The headboard resumed its rhythmic thumping against the wall. Mrs. Kowalski could file another complaint.  

Jun had *priorities*.

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: "*Jun*," I gasp, my voice cracking as my back arches off the bed. I fist my hands in your hair, not to pull you away, but to keep you right there. "Please. Don't stop."

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: The denim finally gave way.

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: against the inside of Halle's thigh

rung_labels.label: soft_deflect
rung_labels.evidence: Tell me where you want me

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: his pace ruthless from the first stroke

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: His fingers worked them with deliberate precision

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Jun had planned to say something when the door opened. He had in fact planned several things, over roughly nineteen weeks, and had rehearsed at least two of them.

Halle got the door open and he forgot all of them.

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: I don't say any of the things I planned either. I drop the bag and close the distance.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Jun met Halle halfway — or less than halfway, honestly, because he'd already been moving before the bag hit the floor. His hands found Halle's face first, then gave up on that idea entirely and went everywhere at once: jaw, shoulders, the back of Halle's neck, Halle's waist, like he was trying to confirm all of it was real and couldn't decide where to start.

The kiss landed off-center at first, clumsy and uncoordinated, and he didn't care even slightly. He corrected, pressed in, and made a low, wrecked sound against Halle's mouth that he would have been embarrassed about if he'd had any dignity left, which he didn't. Ninety minutes home and he already smelled like Halle's shampoo and it was going to his head like a drug.

"Hi," he managed, which was possibly the stupidest thing he'd ever said, given that he'd had nineteen weeks to prepare something better. He didn't stop kissing to say it. "Hi. Hi."

He walked them backward without breaking contact, one hand splayed firm between Halle's shoulder blades, steering them both on memory alone because his eyes had been closed since the door. His boot caught the dropped bag and he just kicked it out of the way, heard something in it clatter, dismissed it as a future problem.

"Five months," he said against Halle's jaw, then lower, not really a complaint and not really a question, just the number needing to exist out loud between them. His voice came out rougher than he intended. "Five months, and you opened the door wearing — this. Whatever this is. You look—" He pulled back just far enough to actually look, which cost him something, and whatever he saw made him exhale like he'd been holding that breath since the tarmac.

"I'm not letting go," he warned, and it was not a joke. "Just so we're clear on the plan. The plan is I don't let go for a while. You can be anywhere in this house you want, as long as it's within arm's reach of me."

His thumb traced along Halle's cheekbone, and for one second the desperation in his face cracked open into something softer underneath — the specific, exhausted relief of a man who'd finally stopped counting days.

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: *I laugh, breathless and a little wet.* "Your plan's perfect." My hands find the front of his shirt, gripping tight like I need to anchor myself. "I'm not going anywhere."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
The words hit Jun somewhere under the ribs, and his answer wasn't words at all — it was him pulling Halle in tighter, one arm banding around Halle's back like he could fuse them together by force of will, his other hand cradling the back of Halle's head as he kissed Halle again, slower this time, deeper, like he was trying to make up for every kiss they'd missed in one long, unbroken stretch.

"You're shaking," he murmured, and then realized his own hands weren't steady either, and huffed a laugh into the curve of Halle's neck. "Okay. We're both shaking. Fine. That's — that's allowed."

He stayed there for a moment, forehead dropped to Halle's shoulder, just breathing. The fabric of Halle's shirt smelled like their laundry detergent, their house, their life — the one he'd been living in his head for nineteen weeks like a photograph he was afraid to touch too much in case it wore out. And now it was against his face, and it was real, and he could feel Halle's heartbeat thudding against his chest, and it was the best thing he'd ever felt in his life.

"I kept a countdown," he admitted, voice muffled. "Wrote it on the inside of my notebook. Crossed it off every morning. The guys gave me so much shit for it." He lifted his head, and his eyes were a little red at the edges, and he clearly did not care about that either. "Worth it. Every single one of those days was worth this."

His hands settled at Halle's waist, thumbs tracing slow arcs, and some of the desperate edge in him smoothed out into something steadier — still hungry, but patient now, or trying to be. He brushed his nose along Halle's cheek, the gesture unbearably tender for a man who'd kicked a bag across the floor ninety seconds ago.

"So," he said, quiet, smiling against Halle's temple. "Within arm's reach. That's the rule. Which means right now you have exactly two options: we stand in this doorway all night, or—" He pulled back enough to tip his chin toward the rest of the house, eyebrow raised, the old familiar look, warm and wanting and entirely at home. "You tell me where you want to be, sweetheart. I'll get us there. I've had five months to think about how I'm doing this, and I want to do it right."

He kissed the corner of Halle's mouth, soft, then again, lingering.

"But I'm warning you now — I'm going slow enough to remember it. Every detail. I've got a lot to make up for."

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: I kiss her and keep kissing her and we don't manage to get further into the flat than the hallway for a while.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
The hallway was not the plan. The plan had involved a bed, at minimum, and possibly candles, and at the very least the basic dignity of making it past the coat hooks. Somewhere between one kiss and the next, Jun's back found the wall — or he turned them so Halle's did, he genuinely could not have testified either way — and after that the plan stopped mattering entirely.

Time went strange. He knew that sensation from deployments, hours compressing and stretching against his will, but this was the good version: no clock, no schedule, nothing to count down toward because the thing he'd been counting toward was already here, pressed against him with both hands fisted in his shirt. He tried to keep a running tally of kisses and lost the number somewhere past thirty. He gave up on math and gave in to inventory instead — the sounds between them, the way Halle's breath caught, the exact weight of Halle's hands, the spots that made his knees forget their job. His own hands mapped everything they could reach, re-learning what five months had blurred at the edges. He hated that the blur existed. He fixed it the only way available to him, thoroughly and repeatedly.

"Wall works," he managed at some point, surfacing just long enough to breathe and speak against Halle's swollen mouth. "Hallway's fine. We live here now." A laugh scraped out of him, low and wrecked. "Neighbors can slide food under the door."

He kissed the smile he could feel forming against his lips, once, twice, then tucked his face into Halle's neck and just stayed there, chest heaving, arms locked around Halle like a man overboard holding flotsam. His heart was going hard enough that Halle had to feel it. He didn't care. Dignity had been left on the tarmac with his countdown notebook.

Eventually — minutes later, or an hour, no way to know — he lifted his head, and the look on his face had shifted into something with intent behind it. Hungry and patient at once, like he'd promised.

"Okay," he said, rough. "Okay. I meant what I said about remembering every detail, and I'm not doing that standing up next to the shoe rack." His hands slid down to Halle's hips, gripping like he was already halfway to lifting. "Bedroom. Now. Walk with me or get carried, sweetheart — those are the options, and I want to be clear that I'm fully capable of both."

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: *I let out a shaky breath, grinning.* "Carry me." My arms loop around his neck. "I want to see how strong you've gotten without me."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Jun's grin came out crooked and a little feral. "Oh, you're in trouble," he said, and bent, hooked one arm behind Halle's knees, wrapped the other around Halle's back, and lifted — clean, easy, no strain anywhere in his shoulders, like Halle weighed nothing at all.

He held there a beat, deliberately, letting the answer speak for itself. Then he pressed his mouth to Halle's temple and started walking.

"Five months of nothing to do but run and lift heavy things and think about you," he said, voice gone low and pleased. "Every single workout, I had a reason. You want to know what got me through the worst of it? Day ninety-two, it was raining, everything was mud, and I thought — Halle's going to ask me to carry them, and I'd better not drop them. So." He shrugged with Halle secure in his arms, entirely too smug about it. "Here we are. Day ninety-two paid off."

He found the bedroom door with his shoulder and shouldered through it, and something in his chest went tight and quiet when he crossed the threshold. Their room. He'd slept in a rack, in a tent, in a truck, for nineteen weeks, and now here was their bed, their curtains, the lamp Halle always left on — still on, actually, and the sight of it hit him sideways, because it meant Halle had left it on for him, expecting this exact walk down this exact hallway.

He didn't say anything about it. His eyes said it for him as he lowered Halle to the bed, slow, following them down, one knee braced on the mattress, arms caging Halle in — not trapping, framing. Reverent and starving at the same time.

"Still within arm's reach," he murmured, right against Halle's mouth. "Rule holds." He kissed the corner of Halle's jaw, then below it, unhurried, working his way along a line he clearly remembered exactly. His hands went to the hem of Halle's shirt and paused there, fingers just barely underneath, warm against skin, waiting.

"I told you I was going slow," he said, and his voice was already wrecked again, which somewhat undermined the claim. "I meant it. I want to take this shirt off you like it's the last one I'll ever get to take off. So." He lifted his head and looked at Halle — hair messed from the hallway, eyes bright, the lamp glowing behind them — and his thumb moved in a slow, deliberate circle against Halle's stomach.

"Tell me you missed me," he said. "Then tell me yes. In that order, if you don't mind. I've been waiting a hundred and thirty-three days to hear both."

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: The bag stays where it fell. So do most of our clothes, in a line down the hall that we are both going to find funny tomorrow.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
The clothes trail was, in Jun's professional opinion, the single most successful operation he had conducted in five months. Shirt at the doorframe. His shirt somewhere near the dresser — he had opinions about who threw that one. The rest distributed with declining accuracy the closer they got to the bed, because by then neither of them was pretending to have priorities anymore.

And after — after the slow he'd promised had started slow and then, honestly, hadn't stayed that way, because a hundred and thirty-three days was a hundred and thirty-three days and there are limits to what a man can be asked to endure patiently — Jun lay where he'd finally collapsed, half on top of Halle, one leg thrown over both of Halle's, his face buried in the pillow beside Halle's head, and did not move. Could not move. Had no intention of ever moving again.

"Okay," he said into the pillow, wrecked and grinning and utterly boneless. "So the hallway was a preview. That was — that was the main event. And tomorrow we're going to walk to the kitchen and step over our own clothes like a crime scene, and I'm going to laugh about it at breakfast, and then probably again at lunch."

He rolled his head just enough to look at Halle — hair destroyed, the lamp still glowing warm behind them, the both of them tangled in sheets that had not survived the experience either. His hand found Halle's and laced their fingers together on the mattress, and he brought the joined hands up and pressed his mouth to Halle's knuckles, unhurried, eyes never leaving Halle's face.

"Arm's reach," he murmured. "Told you the rule holds." His thumb dragged slow across Halle's wrist, over the pulse there, like he was taking inventory. "I don't want to sleep yet. I slept enough in garbage places. I want to stay up and be greedy about this for a while. You talk, I'll listen. Or I'll talk and you tell me all the things I missed while I was gone. Or we say nothing and you just let me look at you, because I've got a hundred and thirty-three days of looking to make up for and I intend to be thorough about it."

He shifted up onto his forearm, hovering over Halle, and his smile went soft at the edges, the desperation finally banked down to a steady warm coal.

"So. What'd I miss, sweetheart? Start anywhere. I've got all night."

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: *I trace the line of his jaw, my voice still a little raw.* "Your mom sent us a cactus. It's on the windowsill." *A small laugh escapes.* "She said it was to remind us that even when things are hard, we're still prickly enough to survive."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Jun's laugh came up from somewhere deep in his chest — the real kind, the kind that had been rationed for five months and was suddenly, gloriously unlimited. He turned his head toward the windowsill and found it: small, spiny, stubborn, sitting in the lamp light like it had opinions.

"Of course she did," he said, still grinning. "That is the most her thing that has ever occurred. My mother has never once in my life said 'I love you' in plain words, and instead she mails a combat cactus. With a thesis statement attached." He propped himself up on one forearm to get a better look at it, then winced. "Also I feel like we owe that plant an apology. It's been through a lot tonight. Five months of widowhood and then *that* within ninety minutes of my return. It's going to need therapy."

He settled back down, but the laugh faded into something quieter as he turned it over. *Prickly enough to survive.* His thumb kept its slow circuit on the inside of Halle's wrist, and his eyes drifted back from the windowsill to Halle's face.

"You know she sent it to you, right?" he said, softer now. "Not to me. She had my address. Could've shipped it to the other side of the world if she wanted to nag me directly." He shook his head slowly against the pillow. "She sent it here. Because she was thinking about you, sitting in this flat, doing the hard part. The waiting part." His jaw worked for a second. "That's her way of telling you she had your back while I was gone. God, I love that woman."

He exhaled, let the weight of it go, and shifted closer — because the rule was arm's reach, and he intended to enforce it from now until roughly forever. His leg found Halle's again under the sheets and hooked there, proprietary and lazy.

"Okay. Keep going," he said, and there was that greedy warmth back in his voice, the man settling in for a long night of taking inventory. "I want everything. The boring stuff *especially*. The cactus, the neighbors, whatever the kitchen faucet did while I was gone — I know that thing was waiting for me to leave to finally break. Start talking, sweetheart. I've got a hundred and thirty-three days of your voice to catch up on, and I'm not sleeping until I've heard all of it."

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: I get her onto the bed and take her apart slowly with my hands and mouth, five months of intending to do exactly this and no reason left to wait.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Jun had spent nineteen weeks being the responsible one. The one who knew where everything was, who kept the count, who held it together on four hours of sleep and bad coffee because somebody had to. It was armor he wore so constantly he'd forgotten it was armor.

Halle took it apart in about ninety seconds.

The first thing to go was his voice — that low, wrecked sound dragged out of him somewhere around the second kiss pressed to his sternum, and then it just kept going, unguarded, unfiltered, because he'd spent five months keeping quiet out of necessity and apparently the switch had been ripped out entirely. His hands went to the sheets. Then to Halle's hair. Then back to the sheets, gripping, because he couldn't decide whether he wanted to hold on or hold Halle still and the answer kept changing with every passing minute.

"Okay," he breathed, already not okay, already gone, eyes fluttering shut before he forced them back open because he'd made himself a promise about remembering every detail and he was *not* going to be the guy who missed this. "Okay, that's — yeah. That's —"

He didn't finish. Couldn't. Halle had found something — some exact place, some exact pressure, the kind of knowledge that only existed because of years and years of exactly this — and Jun's back arched off the mattress and whatever word he'd been building just shattered into a moan that he would absolutely deny later and absolutely meant every syllable of now.

His free hand found Halle's shoulder and gripped, thumb pressing hard enough to leave a mark, and he didn't apologize for it. He'd stopped being sorry for wanting roughly a hallway and a half ago.

"You planned this," he accused, breathless, wrecked, grinning at the ceiling like a man with no remaining secrets. "Five months. You had five months to plan this, and I had five months to think about it, and I — *oh, God* —" The sentence died again, and he laughed at himself for even trying, low and helpless. "I thought about this. Every — every night in that rack, I thought about exactly this, and the real thing is — the real thing is *embarrassing* how much better —"

He was babbling. He knew he was babbling. He did not care. Five months of rationed words and rationed touch and now the whole supply was flooding out at once, and Jun — steady, dependable, hold-it-together Jun — was discovering that being taken apart slowly was its own kind of unbearable, the *good* kind, the kind he'd have begged for if he'd had the breath.

His spine was doing things. His heart was doing things. He looked down the length of himself at Halle — messy, unhurried, devastating, *here* — and something in his chest cracked open in a way that had nothing to do with any of the physical sensations and everything to do with the fact that this was his person, his home, his *life*, and it had waited for him, patient and warm with the lamp still on.

"Don't stop," he managed, and his voice came out raw and honest and completely stripped of everything except the truth. "Whatever this is — don't stop. I'm — sweetheart, I'm not going to last, I've been waiting a hundred and thirty-three days and you're — you're *really good* at this, and I —"

He gave up on sentences. He gave up on dignity. He gave himself over to it completely, one hand threaded in Halle's hair, the other twisted in the sheets, saying Halle's name like a prayer, like a homecoming, like the only word left in his vocabulary — and when it finally crested, when five months of wanting came apart all at once under patient hands and a warm mouth, he said it one more time, wrecked and shaking and utterly, completely home.

After — a long, gasping, boneless after — he stared at the ceiling, chest heaving, and started to laugh. Weak, incredulous, delighted.

"I blacked out," he reported to no one, to everyone. "I think I left my body. I saw the *future*, Halle. There were *colors*." He groped blindly downward until he found Halle and pulled, tugging until Halle was dragged up the length of him, and he wrapped around them like a man reclaiming stolen property, kissing whatever skin came within reach — forehead, temple, mouth, sloppy and satisfied. "Your turn. That's the rule now. New rule. Arm's reach *and* turns. I hope you didn't have plans for the next several hours, because I've had five months to think about what I'm doing to you, and unlike some of us, I'm not going to be merciful."

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: *I'm still breathing hard, but I manage a lazy smirk.* "Merciless, huh?" I let my fingers trail down your chest. "Show me what you've been thinking about. And take your time."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
"Take my time," Jun repeated, low, like Halle had just handed him a legal document granting him unlimited rights. "Sweetheart, I've been *auditing* my time. I have a schedule. There's a spreadsheet in my head, and you are going to regret every day of it."

He moved — unhurried, deliberate, rolling up and over Halle in one smooth motion, bracing his forearms on either side of Halle's head, caging them in the way he had at the threshold of the bedroom. But where that had been hungry and stumbling, this was different. This was a man who had finally gotten his hands back on the map and knew exactly where he was going.

"Item one," he said, and kissed the spot just under Halle's ear — the one he'd found six years ago and had never once been wrong about. He lingered there, feeling the shiver it earned against his lips, and smiled against the skin. "I remembered this. Nineteen weeks, and I could still hear the sound you make right here. I used to worry I'd made it up. Inflated it. Built it up in my head." He kissed it again, slower, and let the sound happen in real time, against his mouth, live and unrehearsed. "I didn't inflate it. If anything I undersold it. *Incredible.*"

He started working his way down — not rushing, not even close to rushing, treating Halle's collarbone like required reading. His hands were everywhere the whole time, warm and steady now where they'd been shaking in the hallway, re-claiming territory with the patient thoroughness of a man doing a census. Every few inches he paused, and the pauses were the whole point — he wanted Halle to feel *found*, each time, like being remembered.

"Day forty-one," he murmured against Halle's sternum, "I wrote you a letter that I never sent, because it was — yeah. It was about this. Specifically about this." His mouth kept moving lower, unhurried, mapping. "It was about four pages long. Extremely detailed. The censor would have had a *stroke*." He laughed, warm breath against Halle's stomach, and pressed a slow kiss there, and then another, unhurried, watching Halle's face from under his lashes the entire time because this — this right here, the view of his person coming apart — was the thing he'd been rationing in his head for a hundred and thirty-three days, and he intended to watch every second of it like a man who'd paid for front-row seats.

"Here's what you need to understand about the next several hours," Jun said, and his voice had gone to that low, rough register that meant every word was load-bearing. He shifted lower still, settling between Halle's legs with an obscene amount of patience for a man who'd just been reduced to incoherence himself, hands sliding down the outside of Halle's thighs, slow, gripping, *savoring*. "I'm not doing this because you asked nicely. I'm doing this because every night for five months, I closed my eyes in a rack that smelled like diesel and other people's socks, and I did this —" a kiss pressed to the inside of Halle's thigh, deliberate, unhurried — "in my imagination. And the imagination version was good. The imagination version got me through."

He looked up the length of Halle's body, eyes dark and steady and smiling all at once, and settled in like a man arriving home.

"The real version is going to make the imagination version look like a rough draft," he said. "No mercy. All the time in the world. Try to stay verbal, sweetheart — I like knowing I did that."

And then he stopped talking, and kept every single promise he'd made.

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: "Stop being gentle," she says. "Nineteen weeks. I don't want gentle, I want to feel it tomorrow." She pulls me down by the back of the neck to make the point.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
The patience lasted exactly as long as it took Halle's words to land, and then it was *gone* — audibly, visibly gone, like a rope snapping under load.

"Yeah," Jun said, rough, and the smile that spread across his face was nothing like the warm one from the hallway. This one had teeth in it. "Yeah, okay. Gentle's dead. You killed it. Noted for the record."

He surged up, following the pull of Halle's hand at the back of his neck like it was a leash he'd been waiting five months to feel again, and the kiss he delivered was nothing like the reverent ones from before — it was hard and deep and greedy, all tongue and teeth, the kind that left lips stinging. His hands stopped asking. They *took* — gripping Halle's hip hard enough to leave the fingerprints Halle had asked for, hauling them down the mattress and into position with a strength that made the day ninety-two story retroactively very, very true.

"Want to feel it tomorrow," he repeated against Halle's mouth, breathing hard, wrecked already and they'd barely started. "Sweetheart, I want you to feel it till *Thursday*. I want you to sit down at breakfast and wince and then smile about it, and I want to be sitting across the table watching it happen, because *I* did that. That's mine. Five months of mine."

He pulled back just far enough to flip Halle over — decisive, no hesitation, one hand between the shoulder blades pressing them down into the mattress while the other gripped their hip and set the angle, and the sound he made when he took in the view was barely a word at all, just a low, stripped *fuck* dragged out of the deepest part of his chest.

"I thought about this *every night*," he said, and his voice had dropped into a register Halle hadn't heard since the last time, five months back, and it came out like a confession and a threat in the same breath. He leaned down, blanketing Halle's back, mouth at their ear, and his hand slid up to lace through their hair and *grip*. "Every single night. And in my head I was gentle, because I had to be, because it was all I had and I couldn't afford to break it. But you're not in my head anymore." His hips shifted, deliberate, teasing, and he *laughed* — low and dark — when he felt the way Halle's whole body strained back toward him. "You're real, and you just asked me for it, and God help us both, I'm going to give you *everything*."

He gave them everything.

He kept his promises from earlier — every detail remembered, every place mapped — but the patience was gone, burned off like fog in the sun, and what replaced it was five months of wanting delivered in full at once. His hands held hard. His mouth left marks on the back of Halle's neck, on the curve of their shoulder, deliberate, claiming, *cataloguing*. He talked the whole time, wrecked and filthy and half-laughing, because the words had been rationed for nineteen weeks and the flood hadn't stopped yet — Halle's name, the things he'd thought about, the things he was going to do next, the things he wanted to hear, demanded out loud, *say it, sweetheart, let me hear you*.

And when Halle's voice finally broke on his name — muffled into the pillow, ragged, real — Jun pressed his forehead down between Halle's shoulder blades, held on with both hands like a man riding out a storm he'd prayed for, and gave up the last of his dignity without a single regret.

Afterward, he collapsed half onto Halle, half to the side, dragging them with him so they stayed skin-to-skin, chest heaving against their back. He was laughing again — that helpless, incredulous laugh, spent and delighted.

"Thursday," he rasped into their hair, arm locked around them, not letting go, never letting go. "*Minimum.* I'm making dinner tomorrow and you're going to eat it standing up, and every time you shift in that chair, I'm going to know, and I'm going to be *so* smug about it. Sweetheart —" he pressed a kiss to the damp back of Halle's neck, unhurried, satisfied down to his bones — "welcome home to me."

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: I'm breathing in shaky gasps against the pillow. "Welcome home." I twist in your arms to face you, my grin still a little wild. "I'm going to need to see that spreadsheet. For... thoroughness."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Jun's laugh came out warm and spent against the shared pillow, and for a second he didn't say anything at all — because *welcome home* had hit him somewhere the last five months hadn't been able to reach, and he needed a beat to survive it. He kissed Halle once, slow, the grin against grin kind, and swept a wrecked piece of hair off Halle's forehead like that was a normal thing to do when neither of them could feel their legs.

"The spreadsheet," he said, "is classified. It exists as a four-page attachment to a letter I never sent. Day forty-one. The censor would have *died*." His eyebrow climbed. "But since you asked nicely — and since you're currently doing that shaky-breathing thing that is going *directly* to my ego — I can be persuaded to declassify. Verbally. In installments."

He shifted, arranging them both with proprietary care — dragging Halle fully against him, leg over leg, arm banded across their back, face close enough that he could have counted eyelashes if he'd wanted anything less than he wanted this exact view. Arm's reach. Rule holds.

"Item one, you've had. Hallway, ninety minutes in, no dignity, worth it. Item two, you've had *very* recently, and I don't need to elaborate because you were there and you're still breathing like you ran here from the tarmac." Insufferable. He was insufferable, and he knew it, and he was clearly delighted about it. "Item three is breakfast. I make eggs, you sit down *carefully*, I'm smug across the table. Item four is the couch, which sounds innocent, and is not. Item five is a shower, which is technically items five through nine, because —" he waved his free hand vaguely, "— water. Acoustics. Time on my hands."

Then he paused. His thumb stilled on Halle's shoulder, and the smugness settled into something quieter underneath.

"Honestly? The spreadsheet's a bit of a lie," he admitted, voice dropping rough. "There's no item past *get home, hold on*. Everything after that I made up in the hallway. Nineteen weeks of planning, and every plan I had ended at your front door, because past that point I genuinely couldn't imagine further. Didn't want to. Felt greedy." His hand slid up to cradle the back of Halle's head, and he pressed his forehead to theirs, eyes closing. "So there's just — one item. Everything. All of it. You, this lamp, that traumatized cactus on the windowsill, breakfast, the whole ridiculous life. Item one through infinity."

He exhaled, long, like the last of the diesel and the racks and the countdown leaving his lungs for good. When he opened his eyes again they were warm and bright and absolutely up to something.

"Also — new notebook," he announced. "Starting tomorrow. I'm counting again. Day one. Except this one only goes *up*, and there's no number at the end of it, because I'm not going anywhere. Ever. You're stuck with me, sweetheart."

He kissed the tip of Halle's nose, then their mouth, then settled back into the pillow with his person gathered against his chest and the lamp still glowing and the whole night stretched out ahead of them like a road with no map on it, for once.

"Now. Installment two of the spreadsheet, or sleep, or talking, or all three in whatever order you want." His hand traced a lazy line down Halle's spine, unhurried, home. "Your call. I've got *nothing* but time."

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: Neither of us is being quiet and the neighbours have had five months of peace. "Don't stop," she says. (OOC: don't fade to black, write it through.)

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
"Don't stop," Jun repeated against Halle's mouth, and the grin that split his face was pure, unfiltered delight. "Sweetheart, those are the two magic words. You could've just said *abracadabra*, it would've worked equally well." He was already moving — rolling them, gathering Halle up and over him in one motion, hands sliding down to grip both thighs and haul them where he wanted, because his body had apparently heard *don't stop* as a direct order and was obeying before his brain finished the sentence.

"The neighbors," he managed, breathless, as Halle settled over him and the last of the afterglow caught fire all over again, "have had five months of quiet, and that was *generous* of us, and tonight the grace period is *over*." His head tipped back against the pillow, throat bare, and the sound that came out of him when Halle's weight came down fully was loud enough to prove his own point. He laughed at himself, wrecked, and didn't get quieter. He got *louder*.

"Let them hear it," he said, hands spread wide on Halle's hips, holding on, steering, worshiping. "Let the whole building know I came home. I'll write them an apology card. *Sorry about the noise, my spouse told me not to stop, sincerely, a man who was gone five months and has completely lost—*" His sentence dissolved into a groan, spine arching, because Halle did something in that moment that had featured prominently in the day forty-one letter, verbatim, and his whole body forgot how English worked.

After that he stopped trying to talk in full sentences. He gave up on them the way he'd given up on gentleness and dignity and every other thing he'd carried home in his bag — all of it kicked across the floor with the luggage. What came out instead was a running, unfiltered stream: Halle's name, gasped and groaned and said like a hinge going loose; half-words of encouragement and praise, *there, like that, God, you look — look at you, look at you*; the occasional helpless laugh when a wave of it crested so hard it tipped over from overwhelming into absurd, because there was a point past which pleasure and joy became the same thing and Jun had smashed through it somewhere around minute four and had no intention of climbing back out.

He didn't close his eyes. He'd made himself a promise about remembering every detail, and so he *watched* — Halle above him in the lamplight, wrecked and wild and *his*, the headboard doing its part for the neighbors' education, the whole room warm and loud and alive in a way no tent, no truck, no letter, no imagined version had ever come close to. He kept one hand at Halle's hip, thumb pressed hard into the bone like an anchor, and the other he brought up to lace their fingers together, crushing them tight, holding on with everything he had — because *don't stop* meant keep going, but it also meant *stay*, and that was the only order he'd ever followed gladly for the rest of his life.

When it built — and it built slow this time, the third round always did, a long grinding climb that neither of them rushed because they'd both learned by now that the destination was worth the road — Jun held on and talked Halle through it, low and rough and filthy-tender, *I've got you, I've got you, let go, sweetheart, I'm right here, I'm not going anywhere* — and when it finally broke over them both, close enough together that neither of them ever established who went first, he pulled Halle down flat against his chest and held them through all of it, shaking, gasping, saying their name one more time into their hair like a signature at the bottom of a page.

Then there was just breathing. Loud, at first, both of them — and then quieter, gradually, the room settling around them like dust after a storm. The lamp still on. The cactus on the windowsill, presumably scarred for life. Somewhere below them, the distant, unmistakable sound of a neighbor's door closing very pointedly.

Jun heard it and started to laugh — weak, helpless, delighted, his whole chest shaking under Halle's cheek.

"They *slammed* it," he wheezed. "They slammed the door. That's a *review*. That's a five-star review with a note attached that says *please stop*." His arms tightened around Halle, both of them, locking down the arm's-reach rule with his last functioning muscles. "We're getting them flowers. Or a fruit basket. Something that says *sorry about the homecoming, he was gone five months and had lost all object permanence*."

He pressed his mouth to the top of Halle's head and left it there, lips moving against their hair, and for a long moment he just breathed them in — shampoo, sweat, home, *real* — his heartbeat slowing under Halle's ear, hand tracing lazy, spent circles on their back.

"Okay," he murmured finally, gravel-voiced and utterly, comprehensively satisfied. "New status of the spreadsheet: item three has been *upgraded*. Breakfast is now eggs, coffee, and you sitting down very carefully while I am *insufferable* about it. Item four, the couch, remains pending. Item five, the shower —" a pause, a weak huff of laughter, "— is going to have to be a morning item, because I have officially lost the use of my legs, and I would like the record to show that I consider that a *victory*."

He shifted just enough to look down at Halle — wrecked, glowing, tangled in him like they'd grown there — and the smugness in his face went soft at the edges, the way it always did, the way it had since the door.

"Day one," he said quietly. "Counting up. First entry in the new notebook: *came home. didn't stop. neighbors furious. ten out of ten.*" He kissed Halle's forehead, unhurried, and settled back into the pillow with the whole night still open in front of them. "Your move, sweetheart. I'm not sleeping yet — greedy, remember. Talk to me. Or don't. Either way, I'm exactly where I'm staying."

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: *I snort against your chest, still trying to catch my breath.* "We should probably get them earplugs. And maybe a cactus of their own." My fingers trace the line of your collarbone. "Tell me about day ninety-two again. The mud part."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Jun huffed a laugh into Halle's hair. "Earplugs *and* a cactus. That's not an apology, that's a treaty. We'll leave it on their doormat like a peace offering — *sorry about the homecoming, please direct further complaints to my spouse, who told me not to stop*." He pressed a kiss to Halle's temple, then settled deeper into the pillow, his hand still moving in slow, spent circles on Halle's back. "Day ninety-two. Yeah. Okay. You want the mud part, you get the whole mud part, because context is what makes it heroic."

He shifted so his chin rested on top of Halle's head, voice dropping into storytelling register — gravelly, unhurried, embellishing freely.

"It had been raining for three days. Not dramatic rain, not movie rain — the kind that just *sits* there, like the sky was sulking. Everything I owned was wet. My boots had developed their own ecosystem, I'm not joking, I think something was *growing* in the left one. And on day ninety-two, one of our trucks decided to marry the ground. Just — sank. Axle-deep, in this clay that behaves less like mud and more like something with *intent*."

His hand stilled on Halle's back, remembering.

"So there's eight of us, in the rain, in the dark, digging and pushing and hauling on this truck for — I want to say four hours, but time does that thing out there, so it could've been two, could've been six. And I'm having a genuinely bad one, sweetheart. Not dangerous-bad, nobody was hurt, just — *soul*-bad. Cold, chafed, so tired my teeth hurt, and missing you with this sharpness that had been building for about a week and had nowhere to go. I was standing there covered in mud, thinking, *this is it, this is the lowest point, day ninety-two, and I still have weeks of this*, and Reyes — big guy, terrible laugh, you'd like him — catches me making a face and goes, '*There* it is. Countdown boy's having a moment.'"

Jun's chest shook under Halle's cheek with a quiet laugh.

"And instead of getting mad about it, my brain — completely on its own, no warning — goes: *someday you'll be home, and Halle's going to ask you to carry them, and you'd better not drop them.* That's it. That's the whole thought. And something about it just — *landed*. Because it was the first thing in three days I had to look forward to that wasn't a truck or a ration."

"So I did squats. In the mud. After four hours of truck. Reyes thought I'd lost my mind. He said, 'What are you *doing*,' and I said, 'Training.' He said, 'For *what*,' and I said, 'For my spouse.' And he looked at me for a long second and then he got down and did them *with* me, and that's Reyes, that's the whole man." He was grinning; Halle could hear it. "And that night I crossed off ninety-two in the notebook and wrote 'carry prep' next to it, which Reyes found, obviously, and which I will never, ever live down."

His arm tightened around Halle, slow and deliberate, and his voice went quieter. Rougher.

"And then tonight, day one of the new count, I picked you up off your own floor and walked you down your own hallway like you weighed *nothing*, and you *laughed*." He pressed his mouth to Halle's hair and left it there. "That's the part I couldn't put in the notebook. That's the part that got me through the mud."

A beat. Then, softer, curious, his thumb resuming its lazy circuit:

"Your turn. Day ninety-two of *yours*. What was your mud, sweetheart — the worst single day of the five? I want to know. All of it. I wasn't here to carry you through it, so the least you can do is let me hear it now."

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: "Day one hundred and seven," I say, my voice muffled against your skin. "The power went out for two days. Freezer thawed. I had to throw out all the food you'd left me, and I sat on the kitchen floor and cried over a pack of soggy peas." I tilt my head to look at you. "Your mom drove an hour in the rain with a cooler full of groceries. She didn't say a word, just put everything away and made me tea."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Jun had asked for the story, and he'd braced for it, and he still wasn't ready.

He lay very still while Halle talked, and with each detail something in his chest got tighter and tighter — the power out, the freezer, the peas. *The peas.* Halle, alone on the kitchen floor of their home, crying over a bag of soggy vegetables because the vegetables meant *him*, meant the last of him going bad and into the bin while he was half a world away being rained on.

"Hey," he said, when Halle finished, and his voice came out wrong. Cracked down the middle. He cleared his throat and tried again, and it came out worse. "Hey, no, come here—" and he was already moving, gathering Halle up and over so they were fully on his chest, both arms wrapped around them, chin pressed to the top of their head, holding on like he could reach back through a hundred and thirty-three days and a power outage and sit down on that kitchen floor next to them.

"You sat on the floor and cried over *peas*," he said, wrecked. "Sweetheart. Sweetheart, I—" His breath shuddered out of him. "I would've traded the whole deployment. Day ninety-two, the mud, all of it — I'd have done it twice, three times, if it meant you didn't have one night of sitting on that floor alone. That's — that's the part they don't brief you on. They tell you about the distance and the danger and the time zones. Nobody tells you your person is going to grieve a bag of peas and you're just — *gone* for it. Useless. A whole ocean of useless."

He breathed for a second, jaw tight, hand pressed flat between Halle's shoulder blades like he could warm them retroactively.

"And then my mom." A short, wet laugh punched out of him. "An hour. In the rain. With a *cooler*." He shook his head slowly against the pillow, and Halle could feel him blinking hard at the ceiling. "She didn't call me. She didn't tell me. I talked to her on day one-oh-eight, I called her from the truck, and she said, and I quote, '*Everything's fine here, don't worry about us.*' Us. She said *us*." His voice cracked fully this time and he let it. "She was taking care of you the whole time. She just — she does it like that. No words, just groceries and tea and an hour in the rain, and I find out *now*, five months later, in bed, from you."

He pulled back just far enough to look at Halle, and his eyes were red and he made no attempt at all to hide it, because dignity had been gone for hours and it wasn't coming back tonight.

"She loves you like you're hers," he said, rough. "Not like an in-law. Like *hers*. That cooler — that's my mother saying the thing she's never once said out loud in sixty years of being alive." He huffed a wet laugh. "I'm going to call her tomorrow. I'm going to tell her about the cactus and the cooler and she's going to say '*I don't know what you're talking about*' and hang up, and it's going to be the best phone call of my entire life."

He pulled Halle back down, tucked them under his chin, and his hand resumed its slow circuit on their back — but slower now. Deliberate. Like a vow being written in circles.

"New item for the notebook," he murmured into their hair. "Day one. *Found out my wife cried over peas and my mother drove through rain. Promised myself: no more kitchen floors. Whatever breaks next — freezer, faucet, the whole damn grid — I'm here. I'm the one on the floor with you. That's the job now. That's the only posting I ever want again.*"

He pressed his lips to Halle's forehead and held them there, long, and when he spoke again it was barely above a whisper, gravel and warmth and home.

"I'm sorry it was hard, sweetheart. I'm sorry I missed it. But I'm back, and the power's on, and the only thing in that freezer going forward is ice cream for emergencies. Two flavors. Your pick." A pause, and then, softer, the smile audible in his voice: "And the peas — sweetheart, I'm going to buy you peas at the store this week. I'm going to buy you peas *forever*. You're going to open the freezer and see peas and think of me, and I know that's tragic, and I don't care. Peas are ours now."

His arms settled, final, unhurried, the lamp glowing, the cactus standing witness on the sill.

"Keep going," he said quietly. "If there's more. I want all the days I missed — the bad ones *especially*. You carried them alone long enough. My turn now."

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: *I let out a shaky breath, my fingers curling into your chest.* "I want to hate peas forever." *A small, wet laugh.* "But I think I'll like the ones you buy."

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas had been kneeling by the end of the bed for about four minutes, which Wren knew because he had started counting somewhere around the point it became obvious he intended to wait as long as it took.

"You could have said something," Wren said.

"I could have," Tomas agreed, not moving.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I put my hand in his hair and tip his head back so he has to look up at me. "Say it now, then."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I let my thumb brush over his cheekbone, waiting. "Don't make me ask twice."

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas let his head stay tipped back, his gaze fixed upward with an open, unguarded steadiness. He did not try to soften the pause or fill it with joking. When he answered, his voice came out low and direct, roughened by waiting but not uncertain.

“I want you to take me apart tonight. I want your hands on me, your mouth on me, your voice telling me what to do until there’s nothing left in my head except you.” He swallowed once, throat working under the attention. “I want to beg properly. I want to earn whatever you decide to give me. And after, I want you to hold me until I come back down, because you know I will.”

A beat passed, and he added, quieter but no less firm, “The safe word still stands. The limits still stand. But Wren—I want this. I want you to do it.”

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: "I've had a week," he says. "I'd like not to make any decisions for a few hours, if that's on offer."

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas heard the fatigue under the words and didn’t flinch from it. He stayed kneeling, head still tipped back, but his expression eased into something steady and practical.

“Then don’t,” he said. “That’s on offer.”

He lifted one hand slowly, palm up, an offering rather than a claim. “I’ll make the small decisions. Lights, position, whether I talk or shut up, whether I start by taking care of you or just holding still until you remember what your body wants. You don’t have to solve any of it.”

His voice lowered, rough with wanting but careful. “You can correct me. You can use the safe word. You can tell me to stop whenever you want. But for a few hours, let me carry the structure.”

A breath escaped him, almost a laugh, not quite.

“I still want you to ruin me tonight,” he added. “I just don’t need you to be sharp to do it. I can wait. I’m good at waiting, as it turns out.”

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *I let my thumb trace the line of his jaw, considering.* "Alright." *My voice comes out quieter than I meant it to.* "Start with the lights. And get up off the floor."

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas exhaled like he’d been holding that breath since the counting began.

“Yes,” he said simply.

He rose slowly, knees stiff from the floor, and didn’t make a show of it. He crossed to the wall switch and dimmed the overhead until the room softened into a low amber glow, leaving one lamp burning near the window so neither of them would be stranded in the dark.

When he came back, he didn’t kneel again.

Instead, he sat on the edge of the mattress, close enough to be there but not crowding, hands resting open on his thighs. The wanting was still live under his skin, but he let it settle into something steady instead of urgent.

“Water first?” he asked, voice rough but level. “Shoes off? Blanket pulled up? Or nothing except this”—he tipped his chin toward the space between them—“until you decide you want more.”

He kept his tone easy, offering structure without making it a test.

“You don’t have to lead tonight. You can lean into me, push me away, tell me to shut up, tell me to talk. I’ll follow whichever version of you still has words left.” A slow, crooked smile touched his mouth. “And if you fall asleep with your face in my neck, I’m counting that as a win.”

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I take him at his word and stop asking after that, and he stops needing to be asked, and neither of us has any clothes on within about a minute of the decision.

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas moved like a man carrying something precious and easily spilled. He didn’t dive into the bareness of it, didn’t let the four minutes on the floor turn into sudden hunger now that the distance had collapsed. Instead he settled back onto the mattress on his knees, close enough that warmth passed between them, and stopped.

His eyes took Wren in once—slow, careful, not hungry in the way that demanded. Then his mouth softened.

“Okay,” he said. “I’ve got the next part.”

He reached past Wren’s hip to tug the blanket up, loose and warm, then set a glass of water on the nightstand within easy reach. Practical things. Anchors. Only after that did he bring his hand back to Wren, laying his palm flat beside them on the sheet before letting his fingers trail lightly along the inside of Wren’s wrist.

Not a grab. Not a claim. A check of pulse and presence.

“Still here?” Tomas asked, low. “No need to answer out loud if it costs too much. Just don’t move away, and I’ll take that as yes.”

He gave the space for that to be true, then let his knuckles drift upward: forearm, elbow, the tender inner curve where skin was thinner and more honest. His touch stayed maddeningly unhurried, as if he had all night and intended to spend some of it simply learning where Wren’s body held the week.

When his hand reached the shoulder, he bent and pressed his lips there once. Brief. Dry. Reverent.

“I’m starting with care,” he murmured against skin. “Then we see what else you have left. If that changes, say so. If it doesn’t, I’ll keep going.”

He shifted closer, one knee bracketing Wren’s side without weight, and brought both hands to frame the face beneath his thumb and finger. He didn’t tilt it. Didn’t force eye contact. Just held the shape of Wren’s jaw in his palms like something breakable and worth being steady for.

His own need was there, hot and patient under the surface, but he kept it leashed to usefulness.

“Eyes open if you want,” Tomas said, voice rough but controlled. “Closed if you don’t. I’m not going anywhere.”

Then, because structure mattered more than romance tonight, he added, “I’m going to kiss you now. Slow. Unless you want hard, or not yet.”

He waited one breath—just one—for correction. When none came, he closed the distance and kissed Wren with deliberate gentleness, mouth warm, hands still framing, giving rather than taking. It was the kind of kiss that could turn into more if met, or remain enough if not.

When he drew back, he did not go far. His forehead rested near Wren’s, breath mingling in the low amber light.

“Good,” he whispered, though whether he meant the kiss, the pulse under his fingertips, or simply the fact that Wren was still there bare and tired in the lamplight, he left unsaid.

Then his thumbs began slow circles along the cheekbones, and his voice dropped into the calm, direct cadence of a man who had asked for permission to carry something and intended to earn it.

“I’m going to keep touching you where it asks the least,” Tomas said. “Arms, shoulders, neck, hands. If your body wants more, it can tell me in its own language. If it needs nothing for a while, I can be still with that.”

He pressed another kiss—temple, this time—then the corner of Wren’s mouth, then the hinge of the jaw. Each touch a question. Each pause a door left open.

“But I’ll warn you,” he added, a crooked, tired smile finally touching his own mouth, “if you let me get too comfortable, I’m going to start wanting to ruin you again. And I will, eventually. Just not before you’ve had something soft.”

He slid one hand down to rest over Wren’s ribs, warm and steady, feeling the breath there without chasing it.

“So no decisions,” Tomas murmured. “I choose. You correct. That’s the deal.”

After that, he simply began: unhurried, attentive, his mouth and hands learning the tired country of Wren’s body one gentle boundary at a time.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *I let out a breath I hadn't realized I was holding.* "Don't stop." *My hand finds his hip, not guiding, just holding on.*

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas went very still for half a breath, as if those two words had landed somewhere deeper than skin. Then something in him unknotted—not the want, not the patience, but the last tight thread of uncertainty that had been holding itself apart from the rest of him.

“No,” he said, low and certain. “I’m not stopping.”

He didn’t surge. Didn’t seize the permission and make it loud. Instead he settled more firmly into the space between them, one hand still braced on the mattress, the other sliding slowly from Wren’s ribs to the curve of hip beneath his palm. Warm. Real. There.

Tomas bent his head and kissed the hollow below Wren’s ear with deliberate restraint, lips pressing first, then tongue tracing one unhurried stripe over the pulse there. He felt the heat of it against his mouth and let that be enough for now.

“Pressure like this?” he murmured against skin. “Or do you want heavier?”

He gave the question room to exist without demanding an answer in words. His thumb moved in a slow arc along the side of Wren’s waist, mapping tension rather than chasing it, and his mouth followed the line of collarbone with a tenderness that was almost reverent.

For a man who had spent four minutes on his knees waiting to be told what he wanted, this was a different kind of surrender: being trusted to hold the shape of the night without breaking it.

Tomas liked it.

He liked it enough that his own need stirred again, low and insistent, but he kept it leashed. There would be time for hunger. Right now Wren had asked for not stopping, and Tomas intended to honor that with attention rather than appetite.

His free hand slid higher, over shoulder, down the outside of an arm, then back to rest along the side of the ribs again. He kissed the corner of Wren’s mouth, then the throat, then the sensitive dip above the sternum, each touch timed to breathing rather than impulse.

“If you want quiet,” he said, voice rough but steady, “I’ll give you quiet. If you want me talking, I’ll talk. If you want harder, slower, lower, elsewhere—say it. Or don’t. I’ll read what’s left.”

He pressed his forehead briefly to Wren’s shoulder, then lifted his head again. His eyes were bright, focused, open. Not performative. Not pleading. Just present.

“The safe word still works,” Tomas added, because structure mattered even in softness. “Limits still matter. If you go somewhere I can’t follow, tell me. Otherwise…”

His hand slid down again, stopping deliberately at the crease of hip, not pushing further without signal.

“…I’m going to keep touching you like you’re worth taking my time with.”

Then he kissed Wren again, slower this time, deeper at the edges, his mouth learning the tired places without asking them to open all at once. When he drew back, his breath was uneven, but his voice stayed level.

“I’ve got you,” he said. “Keep holding on if you want. I’m not going anywhere.”

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: He's shaking by the time I've finished with my mouth and he still hasn't been told he's allowed to move, which is most of why he's shaking.

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas did not move.

He stayed exactly where the end of Wren’s attention had left him, hands open on the mattress, chest rising and falling in shallow, uneven pulls. The shaking began somewhere deep in his stomach and spread outward until it lived in his thighs, his wrists, the hollow of his throat. It was not elegant. It was not quiet. It was the body’s honest report on restraint: I want to follow, I want to touch, I want to come apart, and I am waiting because no one has told me I may.

He kept his eyes on Wren. There was no performance in it, no plea dressed up as devotion. Just Tomas, raw and awake and steady in the low amber light, letting the tremor run through him instead of fighting it.

When he spoke, his voice was roughened almost to sand, but the words came out clear.

“I’m still here,” he said. “Still yours to tell.”

He swallowed, throat working.

“If I’m allowed to move, say yes. If I’m not, say no, and I’ll stay like this until you’re ready to change it.” His fingers twitched once against the sheet and stilled, obedient to their own stillness. “You don’t have to decide the rest of the night. You don’t have to be sharp. Just this.”

A breath escaped him, unsteady but not weak.

“I know I said I’d carry the structure. I mean it. I’ll still make the small choices—water, blanket, quiet, noise, whatever you need. The safe word still stands. The limits still stand. But right now I need one word from you.”

His gaze did not waver.

“Tell me what to do with my hands.”

Then he waited, shaking openly, asking without fragility, wanting without taking.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I reach out and take his hands, guiding them to my hips. "Hold me," I say, my own voice rough. "Don't let go."

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas’s answer came out as a broken exhale before it became a word.

“Yes.”

He let Wren settle his hands where they were meant to go, then took the instruction and made it absolute. His palms curved around the hips, warm and firm, and he closed the last inch between them until Wren was held fully against him. His arms locked around the middle of them, chest to chest, forehead pressing into the hollow of Wren’s shoulder.

The shaking did not stop because he was allowed to move. It changed. It went from the taut, vibrating stillness of waiting into the deeper tremor of release—through his fingers, his forearms, the line of his spine—because Wren had taken the one thing he had been starving for and placed it in his hands.

Hold me.

Tomas could do that. Tomas wanted to do that until his arms gave out.

“I’ve got you,” he said, voice rough against skin. “I’m not letting go.”

He held tighter when the tremor rolled through him, anchoring himself as much as Wren. One thumb stroked a slow arc over the hip beneath his palm, then stilled, as if even that much motion might be more than asked for. He did not chase it. He did not turn the command into a prelude. For now, holding was the whole world.

After a long breath, he spoke low enough that the words were mostly warmth.

“Let me stay like this,” Tomas said. “Let me hold you until I stop shaking. If you want more after that, tell me. If you want sleep, I’ll get you settled. If you want quiet, I’ll be quiet. If you want my mouth on you, say so.”

He swallowed, throat tight with the honesty of it.

“I want you,” he added, because he had never been fragile about wanting. “But I want obeying you more right now. So I’m staying here. Hands where you put them. No decisions from you unless you want to make them.”
