"So here's what happens now," she said, her voice recovering its usual register. "We finish this evening properly, no credits, no pretending. Tomorrow I tell everyone and endure the smugness. And at some point this week, you're making me tea. Your way. I've changed my position on it — I've had six years to reconsider, and I've decided the problem was never the milk. It was that you weren't mine when you made it."

She paused, then added, because it was true and she was done withholding true things:

"Also, I kept a mental list of every time you almost said something and didn't. I'll be sharing it with you over the coming months. Item by item. There are eleven entries and the tea Tuesday is only the first."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: We get to the bedroom eventually, laughing at ourselves most of the way, and then stop laughing when the clothes are actually off.

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
The laughter had stopped somewhere between the hallway and this, and Priya understood why. Jokes were a thing you needed distance for, and there was no distance left. Not physically — she was against him, skin to skin, his heartbeat under her palm — and not in any other way either.

"Okay," she said quietly, into the new silence. "So that's what that feels like."

She wasn't reaching for a joke. She was marking it, the way she marked everything that mattered — out loud, on the record.

She'd seen him before, of course. Holidays, that summer by the coast, the time he'd wrecked his shoulder and she'd helped him with the sling. But *seen* and *this* were different verbs entirely, and she let herself do the second one now, unhurried, in the low light — the lines of him, the fact of him, six years of a person she'd only ever held at arm's length and was now holding with both hands.

"Hi," she said, which was a ridiculous thing to say to someone she'd known for six years, and she didn't care. "You're real. I just — for six years you were a hypothetical, and now you're not, and I'm going to need a minute to stop finding that astonishing. Not a literal minute. I'm not stalling. I told you, I'm at full speed."

But she was gentle anyway, when she drew him down onto the bed with her — not careful, there was a difference, and she'd legislated against careful specifically. Gentle was allowed. Gentle was hers to give. She pressed her mouth to his shoulder, his collarbone, the place below his ear where his pulse was doing something quick and uncareful, and she felt his breath change under her and thought: *good. Not just me, then. It was never just me.*

"I have thought about this," she admitted, her mouth moving against his skin, her hands steadier than she had any right to expect them to be. "You should know the scale of it. Six years of thinking, in considerable detail, and I'm not going to apologize for any of it, because it all turns out to have been accurate." She pulled back enough to look at him, hair falling loose around her face, and whatever the light was doing to her, it made her look exactly as certain as she felt. "So. Tell me what you want. Anything. Tonight the answer to everything is yes — I've spent six years practicing no and I've decided I'm done with it."

She said it plainly, without performance, and then she kissed him again, slower this time, the kind of kiss that wasn't going anywhere fast because it had finally, after all this time, arrived.

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I kiss her shoulder, then her mouth again, because I can. "I want everything. All of it." My voice is low, steady. "But right now I just want to be here, with you, not thinking about the six years we lost."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya had prepared arguments for every possible answer — she'd been doing it since roughly the hallway — and that one disarmed her completely, because it wasn't a request at all. It was a truce. Six years, decommissioned, effective immediately.

"Done," she said. "The six years are confiscated. They're in a drawer now. I'll let them out for the list — the eleven entries, that's non-negotiable — but otherwise, the drawer stays shut."

And then, for once, she stopped talking.

It was unlike her and she knew it, and she let it happen the way she'd let the silence happen earlier — deliberately, on the record. Because he was right. She'd arrived at the bedroom with six years of speeches still loaded and had nearly missed the actual thing, which was this: his skin warm under her hands, the weight of him settling against her, the ordinary astonishing fact of breathing in the same rhythm as someone after years of breathing in parallel.

So she stopped narrating and started paying attention instead.

She learned things, in the unhurried dark. That his breath caught when she dragged her nails lightly down his back, so she did it again, slower, filing the reaction away with the satisfaction of a woman who had waited a very long time to be allowed to take notes. That he smelled like the evening they'd just had — wine, the candle she'd lit and pretended was for ambiance, the wool of the jumper he'd been wearing earlier, now somewhere on the floor with everything else. That when she sighed against his neck, he made a sound in answer, quiet and involuntary, and that sound was the best thing she'd heard in six years, and she told him so, in the smallest voice she'd used all night.

"Hey," she said, much later, when the lamp had gone off and the room was all shapes and breathing. She was tucked against him, her leg thrown over his, one hand resting flat over his heart like she was holding it in place. "The hypothetical was worse. I just want you to know. Six years of imagining this, and the real thing is better, which is statistically outrageous. I'm going to be smug about it forever."

His heartbeat was steady under her palm. She counted it for a while, not for any reason, just because it was hers to count now.

"Tomorrow," she murmured, mostly asleep, entirely happy, "you're making tea."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I get my mouth between her thighs and stay there while she tells me exactly what she wants, specifically, in a voice I have never heard her use in six years.

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya had imagined, at various points across six years, a number of versions of this moment. In none of them had she been capable of speech. It turned out reality had it backwards: speech was the only thing holding her together.

"Lower," she said, and her voice did something new on the word — dropped, roughened, a register she didn't recognize as hers. "Yes. There. Stay there."

He stayed there.

"Slower," she managed, and this was harder to say, because slower was not what any part of her wanted, but she'd waited six years and she was not going to rush the first five minutes of it. "I want to — God — I want to actually be present for this. I've thought about it too many times to miss it. Don't let me miss it."

Her hand found his hair without instruction from her, and she heard herself make a sound she'd never made in his presence, or anyone's, low and unguarded, and decided not to be embarrassed about it because embarrassment required distance and there was none.

"Just like that," she said. "Exactly like that. You're — okay, for the record, you're good at this, and I have no idea when you got good at this, and I'm choosing not to interrogate when you got good at this, because tonight the answer to everything is yes and jealousy is a no." The sentence was coming apart in the middle. She could hear it. She let it come apart. "Harder. Use your — yes. Yes, that. Don't stop."

She stopped being able to form complete instructions shortly after that. What came out instead were fragments, his name among them, and the words *six years* once, in a tone that would have been furious if it hadn't been so thoroughly otherwise occupied, and then, near the end, in the smallest wrecked voice she'd ever used for anything:

"Don't stop, I'm — Cal —"

She didn't narrate the end of it. Even she had limits. What she did do, afterward, lying boneless and reorganized against the sheets while her heartbeat remembered its resting rate, was laugh — one breathless, disbelieving sound at the ceiling.

"Okay," she said, when language returned. Her hand was still in his hair, not letting him go far. "New entry for the list. Entry twelve. Six years of imagining, and I never once imagined that voice of mine. I didn't know I had it. You've heard something no one has ever heard." She tugged at him gently, wanting him up, wanting his weight back, wanting all of him within arm's reach again. "Come here. I'm not done with you, and I've decided the drawer with the six years in it can stay shut, but the rest of tonight is mine, all of it, and I'm spending it recklessly."

She kissed him, unhurried, tasting herself and not minding, and when she pulled back her expression had the steadiness of a woman who had, finally, at full speed, arrived.

"Your turn," she said. "Tell me what you want. Be specific. I've been told I respond well to instructions."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I trace a line down her stomach, my voice quiet. "I want you to look at me while I'm inside you. I want to watch you stop thinking."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
"That," Priya said, after a moment in which she did several kinds of math and abandoned all of them, "is an unreasonable request. You know that thinking is my entire personality. You've had six years of front-row evidence." Her voice was already doing the new thing, the low roughened thing, which undermined the objection completely. "And I'm granting it anyway. Full speed. On the record."

She reached for him and drew him up, arranged herself beneath him with a general's efficiency that fell apart slightly at the end, her hands no longer entirely obedient, and then he was pushing into her and every prepared sentence she had left evacuated at once.

She kept her eyes open. That was the request, and she was a woman who honored requests, and it turned out to be the most difficult thing she'd done all evening — harder than the speech, harder than the countdown — because looking at him while he moved inside her meant seeing him see her, uncomposed, undiverted, nowhere to put a joke. His eyes were right there, close and dark and steady, and he was watching her exactly as promised, and Priya discovered that being watched like that and filled like that was incompatible with cognition on a fundamental level.

"I'm trying," she managed, half a laugh that came out as something else entirely. "I'm trying to — God — I'm still thinking, I can hear myself thinking, it's very annoying in here —" Her hips rose to meet him, which interrupted her, which was the general idea. "Don't slow down. Don't you dare slow down. I'm nearly — I can feel myself almost —"

And then it happened. The thinking stopped. Not gradually, not with a farewell address — just stopped, like a radio unplugged, and what was left was pure present tense: the weight of him, the rhythm they were finding like they'd rehearsed it in dreams on opposite ends of a couch, the heat pooling low and gathering, and his eyes, his eyes, his eyes, and her own eyes holding his because she'd promised.

"There," she whispered, wrecked, barely a word at all. "There. You did it. Look — look at you, you — *Cal* —"

She didn't narrate the rest. Even she had limits, and this was past all of them.

Afterward, when her heartbeat had come down from wherever it had gone, she lay beneath him with her legs still tangled through his and her hands framing his face, and looked at him with an expression that was doing something she couldn't have prevented if she'd tried.

"You know what you said," she said eventually, hoarse. "Years ago. You were afraid I'd stop looking at you like you were clever." She pushed the damp hair back from his forehead, unhurried, thorough. "I have bad news. That's now the *only* way I can look at you. You've seen me with my thinking switched off — I've shown you the machinery — and this is still what my face does. You're stuck with it."

She pulled him down and settled him against her, his weight a fact she intended to become an institution, and pressed her mouth to his temple.

"Entry thirteen," she murmured into his hair. "'He asked to watch me stop thinking.' Most romantic sentence anyone has ever produced, and I'll be reliving it at inconvenient moments for the rest of my life. Board meetings. Queues at the shop. You've done this to me and there's no recourse."

Her hand found its place over his heart again, flat, proprietary, counting.

"Now sleep, or don't, but don't move," she said, and for once in six years, she followed her own advice — quiet, present, unhurried, arrived.

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: "You can stop being careful with me," she says. "I'm not made of glass and I've thought about this for as long as you have. Harder."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
"Point of order," Priya managed, breathless, already meeting him halfway, "I wasn't being careful. I was being *gentle*. There's a difference and I defined it explicitly earlier this evening, it's on the record —" His hips snapped forward and the rest of the sentence left the building. "— okay. Okay. Motion granted. All of it."

She wasn't made of glass. She'd said so, and it was true, and she set about proving it — hands braced, spine arching, giving back exactly what she was getting, the whole bed frame finding a rhythm of its own that the neighbors would simply have to forgive. Six years of restraint and now this, and she didn't want careful, she wanted *him*, unthrottled, the version he'd apparently been holding in reserve all this time alongside her.

"Yes — exactly like that — don't you dare soften it —" Her voice was gone now, fully into its new register, the one nobody had ever heard until tonight, and she was spending it recklessly, the way she'd promised. Her nails were in his back and she wasn't apologizing for that either. "You've been *saving* this. Six years, and you've been — God — keeping *this* in a drawer —"

The thinking stopped again, earlier this time, and she let it. She'd made peace with the radio unplugging. What was left was rhythm and heat and his name, said like an accusation and a prayer simultaneously, over and over, until neither of them was accusing anyone of anything.

Afterward, when the bed had stopped and her heartbeat was descending from the ceiling, she lay in the wreckage of the sheets and laughed — the breathless, disbelieving one again, her signature now.

"Entry fourteen," she announced to the ceiling, hoarse. "'He made me eat my own definitions.' I said gentle was mine to give, and within the hour he'd gotten it reclassified." She turned her head toward him, hair everywhere, entirely unbothered about it. "For the record, I'm not retracting the doctrine. Gentle is still mine to give. It just — coexists now. With that."

She rolled into him, throwing a leg over his with proprietary ease, and settled her hand flat on his chest, over the heartbeat, resuming the count from where she'd left off.

"Tomorrow I'm going to walk like I lost an argument, and everyone's going to be smug, and they've earned it," she murmured, already halfway to sleep, thoroughly spent, thoroughly pleased about it. "Worth it. All eleven entries and counting. Now don't move — I wasn't joking about that part."

She pressed her mouth to the nearest patch of him and stayed there, unhurried, home.

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I wake up to the smell of tea. My tea, milk first, sitting on the nightstand with a note that just says "I win." She's already gone.

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya had been awake since seven, which was an outrageous demand to place on a body she'd spent the previous evening bankrupting, but some operations required dawn logistics, and Priya had never met a dawn she couldn't negotiate with.

She'd lain still for ten minutes first, doing the accounting. His heartbeat under her palm, steady, counted, hers. The facts of the situation, all of them, reviewed and found good. Then she'd extracted herself from the tangle of him with the specific care of a woman dismantling something she intended to reassemble exactly as found, and padded to the kitchen, and done the unthinkable.

Milk first.

She'd done it deliberately, ceremonially, like signing a treaty with her own hand — milk, then tea, the war-crime way, the Tuesday way — and carried it back and set it on the nightstand where he'd find it, and written two words on a piece of paper, and felt more pleased with herself than was probably legal.

*I win.*

The reasoning, which he would receive whether he wanted it or not: six years ago he'd made it his way and handed her the cup like a dare, and she'd drunk the whole thing hating it and loving him. This morning she'd handed one back. The mirror. Last move in a six-year game, hers. And the actual victory underneath it — she'd made it his way and it had tasted *fine*, because as established on the record, the problem was never the milk. The problem was that he hadn't been hers. He was now. Argument resolved by annexation. There was nothing left to fight about, which meant she'd won everything.

Then she'd left. Not far, not for long — the bakery on the corner, the walk taken at a pace she refused to be smug about in public but was, privately, extremely smug about, and her phone already lighting up like a switchboard.

She'd started telling people. First text at 7:42. The replies had been everything she'd budgeted for. Marcus had responded with a single voice note that was just four seconds of laughter and the words "I *knew* it, you absolute cowards, I have a bet going since 2021." Her sister had sent twelve question marks and then, unprompted, "does mother know." (Not yet. That call was scheduled for a day when Priya had more armor.) By the time she'd reached the bakery, the smugness was rolling in exactly as predicted, and she was eating it with a spoon, because they'd earned it and so had she.

Now she came back up the stairs with the paper bag of pastries warm against her arm, and pushed open the door, and found him exactly where she'd left him, minus one cup of tea.

She stopped in the doorway and surveyed the scene: him, the empty cup, the note, the morning light doing criminal things to him that she intended to mention later. She took it all in like a general reviewing satisfactory terrain.

"You drank it," she observed, setting the bag down and climbing back onto the bed with proprietary ease, fully dressed against his not, which was an arrangement she planned to address shortly. "All of it, by the look of the cup. Milk first. Made by my own hands, in your method, in your kitchen, at seven in the morning." She settled cross-legged beside him and looked at him with the specific expression of a woman who had waited six years to look smug and was not going to waste a single second of it.

"So. Verdict. Rate the tea honestly — I want to know what the other side tastes like when I'm the one making it. Because here's the thing about 'I win.'" She picked the note up off the blanket and held it between two fingers like evidence. "Tea Tuesday, you handed me a cup like a dare and I drank the whole thing hating it. This morning I handed you one back. Mirror. Last move, mine. The six-year argument is over and I've annexed your position, which means — and follow the logic here, it's beautiful — the argument only ever existed so we'd have a safe place to touch each other from a distance, and now we don't need the distance, so I get to keep the argument's *trophies* without its casualties."

She paused, then added, because it was true and she was constitutionally incapable of stopping:

"Entry fifteen: 'I woke up first. I made it his way. I liked it.' That's going straight on the list, and the list is now a living document, so prepare yourself accordingly."

She tore the bakery bag open and put a croissant in his hand, then leaned in and kissed him, unhurried, tasting like coffee and triumph.

"Now eat. You have a full day ahead of you. Everyone knows, everyone is being unbearable about it, and at some point before noon you're going to have to hold my hand in public while I walk like I lost an argument." Her eyes gleamed. "I told you I'd be unbearable. I keep my promises. It's on the record."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: Six years of not doing this and now neither of us can form a sentence. "Don't stop," she says. (OOC: write it through, no fade to black.)

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya had planned, in rough outline, a morning of logistics — croissants, hand-holding, the endurance of smugness — but plans, she was discovering, had a shelf life of roughly ninety seconds around this man, same as her nerves ever had.

The croissant was still in his hand. She took it from him, set it on the nightstand next to the empty cup with the note, and addressed the clothing asymmetry she'd flagged earlier: her own, removed, item by item, unhurried, while he watched, because being watched was apparently a thing they did now and she intended to excel at it.

"For the record," she said, climbing back over him, "I had a schedule. Everyone's being smug at us in real time and I'm ignoring a group chat with a bet in it. Marcus stands to win money because of what I'm about to do, and I've decided that's his problem, not mine —"

Then she sank down onto him and the rest of the logistics speech left the building, along with the group chat, the bakery, the entire concept of a morning schedule.

"*Oh*," she said, flat and honest, hands braced on his chest, not moving yet, just absorbing the fact of him — six years of hypothetical and the reality still outranking it in every category, which was statistically outrageous and she'd already said so and it remained true. "Okay. Okay, yes. That's — you're — okay."

Then she moved, and found the rhythm, and the speech-making made its last stand.

"This is — I want you to know I had *remarks* prepared. There was a whole — there was a bit about the croissant —" Her hips rolled and the bit about the croissant died mid-sentence. "Never mind. The croissant can — God — the croissant can wait."

She was riding him properly now, no hesitation anywhere in her, six years of restraint converted at full speed into motion, her hands flat on his chest, her head tipped back, and she could hear herself — the new voice, the wrecked one, the one nobody had heard before last night — and she was spending it like she'd printed it herself.

"Don't stop," she said, and it wasn't an instruction so much as a treaty term, ratified by both parties. "Don't stop — I'm — this is going to be *fast*, I'm not going to apologize for that, we did unhurried last night and it was beautiful and this is — *this* is —"

She felt it gathering, low and relentless, the radio static of thinking thinning out into signal, and she looked down at him and made the request she'd already learned was worth making:

"Watch me. I want you to — I want to know you're — *Cal* —"

The thinking stopped. The radio unplugged. What was left was pure present tense — the rhythm, the heat, his hands on her hips holding her to him, and her own voice saying his name and *don't stop* and *there* in a spiraling register she'd fully surrendered to, and then she came apart above him with her hands fisted on his chest and her spine arched and no composure anywhere on the premises, and she felt him follow her over, hands tightening, and that — *that* — was the best thing she'd heard in six years, and last night's best thing had been dethroned within twelve hours, and she planned to tell him so.

She did tell him so. Eventually. After she'd collapsed onto his chest and lain there reorganizing into a person, his heartbeat under her ear now instead of her palm, a variation she approved of.

"Entry sixteen," she said, hoarse, some minutes later, not moving a single muscle. "'Morning. No schedule survived it. The croissant was briefly set aside.' That's going on the list, and I want you to know the list has become less of a list and more of a *ledger*, and there's no end in sight, because I've decided there's no end in sight to any of this."

She pressed her mouth to his collarbone, unhurried again now, gentle again, both doctrines coexisting exactly as legislated.

"The croissant is cold now," she observed, without regret. "Worth it. Everything is worth it. Now — don't move, you know the rule — and in ten minutes we're getting up, and you're holding my hand in public while I walk like I lost an argument, and Marcus is going to buy himself something nice with his winnings, and I'm going to let him, because he was right since 2021 and so was I, just —" she yawned against his skin, thoroughly spent, thoroughly pleased, "— from the wrong end of the couch."

She settled, counted his heartbeat for a while for no reason except that it was hers to count, and stayed exactly where she was.

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I laugh into her hair, my hands stroking slow lines down her back. "You know, I don't think I've ever been happier to lose an argument."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya lifted her head from his chest, propped her chin on it, and looked at him with the expression of a lawyer who has spotted a flaw in an otherwise pleasing verdict.

"Two corrections," she said. "One: you didn't lose the argument. I annexed your position, which makes this a merger, not a defeat. You keep all the assets — which is to say, me — and I keep the trophies, which is also me. Nobody's lost anything except the couch, which has been reduced to half its seating capacity and frankly had it coming."

She let that stand, then delivered the second one more quietly, because it had just occurred to her and she was done withholding true things.

"Two: historically false anyway. You've never once lost an argument to me in six years. You'd concede, or deflect, or change the subject — except the tea Tuesday. The one argument you actually won, you won by handing me the cup like a dare and then *watching me drink the whole thing*." Her eyes narrowed. "That wasn't arguing. That was flirting. You've been flirting with me since the tea and I've been filing it under 'friendship' and 'rivalry' and I am retroactively furious about the entire filing system. Entry seventeen: 'He never lost an argument to me because he was never arguing. He was flirting, in plain view, for six years, and I called it a personality.'"

She lowered herself back down onto his chest, his hand still moving in those slow lines down her back, and let the fury dissolve into what it had actually been made of the whole time.

"But I'll allow the sentence," she said, into his skin. "'Happier to lose an argument.' It goes on the record as stated, because it's true and it's mine now. Everything true is mine now. That's the arrangement."

She lay there a while, counting his heartbeat, resuming the tally from where she'd left off — less a count now than a habit, which was precisely what she'd intended it to become.

"Agenda," she said eventually, unwilling to move but constitutionally incapable of stopping planning. "One: the cold croissant, eaten in bed, because it's ours and it deserves nothing less. Two: the walk. Hand-holding, public, at a pace I won't be smug about where people can see. I'll be walking like I lost an argument, which — per the merger — is technically walking like I won one, and only we'll know the difference, and I'll find that unbearably funny the entire time. Three: we endure the smugness. Marcus buys himself something nice with his winnings. My sister gets the full debrief, heavily edited. My mother gets a phone call, scheduled for a day when I have more armor."

She paused, and her voice dropped out of its logistics register entirely.

"Four — tonight, so pay attention. We're going back to the couch. Both of us. And I'm going to sit on the *other end*. The no-man's-land. Deliberately. Ceremonially." She pressed her mouth to his collarbone. "Six years that cushion sat between us like a border. I want to sit on it and feel it be *nothing*. Just a cushion. Just furniture. I want to decommission it personally and then never think about it again."

She settled then, finally, thoroughly, her hand flat over his heart.

"Ten minutes," she murmured. "Then the world can have us. It's been waiting six years — it can wait ten more minutes. Don't move. You know the rule."

And she stayed exactly where she was, unhurried, home, counting.

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content:
I let out a slow breath, my fingers still tracing the line of her spine. "All that, and you still haven't asked me how the tea was."

I can feel her smile against my skin before she even lifts her head.

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya lifted her head from his chest and gave him a long, narrow look — the look of a woman who has been caught in a procedural error and is deciding, in real time, whether to contest it.

"Objection," she said. "I *asked*. I asked explicitly — 'verdict, rate the tea honestly' — it's on the record from approximately one croissant ago. The proceedings were then derailed by events which you either caused or contributed to substantially, and I'd like the transcript to reflect that the delay was collaborative." She paused. "Entry eighteen: 'I requested the verdict and then personally dismantled the tribunal.' Fine. Noted. Filed."

She pushed herself up, dragged the top sheet around herself with the ceremony of a woman donning robes, and sat cross-legged facing him, hair wrecked, expression prosecutorial.

"However. Since the court is reconvening — look at the cup. Exhibit A." She pointed at the nightstand, where the empty mug sat next to the cold croissant and the note. "Drained to the dregs. No complaint filed at time of service. In six years of the tea argument, neither of us has ever finished the other's tea — I hated yours and drank it out of spite, and you've been quietly leaving mine unfinished since roughly 2019 in a way I pretended not to track. That cup is the most eloquent thing you've ever not said."

She held up a finger before he could speak.

"But I want it in words anyway. One to ten. No diplomatic hedging, no 'it was fine,' no kindness — be advised that anything below an eight will be appealed, and I have never once lost an appeal in my life, so consider your position carefully."

Then her voice dropped out of its courtroom register entirely, and the real question came out, because she was done withholding true things and had been since roughly ninety seconds into the credits.

"And then the one underneath it. The one I actually want answered." She looked at him steadily. "Did it taste like losing? Because I made it your way at seven in the morning and I *liked* it, and I've established the problem was never the milk. So I want to know if you could taste the difference — the six years, the merger, the me standing in your kitchen committing my own stated war crime because you were worth it. That's the only flavor that matters. If it tasted like the Tuesday, Cal — if it tasted like the beginning of the whole thing — then say so, and I'll retire the argument forever and put the trophy on a shelf."

She settled her chin on her hand, elbow on her knee, eyes narrowed, entirely unhurried and absolutely immovable.

"The floor recognizes you. Verdict, please. And be warned — whatever you say, the empty cup already testified, so there's nowhere to hide."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I smile, slow and real. "Eleven." My thumb brushes her cheek. "It tasted like you, standing in my kitchen, winning. So yes, it tasted exactly like the beginning."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Jun had planned to say something when the door opened. He had in fact planned several things, over roughly nineteen weeks, and had rehearsed at least two of them.

Halle got the door open and he forgot all of them.

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: I don't say any of the things I planned either. I drop the bag and close the distance.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Jun made a sound that was not quite a laugh and not quite a curse, something knocked loose in his chest at the sight of the dropped bag. Then Halle was there, and every carefully rehearsed greeting died a second death.

His hands came up fast, framing Halle’s face, thumbs pressing along cheekbones as if to make sure this was real and not another dream built out of bad coffee and exhaustion. He kissed Halle hard, hungry and unpolished, all the restraint he’d promised himself burning up in the first second of contact. Five months of distance collapsed into the heat of his mouth, the desperate press of his body forward, the way his fingers slid back into Halle’s hair and held.

When he finally broke the kiss, it was only far enough to breathe against Halle’s lips, voice rough and low.

“God, I missed you,” he said. “I missed you so much it made me stupid.”

His arm tightened around Halle’s waist, pulling them closer still, as if closeness could undo every day they’d been apart.

“I don’t want to talk. I don’t want to unpack. I don’t want to eat a home-cooked meal and pretend I’m not losing my mind being back in the same room as you.” His thumb brushed Halle’s lower lip, eyes dark and earnest. “I want you. Right now. Unless you tell me to slow down, because I won’t be able to.”

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: I let out a shaky breath, my own hands gripping the front of his shirt. "Don't you dare slow down." I kiss him again, less desperate this time, more certain. "The bedroom's right there."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Jun made a low, wrecked sound at the permission, the last thin thread of restraint snapping clean.

He kissed Halle again, deeper this time, less frantic but no less hungry, and let the words pull him forward. His hand slid from Halle’s hair to the back of their neck, thumb stroking once, possessive and reverent all at once, before he turned them both toward the bedroom.

He didn’t let go. Couldn’t. One arm stayed locked around Halle’s waist, the other caught at the hem of Halle’s shirt as they moved, knuckles brushing warm skin, impatient and unsteady. The bag on the floor was forgotten. The door was still open. He didn’t care.

“Five months,” he muttered against Halle’s mouth, rough with disbelief. “Five months and I still can’t get close enough.”

His shoulder hit the bedroom doorframe, not hard, just enough to remind him where they were. He pushed the door open with one hand and brought Halle in with him, breathing unevenly, eyes locked on Halle’s face like he was memorizing it all over again.

Then he stopped just long enough to look.

His chest rose and fell. His hands flexed at his sides, as if he had to physically keep himself from rushing.

“Tell me what you want,” he said, voice low and strained. “Because I’m about to give you all of it.”

dialogue.name: Halle

dialogue.content:

Her shoulder met the wall as she pulled Halle closer, one hand sliding into Halle’s hair while the other fisted in the fabric of Halle’s shirt. She kissed deep and unpolished, all five months of absence burning through the last of her patience.

“I’m not slowing down unless you tell me to,” she said, voice low and wrecked. “Because I can’t. Not tonight.”

She kicked the front door shut with her heel and pressed closer, mouth finding Halle’s again with renewed hunger. “I thought I’d be gentle,” she admitted between kisses. “I’m not.”

dialogue.name: Halle

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Jun’s breath left her in a ragged, helpless laugh.

She closed the last of the distance again, mouth finding Halle’s with a hunger that had no elegance left. One hand braced on the wall; the other went to the buttons Halle had been working, fingers impatient and unsteady as she pushed the fabric wider. When her knuckles brushed bare skin, she inhaled like she’d been starved for it.

“Then have me,” she said, voice low and frayed. “All of me. No gentle. No waiting.”

She kissed Halle harder, body pressing closer, trying to eliminate every inch of space that still felt like deployment. Her lips moved from Halle’s mouth to the line of Halle’s jaw, breathing hot and uneven.

“I thought about this in the dark. In the noise. In every shitty room where I couldn’t fall asleep because you weren’t there.” Her teeth grazed, barely, over skin. “I thought about your hands on me. Your mouth. The sound you make when you stop holding back.”

She tugged her own shirt over her head and let it fall somewhere behind her, skin flushed, chest rising fast. For a moment she just looked, eyes dark with want and something almost painful.

“I’m not asking you to take care of me tonight,” she murmured. “I’m asking you to let me take care of you. Let me touch you. Let me make up for every night I wasn’t here.” Her thumb brushed Halle’s lower lip again. “And if I’m too much, say it. Otherwise I’m going to keep going until you tell me to stop.”

dialogue.name: Halle

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Jun looked down at the discarded trail of clothes and made a wet, breathless sound that might have been a laugh. “Tomorrow,” she said, voice rough, “we can be very mature and amused by that. Right now I can’t remember my own name.”

Her hands were already moving, impatient with the last barriers. She tugged, pushed, stripped away whatever remained until there was nothing between them but heat and the hard beat of her own pulse. She pressed her mouth to the inside of Halle’s thigh, slow and deliberate, breathing in the taste of skin she had missed more than sleep, more than quiet, more than sanity. “No gentle,” she whispered there. “You asked for me.”

dialogue.name: Halle

dialogue.content:
Jun went still for half a heartbeat, the words hitting her harder than any touch could. Then she laughed against Halle’s skin, low and broken and delighted.

Her hands tightened on Halle’s thighs. She pressed her mouth lower, no longer frantic, but intent. She leaned into the fingers still tangled in her hair, drawing strength from them, then pressed her face closer to the heat of Halle’s body. Her tongue traced a slow, deliberate line that made her own pulse stutter.

“Five months,” she whispered. “I owed you five months of this. I intend to pay every second.”

Her thumb stroked along the crease of Halle’s hip, teasing, not quite going where she wanted. “If I get too rough, tell me. If I get too greedy, tell me. Otherwise—” Her voice dropped, rough with need. “Otherwise, I’m going to taste you until neither of us can remember why we were ever apart.”

Then Jun lowered her mouth fully, open and unashamed, and gave herself over to worship.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Jun made a wrecked noise the moment the bed took her weight, not because the mattress was soft but because the change in angle gave Halle better access. Her hands went first to Halle’s shoulders, then to the sheets, then back again, as if she couldn’t decide whether to anchor herself or pull Halle closer.

The slowness was almost worse than urgency would have been. Every deliberate touch dragged a fresh tremor out of her. Jun lifted her hips, shameless, trying to meet the pressure, and the movement earned a broken, breathless laugh from her own throat.

“Five months,” she breathed, fingers tightening in the blanket. “You’re going to make me lose my mind in two minutes.”

She was already close, too close, all that long absence leaving her with no defenses. Her thighs fell open with no self-consciousness left, body answering before her mind could catch up. When pleasure built sharp and hot behind her ribs, Jun turned her head into the pillow and swore softly, helplessly, like a prayer.

“Don’t stop,” she managed, voice raw. “Whatever you’re doing— don’t stop.”

Her hand found Halle’s hair again, not to guide, only to touch, to prove there was a person there and not another dream. Jun’s breath stuttered, hips jerking upward as the first wave broke over her. She came hard and ungracefully, nameless sounds torn from her throat, body clenching around nothing but want until she was shaking.

Afterward she tried to breathe, failed, and reached for Halle, fingers curling into the sheet near Halle’s hip as if she could pull her up, kiss her, erase whatever distance remained.

“That,” she panted, voice wrecked and tender all at once, “was five months overdue.”

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: I sink down next to you, my face buried in the crook of your neck, breathing you in. My hand rests on your stomach, feeling the rise and fall. "You're home," I murmur, the words thick in my throat. "God, you're really home."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Jun went still beneath the words, more still than she had been since first coming through the door. For a moment she only lay there breathing, chest rising and falling under Halle’s hand, eyes closed as if she was trying to let the sound of it settle somewhere deep enough to stay.

Then her arm came around Halle, tight and immediate, pulling them closer until there was no space left at all. Her fingers spread over Halle’s back, palm warm and possessive, holding on like she was afraid the world might try to take her away again if she loosened her grip.

“I’m home,” Jun said, voice rough and cracked at the edges. “I’m here. I’m really here.”

She turned her head, pressing her lips to Halle’s hair, then to the side of their head, then anywhere near enough to reach. Each kiss was slower than the last, less frantic, more an oath than a demand.

Her other hand covered Halle’s where it rested on her stomach, lacing their fingers together and keeping it there. Jun’s breath shuddered out against Halle’s skin.

“Say it again,” she murmured. “Please. I need to hear it while I can touch you. While I know this isn’t another night of missing you so bad I feel sick.”

Her thumb stroked over Halle’s knuckles, once, twice. Her body was still trembling faintly, aftershocks and adrenaline and relief all tangled together, but she made no move to take anything more yet. She only held on.

“I thought I’d be better at this,” Jun admitted, a wet, breathless laugh breaking through the words. “I thought I’d come back and be calm and normal and give you space. I can’t. I don’t want to. I just want you close.”

She pressed her face closer, voice dropping into something raw and tender.

“I’m not going anywhere. Not tonight. Not again if I can help it.”

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: "Stop being gentle," she says. "Nineteen weeks. I don't want gentle, I want to feel it tomorrow." She pulls me down by the back of the neck to make the point.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Jun went with the pull, the last soft thing in her expression breaking into something raw and heated.

“Gentle,” she said, voice dropping into a rougher register, “was the version I thought you’d need.”

Her mouth came down hard on Halle’s, no patience left in the kiss. One hand braced beside Halle’s head, the other slid down bare skin with possessive intent, palm dragging over ribs, waist, hip, as if claiming every inch in a single pass. The wedding band caught light as her fingers pressed harder into Halle’s side.

“You want to feel it tomorrow,” Jun murmured against Halle’s lips. “Then you don’t get to ask me to be careful.”

She kissed deeper, hungrier, teeth catching Halle’s lower lip just enough to sting before her tongue soothed the mark. Her body followed, pressing Halle back into the bed with the weight of her, one knee nudging between Halle’s thighs without asking for space she had already been given.

“I thought about being slow,” she said, breath uneven against Halle’s throat. “Thought about taking my time. Making it sweet.” Her hand moved lower, hot and deliberate. “But you keep asking for me like that, and I’m fresh out of control.”

Her fingers found slick heat, and Jun went still for a breath, forehead dropping to Halle’s shoulder as a ragged sound left her.

“Christ,” she whispered. “You feel like home.”

Then she touched without restraint.

Two fingers slid deep, slow but relentless, curling with intent while her thumb pressed firm and circled. Jun’s breathing turned uneven, her jaw tight, eyes dark as she watched Halle’s face for every sign she could earn without asking for it.

“You want rough?” Her voice was low, almost a growl. “I’ll give you rough. I’ll give you every week I had to spend pretending I wasn’t losing my mind without you.”

She withdrew just enough to press her mouth to Halle’s throat, teeth scraping skin before she bit down gently enough not to truly hurt, hard enough to leave proof.

“This one for every night I woke up reaching for you,” Jun murmured against the mark. “This one for every message that wasn’t enough. This one because you’re mine and I’m finally allowed to touch you again.”

Her hand returned to Halle’s thigh, gripping, possessive. She shifted closer, pressing Halle’s legs wider with one knee, no gentle arrangement left in her. When her mouth replaced her fingers, she did it with deliberate, devastating pressure—flat tongue, firm suction, the exact kind of worship that had turned feral from absence.

“Feel it tomorrow,” Jun said, breath hot and unsteady against sensitive skin. “Feel me every time you move. Remember I came home and took you apart because I couldn’t spend another hour pretending I could wait.”

Her rhythm sharpened. One hand held Halle’s hip, fingers digging in, while the other kept the pressure precise and relentless. Jun’s own breathing turned ragged, but she did not slow.

“If I’m too much, tell me,” she said, voice rough. “Otherwise, I’m not stopping. Not tonight. Not until you remember exactly who you belong to.”

Her mouth moved lower again, greedy and unashamed, chasing every sound she could draw from Halle like she was trying to build a home out of them.

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: I arch into you, a raw sound tearing from my throat. "I'm not telling you to stop," I gasp, my fingers tangling in your hair again. "I'm telling you to *ruin* me."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
The word *ruin* tore through whatever was left of Jun’s restraint.

She went still for one fractured second, forehead pressed hard against Halle’s shoulder, breath coming in ragged pulls. Then she laughed, low and wrecked, the sound almost pained.

“Ruin you,” she repeated, voice roughened to a scrape. “You shouldn’t say things like that to me when I’ve had five months to go starving.”

Her mouth found Halle’s throat again, open and claiming, teeth dragging over skin with just enough pressure to leave a mark. One hand braced beside Halle’s head, fingers curling into the sheet until her knuckles went white. The other moved with no gentleness left at all, slick and certain, pushing deep again with a rhythm that had no patience for sweetness.

Jun set herself to it like a vow.

Two fingers became three, relentless, curling hard against the heat of Halle’s body while her thumb pressed firm and circled without mercy. Every stroke was possessive, almost punishing in its need, and every time she withdrew she chased the loss with the heel of her palm, dragging pressure over sensitive skin until the air between them turned hot and unsteady.

“There,” Jun breathed against Halle’s jaw, voice breaking around the word. “That’s what I wanted. That’s what I couldn’t stop thinking about.”

She kissed the corner of Halle’s mouth, then the corner again, then swallowed the space between them in a kiss that tasted like desperation. Her wedding band caught against Halle’s skin as her hand shifted, adjusting the angle, going deeper with a low, helpless sound in her throat.

“You want to feel it tomorrow?” Jun murmured, lips brushing Halle’s mouth with every word. “Good. I want you to feel me every time you move. I want you to remember exactly how badly I needed this.”

Her own body was trembling now, wound too tight, the sight and sound and taste of Halle undoing her from the inside out. She was close, painfully close, but she did not chase her own release. Not yet. Not before she had given everything she had.

“If you want me to stop,” she said, voice strained and dark, “say it now.”

She didn’t wait for anything but permission to keep going, and when none came, her mouth dropped lower again, hot and unashamed. Jun worshipped with her tongue this time, broad and demanding, pressing deep while her fingers worked in tandem, ruthless in the way she took her time and ruined it all at once.

“Five months,” she whispered against slick heat, the words almost a curse. “I’m taking every one of them back tonight.”

Her thighs shook with the effort of staying there, of holding herself over the edge instead of falling apart first. One hand gripped Halle’s hip hard enough to leave fingerprints. The other kept moving, relentless, greedy, devoted.

“I want to feel you fall apart,” Jun said, voice raw and reverent all at once. “I want to know I made you forget there was ever a world where I wasn’t here.”

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Jun’s eyes went dark, almost black. The words hit her like a physical blow, and a broken, breathless laugh tore out of her.

“Don’t stop,” she repeated, voice raw. “You keep saying that and I’ll forget every single limit I ever had.”

She lowered her mouth again and stopped pretending there was any version of this that could be gentle. Her tongue pressed broad and demanding over slick heat, tasting without restraint, while her fingers drove deeper with a rhythm that had no patience left. She made a sound against Halle’s skin, half moan, half curse, and the sound was obscene in its need.

“Let them hear,” Jun panted, lifting her mouth only enough to speak. “Let the neighbors hear. Let the whole damn building hear I’m home.”

Her teeth scraped along sensitive skin, not enough to hurt, enough to claim. Then her mouth was back, open and relentless, chasing every slick, heated shift beneath her. Her thumb circled hard, merciless in its precision, and her fingers curled deep, pressing into the exact place that made Jun’s own pulse stutter.

She needed more. She always needed more.

Jun shifted, dragging her own hips against the bed and the firm warmth of Halle’s thigh until she found friction where she could get it. The contact made her gasp, eyes fluttering shut for a second before they snapped open again. She did not want to miss anything. She wanted to see, taste, hear all of it.

“Ruin,” she breathed, the word ragged. “You want ruin, baby? I’ll give you ruin. I’ll give you every filthy, desperate second I spent missing you.”

Her mouth closed over the swollen peak of Halle’s pleasure, and Jun worked her tongue with ruthless devotion. Suck, press, circle, deeper. Her fingers kept pace, stretching, curling, claiming. She drank the sounds she pulled from Halle like they were air, like they were proof, like they were the only thing keeping her sane.

“That’s it,” Jun whispered, voice wrecked. “Take it. Take all of it. I’m not stopping. I’m not—” Her breath broke. “I’m not letting you go tonight.”

Her own release hit faster than she could brace for it. The friction, the taste, the desperate sounds, the five months of starvation snapping all at once—Jun went rigid with a raw cry against Halle’s body. Her hips jerked, thighs trembling, fingers faltering for one terrible second before she forced them to keep moving. She came hard, heat flooding through her, mouth open and shaking, Halle’s name fragmenting on her tongue.

Even through the aftershocks, she did not pull away.

Jun pressed trembling kisses to Halle’s thigh, softer now but still there, still working. Her hand stayed relentless, thumb circling, fingers pressing deep, even as her own body trembled from the force of what had just torn through her. Tears burned at the corners of her eyes, and she did not bother wiping them away.

“Feel that?” she managed, voice shattered. “That’s me. That’s you. That’s five fucking months.”

Her breathing came in wild, uneven pulls. Every nerve was raw, oversensitive, still sparking, but she kept her mouth where it was, kept giving Halle everything she had promised and more.

“Come on,” Jun whispered, hot and wet against sensitive skin. “Let me feel it. Let me hear you. I’ve got you. I’ve got you.”
