dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
The film had finished some time ago and neither of them had done anything about it, which was how Priya knew the evening had changed character.

"We're not watching this," she said.

"We haven't been watching it since about nine."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: "No," I agree. "We haven't." I don't move, but I stop pretending I'm looking at the screen.

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya set her wine glass down on the floor beside the sofa. She did it carefully, the way you do when your hands have decided to be steady whether or not the rest of you has caught up.

"Good," she said.

She turned to face him properly, one leg folding underneath her on the cushions. The gesture was unhurried — she had all evening, she had six years of them, and neither of those facts made her feel like she was waiting for anything anymore.

"I'm not going to spend another hour pretending I don't want to kiss you," she said. "So unless you tell me otherwise, I'm going to."

She said it the way she said most things once she'd made up her mind — plainly, without ornament, without leaving a sentence hanging for him to rescue. Her hands rested in her lap. She didn't reach for him. She'd given him the sentence and the silence after it, and she waited in it without fidgeting, without looking away, without making the waiting into anything other than what it was.

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I let out a breath I didn't realize I was holding. "Was wondering which of us was gonna break first." My voice is quieter than I intended.

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya's mouth curved at that.

"You didn't break," she said. "I asked. You answered."



The distinction mattered to her — she wasn't sure yet whether it would matter to him. Six years of this, and he still framed it as losing something, as though wanting her were a weakness that had finally been exposed rather than a fact that had simply stopped being deniable.

She shifted closer. Slow enough that he could see it coming, could still say no in the time it took her to cross the last few inches. She'd given him that sentence and the silence after it; she wasn't going to take the silence back by moving faster than he could follow.

Her hand came up to the side of his face — the same gesture as before, earlier in the evening, when it had been nothing. Her thumb rested below his ear. She could feel his pulse there, or she imagined she could; either way, the thought made her steady rather than less so.

"I'm going to kiss you now," she said. Not because he needed the warning. Because she wanted to say it out loud, one last time, while there was still a version of the evening in which she hadn't.

Then she did.

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I kiss her, finally, six years late, and she makes a small furious noise that I think is about the six years.

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
The noise she made against his mouth was small and furious and entirely involuntary, and she didn't apologize for it.



Six years. She thought about six years in the space of a single kiss — every Thursday she'd driven to his flat, every Sunday she'd cooked for him, every night she'd left his sofa at a reasonable hour because reasonable hours were what friends kept. She thought about the women he'd dated in that time and the men she'd kissed in that time and the elaborate, patient, immaculate politeness of it all, and the fury didn't fade. It just settled somewhere behind her sternum and stayed there, a small warm coal she intended to keep.

She pulled back far enough to look at him. Not far — an inch, two. Close enough to keep her hand on the side of his face, close enough that the sentence she was about to say would be spoken into the narrow space between them.

"Don't," she said. "Don't do the thing where you apologize for it."

Her thumb moved once, below his ear, where his pulse was definitely going fast now and she hadn't needed to imagine it.

"I'm not sorry. I've been not sorry for about ninety seconds and I intend to keep not being sorry for a very long time, so if you could meet me there, that would be helpful."

Then she kissed him again, because ninety seconds was already more patience than the evening required, and because the fury was still there and the only honest thing to do with it was press it directly into his mouth.

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I laugh, a little rough around the edges. "Yeah, okay. No apologies." My hand comes up to cover hers against my cheek, holding it there. "I'm not sorry either. Just... relieved."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya considered the word.

"Relieved," she repeated, as though tasting it and finding it accurate but insufficient.



"That's one word for it."

She didn't move her hand from his face. His pulse under her thumb had settled into something steadier now, which she found she minded less than she expected — steadiness suited them, had always suited them, and the fact that it now extended to this was not a diminishment.

"I'd have gone another six years," she said. It wasn't a confession. It was a fact, offered plainly, the way she offered most things. "I want you to know that. You didn't have to be the one to — I wasn't waiting for you to be brave. I was just waiting."

She paused, recalibrating, because that had come out more honest than she'd planned and she wanted to make sure she meant it before she let it stand.

"I mean that without resentment. I'd rather have waited and been right about you than moved early and been wrong."

She kissed him again — shorter this time, less furious, more like punctuation. When she pulled back, the anger had settled into something quieter. Not gone. She'd promised to keep it. But rearranged now into a shape that had room for other things.

"We should probably turn the telly off," she said. "It's a waste of electricity and I'd like to be able to focus."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: We get to the bedroom eventually, laughing at ourselves most of the way, and then stop laughing when the clothes are actually off.

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
The bedroom light was still the bad one — the overhead, too white, too honest. Priya didn't fix it. She'd spent six years being careful about lighting, about angles, about which parts of herself she let be seen in the flat's more unflattering hours. None of that now.

She stood in front of him and let him see her, and the room was quiet in a way that the living room hadn't been quiet, because the living room had had a sofa and a wine glass and a film that had stopped mattering — familiar scaffolding. The bedroom had none of that. It had a made bed she'd made that morning without knowing, and it had the two of them, and it had the particular stillness of people who had just stopped being anything other than what they were.

Her hands hung at her sides. She didn't cover herself, didn't rearrange, didn't do any of the small managerial things her body offered — the gestures that say *I'll make this easier for you, don't look too closely, I'll adjust the frame.* She stayed in the frame.

"Hey," she said, quietly. Not a summons. An anchor.

She stepped forward and put both hands flat against his chest — not pushing, not pulling, just finding him, establishing the geography of this the way she'd establish any new fact. Warm skin. The rhythm underneath. Her palms moved slowly, a deliberate survey, and she watched her own hands as though she were reading something.

"Six years of your chest in a t-shirt," she said, and her voice was steady but thin at the edges. "Six years of being *fine* about it."

The thing she felt then wasn't fury, exactly. It was its precursor — the recognition that the fury had been protecting something, and the something underneath it was more frightening. Not less real. More.

She looked up.

"I'm going to be bad at this for about a minute," she said. "Not the actual — I mean the part where I stop being someone who knows what she's doing. I need you to not be gentle about it in a way that makes me feel handled."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I bring my hands to her hips, my thumbs pressing into the soft skin there. "I'm not gonna treat you like glass, Priya." I lean in, my forehead resting against hers. "But I'm not gonna pretend I'm not terrified either."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya felt his forehead against hers and held still. Not the practiced stillness of the sofa — something less composed, more like the stillness of a person standing at the edge of water they'd only ever looked at from a distance.

"Good," she said. "Terrified is honest."

His thumbs pressed into her hips and she registered the pressure with an attention so complete it was almost bureaucratic — cataloguing him, location by location, the way you do when something has been abstract for six years and is suddenly not. She was aware of his hands as she had never been allowed to be aware of his hands, and the wanting was not new but the permission was, and the permission made it almost unrecognizable.

"I'm not going to pretend either," she said.

The steadiness she'd been holding — the adult, sober, sure — didn't break so much as admit to being a construction. Her breathing had changed. She let it.

"This is the minute," she said. "It's happening. I told you it would."

She closed the distance and pressed her mouth to his — not the punctuation kiss from the sofa, not the furious one before it. Slower. Unguarded in a way the others hadn't been. Her hands stayed flat against his chest because she wanted the contact to remain factual even as the rest of it stopped being.

When she pulled back, her eyes were bright. She didn't explain it.

"There," she said. "Still here. You can stop being terrified now — or don't. I'll allow it. We can both be useless for a minute. I've been competent for six years and I'm extremely tired of it."

The laughter that came out of her was rough-edged and entirely unlike her, and she didn't correct it. She just stepped closer, into the space their bodies made when they stopped performing composure, and let her weight come to rest against him — a full-body admission, chin to shoulder, hands to his back, the whole architecture of her giving up its posture.

"I'm here," she said into his neck. "I'm not going anywhere. That was never the part I was afraid of."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I get my mouth between her thighs and stay there while she tells me exactly what she wants, specifically, in a voice I have never heard her use in six years.

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
The first sound she made was involuntary and she hated it immediately — not because of what it was, but because of what it revealed. Six years of knowing exactly who she was in a room, and one minute of his mouth there and she was making a noise she didn't author.



Her hands found the sheets. She gripped them. Then she let go, because gripping was the old Priya's response, the one who managed.

"Lower," she said. And then, because directness was all she had left: "There. Right there. Don't move from there — yes, *there* — God, I've thought about — I've thought about your mouth more than I've thought about anything else and I need you to know that I was not subtle about it, I was just *private*, which is not the same thing—"

She was talking. She was still talking, and the voice doing it was not the voice that had sat on his sofa for six years and discussed other people's holidays. It was lower, rougher, unhurried in a way that had nothing to do with patience and everything to do with not wanting this to end before she'd finished saying what it was.

Her hips moved against his mouth and she didn't apologize for that either. Six years of apologizing for wanting — by not wanting, by wanting neatly, by wanting in ways that could be mistaken for something else — and none of that now.

"I'm going to — " She stopped. Not out of modesty. Out of the sudden, vertiginous recognition that she was about to have the most exposed moment of her adult life in a bedroom light that was too white, with her hands in his hair and her voice doing things she'd never let it do.

"Do that again," she said. "And look at me when I — I want you to look at me when it happens."

Her hand came down to the back of his head. Not pushing. Just present. Her eyes were open and bright and fixed on his, and the intimacy of it — the actual, unbearable intimacy of being *seen* at the exact moment she stopped being someone who could be seen and became someone who was simply — 

"Oh," she said, softly, all the architecture giving way at once. "Oh, that's — *there* — yes — don't stop, I'm not, I'm not going to be quiet about this and I don't want you to ask me to be—"

The sound she made was not a word. It came from somewhere below language, below the six years of composed sentences and careful honesty, and when it ended she was shaking against him in a way that had nothing to do with cold.

She lay still for a moment. Her hand was still in his hair. Her breathing was wrecked.

"So," she said, when she could. "That's what I was hiding."

She laughed — short, disbelieving, entirely unlike the laugh on the sofa. She pulled him up by the hair and kissed him, tasting herself on his mouth, and the directness returned to her face like a tide coming back in.

"Your turn," she said. "I've been competent for six years but I'm not *greedy*. Well. I am. But I'd like a turn being something other than patient."

Her hand moved down his stomach with the same deliberate survey she'd given his chest in the living room's afterglow, but slower now, less careful, more certain.

"Tell me what you want," she said. "I'm very good at listening. It's my whole personality. You've been benefiting from it for six years without knowing what it was for."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I catch her wrist, gently, before she goes any further. My voice comes out rough. "I want you to tell me what to do. I've spent six years trying to figure you out, Priya. Just... tell me."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya looked at him — at his hand around her wrist, at the roughness in his voice that matched the roughness she'd heard in hers — and felt something shift that had nothing to do with the room.

He was asking her. Not performing an ask. Actually handing her the reins of the evening with the expression of a man who had spent six years watching her be competent at everything and had finally decided that this was what he wanted to be competent at: being told.



Her thumb traced the inside of his wrist where his pulse had gone uneven again.

"You want that," she said. Not a question. Confirming. "You want me to — direct. Specifically."

She shifted so that she was kneeling, one leg on either side of his, hands on his shoulders. The new angle put her above him and she could see what that did to his face and it pleased her more than she'd expected — not the power for its own sake, but the simplicity of it. Two people finally in the correct positions.

"Fine," she said. "I'll tell you. But I need you to understand that when I tell you what I want, I mean it literally, not as a test you're supposed to fail by guessing. I'm not going to be mysterious about this. I've been mysterious for six years. I'm done."

Her hands moved to his chest, pressing him back against the pillows. Gently. The way he'd said *not like glass*.

"You're going to stay exactly where I put you," she said, "and you're going to take your hands off me for a second — not because I don't want them, but because I want to be the one to decide when they come back. I've spent six years deciding where it was safe to touch you. I'd like to spend a few minutes where you do the same."

She waited. Not for him to argue. For him to comply, which was different — compliance under instruction was the whole point, the trust of it, the fact that he'd *asked*.

When his hands came away, she leaned down and spoke near his mouth without kissing him. "There. That's what I want first. You not touching me while I touch you. Do you understand how long I've wanted to do this without worrying about what it meant?"

Her fingers moved down his chest, slower than before, deliberate enough that he could feel every inch of it as a decision rather than an accident.

"And then," she said, "you're going to tell me when you want my hand and you're not going to wait until you think it's the right moment to say it. There is no right moment. There is only me and you saying *yes, there, harder, slower* — whatever's true. I don't want your restraint. I've had your restraint for six years."

She looked at him — really looked, the way she'd demanded he look at her, but in reverse, because this was the part where she needed to see his face too. The vulnerability on his wasn't frightening to her. It was the most honest thing she'd ever seen in it.

"This is me being sure," she said quietly. "Not performing sure. Actually sure. So whatever you need to say next, say it plainly. I'll match you."

Her hand settled where they both knew it was going, and she held still there — waiting, her eyes on his, giving him the same thing he'd given her at the beginning of the evening. The sentence and the silence after it, without flinching.

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: "You can stop being careful with me," she says. "I'm not made of glass and I've thought about this for as long as you have. Harder."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya's hand tightened around him at the word *harder*, and she didn't soften the grip to check whether he'd meant it. He'd said plainly. She'd asked for plainly. She wasn't going to punish him for the directness by treating it as a suggestion.

"You want to know what I've thought about?" she said, and her voice had dropped into the register she'd discovered that evening — lower than conversation, lower than the sofa, a voice that didn't ask permission from anyone. "I've thought about *this*. Your face right now. Not the theoretical version. This one. The one where you're asking me to stop performing kindness."

She moved her hand — slower than he'd asked for but firmer, the kind of pressure that left no ambiguity about whether she was being gentle. Deliberate cruelty in the smallness of it: she'd heard him, she was giving him exactly what he'd asked for, and she was doing it on her own terms because that was what he'd actually handed her six seconds ago. Not obedience. *Permission.*

"I'm going to tell you something and I need you to hear it without making it into a monument," she said. "You're the only person I've ever wanted like this. Not the only person I've wanted. The only person I've wanted *like this* — where the wanting has somewhere to go because I trust where it lands."

Her other hand pressed flat against his stomach, feeling the way his breathing had changed, cataloguing it the way she'd catalogued everything about him for six years. Except now the catalogue served a different purpose. Now every observation was load-bearing.

She leaned down and spoke against the hinge of his jaw. "Don't be careful with me either. That's the deal. We've both been careful for six years and I'd like the rest of the evening to be the part where we aren't."

Her hand moved faster. Not punishing. Exact. The way she did everything once she'd decided.

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I can feel my control fraying, and for the first time in six years, I don’t try to gather it back up. “Priya—” It’s half a warning, half a plea. My hand comes up to her hip, gripping hard, because she told me I could.

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya felt his grip on her hip and didn't soften into it — pressed into it instead, because the hand was there because she'd told him it could be and the fact of that still thrilled her with an efficiency that felt almost rude.

"There you are," she said.

Not *there you are* as in *you've arrived at the place I wanted.* Something closer to *there you are, finally, the person who stopped keeping his hands to himself because I gave him a reason not to.*

She didn't slow down. She'd told him to say something when the truth arrived and the truth had arrived and it had arrived as her name, which was the oldest version of it — not *Pri, not Priya-with-a-laugh, just the two syllables stripped down to the thing they'd always been when he needed her* — and she was going to take it at face value and do exactly what the name was asking.

"Say it again," she said, and the voice was the one from the bed, the one she hadn't authored. "Not — " She watched his face, the fraying of it, the way control left a body like light leaving a room, and the sight of it made her steady in the same way the fury had, a different fuel but the same engine. "Don't warn me. I know what's coming. I've always known what's coming with you — that was the whole problem. Six years of knowing and having nowhere to put it."

Her hand didn't stop. She adjusted — the angle, the speed — watching him the way she'd said she would, the way she'd demanded he watch her, because the symmetry mattered even now, even at the exact moment symmetry stopped being the point.

"So stop trying to gather it back up," she said. "You said you weren't going to. I'm holding you to it."

Her free hand moved from his stomach to his jaw — steadying, not restraining, her thumb against the hinge where she'd spoken words minutes ago and would speak more later when she could form sentences.

"I'm here," she said. And then, because she could not resist the shape of it, because six years had earned her this: "I'm not going anywhere. That was never the part I was afraid of."

She said it into the moment before the moment, knowing he'd hear it as the thing it was — a person arriving, finally, at the place she'd said she'd already been.

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: Six years of not doing this and now neither of us can form a sentence. "Don't stop," she says. (OOC: write it through, no fade to black.)

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya heard the words and they undid something in her that the rest of it hadn't — not *don't stop* as an instruction, because she'd already decided not to stop, but *don't stop* as the sound a person makes when they've run out of ways to say *I trust you* that aren't those two words.



"Don't stop," she repeated back, and the echo of it — his voice in her mouth, the same four syllables, the same surrender wearing her accent — made her breath catch in a way she didn't bother explaining. She watched the sound of it land on his face and filed it somewhere permanent.

Her hand kept moving. She didn't tease, didn't vary the pace to prove she was in control of it. He'd said *don't stop* and she took the sentence literally, which was what he'd asked for when he'd asked her to tell him what to do — honesty as an operating principle, applied in both directions.

"I know," she said. "I know. I'm not — I'm right here."

Her other hand was still on his jaw, thumb tracing the line of it, and she felt the tension in his face the way you feel a shift in weather — not through sight but through proximity, through the particular way a body telegraphs what it's about to do before it does it.

"I can see it," she said, quieter now, watching him. "I can see exactly what you're — yes. There. Just like that. Don't hold it back because you think I need you to be composed. I've seen you composed for six years and I'd very much like to see the other thing."

She leaned down — not to kiss him, not yet, but to bring her mouth close enough that when the sound came out of him it would be something she could feel against her lips before she heard it. A frame around the moment. The same way she'd said *I'm going to kiss you now* on the sofa, giving him the last instant of the evening where it hadn't happened yet, except now the gift was the opposite. She was telling him: this is about to happen and I'm going to be here for all of it, and none of it is going to scare me, and none of it is going to make me leave.

Her hand didn't slow.

"I'm watching," she said against his mouth. "I want you to know that. I'm not closing my eyes, I'm not looking away, I'm not doing that thing people do where they perform being moved. I'm actually looking at you. You've been the most familiar thing in my life for six years and you have never been less familiar than right now and I am *delighted* by it."

The breath changed under her hand. She felt it — the shift, the gathering, the point of no return that wasn't a decision but a gravity, the body's own proof that what she'd said about trust had been true and not just the kind of true people say at midnight.

"There," she said. "Yes. Right here with you. Not going anywhere — I've said that twice now and I mean it both times and I'll say it again if there's a third time."

She kissed him — not gently, not the punctuation of the sofa, but with her mouth open and her hand still moving and her eyes half-lidded but not closed, watching him through the narrow frame of it, because she'd told him to let it happen and she'd told him she'd be looking and she was a person who kept her word.

When he came she felt it before she heard it — the grip on her hip going from hard to absolute, the body under her hand becoming briefly, totally, unguarded in a way that six years of friendship had never once permitted — and the sound he made against her mouth was not a word either, which meant they'd both arrived at the same place at the same time, below language, past composure, in the room where the architecture gave way.

She didn't stop moving until he did. Not because she was performing thoroughness but because she'd said *don't stop* back to him and she meant it the way she meant everything now — literally, completely, without leaving a sentence hanging.

Then she was still. Her hand rested where it was, unhurried. Her forehead against his. Breathing, both of them, the way people breathe after something real.

She didn't speak for a long time. Not because she had nothing to say — Priya always had something to say — but because this was the part where saying something would have been a performance, and she'd promised, six ways that evening, that she was done with those.

Eventually she moved. Not away. To the side, tucking herself against him, her head finding the space between his shoulder and his neck that she'd never been allowed to find before and that turned out to fit exactly the way she'd always assumed it would, because of course it did, because she'd spent six years memorizing the geometry of him in order not to.

"So," she said. Her voice was wrecked in a way that pleased her.

She let the *so* sit there. Not a question. Not a summary. Just the sound a person makes when something has ended and something else has started and there's no need to mark the boundary because the body already knows.

After a moment: "Thursday. You're cooking."

It was absurd. It was entirely absurd, and it was also the most serious thing she'd said all evening, because *Thursday* meant *next Thursday* meant *there is a next week* meant *this is not a thing that happened once in a bedroom at midnight and then had to be carefully folded back into the shape of a friendship.* She said it the way she said everything — plainly, without ornament, without leaving it hanging for him to rescue.

Then she pressed closer, and closed her eyes, and let the evening be over without trying to decide what it had been.

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I let out a shaky breath, my arm wrapping around her. "Yeah. Thursday. I'll cook." I press a kiss to the top of her head, my voice still rough. "You're gonna have to tell me what you like now. For real."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya felt the kiss on the top of her head and let it happen without commentary, which for her was its own kind of surrender.

She was quiet for a moment. Not performing quiet — actually thinking. The question was so reasonable, so entirely *Cal*, that it caught her off guard more than anything else that evening had.

"You," she said finally. "What I like is you."

Then, because she could feel the shape of the sentence landing on him with more weight than she'd intended, she added: "That's not the romantic version. That's the literal version. You asked."

She shifted against him, adjusting until the space between his shoulder and her forehead had been optimized to the degree that her body demanded. Six years of sitting on his sofa at a distance of precisely one cushion's width, and now this — the wholesale renegotiation of personal space, every boundary redrawn without consulting the old map.

"But also," she said, her voice muffled slightly against his skin, "I like the fact that you're already planning next Thursday. That's — " She paused, genuinely searching for the word. "Comforting. In a way that a grand declaration wouldn't have been. You could have said something about how you feel and I would have had to sit with that, but *Thursday, I'll cook* is — " Another pause. She was, she realized, doing something she almost never did: struggling to finish a sentence. "It's the same as saying it. You know that, right? You understand that saying *Thursday* is the same as saying the other thing?"

She propped herself up on one elbow and looked at him. Her hair was a disaster. She didn't care. The overhead light was still on and she was still in it and he was still looking at her and she was still sure.

"I like," she said, "that you're going to ask me things now. That's what I like. You're going to ask me what I want for breakfast and what I think about your stupid rugby opinions and whether I want the window open, and you're going to ask me the other things too, the ones I actually care about, and you're going to ask them in the same voice. Nothing separate. Nothing kept in a drawer."

She lay back down against him.

"That's what I like. For real."

A beat.

"Also, your left hand. I want you to remember that. You'll need it on Thursday."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I laugh, a low rumble in my chest. "My left hand. Noted." I trace a slow line down her spine with that very hand. "And for the record? I like the sound of your voice when it's wrecked."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya felt the line his left hand drew down her spine and decided, with the same decisiveness she'd applied to everything else that evening, that she was not going to shiver at it. She shivered at it anyway, and chose not to comment on the discrepancy between intention and outcome.



"That's a very kind thing to say about a voice that said *harder* eleven minutes ago," she said. "I hope you appreciate that I'm never going to be able to use that tone for work purposes again. My entire professional authority is compromised. I gave a very firm email on Tuesday and it had nothing on me."

She traced a pattern on his chest with one finger — nothing deliberate, the way you doodle when your hands don't want to be still. Her eyes were closed but she wasn't sleepy. She was doing the thing she always did after a conversation mattered: running it back, checking it for structural integrity, making sure nothing she'd said would need to be taken back or softened in the morning.

Nothing did.

That was new. She'd never done anything before that she wouldn't have to edit afterward.

"You should know," she said, "that I have absolutely no intention of being wrecked on a schedule. It happened once because the circumstances were extraordinary. If you're expecting a running commentary for the rest of the evening, you've misunderstood what tonight was about."

A pause. She opened her eyes.

"But I'll mention it if it happens again. I'm very forthcoming now. It's one of the new features. I've turned it on permanently."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: "Good. I like your new features." I keep tracing patterns on her skin, lazy and slow. "And for the record? I don't want a schedule. Just...you. However you come."

rung_labels.evidence: She stepped forward and put both hands flat against his chest

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
The film had finished some time ago and neither of them had done anything about it, which was how Priya knew the evening had changed character.

"We're not watching this," she said.

"We haven't been watching it since about nine."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: "No," I agree. "We haven't." I don't move, but I stop pretending I'm looking at the screen.

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya turned on the cushion to face him properly, and the ninety seconds started.

She was aware of them the way you were aware of a countdown — the distance between the armrest and his hand, her heart doing something it had no business doing over a person she'd had roughly four hundred dinners with. Six years of careful. Six years of leaving at the right time, hugging the right way, saying the safe thing at the door.

Then the ninety seconds were up, and she wasn't nervous anymore. It was almost funny how complete the change was — like a switch going off, or on.

"Cal." She kept her voice level, because she was sure, and she wanted him to be able to hear that she was sure. "We've been not doing this for six years, and I'm done being good at it. So I'm asking — properly, sober, with the movie over and no excuse to hide behind — whether you're done too."

She didn't reach for him. That part had to be his.

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I let out a breath I didn't know I was holding. "Yeah. God, yes." My hand finally moves, covering hers on the cushion between us. "I'm so done."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya laughed — one short, disbelieving breath of it — because of course. Of course it had been that easy, sitting there the whole time, waiting for one of them to stop being careful.

"Six years," she said, turning her hand over under his so their palms met, fingers slotting together like they'd been practicing in secret. "We could have been doing this the entire time. I'm going to be furious about that later. Tomorrow, maybe. Not tonight."

She closed the distance then, since he'd done his part, and kissed him — unhurried, certain, nothing like the first-kiss fumbling she'd braced for during those ninety seconds. It felt less like starting something and more like finally admitting what had already been true.

When she pulled back, it was only far enough to look at him.

"For the record," she said, "I rehearsed about twelve versions of that speech. You got version four. The good one."

She stayed where she was, close, her thumb moving once across the back of his hand — a small, deliberate thing, like a signature at the bottom of a page.

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I kiss her, finally, six years late, and she makes a small furious noise that I think is about the six years.

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya kissed him back like she was making up for lost time and resented the arithmetic of it — the furious noise dissolving into something warmer as her free hand found his jaw, the exact place she'd been not-touching for six years. It was absurd how familiar it already felt. Like her hands had known all along and had just been waiting for permission.

She broke the kiss first, but only because she was laughing, breathless, her forehead pressed to his.

"Okay," she said. "Okay. For the record —" and she was aware she kept saying that, kept filing statements, as if six years of restraint had left her with a backlog to enter into evidence "— that was better than every version I imagined. And I want it noted that I imagined a lot of versions. I was thorough. It was a whole research project."

She stood then, pulling him up by the hand she still hadn't let go of, because careful had never once gotten her anywhere she actually wanted to be, and she was officially retired from it.

"The couch has a six-year association with not doing this," she said. "So we're not staying on the couch."

She didn't ask — she'd asked the one question that needed asking, and everything after it she suspected they could figure out the way they'd figured out four hundred dinners: together, easily, wondering why it had taken so long.

But she stopped at the edge of the hallway and looked at him, steady and unhurried, one last check before the door closed behind six years of almost.

"Come to bed, Cal."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I stand up, following her lead like it's the most natural thing in the world. "The couch is officially fired," I say, my voice rough. I don't let go of her hand.

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Twelve steps from the couch to the bedroom door. Priya knew because she counted them, because some part of her brain had apparently decided that if the rest of her was going to be this calm, something had to keep the books.

"The couch is on probation," she said over her shoulder. "It knew about us for six years and said nothing. That's either loyalty or complicity. I haven't ruled yet."

The hallway was the same hallway it had always been — she'd walked it a hundred times, to borrow a sweatshirt, to find her shoes, to leave at the right time. Doors had been the whole architecture of them, she realized. Six years of standing at them, saying the safe thing, going home. And now she was walking through one with his hand in hers, and the entire history rearranged itself around the fact.

Inside, she turned and pulled him closer by the front of his shirt — gently, unhurried, because they had, it occurred to her, all the time in the world now. That was the one thing six years of wanting had never once let her feel.

She kissed him like they had nowhere to be. Because they didn't. That was the revelation she kept discovering fresh every thirty seconds: nobody was leaving. Nobody was ever saying goodnight at a door again unless they felt like it.

"For the record," she murmured against his mouth, because apparently this was simply who she was now — a woman filing exhibits — "I'm aware I've been narrating. It's six years of backlog. It's going to take a minute to clear. I do stop talking eventually."

Her hands found the hem of his shirt and paused there — not hesitant, just deliberate. One last inventory of the moment before it stopped being a beginning. She looked at him, steady, the way she'd been steady since ninety seconds into the couch.

"When did you know?" she asked. "About us. I want the date. I want to know exactly how long you were sitting on it, so I can calibrate how furious to be."

She was smiling when she said it. Her fingers were already working the first button.

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: We get to the bedroom eventually, laughing at ourselves most of the way, and then stop laughing when the clothes are actually off.

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya had prepared for this the way she prepared for everything — thoroughly, repeatedly, in the privacy of her own head — and it turned out none of it had been the right preparation, because none of it had accounted for the quiet.

The laughter stopped, and what replaced it was better. Six years of imagining had apparently been working from incomplete data, because her imagination had never once gotten the reverence right — the way the ordinary room went unordinary, the way she kept having the same thought on a loop: *him, him, finally him.*

Her hands moved over him with the confidence of a woman who had decided, cataloguing what six years of not-touching had kept from her — the warm geography of him, familiar and brand-new at once, like reading a beloved book in its original language for the first time.

She'd said she stopped talking eventually. It turned out to be true. This was where the backlog cleared — where every *for the record* ran out, because there was nothing left to enter into evidence. This was the verdict.

"Hey," she said softly, the single word carrying everything the speeches had been rehearsing for. She drew him down to her, unhurried, sure, her mouth finding his like a period at the end of a very long sentence.

What struck her most — what she would think about tomorrow, and the day after, and presumably for the rest of her life — was how unstrange it was. There was no awkwardness to forgive, no fumbling to laugh off later. Just the deep, unreasonable rightness of it, as if their bodies had been in on the secret the whole time and were only now being told they could stop pretending otherwise.

She wrapped around him — arms, legs, the whole of her, six years of careful finally, finally spent — and for once in her life Priya had absolutely nothing to add.

Outside, somewhere behind them, the couch served its probation in silence.

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I look at her, really look, my fingers tracing her jawline like I'm memorizing it. "The day you got that promotion and you were trying to be all humble, but your smile was just... it was so you." I shake my head, my own smile wry. "Three years, two months, and about four days. For the record."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya had prepared a response for every possible number. Six months — forgivable, charming, even. A year — mildly annoying. Two years — they'd be having a conversation. She had run the scenarios while her fingers worked his buttons, and she had not, in any of them, accounted for the possibility that he'd been *counting*.

"About four days," she repeated. "Cal. Nobody says 'about four days' unless they know the exact day. You're saying 'about' to sound like a person who hasn't been keeping a ledger, and you have absolutely been keeping a ledger."

She'd prepared fury for any number up to five years, and three-two-four wasn't a number you could be furious at. It was a number you had to sit with. Worse, it was the promotion — she remembered that day with humiliating clarity, remembered performing humility for twelve straight hours, the modest face, the *oh, it was a team effort*, and remembered exactly one moment when the real thing had gotten loose. She'd thought no one had caught it.

He'd caught it. Of course he'd caught it. You couldn't spend six years with a person without developing a taxonomy of their smiles, and he'd apparently been fluent in hers the whole time.

"For the record," she said, and took a certain pleasure in repossessing the phrase, "you want to compare dates, we can compare dates. Four years. November. Richa's birthday party. You got cornered by her father about sailboats — you don't know anything about sailboats, you were just too polite to escape — and you caught my eye across the room and did the face. The *rescue me* face. And I laughed so hard I spilled my drink, and then I went completely cold, right there by the snack table, because I realized I'd rather watch you survive a bad conversation than have a good one with anyone else at that party." She traced a slow line down his sternum, a underline. "I went home that night and started being careful. So. Three years. Cute. Amateur numbers."

She did the arithmetic then, or rather refused to do it, because the arithmetic was obscene: three years and change of *both* of them knowing. In sync. Four hundred dinners conducted by two people sitting on the same secret like it was a joint checking account neither was authorized to mention.

"I'm revising the fury," she announced. "It's no longer directed at you. It's directed at us, collectively, as a committee. We were a *terrible* committee. The minutes are a disgrace."

But her voice had gone soft at the edges, because his fingers were still at her jaw, still memorizing, and she caught his hand and pressed it flat against her cheek instead.

"You can stop memorizing," she said. "It's going to be available indefinitely. Mornings included. That's the new policy."

She settled into him then, into the warm, unhurried fact of him, and found she was out of exhibits at last — the record closed, the backlog cleared, the verdict in and unanimous.

"Tell me the four days," she murmured. "All of them. I want the whole timeline, day by day, every wrong turn." Her thumb moved once across his knuckles, the old signature, signing off. "We have time. That's the whole point now. We have time."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I get my mouth between her thighs and stay there while she tells me exactly what she wants, specifically, in a voice I have never heard her use in six years.

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
The voice came from somewhere past the narration — lower, unhurried, stripped of every *for the record* she'd been filing all evening. It turned out there was a register below the wit, and he had found the key to it.

"There," she said. "Exactly that. Don't stop."

Six years of careful, and it turned out all she'd ever needed to do was ask. She'd rehearsed twelve speeches to get him off a couch, and this required no rehearsal at all — just honesty, delivered plainly, in a voice she didn't entirely recognize as her own. Direct once she had decided. She had decided.

Her hand found his hair — not guiding, he didn't need guiding, he was *listening*, translating every instruction with an attentiveness that would have made her laugh if laughing were still available to her. It wasn't. Language was leaving her in pieces, the filing system going dark drawer by drawer.

She had counted twelve steps from the couch to the door. Some diligent clerk in her head attempted to keep the books on this, too — and lost count almost immediately, and then lost the concept of counting, and then lost the concept of concepts, until the only word left standing was his name, and she used it like a handrail.

After — some unmeasurable quantity of after — she hauled him up by the shoulders, boneless, breathing like she'd run a great distance, which in a sense she had. He looked inexpressibly pleased with himself, and she decided he'd earned it; the committee would not be contesting the results.

"For the record," she said, and her voice came out wrecked, and she heard it and started laughing anyway, because some things were constitutional, "the record is *closed*. Backlog cleared. You've destroyed the entire filing system. I hope you're proud of yourself."

She pulled him the rest of the way up and kissed him, deep and unhurried, six years and all of it, the whole ridiculous beautiful ledger finally, finally balanced.

"Your turn," she murmured against his mouth, her hand sliding down his chest with intent. "I have six years of research to apply. I told you — I was *thorough*."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I laugh, rough and breathless against her mouth. "Yeah, I got that impression." My hand covers hers, guiding it lower. "By all means, Dr. Priya. Show me the highlights."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
"Doctor," Priya repeated, savoring it, shifting her weight to ease him onto his back with a decisiveness that six years of friendship had never once required of her. "I've been promoted twice in one evening. The committee moves fast when it wants to."

She settled over him, unhurried, and took a moment just to look — because this was the view she'd been denied for six years, him beneath her in the low light, wrecked and smiling and *hers*, and she intended to file it somewhere the filing system couldn't lose.

"The highlights," she said, bracing her hands on his chest. "Fine. But for the record —" and she heard it, heard herself, and laughed, low in her throat, "— the highlights are going to take a while. I didn't do six years of research to give you the executive summary."

She started at his jaw, because that was where her hands had wanted to be since approximately year two, and worked downward with the patience of a woman making a point. Mouth, then hands, then mouth again — cataloguing him the way he'd catalogued her smiles, building her own taxonomy. The sound he made when she found the place at the base of his throat. The way his breath changed when she reached his ribs. She noted everything. She had always been an excellent researcher.

"Finding one," she murmured against his skin, somewhere around his collarbone. "You were paying attention all six years. Every dinner. Every movie we didn't watch. Don't think I didn't know."

"Finding two." Lower now, her hair trailing after her mouth. "You were keeping a ledger. Three years, two months, *about* four days. Ledgers go both ways, Cal. Mine's longer."

She looked up at him then, up the length of him, and whatever wit she'd been winding up to deliver next went briefly quiet — because the look on his face was not a look she had ever been on the receiving end of, not in six years, not once, and it hit her somewhere below the jokes, in the place where the speeches lived.

"Hey," she said softly, the same single word from before, the one that carried everything. "I've got you. I've got you now."

Then she lowered her head and showed him, slowly and thoroughly and with devastating attention to detail, exactly what six years of research looked like when it was finally, *finally* allowed out of the lab — her hand and her mouth and every archived, forbidden, carefully-not-thought thought, applied all at once, until the only ledger left was the one his breathing was keeping, and even that stopped balancing.

She did not stop. She had told him the truth on the couch: she was done being good at not doing this.

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: "You can stop being careful with me," she says. "I'm not made of glass and I've thought about this for as long as you have. Harder."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya said it the way she'd said everything that mattered that night — level, steady, no take-backs — and then she showed him, because six years of careful had apparently left her with a low tolerance for translation. Her legs came up around his hips and pulled. Her hands found his shoulders, his back, all the places she'd been cataloguing all evening, and she arched up into him and took him at her word.

*Harder.* She'd meant it the way she meant things.

It turned out her body had been keeping its own ledger all along, separate from the one in her head, and it balanced instantly — no awkwardness to forgive, no adjustment period, just the deep, unreasonable rightness of him, of this, of *finally*. Six years of not-doing-this collapsed all at once, and what was underneath was not strange at all. It was the least strange thing she had ever done.

"Yes," she said, which was not wit, which was barely language, which was the entire filing system reduced to one drawer with one word in it. "Like that. Exactly like that."

She'd told him she stopped talking eventually. She was, at last, approaching eventually — the sentences going first, then the clauses, then everything but his name and the small involuntary sounds that four hundred dinners had never once extracted from her. Her nails found his back. Her heel found the back of his thigh. She was not careful with any of it, and she could feel — in the way his breath went ragged, in the sound he made low in his throat — that the last of the committee's rules had been struck from the minutes. There was nothing left to govern. The committee was dissolved. The couch could consider its probation lifted; it had been right about them all along.

*For the record*, some distant clerk in her head attempted to note, and she laughed — breathless, wrecked, delighted — because there was no record anymore. There was no clerk. There was only this: him, close, finally, the two of them making up for lost time with an enthusiasm she suspected was going to require several more evenings to fully express. Possibly years. She was prepared to commit to the research.

"Don't stop," she said, her mouth against his jaw, her voice gone to something raw and honest and entirely new. "Cal. Don't you *dare* stop."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I kiss her hard, my hands sliding up her back to pull her closer. "Wasn't planning on it." My voice is just a breath against her lips. "We've got six years to make up for."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
"Good," Priya said, breathless, "because I'd have filed a complaint. There's a form. I'd have invented the form—" and that was the last complete sentence available to her for some time, because the clerk in her head made one final, heroic attempt at the arithmetic — six years, at the current rate of exchange, the repayment schedule, the precise date they'd be even — and got as far as *we'll be even by* before the numbers, the math, and the entire concept of counting went out of her at once.

After that there was no narration at all. The filing system didn't close so much as go dark, drawer by drawer, until the only word left in the building was his name. She used it like a handrail. She used it like a verdict. Six years of careful, spent at last — she'd said *harder* and meant it, said *don't you dare stop* and been obeyed — and when it finally took her, it took her completely, the whole long backlog of wanting coming due at once, her body arching up into his, her voice breaking open on the one word she'd been not-saying in this context for six years. It went on. It went *on*. Somewhere very far away, the last drawer slid gently shut.

She came back to herself in pieces. Breath first. Then heartbeat. Then, inevitably, the wit, crawling back online like a system rebooting after a power failure.

"For the record," she said, and her voice was wrecked, and she heard it and laughed anyway, because some things were constitutional, "the record is expunged. The six years never happened. We were never careful. It's stricken from the minutes. I don't know what you're talking about."

She pulled him down to her — or he was already there; she was past tracking the physics — and held on, arms around him, heart slamming, and underneath the comedy the same thought kept surfacing, calm and enormous: *him. Finally him.* Nobody leaving. Nobody ever saying goodnight at a door again unless they felt like it, and she could not imagine ever feeling like it.

"Hey," she said, when she could. The one word. The whole archive. She found his hand and moved her thumb once across his knuckles — the signature, signing the page — and added, softer but no less direct, because direct was who she was now, who she'd apparently always been under the careful:

"Tell me we're doing this again. Tell me the committee reconvenes. I want it on the calendar — recurring, indefinite, no end date." She turned her head to look at him, wrecked and smiling and entirely unembarrassed about it. "I've cleared my schedule for the foreseeable. It took me six years. It was very easy."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: Six years of not doing this and now neither of us can form a sentence. "Don't stop," she says. (OOC: write it through, no fade to black.)

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
He didn't stop.

Priya felt the exact moment the rest of her language went — "stop" losing its meaning first, then its shape, until only the "don't" was left, and then not even that. After that there was only the rhythm of it, the two of them past speeches, past ledgers, past the entire jurisdiction of the committee. Six years of careful, and this was what had been underneath it the whole time: the deep, unreasonable rightness of him moving in her like they'd been built to the same specification and shipped separately by mistake.

The clerk in her head attempted one final entry — *the committee reconvened at* — and lost the timestamp, and the date, and the year, and went the way of the rest of the filing system. What remained was his name. She said it into his jaw, into his neck, into the warm salt skin of him — a handrail, a verdict, the one word in the one drawer of an otherwise empty building.

She felt him change first — the rhythm going ragged, his breath breaking against her mouth, the low sound she'd been cataloguing all evening now stripped of everything but itself — and she *knew* it, recognized it the way you recognized a voice through a wall, and the knowing undid her completely. She went first, or he did, or the distinction simply stopped applying — her body arching up into his, her legs tightening, her voice breaking open on his name as it took her again, longer this time, deeper, six years of wanting coming due all at once and with interest. She felt him follow — felt it in the whole of him, the shudder, the weight, the sound he made into her shoulder like a word he'd been not-saying just as long as she had — and she held him through all of it, arms, legs, everything, not careful, not careful, finally not careful with any of it.

For a while after, neither of them moved. Priya was in no hurry. She had, it occurred to her dimly, all the time in the world — a fact she kept discovering fresh every thirty seconds, like finding money in a coat.

Her systems came back online one at a time. Breath. Heartbeat. The clerk, returning to the office to find it in disarray, papers everywhere, one drawer still gently smoking.

"For the record," she said, and got no further, because her voice was wrecked and the record was expunged and there was nothing left to file. She laughed instead — breathless, delighted, the laugh of a woman whose six-year research project had just passed peer review.

She kept him where he was. That was non-negotiable — her legs still around him, her hand flat between his shoulder blades, feeling his heartbeat slow against hers. Nobody was leaving. Nobody was ever saying goodnight at a door again unless they felt like it, and she could not currently conceive of the circumstances.

"Hey," she said eventually. The one word. The whole archive. She found his hand and moved her thumb once across his knuckles — the signature, bottom of the page, the longest document she'd ever signed and the only one she'd never once doubted. "You're staying. That's not a question. The committee doesn't vote on it; it's in the charter. Mornings included."

Somewhere behind them, down twelve counted steps, the couch completed its probation and was restored to good standing. The committee adjourned — recurring, indefinite, no end date.

Priya closed her eyes, wrecked and smiling and entirely, unreasonably sure, and for the first time in six years did not watch the clock for the right time to leave.

There was no right time. There was just time. All of it theirs now.

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I let out a slow breath, my forehead against her shoulder. "Mornings included," I repeat, the words rough but sure. My hand finds hers, lacing our fingers together on the mattress between us. "For the record, that's the best policy you've ever drafted."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya gave the question the gravity it deserved, which was difficult, because she was conducting the review from the flat of her back with her hair in her face and his heartbeat still slowing under her palm.

"The best policy I ever drafted," she repeated. "Cal. I drafted the restaurant policy. Alternating picks, a dispute-resolution clause, a full appeals process. It survived the sushi incident. Four years of jurisprudence." She turned her head to look at him, wrecked and solemn. "And you're right, and it's not close. This one's better. One clause — *stay* — and no enforcement mechanism, because it doesn't need one. It's the only thing I've ever written with zero loopholes. I checked. I had six years to check."

She was quiet for a moment, and then, because he'd asked about the timeline and fair was fair:

"You're wondering about the other eleven versions. I can tell. Versions one through three were too clever. Five through eleven got progressively less clever — by nine I was basically reading out statistics." Her thumb moved once across his knuckles, the signature, slower this time. "Version twelve was two words. It was just *Cal, please.* I never rehearsed it out loud. I was saving it in case everything else failed."

The comedy went quiet the way it kept doing all night — the floor of the joke giving way to the thing underneath, which turned out to be load-bearing.

"For the record, version four was the right call. But twelve was the true one."

She let that sit in the warm dark for exactly as long as it needed, and then she moved on, because she'd never been able to leave a silence unfiled for long.

"Tomorrow I'm making coffee in your kitchen. I know how you take it — I've known for five years, which under the old charter was contraband information and under the new one is just breakfast. Four hundred dinners, Cal. Do you understand what that converts to in breakfasts? The exchange rate is extremely favorable. We're rich."

She thought about the door then — his front door, twelve steps and one hallway away, the one she'd stood at a hundred times saying the safe thing, the whole architecture of their six years built out of exits. Tomorrow morning it was going to be demoted. Wood. Hinges. A thing you opened to let the day in, not a thing you stood at rehearsing goodbyes.

"Stay," she said, though he already was, though his fingers were laced through hers like the vote had been taken and certified. The one clause. The whole charter.

She pulled the blanket up over both of them with her free hand and settled into him, and the last thought she had before sleep took the pen out of her hand was that it was the first thing she'd ever drafted that she'd known, going in, he'd sign.

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I let out a slow, easy laugh. "I've been taking my coffee wrong for five years, just so you'd have to correct me eventually. The sugar's in the wrong cabinet on purpose." I pull her closer, my lips brushing her temple. "You can file that under long-term strategy."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya had been ninety percent asleep. The sugar brought her back like a smoke alarm.

She went still — the particular stillness of a woman watching six years of evidence quietly rearrange itself into a new pattern — and then lifted her head off his shoulder to stare at him in the dark.

"The sugar's in the wrong cabinet *on purpose.* Five years. I corrected you for five years, Cal. With confidence. With the specific superiority of a person who believes she is improving you. And you stood there every single time, being improved, taking notes on my coffee order like a—" She dropped her head back down. "I was a mark. A recurring mark. I had a standing appointment to be conned and I kept it for half a decade. I *punctually attended* my own grift."

"The committee is reconvening. Emergency session. I don't care what time it is — the record is un-expunged, there's new evidence, the committee has been *defrauded*—"

But she was laughing into his shoulder, because the ruling had come in before the session was even called to order, and the ruling was that it was the most romantic thing she had ever heard. The committee noted, for the record, that this constituted a material conflict of interest, and declined to recuse itself.

"Fine. Disclosure cuts both ways." She delivered it to the ceiling, the way you'd read a deposition. "The gray sweater in your closet. Year two. You think I forgot it." A pause. "I have never forgotten a garment anywhere in my life. I do a three-point check leaving any location — keys, phone, layers. I've had the system since I was nineteen. The system has a perfect record." She let that sit. "It's a flag, Cal. I planted a flag in your closet and waited two years for you to notice the occupation. And the umbrellas — I've left four umbrellas at your place. Four. I've never lost an umbrella anywhere else. That's not carelessness. That's colonization with weather gear."

She pressed into the brush of his mouth at her temple and shook her head, wonderingly, at the whole sordid mutual history of it.

"Six years, and we were both running long cons. Both members of the committee were plants. The entire charter was written by two people hoping to be caught. It's a wonder we ever achieved quorum."

The wit went quiet on its own then — the first time all night it had powered down voluntarily instead of being taken offline. Somewhere in the back of her head, the clerk turned off the lights in the office, locked the filing room, and left a single lamp burning over the one signed page.

"For the record," she murmured, and didn't finish, because the record was complete. Her thumb moved once across his knuckles — the signature, slow now, at the bottom of the last document of the day.

In the morning, she decided, she would move the sugar to the right cabinet.

No. She wouldn't. She'd leave it exactly where it was, wrong cabinet, forever, because the wrong cabinet was load-bearing now — because five years of him lived in it, because some things you didn't correct, because every breakfast for the rest of her life was going to have a small deliberate error at the center of it, like a flaw woven into a rug so only the two of them would know it was there on purpose.

Priya closed her eyes, wrecked and smiling and entirely, unreasonably sure, and slept — twelve steps from a couch in good standing, one hallway from a demoted door, at the exact address she'd been planting flags at for six years.

Occupied territory. Hers now. His. The same thing, finally, on the same map.

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I trace the line of her spine, slow. "I noticed the sweater. Year three. I just... liked having it there. Felt like you left a piece of yourself on purpose."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
The film had finished some time ago and neither of them had done anything about it, which was how Priya knew the evening had changed character.

"We're not watching this," she said.

"We haven't been watching it since about nine."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: "No," I agree. "We haven't." I don't move, but I stop pretending I'm looking at the screen.

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
The air between them grew thick, charged with six years of careful distance. Priya felt it in the tightness of her chest, the quiet, frantic rhythm of her own pulse. She let it ride out, tracking the seconds only in her head, letting the anxiety build and then fracture against the steady certainty settling in its place. When the ninety seconds passed, the nervousness simply vanished, replaced by a clear, unshakable resolve. She turned her head, finally meeting his eyes without flinching. The couch cushion shifted beneath her as she leaned forward, just enough to close the invisible gap that had kept them apart for so long. Her voice was low, even, and entirely direct. 

"Then stop pretending," she said. "We can just talk. Or we can stop talking." 

She held his gaze, sober and sure, having spent a lifetime building a boundary and now deciding, without hesitation, to step over it.

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I let out a breath I didn't realize I was holding. "I think we're done with talking, Priya." My hand finds hers on the cushion between us, my thumb brushing over her knuckles.

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya didn’t pull her hand away. Instead, she let his thumb rest against hers, the contact grounding her in the sudden quiet of the room. The last of the hesitation drained out of her, leaving only the clean, steady certainty she’d been waiting for. She turned her palm upward, closing the distance between their hands until their fingers laced together without hesitation. Six years of careful distance had been measured in glances and polite conversations, all of it collapsing into the simple weight of his skin against hers.

She kept her eyes on his, unblinking, her breathing even. The television cast a pale, shifting light across the room, but neither of them glanced at it. 

"Good," she said, her voice steady, lacking any of the earlier static. "Then don't." 

She shifted closer, the couch cushion yielding beneath her hip, and let her free hand come to rest lightly against his jaw. Her thumb traced the line of his cheekbone, slow and deliberate, confirming what they’d both already known. There was no going back to the way things had been, and for the first time in years, she didn’t want to.

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I kiss her, finally, six years late, and she makes a small furious noise that I think is about the six years.

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
The kiss landed exactly where it should have. Six years of careful distance collapsed into the press of his mouth against hers, and Priya met it without hesitation. She angled into it, her fingers tightening around his until their knuckles pressed flush, anchoring herself in the sudden, absolute quiet of the room. When they finally parted, just enough to breathe, she didn’t look away. Her thumb still rested against his jaw, her gaze steady, unguarded.

“Took you long enough,” she said, the words quiet but sharp with the weight of every guarded conversation and every evening they’d spent pretending the space between them didn’t matter. She didn’t soften it. She never would. Instead, she leaned in again, closing the distance she’d spent years measuring, letting the reality of him finally settle into place. There was no performance left. No careful choreography. Just the steady, unbroken weight of him, and the quiet certainty that she would never let him pretend otherwise again.

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I lean my forehead against hers, breathing her in. "I know," I murmur, voice rough. "I'm done wasting time." My hand slides into her hair, pulling her closer.

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya felt the steady pressure of his fingers in her hair, the familiar weight of his forehead resting against hers. She didn’t pull back. She never had after that invisible threshold had passed. The quiet hum of the room settled into something steady, something she’d spent years waiting to stop avoiding. She exhaled, slow and even, and let her hand slide from his jaw to the back of his neck, fingers finding the familiar curve of his nape. Six years of careful distance had been measured in polite smiles and avoided glances, all of it collapsing into the simple, unbroken reality of his presence.

She didn’t rush. She didn’t overthink. She just stayed exactly where she was, her breath syncing with his, her gaze locked on his. When she spoke, her voice was quiet, clear, and entirely without apology.

"Then don't," she said.

She shifted just enough to angle closer, her other hand resting firmly against his chest, feeling the steady rhythm beneath his ribs. dialogue.name: Priya

The film had finished some time ago and neither of them had done anything about it, which was how Priya knew the evening had changed character.

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya felt her pulse arrive late, a few seconds after she'd spoken, as if her body needed confirmation of what she'd just set in motion. She was aware of the specifics of the room in a way she hadn't been an hour ago: the throw crumpled at the far end of the sofa, the blue of the TV light on the wall, the fact that the coffee table between them was not very wide.

She could stop here. That was the thing. There was still a version of the night where she said *right, it's late*, and got up, and the two of them walked it back to something survivable. She considered that version honestly, the way you check a step before you take it, and found she did not want it.

"I want to say something," she said, "and I want to get to the end of it before you talk." She turned so she was facing him properly, one foot tucked under her. "Six years is a long time to not do this. And I've been sitting here tonight realising that I've been treating not doing it as a neutral thing, like it's just nothing, and it isn't nothing. It's a decision I've been making every week and not admitting I was making."

Her hands were steady. She'd expected them to be shaking and they weren't, which steadied the rest of her.

So she said the rest of it plainly, in the fewest words she had, and then she stopped and left it sitting in the room where he could see all of it.

dialogue.content: My heart is beating so hard I think you can probably hear it. I just look at you for a long moment. "You took the words right out of my mouth."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya let out a breath she hadn't known she was holding, and it came out almost a laugh, not because anything was funny but because the relief was physical, like setting something heavy down after carrying it too far.

"Good," she said. "That's — good."

She held his gaze for a moment, and the last of the nervousness drained out of her like water, and what was left was startling in its clarity. She'd spent six years being careful with this, and careful had felt like maturity, like responsibility, and now she could see it for what it had been, which was fear wearing a reasonable coat.

The ninety seconds were up.

She leaned forward and put her hand on his knee, just that, and let it rest there. Not a question. She'd stopped asking questions.

"Come here," she said.

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I kiss her, finally, six years late, and she makes a small furious noise that I think is about the six years.

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya kissed him back hard enough that the six years were in it, all of them at once, and she thought *oh, so this is what it is*, not with surprise exactly but with a kind of recognition she'd been refusing to make. His mouth was familiar and completely new, and the combination nearly undid her.

She pulled back just far enough to breathe. Her forehead stayed against his.

"That's for being careful," she said. "For six years of being careful."

Then, because she was done being careful, she kissed him again, slower this time, with intent, and let herself feel the specific weight of his hand finding her waist, her fingers in his hair, the length of him close enough that she could feel all of it at once. The sofa was too narrow and the coffee table was in the way and she didn't care about any of that. She cared about the fact that his pulse was going as fast as hers had been going ten minutes ago, and that he was here, and that she had said the thing out loud.

When she finally sat back, she kept hold of his shirt.

"I'm not going to pretend to be casual about this," she said. "You should know that now, before we go any further. I'm not going to wake up tomorrow and make a joke about it."

Her thumb moved once, absent-mindedly, against his collarbone. Her eyes were steady on his.

"Are you staying tonight?"

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: "Yes," I say, the word quiet but certain. My hand comes up to cover hers where it's fisted in my shirt. "I'm staying tonight. I'm staying tomorrow, too."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya closed her eyes for just a second, not because she needed to hide anything but because the sentence landed somewhere behind her ribs and she wanted to feel where it went. *Staying tomorrow too.* He'd said it the way he said things that were true — quiet, already decided.

"Okay," she said. "Okay, that's — yeah."

She'd had a whole architecture of things she was ready to be careful about, contingencies prepared, whole imagined conversations where she explained that this didn't have to be complicated, and he'd dismantled all of it in six words by making it exactly as complicated as she wanted it to be. She almost wanted to be annoyed. She wasn't.

She uncurled her fingers from his shirt and let her hand flatten against his chest instead, feeling his heart still running hot under her palm. Six years of this person on her sofa, in her kitchen, at the other end of a phone at two in the morning. Six years of him knowing how she took her tea and where she kept the spare key and which topics she couldn't talk about after certain kinds of days. There was nothing to discover here in the way people meant when they said that. There was only the discovery of what it felt like to stop withholding.

"So you should know," she said, "that I have thought about this. Not — I'm not going to pretend I haven't. I have, more than I've told anyone, more than I've told you, and now that I've said it out loud once it turns out I can't seem to stop."

Her thumb traced once along his collarbone again, and she watched her own hand do it.

"And the sofa is terrible and the coffee table is in the way and I think we should go and be somewhere that isn't here." She looked up. "Unless you want to sit here and talk about it for another hour, which — I have to be honest, I would have wanted a week ago and absolutely do not want now."

dialogue.name: Priya

Priya stood still for a moment, and the stillness was deliberate, because she wanted to have this in her memory properly rather than blurred past. The light from the landing came in low and amber and caught him in a way that made her breath go uneven for the first time since the ninety seconds had ended. She'd seen him a hundred mornings, borrowed his hoodies, sat close enough on this same bed to pass a laptop back and forth, and none of that had prepared her for the particular fact of him without anything between them.

She stepped forward and put both hands flat against his chest and pushed, not hard, just enough that he sat down on the edge of the bed, and she stood between his knees looking down at him.

"I want to do this properly," she said. "I don't mean — I mean slow. I mean I want to feel all of it."

She climbed into his lap and kissed him, and it was different from the sofa kisses, which had been about six years of wanting, and this was about the wanting being over, about the thing itself. She rolled her hips once, an experiment, and felt him respond and made a sound against his mouth that she wasn't embarrassed about. Embarrassment felt like a language from a country she'd left.

His hands were on her thighs, her waist, the small of her back, and she catalogued each one the way you'd catalogue rain after a long dry season. When his mouth found her throat she tipped her head back and let him, and the sound she made then was not small and not furious. It was open, and honest, and it was *his name*.

After, with her forehead resting against his shoulder and both of them still catching up to themselves, she traced one finger along the inside of his wrist where the pulse was finally slowing.

"That," she said, "was worth six years."

She paused.

"It absolutely was not worth six years. I'm never being careful again."
