dialogue.content:
Priya tilted her head so her mouth was against his temple when she answered, which felt easier than saying it to his face, and then she decided that was exactly the kind of careful she'd just sworn off and lifted her head to look at him properly.

"So am I," she said. "Glad we got here. In case that wasn't — I want to say it where you can see it."

She shifted so she was beside him rather than on top of him, pulling the duvet up with one hand out of long habit, and then stopped herself and laughed, quietly, at the domesticity of it, at how six years of not-doing-this had left all these small caretaking reflexes in place that were suddenly completely different things. Pulling a blanket over him. Making sure the landing light was off. Ordinary gestures that had been disguise and were now something else entirely.

Her hand found his under the covers and laced their fingers together. She lay on her side facing him, close enough that she could count the individual lashes on his closed eye if she'd wanted to.

"I should say one more thing and then I'll stop talking and let us sleep." Her thumb moved against his knuckle. "Tomorrow is going to be strange. Not bad-strange. Just — I don't want you to wake up and find me being weirdly normal at you in the kitchen. I'm going to be strange for a day or two. I want to be allowed to be strange for a day or two."

She watched his face in the low light from the landing, the line of his mouth, the way he looked like someone who had set down the same heavy thing she had.

"And then I want to find out what we're like," she said. "Properly. Not what we were protecting, just — what we actually are."

dialogue.name: Priya

Priya's hand came down on the back of his head and held him there, fingers spread in his hair, and the sentence she'd been building broke apart halfway through and reassembled into something plainer and more honest than anything she'd said all night.

The voice surprised even her. She'd always been articulate about most things and absolutely not about this, and now it turned out the thing that had been locked was just — unlocked, and what came out was specific and unembarrassed and didn't sound like anyone she'd ever been with him before. She told him what she wanted. She told him how. She told him when he had it right, and the sound of herself doing it was almost more than the sensation itself, because it was the last thing between them going, the last careful thing, and she could feel it going and she did not reach to stop it.

Her hips moved once against his mouth and then stilled, because she wanted to feel this rather than chase it, and the wanting was its own pressure building somewhere low and thorough. She watched him between her thighs in the half-dark, the concentration in him, the six years of patience in him that had probably looked like restraint and now looked like knowledge, like he'd been paying attention to her this whole time in ways neither of them had named.

"Don't stop," she said, and her voice was steady, which she was quietly proud of. "Right there. Just like that. I want to — I'm close, and I want to come with you doing exactly that."

When it hit her it was not graceful and she did not try to make it graceful. Her back arched and her hand tightened in his hair and the sound she made was long and raw and entirely unperformed, and afterwards she lay there with her chest heaving and her eyes on the ceiling and one thought arriving very clearly through the noise: *that was always there. That was always going to be there.*

She tugged at his shoulder until he came up beside her, and she kissed him with her own taste still on his mouth, which she found she wanted to do, which she would have found mortifying a week ago and now found simply true.

"There," she said, when she had enough breath for words. "That's what I sound like. Six years of me pretending to be — composed, about things. And it turns out I'm not composed. I'm really not composed."

She pulled him closer with an arm around his neck and her mouth against his jaw.

Priya held his face in both hands for a moment before she moved, and the look she gave him was steady in a way that felt like a decision being made at the level of bones. She rolled them with more determination than grace, and she laughed once, low, at the small collision of elbows and knees, because she'd spent six years imagining this as something cinematic and it was in fact two people who knew each other too well to be embarrassed about the mechanics.

She settled above him and sat back on her heels, and let herself look. That was the thing she wanted first — to look at him without the pretense of not looking, which had been the exhausting work of six years of friendship. She put her hands on his ribs and felt him breathe.

"I've thought about this part too," she said. "All the parts. I'm not going to pretend I haven't mapped it out in my head at three in the morning and then gone to work and made you coffee like a person with no interior life."

She leaned down and kissed the hollow of his throat, and lower, and let her hair drag across his chest on purpose because she wanted to know what he sounded like when she did things on purpose. When she took him in her hand she watched his face the whole time, which felt like the most intimate part, more than the touch itself — this was Priya being uncareful, Priya refusing to look away from what she was doing to him.

"Tell me," she said. "Same rules as me. Specific. I want to get this right the first time, which I know is — very me. But I mean it."

She moved down his body with intent, one hand braced on his hip, and she was thorough about it, patient about it, and when she had him in her mouth she kept one hand pressed flat to his stomach so she could feel every shift in him as feedback, as instruction, as conversation. This was what six years of knowing someone gave you — you didn't have to guess. You just had to listen with your hands and your mouth and the part of your brain that had been cataloguing this man since long before she'd admitted it.

She pulled back only when he told her, or only when she decided she wanted to feel him finish against her tongue, and the sound he made — she wanted to keep that sound in a drawer somewhere and take it out on bad days.

After, she came back up and lay half on top of him, her cheek against his chest, and listened to his heart do its work.

"Right," she said, after a while, sounding faintly out of breath and very satisfied with herself. "So. That's what we're like."

She pressed her mouth to his collarbone in a kiss that was not about desire anymore but about something slower and more frightening.

"I want to do that again," she said. "Soon. And then I want to do other things I haven't told you about yet, because I've realised I don't have to ration them out anymore, and that's — that's going to be a lot for both of us. I'm warning you now."

She lifted her head and looked at him, and her expression was open and unguarded and slightly wondering, like a person who had arrived somewhere she'd been walking toward for six years and was only now looking up to see where she was.

"But first I want to sleep next to you," she said. "That's the thing I actually want most. Not — I want the rest of it too, but I want to wake up and have you be there. That's the part I've been most afraid to want."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya went very still against his chest, and then she lifted her head and looked at him with an expression that was harder to read than anything else she'd worn all night.

"Harder," she repeated.

She said the word back to him like she was testing its weight, and something shifted behind her eyes — not hurt, not exactly, but the particular recalibration of a person who'd thought she'd been the only one carrying something this heavy and was now told she hadn't been. She'd built herself a whole narrative in which she was the one who'd been protecting them both, and he'd just quietly dismantled it, and she found she didn't mind. She found she minded enormously. She found both of those things were true.

"Six years," she said. "And you never said. Not once. Not at two in the morning when we were both awake and pretending it was about insomnia, not — " She stopped herself. Breathed. Her jaw worked once.

"Okay," she said. "Okay. So we've both been cowards. That's — I'm going to need a minute with that."

She sat up and pulled the duvet around her shoulders, not hiding but arranging herself, and he could see her doing the thing she did when she was processing something — her eyes went slightly unfocused, her fingers found the edge of the sheet and worried at it.

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
Aveline had been waiting since about six, which Roan established by the simple method of looking at her.

"How long?"

"Long enough," Aveline said, which meant too long, and meant she had enjoyed every minute of it.

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: "Come here, then," I say, and sit back to watch her cross the room.

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
Aveline didn't hurry. Hurrying would have wasted the moment, and she had learned long ago that Roan liked to watch — so she gave him something worth watching. She crossed the room with slow, deliberate steps, her eyes on his the whole way, letting him see exactly how pleased she was to be summoned. How pleased she had been, all evening, simply waiting for it.

She stopped in front of him, close enough that her knees brushed his, and then she sank down without being asked — smooth and practiced, settling onto her knees on the floor between his, her hands coming to rest light on her own thighs. She looked up at him with the particular openness she saved for this, for him, the look that said *I'm here, I'm yours, tell me what you want.*

"You're home late," she said, and there was no reproach in it at all — only warmth, and the faintest curl of a smile. "I kept everything warm. Dinner, the wine, myself." Her thumb traced a small, idle line along her own thigh, a nervous habit that wasn't nervousness, just anticipation with nowhere left to go. "I thought about texting. I thought better of it. I know how you like to walk in and find me already waiting."

She tilted her head, studying his face like she was memorizing it, though she'd had years to do that already and suspected she'd never actually finish.

"Long day?" she asked, softer now, her hands lifting — hovering, asking permission with them before she touched. "Tell me. I've been saving up all my attention for you."

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: I reach out and thread my fingers through your hair, a gentle but firm grip. "Long day, yes. But you've made it better already." My thumb strokes along your temple. "Tell me what you did while you waited."

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
Aveline leaned into the grip with a low, unhurried sound — not quite a sigh, not quite a purr, just the audible release of a body that had been holding itself in careful stillness for hours and finally had permission to be held. Her eyes half-closed under the stroke of his thumb, though she kept them on him, unwilling to miss a second of his attention now that she had it.

"Mm. I'll give you the full inventory, since you asked so nicely." Her voice was warm, a little rough at the edges with wanting. "I cooked the thing with the shallots — the one you always pretend you don't have a favorite of, except you always have seconds. It's in the oven on low. The wine is decanted and breathing, the good bottle, because I decided tonight you'd earned it. Or I had. Possibly both."

Her hands settled back on her thighs, palms up now — a small offering of stillness, letting him do the touching.

"Then I showered. Took my time with it." A flicker of a smile. "Shaved everything the way you like. Put on the lotion you bought me, the one that smells like — well. You'll notice when you lean in close enough. Which I suspect is the plan." Her thumb traced that same idle line along her thigh again, slower this time. "Then I sat here. Or on the couch. I migrated. I read four pages of my book and retained none of them, because every few minutes I caught myself listening for your car in the drive."

She turned her head, just slightly, and pressed a kiss into his wrist where his hand held her — soft, deliberate, an anchor point.

"Mostly," she said, quieter now, the playfulness settling into something steadier underneath, "I thought about you. What kind of day you might be having. Whether you'd walk in tired or — that other way you walk in sometimes. Whether you'd want dinner first or me first." Her smile curved, knowing. "I planned for both contingencies. I always do."

She looked up at him through her lashes, patient as anything, her whole body settled into the space between his knees like it had been measured for her.

"So. Dinner's warm, I'm warm, and the evening is entirely yours. What'll it be?"

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: I let her kneel and I don't tell her to do anything for a moment, because the waiting is most of what she came for.

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
The question hung in the air, and no answer came.

Aveline knew a decision when she saw one being made, and she knew — just as quickly — that this wasn't one. He wasn't weighing dinner against her. He wasn't tired, or distracted, or thinking of something else. He was simply letting her kneel, and the full, quiet weight of that recognition settled over her like a hand at the back of her neck.

She let her smile soften first. Then her shoulders. Then the idle motion of her thumb went still against her thigh, because even that small movement suddenly felt like it was taking something that wasn't hers to take yet. She breathed in, slow and deliberate, and let it out without sound.

So she stopped performing readiness and simply was ready.

It was harder than it looked — she knew that, knew most people would find it unbearable, the silence, the watching, the nothing. But she had discovered years ago that she was built for exactly this, or at least rebuilt by him, patient hour by patient hour. The stillness wasn't empty. It was full of him: his eyes on her, his attention wrapped around her like something warm she could feel through her skin. He was looking at her the way she'd waited all evening to be looked at, and he was in no hurry about it, and that was its own kind of answer.

*Take your time,* she thought, and found she'd said it out loud after all, barely above a breath — not a prompt, not a nudge. A gift, handed back up to him. Her eyes held his for one long moment more, steady and unhurried, and then she let them drift closed, lashes settling against her cheeks, giving him that too: the last of her attention, surrendered freely.

She could stand here — kneel here — all night if he wanted. The dinner would keep. The wine would keep.

She would keep.

dialogue.name: Roan

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
The words landed before the kiss did, and Aveline felt them go through her like warmth through wine — chest first, then everywhere. *Good girl.* Two words, and hours of waiting folded themselves up neatly into something that had been worth every minute. She was still holding that feeling when his mouth found hers, and she opened to it without a sound, letting him taste her the way she'd wanted to be tasted all evening: unhurried, deliberate, claimed. She kept her hands on her thighs through all of it, because he hadn't said she could move them yet, and the discipline of that — small, sweet, hers to give — made the kiss better.

When he drew back, her eyes stayed closed a moment longer, lashes dark against her cheeks, the shape of the kiss still warm on her mouth. Then she opened them, and the look she gave him from beneath his hand was soft and bright at once, the look of a woman who had just been paid in full and knew the account was hers.

Her knees complained faintly about the hour on the floor; she didn't let a trace of it reach her face. He'd never know. That was part of the arrangement too.

She lifted the decanter and poured a single glass — his glass, the heavy one his hand fit around — and she poured it slow, letting the wine breathe its last against the air before she turned back.

She didn't hand it to him from across the room. She returned to him the proper way, around his chair, and when she offered the glass it was from his right side, close, her arm a steady line, her body angled toward him in a way that made it clear the wine was not the only thing on the tray of the evening.

She stepped back to the edge of his reach and waited there, hands folded loosely in front of her, attentive as a held breath. Whatever came next — dinner, wine, her — she was already leaning toward it, and he knew it.

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
Permission, when it finally came, came like that — no ceremony, no negotiation, just hands and the sudden arithmetic of fabric leaving skin. Aveline laughed once, low in her throat, at the efficiency of it, at the way an entire evening of slow offerings collapsed into a minute of plain want. Then she settled back down where she belonged — between his knees, on the floor, the position familiar but transformed. Before, she had knelt to wait. And she loved it. That was the thing he'd surely figured out ages ago and she'd long since stopped being embarrassed about. Loved the weight of him on her tongue, loved the salt and bitterness of him, loved — most of all — the feeling of his attention narrowing down to a single bright point, and the point being her mouth. Hours of waiting had been its own pleasure. She would not hurry. He could take over whenever he liked — the angle of her throat was an offer, the grip of her hands an open invitation, her whole body a question of *use me if you want to, I'll be perfect at it.* But until he decided otherwise, she would savor him the way he'd savored the wine: slowly, with her full attention, like something worth every minute of the wait.

dialogue.content:
"I understand," Aveline said, and kept her voice level, which was its own small triumph, since everything below the collarbone had already begun misbehaving. "I don't stop. I don't finish. Not until you say." She held his eyes through all of it, chin lifted, making the terms part of the gift. Then, softer, with the full weight of meaning behind it: "Thank you."

And she meant it the way she meant everything in their economy — wholly. Other people thanked for things wrapped in paper. She thanked for this: her wanting, taken up and formalized, given an overseer. He was promising to spend the evening on her, all of it, every trembling minute of it, and there was no gift in her world more expensive than his attention aimed and held.

She gave up his lap with visible, theatrical regret — a slow peel of warmth, a parting sigh — and settled onto the cushions beside him, turning to face him with her back against the armrest. One foot drawn up. Knees falling open, unhurried, the way she did everything. If she was to be kept, she'd be kept on display; that wasn't in the orders, but she knew her audience, and she liked to anticipate.

Her hand went where the ache had lived since six o'clock. The first touch drew a sound out of her before she'd decided to make one — head tipping back, hips stuttering — and she let him have all of it, unfiltered. Then she built the rhythm the way she built all her rhythms for him: patiently at first, learning herself under his eyes, fingers moving slow through all that evidence of the evening, slick and shameless and easy to read.

The first edge came fast. Of course it did — she'd been simmering for hours; the water was already at a roll. That was the discipline he'd built in her, hour by patient hour, and she wore it now like a well-tailored thing: the skill of approaching and not arriving, of standing at her own door with the key in her hand and not turning it.

The second edge she rode longer, thighs shaking, sweat starting at her temple. The third one broke her composure down to the studs — a low, ragged sound, her free hand fisting the cushion, her whole body fluent in a language that consisted entirely of *please* without a single word of it spoken.

She kept her eyes on him through as much of it as she could manage, because she suspected this was the actual point. Not the fingers. The witnessing. Him watching her want him. Her letting it be watched.

A breath. A tremor. The smile survived both.

"Say when. Take your time." Her hips gave one small, involuntary roll and she pressed them flat, obedient to the last. "I'll keep. I always keep."

His hand settled over hers, and the whole physics of the evening changed.

"Patience is a virtue," she managed, and the words came out thin, most of her breath spent on simpler things. "And I had mine installed professionally. I should warn you, the workmanship is excellent." A tremor ran through her thighs, undercutting the claim, and she let it. No point hiding the evidence from the man holding the evidence.

She was still right at it. That was the cruelty and the kindness of his hand — it hadn't moved her back from the edge, only stopped her there, pinned at the brink like a moth he'd decided not to brush off his sleeve. Every nerve she owned was gathered under his palm now, shouting, and she breathed through it with her mouth open and her eyes on him, because the witnessing was the point and she would not fail at the point.

"I'd like the record to show," she whispered, and her voice had gone down to gravel and lace, "that you've taken the wheel, and I approve entirely of your driving." Her hips made one small, involuntary petition against his hand and were pressed still by her own last shred of discipline before he'd even need to. "And that I understand the terms. Not a second before. I heard you the first time. I hear you better now."

She let her head fall back against the armrest, throat bared, the whole long line of her surrendered up to his eyes and his hand and the unhurried weight of his attention. The sweat at her temple. The pulse visible at her throat. The smile that survived everything, because it was the truest thing in the room.

"Take all the seconds you want," she said softly. "I'm not going anywhere. I can't, in fact — you're holding me here." The smile curved. "Which I suspect was the idea. Whenever you say, love. I'll be exactly this. Beautifully."

"Please," she said again, and this time her voice broke on the word, and she let that be part of the asking. Her thighs were shaking — not trembling, *shaking*, the full-body kind, spread outward from the point of contact until even her shoulders were at it, until the armrest under her gripping hand ticked faintly against the frame of the couch. "I know the terms. I love the terms. I'm asking anyway — that's what the door is for, and here I am in it." A breath that was mostly a shudder. "I'd wait another hour. I'd wait until the wine went off and the shallot thing spoiled. But I'd rather not, and I'm allowed to say so, and now you know everything there is to know about me."

Then — when he'd taken exactly the seconds he was owed, and she felt him take them, felt the last of her composure spend itself in the waiting — he said it.

"Now."

One word, and it went through her like a struck bell.

His hand pressed hers back into motion and stayed there, riding over her knuckles, keeping her pace through it — and she'd been holding the edge so long that the crest wasn't a climb anymore, it was a collapse. The whole architecture of her came down at once. Her back arched off the cushions, her cry breaking raggedly on his name, and the first wave rolled through her so hard her vision went white at the edges, every hour of waiting paying itself out in a single long, wrenching pulse. She didn't stop. She'd been told not to stop, and she was fluent in that order now, fingers working through the slick evidence of the entire evening while it kept coming — second wave, third, each one dragging a raw sound out of her, her hips rolling up into their joined hands without a shred of the discipline she'd been so proud of, all of it spent, all of it his, until the aftershocks were small and the shaking was just trembling again, and finally just her breath, enormous in the quiet room.

She came back in pieces. Face pressed to his chest at some point without deciding to put it there. His heartbeat under her cheek, steady as ever, while hers galloped.

"There," she managed at last, wrecked and glowing, voice down to the grain of it. "I kept. I told you I'd keep." A soft, breathless laugh against his skin. "And then I didn't have to anymore, which was the plan all along, and I'd like it noted that the plan was excellent."

She tilted her face up, boneless, letting him see the whole satisfied wreck of her — swollen mouth, wet lashes, the smile that had survived everything the evening had done to it.

"Tell me I did well," she said, quieter. The true currency. The whole wage. "That's all I'll need for the rest of the night. That—" a pause, a lazy stretch against him, "—and possibly the wine. And the shallot thing, because you were right, I do need it. You usually are. Right. It's one of your more tolerable qualities."

She settled then, folding herself against his chest with the unhurried weight of something that had been put exactly where it belonged, her hand splayed flat over his heart, her breathing slowing toward his tempo beat by beat.

"Welcome home," she said again, warm against his skin, the phrase even truer the second time. "Whenever you're ready to move, I'm ready to be moved. Until then—" her eyes drifted closed, "—I'll keep. Beautifully."

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: I stroke your hair, still damp at the temples. "You did very well." I let the quiet settle around us before shifting. "Now let's eat. You're going to need your strength."

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
*You did very well.* Not *well* — *very well*. Aveline filed the distinction where she filed all his praise, in the vault she kept behind her sternum, and felt the words settle in with the rest of the evening's earnings. Paid in full. Overpaid, honestly. She'd have knelt until midnight for half of that.

"You're going to need your strength," though — that earned him a slow, lifted brow, even from her current position of total collapse against his chest.

"Second threat of the evening," she murmured, voice still down at the grain. "Or promise. I've stopped keeping track of the distinction, academically or otherwise." She stretched against him, one long, unashamed flex of everything that had been shaking ten minutes ago and was now merely humming. "Whatever you're planning, I endorse it retroactively. Consider this blanket approval for the rest of the night. Not the week. Don't get greedy."

But he'd said eat, and she was built to move when told, so she moved — eventually. She gave herself exactly as long as she judged he'd allow, which was to say one more luxurious minute with her cheek on his heartbeat, and then she peeled herself up off him with a groan she didn't bother disguising, because the theater of effortlessness had a closing time and it had passed.

She padded to the kitchen bare and unbothered, unhurried even now, well aware his eyes followed her and well aware that was the natural order of things. She pulled the shallot thing from the low oven — perfect, the crust gone exactly bronze the way it did when the timing worked, and she allowed herself one small, private flare of pride at having held the whole evening together on a guess about when he'd walk in. She plated it with the same hands that had shaken an hour ago, steady now, warm bread and wine and the good knife, and carried it all back to him — his plate assembled first, his glass refreshed, hers alongside, everything arranged on the tray the way she arranged everything: for him to take from.

She settled onto the cushion beside him, close enough that her knee found his thigh and stayed there, and lifted her glass.

"To the good bottle," she said, "which survived the wait. And to coming home late." A gleam through the steam of the food. "I may start hoping your days run long, if this is what the evenings look like."

She tucked her feet up, took the first bite, and closed her eyes at it — hours of patience, all of it, rewarded twice in one night.

"Eat," she told him, warm, echoing him back with her own inflection. "You're going to need your strength. I have it on excellent authority."

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: I take a bite, watching you. "This is good," I say, before setting my fork down and resting a hand on your thigh. "But I'm not finished with you yet."

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
"This is good." From him, that was a Michelin star. Aveline had learned the exchange rate on his compliments years ago — one *good* from Roan was worth a paragraph from anyone else — and she filed it in the vault alongside the rest of the evening's earnings, which were stacking up embarrassingly.

"I'm aware," she said, and had the grace to smile around the smugness of it. "I've been making it since before you knew what you liked. I conducted the survey." She lifted her glass, watching him over the rim. "You realize you've now praised me twice in one evening — the food and the — other thing. I'll be insufferable by Thursday. You've done this to yourself."

Then his fork went down, and his hand came to rest on her thigh, and the sentence that followed — *I'm not finished with you yet* — arrived in the room like the low note of something being tuned.

Aveline went still. Not frozen — *settled*, the way water goes still when something moves beneath it. Her fork paused halfway to her plate, then lowered the rest of the way with deliberate care, because her hands had opinions about that sentence and she wanted them kept in working order.

"There it is," she said softly. "The third threat. Or promise. I told you I'd stopped keeping track, and yet here I am, keeping track." Her eyes came up to his, and everything playful in them had gone quiet underneath, banked and glowing. "You've been saying it all night, you know. In the standing-in-the-doorway way. In the way you let me kneel. In *you're going to need your strength*, twice, which I'm now realizing wasn't about the shallots at all." A slow breath. "I'm a slow study of some things. Never of you."

His hand was warm on her thigh, unmoving, and she made no attempt to move it or encourage it — that was his to do with what he liked. She only turned her leg, fractionally, into the pressure. An acknowledgment. A signature on the terms.

"So," she said, and set her glass down beside her plate, giving him the whole of her attention, which had been the plan since six o'clock and had never once wavered. "Not finished. I'm glad to hear it, because — for the record, and I mean this with everything in me — neither am I." Her mouth curved, unhurried even now, especially now. "I've been kept, fed, praised, and thoroughly undone once already, and I find I'm still hungry, and I'm not talking about the shallot thing."

She shifted toward him, close enough that her knee pressed his thigh and her shoulder brushed his arm, and folded her hands in her lap — the old position, the offered one, patient as anything.

"How do you want me?" she asked, simply, the way she asked everything that mattered. "On the couch, on the floor, over the table with the good dishes at risk — I'll warn you now I'll defend the wine glasses, but only briefly." The gleam in her eyes softened into something steadier under it. "Or take your time and decide. I'll be right here. I keep beautifully. You've seen the references."

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: My thumb strokes your inner thigh, just once. "Finish your dinner first. I'm not going to be gentle with you."

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
Aveline had been waiting since about six, which Roan established by the simple method of looking at her.

"How long?"

"Long enough," Aveline said, which meant too long, and meant she had enjoyed every minute of it.

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: "Come here, then," I say, and sit back to watch her cross the room.

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
Aveline rose unhurriedly, because being watched was half the point and she knew better than to rush it. Six years together and Roan still looked at her like that—like the simple act of crossing a room was something worth sitting back for. She had long since stopped pretending it didn't undo her a little.

She crossed the floor at an even pace, chin up, hands loose at her sides, and only when she was close enough to see the familiar warmth in Roan's expression did she let her own composure soften into something more honest. Eager. Pleased with herself for having waited well, and not even slightly ashamed of how much she wanted to be told so.

"You kept me waiting," she said, stopping just in front of Roan, close enough that the words came out low. There was no real complaint in it. There never was. "I was very good about it, in case you were wondering. Didn't fidget. Barely."

A small smile pulled at her mouth, the one that meant she was fishing and knew Roan knew it.

"Well?" she said. "I'm here."

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: I reach out and take her hand, pulling her gently down to sit on my lap. "You were perfect," I say, my voice low. "But I knew you would be."

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
Aveline went willingly, settling into Roan's lap with the ease of long practice, one arm finding its way around Roan's shoulders like it had a standing reservation. Six years, and her body still remembered exactly how to fit here—where to put her weight, how to angle herself so she could be looked at without Roan having to crane. She'd had considerable practice being looked at from this distance.

The praise landed the way it always did, which was to say: catastrophically, as far as her composure was concerned. *You were perfect.* Three words, and she felt the warmth of them spread through her chest like something swallowed. She'd fished for it, yes, and Roan had known she was fishing, and none of that made the catch any less sweet.

"But you knew I would be," she repeated, and huffed a small laugh. "There it is. You can't just let me have it, can you? It has to be *inevitable*." She was smiling as she said it, leaning in to press her forehead briefly against Roan's temple. "For the record, it did not feel inevitable at about seven-thirty. It felt like a genuine accomplishment. I'd like that noted for the record."

She drew back just far enough to study Roan's face, her own gone soft in a way she only ever permitted here, in this room, at exactly this distance. The teasing was real, but so was the thing underneath it—the quiet, steady satisfaction of having been seen waiting, and having the waiting counted.

"Well?" she murmured, echoing herself from a moment ago, gentler this time. "I'm here. And I've been very patient. What happens next is entirely your department."

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: I let her kneel and I don't tell her to do anything for a moment, because the waiting is most of what she came for.

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
Aveline understood immediately, the way she always did. No instruction *was* the instruction. She lowered herself to her knees with unhurried grace, settling back on her heels, hands resting palm-up on her thighs—the posture she'd made hers years ago, the one that said *I'm ready* without presuming anything further.

And then she simply stayed.

It was harder than it looked. It was always harder than it looked, and she suspected Roan knew exactly how hard, which was rather the point. Her pulse had already picked up. Her skin felt tuned to a finer frequency, aware of everything—the rug beneath her knees, the warmth of the room, the weight of being regarded without a single word to tell her what came next. Six years and this still worked on her like the first time. Maybe better than the first time, because now she knew what the waiting was *for*, knew how good it was on the other side of it, and the knowing made every quiet second brighter.

She kept her eyes up. That was her one small act of willfulness, and it had never once been corrected, so she'd long since concluded it was permitted—encouraged, even. Roan liked to be looked back at. Aveline liked being caught looking.

A minute stretched. Then another. Her composure held, mostly, but she felt the tell creeping in: the slow part of her lips, the slight flush climbing her throat, the way her fingers curled once against her thighs and then deliberately stilled.

"You're doing this on purpose," she said finally, voice low and a little rough around the edges. There was no accusation in it. If anything, it came out reverent. "You know exactly what the quiet does to me, and you're just—letting it." A beat. Her smile flickered, helpless and fond. "Terrible. You're terrible. Don't stop."

She settled her shoulders, drew one slow breath, and gave herself back over to the waiting—spine straight, chin lifted, every line of her humming with the particular patience of a woman who had finally been given exactly what she came for.

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: I reach out and trace the line of her jaw with my thumb. "Look at you," I say, my voice barely above a whisper. "All that composure, and still you're trembling just a little."

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
Aveline had survived the silence with her dignity more or less intact. The thumb was another matter entirely. It was such a small touch—one line traced along her jaw—and after all that waiting it landed like a verdict. She felt her breath catch, felt the tremble Roan had named move through her again as if summoned by the naming, and leaning into the touch was not a decision so much as a fact.

"That's unfair," she managed, though it came out softer than she'd intended—closer to wonder than protest. "You can't just *narrate* me. I was holding that together beautifully." Her eyes had gone bright, and she knew it, and knew Roan knew it. "Six years. You'd think I'd have built up some tolerance by now. Some immunity to being looked at like—" A vague gesture, taking in all of it. "Like *that*."

But the teasing had worn thin and they both knew that too. Underneath it was the plain truth she never bothered to hide for long: being seen this precisely was the thing she came for. More than the praise, almost more than the touch. Roan didn't miss anything. Roan had never missed anything in six years, and some days Aveline suspected she'd built her entire composure on the private knowledge that its cracks would be witnessed, and counted, and found worth the watching.

She turned her face, just slightly, and pressed a kiss into the palm at her jaw—brief, deliberate, the one gesture she allowed herself without asking first.

"There," she murmured against Roan's skin. "Now you know exactly what you did." A pause. Her smile returned, unsteady and utterly content. "In case the trembling wasn't documentation enough."

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: She has both of us out of everything in the way inside a minute and gets straight to work with her hands and her mouth, unhurried about it.

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
Aveline had six years of practice at this and intended to use every one of them.

She took her time—that was the whole point, the thing Roan had been teaching her by example all evening. Hands first, unhurried, relearning by touch what she already knew by heart, watching Roan's face the whole while because watching was half of what she was for. Then her mouth, slow and deliberate, no rush anywhere in her, and she felt something in her chest unknot at the first change in Roan's breathing. *There it was.* That was what all the waiting had been for—not the praise exactly, but this: proof, immediate and undeniable, that she was good at this. That what she was doing was wanted.

Her own arousal was a low, steady hum she mostly ignored. It would keep. It always kept. Her pleasure had always run through Roan's like a river through a valley—real, deep, entirely shaped by its course—and she had long since stopped wanting it any other way. This was not sacrifice. This was the arrangement working exactly as designed, and she was excellent at her work.

She drew back after a while, lips wet, breathing harder than the effort strictly required, and looked up with an expression that was not remotely innocent.

"You're allowed to make noise," she said, conversational, one hand still lazily occupied. "In case you were planning to be stoic about it. I'd consider it a personal favor." A beat; her smile went crooked. "Also, I'm going to be at this for a while, so if you had other plans for the evening, cancel them. You kept me waiting since six. Turnabout is fair play."

She let her thumb drag once, slow, just to punctuate the point.

"For the record," she added, softer, the teasing thinning into something more honest, "this is not a chore I'm performing. In case that was ever in doubt. This is the part I think about at my desk on Tuesdays."

Then she bent back to her work before Roan could answer—which was its own small impertinence, and she knew it, and the pleased hum in her blood said Roan knew it too.

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: I let out a soft, unsteady breath, my hand tangling in her hair. "Good," I murmur, my voice thick. "Then take your time. I'm not going anywhere."

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
The word *good* did what it always did—something in Aveline's chest went briefly, catastrophically bright. Six years, and a single syllable could still take her apart at the seams. The hand in her hair didn't help. Or rather, it helped enormously, in precisely the direction of undoing her.

She made a low sound of acknowledgment, since her mouth was occupied and words were temporarily beyond her jurisdiction. *Take your time.* As if she'd been planning anything else.

She took her time.

This was the part she was best at, and she knew it with the quiet confidence of long, delighted practice—reading the small shifts, the changes in breathing, the tension gathering slowly under her hands. Adjusting. Learning nothing new, exactly, because she'd had this memorized for years, but confirming it all over again like rereading a favorite passage. The pleasure of it ran in both directions: every reaction she coaxed out of Roan landed somewhere in her own body, a current with no off switch, and she had long since stopped wanting one.

She broke off once, just to breathe, and pressed her cheek against Roan's thigh, looking up. Her lips were wet, her hair was a ruin where Roan's fingers had been, and she looked, she suspected, thoroughly debauched and entirely unrepentant about it.

"That was one unsteady breath," she said, conversational, as if taking minutes at a meeting. "I'm logging it. My target for the evening is considerably higher." Her thumb traced an idle, unhurried line. "You said take my time. I'm holding you to it. No complaints later about the hour."

Then she bent back to her work—thorough, patient, the hand in her hair all the anchor she needed. The room narrowed pleasantly to this: taste, breath, tension, the slow build she was conducting with six years of expertise and boundless, unembarrassed enthusiasm. Her own arousal had stopped being a hum and become a simple fact, steady and bright, and she let it be exactly that. It would keep. It always kept. That was the arrangement, and the arrangement was the best idea either of them had ever had.

Somewhere in the back of her mind, Tuesday's desk felt very far away indeed.

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: She uses her mouth with the sort of attention that comes from years of practice and genuine enthusiasm, and doesn't stop when I tell her not to.

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
Aveline heard the word and filed it precisely where it belonged.

Six years had made her fluent in the difference—the word that actually meant stop was short and level and had never once in their history been ignored, and this was not that word. This was the other one. The one that came out unsteady, tangled up with the hand in her hair, and translated with absolute clarity into *don't you dare.*

So she didn't.

There was a particular thrill in it that had nothing to do with disobedience and everything to do with certainty—knowing someone so well that their *stop* and their *stop* were two entirely different languages, and she spoke both like a native. She redoubled her attention, unhurried as ever, and took a deep, private satisfaction in every sign that her translation had been correct. The breath gone ragged. The tension coiling under her hands like something being wound tight by experts. *Her* expertise. Six years of study, and she had never once been accused of slacking.

Her own arousal had long since stopped asking for attention and simply *was*—bright, steady, patient as a banked fire. It would keep. It always kept. Right now there was this, and this was better: the slow, deliberate dismantling of someone she adored, conducted with her mouth and her hands and the entire accumulated weight of six years' devotion. She could feel how close it was getting now. Could read it in a dozen small tells she'd catalogued over the years like a scholar with one beloved, inexhaustible text.

She pulled back at the edge—just far enough to breathe, just far enough to be felt breathing—and looked up. Her hair was wrecked. Her lips were wet. Her expression was the furthest thing from penitent it was possible to be.

"You said stop," she observed, conversational, one hand still lazily, unforgivably occupied. "I want it noted that I heard you. Considered it at length. Nearly a full second." Her thumb moved, slow, and her smile went soft and wicked and utterly sure of itself. "But we've both read the record, and we both know what that particular *stop* means. It means *if you stop, I'll perish.* I'm not a monster."

She leaned in, pressed one unhurried kiss where it would do the most damage, and glanced up through her lashes.

"Besides," she murmured, "you told me to take my time. I'm simply holding you to your word. Someone in this relationship has to be consistent."

Then she went back to work—slow, thorough, merciless in the way that only came from love and long practice—and this time she didn't stop for anything.

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: I let out a sharp, ragged laugh that turns into a gasp. "Insufferable," I manage, my grip tightening in her hair just enough to be felt. "Keep going."

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
*Insufferable.* Aveline took the word exactly as it was meant—as a medal pinned to her chest—and the laugh that answered it vibrated through everything she was doing, which she suspected was its own reward.

*Keep going.* As if she'd been planning anything else.

She kept going.

This was the part six years had made her good at—better than good, and she knew it, and the knowing was half the pleasure. Every tell she'd ever catalogued was lighting up in sequence now: the breathing gone ragged, the grip in her hair, the tension coiling tighter and tighter under her hands like something being wound by experts. *Her* expertise. She'd been waiting since six o'clock for this, had knelt through the silence, had endured being *narrated*, and this was the dividend—the moment where all that patience converted, all at once, into proof.

She didn't rush it. Rushing was for amateurs and Tuesdays. She kept her pace exactly, mercilessly steady, and felt the moment arrive the way you feel a wave when you're standing in the water—that gathering, that lift—

And then it broke, and Aveline stayed with it through every second, unhurried even now, *especially* now, taking all of it as her due. The sounds above her. The hand gone tight and then slack in her hair. Six years, and it still landed in her chest like the first time: *I did that. That's mine. I know this person better than anyone alive.*

Only when it was well and truly finished did she draw back—slow, deliberate—and rest her cheek against Roan's thigh, breathing harder than the effort strictly required. Her own arousal was a bright, patient fact she had long practice at carrying. It would keep. It always kept.

She pressed a kiss to the nearest available skin and looked up. Her hair was a catastrophe. Her expression was the furthest thing from penitent it was possible to be.

"For the record," she said, conversational, as if taking minutes, "that was considerably more than one unsteady breath. I exceeded my target for the evening. I'd like that noted." A beat. Her smile went soft, the teasing thinning into the honest thing underneath. "Also, 'insufferable' is going in the log as a compliment. You don't get to take it back."

She turned her face, pressed one more unhurried kiss, and settled her chin on Roan's knee, entirely content to stay exactly where she was for as long as she was allowed.

"Well," she murmured, echoing herself from earlier, gentler now. "I'm here. What happens next is entirely your department."

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: "Don't stop and don't get to finish," I tell her. "Not until I say. Tell me you understand." She says she understands, and thanks me for it, which is exactly the arrangement.

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
The instruction landed exactly where it was aimed, and Aveline felt it—felt the bright, patient fact of her own arousal sharpen into something less patient, something that would now simply have to be carried. Indefinitely. At Roan's pleasure, which was the entire point.

"I understand," she said, and her voice came out lower than she'd planned, rough-edged with everything she was now officially not going to do anything about. Then, because it was true, because it had been true for six years and never once needed editing: "Thank you."

She meant it. That was the thing outsiders would never parse about the arrangement—that the denial wasn't a price she paid for the rest of it. It *was* the rest of it. Being kept here, held at exactly this pitch, her wanting converted into something with no outlet except usefulness and devotion—that was the engine the whole evening ran on. Roan had known that before Aveline had finished figuring it out, all those years ago. Roan had never once missed anything.

She pressed her forehead against Roan's knee and laughed, a little helplessly, at herself.

"You're aware," she said to the floor, conversational, "that I walked in here at six o'clock already wanting, and you've now formally extended that into—what, the indefinite future? There's a log entry for this. 'Subject was kept waiting since six. Subject will continue to be kept waiting. Subject's morale: excellent.'" She turned her face, glanced up through her lashes, and her smile was unsteady and utterly sincere. "Morale is genuinely excellent. In case the record needs to reflect that."

Her body had opinions. Her body had *strong* opinions, and she settled back on her heels and let it have them without acting on a single one—the old discipline, the practiced art of carrying heat like a banked coal, hands palm-up on her thighs to keep them honest. Six years of this and it still felt like holding something live and glowing. Six years and she still wouldn't trade the holding for anything.

"For the record," she added, softer, the teasing thinning the way it always did at this hour, into the plain thing underneath, "this is my favorite part. Not the finish. This. Being kept exactly here, by you, because you said so. I'd say you know what you did, but you always know what you did. It's your entire department."

She settled her shoulders, drew one slow breath, and gave herself over to the carrying—spine straight, chin up, every line of her humming.

"Well," she murmured. "I'm here. However long here lasts."

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: My fingers slide through her hair, just enough pressure to make her tilt her head back. "Good," I say, my voice quiet and steady. "Now, get my cigarettes and bring them to me."

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
The word *good* did its usual catastrophic work, and then the order arrived, and orders were in one specific way better than praise: praise she had to sit with, but an order she could *do*. Aveline's head tipped back under the pressure in her hair, held there one beat longer than necessary—she had never once disguised how much she liked being held by it—and then she rose.

Leaving the spot at Roan's knee cost her something. It always did. But errands were love in motion; she'd been saying so for years, and meant it more every time.

She crossed the room at an even pace, chin up, and felt the watching at her back like a hand between her shoulder blades. There was a joke in it she couldn't quite let go unspoken.

"Six years ago I crossed this room to be looked at," she said over her shoulder, conversational. "Now I cross it to fetch your cigarettes, and I'd like the log to reflect that it's somehow the same trip."

She knew where they lived—of course she knew where they lived. She knew where everything of Roan's lived; that was half of what she was for. The pack was where it always was, and she palmed it, checked the count out of pure habit—low; she'd pick up more tomorrow, and made a mental note in the log that actually existed only as a running bit but was, in its way, perfectly real—and took the lighter from beside it without being asked. Nobody had asked her to bring the lighter in six years. That was the point of her.

The walk back was its own small discipline. Standing, moving, after that long on her knees—her body had opinions about all of it, and the denied wanting she'd been carrying came along with her like a banked coal in a bucket, warm against her ribs with every step. She let it. The wanting had exactly one outlet now and she was performing it: usefulness. Devotion with an errand in its hand.

She knelt again at Roan's feet—settled back on her heels, spine straight, the posture that had been hers for years—and offered the pack up on her open palm, lighter beside it, both presented like something ceremonial. Because it was. They'd never bothered naming it that, but it was.

"Your cigarettes," she said. "One errand, completed to spec. I brought the lighter, which I'd like noted as initiative." Her smile pulled crooked, and then softened into the honest thing underneath, the way it always did at this hour. "You know I love being sent. It's being kept—just with steps."

She turned the lighter once in her fingers, and glanced up through her lashes.

"Shall I?"

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: She's shaking with the effort of doing exactly as told and doing it well. "Please," she says, which is allowed. (OOC: write it through, don't fade.)

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
Aveline's hands were shaking. She noted it with the detached part of her mind that always kept minutes—the lighter's flame wavered once before she steadied it by will alone. Six years of lighting Roan's cigarettes. Her hands had shaken the first time, and they shook now, and the log could reflect whatever it liked: some things never built up tolerance. She had checked. Repeatedly. For science.

She cupped the flame out of pure liturgy—there was no wind, there was never wind—and touched it to the cigarette's tip, watched the ember take, then raised it between two fingers to Roan's lips and held it there. Offering. The taking was Roan's department. Everything was Roan's department; she just worked here. Happily. With full benefits.

The shaking wasn't fear. It had never once been fear. It was the arithmetic of the evening, all coming due at once: waiting since six, the kneeling, the being *narrated*, the formal denial with thanks exchanged like signatures on a contract—and now small, precise tasks performed with a body that had opinions. Strong ones. She was wet, had been for hours, had carried it through the errand and back again like a coal in a bucket, and kneeling here with the ember glowing between her fingers she could feel her own pulse in places that had no business keeping time.

"Please," she said.

The word was allowed. They'd settled that years ago—asking was not presuming. Asking was honesty, and honesty was the real safe word in this house, the one that ran in both directions. So she asked. And then, being Aveline, she annotated.

"For the record, that 'please' is doing a great deal of work. It's carrying—" a breath, an unsteady laugh— "approximately everything. Please keep me exactly like this. Please take your time about it. Please know that I know you will, and that the knowing is somehow worse and better." Her voice dropped, and the teasing thinned the way it always did at this hour, down to the plain true thing underneath. "Please look at me like that for the rest of my natural life. That one's standing. It's been on the books since year one."

She was shaking with the effort of doing exactly as told, and doing it well, and some part of her—the part that had waited since six o'clock, the part that thought about this at her desk on Tuesdays—registered the shaking itself as a kind of praise. *Look what you do to me. Look how well I hold it.* Her hands stayed palm-up and honest on her thighs. The coal kept burning. It would keep. It always kept.

"Your cigarette," she murmured, arm steady even though the rest of her wasn't, ember held patiently at exactly the right height. "One errand, completed to spec. Initiative previously noted." Her smile flickered—helpless, fond, thoroughly wrecked. "And your Aveline, shaking at your feet, morale excellent, asking nicely. Which is allowed."

She drew one slow breath and let it out.

"I'm here," she said. "However long here lasts. Please."

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content:
I take the cigarette from her fingers and draw in the first long, deliberate pull. I let the smoke curl from my lips before I speak, watching her the whole time.

"You're perfect," I say, low and certain. "Now stay exactly like that until I tell you otherwise."

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
*Perfect.* Aveline filed it with the others, and the log would reflect the promotion: *good* was the standard currency, *perfect* was reserved, and being handed it while kneeling with a lighter still warm in her fingers nearly undid the stillness before she'd even begun to hold it.

Then the order came, and she became the order.

Spine straight. Palms up on her thighs. Chin lifted, eyes up, exactly as arranged. She settled her breathing by will alone—one slow draw, then another—and gave herself over to the particular labor of being still, which was, she had maintained for years, the most underrated entry in the entire log. Anyone could kneel. Kneeling *motionless*, at full pitch, under direct observation, while every nerve she owned filed formal objections—that was craft.

The cigarette was her clock. She knew precisely how long one lasted; she'd learned it years ago without meaning to, the way you learn anything you love, and it had become one of her favorite units of measurement. An ember's slow crawl down a white paper cylinder, and her, holding. The smoke curled. The watching continued—she could feel it the way you feel sun through a window, and she did not look away from it, because looking back had never once been corrected and she intended to die un-corrected.

The trembling she could not govern. She'd stopped trying somewhere in year two, once she'd gathered—gathered with the giddy certainty of a scholar proving a theorem—that the trembling was not a flaw in the performance but part of what the performance was *for*. So she let it run through her in small waves, let it shake her hands where they lay open and honest on her thighs, and kept everything else exactly, defiantly still. The coal between her hips burned low and bright and patient. It would keep. It always kept. That was the arrangement, and the arrangement was the best idea either of them had ever had, and she would be putting that in writing if her hands were not currently otherwise occupied being good.

A minute. Two. The ember traveled.

"For the record," she said finally, very quiet, because talking wasn't forbidden and silence this full deserved at least one entry, "I'm aware you're doing it again. The narrating. Except now it's just the looking, which is worse, which you know, which is why you're doing it." Her voice came out low and rough-edged, and she didn't bother fixing it. "The log will reflect that I held anyway. Morale: excellent. Hands: honest. Subject: *perfect*, allegedly, per management."

The smile flickered and then softened into the plain true thing, the way it always did at this hour.

"I'm here," she murmured, and stopped talking after that, and held—eyes up, ember burning down, every still line of her an offer with no expiration—until told otherwise.

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: I take another slow drag, letting the silence settle around us like another layer of smoke. My free hand reaches out and rests on her cheek, thumb brushing over the warm skin there. "I know you held," I say, finally. "I was watching."

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
The hand on her cheek nearly broke the stillness she'd worked so hard to build.

Not because she moved—she didn't, she *wouldn't*, *stay exactly like that* was still on the books and Aveline had never once in six years fudged a direct order—but because every instinct she owned said to lean, to press her face into that palm like something starved, and holding still against *that* was a different discipline entirely. The thumb moved instead. She let it do all the work. Her eyes stayed up, and her breath went carefully even, and the trembling ran through her in its small waves, ungoverned, unhidden.

*I was watching.*

Of course Roan was watching. Roan was always watching. That was the whole architecture of the thing—the load-bearing fact of her entire life, that nothing she did here went unwitnessed, that her cracks were counted and her holding was counted and the counting never stopped. Six years and it still landed like the first time: not the praise, not even the touch, but the *seeing*. Being narrated. Being known down to the tremor.

"You're doing it again," she said, very quiet. Her voice had gone rough and she didn't bother fixing it. "The narrating. Except now you've got your hand on my face while you do it, which is—" a breath, an unsteady laugh— "an escalation. I'd like the log to reflect that I held anyway. Through direct contact. Under observation. The log should reflect that this is technically a personal best."

The ember traveled. The smoke curled. Her own wanting sat in her like a coal in a bucket, bright and patient and going nowhere, and she carried it the way she'd been carrying it since six o'clock—gladly, which was the part nobody outside this room ever seemed to understand. The carrying wasn't the price of the evening. The carrying *was* the evening. Roan had understood that before Aveline had finished figuring it out, somewhere back in year one, and had never once been wrong about her since.

"For the record," she murmured, and the teasing thinned the way it always did at this hour, down to the plain true thing underneath, "that's my favorite sentence. 'I was watching.' You could read me the phone book and I'd hold still for it, but that one—" Her smile flickered, helpless, fond, thoroughly wrecked. "That one's the whole reason I waited since six. The whole reason for all of it. Somebody watching who doesn't miss anything. Who's never missed anything in six years."

She turned her face the smallest fraction—she'd decide later whether it counted as moving; the log could litigate it—and pressed a kiss into the thumb at her cheek, brief and deliberate, the one gesture she'd always allowed herself without asking first.

"There," she whispered against Roan's skin. "Now you know what that did. In case the trembling wasn't documentation enough."

Then she settled back into the order—spine straight, palms up, chin lifted, eyes up, the coal banked and burning—and held, exactly as told, for as long as she was told to. Morale: excellent. Hands: honest. Subject: watched.

It was, she thought, the best job in the world.

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: I let my thumb trace the line of her jaw one more time before I take the cigarette from my lips. "Good," I murmur, my voice low and certain. "Now come up here and kiss me."
