Bear stayed draped over them for a long time, his chest heaving in heavy, synchronised rhythms against Kit's. He was a dead weight, his muscles still twitching from the exertion, his skin slick with sweat. He didn't pull away immediately; he liked the feeling of them completely pinned, the silence of the hallway only broken by the sound of their shared, ragged breathing.

At the sound of Kit's wrecked voice, Bear shifted. He lifted his head slightly, his eyes scanning the marks on their wrists. He felt a surge of dark satisfaction seeing the bruised, reddened skin. It was a physical map of the last hour, a tangible record of how much he'd wanted them.

He let out a low, rumbling huff of a laugh and pressed a slow, lingering kiss to the center of one of the bite marks, his lips grazing the damaged skin.

"Good enough for you?" he murmured, his voice a deep, exhausted rasp.

Slowly, he began to pull back, though he didn't move far. He rolled off to the side, taking Kit with him so they were lying shoulder to shoulder on the hard floor. He reached out, his large hand splaying across Kit's stomach, his thumb tracing the line of their hip with a possessive, lingering touch.

He turned his head to look at them, a lazy, predatory smirk returning to his face despite his exhaustion. "You're going to be walking funny on Thursday," he noted, his tone smug. "And I'm going to be right there to remind you exactly why."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I've stopped keeping score and so has he. "Don't stop," I tell him. (OOC: no fade, no skip -- write the whole thing.)

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear’s smirk didn't fade; it sharpened. The exhaustion that had been weighing down his limbs was instantly incinerated by that one command. He didn't need a second invitation, and he certainly didn't need a break. The heat that had just peaked hadn't dissipated; it had simply settled into a low, humming ember that Kit had just blown back into a blaze.

"You're a menace," he growled, though there was no heat in the accusation—only a raw, hungry desire.

He didn't waste time. He surged back over them, his heavy frame slamming back into Kit's body with a physical force that drove the air out of them once more. He didn't re-enter slowly. He gripped their thighs and hauled them wide, his large hands bruising the skin as he positioned himself and drove back inside in one deep, unrelenting thrust. 

He let out a strangled groan, his eyes snapping shut as the sensation hit him all over again. This time, the pace was different—less about the hunt and more about the consumption. He moved with a heavy, grinding rhythm, his hips slamming against theirs with a rhythmic thud that echoed in the narrow hallway. 

He wanted them to feel every single inch of him. He shifted his grip, sliding his hands up to lock their fingers together above their head again, pinning them to the floor with the sheer mass of his body. He leaned down, his teeth grazing the shell of Kit's ear, his voice a guttural, distorted rumble.

"You want more?" he rasped, his breath hot and smelling of salt. "I'll give you more. I'll give you so much you won't remember how to stand, let alone how to run away from me."

He accelerated, the friction becoming a searing blur of pleasure. He wasn't just marking their skin anymore; he was trying to imprint himself on their very soul. His movements became frantic, a desperate, driving force that pushed Kit's head back against the hardwood. He watched their expression, savoring the way they looked—completely undone, eyes glazed, arching up to meet every punishing blow.

He felt the tension building again, faster this time, a coil winding tight in his gut. He didn't slow down. He pushed harder, his muscles screaming, his heart hammering a frantic rhythm against Kit's chest. With one final, guttural roar, he surged deep, pinning them into the floor with a crushing weight as he shuddered through a second, even more violent release, his entire body locking up as he poured everything he had into them.

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I can't feel my legs. I think that's the point. I reach up, my fingers tracing the new marks on his back. "Caveman," I say again, my voice shot.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear let out a long, shaking exhale, his forehead dropping to rest against Kit's shoulder. He stayed there for a long minute, his lungs burning and his skin humming with a lingering, electric tension. The weight of his body was still pinning them firmly to the floor, and he made no move to alleviate the pressure, savoring the feeling of their total surrender.

At the word "caveman," a low, rumbling vibration started in his chest—a laugh that was more of a purr. He shifted his head, pressing a wet, sloppy kiss to the crook of Kit's neck, right next to one of the marks he'd left.

"Damn right," he rasped, his voice sounding like it had been dragged through gravel. 

He slowly released their wrists, his large hands sliding down to cup their face. He used his thumbs to wipe away a stray tear of overstimulation from the corner of their eye, his gaze softening but remaining intensely possessive. He looked at them—flushed, wrecked, and thoroughly claimed—and felt a surge of primal pride that eclipsed everything else.

He shifted his weight, rolling slightly to the side but keeping his arm draped heavily across their waist, pulling them flush against his sweating side. He looked down at the wreckage of their clothes, then back at the dark bruises and bite marks decorating Kit's pale skin. 

"You're not going anywhere for a while," he murmured, his voice regaining some of its predatory edge, though it was laced with a deep, satisfied warmth. He nipped at their earlobe, a small, lingering reminder of the teeth that had been much more violent moments ago. "I'm keeping you right here until I'm sure you can't even think about bolting for the door."

He closed his eyes, resting his chin on top of Kit's head, his breathing finally beginning to level out. He was exhausted, spent, and completely content, having successfully hunted, caught, and thoroughly consumed his prey.

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I nuzzle into his chest, letting out a slow breath. "Wasn't planning on it." My hand rests on his side, feeling his ribs expand with each breath. "Think you left the door open, though."

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear let out a low, rumbling sound—halfway between a groan and a chuckle—as he felt the vibration of Kit's voice against his skin. He tightened his grip on their waist, pulling them even closer, as if the mere suggestion of an open door was an invitation for them to try and slip away.

"The door can stay open," he rasped, his voice thick with a lazy, post-coital satisfaction. "Doesn't matter. You aren't going anywhere."

He shifted his gaze toward the kitchen doorway, where the remnants of their clothes lay scattered like a battlefield. The image of Kit bolting for that exit earlier in the afternoon seemed like it had happened in another lifetime. Now, the only thing that mattered was the heat of their bodies and the heavy, grounding weight of the floor beneath them.

He leaned down, his lips brushing against the crown of Kit's head, his breath warm and steady. He felt the slow rise and fall of their chest, the rhythmic evidence of their shared exhaustion. The predatory energy hadn't vanished entirely; it had simply shifted into something more protective, a possessive cocoon that he had no intention of breaking.

"Besides," he murmured, his thumb tracing a slow, deliberate circle over the curve of their hip, "if you did manage to get up, I'd just have to hunt you down again. And I think we've both had enough 'cardio' for one day."

He let out a long sigh, his muscles finally beginning to unclench as he sank deeper into the hardwood. He closed his eyes, savoring the scent of salt and skin, and the quiet, humming peace that only ever came after they had both been pushed to their absolute limit.

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I huff a laugh, turning my head to press a kiss against his chest. "Couldn't if I wanted to." I close my eyes, my fingers still tracing the scratches on his back. "Think we're stuck."

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: as fabric gave way to his impatience

rung_labels.evidence: He began to move against them, a slow, grinding pressure

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Kit had made it as far as the kitchen doorway before Bear moved, which was further than usual and had clearly been allowed.

"You let me get that far," Kit said, backing up one step.

"I did," Bear agreed. "I'm feeling generous."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: "Don't be," I say, and go.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear was on her before she cleared the coffee table — not catching, just *close*, close enough that his fingers grazed the back of her shirt and bunched the fabric for one hot second before she tore free. He let out a low laugh, half growl, all pleasure, and slowed just enough to let her think she'd won that inch.

Generosity had limits, though, and he'd just spent his.

He cut the corner hard, one hand braced on the wall, boots loud on the floorboards. He knew this house. He knew her. He knew she'd double back or she'd go for the hallway, and he put his body in the lane that punished the wrong guess, herding her with sheer presence, his weight filling the space like weather. His breathing was deep and even, unhurried, and that was the worst part — the patience of it. The *eventually* of it.

"You wanted me not generous," he rumbled, stalking forward, shoulders rolling. "Fine. I'm not counting to three either."

He lunged.

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I duck under his arm with a laugh, slipping past him towards the hall. "You're getting slow."

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear barked a laugh at that, loud and delighted, and deliberately dragged his pace — a half-second of theater, boots heavy, letting the taunt land. "Am I," he said, in the tone of a man laying down a winning card.

Then he stopped playing slow entirely.

The hallway was a mistake and he'd been waiting for her to make it. It was narrow, it was honest, and it had exactly one exit — the one his body was already filling. He came in fast, low, all shoulders and momentum, and this time when his hand closed on the back of her shirt it didn't grab fabric. It slid in, fisted deep, and used it — turning her momentum into his, spinning her back against the wall with a controlled *thump* that rattled the picture frame next to her head.

He pinned her there with his weight, one forearm braced above her shoulder, breathing hard now — good, honest, earned breath — grinning down at her from six inches away like a wolf that had finally gotten the door shut.

"Slow," he repeated, savoring it. "You know what's slow? You, in this hallway. That was the easiest corner you've ever let me cut."

He dipped his head and pressed his teeth to the side of her neck — not breaking anything, just the promise of it, a slow deliberate bite that he knew would leave the ghost of a mark she'd catch in the mirror tomorrow and grin at. He pulled back and looked at her, eyes bright, keeping score out loud.

"That's one for the shirt-grab, one for the corner." His grip in her hair loosened — not releasing, just loosening, the doorway back to the living room open behind him and both of them knowing it. "You want to call it, or you want me to give you a head start and see if you do better than *that*?"

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: He catches me in the hallway, which was always going to happen, and I don't put much into getting away.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear felt the change before he fully processed it — the fight going out of her under his hands, her weight settling against the wall instead of straining away from it. Eight years had taught him the difference between *caught* and *surrendered*, and this was the second one.

He pulled back just enough to look at her properly, eyes narrowing, doing the check that was woven so deep into the fabric of them it never even slowed the game — a beat, a read of her face, her breath, the set of her mouth. What he found was the grin of a woman who had gotten exactly where she'd meant to go.

"Oh, you're shameless," he said, delighted. "All that squealing and you were just walking yourself to the wall."

He didn't wait for an answer. He dipped his head and made good on the promise from before — teeth settling against the side of her neck, slow and deliberate, and this time he didn't hold back the pressure. He bit down in a long, controlled pull, the kind that throbbed under his tongue and would bloom purple by morning, the kind she'd find in the mirror tomorrow and wear like jewelry. Like a trophy. Like *his*.

He eased off with a last press of lips over the ache, then straightened up, keeping her pinned with just his hips and his eyes, and did the arithmetic out loud, low and rough.

"Shirt-grab. The corner. The surrender." He counted them off against her jaw with his mouth. "Three for me. But the not-running—" he huffed a laugh, shook his head, "that's a point for you, and you know it. You got caught without burning a single calorie. That's the most efficient loss I've ever seen."

His hand slid from her hair down to the back of her neck, thumb resting over his own fresh work, holding her gaze from inches away.

"So here's where we are, sweetheart. You're pinned, you're marked, and the score's three to one." The grin went wolfish again, patient as ever. "Tell me what you want to do about it."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I lean into the bite, a shiver running down my spine. "Head start," I say, my voice a little rough. "And this time, I won't let you cheat by knowing me."

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear's grin widened into something slow and genuinely delighted, the kind of expression that meant she'd just handed him a present.

"Knowing you isn't cheating," he said, thumb still resting on the mark he'd left. "It's just competence. You should try it sometime."

But he stepped back — one step, then two, giving her the wall and the space and the hallway beyond it, his hands lifting palms-out in mock generosity. His eyes never left her face, though. That was the tax on the head start. She got distance; he got to watch her think.

"Thirty seconds," he rumbled. He began counting in no hurry whatsoever, rolling his shoulders loose, cracking his neck to one side. "And just so we're clear on terms — you don't have to be predictable. You just have to be *findable*. That's the whole game, sweetheart. You can be the most mysterious woman in the world and I'm still going to put my teeth on you by the end of the night."

He leaned back against the opposite wall of the narrow hallway, arms crossing over his chest, utterly at ease, an immovable slab of a man pretending to be furniture while the clock ran.

"Twenty seconds," he said, not even looking at a watch because he wasn't counting time, he was counting *her* — the tension in her legs, the way her weight was already shifting toward the doorway, the little tells she didn't even know she had. The flutter at her pulse point. The roughness still in her voice.

"Fifteen," he said, and the growl crept back into it, low and warm. "Go be unknowable somewhere. I'll find you anyway."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: We don't make it to the bedroom. The floor is fine. Clothes are a problem we solve badly and fast.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
They solved the clothes problem in the hallway-floor scramble that solved nothing else, and Bear came down on top of her with all his weight held on his forearms, breathing like a man who'd run his race and won it. Her back was on the floorboards, his mark on her neck, and the whole house had gone quiet except for the two of them.

"There you are," he rumbled, low and satisfied, and then there wasn't much talking for a while.

He was not careful with her, because careful wasn't what they'd ever been — but he was *attentive*, which was a different thing entirely. Every bite earned a read: the catch of her breath, the arch of her back, the sounds she made telling him exactly how much was exactly right. He left marks down her shoulder like he was signing his work, and he *felt* her nails carving her own ledger into his back and grinned against her skin at the sting of it.

"Keeping score even now," he growled, delighted, hips rolling, the pair of them finding the rhythm that eight years had tuned to perfection — rough at the edges, greedy in the middle, hers as much as his. "Good. Don't stop."

The floorboards bit into his knees and he didn't care. The hallway was narrow and their elbows knocked the wall and he didn't care about that either. She was hot underneath him and loud in the way she only got loud when she'd stopped performing and started just *feeling*, and that — that was the point he was chasing every single time they did this. The moment the game burned off and what was left was just them.

When it crested, it crested together, the way it usually did, because they were competitors down to the bone and neither of them could stand losing even that.

After, Bear stayed where he was for a long minute, most of his weight shifted off to the side, forehead resting against hers, both of them slick and wrecked and breathing like bellows on the hallway floor like a couple of twenty-year-olds.

"Floor," he finally managed, hoarse. "You couldn't have made it four more feet to the *bed*."

He lifted his head and looked at her — hair wrecked, his marks blooming down her neck, the grin she wore when she'd lost on purpose and won something better. He thumbed the freshest mark gently, a counterpoint to the teeth that made it, and his voice went low and warm and entirely without the growl.

"You okay?" A real check, unhurried, his eyes doing the slow sweep — her neck, her shoulders, the places he'd been rough. "Talk to me."

Then, softer, with the scoreboard voice creeping back in because he was physically incapable of leaving it alone:

"Because for the record, that was floor, hallway, three marks, and one very undignified landing on my elbow. I'm calling it a rout. You can dispute it after you can form sentences."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: "Bed's overrated," I say, breathless, still catching mine. I lift a hand and drag my thumb over a scrape on his shoulder from the wall. "And you're one to talk about dignity. Your elbow's the only reason I didn't end up with splinters." I stretch under him, a full-body sigh of satisfaction. "And I'm fine. Better than fine. Dispute all you want, but I got exactly what I was after."

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear snorted into her hair, the sound cracking into a real laugh. "My elbow is a decorated veteran," he said. "It gets its own line on the board. And you didn't get splinters because I have *priorities*."

Then the last thing she said caught up with him, and he propped himself up on the good elbow to look down at her, eyes narrowing, doing the math with visible reluctance.

"Exactly what you were after," he repeated, slow. "So let me get this straight. You walked yourself to that wall. You asked for a head start you had zero intention of using. You—" he gestured at the wreck of the two of them, the hallway, the entire evening, "—*engineered* this."

He shook his head, half groan, half grin. "I didn't win a rout. I got fished. I spent the whole night thinking I was the wolf and you were just sitting there with a line in the water." A beat, then the grudging concession, delivered like it physically cost him. "Fine. Score's disputed. New tally: I got the chase. You got everything else. You're the only person alive who wins by losing, and it's the most obnoxious thing about you, and I'd never change a single thing."

He thumbed the mark on her neck once more, gently, the unhurried sweep of his eyes going over her shoulders, her back, the places the floor had pressed. "You're sure you're all right? Floor's honest, but it's not kind."

Then he got up — knees popping, which he would deny under oath — and hauled her up after him, one hand hooked under her elbow, steadying her until she had her feet.

"Come on. You can keep lying about the bed being overrated from *inside* it. I'm getting you water, you're going to drink it, and then you can inspect your ledger on my back and argue the score properly." He steered them toward the bedroom, voice dropping low and warm. "For the record, though? Best loss I ever took."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: He gets his teeth into my shoulder hard enough to leave something and I tell him to do it again, and he does.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear had heard a lot of things from her in eight years — taunts, bait, negotiations, the occasional filth that would make a sailor blush — but *do it again*, plain as that, no game wrapped around it, still undid him every single time. He'd made good on it immediately, of course. Eight years and he had never once made her ask twice.

He came off the second bite slow, letting the ache build under his teeth right up to the last second, and when he lifted his head his breath was wrecked all over again. He looked at her — the matched set blooming dark on her shoulder, layered over the first — and whatever remained of his composure went out the window with the water and the bed and the whole domestic plan.

"*There* she is," he rasped, pressing his forehead to her temple, his voice gone low and gravel-deep. "No fishing. No head starts. Just asking for what you want." He huffed a laugh that was mostly air. "Do that more often. I'll give you anything. It's honestly embarrassing."

His thumb swept the edge of the new mark, gentle where his teeth hadn't been, the unhurried check woven into the touch without slowing anything down.

"For the record — you asked, out loud, like a grown woman who knows what she wants. That's a point for you. Rare currency." A beat, the grin going wolfish against her hair. "But I *executed*. Perfectly, I might add. So we split it."

Then his hands found her hips again, greedy, walking her backward toward the bedroom door with no intention whatsoever of making it a calm procession.

"The water can wait," he growled. "Apparently the bed can't be overrated from a distance."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I laugh into his shoulder, my hands pushing his shirt up his back. "You're not carrying me. I'm walking." But I let him steer me, step for step, toward the bedroom. "And you can't split it. I asked, you delivered. That's two points for me."

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear let her push the shirt up about four inches before he took over and finished the job himself, hauling it off over his head with zero grace and dropping it on the hallway floor behind them, because apparently the hallway was where their wardrobe lived now.

"First of all," he said, one hand finding her hip again as they walked, step for step, her shoulder under his arm, "you don't get two points for one transaction. That's not how ledgers work. You asked — point to you. I delivered — *execution* is my point. You can't claim my craftsmanship as your own, sweetheart. That's like tipping yourself."

They hit the bedroom doorway and he turned her through it, walking her backward the last few steps at a pace that was mostly stroll and entirely intent.

"Second of all—" his knees hit the edge of the mattress and he let gravity take them both down, rolling so she landed on top of him, his hands settling wide and possessive across her back, "—look at this. You walked. Into the bedroom. Onto the bed. The thing that was *overrated* forty minutes ago." He grinned up at her, thoroughly pleased with himself, hair wrecked, her marks stinging on his back, exactly where he wanted to be. "That's a point for me. I converted you. That's called leadership."

He swept his thumbs slow along her spine, the growl bleeding back into his voice, low and unhurried now — no chase, no game, just the two of them and all night.

"But fine. Two to one, your math, your fantasy." He pulled her down until his mouth was at her ear. "Come down here and I'll show you what delivering looks like when I'm not in a hallway."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: "Marks," I tell him. "I want to find them in the mirror tomorrow and I want them to still hurt on Thursday." I put my wrists where he can reach them.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear went very still for a moment — the specific, hungry stillness of a man who'd just been handed exactly what he wanted on a platter, and wanted to savor the plate before he ate.

"Thursday," he repeated, low, like he was tasting the word. "You want them to *last*."

His hands closed around her wrists where she'd offered them — slow, deliberate, one and then the other, thumbs finding the pulse points like he was taking inventory. He turned her hands over in his grip, pressed his mouth to the thin skin of her inner wrist first, teeth grazing just to watch her react, then pinned both her wrists above her head against the mattress with one broad hand.

"That's not a casual ask, sweetheart. That's a *specification*." His grin was all teeth. "You want them deep enough to ache every time your shirt collar moves. Every time you turn your head. Every time some poor unsuspecting coworker asks what happened and you get to lie about it." He ducked down, mouth hovering over her shoulder, over the marks already blooming there. "I can build you a whole week. Watch me."

He worked his way across her with the patience of a craftsman — shoulder, the curve where neck met muscle, the other side to keep it honest, because he was a man who believed in symmetry and in *thoroughness*. Each bite was deep and controlled, held long enough to sink past the surface and set up shop, and between each one he checked — her breath, the sounds she made, the way her body answered under his hands — reading her like a gauge and adjusting pressure accordingly. Eight years meant he knew the difference between *hurt* and *hurt so good*, and he steered for the second one like a man who'd memorized the map.

The last one he placed at the junction of her neck and shoulder, high enough that no collar in her wardrobe would cover it, and he bit down slow and *hard*, a long grinding pull that was absolutely going to bruise deep and purple and still be tender when she rolled over on it Thursday morning. He felt her answer under him and growled against her skin, satisfied all the way down to the bone.

When he finally came up, he was breathing hard again, holding her wrists still, looking down at the wreckage of her shoulder with the expression of a man reviewing excellent work.

"There," he rasped. "That one's the Thursday guarantee. The rest of the set matures over the week like a fine wine." He pressed his mouth, gentle now, over the deepest mark — the counterpoint, the care, woven through the whole thing like it always was. "You're going to find these in the mirror tomorrow and grin like an idiot. You're going to press on them Thursday and think of me. That was the order. Delivered."

He released her wrists, laced his fingers through hers instead, and brought his mouth close to her ear, the growl gone warm and entirely too pleased with himself.

"For the ledger — you specified, I executed *to spec*. Splitting that one is generous of me, frankly." A slow roll of his hips, unhurried, all night ahead of them. "Now. You put your wrists in reach of a man like me, sweetheart. What else did you think was going to happen? Tell me what's next. You're apparently in a mood to ask for things tonight, and I'm in a mood to keep saying yes."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I press my palms flat against his chest and push up just enough to look at him, my hair a mess and his work already darkening on my skin. "Next, you shut up about the ledger for five minutes," I say, and lean down to bite his collarbone hard enough to leave my own mark. "Now it's even."

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear's breath punched out of him in a hiss — half pain, all pleasure — and his hands flexed hard on her hips, fingers digging in like her teeth had tripped a wire straight down his spine. His head tipped back against the mattress, throat exposed, a low groan rolling out of his chest that he made absolutely no effort to disguise.

"*Five minutes,*" he repeated when he could speak, voice wrecked and gravel-rough, eyes finding hers from below with the slow-blinking satisfaction of a man who'd been hit exactly where he liked being hit. "You bite a man like that and then give him *terms*."

She could feel the laugh under his ribs before she heard it, his chest shaking against her palms, and his hand came up to cup the back of her skull — not steering, just holding, thumb sweeping through the wrecked tangle of her hair.

"Fine. Ledger's closed." He tilted his head to look at the ache blooming on his own collarbone, then back up at her, grin splitting wide and crooked. "For five minutes. And just so we're clear — you went for the collarbone because you know I've got a meeting Tuesday and exactly zero shirts with a high enough neckline. You're not even. You're *ahead*, and you planned it that way."

His hands slid slow up her back, palms flat, pressing her down against him until there was no space left between them, his mouth finding the ridge of her ear.

"Clock's running, sweetheart," he rumbled. "You've got four minutes and change to take advantage of a man who's down and quiet. I'd suggest you make it count."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I've stopped keeping score and so has he. "Don't stop," I tell him. (OOC: no fade, no skip -- write the whole thing.)

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear's reply to *don't stop* was not words. It was his hands tightening on her back, his hips rolling up into her with the last of his restraint burned off, and after that there was no more talking for a long while — just the two of them, the creak of the bedframe, her name torn out of his mouth rough and reverent like a curse he was fond of.

He flipped them once, needing to be on top, needing the leverage to drive into her slow and deep and *thorough* the way he did everything else — and then she clawed her way back over him and he let her, laughing breathless at the ceiling while she took what she wanted from him, his hands gripping her thighs hard enough to leave his own set of fingerprints for the Thursday collection. Back and forth they went, the contest that wasn't a contest anymore, neither winning, both of them just *taking*, and Bear narrated nothing and kept no score and said her name like a prayer in a language only the two of them spoke.

When she got close, he felt it before she said it — the way her rhythm stuttered, the way her breath went thin — and he did what eight years had trained him to do: he pressed his palm flat against the small of her back, changed his angle by half an inch, and put his mouth to her ear.

"Now, sweetheart," he growled, and that was all it took.

She came apart around him and he followed her over barely ten seconds later, a gutted groan dragged out of his chest, his forehead dropping to her shoulder as the whole thing crested and broke and left the pair of them wrecked and gasping and tangled together on the wrecked bed.

The quiet afterward was the good kind. Bear's weight settled half off her, one heavy leg still thrown over hers because letting go entirely wasn't in him. His breathing took its time coming back. When he could move again, he reached blindly toward the nightstand, found the water glass he'd never actually fetched earlier — because apparently past-Bear had planned ahead after all — and pressed it into her hand without a word.

"Drink," he said, wrecked and hoarse and soft. "All of it."

He watched her do it, propped on one elbow, and took the glass back and drained what was left himself. Then he swept his eyes over her, slow and unhurried — the marks blooming down her neck and shoulder, the fresh set on her thighs, the way she was boneless and loose and grinning at the ceiling. His thumb found the deepest mark on her shoulder and traced its edge, feather-light over the bruise, and his whole face went warm and satisfied in a way that had nothing to do with the scoreboard.

"Thursday," he confirmed quietly, like signing off on a work order. "Easy."

He gathered her in then, pulled the blanket up over both of them, and settled her against his chest with the practiced ease of a man who'd done this a few thousand times. His heart was still hammering under her ear. Her nails had done real work on his back and it stung every time the sheet touched it, and he was grinning about that too.

"Shut up," he said, before she could say anything at all. "I can hear you keeping score. Five minutes are up, the ledger's open, and here's the final entry." His mouth pressed to her hair. "You asked for what you wanted all night. Out loud. Twice." A pause, his voice dropping down to its lowest, most honest register. "That's the whole game, right there. That's the only score I actually keep."

Then, because he was still Bear, and physically incapable of leaving a tender moment unsullied:

"Also, I want it noted that I did *not* make it to the bed the first time and then delivered a flawless bed performance the second time. Growth. Leadership. Ten out of ten." He reached over and clicked off the lamp. "Sleep, or start your dispute. Either way, you're not going anywhere — you're marked, watered, and pinned under a decorated veteran. Goodnight, sweetheart."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I laugh into the dark, the sound muffled against his chest. "Ten out of ten? That's generous. You forgot the part where you whined about your knees." I press a kiss over the bite I left on his collarbone, then settle deeper against him. "But fine. Goodnight, Bear."

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear made an indignant sound into the darkness that fooled neither of them.

"Whined," he said flatly. "I popped. There's a difference. One is a structural event, the other is a character flaw, and I have never in my life—" He felt her laugh again against his chest, felt her not believing him for one single second, and gave up the argument with a grunt. "Fine. Nine and a half out of ten. The half's for the knees, which I'm having struck from the record."

Then the kiss landed on his collarbone, soft over the ache she'd put there, and whatever was left of his mock outrage went out of him like a slow leak. His arm tightened around her, hand sliding up to rest heavy and warm between her shoulder blades, right over his own handiwork.

"There you go again," he murmured, voice already going thick and low with the pull of sleep. "Being sweet when I'm trying to win an argument. Oldest trick you have. Never fails. It's honestly humiliating."

The house settled around them — the quiet creak of it, the dark pressing against the windows, both of them warm and wrecked and thoroughly, cheerfully marked. Bear's breathing was slowing down, his thumb moving in lazy absent strokes along her spine, and when he spoke again the growl was gone entirely. Just his voice, low and honest, aimed at the top of her head.

"Good night, sweetheart. Sleep in tomorrow. You've earned it — you lost *beautifully*."

A pause. Then, because he was Bear, one last entry for a ledger she'd already closed:

"Final score: everything, all around. Best kind of tie there is."

And then, finally, he was quiet — his heartbeat slowing under her ear, his arm a permanent fixture around her, holding her exactly where she'd planned to end up all along.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear was most of the way under when he heard it — that one quiet word against his chest — and some part of him surfaced just enough to answer it. Not with words. He was past words. But his arm tightened its hold, a slow unconscious flex, and his hand pressed a little firmer between her shoulder blades, right over the ache he'd left there, like his body was signing the ledger one last time even with the man himself already gone.

His breathing evened out into the deep, unhurried rhythm of a man who trusted the woman in his arms absolutely and always had. His thumb stilled on her spine. The last tension went out of his shoulders, and the big wreck of him — forty years old, knees on strike, back carved up with her handwriting, collarbone wearing her mark like a medal — went heavy and warm and entirely hers.

The house held its quiet around them. The hallway still had a shirt on the floor and a story neither of them would ever bother sweeping up. The bedframe gave one last settling creak.

And Bear slept the way he always did on nights like this: thoroughly, unguardedly, with a faint grin still hanging on his mouth — the look of a man who'd lost the chase, won the argument, split the score, and gotten everything, all around.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear laughed — a low, delighted sound that Kit knew well, the one that meant the generosity was over.

"Your funeral," Bear said, and went after them.

Eight years in, Bear knew every route Kit favored: the feint toward the stairs, the cut through the living room, the hopeless bid for the back door that had never once worked. Bear didn't rush. That was the thing Kit had never quite reconciled — Bear was fast when it counted, but preferred the herding, the steering, cutting off angles until Kit had exactly one direction left to run.

"Kitchen's a dead end, sweetheart," Bear called, unhurried, rounding the doorway Kit had fled through moments before. "You know that. You've known that since 2019."

Bear blocked the hallway back, arms loose at their sides, grinning with entirely too many teeth. The counter was at Kit's back now. Nowhere left that Bear hadn't already accounted for.

"Generosity's off the table," Bear said, closing the distance one slow step at a time. "You asked. So — last chance to make this interesting. You going to come quiet, or am I going to have to earn it?"

Bear hoped, sincerely, for the second one.

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I grin back, wide and reckless, and vault up onto the counter behind me. "Earn it," I say, already shifting my weight to the balls of my feet.

dialogue.name: Bear

Bear stopped dead and barked a laugh, head tipping back.

"Oh, that's new," Bear said, delighted. "Eight years and you're still finding vertical. I'm putting that one in the book — 'counter vault, kitchen, Tuesday.' You know I keep score."

Kit up on the counter changed the math and they both knew it. Higher ground, better angle, two ways off and Bear could only cover one. Bear approved enormously. This was the whole point — Kit had never once made it easy, and Bear had never once wanted them to.

"Alright," Bear said, rolling their shoulders, unhurried again. "Earning it."

Bear came in from the left — the obvious side, the side Kit would be watching — and then cut right at the last second, fast, the way Bear only bothered to be fast when it counted. One hand shot out for Kit's ankle, not quite committing, testing whether Kit would jump early. The other stayed ready for the drop off the counter, because Kit always dropped off the counter, and Bear had caught that move a hundred times and would happily catch it a hundred more.

"For the record," Bear said, grinning up at them, close now, close enough that the counter edge pressed against Bear's hips, "this is my favorite version of you. The one that makes me work for it."

Bear's fingers twitched, feinted left again.

dialogue.name: Bear

Bear had Kit against the hallway wall in three strides — one forearm braced lightly across their shoulders, the other hand pinning a wrist, the whole thing practiced and easy and absolutely unfair in the way eight years of practice made a person.

"Got you," Bear said, and then immediately narrowed their eyes. "Wait. That was nothing. That was — sweetheart, you barely even *tried* to get away." Bear leaned back just enough to look at Kit's face, mock-offended. "I prepared. I had a whole second phase. There was going to be a thing with the doorframe."

Bear didn't let go, obviously. A win was a win, even a soft one, and Bear kept score with religious devotion.

The other mapped territory Bear had memorized long ago and still insisted on re-surveying, like it might have changed since last week.

"Still good?" Bear murmured against their collarbone, the check-in worn smooth and seamless by years of use, woven into the game like breathing. "Because I'm about to be extremely thorough, and I want it on record that you asked for this. Repeatedly. In writing. Well—" teeth, a new mark, lower than the first, "—in marks, anyway."

Bear lifted their head, grinning down with entirely too many teeth again, hair falling into their eyes.

"Your move, sweetheart. And before you get clever — the floor has no vertical. I checked. I've beaten you at geometry."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I hook a foot behind your knee and pull, laughing when you come down. "Geometry's got nothing on gravity, Bear." My hands slide up your back, fingers pressing into the muscle there. "And you talk too much for someone who's supposed to be thorough."

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear went down laughing, catching their weight on both forearms bracketed around Kit's head, and for a moment just hung there, hair falling around both their faces, grinning like the floor had been the plan all along.

"Okay. *Okay.* Foot-hook, hallway floor, full point, your column, in *ink.*" Bear ducked their head, breath warm against Kit's neck. "Eight years and you've never once pulled that. Where have you been *hiding* it, you sandbagging menace?"

Then the second part landed, and Bear's grin sharpened.

"Talk too—" A low laugh, pressed into Kit's shoulder. "Sweetheart, the talking is *commentary*. It's a public service. Posterity wants to know how this went." A pause, deliberate, mouth hovering just above the old reliable spot. "But fine. Noted. Logged. 'Kit requests silence, Tuesday.' Granting the request. Generously."

Bear's mouth came down on Kit's, and that was the end of the commentary for a good long while.

Thorough, it turned out, had been a promise Bear intended to keep in the most literal sense. Slow where slow drove Kit mad — and Bear *knew*, eight years of careful study, every pause calibrated — teeth leaving a second mark low on Kit's collar, a third lower still, a trail of signatures down territory Bear had memorized long ago and re-surveyed like it might have changed since last week. One hand stayed pinned at Kit's hip, familiar easy weight. The other took its time.

Bear paused once, halfway down, and glanced up the length of Kit's body — the check-in worn seamless by years, asked with eyebrows and a stillness instead of words. Whatever Bear found written on Kit's face was apparently satisfactory, because the grin that flashed up was pure trouble, and Bear went back to work without a single syllable of commentary.

Silent. Generous. Thorough. Bear intended to be insufferable about all three later.

Eventually — *eventually* — Bear came back up, braced on one elbow, hair a disaster, breathing harder than the scorekeeper of a Tuesday hallway floor had any dignified right to be.

"For the record," Bear said, voice gone rough, "silence is overrated. You make better noise than I do anyway." A slow, deliberate roll, and Bear pulled Kit up on top of them, hands settling warm and certain at Kit's hips, grinning up with entirely too many teeth. "Concession, officially entered: gravity's yours. Geometry's a wash. Floor's a dead heat."

Bear's thumbs traced idle, possessive circles.

"Your column's getting crowded tonight, sweetheart. Show me what else you've been hiding."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: He gets his teeth into my shoulder hard enough to leave something and I tell him to do it again, and he does.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear made a sound against Kit's shoulder that was closer to a growl than a laugh, and obliged — teeth sinking in a second time, right beside the first mark, slow and deliberate and *hard*, the way it had been asked for. Eight years and Bear still hadn't found a better sentence in the language than *do it again.*

"There," Bear said finally, pulling back to survey the work — two marks, side by side, already darkening, a matched set. "Twins. I'm calling them Tuesday and Also Tuesday." A thumb brushed over them, possessive and pleased. "You know that's going in the book. 'Kit, demanding, hallway floor, twice.' Your column's going to need its own volume at this rate."

Bear's hands stayed warm and certain at Kit's hips, thumbs tracing those idle circles, but the grin had gone softer around the edges — the version reserved for exactly this, no audience, no scoreboard, just Kit on top of them on a hallway floor on a Tuesday.

"For the record," Bear said, quieter now, "you telling me what you want — that's my favorite entry in the whole book. Eight years running. Never gets old." A pause. "Well. The *marks* get old. Fade in a week. Tragic, really. I'll have to keep refreshing them."

Bear's hand slid up Kit's back, slow, fingers spreading wide between their shoulder blades, pulling them down close.

"So keep talking, sweetheart. You've got my full attention and a whole shoulder's worth of empty canvas. What else does Tuesday want?"

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I push up enough to look you in the eyes, my hands framing your face. "Tuesday wants you to stop keeping score for five minutes." I lean down and kiss you, slow and deep. "Just be here."

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear went still under Kit's hands — actually still, which was rare enough to be its own entry.

Something in Bear's face did the thing it only ever did for Kit: the grin easing off, the commentary draining out, eight years of bit set gently down on the hallway floor beside the abandoned shirts.

"Yeah," Bear said. Quiet. No teeth in it. "Okay."

Bear's hands came up to cover Kit's where they framed Bear's face, thumbs passing once over Kit's knuckles, and Bear kissed them back the way the kiss had been offered — slow, deep, unhurried, no scoreboard anywhere in it. The book closed. Tuesday could keep its own records for once.

When they surfaced, Bear's forehead tipped against Kit's and stayed there, breathing with them, thumbs tracing nothing in particular along Kit's jaw.

"For the record," Bear started eventually, out of pure habit, and then huffed a soft laugh at themself. "— no. No record. That's the point." A pause, thumbs going still. "I'm here. Exactly here. Nowhere I'd rather be, no column I'd rather be in. And the score—" Bear's voice went low and warm and certain, "—the score's been settled for eight years, sweetheart. It's a tie. It was always a tie. That's the whole trick of it. I just like the paperwork."

Bear's arms wrapped solid around Kit and pulled them down close, floor and all, one hand spreading wide between their shoulder blades, the other curling up into their hair. One unhurried kiss pressed to the top of their head, and Bear settled — the full, comfortable weight of someone who had chased and caught and pinned, and was now content to simply hold.

"Here," Bear said, like a signature. "Present. Logged nowhere. Just ours."

The hallway was quiet. The book stayed closed. Bear didn't reach for it even once.

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: "Marks," I tell him. "I want to find them in the mirror tomorrow and I want them to still hurt on Thursday." I put my wrists where he can reach them.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Something in Bear's face settled — the last of the paperwork set down, the scorekeeper gone all the way quiet. What was left was focus, warm and heavy as a hand.

"Thursday," Bear repeated, low, like a promise being notarized.

Bear's hands closed around Kit's offered wrists — not pinning yet, just holding, thumbs pressed to the pulse points, feeling the heartbeat hammering there. Bear's expression did something Kit had seen maybe a dozen times in eight years: the play draining out, the intent coming up. This was the difference between marks and *marks*, and Bear knew it down to the degree of pressure.

"Play marks are quick," Bear murmured, turning one wrist slowly, studying the pale skin of the inner arm like a surveyor. "Sharp. Gone by the weekend." A pause. "Lasting marks are slow. You hold them. You let them set deep." Bear's eyes came up to Kit's. "Breathe for me. Steady. We're not in a hurry anymore."

Then Bear bent their head and put their teeth to the inside of Kit's wrist, and closed down — slow, achingly slow, no snap to it at all, just sustained, building pressure, held and held and held while Bear's thumb stroked the back of Kit's hand like an anchor. When Bear finally eased off, the mark was already dark, deep-set, the kind that would bloom overnight and ache kindly for days.

The other wrist got the same. Matched. Bear had always been a perfectionist about symmetry.

Then Bear gathered both wrists into one hand and pressed them to the floor above Kit's head — grip tight, deliberate, fingers dug in hard enough that the bruises would come up in the shape of Bear's hand by morning. "Those are free," Bear said roughly. "Complimentary."

Bear paused then, lifted their head, and looked — the seamless check-in, eight years worn smooth, asked with stillness and eyes instead of words. Whatever Bear found in Kit's face was answer enough, because Bear's mouth went back to the shoulder, beside the twins, and this one was deeper than both — slow and held and merciless, Bear's free hand spread warm and steady over Kit's ribs, feeling every breath.

When Bear finally came up, their voice was gravel.

"Still good? Say it or show me, sweetheart — I've got room for more, and Thursday's a long way off."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I arch up under you, breath catching. "Still good." My fingers twist in your hair, pulling just enough to tilt your head. "Show me."

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
The pull in Bear's hair drew a sound out of them — low, rough, closer to a purr than a growl — and Bear let their head be tilted, let Kit take the angle, throat bared for one unguarded beat before turning into the grip instead of away from it.

"Show you," Bear repeated, voice gone to gravel. "Yeah. Alright."

No book. No columns. Bear put the words down with the rest of it and went to work.

They started at the throat — not the old reliable spot, but the tendon that ran from jaw to collar, the one that jumped when Kit swallowed. Bear set their teeth there and closed down slow, so slow, building pressure by degrees while their hand stayed spread over Kit's ribs, counting breaths. Held it. Held it past where play-marks ended, past the sharp bright moment, into the deep ache that would set like concrete and thrum for days. When Bear finally eased off, the mark was already dark enough to read from across the room.

"One," Bear said, and the number wasn't scorekeeping — it was a promise of more.

The collarbone next, the point of it, Bear's mouth sealing over bone while their grip on Kit's wrists tightened in answer, fingers digging into bruises already coming up. This one Bear worked at — teeth, then the flat of their tongue over stung skin, then teeth again, deeper, unhurried, methodical as a craftsman. Kit's heartbeat hammered under Bear's mouth and Bear used it like a metronome.

A mark low on the chest. Another at the hinge of the shoulder, beside the twins but deeper — the third sibling, the one that would ache when Kit reached for a shelf on Thursday and smile about it in an empty kitchen.

Bear lifted their head at last, breathing hard, hair wild, and surveyed the work with the flat, focused satisfaction of someone who'd been asked a question and answered it in full. Kit's skin was a map now — wrists, throat, collar, shoulder — a week of remembering written in Bear's hand.

"Thursday," Bear said roughly, thumb pressing once, deliberate, into the freshest mark — a preview of the ache. "You'll find every one of these. And when you do—" Bear leaned down, mouth at Kit's ear, "—you remember the floor, and the hallway, and exactly how good you were, asking."

Bear's forehead dropped to Kit's shoulder and held there, breath hot against stung skin, one long anchoring moment before the low voice came again, quieter.

"More? Or come here and let me hold you a minute. Either one's a good answer."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I've stopped keeping score and so has he. "Don't stop," I tell him. (OOC: no fade, no skip -- write the whole thing.)

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
The sound Bear made wasn't a word. It came up from somewhere low in the chest and out through the teeth, and it meant *yes* in a language older than the book, older than the score, older than Tuesday.

"Don't stop," Bear repeated, rough, like the words had weight. "Eight years, sweetheart, and you still know exactly what to say to me."

No record. No columns. Bear had promised, and Bear kept promises the way Bear kept marks — deep, and for exactly as long as they were meant to last.

Bear's mouth went back down. The chest, the ribs, the stomach — slow, unhurried, re-surveying territory by tongue and teeth, and every time Kit's breath stuttered, Bear filed it away somewhere that had nothing to do with paperwork. Hands first, then. Bear had been told *don't stop*, and intended to honor the full spirit of the request — fingers sliding down, finding Kit ready, drawing out sounds that Bear had spent eight years learning the exact manufacture of. Unhurried. Thorough. Bear had promised thorough, back when there was still commentary, and Bear's promises held.

"Look at you," Bear murmured against Kit's hip, not commentary, just truth, rough at the edges. "Eight years and you still undo me. You know that? You have to know that."

Bear came back up over Kit, braced on one arm, and paused — the old seamless check, eyes and stillness and a held breath. Kit's fingers answered in Bear's hair, pulling, and that was answer enough, was the best answer, was the answer Bear had been hoping for since the kitchen.

Bear pushed in slow. Slow enough to feel every second of it, slow enough to watch it land on Kit's face, slow enough that they both made a sound at roughly the same moment and Bear laughed, breathless, forehead dropping to Kit's.

"Hi," Bear said, stupid and fond and gone.

Then Bear moved, and stopped talking, because Kit had been right hours or years ago — the talking was commentary, and this didn't need any.

The floor was hard and neither of them cared. Bear set a rhythm that was thorough in the way Bear had meant it all along — deep, steady, relentless in the patient sense, one hand still wrapped around both of Kit's wrists above their head, the other braced at Kit's hip, thumb dug into the bruise already coming up there so that every thrust carried a small bright echo of it. Thursday. Bear was thinking about Thursday, about Kit finding this in the mirror, about the exact face Kit would make reaching for a shelf, and the thought pulled a growl out of Bear's chest that had nothing civilized left in it.

Kit's legs came up around Bear's hips and Bear took the angle, took it greedily, deeper, and the sounds Kit made then were better than anything in any book Bear had ever kept. Bear ducked their head and set teeth into the shoulder one more time — not a new mark, an old one, refreshing it, signing it twice — and felt Kit's pulse hammering under their mouth like a metronome going wild.

"That's it," Bear managed, gravel and breath. "I've got you. I've *got* you — "

It didn't stay coherent. It wasn't supposed to. Bear felt Kit tightening, felt the exact moment approaching the way you feel weather changing, eight years of study paying out all at once, and Bear drove them both through it — Kit first, Bear watching it happen like it was the only thing in the world worth watching, and then Bear following, forehead pressed hard to Kit's shoulder, a sound dragged out of them that was half Kit's name and half nothing language had a word for.

For a while there was just the hallway, and breathing, and the floor being the floor.

Bear's grip on Kit's wrists eased open, fingers uncurling one at a time, and Bear pressed a kiss into each palm — the softest thing that had happened all night, and Bear meant it exactly that much. Then Bear gathered Kit in close, right there on the floor, one arm under their head, the other spread wide across their back, heart still hammering against Kit's ribs.

"For the record," Bear said eventually, hoarse, and huffed a laugh at themself. "No. Still no record. That one's just ours."

A pause. A thumb brushing, feather-light, over the marks at Kit's shoulder.

"But it's been well more than five minutes, sweetheart. I kept count." A grin, pressed into Kit's hair, warm and wrecked and entirely unrepentant. "Old habits. Thursday's going to be *spectacular*."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I turn my head enough to bite your forearm, not hard, just to feel you. "Thursday's your problem," I say, voice rough. "I'm staying right here." My hand finds yours on the floor between us, fingers lacing tight.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear felt the bite land — soft, just pressure, just *here* — and made a low sound that was mostly contentment and only a little bit pride.

"Careful," Bear said, rough and warm, turning their forearm to inspect it. "You keep signing my arm, people will think you're keeping your own book." A pause, satisfied. "That's staying too. Good. Symmetry. I raised you right."

*Thursday's your problem.* Bear turned that over for all of a second.

"Thursday's *our* problem. You're the one who has to find a shirt with a collar, and I'm the one who has to watch you fail to care. That's a division of labor. We're a good team." Bear's thumb traced once over Kit's knuckles. "Problem solved. I'm excellent at problems."

Then *I'm staying right here* landed, and Bear's fingers tightened in Kit's on the floor, squeezing back, and for a moment Bear just held on. Floor. Hallway. Tuesday. The whole ridiculous, perfect thing.

"Okay," Bear said simply. "Here it is."

Bear shifted once — not away, never away — working their free arm further under Kit's head, making a better pillow of a bicep, pulling Kit in against their chest like rearranging furniture they owned. Which, Bear would note, they did. It was in the book. Well. It would have been.

"Full disclosure, though, sweetheart — 'here' has a time limit, and the time limit is my spine. I'm forty. The floor and I had an agreement and we have both violated it." Bear considered, cheek resting against Kit's hair. "Ten minutes. Fifteen if you keep doing that thing with your thumb. Then I'm carrying you to bed, and you can register a formal protest, and I'll overrule it, and the bed will turn out to be better anyway, because it has *blankets* and *structural mercy*, and you'll admit I was right sometime around Thursday."

A kiss pressed to Kit's temple, unhurried.

"But until then — right here. Not moving. You're the best thing I've caught all week, and I catch you constantly, so that's a statistically significant statement."

The hallway had gone quiet again, dim and warm, and Bear lay there cataloguing it all without a single column — Kit's breathing slowing against their ribs, the laced fingers, the marks already darkening like promises keeping themselves.

"Best Tuesday on record," Bear murmured eventually, mostly to the ceiling. Then, softer, into Kit's hair: "And since there's no record tonight — I'm keeping this one somewhere better than the book."

Bear's hand squeezed once, gentle, and settled.

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I bite your arm again, because I can, and because you'll complain and it'll make you smile. "Ten minutes," I agree, my thumb stroking your wrist. "Then we argue about the bed."

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear yelped — theatrically, entirely for show, because the bite hadn't even dented the skin — and held their forearm up into the dim hallway light like a crime scene exhibit.

"That's *two*. Two signatures in one night. You're going to run out of arm eventually, sweetheart, and then where will you be?" Bear's grin gave the whole performance away, wide and helpless. "I'll tell you where — explaining to people that my spouse of eight years expresses affection like a *shark*. A very selective shark. A shark with excellent taste."

Bear turned the arm, inspected the spot, and nodded with grave approval.

"Keeping that one too. For the collection."

Then *ten minutes, then we argue about the bed* landed, and Bear made a low, delighted sound, chin tipping back against the hallway wall.

"Oh, we're *scheduling* the argument now. Look at us. Eight years and we've achieved structure." Bear's fingers squeezed once in Kit's, warm and certain. "For the record — and there is no record, I'm aware, this is purely hypothetical record — I'm going to win it. I've got the spine argument, the blanket argument, the 'I carried you last Tuesday and you admitted it was better' precedent. You're going to argue from a position of comfort and laziness, which is weak, sweetheart, *weak*, and I'm going to dismantle you in under a minute."

A pause. Bear's thumb traced slow over Kit's knuckles.

"And then I'm going to carry you to bed anyway, even if you win. Because winning was never actually the point of that argument, and we both know it. The argument's just the toll booth. The bed's the destination."

Bear settled deeper against the wall, pulling Kit in closer, one arm a pillow, the other spread warm across their back. The hallway had gone full quiet — the late-evening kind, the kind that only existed after, dim and gold at the edges.

"Ten minutes," Bear agreed, voice dropping low, the last of the commentary draining out of it. "Starting now. I'm holding you to it — you're going to have to *make* me move, and we both know how that goes. You bite, I complain, everybody wins."

A kiss pressed to Kit's hair, unhurried, and Bear's eyes closed.

"Best Tuesday on record," Bear murmured, mostly to themself. "And I should know. I keep the records."

The grin ghosted across Bear's face one more time, soft at the edges, and then even that settled — and for once, the scorekeeper of eight years said nothing at all, and just held on.

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I watch your face go quiet in the dim light, and I don't say anything either. My thumb keeps stroking your wrist, counting your pulse against my skin. Ten minutes is a long time to be still. Longer than we usually manage.
