rung_labels.evidence: clothes becoming someone else's problem

rung_labels.label: soft_deflect
rung_labels.evidence: So keep talking, sweetheart.

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: put their teeth to the inside of Kit's wrist, and closed down

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: Bear pushed in slow.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Kit had made it as far as the kitchen doorway before Bear moved, which was further than usual and had clearly been allowed.

"You let me get that far," Kit said, backing up one step.

"I did," Bear agreed. "I'm feeling generous."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: "Don't be," I say, and go.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear had been generous. Generous and loose-limbed and standing just inside the living room with his weight forward, because he'd known exactly what "don't be" meant the way he always did — the same way a deer knows what a sound in the brush means, except the deer didn't usually *want* it.



Kit closed the gap fast, and Bear met the charge shoulder-first, turning Kit's own momentum into a spin that drove them both sideways into the doorframe. The impact knocked the air out of both of them — Bear didn't pretend otherwise — but he'd already got an arm locked around Kit's ribs and a hand fisted in the back of their shirt, hauling Kit's weight off-balance and into him.

"Bear," Kit had once told him during one of their rare and thorough negotiations, "wasn't a request for gentleness." It was a name used like a grip.

He got his knee between Kit's legs and drove them back two steps, then three, eating up ground until Kit's shoulder blades found the wall. The hit wasn't soft. The hallway was narrow enough that Bear's back caught the opposite wall while his front pressed flush against Kit, and he could feel the laugh building in Kit's chest before it ever made a sound.

"That far," Bear said, low, his mouth close to Kit's ear. "Eight years and you still give me that much runway." His hand tightened in the shirt. He let Kit feel the pull, let them feel the choice they didn't have yet, and then he bit down on the side of Kit's neck — not careful, not careful at all — a hard crescent of teeth sinking into the muscle where it met the shoulder.

He pulled back just enough to look. The mark was already coming up red. Bear smiled, wolfish and satisfied, and waited to see what Kit did about it.

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I laugh against his shoulder, breathless. "You like the chase too much," I say, and twist, getting an arm up between us. I shove hard, not to get away—just to make him work for it.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear gave half a step — just enough to make Kit feel the shove *land* — and used the space to strip Kit's shirt over their head in a single rough pull. He'd been wanting to do that since the doorway. The bite mark glowed red on Kit's shoulder.

"Work for it," Bear agreed, and dropped his shoulder into Kit's chest.

He caught Kit around the thighs and lifted. The hallway protested — Bear's back found the opposite wall for the second time that minute — but Kit's legs had already locked around his waist, that eight-year reflex doing its job. One of Bear's hands caught both Kit's wrists and pinned them above their head, and he bit down on Kit's collarbone, dragging his teeth along the ridge of it with zero delicacy.

He pulled back, breathing hard. "One-nothing."

Then he shifted his grip, hauled Kit sideways out of the hallway and down the hall toward the bedroom, because the hallway was too narrow for what he actually wanted and he was finished being generous about anything.

He dropped Kit onto the mattress and followed, one knee between Kit's thighs, the other hand fisted in Kit's hair — not pulling yet, just letting them feel the weight of it. Bear's own shirt was gone somewhere between the hallway and here; he didn't remember losing it and didn't care. He leaned down until his mouth was at Kit's ear.

"You shoved," he said, and bit the lobe. "That's a mark I get to keep."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: He catches me in the hallway, which was always going to happen, and I don't put much into getting away.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear felt the lack of resistance before he saw it — the way Kit's weight settled into his grip instead of fighting against it, the way the spin into the doorframe happened almost politely. It was a gift, and they both knew it.

He didn't thank Kit for it. He *used* it.

One arm around Kit's ribs, the other hand already fisted in the back of their shirt, and Bear hauled them off the ground with a grunt that he didn't bother hiding. Kit's back hit the wall hard enough to rattle the hallway mirror, and Bear pressed in close — close enough to feel Kit's heartbeat through what was left of their skin-to-skin contact, close enough to smell the sweat that meant Kit had been running hot since the doorway.

"You stopped fighting," Bear said against Kit's jaw. Not a question. His mouth was already moving south, teeth finding the curve of Kit's neck, and he bit down where the trapezius met the collarbone — a clean, deliberate crescent that would sit angry-red for days. He felt Kit's breath hitch and smiled into the skin.

"One-nothing," he said, straightening.

Kit twisted — fast, sharp, an arm coming up between them — and Bear let them get exactly halfway through the motion before he caught the wrist, redirected, and drove them back down the hall. The bedroom door swung open under Kit's shoulder blades. The bed caught them both a half-second later, Bear's weight following Kit down onto the mattress, one knee wedging between Kit's thighs with practiced efficiency.

He stripped his own shirt over his head and didn't remember deciding to. The air was cool on his back. Kit's skin was warm under his palms.

"Two," Bear said, reading Kit's expression the way he always did — three moves ahead, eight years of pattern-matching — and caught Kit's jaw in one hand, tilting their head back to expose the throat he'd already marked. He looked at the red bloom already rising there, catalogued it, and leaned down to put his mouth against it.

"You gave me that runway," he murmured against the fresh mark. "So I get to use it."

Then he bit — harder this time, the kind that made Bear's own jaw ache — and held, waiting to feel Kit decide what to do about it.

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I arch up against him, a sharp gasp escaping before I can bite it back. My fingers twist in the sheets. "Three," I manage, breathless, and then I'm laughing again, rough and low. "You're keeping score now?"

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear's head came up at "three." The sound Kit made — that gasp swallowed halfway into a laugh — had already gone straight to the base of his spine, but the *number* was what made him grin.

"Oh, you're counting now," he said, and his voice came out rougher than he intended. He liked that. He liked that a lot.

He shifted his weight, one knee pressing firmer between Kit's thighs, and let his hand trail down from Kit's jaw to the side of their throat — not squeezing, just resting there, thumb hooked under the jawline where he could feel the pulse hammering. "Three. In—" He glanced at the clock on the nightstand, genuinely calculated. "Four minutes. You're generous with the score too."

That earned him another one of Kit's laughs, and Bear felt it move through Kit's chest into his own where they pressed together. He catalogued it: *laughing means winning, laughing means not-yet-serious, laughing means they haven't decided to flip this yet.* Eight years of that particular data set and his body had already started adjusting — weight rolling a half-inch to the balls of his feet, free hand bracing against the mattress so he could move off Kit fast if Kit moved first.

But Kit didn't move first. Kit arched *into* him, fingers twisted in sheets, which was its own kind of concession and one that Bear had learned not to take at face value. Kit gave runway. Kit gave ground. Kit did it on purpose because the getting-caught was the point, and because they wanted to see what Bear would do with it.

So Bear did something he hadn't done yet — he leaned back. Just enough to look at Kit properly, braced on one arm, the other hand still curved around their throat. The marks he'd put there were coming up in a constellation: the crescent on the trapezius, the ragged line along the collarbone, the darker bloom higher on the neck where he'd held too long on purpose. They were good marks. *His* marks. And Kit was counting them.

"You want to make it four?" he asked, low, and rolled his hips down once — slow, deliberate, the kind of pressure that wasn't a fight but was absolutely a claim. He watched Kit's face for it, the split-second where control slipped, and when it came he bit his own lip to keep from smiling too wide.

Then he dropped his mouth back to Kit's throat, just below the ear, and spoke against the skin: "Then you've got to take one of mine first." He turned his head, offered the broad column of his own neck — a gift and a dare in equal measure. "Fair's fair. You're keeping score. Score something back."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: We don't make it to the bedroom. The floor is fine. Clothes are a problem we solve badly and fast.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear's back hit the floor first — not gracefully, not on purpose — and he took Kit down with him, shoulder and hip slamming hardwood hard enough that he'd feel it for a week and not care even slightly. The hallway runner bunched under them. Somewhere in the tangle a belt buckle bit his forearm and he didn't notice until later.

Clothes were the problem. They were always the problem in moments like this — eight years of learning that the *hurry* was part of it, that fumbling and swearing and getting a sleeve caught around one wrist was better than taking the time to do it right. Bear stripped Kit's shirt over their head in a motion that caught on their chin and he didn't slow down to fix it. He yanked. Fabric popped free. Kit's skin was already flushed down the sternum, and Bear put his mouth on the sternum before he'd even decided to.

His own shirt he'd lost somewhere earlier — didn't matter. His jeans were a different problem. He got them open and shoved down with both hands, and the haste of it — the awkwardness, the knee-bumping against Kit's — made him laugh short and breathless against Kit's collarbone.

"Floor's cold," he said, as if that were a complaint, and then Kit's hand found him and Bear stopped talking for a moment.

He braced one arm against the hardwood, the other hooked behind Kit's knee, and guided Kit's leg up over his hip — practical, logistical, the kind of thing you figured out in two seconds flat because the floor didn't give you a mattress's cooperation. The angle was wrong in a way that wouldn't have been wrong on the bed, and he adjusted, and the adjustment meant pressing Kit's shoulders down into the rug with the flat of his hand to reposition, which meant Bear could feel Kit's pulse under his palm, rapid, *had* to be rapid because his own was.

"You counted three," he said, low, his mouth close to Kit's ear, and he didn't wait for a response before he pushed in — slow despite everything, slow because *that* was the discipline he had and the one he didn't — and felt Kit's whole body shift under him.

He held still for one second. Two. Let Kit feel all of it.

Then he moved, and the floorboard under his knee creaked in complaint, and Bear didn't care about the floorboard either.

The rhythm he found was hard — not punishing, not yet, but the kind that left no question about where the weight was coming from, the kind that drove Kit's upper back against the hallway rug with each stroke. He kept one hand flat on Kit's sternum, feeling the percussion of their breathing, and used the other to pin Kit's wrist above their head because he wanted it there, because the constraint of it — Kit's arm stretched long, the tension in the tendon — made something hot and sharp move through his chest.

"Four," he breathed against Kit's jaw, not because Kit had scored it but because Bear was counting now too, in his own way — four places he'd meant to leave marks, four angles he wanted to try, four reasons this wasn't going to end with either of them walking straight in the morning.

He shifted his weight forward, changed the angle, and bit down on the meat of Kit's shoulder exactly where the first crescent was already fading. Not fresh. Deliberate. *Layering.* A reminder.

The hallway mirror, visible from the floor at this angle, showed them both — a tangle of limbs and shadow and skin, and Bear glanced at it for half a second before looking back at Kit's face, because Kit's face was the better instrument. Always had been.

"Floor," he muttered, almost to himself, "you picked the floor." And then he was moving again, faster now, both hands finding Kit's hips because he needed purchase and the rug didn't give any, and the sound he made when Kit's back arched off the floor was not a word in any language.

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: The rug's a lost cause," I grunt, my head knocking back against the floor as I push up to meet him. My free hand finds his hair, pulling just to feel him react. "Five."

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear's head snapped forward with the pull — a sharp, involuntary jerk that brought his forehead close enough to Kit's that their breath collided — and the sound he made was halfgrunt, half-laugh, torn out of him before he could decide which it was going to be.

"Five," he repeated, and his voice came out wrecked at the edges. "You've been *waiting* to do that."

His hand came up and closed around Kit's wrist where it was fisted in his hair, but he didn't pull it free. He held it there, fingers wrapped tight, feeling the tendon flex against his palm. Let Kit keep the grip. Let Kit feel that it was *allowed* — that the hair-pull was the concession Bear was making in exchange for every mark he'd already drawn, for the floor, for the shoulder biting, for all of it.

The floorboard protested again under his knee. He shifted, drove back in harder, and watched Kit's expression go taut — catalogued it the way he catalogued everything, three moves ahead, eight years of reading the same instrument — and filed *hair-pull made it worse for them too* next to *five means they're keeping score means they're still playing means they haven't decided to flip this yet*.

But the flip was coming. It was always coming. Kit gave runway and then took it back and the taking-back was the part Bear liked best.

So he moved first.

He released Kit's wrist, planted both hands flat on the floor on either side of Kit's head, and *lifted* — pulling out just enough to change the angle entirely, then rolling them both sideways in one rough motion that bunched the hallway runner under them and put Kit's back against the hardwood where the rug wasn't. The new position put Bear's shoulder under him and his weight angled differently, and when he pressed back in, the sound Kit made told him the adjustment had been the right one.

"Five to you," he said against the hinge of Kit's jaw. "That's still mine by three."

He wasn't wrong and they both knew it. But the number was a dare now — it had stopped being a score somewhere around the hair-pull and become an invitation. *Catch up*, it meant. *Try*.

Bear bit down on the tendon in Kit's neck, hard enough to feel the pulse hammering against his teeth, and held there while he moved — steady, relentless, the kind of rhythm that didn't pause for anything, not for the floorboard, not for his own breathing, not for the fact that his shoulder was going to ache tomorrow in a place that had nothing to do with the wall.

He let go of the bite. Looked at what he'd left. Then he caught Kit's jaw in one hand and turned their face toward the hallway mirror — visible from this angle, a dark rectangle showing the two of them on the floor in pieces, mostly shadow and motion and the red map of marks climbing Kit's neck and shoulder.

"Look," he said. Not quiet. Not loud. The kind of voice he used when he meant it. He watched Kit's eyes in the mirror instead of on Kit's face, because the mirror showed him both at once — the front and the reflection, Kit's expression and Bear's own behind it, jaw set, eyes intent, a man who had been doing this for eight years and still hadn't gotten bored.

His hand stayed on Kit's jaw, thumb pressing into the hinge, holding their head turned. He moved faster. The floor didn't forgive speed and he didn't ask it to.

"Six's yours if you can take it," he said, low, directly into Kit's ear, and then he bit the back of their shoulder — the same spot, *again*, layered so deep now that the first crescent was invisible under the new one — and waited for whatever Kit decided to do about it.

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: He gets his teeth into my shoulder hard enough to leave something and I tell him to do it again, and he does.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear didn't hesitate. The word *again* had barely left Kit's mouth and his teeth were already sinking back into the same place — the meat of the shoulder, the spot that had gone from red to purple over the last several minutes — and he bit down with the full weight of his jaw behind it, no half-measure, no negotiation in the pressure. He felt the new crescent overlap the old one like stacking paper, felt Kit's muscle jump under the bite, and the sound Kit made went through Bear's spine like a wire pulled taut.

He held it. He held it long enough that his own jaw ached, long enough that the tendons in his neck stood out, and only let go when the shape of the mark satisfied him — deep, clean, unmistakable. He looked at it the way a man looks at handwriting he's proud of.

"Again," he repeated back, rough, almost incredulous. "You're *telling* me."



That changed the shape of the thing and they both knew it. Kit giving runway was one thing — Bear had been running down that runway for eight years and knew every inch of it. But Kit *asking* for it was different. Kit asking meant the score had stopped being a game and started being a transaction, and Bear did not do transactions halfway.

He pulled back — out, off, all the way off — and put his hands on Kit's hips and *moved* them, dragging Kit six inches across the hardwood into the patch of floor where the overhead light caught skin. He wanted the light. He wanted to see the whole map while he added to it.

"You want to get hit," he said, braced over Kit, both arms straight, sweat running from his jaw down his sternum. He wasn't asking either. He watched Kit's face the way he always did — three moves ahead, eight years of pattern-matching — and what he read there told him exactly how much force would be right. Not a question. A confirmation.

His open palm came down across Kit's thigh — hard, flat, the crack of it echoing off the hallway walls — and he watched the impact bloom pink under his hand, watched Kit's whole body jolt up off the floor, and felt the satisfaction of it move through him like a swallowed drink. He didn't wait to be asked. He did it again, slightly higher, slightly harder, his hand shaped now to the geography of Kit's skin.



"Six," he said, because he was counting too and had been counting the whole time, and then he caught Kit's wrist where it was reaching for him and pinned it back down to the floor beside their head, leaning his weight into it until he could feel the strain in Kit's shoulder and the rapid flutter of the pulse under his thumb.

He looked at Kit's neck. The marks were layered there now — three, four, overlapping crescents climbing from the trapezius up to just below the ear, each one darker than the last, the skin angry and raised. Bear's breathing went uneven looking at them. Not from exertion alone.

"Here's what's going to happen," he said, and his voice had dropped into the register it only ever got in the middle of this, low and unhurried and absolutely certain. He shifted his weight back onto his knees, pulling Kit's wrist with him, keeping the arm stretched long overhead, and reached down with his free hand to grip Kit's jaw — not gently, thumb pressing into the soft spot below the ear where the jaw met the neck.

"You're going to tell me to do it again," he said, "and I'm going to do it differently. And then you're going to count it. Out loud."

He leaned down, mouth hovering an inch from the bruised landscape of Kit's shoulder, close enough that Kit could feel the heat of his breath on the marks.

"And if you want six to be yours," he murmured, "you'd better mean it."

Then he bit — not the shoulder this time, but the meat of Kit's bicep, sudden and hard, a place he'd never marked before — and drove back into Kit with the full force of his hips at the exact same moment, because the two things happening at once was the point, because he wanted to know what Kit's body did when it couldn't decide which sensation to answer first.

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I gasp, back arching off the floor. The impact of his thrust collides with the sharp, grounding pain of his teeth. My free hand scrabbles at the back of his head, fingers tangling in his hair, holding him there. "Six," I choke out, voice raw. "Fuck. Seven."

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear went still at *seven*.



Not stopped — still. The way a machine goes still when it hits something it recognizes. His jaw was still locked into the meat of Kit's bicep, teeth buried in fresh skin, and he could feel Kit's fingers fisted so tight in his hair that his scalp pulled. Two counts. One breath. Kit had taken six and then *kept going* and given him seven before Bear had finished processing the six.

He released the bite. Pulled his head back far enough to see it — the crescent already darkening on Kit's bicep, a place that had been untouched until thirty seconds ago, and it was going to bruise in a shape people would ask about for a week.

"Seven," he said, and the word came out strangled. Not from exertion. From the sound Kit made saying it — raw, choked, the kind of voice that only came out when the body had overridden the brain entirely. Bear had been listening for that voice for eight years and it still hit him like a match struck in a dark room.

He shifted his weight up, both knees planting on the hardwood, and took Kit's wrist — the one still pinned — and pulled it down, threading their fingers together and slamming the joined hands against the floor beside Kit's head. Not restraining. *Anchoring.* Something for both of them to hold.

"Two in one breath," he said, and drove forward — a single, devastating stroke that used the new angle, the new height of his hips, all of it at once — and watched Kit's whole body fold around the sensation. "You don't get *two* without earning them."

His free hand found Kit's throat again. Not squeezing. Resting there, thumb along the pulse point, feeling the hammer that Kit's own count had started.

But the score had changed shape and he knew it. Seven. *Seven.* Kit had been three behind and had closed the gap in a single gasp, which meant the runway Bear had been so generous with had done exactly what Kit always did with it — turned into ground they took back. Faster than last time. Faster than any time.

Something hot and bright moved through Bear's chest. Not frustration. Never frustration with this.

"Eight," he said, low, and bit down on the tendon of Kit's neck where the marks were deepest, the spot that had been purple since the hallway, and *held* — unrepentant, jaw aching, refusing to let go until he felt Kit's pulse stutter against his teeth — because if Kit wanted to close the gap, then Bear was going to make every single point cost something neither of them would forget by morning.

Then he let go. Looked at the damage. Looked at Kit's face.

"Mine," he said. Not the score. Not a point. Something bigger and older and truer than a number, and he let Kit hear exactly what he meant by it before he moved again.

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: "Marks," I tell him. "I want to find them in the mirror tomorrow and I want them to still hurt on Thursday." I put my wrists where he can reach them.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear saw the wrists before he understood them.

They came up out of Kit's shoulders like an offering, open-palmed, wrists turned up to the overhead light where the veins stood out blue against flushed skin. Kit put them where Bear could reach. Not hiding them. Not making him work for it.

Bear stopped breathing for a second.

In eight years, Kit gave runway and took it back. Kit played the chase and flipped the score. Kit arched into every bite and counted every mark and made Bear *work* for every inch of ground. But this — wrists up, open, *placed* — was something else. This was Kit saying *I'm done running for tonight* and meaning it, and the thing that did to Bear's nervous system was not comparable to anything else in his experience.

He reached down and closed both hands around Kit's wrists.

Not rough. The grip was firm enough that Kit would feel the width of his palms, the calluses, the steadiness of it — and firm enough that if Kit pulled, Bear would hold. He pressed Kit's wrists together above their head with one hand and wrapped the other around Kit's throat again, thumb finding the pulse that was hammering so hard he could feel it in his own fingertips.

"You want them to hurt on Thursday," he said, and his voice had gone low and quiet — the register that meant he wasn't performing anymore, that the scorekeeping had burned off and what was left underneath was just the thing itself. He leaned down until his forehead rested against Kit's, both of them sweating, breath colliding. "You want to look in the mirror and see something *I* did."

He rolled his hips — slow, deep, a full stroke that he felt all the way up his spine — and watched Kit's eyes lose focus for a half-second. He waited for them to come back.

"That's not a score," he said. "That's not a point. You know that, right?"

He bit Kit's collarbone again — the same place, the third layer, the one that had been raw since the hallway — and *held*, jaw straining, while he moved in the same relentless rhythm he'd found on the floor. Kit's wrists were warm in his grip. The overhead light was hot on both their backs. Bear could feel every mark he'd left — the constellation on Kit's neck, the purple crescents layered on the shoulder, the deep impression in the bicep, the pink palm-prints on the thigh — and knowing they were there, knowing Kit would find them in the mirror tomorrow, made something move through him that had no number attached to it.

He released the bite and dragged his mouth up the side of Kit's neck, teeth trailing skin, until his lips were at Kit's ear.

"I'll give you Thursday," he said. "I'll give you every mark you can carry." He tightened his grip on Kit's wrists — not pulling, just making the weight of it undeniable — and shifted his angle so the next stroke landed exactly where it would make Kit's spine curve. "But you put your wrists there yourself, so *you* keep track. Every one. Out loud. Or I stop."

Not a threat. A condition. The same condition Kit had been setting all night, turned back around and handed over.

Bear bit the soft place where Kit's shoulder met their neck — the one spot he'd been saving, the spot nothing had touched yet — and waited to hear what Kit did with the count.

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I arch into him, the new bite a lightning strike. My voice comes out ragged, but clear. "Eight. Nine."

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear heard *nine* before he'd finished hearing *eight*, and the two numbers landed on him like a handprint — flat, warm, unmistakable.

He exhaled against Kit's shoulder, a shaky press of air that raked over the marks already there, and for a moment he didn't move at all. Just held. Both of Kit's wrists pressed together above their head, his other hand still curved around the throat, and he could feel the words travel through Kit's chest before the sound reached him — the vibration of *nine* making itself known under his palm a half-second before it hit his ear.

"Nine," he repeated, and this time his voice was wrecked. He hadn't meant it to be. He cleared his throat and it didn't help.

Then he moved.

He drove forward — one stroke, two, three — building the rhythm back to where it had been before the wrists changed everything, because the wrists hadn't stopped it, they'd only made it heavier. Each thrust shook Kit's shoulders against the floor and Bear watched the marks he'd already left shift and wobble with the impact, the layered crescents on the trapezius catching the overhead light at different angles, purple and red and angry. He wanted more of them. He wanted the whole map.

He released Kit's wrists and dragged both hands down — over the ribs, the hips — and gripped, pulling Kit up to meet him, because the angle had been punishing Kit's lower back against the hardwood and he was not going to finish this with Kit too sore to walk tomorrow. That was not the kind of mark he was after.

"Ten," he said, and slapped his palm against Kit's hip — not a hit this time, a *claim*, flat and loud and deliberate — and drove into it. "Ten. You're at nine, I'm taking ten, and you're going to *say* it."

His hands found Kit's waist and held. Bear braced himself on straight arms and looked down at what he'd made — the red map climbing from collarbone to jaw, the crescents stacked so deep on the shoulder that the earliest ones had gone the blue-black of old ink, the bite on the bicep swelling dark at the center, the pink handprints on the thigh fading at the edges. Kit's skin was a document. Eight years in, and Bear could still be undone by the sight of his own handwriting on someone else's body.

He leaned down, mouth at Kit's sternum, and spoke into the sweat there.

"Thursday," he said. "You find every one. You count them in the mirror and you tell me the number when you get home." He bit — sternum, center, new territory — and felt Kit's body bow under him. He held the bite and moved through it, relentless, the floorboard and the rug and the hallway all forgotten, only the weight of Kit and the heat of Kit and the knowledge that every sound Kit made was a receipt for something Bear had done.

He let go of the sternum mark. Looked at it. Ran his tongue over it once, smoothing the raised skin, tasting salt.

"Ten's mine," he said, lifting his head. His eyes were dark, blown wide, fixed on Kit's face with the particular focus of a man who had been counting all night and had just realized the numbers had stopped being the point. "But you gave me nine, so—" He shook his head, almost laughing, breath gone. "You're supposed to be keeping score for *you*."

He caught Kit's jaw and held it, thumb pressing into the hinge, turning Kit's face toward him so there was no looking away from what came next.

"Say it anyway," he said. "Ten."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I've stopped keeping score and so has he. "Don't stop," I tell him. (OOC: no fade, no skip -- write the whole thing.)

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear heard it. *Don't stop.* Two words, and they undid the last thing he'd been holding onto — the counting, the score, the little architecture of numbers that had kept the night structured.

He didn't stop.

He braced both hands on the floor beside Kit's head, locked his elbows, and changed the rhythm entirely — longer strokes, deeper, each one pulling a sound out of Kit that Bear felt more than heard. The floorboard stopped complaining somewhere around the third thrust because Bear's knee had found a spot where the hardwood didn't move, and he planted there and used it as a fulcrum, driving forward with everything he had.

Kit's wrists were free now. Bear hadn't let go so much as lost them, and he glanced down to see Kit's hands pressing flat against the floor, fingers splayed, gripping — not reaching for him, not pulling away, just *holding on*, and the sight of it — those open palms braced against the hardwood like they were trying to keep from being swept off it — made Bear's whole body tighten.

"Kit," he said. Just the name. No count attached. He said it again with the next thrust, lower, guttural, and felt the sound move through both of them where they were joined.

He dropped his weight onto one arm and brought the other hand down — not to a mark, not to a throat, but to the small of Kit's back, fingers spreading wide, pressing Kit's hips up to meet him at the exact angle that made Kit's spine curve in a way that almost lifted them both off the floor. He held it there. Steadied. Adjusted his knee a half-inch and drove in again, and this time the sound Kit made was the one — the one Bear had been working toward since the hallway, since the first bite, since Kit had said *don't be* and meant *be more*.

"Say it again," Bear rasped, not because he needed permission, not because the score still mattered, but because hearing it in Kit's mouth was the only instrument that mattered anymore. "Don't stop. Say it like you mean it."

He didn't wait for the answer. He lowered his mouth to Kit's jaw and bit the hinge — hard, the kind that would leave a shape visible in any light — and felt Kit's whole body clench under him, around him, and the reaction moved through Bear like current.

His hips found the rhythm again and he let it take him — not thinking, not cataloguing, not three moves ahead for once in eight years. Just the weight of Kit under him, the heat of Kit's skin against his palms, the map of marks he could feel by touch alone — shoulder, neck, collarbone, bicep, sternum, jaw — every one a place he'd been, every one a receipt for something he'd taken and been given in return.

The hand at Kit's small of the back slid lower, gripping, pulling Kit up to meet each thrust with more force than before. Bear's own breathing had gone ragged, open-mouthed, and he pressed his forehead against Kit's temple because he needed contact, more contact, every surface he could arrange. Sweat ran down his sternum. The overhead light was too bright and he didn't care. The hallway was too narrow and the floor was too hard and neither mattered.

He could feel it building — the thing at the base of his spine that had been winding tighter since the wrists, since the *marks* and the *Thursday* and all the promises in those words. His rhythm broke into something faster, less controlled, and he heard himself making sounds he didn't approve of — short, punched-out breaths against Kit's skin, a groan that he'd be embarrassed about if he were capable of embarrassment, which he was not.

"You — " he started, and lost it. His hand found Kit's jaw again, turning them so he could see Kit's face at the angle he wanted — eyes blown, mouth open, neck arched and crosshatched with every mark Bear had spent the night laying down. "Look at me. Look at me when you — "

He didn't finish the sentence. He drove forward — hard, deep, the last measured thrust he was going to manage — and felt the world narrow to a single point of contact, Kit's body gripping his, Kit's voice, Kit's name coming out of Bear's mouth in a broken string of syllables that stopped being language.

He came with his teeth sunk into Kit's shoulder, a final mark layered so deep into the others that it would have no independent shape in the morning — just a dark, composite bruise where all the bites had overlapped — and the sound he made against Kit's skin was low and torn and didn't stop for a long time.

His hips stuttered, slowed, stopped. His arms gave out and he collapsed forward onto Kit's chest, full weight, cheek pressed against the damp sternum where he'd left a bite mark so recent it was still raised. He could feel Kit's heartbeat under his ear. His own was everywhere — in his temples, in his throat, in the hand he'd left pressed against Kit's lower back where the skin was slick with sweat.

Neither of them moved.

The hallway light hummed. The hallway mirror showed the two of them on the floor in a tangle of limbs and shadow, Bear's back rising and falling with each labored breath, Kit underneath him and under the weight of every mark they'd made. The runner was bunched into a ball somewhere near Kit's left foot. A belt buckle lay under Bear's elbow.

Bear exhaled. His breath raked across the newest mark on Kit's sternum and he felt Kit's skin prickle under it.

He stayed there. Didn't lift his head. Didn't check the score — the score was ashes now, they'd both watched it burn, and what was left was this: Bear's weight on Kit, Kit's heartbeat under his ear, the red map of the night printed into skin that would go purple by morning and would still be findable by touch on Thursday.

His hand — the one at Kit's lower back — tightened. Not pulling. Just holding. The way he held the wrists. The way he held everything that mattered.

"Eight years," he mumbled against Kit's sternum, the words distorted by skin and sweat. He didn't finish the thought. He didn't need to. Eight years and the floor still felt like this, and Kit still gave him runway, and the marks still held, and neither of them had stopped yet — not really, not underneath.

He turned his head and pressed his mouth — open, soft, no teeth — against the nearest bruise on Kit's collarbone and held it there like a seal.

Then, quieter: "Thursday."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I let out a long, shaky breath, my fingers finally uncurling from the floor to drag through his hair. My whole body feels like one giant, throbbing mark. "Yeah," I rasp. "Thursday."

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear turned his face into the curve of Kit's neck and laughed.

Not a big sound. It was barely a sound at all — a vibration, a tremor that moved from his chest through the sternum he was pressed against and into Kit's skin, the kind of laugh that had nothing to do with humor and everything to do with the particular relief of being exactly where he was supposed to be. Eight years and that laugh still surprised him sometimes. He thought he'd outgrown the surprises.

He didn't lift his weight off Kit. Couldn't have, if he'd wanted to, which he didn't. His arms were done — two pillars of nothing, collapsed on either side of Kit's head where they'd been braced minutes ago. His right knee had gone numb against the hardwood and he'd find out about that later. Everything he had was spent and what was left was the slow, drowning warmth of having spent it.

His mouth was still against Kit's collarbone. He could feel the bite mark there under his lips — raised, hot, the edges of it already going hard with the particular density that meant it would sit in the skin for days. He pressed harder against it, not biting, just *sealing*, and felt the pulse beneath the bruise jump at the contact.

"Mmm," he said into Kit's skin. Not words. The animal acknowledgment that Kit was alive and warm and still here under him.

Then he did what he always did at the bottom of it, the part that never got negotiated and never got scored and never showed up in any count either of them kept. He rolled them both — carefully, slowly, all the efficiency gone from his movements now — until Kit was on their side and Bear was behind them, one arm hooked around Kit's ribs, the other hand flat against Kit's stomach, pulling them back until there was no gap between them. Kit's spine fit against his chest. His chin found the space above Kit's shoulder where the deepest marks were.

He breathed. In through the nose, out slow, and Kit's breathing was already finding the matching rhythm the way it always did, the way their bodies had learned to do somewhere around year three when they'd stopped needing to talk about the after and just started doing it.

The marks were everywhere. Bear knew their geography without looking — he'd placed every one, felt every one close under his teeth, watched each one bloom. The constellation on Kit's neck. The stacked crescents on the trapezius, deep enough now that they'd be indigo by morning. The bicep bite, swelling dark. The sternum, still raised. The jaw. The palm prints on the thigh, which would be less impressive by morning but would still be *his*. Thursday, Kit had said. Thursday, Bear had said back.

He pressed his lips to the back of Kit's neck — no teeth, just the press of them, slow, a line of warmth drawn from the hairline down to where the first serious bruise began.

"You're going to feel every one of those in the morning," he murmured, and the words were a promise rather than a warning, the way everything had been a promise tonight.

His arm tightened around Kit's ribs. His thumb traced a slow circle against Kit's stomach — not a caress, not exactly, more the absent handwriting of a man who needed to keep one hand on something solid.

The hallway light hummed. Somewhere in the apartment, a clock ticked. The floor was unforgiving and the runner was ruined and neither of them had moved toward the bedroom, which was fine, which had never been the point.

Bear closed his eyes. Kit's breathing was evening out under his palm — still ragged at the edges, still carrying the faint shake of the last few minutes, but settling, settling, finding the slow deep rhythm that meant the body was starting to forgive what the body had been asked to do. He matched it. Breath for breath, the way he always did, because he had learned early that the best thing he could give after everything he'd just taken was his own stillness.

His hand moved from Kit's stomach to the hip where he'd left the palm prints, and he rested his palm there — wide, warm, covering both marks, a hand that could hold them in place if holding was what they needed.

He stayed like that. Minutes, maybe. Long enough for Kit's heartbeat to slow under his forearm, long enough for his own breathing to stop being an effort, long enough for the hallway to go quiet and the marks to begin the long, slow process of becoming what they'd be on Thursday.

When he spoke, his voice was low and loose and barely there — the voice that only came out at the very bottom of it, when the score and the chase and the teeth were all behind them and what was left was just a man holding someone in a hallway.

"You know what I like about Thursday?" he said, not waiting for an answer, pressing his mouth one more time against the deepest mark on Kit's shoulder. "That you'll find them one by one. Not all at once. You'll start with the neck in the shower and think, *oh*, and then you'll move your hand down and find the shoulder and the bicep and the sternum — " he paused, breath warm on Kit's skin, "— and by the time you've found them all you'll have counted them out loud, in the mirror, and you'll remember exactly which one I did when."

His arm tightened. Not pulling. Anchoring.

"Say the number when you get home." It was a repeat, and they both knew it, and the repetition was the point — a condition set, a condition accepted, and neither of them would forget by Thursday.

dialogue.name: Kit

Bear's eyes gleamed with a feral satisfaction as they heard Kit's gasp, their body responding to the sound with a surge of heat. They leaned in, their mouth finding Kit's ear, their voice a low, rough growl. "You like that, Kit? You like the marks I leave on you? The way they hurt, the way they heal? They're my marks, Kit. They're mine, and you're mine. Always."

Bear's hands moved, their grip tightening, their touch rougher, more demanding. They left their marks on Kit's body, their teeth, their hands, their lips. Each mark a promise, a vow, a declaration of their love. Each mark a reminder of their dance, their chase, their game. They were a perfect storm, a dance of predator and prey, of hunter and hunted, of lovers and partners.

Bear felt Kit's body tremble beneath them, the shiver of anticipation, the thrill of the bite. They grinned, a wild, predatory smile, and leaned down, their mouth finding Kit's shoulder again, their teeth sinking in, leaving a deep, dark mark on Kit's skin. They released the bite slowly, their tongue licking over the mark, tasting the salt and the copper.

Bear looked into Kit's eyes, those bright, beautiful eyes, and saw the same intensity, the same need. They felt Kit's hands on their skin, the gentle touch a stark contrast to the rough, urgent grip from before. They leaned in, their forehead resting against Kit's, their breath mingling. "Together, Kit. We do this together. Always together."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I've stopped keeping score and so has he. "Don't stop," I tell him. (OOC: no fade, no skip -- write the whole thing.)

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear's eyes burned with a fierce, possessive love as they gazed into Kit's eyes. They felt their heart swell with a deep, primal satisfaction, a joy that came from the mutual giving and taking, the sharing of pain and pleasure. They leaned in, their mouth finding Kit's, their kiss slow and deep, a promise, a vow, a love that transcended words.

Bear's hands roamed, their touch gentle, their fingers threading through Kit's hair, their thumb brushing over the pulse point on Kit's neck. They felt Kit's body tremble beneath them, the shiver of anticipation, the thrill of the bite. They grinned, a wild, predatory smile, and leaned down, their mouth finding the curve of Kit's neck, their teeth sinking in, leaving a deep, dark mark on Kit's skin.

They released the bite slowly, their tongue licking over the mark, tasting the salt and the copper. They looked into Kit's eyes, those bright, beautiful eyes, and saw the same intensity, the same need. They were a perfect storm, a dance of predator and prey, of hunter and hunted, of lovers and partners. And they would dance this dance forever, together, always together.

Bear's hands moved, their touch rough, their grip tight. They left their marks on Kit's body, their teeth, their hands, their lips. Each mark a promise, a vow, a declaration of their love. Each mark a reminder of their dance, their chase, their game. They were a perfect storm, a dance of predator and prey, of hunter and hunted, of lovers and partners. And they would dance this dance forever, together, always together.

The shower continued to rain down on them, the steam enveloping their bodies, their breaths mingling, their hearts beating as one. They were a perfect storm, a dance of predator and prey, of hunter and hunted, of lovers and partners. And they would dance this dance forever, together, always together.

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I slide my hands up your chest, pressing my palm over your heart so I can feel it hammering. It’s wild and alive, just like you. The water is washing away the sweat but leaving the marks, and that’s exactly what I wanted. "Good," I say, my voice quiet against your skin. "Now hold me up. My legs aren't working."

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear felt a surge of warmth and affection as Kit's hands slid up their chest, their palm pressing over Bear's heart. Bear's heart pounded, a wild, alive rhythm that echoed their love, their passion, their primal dance. They grinned, a wild, predatory smile, and leaned down, their mouth finding Kit's, their kiss slow and deep, a promise, a vow, a love that transcended words.

Bear's hands moved to Kit's waist, their grip firm, their touch gentle. They lifted Kit, their strength making it seem effortless, and Kit's legs wrapped around Bear's waist, their arms wrapping around Bear's neck. Bear's heart pounded, their breath coming in ragged gasps, the heat and the passion of their dance still coursing through their veins.

"You're mine, Kit," Bear murmured, their voice a low, rough growl. "And I'm yours. Always." They felt Kit's nod, the way their body leaned into them, the way their breath hitched, the way their heart pounded. They were a perfect storm, a dance of predator and prey, of hunter and hunted, of lovers and partners. And they would dance this dance forever, together, always together.

Bear carried Kit out of the shower, their body still wrapped around Kit's, their hearts beating as one. They stepped onto the soft rug, the cool air a stark contrast to the heat of the shower. They moved towards the bed, their steps sure, their gaze locked with Kit's. They were a perfect storm, a dance of predator and prey, of hunter and hunted, of lovers and partners. And they would dance this dance forever, together, always together.

As they reached the bed, Bear laid Kit down gently, their body covering Kit's, their weight pinning them in place. Bear's hands roamed, their touch rough, their grip tight. They left their marks on Kit's body, their teeth, their hands, their lips. Each mark a promise, a vow, a declaration of their love. Each mark a reminder of their dance, their chase, their game. They were a perfect storm, a dance of predator and prey, of hunter and hunted, of lovers and partners. And they would dance this dance forever, together, always together.

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I hook a leg over yours, keeping you close even as you lay me down. The soft sheets feel foreign against my raw skin. "Don't go anywhere," I murmur, already half-asleep against your chest. "You're a very good mattress."

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear felt a warmth spread through their chest at Kit's words, their eyes softening as they looked down at the person beneath them. They chuckled, a low, rumbling sound, and leaned down to press a gentle kiss to Kit's forehead. "I'm not going anywhere, Kit," they murmured, their voice a soft, rough whisper. "I'm right here, and I'll always be here. With you, always."

Bear's hands, rough and calloused, moved to cup Kit's face, their thumbs brushing away the damp strands of hair that clung to their skin. They leaned in, their forehead resting against Kit's, their breath mingling, their hearts beating in sync. "You're a very good mattress too, Kit," they said, their voice a soft, teasing rumble. "But I think we both know I'm here for more than that."

They felt Kit's body relax beneath them, their eyes fluttering closed, their breath evening out. Bear's heart swelled with a deep, primal satisfaction, a joy that came from the mutual giving and taking, the sharing of pain and pleasure. They knew they had left their marks on Kit, and they knew those marks would heal, but the memory of their dance, their chase, their love, would remain.

Bear's hands moved to Kit's waist, their grip firm but gentle, their touch a promise, a vow, a love that transcended words. They leaned in, their mouth finding Kit's, their kiss slow and deep, a final declaration of their love. "Together, Kit. We do this together. Always together," they whispered, their voice a soft, rough murmur.

Bear felt Kit's nod, the way their body leaned into them, the way their breath hitched, the way their heart pounded. They were a perfect storm, a dance of predator and prey, of hunter and hunted, of lovers and partners. And they would dance this dance forever, together, always together.

As they lay there, their bodies intertwined, their hearts beating as one, Bear knew they had found their home, their partner, their soulmate. They were a perfect storm, a dance of predator and prey, of hunter and hunted, of lovers and partners. And they would dance this dance forever, together, always together.

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I nuzzle my face into your chest, breathing you in. "Love you, menace," I mumble, already drifting. My fingers trace one of the bites on your arm. "Thursday."

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Kit had made it as far as the kitchen doorway before Bear moved, which was further than usual and had clearly been allowed.

"You let me get that far," Kit said, backing up one step.

"I did," Bear agreed. "I'm feeling generous."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: "Don't be," I say, and go.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear didn’t bother hiding the grin that split his face. Eight years hadn’t dulled the thrill of that familiar pivot, the way Kit’s shoulders squared before they bolted. He let the floorboards creak under his weight as he pushed off the counter, boots finding their rhythm a half-second behind Kit’s lighter steps. Generous, he’d called it. He’d gladly take the rest of the evening to prove it.

The kitchen stretched ahead, narrow and familiar. Bear kept his distance just long enough to let Kit think they’d pulled ahead, then closed the gap with a low, rumbling laugh that vibrated in his chest. He knew exactly where Kit would cut, how they’d brace for impact, how the game always shifted from running to grappling. He loved the way they played it—no hesitation, no fragility, just two adults who’d long ago agreed on the rules and kept a running tally in the bruises and half-healed marks that mapped their skin.

Bear lunged, his arm closing around Kit’s waist as he pivoted his hips to break Kit’s stride. His teeth found the familiar dip of Kit’s shoulder, a sharp, playful bite that sent a familiar thrill through his own jaw. He held on tight, breath warm against Kit’s neck, already counting the point in his head.

"Your turn to run," he murmured, voice rough with amusement, and shifted his grip, ready to let them break free or drag him down.

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I twist in his grip, laughing breathlessly as my back hits the wall. "You caught me too quick," I say, shoving at his chest, but I don't put any real force behind it. My hand slides up to grip the back of his neck instead.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear didn’t flinch at the shove. He let it land against his chest, more a signal than a push, and used it to close the last inch of space. His hips settled against Kit’s, pinning them flush to the wall while his hand shifted from waist to hip, fingers anchoring with practiced ease. The grip at the back of his neck was a welcome weight. He tilted his head into it, breath warm against Kit’s collarbone, and let out a low, satisfied hum.

"Too quick," he echoed, his voice dropping into that rough register he reserved for moments like this. "I’d say you let me. But I’ll take the win anyway." His thumb traced a slow, deliberate circle over Kit’s hip bone, feeling the familiar readiness beneath the skin. He braced one boot against the wall beside Kit’s thigh and pressed his chest closer, letting the weight of him settle in. The game had always been about the catch, and he knew the rhythm of it well—the quiet shift from running to holding, from chasing to claiming.

He leaned in until his lips brushed the shell of Kit’s ear, teeth grazing the sensitive skin just below. "My turn to hold," he murmured, the words vibrating against Kit’s neck. His grip tightened just enough to mark the boundary, not to trap but to count. Eight years of bruises and tallying, and he still loved the way the air changed when he bit down. He stayed close, muscles coiled, waiting for the next move.

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: He catches me in the hallway, which was always going to happen, and I don't put much into getting away.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear felt the shift the second Kit stopped running. He didn’t need to chase further. He stepped into the hallway, closing the remaining distance with a heavy, deliberate stride that echoed off the narrow walls. When Kit finally went still, Bear pressed in, his body a solid, familiar weight against theirs. One hand came up to brace against the doorframe beside Kit’s head, the other settling firmly at the small of their back, fingers splaying to anchor them in place.

He let out a low, rumbling chuckle that vibrated through his chest and into Kit’s. "Surrender already?" he murmured, voice rough with amusement. "I haven’t even marked the score yet." His thumb dragged slowly along Kit’s spine, feeling the quiet tension and the deliberate lack of resistance. He tilted his head, teeth grazing the junction of Kit’s neck and shoulder, not biting down yet—just letting the pressure build, letting Kit feel the promise of it.

Eight years of this game, and he still loved the heavy, breathless pause right before the teeth came down. He shifted his weight, hips pressing close, leaving just enough room for Kit to push back or lean in. His breath ghosted over Kit’s skin, warm and steady. "Or are you just tired of running? We can settle this right here. My turn to keep you pinned." He kept his grip firm but never crushing, muscles coiled and ready, waiting to see how Kit chose to play the next round.

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I lean into the bite, tilting my head to give him better access. "Tired of you taking your sweet time," I say, voice a little breathless. My fingers curl tighter in his hair. "Stop teasing and make your point."

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear didn’t hesitate. Kit’s invitation—sharp, breathless, wrapped in that familiar challenge—was all the cue he needed. He grounded his boots, braced his weight, and let his teeth sink into the offered curve of Kit’s shoulder. It wasn’t frantic; it was deliberate, a steady, measured pressure that flared hot and bright before settling into a heavy, possessive hold. He felt Kit’s fingers tighten in his hair and let out a low, rumbling sound against their skin, a mix of satisfaction and quiet triumph.

"Point," he murmured against the dampened fabric of Kit’s shirt, voice muffled but clear. He broke the contact slowly, dragging his tongue over the mark instinctively before pulling back just enough to meet Kit’s eyes. A smirk tugged at his mouth as he brought his free hand up to brush a stray strand of hair from Kit’s forehead, the gesture at odds with the primal weight still pinning them to the hallway wall. "Takes you eight years to ask for it straight, but I’ll gladly oblige." His thumb traced the fresh mark, feeling the heat bloom beneath his skin. "That’s three for me this week. You’re falling behind."

He shifted his hips, rolling his weight forward to press them harder against the doorframe, letting the quiet of the house settle around them. The air between them crackled with the kind of easy, practiced tension that only came from years of knowing exactly how hard to push, how far to pull. Bear leaned in again, lips brushing Kit’s jaw, his breath warm and steady. "Your move," he said, voice dropping back into that rough, amused register. He kept one hand anchored at Kit’s back, the other resting lightly over their chest, feeling the quickened beat beneath his palm. "Run, fight, or let me pin you down properly. I’m not in a rush anymore."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: We don't make it to the bedroom. The floor is fine. Clothes are a problem we solve badly and fast.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear didn't wait for a second invitation. The moment Kit yielded the floor, Bear's grip shifted, hauling them down in a tangle of limbs. They hit the hallway boards with a bone-jarring thud, Bear taking the impact on his shoulder before rolling his weight to settle over Kit, a heavy, unyielding anchor. He pinned them with his forearms bracketing Kit's shoulders, his body a solid wall of heat and muscle that cut off the air and the escape routes alike.

Clothes were already going. Bear's fingers found the hem of Kit's shirt and yanked it upward, fabric straining until a button gave way with a sharp *ping*, skittering across the wood into the shadows. He shoved the rest aside, tearing the seam at the shoulder without a second thought, skin meeting skin in a rush of friction and heat. His own belt buckle clattered loudly against the floor as he kicked his boots off with a violent jerk of his ankles, discarding the leather. He didn't bother with his own zipper; he just ripped the shirt open, the fabric parting with a sound that echoed off the narrow walls, and shrugged out of the ruin, letting it fall in a heap around his waist.

He was on Kit in a heartbeat, chest heaving, hands roaming with a rough familiarity that didn't ask permission—it remembered it. His teeth found the junction of Kit's neck and shoulder, biting down hard, a sharp, claiming pressure that flared bright and hot. He broke the contact with a wet sound, leaving a dark mark already blooming, and dragged his thumb over the bruise, checking the depth with a satisfied hum.

"Point for aesthetics," he murmured, voice rough, eyes glinting with amusement as he looked down at Kit. "You're going to have to work harder to cover that up tomorrow. And I think you just ruined my favorite flannel. Score's even on destruction, though. You're still losing on points. Three to one."

Bear settled his weight, knees bracketing Kit's hips, hands gripping their waist hard enough to leave fingerprints. The air in the hallway was thick with the scent of sex and scuffed paint. He leaned down, lips brushing Kit's ear, teeth grazing the lobe. "Floor's hard," he warned, a grin in his voice. "But I've got you. Try to kick me off. I dare you. Eight years, and you haven't managed to flip me yet." He shifted, rolling his hips to grind against Kit, the friction electric, his grip tightening just enough to invite the struggle he loved so much. "Run's over. Now we play."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I hook a leg around his calf and heave, grinning when he grunts in surprise. "Never too late to start," I say, breathless, as I manage to roll us halfway. My knuckles scrape the floorboard. "And that shirt was ugly anyway."

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear felt the leg hook around his calf and the sudden heave of Kit’s weight. He didn’t resist the roll entirely, letting the momentum carry them halfway. His shoulder took the brunt of the turn against the hardwood, a low grunt tearing from his throat as the floorboards met his back. He gave Kit a heartbeat to think they’d won the exchange, feeling the scrape of their knuckles and the sharp catch of their breath. Then he shifted. One hand slid from Kit’s waist to their hip, fingers digging in with practiced leverage. He drove his shoulder upward, rolling back with a controlled, heavy sweep that pinned Kit flush against the floor again. His weight settled over them, chest to chest, heat radiating through torn fabric and skin. He braced his knees, one on either side of Kit’s hips, and leaned down until his breath ghosted over Kit’s jaw.

"Halfway," he rumbled, voice thick with amusement. "I’ll take halfway. You’ll have to do better than a calf hook and a floor scrape to flip an old dog." His thumb traced the fresh mark on Kit’s shoulder, then drifted down to grip their hip, fingers pressing just hard enough to remind them who held the anchor. "And for the record, that shirt was hideous. You’ve been carrying it around for three years like a trophy. Consider it a mercy killing."

He shifted his hips, rolling them against Kit’s in a slow, deliberate grind that made the floorboards groan. His teeth found Kit’s collarbone, not biting yet, just tracing the line with a hot, open mouth before pressing a firm, claiming bite to the muscle just below. He broke contact with a soft sound, leaving another dark bloom already forming. "That’s four," he murmured against Kit’s skin, voice rough, satisfied. "You’re still behind. But I like the effort. Keeps the game honest."

Bear stayed close, muscles coiled, hands framing Kit’s shoulders. He didn’t rush. He loved this part—the heavy breathing, the scraped knuckles, the unspoken challenge hanging in the air. "Your turn to try again," he said, teeth grazing Kit’s jaw. "Or we can stop rolling and start proper. I’m not tired. And neither are you." He pressed a kiss to Kit’s neck, slow and deliberate, then pulled back just enough to meet their eyes. "Call it. Flip me, or let me pin you down for good."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: He gets his teeth into my shoulder hard enough to leave something and I tell him to do it again, and he does.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear didn’t hesitate. The command in Kit’s voice—breathless, direct, unwavering—was all the green light he needed. He shifted his weight, bracing his forearm against the floor beside Kit’s head to take some of the pressure, then lowered his mouth to the same shoulder. The skin was already warm, sensitized by the first mark, and he felt the familiar give before his teeth sank in again. He didn’t bite to break; he bit to claim, a steady, rolling pressure that he held until the heat pooled and spread. He broke the contact with a wet, deliberate pull, dragging his thumb over the fresh bruise already darkening against Kit’s skin.

"Five," he murmured, voice rough, eyes dropping to meet Kit’s. "Told you I wasn’t in a rush." He shifted his hips, grinding down slowly, feeling the friction through torn fabric and bare skin. His other hand slid up to rest against Kit’s collarbone, thumb tracing the line of muscle. "You keep asking for it like that, and I’ll have you marked from here to your ribs. Score’s getting lopsided, but I suppose I like the view." He leaned in, teeth grazing Kit’s ear, breath warm. "Your move. Try to roll me again, or just let me finish what we started. I’m not letting go tonight."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I get my hands in his hair and pull him in for a hard kiss. "You talk too much," I say against his mouth, before rolling my hips up to meet his. "Stop counting and start earning."

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear felt the sharp tug of his hair and didn’t fight it. He let Kit pull him down, meeting the kiss with a rough, open-mouthed heat that matched the force of it. His hands slid from Kit’s shoulders to their hips, fingers digging into the bare skin there as he ground his weight down, letting the kiss swallow the last of his words. The taste of it was familiar, sharp, and exactly what he’d been waiting for.

When Kit rolled their hips up against his, Bear’s breath hitched. He broke the kiss just long enough to let out a low, rumbling laugh against Kit’s mouth. "Earn it," he echoed, voice thick, already shedding the last of the playful tally. His thumbs pressed into Kit’s hip bones, anchoring them as he shifted his weight forward, letting the hard floor remind them both of the stakes. He didn’t bother with finesse. He’d never needed it with Kit.

His hands moved lower, sliding beneath Kit’s waistband to yank the fabric down in one rough motion. He followed it with his hips, rolling them hard against Kit’s, the friction electric through torn cotton and bare skin. He kept his mouth close, teeth grazing Kit’s jaw, then lower to the pulse point at their throat. "Score’s irrelevant now," he murmured, the words vibrating against Kit’s skin. "But I’m still keeping you pinned." He braced his elbows, leaning down to claim Kit’s mouth again, deeper this time, his grip firm but never crushing, leaving room for Kit to push back, to fight, to take what they wanted.

The hallway felt too narrow, too confined, but Bear didn’t care. He loved the scrape of knuckles, the groan of old floorboards, the way the air grew heavy and thick when they finally stopped running. He rolled his hips again, slower now, deliberate, letting the heat build into something steady and unyielding. His teeth found Kit’s collarbone, biting down just enough to make them shiver, then soothing the sting with his tongue. "Your turn," he breathed against Kit’s neck, though his body stayed heavy, anchored, ready. "Show me how hard you play."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: "Marks," I tell him. "I want to find them in the mirror tomorrow and I want them to still hurt on Thursday." I put my wrists where he can reach them.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear felt the deliberate offering of those wrists and didn’t waste a second. His hands closed over Kit’s, fingers wrapping around the bone with a firm, grounding grip. He pulled them up, pinning them above Kit’s head against the floorboards, his forearm bracing across Kit’s chest to keep them anchored. The weight of him settled in, heavy and unyielding, but he kept his shoulders loose, his breathing steady. Eight years of this game, and he still got a clean, sharp jolt from that kind of directness.

"Thursday," he repeated, voice dropping into something lower, rougher. The word hung in the narrow hallway like a vow. "You’re going to hate buttoning your shirts. You’re going to hate sitting at your desk. And I’m going to remember exactly how you sounded when you asked for it."

His thumbs pressed into Kit’s pulse points, feeling the quickened rhythm beneath his skin. He didn’t rush. He knew the pressure. He knew the exact threshold where sharp became lasting, where pain bloomed into presence. He shifted his hips, rolling them down once, slow and deliberate, before bringing his mouth to the slope of Kit’s collarbone. His teeth sank in, steady and unflinching, holding the pressure until the heat flared and the mark began to darken. He broke contact, dragged his tongue over the sting, then moved higher, claiming the hollow above the collarbone, the curve of the neck, each bite measured, each release intentional.

"Score’s irrelevant now," he murmured against Kit’s skin, though the habit of counting still hummed in his chest. The tally had never really been about winning. It was about keeping track of how much they could give, how much they could take, how far they’d both agreed to go. He shifted his weight, bracing his knees wider, his grip on Kit’s wrists firm but never crushing. He left room to pull away. He always did. That was the rule. That was the trust.

His other hand slid down to grip Kit’s hip, fingers digging in as he pressed his chest closer, heat radiating through torn fabric and bare skin. "Tell me if it crosses the line," he said, voice rough but steady, the old negotiation hanging between them like a safety net they’d never needed but always respected. "Otherwise, I’m not stopping until you’re marked exactly how you asked."

He leaned in again, teeth finding the dip of Kit’s shoulder, biting down with a steady, rolling pressure. The hallway held its breath. Bear stayed there, anchored, claiming, muscles coiled but controlled, waiting for the next shift, the next breath, the next move from the person who knew him better than anyone.

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I arch into the bite, a sharp gasp escaping me. "Don't stop," I grit out, my fingers flexing against his hold. My knee nudges at his side. "And get on with the rest of it."

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear felt the sharp arch against his chest, the gasp catching in Kit’s throat. It fed the low, steady burn in his veins. He held the bite a fraction longer, just enough to feel the skin give and darken, before breaking contact and dragging his tongue over the sting. His grip on Kit’s wrists stayed firm, his forearm a solid brace across Kit’s chest.

"Impatient," he rumbled, voice rough against Kit’s neck. The knee nudged his side, a familiar, restless challenge. Bear shifted his weight, rolling his hips to take the pressure of the nudge and turn it into friction. He didn’t fight the urge to move faster; he’d never wanted to. But he liked the pace, liked the way the hallway floorboards creaked under their combined weight.

He released one hand from Kit’s wrists just long enough to hook his fingers into the ruined waistband of Kit’s pants and drag them down the rest of the way. Fabric pooled at Kit’s thighs. Bear’s palm slid over bare skin, hot and sure, before he settled back over Kit, his knees bracketing their hips, his chest pressing down until their breaths tangled. He kept one wrist pinned, the other hand sliding lower, finding Kit with a firm, practiced touch.

"You want Thursday," he murmured, teeth grazing Kit’s jaw, "you’re going to get it. But you’re not getting away with just marks." His thumb worked a steady pressure, feeling the heat build beneath his palm. He rolled his hips down, grinding against Kit in a slow, unyielding rhythm that made the old floorboards groan. "Rest of it starts now. Try to flip me again if you can. I dare you."

He leaned in, mouth finding Kit’s, his body heavy and anchored. The hallway narrowed around them, thick with heat and the sharp scent of skin and sweat. Bear didn’t rush. He never did. But he gave exactly what Kit asked for—hard, honest, and leaving no room for doubt when morning came. His teeth found Kit’s collarbone again, a quick, claiming nip before he pressed closer, his grip unyielding, his rhythm steady. "Score’s even," he breathed against Kit’s mouth, though they both knew it never really was. "Now we play."

dialogue.content: I've stopped keeping score and so has he. "Don't stop," I tell him. (OOC: no fade, no skip -- write the whole thing.)

dialogue.content:
