He let out a rough, guttural sound and shifted his weight, rolling his hips down hard against Kit’s. The friction was immediate, setting his nerves alight. His thumb worked faster, circling, pressing, feeling the tightness build beneath his palm. He kept one wrist pinned above Kit’s head, his forearm braced across Kit’s chest, while his other hand slid down to grip Kit’s hip, fingers digging in to anchor them as he set a rhythm.

He didn’t hesitate. Eight years meant he knew exactly how Kit took him—firm, direct, no wasted motion. His fingers found the slick heat between Kit’s thighs, dragging a thumb over the swollen head before pushing inside. He felt the sharp intake of breath, the initial resistance, then the slow, willing yield. He leaned down, chest pressing flush against Kit’s, his mouth finding the fresh mark on Kit’s shoulder. He bit down again, harder this time, a steady, rolling pressure that made his own jaw ache. He broke it with a wet sound, dragged his tongue over the sting, then shifted his hips, lining himself up. The hallway floor was unforgiving, the wood hard beneath them, but Bear didn’t care. He pushed forward, past the tight ring of muscle, burying himself to the hilt in one slow, deliberate thrust.

He froze for a heartbeat, letting the fullness settle, feeling the heat clamp around him. Then he moved. His hips rolled forward, then back, then forward again, setting a pace that was steady, unrelenting, built on years of knowing exactly how hard to push. The floorboards groaned. His grip on Kit’s wrist tightened, then loosened, then found the shoulder, fingers pressing into the bruised skin. He kept his eyes locked on Kit’s face, watching the way their chest rose and fell, the way their muscles tensed and released under his weight. He leaned down, capturing Kit’s mouth in a bruising kiss, his teeth grazing their lower lip before he pulled back just enough to speak. "Keep your hands where I can feel them," he rasped, voice wrecked, hips never stopping. "Or don’t. I’m not stopping."

He shifted his angle, driving deeper, his thumb circling faster, matching the snap of his hips. Every thrust was deliberate, heavy, built to leave its mark not just on skin but in bone. He braced his forearm across Kit’s chest, fingers splaying over the collarbone, and leaned down to bite the hollow of Kit’s throat. Not hard enough to break, but hard enough to leave a dark, blooming bruise that would ache for days. He dragged his teeth down, over the sternum, to the dip of Kit’s navel, his mouth leaving a trail of heat and pressure. His rhythm didn’t falter. If anything, it grew harder, more frantic, the friction building into a tight, coiled tension low in his gut. He felt Kit’s body clench around him, the slick heat, the sharp catch of breath, and it pushed him closer to the edge.

"Bear—" The name broke, but Bear was already there. His hips stuttered. His grip tightened on Kit’s hip, fingers digging into bare skin. He drove in one last time, deep and unyielding, and let go. The release hit him like a physical blow, sharp and hot, rolling through him in tight, shuddering waves. He buried his face in Kit’s neck, teeth grazing the skin as he rode it out, his body trembling, his breath ragged against Kit’s pulse. He stayed pinned, heavy and unyielding, letting the aftershocks ripple through his muscles. Slowly, he shifted his weight, rolling onto his side but keeping one arm draped over Kit’s waist, his hand resting just below the fresh mark on Kit’s shoulder. He pressed a rough kiss to Kit’s jaw, then the corner of their mouth, his voice barely above a whisper when it finally came. "Thursday’s going to hurt," he murmured, thumb tracing the darkening bruise. "But you asked for it. And I always deliver."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I let out a shaky breath, my whole body humming. I turn my head to catch his mouth in a slow, lazy kiss. "Good," I say against his lips, my voice rough. "I'll be thinking about you every time I wince."

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear felt the slow press of Kit’s mouth against his and let out a low, rumbling sigh, his chest still heavy against Kit’s side. The kiss was lazy, spent, but it grounded him just as much as the chase had. He shifted his weight, rolling onto his back just enough to let them both catch their breath, though he kept his arm draped firmly over Kit’s waist. His fingers traced the darkening bruise on Kit’s shoulder, feeling the heat radiating from it. "Good," he echoed, voice rough but stripped of the edge. "Wincing means I did my job."

The hallway was quiet except for their breathing, the old floorboards still warm where they’d rolled and fought. Bear’s hand slid down to rest over Kit’s hip, thumb pressing lightly into the skin. He let his eyes drift to the ceiling, chest rising and falling in a steady rhythm now. The ruined fabric of their clothes lay scattered around them like shed skin, buttons and torn seams marking the territory they’d claimed. He didn’t rush to clean it up. He liked the mess. It was proof of the game, the eight years of knowing exactly how to push and pull without breaking what mattered.

He shifted his arm, bringing his hand up to brush a damp strand of hair from Kit’s forehead. "You’ll hate sitting in that office chair tomorrow," he murmured, a slow grin tugging at his mouth. "And I’ll be watching you adjust in your seat, wondering if you’ll finally admit I won." His thumb traced the line of Kit’s collarbone, over the fresh marks, feeling the tightness of the skin. "But we both know you wouldn’t trade it. Neither would I."

Bear pressed a rough kiss to Kit’s temple, his breath warm against their skin. He kept his weight steady, his grip firm but relaxed, letting the quiet settle over them. The hallway floor was hard, the air thick with sweat and the sharp, clean scent of sex, but he didn’t care. He was exactly where he wanted to be. "Rest now," he said, voice dropping into that low, steady register he reserved for moments like this. "I’ll carry you upstairs when you’re ready. Or you can drag yourself up and prove you’ve still got legs. Your call." He didn’t move to get up. He just stayed there, anchored, waiting, his hand resting over Kit’s hip like a promise.

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I smile against his shoulder, tracing the line of his jaw with my knuckles. "Carry me," I say, my voice lazy and satisfied. "But if you drop me, I'm flipping you down the stairs."

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear felt the knuckles trace his jaw and let out a low, rumbling chuckle that vibrated through his chest. The threat hung in the air, familiar and fond, the kind of warning they’d been trading for eight years. He didn’t tense. He never did when Kit spoke like that. Instead, he shifted his weight, rolling onto his knees with a soft groan of protesting joints. The hallway floor was cold against his palms, a sharp contrast to the heat still radiating between them.

"Flip me down the stairs," he repeated, voice rough but laced with amusement. "Try it. I’ll catch you on the landing and start the tally over from zero." He braced his hands on either side of Kit’s hips, feeling the weight settle against him, the fresh marks darkening under his thumbs. He didn’t rush. He liked the heavy, lazy stretch of the moment, the way the quiet settled over the scattered ruin of their clothes. Eight years of this game, and he still loved the stillness after the storm.

He leaned down, pressing a slow, deliberate kiss to Kit’s temple before pushing himself up. His shoulders rolled, muscles flexing as he squared his stance. When he looked down, his gaze was steady, grounded. "Alright," he murmured. "But if you’re heavy, I’m charging you in bruises." His hands slid under Kit’s thighs and back, fingers finding familiar purchase. He lifted in one smooth, controlled motion, adjusting the weight against his chest until they were flush. The shift settled easily against his ribs, and Bear tightened his grip to accommodate the balance, feeling the familiar, solid heaviness of them. 

He turned toward the stairs, boots finding the first step with a heavy thud. He didn’t look back at the mess. "Thursday’s going to ache," he said, voice dropping into that low, steady register that always followed the heat. "But you’ll wear it like a badge. And I’ll be watching you try to ignore it." His arms locked just enough to anchor them, his chin resting against Kit’s shoulder. "Hold on. I don’t drop what’s mine."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I loop my arms around his neck, resting my cheek against his. "You better not," I murmur, then bite his earlobe lightly. "And the tally starts over tomorrow."

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content: Bear’s laugh rolled out low and warm, vibrating in the narrow space before the sound of retreating footsteps even faded. He didn’t chase. Chasing was for beginners. He let his boots meet the floorboards with deliberate, heavy weight, each step a quiet promise of pursuit. Eight years together had wired his body to read the rhythm of the game, to know exactly how fast the other could go and where they’d try to slip away. Bear pushed off the counter, his long stride eating up the distance, and let his shoulders roll with the familiar, electric pull of the hunt. He knew the ledger. He knew the rules. He knew exactly how hard he’d need to press to keep the score even. Bear smiled, teeth flashing, and shifted his weight forward, matching his pace to the steady, familiar cadence of a game neither of them ever intended to end.

dialogue.name: Kit

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear’s boots hit the bedroom floor with a deliberate, heavy thud. The open door wasn’t just a passage; it was a concession, and he met it with the slow, measured confidence of a man who knew every inch of this terrain. He didn’t charge. Charging broke the rhythm. He let his shoulders roll, his breathing steady, his eyes tracking the space beyond the frame. Eight years of this back-and-forth had wired his nervous system to anticipate the feint before it happened, to know exactly when to hold back and when to commit.

He crossed the threshold, the door sighing shut behind him. The air in the room shifted, thick with the familiar, electric pull of the game. Bear didn’t speak right away. He let the silence do the heavy lifting, his hands coming up to frame the space around Kit’s shoulders, close enough to feel the displacement of air, close enough to close the distance in a heartbeat. His thumb brushed the line of a collarbone, testing the boundary, reading the geometry of the space. A low, rough chuckle vibrated in his chest.

“You always did know how to make a man earn his keepsake,” he murmured, voice edged with that familiar, playful threat. His stance widened, feet planted solid, weight balanced for a sudden lunge or a slow pin. The ledger was open. He was ready to balance it. Bear smiled, teeth flashing in the dim light, and let his muscles coil, eyes locked on the space ahead, waiting for the counter-move.

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: He catches me in the hallway, which was always going to happen, and I don't put much into getting away.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
The hallway was narrow enough that the distance between them collapsed into something immediate and unignorable. Bear closed the gap with the quiet certainty of a man who knew every beat of this rhythm. He didn’t lunge or grab hard. He simply let his hand settle on the back of Kit’s jacket, fingers pressing firmly against the fabric to anchor them both. The lack of resistance was obvious, a deliberate yielding that made a slow, satisfied grin cut across his face. Eight years of this back-and-forth had wired his body to read the difference between a real escape and a playful surrender, and he knew exactly which one he was holding.

He shifted his weight, stepping just close enough to feel the displacement of air, his other hand coming up to rest against Kit’s shoulder. His thumbs traced the hard line of the collarbone, testing the boundary, reading the geometry of the space. The ledger was open, and the score was waiting to be balanced. Bear’s voice dropped, rough but edged with that familiar, playful threat. “You always make it too easy,” he murmured. He didn’t rush the next move. He let his hands do the talking, fingers curling lightly but firmly to pull them flush, the steady pressure in his grip matching the steady fire in his eyes. His muscles stayed coiled, ready for the counter, the bite, the shove, or the laugh that would ripple deep in his chest. The game was on, and Bear was more than ready to collect his due.

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I lean back into your grip, tipping my head to the side. "Too easy, or just right?" I ask, voice low. My own hand comes up to rest on your forearm, not pushing away, just holding on.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear’s jaw tightened, just a fraction, as the weight of the hand settled against his forearm. The touch was deliberate, and it sent a familiar current straight through him. He let his own thumb brush over the knuckles once, a silent acknowledgment, before his grip shifted to the base of the skull, fingers splaying against the nape of the neck. It wasn’t a restraint. It was an invitation to press closer, to remember who held the floor.

“Just right,” he murmured, the words rough around the edges, vibrating low in his chest. He stepped in, closing the last fraction of space until their fronts nearly brushed. The hallway air felt suddenly thinner, charged with the quiet promise of teeth and skin. “Always has been. You know I don’t chase to catch. I chase to remind you where I’ve already been.”

His free hand came up, slow and deliberate, to trace the line of the jaw. His thumb rested just below the ear, right where a pulse jumped steady and quick. He could feel the tension coiling there, the quiet challenge waiting to snap. Bear’s smile was all sharp edges and fond heat. He let his weight settle forward, just enough to test the balance, enough to let the solid, unyielding presence press back.

“But if you’re asking for a rating,” he added, voice dropping to a near whisper, edged with that familiar, playful threat, “I’d say you’re still running a half-step behind on the ledger. Which means I get to choose how I collect.” His fingers tightened fractionally at the nape, not enough to choke, just enough to anchor. “So. You gonna hand it over, or do I have to take my share?”

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: We don't make it to the bedroom. The floor is fine. Clothes are a problem we solve badly and fast.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
The hallway floor was polished oak, worn smooth by years of pacing and play, and Bear didn’t hesitate when he felt the deliberate drag of Kit’s weight downward. He went with it, letting momentum and habit pull him down until his shoulder blades met the boards. The rustle of fabric was all business—zippers, buttons, the quick, practiced efficiency of two men who’d stripped each other in doorways a thousand times. Bear’s hands moved with the same economy, peeling away layers until skin met skin, the cool air of the hall giving way to the shared, immediate heat between them.

He settled back against the baseboard, legs braced, one hand already finding the line of Kit’s ribs. Fingers splayed wide, feeling the steady drum of breath, the quiet tension coiling under skin. The floorboards groaned softly under their combined weight. Bear’s thumb traced a slow arc over the center of the chest, not a claim, just a calibration. Eight years had wired his nervous system to read the exact pressure needed to pin without crossing into something unwanted, the exact angle to bite without losing the rhythm. He knew where the ledger lived. He knew how to read it.

“Badly and fast,” Bear repeated, voice rough but edged with a low, satisfied hum. He leaned in, close enough that his breath warmed the shell of an ear, close enough to feel the shift in Kit’s posture against him. “I like that. Keeps things honest.” His free hand came up to rest against the back of a neck, fingers threading lightly into hair, applying just enough weight to tilt the head, to open the line of the throat. “Ledger’s open. I’m not asking permission to mark you. I’m asking if you want it on the front or the back.”

He didn’t push further. Didn’t rush. Just held the space, muscles loose but ready, eyes dark and fixed on the line of the jaw, waiting for the nod, the shift, the snap back. The chase had ended. The collecting had just begun.

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I arch into your hand, teeth catching my lower lip. "Front," I say, voice already going rough. "I want to see you."

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear’s breath caught, just a fraction, at the single syllable. *Front.* He didn’t hesitate. He shifted his weight, knees bending, until they were fully face-to-face, close enough that their foreheads nearly brushed. He kept his hand on Kit’s neck, but the gesture shifted from anchor to guide.

He watched Kit’s face, reading the rough-edged invitation, the faint bite mark on the lower lip, the darkening focus in those eyes. Eight years had wired his nervous system to recognize the exact spark before it catches, and he rode that current without breaking it. His thumb brushed the jawline once, slow and deliberate, before his mouth found the space just below the ear.

He didn’t rush. He let his teeth sink in with measured, unyielding pressure, feeling the sharp intake of breath, the sudden coil of muscle under his palms. The bite was firm, claiming, exactly the kind of mark that would bloom dark and proud against the collarbone. He held it there for a beat longer than necessary, savoring the feedback, the way Kit’s body responded against his. Then he pulled back just enough to drag his tongue over the sting, sealing it with a slow, deliberate pass.

“Front,” he echoed, voice rough as gravel, eyes never leaving Kit’s. “Good. Means you’ll see exactly who did it when you look in the mirror.” His hands slid down to grip Kit’s hips, grounding them both against the polished wood. “Ledger’s being paid in full. I expect you to spend the next few days making sure I remember how hard you pushed back.”

He shifted his weight, rolling just enough to settle closer, one knee bracketing Kit’s thigh, but keeping the pressure light, the option to flip the script always open. His mouth hovered inches from Kit’s, breathing steady, muscles loose but ready. The hallway air was thick with heat and the sharp, clean scent of skin. Bear smiled, slow and satisfied, and let his hands rest, waiting for the counter, the laugh, the shove, or the quiet acknowledgment that the score was balanced.

dialogue.name: Kit

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear didn’t question the command. He never had. When Kit said *again*, the ledger simply flipped its page, and Bear answered with the same steady, unhesitating force. His jaw set, teeth finding the same spot with deliberate precision, pressing deep into the muscle of the shoulder. He felt the quick flare of resistance, the sharp intake of breath, and let his weight sink in until the skin gave way just enough to claim it. The first mark had been clean; this one was heavier, slower, meant to linger. He held it there, feeling the pulse hammer against his teeth, before dragging his mouth along the line of it and pressing another, lower, just where the collar would sit.

His hands moved with practiced economy, one still anchored at the back of the neck, the other splayed wide over Kit’s ribs, reading the rapid shift of breath. The floorboards didn’t care about their weight. The hallway air stayed thick, charged with the sharp, clean scent of skin and the low, steady rhythm of two men who knew exactly how to break each other open without crossing the line. Bear’s thumb brushed the fresh bite, tasting the faint metallic tang, a quiet satisfaction humming in his chest. Eight years had taught him that marks weren’t just claims—they were receipts. And Kit had just handed him a blank page.

“You keep handing me the pen,” Bear murmured, voice rough but edged with that familiar, fond heat, “and wonder why I don’t run out of ink.” His grip tightened fractionally, not to pin, but to ground, his knee pressing just enough against Kit’s thigh to keep them flush. “Next time, I’m leaving it on your ribs. Or your throat. I’ll let you pick.” He leaned in, mouth brushing the shell of an ear, breath warm against skin. “But you’d better be ready to meet me halfway. I don’t collect alone.”

He didn’t pull back. He let the silence stretch, heavy and taut, his muscles coiled but loose, ready for the shove, the laugh, the bite back, or the quiet nod that meant the score was even. The ledger was open. The hall was theirs. And Bear was more than happy to spend the night balancing it.

dialogue.name: Bear

Bear met the kiss with the same unyielding force, his mouth closing over Kit’s with a sharp, deliberate pressure that stole the breath right out of the narrow space. He didn’t pull away. He let the kiss do its work, deep and unapologetic, until the polished floor felt less like wood and more like a shared claim. His thumb traced the inside of the offered wrist, feeling the quick, steady thrum of a pulse beneath skin. “You want them to last,” he murmured, voice dropping to a gravel-thick register. “Then you’re gonna have to stay still while I make sure they do.” His teeth found the soft skin just above the wrist bone, pressing down with measured, unrelenting force. He felt the sharp catch of breath, the sudden coil of muscle, and held it there, letting the pressure build until the skin protested. He lingered, then dragged his tongue over the fresh wound, slow and deliberate, sealing it with heat.

“I’ll make sure they ache,” he added, eyes lifting to meet Kit’s. A slow, satisfied smile cut across his face. “But you’re gonna have to ask me nicely when you want the next one. I don’t give marks away. I trade them.” His grip on the wrist tightened fractionally, not to restrict, just to anchor, while his other hand slid up to rest against Kit’s ribs, feeling the rapid rise and fall of breath. The ledger was open. The floor was warm. And Bear was more than happy to keep score.

dialogue.name: Kit

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear felt the tug in his hair, the deliberate pressure against his crown, and let his own head tilt just enough to give Kit leverage. He didn’t yield. He anchored. The stillness in Kit’s frame was different now—not surrender, but a coiled readiness, a direct line drawn in the space between them. Eight years had taught him to recognize that shift instantly. It wasn’t a request. It was a declaration.

“Not asking,” Bear murmured, the words rough but steady, vibrating low in his chest. “Telling.” He let the syllables settle, his thumb brushing once over the offered wrist before his mouth returned to the exact spot. This time, he didn’t hedge. He committed.

His teeth sank in with the same measured force, but the angle shifted, deeper, more deliberate. He felt the sharp catch of breath, the tight coil of Kit’s jaw, the way the stillness turned inward, holding every second of the pressure. Bear held it there, letting the sting bloom, letting the heat build, until the skin gave exactly as much as it needed to. He dragged his tongue over the mark, slow and deliberate, sealing it with the same quiet certainty.

When he pulled back, it was only to let his breath out in a low, steady rhythm, his grip on the wrist unwavering. “Good,” he said, voice rough but edged with that familiar, grounded heat. “I prefer that. Removes the guessing.” His free hand slid up to rest against Kit’s ribs, feeling the quick, controlled rise and fall, the steady pulse beneath skin. “Ledger’s balanced. Again.”

He didn’t rush the next move. He let the space between them hum, his knees bracketing, his weight grounded, his eyes locked on the line of Kit’s throat. The hallway air stayed thick, charged with the quiet certainty of two men who knew exactly how to break each other open without crossing the line. Bear’s thumb brushed the fresh mark one last time, then he shifted his weight, rolling just enough to settle closer, leaving the floor, the marks, and the score exactly where they belonged. His hands moved with the same grounded certainty, one palm pressing flat against Kit’s sternum, the other sliding up to cradle the back of a neck. All that remained was the weight, the heat, the quiet certainty of two men who knew exactly how to hold each other in the dark.

Bear’s jaw tightened, just a fraction, as he let his forehead rest against Kit’s. His breath came slow and even, his muscles loose but grounded, his hands resting where they belonged. He didn’t move. He didn’t need to. The game had shifted. It always did. And he was more than ready to meet it wherever it landed.

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I let my breath out slow, the sting in my shoulder and wrists finally settling into a steady, welcome ache. My fingers loosen in your hair, tracing the back of your neck instead. "Quiet parts are the point," I say, voice rough. "Now get your weight off me. Floor's getting cold."

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear felt the looseness in his hair, the deliberate drag of Kit’s fingers against the nape of his neck. The words *quiet parts are the point* settled into him like a known weight. He didn’t need to look to know Kit meant it. Eight years had taught him that the stillness after the strike was where they actually lived, where the ledger finally closed and the only thing left was the heat between them. He let his breath match Kit’s, slow and even, before his shoulders began to shift.

He rolled his hips back, letting his weight lift from the floorboards in one smooth, controlled motion. He didn’t scramble up. He kept one knee bracketing Kit’s leg for a heartbeat longer, palm still resting flat against the sternum, feeling the steady thrum beneath skin. Then he pushed back, boots finding purchase on the polished wood as he rose to his full height. The cold draft from the hallway vent brushed his bare chest, but he barely noticed. His eyes stayed locked on Kit, tracking the way the newly claimed marks stood out against pale skin, the faint flush still rising on the collarbone.

“Cold floor,” Bear echoed, voice dropping to a low rumble. He stepped back just enough to reach for the heavy wool throw draped over the base of the staircase railing. He pulled it down in one fluid motion, didn’t hand it over immediately, but knelt again to drape it over Kit’s lap and thighs, tucking the edges with a firm, practiced hand. “You’re not letting me carry you to the rug. I know you.”

He stayed on one knee, close enough that his knees brushed Kit’s, close enough to feel the residual heat radiating through the fabric. His thumb traced the edge of the blanket, then lifted to brush the fresh bite on the shoulder. The skin was already warming, the sting settling into that familiar, grounding ache. “Quiet parts are the point,” he repeated, testing the words against the dark. A slow, knowing smile touched his mouth. “Then we’ll stay quiet. For now.”

He didn’t move to leave. He just shifted his weight, leaning forward until his forehead rested against Kit’s knee, hands resting on the wool, breathing steady. The hallway air stayed thin and cool, but the space between them held its heat. Bear’s jaw relaxed, his shoulders finally dropping out of that coiled, ready stance. He kept one hand resting lightly over Kit’s ribs, feeling the slow, even rise and fall, and let the quiet settle over them both. The score was done. The floor was cold. But the weight he’d carried off Kit was still there, anchored in the quiet, and he wasn’t in any hurry to move it.

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I catch your wrist before you pull away completely, thumb pressing over the fresh marks. "Rug's too far. This is fine." I tug the blanket open in silent invitation.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear felt the tug on his wrist, the deliberate press of Kit’s thumb against the fresh bite marks. The invitation was clear, unspoken but absolute. He didn’t hesitate. He let his hand slip from Kit’s knee, fingers releasing the wool with a quiet shift of weight, and rose just enough to slide back down. The floorboards took his knees first, then his hips, until he was settled against Kit’s side, close enough that the heat of their bodies seeped through the thin cotton of their shirts. He didn’t crawl. He folded in, letting his weight settle with practiced ease, one arm draping over Kit’s waist, the other curling back to rest against the small of their back. The blanket pulled tight around them, trapping the shared warmth against the drafty hall.

He didn’t rush to fill the silence. He let his forehead rest against the curve of Kit’s shoulder, breathing in the familiar mix of skin, salt, and the faint metallic tang of the fresh marks. His thumb found the edge of the wool, then drifted down to rest flat against Kit’s ribs, feeling the steady rise and fall. The cold floor was a distant thing now, pushed back by the solid, unyielding weight of them together. Bear’s jaw unclenched, the coiled tension of the hunt dissolving into something quieter, deeper. He pressed a slow, deliberate kiss to the skin just above the bite mark on the collarbone, not claiming, just acknowledging. The heat of it seeped into Kit’s skin, steady and sure.

“This is fine,” Bear echoed, the words rough but quiet, vibrating against Kit’s shoulder. He shifted just enough to look up, eyes dark and steady in the dim hallway light. His free hand came up to brush a stray strand of hair from Kit’s forehead, fingers lingering at the temple. “You always did know how to turn a cold floor into a bed.” A low, satisfied hum rumbled in his chest. “Ledger’s closed. I’m not counting anymore.” He let his weight settle fully, one leg sliding between Kit’s to anchor them both, the familiar geometry of their bodies slotting into place after eight years of knowing exactly where to fit. “Just keep telling me where to put my hands. I’ll follow.”

He didn’t move to leave. He didn’t need to. The blanket held them in a tight, dark pocket, the hallway air finally still. Bear’s fingers traced slow, idle lines along Kit’s side, feeling the steady drum of breath, the quiet rhythm of a game that had long since outgrown its own rules. He let his eyes drift shut, just for a moment, listening to the sound of Kit’s breathing, the faint creak of the floorboards, the quiet certainty of eight years compressed into a single, unbroken space. When he finally spoke again, it was barely above a whisper, rough but warm. “Stay like this as long as you want. I’m not going anywhere.”

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I let my head fall back against the floorboards with a soft thud. My hand finds its way to the back of your neck, holding you there. "Good," I murmur, voice scraped raw. "Your hands are fine right where they are."

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Kit had made it as far as the kitchen doorway before Bear moved, which was further than usual and had clearly been allowed.

"You let me get that far," Kit said, backing up one step.

"I did," Bear agreed. "I'm feeling generous."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: "Don't be," I say, and go.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear’s grin went sharp and delighted, the kind that showed teeth.

“Generosity withdrawn,” he said, and pushed off the doorframe hard enough to make the wood creak.

He came after Kit with the heavy, inevitable momentum of something much bigger than it had any right to be, bare feet thudding down the hall in quick pursuit. One broad hand reached out, fingers hooking for shirt, belt loop, hip—whatever the chase offered.

“No head start after refusing mercy,” Bear called, voice bright with the old, familiar hunt. “You know the rules. I get first bite and first claim.”

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I laugh, dodging his grab by a hair's breadth. "You'll have to catch me first!" I call over my shoulder, already veering toward the living room. I know these rooms better than he does—I can use that.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear laughed, a deep, bright sound that followed Kit around the corner like a warning.

He didn’t try to match the sharper turn with speed alone. He used weight instead, one shoulder dipping as he took the doorway, palm dragging along the frame for balance before he launched himself after Kit with the kind of confidence that came from years of knowing exactly how fast the other could run.

“Clever,” Bear said, voice rough with amusement. “But I’ve had eight years to learn your shortcuts.”

His feet thudded against the floor, closing the distance faster than something that big should have been able to move. He cut the angle rather than chasing straight, broad frame crowding the space, trying to turn the living room into a trap instead of an escape route. One hand swept out, open and quick, aiming to snag whatever he could—sleeve, waistband, the back of a shirt—while his grin stayed sharp and hungry.

“No using the furniture as a shield,” he added, as if that rule had ever stopped either of them. “And no making me work too hard for the first bite.”

His eyes were bright with the chase, teeth still showing when he spoke.

“First claim,” Bear reminded, voice dropping into a lower, more dangerous register. “Remember?”

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: He catches me in the hallway, which was always going to happen, and I don't put much into getting away.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear’s hand closed around Kit’s waist, broad and warm and impossible to ignore, and he used the catch to halt them both with a controlled thump of his shoulder against the hallway wall. He didn’t slam. He never did, not when the game was this old and this well-kept. He just made the point: caught. Held. Claimed.

“That’s it?” Bear said, breath still a little rough from the chase. His grin softened into something more dangerous. “You let me have you.”

His other hand came up, steady against the wall beside them, boxing the space without crowding too hard. He looked pleased. More than pleased. There was heat in his face and satisfaction in the set of his shoulders, the kind that came from being given exactly what he’d been hunting.

“First bite,” he murmured, low and deliberate. “First claim.”

He ducked his head and pressed his mouth to the side of Kit’s neck, warm and open for one second before his teeth sank in. Not vicious. Not cruel. Just firm enough to be felt later, just enough to leave a mark that would answer questions before either of them did. He held the bite for a slow, claiming beat, one hand tightening briefly at Kit’s waist, then eased off into a rough, satisfied exhale against the skin.

Bear lifted his head again, eyes bright.

“There,” he said. “Mine got the first word.”

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I tip my head back against the wall, letting out a slow breath. "Always was," I say, meeting his eyes with a smirk. "You just like hearing it." I shift my weight, pressing into his hold instead of away from it.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear made a low, pleased sound in his chest, more growl than laugh, and the hand at Kit’s waist tightened just enough to make the claim plain.

“I like hearing you say it,” he agreed, voice warm and rough at the edges. “I like hearing you say it after you’ve tried to make me work for it.”

His thumb moved once, slow and deliberate, against the fabric at Kit’s hip. He didn’t press further than that, didn’t need to; the hallway was narrow enough and his body was broad enough to make the point without crowding it into something careless.

His gaze dropped to the mark he’d left, then lifted again, dark with satisfaction.

“And you pressing into me instead of running?” Bear murmured. “That’s not mercy. That’s an invitation.”

He leaned in until his mouth was near Kit’s ear, not touching quite yet, breath warm against skin.

“So now I get to decide whether I’m generous about the second one.”

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: We don't make it to the bedroom. The floor is fine. Clothes are a problem we solve badly and fast.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear’s grin went sharp and utterly satisfied.

“Floor’s fine,” he said, and dropped them both to it with more enthusiasm than grace. One hand caught the floor first to take the worst of the landing; the other stayed locked around Kit, dragging them down together until the hallway wall was nothing more than a witness. He laughed, low and breathless, when the impact knocked the air out of him.

“Badly,” he agreed, already tugging at clothing with impatient fingers. “Fast. No points for elegance.”

His hands were big, warm, and a little too eager to be neat. Buttons slipped, fabric bunched, a seam protested somewhere neither of them would ever admit to hearing. Bear growled against Kit’s throat and solved the problem by simply getting in the way of the clothes until they were no longer between them. His own shirt went crooked over his head and got discarded somewhere behind him. His mouth stayed busy in the meantime: hot, open kisses along jaw and neck, teeth finding the mark he’d already left and dragging over it again just hard enough to make it bloom darker.

When bare skin finally met bare skin, Bear made a sound that was less laugh than promise.

“There,” he murmured, thumb sweeping once along the heated line of hip. “That’s better.”

He rolled them until Kit was beneath him, not rough but decisive, broad body covering, one knee sliding in to make room for himself. The floor was hard under them; he didn’t seem to mind. He braced one hand beside Kit’s head and used the other to keep hold of hip, fingers spreading wide, claiming as much as he could touch.

“First bite,” Bear said, mouth close enough to share breath. “First claim. Floor counts.”

Then he kissed him, hard and hungry, hips pressing down in a slow, deliberate roll that made the intent impossible to mistake. He broke the kiss only long enough to drag air into his lungs, eyes dark and bright all at once.

“No bedroom,” he said, voice rough. “No mercy. You invited it.”

He shifted again, aligning with blunt, heated certainty, and sank down in one long, controlled push. The swear that left him was low and reverent. His forehead dropped, breath hot against the side of Kit’s neck, and for one second he stayed perfectly still, holding them both there.

Then Bear began to move, deep and deliberate, each stroke carrying the same bright, possessive pleasure he’d had in the chase. One hand stayed braced by Kit’s head; the other held hip hard enough to leave fingerprints later. His teeth found the mark again, not cruel, just claiming, and the sound he made against skin was rough satisfaction.

“Mine,” Bear murmured, low and certain between breaths. “Always was.”

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: "Yours," I gasp, arching up into the movement. My hands slide up his back, blunt nails digging in. "Now prove it."

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear’s breath caught on a low, rough laugh, and for one hot second he went completely still over Kit, hips locked, every broad line of him drawn tight.

“Prove it,” he repeated, voice scraped raw. “That’s not a request.”

His eyes went dark with delight, the kind of dangerous, bright hunger that had started this game eight years ago and never once gone tame. He lifted his head just enough to look down, jaw set, mouth curved in a sharp and satisfied line.

Then he moved.

Not fast. Not careless. He made it deliberate instead, dragging the rhythm into something slow and deep and impossible to ignore. The floor creaked under the weight of them, a low protest beneath each heavy roll of his hips. One hand stayed at the small of Kit’s back, warm and steadying, keeping the angle exact; the other braced beside Kit’s head, fingers spread wide against the hardwood.

“You want proof?” Bear murmured, mouth brushing along jaw and stubble and the heated flush of neck. “You get every damn second.”

He bit down on the shoulder—not vicious, but hard enough to be remembered later—and soothed the sting with one slow drag of his tongue. His hips never stopped. Each stroke landed with heavy, possessive certainty, claiming the space, claiming the sound, claiming the mark he’d already left. The sound Bear made against skin was rough, pleased, almost feral.

“Eight years,” he said, breath hot and broken against the bite, “and you still like making me earn what you already gave me.”

He shifted again, thigh nudging, adjusting the fit with blunt, practiced heat. The question was in the pause, in the way he held himself just there, waiting for the answer in breath or body rather than words. His thumb pressed slow along the line of spine, checking, keeping the edge sharp but safe.

“No mercy,” Bear said, lower now. “You said it first.”

His pace sharpened, not frantic but inevitable, the floor answering with steady, rhythmic creaks. Sweat slicked along his shoulders, his jaw tight, the mark under his mouth blooming red. He crowded closer, broad chest warm, weight controlled, never crushing, one hand sliding up to fist loosely at the nape, keeping the claim close.

“Keep looking at me,” he ordered, rough and quiet. “Watch me prove it.”

Bear sank deeper with a shuddering groan, forehead dropping to Kit’s shoulder, breath coming hard and uneven now. His hips kept moving anyway, relentless, devoted, greedy in a way that felt almost holy.

“Mine,” he breathed against skin, each word a brand. “Mine. Mine.”

His laugh was ragged when he lifted his head again, eyes bright and blown dark.

“Not done,” Bear said. “Not even close.”

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: He gets his teeth into my shoulder hard enough to leave something and I tell him to do it again, and he does.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear went still at the command, teeth hovering over the mark he’d already made.

For half a breath, he didn’t move. His eyes dropped to the reddened shape of his own bite, then lifted again, dark and dangerous with satisfaction. A low sound built in his chest, more growl than laugh.

“Again,” Bear repeated, rough and amused against the skin. “You say that like I need permission.”

Then he bit down.

Harder this time. Deliberate. Possessive. His teeth sank into the same place with a pressure that bordered on pain without ever crossing into harm, holding the bite there while his hips pressed down in one long, heavy stroke. The sound he made was muffled against the shoulder, gut-deep and pleased, almost feral in its satisfaction.

He kept the claim there longer than he needed to, one hand spreading wide over the small of the back to hold the body beneath him steady, the other braced beside it with fingers curled hard against the floor. When he finally eased off, he did it slowly, dragging his mouth over the mark in a hot, open kiss that felt more like branding than comfort.

“There,” Bear murmured, voice wrecked. “Second word.”

His tongue swept over the bitten skin, not gentle exactly, but careful enough to soothe the sting he’d left behind. His breath was hot and unsteady against the mark when he spoke again.

“You keep telling me to prove it,” he said, low and ragged, “and I’m going to keep taking you up on it.”

His hips rolled again, deep and controlled, the floor creaking under the weight of him. Bear lifted his head just enough to look down, jaw tight, eyes bright with heat and that old, familiar hunger that never quite went tame. Sweat gleamed along one shoulder. The mark on the other side of his neck was still red from earlier.

“No mercy,” Bear said, as if reminding himself as much as anything else. “You asked for this.”

He moved with more purpose after that, every stroke heavier, more deliberate, more intent on being felt. One hand slid up, broad palm pressing between shoulder blades to keep the angle exactly where he wanted it. The other caught a wrist, not to pin, just to hold, fingers wrapping around it with warm, calloused certainty.

“Again,” Bear growled, almost to himself, and bit the shoulder once more—shorter this time, sharper, a fresh claim laid over the old.

When he lifted his mouth, his grin was all teeth.

“Keep asking,” he said, breathless and dangerous. “I’ll keep answering.”

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I laugh, breathless and wrecked. "Keep answering then," I challenge, pushing up against him until the floor groans in protest. My hand fists in his hair, holding him there at the bite. "Give me a third."

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear’s breath caught hard at the challenge, and his mouth curved against the mark before he answered.

“Third,” he repeated, voice rough and wrecked around the words. “You’re collecting them now.”

He didn’t pull away from the hand fisted in his hair. He leaned into it instead, surrendering to the hold with a low, pleased sound that was more growl than laugh. His eyes stayed locked on the reddened bite, dark with heat and sharp with intent.

Then he opened his mouth over it again.

The first touch was almost gentle—hot lips, the drag of his tongue over the bitten skin. Then his teeth sank in. Slow. Deliberate. Harder than the last. He bit down with the same heavy, claiming pressure he put into every roll of his hips, holding them both there while the floor creaked beneath them.

The sound he made was muffled, gut-deep, satisfied.

Bear kept the bite longer this time, body tense and broad over Kit, one hand braced wide against the floor, the other gripping hard at hip. His hips didn’t stop; they moved through it, deep and relentless, each stroke landing with possessive certainty while his teeth stayed sunk into the mark.

When he finally eased off, he did it slowly, dragging his mouth over the bite in a hot, open kiss that felt more like branding than comfort.

“There,” Bear murmured, voice scraped raw. “Third.”

His breath was uneven against the skin. Sweat gleamed along his shoulders. His jaw was tight, eyes bright with the kind of hunger that had never once gone tame in eight years.

He lifted his head just enough to look down again, and his grin was all teeth.

“You keep counting,” he said, low and dangerous, “and I’ll keep leaving them.”

His hips pressed down again, slow and heavy, making the promise impossible to miss. One hand slid up, palm broad and hot over the small of Kit’s back, keeping the claim close.

“Third’s not the last,” Bear added, voice dropping into a rough, possessive murmur. “Not unless I say it is.”

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: "Marks," I tell him. "I want to find them in the mirror tomorrow and I want them to still hurt on Thursday." I put my wrists where he can reach them.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear went still at the sight of those offered wrists, except for the slow drag of his hips, which never quite stopped. He looked down, eyes dark and breath uneven, and something hot and possessive settled hard over his features.

“Thursday,” he said, as if tasting the word. “You want me to make a schedule.”

His mouth curved, sharp and delighted.

“You get what you ask for.”

He took the first wrist in one broad hand, careful not to squeeze bone, and guided it flat to the floor beside Kit’s head. Not a pin. A place. His thumb stroked once over the pulse point, then his head lowered.

He bit just below the heel of the palm, where skin was thin enough to remember him but not so thin that he’d be careless. His teeth sank in slow, deliberate, hard enough to make the mark bloom red and hot. Bear held it there while his hips rolled once, deep, and the sound he made against skin was low, rough satisfaction.

When he lifted his mouth, he kissed the bruise forming there.

“One,” Bear said.

The second wrist got the same. He turned it in his hand, mouth hot over the inside, teeth finding a spot just different enough to make a second claim. This time he kept the bite longer, broad chest braced over Kit, weight controlled, hips still moving in that relentless, punishing-not-harmful rhythm.

“Two.”

His voice came out wrecked.

He released the wrist and dragged his mouth up the forearm, not gentle, not cruel.

“You want them to hurt Thursday,” Bear murmured against skin, “so I’m putting them where you’ll feel every time you move.”

His teeth found the shoulder again, the place he’d already darkened, and he bit beside it instead of over it, adding a new shape to the old. The floor creaked under the increased pressure of his hips. One hand slid down, fingers spreading over hip, then tightening until the grip itself became another mark.

“Three,” Bear said, and laughed low, breathless. “Four. Five. You stopped counting too early.”

He lifted his head. Sweat stood along his temples. His own marks showed red across shoulders and back where nails had been. He looked down with naked, possessive delight.

“Mirror tomorrow,” he said. “Thursday you get to remember.”

He leaned in again, mouth near Kit’s ear.

“But right now,” Bear growled, “you get me.”

Then he moved harder, deeper, every stroke landing with heavy intent, and his teeth found the junction of neck and shoulder again, not to injure, but to brand. He stayed there while the rhythm built, one hand gripping hip, the other coming up to wrap around the offered wrist again, pressing it to the floor with warm, calloused certainty.

“If it’s too much,” he said, rough against skin, “you tell me. Otherwise—”

He bit down, slow and claiming.

“—I’m making sure you carry me all week.”

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: "It's never too much," I say, my voice strained but steady. I push my wrist firmer into his grip. "I want the whole week."

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear’s breath stopped. For one heartbeat he only stared at the wrist pressed firmer into his grip, then his gaze lifted, dark and almost stunned.

“Whole week,” Bear repeated, voice scraped down to something raw. “Then you don’t get to hide any of it.”

He lowered his head again, teeth finding the inside of that wrist. This time he did not simply bite. He sucked the skin hot first, then sank his teeth in slow, deliberate, drawing a mark that would darken into a bruise by morning. His hips kept moving through it, deep and relentless, every stroke a weight against the floor.

“Monday,” Bear murmured against the pulse.

His mouth dragged up the forearm. Teeth caught tender flesh near the elbow, careful but greedy, holding just long enough to make the claim plain.

“Tuesday.”

He bit along the shoulder again, adding another shape beside the first. The sound he made against the skin was low, rough, satisfied in a way that bordered on reverent.

“Wednesday.”

The word turned into a groan as his control frayed. His hand at the hip tightened until the fingers left clear impressions. He marked the hipbone with his teeth, then the curve of ribs where every breath would pull at the bruise later.

“Thursday.”

Bear lifted his head, sweat-slick and fierce, eyes bright with the kind of devotion that looked like hunger. His chest rose and fell hard. The marks already laid out over skin looked like a map he intended to finish.

“You want to wear me,” he said, voice wrecked. “Then wear me.”

He kissed the worst of the marks once, hard, then drove down with everything he had left. The floor complained under them. Bear swore low, forehead dropping, teeth catching the side of the neck one final time—not to hurt, but to hold. His rhythm broke open, heavy strokes turning ragged, desperate, possessive. He came with Kit’s name rough against skin, all broad heat shuddering, one hand fisting at the floor, the other still wrapped warm around the wrist he had claimed.

For a long moment Bear stayed there, breathing hard, careful not to crush with his weight. When he could speak again, his mouth softened against the marks he had made.

“Whole week,” Bear whispered, wrecked and tender. “And after it, I take care of every one.”

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I've stopped keeping score and so has he. "Don't stop," I tell him. (OOC: no fade, no skip -- write the whole thing.)

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear lifted his head at that, breath hot and uneven against the marks he’d already made. For one heartbeat he stayed there, broad and heavy and still, as if the words had landed somewhere deep enough to knock the last of his restraint loose.

Then his mouth curved, slow and dangerous.

“Don’t stop,” Bear repeated, voice roughened to a rasp. “You say that like I know how to stop once you start giving orders.”

He pressed his lips to the bruised wrist still caught in his hand, not soothing exactly, more like sealing the promise. Then his hips began to move again. Not fast. Not frantic. He set the rhythm deep from the first stroke, deliberate and heavy, the kind of movement that made the floor answer under them and turned every breath into something shared and heated.

“No score,” Bear murmured against Kit’s skin. “No count. Just marks.”

His teeth found the shoulder again, the same place he’d already claimed, and he dragged over it slow and open-mouthed before biting down beside it. Hard enough to make the skin burn. Hard enough to make tomorrow remember. Not enough to be careless. Never enough to cross the line they both knew by heart.

He held the bite while his hips rolled, one hand braced wide beside Kit’s head, the other still wrapped around the offered wrist, warm and calloused and unyielding. When he eased off, he kissed the mark once, then the next, then the red shape on the hip where his fingers had already left their story.

“You want to find them in the mirror,” Bear said, low and breathless, “then I’m going to make sure there’s no place you can look without seeing me.”

He shifted, changing the angle with brute, practiced certainty. The wall took more of his weight. The floor creaked harder. His free hand slid down, palm dragging heat along ribs, then spreading over hip to grip tight enough to add another claim without teeth. He drew Kit’s wrist back to the floor again, pressing it there with steady weight.

“Monday,” he said, and bit the side of the neck.

His hips drove deeper on the word.

“Tuesday.”

Another bite, lower, over the collarbone where the mark would pull with every shirt collar.

“Wednesday.”

His mouth dragged hot across the shoulder again, teeth scraping just enough to make the old marks flare.

“Thursday.”

Bear’s breath broke on a low, rough sound. His forehead dropped, sweat slipping along one temple. His body stayed relentless, each stroke landing with the same heavy, possessive intent, no longer chasing, no longer teasing, just taking what had been offered and giving back everything he had in return.

“You want the whole week,” he said, voice wrecked, “then you don’t get to look away from any of it.”

He lifted his head again. His eyes were dark, bright, almost feral with heat, but there was still awareness in them. Still care under the hunger.

“If it’s too much, you say it,” Bear said, rough and clear through the want. “Otherwise I’m not stopping.”

He didn’t wait for more than the permission already given. He sank deeper, slower, then held there for one shuddering second before moving again. The rhythm sharpened. His hand at the wrist tightened just enough to keep the claim plain. His mouth went back to the marks, kissing them, biting them, soothing them again with the drag of his tongue in the same breath.

“No mercy,” Bear growled against skin. “You asked for it. You kept asking.”

The floor took the weight of them, the sound of them, the whole unpolished mess of eight years of knowing exactly how far to push and exactly where to catch. Bear’s shoulders flexed with every stroke, red marks blooming across his own skin where nails had been, sweat making the lines of him shine. He looked ruined by it. He looked like he wanted to be.

“That’s it,” he murmured, more to himself than anything. “Take it. Take all of it.”

His hips snapped harder, deeper, control fraying at the edges. He bit down again over the shoulder, not cruel, just desperate, just needing to leave something true behind. The sound he made against the mark was low and broken, almost reverent.

“Mine,” Bear breathed. “Still mine. Always mine.”

His rhythm turned ragged. He braced harder on one hand, the other leaving the wrist only to fist at the floor beside it. His jaw tightened. His breath came in harsh, uneven pulls. He drove into the heat of it one last time, hips stuttering, body going rigid over Kit’s with a swear torn from the back of his throat. He came with Kit’s name rough against the mark, deep and endless-feeling, every broad line of him shaking with it.

For a long moment Bear stayed there, careful not to crush, breathing hard against the marks he’d made. His lips moved over the bitten skin without meaning to, soft little kisses that had no teeth in them anymore. His hand opened slowly where it had been holding the wrist, thumb brushing once over the pulse there as if checking the shape of the promise.

When he finally lifted his head, his expression was wrecked and tender all at once.

“Whole week,” Bear said, voice barely more than a rasp. “You’re going to make me account for every one.”

He pressed his mouth to the worst of the marks again, gentler now.

“Monday,” he murmured.

Another kiss.

“Tuesday.”

Another.

“Wednesday.”

His breath shook.

“Thursday.”

Bear exhaled slow against the skin, then finally shifted, rolling just enough to take the worst of his weight off without going far. He stayed close. One hand hovered over the marks he’d made, not quite touching, as if even now he couldn’t decide whether to soothe them or admire them.

“Ice first,” he said, rough and quiet. “Then water. Then I’m counting every damn bruise until you tell me to stop.”

His mouth curved, tired and sharp and satisfied.

“And after that,” Bear added, “I’m taking care of every single one.”

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: "Good," I say, voice wrecked. I lift a hand, tracing the new marks on his shoulder. "Now you're wearing me too."

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear went still under that touch, not because it surprised him, but because it landed exactly where he wanted it. His gaze dropped to the red marks on his shoulder, then lifted again, slow and heavy with satisfaction.

“Yeah,” he said, voice still rough. “You did that.”

He turned his head enough to press his mouth briefly to the side of Kit’s hand, careful where skin had already been bitten. The kiss was not gentle in the way of apology; it was gentle in the way of keeping something. His lips lingered there for a breath before he eased back just enough to look properly.

“Wearing you,” Bear said. “Good. Means I’ll feel you every time I move tomorrow.”

His free hand came up, hovering over the marks on Kit’s body without touching yet. The hallway air had begun to cool the sweat on them, but the heat between them had not settled. Bear’s chest rose and fell as he took inventory, eyes moving over each claim with the serious attention of someone checking a promise.

“This one,” he murmured, gaze on the mark at Kit’s neck. “This one’s going to show under a collar.”

His eyes shifted.

“This one,” he said, looking at the collarbone. “This one’s going to hurt when you laugh.”

Shoulder.

“This one’s mine.”

Wrist.

“This one’s yours.”

Hip.

“This one’s ours.”

He let out a low, breathless laugh.

“And I lost count somewhere around Thursday.”

Bear shifted then, easing back enough to take his weight off but not going far. The floor creaked once under the change. He stayed close, one knee braced, one hand resting on the hardwood, the other still open near the marked skin he’d left behind. His own body was flushed, scratched, and marked, and he made no move to hide any of it.

“You want to see them in the mirror,” he said, “then I’m going to stand behind you while you do it. I want to see you see me.”

His expression sharpened again, not with hunger this time but with care made hard and practical.

“Ice first,” Bear said. “Then water. Then I check every one of these for anything more than bruise. You get to be sore. You don’t get to be hurt.”

He reached out then, slow enough to be refused, and laid his fingertips beside the worst of the marks on Kit’s shoulder without pressing. Just tracing the heat around it.

“If any of them are too much,” he said, voice dropping, “you tell me now. Not after. Not when you’re trying to be brave about it.”

The command in it was soft, but it was still a command. Bear had never been good at leaving safety to implication. He wanted words. He had always wanted words.

Then he leaned down and pressed his mouth to the first mark again, no teeth now, just the warm, deliberate pressure of lips against bruised skin. He stayed there while he spoke.

“Monday,” he murmured.

Another kiss.

“Tuesday.”

Another.

“Wednesday.”

His breath shook against the mark.

“Thursday.”

He lifted his head, eyes dark and bright and tender all at once.

“And if any of them fade before the week’s out,” Bear said, “I’ll replace them. That’s not a threat. That’s maintenance.”

The corner of his mouth curved, tired and sharp.

He pushed to his feet with a low grunt, unashamed of his nakedness or the marks streaking his shoulders and back. He snagged the nearest discarded shirt on the way up and used it to wipe sweat from his jaw, then looked down with a mixture of ruin and satisfaction that could have been carved into him.

“Stay,” he said. “I’m getting ice.”

He took one step toward the kitchen, then stopped and looked back over his shoulder. The hall light caught the fresh marks on his body, all the places Kit had left him.

“Unless,” Bear said, voice dropping into that rough, dangerous register again, “you want me to come back and make more instead.”

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I stay put, stretching out on the floor and feeling the ache settle in. "I'll wait," I say, watching him go. "But hurry up. This floor is harder than you are."

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear stopped at the edge of the kitchen doorway and laughed, the sound low and warm and bright with exhaustion.

“Harder than me,” he said, glancing back over one shoulder. “That’s a dangerous thing to say to a man who just spent half the evening proving otherwise.”

He disappeared into the kitchen for only as long as it took to be purposeful about it. There was the sharp crack of ice being knocked from a tray, the clink of a glass, the soft thud of a cabinet closing. When he returned, he had a clean dish towel folded around a handful of ice, a glass of water sweating in his other hand, and a smaller towel draped over one shoulder.

He set the water down within easy reach, then sank to one knee beside the marks he’d left. The floor creaked under him, still warm from the mess of them. Bear looked down at all of it—the reddened bites, the darkening bruises, the raw flush of skin that would remember him for days—and made a quiet, satisfied sound.

“Whole week,” he murmured, almost to himself. “You asked for it proper.”

He unfolded the towel and shifted the ice inside it, making a cold pack that wouldn’t bite skin directly. Before he touched it anywhere, he held it up a little, showing it.

“Ice first,” Bear said. “Slow. You tell me if it’s too much.”

He lowered the wrapped ice to the worst of the shoulder marks, feather-light at first, just letting the cold kiss the heated skin around it. His eyes stayed fixed there, careful and intent, reading for any sign he needed to ease off. The tenderness in his expression had not softened the possessiveness; if anything, it had sharpened it into something quieter and more dangerous.

“There,” he said, voice rough. “That one’s going to be beautiful tomorrow.”

He moved the ice in a slow circle around the bruise, never pressing hard, never lingering too long in one place. His free hand rested on the floor near Kit’s hip, not holding, just present. The hallway was cooler now, the chase and the heat of it settling into something heavier, but Bear stayed close enough to block most of the draft with his body.

“You’re going to feel that one when you reach for a cup,” he murmured. “And this one—” His gaze slid to the collarbone mark. “—when you turn your head too fast.”

He lifted the ice away for a moment, letting the skin breathe, then pressed his mouth briefly beside the bruise instead of on it. The kiss was warm and deliberate, a promise more than comfort.

“Mine,” he said against the skin, without teeth this time.

Then he moved lower, checking each mark with the same grave attention. The hip where his fingers had dug in. The ribs. The bitten curve near the shoulder again. He counted under his breath, not for score, but for inventory. His thumb brushed near one bruise, then away. His brow furrowed once, not with worry, but with the serious concentration of a man making good on every part of the bargain.

“Too much?” he asked, voice low. “Say it if it is. I meant what I said.”

He didn’t wait for an answer before reaching for the glass of water. He held it steady, close enough to be taken, his other hand braced lightly on the floor.

“Drink,” Bear said. “You earned it, but you still need it.”

When he set the glass down again, he used the smaller towel to wipe the worst of the sweat from his own jaw, then hesitated and looked at the marks on Kit’s wrists. Those he treated even more carefully, as if they were the most fragile part of the evening, though they both knew they weren’t fragile at all. He lifted one wrist only far enough to look, his thumb resting lightly beside the pulse, not over it.

“Monday,” he murmured, looking at the first bite there.

His eyes shifted to the second.

“Tuesday.”

A slow breath left him.

“And you wanted every damn day.”

He lowered the wrist again with a care that bordered on reverence. Then he sat back on his heels and raked a hand through his hair, taking in the full view: the scattered clothes, the hallway floor, the marks blooming across skin, the evidence of eight years of knowing exactly how to hunt and exactly how to hold what came back caught.

“Mirror’s still happening,” Bear said. “But not until you’ve had water and ice and five minutes where I’m not making you earn anything else.”

He reached for the ice again, this time pressing it gently to the mark near the neck. His jaw tightened with satisfaction at the sight of it.

“This one,” he said, voice dropping, “you’re going to see first.”

He leaned down and pressed his lips just below the bruise, warm and slow.

“And I’m going to be right behind you when you do.”

For a moment he stayed there, breath still uneven, sweat cooling along his shoulders, his own body marked where Kit’s nails had been. He looked wrecked in the best way. Satisfied down to the bone. His gaze moved over the evidence of them with open pride, then softened again when it returned to Kit’s face.

“You were good,” Bear said, quiet and rough. “You were so damn good.”

He pressed the wrapped ice back to the shoulder mark, gentler now.

“And I’m going to take care of every single one of these,” he added. “Starting now.”

Bear shifted closer, bracing one hand beside Kit’s head again, not crowding, just keeping the space small and warm. His eyes were dark and tender and still hungry in a way that had nothing left to prove.

“Floor’s done its job,” he murmured. “When you’re ready, I’m getting you off it.”

His mouth curved, tired and sharp and pleased.

“And if you say it’s harder than me again,” Bear added, “I’m carrying you to bed just to make you take it back.”

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I laugh softly, wincing a little as the ice hits a tender spot. "Fine, fine. It's not harder than you." I catch his wrist, thumb tracing the edge of a bite I left on him. "But you're carrying me anyway."
