dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Kit had made it as far as the kitchen doorway before Bear moved, which was further than usual and had clearly been allowed.

"You let me get that far," Kit said, backing up one step.

"I did," Bear agreed. "I'm feeling generous."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: "Don't be," I say, and go.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear’s laugh came out low and rough, more vibration than sound. He crossed the kitchen in two strides and stopped just inside Kit’s reach, close enough that the heat of him radiated between them. One hand lifted, slow and deliberate, and settled on the doorframe beside Kit’s head; the other braced low on the opposite side, boxing the narrow space without touching.

He dipped his head, mouth curving near Kit’s ear. “Bad idea,” Bear murmured, teeth skimming the air just shy of the tendon there. “You tell me not to be generous, and now I’m spoiled.”

His gaze held, dark and amused. “Again,” he said. “Make me work for it.”

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I grin, sharp and unrepentant. "Work for it?" My hand snaps up, pushing against his chest — not to shove him away, but to brace, digging my fingers in. "You're about to."

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear held perfectly still under the pressure, letting the challenge settle in his bones. Then his smile changed—slower, sharper, the kind that promised teeth.

“Good,” he said.

He peeled one hand from the doorframe, dragging his knuckles along the wood with deliberate slowness, and stepped back just enough to open the corridor between them. Not retreat. Invitation.

His gaze kept hold, dark and amused. “I like being made to work.” A rough note threaded through it. “Especially when the reward’s worth the bite.”

He turned toward the hall, rolling his shoulders as he went, and looked back over one shoulder with a lazy, dangerous grin.

“Come get it.”

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: He catches me in the hallway, which was always going to happen, and I don't put much into getting away.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear’s laugh chased Kit down the hall a half-step ahead of his feet. He closed the distance in two long strides, one hand shooting out to catch the front of Kit’s shirt—not yanking, just stopping, fingers bunching fabric tight enough to make the point. The other braced against the wall above Kit’s shoulder, turning the narrow hallway into a hot, timber-walled cage.

“Cute,” Bear said, rough and fond. He leaned in until his mouth hovered at the tendon below Kit’s ear. “You run like you already know I’m faster.”

Then he took the bite.

It was a good one—sharp, deep, deliberate, the kind that left a claim without needing the word. Bear held the gathered fabric for a breath after, letting the heat of it sink into his palm, then eased his teeth away and dragged his tongue over the mark once, slow and possessive.

His gaze lifted, dark and amused. “That’s for making me cross the kitchen twice.” The grin that followed was feral, easy, and entirely unrepentant. “Now. Are we doing this properly, or do I have to teach you manners?”

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I laugh, breathless, and tip my head back against the wall. "Teach me manners," I say, meeting his eyes. "I'm a terrible student."

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear’s grin went wider, showing teeth.

“Terrible students are my favorite kind,” he said.

He let go of Kit’s shirt, but he didn’t give an inch of space. Instead, he crowded the narrow hallway even closer, one palm braced high on the wall, the other coming up to rest against the hinge of Kit’s jaw—thumb brushing once, slow, almost gentle, against the pulse there.

“The first rule,” Bear murmured, leaning in until his breath warmed the fresh mark below Kit’s ear, “is that when I’ve caught you, you stop pretending you wanted to escape.”

His teeth closed over the tender spot again, lighter this time, a teasing pressure rather than a claim. Enough to sting. Enough to promise worse.

He soothed it with his tongue, then drew back just far enough to look at Kit, eyes dark and bright with amusement.

“Second rule,” he said, voice roughening. “Manners mean you thank your teacher.”

A pause. His thumb traced once more along Kit’s jaw before dropping away.

“So,” Bear said, nodding toward the bedroom down the hall. “Bed. Now. Unless you’d rather I keep marking you in public and see how long your ‘terrible student’ act lasts.”

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: We don't make it to the bedroom. The floor is fine. Clothes are a problem we solve badly and fast.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear’s laugh scraped low through the hallway. “Fast, then,” he said, and dropped to his knees on the boards. He caught the hem of Kit’s shirt with both hands and dragged it up in one rough, efficient motion, then tossed it toward the bedroom without looking.

The newly bared skin got exactly one second of cool air before Bear bent his head and bit.

It was a good bite—deep, deliberate, the kind that left a claim without needing poetry. Bear held his teeth there for a heartbeat, then soothed the sting with his tongue, lips curling against the warm mark.

“One,” he murmured against Kit’s shoulder. “I’m keeping score.”

He shed his own shirt next, letting it join the first somewhere behind him, then returned with both palms set firm on Kit’s hips. His thumbs pressed into the edges there, holding, grounding, while he tipped his face up with that feral, easy grin.

Bear kissed him then, hot and unhurried, taking the shape of the kiss like he owned the right to it—because he did, because they had built that right out of teeth, laughter, and eight years of refusing to be polite about want. When he broke away, his forehead stayed braced to Kit’s, breath rough in the narrow space between them.

“Floor’s fine,” he said, voice darker now, amused and impatient all at once. “But if we’re doing this properly, you remember the lesson.” His grip tightened just enough to make the point, then one hand slid lower to press flat against the small of Kit’s back. Bear eased himself backward until the hallway floor took his shoulders, never losing the contact, never losing the grin.

He looked up from the boards, eyes bright and wicked. “Thank your teacher,” he said. “Then show me how terrible you can be.”

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I sink down with him, knees hitting the wood on either side of his hips. "Thank you," I say, breathless already, and lean in to bite his shoulder in answer.

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: He gets his teeth into my shoulder hard enough to leave something and I tell him to do it again, and he does.

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I arch into the bite, a sharp gasp escaping me. "Harder," I demand, fingers digging into his back.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear’s grin sharpened, all humor burning down to something darker. He settled heavier over the hallway floor—not crushing, just weight, just proof—and brought one hand up to cradle the back of Kit’s neck. His thumb stroked once along the spine there, slow and steadying, before his mouth closed over the fresh mark again.

This time he didn’t tease.

He bit deep, the pressure sudden and exact, and held it with a low groan vibrating through his chest. Heat, salt, the familiar taste of want—eight years of it, still enough to ruin him. Bear eased off and dragged his tongue over the sting in one long, possessive sweep.

“Careful,” Bear murmured against skin, voice wrecked around the edges. “You keep asking for trouble and I’ll start thinking you meant it.”

He shifted, bracing his forearms on either side of Kit’s head, and looked down with eyes full of feral amusement. “Harder isn’t a request,” he said. “It’s a dare.”

Then he took the dare seriously.

His teeth found the slope of Kit’s other shoulder, grazed once, twice, and sank in again—harder, cleaner, a claim stamped without apology. Bear held the bite until his own breath shook, then soothed the mark with kisses that were anything but gentle.

When he finally lifted his head, his mouth curved near the spot he’d just ruined. “That’s two,” he said, rough and satisfied. “And I’m not done teaching.”

He kept one hand fisted lightly in the shirt he hadn’t managed to remove yet, using it to tug Kit closer by inches. “You want harder?” Bear asked, though the question was more promise than permission. “Then stop talking and take it.”

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: "Marks," I tell him. "I want to find them in the mirror tomorrow and I want them to still hurt on Thursday." I put my wrists where he can reach them.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear’s gaze dropped to the wrists offered like a dare and a benediction. Something in him answered before thought did—old, hungry, fond.

“Thursday,” he repeated, voice low. “Ambitious.”

He took the wrists. One hand closed over both, warm and firm, and he eased them down to the boards beside Kit’s head. Not a crush. Not a trap. A claim, steady as the eight years underneath it. His thumb swept once over the captured pulse, checking the rhythm there the way he always did when the chase got sharp: still here, still choosing this, still his to answer.

“Then I’d better make them worth finding.”

Bear lowered his mouth to the shoulder Kit had bitten first. His teeth scraped over the tender ridge, once, twice, and then sank in. Slower than before. Deeper. The kind of bite that would bloom dark and stubborn, that would ache under a shirt sleeve and remind Kit every time he moved. Bear held it until his own breath roughened, then soothed the mark with his tongue, lips pressing over the sting in a long, possessive sweep.

“Four,” he murmured against skin. “Score’s still open.”

He shifted, bracing one forearm high on either side of Kit’s pinned wrists, and brought his mouth to the hollow beneath Kit’s ear. The fresh mark there was hot under his teeth. Bear worried it gently at first—just enough pressure to make the skin blanch—then closed down harder, a clean, deliberate bite that left no room for politeness.

When he lifted his head, his grin was feral and satisfied.

“If you want mirror marks,” Bear said, “I’m going to have to stop being sweet about it.”

He released the wrists slowly, dragging his palm over the captured skin as he went, then cupped Kit’s jaw with one hand, thumb brushing the corner of Kit’s mouth before letting his hand fall away. His eyes searched Kit’s face—not uncertain, never uncertain, just attentive in the way eight years had taught him to be when teeth and trust shared the same space.

“Still mine to mark?” he asked, rough and light at once.

After a beat—enough space, enough air—he rolled onto his back with a low laugh, one arm tucked behind his head, the other reaching out palm-up over the hallway floor. An invitation. A scoreboard. A dare dressed as rest.

“Your turn, terrible student,” Bear said, gaze glinting up at Kit from the boards. “Bite me like you mean Thursday.”

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I catch his offered hand and press my teeth into the heel of his palm, hard enough to leave a crescent. "Yours," I say, letting go. "Always." Then I lean down and kiss the mark I just made, soft against the sting.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear went very still at the word.

Not startled—never startled—but caught, in the way a man is caught when something old and true lands exactly where he hasn’t bothered to armor himself. The bitten heel of his palm throbbed, bright and welcome, and for one reckless second he simply looked at Kit with the mask off: fond, hungry, wrecked by eight years of being chosen in teeth and whispers.

Then he laughed, low and rough.

“Cheater,” he said, though there was no accusation in it. Only delight, and the particular pleasure of a rival who had just scored where he wasn’t supposed to. “You get to say that right after I’ve been good?”

He brought his hand up, studying the crescent with mock severity. The mark was already angry, perfect, a small dark promise pressed into skin. Bear touched it once with his thumb and hissed softly through his teeth, more pleased than pained.

“That’s one for you,” he admitted. “Maybe two. I’m biased.”

His gaze lifted, dark and amused. “And if you keep kissing it like that, I’m going to forget I’m supposed to be teaching.”

Bear shifted closer, collapsing the remaining distance with intent. One hand slid into the hair at the nape of Kit’s neck, fingers threading slow and certain, and he left it there—warm, heavy, an anchor rather than a command.

“Thursday,” he murmured, tasting the word. “You want to hurt on Thursday?”

His mouth brushed the shell of Kit’s ear, barely there. “Then I’m going to need you very still for one minute.”

He kissed the corner of Kit’s mouth once, soft and profane at the same time, then drew back enough to look at him.

“Not forever,” Bear added, grin returning sharp. “Just long enough to make sure tomorrow’s mirror gets a proper show.”

His hand left Kit’s neck and traveled down, fingertips tracing the line of collarbone before pausing over the shoulder Kit had bitten first. Bear pressed his mouth there instead, tongue sweeping the mark clean before his teeth closed again—deeper this time, slower, a bruising claim laid over the memory of Kit’s own.

When he lifted his head, his voice was rough with satisfaction.

“Five,” he said. “And I’m still keeping score.”

He cupped Kit’s jaw, thumb brushing the hinge with a gentleness that belied the heat in his eyes.

“Your turn to be good,” Bear said. “Or don’t. I’m flexible.”

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
The party had reached the stage where nobody would notice two people missing, which Odile pointed out approximately four seconds before doing something about it.

"The bathroom upstairs has a lock," she said, into Fen's ear, over the music.

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: "Does it work?" I ask, already moving toward the stairs.

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
Odile let out a low, humming laugh, her breath warm against Fen's skin. She didn't answer immediately, instead letting her hand slide down from Fen's shoulder to give a firm, playful squeeze to their hip, urging them forward. 

She followed close behind, her heels clicking rhythmically against the floorboards as they ascended. The music became a muffled thrum in the background, replaced by the sudden, charged silence of the upper hallway. Odile didn't wait for Fen to reach the door first; she stepped around them with a mischievous glint in her eyes, reaching out to turn the handle and slip inside.

Once they were both in, she clicked the lock shut with a decisive *snap* that sounded far louder than it actually was in the small space. She leaned back against the door, crossing her arms and tilting her head. A small, daring smile played on her lips.

"I'm fairly certain it does," she whispered, her voice humming with a thrill of anticipation. "But I think the real question is whether we can keep the noise down enough that the host doesn't come knocking."

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: I grin, moving closer and caging her against the door with my hands on either side of her. "You're the loud one, not me," I say, my voice low.

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
Odile threw her head back, a short, breathless laugh escaping her. She didn't deny it; instead, she looked up at Fen with an expression that was purely provocative, her eyes dancing with the risk of it all. The thought of someone walking past the door and hearing a muffled moan or the frantic beat of a heart was, to her, the most intoxicating part of the entire evening.

"Is that a challenge?" she murmured, her voice dropping an octave.

She reached out, her fingers curling around the lapel of Fen's clothes to tug them firmly closer, closing the remaining gap between their bodies. Odile shifted her weight, pressing herself flush against them, the cool surface of the door at her back contrasting with the sudden heat of their proximity. 

She tilted her chin up, her smile widening into something more hungry as she breathed in the scent of them. "I can be very quiet if I want to be," she lied, the words vibrating against Fen's lips just before she bridged the distance to kiss them, the gesture far more aggressive and impatient than her claim suggested.

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: I get the door shut and her against it, and downstairs somebody turns the music up, which helps.

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
Odile let out a soft, muffled sound of approval against Fen's lips as the bass from downstairs kicked back in, the vibration rattling faintly through the floorboards. The sudden surge of volume felt like a green light, a shield of noise that emboldened her. 

She broke the kiss for a fleeting second, her breath hitching as she looked up at Fen. The thrill of the situation was humming through her veins, making her feel lightheaded and daring. She loved this—the precariousness of it, the way they were tucked away in a small, sterile room while their friends were just a few dozen feet away, completely oblivious.

"Perfect timing," she whispered, though it was more of a breathless giggle.

Her hands didn't stay idle; she slid them from Fen's lapels down to their waist, her fingers digging in with a sudden, needy urgency. She arched her back, pressing her chest firmly against theirs, and let out a small, shaky sigh that was far louder than she intended. She didn't seem to care. In fact, the risk of the sound escaping the room only seemed to make her more fervent.

Odile tilted her head, seeking out the sensitive skin of Fen's neck with her lips, nipping lightly at the junction of their shoulder. "I bet they're all wondering where we went," she murmured against their skin, her voice laced with a playful, wicked sort of pride.

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: My breath catches at the nip against my neck. "Let them wonder," I manage, sliding a hand up to tangle in her hair, gently guiding her mouth back to mine. The thrum of the bass vibrates through the door at my back.

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
Odile melted into the touch, a soft, needy sound vibrating in her throat as Fen guided her back to a kiss. She leaned into them with everything she had, her body molding against theirs as if she wanted to merge into the very door she was pinned against. The bass from downstairs was a steady, rhythmic pulse, and Odile found herself timing her own quickening heartbeat to the beat of the music.

She was far past the point of wanting to be discreet. The danger was an aphrodisiac, and every time she heard a distant laugh or the faint sound of a door closing in the hallway, she felt a surge of electricity shoot through her.

Her hands wandered, sliding down to the hem of Fen's shirt, her fingers hooking under the fabric to pull it up, desperate for more direct contact. She let out a sharp, airy gasp when Fen's hand tightened in her hair, her eyes fluttering shut.

"You're far too... indulgent," she breathed against their lips, her voice trembling slightly. She pulled back just an inch, a daring, wide-eyed look on her face. "I wonder... how many people have to walk past this door before someone notices it's locked?"

The question was a tease, a gamble. She let out a small, giddy laugh, the sound far too loud for the small room, and immediately pressed her forehead against Fen's, her breath coming in short, jagged bursts. She was practically vibrating with excitement, her body humming with a hunger that the risk only amplified.

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: There isn't room to do this properly and we don't let that stop us. Enough clothes come off to be a problem if anyone knocks.

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
Odile didn't care about the lack of space; in fact, the cramped quarters only added to the friction, forcing them into an intimacy that felt frantic and urgent. Every time she shifted, her back pressed harder against the door, the wood creaking slightly under her weight. The sound made her heart leap into her throat, but instead of pulling back, she leaned further into the sensation, a small, triumphant smirk crossing her face.

As clothes were discarded with haphazard haste, landing in a heap on the cold tile floor, Odile felt a rush of pure, unadulterated mischief. The thought of the sheer panic—or the awkwardness—of having to explain their state of undress to a confused guest if the lock failed was almost as stimulating as Fen's touch.

She let out a sharp, uncontrolled moan as they finally connected, the sound echoing off the small bathroom walls. She immediately clamped a hand over her own mouth, her eyes widening, but the gesture was more of a performance than a genuine attempt at silence. She was shaking, her breath coming in ragged, shallow hitches that she made no effort to stifle.

"Oh god," she whispered, her voice thick and strained, barely audible over the thumping bass from below. She arched her hips, pressing herself closer to Fen, her fingers digging into their shoulders. 

She tilted her head back, her gaze drifting toward the door. Every muffled footstep in the hallway felt like a lightning strike. She let out another soft, giddy sound—half-laugh, half-gasp—as she closed her eyes, completely surrendered to the heat of the moment and the delicious, dangerous possibility of being caught.

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: I stifle a laugh against her shoulder. "If someone knocks, you're answering it," I murmur, shifting my weight against her with the rhythm of the music. The door groans softly in protest.

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
Odile’s eyes snapped open, a flash of genuine, manic amusement crossing her features at the suggestion. The idea of opening the door in this state, breathless and half-naked, was absolutely absurd—and the thought of it made her blood sing.

"I would," she gasped, her voice strained and trembling. "I'd love to see the look on their face."

She let out a shaky, breathless laugh that turned into a sharp cry as Fen shifted their weight, the rhythm of the music downstairs syncing perfectly with the friction between them. The door groaned again, a loud, wooden protest that vibrated through her spine. Odile didn't flinch; instead, she gripped Fen's shoulders tighter, her nails digging in as she pulled them closer, as if trying to eliminate any remaining air between them.

The risk was peaking now, the adrenaline making every sensation feel amplified, almost overwhelming. She was far beyond the point of modesty or caution. As the bass thudded through the walls, Odile threw her head back against the door with a dull *thump*, her expression one of pure, blissful desperation.

"I can't... I can't be quiet," she confessed, her voice breaking into a low, needy whimper. She didn't try to cover her mouth this time. Instead, she let out a long, shuddering moan that echoed clearly in the small space, her body arching violently. She was practically glowing with the thrill of it, her eyes half-lidded and hazy as she surrendered entirely to the heat and the wonderful, terrifying possibility of a knock at the door.

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: I get my hand between her legs and she bites down on my shoulder to keep quiet, which works for about thirty seconds.

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
Odile’s eyes flared, the pupils blown wide as the sudden, direct contact sent a jolt of electricity straight through her. She clamped her teeth down on Fen’s shoulder, her knuckles whitening where she gripped them, her entire body tensing into a rigid, trembling line. For a few moments, she was a portrait of forced restraint, her breathing coming in jagged, nasal huffs, her gaze locked onto Fen’s with an intensity that was almost feral.

But the effort was unsustainable. The combination of the thumping bass, the cramped heat of the room, and the sheer, overwhelming sensation of Fen’s hand of her was too much for her to contain. 

The dam broke with a sharp, guttural cry that she couldn't have stopped if she'd tried. She let go of Fen's shoulder, her head snapping back against the door with another loud *thud* as she shuddered violently. The sound was unrestrained, a loud, needy sound that surely would have carried into the hallway had the music not been at its peak.

"Oh, *fuck*," she gasped, her voice a wrecked, breathless whisper. She was shaking, her legs feeling like water as she clung to Fen for support. A small, delirious laugh bubbled up in her throat, a sound of pure, giddy triumph. She looked up at Fen, her face flushed and her expression utterly wrecked. "I told you... I'm terrible at this," she breathed, her eyes shimmering with the thrill of how loud she had just been.

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: I press my forehead against hers, breathing heavily. "We're lucky they're all too drunk to notice," I mutter, my voice rough. The music downstairs shifts to something slower, making the sudden quiet in the hallway outside feel more dangerous.

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
Odile froze, her breath still coming in ragged, shallow hitches. The sudden shift in the music acted like a spotlight, stripping away their auditory cover and leaving the silence of the upper hallway feeling heavy and oppressive. The contrast was electric; the sudden quiet didn't make her want to hide—it made her feel exposed in the most exhilarating way possible.

She stayed pressed against Fen, her skin damp and humming, her heart hammering against her ribs like a trapped bird. She tilted her head slightly, straining her ears to listen. Every tiny sound—the distant hum of the AC, the faint clink of a glass downstairs—felt magnified. 

A small, daring smile curled her lips. The danger had just spiked, and the adrenaline surge was almost as potent as the climax she had just experienced.

"Lucky?" she whispered, her voice a low, sultry rasp. She didn't move to pull away; instead, she shifted her hips just a fraction, a slow, provocative grind that was a blatant challenge to the new silence.

She looked up at Fen, her eyes dancing with a wicked sort of mischief. "I don't know... I think the silence makes it more interesting. Imagine if someone walked by *right now* and heard us breathing like this."

She let out a soft, airy giggle, the sound dangerously clear in the small room. She knew she was being reckless, practically begging for an interruption, but the risk was a drug she couldn't stop taking. She leaned in, her lips brushing Fen's ear as she murmured, "Do you think we should stay in here a little longer? Just to see if we get caught?"

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: "Stop worrying about the noise," she says, "and get on with it," so I get her leg up over my hip and stop being careful about how much sound either of us is making.

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
Odile let out a sharp, delighted gasp as Fen hoisted her leg up, her body reacting instantly to the sudden shift in intensity. The command to stop worrying about the noise was exactly what she wanted to hear; it was like a permission slip for her to completely lose herself. 

She didn't just stop being careful—she leaned into the chaos. 

As Fen drove back into her with renewed, unapologetic force, Odile’s head hit the door with a rhythmic, steady *thump-thump-thump* that echoed through the small bathroom. She wasn't biting her lip or stifling her breath anymore. Instead, she let out a series of loud, unrestrained moans, her voice filling the room and likely spilling out into the hallway. 

"Yes!" she cried out, the word a ragged, breathless exclamation. 

The sensation of the cold door against her back and the searing heat of Fen's body was overwhelming. She wrapped her arms tightly around Fen's neck, pulling them in so close there was no space left for air. Every time the door groaned or the wood rattled, Odile felt a surge of manic energy, a giggle of pure adrenaline escaping her lips between her heavy, sobbing breaths.

She was completely gone, her eyes rolled back in a state of blissful, reckless surrender. She didn't care who was in the hallway, who might be heading toward the bathroom, or whose curiosity might be piqued by the commotion. All she could feel was the friction, the noise, and the intoxicating thrill of being utterly undisguised.

"Right... right there," she whimpered loudly, her fingers digging into Fen's back, her voice echoing off the tiles in a way that made her heart race with a dangerous, wonderful pride.

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: I let out a low groan, the sound ragged against her neck. The door rattles with our rhythm, and for a second I'm sure it's going to give way entirely. "Fuck, Odile," I gasp, my own control slipping completely.

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
Odile’s entire body shuddered at the sound of her name, his voice rough and stripped of all patience. The feeling of the door rattling behind her—the precariousness of the lock, the thin barrier between them and a room full of people—pushed her over the edge. It was the final, perfect catalyst.

She let out a loud, piercing cry that she didn't even attempt to stifle, her voice echoing sharply against the white tiles. She didn't just surrender to the sensation; she chased the risk, her hips bucking back against him with a desperate, frantic urgency. 

"Don't... don't stop," she sobbed, the words barely coherent, a mixture of pleasure and a wild, giddy adrenaline. 

As the tension reached its breaking point, Odile gripped Fen’s hair, pulling them closer as she collapsed into a series of violent, shaking tremors. Her head hit the door one last time with a definitive *crack*, and she let out a long, shuddering moan that seemed to vibrate through the very walls of the house. 

For a few seconds, the only sounds were their combined, ragged breathing and the distant, muffled thumping of the music downstairs. Odile slumped against the door, her limbs feeling like lead, her chest heaving. A slow, dazed smile spread across her face as she looked up at Fen, her eyes glassy and pupils dilated.

She let out a soft, breathless laugh, the sound echoing in the sudden silence of the room. "I think..." she whispered, her voice a wrecked, satisfied rasp, "I think we might have actually woken the neighbors."

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: Somebody tries the handle and neither of us stops. "Don't," she says, meaning don't stop. (OOC: write it through, no fade to black.)

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
The sudden, sharp *clack* of the door handle being turned sent a jolt of pure electricity through Odile’s spine. She froze for a split second, her heart hammering against her ribs with a violence that felt almost physical. But as the handle rattled—someone on the other side trying to force their way in—the panic didn't set in. Instead, a wave of manic, intoxicating heat flooded her system.

When Fen whispered that one word—*"Don't"*—Odile felt her breath hitch in a jagged sob of desire. 

She didn't pull away. She didn't even try to hide. Instead, she arched her back, pressing her spine harder against the rattling wood of the door, her eyes wide and shimmering with a reckless, wild light. The sensation of someone being *right there*, separated from them by only an inch of mahogany, turned the pleasure into something blinding.

"Oh god," she gasped, the sound loud and clear, intentionally projecting it toward the door. 

As Fen continued, ignoring the intruder and pushing deeper, Odile let out a loud, unrestrained moan that was practically a shout. She wrapped her legs tighter around Fen's hip, her fingers digging painfully into their shoulders, her head tossing back against the door with a rhythmic, punishing *thump*. 

The handle rattled again, more insistently this time, and Odile let out a high, giddy laugh that broke into a moan. The risk was no longer a game; it was a reality, and it was the most erotic thing she had ever experienced. She was practically vibrating, her body shaking with a combination of climax and adrenaline.

"They know!" she whimpered, her voice strained and breathless, a smirk playing on her lips even as she trembled. "They know we're in here!"

She didn't care who it was—a friend, the host, a stranger. The thought of them listening to her unravel, hearing the wet slap of skin and the frantic, heavy breathing, pushed her over the final precipice. With one last, violent shudder, Odile screamed into the quiet of the hallway, her body collapsing against Fen in a series of crashing, rhythmic waves. She clung to them as if they were the only thing keeping her grounded, her breath coming in ragged, sobbing gasps, a look of absolute, triumphant delirium on her face as the handle finally stopped rattling and the footsteps retreated.

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: I listen to the retreating footsteps, my own breathing still harsh against her damp skin. "We're going to have to go out there eventually," I murmur, reluctantly pulling back.

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
Odile stayed slumped against the door for a long moment, her chest heaving in sync with Fen's. Her skin was flushed a deep, burning pink, and her hair was a chaotic mess, clinging to her forehead and neck. The silence that followed the retreating footsteps was heavy, but to Odile, it felt like a victory.

She let out a slow, shaky exhale, a small, mischievous giggle escaping her as she slowly opened her eyes. The adrenaline was still humming in her veins, leaving her feeling lightheaded and wonderfully reckless.

"Eventually," she repeated, her voice a wrecked, sultry whisper. She didn't move to let Fen go immediately; instead, she tightened her arms around their neck for one last, lingering squeeze, savoring the lingering heat between them.

She finally leaned her head back against the wood, staring up at the ceiling with a dazed, triumphant expression. The thought of walking back into the party—of seeing who had tried the handle and seeing the look of recognition or suspicion on their face—was almost as exciting as the act itself.

"I wonder if they'll be too embarrassed to ask where we were," she murmured, a wicked glint returning to her eyes. 

With a slow, languid movement, she began to slide her leg down from Fen's hip, the cool air of the bathroom hitting her skin. She looked at the heap of discarded clothes on the floor and then back at Fen, her smile widening into something playful and daring.

"Do we look like we've been 'fixing the plumbing'?" she teased, her voice regaining its usual playful lilt. "Because I think we might need a few more minutes to... compose ourselves. Just in case they decided to wait in the hall."

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: I let out a soft laugh, already bending to pick up her shirt from the floor. "We look like we lost a fight with a tornado," I say, handing it over. My own shirt is hopelessly wrinkled, and I run a hand through my hair. "Think we can sneak out the window?"

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
Odile took the shirt with a slow, languid grace, her fingers brushing Fen's as she pulled the fabric over her head. She didn't immediately smooth down her hair or fix her clothes; instead, she stood there for a moment, basking in the afterglow and the lingering scent of their exertion. 

At the mention of the window, she paused, her head tilting as she looked toward the small, frosted pane of glass high up on the bathroom wall. A small, thoughtful hum vibrated in her throat, and a slow, wicked grin spread across her face.

"The window?" she echoed, her voice regaining its playful, melodic quality. "And miss the chance to walk back into that living room and see who was brave enough to try the door? That would be a tragedy, Fen."

She stepped closer to him, reaching out to straighten his collar with a lingering, possessive touch. Her eyes were still bright, the pupils not yet fully returned to normal, reflecting a lingering spark of the chaos they'd just created. She leaned in, pressing her forehead against his and letting out a soft, contented sigh.

"Besides," she whispered, her breath warm and smelling of the wine they'd had earlier. "I want them to wonder. I want them to see my hair a little messy and your shirt wrinkled and spend the rest of the night trying to piece together exactly what happened in here."

She stepped back, finally smoothing her dress down with a decisive pat, though she intentionally left one small crease of fabric tucked in a way that suggested haste. She looked at him with a look of pure, unadulterated mischief.

"Let's go back down. But," she added, her voice dropping to a conspiratorial murmur as she reached for the lock, "if we see the person who tried the handle... I might just give them a little wink."

With a decisive *click*, she unlocked the door and swung it open, stepping out into the hallway with a triumphant, beaming smile.

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: I pull my shirt on, giving you a look that's half amusement, half disbelief. "You're a menace," I mutter, but I follow you out, my hand settling low on your back as we head for the stairs.

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
The party had reached the stage where nobody would notice two people missing, which Odile pointed out approximately four seconds before doing something about it.

"The bathroom upstairs has a lock," she said, into Fen's ear, over the music.

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: "Does it work?" I ask, already moving toward the stairs.

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
"Define 'work,'" Odile said, which was not reassuring, and she knew it, and said it anyway because the look on Fen's face was worth more than accuracy.

She followed up the stairs two steps behind, close enough to hook a finger through Fen's belt loop. "It worked at New Year's. It worked at the barbecue. It's a bolt, not a bank vault — the point is it makes a noise when someone tries the handle, and the noise gives us time to—" she gestured vaguely, "—look innocent."

Halfway up she was already grinning. The music swallowed the creak of the stairs, which was lucky, because Odile's whisper had a well-documented tendency to carry, and she was deploying it at full volume.

"Also, if anyone asks, you're helping me find my earring," she added at the top of the landing, not quietly. "I lost it hours ago. Very believable story. I've told it to zero people."

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: "The more you talk, the less believable this is," I laugh, pulling her with me towards the bathroom door. I test the bolt—it sticks a little, but it slides shut with a satisfying *thunk*.

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
The thunk of the bolt was, in Odile's professional opinion, the sexiest sound in the world, narrowly beating out a cork popping and someone else's key in a front door.

"See?" she said, crowding Fen back against the sink, both hands already at work on Fen's shirt buttons with the confidence of a woman who had done this in worse bathrooms. "Fortress. We're basically in a castle."

The bathroom was, in fact, approximately the size of a wardrobe, lit by one flickering vanity bulb, and smelled faintly of someone else's expensive candle. Odile had never felt more romantic in her life.

"Okay, ground rules," she said, which was rich, coming from someone currently unbuttoning with one hand and pulling Fen's collar aside with the other. "One: if someone knocks, I'm a sick friend and you're holding my hair. Two: if someone knocks twice, we've both fainted. Three—" she got the last button and spread the shirt open, and her voice went slightly less steady, which she would later deny, "—I am going to be *so* quiet. Historically quiet. People will write songs."

She was, at that moment, speaking at roughly her normal volume, which at parties had once been described as "projecting."

Then she kissed Fen like the music downstairs was a countdown, all grin and no patience, one hand fisted in the shirt she'd just opened and the other braced on the sink. Something small rolled off the counter and landed in the basin with a tiny clink, and Odile broke the kiss to laugh about it directly against Fen's mouth.

"That was the earring," she whispered, at a volume audible in the hallway. "Found it. Mystery solved. We can go now."

She did not go anywhere.

dialogue.name: Fen

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
Being pinned to the door was, in Odile's assessment, an excellent development, and she said so, and then said it again quieter when the first version came out at a volume that could have been heard in the garden.

"The music's helping," she murmured, which for Odile meant a stage whisper with full orchestral backing. "Whoever's DJing deserves a raise. Is this the same playlist from the barbecue? Because I have memories attached to this song. Several. Most of them involve a shed."

She got both hands back in Fen's collar and pulled, kissing like she was trying to win something, one heel hooked behind Fen's leg, the door rattling faintly in its frame every time she moved. The vanity bulb flickered in Morse code. The expensive candle was losing its fight with adrenaline. Odile had never been happier in a bathroom in her life.

Then — footsteps on the stairs.

Odile froze with her mouth an inch from Fen's, eyes gone enormous and delighted, a laugh already loading in her chest that she physically suppressed with a fist pressed against her own lips. The footsteps reached the landing. Stopped. The handle turned, and the bolt did its one job with a loud, dignified rattle.

"*Occupied!*" Odile called, in the voice of a woman announcing a departing train. A pause. "Someone's in here! There's a queue! There's no queue! Go away, kindly!"

A muffled "sorry," retreating footsteps, and Odile folded forward against Fen's shoulder, shaking silently with the effort of not howling. "Did you hear that? The bolt *worked.* I owe that bolt a drink. 'There's a queue, there's no queue'—" she wheezed, tears of pure joy in her eyes, "—I'm a disaster, you're an enabler, and we've got maybe four minutes before someone sends a search party, so—"

She didn't finish the sentence. She was kissing again, grinning straight through it, one hand flat against the door behind her as if holding it shut by force of will alone.

dialogue.name: Fen

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
"Four minutes," Odile repeated, with the reverence of a woman who had just been handed a sacred quest. "That's ages. That's *so much* time. I've done incredible things in four minutes. There was a coat check in Leeds—"

She abandoned the anecdote in favor of action, which for Odile meant attempting both simultaneously and narrating throughout. Her hands went to Fen's belt with the focus of a safe-cracker, her mouth to Fen's neck, her heel still hooked behind Fen's leg like she was mooring a boat in rough weather.

Because when someone comes up those stairs — and someone is *always* coming up those stairs, this house has one bathroom and forty guests, the maths is a horror film — I am not stopping, and I want it on record that this was *your* instruction—"

The permission changed everything. Odile ungagged was a force of nature. The commentary returned at full party volume, the laugh ran free underneath it like a river breaking through a dam, and all the small high sounds she'd been biting back came out at once, like she'd been saving them in a jar. The bolt rattled a tattoo in its housing. The bulb flickered in applause. The candle surrendered its last pretense of relevance.

Her eyes went enormous and luminous and she pulled Fen closer by the shirtfront and narrated, hoarse and wrecked and radiant: "Don't you dare slow down. dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
"I'm keeping you" did what the footsteps, the knocking, the bolt, and the entire population of the party had failed to do all evening: it shut Odile up.

For three whole seconds.

"You can't—" breathless, fingers twisted in Fen's collar, eyes gone enormous, "—you can't just *say* things like that mid— that's a *finishing* sentence. That's a violins sentence. That's the sentence at the end of the film—" her voice cracked clean through, "—*keeping* me. Like a stray. Like a raccoon that's been living in your attic and you've decided to just— *feed* it—"

The sincerity ambushed her mid-bit, the way it kept doing, and she got Fen's face in both hands and kissed her like the violins were actually playing — no commentary, no countdown, the laugh gone somewhere warm and quiet at the bottom of her chest.

"Good," she said, hoarse, against Fen's mouth. "Keep me. I was going to keep you first — I said it in my head *weeks* ago, so it's mine, you're only borrowing it, there's a waiting list—"

And then, downstairs, the party saved them.

The song came on — *the* song, the one everybody knew, the one that turned forty drunk people into a single choir — and a cheer went up through the floorboards, and the whole house started singing, and Odile realized what was happening halfway through a gasp and nearly died of it.

"They're *singing,*" she wheezed, delighted, wrecked, forehead knocking against Fen's. "The whole party. That's *cover.* That's a gift. That's the house giving us its blessing—" her head tipped back, her heel dug in, her hand slapped flat against the door one last time, "—oh, I'm going to be so loud and *nobody will ever know*—"

And she was. The one time all night she could have been as loud as she liked, with the chorus bellowing up through the floor and the bassline rattling the bolt in time, Odile finally let the whole jar open — the laugh and everything else tangled together past separating, both arms locked around Fen, the door taking its beating like a decorated veteran, the bulb flickering like the world's smallest strobe light. The irony — that she'd spent the entire evening muffling herself for *this* moment of total acoustic freedom — occurred to her mid-everything and made it all worse and better, and she rode it out shaking, radiant, tears standing in her eyes, Fen's name in there somewhere, cracked and fond and completely unguarded.

When it was over, she stayed exactly where she was, pinned between Fen and the door, breathing like she'd taken the stairs four times, and conducted a quiet internal survey.

"Report," she said hoarsely, to no one. "Legs: gone. Voice: gone. Bit: gone." A pause, forehead tipping against Fen's. "Update on the maths. It's all you now. There's no door. There's no bit. The scientists have been informed."

She stayed there until the song downstairs ended and the next one started, because moving had been taken off the table by her own body, and because Fen's arms were around her, and because the cupboard smelled of sandalwood and victory.

"Okay," she said eventually, with the solemnity of a woman returning to her own life from a great distance. "Exit strategy. Real one this time. You go first, cough if it's clear, I'm a sick friend, you're a hero, we've never met." She reached past Fen and patted the bolt, a comrade thrice decorated. "And if anyone asks about the noise, the toe made a full recovery. The toe's *fine.* The toe's had the best night of its life."

She slid the bolt back — the little dignified *thunk* — and cracked the door one inch, one eye to the gap, shoulders already shaking.

"Coast report," she whispered, at a volume audible in the garden. "And Fen—" a glance back, hair a crime scene, grin enormous, "—keep me. It's mutual. There's paperwork. I'll have it drawn up at breakfast."

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: Somebody tries the handle and neither of us stops. "Don't," she says, meaning don't stop. (OOC: write it through, no fade to black.)

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
The handle turned.

Third time. The bolt gave its dignified rattle — a veteran of two campaigns, called upon to hold the line once more — and Odile's eyes went enormous, luminous, *vindicated*, because she had said it, she had literally *said* it, someone was always coming up those stairs, the maths was a horror film—

"Don't," Fen said.

"You don't—" Odile's voice cracked clean through, her heel digging in, her fingers twisting in Fen's collar, "—have to tell me. You never have to tell me. This is the prophecy. This is what I was *for*—"

A muffled voice, inches away, on the other side of a door that was currently moving in its frame: "Hello? Someone in there?"

And the glorious, unholy, life-affirming thing was that nobody stopped. Fen didn't stop. Odile didn't stop. The rhythm against the door didn't so much as stutter, and Odile had to compose an entire face and an entire voice while being comprehensively undone, which she would later describe as the greatest acting challenge of her career.

"*Occupied,*" she called, and it came out remarkably steady for approximately one syllable. "Still occupied! Same toe! Ongoing toe situation! It's—" a hitch, a gasp, her head thumping back against the wood, "—it's a *whole* thing in here!"

"Are you... okay?"

"*Never better,*" Odile said, which was the literal truth, which was the problem, which made the laugh come up through her chest like a geyser and had to be bitten back against Fen's shoulder mid-sentence. "Genuinely! Genuinely never better! Use the— there's a downstairs one! Behind the kitchen! It's *lovely,* it's got a *window*—"

A pause. A long, thoughtful pause, during which the door continued to do its work and the bolt continued to rattle its small metallic protest and Odile's eyes streamed with the effort of holding her entire personality inside her own body.

"...Right," said the voice, with the tone of a person who had decided to simply never know. "Sorry."

Retreating footsteps. The stairs. Gone.

Odile lasted exactly as long as the footsteps did, and then she came apart like a firework in a cupboard.

"He *knows,*" she wheezed, delighted, wrecked, not stopping, never stopping, her leg hooked higher over Fen's hip and the door taking the rhythm like a drum. "He knows and he's *going anyway,* he's going to tell this story at every party for the rest of his life and nobody will ever believe him— *oh*—" her hand slapped flat against the wood, fingers spread, the bolt rattling in time, "—don't you dare slow down, this is the best thing that's ever happened to me, and I include the *shed*—"

There was no muffling it now and no point. The music downstairs swallowed nothing and Odile didn't care. Every sound she'd bitten back all evening came out of her at once, the laugh running underneath all of it like a river, warm and helpless and incurable, her head tipped back against the door and her hair a crime scene and the bulb flickering over both of them like the world's smallest, most supportive strobe light.

"Fen," she got out, cracked and fond and completely unguarded. "Fen, I'm—"

The sentence didn't survive. It had never once survived. It went somewhere bright and shattered and took her with it, her whole body seizing, her teeth finding Fen's shoulder and her arms locking tight and the laugh breaking into something else entirely — something with no bit attached, no commentary, no plaque, just Fen's name said into Fen's skin like a password, like the one true thing in a house full of strangers, while the door rattled its applause and the bolt held the line and downstairs forty people sang the wrong words to a song.

She rode it out shaking, radiant, tears standing in her eyes, and when it finally let her go she stayed exactly where she was — pinned between Fen and the door, breathing like she'd taken the stairs six times, leg still hooked, unwilling on a spiritual level to stand under her own power ever again.

"Report," she said hoarsely, to the ceiling. "New report. That was the single greatest moment of my life and I've *been to Leeds.*"

Her forehead tipped against Fen's. Her voice, when it came, was wrecked and smug and softer than she'd have admitted to any jury.

"Worth it," she said. "Whatever's waiting on the other side of that door. Whatever that man tells people. Whatever the plaque costs to have engraved." A beat. The grin, audible. "*She was given every opportunity to stop, and did not.*"

She patted the bolt without looking, a comrade thrice decorated, now legendary.

"You're getting a plaque too," she informed it. "Load-bearing. Like you."

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: "Shut up," I tell the door, breathless and grinning. I lean my forehead against yours for a second. "Let's go downstairs and get a drink before your toe develops a limp."

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
"You just told the door to shut up," Odile said, with enormous pride. "Six hours in this house and you're already talking to the fixtures. That's my influence. I'm a contagion. There's going to be a whole outbreak of us by Christmas."

"A limp," she repeated, getting her jeans up for the second time in what she now considered the same continuous emergency. "The toe's absolutely going to have a limp. I'm going to walk down those stairs like a woman who has *survived* something. Method acting. I've already got the face."

She did not have the face. The face, consulted in the mirror over the sink, was a full confession: hair describing events in iambic pentameter, mouth wrecked, eyes bright enough to read by. She attempted repairs with wet hands and optimism, achieved nothing, and declared the result "a look" and "honestly, at this point, a tribute."

"How caught am I — don't answer, I can see it. Extremely. Nobody has ever looked this pleased about a toe. If anyone asks, the toe was *wonderful.* Life-changing toe. I'd do it again."

The earring went back in. Evidence. Heirloom. She pointed at it in the mirror and informed her reflection that it would be buried with her, along with the bolt, which she patted on her way past, a comrade now beyond decoration, into legend.

"Okay. Real exit strategy. Final one. Signed, sealed—" she cracked the door one inch, one eye to the gap, shoulders already shaking. "Landing's clear. Staircase: clear. Bottom of the stairs: one man, back turned, holding a—" a pause, her voice dropping to what she believed was a whisper, "—oh no. That's him. That's toe man. He's *lingering.* He's waiting for the show. Well, he's getting one, because I'm going first, I'm the decoy, if he looks at me I'll faint dramatically and you walk over my body. It's what I would've wanted. We've known each other a while, you can trust me on that."

She slipped out onto the landing, pressed herself to the wall like a jewel thief in a pantomime, and beckoned with one entire arm, a signal visible from the street.

At the top of the stairs she stopped, because downstairs the party was doing that thing parties did — someone had opened something expensive, someone else was already singing again, the whole house warm and loud and oblivious — and the sheer normalcy of it nearly finished her off. She gripped the banister and breathed through it like a woman in labor with a joke.

"Drink," she agreed, hoarse, resuming the descent at a pace she clearly believed was casual and which was, in fact, the walk of a person leaving a casino. "One drink. Two maximum. And if anyone — *anyone* — mentions a queue for the bathroom, I'm going to look directly at you with a completely straight face, and that's going to be the hardest thing I've ever done, and I once carried a sofa up four flights of stairs in *Leeds*—"

Halfway down, the toe man turned around.

Odile made eye contact with him over the banister, held it for one full second with the serene dignity of a fallen saint, and received — there was no other word for it — a small, slow, deeply respectful nod. The nod of a man acknowledging a colleague.

She made it three more steps before folding silently over the banister, shoulders shaking, one hand flapping behind her in Fen's general direction, unable to speak, tears standing in her eyes.

"He *nodded,*" she wheezed, barely audible, a personal best. "He knows. He *knows,* and he nodded. That's the greatest moment of my life and I've been *in* this bathroom—"

She pulled herself upright by force of will, wiped her eyes, and caught Fen's hand at the bottom of the stairs, lacing their fingers together with the unselfconsciousness of a woman who had stopped being able to pretend she wasn't keeping this.

"Plaque's going on the landing," she decided, steering toward the kitchen, toward drinks, toward the rest of the night, hair a crime scene, limp fully committed to. "*Here stood two heroes. The toe recovered. The bolt held. Nobody stopped.*" A beat, a sideways glance, the grin going soft at the edges in a way she'd have denied under oath.

"Breakfast," she added. "Paperwork. I'm having 'keep me' drawn up by a solicitor. Witnessed. Notarized. The nodding man can countersign — he's earned it."

She raised their joined hands like a victorious doubles team and walked them both into the kitchen, into the noise, limping with tremendous dignity about a toe that had never been injured in its life.

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: I squeeze your hand, nodding at the man by the fridge as we pass—no words, just a look that says we're in the same secret club now. "Two drinks," I agree, reaching past someone for a bottle. "And then I'm taking you home before you get that plaque notarized in front of everyone."

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
The nod was returned, and Odile watched the entire exchange with the hushed fascination of a naturalist witnessing a ritual no one had ever documented before.

"You've been inducted," she said, awed, accepting her drink. "You don't even know what the club is. *Nobody* knows what the club is. That's the club. There are no meetings. There's no membership card. There's just a man by a fridge who knows what he heard and respects it." She raised her glass toward him across the kitchen; without turning around, he raised his own in reply, and Odile nearly dropped hers. "Did you see that. Did you *see* that. That's the coolest thing that's ever happened to me and I've been *in* that bathroom."

She poured with the ceremony of a woman who had survived something, and proposed a toast to the bolt, to the toe's full recovery, and to the house, "which gave us its blessing in the form of a singalong and will never receive a thank-you card, because how would you even *phrase* it."

"And for the record," she added, delighted, "you absolutely think I won't get the plaque notarized in front of everyone. That's adorable. You've known me how long? There's a stationery drawer somewhere in this house and I *will* find it. I'll officiate myself. The fridge man can witness. He's already witnessed so much."

Then, from across the kitchen, a stranger's voice: "Hey — is the upstairs bathroom free?"

Odile's entire body went rigid with effort. She turned to Fen with a face of such heroic, trembling neutrality — eyes enormous, lips pressed into a line of pure structural will — and held it, and held it, and answered, "Think so! Toe's better!" in a voice only slightly higher than a piccolo, and survived it. The stranger wandered off. Odile exhaled like a diver surfacing.

"The hardest thing I've ever done," she whispered, hoarse. "The sofa in Leeds was *nothing.* Put it on the plaque. *She kept a straight face once, in a kitchen, and it nearly killed her.*"

Then "home" caught up with her — Fen had said it, casually, like it was one place, like it was theirs — and the violins ambushed her right there between the fridge and the crisps.

"You're doing it again," she accused, quieter, pointing at Fen's chest with the hand not holding her drink. "The finishing sentences. You can't just say *home* like that in the middle of a kitchen. I'm going to need a whole drinks cabinet for the violins at this rate."

She finished the drink in a manner she described as pacing herself, collected their coats with the regal bearing of a woman whose hair was still describing events in iambic pentameter, and paused at the front door for one last look up the stairs. The landing stood empty. The bathroom door was shut. The bolt, presumably, was at rest, its watch ended.

She saluted it. A comrade retired with highest honors.

Out in the cold air she laced her fingers back through Fen's and committed to the limp all the way down the front path, even though nobody was watching anymore, because "the toe has to be consistent. The toe is *method.* If we pass the nodding man on the pavement, I want him to believe."

"Breakfast," she said, swinging their joined hands, heading for the end of the street and the rest of everything. "Paperwork. *Keep me,* witnessed and notarized, both copies, fridge door." A beat, and the grin went soft at the edges in the way she'd have denied under oath. "Best party of my life. Five stars. The review's going to be glowing and completely unusable."

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: I glance back at the house, then tug you closer by your hand. "Let's get out of here before your review makes the papers."

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Kit had made it as far as the kitchen doorway before Bear moved, which was further than usual and had clearly been allowed.

"You let me get that far," Kit said, backing up one step.

"I did," Bear agreed. "I'm feeling generous."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: "Don't be," I say, and go.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear wasn't generous. Bear was never generous. That was the whole point.

He moved before Kit's second foot hit the hallway floor, covering the distance in three strides — not running, not yet, just *closing*, the way he'd done ten thousand times before in this house and others. The kitchen doorframe blurred past his shoulder. Kit had a head start of maybe four feet and a leaner turn of speed and absolutely no respect for baseboards.

The hallway narrowed. Bear grinned. He liked it narrow.

He didn't reach for Kit's arm — too easy, too clean. Instead he hooked an arm around the midsection and drove forward, turning his own momentum into the catch, letting them both go down in a controlled crash against the wall by the coat hooks. Something fell. A coat. A scarf. He'd find it later.

Kit thrashed and twisted and got an elbow somewhere near Bear's ribs, which was fair, which was the deal, and Bear took it and didn't let go. His teeth found the back of Kit's neck — not gently, never gently — and he pressed down just hard enough to say *got you* and *mine* and *not generous at all*.

His own pulse hammered. Eight years and his pulse still hammered.

He breathed against Kit's skin, held the bite, and waited to see what it would cost him to keep it.

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I twist in your hold, gasping as your teeth dig in. "See?" I say, breathless. "That's more like it." I shove back against you, testing your grip.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
The shove back into him was exactly the right answer and Bear growled against the nape of Kit's neck — low, appreciative, the sound of a man who'd just been handed a receipt.

He gave ground. Half a step, deliberate, letting Kit feel like something had shifted. Then he drove forward again and took the space back and then some, his forearm sliding up across Kit's collarbone, his knee nudging hard between Kit's heels to widen the stance. The wall was cold against his knuckles. Kit was not cold against him. Kit was warm and swearing and already squirming for leverage.

He released the neck — long enough to breathe, long enough to hear what else Kit would say — and then re-bit, lower this time, the meat of the shoulder where the shirt pulled taut. Harder. He felt the fabric give a little before skin did and he did not care about the shirt. Shirts were replaceable. This was not.

His other hand found Kit's hip and *squeezed*, fingers digging in with the kind of pressure that would say *here* tomorrow morning when Kit reached for something on a high shelf and grinned about it.

Eight years and he still kept score. Currently: Kit one, for the elbow. Bear one, for the wall. The night was young and the hallway was narrow and he had every intention of running up the tally.

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: He catches me in the hallway, which was always going to happen, and I don't put much into getting away.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear felt it before he understood it — the going-limp wasn't giving up, wasn't losing. Kit's body told him *not much into this* the way a hand of cards told him *I'm not bluffing, I just don't care about this round*. Different game. Same table.

He eased the bite. Not off — never all the way off — but the pressure backed down from *tomorrow's bruise* to *tonight's warmth*, and his jaw unclenched around the muscle of Kit's shoulder. His hand on Kit's hip loosened from grip to weight, just a palm, just a claim laid flat.

He didn't move away. Moving away would've been a different message entirely, and that wasn't what Kit had asked for. Kit had asked for *here, like this, less*.

So he stayed. Forearm still across the collarbone but resting now, not pressing. Knee still between Kit's heels but no longer driving. The wall was still at his back and Kit was still in front of him and the hallway was still narrow, and Bear breathed slow against the damp mark his teeth had left on the shirt.

"Say the word," he murmured into Kit's shoulder. Not a question. A standing offer, eight years old and never once expired.

He turned his face just enough to press his mouth flat against the same spot — no teeth this time, just pressure, just heat — and waited. Scorekeeping still on. Scorekeeping always on. But some rounds you won by not running up the tally.

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I lean my head back against your shoulder, letting out a slow breath. "Nah," I say, my voice quiet but clear. "Just hold still a minute."

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear held still.

It wasn't nothing. Eight years ago he'd have had to learn it, and he had, badly at first and then better, and now he knew exactly what *hold still* cost Kit to ask for and exactly what it cost Bear to give. Both prices were fine. Both prices had always been fine.

So he became a wall. Warm one, breathing one, with a heartbeat still going too fast behind Kit's shoulder blade, but a wall all the same. Forearm resting across the collarbone. Palm flat on the hip. Mouth against the damp mark on the shirt. No teeth. No squeeze. No shifting his weight to see if Kit would shift first.

He breathed. Kit breathed. The hallway smelled like the coat that had fallen and the faint ghost of whatever Kit had been cooking before the running started, and underneath both, that warm specific smell that Bear had been tracking across rooms and years and never once gotten tired of.

His thumb moved. Once. A single slow pass across Kit's hip bone. Not a demand. Not a signal. Just the kind of thing a hand does when the rest of the body has been told to stay put — a small allowance, like letting a dog have one paw off the rug.

Outside, a car went past. Inside, the fridge ticked and hummed its long low note. Somewhere near Bear's feet lay the evidence of a scarf's disagreement with gravity.

He waited. He was good at waiting now, which had taken him most of the eight years and was, in his private accounting, the single most expensive skill he'd ever bought.

The score stood where it stood. Kit one, Bear one, and the rest of the night hanging in the hallway like something neither of them had to catch yet.

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: We don't make it to the bedroom. The floor is fine. Clothes are a problem we solve badly and fast.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear had never been good at clothes. Clothes were the enemy. Clothes were a problem to be solved by force and impatience and, when those failed, by the specific and time-honored technique of not caring what survived.

Kit's shirt had already lost the argument with his teeth somewhere in the hallway. The rest of it went the same way — fast, graceless, half-tugged and half-abandoned in a trail from the coat hooks to the place where the hallway opened into the front room and the rug did its inadequate best. Bear's own shirt caught on his wrist and he yanked it the rest of the way off with a grunt that was closer to a laugh. Somewhere behind him a button hit the baseboard. He'd find it with his foot in three days and feel a small satisfied thing about it.

Kit was faster at this part. Kit was faster at most parts. Bear had made his peace with it and instead made up the difference in weight and in grip and in the specific cruelty of knowing exactly where to put a hand so that Kit's speed didn't matter.

He got them down. Not gracefully — never gracefully — but with intent, one forearm taking the impact of the floor and the rest of him taking the impact of Kit, and the rug bunched under his knee and he didn't care, and the floor was hard under his back when Kit got the better of the angle and he didn't care about that either.

He cared about exactly one thing and it was warm and swearing and currently winning.

His mouth found the mark he'd left in the hallway and pressed it flat again, tongue over the bruise forming there, and felt Kit shiver into him. He bit again — lower, new real estate, the kind that would make sitting at the kitchen table tomorrow morning an interesting proposition for both of them. His hands were everywhere and not gentle and exactly as precise as they needed to be. Eight years of cartography. He knew every elevation and every fault line and he played them like a man who intended to win.

The score, by his reckoning, was now: Kit one, for the angle reversal. Bear two, for the floor. But he'd stopped keeping strict count somewhere around the second mark, which happened sometimes and which he counted as its own kind of score — the kind you lost on purpose and won anyway.

He pressed his forehead against Kit's shoulder and breathed and held on and let the floor be the floor and the night be whatever Kit decided it would be next.

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I push you onto your back, straddling your hips. "My turn," I breathe, hands on your chest, fingers digging in.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear hit the floor on his back and grinned up at the ceiling like a man who'd just been handed a gift he fully intended to regift.

"Yours," he agreed, and the word came out rougher than he meant it to, dragged over gravel somewhere south of his ribs where Kit's fingers were currently making their case.

He didn't fight it. That was the thing about eight years — he knew the shape of *my turn* the way he knew the shape of the hallway, and he knew that the worst thing he could do right now was make it easy and the second worst thing was make it hard in the wrong way. So he lay back and *took* it, and the taking was its own kind of work, muscles held taut under Kit's palms, jaw set, breath going shallow through his nose because deep breathing felt like conceding something and he wasn't in a conceding mood.

His hands found Kit's thighs. Not pushing. Not pulling. Just *there*, heavy, the way a tree is there — something for weather to happen against. His thumbs pressed into the muscle and held.

The floor was hard under his shoulders and he liked it. The rug had given up entirely somewhere near his hip. A corner of it dug into his back and he didn't move it, because moving it would mean moving, and he'd been told whose turn it was.

Kit's fingers dug in and Bear's chest hitched — once, involuntary, the body's small betrayal — and he let it happen and didn't cover it. Scorekeeping: Kit one, for the sound he'd just made out of Bear without touching anything that mattered. Fair. Fine. He'd collect later. He always collected later.

He looked up at Kit with the particular expression he saved for exactly this — not soft, not yielding, but *present*, wide open and entirely unwilling to be anywhere else. The mark on his own collarbone from some earlier round was fading. The marks he'd left on Kit were not. He could see one from here and it pleased him in a way he didn't bother to hide.

"Take it then," he said, low, and the dare in it was real and so was the welcome, and after eight years he'd stopped trying to make those two things make sense to anyone who wasn't Kit.

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: He gets his teeth into my shoulder hard enough to leave something and I tell him to do it again, and he does.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
The second time he didn't stop to make it pretty.

Bear's mouth found the first mark by memory — the wet place where his teeth had already been, where the skin was already confused and tender and sending back signals that weren't entirely pain and weren't entirely not — and he bit into it again like he was finishing a sentence he'd started in the hallway. Harder. Deeper. The kind of harder that meant the sound Kit made wasn't a word and the kind of deeper that meant Bear's jaw ached already and he was going to keep going anyway.

He tasted salt and heat and the particular electricity of skin that had been asked for twice.

His hands held Kit's hips down against him and he wasn't gentle about it — fingers digging in, wrists locked, the whole long architecture of his arms turned into brackets around Kit's body. Not trapping. *Holding*. There was a difference and they both knew it and neither of them had needed to say it out loud since somewhere around year two.

He released the bite slowly. That was new — that was the last few years, the slow release, the drag of teeth instead of the snap of them. He felt Kit shudder through it and filed that away in the place where he kept the evidence. Then he pressed his tongue flat against the ruin he'd made and breathed hot over it and felt the gooseflood rise up under his mouth like weather.

"Again?" he murmured against the mark. Not asking permission. Asking *what else*. Asking *what's next* and *how much* and *where*, all in one low rough syllable that vibrated against bruised skin.

He grinned against Kit's shoulder. He could feel his own pulse in his throat and his wrists and the places where Kit's fingers had been. The score was — the score didn't matter. The score was a game they played to get here, and here was the floor and the bunched-up rug and the shirt he was never finding the button for, and Kit's weight on his hips and Kit's skin under his mouth and the whole long night still lying open in front of them like country neither of them had finished mapping.

He waited, mouth hovering a half-inch off the mark, breathing on it. His teeth were right there. They both knew it. That was the point.

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I reach back, fingers tangling in your hair. "Yeah," I breathe, pulling your mouth back to my skin. "Keep going."

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear went.



Not gentle. Not slow. The fingers in his hair were a leash and a permission slip and a *go*, and he took the *go* like a man who'd been waiting his whole life for exactly this instruction, which — eight years in — wasn't even a lie.

His mouth closed on the mark and he bit down and *held*, jaw set, breathing through it, the muscles in his temples standing out like cable. He tasted the bruise forming underneath his teeth — that deep hot flavor that was Kit's and only Kit's, the one he could have picked out of a lineup of a thousand shoulders in a dark room. He bit down harder. Felt the give. Felt the sound Kit made come up through the skin and into his mouth like something swallowed.

His hands released Kit's hips and went instead to Kit's back — palms flat, spreading wide, fingers dragging slow down the ridge of spine and out along the ribs. Not tickling. Not soothing. *Reading*. Eight years of braille and he still found new things, still found the exact place where the muscle jumped when he pressed, the exact place where Kit's breath stuttered when he dragged a thumbnail slow across it.
