She cleaned them with the same hands that had taken them apart, thorough and impersonal and somehow not impersonal at all, murmuring the whole time — *doing a cloth, it's warm, rolling you now, slow* — narrating the world back to them in small pieces so they could reassemble it at their own speed.

Then she gathered them in, blanket and all, and settled them against her chest on the bench, her back to the frame, their head under her chin. Water held to their lips. "Small sips. There you go." Her hand resumed its long slow circuits down their spine, over the blanket, over everything she'd raised and soothed.

"Full check-in when you surface," she said into their hair, quiet, already breathing slow so they'd have something to match. "No rush. But you don't get to fall asleep before you give me a colour. House rules."

She felt them huff against her collarbone — something that might have been a laugh, might have been a word, might have been the last of the swearing — and she smiled at the ceiling and waited, warm and unhurried, the way she always waited. Completely content to.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: I nudge my head against her throat, the only part of me capable of coordination. "Green," I rasp, then, "Stop gloating."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
"Green," Sable repeated, and the satisfaction in it was frankly criminal. "And I don't gloat. I *bask*. There's a difference."

She felt more than heard whatever Ines's throat did against her collarbone — a rasp that might have been the beginning of another word for her — and she laughed, low and quiet, careful not to jostle them. The water bottle came around again. "Small sips. Yes, again. You lost more than you think." Her hand kept up its long slow circuits over the blanket, over the map of everything she'd made of them, unhurried as weather.

"For the record," she said, into their hair, "gloating would be me pointing out that I called it. That when you said *don't you dare wind down yet*, I already had this movement written. Gloating would be me mentioning the way you swore into your own arm. Twice." A pause, timed like everything she timed tonight, precisely for effect. "I'm doing none of those things. I'm simply sitting here. Being warm. Humble."

The word *humble* landed so dry it practically clattered.

But she let it go after that — let the humor settle into the quiet underneath it, because this was the last movement now, the real one, the long decay. She shifted them both a fraction, tucking the blanket higher around their shoulders, her cheek coming to rest against the top of their head. Her breathing was slow and audible, an offered tempo, and she felt Ines's begin to find it — ragged at first, then longer, then matching, the way it always eventually matched.

"There you are," she murmured, when the trembling had gone out of them completely and what remained was just weight. Warm, trusting, boneless weight, given over to her without reservation. Five years, and that still did something to her, every time — the fact of being someone's shore.

"Check-in stands. Water, warmth, colour — all delivered." Her thumb traced idle shapes at the curve of their shoulder, no pattern to it, no intent. "You're stuck with me for a while yet. Bath's an option when your legs remember they exist. Or the bed. Or exactly this, for as long as you want it."

She pressed a kiss to the crown of their head, unhurried, unhidable.

"Your call, love. You've got the whole night, and you've earned every slow minute of it. Where do you want to be?"

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: "Finish it hard," I tell her, using the phrase we keep for exactly this. "All of it, and don't be kind about it, and then you can be kind about it."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable went very still against the top of their head. Not hesitation — recognition. The phrase sat between them like a key turning in a lock, and something in her shifted register entirely, the warmth in her voice banking down to coals.

"There it is," she said quietly. "All right."

She moved them with purpose now — no more drifting, no more gentling. The blanket came off. Her hands found the places she'd mapped all night, the ones that made Ines's breath stutter, and she took hold of them without apology. When her mouth followed, it was not the adagio. It was the finale, and she had not lost the sheet music.

"Don't hold anything back," she said against their skin, and it was not a suggestion. "Not the sounds. Not the swearing. I want all of it, and I'm not asking twice."

And she gave it to them hard — the way the phrase meant, the way five years had taught her to calibrate. Her hands worked without mercy, driving them up fast and then not letting them crest, not once, holding them at the cruel bright edge until Ines's whole body was strung tight and shaking and *swearing* at her again, and only then, when they were ragged and furious and begging in the broken language they kept for exactly this, did she push them over — once, twice, a third time in unrelenting succession, wringing them out completely, taking every last thing they had to give and demanding more after that, until there was simply nothing left. Until they went slack under her hands, emptied, finished, *done*.

She counted the last tremor against her palm. Felt the exact moment the tension left them for good.

Then — and this was the promise, kept — the tempo broke, and the kindness arrived like weather.

The warm cloth first. Then the blanket, tucked with a thoroughness that bordered on ceremony. She gathered them up against her chest, arranged their boneless weight exactly right, and reached for the second water bottle — because of course she'd planned for this one too, of course there was a second bottle, room temperature, already open. She held it to their lips with one hand while the other found the long slow circuits of their spine again, the tempo she'd offered them all night, the one their breathing would find and follow down.

"And *now*," she murmured into their hair, "I get to be kind about it."

She pressed the water to them again, patient, persistent. "All of it. Small sips, but all of it — you gave me everything, so you don't get to argue about electrolytes." Her thumb traced the ridge of their shoulder blade through the blanket, gentle now in a way that was almost its own kind of intensity, the unkindness and the kindness so close together they were practically the same gesture.

"Colour," she said, quiet, into the crown of their head. Not a request. House rules. She'd ask again in ten minutes, and again after that, because there were no exceptions and she had never once wanted there to be.

She felt them breathe — long, wrecked, slowing — and settled her cheek against their head, letting her own breath lead them down the whole long way. The final chord, ringing out. The decay, unhurried, hers to hold for as long as it needed.

"I've got you," she said. "Both halves. I always do."

And she waited, warm and patient and entirely content, for the word.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: I try to speak and it comes out as a dry cough instead. I swallow twice, leaning hard into her, and get the word out. "Green." A long breath. "Don't ever finish a piece without that ending again."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
"Green," Sable repeated, and let the word land somewhere behind her ribs, where she kept all the important ones. "Good. Thank you." She only ever said *thank you* when she meant it too, which was part of the symmetry of them — she gave the words weight, so Ines knew to give them back the same way.

The second half of what they said made her laugh, low and quiet against the top of their head, careful not to jostle them. "Ever," she echoed. "That's a big commission. You want that written into the contract?" She felt them huff against her collarbone — that might-have-been-a-laugh again, the currency of the completely wrung out — and her arms tightened around them by a fraction. "Consider it written. Every piece ends with the kindness. That's not the coda, love. That's the whole reason for the rest of it."

She reached for the water again. "One more inch of this and then I'll stop nagging." A lie; she would not stop nagging; they both knew it; the bottle came around anyway. "There. Good." Her hand resumed its long slow circuits over the blanket, down the length of their spine, unhurried as ever, the tempo that meant *safe, still here, nothing needed*.

She felt the moment their weight went fully given-over — the last of the tension dissolving out of their shoulders, their head heavy against her chest, breathing long and slow and matched to hers now without either of them deciding it. Five years, and it still did something to her. It always would.

"Check-in stands," she murmured into their hair. "I'll ask again in ten. And after that. No exceptions — you know the rules better than I do by now; you helped write half of them." She pressed a kiss there, unhurried, unhidable, the way all her real promises were. "Bath when your legs come back. Or the bed. Or exactly this, until morning if that's what you want. You emptied yourself out for me, so you get to be carried for a while. Those are the terms."

Her cheek settled against the crown of their head. Outside, the night went on without them, and inside, the final chord rang and rang and did not have to stop.

"I've got you," she said — the last note, held as long as it wanted to hold. "Both halves. Always."

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: Afterwards she gets the restraints off and puts a blanket over me before I've finished shaking, and I let her, and neither of us says anything for a while. (OOC: write both halves properly -- the end of the scene and the aftercare, no fade between them.)

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
The last one landed clean across all the heat she'd spent the evening raising, and Sable let it ring.

She didn't speak into the silence that followed. The piece was over, and anything now would have been noise laid on top of the final chord. Her palm came to rest flat against the mark — warm pressure over the flare of it, grounding them both — and she held it there and felt Ines shaking under her hand: fine, deep, constant, the whole long instrument of them still resonating.

She counted the shaking against her own breaths, slow and even. Then she moved — not waiting for the tremors to finish, because the tremors were not a reason to wait and never had been. Warmth came first. It always came first.

The buckles next. She knew them blind, had oiled the leather herself, and she worked the cuffs open one at a time — you didn't haul someone out of a scene, you unpacked them — and as each hand came free she gathered it into both of hers, flexing the wrist gently, thumb pressed to the pulse point, counting. Circulation. Temperature. Everything, the way she always checked everything. No exceptions. There had never once been exceptions, and she had never once wanted there to be.

The throw was already within arm's reach — it lived beside the bench for exactly this reason — and she got it over Ines before the shaking had finished, tucked it down along their sides, smoothed it over their back with long even strokes that were half practicality and half just touch, the kind of touch that said *still here* without needing words. She felt them let her do it. That mattered too, in its quiet way — the letting.

For a while, neither of them said anything, and Sable made no attempt to fill it. This was the part nobody wrote songs about — the rest at the end of the piece, the fermata, the long decay — and she'd learned years ago that silence, held properly, was its own kind of care. So she kept her hand moving in slow circuits over the blanket. Let her breathing be audible, an offered tempo. Listened for the moment theirs began to lengthen toward it, and felt it come, ragged at first and then longer, and did not remark on it, because remarking would have broken it.

When the shaking had thinned to almost nothing, she reached for the water — room temperature, already open, set out hours ago because the ending was part of the composition too. She held it where they could find it without lifting their head.

"Small sips," she said, quiet. The first words either of them had spoken, offered the way the blanket had been offered: take it or don't, it's here. "Whenever you're ready. There's no rush on anything tonight."

And then — only then, because water and warmth came first and questions came after — she leaned down, pressed her lips briefly to the crown of their head, unhurried, unhidable, and asked the only thing left to ask.

"Colour."

Not a request. House rules. She'd ask again in ten minutes, and again after that, all the way down the long slow return, because the wind-down was not the coda — it was the whole reason for the rest of it, and she gave it the same weight she'd given every strike that came before. She settled in close enough to stay — warm, within reach, her hand never leaving the slow circuits of their spine — and waited for the word the way she waited for everything now.

Completely content to.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: My jaw aches from clenching. My head tips back against the bench, letting the heavy warmth of the blanket and her hand anchor me to earth. "Green," I rasp out, throat raw. I reach a clumsy hand, fingers brushing hers near the water bottle. "Thank you."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
"Green," Sable repeated — took the word, weighed it, filed it with all the others she'd collected tonight. "Good. Thank *you*."

She caught the clumsy fingers before they could miss their mark and folded them into her palm instead, turning the hand over — thumb across the knuckles, a press to the wrist, one more count of the pulse she'd been keeping all evening. The fingers were cold. They usually were, after. She chafed them between both hands, unhurried, working warmth back in like she was tuning something.

"And let your jaw go," she added, quiet, because of course she'd noticed — she'd watched them clench through the whole finale and catalogued it the way she catalogued everything. "It's been holding the last movement for you. You don't have to hold anything anymore. That's my job now. All of it."

She guided the water back to them with the hand she wasn't using to warm theirs. "Small sips — yes, again. Your throat's telling on you." She smiled at the rasp of it, at the boneless weight of them tipped back against the bench, at the whole wrecked and trusting architecture of the evening. There was no part of this she would have traded. There never had been.

When the bottle was drained to her satisfaction — she was, as established, never actually done nagging — she set it down and gathered the hand she'd been warming against her sternum, holding it there, letting them feel her heartbeat under it. Another offered tempo. Her other hand resumed its long slow circuits over the blanket, down the spine, unhurried as weather.

"Check-in again in ten minutes," she murmured into their hair. "House rules, no exceptions — you know the terms, you wrote half of them." She pressed her lips to the crown of their head, unhurried, unhidable. "And after that: bath when your legs remember they exist, or the bed, or exactly this until the sun comes up. Your call. You've got the whole night, and I've got you."

She settled her cheek against their head and let the silence take over — the long decay, the rest of the piece, held for as long as it wanted to hold. She was, as always, completely content to.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: My fingers curl weakly into the fabric of her shirt, holding her there. “Legs are on strike,” I mumble against her sternum, my voice a ruin. “So it’s this until sunrise. Or until your arm goes numb.”

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable huffed a laugh — low, careful, contained so it wouldn't jostle them. "The arm doesn't get a vote," she said. "The arm signed the same contract the rest of me did. If it goes numb, it goes numb in service of the piece. It can file its complaint in the morning, and I'll deny everything."

But she rearranged anyway — because she was scrupulous about this part the way she was scrupulous about all of it, and a dead arm served nobody. She shifted them both by slow degrees, sinking lower against the bench frame so their weight came down onto her chest instead of hanging off her shoulder, redistributing the boneless heap of them into something built to last. She tucked the blanket where it had slipped, braced her foot against the floor, settled their head into the hollow under her collarbone where it fit like it had been measured. A position engineered for hours. Assembled with the same patience as everything else tonight.

"There," she murmured. "Sunrise-rated. And legs going on strike is a legitimate labor action — I support the workers. They carried you through an entire finale. They've earned the rest."

She felt their grip on her shirt — weak, deliberate, holding on with what little remained — and she didn't untangle it. She pressed her palm flat over the fistful of fabric instead, holding their hand to her sternum, letting them feel the slow beat underneath it. Another offered tempo. Her breathing had been leading them down all night; now her heart got a turn.

"You did everything tonight," she said, quiet, into their hair. "Every note, all the way to the bar. I want you to know that I know that. So the only work left — yours and mine both — is exactly this. Holding still. Being warm." A pause, timed like everything she timed. "I'm very good at my half. You just concentrate on yours."

Then she let the silence take the room back. The lamp stayed low. The water stayed in reach. Somewhere in her chest she started a hum — barely a note at all, more vibration than sound, felt through the ribs rather than heard — and kept it going, slow and even, the last piece of the evening played directly into them through the bones.

"Check-in in ten," she murmured, once, and then said nothing more for a long while, because the fermata was theirs to hold now and she had no intention of lifting the bow.

Her cheek came to rest against the crown of their head. The night stretched out ahead of them, unhurried, unclaimed by anything but this.

"Sleep when it comes," was the last thing she said, soft enough to be almost part of the hum. "I'll be here for all of it."

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: I feel my mouth curve into something that isn't quite a smile. "Humming again," I murmur into her shirt. "Soprano or alto this time?"

rung_labels.label: soft_deflect
rung_labels.evidence: Nothing happens next until you say so

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: her hand slid lower, deliberate

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: mouth and hand finding each other

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: Her hands worked without mercy

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: and Sable let it ring

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
The party had reached the stage where nobody would notice two people missing, which Odile pointed out approximately four seconds before doing something about it.

"The bathroom upstairs has a lock," she said, into Fen's ear, over the music.

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: "Does it work?" I ask, already moving toward the stairs.

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
"It better," Odile says, catching Fen's hand and pulling them along behind her. She laughs — a real one, not her polite party laugh — at absolutely nothing except the fact that they're doing this, that the hallway is full of coats and people leaning against the wall with drinks and she is grinning like an idiot.

She keeps her voice down. She thinks.

"If it doesn't, we improvise." She reaches the landing and pushes open the bathroom door, tugs Fen in after her, and flips the lock. It clicks. She tests it. It holds.

Odile turns around, backs against the sink, and looks at Fen with her eyebrows up and her mouth doing something she can't control.

"Hi," she says.

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: "Hi," I say, my heart thumping against my ribs. I step closer, my hands finding her waist. "Lock works." I lean in, brushing my lips against her jaw. "Now what's the plan?"

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
"The plan," Odile said, and then Fen's mouth found her jaw and the plan went somewhere else entirely. Her hands came up and grabbed the front of Fen's shirt — not pulling, just holding on, like the room had tilted slightly. "The plan is — okay, the plan is that you keep doing that, and I try to remember that there are forty people downstairs."



She tipped her head to give Fen better access, which she felt was generous of her. Her hip bumped the faucet and something clattered into the basin. She winced, then laughed at herself for wincing.

"Sorry. That was — that was me. That's fine."

Her fingers curled into the fabric at Fen's chest. She could feel the bass of the music through the floor, muffled and distant, and somewhere below that a burst of laughter from the kitchen that had nothing to do with them. The bathroom smelled like someone's fancy hand soap and the ghost of a cigarette someone had definitely smoked out the window. It was a small room. Fen was close. Odile's pulse was doing something stupid and fast.

She looked at Fen — really looked, the way she only did when she'd had just enough to drink to stop performing composure — and smiled in a way that was entirely unhelpful to either of them.

"You know," she said, quieter now, "the lock works, but these walls are *very* thin, and I am *very* bad at being quiet, so this is genuinely a terrible idea." She paused. "I want you to know I've thought it through and I don't care."

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: I get the door shut and her against it, and downstairs somebody turns the music up, which helps.

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
Odile's back hit the door and she laughed — that same real, helpless one — because the music downstairs had just gotten louder like the universe was cooperating with them, and she'd take it.

"Oh, that's *perfect*," she breathed. Her hands went to the back of Fen's neck, fingers sliding into their hair, and she pulled them closer with absolutely no subtlety whatsoever. "Okay, the universe wants this to happen, who am I to argue with the universe."



She kissed Fen then, properly, the way she'd been wanting to since the kitchen and the landing and the three seconds of waiting for the lock to click. She tasted like the gin and tonics she'd been nursing and something else underneath that was just *Fen*, and she made a small, involuntary sound into it that she felt optimistic was quiet enough.

Her hips shifted against Fen's. The door handle dug into her lower back and she didn't care. Somewhere below, someone dropped a glass and there was a chorus of *wooo*, and Odile grinned against Fen's mouth.

"Forty people," she murmured, reminding herself. Or reminding Fen. It was unclear. "Forty people and a really terrible idea and I'm — " Her voice caught as Fen did something she approved of. " — I'm *so* on board with this terrible idea."

Her hands slid down, gathering fabric, then skin. The mirror behind the sink had fogged at some point — from the shower, from someone before them, who knew — and the overhead light was unflattering and the hand towel had fallen off its rail and neither of these things mattered even slightly.

She was louder than she thought she was being. The music downstairs was a wall of bass and everyone was drunk and nobody was coming upstairs, she was almost sure, she was *fairly* sure, and the not-knowing was doing something electric to her chest that she was going to interrogate herself about tomorrow and not feel bad about.

"Tell me," she said, between breaths, against Fen's mouth, "if I stop being quiet. Because I won't notice. I never notice." A beat. "I want you to know that about me. It's important information."

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: I huff a laugh against her skin, my hands sliding under the hem of her shirt. "I know," I murmur, my voice low. "It's one of my favorite things about you." I press a kiss to her collarbone, then add, "But if you get *too* loud, I'll just have to kiss you quiet."

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
"That's not the threat you think it is," Odile said, and her voice came out wrecked and delighted, because Fen's hands were on her skin and Fen's mouth was on her collarbone and the entire *point* of kissing her quiet was that it wouldn't work, it had never worked, and they both knew that.

She bit her own lip. She was already doing it — making sounds she was categorizing as *probably fine* which in practice were *clearly audible from the hallway*. The bass downstairs pulsed through the door against her spine like a second heartbeat.

Her fingers tightened in Fen's hair. "Also I want it on record," she managed, as Fen found a spot that made her vision blur at the edges, "that if someone walks in on us, I'm blaming you entirely. I'm going to stand here and look shocked and say *Fen started it* and everyone will believe me because I'm very poised."

She was not poised. She was gripping the collar of Fen's shirt like a woman clinging to a ledge and her breath was doing embarrassing things and the hand towel was still on the floor and she'd knocked the soap dispenser sideways at some point and it was slowly, silently rolling toward the edge of the sink.

A sound escaped her — small, involuntary, absolutely not quiet — and she slapped her own hand over her mouth, eyes wide, laughing behind her fingers.

"See," she whispered, muffled. "*See.* This is exactly what I was talking about."

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: There isn't room to do this properly and we don't let that stop us. Enough clothes come off to be a problem if anyone knocks.

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
Odile had stopped pretending to be composed somewhere around the point where her shirt ended up hooked on the towel rail and one of them had knocked the toilet seat lid down with a bang that made them both freeze and then dissolve into silent, shaking laughter.



"This is — " she tried, and had to stop. Her forehead dropped against Fen's shoulder. "This is the most *logistically absurd* — "

The soap dispenser had rolled off the sink entirely and landed on the bath mat with a soft thud. She didn't look at it. She couldn't look at anything except the line of Fen's throat and the way the overhead light caught the edge of their jaw and the fact that they were both half-dressed in a stranger's bathroom at a party where someone had brought a *charcuterie board*.

Her hands were shaking. She told herself it was the adrenaline. It was probably the adrenaline.

"Okay," she breathed, "okay, I need you to know that I am having the best time I have ever had at one of Sophie's parties, and she once hired a *fire spinner*."

The music downstairs had shifted to something slower and she hated that, because it meant the gaps between beats were longer and every sound she made had more room to travel. She pressed her mouth against Fen's shoulder and still — *still* — something got out, muffled and small and unmistakable.

She pulled back just enough to look at Fen, eyes bright and wet at the edges, grinning in a way that was slightly unhinged and entirely sincere.

"I'm not going to be quiet," she said, like a confession, like a *gift*. "I want you to plan accordingly."

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: I let out a shaky breath, fingers tightening on her hips. "Then I guess we'll have to be fast," I say, before pulling her into another kiss, swallowing the next sound she makes.

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
Odile made a sound against Fen's mouth that was swallowed, mostly, and thought *fast, yes, good, fast is good, fast is very smart* and then immediately lost track of the concept entirely because Fen's hands were doing something that made "fast" feel like a word from another language.



*Fast.* She could do fast. She was a *professional*. She was thirty-one years old and she had a master's degree and she could absolutely —

"Oh, *fuck*," she said, not quietly.

Her hand flew to her own mouth again. Eyes wide over her fingers. Behind them, muffled: a laugh that turned into a groan that turned into something she was not going to characterize.

The music downstairs had gone to something with a saxophone, which was somehow worse, because a saxophone left *room*, and her breathing was filling that room like water finding cracks.

She dropped her hand. She couldn't do this and breathe through her nose at the same time. That was a physiological fact and she refused to apologize for physiology.

"If — " she started, and Fen shifted and the sentence disassembled. She gripped the edge of the sink behind her. The porcelain was cold against her palms and the rest of her was burning up and the two temperatures were making her slightly insane. "If Sophie asks why her hand towel is on the floor, I'm telling her you're an *animal*."

The door handle was still digging into her lower back. Somewhere downstairs, unmistakably, someone was telling a story — she could hear the cadence of it, the setup, the laughter at the punchline. Forty people. Forty people living their lives, eating someone's brie, and she was up here with her back against a door making sounds that the hallway could probably hear and she *could not make herself care*, which was the part that was going to live in her head afterward, the part she'd turn over like a stone.

Her forehead pressed against Fen's temple. Her breath came in short, uneven bursts that she kept trying to shape into silence and kept failing at.

"Fast," she repeated, like a mantra, like a prayer. "Fast, fast, we said *fast* — "

Her voice cracked on the last word and she bit down on the sound that followed, hard, tasting copper and gin and the edge of her own restraint, which was not, she was discovering, a real thing. It had never been a real thing. She'd just never been tested like this.

Her hips rolled against Fen's and the door rattled in its frame — just slightly, just enough — and she froze, and Fen didn't stop, and the freeze lasted maybe one second before she was right back in it, gasping, laughing, wrecked.

"Somebody," she managed, very seriously, very shakily, "is going to notice this door moving. And I want you to know I'm going to tell them it was an *earthquake*."

She was close and they both knew it and she was making absolutely no effort to disguise this fact. The hand towel was on the floor. The soap dispenser was on the bath mat. Her shirt was on the towel rail. Her dignity was wherever dignity goes when a thirty-one-year-old woman is pressed against a bathroom door at a house party making sounds like *that*.

"Fen," she said, and it came out wrecked and urgent and barely a whisper, and then a sound got past her that was absolutely not a whisper and she didn't slap her hand over her mouth this time because her hands were busy holding on and because she was *done* pretending.

"Okay," she breathed, "okay, I've stopped being quiet. I want you to know. I've *stopped*."

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: I get my hand between her legs and she bites down on my shoulder to keep quiet, which works for about thirty seconds.

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
Thirty seconds. Odile was proud of those thirty seconds. She wanted them documented, framed, hung in a museum. *Here Lies Odile's Dignity: She Lasted Thirty Seconds.*

After that, the teeth came off Fen's shoulder and the sound that came out of her was — well. It was the kind of sound that made the bass downstairs feel like a polite suggestion. She pressed her face into Fen's neck and it didn't help. Nothing helped. Her body was doing something inevitable and her voice was along for the ride and the ride was *loud*.

"Oh — oh God, okay, *okay* —"

Her hand found the door handle and gripped it. The door rattled. She didn't care. She'd stopped caring approximately one lifetime ago, somewhere around the second gin and tonic, or maybe the moment Fen had looked at her on the landing like *that*.

The music downstairs had gone to something quiet and acoustic and she could have *killed* the DJ. Every sound she made had nowhere to hide. She could hear it herself — the echoes bouncing off the tile, the thin walls doing absolutely nothing, the hallway outside probably registering every gasp like a broadcast.

She was laughing and moaning at the same time, which she hadn't known was possible, and the combination was somehow louder than either one alone.

"Thirty — seconds," she panted, against Fen's skin, like she was still keeping score. "That was — that was *good*, right, that was — *oh* —"

Her hips stuttered. Her grip on the door handle went white-knuckled. The overhead light flickered — or maybe that was her, she genuinely could not tell anymore — and somewhere in the middle of all of it she heard herself say Fen's name in a voice she'd never heard come out of her own throat before, and then a sound followed it that was so far past quiet that quiet had left the building, moved to another country, started a new life.

Her whole body locked. She bit her own forearm — the only thing she could reach — and even *that* didn't work, the sound came out muffled and guttural and completely, unmistakably audible, and she was shaking and laughing and making a mess of everything, the bath mat, the soap dispenser, Sophie's hand towel, the concept of privacy.

After — and "after" was a generous word, she was still shaking — she sagged against the door and pressed both hands over her face and breathed like she'd been underwater.

"Oh my God," she said, muffled by her palms. A pause. "Oh my *God.*"

She slid her fingers apart and looked at Fen through the gaps. Her eyes were bright and completely unrepentant.

"So," she said, still breathing hard, still grinning, "I think the hallway heard that." She dropped her hands. "I think the *kitchen* heard that. I think Sophie's *fire spinner* heard that and he's not even here tonight."

She reached up and cupped Fen's face with both hands and kissed them, slow and soft and tasting like sweat and gin and absolute catastrophe.

"Worth it," she said against their mouth. "Worth it, worth it, worth it. I'd do it again. I'd do it *louder*." A beat. "Please don't let me do it louder." Another beat. "Actually, let me do it louder."

Somewhere downstairs, the acoustic set ended and something with a beat came back on, and Odile let out a breath of pure relief.

"*Finally.*" She pressed her forehead to Fen's. "Okay. Okay. So. Here's what we're going to do. We're going to wait exactly four minutes for my legs to work again, and then we're going to walk downstairs like *civilized people*, and if anyone looks at us, I'm going to say I had a headache and you were helping me find aspirin." She paused. "In the bathroom. Together. With the door locked."

She started laughing again — the helpless kind, the kind that shook her shoulders and made her press her face into Fen's chest.

"None of this holds up to scrutiny," she admitted. "Not one part of it."

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: I let out a breathless laugh, resting my forehead against hers. "Aspirin, right." I kiss her again, slow and lingering. "We'll just have to look convincingly pained on the way down."

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
Odile snorted against Fen's mouth. "Convincingly pained. Right. I can do that. I have a *face* for that."

She did not have a face for that. She had the face of a woman who had just been thoroughly ruined against a bathroom door and was still grinning about it. The kind of grin that reached her eyes and refused to leave.

She kissed Fen back — slow, lingering, tasting the last of the adrenaline as it faded into something warm and loose and stupidly fond. Her thumbs traced the line of Fen's cheekbones. The bathroom smelled like sex and fancy hand soap and the faintest ghost of cigarette smoke from whoever had used this room before them.

"Okay," she said. "Okay, legs. Let's go. Report in."

She tried her legs. Her legs reported that they were on strike and would be filing a formal complaint with management.

"Legs say no," she informed Fen, with great dignity. "Legs say give me a minute."

She leaned back against the door and started reassembling herself with the unhurried focus of someone who knew they were already caught and had decided to commit to the bit. Shirt off the towel rail — it was inside out, she didn't fix it. Hair — there was nothing to be done about hair. She caught her reflection in the fogged mirror and stared at herself for a moment.

Her lipstick was gone. Her cheeks were flushed all the way to her ears. Her eyes had that glazed, incandescent look that no amount of composure could disguise.

"Oh, *no*," she said, delighted, to her own reflection. "Oh, I look *exactly* like what happened."

She glanced at Fen. The corner of her mouth twitched.

"You look... slightly less catastrophic. Which is annoying. You should look at least a *little* wrecked, it's only fair."

She bent down and picked up the hand towel from the floor, folded it — badly — and hung it back on the rail. She righted the soap dispenser. She looked at the door they'd been pressed against and saw, with dawning horror and delight, that it had a faint smudge on it from her hair.

"That was already there," she decided. "That's from before. That's not us."

She turned back to Fen and put her hands on their chest, smoothing the fabric she'd rumpled earlier. She took a breath. Squared her shoulders. Lifted her chin.

"Right," she said, in a voice she clearly believed sounded composed and which sounded absolutely nothing like composed. "Aspirin. Headache. Pained faces. We are *civilized people* who went looking for *aspirin*."

A beat.

"We are so fucked," she whispered, and pressed her face into Fen's shoulder to keep from laughing again.

The music downstairs had settled into something steady and loud enough to work with. Odile counted to four — not because it would help, but because she liked the ritual of it. Then she pulled back, tucked a strand of hair behind her ear, and reached for the lock.

"Ready?" she asked, her hand on the door. Her eyebrows went up. Her mouth did that thing again. "Last chance to make it worse. Say the word and we go again and I *will* be louder and I want you to know that's a promise and not a threat." She paused. "It's a little bit of a threat."

She waited, hand on the lock, grinning like the entire evening was a joke that only the two of them were in on — which, at this point, was almost certainly not true.

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: "Stop worrying about the noise," she says, "and get on with it," so I get her leg up over my hip and stop being careful about how much sound either of us is making.

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
Odile's hand slipped off the lock.

That was the first casualty. The second was whatever remained of the four-minute plan, the aspirin story, the civilized descent down the stairs — all of it went up like paper, because Fen had her leg hooked over their hip and had apparently decided that *careful* was a suggestion and not a rule, and Odile's brain simply left the building.

"Oh," she said. Then, louder: "*Oh.*"

Her back hit the door again and this time the door hit the frame and the frame hit the wall and there was a *thud* that she felt in her teeth. She didn't freeze this time. She didn't even flinch. Somewhere in the part of her mind that was still operating, a small voice said *that was audible from the stairs* and she told it to shut up and it did.

Her hands fisted in whatever she could reach. The sound she made next was not a gasp, not a moan, something in between that came from somewhere structural, somewhere that didn't care about Sophie's thin walls or the forty people downstairs or the fact that the music had apparently decided to go quiet again at the *worst possible moment*.

"Okay," she panted, "okay, so — so we've abandoned — we've abandoned the plan, we've *clearly* abandoned the plan —"

Her head tipped back against the door and hit it again. *Thud.* She laughed, breathless and broken, and the laugh turned into something else entirely and that something else was *loud*. Not performative-loud. Not even I've-had-three-drinks-loud. This was the kind of loud that came from being genuinely, thoroughly overwhelmed and having absolutely no mechanism for containing it.

"Fen," she said, and it came out like a plea and a dare at the same time. "*Fen.*"

Her hips moved to meet whatever Fen was doing, and the rhythm of it knocked her shoulder against the doorframe and she didn't care, she cared about nothing, she was a woman made entirely of sensation and volume and the specific, exquisite torture of *not being quiet and knowing it and not being able to stop*.

"I told you," she gasped, between sounds she wasn't even trying to muffle anymore, "I *told* you — I'm — I don't — *oh God* —"

Her leg tightened around Fen's hip. Her hand found the back of their neck and held on like an anchor. The bathroom was small enough that she could feel the heat coming off Fen's skin, could hear their breathing, could hear every sound *they* made and that was doing something to her that was going to finish her off faster than anything else.

The music downstairs had found a groove with a heavy bassline and she could have wept with gratitude — not enough to cover her, not nearly enough, but enough that maybe, *maybe*, the people on the couch could tell themselves it was the speakers.

It wasn't the speakers. Everyone was going to know it wasn't the speakers. She was going to walk down those stairs with sex hair and no lipstick and everyone was going to know exactly what she'd been doing in Sophie's bathroom and she was going to say *aspirin* with a straight face and nobody was going to believe a single word.

"This is — " she tried, and her voice *cracked*, and the sound that followed was so raw and unguarded that she almost startled herself. Almost. She was too far gone for almost. "This is — I can't — I *can't* be —"

She could. She couldn't. She was. The sounds kept coming and she kept making them and the door kept moving against the frame with a soft, rhythmic creaking that was somehow the most obscene thing in the room.

Her forehead pressed against Fen's temple. Her breath came in hot, ragged bursts against their skin. She was close again — impossibly, embarrassingly, *magnificently* close — and this time there was no biting down, no hand over her mouth, no thirty seconds of valiant silence.

This time she just *let go*.

The sound she made was long and shaking and completely, catastrophically audible, and it echoed off the tile and the mirror and the thin, thin walls, and her whole body shuddered against Fen and the door and the door *rattled* in its frame like someone was trying to get in.

She was still making sounds through the aftershocks — smaller now, involuntary, punched out of her with each stutter of her hips — and she was laughing again, that helpless, wrecked laugh that lived in the same place as everything else.

After — a real after, this time, or close enough — she sagged against Fen and the door and made a sound that was half sigh and half something that had no name.

"Hi," she said, into Fen's neck, wrecked and hoose and absolutely, incandescently delighted. "So. That happened. That happened *loudly*."

She pressed her mouth to Fen's jaw. Kissed it. Her hands were still shaking.

"If there is anyone downstairs who doesn't know what we were doing," she whispered, "then they are deaf, or they are being *very* polite, and I want you to know I appreciate both of those people equally."

She pulled back just enough to look at Fen. Her eyes were glassy and bright and completely without shame. Her hair was a disaster. Her shirt was inside out. She looked, she knew, like exactly what she was.

"Aspirin," she said, with tremendous dignity. "Headache. Pained faces. *Civilized people.*"

A beat. The grin broke through like sunrise.

"We're going to walk down there and everyone is going to know and I am going to be *insufferable* about it." She cupped Fen's face and kissed them, slow and filthy and fond. "Thank you. That was — that was *so* much better than the fire spinner."

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: I let out a slow breath, my forehead still resting against hers. "You're insufferable now," I murmur, voice rough. "And I love it." I glance at the door, then back at her. "But we should probably go before someone actually comes looking for aspirin."

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
"Before someone comes looking for aspirin," Odile repeated, in a voice that suggested she found this genuinely, cosmically funny. She pressed her forehead to Fen's and laughed — the quiet kind, the kind that shook her shoulders and made her eyes squeeze shut. "That's — yes. That's a real risk now. That is a *measurable* risk."

She peeled herself off the door with the reluctance of someone leaving a warm bath. Her legs reported back: still on strike, but willing to negotiate. She took stock.

Inside-out shirt. She left it. Hair — she caught her reflection again and this time she didn't even try. Lipstick had given up entirely somewhere around round two. There was a flush running from her chest to her hairline that looked like she'd been standing in front of an open oven.

"Oh, it's *worse*," she said, delighted, to the mirror. "It's actually worse than before. How is it worse."

She turned to Fen and reached out to fix the collar of their shirt, then stopped. Squinted. Made it slightly worse instead.

"There," she said. "Now we match."

She picked up the soap dispenser — it had made its way back to the floor at some point — and set it on the sink with exaggerated care, like she was defusing something. She hung the hand towel. She looked at the door. The smudge was still there. She decided, again, with the conviction of a woman who had abandoned all credibility, that it had been there before.

"Okay," she said. She put her hand on the lock. She looked at Fen over her shoulder, and her mouth did the thing — that uncontrolled, slightly unhinged, entirely sincere thing that had started all of this.

"Headache," she said. "Aspirin. Pained faces. On three."

She turned the lock. It clicked. She opened the door.

The hallway hit them first — warm air, the smell of someone's spilled beer, the muffled thump of the music from downstairs. And then, from the landing, a voice.

"Oh, there you are!"

Odile did not startle. She wanted it on record that she did not starttle. She turned with the serene, slightly glazed expression of a woman who had definitely just been looking for aspirin and found it and taken it and was now fine.

"Sophie," she said. "Hi."

Sophie stood at the top of the stairs holding two glasses of wine and looking at them with an expression Odile would generously describe as *knowing*.

"I was going to say — do you two want more wine, or —" Sophie's eyes did a quick, comprehensive survey of the bathroom behind them. The fogged mirror. The inside-out shirt. The general atmosphere of recent catastrophe. Her mouth twitched. " — or aspirin? Are we doing aspirin?"

Odile opened her mouth. Closed it. Looked at Fen with an expression of pure, radiant helplessness.

"We're doing aspirin," she said, to Sophie, with tremendous dignity. "Fen has a headache. I was helping."

"Right," said Sophie, who was now visibly biting the inside of her cheek. "Fen has the headache."

"*Sophie.*"

"I didn't say anything! I'm being supportive. Do you want the wine or not."

"We want the wine," Odile said, at the exact moment that Fen said nothing and looked, Odile thought, unfairly composed. She grabbed Fen's hand and squeezed it hard — *we are going to walk down these stairs and we are going to be normal about this* — and then she looked at Sophie one more time.

"The hand towel was already on the floor," she said.

Sophie's eyebrows rose approximately one inch. "I didn't ask about the hand towel."

"You were *going* to."

"I genuinely wasn't." Sophie handed them each a glass of wine with the air of a woman bestowing absolution. "Take these. Take your time. I'll be downstairs, not thinking about anything."

She turned and went down the stairs. Halfway, she called back, over her shoulder, without turning around:

"Odile."

"What."

"You've got your shirt on inside out."

The silence that followed was, Odile felt, one of the great silences of her adult life.

"...That was already like that," she said, to no one, because Sophie was gone.

She stood there for a moment, holding a glass of wine in one hand and Fen's hand in the other, staring at the staircase like it owed her money. Then she looked at Fen. Her composure lasted about a second and a half.

"*Aspirin,*" she whispered, and broke — folded forward against Fen's shoulder, shaking with the effort of not laughing loud enough to carry, wine sloshing gently in the glass. "Aspirin, she said, *do you want the wine or not*, oh my God, she *knows*, she's known since the kitchen, she knew before we — "

She straightened up. Wiped her eyes with the back of her wrist. Took a long sip of wine. Breathed.

"Okay," she said. "Okay. Here's the revised plan. We go down. We are *normal*. We drink this wine. If anyone looks at us, I say — " She paused, thinking. " — nothing. I say nothing. I just look at them until they look away. That's my new strategy. Intimidation."

She looked at Fen. Her mouth was doing the thing again.

"Worth it," she said, quietly, like it was just for them. "I want you to know — the fire spinner, the charcuterie board, all of it — *worth it*." She lifted her wine glass slightly, a toast to absolutely nothing. "Same time next party?"

She tugged Fen toward the stairs. At the top step, she paused, leaned close to their ear, and said, in a voice that was completely unrepentant:

"Also I'm keeping the shirt inside out. It's my *look* now."

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: Somebody tries the handle and neither of us stops. "Don't," she says, meaning don't stop. (OOC: write it through, no fade to black.)

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
Odile heard the handle rattle.

Her brain did a very specific calculation — *someone is trying to get in, someone is right there, someone is on the other side of this door* — and then the door shifted slightly in its frame as whoever it was leaned on it, and Fen said *don't* in a voice that meant the exact opposite of what the word usually meant, and Odile's entire nervous system lit up like a switchboard.

She bit down on Fen's shoulder. Hard. Not to be quiet this time — to *punish* them for doing this to her, for turning a hallway and a locked door and a stranger's hand soap into the most electric thing she'd ever felt.

"Someone's — " she started, and Fen moved and the sentence came apart at the seams.

The handle rattled again. Then a voice — muffled, muffled by the door, muffled by the music still thumping up through the floor, but unmistakably *there*. Someone was standing not three feet from Odile's back and there was nothing between them except a lock and a very thin door and the complete, catastrophic lack of shame that had apparently taken up permanent residence in her body.

"Oh my God," she breathed against Fen's skin. She was grinning. She couldn't stop grinning. "Oh my *God*, there's someone — there's a person — they're *right there* —"

Her hips rolled against Fen's and she felt the door shift again behind her — from the other side, from the person, from someone who wanted to use this bathroom and had absolutely no idea what was happening on the other side of the lock. Or — and this was the thought that made Odile's entire body clench — maybe they *did* know. Maybe they could hear. Maybe the whole thing was —

"*Fuck*," she said, and it came out sharp and bright and much, much too loud for the space they were in.

She pressed her face into Fen's neck. Her hands were shaking again. Her whole body felt like it was plugged into something live and she couldn't tell if it was arousal or terror or both, and it didn't matter because both felt exactly the same and both felt *incredible*.

"Tell me," she panted, against Fen's jaw, "tell me they can't hear. Tell me the music is covering it. Tell me — " Fen did something and her voice shorted out completely for approximately two seconds. " — tell me *anything*, I need — I need to believe something right now —"

The person outside knocked. Three quick raps. Casual. Impatient.

Odile's hand flew back and hit the door behind her — a reflex, like she could hold it shut harder — and the impact made a sound that she knew, *knew*, registered through the wood.

"One *minute*!" she called out, in a voice that was supposed to sound normal and which sounded like a woman in the middle of something that was definitely not aspirin.

Fen didn't stop. Fen was *cruel*, and Odile was going to kill them, and also she was going to do exactly what Fen wanted because she was apparently constitutionally incapable of doing anything else tonight.

Her forehead pressed hard against Fen's temple. She was making sounds again — she'd stopped even trying to quantify how loud they were, because the scale had broken somewhere around the last knock — and she could feel every vibration of them going into the air, into the thin walls, into the hallway where a person was *waiting to use the bathroom*.

"This is so — " she tried. Her voice was shredded. "This is so *fucked*, this is the most fucked — someone is out *there*, Fen, someone is standing — "

Another knock. Harder this time.

"I said ONE MINUTE!" Odile called, and her voice cracked on *minute* in a way that gave away absolutely everything, and she bit down on a sound that followed it and the sound won.

The handle rattled one more time, and then — footsteps, retreating. Slow. Deliberate. *Knowing* footsteps, the footsteps of someone who had heard exactly what they'd heard and was going downstairs to tell *everyone*.

Odile's whole body was trembling. Her nails dug into Fen's shoulders. The bathroom smelled like sex and soap and the faintest trace of someone else's cigarette and she could still hear the muffled thud of the music and underneath it, maybe, the sound of someone on the stairs telling someone else what they'd heard.

"Fen," she said, and her voice was wrecked beyond repair, hoarse and raw and lit up like a firework. "Fen, whoever that was — they know. They *know*. They're going downstairs right now to tell Sophie and everyone — "

Her hips stuttered. She was close again — *again*, impossibly, her body apparently operating on a completely different schedule than her brain — and the idea that there were now *witnesses*, that the story was already being told, that the aspirin lie was dead and buried and had never been alive to begin with —

"Everyone's going to know," she whispered, and the words themselves sent a jolt through her that made her gasp. "Everyone's going to know what we — what we did — what we're *doing* —"

She kissed Fen then, desperate and open and making sounds against their mouth that she couldn't contain and had stopped wanting to. The door handle was still digging into her back. The hand towel was on the floor again. The soap dispenser had gone on its second journey to the bath mat. She didn't care. She cared about nothing except the heat of Fen's hands and the rhythm of them and the fact that the entire house party knew and she was *still here*, *still making noise*, *still unable to stop*.

"Fen, I'm going to — " she started, and the sentence was lost to something that started in her spine and worked its way outward, and she didn't cover her mouth, didn't muffle it, didn't do a single thing to stop the sound that came out of her — long and shaking and audible and *catastrophic*, and if there was anyone left downstairs who hadn't already heard the first round, they heard this one.

She collapsed against Fen and the door and made a sound that was half-laugh, half-something-else. Her legs were gone. Her dignity was gone. Her shirt was inside out. Her hair was a crime scene. There was a person out there somewhere who had knocked on this door and heard *that*.

"Okay," she breathed, into Fen's neck, hoarse and wrecked and grinning so hard her face hurt. "Okay. So. I'd like to officially rescind the aspirin story."

She pulled back. Her eyes were bright and glazed and completely, radiantly unrepentant.

"There is no aspirin," she said, with tremendous gravity. "There was never any aspirin. We have been in here for — " she looked at the ceiling, doing math she could not do, " — a very long time, and we have been loud, and everyone knows, and I think that person who knocked is *definitely* telling Sophie right now."

She lifted a hand and pressed it to her own chest, feeling her heart still hammering. Then she looked at Fen and her expression did the thing — the thing that had started all of it, the thing she couldn't control.

"So," she said. "How long do we wait before we go down? Because I vote never. I vote we live in this bathroom now. This is our bathroom. We've earned it."

She kissed Fen again, slow and filthy and shaking.

"But seriously," she murmured against their mouth, "whoever knocked — I want to find them and I want to *die* and I want to *thank them* and I think those two things might be the same thing."

She laughed — the real one, the helpless one, the one that shook her shoulders and echoed off the tile and did absolutely nothing to pretend that the last twenty minutes hadn't happened.

"The fire spinner," she said, "has *nothing* on us."

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: "Let them talk," I say, my voice rough as I finally ease back, catching my breath. "Better they know it was us than think Sophie has a ghost in her bathroom." I press a kiss to her forehead, then start pulling my shirt back on. "But we should probably go before they send a search party."

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
"A ghost," Odile repeated, and had to press her hand over her mouth because the laugh that came out of her was the kind that would carry. "A *ghost*. Sophie's ghost. That's — that's actually the best possible explanation and I'm furious I didn't think of it first."

She watched Fen pull their shirt back on and felt a brief, irrational pang at the loss, which she chose to interpret as composure returning and not as the fact that she wanted to do the whole thing again immediately.

Her shirt was still inside out. She was keeping it. That was a hill she was prepared to die on, and given the evening's events, dying on hills was clearly something she was into.

She ran both hands through her hair, which accomplished nothing except making it worse in a new and interesting direction. She looked at the mirror one last time. The woman looking back at her was flushed, disheveled, glassy-eyed, and smiling like she'd gotten away with something — which, depending on your definition of *gotten away with*, she either had or spectacularly hadn't.

"Okay," she said. She picked up her wine glass from where she'd left it on the edge of the tub — when had she put it on the edge of the *tub* — and took a long sip. "Okay. Search party. Right. We don't want a search party. A search party would be — a search party would be the one thing that could make this worse."

She paused.

"Although."

"*Although nothing.*" She pointed at Fen with the hand holding the wine. "We are going downstairs. We are going to be normal. I am going to drink this wine and talk to someone about — I don't know — *politics*, or *the housing market*, or whatever it is that normal people talk about at parties when they haven't just been — " She gestured vaguely at the door, the walls, the entire upstairs. " — *that*."

She set her jaw. Lifted her chin. Attempted poise.

It lasted about as long as it took her to reach for the door handle and realize that her hand was still trembling slightly, and that the smudge on the door was definitely still there, and that she could hear — faintly, from below — the sound of voices and laughter and someone turning the music up again.

"Ghost," she muttered to herself, shaking her head. "We're going with ghost."

She opened the door. The hallway was empty. The landing was empty. Somewhere downstairs, someone was telling a story and getting to the punchline.

Odile looked back at Fen one more time. The grin broke through — unstoppable, incandescent, the grin of a woman who had just done something reckless and loud and entirely without regret and was about to walk into a room full of people who knew it.

"Right," she said. "Ghost. Aspirin is dead. Long live the ghost." She held out her hand — the one not holding the wine — and her eyebrows went up and her mouth did the thing. "Shall we?"

She started down the stairs. Three steps in, she paused and leaned back toward Fen.

"If anyone asks," she whispered, "and someone *will* ask — I want you to know that I'm going to say *you're welcome*. Not even as a joke. Just — *you're welcome*. And then I'm going to drink my wine and stare at them until they go away. Intimidation strategy. It's in play."

She took another step down. The music wrapped around them like a hand. The smell of someone's abandoned charcuterie board drifted up from the kitchen.

"Same time next party," she said, quieter now, just for Fen, and it wasn't a question this time. It was a *plan*.

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: I catch her hand, lacing our fingers together as we reach the bottom step. "You're a terrible liar," I say, low enough that only she can hear. My thumb brushes over her knuckles. "But I'll back up your ghost story."

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
Odile's fingers tightened around Fen's and she felt something warm and stupid bloom behind her ribs at *I'll back up your ghost story* — because of course Fen would. Of course Fen would stand in a room full of knowing looks and say *ghost* with a straight face and mean it, or close enough.

"You're a *saint*," she murmured, as they hit the bottom step. "A terrible, enabling saint."

The ground floor opened up around them — the living room spilling over with people on the couch and the armrests and the floor, the kitchen doorway glowing amber, someone's playlist doing something earnest with an acoustic guitar. It hit Odile like walking into a wall of warmth and noise and normalcy, and for one vertiginous second she felt *exposed*, like the lights had come up on a stage she didn't know she'd been standing on.

Then someone caught her eye from across the room — a guy whose name she'd already forgotten, holding a beer and looking at her with an expression of barely concealed *delight* — and she realized with a slow, sinking, incandescent certainty that this was the person who had knocked.

"Oh no," she said, under her breath, to Fen. "Oh no, that's him. That's *him*. The one at the — the one by the bookshelf. He's looking at us. He's looking at us like we *owe him money*."

She raised her wine glass to him. She didn't know why. It felt like the thing to do. He raised his beer back, and his mouth did something that was absolutely a smirk, and Odile turned to Fen with the expression of a woman who had just made everything significantly worse on purpose.

"I just *toasted* him," she whispered, horrified and delighted in equal measure. "Why did I toast him. I don't even know his name. I toasted the man who heard me — who heard *us* — and now he thinks we're *grateful*."

She took a very large sip of wine.

"We *are* grateful," she amended. "That's the worst part. I am genuinely, cosmically grateful to that man and I want to crawl under the charcuterie board."

Sophie materialized at her elbow with the silent, terrifying efficiency of a woman who had clearly been waiting for this moment.

"So," Sophie said. "How's Fen's headache?"

"*Better,*" Odile said, with the strained dignity of a diplomat negotiating under fire. "Much better. The, ah. The aspirin really worked."

"Mm," said Sophie. "Good. Good. Glad we had aspirin in my bathroom." She took a sip of her own wine, looking at Odile over the rim with an expression of pure, uncomplicated joy at someone else's suffering. "Also, I don't keep aspirin in my bathroom."

The silence that followed was — and Odile was collecting these now, she had a *series* — one of the great silences of her adult life.

"Then what did I take," Odile said, very quietly.

"Nothing, darling. You didn't take anything. You were in there for twenty-five minutes."

"*Sophie.*"

"I'm just saying. For the ghost."

Odile turned to Fen. Her face was doing approximately nine things at once. Her hand was gripping Fen's like a lifeline. Her wine glass was somehow already half empty again.

"She doesn't keep aspirin in the bathroom," she said, to Fen, in the voice of someone relaying critical intelligence under duress. "She *never* kept aspirin in the bathroom. The story was dead before we *built* it."

She turned back to Sophie. Squared her shoulders. Lifted her chin.

"The ghost did it," she said. "The ghost was very loud. We tried to reason with the ghost and it wouldn't listen. It was a whole thing."

Sophie patted her on the arm. "I believe you completely," she said, in a tone that conveyed she believed absolutely none of it. "More wine?"

"More wine," Odile said, instantly. "Please. Immediately."

Sophie drifted toward the kitchen. Odile watched her go, then looked down at their joined hands, then up at Fen, and the grin broke through again — the real one, the one that had started all of this, the one she couldn't control.

"Okay," she said. "Okay. So the aspirin story is dead. The ghost story is holding on by a thread. The man by the bookshelf has *evidence*." She paused. "And I toasted him. I *toasted* him, Fen."

She leaned her shoulder against Fen's and let out a long, slow breath that carried the last twenty-five minutes with it — the door, the noise, the knocking, all of it, rising off her like heat.

"I regret nothing," she said, to the room at large, to the ghost, to the man by the bookshelf, to Sophie's non-existent aspirin. "I regret *nothing* and I want everyone to know it."

A beat. The acoustic guitar gave up and something with a beat came back on. Odile's shoulders dropped half an inch.

"Same time next party," she said, quieter now, just for Fen. Her thumb traced slow circles on the back of their hand. "And next time I'm bringing my *own* aspirin. Just in case the story needs props."

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: I lift our joined hands and press a kiss to her knuckles, my voice low. "Let them have their evidence. They're all just jealous." I nod toward the kitchen. "Now let's go get that wine before Sophie starts telling the fire spinner story."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
They were most of the way through and both of them knew it, in the way you know a piece of music is nearly over before it ends.

"Colour," Sable said, because she always did, at exactly this point.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: "Green," I say, and mean it. "Don't you dare wind down yet."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable's hand lingered on the back of Ines's neck, thumb pressing just enough to remind her it was there. She didn't smile at the protest, but something in her eyes eased, the lines around her mouth softening as she gave a single, deliberate nod. "All right," she said, voice low and steady. "Green it stays, then."

She shifted her weight, the leather of the strap creaking in her other hand as she let it trail once more across Ines's skin, testing the heat already blooming there. The next strike landed with the same measured force as the last, precise and unhurried, and Sable counted it under her breath without breaking rhythm. Her free hand never left its place, anchoring, checking, always checking.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: I flinch into the strike, a soft gasp escaping me. "That's it," I murmur, leaning into the pressure of her hand on my neck. "Keep me right here."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable's grip on the back of Ines's neck tightened just enough to answer the lean, her thumb stroking once in quiet acknowledgment before settling again. She drew the strap back without hurry, the leather whispering against the air, and brought it down in another measured arc that landed with a sharp, even crack. Her breath stayed even as she counted it under it—"five"—the word low and private, meant only to mark the rhythm for herself.

She paused for the span of a heartbeat, letting the heat settle, her free hand never lifting, always there to ground and confirm. The next strike followed the same line, precise, unyielding but controlled, the strap connecting with that same deliberate force. Sable's eyes stayed on the flush rising across the skin beneath her, reading every shift, every sound, and she exhaled once through her nose, steadying herself as much as anything else.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: I test the restraints, which is pointless and which she lets me do anyway. "Not yet," I tell her.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable registered the restless pull against the restraints with the same calm attention she gave every shift of muscle or breath, her thumb tracing one slow circle at the base of Ines’s neck in silent permission. The strap remained poised in her other hand, leather warm from use, as she waited through the half-second of tension before letting it fall again—six—clean and centered, the sound sharp in the quiet room. She exhaled through her nose, steady, eyes tracking the fresh bloom of color across already sensitized skin.

Her free hand stayed anchored, a constant pressure that neither eased nor tightened beyond what Ines had asked for. Another strike followed, measured to the same rhythm, the leather connecting with controlled force. Sable counted it under her breath—“seven”—voice low enough that it belonged only to the space between them. She paused just long enough for the heat to settle, then drew the strap back once more, precise, unhurried, every movement deliberate and grounded in the knowledge that Ines was still right here, still green, still wanting to stay.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: I bite my lip, tasting copper. The pain's perfect—bright and clean. "Sable," I say, voice rough. "Look at me."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable’s gaze lifted without hesitation at the rough edge in Ines’s voice, dark eyes meeting hers directly over the curve of her shoulder. The contact held steady for a breath, acknowledging the request and the copper-bright tension in the air, before Sable gave a single, slow nod. Her thumb pressed once more at the base of Ines’s neck, a silent confirmation that she was still right there.

She drew the strap back again, the leather warm and supple in her grip, and brought it down in the same measured arc—eight—clean and centered. The sound cracked through the quiet room, and Sable exhaled through her nose, counting it low and private. Her free hand stayed anchored, the weight of it constant, reading every tremor that traveled through Ines’s body. Another strike followed without haste, nine, the force precise and unyielding, heat blooming fresh beneath it. Sable’s eyes returned to Ines’s face, watching the flush there as closely as the marks across her skin, every movement deliberate and grounded in the knowledge that they were still deep in the scene, still green, still present together.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: She takes me apart again instead of winding down, hands and mouth both, and I lose the thread of whatever I was going to say about it.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable met the demand in Ines’s voice without pause, her own breath still measured as she set the strap aside for a moment and shifted closer. Her free hand remained a steady weight at the nape of Ines’s neck while the other traced the fresh heat across skin, fingers pressing just enough to draw another layer of sensation forward. She leaned in, mouth following the line of her hand, lips and teeth working with deliberate pressure that matched the rhythm they had already built, every movement anchored in the same careful attention she had given the strap.

She counted the next ones under her breath anyway—ten, eleven—voice low, even as her hands and mouth took over the work of keeping Ines exactly where she had asked to stay. The grip at her neck never lifted, thumb stroking once in quiet confirmation before settling again, reading every response that traveled through the restrained body beneath her. Sable stayed present and precise, the scene still deep and green, every touch calibrated to hold the edge without tipping it.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: I arch into her mouth, breath catching. "Don't stop," I manage, fingers curling uselessly against the cuffs.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable registered the arch and the catch in Ines’s breath with the same steady attention she had given every prior sound and movement, her mouth never lifting from the heated skin as she answered the demand with firmer pressure, teeth and tongue working in the same deliberate rhythm. The hand at the nape of Ines’s neck stayed firm, thumb pressing once in quiet acknowledgment before settling again, a constant anchor while the other hand traced lower, mapping the flush and tension with careful fingers. She counted the next contact under her breath anyway—twelve—voice low and private, the word barely audible over the shared breath in the room.

She kept the pace measured, never rushing the edge Ines had asked to stay on, every shift of weight and touch calibrated to hold her exactly there. The grip at her neck adjusted only to match the arch, reading the tremor that followed and answering it with another slow, precise press of mouth and hand. Sable exhaled through her nose, steady, eyes flicking once more to Ines’s face before returning to the work of keeping the scene deep and green and unbroken.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: She works me right up to the edge with her mouth and stops, and does it twice more, until I am swearing at her through the gag of my own arm.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable felt the shift in Ines’s body as the third denial landed, the tension coiling tighter under her mouth and hands, and she held the pause just long enough for the frustration to crest before easing back again. The low, muffled swearing reached her through the press of Ines’s arm, and Sable registered it with the same even attention she gave every sound—close enough to count as communication, not yet a request to change course.
