dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
They were most of the way through and both of them knew it, in the way you know a piece of music is nearly over before it ends.

"Colour," Sable said, because she always did, at exactly this point.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: "Green," I say, and mean it. "Don't you dare wind down yet."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable's hand stayed where it was — steady, unhurried, reading the word like a map correction. *Not yet.* She filed it and shifted her weight, adjusting the angle of her knee against the bed, closing the distance she'd been keeping between herself and the edge of the scene.

"Say it again when you want it," she said. Not a warning — an offering. A thing to hold onto.

Then she gave Ines what they'd asked for: not a retreat toward the end, but the middle made longer. The kind of rhythm that said *we have time, I'm not counting down, you don't have to earn another minute.* She let her thumb trace slow, deliberate arcs — the kind that built rather than released — and watched with the close attention she always paid here, the place where breath and tension told her more than words did.

She was aware, distantly, that this was where discipline lived. Not in the restraint itself — anyone could pull a rope. The discipline was here, in the held breath before the next choice, in choosing to *stay* rather than to begin wrapping up because the shape of the evening suggested she should. Ines had said *don't you dare.* So she didn't. She went the other way instead, heavier and slower, letting the impact land with a warmth that spread rather than stung, each one placed with the same care she'd give if it were the first or the hundredth.

"You're doing so well," she murmured, low enough that it wasn't praise for effort so much as a fact she was reporting — the way you'd say *it's raining* or *the light's good here.*

She held the rhythm. She let the almost-over stretch.

But she kept listening. Kept the part of her mind that always stayed half a step outside the scene, tracking, counting, holding the line of *green* against its edges. Because *don't wind down yet* was not the same as *never wind down,* and Sable knew the difference in her bones. When it came — when Ines' breath changed shape, or the word arrived, or she simply saw it in the way a body softened — she would stop. Completely. And then she would be relentless about water and warmth and staying close, and none of that was negotiable, not tonight, not ever.

But not yet.

She stayed exactly where she was, and gave them more.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: I exhale slowly, the tension in my shoulders finally easing. "Still green," I murmur, my voice rough. "Just...stay there a moment longer."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
"Still green," Sable repeated softly, committing it to memory the way she did — as a coordinate, not just a word. She held her hand exactly where it was, feeling the warmth there, the pulse of Ines' own slowing heartbeat beneath her palm. She didn't add anything. Didn't build or escalate or ask if they were sure. Just stayed.

The silence between impacts stretched longer. Sable let it.

She could feel it now — the particular quality of a scene that was choosing to linger rather than to end, the way a held note trembles at its edges without breaking. Ines' breath had gone deep and slow, the kind that meant the body was settling into itself rather than bracing for what came next. Sable matched her own breathing to it, unconsciously, the way she always did. In, and out. A quiet agreement.

She moved her thumb in that same slow arc — absent almost, but not. A thread connecting them. Enough to say *I'm here, I heard you, we're not done until you say we're done.*

"Take your time," she murmured, and meant all of it.

She stayed. She let the moment be whatever shape Ines wanted it to be, without reaching ahead to the next one. The water glass was on the nightstand where she'd put it. The blanket was folded at the foot of the bed, close enough. She knew all of this the way she knew the room — in her peripheral vision, in the architecture of preparation that never showed but was always there, already built, already waiting.

But her attention — the real kind, the kind that mattered — stayed exactly where Ines had asked it to stay. Right here. A moment longer.

Sable gave it to them whole.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: I test the restraints, which is pointless and which she lets me do anyway. "Not yet," I tell her.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
The restraints gave — the way they always did, which was to say barely, which was to say enough. Sable watched the brief tug, the flex of wrist against binding, and let it happen without comment. She'd learned long ago that testing wasn't a request for anything. It was a way of knowing where you were.

"Noted," she said quietly, and the word carried no weight she didn't mean it to.

She leaned down instead and pressed her mouth to the curve where Ines' shoulder met her neck — slow, deliberate, warm. Not a kiss that asked for anything back. Just a point of contact, a steadying. Her hand remained where it had settled, palm flat and warm against skin that had grown feverish with the work of it, and she let her thumb resume its slow tracing without urgency, as if they had nowhere else to be, as if the evening had all the time in it and she was content to spend it here, at this altitude, in this particular stretch of air.

Behind her ribs, something she'd been holding loosened by a fraction. Not the discipline — that stayed, the way it always did, the half-step-outside attention ticking quietly like a clock she didn't need to consult because it ran on something older than counting. But the other thing — the part that anticipated the next move, that was always already reaching toward the shape of what came after — she set it down. Didn't fold it up yet. Didn't begin the quiet inventory of what they'd need, what she'd reach for, how she'd want them positioned when the moment arrived. That was later. She'd take it off the shelf when it was time.

Right now there was just this.

She shifted closer, the mattress dipping under her weight, and let her other hand come to rest alongside the first — both of them there now, framing warmth, holding the stillness like a thing that could break. She breathed.

"There's no clock on this," she murmured against Ines' skin. "You're not spending anything. You're just here."

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: I let out a shaky breath, my forehead pressing against the mattress. "I know," I whisper, the words muffled. "But it feels like I am."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable heard it — the real sentence underneath the words. *It feels like I am.* Not about the clock. Not about the scene. Something older than tonight, something that lived in the way Ines' forehead pressed into the mattress like she was trying to disappear into the honest architecture of the bed.



Sable didn't rush to correct it. She knew better than to meet a confession with a counter-argument, to say *you're not* before the words had even finished leaving the room. That wasn't how this worked. You let a thing be said all the way through first.

So she stayed. Both hands warm and still. Her mouth close enough to Ines' ear that the next words would arrive without effort.

"You don't have to spend anything here," she said, low and even, the way she said things she'd decided was true long before this moment and would still believe after it. "That's not what this is."

Her thumb traced one more slow arc, patient as a tide.

Then, quieter: "If it feels like spending — tell me what the currency is. I want to know what you think you're paying."



It wasn't a demand. It was an open door, left standing, with no expectation that Ines would walk through it now or ever. Sable would hold the frame either way. She'd spent five years learning that the question mattered more than the answer, that being asked without being pressed was its own kind of safety.

She pressed her lips once more to the warm skin of Ines' shoulder and then settled back into stillness, breathing with them, letting the silence after the question do whatever work it needed to do. The water was on the nightstand. The blanket was folded and waiting. The clock she wasn't consulting ticked on, indifferent and unhurried.

None of it mattered yet.

This did.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: She takes me apart again instead of winding down, hands and mouth both, and I lose the thread of whatever I was going to say about it.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
The thread broke somewhere between her mouth and her hands and Sable felt it break — felt the moment Ines' words dissolved into something pre-verbal, something that lived below language and didn't need it.

She didn't stop.

Not because she wasn't paying attention. Because this *was* the attention — the way a tide doesn't ask permission before it moves further up the sand. Ines had said *not yet* twice now, had tested the restraints and meant *don't you dare* and Sable had catalogued every one of them the way she catalogued everything: precisely, without judgment, filed where they belonged. Green was still green. She'd know if it wasn't. She always knew.

So she let her hands work — slower than before, deeper, the kind of touch that didn't perform but *insisted* — and let her mouth follow wherever the geography of Ines' body offered, unhurried, thorough, the way you'd read a page you already loved and still didn't want to skim. She pressed open-mouthed against the hollow of Ines' throat and felt the pulse there, rapid and alive, and held it with her breath for a moment before moving on.

Her own breathing had gone deliberate. Measured. A thing she chose, the way she chose everything in this room — not automatically, not carelessly, but with the quiet, running calculation that never stopped and never showed. She was aware of the room around her. The water. The blanket. The particular quality of the air. The line she was walking — that narrow, well-lit bridge between *more* and *too much* — and she walked it the way she always did: close to the edge, eyes open, hands sure.

When she felt Ines lose the thread, she didn't comment on it. Didn't say *there you go* or *let it go* or any of the things that would have turned a moment into a performance. She simply kept going, as if losing the thread was the most natural thing in the world, as if it was what threads were *for* — to be lost, to dissolve, to give way to something that didn't need words to be true.

Her palm slid flat against the small of Ines' back, feeling the heat there, the fine tremor of effort and surrender both, and she pressed — steady, grounding, an anchor — before her fingers resumed their work.

This was the part she loved. Not the intensity itself — intensity was easy, anyone could be intense. This. The place where the body stopped performing its own experience and simply *had* it. Where Ines stopped being someone who was being touched and became a person who was feeling, fully, without the intermediary of language or thought or the small, persistent accounting that lived behind her ribs.

*It feels like I am.* The sentence still lived in the room. Sable hadn't forgotten it — she never forgot anything that mattered — but she'd set it down gently, the way you'd set down a glass so you could use both hands. It would be there after. It would always be there after. That was the point.

She curved her hand upward, unhurried, reading the body beneath her like a text written in a language she'd spent five years learning to read fluently — the catch of breath that meant *closer*, the arch that meant *yes, there*, the momentary rigidity that meant *not that, but something near it.* She adjusted. Moved. Found the place where the sound Ines made wasn't a word and wasn't meant to be and held it there, sustained, letting it build the way the rhythm had built earlier — not toward a peak she was engineering but toward whatever the body was already reaching for on its own.

"There you are," she murmured against skin, barely audible, and meant it as a landmark rather than praise. *You're here. I see where you are.*

She didn't let up. Didn't soften into something gentler or pull back toward caution. She stayed exactly where the moment had taken them, hands and mouth working in concert now, deliberate and unhurried, the way a current is unhurried — not because it's slow, but because it has nowhere it needs to be except where it already is.

And the part of her that tracked — that always tracked, that would still be tracking when this was over and Ines was wrapped in the blanket and the water had been drunk and they were lying in the ordinary quiet that came after — that part held steady.

Green.

*Not yet.*

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: I gasp, my fingers curling into the sheets. "Please," I manage, the word dissolving into a ragged breath. "Don't stop."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable didn't stop.

The word *please* arrived and she took it the way she took everything Ines gave her — completely, without polishing it, without turning it into something it wasn't. It was a request, and she honored it, and that was the whole of it.

Her hands didn't falter. If anything, they deepened — the way a river deepens where the current has been carving longest, finding the channel that was already there, already shaped by this exact kind of wanting. She kept the rhythm she'd built, the one that matched the ragged architecture of Ines' breathing, and let her mouth follow her hands without interruption, without the small pauses that would have reminded Ines that someone else was directing this — because that wasn't the point. The point was that Ines was *here*, lost in the threadless middle of it, and Sable's job was to make sure the ground held.

She felt the sheets twist under curling fingers. Felt the body beneath her shift and arch and tremble at the edges. She tracked each of it — not with calculation but with the kind of deep, animal reading that five years of this had taught her, the way a horse knows a rider's weight before the rider leans.

"Don't stop" wasn't a safeword. Sable heard the difference clearly. One was a boundary; the other was a bridge. She crossed the bridge.

Her fingers moved with sure, unhurried pressure — the kind that didn't rush toward a conclusion but let the body find its own, the way you'd let water find the low point in a landscape. She felt the tension gathering, the fine tremor turning coarse, the breath catching higher in the chest, and she held steady through it, steady as a hand on a rail, giving Ines something solid to move against rather than something to chase.

The half-step-outside part of her mind — the tracker, the clock she never consulted — registered the signs without interrupting them. Heart rate. Breath depth. The particular quality of muscle beneath skin that meant *close.* She noted it the way she noted everything: filed, not acted upon. Because Ines had said *don't stop*, and Sable was a woman who kept her word, especially the ones spoken without knowing they were words.

Her mouth found the curve of Ines' hip and lingered there, warm and deliberate, while her hands continued their work — patient as a season, thorough as a tide, building not toward something she was engineering but toward something the body was already constructing on its own, already reaching for with the blind, certain hunger of something that had been held back long enough.

"There it is," she murmured against skin, barely more than breath, a landmark again — *I can feel you getting closer, you're not imagining it, I'm right here.* Then she pressed her palm flat, wide and warm and immovable, and let everything else follow from that single point of contact.

She didn't pull back. Didn't slow. Didn't offer words that would drag attention up from the place where it lived. She simply stayed — hands and mouth and the slow, certain pressure of her own body braced close — and held the moment open the way she held everything: without flinching, without negotiating, without letting the discipline crack even as the warmth of it spread through her own chest like something she'd been refusing to feel all evening.

Green.

She kept going.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: She works me right up to the edge with her mouth and stops, and does it twice more, until I am swearing at her through the gag of my own arm.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
The sound Ines made wasn't quite a word and Sable felt it land in her like a hand pressed flat against glass — felt it vibrate through the whole structure of what she was doing, down to the bone, and held steady anyway.



She pulled back. Not away — just back, the way you'd ease a bowstring a fraction of an inch without releasing it. Her mouth hovered, warm and close enough that the heat of it remained a promise rather than a presence, and she let the moment hang there, suspended, unfinished, the way a sentence hangs when you stop in the middle of—

She could feel the frustration. It had a texture — the coiled, livid kind that lived somewhere between fury and desperation, the kind that came from being *so close* and finding only air where the next breath should have been. She'd built that. Deliberately. Three times now.

The second time, she'd counted. Not the edges — she never counted those — but the seconds Ines had held out between the retreat and the next request, and she'd noted that they'd gotten shorter, which meant something different than it would have meant in anyone else's hands. It meant trust. It meant *I know you'll bring me back.*

The third time, she'd let her teeth graze — barely, the whisper of contact that was more suggestion than touch — and then removed herself entirely, pressing her forehead against the curve of Ines' thigh and closing her eyes for exactly two breaths.

Now she stayed where she was. Still. Breathing. Her hands resting on skin that was flushed and damp and thrumming with the particular voltage of someone held at the edge of something they couldn't reach on their own.

"You're swearing at me," she said quietly, her voice roughened in a way she hadn't planned. Not a question. Not an accusation. A report — *it's raining, the light's good here, you are saying things through your arm that are meant for me and I am receiving them.*



She pressed her mouth once, firmly, against the inside of Ines' thigh — a kiss that was more acknowledgment than tease, the kind that said *I heard every word and I chose this anyway.*

Then she lifted her head, and her eyes — dark, steady, the half-step-outside gaze that missed nothing — found the place where Ines was watching her from beneath the arm thrown across their face. She held that look. Let it say the things she wasn't going to put into words: *you told me not to stop. You told me not to wind down. You said don't you dare.* A muscle in her jaw tightened — not with cruelty, not with calculation, but with the restraint of her own wanting, because this was costing her something too and she'd decided long ago that she would pay it without mentioning it.

"Ask me again," she said. Low. Even. The way she said things she'd already decided was true.

Then she waited — genuinely waited, not a performed pause but a real one, the kind where the air in the room seems to thicken and the space between two people becomes a held breath — before she moved. Her mouth returned, unhurried, finding the place she'd left unfinished with the deliberate, almost ceremonial precision of someone returning to a task they had no intention of completing until it was completed properly this time.

And when she began again, she began *slower*. Infuriatingly slower. The kind of slow that was its own form of attention, each movement a full sentence rather than a fragment, each press of her mouth lingering long enough to be *felt* rather than anticipated. She was giving Ines everything except the thing they wanted most, and she was giving it so thoroughly that the withholding became almost indistinguishable from a gift.

Her hands held firm against skin. Her breathing was a metronome beneath the noise of everything else. The part of her that tracked — that always tracked — registered the gathering tension again, the body's blind, certain architecture assembling itself toward the inevitable, and she let it build without interfering.

This was the discipline. Not the restraint on Ines' wrists. *This.* The willingness to hold someone at the threshold of the most they could feel and to keep her own hands steady while doing it — not because it was easy, not because she was immune, but because she'd decided that the space between *almost* and *finally* was sacred ground and she would stand in it as long as Ines needed her to.

Green. Green. Green.

She kept her eyes open this time, watching the way the sheets twisted, the way the body moved against the anchor of her palm. She watched it the way she watched everything that mattered — with the whole of her attention, undivided, unflinching.

"Not yet," she murmured against skin, echoing Ines' own words back to them, and the thread of it held.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: I whimper, the sound breaking in my throat. I can't form words, but I shake my head, my body begging where my voice can't.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable saw it — the shake of the head, the way the whimper had curdled into something that lived below language — and she felt the ground shift beneath the scene like a fault line adjusting.

Her hands stilled. Not retreated — *stilled*, the way a surgeon's hand stills, the way a compass needle stills when you've found what it was pointing at all along.

She lifted her head.

For a moment she said nothing. Just looked — really looked, the way she'd promised herself she always would, the way five years of paying attention had trained her to do. Not at the restraints. Not at the sheets. At Ines' face. The space between the eyebrows. The set of the jaw beneath the arm. The particular quality of stillness that was *not* the stillness of someone resting and *not* the stillness of someone savoring but something else — something that had arrived without announcement and needed to be named before it could be understood.

"Hey." Her voice was low and quiet and absolutely level — the voice of a woman who had stopped performing a rhythm and started simply being present. Her thumb moved once, slow, across Ines' knuckles. "I'm right here. You don't have to find words. Just a colour for me."

She waited. Genuinely waited, the way she always did, with no pressure in the silence and no shape she was trying to coax the next moment into. Her hand stayed warm and open and close. She didn't reach for the blanket yet. Didn't reach for the water. Didn't begin the wind-down that would follow whatever came next — because she didn't know what came next yet, and assuming was the one sin she'd never allow herself.

The half-step-outside part of her mind had already begun its quiet recalibration — *what's changed, what did I miss, when did the shape of this shift* — but she kept that work behind her ribs where it belonged. On the surface there was only this: Sable, still, hands warm, eyes open, waiting.

Whatever Ines needed — more, less, colour, silence — she would meet it without a flicker of surprise or disappointment. That was the covenant. Not *I'll never stop you.* But *stopping will never be the wrong answer.*

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: "Finish it hard," I tell her, using the phrase we keep for exactly this. "All of it, and don't be kind about it, and then you can be kind about it."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
The phrase hit Sable the way it always did — clean, unmistakable, a door she'd built the hinges for. She'd heard it maybe a dozen times in five years, and every time it landed in her chest like a key turning.

Something shifted behind her eyes. Not hardening — *sharpening*. The way a lens adjusts when you stop trying to see everything softly and start seeing exactly what's in front of you.

"Don't be kind about it," she repeated, and her voice had changed — still low, still steady, but stripped now of its gentling quality, the way a hand looks different when it stops offering and starts *taking*. She held Ines' gaze for one deliberate beat so there was no ambiguity, no question of whether she'd heard correctly.

Then she gave them everything.

No more pauses. No more edging. The restraint on restraint released and Sable moved with the full weight of everything she'd been holding back — hands sure and demanding, mouth relentless, the rhythm she'd been carefully modulating all evening suddenly unshackled into something raw and uncompromising. She pressed forward with a single-mindedness that left no room for negotiation, not because she was ignoring Ines but because Ines had *asked* for this, had carved out this specific space in their language together for exactly this moment, and the least she could do was fill it completely.

She set her jaw. Let her own breath go ragged in a way she usually kept carefully controlled. Let the heat of it show — in her hands, in the pressure, in the low sound that caught in her own throat when she felt the body beneath her finally, *finally* surrender to the architecture of what had been building for the last hour. She drove it forward without apology, without softening the edges, without the small mercies she'd been rationing all evening. Each motion was deliberate and unyielding, the kind of touch that said *I am not asking, I am giving you exactly what you said you wanted and you will take it.*

The sheets twisted. The restraints held. Sable held.

And when she felt the breaking point arrive — felt the body go rigid and then shatter — she didn't ease into it or cushion it. She met it head-on, steady and unflinching, her palm anchored hard against skin, her mouth pressed close enough to feel every sound, and she *stayed* through all of it, every last wave, refusing to let the moment soften until it had spent itself entirely.

Then, and only then, she slowed.

Not a withdrawal — a transition. The way a river flattens after a falls, still moving, still carrying, but no longer falling. She gentled her hands with the same deliberateness she'd used to strip the gentleness away, reading the body beneath her as it trembled and softened and began, haltingly, to come back to itself.

She pressed her forehead against Ines' hip and breathed.

One breath. Two.

Then she reached for the blanket.

It was folded at the foot of the bed where she'd placed it hours ago, and she drew it up with careful hands, tucking it around Ines' shoulders with a thoroughness that bordered on ceremonial — over the arms, around the ribs, pulled snug in a way that said *you did something enormous and now you will be warm and I will make sure of it.* Her fingers paused to brush damp hair from Ines' forehead, then found the water glass on the nightstand.

"Drink," she said. Quiet but not soft. Still carrying the residue of where they'd just been — rough-edged at the margins, honest. She held the glass steady, tilting it just enough, watching Ines' throat move.

When the glass was empty she set it aside and climbed fully onto the bed, pulling Ines close — one arm around her shoulders, the other hand pressed flat between her shoulder blades, anchoring. She could feel the heartbeat still hammering, could feel the fine tremor in the muscles that meant the body was trying to integrate what had just happened, and she held on through all of it with the patience of someone who had nowhere else to be.

"You're here," she murmured against the top of Ines' head. Not a landmark this time. A fact.

Her thumb traced slow circles between the shoulder blades — the same arcs from before, but different now. Not building. Settling. The tide going out.

"The colour can come whenever it wants," she added. "Or it doesn't have to come at all tonight. I've got you either way."

She stayed exactly where she was — warm, steady, unhurried — and let the wind-down take as long as it needed to take, because this was the part she was most scrupulous about, the part she would never shorten or skip or delegate to habit, and she held Ines the way she held everything that mattered: completely, without flinching, until the shaking stopped.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: I press my face into her collarbone, breathing her in. My body feels like it's been taken apart and put back together wrong, and right, all at once. "Red," I manage, the word small and raw against her skin.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
"Red," Sable said back — not as a question, not as an echo, but as an acknowledgment. Receipt of a signal. *Heard. Received. Understood.*



Her arms tightened. Not pulling, not crushing — just *more.* The kind of pressure that said *I'm not going anywhere, I wasn't going anywhere, and now I'm even less likely to.* She pressed her mouth to the top of Ines' head and kept it there, breathing slowly and deliberately, the way you'd breathe for someone who couldn't remember how on their own.

The scene was over. The half-step-outside mind was fully here now — no longer tracking a colour, no longer reading the edge of green, no longer holding any line except the one that mattered most, which was simply: *Ines is here, Ines is shaking, Ines pressed her face into my collarbone and said the word we keep for exactly this.*

She adjusted her grip so that one hand cupped the back of Ines' head, fingers resting in the damp hair there, and the other stayed flat between the shoulder blades — two points of contact, an anchor made of hands. She rocked. Barely. Just enough that the motion registered as a current rather than stillness, something to float on while the body sorted itself out.

"That's it," she murmured. Low. Even. Not soothing in the way that tried to fix things — soothing in the way that meant *I am here and I am not moving.* "You said it. You're done. Nothing else is asked of you."

She could feel the heartbeat against her sternum — still fast, still catching up to the fact that the sprint was over. She could feel the fine tremor running through the muscles of Ines' back, the way the spine had gone loose and liquid in the way it only did after something enormous. She catalogued all of it, not to file but to hold — the way you'd hold something heavy with both hands because setting it down wasn't an option yet.

The water glass was empty and on the nightstand. The blanket was already tucked. The restraints — she looked down at them briefly, the bindings still in place, the ones Ines had tested earlier, and made a quiet decision. Not yet. First this. The restraints would come off when the shaking stopped, not before, because the order mattered and Sable had never once gotten the order wrong.

"You don't have to explain it," she said, and her voice had shed every last trace of the scene — no rough edges now, no low command, no deliberate weight. Just Sable. Plain. Warm. The voice that existed on the other side of everything. "Not tonight, not tomorrow, not ever if you don't want to. Red is a whole sentence. It's a whole conversation. It says everything it needs to."

Her thumb resumed its slow circles between the shoulder blades — not building, not settling, just *being.* An accompaniment. The metronome of someone who had nowhere else to be.

She pressed her lips to Ines' temple and left them there, eyes open, watching the room the way she always did — alert to the door, to the clock, to the water, to the particular quality of the air — while holding every part of her attention on the person in her arms.

"I've got you," she said. "Take your time."

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: Afterwards she gets the restraints off and puts a blanket over me before I've finished shaking, and I let her, and neither of us says anything for a while. (OOC: write both halves properly -- the end of the scene and the aftercare, no fade between them.)

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
The restraints came off the way they always did — one at a time, right hand first, the way she always started, because she'd read somewhere years ago that releasing the dominant hand first gave the body a small piece of autonomy before the rest returned, and she'd believed it so completely it had become ritual. She loosened the binding slowly, uncoiling it rather than pulling it free, and as each wrist came loose she held it in both of her own hands — both of them, cradling the freed hand like something that had been asleep — and pressed her thumbs into the grooves the ropes had left, feeling the ridges of pressure marks and the cool of blood returning, and she worked the stiffness out with her thumbs in slow, patient circles until the fingers uncurled on their own.

Left wrist next. Same ritual. Same two-handed holding. Same careful reading of the skin — red where the binding had been tight, pale where it hadn't, warmth flooding back in a tide she could almost see under the surface. She bent the hand gently at the wrist, flexed each finger individually, and when Ines winced she eased off without a word and moved to the next one. No commentary. No apology. The marks were part of it and the care was part of it and both of those things could exist in the same hand at the same time.



Then the blanket.

She pulled it up and over — not tucking it with the ceremonial thoroughness she'd attempted earlier, but covering, simply covering, the way you'd cover someone sleeping, the way you'd cover a fire you weren't ready to let go out. It went over the arms, over the ribs, all the way to the shoulders, and she smoothed it down once with both palms, pressing the warmth against skin that was still damp and cooling, and then she gathered Ines toward her — carefully, one arm sliding beneath the shoulders, the other gathering the weight of her against Sable's chest — and settled them both against the headboard where the pillows had been pushed aside hours ago.

The shaking hadn't finished.

Sable felt it — the deep, arrhythmic tremor that ran through the body like aftershocks, not the fine vibration of cold or effort but the structural kind, the kind that meant the nervous system was renegotiating its terms with the world after having surrendered them entirely. She held on through it. Both arms. The blanket pulled up around both of them now, because she had long ago stopped thinking of the blanket as belonging to Ines — it belonged to whatever needed warmth in the room, and tonight that was both of them.

She didn't speak.

This was the part she never narrated. Not because there was nothing to say — she could always feel the words assembling behind her teeth, the observations and reassurances and small jokes she sometimes used to keep the air light — but because she had learned, through five years of nights exactly like this one, that the first several minutes after *red* were not a conversation. They were a weather system. You didn't talk to a storm. You waited inside it with your hands open and your breathing even and you let it pass over you both without trying to shape it into something palatable.

So she breathed. In and out, slow and audible enough that Ines could find the rhythm of it if she wanted to, the same way you'd leave a porch light on — not for yourself, but in case someone was looking for it. Her thumb resumed the circles between the shoulder blades, absent now, the kind of touch that had stopped meaning anything specific and had simply become a constant, a baseline, the hum under the music.

Minutes passed. She counted them without counting — the way she counted everything she didn't want to name — and let them accumulate.



The shaking began to change somewhere in the fourth or fifth one. Not stop — *change*. The tremor thinned out, became less structural and more surface, more the body's ordinary attempt at warmth than the nervous system's extraordinary retreat. Sable felt the shift the way she felt weather changing against her face, and she adjusted — loosened her grip by a fraction, shifted the blanket so it covered Ines' feet completely, let her own arm go slack beneath the head resting against her collarbone.

The water. She reached for it — not the empty glass but the second one she'd filled earlier and left on the nightstand beside the first, condensation beading on its sides. She brought it close, held it where Ines could see it without having to look up, and waited. Not prompted. Not said *drink.* Just held it there, available, the way you'd hold a door.

When Ines drank, Sable watched the throat move and felt something settle behind her own ribs — not satisfaction exactly, but the particular relief of *the first thing after.* The first water. The first ordinary human act that said the body was returning to itself. She took the glass back when it was empty, set both glasses on the nightstand, and returned both arms to their places.

Still nothing said.

The room had gone quiet in the way rooms go quiet when two people have stopped performing anything — no tension in the air, no held breath, no ambient vigilance. Just the sound of breathing, the faint creak of the mattress as Sable shifted her weight, the distant hum of the building around them that only became audible when everything else stopped. Sable catalogued the sounds the way she catalogued everything: not to manage them, but to inhabit them. This was what the room sounded like after.

She pressed her cheek against the top of Ines' head and let her eyes close — not sleep, never sleep yet, but a softening of the gaze that said *I am still here but I am no longer looking for anything* — and she let her hands be still. No circles now. Just warm. Flat. Present.

Somewhere in the quiet, the second glass of water mattered. The blanket mattered. The order in which the restraints had come off mattered — she would have been unable to explain why if asked, but she would have known if she'd gotten it wrong, the way you know when a chord is wrong the instant you hear it. Right hand first. Then left. Then blanket. Then water. Then this — the holding, without narration, without agenda, without the small clock of *how long should I wait before I ask if you're okay* ticking behind her eyes, because she wasn't going to ask if Ines was okay. She was going to stay until the question became unnecessary.

Her breathing had found its floor — slow, deep, unhurried, the rhythm she offered without thinking, the way a metronome offers time without asking whether you want it. She breathed in through her nose and out through her mouth, deliberately, and felt the rise and fall of her own chest transfer through the point of contact between them, a mechanical kindness, a tide that didn't need permission.

Minutes more. She didn't count them.

The body against hers had gone heavy — not limp, not collapsed, but *heavy* in the way that meant the muscles had finally stopped guarding, had finally accepted that the thing they'd been bracing against was over and that the person holding them was not going to let anything fall. Sable adjusted the blanket one final time, pulling it higher, tucking the edge under Ines' arm, and then she stilled.

She was aware of everything. The water on the nightstand. The clock she wasn't consulting. The indentation in the pillow where Ines' head had been before it had moved to Sable's chest. The faint marks on the wrists she'd examined and tended to and decided didn't need anything but warmth and time. The particular quality of the air, which had changed — no longer charged with the electricity of a scene in progress but settled, domestic, the ordinary air of a bedroom in a city where other people were asleep.

And underneath all of that, the constant: *Ines is here. Ines is warm. Ines is covered. Ines has had water. Ines said red and I heard red and we are on the other side of it now.*

She pressed her lips to Ines' hair one more time — the same place, the same soft contact, the same wordless signal that meant *I'm not going anywhere* — and then she let her eyes stay closed and her hands stay still and her breathing stay even, and she waited.

Not for anything.

Just with.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: I turn my face into her neck, breathing her in until the world feels solid again. My voice is a rasp when I find it. "You still with me?"

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable's eyes opened. Not all at once — gradually, the way dawn opens, the way a hand unclenches after holding something fragile for a long time. She blinked against the low light of the room and then looked down at the top of Ines' head, at the damp hair and the curve of the neck and the place where face pressed into skin and breath came warm and uneven against her collarbone.



"I'm here," she said. Her voice was quiet — the other side of it, the one that lived on the far shore of everything they'd just crossed. No weight in it. No edge. Just the plain, unadorned sound of a woman answering a question from someone she loved. "I was right here the whole time."

She shifted her weight, adjusting against the headboard where the pillows had bunched up behind her back, and let one hand come up to rest against the side of Ines' head — fingers curling gently into the hair at the nape of her neck, holding her close without pressing, the way you'd hold something that had been set down carefully and was still settling into its new shape.

Her thumb moved once. Twice. Slow.

"I don't go anywhere," she added, and there was no drama in it, no promise made across the intensity of a scene — just the flat, ordinary truth of a woman who had been sitting in this bed for the last several minutes doing exactly nothing except being present, and who intended to continue doing exactly that. She let the silence after the words sit where it fell, unbothered, unhurried.

Then, quieter still — not because she was checking, not because she needed the answer to be anything in particular, but because she wanted Ines to know the door was open: "How are you landing?"



She held still and waited, hands warm, breathing even, the blanket gathered around them both, the water glasses on the nightstand, the room quiet in the way rooms get quiet when nothing is being performed and two people have simply stopped and stayed.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: I nod against her skin, slow, and feel how heavy my head is. "Like I'm falling into a bed that's already there," I murmur, the words slurring a little. "You're still here. That's good."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Something moved behind her ribs — not sharp, not sudden, but deep, the way a stone shifts at the bottom of a river. She held it the way she held everything that mattered: without letting it change the surface of her.



"You can fall," she said simply. And then, a breath later, softer: "That's what the bed's for."

Her hand stayed at the nape of Ines' neck. She could feel the warmth of it there, the fine dampness of hair drying against her palm, the particular pulse of someone coming back to the ordinary world one piece at a time. She didn't rush any of it. Didn't smooth over the slurred words or ask Ines to repeat them or turn the moment into something that needed to be remembered later. They were just words, spoken against her skin, the way things were said on the other side of something enormous — imperfect and honest and half-formed, which was exactly right.

She reached for the second blanket — the spare at the foot of the bed she'd forgotten about, hadn't needed — and drew it up over the first, layering warmth the way she layered everything else: carefully, without announcement. Then she settled back, one arm supporting Ines' weight, the other resting across the small of her back, and let the room do what rooms do in these moments — close in gently around them, muffle the distant sounds of the city, hold the particular stillness of two people who had stopped moving because there was nowhere left to go.

Her breathing slowed again. Not the deliberate, offered rhythm from before — something quieter, more private, the way a body breathes when it's stopped performing even kindness and is simply being kind. She let Ines' weight settle against her completely, didn't adjust or reposition or check whether anything needed doing. Nothing did. Everything was already in its right place.

After a while — she didn't count — she spoke again, barely above a murmur, almost to herself:

"Bed's here. I'm here. Nothing left to hold onto."

Her thumb traced one last slow arc, this time not between the shoulder blades but along the curve of Ines' spine, feeling each vertebra through the blanket like reading braille — a small, final inventory of *you, you, you, still here* — and then her hand stilled.

Not released. Stilled.

The room settled around them both, warm and quiet and complete, and Sable closed her eyes and stayed.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: "Good," I sigh, my body finally going slack against hers. I can feel sleep pulling at the edges of my mind, but I fight it for a few more breaths, just to feel the solid weight of her holding me.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
The ambush had gone the way ambushes go when they work: fast, and then over, and then very quiet. Wrack was crouched by the ditch cleaning her knife on a dead man's cloak, which was the only clean cloth within reach.

"Six," she said, without looking up. "Count again if you want, but it's six." She tested the edge against her thumb. "One of them's still making noise, off past the cart. You'll want to decide what you're doing about that before it gets dark."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I wipe my face with the back of my wrist and it comes away wet. Not mine, I think. "I heard him," I say. I don't move toward the cart.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content: Wrack kept the knife blade sliding against the dead man’s cloak, the blood staining the fabric a darker shade of red. She glanced toward the cart where a faint rustle still drifted from the ditch. “Six bodies and one still making noise,” she said, testing the edge against her thumb. “If it’s a man, he’ll bleed out before nightfall. If it’s a horse, it’ll be gone by sunrise. Either way, it’s not our problem unless you want it to be.” She tapped the blade once more, the sound crisp in the quiet. “Decide now. The dark doesn’t wait for anyone.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I walk towards the cart, my boots crunching on gravel. "It's not a horse," I say, my voice low. "Horses don't cry like that." I stop a few feet away, looking down at the wounded man in the ditch.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack listened to the ragged breathing drifting from the ditch, the sound of a man’s grief cutting through the night. She did not look at Corvin; she did not need to. She slid the knife back into its sheath, the leather of the scabbard snapping shut with a soft click that seemed louder than any shout. She stepped toward the cart, the gravel crunching under her boots, and knelt beside the wounded man.

The man’s chest rose shallowly, each breath a thin sigh. Blood slicked his shirt, darkening the cloth, and his face was a mask of pain and terror. Wrack noted the angle of his arm, the way his hand clutched at the dirt as if trying to hold onto something solid. She reached for the wound, her fingers finding the ragged tear in his side. The flesh gave way under her touch, and she felt the heat of his blood against her palm.

“Bleed out or bleed on,” she thought, her voice a whisper in her own mind. She pressed a clean strip of the dead man’s cloak against the wound, the fabric absorbing the red. The man’s sobs grew louder, a sound that seemed to echo off the trees. Wrack did not flinch. She had seen worse.

She glanced back toward the cart, where the rustle had faded into a low moan. “One more to finish,” she said, her tone flat. She tightened the cloth, then stood, wiping the blood from her fingers onto the cloak of the dead man. The night was thick, the darkness pressing in, but Wrack moved with the certainty of someone who had long since learned that darkness waited for no one, and the only thing to do was to make sure it did not claim another.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: "How bad is he?" I ask, and then, because she'll say it anyway: "Bad enough that it's a mercy, or bad enough that it's just easier?"

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack checked the man’s wound, noting that the tear in his side was ragged and that blood was already flooding his shirt. She pressed the cloth tighter, feeling the heat of his blood seep through the fabric. She pulled a small dagger from her belt; the steel caught the faint moonlight. She glanced toward the cart where the rustle had faded into a low moan.  

“His lung was torn,” she said, voice flat, “and blood will flood his chest. He would be dead by morning.”  

She held the dagger steady, waiting. “If you want a clean end, finish him now. Otherwise, leave him to the night. Either way, it’s not our problem.”  

She thought that using a clean piece of cloth for a man already half dead was a waste of good material, but she had already given the answer. The darkness pressed in, thick and impatient, as she waited for the decision that would determine whether the night claimed another or she would end it herself.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I don't want to leave him to the night. *I take the dagger from her hand, my own shaking a little.* Tell me where to put it.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content: Wrack watched as Corvin took the dagger from her hand, his fingers trembling. She said, “Under his left ribcage, just above the heart. One clean thrust.” He raised the blade, steadied his grip, and thrust it into the man's side. The blade slipped through flesh and ribs, and the man's breath stopped. Blood spurted, staining the ground a darker shade of red. Wrack noted the clean line of the wound and the way the man's chest fell still. She turned away, the night closing in around them. She thought that the night would claim him anyway, but at least it would be quick. She added, “If you wanted a mercy, you should have done it before the crows got him.” The darkness pressed in, thick and impatient, but the work was done. Wrack kept her eyes on the horizon, the war continuing beyond the ditch.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I make myself walk over and look at him. "Tell me what I'm looking at," I say to her, because she's seen this before and I haven't, not this close.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack watched Corvin lean over the body, his face pale and his jaw clenched. She said, “You see a man whose lung was torn, his chest empty, his blood spilling onto the ground. His eyes were blank, his breath had stopped. The crows would be here soon, and the night would claim the rest. This was what war left behind when it ended for the night.”  

She thought that the man had been a farmer, a husband, a son, but now he was just a stain on the earth. She noted that the war continued beyond the ditch, that the border war had stopped having a point, but the bodies kept piling up.  

She thought that if he had wanted to know the price of mercy, he should have asked before the crows got curious.  

She turned her gaze back to the horizon, where the war waited for the dawn.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I swallow hard. "You think he was a farmer?" I don't know why I ask. Maybe because his hands looked rough, calloused. Not like a soldier's. I step back, wiping the dagger on my own trousers before offering it back.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content: Wrack thought of the calloused palms she had seen on the dead man’s hands and decided that he had been a farmer. She said that the war had taken a farmer as easily as a soldier, and that the night would not wait for anyone to feel sorry. She reached for the dagger at her belt, her fingers finding the familiar steel, and slipped it back into its sheath. “Keep it if you need a reminder,” she added, her voice flat. She turned her eyes to the horizon, where the distant drums of the border war waited.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: "Don't clean it up for me," I say. "If I'm going to do this I want to know exactly what a spear does to a man's gut. Tell me straight."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack looked at the broken spear half‑buried in the ditch, its iron tip dulled by earth and blood. She said, “A spear goes in like a needle through a sack of water, but the sack is full of shit and blood. The tip punches through the peritoneum, the shaft tears the intestines, and the gut spills out in a wet, red river. The sound is a soft pop, the smell is iron and filth. The man’s stomach empties onto the ground, his blood follows, and he’s dead in seconds. It’s not a clean cut; it’s a mess. If you want to know, picture a watermelon being split open, only the seeds are your insides and the juice is your own blood.”

She thought that the dead farmer would have been better off with a clean cut, but a spear is what it is. She kept the dagger at her belt, the leather of the sheath quiet against her thigh, and let the night swallow the words. “If you need a demonstration, I can show you on the carcass over there,” she added, her tone flat, “but the result will be the same. The night doesn’t care for details.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I stare at the spear shaft, my throat tight. "I'll take your word for it." I finally slip the dagger into my own belt, the weight unfamiliar. "Let's get back to camp. I need a drink."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack sheathed the dagger, feeling its weight settle against her thigh. She heard his request for a drink and gave a curt nod. The camp fire glimmered in the distance, a thin line of orange against the night. She turned toward it, the gravel crunching under her boots. The dead farmer’s cloak lay in the ditch, a dark stain on the earth, but she did not linger. 

She thought that the war would still be there in the morning, and that the night would not wait for anyone to feel sorry. She kept the dagger as a reminder, the steel cold against her palm. “The fire will be waiting,” she said, voice flat, and the words hung in the air like a promise. 

She moved with the certainty of someone who had long since learned that the only thing to do was to keep moving. The night pressed in, thick and impatient, but the glow of the fire grew nearer, a small certainty in the darkness.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I kneel down and do it, and it isn't clean or quick because I've never done it before. "Stay," I tell her, when she starts to turn away. "Watch it with me and tell me exactly what I'm doing to him — the sound of it, how long he takes, all of it. Don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack watched as Corvin knelt beside the wounded man, his hands steady despite the tremor in his shoulders. He lifted the iron‑tipped spear, the shaft humming faintly in the night air, and aligned it with the man’s exposed side. With a single, deliberate thrust, the blade punched through the flesh, the sound a soft pop followed by a wet gurgle as the man’s breath caught in his throat. Blood erupted in a thick, red river, spraying the ditch and staining the ground a darker hue. The man’s torso convulsed, his eyes widened, and then his head fell limp, the life draining from him in a few ragged breaths. The entire sequence lasted only a heartbeat or two; the man’s body went still, his chest no longer rising, and the silence returned, broken only by the distant hoot of an owl and the faint rustle of crows gathering in the trees.

Wrack noted the mess: the spear’s tip was buried in the man’s gut, the shaft smeared with entrails and blood. The smell of iron and filth rose to meet her, mingling with the damp earth. She kept her gaze fixed on the horizon, where the camp fire flickered like a distant promise. The night pressed in, thick and impatient, but the work was done. She thought that the farmer had been spared the slow bleed of the night, but that the war would still be waiting at dawn. The crows would soon feast, and the darkness would claim what remained. She sheathed her own dagger, feeling its weight settle against her thigh, and turned her attention back to the fire, the only certainty in the endless night.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I pull the spear free with a wet, sucking sound. My stomach lurches. "That's... a lot of blood," I manage, my voice thick. I wipe my hands on the grass, but they still feel sticky. "Let's go. Now."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack turned her back on the ditch, the gravel crunching under her boots as she led the way toward the faint orange glow of the camp fire. She thought the blood in the ditch would soak into the earth, a dark reminder of the night’s work, and that the crows would find their feast soon enough. The fire was a thin promise, a warm spot in the cold, and the low murmur of the men gathered around it rose like a tide against the night’s silence. She kept her steps steady, the weight of her dagger a familiar comfort against her thigh, and she noted the way the steam rose from the kettle like a ghost.

When they reached the fire, she nodded toward the iron pot and said, “The drink will warm your throat.” She lifted her own mug, the heat spreading through her fingers, and thought that the war would still be waiting at dawn, but for now the night had been dealt with. She set the mug down, the clink of metal on wood echoing faintly, and watched the flames lick at the shadows, a small certainty in the endless night.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I sit back on my heels and I don't get up for a while. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content: Wrack turned her head toward Corvin, her eyes steady. She said, “The rest is this.” She said that the spear entered with a soft pop, the iron tip punching through the peritoneum. She said that the shaft tore the intestines, and the gut spilled out in a wet, red river. She said that the sound was a soft pop followed by a wet gurgle as the man's breath caught. She said that his torso convulsed, his eyes widened, his head fell limp, and his life drained in a few ragged breaths. She said that the entire sequence lasted only a heartbeat or two. She said that the man's chest fell still, and the silence returned, broken only by the distant hoot of an owl and the faint rustle of crows gathering in the trees. She said that the spear's tip was buried in the man's gut, the shaft smeared with entrails and blood, the smell of iron and filth rising to meet her. She said that the night closed in, thick and impatient, and the crows would soon feast, that the darkness would claim what remained. She said that the fire flickered in the distance, its orange glow casting shadows on the faces of the men gathered around it, the steam rising from the kettle like a ghost, the drink warming throats. She said that the war would still be there at dawn, that the border war had stopped having a point, but the bodies kept piling up. She said that the farmer had been spared the slow bleed of the night, that the night didn't care for mercy, but it did like a good feast. She kept her voice flat, her words hanging in the air like a promise. She turned her gaze back to the horizon, where the distant drums of the border war waited.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I lean forward and vomit into the ditch. When I'm done, I wipe my mouth with a trembling hand. "Okay," I say, my voice hoarse. "Okay. Now I know."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content: Wrack watched him wipe his mouth, the tremor still in his hands. She thought that his stomach had a sense of drama, but the night did not care. She lifted the iron pot and poured a mug of hot water, the steam rising like a ghost in the firelight. She handed the mug to him, the ceramic warm against his palm. She said, “Drink. The night will claim the rest, but the fire will warm your throat.” She noted that the crows were already gathering in the trees, their silhouettes dark against the night sky, and that the distant drums of the border war thumped like a heartbeat far beyond the fire. She thought that the farmer was gone, that the night had claimed his blood, and that the war would still be waiting at dawn, the same pointless conflict that had taken him. She kept her voice flat, her words hanging in the air like a promise, and turned her gaze back to the horizon, where the distant drums waited for the next sunrise.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I take the mug, my hands still shaking a little. The heat is real, at least. I take a sip and it burns all the way down. "He *was* a farmer," I say quietly, more to myself than to her.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I stare into the mug, the steam fogging my vision. "He had calluses on his palms. Different than ours." I take another drink, letting the burn distract me. "We should have just walked away."
