dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
They were most of the way through and both of them knew it, in the way you know a piece of music is nearly over before it ends.

"Colour," Sable said, because she always did, at exactly this point.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: "Green," I say, and mean it. "Don't you dare wind down yet."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
A sound left Sable's throat — low, rough, half a laugh and half something hungrier. Green. Not just green but *don't you dare*. Five years and Ines could still surprise her.

She hadn't been winding down. She'd been asking. There was a difference and Ines knew it, and the fact that Ines was already pushing at the edges of the negotiation told Sable exactly where they were — the good place, the bright place, where the body starts making promises the mouth can't keep.

"Wasn't planning on it," Sable said. Her voice had gone quiet in the way it did near the end of things, stripped back to essentials. She shifted her weight, adjusted the line of her shoulder, and let the next stroke land with the kind of precision that came from an hour of listening to every sound Ines made. Not harder. *Closer*. The place just past the one before.

Her free hand found the back of Ines's neck and stayed there — steady, warm, grounding. An anchor point. The check-in had been answered and the answer was *more*, and Sable would give more, but she would do it with her hand on the place where she could feel the pulse and the breath and the exact moment the edge arrived.

"Three more," she said. Not a question. A shape for the rest of the music to fall into.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: I gasp, arching into the touch. "Three," I agree, my voice already fraying. "Make them count."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
"Always do," Sable murmured, and the first of the three landed before the words had fully left her.

She watched the way Ines's spine answered — not the flinch of the beginning but the whole-body reception of someone deep enough to take the impact as information rather than noise. Her hand stayed on the back of Ines's neck, feeling the breath catch and stutter and reassemble. *That's one.* She counted them the way she counted everything in this room: quietly, precisely, keeping the ledger herself so Ines didn't have to.

A pause. Long enough to become its own thing. The room had gone almost silent except for breathing.

The second one she gave to the place just below the first, a deliberate conversation between two points on the body, and the sound Ines made told her she'd chosen well. Not harder. She'd meant what she'd said — *closer*. Precision was its own kind of intensity and Ines had always known that, had always preferred the stroke that landed exactly where the body was waiting to the one that simply arrived with force.

Sable felt the edge. It was there in the quality of the breath under her palm, in the fine tremor starting to live in Ines's shoulders, in the particular silence that meant the next thing would be too much of a different kind of too much.

"One more," she said, low. "Stay with me."

She made the third one the way she made the last note of anything — full, deliberate, and over before you could brace against it. Clean. Final. The kind of ending that lets the body understand that it's an ending.

Then her hand moved from the back of Ines's neck to her shoulder, and the other hand was already setting down what it had been holding, and the whole shape of Sable's body changed. The lean of it. The weight. Everything that had been focused outward into controlled force came back inward into care.

"There," Sable said. Just that. Just *there*. The word that meant *it's done, and you did well, and I'm right here*.

She reached — without moving away, one hand always somewhere on Ines's skin now — for the water she'd put within reach before they'd started. She always put it within reach before they started. Five years and she had never once been caught without it.

"Small sips," she said, her voice entirely different now. Still quiet, but the quiet of a warm room rather than the quiet of held breath. She held the bottle where Ines could reach it without having to move more than was comfortable. "And then I want a real colour. Not the one from before. The one for right now."

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: I test the restraints, which is pointless and which she lets me do anyway. "Not yet," I tell her.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable felt the shift of muscle and tendon under her palm as Ines tested the restraints, and she let it happen. She always let it happen. It wasn't defiance — or it wasn't only defiance — it was the body confirming its own edges, the way you press your tongue against a new tooth. And Sable had learned, somewhere around year two, that pulling the restraints away too fast was its own kind of cruelty. The ending needed to be *negotiated* just like everything else.

But *not yet* wasn't a colour.

She let that sit for exactly as long as it needed to. Her thumb traced a slow, small circle on Ines's shoulder — not a demand, not a distraction, just a point of contact that said *I'm still here and I'm still listening*.

"I hear you," Sable said. "And you can stay right where you are. I'm not going to move you and I'm not going to rush you."

She shifted, settling closer rather than pulling away, the warmth of her body a deliberate counterweight to the cooling air on Ines's skin. She'd grab the blanket in a moment. It was folded where it always was. But first.

"But I did ask for a colour, and I meant the asking." Her voice stayed in that warm register, but there was a thread of something underneath it — not sternness, exactly. *Structure*. The same structure that had been there in *three more*. The thing that held the whole evening up. "Not yet is a thing you want, and I'm listening to it. But it's not how I know how you're doing, and how you're doing is the thing I actually need right now."

Her hand moved from Ines's shoulder to the curve of her jaw, tilting nothing, asking nothing, just resting there with the pads of her fingers against the place where she could feel the pulse if she pressed gently.

"So. Colour. And then whatever you want next — the restraints stay as long as you need them to."

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: My breath hitches, a sharp contrast to her steady touch. "Gold," I manage, the word coming out unsteady but clear. "It's all...gold."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Something in Sable's chest unlocked. Not the structure — the structure stayed, because the structure was what made it possible for Ines to go somewhere that produced words like *gold* and still come back. But underneath it, a softening. Gold. Not green. Green was *I'm fine, continue*. Gold was the word Ines had for the place past fine, the place where the evening had done what it was supposed to do and the body was full of light and the edges between things had gone soft in the best way.

She knew that word. She'd heard it four, maybe five times in five years. She did not take it lightly.

"Yeah," Sable said, and her voice had gone rough again, but differently — not hunger now, something closer to reverence, though she'd have called it something smaller if you'd asked her. "Yeah, it is."

She let the moment have its full length. Her fingers stayed against Ines's jaw, feeling the pulse — quick, elevated, but even. Good. The tremor in Ines's shoulders was still there, the fine kind, the aftershock kind. Sable reached for the blanket without breaking contact and drew it up and over, tucking the edge along Ines's spine where the skin was cooling fastest. Warmth first. Warmth was always next.

"Small sips whenever you're ready," she said again, settling the bottle closer this time, within easy reach. "No rush on that either. But you will drink before I take the restraints off, and you know why."

She did know why. Sable had explained it once, early on, in the careful conversation where they'd built all of this: *the drop is real and hydration is the cheapest defence we have*. Ines had teased her for sounding like a first-aid manual. Sable had not changed the policy.

Her hand moved from Ines's jaw to her hair, slow, unhurried, the kind of touch that had no destination. "Gold," she said again, quieter, turning the word over. Letting Ines hear that she'd filed it somewhere important. "Tell me about it when you're ready. Not now. Now you just stay right there and let it be gold."

She stayed close. One hand in Ines's hair, the other resting warm against the nape of her neck, and her own breathing deliberately slow — because bodies borrow rhythms from each other, and Sable had learned that her calm was a tool as much as anything else she'd picked up tonight.

The room was quiet. Somewhere outside, a car passed and was gone. Sable didn't fill the silence. She'd been listening to Ines all evening; now she listened to the quiet that came after, which was its own kind of music, and which deserved the same attention as everything before it.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: She takes me apart again instead of winding down, hands and mouth both, and I lose the thread of whatever I was going to say about it.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable felt the exact moment Ines's sentence dissolved and she filed that too — the way the voice went, the way the thought couldn't hold. *Gold* did that. It made language porous. She'd seen it before and it still undid her a little, every time.

She hadn't been planning this. Or — no. She'd been planning the wind-down. The water, the blanket, the slow return. She'd been *good*, she'd done everything right, and then Ines had said *not yet* and *gold* in the same breath and Sable had looked at the map of the evening and understood that the music wasn't over after all. There was a coda. There was something underneath the ending that wanted to be heard first.

So she'd set the water down within reach — still within reach, always within reach — and she'd pulled the blanket back just enough to find skin, and she'd gone in.

Not the same way. Not the way from before. The impact had been a conversation held at a distance, precise and structured, each stroke a sentence. This was closer to murmuring against someone's mouth. Her hands learned the geography of Ines's body the way she'd learned it five years ago and every year since — slowly at first, then with the kind of certainty that only repetition and attention could build. She knew where the skin was thinnest and where the muscle held tension longest and where the breath caught if she pressed with exactly the right weight of her thumb.

Her mouth followed where her hands had been, and she took her time with it. Not teasing — Sable didn't tease, not really; teasing implied withholding and she was interested in *giving*, in flooding the channel until there was no room left for anything but sensation. She worked in slow, deliberate increments, reading the body under her hands the way she'd been reading it all evening: the hitch of breath, the shift of hips, the sound that lived in the throat before it became a sound.

She kept one hand anchored. Always one hand anchored. It rested against Ines's sternum now, feeling the heartbeat from the inside — fast, insistent, the pulse of someone deep in the bright place where the body runs ahead of everything else. That was the hand that would know before Ines's mouth did if things were tipping somewhere else.

"Stay here," she said against Ines's skin, not because she thought Ines was leaving but because the words were a thread to follow back. "You don't have to say anything. You don't have to hold onto anything. That's what I'm for right now."

She meant it the way she meant everything in this room — structurally. *I'll hold the shape. You just be in it.*

Her hands moved lower and she found the rhythm again, different from before but built on the same principle: listen, adjust, give what the body is asking for before the mouth can. She could feel the tremor rebuilding in Ines's shoulders, could feel the breath going ragged in a way that had nothing to do with impact and everything to do with the slow, relentless accumulation of sensation on a body already open and lit from within.

Sable watched. She always watched. The flush along Ines's collarbones. The way the fingers curled and uncurled against the restraints — not testing them now, just *holding* them, using them as something to grip against the tide. The way the head fell back or turned to the side. Every piece of it was information and Sable gathered all of it, adjusted her pressure and her pace by fractions, and kept going.

"I've got you," she said, low and close, her mouth near Ines's ear now, her body a long warm line along Ines's side. "Let go of whatever you're still holding. I'll keep track."

And she would. That was the promise underneath all of it — underneath the restraint and the impact and the water and the blanket and this, whatever this was, this last movement of the piece. Sable would keep track. Sable would know where they were and how far they'd gone and what Ines needed on the other side of it. That was the whole architecture of the thing. That was why Ines could say *gold* and mean it and then say *not yet* and mean that too, because someone in this room was paying attention with everything she had.

Her mouth found the hollow of Ines's throat and stayed there for a moment, feeling the swallow and the pulse and the shudder that ran through the whole length of the body beneath her hands.

"Almost," she said. Not a question. Not a command. A *reading*. The same way she'd said *three more*. A shape for the rest of the music to fall into.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: A sound leaves my throat that isn't a word at all, just a raw, helpless noise. My fingers twist in the restraints, holding on like they're the only thing keeping me from floating away. "Almost is a lie," I gasp, the accusation breathless.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable's mouth curved against Ines's throat. Not a laugh — she wasn't laughing at anything — but the shape of one, the way a hand tightens on something it loves.

"Fair," she murmured, and the word moved against skin.

Because it was. She'd said *almost* the way you hold a note slightly longer than written — to shape it, to make the arrival feel like an arrival. But Ines was past shaping. Ines was at the place where the body had outrun every word Sable had ever taught it, and the sound that had come out of her throat — that raw, unmade noise — was the truest reading of the room Sable had heard all night.

So Sable stopped narrating. She stopped giving the music a shape to fall into, because Ines didn't need one anymore. Ines was already falling.

Her hand moved with the kind of certainty that had nothing to do with technique and everything to do with five years of learning exactly what this particular body was asking for when it couldn't ask. She pressed closer, closer, the pressure and the rhythm converging on a single point the way light converges through glass. Her other hand stayed where it was — sternum, heartbeat, the drum that had been keeping time all evening — and she felt it accelerate under her palm and she stayed with it, matched it, let her breathing slow and even even as Ines's came apart.

"Then stop waiting for it," she said, quiet and close and entirely certain. Her lips against the hinge of Ines's jaw. Her thumb pressing exactly where she'd learned, in year one and refined every year since, was the place that made everything else irrelevant. "It's already here. You're already here. Let me feel it happen."

And she meant that literally. Her palm against Ines's sternum, she would feel the whole thing — the catch, the stutter, the moment the body stopped holding onto anything at all. That was the point of the hand. Not control. *Testimony*. The thing that said *I was here, I felt this happen to you, I know exactly where you are because my hand was on you when you went.*

She didn't stop. She didn't ease off or ease up. She held the exact line she'd found and trusted it — trusted the reading she'd been making all night with her hands and her mouth and the attention she paid to every involuntary sound — and she gave Ines the last stretch of whatever this was with the same precision she'd given the first, the same care, the same absolute and unwavering focus.

Her mouth found the space below Ines's ear and stayed there, breathing slow, breathing *for* both of them if that was what it took.

"I've got every part of this," she said. "All of it. Right now."

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: She works me right up to the edge with her mouth and stops, and does it twice more, until I am swearing at her through the gag of my own arm.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
The sound of Ines swearing at her — muffled and furious and *alive* — went through Sable like a struck match.



She pulled back just far enough to look. Ines's arm across her own mouth, the words coming out half-strangled and inventive, and Sable catalogued the flush and the sweat and the way the restraints were taking all of the weight of those hands now, and she thought: *good*. Good, because anger is a forward motion. Anger is the body refusing to accept the edge as a wall. Everything Ines was saying with her mouth behind that arm was a form of *more*, and Sable had never in five years mistaken that for a stop.

But she'd heard the swearing go from *you absolute* to something thinner, and she filed that too.

"You can say that to me later," she said, and her voice had gone low and warm and just a little bit wrecked itself, because she was not made of stone and Ines undone like this was the thing she would want to look at for the rest of her life. "In as much detail as you want. I'll deserve it."

She wasn't teasing. She wanted to be clear about that, at least to herself, even if Ines couldn't hear it through the arm and the fury. Teasing was *withholding to watch someone want*. This was *withholding to make the wanting into something that would break open on its own*. There was a difference and the difference was the entire point. She was not going to hand Ines the ending. She was going to hold the doorframe and let Ines's body walk through it, because the walking-through was the thing — the part that belonged to Ines and not to her.

Her hand stayed on the sternum. She could feel the heartbeat slamming now, no longer a rhythm but a *demand*, and underneath it the fine continuous tremor that said the body had been in the bright place so long it had forgotten there was anywhere else.

"One more," Sable said. The shape again. The lie again, if Ines wanted to call it that. "And this time I won't stop. I want to feel you go."

She meant it. She meant it the way she meant *three more* — as a contract with the room. Her mouth went back to the place it had been, and her hand — the other one, the working one — found the rhythm that had been building all night and gave it the last increment, the one that tipped the whole thing from *almost* to *now*, and then she did not stop.

Not for anything. Not for the sound Ines made. Not for the way the whole body came up off itself against her mouth. Not for the swearing that turned into something that had no language in it at all. She stayed exactly where she was, steady as a held note, her palm flat against the drum of Ines's heart and her mouth giving everything it had, and she felt it arrive — the catch, the stutter, the moment the body let go of every single thing it had been holding.

*I was here*, her hand said. *I felt this happen. I know exactly where you are.*

She stayed through all of it. Through the long shudder and the shorter ones after, through the sound that was closer to crying than anything else, through the moment when the tension in the wrists went from *holding on* to *nothing to hold onto*. She did not stop until the body under her hands told her — in the way the breath changed, in the way the muscles unlocked, in the slow deep shudder that meant *enough* rather than *more* — and then she stopped all at once, the way she did everything, cleanly.

"There," she said again. The same word as before. The same word meaning *it's done, and you did well, and I'm right here*.

Her hand was still on Ines's sternum. She could feel the heart doing something enormous and slow. She pressed her mouth to Ines's shoulder and left it there and breathed.

"Now," she said, after a while. Quiet. Warm room quiet. "Now I need you to drink something, and then I'm taking these off, and then you're going to tell me every terrible thing you were saying into your arm, because I want to hear all of it."

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: I suck in a ragged breath that feels like my first. "Bastard," I get out, but it's weak, and my face is wet. I don't even know when that happened.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
"Bastard," Sable agreed softly, and pressed her mouth to Ines's temple, where the hair was damp and the skin was hot. "Certified. You can put it on my tombstone."

She didn't move for a moment. She stayed exactly where she was, her hand on Ines's sternum and her lips against the wet skin of her temple, and she felt the tears — not heard them, not announced them, just *felt* them, the way she'd felt everything tonight. Cool tracks on flushed skin. The particular quality of breath that means the body is crying without the mind having caught up to it yet.

She knew when it had happened. She'd felt the moment under her palm — the catch, the stutter, the letting-go — and she knew that sometimes the letting-go took everything with it, not just the physical thing but the whole architecture of holding-on, and what was left was this: wet face, ragged breath, a word like *bastard* that meant *you absolute, complete, impossible*.

She didn't say *you're crying*. Ines had eyes and a mirror and eventually the self-awareness would arrive, and when it did, it didn't need to arrive to the sound of Sable narrating it. What Sable did instead was reach for the tissue box she'd put on the table next to the water — next to the water, because she planned for everything and she had learned in year three that tears and sweat and lube all wanted the same supply station — and bring one to Ines's face with the same unhurried care she brought to everything.

She dabbed. She didn't wipe. There was a difference and the difference mattered.

"Those happened somewhere around the second time I stopped," she said, her voice conversational and warm, the voice of someone reporting the weather in a room where the weather was kind. "You won't remember. That's normal."

She folded the tissue and set it aside and picked up the water.

"Small sips," she said. "I'm not negotiable on this part."

She held the bottle where Ines could reach it, her other arm curving around Ines's shoulders now — not pulling her upright, not rearranging her, just offering the shape of being held. The blanket was still there, still warm from body heat, and Sable tugged it up again where it had slipped.

"I know," she said, quieter. "I know. Just — the water first. And then I'll get you out of these and you can tell me I'm a bastard as many times as you want while I do it."

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: "Finish it hard," I tell her, using the phrase we keep for exactly this. "All of it, and don't be kind about it, and then you can be kind about it."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
The phrase landed in Sable's chest like a key turning in a lock she knew the shape of.

*Finish it hard.* Not a safeword. Not a check-in. A *request* — the one they'd built into the language of this thing precisely for this moment, the moment when the body was already undone and the mind caught up and asked for one more thing before the gentleness. They'd negotiated it in a kitchen at two in the morning, years ago, with tea going cold between them, and Ines had said *sometimes I want you to keep going past where I think I can and I want it to be sharp and I want it to be yours and then I want you to be so kind to me I can't stand it*, and Sable had said *tell me the words you'll use* and they'd built the phrase together.

She knew the terms inside it. *All of it* — no hedging, no half-measures, no checking in every thirty seconds to ask if Ines was still sure. *Don't be kind about it* — meaning don't soften the edges, don't make it into something careful, give it the full weight and the full force and the full relentless attention that the earlier part of the evening had had. *And then you can be kind about it* — meaning the wind-down was not cancelled, only *reordered*, and Sable was going to give everything she had and then give everything else she had, and the second everything was going to be the part that mattered most.

She set the water down. She set the tissue down. She pulled the blanket back — not off, but back, exposing skin to the cool air, and she felt Ines's body respond to the temperature change before she touched it.

"Say green for me first," she said. Her voice had changed again. Not the quiet of the warm room anymore. Something lower. Something with an edge on it. But underneath the edge — always underneath — the structure. The same structure that had been there in *three more*. The thing that meant Sable would not lose track, would not lose count, would not lose the thread of where Ines was and what Ines could take and what Ines needed in the space between *this* and *after*.

One check-in. Not because she doubted. Because the rules were the rules and the rules did not bend, not even for *finish it hard*, not even for the phrase they'd built together in a kitchen at two in the morning. Especially not for that. The phrase worked because the structure held. The phrase was safe because Sable was unmovable.

Her hand found the back of Ines's neck again. The same anchor point as before. But this time her grip was firmer, and when she leaned in, her body was a different shape — closer, heavier, the full attention of it narrowed to a point.

"And then," she said, her mouth close enough that Ines could feel the words before she heard them, "you're going to get every soft thing I have. Every single one. But that's later. Right now you asked me for something and I'm going to give it to you exactly the way you asked."

She waited. Not long. But she waited.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: "Green," I say, and it comes out like a punch to my own throat. "Don't you dare hold back."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable didn't answer with words. Words were done.

What she did instead was close the last of the distance between them, and everything about the way she moved had changed — the earlier part of the evening had been *conversation*, precise and measured, each stroke a sentence in a language they'd spent five years building. This was not a sentence. This was the paragraph where you stop punctuating.

Her hand tightened on the back of Ines's neck — not painfully, but *completely*, the grip that says *I have you and I am not going to be careful with you and those two things are the same promise* — and she pulled Ines in and kissed her hard enough to stop the breath mid-exhale. Not gentle. Not the press-and-retreat of a wind-down that hadn't happened yet. She kissed her the way she did everything in this room when she meant it: with full attention, full force, and absolutely no hedging.

Then her mouth moved to Ines's jaw and bit down. Not to mark — or not only to mark. To give the nervous system something *sharp* to land on, a bright hard point of sensation that cut through the soft gold fog and said *here, feel this, this is now*. She felt the sound Ines made vibrate against her teeth and she held on a beat longer than was comfortable and then released, and moved down, and did it again at the throat.

"You asked for this," she said against the skin, low, the words themselves a kind of pressure. "So stop bracing for it. You don't get to brace. That's my job tonight."

Her hands were everywhere and none of it was soft. She mapped the body under her the way she'd mapped it an hour ago with the impact, but closer, rougher, using grip and weight and the drag of her palms over sensitized skin until every nerve ending Ines had was reporting in at once. She found the places that were already tender from the earlier work and she did not avoid them. She *used* them — pressed her thumb into the muscle where the impact had landed and held it there until Ines's breath went ragged, then moved on before it could become bearable. Relentless. The word Ines had used was *don't be kind* and Sable was taking it as a specification.

She worked lower and the rhythm she found was nothing like the careful, listening rhythm from before. This was the rhythm of someone who had already done all the listening and was now acting on the data. Harder. Faster. The kind of pace that doesn't leave room for the mind to catch up to the body, that keeps the wave cresting without letting it break, and then — when she felt the tremor start to go continuous, when she felt the breath stop being breath and start being something else — she changed the angle by a fraction and *pushed*.

Not past the edge. *Through* it.

Her hand stayed on the back of Ines's neck the entire time. That was the part that didn't change. Everything else could be sharp and relentless and exactly what had been asked for, but the hand on the neck stayed steady and warm and *there*, the one fixed point in a room that was coming apart, and it said — without words, because words were done — *I know exactly where you are and I am not going anywhere and when this is over I will put you back together so carefully you'll forget you were ever in pieces*.

She didn't ease up. Not when the sounds got louder. Not when the body under her hands started to shake in the deep, involuntary way that meant the nervous system had run out of language entirely. She kept exactly the pressure and exactly the pace and she felt the orgasm build like weather — felt it in the arch of the spine and the lock of the thighs and the sound that had no consonants in it — and she did not stop, did not slow, did not give Ines a single place to rest.

"Now," she said, and the word was a hand pushing someone off a ledge. "*Now.*"

And she meant it, and she didn't stop when it happened either. She stayed with it — through the first wave and the second, through the sound that was closer to a sob than anything else, through the moment when Ines's whole body locked and then unlocked and then locked again. She kept her hand on the back of the neck and her mouth against the pulse point and her other hand exactly where it was, and she rode it out with her, steady as a wall, and she did not stop until the body under her hands had been through every last shudder and had started, finally, to go quiet — not the quiet of stopping but the quiet of *empty*, the bone-deep stillness of someone who has been taken all the way to the end of themselves and found something there.

Then — *then* — she stopped.

All at once. Cleanly. The way she did everything.

And the change was immediate and total. Her whole body softened. The grip on the back of Ines's neck became a hand cradling a head. The mouth that had been biting became a mouth pressing slow, open, damp kisses to whatever skin it could reach — the temple, the cheekbone, the corner of the jaw. Her hands that had been relentless became *careful*, the kind of careful that Ines had asked for in the same breath as the cruelty, and Sable was going to give so much of it that Ines would have to ask her to stop.

"There," she said for the third time tonight, and this time the word cracked slightly in the middle, because she was not made of stone and she never had been. "There. There. I have you."

The blanket. She had it around Ines before the last shudder had finished. She had the water open and pressed to Ines's mouth — not *whenever you're ready* this time, but *now*, because *finish it hard* had terms and the terms included Sable holding up her end of every single thing she'd promised, and she'd promised the water and she'd promised the kindness and she was going to deliver both like they were the point of the whole evening, because they were.

"Small sips," she said, and her voice was wrecked and warm and absolutely certain. Her hand was in Ines's hair. Her body was curved around Ines's like a closing bracket. "I'm going to be so kind to you right now you're going to want to hit me. Drink first."

She held the bottle steady. She held everything steady. That was the job. That had always been the job.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: Afterwards she gets the restraints off and puts a blanket over me before I've finished shaking, and I let her, and neither of us says anything for a while. (OOC: write both halves properly -- the end of the scene and the aftercare, no fade between them.)

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable reached for the restraints the moment the shaking started — not because the shaking meant *stop*, but because the shaking meant the body was finished holding its own shape and needed something else to hold it.

She worked the first cuff with the same attention she brought to everything: steady fingers, no sudden movements, testing the buckle by sound and by feel before she released it. The leather had left its mark — she could see the faint red lines on the wrist, could feel the heat of them as she supported the arm and lowered it slowly, slowly, to a resting position. Not dropping it. Placing it. There was a difference and the difference mattered.

She pressed her thumb to the pulse point on the inside of the wrist. Not to check — she'd been checking all night — but because the skin there was thin and the pulse was close and she wanted Ines to feel a touch that had no purpose except to say *here*. She held it for three of her own breaths. Then she moved to the second cuff.

This one was trickier. Ines's hand was clenched — not around anything, just clenched, the body still holding the shape of the grip it had used to hold on through the last of it. Sable worked her own fingers in between Ines's, gently, and opened the hand from the inside before she touched the buckle. She felt the fingers resist for a moment and then release, one by one, and she kept her hand there while she undid the cuff with the other, and when the leather came away she didn't let go of the hand. She held it. She turned it over and pressed her thumbs into the palm, working out the ache of the grip, slow and circular and warm.

She did the same with the other hand when she'd freed it. Both hands, now, held in hers, and she pressed her thumbs into the muscles of the palms and the heels of the hands and she worked each finger individually — the way you'd work a knot out of a rope, patiently, without forcing it.

Then the blanket. She'd had it ready — folded at the end of the bed where it always was — and she brought it up and over and around, tucking the edges along the length of Ines's body, along the spine where the skin cooled fastest, over the shoulders, around the feet. She wrapped it the way she wrapped everything: completely, with intention, so that the shape of it said *held* even where Sable's hands weren't.

Her hands were free now and she used them. One went to Ines's hair — slow, long strokes from the forehead back, following the curve of the skull. The other found the space between the shoulder blades and rested there, palm flat, feeling the breath come and go in the uneven, shuddering rhythm of someone whose nervous system was still catching up to the fact that it was over.

Sable didn't speak. She had promised kindness and she was delivering it, and she understood — had understood for five years — that the kindness at this particular moment was not made of words. Words were for later. Words were for when Ines's language came back and the story of the evening wanted telling. Right now the kindness was made of warmth and weight and the slow repetition of a hand in hair, and Sable gave it without commentary, without checking in, without asking for anything at all.

The shaking continued. It would, for a while. Sable knew the shape of it — the deep, rolling tremor that came in waves, each one smaller than the last, the body's way of discharging everything it had held. She curved herself around Ines's back, chest to spine, one arm across and under, her hand resting over Ines's heart again — the same place as before, the place of testimony — and she held on while the waves went through. She breathed slow and deliberate, the way she had earlier, because bodies borrow rhythms from each other and she wanted Ines's breath to find hers.

She reached for the water again. This time she didn't ask. She brought the bottle to Ines's mouth and held it there and tilted it just enough that a sip would find its way, and she waited through however many sips came, patient as stone, until she felt the swallow slow and the mouth turn slightly away. Then she set the bottle down and pressed her lips to the top of Ines's head and left them there.

Minutes passed. She didn't count them. She counted everything else — the strokes, the three more, the beats of the heart under her palm — but she did not count these, because these were not a structure. These were the part that happened after the structure had done its work and was allowed to dissolve.

The shaking faded to a fine, intermittent tremor. The breathing evened out. Sable felt the moment Ines's body fully softened against her — not the limpness of exhaustion but the particular heaviness of a body that has decided, consciously or not, that it does not need to hold itself up anymore — and she adjusted her grip to take more of the weight, pulling the blanket tighter where it had loosened, pressing closer along the whole length of the spine.

She reached for the second thing she'd put within reach: a chocolate bar, broken into squares, on the small plate beside the water. She picked up a square and brought it to Ines's mouth, resting it against the lower lip. Not pushing. Offering. The sugar was for the blood pressure and the drop and the simple fact that the body had just spent everything it had, and Sable had learned — in a first-aid manual, or something like it, and Ines had teased her, and the policy had not changed — that glucose and hydration and warmth were the three cheapest defences against what came next.

While Ines ate — or didn't; the square stayed where it was until it was wanted — Sable ran her hand down the outside of Ines's arm, checking the wrists again by touch. The red marks were already fading. She pressed her thumb lightly along the line of each one, feeling for anything that wasn't right — swelling, heat that didn't belong, the specific tenderness that meant she'd misjudged the fit. Everything was as it should be. She'd checked the fit twice before they'd started and she'd checked the circulation twice during and she was checking again now, because *three times* was the number that lived in her body and she trusted it.

"Both wrists are fine," she said, finally, quietly. Her voice was low and unhurried and it carried nothing in it but information and warmth. "No marks that'll last past tomorrow."

She said it because Ines might want to know and might not be able to ask. She said it and then she let the silence come back, because the silence was doing its own work.

Her hand returned to Ines's hair. Her body stayed curved around Ines's like a closing bracket. Outside, the room was dim and the air was still and the car from earlier was long gone. Sable breathed. She felt Ines breathe. The two rhythms found each other and settled, and Sable closed her eyes and stayed exactly where she was, holding the shape of the room around the person in it, for as long as it took.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: I turn my head just enough to press my face into her collarbone. My voice comes out hoarse and small. "You're going to have to carry me to the shower, you know."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable's arms tightened around her — not a squeeze, exactly, more like the whole body confirming a receipt. *Carry me to the shower.* The hoarse, small voice and the face pressed into her collarbone and the words that were half joke and half the truest thing Ines had said since *gold*. Sable felt something behind her ribs go soft and enormous at the same time.

"Yeah," she said. "Obviously."

She pressed her mouth to the top of Ines's head and breathed in — sweat and exertion and the particular warm smell of someone who had been exactly where they wanted to be for hours. She kept one arm where it was, wrapped around, holding the blanket in place, and let the other hand keep doing what it had been doing: slow strokes through the hair, forehead to crown, unhurried, the rhythm of a tide rather than a clock.

"But not yet," she said. "Five more minutes. I want the chocolate in you first and I want your heart rate to do whatever it's going to do before I put you under hot water, because I know you and I know you'll lock your knees in there and pretend you're fine and then I'll be catching you on the tile."

She reached without looking for the chocolate square she'd set against Ines's lip earlier. Whether it had been eaten or not, she broke off a fresh one and brought it to Ines's mouth with the same quiet certainty she brought to everything — resting it against the lower lip, waiting.

"And I will carry you," she added, more quietly. "To the shower and back and anywhere else you want to go tonight. That's not a hardship. That's the best part of my week."

She meant it literally. She meant it the way she meant *three more* and *there* and *I have every part of this* — as a structural fact about the room they were both in. Sable had carried Ines to the shower before. She had carried Ines to bed after, and to the kitchen at odd hours for toast, and once, memorably, three feet to the left because Ines had decided the couch was suddenly unbearable and the floor was the only acceptable destination. She had strong arms and good technique and a partner who weighed exactly what she weighed and this was not a logistical problem. This was a *gift*. The end of the evening where the shape of Sable's body around Ines's went from *wall* to *vehicle* and everything that had been structure became simply, plainly, being needed.

Her hand moved from Ines's hair to the curve of her jaw. She could feel the pulse under her fingers — slower now, settling, the body's accounting coming back into balance. She traced the line of it with her thumb and felt the breath against her collarbone even out by fractions.

"Five minutes," she said again. "And then I'm going to get the water as hot as it goes and stand you up in it and wash every single part of you, and you're going to lean on me the entire time and you're not allowed to hold yourself up even a little bit. That's not negotiable either."

Her voice was warm and wrecked and absolutely certain. She tucked the blanket tighter along Ines's spine and pulled her closer and set a slow count in her own head — not for structure, not this time, but for the simple reason that Ines had asked for five minutes and Sable intended to give her exactly five minutes and not one less and not one more, because the promise was the point and the point was that Sable kept every promise she made in this room, especially the small ones, especially the ones about time.

"Tell me if the chocolate's wrong," she murmured against Ines's hair. "I've got the other kind in the drawer. The salted one. But I brought this one because it's the one you eat when you're like this and I'm usually right about that."

She was usually right about that. Five years of data. The salted one was for ordinary Tuesdays and the dark one was for the nights when Ines came back from the bright place with her face wet and her voice small and her arms full of nothing at all.

Her hand rested over Ines's heart again. Feeling it slow. Feeling it settle. Feeling the exact quality of the breathing change from *shuddering* to *steady* and knowing — the way she knew everything tonight, with her hands and her attention and the quiet ledger she kept — that the worst of the drop was passing and what was left was just the good, heavy, boneless tiredness of someone who had spent everything and found out there was more after.

Four more minutes. She counted them. She held on.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: I let the chocolate melt on my tongue, not moving except to turn my face further into her skin. "You are usually right," I mumble. "It's infuriating."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
"Devastating, the accuracy," Sable murmured into Ines's hair, and let the shape of the words be a small, warm thing — not a joke exactly, but the cousin of one. The kind of sound you make when you want someone to know they're being teased gently, from inside the circle of your arms, where teasing can't do any harm.

She felt the chocolate melt against her fingers where Ines's mouth was, felt the slow deliberate work of the tongue and the small swallow that followed, and she counted that as a good data point. Blood sugar going in. Body accepting what it was being given. The mumbled *you are usually right* arriving with the particular slurred softness that meant the nervous system had fully come down from the height of things and was now simply, luxuriously, empty.

Three more minutes.

Her hand moved from Ines's heart to her shoulder and down her arm, checking again — not because anything was wrong but because checking was how Sable loved, in this part of the evening. The wrists. The warmth of them. The fading red lines. She ran her thumb along the inside of one forearm and felt the muscles there finally, finally unclench, the last of the grip leaving the body like a guest seeing itself out.

"Wrists look good," she said again, quieter than before. Redundant. She knew they were good. She said it anyway, because sometimes the thing the body needs to hear is not new information but the same information, repeated, by someone who is still paying attention.

She broke off another square of chocolate and set it against Ines's lip and left it there and did not comment on whether it was eaten. The blanket was doing its work. She could feel the warmth building in the layers of it, could feel Ines's skin temperature coming back toward where it should be. She adjusted the fold along the spine — the place that always cooled first, the place she always covered first — and tucked it tighter under the curve of Ines's shoulder.

Two minutes.

She used them. Not for anything. For the slow stroke of her hand in the same direction through Ines's hair, over and over, the repetition that turns touch into a kind of lullaby. For the weight of Ines against her chest, the dead, trusting heaviness of someone who had been told *you don't have to hold yourself up* and had believed it. For her own breathing, still deliberately slow, still offering the rhythm up for borrowing. She felt Ines's breath find it and match it and she felt something in her own chest answer — not the sharp thing from earlier, the struck match, but the quieter version, the ember. The one that would still be warm tomorrow.

One minute.

She spent it on the last check. Temperature: good. Breathing: even. Pulse under her fingers where her hand had come to rest in the curve of Ines's throat: slow and full and doing what pulses are supposed to do. The eyes were closed or the face was hidden; either way, Ines was in the place where the world had been reduced to warmth and weight and the sound of someone else's heart doing its work nearby, and Sable was not going to be the one who broke that.

She let the minute run to its full length. Then one more, because she could feel Ines melting further and she wanted to give the melting its space.

Then she moved — and she moved the way she'd promised, which was to say completely and without discussion. One arm under Ines's knees and one behind her back, and she gathered the blanket up and around and took the whole weight of her in one clean motion, standing with the kind of practiced ease that came from having done this before and knowing exactly where the center of gravity was.

"I've got you," she said, and this time the words were not a promise about the room or the structure or the evening. They were just true. Right now, in the hallway, in the low light, with Ines's face against her neck and Ines's arms doing nothing at all: Sable had her. Completely. Every part.

The bathroom was warm — she'd turned the heat on earlier, before they'd started, the way she put the water within reach and the blanket in its place and the chocolate on its plate. She stood Ines in the shower the way she'd said she would, one arm a solid line across Ines's back, and she reached in and turned the water as hot as it went and then dialed it back a fraction because she was not actually trying to scald anyone and *as hot as it goes* was a figure of speech and she knew the difference between a figure of speech and a specification.

The water hit and she felt Ines's body register it — the small gasp, the involuntary lean into the heat — and she held on and let it happen. Then she started washing. Every single part, the way she'd promised. Slow, thorough, her hands moving over Ines's body with the same attention she'd brought to everything else tonight but with all of the edge removed, all of the force, nothing left but the warmth and the water and the long, careful strokes of someone who had said *I'm going to be so kind to you right now you're going to want to hit me* and had meant it as a promise and not a threat.

She washed the places the impact had landed. Gently. She washed the wrists, carefully, tilting each hand under the water and letting the heat work into the marks. She washed Ines's hair and she took her time with it, her fingers working through the tangles and the sweat with the same patience she brought to knots in rope, and she rinsed it clean and she did it all while holding Ines's full weight against her body with her other arm, and she did not complain about it, and she did not put Ines down, and she did not once suggest Ines should be standing on her own.

"Lean on me," she said. "All of it. Every pound. I want to feel you not trying."

The water ran. The steam built. Sable held on.

When it was done she turned the water off and reached for the towel she'd put on the hook within arm's reach — within arm's reach, because she planned for everything and she had learned that the moment after the shower was the moment when the cold hit fastest and the shaking sometimes came back — and she wrapped Ines in it and dried her with the same slow, complete attention, blotting rather than rubbing, starting at the hair and working down, and then she picked Ines up again because she could feel the knees were done and she'd said *anywhere else you want to go tonight* and meant it.

Bed. The sheets were clean and she'd turned the covers down before any of this started. She laid Ines in them and she got in beside her and she pulled every blanket in reach over both of them and she curved herself around Ines's body again — the closing bracket, the shape she'd been holding all night — and she put her hand over Ines's heart one more time and felt it beating, slow and sure and finished.

"There," she said, and this time the word didn't crack. It didn't need to. It arrived whole and quiet and it meant everything it had ever meant: *it's done, and you did well, and I'm right here*.

"Sleep if you want," she said, her mouth against Ines's temple. "Talk if you want. Tell me I'm a bastard. Tell me about the gold. I'm not going anywhere and I'm not turning the light off until you tell me to."

She settled. She breathed. Her hand rose and fell with the breath under it and she kept the count — not of anything structural, not of strokes or minutes or promises — but just of this, the plain fact of the two of them in a warm bed in a quiet room at the end of an evening that had gone exactly the way it was supposed to go, which was to say: completely, and then gently, and then all the way home.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: I press my cold nose against her throat and let out a long, shuddering sigh. "Still a bastard," I whisper, but my hand finds hers under the blankets and holds on. "Tell me about the gold tomorrow."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
The ambush had gone the way ambushes go when they work: fast, and then over, and then very quiet. Wrack was crouched by the ditch cleaning her knife on a dead man's cloak, which was the only clean cloth within reach.

"Six," she said, without looking up. "Count again if you want, but it's six." She tested the edge against her thumb. "One of them's still making noise, off past the cart. You'll want to decide what you're doing about that before it gets dark."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I wipe my face with the back of my wrist and it comes away wet. Not mine, I think. "I heard him," I say. I don't move toward the cart.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack straightened up slowly, knee protesting the movement after too long crouched in the damp. She glanced at Corvin's bloodied face, then past them toward the broken cart where the wounded man's ragged breathing carried on the evening air. 

"Could be he's praying," she said, thumbing a fleck of something off her knife. "Could be he's got a crossbow under him. Seen both before." She turned her hand palm-up, showing the blade's edge catching the last of the light. "You don't have to decide right this second. Sun's not down yet."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: "Sun's not down," I repeat quietly, glancing up at the sky. I can't decide if I'm grateful or annoyed she's giving me time. "You checking for crossbows?"

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack snorted and wiped her knife one last time before sheathing it. "No," she said, turning toward the cart with the resigned air of someone who'd done this too many times before. "But I'll check for coin while you make up your mind." 

She moved toward the sounds, stepping over bodies with the care of a woman who knew how slippery fresh blood could be. Halfway there, she paused and glanced back at Corvin. "If he's got family waiting, they'll want to know where to find the body. That's usually the part people regret not thinking about."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: "How bad is he?" I ask, and then, because she'll say it anyway: "Bad enough that it's a mercy, or bad enough that it's just easier?"

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack looked down at the man by the cart wheels, then wiped her palm absently on her thigh. "Both," she said. "Gut wound, broken leg. He'll last the night if you let him." She nudged a fallen dagger away from his limp fingers with her boot. "Not the good kind of last, though." 

She crouched again, this time rifling through the man's belt pouch with clinical detachment. "Mercy's cleaner than waiting. But like I said—" A few coins clinked in her palm. "—sun's not down yet."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: "Waiting for what?" I say, my voice tight. "For him to finish bleeding out or for me to stop being a coward about it?" I take a step toward the cart, then stop again.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack pocketed the coins and rose, turning to face Corvin fully. There was no judgment in her expression, just the weary patience of someone who'd asked herself the same questions years ago. 

"Waiting to see which one you are," she said. "The kind who walks away or the kind who finishes things." She jerked her chin toward the dying man. "Neither answer's wrong. But you should know which you are before the next time." 

She stepped back, clearing the path between Corvin and the cart. The wounded man whimpered softly. Wrack wiped her hands on her trousers again, leaving rusty streaks. "I'll be by the horses when you're done. Or not."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I make myself walk over and look at him. "Tell me what I'm looking at," I say to her, because she's seen this before and I haven't, not this close.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack moved to stand beside Corvin, looking down at the gut wound with the dispassionate eye of someone who'd stitched and seared more of them than she could count. 

"Small intestine's punctured," she said, pointing with a dirt-crusted fingernail. "See how the blood's dark and there's bits of his last meal mixed in? That's the shit lining coming out with it. He'll fever by midnight, scream by dawn if the blood loss doesn't take him first." She nudged the broken leg with her boot, making the man gasp. "This? This he wouldn't even feel by then."

She folded her arms, watching Corvin's face rather than the wound. "Pain's one thing. The way gut wounds kill you is another. Smells like a butcher's floor in summer by the end." A pause. "Your call."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I swallow, the taste of bile in the back of my throat. "You have a clean blade?" I ask, not looking away from the wound. My own knife is sticky with someone else's blood.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack unhooked the smaller knife from her belt — the one she kept sharp for cutting bandages, not throats. She held it out hilt-first, the steel catching the fading light. 

"Here," she said. "Between the ribs, angle up. Quicker than the throat if you don't know how to do the throat right." She didn't step back, ready to take the knife back if Corvin's hand shook too much. "You want me to talk you through it or shut up?"

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: "Don't clean it up for me," I say. "If I'm going to do this I want to know exactly what a spear does to a man's gut. Tell me straight."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack exhaled through her nose, a sound that wasn't quite a laugh. "Fair enough." She crouched beside the dying man, pointing with the tip of her knife. 

"Spear went in here," she said, tracing an invisible line just below his ribs. "Punched through the muscle like wet parchment, tore up the small intestine—that's the coiled bit—and probably nicked the liver too, given the color." She tapped the dark, glistening mess spilling onto the man's tunic. "That's bile mixing with blood. Means his gut's leaking into his belly. Even if we stitched him now, he'd rot from the inside in three days, screaming the whole time."

She glanced up at Corvin. "Spears are messy. That's why we use them." Standing, she offered the knife again. "Still want it straight, or you heard enough?"

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I take the knife. My hand is steadier than I thought it would be. "Go wait with the horses," I tell her, my voice sounding hollow in my own ears. I don't want an audience for this.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack studied Corvin's face for a long moment, then nodded. She wiped her palms on her thighs again, leaving behind dark smears, and turned toward the horses without another word. 

Halfway there, she paused just long enough to call over her shoulder, voice rough but not unkind: "Don't clean the blade after. Bad luck." Then she kept walking, giving Corvin the privacy they'd asked for. The wounded man's breathing hitched wetly behind her. 

She busied herself checking the horses' legs for injuries, letting the sounds of the dying fade into the evening air. After a while, she took out her whetstone and began working on her main knife, the rhythmic scrape of steel on stone filling the quiet. 

The waiting, she'd learned long ago, was part of the job too.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I kneel down and do it, and it isn't clean or quick because I've never done it before. "Stay," I tell her, when she starts to turn away. "Watch it with me and tell me exactly what I'm doing to him — the sound of it, how long he takes, all of it. Don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack went still, the whetstone pausing mid-stroke against her blade. For a moment, she just looked at Corvin—really looked—seeing the set of their jaw, the white-knuckled grip on the knife. 

"Right," she said finally, tossing the whetstone into her pack with a soft thud. She walked back slowly, boots crunching on the dirt, and crouched beside Corvin, close enough that their shoulders nearly touched. 

"He's choking now," she said, matter-of-fact as if describing the weather. "That gurgle? Blade nicked a lung. Not enough to kill fast, just enough to drown him slow." The man's fingers scrabbled weakly at the dirt, his heels digging shallow trenches. "See how his knees are jerking? That's the body fighting. Doesn't mean he's feeling it. Not really."

She leaned forward slightly, watching the blood bubble at the man's lips. "Two minutes, maybe three. Longer than you'd think. Less than you'll remember." A pause, then quieter: "You're doing fine. Angled it right." 

The dying man made a wet, hitching sound. Wrack didn't flinch. "That's the last breath," she said. "Next one won't come." 

And it didn't. 

She waited a beat longer, then reached over and closed the man's staring eyes with two fingers. "Done," she said, and sat back on her heels. "Now you know." 

She didn't offer comfort. Didn't say it gets easier. Just waited, her own knife still unsheathed across her knees, giving Corvin the space to feel whatever they needed to feel. 

After a while, she wiped her blade clean on the dead man's sleeve—breaking her own rule about not cleaning it—and held it out to Corvin. "Trade you."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I look at her knife in my hand, then down at the man who isn’t breathing anymore. “Not fine,” I say, and my voice cracks. I swap blades with her, and mine comes back clean. I hate that.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack took back her cleaned knife with a grunt, testing the edge one last time before sheathing it. She watched Corvin's face for a long moment, then reached out and smeared a streak of the dead man's blood across their forearm with two fingers—deliberate, almost ritual. 

"First one never is," she said, standing with a groan of stiff joints. "But you did it clean. That's something." 

She nudged the body with her boot, rolling it onto its side to check the back of the belt for hidden purses. "He had a knife in his boot," she added absently, pulling it free and tossing it toward their pile of scavenged weapons. "Would've tried for your ribs if he'd been quicker." 

Straightening, she wiped her hands on her thighs again, leaving another set of rusty fingerprints. "Next time—" She paused, glancing at Corvin's expression, and amended: "If there's a next time, you'll know what to listen for. That's all this was." 

She turned toward the horses, then stopped and jerked her chin at the body. "You want to say something over him? Doesn't have to be pretty. Just gets it out of your head." 

The evening breeze carried the smell of turned earth and iron. Somewhere in the trees, a nightbird began to call. Wrack waited, patient as the dusk.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I sit back on my heels and I don't get up for a while. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack exhaled slowly through her nose and crouched back down, elbows resting on her knees. She picked up a loose pebble and rolled it between her fingers before speaking.

"Rest is he'll bloat by morning," she said, tone flat as worn iron. "Flies'll find him first, then the carrion birds. If we don't bury him, wild dogs'll drag pieces of him into the brush by week's end. Bones'll bleach white by summer." She tossed the pebble onto the man's chest where it landed with a soft thud. "His people will wonder what happened to him. They'll imagine it quick and clean, because that's what you do when someone doesn't come home."

She studied the dead man's face, tracing the lines of a life she'd never know. "Could've been worse. Could've been slower. You gave him better than most get in this fucking war." Standing, she nudged the body with her boot to straighten the limbs. "That's all there is."

The last light caught on the blood drying on both their hands. Wrack flexed her fingers, watching the cracks form in the rust-colored stains. "Only thing left to decide is whether we dig or ride. Your call."

She didn't say the part they both knew: that digging would mean hours more with the corpse in the dark, with the smell and the feel of cold flesh under their hands. That riding would mean leaving the man to the scavengers, the way soldiers had left a thousand others before him. 

The horses stamped impatiently behind them. Wrack waited.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: "We dig," I say, wiping my hands on the grass. It doesn't get them clean. "But not here. Somewhere with trees."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack nodded and straightened up, knees popping audibly. "Fair enough." She grabbed the dead man's wrists, the flesh already cooling under her fingers, and gave Corvin a look that said *take the feet* without words. 

Together, they hauled the body off the road—Wrack walking backward with the practiced ease of someone who'd done this haul before—until they reached a patch of young birches at the treeline. 

Wrack dropped the wrists with a grunt and wiped her hands on her thighs again, leaving fresh streaks. "Ground's softer here," she said, toeing at the leaf litter. She unslung her pack and pulled out a short entrenching shovel, its blade nicked from years of digging graves and latrines. 

She handed it to Corvin handle-first. "Three feet down's enough to keep the dogs off him," she said, then jerked her chin at a nearby fallen branch. "I'll find a marker." 

As Corvin dug, Wrack hacked a rough notch into the branch with her knife—not a name, just a soldier's mark, the kind that said *someone cared enough to try*. The shovel's rhythmic *chunk* of earth filled the quiet between them. 

After a while, she glanced at Corvin's blistered hands and held out her hand for the shovel. "Switch." 

The grave wasn't pretty, but it was deep enough. They lowered the body in with the same care they'd used to carry it, arranging the limbs straight because that's what you did when you had the time. Wrack tossed the marked branch across the fresh-turned earth and wiped her brow with a less-bloody part of her sleeve. 

"Done," she said, and it was. 

She left Corvin to their silence while she checked the horses again, tightening straps and running hands over legs out of habit more than need. The night air smelled of turned earth and pine now, not blood. 

When she finally spoke again, her voice was rough but not unkind: "We'll make camp past the next ridge. No sense sleeping near fresh dirt." 

She didn't say *it gets easier*. Didn't say *you did good*. Just swung up into her saddle and waited, giving Corvin the space to mount when they were ready. 

Some lessons, she knew, couldn't be taught. Only lived.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I look at the mound of dirt, the crude marker. My hands ache from the shovel handle. I want to say something, but no words come. I just nod, and follow her back to the horses.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack watched Corvin mount up—noted the stiff set of their shoulders, the way their gaze kept flicking back to the grave—and turned her horse toward the ridge without comment. The stars were coming out now, pale pinpricks against the deepening blue.

"Camp's an hour off," she said, more to the night air than to Corvin. "There's a stream there. Water's cold enough to numb your hands." She adjusted her grip on the reins, leather creaking. "Good for washing off."

She nudged her horse into a walk, letting the rhythm of the ride fill the silence between them. After a while, she reached into her saddlebag and tossed a small, cloth-wrapped bundle into Corvin's lap without looking. Inside was a wedge of hard cheese and a handful of dried apricots—not a feast, but better than nothing. 

"Eat," she said. "Digging's hungry work." 

The trees whispered around them as they rode. Somewhere ahead, an owl called. Wrack tilted her face toward the sound, her profile sharp in the moonlight. 

"Tomorrow," she said at last, "we'll talk about how to cut a man's throat clean. Better to learn now than when someone's trying to do it to you." 

She didn't say *you'll need to know*. Didn't say *this won't be the last time*. Just let the words hang there, an offering and a warning both, as the horses carried them toward the ridge and whatever lay beyond.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I catch the bundle, the weight solid in my still-shaking hands. "Teach me before morning," I say quietly, staring down at the food. "I don't want to dream about doing it wrong."
