dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I wipe my face with the back of my wrist and it comes away wet. Not mine, I think. "I heard him," I say. I don't move toward the cart.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack finally looked up, her eyes scanning Corvin with a flat, clinical neutrality. She didn't offer a hand or a word of comfort; instead, she noted the spray of blood on his face with the same detachment she might use to check the weather. 

She sheathed the knife with a metallic *snick* and stood up, her joints popping. She was a woman made of old scars and hard lessons, her armor dented and dull from years of utility over vanity. 

"If you're waiting for him to start singing hymns, you're wasting time," she said, her voice a low, gravelly rasp. "He's probably just leaking from the gut. They always make a lot of noise when the stomach opens up—sounds like a wet bellows."

She stepped away from the ditch, her boots crunching on the grit. She didn't move toward the dying man herself; that was a decision for the one who felt the need to be merciful, or the one who needed to practice their finishing stroke. Wrack just leaned back against a charred fence post and crossed her arms, watching Corvin.

"He's not going to be a problem for long," she added dryly. "But he's a problem right now. He's a beacon for anyone else they left in the woods."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I shake my head, trying to get the sound of that wheezing out of my ears. "I'll do it," I mutter, but my feet still feel stuck. "Just... give me a second."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack didn't move to help him, nor did she push him. She simply shifted her weight, the leather of her brigandine creaking. She had seen that look on a hundred faces over a decade of border skirmishes—the hesitation that came when the adrenaline dipped and the reality of the meat set in. It was a luxury she had stopped affording herself somewhere around her thirtieth year.

"Take your second," she said, her tone devoid of judgment but stripped of patience. "But do it quickly. The wind is shifting, and if it carries that sound toward the treeline, we're not the ones doing the ambushing anymore."

She reached into a pouch at her belt and pulled out a piece of dried, salted meat, chewing on it slowly. Her gaze remained fixed on Corvin, watching the way he stood. She was gauging his stability, checking for a tremor in the hands or a wobble in the knees. If he broke now, she'd have to do it herself, and she'd rather not waste the energy if he was capable of the task.

"Don't go sawing at him," she added around a mouthful of jerky, her voice flat. "One clean thrust through the base of the skull or a deep cut across the throat. Anything else just makes a mess and keeps them screaming. Efficiency, Corvin. It's the only thing that makes this job tolerable."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: "How bad is he?" I ask, and then, because she'll say it anyway: "Bad enough that it's a mercy, or bad enough that it's just easier?"

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack stopped chewing for a moment, her jaw pausing mid-grind. She looked toward the cart, listening to the ragged, bubbling sound of the man's breathing, then looked back at Corvin. A small, ghost of a smirk touched the corner of her mouth, though it didn't reach her eyes.

"Both," she answered. "The overlap is where the efficiency is."

She swallowed the meat and spat a piece of gristle onto the dirt. "He's got a belly wound. I can tell by the rhythm of the wheeze. He's leaking everything he ever ate into his own abdominal cavity. He'll be shivering in five minutes, then he'll be delirious, and then he'll spend the next three hours praying to a god who isn't listening while he slowly rots from the inside out."

She shrugged, a slow movement of her heavy shoulders. To her, this wasn't a philosophical debate; it was a matter of anatomy.

"It's a mercy because it stops the pain, and it's easier because I don't want to listen to him do it for the next three hours," she said plainly. "The distinction is for people who get paid to write poems about the war, not for people who have to walk through it."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I nod, my mouth dry, and finally start walking toward the cart. "Efficiency," I echo, my voice coming out a little hoarse. "Right."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack watched him go, her eyes tracking the stiff, uncertain gait of his stride. She didn't call out a word of encouragement; encouragement was for recruits and children, and Corvin was currently neither. She simply waited, leaning against the fence post, the silence of the woods returning to swallow them as the dying man's gasps became the only audible thing in the clearing.

She reached down and adjusted the strap of her gauntlet, tightening it with a sharp tug. As the first sound of the struggle reached her—the frantic scrape of boots on dirt and a sudden, sharp intake of breath—Wrack didn't flinch. She didn't even blink. She just stared at the treeline, her ears tuned to the perimeter, listening for the snap of a twig or the distant call of a horn.

When the noise from the cart finally ceased, replaced by a heavy, definitive silence, Wrack let out a slow breath through her nose. 

"About time," she muttered.

She pushed herself off the fence post and walked toward him, her boots heavy and deliberate. She didn't look at the body as she passed, treating it as nothing more than a piece of discarded gear. She stopped beside Corvin, glancing at the blood on his hands and the expression on his face.

"Wash that off in the ditch," she said, gesturing vaguely toward the water. "Blood attracts flies, and flies attract things we don't want to deal with. Then check his pockets. If he was carrying the dispatch, it'll be in a waterproof tube. If he wasn't, we're just wasting our afternoon."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I make myself walk over and look at him. "Tell me what I'm looking at," I say to her, because she's seen this before and I haven't, not this close.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack sighed, a sound of genuine boredom. She stepped closer, her boots planting firmly in the blood-soaked dirt, and peered down at the man. She didn't recoil; she didn't even lean away. She looked at the body with the same professional interest a cobbler might show a ruined boot.

"You're looking at a mess," she said, her voice flat. She pointed a calloused finger toward the jagged tear in the man's tunic, where the blood had pooled and darkened. "The gut wound did the heavy lifting. It's a slow way to go, but it's certain. The blood you're seeing now is just the runoff. Most of it's inside, filling up the gaps."

She shifted her gaze to the neck, where Corvin had delivered the final blow. She leaned in, squinting at the angle of the cut.

"A bit shallow on the left," she noted, as if grading a schoolboy's penmanship. "You hesitated. He probably felt the cold of the steel before he felt the edge. Next time, commit to the motion. Don't think about the skin; think about the spine. You want to sever the connection between the brain and the lungs. That's how you get the silence you're after."

She stood back up, her expression unchanging. There was no malice in her critique, only the cold reality of a trade. 

"But he's dead now, so the lack of technique is a moot point," she added, glancing back toward the woods. "Now, stop staring at him. The dead are the easiest people in the world to talk to—they never tell you anything you don't already know. Check the pockets. Now."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I swallow hard, looking away from the neck wound. My hands feel clumsy as I start patting down the dead man's clothes. "I don't see a tube," I say after a moment, my voice still too tight.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack let out a sharp, clicking sound with her tongue, a noise of pure annoyance. She stepped forward, shoving Corvin aside with a blunt shoulder to get a better look. She didn't do it with aggression, but with the efficient displacement of an object that was in her way.

"You're patting him like you're looking for a misplaced coin," she muttered. 

She didn't just feel the clothes; she probed. Her hands moved with a practiced, clinical speed, sliding beneath the lining of the man's tunic and digging deep into the waistband of his trousers. She knew where soldiers hid things—not where they *should* be, but where they actually put them when they were terrified of losing a dispatch in a muddy ditch.

Her fingers snagged on something hard and cylindrical tucked tight against the small of the man's back, hidden beneath the belt. With a swift, rough tug, she yanked a leather-wrapped tube from its hiding place.

"Too much faith in the obvious," she said, holding the tube up for Corvin to see. She didn't hand it over immediately; she held it just out of reach, her gaze sliding back to his face. "You're shaking. Stop it. The dead man isn't going to jump up and bite you, and the living ones in the woods don't care about your conscience."

She finally pressed the tube into his hand, the leather still warm from the dead man's body. 

"Go wash your hands. I'll start stripping the boots and the gear. Good leather is hard to come by these days, and I'm not leaving a perfectly good pair of cavalry boots to rot in the dirt just because the owner didn't have the sense to stay out of our way."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: "Don't clean it up for me," I say. "If I'm going to do this I want to know exactly what a spear does to a man's gut. Tell me straight."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack paused, her hands already hovering over the dead man's laces. She looked up at Corvin, her expression shifting from annoyance to something that might have been respect if she were a woman prone to such things. It was a look of recognition—the moment a man decided he was tired of pretending the blood wasn't there.

"Straight it is," she said. She didn't move to comfort him; she simply stepped back and gestured toward the wound with a flick of her wrist. "A spear isn't like a sword. A sword slices, it peels. A spear... a spear is about displacement. It doesn't just open you; it pushes everything aside to make room for itself."

She crouched down, pointing to the entry point. "When the head hits the gut, it doesn't just stop. It punches through the muscle, tears the peritoneum, and then it starts sliding through the loops of the bowel. If the man is unlucky, it hits the spine and pins him like a moth to a board. If he's lucky, like this one, it just shreds the plumbing."

She looked Corvin in the eye, her voice dry and devoid of sentiment. "The real horror isn't the hole. It's the leak. The stomach and intestines are full of filth—half-digested grain, bile, waste. When that spills into the abdominal cavity, it's like pouring acid on a raw nerve. It triggers a systemic shock. The body tries to fight it, but it can't. That's where the shivering comes from. The cold isn't from the wind; it's the body shutting down because it knows it's already a corpse."

She stood up, the leather of her armor creaking. "He spent his last ten minutes feeling his insides turn into a swamp. That's what a spear does. It turns a man into a leaking bag of meat and regret."

She blinked, her gaze returning to the boots. "Now that you've had your lesson in anatomy, get your hands clean. The blood is starting to tack up, and if it dries on your skin, you'll be scrubbing it off with sand for an hour."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I stare at the wound for another few seconds, then nod stiffly. My hands are sticky and red. I turn and walk to the ditch, crouching to plunge them into the cold, muddy water. I scrub until the skin feels raw.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack didn't watch him go. She had already returned to her work, her movements methodical and devoid of hesitation. She knelt by the body and began the process of stripping the gear, first unbuckling the belt and then working the heavy cavalry boots off the dead man's feet. She did it with a practiced indifference, treating the corpse as nothing more than a trunk of clothes that needed unpacking.

"Rub a bit of grit into your palms if the blood won't budge," she called out over her shoulder, her voice flat. "Water alone just smears it. Use the sand at the bottom of the ditch."

She set the boots aside, checking the soles for wear. They were high-grade leather, still sturdy, though stained with the red mud of the borderlands. She gave a small, approving grunt. In this war, a good pair of boots was often worth more than a soldier's life; one was a tool for survival, the other was just a liability that bled.

As she moved on to the man's cloak, she glanced back at Corvin. He looked smaller in the ditch, stripped of the adrenaline that had carried him through the fight, now just a man scrubbing his hands in the mud. She didn't feel pity—pity was a heavy emotion that slowed a person down—but she recognized the stage he was in. The "scrubbing" phase. The desperate hope that if you could just get the red off your skin, you could get the memory of the smell out of your nose.

"Once you're done playing in the mud, open that tube," she said, tossing the man's cloak onto a pile of loot. "I want to know if we're heading toward another ambush or if we can actually find a place to sleep that isn't under a hedge."

She stood up, scanning the treeline again. The silence of the woods was deepening, the shadows stretching long and thin across the road. The window of safety was closing. 

"And don't spend too long on your hands," she added, her voice dropping an octave, becoming a warning. "I can smell the copper from here, and so can every scavenger within three miles. Move it."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I kneel down and do it, and it isn't clean or quick because I've never done it before. "Stay," I tell her, when she starts to turn away. "Watch it with me and tell me exactly what I'm doing to him — the sound of it, how long he takes, all of it. Don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack stopped. She didn't turn around immediately, her shoulders squaring as she processed the request. She had spent a decade stripping the illusions away from the men she served with, usually through blunt correction or the sheer, crushing weight of reality. Most men begged for the opposite—they wanted the lie, the romanticized version of the "soldier's death," or they wanted to forget the sound of a throat closing up.

Slowly, she turned back to him. She didn't look disgusted, nor did she look sympathetic. She looked at him with a clinical curiosity, as if he were a peculiar piece of equipment she was trying to figure out how to use.

"You want the full ledger," she said, her voice a low, gravelly hum. "No shortcuts, no polishing the edges."

She walked back toward him, her boots crunching on the grit, and stopped just a few feet away. She didn't crouch; she stood over him, her presence a heavy, grounding weight.

"Fine. But don't come whining to me when you can't taste your dinner because you can still smell the bile," she warned. She gestured toward the body with a tilt of her chin. "The sound you heard—that wheezing—that's the 'death rattle.' It's not actually the soul leaving the body, despite what the priests say. It's just fluid. The lungs fill with blood or edema, and every breath becomes a struggle to push air through a straw full of syrup."

She stepped closer, her gaze flat. "As for the timing... a gut wound is a slow burn. If you hadn't stepped in, he would have lasted hours. He would have gone through the shivering, then a period of deceptive calm where he might have even thought he was getting better, and then the sepsis would have hit. His skin would have turned a grey-yellow, his eyes would have sunk, and he would have started hallucinating. He would have called for his mother or his dog, and he would have screamed for water that would have only made him vomit."

She paused, letting the silence of the woods emphasize the grimness of the description.

"The sound of your knife? That was the only mercy he got. The *shick* of the steel through the cartilage and the sudden, wet hiss of the windpipe opening. That's the sound of the clock stopping."

Wrack looked down at his raw, scrubbed hands. 

"That's the anatomy of it. No glory, no poetry. Just a series of failures in the machinery of the body until it finally stops fighting. Satisfied? Or do you want me to describe the way the skin feels when it starts to cool?"

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I stare at my hands in the muddy water. "Yeah," I say, my voice quiet. "Satisfied." I finally stand, shaking the water off my fingers. "Let's see what's in the damn tube."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack didn't offer a hand to help him up. She simply stepped aside, giving him room to breathe, though her eyes remained fixed on him for a heartbeat longer. He had asked for the truth, and he had taken it; whether that would harden him or break him was a question for a different kind of professional. For her, the only thing that mattered was that he was no longer shaking.

"Good," she said, her voice returning to its usual dry, clipped cadence. "The staring is for the dead. The doing is for us."

She moved back toward the pile of stripped gear, picking up the cavalry boots and slinging them over her shoulder with a practiced ease. She didn't look at the body again. To her, the man had ceased to be a person the moment his heart stopped; he was now just a source of supplies and a cautionary tale.

She fell in step beside Corvin as he approached, her gaze scanning the perimeter of the clearing one last time. The light was failing, turning the greens of the forest into a bruised purple. The air was growing colder, the kind of damp chill that seeped through leather and wool to settle in the marrow.

"Well?" she prompted, her tone impatient. "Open it. If it's a request for reinforcements, we're in for a long night. If it's orders to retreat, we can actually start thinking about a decent meal."

She stopped a few paces away, leaning her weight onto one hip and crossing her arms. She didn't crowd him, but she didn't move away either. She waited, the silence of the woods pressing in around them, her ears tuned for the sound of something moving in the brush. In this land, the only thing more dangerous than a dying man was the silence that followed him.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I sit back on my heels and I don't get up for a while. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack didn't move. She didn't sigh or roll her eyes, though the request was an indulgence she usually wouldn't tolerate in the field. She simply shifted her weight, her gaze dropping to the corpse and then back to Corvin. She recognized the hunger in his voice—not for food, but for the grounding weight of the worst possible truth. He wanted the full map of the horror so he could navigate it.

"You want the cooling," she said, her voice a low, rhythmic rasp. "Fine. Sit tight."

She stepped closer, her boots clicking on a stone. "The first thing you'll notice is the temperature. It doesn't happen all at once. It starts at the extremities. The fingers and toes go first, then the nose and the ears. It's a slow migration toward the core. If you touch a man who's been dead for an hour, he doesn't feel like ice; he feels like damp clay. There's a specific kind of clamminess to the skin—a waxen quality. The blood stops circulating, and gravity takes over. It all sinks to the lowest point of the body. That's why the back and the underside of the limbs turn that deep, bruised purple. We call it livor. It's the body's final way of showing you exactly where the ground is."

She looked at the dead man's slack jaw, her expression clinical. 

"Then there's the settling. The muscles lose their tension. The jaw drops, the eyelids flutter or sink. If you try to move a limb after a few hours, it'll feel heavy, then it'll snap back. That's the rigor setting in. It starts in the neck and the jaw, then works its way down. It's the chemistry of the muscles locking up because there's no more energy to tell them to relax. You can fight it if you have to—you can break the rigor by forcing the joint—but it’s like trying to bend a piece of old wood. It doesn't want to move."

Wrack paused, her eyes narrowing slightly. 

"And then, the smell changes. Right now, it's just copper and bile. But soon, the internal bacteria—the things that helped him digest his last meal—start eating him from the inside out. They don't care that he's dead; they just see a feast. The abdomen will start to bloat. The skin will tighten and turn a strange, sickly green. That's when the air starts to smell sweet. Not like flowers, but a cloying, heavy sweetness that sticks to the back of your throat and stays there for days. Once that starts, you don't want to be anywhere near the body unless you're paid enough to ignore the urge to vomit."

She stepped back, the description complete. She didn't look away from Corvin, her gaze flat and unwavering. 

"That's the rest of it. From the first wheeze to the final rot. No magic, no ghosts, no great transition. Just a machine breaking down and being reclaimed by the dirt."

She stood there for a moment, the silence of the woods returning, heavier than before. 

"Now," she said, her voice returning to its sharp, impatient edge. "The tube. Before the scavengers decide we're the next meal on the menu."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I nod, wiping my hands one last time on my trousers. My fingers are still a little numb as I break the wax seal on the tube and pull out the parchment inside. I unroll it, squinting in the fading light.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack didn't lean in to read over his shoulder. She stayed where she was, her arms crossed, her eyes scanning the treeline. She had learned long ago that the contents of a dispatch rarely changed the immediate reality of the mud beneath her boots, but she remained attuned to the shift in Corvin's posture. She was listening for the change in his breathing, the moment the ink on the page translated into a new set of problems.

"Well?" she pressed, her voice a low, impatient grate. "Is it a map to a gold mine or a death warrant for the lot of us? Don't make me guess. I hate guessing; it's a waste of mental energy."

The wind picked up, whistling through the skeletal branches of the nearby oaks and carrying the scent of damp earth and old blood back toward them. Wrack shifted her weight, the leather of her gear creaking. She felt the prickle of the evening chill and the instinctive, ingrained need to be moving. Standing still in a clearing with a fresh corpse was an invitation for every opportunistic predator in the province—be they men or beasts.

"If you can't read it in this light, hold it up," she added, her tone devoid of helpfulness. "Or just tell me the gist. Names, numbers, and directions. I don't care about the flowery prose or the 'by the grace of the crown' nonsense. Give me the meat of it."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I hold it up toward the last of the light. "It's a roster," I say, my voice steadier than I expected. "Names, supply cache locations... there's a rendezvous point marked for two days from now." I look at her. "It's for their scouts. We're sitting in the middle of their mail route."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack didn't react with surprise; she simply closed her eyes for a second, a slow blink of resignation. She let out a long, tired breath that misted in the cooling air.

"Wonderful," she muttered. "We've stumbled into a postal service for the enemy."

She finally stepped forward, her eyes narrowing as she looked at the parchment in his hand. She didn't take it, but she leaned in just enough to scan the coordinates. Her mind began to map the terrain—the ridges, the creek beds, the narrow passes that would make a rendezvous point viable for scouts.

"A roster is a goldmine, but a rendezvous is a trap if you're not the one setting it," she said, her voice returning to that clinical, flat tone. "If this was their mail route, there's another group of them expecting this man to arrive at that point. When he doesn't, they'll start looking backward along the trail. They'll find the cart, they'll find the bodies, and they'll find our tracks."

She straightened up, her gaze shifting sharply to the woods. The urgency had returned, no longer just a matter of comfort, but of survival. 

"We can't stay here another minute. If we move now, we can put a ridge between us and them before first light." She looked at the dead man, then at the gear she had piled up. "Forget the heavy stuff. Take the boots and the dispatch. Leave the rest for the crows."

She started to move, not waiting for him to agree. She began to backtrack toward the road, her steps light and deliberate, her hand already resting on the hilt of her blade.

"Two days to the rendezvous," she called back over her shoulder. "That gives us forty-eight hours to decide if we're going to use that roster to hunt them, or if we're going to use it to find a way out of this godforsaken border before someone decides to do to us what you did to that man's neck."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I fold the parchment and shove it into my belt. "We hunt them," I say, following her. The words come out before I can second-guess them. "If we run now, they'll just keep sending scouts."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
The ambush had gone the way ambushes go when they work: fast, and then over, and then very quiet. Wrack was crouched by the ditch cleaning her knife on a dead man's cloak, which was the only clean cloth within reach.

"Six," she said, without looking up. "Count again if you want, but it's six." She tested the edge against her thumb. "One of them's still making noise, off past the cart. You'll want to decide what you're doing about that before it gets dark."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I wipe my face with the back of my wrist and it comes away wet. Not mine, I think. "I heard him," I say. I don't move toward the cart.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack got the blade clean, sheathed it, and stood with the small cracking noise her knees had started making two winters back. The sound from past the cart had settled into a rhythm now — wet, hitching, a man breathing around a hole in himself. She'd heard it enough times to know roughly what it was before she looked.

She looked anyway. Knowing mattered.

She walked over, boots deliberate on the gravel, and crouched beside him. Nineteen, maybe twenty. Patchy beard, hands slick and red where he'd been holding himself together. His eyes found her and he said something — water, or mother, or please; it came out the same. She didn't answer him. She just pulled his hand aside long enough to see, then put his hand back where it was.

"Gut," she called back toward Corvin, not raising her voice much. "Low, on the left. He's got three hours, maybe four, and he'll spend every one of them getting louder. Sound rolls down this valley at night like water. His friends are somewhere back down that road, and they've got ears."

She stood and came back, unhurried, stopping a few feet from him. She looked at the blood on his face the way she'd looked at the dead man's cloak — measuring it, filing it.

"First time the decision's landed on you?" she said. Not unkind, exactly. The question came out flat, like asking about the weather. "Doesn't matter if it is. It doesn't get easier and it doesn't get harder. It just gets faster."

She drew the knife again and held it out, handle first.

"You go do it, or I do it, or we leave him out here ringing like a dinner bell for whoever's marching up that road. Nobody with sense picks the third." A pause. "And some men will tell you the first option's mercy. It isn't. It's just quieter. Quieter's what we need by dark."

She kept the handle steady in the air between them, and waited.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I stare at the knife, then past her at the cart. My jaw feels tight. "You're right about the noise," I say, but I don't take it. "I'll do it. Just... give me a minute."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack turned the knife around and slid it back into her own sheath — no sense in him standing there holding it while it went cold in his hand. That was a thing she'd seen happen. A knife in the hand of a man who isn't ready weighs about fifty pounds.

"You've got one," she said, and meant it. She tipped her chin at the sky, where the light had started going the color of old bruises. "Maybe less. Sun's not waiting on you."

She walked back toward the cart as she talked, not hurrying, and started turning out the dead men's pockets with the efficiency of a woman checking a ledger. Coins went in her pouch. A good pair of boots she set aside. She kept her voice level and matter-of-fact, the way you talk through work.

"When you go over — kneel on his right. Left hand on his shoulder. He'll grab your arm when he understands. Let him. Doesn't change anything." A pause while she worked a buckle. "Blade goes under the ribs on his left, angled up toward the far shoulder. The angle does it, not the strength. You push like you mean it and it's over before he's done being surprised."

She stood, wiped her hands on her thighs, and looked at him properly for the first time since the ambush ended.

"He'll talk to you. Water, mother, please — it all sounds the same. Don't answer him. I mean that. Answering makes it long, for both of you." Her voice didn't soften, but it didn't sharpen either. "And when it's done, walk away straight. Don't look back at him. That's not mercy either, that's just sense. You'll look plenty later, in your own time, for free."

She rolled her shoulders and glanced down the road, at the long shadows pooling in the valley like spilled ink.

"Then we strip the rest and we're gone before full dark. So." She checked the sky once more, as if it owed her an answer. "That minute's burning."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: "How bad is he?" I ask, and then, because she'll say it anyway: "Bad enough that it's a mercy, or bad enough that it's just easier?"

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack didn't answer right away. She looked down the slope at the cart, where the wet hitching sound kept on, steady as a man sawing something, and then back at him.

"Bad enough that he's dead either way," she said. "That's the honest answer. Ball went in low on the left and came out somewhere it shouldn't have. There's things in a man's belly that, once they're torn, everything in there starts going sour. Takes hours. Sometimes a day if he's strong, and he's young, so he's strong." She paused. "He'll fever, he'll swell, he'll start smelling before he finishes. That's not a wound. That's a sentence."

She shifted her weight, and her knees cracked again, and she ignored it.

"There's no surgeon within forty miles, and if there were, there's nothing a surgeon does for a gut but make you comfortable while it kills you. So no. It's not easier dressed up as mercy. It's just that the two things happen to be the same thing today." She shrugged, a small economical motion. "They're not always. Sometimes a man's got a chance and you take it anyway because it's convenient — that's when it's just easier, and you ought to know the difference so you can live with yourself after."

The sound from the cart hitched, caught, resumed.

"He's not going to get quieter," she said. "And I'll tell you one more thing, since you asked straight." Her eyes settled on him, level, no judgment in them, the way she'd look at a knot in a rope before cutting it. "The longer you stand here working out whether it sits right with you, the more of those three hours he does alone on that ground, in that much pain. You're not sparing him anything by waiting. You're just spending his time on your conscience."

She let that sit exactly as long as it needed to, then turned back toward the bodies, unhurried.

"So. You do it, or I do it. But decide like a man who knows the whole picture now, because you've got it."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I let out a slow breath and walk toward the cart. "Alright." My voice comes out steadier than I thought it would. I don't look back at her.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack watched him go about ten paces, until she was sure he wasn't going to stop again, and then she turned back to the bodies. She didn't follow. A man did that walk alone or he didn't do it at all, and standing over his shoulder would only make it two people's weight instead of one.

She worked. A second pouch of coins. A knife worth keeping, a knife worth leaving. She rolled the dead man out of the good boots and set them by her kit, laces tucked in. All the while her ears were somewhere else entirely, the way they'd learned to be, split between the road down the valley and the cart up the slope.

The boy's voice rose once — that same word, water, mother, please, it didn't matter which — and Wrack's hands went still on a dead man's belt buckle for exactly as long as it took to breathe in and breathe out.

Then the sound stopped.

Not the gasping-hitched-and-slowing kind of stopping. The clean kind. She went back to the belt buckle.

She gave him until she heard his boots on the gravel coming back before she looked up, and when she did, her face was the same as it had been all afternoon — flat, busy, half-turned toward the road.

"Boots are yours if they fit," she said, nodding at the pair by her kit. "Water's in the skin on the cart horse. Drink some. That's not a request, that's maintenance."

She cinched her pouch shut and swung it onto her hip, then looked at the sky one last time. The bruise-color had gone to iron. Down the valley the shadows had joined up into one solid dark.

"Two more to strip and then we move," she said, shouldering past him toward the bodies, unhurried as ever. "You did it clean. That's all there is to say about it. Walk."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I make myself walk over and look at him. "Tell me what I'm looking at," I say to her, because she's seen this before and I haven't, not this close.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack came and stood beside him, close enough to look but not so close they'd be in each other's way. She looked down at the boy the way she'd looked at the wound earlier — measuring, filing — and then she started talking in the same flat, unhurried voice she used for everything.

"You're looking at it done right," she said. "Angle took him quick — see how he's not twisted up? A man who goes slow fights at the end. Kicks, claws, grabs whatever's near. He's flat. His hands are open." She nodded at them. "That's the shape of a fast end. You gave him that, whether you meant to or not."

She crouched, not touching anything, and tilted her head at the boy's face.

"His eyes. You'll want to close them — most men do, first time. It doesn't do anything for him. He's done with them. But it's not for him, it's for you, and there's no shame in doing a thing for yourself at a time like this." She paused. "Use your left hand, and go from the temple down, with the grain of it. Top lid first, then bottom against your thumb. If you do it wrong it pops back open and that's worse than leaving it, so if you're going to do it, do it right."

She stood again, knees cracking, and swept her eyes over the rest of it — the blood gone flat and dark, the patchy beard, the hands still slick where he'd held himself together.

"You'll want to remember him," she said, matter-of-fact. "You won't be able to stop it. Not tonight — tonight you're too busy moving and that's a mercy of its own. But in a week, or a month, you'll be eating or taking a piss or just walking, and his face will come back whole. That's normal. That's the toll. It doesn't mean you did wrong." She looked at him sideways. "Doing wrong sounds different. Doing wrong, you don't get the face. You get the moment — the surprise on it, the sound of it. You get that instead. So if it's the face that comes, count yourself lucky."

She let him stand there a moment longer, because he'd earned a moment, and then she nodded down at the boy.

"He was on the wrong road in the wrong war at nineteen. That's the whole of his story and it's not your fault and it's not ours either. We were on our road and he tried to take it off us." She turned back toward the bodies and the deepening dark. "Now say whatever you say to your dead — some men do, some don't, both are fine — and then close him or don't, and let's go. The valley's filling up with night, and I don't intend to be in it when his friends come looking for their dinner bell."

She walked a few paces, then stopped, not looking back.

"You did it clean," she said again. "Faster than most, first time. That'll mean something to you later. It doesn't have to mean anything tonight."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content:
I crouch down and close his eyes like she said. My left hand feels steady. I don't say anything to him. There's nothing that fits.

When I stand, I wipe my hand on my trousers and walk back to her. "Boots'll do," I say, my voice low. I pick them up and start working on the next body. My fingers move quick, like I'm trying to outrun something.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack watched his hands for a moment — the quick, scrabbling speed of them — and didn't say anything for the length of one body. Then he fumbled a buckle and dropped a coin in the dirt, and that gave her the excuse she'd been waiting for.

"Slow down," she said. Not sharp. Just an instruction, like the angle of the knife had been. "Fast hands miss seams. Men sew things into waistbands. They tuck coin under collars, behind the leather in their boot tops. You go at it like a dog on a bone and you'll walk past a month's pay and leave it for his friends to find, and then they'll know exactly who beat them to it." She worked the dead man's belt in front of her loose with two fingers, unhurried. "It's not a race. The trick is to be thorough and gone. Not quick and stupid."

She turned out the next pocket herself, flat and methodical, talking the way she'd talk through any work.

"Anything that takes both hands to get, leave. Rings on swollen fingers, boots that won't come — leave them. Time's worth more than silver tonight. Weapons we take even if they're poor — poor steel still sells, and more to the point, it doesn't sell to *them*." She nodded down the valley road without looking at it. "Count of six men doesn't march alone. Whoever they answer to will want to know what happened here, and I'd rather he found six bare corpses and no answers than six armed ones."

She worked in silence for a stretch then, letting the quiet do some of its own work, and when she spoke again her voice hadn't changed at all, which was how you could tell she'd chosen the words already.

"You can't outrun it tonight," she said, to the body in front of her. "I see what you're doing. Everybody tries it once. The work helps, I won't lie — keeps the hands busy so the head gets no room. But you're not going to out-march him by dark. He'll catch you in three days, over a bowl of something, and you'll sit there for a minute with your spoon down. That's the toll I told you about. You pay it and you finish eating. That's the whole trick of it." She rolled a dead man's shoulder to get at the purse under it, easy as turning a ham. "The ones who go wrong are the ones who think they can dodge the toll. They get strange. Start drinking too much or praying too hard or picking fights so the head's got something louder in it. You pay the toll, you keep eating. Write that down somewhere in yourself."

The last body was done. She stood, knees cracking, and swept the ground once with her eyes — coins, kit, boots, the good knife, the horse standing patient at the cart with its ears doing slow circles.

"We walk the ridge, not the road," she said, tightening her kit's straps. "No fire tonight. Light travels down a valley the same as sound does, and tonight I'd just as soon be nobody. Cold camp, hard ground, and you sleep when I tell you to, because sleep's the same as water — maintenance, not a favor." She took the horse's lead and started up the slope toward the treeline, then glanced back at him, her face half-lost in the last iron light.

"Tomorrow you'll feel like an old man and you're what, twenty-some? That passes too." A pause, and the dry ghost of something that wasn't quite a smile. "The knees, though. Those you get to keep."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: "Don't clean it up for me," I say. "If I'm going to do this I want to know exactly what a spear does to a man's gut. Tell me straight."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack kept walking for a few paces before she answered — long enough to get them off the open gravel and into the trees, where the dark started doing some of the work for them. She dropped her voice to match it. Not hushed. Just scaled down, the way you talk when sound rolls downhill like water and you'd rather it didn't.

"All right," she said. "Straight, then."

She handed him the horse's lead so her hands were free, which was also a way of saying *keep walking while you hear this, don't stand still with it.*

"Spear goes in easier than you'd think. Body gives to it. Point finds the belly wall and the man's own weight does most of the work — they run onto it more than it's run into them. Half of them don't even feel it at first. They look down and see the shaft sticking out of them and their mind takes a moment to catch up. That moment's the quietest they'll ever be again."

She stepped over a deadfall, not breaking cadence.

"Here's the thing that surprises people: it barely bleeds. Little hole, seeps more than pours. It misses all the fast ways to die. That's the cruelty of it. It doesn't touch anything that kills you quick — it touches the bowel. And the bowel is full of filth. Not dirt — the body's own rot, the waste of digestion, sitting in a bag that's meant to hold it. Tear the bag and it spills into the belly cavity, and the cavity's meant to be clean. Once it's soiled, the body turns on itself. Fevers. Swells. The belly goes hard as a drum — you can tap it and it sounds like one. The pain gets so a man screams at the weight of a blanket."

The horse's hooves went soft on pine needles. She went on in the same level tone.

"And the shaft drags everything in with it. Whatever's on that wood — dirt, rust, a week of a soldier's hands — it pushes in ahead of the head. Then some friend of his gets brave and pulls it out, which is worse, because the head tears more coming than going. If a man's speared through the gut and you want him to live longest, you leave the thing in and you don't touch him. Nobody does that. Everyone pulls."

She glanced sideways at him, measuring how he was taking it, and apparently decided he could take more.

"They beg for water. Constantly. Body knows it's dying of thirst even while it's filling up with poison. They stay awake — pain won't let them faint, which is a mercy the wound denies them. Strong ones last a day, two. The boy today had it from a ball, which tears more and drags cloth in with it, so he was on the short end of it. Three hours was generous."

A few more steps. Her voice stayed flat as a ledger.

"I've packed a man's bowel back in with a wet clean cloth and strapped a pad over it and held his hand, and he died four days later anyway, tidy. There's nothing a surgeon does for it but opium, if he's got it, and most don't. So hear the practical end of it, because this is the part worth carrying: if it's ever you with a hole below the ribs, you ask for the knife, not the surgeon, and you ask early while you've still got the voice to."

They came out onto the ridge line, the valley gone black beneath them. She stopped, looked at the sky — clear, cold, no moon worth the name — and nodded once, satisfied.

"That's the straight of it," she said. "There wasn't anything to dress up. Now you know why I didn't bother." She took the lead back from him and started picking her way toward a shelf of ground that would hold no light and no sound. "Camp's there. Blanket out, boots off, and no — we're not talking more tonight. You've had your ration of truth for one day. Eat it and sleep."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I follow her, quiet. When the blankets are out and the horse is tied, I sit with my back against a rock. "I don't feel lucky," I say, to the dark.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack didn't answer right away. She was already down on her blanket, sword laid along her side where her hand would fall on it without hunting, her eyes on the treeline rather than the sky. She let the dark sit between them for a long moment, the way she let most things sit.

"Didn't say you would," she said finally. "Tonight you're not supposed to feel anything. Tonight's for lying still and letting the body do its dumb animal work — heart slowing, hands cooling, all of it. The feelings turn up later, on their own schedule, and they don't consult you."

She shifted once, found the flat spot she'd already mapped in the ground, and settled.

"Lucky's not a feeling anyway. It's an accounting. You do it later, when the book's got more entries in it." A pause. "My first went wrong. Man was down and done fighting and I made it slow anyway — bad angle, bad nerve, three tries. I didn't get his face. I got the sound, and the surprise on him, and I kept those for years — they'd come find me at the worst times, over a fire, mid-conversation, once in the middle of buying bread." Her voice stayed level as a floor the whole way through it. "So when I tell you count yourself lucky, I'm not flattering you. I'm telling you the difference between what I carry and what you're going to carry, because I've weighed both."

She rolled her head just enough to look at him, one eye finding him against the rock.

"You did it clean, first time, on a boy who was dying regardless, and you closed his eyes after. There are men twenty years in this trade who can't put all three of those in a sentence about their first." She rolled her head back toward the trees. "That's your luck. You don't have to feel it. It's just true, and true things keep whether you believe in them or not."

Somewhere below, the valley made its night sounds — wind working through the pines, one far-off thing that might have been a bird. Wrack let it all wash past without comment.

"I take first watch. You wake when I kick your boot — there's no moon to go by, so that's the arrangement." Her voice had started going down toward sleep the way other people's went, dropping register by register. "And eat something before you lie down. Hard bread's in the saddlebag. Grief burns through a man same as marching does, and I'm not carrying you tomorrow."

A long quiet. Long enough that he might have thought she was done.

Then, from the blanket, flat as ever: "You did right by him, Corvin. Both times — the asking and the doing. Now do the third right thing and sleep, because I'm not spending my watch listening to you think."

And that was the end of the conversation, because she'd decided it was.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I kneel down and do it, and it isn't clean or quick because I've never done it before. "Stay," I tell her, when she starts to turn away. "Watch it with me and tell me exactly what I'm doing to him — the sound of it, how long he takes, all of it. Don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack stopped mid-turn. She looked at him for a long second — the knife in his hand, the boy under him, the request hanging in the air between them — and something in her face shifted and settled, the way a decision does when it's already been made before it's spoken.

"All right," she said. She came back and crouched on the boy's other side, forearms across her knees, close enough to reach and far enough to stay out of his way. "You asked for it straight. You'll get it straight, all of it. Go."

He went in wrong. She saw it before the blade touched skin.

"Stop. Your angle's flat." Her voice stayed level, the same voice she'd used for everything all day, the voice for work. "You're going in like you're stabbing a table. Tilt it — up, toward his far shoulder. Like you're trying to reach his heart from underneath the ribs. The angle does it. I told you that. The angle, not the arm."

The boy came alive under it the moment the steel found skin. His hand shot up and closed on Corvin's forearm — slick, gripping, impossibly strong for a dying man — and his eyes went wide, and the word came out again, water, mother, please, all the same word.

"He's got your arm. Let him keep it. He's not strong enough to matter and it gives him something to hold that isn't the knife." She didn't move. "Don't answer him. I told you that too. Answering makes it long."

The blade went in and Corvin stopped — halfway, the instinct of every first-timer, the body refusing what the mind had ordered — and Wrack's voice came in flat over the boy's noise.

"Push. All the way. Don't stop there — halfway is the cruelty, not the mercy. You've done the hurting, now finish the work." A beat. "Push like you mean it."

The sound came when the blade found its depth — a long wet exhale, air rushing out around the steel, and beneath it something smaller and worse, a bubbling in the throat.

"That sound's his lung, not his voice. The blade's let it off its leash. It's not pain, it's pressure leaving. Don't put that in your ledger as pain." Her eyes never left the work. "He's going to fight for about ten more of your breaths. Hold still. Hold the angle. Don't pull out early — you'll tear more coming than going and then you'll owe him another."

The boy's grip went from iron to something less, then to nothing. The hand slid off Corvin's arm and landed open in the dirt. The surprise stayed on his face — it hadn't left; it had been the last thing he wore.

Wrack counted the last of it in her head, the way she always did, and then let a silence sit over the three of them for exactly three breaths.

"Done," she said. "Count of about fifteen from first cut. Slow for the work, fast for the man — he was gone before he finished being surprised, whatever his face is telling you now. Faces lie. They stay at whatever scared them last."

She leaned in and looked at the wound, measuring, filing — a craftsman checking another man's joinery.

"You went in flat, corrected, went deep, stopped halfway once. That's three faults." She held up the accounting the way she'd hold up fingers. "None of them were cruelty. All of them were inexperience. There's a difference, and it matters later, so hold onto it: cruelty is a choice. You didn't make it once in there."

She straightened, knees cracking, and stood over them both for a moment.

"You wanted to know what you'd carry. Now you know. You'll get the sound — that air, the bubbling. You'll get the grip on your arm and the surprise. That's my first, what I told you about, and now it's yours too, and I'm sorry for that, and being sorry doesn't lift it off you." She said *sorry* the way she said everything — flat, unadorned, a fact about her and not a performance for him. "But you asked to see it true instead of walking away with a clean story, and I'll tell you the last straight thing I've got: the men who go strange aren't the ones who saw it. They're the ones who guessed at it afterward, alone, and let the guessing rot. You saw it. It's worse and it's better. Both. That's how most true things come."

She nudged his boot with hers — not unkind. An instruction with a foot.

"Close his eyes if you're going to — left hand, temple down, I told you the way of it. Then stand up and walk away straight, and don't look back, and that part's not for him and it's not for your conscience either. It's for me, because it's getting dark, and I'm not standing on this road when his friends come up it."

She was already turning toward the bodies, unhurried, voice dropping back into the register of work.

"You did it slow and you did it anyway. First time, with a man begging at you and his hand on your arm." She paused, half-turned, and the dry ghost of something moved through her voice that wasn't quite a smile and wasn't quite pride but lived in the same county. "There are men twenty years in who couldn't have finished that push. Write that down somewhere in yourself, next to the sound. You'll want both entries when the book gets long."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I close his eyes. My hand shakes just once, right at the end, but they stay shut. I stand up and walk back to her without looking. "They taught us angles in training," I say, my voice rough. "They didn't tell us about the sound."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack didn't look up from the belt she was working loose. "No. They never do."

She got the buckle free, turned the pouch out into her palm, counted by feel. "Training teaches you the parts that don't cost anything. Angles, stances, how to hold your wrist. Wood and straw men. That's deliberate, before you go blaming whoever trained you. You put a recruit in front of a man who begs and you teach him the sound first, you get one of two things. A man who freezes when the sound comes — and the sound always comes — or a man who can't be made to do it at all. Both of those are worse in the field than what you were this afternoon, which is a man who went in wrong and finished anyway."

She moved to the next body, talking the way she'd talk through any work, because that's what it was.

"The sound's not a lesson. It's a toll. Nobody can teach it to you. You pay it in person or you don't, and every man who's paid it has stood exactly where you're standing, saying some version of *nobody told me.*" She paused. "The ones who say nobody told me and stay are soldiers. The ones who say it and leave — that's fine too. Better to know in your first month than your fifth."

She stood, knees cracking, and swept the ground once with her eyes. Boots, coins, the good knife, the horse standing patient with its ears doing slow circles.

"Here's the thing about the sound they also don't tell you." She shouldered her kit and took the horse's lead. "It fades. Not the memory of it — the weight of it. First few times it sits in your ears like water from a bad swim. Then one day you notice you heard it and kept your hands moving. That's not you going hard. That's just the ear learning what it is — pressure leaving, like I said. A body sound, same as coughing. You'll file it wrong for a while. Then you won't."

She started them up the slope toward the treeline, voice dropping as the dark thickened around them.

"They didn't tell you about the sound because the sound can't be taught. But you know it now, and you asked for it on purpose, which is more than most men can say about their first." She glanced back at him once, half-lost in the last of the light. "You went and paid full price with your eyes open. That's the most expensive way to buy it and the only way that keeps."

A few steps in silence, gravel giving way to pine needles.

"Now walk. Ridge, cold camp, no fire, and you sleep when I tell you to." The dry ghost came back into her voice, the not-quite-smile. "And eat something. You've earned it, which I don't say often, and you'll need it, which I say always."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I sit back on my heels and I don't get up for a while. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack looked at him for a long moment — sitting back on his heels in the middle of the road with the dark coming down and the knife still in his hand, going cold on him the way knives do when a man stops remembering he's holding one. She'd seen men pay the toll standing, walking, over a bowl of stew three days late. She'd never once seen one sit down in the road and ask for the whole bill up front.

So she stopped working. That was the first thing. All day she'd talked with her hands moving — buckles, boots, pockets. Now she came over, lowered herself onto a flat rock across from him with the cracking of her knees, and let the silence stand for exactly as long as it needed to.

"All right," she said. "The rest."

She settled her forearms on her knees.

"The sound fades. I told you that. Here's what I didn't tell you: what comes after it fades. Nothing. That's what comes. First few years, the faces find you — his, others — and they cost you a minute here, a spoon set down there. Then they come less often. Then one night you notice you can't remember whether the face that came to you over dinner was this boy or a different boy, and that will scare you worse than the sound did." She let it sit a breath. "It shouldn't. Forgetting isn't the wound. Forgetting is the scar. It's what a healed thing looks like, and healed things are ugly and flat and don't hurt, and men spend years thinking they're rotting because the pain stopped. Pain stopping isn't rot. Rot is when the pain stops and you can't remember it was ever pain. Learn the difference now and you'll save yourself some bad nights."

She shifted her weight on the rock.

"I counted, my first four years. Kept it exact, like the number owed me something. Stopped at a hundred and something — not because I lost count. Because I noticed I'd stopped feeling the count, and a number you don't feel is just noise. That's the day I started keeping a different ledger. Not how many. How. Clean or not." Her eyes went to the boy behind him, then back. "The count belongs to the war. The how belongs to you. That's the only column in the book that's yours, and it's the only one you'll want to read when you're old and stupid like me."

The valley below had gone black. She talked on into it, flat and unhurried.

"You asked for the rest, so here's the rest of the rest. This war. Nobody you're bleeding for can tell you what it's over. Ten years on this border and I've heard three different reasons from men wearing the same colors, and the border's moved twice and moved back twice, and the only things that have changed are the price of bread and the names on the muster rolls. I don't fight for the border. I don't fight for the reasons. I fight because it's the trade, and I'm good at it, and the pay's honest, and because there's maybe four people left breathing I'd take a blade for, and every one of them is in the trade too. That's the whole of my patriotism." A small shrug. "It's small. Small things hold up. Big ones crack and drop you. Small ones you can carry in a kit."

She was quiet for a moment, and when she spoke again her voice hadn't changed at all, which was how he could tell she'd chosen these words a long time ago and never had anyone worth giving them to.

"Last thing, and this is the one to keep. The work stays work. That's not a description. That's a discipline. Killing is work, and work has details — the angle, the count, the closing of eyes — and you give it the details because details are how you keep a thing the right size. The day you let it be more than work — a craft you take pride in, a hunger, a story you tell — that's the day you start going strange. And you won't notice, because going strange feels like getting good. That's the trap of it. So you test yourself. Night before a fight, check. Tired, fine. Scared, fine. Hungry, fine. Eager — eager's the one to watch for. The day you catch yourself looking forward to it, that's the day you quit the trade, because past that line you won't want to come back, and wanting is the whole of the road back."

She looked at him the way she'd looked at the wound. Measuring. Filing.

"And the other half, because it's got two. You keep it work so the rest of you can stay whatever it is. Somewhere in there is a man who closed a stranger's eyes for no reason the stranger would ever know about. That part isn't work. That's the thing the work pays for. You do the killing clean because clean is the only thing the dead ever get off of you, and you do the living — the eating, the sleeping, the four people — because that's what the killing's *for*. Men who forget the second half go strange too. Different strange. They go quiet and careful and they die tidy deaths and nobody mourns them, because there wasn't anything left in them to mourn. Some hard night you'll want to be one of those, because it looks like peace." She shook her head once. "It isn't. It's just work with the pay stopped."

She let that be the end of it for a moment. Then she stood, knees cracking, and the working voice came back like a door closing.

"That's the rest. There's nothing under it — no secret beneath the secret. That's the whole of what twenty years teaches, and you got it in an afternoon, which some would call a shame and I call a bargain, because you paid for it in person." She nodded at the knife in his hand. "Clean it before we walk. On his cloak, same as I did. That's not a chore. That's your first entry in the how-column."

She took up the horse's lead and stood waiting, half a silhouette against the last iron light, and when she spoke again it was dry as the gravel.

"Now get up. Not because you're fine — you're not. Because the dark's here and his friends are on that road, and the dead don't mind waiting." She turned up the slope toward the treeline. "The living get killed by it. Walk."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I clean the knife on the dead man's cloak. The motion is slow, deliberate. "Thank you," I say, my voice rough. "For all of it." I stand, sheathe it, and pick up the boots. "Let's go."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack took the thanks the way she took most things — a pause to weigh it, then a verdict.

"Don't thank me," she said, taking the slope at her usual pace, which was the pace of a woman who'd decided long ago that hills didn't get a vote. "I didn't do anything but talk, and talking's free. You did the work. Both parts — the asking and the pushing." A few steps of pine needles, soft underfoot. "If you want to pay me, pay me in a week. His face will find you somewhere — over a bowl, at a stream, mid-sentence. Take the minute it costs. Then finish what you were doing. That's the payment. Nothing else clears."

She didn't look back to see how that landed. She was listening to the woods instead — one ear on the trees, one on the road below, the split she'd worn so long it wasn't effort anymore. Twice she stopped without warning, just stopped, and stood for three breaths with her head tipped, and then moved again. Nothing explained. He'd learn what she was listening for, or he wouldn't.

The camp shelf was where she'd said: flat rock, pine cover, a wall of deadfall on the windward side that would take the weather and give back nothing. She tied the horse short where it couldn't tangle, dropped her kit, and started dealing out supper the way she'd dealt out everything that day — no ceremony, just ration.

"Half the bread's yours. Cheese with it. Water first." She pushed the skin at him and then sat back against the deadfall, forearms on her knees, watching the dark come up out of the valley like it was filling a bowl. "And that's the last of the ledger today. Book's closed. I mean it — you've had a full day's ration of truth and a double ration of everything else. All that's left tonight is bread and ground, and neither one wants your opinion."

She ate her own share the way she did everything, quick and uninterested, and then settled into the shape she made at night — back to something solid, sword flat along her thigh where her hand would find it blind, eyes on the treeline and not the stars. Her breathing slowed. It never went all the way down to sleeping. It never had, even before the war.

Sometime deep in the black, far down the valley, light moved on the road. Small, orange, more than one — torches, coming up the way they'd come hours ahead of schedule. Wrack watched them for a long time without moving anything but her eyes. Measuring the spacing. Filing it.

"There they are," she said quietly, to the dark, to whoever was still awake to hear it. "Right on time, which I'd admire if I didn't dislike them."

The lights crawled and shrank and passed below, and she kept watching the road long after they were gone, the way a woman checks a knot twice.

Then she settled back, and her voice came out of the dark one more time, flat as ever, dry as the gravel.

"Sleep, Corvin. You did the day clean. Now let the day go — it's not yours anymore. It's mine. I'm on watch, and nothing's getting past me tonight that didn't already."

And that was the end of it, because she'd decided it was.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I watch the torches move until they're gone, then close my eyes. "Alright," I say into the dark. I don't thank her again. I just lie down and try to do what she says.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack heard him not sleeping for a long time. That was fine — she'd told him to sleep, but bodies don't take orders, they take time. The breathing over on his blanket was too even, too measured, the breathing of a man working at it. She let him work. Somewhere in the working, the body usually won, because the body didn't care what the head had seen. It only knew marching, and blood loss, and bread. It would drag him down when it was good and ready.

She kept the watch the way she kept every watch — in pieces. An hour on the treeline. A check of the horse, done by feel in the dark, a hand along its neck to keep it settled. An ear on the valley, sorting what came up out of it: wind in the pines, which meant nothing; the far-off thing that might have been a bird, which came twice more at even intervals and so was a bird; a rock shifting somewhere below, which was a rock, because rocks shifted in the cold and men in ambush didn't. Twenty years of sorting sounds into harmless and not, and the trick of it was that the sorting never got interesting, and that was the point. A watch that got interesting was a watch gone wrong.

Somewhere in the middle hours, her own toll came due. It always did, in the dark, on watch, when the hands had nothing to do. Not the boy — the boy was Corvin's to carry now, paid in person, his entry. Hers was older. The sound of her first, the three tries, the surprise on a face that had done nothing to her but be on the wrong end of her bad angle. She sat with it the way she'd told him to sit with his — took the minute it cost, didn't fight it, didn't feed it. Then she checked the treeline and let it go back to wherever it lived. That was the whole of the ritual. It had never once been more dramatic than that, and men who made it dramatic were men who'd stopped paying the small tolls and let them pile up.

The cold came down off the ridge around the deep of the night, the way it did in that country, quick and dry. She pulled her cloak closer one-handed, kept the other where it was. The horse dozed standing. The stars did their slow wheel. Nothing else moved, and nothing else was going to, and she was as near to content as she got, which was a flat, unhungry kind of quiet that most people would have mistaken for nothing at all.

She thought, once, about the four. The ones she'd take a blade for — one dead since spring, which made it three, and she hadn't updated the count in her head until just now, sitting on a cold shelf above a valley full of the enemy's road. She filed that too. Three. Filed it, took the minute, let it go. That was the other ledger, the private one, and it didn't get entries often, and never out loud.

Toward the last of the black, when the sky went from iron to ash at the east edge, she gave it up. She'd promised him the arrangement, and arrangements were the only thing in the trade that held value — the pay fluctuated, the border moved, the reasons rotted, but a deal kept was a deal kept. She stood, knees cracking, and crossed the shelf, and stood over his blanket for a moment first. Checking, the way she checked everything. Breathing slow and deep now — the body had won, hours back. Good. Sleep had done its maintenance.

She toed his boot. One knock, deliberate, no more.

"Up," she said, flat, at whatever volume wakes a soldier and not a valley. "Your watch. Treeline's the front, the road's been empty since the torches passed, and the horse will tell you before I would if that changes — watch its ears, not the dark. Nothing's moved. Keep it that way."

She was already back at her blanket, sitting down against the deadfall, sword laid along her thigh, settling into his spot in the arrangement like a stone fitting a hole it had worn for itself.

"I'll be asleep, which is a figure of speech. Wake me for anything that breathes wrong." She pulled the cloak up. "Wake me for nothing else. Dawn's not far off, and I've been generous with the truth already. Don't spend it asking questions at this hour."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I sit up, the cold hitting me all at once. "Treeline, road, horse's ears. Got it." My voice sounds like gravel. I get to my feet and take her place by the deadfall, staring out into the gray nothing.
