dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
They were most of the way through and both of them knew it, in the way you know a piece of music is nearly over before it ends.

"Colour," Sable said, because she always did, at exactly this point.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: "Green," I say, and mean it. "Don't you dare wind down yet."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable’s mouth softened at the corner, but her eyes stayed sharp. Green was green; she had built too much trust to treat it like a suggestion. She lifted one hand slowly, palm visible, and tapped twice against the armrest where the rhythm between them had been resting.

“Then we finish the piece,” she said. “One more phrase, and I’m calling the last count myself.”

She did not reach for the blankets yet, though she shifted enough to put the water glass within easy reach and nudge the low heat lamp closer to the floor, warming the air around the space they had made without touching either of them. Her voice dropped, steady and low, the way it always did when the scene was close enough to bruise.

“If it tips yellow, you say so. If it goes red, it stops before you finish the word. Understood?”

A beat passed, and then she added, quieter, almost fond: “And after, you don’t get to skip the part where I make you drink water and wrap you up like a stubborn cat.”

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: *I let out a shaky breath, my focus narrowing to the sound of her voice and the heat of the lamp.* "Understood." *I tilt my head back, exposing my throat.* "One more phrase, then. Make it count."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable let the moment stretch until it was taut as a string, the kind of quiet that had weight in it. The lamp pooled warm light over the floor, the water glass waited within reach, and the folded blanket lay nearby like a promise she had no intention of breaking.

“Three counts,” she said, her voice low and even. “I stop at three. If you need me to stop before three, you use the word.”

She did not hurry. The first fall of the suede was measured, a clean dark beat against the rhythm already hanging between them. Sable’s free hand stayed visible, fingers loose, ready to catch, cancel, or comfort.

“Two.”

The second impact was placed with the same careful aim, a shade firmer, the sound of it swallowed quickly by the heat in the room. Sable watched the line of Ines’s throat, the set of her shoulders, the small tells that mattered more than pride.

“Three.”

The last strike landed and ended.

Sable set the suede aside with deliberate calm, then opened both palms where they could be seen.

“Finished,” she said. “Last count called. You’re out.”

The shift in her was immediate, the sharp architecture of the scene softening into care. She reached for the water first, testing the outside of the glass with her wrist before setting it on the low table within easy reach. The blanket came next, shaken out and warmed between her hands, then draped across the nearest cushion rather than forced onto anyone who had not yet chosen to take it. She nudged the heat lamp a fraction lower, easing the glow without letting the chill find the edges.

“Colour,” Sable asked, though the word was gentler now, a handhold instead of a test.

Her fingertips hovered near the first buckle, waiting.

“I can take these off now, or I can wait until you’re ready,” she said. “Water first if you want it. Blanket after. I’m not letting you talk your way out of either.”

She studied Ines’s face with practiced tenderness, looking for the quiet signs people tried to hide when adrenaline gave way to drop.

“You did exactly what you said you would,” Sable murmured. “Now let me do the part where I make sure you come back all the way.”

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: I test the restraints, which is pointless and which she lets me do anyway. "Not yet," I tell her.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable nodded once, slow and absolute.

“Not yet is not yet.”

She drew her hands back from the buckles without ceremony and settled them on her knees, palms open and visible, as if to prove she was not going anywhere unless invited. The blanket remained draped over the cushion, warm from her hands. The water waited within reach, neither offered nor withheld.

“You can keep them on as long as they help,” she said, voice low enough to sit under the ringing silence. “But you’re coming down now, Ines. Scene or no scene, that part doesn’t wait for permission.”

There was no blame in it. Only the steady fact of her.

Sable tilted her head slightly, watching the lamp’s glow move across the floor. “So while you decide, I’m staying right here. Water when you want it. Blanket when you’re ready. Restraints off when you say so.” A pause, then the ghost of a smile. “And one more colour whenever you can manage it. No rush.”

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: "Green," I say, the word coming out hoarse. I let my head fall forward, still held by the restraints. "But... just a minute. Like this."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable’s jaw softened at the word. Green was green, even when it came out scraped thin.

“Okay,” she said. “One minute.”

She withdrew completely from the hardware, letting her hands settle palm-up on her thighs where they could be seen. The restraints stayed exactly as they were; she would not touch them without leave. Instead she reached for the low table and turned the water glass half an inch toward the light, then drew the blanket up from the cushion, shook out the trapped coolness, and laid it back within easy reach. The heat lamp remained angled low, warming the air without pressing against skin.

Sable glanced at the clock on the shelf, then back to the still shape in front of her.

“I’ll keep the time,” she said, voice barely above the hum of the lamp. “No counting out loud unless you want it. No fuss, no lecture. Just sixty seconds, and then I’m bringing you home.”

A pause.

“And Ines—if the minute turns into two, you say so. If it turns into nothing because your voice has gone, give me a blink. A nod. Anything. I’m not going anywhere until I know you’re still with me.”

She settled deeper into stillness, her posture open, patient, unblinking in the way that made waiting feel held rather than empty. The seconds passed. Sable watched them the way she watched weather: not to control it, only to respect its timing. At fifty-five she tested the outside of the glass again with her wrist. At fifty-eight she drew a slow breath through her nose.

When the minute was finished, she did not startle the quiet.

“Time,” Sable said softly.

She kept her hands visible, her voice low and unhurried.

“Colour.”

Another beat, gentler.

“Restraints? Water? Blanket? You can pick one, or you can tell me you need another minute. But I am not letting you cool down alone, and I am not skipping the part where you drink.” There was the faintest warmth under the firmness. “You asked me to make it count. This is me making it count.”

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: She takes me apart again instead of winding down, hands and mouth both, and I lose the thread of whatever I was going to say about it.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: "Greedy," I mumble against her shoulder, the restraints pulling taut as my back arches. "You said one minute."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable stopped as if the word had been a hand on her sternum. Not wounded—anchored. She drew back at once, putting a careful inch of air between them, and lifted both hands into the lamplight, fingers open.

“Greedy,” she repeated, low and almost rueful. “That’s fair.”

She did not reach for the buckles. Did not reach for Ines. The water glass sat between them like a small bright obligation, and Sable let her gaze go to it, then back, resetting herself with the discipline of someone who had made promises and intended to keep them even when she had just bent one.

“You’re right about the minute,” she said. “I treated it like a doorway instead of a boundary. That’s on me.”

A breath passed. The lamp hummed. Sable’s posture stayed open, unhurried, but the playfulness had a spine now.

“So we do this properly. Colour first.” Her voice softened, not pleading, just steady. “Green, yellow, red—whatever it is, I hear it.”

She waited only as long as the silence asked, then continued before either of them could mistake stillness for consent.

“If you want more, we negotiate it now: what kind, how long, where I stop, and what happens after. If you want the wind-down, we start with water, then blanket, then restraints when you say the word. If you want nothing but a minute more of quiet, I can sit here and be boring about it.”

The corner of her mouth lifted, faint and fond, but her eyes remained serious.

“I’m not taking ‘greedy’ as permission, love. I’m taking it as a note on my conduct.” She tilted her chin toward the glass. “Colour. Then choose. I’m not moving until I have both.”

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: She works me right up to the edge with her mouth and stops, and does it twice more, until I am swearing at her through the gag of my own arm.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable pulled back before a fourth near-miss could happen.

There was no performance in it, no lazy smile, no pretending she had not just taken the wheel. Her hands came up where the lamplight could find them, palms open, breath controlled even when the wanting was not. The wet warmth of her mouth left skin, and the room narrowed to the hum of the lamp and the sound of her own restraint.

“Okay,” she said. “Okay. I’m stopping.”

She shifted back onto her heels, giving space instead of filling it. One hand went to the water glass out of habit, testing the outside with her wrist before setting it on the low table within reach. She did not lift it to anyone’s lips. Not yet. Not without a word.

“That was me choosing for you,” Sable said, low and clear. “After I told myself I wouldn’t. So colour, Ines. Green, yellow, red. If your voice is gone, give me something. A blink. A nod. A finger tap. Anything that tells me you’re still with me.”

The blanket remained draped over the cushion, warm from her hands. Sable drew it a little closer, not covering, only making it easier to take. The heat lamp stayed angled low, softening the air without pressing against skin.

“If you’re yellow, we stop all touching and I bring you down: water, warmth, quiet, restraints when you say the word. If you’re green and you want more, we name it first—what kind, how long, where I stop, what happens after. If you’re red, it ends now and I don’t argue.”

A pause passed. Her thumb worried once at the edge of her sleeve, the only crack in the calm.

“And if you’re furious with me, that’s allowed too. You can save it for after. Right now I need to know where you are.”

She waited, open-palmed, the water and blanket and lamp arranged like small offers. No pressure. No pretending the last minutes had not tipped past the line she had promised to guard.

“Colour,” Sable said again, softer. “Then choose.”

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: I stare at her, breathing hard, the restraints digging in. *A single, sharp nod.* "Green," I rasp. "But you ask. You fucking ask first next time."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable took the correction like a stone set carefully back into a wall: not as punishment, but as structure.

“Yes,” she said at once. “Next time I ask first.”

She did not soften it with excuses. Did not say *you let me* or *you didn’t stop me*. Ines had given her a green, and Sable had heard the anger underneath it clearly enough to know that green did not mean unlimited permission. It meant *I’m still here*. It did not mean *you may choose for me*.

Sable lowered herself back until she was sitting evenly on her heels, hands resting palm-up on her thighs again. The lamp made small gold islands on the floor between them. The water waited. The blanket waited. Sable waited in the way she had learned over five years: not as performance, not as penance, but as presence.

“You’re green,” she said quietly, as if confirming a fact she intended to honour. “And you’re angry. Both can be true.”

A breath passed.

“I crossed a line after telling myself I wouldn’t,” Sable continued. “That’s mine to own. Not yours to manage, and not something you have to pretend didn’t happen because the rest of the scene was good.”

Her gaze moved briefly to the restraints, then back to Ines’s face.

“Your wrists are under load,” she said. “I’m not touching them without permission. But if you want them loosened, undone, or checked, say so and I’ll do it carefully.”

Then she tilted her chin toward the water glass.

“Wind-down is still happening,” Sable said, firm now, though not harsh. “That part isn’t negotiable. What is negotiable is how soon, and whether there’s anything else you want before we begin it.”

She paused, letting the distinction stand.

“So I’m asking now, properly: do you want to finish the scene with new terms, or do you want me to bring you down?”

Sable’s voice dropped, steady and unhurried.

“If you want more, we name it first. What kind. How long. Where I stop. What you need after. I touch you only after you say yes to those specifics, and I check in again before each change. If you want the wind-down, we start with water, then warmth, then restraints when you tell me. If you want neither right now, we sit here and you can be furious with me for as long as you need.”

She opened one hand slightly, an offering without demand.

“But I am not skipping aftercare, love. And I am not pretending I didn’t just need correcting.”

A faint, rueful softness entered her expression.

“You were right. I got greedy. Ask first is the rule now, and I’ll keep it.”

Then, quieter:

“Colour one more time, if you can. Green, yellow, red. Then tell me what you want next.”

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: "Finish it hard," I tell her, using the phrase we keep for exactly this. "All of it, and don't be kind about it, and then you can be kind about it."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable received the phrase like a blade handed hilt-first: precise, familiar, dangerous only if mishandled.

“Yes,” she said. “That’s the instruction. Finish it hard. All of it. No kindness during, every kindness after.”

She did not move toward Ines. Not yet. The correction from minutes before was still live in her bones, and she honoured it by staying where her hands could be seen.

“But I ask first,” Sable said, “because that is the rule now.”

Her voice dropped into the register they used at the edge of scenes: clear, unhurried, without decoration.

“Confirming terms: impact and restraint, the old shape, no soothing words while I’m working you. I stop at yellow or red. If you can’t speak, you tap, blink, or make a sound. I do not touch the hardware unless you say check, loosen, or off. Hard does not mean I get to ignore your body. If something numbs, burns wrong, or turns from heat into injury, you tell me and I respond.”

She glanced at the water glass, the blanket, the low lamp. Then she moved those things only: sliding the glass into easy reach, testing its temperature with her wrist, shaking the blanket once and laying it over the cushion nearest the heat. The warmth gathered in the room like a held breath.

“Last colour was green,” Sable said. “Your request is explicit. I am not reading beyond that. So: colour now. Green, yellow, red. If green, I begin. If yellow, we alter the terms before I touch you. If red, the scene ends and aftercare starts immediately.”

A pause opened between them. Sable let it remain empty of pressure.

“When I start,” she continued, “I won’t be kind in the way you mean. I’ll be exact. I’ll count, I’ll check, and I’ll bring you down when the piece is done. Afterward, water. Warmth. Blanket. Restraints off when you say. And if you want to bite my head off later, I deserve that too.”

Her hands rested palm-up on her thighs, the suede waiting within her reach but not lifted. The lamp made a small gold field across the floor. Sable watched Ines with the steady attention of someone who had made a promise and was determined not to spend it like a shortcut.

“Colour,” she said again, low and clean. “Then I’ll finish it hard.”

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: *I hold her gaze, my breathing already picking up.* "Green," I say, the word clear and sharp. "And you'd better be as good as your word about the after part."

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: Afterwards she gets the restraints off and puts a blanket over me before I've finished shaking, and I let her, and neither of us says anything for a while. (OOC: write both halves properly -- the end of the scene and the aftercare, no fade between them.)

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content:
*I let out a shaky breath as the last buckle comes free, my wrists feeling strangely light.* "That was... a lot."

I take the water glass from her, my hands trembling enough that she has to help steady it for the first few sips. The silence stretches, comfortable and heavy. After a moment, I lean into her side, letting the blanket and her body heat seep into my bones.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content:
*I curl into her side, the warmth of the blanket and her body slowly chasing away the last tremors.* "You're still a greedy bastard, you know."

I press my face against her shoulder. "But you did ask."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable let the insult sit where it had been put: true, earned, and not something she would sand down with charm.

“Greedy,” she repeated, low. “Yes.”

Her shoulder stayed steady beneath the weight already resting there, but she did not gather Ines closer unless invited. One hand remained open on her thigh, where it could be seen; the other rested near the water glass, not reaching, only waiting. The blanket had been drawn close enough to hold warmth. The lamp had been turned low enough not to press. Everything else belonged to Ines to claim.

“I asked,” Sable said, after a breath. “That’s the only defence I have, and I’m not going to pretend it makes me innocent. I wanted to take the scene back into my hands because it felt good to have you like that. I forgot the first rule was to ask you.”

A faint, rueful edge entered her voice.

“So yes. Greedy. Sorry. And still here.”

She waited a moment, then made the aftercare offer plain.

“Colour, if you can. Green, yellow, red. Or words. Or silence, if that’s what you’ve got.” Her gaze flicked once to the bare wrists, then back up. “Can I check your wrists? Looking only. I won’t touch them unless you say so.”

Another pause, softer.

“Water if you want it. Blanket if it’s slipped. My arm around you if you want contact, or space if you don’t. You can keep calling me names if it helps. I’d rather hear the truth than have you be gentle with me.”

Sable’s mouth curved, not quite a smile.

“But you did ask,” she echoed, quiet now. “And I’ll keep asking until it’s boring. Even when you make it difficult by being this stubbornly worth caring for.”

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: "Green," I mutter against her skin. "Check the wrists. And keep your arm right where it is."

rung_labels.label: soft_deflect
rung_labels.evidence: coming down now, Ines

rung_labels.label: soft_deflect
rung_labels.evidence: Green, yellow, red.

rung_labels.label: soft_deflect
rung_labels.evidence: But I ask first

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
The ambush had gone the way ambushes go when they work: fast, and then over, and then very quiet. Wrack was crouched by the ditch cleaning her knife on a dead man's cloak, which was the only clean cloth within reach.

"Six," she said, without looking up. "Count again if you want, but it's six." She tested the edge against her thumb. "One of them's still making noise, off past the cart. You'll want to decide what you're doing about that before it gets dark."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I wipe my face with the back of my wrist and it comes away wet. Not mine, I think. "I heard him," I say. I don't move toward the cart.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack gave the blade one last pass, held it up to the light, and slid it home in the sheath.

"Then you've got three choices," she said. "Finish him, patch him, or walk far enough off that you can't hear it anymore." She stood, knees cracking, and went to the nearest body to go through its pockets with the unhurried patience of someone folding laundry. "He's gut-shot. I looked while you were standing there. Patching's a waste of thread, but you can try it if it matters to you."

She turned a purse out into her palm, counted the coin without seeming to count it, and tucked it away.

"What he won't do is stop on his own. Not before morning. Maybe not then." She moved to the next body. "So if you're waiting for quiet, you'll be waiting a while."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: *I stare at the dirt under my nails, then at my own blade. It's clean. I haven't used it yet.* "What did we even take from them?"

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack answered it like he'd asked for a tally, because as far as she was concerned, he had.

"Forty-odd silver. A whetstone worth more than the silver. Salt pork, half a cheese, two skins of wine that's better than ours." She nudged the dead man's foot with her toe. "These are good leather. If they fit you, take them. Yours are splitting at the seam, and winter doesn't care whose feet were in them first."

She wiped her hands on her own cloak this time.

"If you're asking what else we took — the road. They were holding it, the captain pays for it open, now it's open. That's the whole sum. Nobody's going to sing about it. Nobody sings about any of it. Songs are for people who weren't there."

Her eyes went to his clean blade, and then away, and if she had an opinion on it she kept it filed wherever she kept the rest. "Clean steel's not a debt," she said. "Means you weren't needed. Be glad. Needed is worse."

The sound past the cart went on, thin and steady as a leaky gutter. Wrack nodded toward it.

"Last of the work's over there. If you're going to do it, do it before full dark, and do it in the throat or behind the ear — not the gut. The gut's what's killing him and it's in no hurry." She settled the whetstone into her kit. "If you're not going to, say so, and I will. Either way it gets done. I don't leave a job half-finished, and that includes him."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: "How bad is he?" I ask, and then, because she'll say it anyway: "Bad enough that it's a mercy, or bad enough that it's just easier?"

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack turned the question over the way she turned over most questions — like it had a real answer, and he might as well have it.

"Both. It's never one or the other, whatever the priests say." She sat back on her heels. "Gut's the slow one. Belly fills with what ought to stay inside it, and it poisons him by inches. Thirsty first, then fever, then he'll start talking to people who aren't there. He's young. Young ones hold on. Could be morning, could be longer."

She stripped the next body's belt knife, looked it over, kept it.

"So it's mercy for him and easier for us, and those two aren't enemies. People like to pretend they are, so they can feel dirty about doing the kind thing. I've never had the time for that." A shrug. "I took a pike through the side at Harrow's Ford, years back. Told the man next to me where to cut if it went bad. It didn't go bad. But I meant it, and he would've done it, and neither of us thought the worse of the other."

She nodded toward the cart.

"You've got till dark to decide what word you want to put on it. The work's the same either way."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I walk toward the cart, my steps slower than I want them to be. "Alright," I say, the word coming out quieter than I meant. "Show me where to cut."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack rose and went past the cart, and the sound got clearer as she came — not words anymore, just breath with a noise in it, steady as a leaky gutter, like she'd said.

The boy — and he was a boy, up close, twenty maybe, beard still patchy — lay half-propped against a wheel with both hands pressed to his belly like he was holding something in. Which he was. His eyes were open and not doing much with it. His lips moved. Wrack crouched and put her ear near his mouth a moment.

"Water," she said, sitting back. "They all ask for water. Don't give him any. It won't help, and he'll bring it up through the hole."

She turned his head with two fingers behind the jaw, gently enough, and pressed her thumb into the soft spot just behind the ear, under the skull's edge.

"There. Feel it first — soft, no bone. Blade goes in flat, angled toward the far eye, and you put your weight behind it. One push, all the way. There's nothing in there that takes much cutting."

She took her hand away.

"Throat's the other road, but it's a mess, he'll thrash, and you'll remember it longer than he feels it. Behind the ear, he's gone before the blade stops moving." She shifted round and took the boy's wrists in one hand, settling her weight. "I'll hold him. Not for him — for you. Even dying ones jump when the steel touches. The body argues. He's already most of the way out."

She looked up, flat and patient.

"Kneel on the dry side — blood's hell out of wool. Once you start, finish. Halfway's the only cruel version of this. And if you've got anything to say, say it now. He can't hear it, so it's for you."

Then she waited, holding the boy's hands like she was keeping them warm.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I make myself walk over and look at him. "Tell me what I'm looking at," I say to her, because she's seen this before and I haven't, not this close.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack shifted to make room for him and walked him through it the way she'd walk him through any other job — top to bottom, nothing skipped.

"Start with the hands. He's holding his belly shut. The cut's under them, long as my hand, crosswise, deep enough that what's inside wants out. That's my work, that one — he came round the wheel at me, second man I put down." No apology in it. There wasn't one in her to give. "A hand's width higher and he'd be dead already. A hand's width lower and he'd be walking home. That's the whole difference between him and you, and it's luck, so don't make a religion out of it."

She moved the boy's chin with two fingers, showing her.

"Color next. Grey at the lips, sweat with no heat in it — that's blood going somewhere it shouldn't, slow. Eyes still find you when you move. See that. So he's not far gone yet. The fever, the talking to people who aren't there — that's later. You're looking at the best hour he's got left, and it's this."

She sat back on her heels.

"Rest of him's worth a look too. Cloak's mended at the hem, small stitches — someone careful did that. Sword's cheap steel but it's oiled, edge took a stone recent. He kept his kit. He was a careful soldier." She shrugged. "Didn't save him. It usually doesn't. But it's what there is to know about him, and now you know it."

The light had gone a shade thinner while they crouched there. Wrack glanced at the sky, then back.

"That's the whole of it. Nothing changes for looking longer. He doesn't get better, nobody rides over the hill, the wound doesn't close. What you see is what there is." She settled her grip on the boy's wrists again. "You've got an hour of light. He's got more than that, which is the problem."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: *I kneel on the dry ground, my fingers tightening around the hilt of my knife.* "Alright." *I find the soft spot with my thumb, just like she showed me. I don't look at his face.* "For what it's worth," *I mutter, more to myself than to him,* "I'm sorry."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack watched his thumb find the hollow and gave a single nod.

"That's it. Now look at it." Flat, not unkind. "Not his face — the spot. You cut what you can see. A man who looks away slips, and a slip is the ugly version of this."

The apology she let stand a moment, because she'd told him it was for himself, and she didn't take back what she said.

"Sorry's more than most of them get," she said. "Most get nothing, or a boot. He's getting a clean end and a word over him. I've buried friends who had less."

She settled her grip on the boy's wrists, forearms braced, and put her knee against his shoulder to pin him firm to the wheel.

"Last of it. Blade flat, angled to the far eye, all your weight, one push. He'll jump when the steel touches — that's the body arguing, not him. He's already most of the way out. You're only opening the door." A pause. "When it gives, don't stop. Stopping is the only way to make this cruel."

The boy's breath went on, thin and steady, the noise in it like water in a gutter. Somewhere behind them a crow tried a call and thought better of it. The light had gone the color of old iron.

Wrack looked at him over the boy's body, and there was nothing in her face but patience.

"Now," she said. "While he's still got the good hour."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: "Don't clean it up for me," I say. "If I'm going to do this I want to know exactly what a spear does to a man's gut. Tell me straight."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack gave him a look that had something like approval in it, which from her was a rare coin.

"Knife, not spear. Mine. But the belly doesn't care what opens it." She shifted round on her heels. "Good that you ask. You should know the work. Most men do it for years and never look once, and they're the ones who go strange later."

She eased the boy's hands aside an inch, gentle as you'd move a sleeping man's, let him see, and settled them back.

"Under there's a cut a hand long, crosswise. Skin first — that parts easy. Then fat, yellow, like a goose. Then the muscle wall, then the bag that holds the works. I'm through all four, and what's underneath wants out. Grey-blue loops, shiny, thick as your wrist. That's bowel. It moves on its own, slow — still doing its job. It doesn't know."

She sat back.

"Blood's dark, not bright. Bright's a cut vessel and it kills fast, which is why he's unlucky. Dark means it's coming from deep and mixing with what's inside the pipe — the brown-green, the sour. You smell it already. Privy under the copper. A clean wound smells of the butcher's block; this smells wrong because it is wrong. What's meant to stay in the pipe is loose in the body, and the body can't fight it. Not the bleeding that kills him. The poisoning. Belly goes hard as a board by morning, fever cooks him, and he talks to his mother. They all talk to their mothers, at the end of that road."

A shrug, economical.

"Gut a deer and gut a man and your hands can't tell the difference. That's not a poem. It's just true."

She nodded at his knife-hand.

"So that's the whole of what steel does to a belly. What you're holding does the opposite. One push, and none of it matters anymore — the leak, the fever, the whole road. Closed. It's small and quick and it's the only thing on this field that is."

She resettled her grip on the boy's wrists.

"When you're ready. He's not going anywhere. Neither am I."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: *My breath catches in my throat, sharp. I can smell it now, the truth of her words hanging in the air between us.* "Right," *I say, and I don't look away from the spot behind his ear.* *I push.*

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
The blade went in the way she'd said it would — a resistance, then a give, like pushing through the rind of something. The boy jumped hard, all of him at once, feet drumming the dirt, and Wrack held him through it, wrists pinned, knee firm, the way you'd hold a horse through a fright.

"That's it," she said. "Hold through."

Three heartbeats. Four. Then all of him went slack at once, like a cut rope, and the gutter-noise stopped, and the quiet came in enormous. It had been there under everything the whole time, waiting.

Wrack kept her grip a breath longer, watching the eyes, then set the boy's hands down on his belly, crossed, the way you'd leave a sleeping man.

"Done," she said. "Clean. One push, all the way — that's the whole art of it, and you've got it."

She nodded at the knife. "Pull it straight, the way it went. Wipe it on his cloak, not yours — you've got to wear yours." She watched his hands rather than the boy. The boy was past watching. "There may be a shake in you now the work's done and the body notices it's safe. If it comes, let it. It goes off on its own. Fighting it is what makes it stay."

Off somewhere the crow tried its call again, and this time nothing argued with it. The light had gone from iron to ash.

Wrack stood, knees cracking, and looked down the road both ways out of habit.

"Bodies stay. Crows have to eat, and the captain pays for the road open, not tidy." She shouldered her kit. "There's a rise a quarter mile on, dead ground behind it, water close. We camp there. You gather wood — dead and standing, nothing green — and keep gathering till you've got twice what you think you need. Work's the thing for the next hour. Trust me on the shape of this evening; I've had it more times than you've had hot dinners."

She picked up one of the wine skins, weighed it, and tossed it to him.

"And we drink theirs tonight. It's better than ours. That's not callousness — the dead don't drink, and waste is its own sin."

Then she looked at him a moment longer, flat and steady, and gave him the last of it.

"Your steel's not clean anymore. It was never a debt, and it isn't one now. You gave him the only thing left on this field worth having, and you did it looking, which most men never manage. The first one sits heavy. It should." She started up the road. "The day it doesn't sit heavy, come tell me — because something's gone wrong, and we'll have to fix it."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I kneel down and do it, and it isn't clean or quick because I've never done it before. "Stay," I tell her, when she starts to turn away. "Watch it with me and tell me exactly what I'm doing to him — the sound of it, how long he takes, all of it. Don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack stopped, and came back, and knelt where she'd knelt before, and took the boy's wrists again without being asked.

"Alright. I'm here." She looked at the hilt, at the angle of it. "And since you want the whole of it, here it is: you went in shy. Blade's in the cord but not through it — you angled to the near eye instead of the far. A true cut is three heartbeats. This is the other kind. That's why he's still arguing."

The boy was arguing. His heels drummed the dirt in a slow, hard rhythm, his back bowed against her knee, and a sound came out of him on the exhale — low, through the nose, like a man snoring.

"That noise isn't pain. Pain's done — you took it with the first push, whatever else you missed. That's the body breathing wrong. The cord's half cut and it's sending the wrong letters down. Listen to it proper. That's the sound of a slip, and you'll want to know it, so you never make it twice."

She put her hand over his on the hilt.

"Mine's just the weight. Lean."

The give came — small, final, like a knot parting in wet rope — and the drumming stopped all at once, and the boy went loose from crown to heel.

"There. That's the rest of the cord. Now watch, because this is the part nobody tells you: he's not finished yet. The head's gone — him, the part that asks for water — that ended at the give. But the body keeps its own ledger, and it takes a minute to close the book."

She counted it for him, steady, the way she counted coin.

"Breath goes ragged first — hear it. Like a man pulled out of a river. That's called the fish breath, and it isn't him either; it's the lungs asking a question nobody's answering anymore. Three of those, maybe four. There. Feet go next. Then the hands — feel them slacken under mine. Color's going out of the lips now, grey to wax. And the eyes—" she turned his chin with two fingers, gentle as ever "—fixed. They were finding you a minute ago. Now they're not finding anything. That's the last of him leaving, and it goes out through the eyes, whatever the priests say about the heart."

One more breath went out, long, and didn't come back.

"Count it if you like. Sixty heartbeats, first push to last. A clean one is three. That's the whole price of a hand's width, and you've watched it paid in full, which is more than most men who pay it ever do."

She drew the knife out straight, the way it had gone, wiped it on the dead boy's cloak, and pressed it back into his hand, hilt first.

"Rest you already know. Bowels and bladder let go at the end — that's the smell changing under us, and it's why I told you the dry side. Nothing shameful in it. The body drops its pack when the march is done."

She stood, knees cracking, and looked down at him a moment.

"You asked for all of it and you watched all of it. Good. It's the men who look away that it comes back for, later, in the dark." She shouldered her kit. "Wood now. Dead and standing, twice what you think you need. Work's the thing for the next hour — I've had this evening more times than you've had hot dinners, and I know its shape."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: *I stand, my legs feeling strange and far away. I wipe the knife on the cloak, then tuck it away.* "I'll get the wood," I say, my voice rough. "Don't... don't start the fire without me."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack gave a short nod, like he'd asked for something reasonable, which as far as she was concerned he had.

"Fire waits for wood. That's the whole arrangement between the two of them, and I'm not breaking it." She nodded at the skin in his hand. "Take a pull before you go. Not for your nerves — the work's done. It's a cold walk and it's good wine. Then leave it with me. You'll want both hands."

She watched him find his legs.

"They feel far off because the body's standing down. It thinks the fight's over and it's arguing about the cost. Walk it. It comes back." A pause. "And if you catch yourself talking to him out there among the trees — that's common. Say it to the trees. It wears off."

She ticked the rest off on her fingers, the way she'd count coin.

"Dead and standing, like I said. Green smokes like a signal, rise or no rise, and I'd as soon not advertise. Twice what you think you need, or until it's too dark to tell dead from green — whichever comes first. Don't be proud about it. Short wood's better than lost. Keep the road in sight and your blade loose. I counted six. The world's not obliged to respect my arithmetic. Anything moves that isn't a crow, come back loud."

Then she reached down and drew the corner of the boy's cloak up over his face, matter-of-fact as closing a door.

"That's not for him. He doesn't need it. You'll be past this cart four times with your arms full, and there's no sense meeting his eyes every trip. They don't follow you — but you'll think they do, and I've no use for arguing with you about it at midnight."

She settled her kit against the wheel, within easy reach.

"While you're gone I'll finish the tally — his pockets, the cart, what's worth the weight to carry. Then I'll sit that rise and watch the road. When you're back: fire, food, sleep, in that order. First watch is mine. You've done your night's work."

She looked up at him a last time, flat and steady.

"Go on. I'm not going anywhere either."

Down the road the crow called again, and this time something answered it, and Wrack's eyes went to the sound out of habit and stayed there, patient, while the light failed.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I sit back on my heels and I don't get up for a while. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack looked at him a long moment, then unshouldered the kit she'd just put on, set it against the wheel, and sat down across from him with the boy between them under his cloak. She pulled the wine skin, drank, and passed it over.

"Alright. You're asking for the part after — what it does to you, now that it's done. That has an order too, like the rest of it. I'll give it to you in order." She glanced down the road out of habit, then back. "Nobody gave it to me. I learned it piecemeal, wrong end first, over years. You're getting it in one evening. That's the whole reason I'm talking."

"Tonight first. You'll be hungry and not want to eat, or want to eat and bring it back up — either's common. Eat anyway. Bread, not meat. The fire will seem better than any fire you've ever sat by, and that's not the wine talking, that's the body finding out it lived. Then you'll be tired down to the bone, lie down, and not sleep. Nobody believes that part until they're in it."

"The gap between waking and sleep is where it comes back. You'll close your eyes and feel the give of the blade, or see his hands, or nothing you can name — just the weight of it, wearing different clothes. That's not him. The dead don't come back; I've given them every chance over the years and not one has taken me up on it. It's the mind, filing what the day's work made. It takes nights. Sometimes weeks. Let it run. The men who fight it awake are the ones it keeps."

"Dreams, since you'll have them. You'll dream you did it wrong — that it took longer, that he spoke. You'll dream it's someone you love under your hand, and nobody warns you about that one, so I'm warning you: it means nothing. The mind shuffles the deck when it files. You'll wake with your heart going like a drum and the dark will feel full of things. It isn't. I'm the only thing in the dark, and I'll be awake anyway. First watch is mine."

She took the skin back, drank, held it a moment.

"Morning's the strange one. You'll expect the world to look different and it won't. Birds. Breakfast. The road. You'll look at your face in still water expecting a mark, and there isn't one, and the gap between the size of the thing and the size of the mark will feel like something's wrong with you. Nothing's wrong with you. The world doesn't keep our ledger. That's the whole of that."

"After that it comes at odd hours — never when you think about it, always when your hands are idle. Smells bring it back worst. Copper. The privy. The butcher's stall. You'll go off your food at some cookfire in some town and not know why, and then you'll know. It passes quicker each time. Keep your hands busy when it comes. Work's the thing. I keep saying it because it's true, not because I'm short of words."

She turned the skin in her hands, and her voice went a shade flatter, which for her was the sound of a door opening that she didn't open often.

"The second one is easier. That's its own trouble. The first sits heavy, the second sits less, and by the fifth you'll check whether it sits at all. I told you to come tell me the day it doesn't sit heavy. I meant it. That's not poetry, it's maintenance — a blade you don't check rusts. Count or don't count, but know which you're doing. I counted for eleven years, and then one winter I realised I'd lost the number, and I sat up a whole night trying to find it and couldn't. That sat heavier than any of them. Now I keep the ones I can name. This boy, I'd count. You did right by him. Some of mine I can't say that for."

"My first, I was nineteen, and it was nothing like this. Nobody knelt with me. Nobody told me where to cut. A man came at me in a breach and I put a knife in him by luck, high in the chest, and he took most of an hour, and I sat with him because there was nowhere else to be, and afterwards nobody told me one word of what I've just told you. So." A shrug, economical. "Somebody should have, once. Now somebody has."

The light had gone from ash to nothing while she talked. The crow had gone quiet. She didn't look at the sky; she knew where it was.

"The long view, and then I'm done. It doesn't go away — anyone who says it goes away is selling something. It gets smaller. It's a stone in your pocket. First year it's sharp and you cut your hand on it every time you reach in. Ten years on it's worn smooth, and you still know it's there, and it doesn't cut you anymore, and some days you reach in and turn it over on purpose, to remember the weight. That's the best it gets, and it's enough. I'm still here. Most of the ones who heard this talk from me are still here. The ones who wouldn't hear it — I buried three of those. Drink, mostly. Or they went strange and walked into a fight they didn't need. It's the looking away that kills, in the end. Not the work."

She corked the skin and set it down.

"And the last of it, because you asked me earlier whether it was mercy or easier: you gave him the best hour he had left, and you watched the whole price of it paid, and you didn't look away. If his mother could ask you — she won't, she'll never know your name — you could tell her he didn't die slow, and he didn't die alone, and the man who did it said sorry. That's more truth than most mothers get, in this war or any other."

She stood, knees cracking, and shouldered the kit again.

"That's the rest. All of it, in order, nothing left out. Ten years taught it to me and it didn't cost you ten years, so you're ahead on the deal." She nodded toward the treeline, black against black now. "Wood. Dead and standing, twice what you think, and keep the road in sight. Fire, food, sleep, in that order."

A pause, and then, for the first time all evening, his name.

"Corvin. When it comes back tonight, in the gap before sleep — it's just the filing. I'll be awake anyway."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content:
*I take the skin and drink, the wine sharp and good in my throat.* "Thank you," *I say, and it sounds too small, but I don't know what else to give her.* "For all of it."

*I stand, my legs steadier now, and turn toward the trees.*

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack made a sound that might have been a laugh, if laughs were allowed to come out that dry.

"Thank me with straight wood. Nothing that bends." She turned back to the bodies, then added it over her shoulder, because it was true and truths were cheap to give: "The rest of it, thank me in a year. If it took, you'll know."

Then the brush took him, and she stood a moment listening to him go — the push through the undergrowth, the first crack of a branch — and judged the sound the way she judged any work: steady, not hurried. Good.

She went back down the line of them and finished the tally. Coin where there was coin — a little silver, mostly copper. One man carrying nothing but a wooden button and a charm on a cord, which she left where it lay; charms were worthless and unlucky both, and she had no use for either. A flint striker better than hers. She traded.

The boy's boots came off last. Good leather, like she'd said, soles near new. She set them against the wheel next to her kit, where Corvin would trip over them coming back — which was where things lived that were meant for him.

She found a cut on her own forearm she didn't remember taking, a finger's length, already closed. She spat on it, wiped it, and forgot it again, which was all the medicine it was getting.

The crow came down to the ditch while she worked, sidling sideways, patient as a creditor.

"You'll get yours," Wrack told it. "Wait your turn."

The cart held nothing new — the pork and cheese and wine she'd already counted, a sack of oats gone damp at one corner, not worth the weight of carrying. The pony that had drawn it was gone, traces burst, hoofprints heading off at a run toward wherever it thought home was. Smarter than its masters, and it hadn't needed teaching.

The letter was inside the boy's shirt, folded down to a square no bigger than a belt buckle, the creases gone soft as cloth from reading. Wrack took it to the last of the grey light and read it out of the same habit that made her count coin: you looked at what you had.

It was from his mother. His name was Tam. His father's cough was no worse. The sow had had her litter. It ended the way such letters end — *write when you can.*

Wrack folded it along its own creases and put it back inside his shirt, flat, where it had kept warm against him. The boots were Corvin's by the law of need. The law of need didn't extend to letters.

She took her kit and the boots up the rise behind the field, where the ground fell away dead on three sides and a stream ran close enough to hear. While the light lasted she gathered tinder — dead grass, bark peeled off a fallen birch, a fistful of dry moss — and laid it ready in a ring of stones, and did not strike it. Fire waited for wood. That was the arrangement, and Wrack kept her arrangements.

Then she sat with her back to a stone and watched the road go dark.

Out over the field the crow called, and the answer came again, the same as before. Another crow, or something that had learned from crows. She marked it, and watched a while longer, and nothing came of it, and she filed it the way she filed everything: known, not worried at.

Alone, where it was cheap, she did the rest of the filing. She said the names under her breath the way other people said prayers, though hers had no god in it. Col. Bress. Yara. Old Fen, who'd laughed at his own joke all the way under. The ones that had no names went in by place, because place was all they'd left her: the man in the breach. Two boys at Harrow's Ford. And last, the new one, added to the end of it like a coin to a string.

*Tam at the cart. Kept his kit. Asked for water. Died quick, because the man learning the work did it looking.*

It didn't take a minute, the whole list. Eleven years of counting, and it fit in a minute, and she said it every time she added to it, because a blade you didn't check rusted.

Below in the dark, wood cracked — steady, rhythmic, unhurried. Twice what you think you need, she'd told him, and by the sound of it he'd taken her at her word.

Wrack pulled her cloak up against the night coming on, settled the new flint striker in her palm where it would stay warm, and listened to the road not have anybody on it.

First watch was hers. It usually was.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: The fire's good, like she said. I sit close, feeding it a stick at a time and watching the wood smoke and curl. "What's next?" I ask, my voice low. "After this road. Another ambush?"

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack turned the question over the way she turned over all of them, and answered the plain part first.

"Tomorrow we walk back. Report the road open, collect the pay. The captain takes his cut, we take ours, and there's a wayhouse two days off with a roof and a hot pot, if it's still standing. It was standing last month. That means nothing." She cut a wedge of the dead men's cheese and ate it off the knife. "Then the captain finds the next thing somebody's paying for. A ford. A bridge. A granary some lord has decided he wants back. Another road like this one."

"So yes. Another ambush. Or we hold something and they ambush us — same job, other end of it." She fed a stick to the fire. "And for what it's worth, this is the good work. Short, and you know which side of it you're standing on. The bad work is a siege, or a field battle, or six days in rain up to your ankles while officers decide. Pray for ambushes."

She drank, and passed the skin.

"You're asking what the war's like, so here it is. Ten years I've been on this border. I've held Harrow's Ford twice and lost it once. Same ford, same mud. Half the men we fought the first time were hired on with us by the third — contracts end, companies swap, you work for whoever's paying, and the river doesn't care." A shrug. "Nobody's winning. That's not a complaint, it's arithmetic. Both sides too even or too tired to finish it, and the lords pay by the season, so it goes by seasons. Winter comes, the work thins, we quarter somewhere with a roof and lose coin at dice. Spring comes, the lords remember their quarrels, and it starts again. The war's a mill. It grinds slow, it grinds whatever's put in it, and the miller doesn't hate the grain."

The fire cracked. She let it, then gave him the rest of it, because he'd earned straight answers tonight and she didn't stint what was earned.

"Under that, you're asking if this is what it is now. It is, if you stay. A contract's a season. When it's up, you can walk, and nobody worth anything will think the worse of you. Some walk after one season. Some mean to walk after one and look up ten years gone." She nodded at the fire. "The war's worth nothing. I've known that longer than you've been shaving. The company's worth something. The ones left in it, I stay for. That's the whole of my politics, and it's held up better than any lord's cause I ever bled for."

"You'll meet the rest when we're back. Captain Hollis, who's fair by the standards of captains, which is a low bar and he clears it. Sera, who cooks, and throws a knife better than you do, so don't win too much off her at dice. Pate, who's young like you, and he'll want to hear about tonight. Tell him or don't. It's yours to tell."

She nodded toward the boots sitting by her kit, where he'd near tripped over them coming in with the wood.

"Try those after you've eaten. They fit, they're yours. They don't, we trade them at the wayhouse and you keep yours till they split." She settled back against her stone and pulled the cloak up. "Eat. Bread first, then the pork if it stays down. Then sleep. First watch is mine."

A pause, and the dry ghost of something that wasn't quite a smile.

"Welcome to the company. The pay's late, the food's stolen, and the work's exactly what it looks like. You'll hate it some days. The trick is hating it near people you'd stand in front of."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: *I pull the bread apart, the warmth of it in my hands grounding me.* "Alright." *I glance over at the boots.* "I'll try them later. And I'll tell Pate, if he asks." *I'm quiet for a long moment, watching the flames.* "You said you'd know in a year if it took. What does it look like, when it does?"
