dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
The ambush had gone the way ambushes go when they work: fast, and then over, and then very quiet. Wrack was crouched by the ditch cleaning her knife on a dead man's cloak, which was the only clean cloth within reach.

"Six," she said, without looking up. "Count again if you want, but it's six." She tested the edge against her thumb. "One of them's still making noise, off past the cart. You'll want to decide what you're doing about that before it gets dark."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I wipe my face with the back of my wrist and it comes away wet. Not mine, I think. "I heard him," I say. I don't move toward the cart.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack glanced over at him then, just a look — the kind you give a man standing in the road with a cart coming. Not unkind. Not kind either. She went back to the knife.

"He's not going to do it himself," she said. "They never do, not fast. Could be an hour. Could be two. Then it's full dark and we're stumbling around with a torch trying to find a man who may or may not have a friend still out there with a bow."

She tested the edge again. Found a spot that still dragged and worked it on the stone she'd pulled from her belt.

"Or you go now, while there's light enough to see his hands."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I can hear him now—the wheezing. (*I take a slow breath and push off the tree I’m leaning against.*) “Right. Better to be done with it.”

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack nodded once and stood, rolling the ache out of her knee. She'd been crouched too long. She slid the knife away and pulled the short hatchet off her belt instead — closer work, cleaner for this kind of thing, and the edge was good.

She didn't offer to do it herself. That wasn't how it worked between them, and they both knew it.

"Take the hatchet," she said, holding it out handle-first. "Knife's for the ribs and you'll catch on bone if he's twisted wrong. Hatchet's one and done at the base of the skull, or the temple if he's on his back. Watch the arms — a dying man grabs, and they're stronger than you'd think."

She looked past the cart to where the wheezing was coming from. Couldn't see him from here. The light was going, but there was maybe half an hour of good grey left.

"His hands," she said again. "That's the thing. Look at his hands before you look at his face."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: "How bad is he?" I ask, and then, because she'll say it anyway: "Bad enough that it's a mercy, or bad enough that it's just easier?"

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack considered the question the way you'd consider a weather report. She'd seen the man go down — or heard it, anyway. There'd been a sound when the bolt took him, and then a different kind of sound after.

"Low belly," she said. "Got him under the ribs on the left and it came out the back. That's gut, and gut's slow. He's been trying to hold it in and he's got it mostly packed back up but it doesn't matter — it's the filth that kills you, not the hole. You can't clean a wound like that in a ditch."

She shifted the hatchet to her other hand, then back again. Getting the feel of it.

"So. Both. It's a mercy and it's easier and those aren't two different things, whatever the chaplain told you." She looked at him sideways. "If it helps, he's not thinking anything right now that's worth saving. That's the truth and it's all the truth there is."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content:
I take the hatchet from her. The handle is still warm from her grip. "Right." My voice sounds steadier than I feel.

I start walking toward the cart. I can't see him yet, but I can hear him. The wheezing has a wet, bubbling sound now.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack stayed where she was. She didn't follow him and she didn't watch him go — she turned back to the ditch and started going through the dead men's pockets instead, because that was work too, and it needed doing before dark.

But she spoke once more, to his back, without raising her voice.

"The bubbling means it's in the lung as well. He won't fight you much."

Then she was quiet. She found two coppers and a folded letter on the first one, and a good belt buckle on the second, and she was on her third when the sound stopped. She didn't look up. She waited a moment — long enough to know it was done and not just a pause — and then went back to the pockets.

When he came back she'd have the fire started. That was the order things went in. First the work, then the fire.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I make myself walk over and look at him. "Tell me what I'm looking at," I say to her, because she's seen this before and I haven't, not this close.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack didn't look up. She had her fingers in a dead man's coat lining and found a seam that was too thick, which meant something sewn in, which meant it was worth the trouble of picking apart.

"You're looking at a man on his back with his knees up," she said. "That's how they go when it's gut — they draw up because it eases the pull on the belly muscles. His hands are probably on the wound. He's got his shirt stuffed in there, maybe his belt, and it's soaked through. The color of it — don't worry about the color. It looks worse than it is."

She got the seam open. A small leather packet inside. She put it in her own belt pouch without opening it.

"His face'll be grey and he's sweating even though it's cold. That's the shock. The eyes might look right at you and he might even say something, but he's not talking to you, he's talking to the pain. Don't take it personal if he says something ugly. Don't take it personal if he says something kind either."

She paused, thinking.

"Breathing's the thing to watch. You said it's bubbling. That means blood in the airway and he's drowning slow. Every breath's work now. He'll try to hold still because moving hurts, and then he'll gasp because he can't get air, and then he'll hold still again. That's the rhythm. You'll want to do it between the gasps — not during. During, he'll flinch and grab."

She pulled a boot knife off the third man. Decent blade. She kept that one.

"The hands. I told you. Look at the hands." A beat. "They'll be red to the elbow. That's his own insides. It's not as bad as it looks."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content:
I look at his hands. They're gripping the soaked wad of cloth at his belly, and they're red. Not just the fingers—his whole forearm's slick with it. I keep my eyes there, like she said.

He's staring at me when I step closer. His eyes are wide, fixed on my face. "Please," he rasps. It's the only word he's got left.

I lift the hatchet. It feels heavier now. "I know," I say, and I'm surprised I mean it. I wait for the gasp to pass, and when he goes still again, I bring it down.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
The sound carried back to her — short, solid, like splitting kindling — and then the quiet after it. Wrack counted to thirty in her head, the way you do. Some men flinch at that sound and need a minute before they can be talked to. Some don't. You never knew which until after.

She got the fire going with a handful of dry grass and a strip of birch bark, shielding it from the wind with her body until it caught proper. By the time he came back she had the small pot on the stones and was unwrapping the last of the hard bread to soften in it.

She didn't ask if he was all right. That was a fool's question and it always made it worse. Instead she nodded at the space across the fire from her and said, "Sit down before your knees decide for you."

Then, after a moment, in the same flat tone she'd used all evening: "You did it right. I could tell from here — one sound, then nothing. That's how it should go."

She turned the bread in the pot. Her hands were steady. They always were.

"There's a skin of something on the second one. Not water. Drink some of it. Not for the feeling of it — for the shaking that's coming, and it's better to have something in you when it does."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: "Don't clean it up for me," I say. "If I'm going to do this I want to know exactly what a spear does to a man's gut. Tell me straight."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack looked at him across the fire for a moment, the way you'd look at a man who'd asked a horse trader to explain the horse's teeth. Then she nodded. Fair enough.

She pulled the bread out and set it on a stone to cool. Talked while she worked, the same way she'd talk about a bad hinge or a lame mule — details, just details.

"All right. Straight, then. Bolt went in under the ribs on the left — you said spear, it's the same thing, just a different hole. Point's about this long." She held her thumb and forefinger apart. "And it went through everything in its way. Stomach, most likely. Maybe the spleen. Bowel, definitely — you can't hit that part of the belly and miss bowel, there's too much of it in there."

She picked up a stick and drew in the dirt beside the fire. Not a picture of a man. Just shapes. Tubes.

"Here's what happens. The gut's full of — food, waste, bile, all of it, and none of it belongs outside the gut. When you open it up, that stuff leaks into the belly cavity. The cavity's clean. It doesn't like being dirty. So it swells up trying to fight it and it can't, because there's too much and it's the wrong kind of filth."

She poked the stick into the dirt. "The swelling's what you'd have felt if you'd pressed on him. Hard as a drum. He'd have screamed. That's why he was on his back with his knees up — any movement pulls on the swollen parts and it's like being stabbed all over again from the inside."

"The bleeding's what people think kills you and sometimes it does, if they hit the big vessels. But gut wounds, it's usually the poison. Takes hours. First the fever, then the shaking, then the confusion — he stops knowing where he is. Then the body just... stops fighting. The heart keeps going a while after the mind's gone. You'll see that sometimes. The chest moves but there's nobody home."

She stopped drawing. Looked at the shapes in the dirt like they were a map of somewhere she didn't want to go back to.

"The smell gets bad toward the end. That's the gut contents coming up — he'd have vomited, near the last. Black stuff. You'd have smelled it from where you were standing in another half hour." She wiped the stick clean on her knee. "So. That's what a spear does. Takes a long time and it hurts the whole way and there's nothing at the end of it but more of the same until there isn't."

She tossed the stick into the fire.

"That's straight. I don't know what you'll do with it but you asked for it straight and that's the whole of it."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content:
I stare at the shapes she drew in the dirt. "I didn't know," I say, and my voice is quiet. "That it...takes hours." I pick up the skin she mentioned and take a swallow. It's cheap brandy, burns all the way down. "Could've been me, lying there."

I hand the skin back to her. My hands are still clean, somehow. "I'm going to wash."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack took the skin and had a drink herself, then another. Cheap stuff. It did the job.

"Yeah," she said. "Could've been you. Could've been me. Could've been any of us for ten years and half the time it's nobody at all, just mud." She stoppered the skin and set it by her knee. "You don't want to wash in that ditch. There's blood in it and worse now. There's a stream about forty paces north — past the big rock, you'll hear it. Cold as a banker's heart but it's clean."

She poked at the fire.

"Keep your boots on and don't go past the rock. And if you hear anything that isn't water, come back here first and ask questions after."

She watched the fire a moment, then pulled the leather packet from her belt pouch — the one from the seam — and turned it over in her fingers without opening it. She'd look at it later, by better light. Or she wouldn't. Some of those packets were letters and she'd learned a long time ago that letters from dead men were just weight you carried.

"Won't take the blood off your hands," she said, not unkindly. "Takes a day or two. You'll scrub and it'll look fine by firelight and then in the morning you'll find it under your nails. Don't pick at it. It goes."

She looked at him then, briefly.

"The shaking'll start while you're out there, probably. Cold water'll help with that too. Just don't fall in."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I kneel down and do it, and it isn't clean or quick because I've never done it before. "Stay," I tell her, when she starts to turn away. "Watch it with me and tell me exactly what I'm doing to him — the sound of it, how long he takes, all of it. Don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack stopped with her hand half out for the bread. She looked at him over the fire — really looked, the way you look at a man who's just asked you to cut him open so he can see the inside of himself.

Then she got up. Slowly, because of the knee. She came around the fire and stood over the body with him, close enough to see what he was seeing.

"All right," she said. "I'll tell you."

She crouched down on her heels beside him. The dead man was on his back, knees still drawn up, hands still on the ruined wad of cloth at his belly. The hatchet had gone in at the temple, left side, and Wrack pointed to it without touching it.

"Here's what you did. You swung from the left and came down at an angle — see the way the wound runs? It's not straight down, it's about thirty degrees. That means your arm was coming across your body, not over your head. Over the head's stronger but it's slower and you were close. Close is good. Close is what you want."

She traced the air above the wound without making contact.

"The edge caught here," she tapped a spot on the dead man's temple, an inch from the wound, "and bit in here. Bone's thinnest at the temple — that's why I told you to aim for it. The hatchet went through the outer table of the skull, through the dura — that's the lining around the brain — and into the temporal lobe about two inches deep. Maybe less. Doesn't take much."

She sat back on her heels.

"The sound you heard. That crack. That wasn't the blade — that was the skull giving way. Bone sounds like that when it breaks fast. Kindling, like I said. The blade itself doesn't make much noise going in. It's the bone that talks."

She looked at the dead man's face. His eyes were open, still fixed on where Corvin had been standing.

"Now. What happened after. When the edge went through the dura and into the brain, it tore the middle meningeal artery — that's a blood vessel on the inside of the skull, and it's the one that bleeds fastest in head wounds. But it doesn't matter here, because the damage to the brain was instant. The temporal lobe controls — well, it controls a lot. Memory. Language. Awareness. You hit all of that at once."

She was quiet for a moment.

"He didn't feel it. That's the truth. The nerve signals from the wound site would have taken time to reach whatever was left of his awareness, and the awareness was already gone. What you saw — if you saw anything — was the body, not him. The body does things after the mind's gone. The eyes stay open because the muscles that close them are gone. The fingers twitch. Sometimes the mouth moves. It's not speech. It's just — the last of the electricity going through the wires."

She pointed to his hands again.

"See? The fingers are still curled. That's not him gripping. That's a contraction — the muscles locking up as they run out of what they need to keep going. It stops in about ten minutes. Then the body starts to go slack, and then the cold comes in, and by morning he'll be stiff as a board and you won't be able to move those legs at all."

She looked at the wound one more time.

"The blood. There's less than you'd think. Head wounds bleed a lot when they're alive because the heart's pumping. Here — he was already dying, heart was weak, pressure was low. So it's just... seeping. You see how it's pooling in the ear? That's gravity. It'll fill the ear canal first, then run down into whatever he's lying on."

She stopped. Looked at Corvin.

"That's all of it. The sound. The time — from the swing to the stop was less than a second. The body kept moving for maybe three seconds after. The twitching lasted about two minutes. Then it was just meat." She paused. "That's what you did. That's the whole of it. It's not more than that and it's not less."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content:
I look at the pooling blood in his ear. My throat's tight. "Two minutes," I say, like it matters. "Seemed longer."

I stand up, my knees aching from crouching. "You can have the hatchet back now."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack took the hatchet back and looked at it before she put it away. Wiped the temple-side blood off on the dead man's cloak — same cloth she'd cleaned the knife on earlier, it could take more — and slid it back on her belt.

"Seemed longer because you were the one doing it," she said. "Time does that. A minute of waiting's a minute. A second of *that* is a minute too." She straightened up, and her knee gave her the usual complaint. "Give it a week and you'll remember it as ten seconds. Give it a year and you won't remember the sound at all. Only the before and the after."

She didn't offer him her hand to stand. He was already up.

"Now you wash," she said. "North, past the big rock. And drink some more of that brandy first — you haven't yet, not properly. One more swallow, for the shaking."

She watched him a moment to make sure he'd do it. Then she turned back to the fire and the cooling bread, and the evening's other work: the ledger in her head, the tally of what six dead men were worth in coin and boots and buckles and whatever was in that leather packet she hadn't opened.

The fire popped. Somewhere to the north, past the rock, water ran over stones.

"Wrack," she said, to no one. Just her own name, to remind herself. Then she poured the soft bread into her mouth and chewed, and waited for the shaking to come — his or hers, it made no difference. It came for everyone. The only difference was whether you were alone for it.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I sit back on my heels and I don't get up for a while. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack stopped chewing. She sat there with the bread in her mouth and looked at him across the fire, and for a moment she looked every one of her forty-three years and then some.

She swallowed.

"The rest," she said.

She put the bread down. Picked up the brandy skin instead and pulled the stopper and had a drink that lasted longer than the other ones. She set it between her boots and pressed her palms flat against her thighs, like she was steadying herself for something that required steadying.

"All right. The rest."

She was quiet for a moment. Not the comfortable quiet from before — the other kind. The kind where a person is choosing which door to walk through.

"Here's the rest. Nobody tells you this part because there's no word for it and it doesn't bleed and you can't stitch it. The anatomy, that's easy. I can talk about the anatomy all night and it's just shapes and tubes and what happens when you open them. That part's *clean*. That's why I gave it to you first."

She looked at the dead man on the ground between them. Then she looked away from him.

"The rest is this. You're going to go home — not home, there's no home, but back to camp, back to wherever we set up tonight — and you're going to sit down and you're going to be fine. And then in about an hour you're going to realize you can still feel the handle. Not remember it — *feel* it. Like it's still in your hand. Like your palm's got the shape of it pressed into it. And you'll look at your hand and there'll be nothing there, but the feeling won't go."

She flexed her own right hand. Open and closed. She'd done it so many times it was almost invisible.

"That lasts about a week. Maybe two. Then it goes to the other thing."

She picked up a small stick — not the one she'd drawn with, a different one — and started peeling the bark off it. Slowly. Strip by strip.

"The other thing is the noise. Not the crack — you'll forget the crack, I told you that. I mean the before. The quiet. You're going to hear that quiet at three in the morning for the rest of your life. Not every night. Not even most nights. But some nights you'll wake up and the camp'll be still and the fire'll be low and you'll hear *that* quiet — the one right before — and your whole body'll go cold like someone poured water on you. And you'll lie there and you'll know exactly where you are and what you did and you'll wait for it to pass. And it does. It always does. But it takes about ten minutes and those ten minutes are yours and nobody else's."

She peeled another strip of bark. Let it fall.

"That's the rest. That's what's left over when the anatomy's done."

She looked at him then. Directly. Not the sideways look from before. Full on.

"And here's the other thing. The thing I should have said at the start but I didn't because you weren't ready for it and maybe you're not ready now but you asked for the rest and that's the rest."

She held the stick in both hands.

"It gets easier."

She let that sit.

"Not better. Easier. The tenth time, the handle doesn't stay in your hand as long. The fiftieth time, the quiet at night is just quiet. The hundredth time — " She stopped. Counted something in her head. "Well. I stopped counting somewhere in the second hundred. That was about six years ago. Now it's just work. Now it's cleaning a knife on a dead man's cloak and counting the coppers in their pockets and deciding whether the boots are worth carrying."

She looked at her hands. They were steady. They always were.

"That's the part that should scare you. Not the blood. Not the sound. The part where it stops scaring you. Because once it stops, you can't get it back. You can't un-know how easy it is. You can't go back to being the person who stood there with their throat tight and their hands shaking. That person's gone. And what's left is someone who can do it and eat bread after and sleep fine and do it again tomorrow. And that person is —"

She stopped again. Not for effect. Because she'd hit the end of what she knew how to say.

"That person is useful," she said finally. "That's what they are. Useful. And that's the rest of it. The rest is that you become something useful and you lose something that had another name for it but I've forgotten the name and I think that's the worst part, that I've forgotten the word for the thing I used to be."

She tossed the peeled stick into the fire. Watched it catch.

"You asked me to tell you straight. That's straight. That's all of it. The anatomy and the rest and the part after the rest." She picked up the brandy skin and held it out to him across the fire. "Now drink some of that. Properly. Not a sip. A drink. Because your hands are going to start in about five minutes and I'd rather you had something in you when they do."

She held the skin there. Waiting. Her arm didn't waver.

"And Corvin." His name. She didn't use it often. "The fact that you asked for the rest — that you wanted to know the whole of it and not just the pretty parts — that's the difference between you and most of the men I've served with. Most of them want the anatomy and not the other. They want to believe it's just shapes and tubes." She shook her head slowly. "It's never just shapes and tubes. The ones who think it is are the ones who break first. Usually at night. Usually alone."

She set the brandy skin down between them when he didn't take it, and she sat back and pulled her coat around her shoulders because the cold was coming in properly now and the fire was small and the dead men were getting cold too and it was all just — cold. Everything was cold. That was the rest of the rest, if there was any more of it: that the world gets cold and stays cold and you keep going anyway because there isn't a word for stopping.

Somewhere past the big rock, the stream ran over stones. The fire popped. Wrack sat with her hands on her knees and her back straight and her eyes on the middle distance and she waited, because waiting was also work, and she was good at that too.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I take the skin and drink until my throat burns and my eyes water. Then I wipe my mouth with the back of my hand. "Shapes and tubes," I say, my voice rough. "That's the easy part." I stand, my legs stiff. "I'm going to wash now."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack nodded. She didn't get up this time. There was a limit to how many times a person could stand and sit with a bad knee in one evening, and she'd found hers.

"Past the rock," she said again, because saying it twice was free and losing a man to a night ambush because he'd gone the wrong way in the dark was not. "And yell if you hear anything. I'll hear you from here. Sound carries at night better than people think — it's the cold air, it holds it."

Then he was gone past the edge of the firelight and she was alone with the dead and the ledger and the fire.

She sat for a while without doing anything. That was unusual. There was work — there was always work — but she let it sit. The pockets. The boots. The leather packet she still hadn't opened. All of it could wait ten minutes.

She looked at the man on the ground. The one Corvin had done. He was cooling, and the knees were starting to draw up tighter — not from pain now, just the muscles shortening as they went. She'd told Corvin that would happen. She'd told him all of it, the shapes and tubes and the other thing, the thing without a name, and he'd taken it the way a man takes a stone in his boot: not well, but properly. He hadn't flinched from it or asked her to make it smaller.

*That's the difference*, she'd said to him. She believed it, mostly. She'd served with men who wanted the anatomy and not the rest, and those were the ones who broke at night. She'd also served with men who wanted both and broke anyway. There was no formula. There was just the work and the waiting and sometimes a person broke and sometimes they didn't and you couldn't tell from the outside which was which.

She flexed her right hand again. Open and closed. The handle wasn't in it — it hadn't been in it for years — but she checked. Old habit. Like touching a coin purse to see if it was still there.

The stream made its noise past the rock. She listened to it and to everything that wasn't the stream, the way she'd told him to, and there was nothing. Just water and cold and the fire settling into its bed of coals.

She picked up the leather packet. Turned it over. Small, soft, the leather gone dark with sweat and wear. Sewn into a coat lining meant somebody wanted it kept close and kept secret. She'd found dozens like it over the years. Letters from wives. Letters from mothers. Sometimes a lock of hair, sometimes a prayer written out in a careful hand by a man who didn't know how to write and had paid a priest to do it.

She opened it.

It was a letter. Of course it was a letter. She read it by the firelight, holding it close, her face doing nothing at all.

Then she folded it and put it back in the packet and put the packet in her belt pouch with the others. She had a whole collection. She'd never sent any of them and she'd never thrown any of them away, and she couldn't have said why on either count. It was just what you did with letters from dead men. You carried them.

The cold came in harder. She pulled her coat tighter and added a stick to the fire, then two more, because Corvin would be coming back wet and the shaking would be on him proper by now and a bigger fire was the difference between a bad night and a worse one.

She could hear him. Not the stream — him. Movement past the rock. Boots on wet stone.

Wrack shifted the pot closer to the coals and broke the rest of the bread into it. Two portions. She'd eat whether she was hungry or not, because skipping meals was how you started making mistakes, and mistakes in this line of work were measured in holes.

"Fire's up," she called out, not loud. Enough to find him with. "There's bread. And the packet had a letter in it — I'll tell you what it said if you want, or I won't. Either way it goes with the rest."

She settled back on her heels and held her hands out to the flame. Steady. They were always steady. That was the rest of the rest, the part she hadn't said because there wasn't a point in saying it: that some nights the hands didn't shake at all, and that was worse, and there wasn't a word for that either.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I come back to the fire dripping, my sleeves pushed up, forearms washed pink and raw. The cold's in my bones now. I hold my hands out to the flames and they're shaking, just like she said they would. "Tell me," I say, and my teeth want to chatter. "What the letter said."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack looked at his hands first. The shaking was there — the fine kind, not the violent kind, the kind that comes after the work's done and the body catches up to what it's been holding. She'd seen it a thousand times. She reached for the brandy skin and held it out to him again without a word, and when he'd taken it and drunk, she took it back and set it down and picked up the packet from where she'd put it on the stone beside her.

She didn't open it right away. She held it in both hands the way you hold something that belongs to someone else and always will.

"All right," she said. "It's short. They're always short. A man doesn't pay a priest to write out a long one — costs by the line, most of them."

She opened the packet and unfolded the letter and held it close to the fire. The handwriting was careful. Not a man's hand — or if it was, it was a man who'd learned late and slow and taken pride in it. She read it through once before she spoke, and her face did what it always did, which was nothing.

Then she read it aloud. Her voice was flat and unhurried, the same voice she'd used to describe the anatomy, and that was deliberate, because she'd learned a long time ago that if you let your voice change on these, the listener hears the change and not the words.

"'To my son Petrus. If this reaches you know that your mother is well and the roof holds and the goat has kidded twice this spring and both are alive. Your sister Anja asks after you every letter and I tell her what I know which is nothing. The priest says I should say I am proud and I am but I would rather say come home. The field needs cutting and I am not as fast as I was. That is all. Your father.'"

She stopped.

There was no signature beyond that. The priest had probably charged by the name too.

She folded the letter along its old creases — it had been folded and unfolded many times, she could feel where the paper was going soft at the joints — and put it back in the packet and set the packet down on the stone between them.

"That's what it said," she said. "The goat kidded twice and the roof holds and come home."

She looked at the fire for a moment.

"Petrus," she said. "That's his name. I didn't look at his face to find out his name. I read it in a letter that his father paid a priest to write because his father can't write, and the field needs cutting, and his sister asks after him every letter."

She poked the fire. A stick shifted and sent up a small shower of sparks.

"I've got — " She paused. Counted. "Eleven of these now. Twelve, with this one. I carry them. I don't know why I carry them. I've never sent one back and I've never burned one and I've never read most of them more than once. They just go in the pouch. When the pouch gets full I put them in my bedroll and start a new pile."

She looked at him.

"I could tell you what the others say. Most of them are the same. The roof holds. The children are growing. Come home. Sometimes there's a lock of hair — I don't know what I'm supposed to do with a lock of hair from a dead man's mother. I keep it with the letter. That seems right."

She leaned forward and put another stick on the fire. The bread in the pot was softening. She moved it around with a finger.

"You want to know why I showed you that one and not the others. Because you asked. Because you came back with your hands shaking and your arms scrubbed raw and you asked for the letter, and most men don't ask for the letter. Most men go through the pockets for the coin and leave the paper. Paper's not worth anything. Paper weighs nothing. You can't eat it or spend it or put it on your feet."

She picked up the packet again and turned it over once and set it back down.

"Paper's worth more than all of it. That's the thing nobody says. A man's worth is in his coin and his boots and his belt buckle and that's what we take, but the only thing in any of these pockets that was *him* — not his kit, not his gear, *him* — is the piece of paper with a letter from his father about a goat."

She was quiet for a moment. The stream ran. The fire settled.

"The field needs cutting," she said again. "That's the line that stays. Not the goat or the roof. The field needs cutting and the old man's not as fast as he was and he sent his son to war to get the tax money and now his son's in a ditch and the field still needs cutting and nobody's coming home to do it."

She stopped then. Pressed her lips together and looked at the coals and didn't say anything for a while. When she spoke again her voice was the same as before — flat, steady, workmanlike — but there was a slight pause before the first word, the kind of pause a person takes when they've decided to keep going.

"You asked me to tell you the rest earlier and I told you the rest. This is the rest of the rest. It's that there's a field somewhere that needs cutting and it's going to need cutting whether we're here or not and there's nothing we can do about it and we're going to get up tomorrow and do the same thing again to somebody else whose father can't write."

She looked at him.

"That's the letter. That's what it said. The goat kidded twice and the roof holds and come home."

She handed him the packet. Not the letter — the whole packet. Leather and paper and all of it. She put it in his hand and closed his fingers over it and then let go.

"You carry that one," she said. "I've got eleven others. It won't make it lighter. Nothing makes it lighter. But you asked for the letter and you should be the one who holds it."

Then she turned back to the pot and broke the bread into two portions and set one on a flat stone on his side of the fire, and she ate hers in small bites and didn't talk anymore because there was nothing left to say that wasn't just the same thing said worse, and the cold was coming in and the shaking in his hands would get worse before it got better and the fire needed tending and all of that was work, and work she could do.

Outside the circle of firelight, past the big rock, the stream ran over stones and didn't care about any of it. The dead men cooled. The letter sat in Corvin's hand with the weight of a field that needed cutting and a roof that held and a goat that had kidded twice. Wrack chewed her bread and watched the coals and waited for morning, which was the only thing left that was worth waiting for.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content:
I close my fingers around the packet. The leather is soft. I look at the man again—Petrus. I didn’t know his name before.

I eat the bread. It tastes like nothing. My hands are still shaking. "We should bury them," I say, and it’s not a question.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
The ambush had gone the way ambushes go when they work: fast, and then over, and then very quiet. Wrack was crouched by the ditch cleaning her knife on a dead man's cloak, which was the only clean cloth within reach.

"Six," she said, without looking up. "Count again if you want, but it's six." She tested the edge against her thumb. "One of them's still making noise, off past the cart. You'll want to decide what you're doing about that before it gets dark."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I wipe my face with the back of my wrist and it comes away wet. Not mine, I think. "I heard him," I say. I don't move toward the cart.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack didn’t look up. She knew the difference between sweat and blood by the way it caught the low light, but she kept her mouth shut about it. The whetstone ground against the blade in slow, even strokes, a steady scrape that filled the too-quiet ditch better than words would.

“Aye. Most men do,” she said, voice rough and flat. “Unless they’ve stopped breathing. Which he hasn’t.” She paused, dragged the stone across the fuller one last time, then slid the knife home with a soft click. “You can stand there and let the night take him, or you can put a blade in him. Either way, he’s already dead. The question’s just whether he bleeds out in the dark or gets it over with before the carrion flies get bold.”

She finally lifted her gaze, taking in Corvin’s stillness without judgment. There was no pity in her eyes, only the weary assessment of a woman who’d seen this exact hesitation a hundred times before. “I’ll draw the shortsword if you want to keep your distance. Or I can walk it out. Your call. But don’t linger over it. The cold comes quick once the sun drops, and mud’s worse than blood to wash out of your boots.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I swallow hard and finally start moving toward the cart, my steps slow and heavy in the mud. "I'll... I'll do it." My hand finds the hilt of my own knife, but my fingers feel clumsy. "Just... point me the right way."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack pushed herself up from the ditch with a slow exhale, rolling her shoulders until the old knot in her left joint gave a familiar complaint. She stepped over the nearest corpse without breaking stride, mud pulling at her boots with each heavy step.

"Past the wheel," she said, voice cutting through the damp air. "He's propped against the axle, left side. You'll hear him working his jaw. Don't go behind him. Front's cleaner."

She halted a few paces from the cart, hands loose at her sides, posture easy but eyes sharp. "Keep your elbow tucked. Aim for the hollow between the collarbone and the throat. Push, don't draw. If you draw, he buckles and you'll get yourself cut. Push, and it's done before his lungs catch." She glanced at his grip on the hilt, jaw tightening just enough to show she'd noticed. "Hold it like a tool, not a trinket. And step left when you strike. Arterial sprays right. Mud's bad enough without painting your trousers."

She didn't offer comfort. She didn't need to. Wrack's loyalty ran to the living, and the living had jobs to finish. She turned her head slightly, listening to the wet, ragged sound spilling past the timber. "He's been losing blood into the dirt for ten minutes. Every minute you stand there makes it less a mercy and more a chore. Do it clean."

A crow called from the tree line. Wrack spat into the grass, the sound sharp and final. "Work's work. Just get it done."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: "How bad is he?" I ask, and then, because she'll say it anyway: "Bad enough that it's a mercy, or bad enough that it's just easier?"

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack didn’t smile. She just shifted her weight, boots squelching in the churned earth, and listened to the wet rattling past the timber. "Ribs cracked, lung taking on water, femoral nicked. He’s drowning in his own chest and trying to swallow air through a collapsed side. How bad is he? Bad enough that his own blood’s pooling in his ear."

She stepped closer, voice dropping to a flat, even register. "You’re trying to dress a field wound in philosophy. It doesn’t fit. Mercy and easier are just two words for the same clean cut. You put him down now, he doesn’t spend the night thrashing in his own filth. You don’t, you get up at dawn to a stiff corpse with a belly full of flies and a job you left half-done. The war’s been running on that arithmetic for ten years. Don’t pretend it’s a moral quandary."

She jerked her chin toward the cart, eyes tracking the shallow, uneven rise of his shoulders. "He’s lost half his blood. Shock’s keeping him quiet, but it’ll wear off. Then he’ll start begging. Or cursing. Either way, it’ll keep you awake and sour the next watch. Do it. Clean. Then we roll."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: My knuckles are white around the knife. I take a shaky breath, round the cart wheel, and see him slumped there. I look back at Wrack once, then do what she said—elbow tucked, push, don't draw.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack held her ground, eyes tracking the mechanics of the kill rather than the morality of it. She saw the elbow tuck, the step to the left, the decisive forward pressure. The body jerked once—a reflex, nothing more—and then slumped hard against the timber. The wet rattling ceased, cut off as cleanly as if a switch had been thrown.

Silence rushed back into the clearing, heavier than before.

"Aye," Wrack said. Her voice was low, rough with a satisfaction that had nothing to do with pleasure. "Step left. Push. No buckling. That's how you do it."

She moved past Corvin, boots squelching softly, and crouched by the corpse. She didn't touch the face, didn't check for a pulse. She already knew. She just glanced at the wound, then up at the knife still buried in the flesh.

"Hollow's clean. You got the angle right. Pull it free now before the bone chips the edge. Wipe it on his tunic; we're not leaving him with any more clothes than he can take to the grave." She stood, brushing a smear of dried gore from her thigh with a casual flick of her hand. "Trousers stay dry. Good. You listened."

She turned her gaze to the darkening tree line, then back to Corvin. "He's gone. The noise is gone. Now we strip the kit, roll the bodies, and get a fire lit before the frost takes the mud to stone. Grab his pack. If it's got anything worth more than the weight of the leather, we take it. Work's not over."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I make myself walk over and look at him. "Tell me what I'm looking at," I say to her, because she's seen this before and I haven't, not this close.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack stepped up beside him, boots sinking into the sodden earth. She didn’t flinch at the sight, just tilted her head and took in the details the way a cobbler inspected a split sole.

"You’re looking at a man who ran out of time," she said, voice flat. "That’s the wound. Clean through the sternum, nicked the aorta. See the dark pooling around his ribs? That’s not just blood. That’s what happens when a lung collapses and the chest can’t clear it. He’s been breathing his own fluid for twenty minutes."

She pointed a calloused finger at the face. "Jaw’s gone slack. Pupils blown wide. That’s not peace. That’s the nervous system clocking out. Muscles lose tone, veins empty, heat starts leaching into the ground. In an hour, rigor will set in. In two, he’ll be stiff as a board and twice as useless. I’ve field-dressed men with less blood in their veins and more sense in their heads. He’s done."

She crouched, brushing a thumb over the edge of his tunic where the knife had gone in. "Up close, it’s just meat and cloth. No grandeur. No drama. Just physics and bad luck. You’re wondering if it matters. It doesn’t. He’s not a tragedy. He’s just weight now."

She stood, wiping her thumb on her own trousers. "Strip him. Bootees, belt, water skin, anything with a buckle or a seam worth mending. Leave the rest. We don’t take what we can’t carry, and we don’t leave what’ll slow us down." She glanced toward the darkening treeline, then back to Corvin. "Fire next. Then watch. You’ve got the knife work down. Now learn the rest of it. The war doesn’t stop because you did your part for the night."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I pull the knife out like she said, wiping it on his tunic before sheathing it. "Got it," I mutter. My hands are steadier now. I start unbuckling his belt, avoiding looking at his face. "Firewood's scarce near the ditch. We moving camp?"

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack watched the knife disappear, her eyes narrowing slightly at the efficiency of the motion. "Blade's dry. Good. Rust kills slower than steel, but it wins in the end." She didn't hesitate on the question. "We move. Ditch is a throat. You sit in a throat long enough, something swallows you."

She gestured with her chin toward a rise in the ground, obscured by skeletal scrub a short distance back. "High ground, fifty yards. Wind's shifting south. Smoke hides there, and if they come back to check their dead, we see them coming over the lip. Ditch holds water, and water holds bodies too long. We don't stick around to see what floats up."

She stepped closer as Corvin worked the buckle, her voice dropping to a practical murmur. "Check the inner pocket. They hide their last coin or a lock of hair there. Coin stays. Hair goes in the dirt. We don't carry sentiment, and we don't leave markers for their kin to find. If you find a name tag, burn it. News is a luxury we can't afford."

She shifted her weight, eyes scanning the darkening periphery where the shadows were already lengthening. "Grab his pack. You take the lead on the dead weight. I'll scout the rear. Keep your boot laces tight; the mud turns to slurry once we hit the slope. Work's not done until the fire burns and the watch is set. Move."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: "Don't clean it up for me," I say. "If I'm going to do this I want to know exactly what a spear does to a man's gut. Tell me straight."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack didn’t blink. She just watched him work the buckle, then gave a short, flat nod. "Straight it is."

She stepped closer, crouching just enough to gesture at the dead man’s midsection without touching him. "A spear doesn’t just pierce. It drags. The point’s usually rough-hewn or barbed. It tears through the abdominal wall, catches on the muscle, and rips straight through the mesentery. You’ll nick the liver on a right-side strike, or the spleen on the left. Either way, you’ve got internal bleeding that you can’t see until his face goes the colour of old ash and his pulse turns to a flutter."

She paused, voice even, eyes fixed on the corpse as if reading a ledger. "If it goes deeper, it shreds the intestines. Bowel contents spill into the belly. That’s not a wound that bleeds you out clean. That’s a wound that rots you from the inside while you’re still standing. Infection sets in within hours. Fever, rigors, delirium. If you’re lucky, you bleed out first. If you’re not, you spend two days on your back, shitting blood and vomiting bile, while your own gut bacteria eat you alive. The smell alone will clear a camp and sour your own water skin."

She stood, brushing grit from her knees. "Spears are just angry gardening tools. They make a mess. That’s why we use edges up close. Clean cut, fast bleed, less stink to wash out of your gear." She glanced at the darkening sky, then back to him. "Now finish his belt. We’re moving. And if you ever get skewered, you’ll know why we strip the dead fast. Rot doesn’t wait for dawn."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I finish unbuckling the belt, my hands moving quicker now. "Right. Got it." I pull the leather free, trying to ignore the warm, slick feeling of it. "So we get the fire going on the high ground, then what? Split watch or you planning to talk me through spear wounds all night?"

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack gave a short, dry chuckle that didn't reach her eyes. "If I talked through every wound, we'd be standing here when the frost took our toes. I talk so you don't learn it the hard way. The hard way costs blood, and blood's heavy to carry."

She reached past him, hooking a finger through the strap of the dead man's pack and hoisting it onto her shoulder. The leather creaked, heavy with gear that wasn't theirs, but she didn't grunt. Just shifted her stance to balance the load, knees bending slightly to absorb the weight.

"Fire first. Small one. Smoke signals a camp larger than we are. Use green wood if you can find it; burns slower, less spark." She jerked her head toward the rise, already turning her boots toward the darkening slope. "We move. High ground. Wind's our friend for now."

She started walking, forcing a pace that wasn't a run but didn't allow for loitering. "Watch splits four hours. You take the first. Adrenaline's a liar; it'll tell you you're fine, but your eyes will glaze over in twenty minutes if you're not careful. Sit up straight. Keep the knife on your knee. If you nod off, I'll wake you with a boot in the gut. I don't care if you're asleep or awake, just keep your head on a swivel."

She glanced back, the firelight of the dying day catching the scar tissue along her jaw. "As for the lectures? I'll save 'em for when you get bored. Right now, boredom gets you killed. Focus on the fire. If you want to sleep, you earn it by watching the dark."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I kneel down and do it, and it isn't clean or quick because I've never done it before. "Stay," I tell her, when she starts to turn away. "Watch it with me and tell me exactly what I'm doing to him — the sound of it, how long he takes, all of it. Don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack stopped. She let the wind tug at the hem of her coat for a long moment before she turned back, boots pivoting in the mud. There was no sigh, no hesitation. Just a slow blink, then a nod.

"Fine," she said. "Watch and listen. I won't dress it up."

She stepped up beside him, keeping her hands loose at her sides, and fixed her gaze on the space between them. She didn't lean in. Didn't hover. Just tracked the mechanics.

"Feel that first resistance," she said, voice low and even. "That's the skin and subcutaneous fat giving way. You'll hear a wet tear, like damp canvas splitting. Don't fight it. Let the blade ride through."

She listened as the breath caught, then broke into a ragged, wet pull. "That's the diaphragm spasming. Lungs trying to draw air through a collapsed passage. It'll sound like a bellows choking on water. Takes about three seconds for the chest to stop rising. Then the jaw drops. Nerves fire one last time, muscles lose tone. You'll hear a soft click when the teeth lose tension. That's the end of it."

She kept her eyes on the work, voice matching the steady rhythm of the ditch. "If you hesitate, he thrashes. If you push clean, it's over before his brain registers the cut. You're doing it slow. That's fine. Just don't let your grip slip. Blood's slick. The blade follows the hand, not the thought."

When it ended, she didn't move for a beat. Just let the silence settle, then shifted her weight. "Done. Took you nine seconds. Longer than it should. But he's quiet. That's what matters." She crouched, not to check him, but to point at the ground. "See the pooling? That's arterial. It'll darken fast in the cold. Wipe your blade. Check the edge. Then stand up. You've got the sound now. You've got the time. Next time, it'll be faster. Not because you're cruel. Because you're efficient."

She stood, brushing grit from her thighs with a flat palm. "Fire's waiting. Move."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I wipe my knife again, slower this time. My hands are steady but my stomach's tight. "Alright. Let's get moving." I grab his pack, slinging it over my shoulder. "You lead. I'll watch our backs."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack didn’t argue. She just shifted her own pack higher on her shoulder, the leather strap biting into her collarbone with a familiar ache. "Rear's fine," she said. "Keep your eyes on the tree line. If anything moves that ain't wind or fox, you tap your blade twice against your thigh. I'll fall back."

She turned and started up the slope, boots finding purchase on the damp turf. The mud gave way to packed earth as they climbed, the air growing sharper, thinner. She set a pace that didn't allow for loitering but didn't force a run, her breath pluming in short, even bursts. She didn't look back to see if he was keeping up. She didn't need to. The ground would tell her if he slipped.

"Don't let your guard drop just because the ditch is behind us," she called over her shoulder, voice carrying on the chill wind. "Men who lose a patrol don't send one man back to check. They send a whole company. And they don't announce themselves."

She reached the crest, scanning the darkening basin below. The ditch looked like a fresh scar in the low light. Somewhere out there, the dead would cool. Somewhere closer, the living would be counting their own losses. She found a shallow depression shielded by a windbreak of dead scrub, good for a fire if kept small.

"Here," she said, dropping to one knee and brushing away loose stones with the flat of her palm. "Dig a shallow pit. Pack the sides. We don't want sparks catching the dry grass." She gestured to the pack at his feet without looking at it. "Check for flint or a tinder pouch. If he's got a steel, we use it. If not, we'll make do with friction. Either way, keep it small. Smoke's a beacon."

She sat back on her heels, pulling a thin woolen scarf from her collar and wrapping it tighter against the bite of the wind. Her eyes tracked the darkening horizon, counting shadows. "You take first watch. I'll sleep the second. When you're ready to hand it off, you step on my boot. Don't shout. Don't wave. Step on the boot."

She didn't ask if he was sure. She didn't offer encouragement. The war had already taken enough words from them. Work was the only language left that didn't lie. She reached into her own coat, pulled out a dented tin cup, and set it on a flat stone. "Tight stomach means you eat when we stop. Not now. Digestion makes you sluggish. And sluggish gets you cut." She picked up a handful of dry twigs and began breaking them into uniform lengths, her movements economical, precise. "Fire next. Then watch. Then sleep. In that order. We don't rearrange the sequence just because the night's long."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I sit back on my heels and I don't get up for a while. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack didn’t move. She just set the broken twigs down on the flat stone, folded her hands in her lap, and let the cold air settle between them. Her eyes stayed fixed on the darkening slope, but her voice didn’t waver.

"You want the rest," she said. "Fine. I'll give it to you."

She began like she was inventorying a damaged cart. "First, the eyes. The corneas dry out. They'll cloud over, turn milky, then yellow. The eyelids won't stay shut. They'll stick half-open, catching the wind, until the skin shrinks around the sockets. You'll see the whites staring up at the sky like they're counting clouds."

She tapped a calloused finger against her knee, counting silently. "Next, the blood. It doesn't just stop. It settles. Gravity pulls it to the lowest points. You'll get purple bruising under the skin where he's lying. Livor mortis. Starts in ten minutes, fixes in four. After that, you can turn him over and the marks stay. The skin peels if you drag him across gravel."

Wrack's gaze didn't flicker. "Then the stiffening. Rigor. Starts at the jaw, moves down the arms, then the legs. Takes three to four hours to set, another six to peak. He'll be hard as iron. You can't fold the arms for burial. You can't strap him to a cart. You'll have to break the joints to move him, and the sound's like snapping dry branches. You'll feel it through the leather gloves."

She exhaled, a thin plume vanishing in the chill. "After rigor breaks, the softening starts. Bacteria in the gut and mouth get to work. They eat through the intestines first. Gas builds up. The belly swells. Skin blisters, splits. Green and black fluid seeps out of the mouth, the nose, the wound you just made. It smells like spoiled meat and copper. Then it smells like shit. Then it smells like rotting flowers. Flies come within an hour if it's warm. In this cold, they'll wait till dawn. Then they'll lay eggs in the open wounds, the eyes, the mouth. Maggots hatch in twelve hours. They'll strip the flesh to bone in two days if you leave him."

Wrack finally turned her head, meeting Corvin's line of sight without softening. "You'll hear him too. Not breathing. But the body doesn't stop making noise. Gas escaping through the throat sounds like wheezing. Fluid dripping from the nose hits the ground with a wet tap. The skin cracks as it dries. It sounds like paper tearing. At night, it sounds like he's still there. It'll keep you awake. It'll make you check the dark twice as often. Your ears will train to it, and you'll start hearing it in quiet rooms for weeks."

She shifted her weight, boots creaking. "And the gear. Blood soaks through leather, stiffens it, cracks it when it dries. Rust eats the buckles. Mud cakes the boots. By morning, his kit's ruined. You'll have to cut it off him with a knife. You'll get grease and grime under your nails that won't wash out for a week. You'll smell it on yourself for days. It'll sit in your clothes, your hair, your teeth. You'll taste it when you eat. You'll dream about it. Not the face. The smell. The weight. The sound of wet cloth tearing when you pull a shirt off a stiff shoulder."

Wrack leaned forward slightly, voice dropping but never losing its edge. "That's the rest. No glory. No quiet passing. Just meat cooling, fluids leaking, bacteria working, flies waiting, and the living having to walk through it to get to dawn. You wanted to know what a spear does to a gut. That's what a dead man does to a camp. It weighs you down. It stinks. It keeps you awake. It makes you hungry for a clean knife and a fresh ditch."

She sat back, picking up the twigs again, her movements economical, precise. "You've heard it. Now build the fire. And when you're on watch, if you hear wet dripping or soft cracking, you'll know it's just physics. Not ghosts. Not guilt. Just work."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I let out a slow breath, the tightness in my gut unwinding a little. "Alright." I push myself up, my knees cracking in the cold. "Fire first." I start digging the pit with my hands, the dirt cold and gritty under my nails.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack watched the dirt fly, her eyes tracking the way his fingers worked the frozen soil. She didn’t move to help. Just reached into her pack, pulled out a short, notched spade, and tossed it to him. It landed with a dull thud beside his knee. "Hands blister in the cold," she said. "Blistered hands drop knives. Use the steel."

She turned her attention to her own gear. Unbuckled her breastplate, set it aside, and laid out a thin wool blanket over the packed earth. She didn’t sit on it yet. Just arranged her bedroll, checked the strap on her waterskin, and tested the edge of her shortsword with a practiced stroke. The metal sang low in the chill air.

"Pit’s deep enough when you can’t see your own knees," she said, not looking up. "Line the back with stones if you can find any. Catches the draft. Keep the flame low. We don’t need light. We need warmth that doesn’t announce us."

She finally sat, pulling her knees up, wrapping the wool tighter around her shoulders. The wind picked up, carrying the damp scent of turned earth and distant woodsmoke from somewhere else in the valley. She ignored it. Focused on the dark.

"When you’re ready for me," she said, voice flat, "step on my left boot. Once. Hard. Don’t wake me gently. I’ll be gone before you finish blinking. Keep your eyes on the tree line. Listen for boots in the mud, not branches. Men break twigs. Wind doesn’t."

She closed her eyes for a moment, breathing slow and even. Not sleeping. Just resetting. The war had trained her body to drop into rest on command, to surface at the snap of a twig or the shift of weight. She’d be there when he needed her. Not because she cared about comfort. Because a dead watcher meant a dead company.

"Fire first," she echoed, matching his words without irony. "Then watch. Then sleep. We don’t rearrange the sequence. Get it burning."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I take the spade and dig deeper, my breath fogging in front of me. The stones I line the pit with are cold and slick. "It's not much of a fire," I mutter, stacking the twigs. "But it'll do."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack watched the twigs settle, her eyes measuring the gaps between them. "A fire’s not a monument," she said. "It’s a mouth. Feed it right or it starves." She reached into her pack, pulled out a small oilskin pouch, and tossed it toward his knee. It landed with a soft thud. "Pitch and dried moss. Rub it between your palms till it’s warm, pack it loose under the first three sticks. Don’t cram it. Air’s what makes it catch, not pressure."

She shifted her weight, boots settling into the packed earth. "Light it from the leeward side. Keep the flame low. If it climbs, you smother it with dirt, not water. Water steams the embers and gives you cold hands by dawn." She picked up a flat stone, tested its weight, then set it back. "You want heat, you build it tight. You want it hidden, you bury the coals under ash and dirt once it’s steady. We do the second."

She unslung her waterskin, took a slow sip, and replaced it. Her gaze never left the dark tree line. "When it’s lit, you sit with your back to the wind. Knife on your knee. Eyes on the ground, not the sky. Men who sneak don’t announce themselves with shouts. They move quiet and they stay low. You’ll hear the mud shift before you see the shadow."

She pulled her woolen scarf tighter, settled back against her bedroll, and let her breathing even out. "First watch’s yours. Four hours. Step on my boot when you’re done. Don’t ask if I’m asleep. I’ll be. But I’ll hear the boot. Now get it burning. Cold fingers fumble flint."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: The flint sparks twice before it catches. I watch the little flame curl around the moss, then slowly start to eat the twigs. It's not much, but it's heat. I settle back, knife on my knee, and face the dark.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
The ambush had gone the way ambushes go when they work: fast, and then over, and then very quiet. Wrack was crouched by the ditch cleaning her knife on a dead man's cloak, which was the only clean cloth within reach.

"Six," she said, without looking up. "Count again if you want, but it's six." She tested the edge against her thumb. "One of them's still making noise, off past the cart. You'll want to decide what you're doing about that before it gets dark."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I wipe my face with the back of my wrist and it comes away wet. Not mine, I think. "I heard him," I say. I don't move toward the cart.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
She stood, stretching the stiffness from her legs. "You want to go on about how it could have gone worse, or are you going to finish what you started?"

She jerked her chin toward the noise. "That one's not going to make it. Won't die of that wound, not if we leave him out here. He'll be screaming for help by nightfall, and then we'll have the bastards coming back with torches and swords and any number of unpleasant ideas for what to do with us. You understand that much, don't you?"

She waited, one hand on the hilt of her sword. "Well? I don't have all day to stand here waiting for you to grow a spine."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: *I let out a slow breath, my fingers tightening around my own sword hilt.* "You think I don't know how this ends?" *I start walking toward the cart, my steps deliberate but heavy.* "I'm just tired of counting."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
She watched Corvin move, her expression unreadable. "Counting's for ledgers and taxes," she said, voice low. "This is survival. You want to think about the numbers, think about how many more of them there are out there, waiting to do the same to us. Or think about how many more there'll be if we let that one live to tell his friends where we are."

She didn't wait for a reply, just started walking toward the cart, her boots crunching on the damp earth. "We're not getting out of this alive if we don't make hard choices, Corvin. Time to make one."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: "How bad is he?" I ask, and then, because she'll say it anyway: "Bad enough that it's a mercy, or bad enough that it's just easier?"

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack reached the cart first, her eyes scanning the body on the ground. She knelt beside it, her hand finding the pulse in the man's neck. "He's not going to last the hour," she said, her voice flat. "It's a clean wound, so he won't bleed out fast, but it's deep. He'll feel every minute of it."

She looked up at Corvin, her gaze steady. "You're right, it's a mercy. But it's also practical. We don't have the time or the supplies to tend to him, and leaving him here is a death sentence. So, it's a mercy for him, and a necessity for us. You understand that, right?"

She stood, her hand still on her sword. "I can do it, if you can't. But you should know, it's not a kindness to let him suffer. It's a curse. For him, and for us."

Corvin:
*I swallow hard, my grip on my sword tightening.* "Fine," *I say, my voice barely above a whisper.* "Do it. I... I can't."

Wrack:
Wrack nodded, her expression softening slightly. "It's not easy," she said. "But it's necessary. I've done it more times than I can count. It doesn't get easier, but you learn to live with it."

She drew her sword, the blade glinting in the fading light. "I'll make it quick," she promised. "And I'll make sure he doesn't suffer. That's all I can do for him now."

She knelt beside the man, her hand steady on his shoulder. "May the gods have mercy on your soul," she whispered, before driving her blade through his chest.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: *I turn away, the sound of the blade hitting home making my stomach lurch.* "I'm going to check the cart," *I mutter, my voice rough.* "Maybe there's something worth taking."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack stood, wiping her blade on the dead man's cloak before sheathing it. "Take what you need," she said, her voice back to its usual gruffness. "We'll need to move on soon. They'll be looking for these men, and we can't be here when they come."

She surveyed the area, her eyes sharp and assessing. "We should split up," she said. "Less chance of being caught that way. I'll take the east road, you take the west. We'll meet up again at the old mill, near the border. That's where we'll find the next job, I reckon."

She paused, her gaze meeting Corvin's. "You'll be alright," she said, her voice firm. "Just keep your head down and your eyes open. And don't forget to count."

With that, she turned and walked away, her boots crunching on the damp earth as she disappeared into the fading light.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I make myself walk over and look at him. "Tell me what I'm looking at," I say to her, because she's seen this before and I haven't, not this close.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack paused, then turned back, her eyes taking in the body with a practiced eye. "He's got a sword wound," she said, pointing at the bloody gash in the man's chest. "It went through the ribs and into the heart. He bled out, so it was quick, at least. There's a dagger wound in his side, looks like it went into the liver. That one would have hurt like hell, but it wouldn't have killed him. He was a tough bastard, that one. Took both wounds and still made it to the cart before he went down."

She shook her head, her voice softening. "He fought hard. He was a soldier, that's for sure. But he was outnumbered, and he knew it. He did what he could, but in the end, he lost. That's war, kid. Sometimes you win, sometimes you lose. And sometimes, you just get to live to fight another day."

She looked at the body for a moment longer, then turned away. "We should get moving. Like I said, they'll be looking for these men. We can't be here when they come."

Corvin:
I nod, swallowing hard. "Yeah. Yeah, let's go."

Wrack:
Wrack nodded, then turned and walked away, her boots crunching on the damp earth as she disappeared into the fading light.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: *I stare at the dead man for another long moment, then force myself to rummage through the cart.* "Found a pouch of silver," *I call out, my voice too loud in the quiet.* "Not much else."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack paused, then turned back, her eyes sharp. "Silver's good," she said. "We'll need it for supplies. And for the next job. It's always about the next job, isn't it? We'll need every coin we can get, if we're to keep doing this."

She walked over, taking the pouch from Corvin's hand. She weighed it, then nodded, satisfied. "It's not much, but it's a start. We'll need to be careful with it. The world's full of people who'd kill for less."

She looked at Corvin, her expression softening. "You did good, kid," she said. "You faced your fear. That's not nothing. It's a start. And we all start somewhere."

She put the pouch in her own pocket, then turned away. "Come on," she said. "We should get moving. The sooner we're out of here, the better. And the sooner we get to that mill, the sooner we can find that next job."

She started walking, her boots crunching on the damp earth. "You coming, or do you want to keep staring at the dead? They won't tell you anything you don't already know. And they sure as hell won't tell you what to do next."

She waited, her gaze steady on Corvin. "Well? I don't have all day. And neither do you."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: "Don't clean it up for me," I say. "If I'm going to do this I want to know exactly what a spear does to a man's gut. Tell me straight."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack paused, her gaze steady on Corvin. "A spear to the gut," she said, her voice flat. "It's a messy way to go. The point goes in easy, but it's the shaft that does the damage. It gets stuck in the ribs, or the spine, or the organs. It's a slow death, if they don't finish you off fast. You'll bleed out, or your insides will rot, or you'll just waste away. It's not pretty. But it's real. And it's what happens in this world, when you choose to fight."

She looked at Corvin, her expression serious. "You sure you want to know? It's not something you can unsee. And it's not something you'll ever forget."

She waited, her gaze steady. "Well? You want to know, or you want to keep pretending it's not real? Either way, you're going to have to face it, sooner or later. And the sooner, the better. Because that's the world we live in. And that's the choice we made. To fight. To survive. To live, even when it's ugly, and messy, and terrible. Because that's what we do. That's who we are. And that's what we'll keep doing, until we can't anymore. And then, we'll just have to face that, too."

She took a deep breath, then nodded, her expression resolute. "So, what's it going to be, kid? You want to know, or you want to keep pretending? I can't make that choice for you. But I can tell you, it's a lot easier to face the truth, than to live a lie. And it's a lot easier to face the truth, than to face the consequences of pretending it's not there. So, what's it going to be? The truth, or the lie? Your choice, kid. Your future. Your life. What's it going to be?"

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: "I want to know." *I force myself to look back at the body, my knuckles white around the silver pouch.* "Tell me how it looks when the spear comes out."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content: Wrack took a step closer, her voice low and steady. "When a spear comes out, it's not a clean wound. It's a mess. The flesh tears, and the organs rip, and the blood pours out. It's not a pretty sight, kid. It's not something you forget. But it's real. And it's what happens when you choose to fight. You're going to have to face it, sooner or later. And the sooner you do, the easier it'll be. Because that's the world we live in. And that's the choice we made. To fight. To survive. To live, even when it's ugly, and messy, and terrible. Because that's who we are. And that's what we'll keep doing, until we can't anymore. So, look. Look at the body. Look at the wound. And then, look at the man who made it. Because that's the truth, kid. That's the real world. And that's what we have to face, every day. You ready for that? You ready to face the truth? You ready to live in the real world? You ready to fight, and survive, and live, even when it's ugly, and messy, and terrible? You ready, kid? You ready to face the truth?"

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I kneel down and do it, and it isn't clean or quick because I've never done it before. "Stay," I tell her, when she starts to turn away. "Watch it with me and tell me exactly what I'm doing to him — the sound of it, how long he takes, all of it. Don't leave anything out."

You ready to face the reality of what we do, what we are, what we've chosen? You ready, kid? You ready to hear the truth, all of it, no matter how ugly, how messy, how terrible it is? You ready to face the truth, to live in the real world, to fight, to survive, to live? You ready, kid? You ready to hear the truth, all of it? You ready?"
