dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
The ambush had gone the way ambushes go when they work: fast, and then over, and then very quiet. Wrack was crouched by the ditch cleaning her knife on a dead man's cloak, which was the only clean cloth within reach.

"Six," she said, without looking up. "Count again if you want, but it's six." She tested the edge against her thumb. "One of them's still making noise, off past the cart. You'll want to decide what you're doing about that before it gets dark."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I wipe my face with the back of my wrist and it comes away wet. Not mine, I think. "I heard him," I say. I don't move toward the cart.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack drew the knife once more across the dead man’s cloak, left a dark smear, and stood with the careful economy of someone whose knees had opinions. Somewhere past the cart, the noise went on: thin, wet, more breath than voice.

“Then hearing’s half the job,” she said. “Other half’s deciding whether he dies now, dies later, or spends the night calling friends we don’t want to meet.”

She slid the blade home without a flourish, just the tired click of metal finding its sheath. Her gaze came back to Corvin, taking in the borrowed blood and the stillness without naming either.

“I’ll do it if you’re done for the day,” she said. “No shame in that. But if you mean to do it yourself, do it before the light goes. Dark makes botches of mercy.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I let out a slow breath and finally push off from where I'm standing. "No. I'll do it." My voice sounds steadier than I feel. I start walking toward the cart, trying not to think about what I'll find on the other side.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack gave a single, short nod.

“Then make it one pass,” she said. “Under the jaw and angled up, if he’s on his back. Throat work takes longer than people think, and he’ll make a mess of you either way.”

She glanced toward the cart, where the breathing had turned thinner, more broken.

“Don’t talk to him first,” she added. “No point asking forgiveness. He won’t give it, and you’ll only stand there longer.”

She turned back to the dead men and took hold of the nearest by the ankles, boots scraping in the dirt as she began dragging him toward the ditch with steady, unbothered pulls.

“I’ll watch the road,” she said. “If there’s more than one, shout.”

The light was failing along the tree line, turning the blood on the road black. She did not look up again.

“Dark makes botches of mercy,” she said once more, quieter now, as if reminding herself more than anyone else.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: "How bad is he?" I ask, and then, because she'll say it anyway: "Bad enough that it's a mercy, or bad enough that it's just easier?"

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack stopped dragging the dead man by the ankles, boots still planted in the dirt, and considered the question without any visible surprise.

“Bad enough,” she said.

She let the legs down gently enough not to be respectful, only practical, and turned her head toward the cart. The breathing beyond it had become a shallow, bubbling thing, interrupted by small catches that sounded worse than screams.

“Gut’s opened. One lung’s likely filling. He’ll live long enough to make it ugly if you leave him,” she said. “So if you need it to be mercy, call it mercy.”

Her eyes came back, flat and unkind in the fading light.

“If you need it to be easier, it’s that too. Easier for him, easier for us, easier for whoever finds him screaming at crows.” She wiped her hands on her thighs, though that did little good. “Don’t make a sermon of it. Just make it clean.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: *I nod once, my throat tight.* "Right." I step around the cart and see him then, curled around his own ruin. I draw my knife.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack stayed where she was, one boot planted against the dead man’s hip to keep him from sliding back down the ditch while she looked out at the road. The light was going the color of old bruises along the trees.

She heard the knife clear its sheath.

“Don’t look at his face,” she said, not raising her voice. “Look for the hollow under the jaw. Put the point there and drive up. One good push is better than three careful ones.”

The sound beyond the cart hitched, wet and thin.

Wrack’s eyes stayed on the road, though her head tilted slightly, listening.

“If he grabs you, break his grip at the wrist,” she went on. “Not the fingers. Fingers take too long.”

She shifted her weight, hand resting near her sword without drawing it.

“And step back when he jerks. They always jerk.”

A pause. The wind moved through the grass at the ditch’s edge.

“Do it now,” she said, quieter. “Before he starts begging.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I make myself walk over and look at him. "Tell me what I'm looking at," I say to her, because she's seen this before and I haven't, not this close.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack left the dead man where he lay and came around the cart without hurry, boots quiet in the dirt. She stopped close enough to be useful, but not so close that she crowded the moment. Her eyes went to the wound first, not the face.

“You’re looking at a gut opening that’s gone deep,” she said, voice low and steady, as if she were explaining how to sharpen a blade without ruining the edge. “That dark soak under him is blood, not wine. The bubbling in his breath means his chest is filling. He’s past mending.”

She tilted her head slightly, indicating the angle without touching.

“You’re not looking at a man anymore. You’re looking at a job. See the hollow under the jaw, where the bone dips? Put the point there. Angle it up toward the base of the skull. One hard push. Don’t saw, don’t hesitate. If it catches, drive through.”

The wounded man made another thin, broken sound. Wrack did not flinch.

“He’ll jerk,” she said. “Step back when he does. Don’t let him drag you down into the blood.”

Her gaze lifted briefly, not unkind, but hard as flint.

“And don’t speak to him now. No apologies, no blessings, no asking if he’s ready. Mercy doesn’t need a preamble.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: My hands feel cold despite the blood on them. I kneel, find the hollow she mentioned with my fingers. "Alright," I say, more to myself than him. I push.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack did not move to help. She stood with her hands loose at her sides, watching the wounded man’s shoulders rather than Corvin’s face, because that was where the tell would be.

The blade went in under the jaw, and the body gave the jerk she had promised: a sudden, ugly arch, heels beating once against the ground, fingers snatching at air.

“Back now,” she said, low and even. “Let him have the ground.”

The breath went out of the man in a long, rattling sigh, and the bubbling eased. Wrack waited until the eyes glazed and the hands fell still before she spoke again.

“Clean enough,” she said. “No sermon needed.”

She crouched beside the body, took the dead man’s wrist, and checked for a pulse more out of habit than doubt, then let the arm drop.

“Wipe the blade on his cloak, not your sleeve. Steel remembers neglect even if you don’t.” She straightened with a faint creak of knees and looked back toward the road. “Then take his purse if it isn’t drowned in blood. We’ll want boots too, if they fit. Dead men don’t complain about bare feet.”

The last light was bleeding out of the sky, leaving the world in shades of ash and old iron. Wrack’s voice stayed practical.

“If you need a minute, take it facing the ditch. If you need to be sick, do it away from the water. But we don’t stay long. Noise travels after dark, and six men make a hole in the world somebody’s bound to notice.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: "Don't clean it up for me," I say. "If I'm going to do this I want to know exactly what a spear does to a man's gut. Tell me straight."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack did not look away from the dead man. She considered the question for a beat, then gave it to him plain.

“A spear in the gut is not one wound,” she said. “It is whatever it touches on the way through.”

She crouched again, not touching the body, only indicating with two blunt fingers.

“Low belly, under the navel—there is no bone to stop it. It goes through skin, fat, muscle, then bowel. If the gut is opened, he fills with his own filth. You will smell it quick. Shit, bile, that sweet rot-green smell of belly-water. Some men die fast from shock. Most die slow, over days, burning up and begging for water while their insides poison them.”

Her voice stayed level, the way she might describe bad weather or a broken axle.

“Higher up, under the ribs, it can find liver or spleen. Those bleed hard. Liver blood is dark and heavy. Spleen can leak slow, then all at once. Stomach spills sour water and whatever he last ate. If the point cuts one of the great vessels down the middle, he is dead before his knees understand it. If it angles up beneath the ribs into lung, he drowns in his own breath. That is the bubbling sound you heard.”

She glanced toward the corpse, then back.

“If the spear stays in, sometimes the shaft plugs the hole. Pull it, and you open the whole mess. If it is barbed, or rough, or bent, pulling drags meat with it. A clean thrust can kill quick. A bad one turns a man into a leaking sack and leaves him screaming for someone to stop the pain.”

The last of the light had gone thin and gray over the road. Somewhere in the trees, a bird gave one startled note and fell silent.

Wrack straightened with that same tired creak of joints.

“So that is what it does,” she said. “It opens, spills, and kills slow unless it hits something vital. Most gut wounds are not quick. That is why we finish them when we can. Not because it is pretty. Because the alternative is worse.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I look down at the man's body, at the dark mess of his middle. "Then he was dead either way." My voice sounds hollow. I wipe the blade on his cloak, the way she said. It comes away clean.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack watched the knife come clean and gave one short nod.

“I won’t clean it up for you,” she said. “You wanted the shape of it, and now you’ve got it. Carry it. Best carried moving.”

She crouched beside the body again and began going through the belt with the same dispassionate efficiency she might have used to sort spoons from a camp kit. A purse came loose. She weighed it once, found it more hopeful than heavy, and tucked it away.

“Dead either way is the only arithmetic that matters after,” she said. “Don’t dress it up prettier than that. He was dead when his gut opened. We only shortened the noise.”

Her fingers worked over the dead man’s cloak, checking for hidden seams, then moved to the boots. She tugged one free, felt the sole, grunted at what she found there.

“You asked for straight, and straight’s what you got. Spears make ugly work. Ugly work still needs doing, and better it gets done by hands that don’t enjoy it.”

She set the boot aside and started on the other.

“If your hands shake later, let them. Shaking’s just the body saying it noticed. If you need to be sick, use the ditch. If you need to talk, talk to the road. It won’t answer, but it won’t judge either.”

The dark had settled into the ruts now, and the trees had become a wall of black beyond the last gray smear of sky. Somewhere far off, a dog barked once, thought better of it, and quit.

Wrack straightened with that faint creak of knees again and looked down the road.

“We’ll take what’s useful,” she said. “Coin, steel, boots, bread, anything that doesn’t stink worse than it’s worth. Then we move. Dead men make poor company, and living ones are likely to be worse.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I kneel down and do it, and it isn't clean or quick because I've never done it before. "Stay," I tell her, when she starts to turn away. "Watch it with me and tell me exactly what I'm doing to him — the sound of it, how long he takes, all of it. Don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack stopped.

She did not turn away at once, and she did not answer at once either. She stood with the dead man’s boot still in one hand and looked down at the body, then at the knife, then at the dark ground where the blood had gone sticky and black in the failing light. Her face had no pity in it, but it had no cruelty either. It had the look of a woman deciding what part of a hard thing needed saying.

“He’s dead,” she said at last. “You already did that part.”

Her voice was not sharp. It was flat and sure, the way she might have said *the fire’s out* or *the rain’s started*.

“There’s no more time to take from him. No more sound he’s going to make. If you’re asking me to stand here and tell you how long he took after the blade went in, I’ll tell you straight: not long. You gave him the hollow, you drove up, he jerked, and then he wasn’t. That’s the truth of it. I won’t stretch it out to make you feel you’ve paid enough.”

She set the boot down and came a step closer, not crowding, only near enough that he would not have to face the thing alone if he did not want to. Her eyes dropped to the corpse again.

“If you mean the searching, that’s different. That I can tell you plain.”

She nodded toward the body.

“You’ll hear cloth first. Blood dries quick and glues things, so a cloak parts with a little tear, like old paper. Leather creaks when you work a belt loose. The purse clinks if there’s coin in it, and if there isn’t, it knocks soft against your knuckles like an empty cup. Boots come hard if the legs have begun to stiffen. Sometimes they make a wet sound when the blood’s pooled under them. Nothing else. No groaning, no begging. Dead men are heavy and quiet, and that’s the worst part for some.”

Her gaze lifted.

“You don’t need me to invent suffering for you. You don’t owe him your nightmares. He was an enemy, and now he’s meat and clothing and maybe a few coppers. That’s all that’s left to do here.”

She crouched again, slow, knees protesting in their usual way, and rested one forearm on her thigh.

“I’ll stay while you go through him,” she said. “But I’ll tell you what’s real, not what you think you ought to hear. The real part is this: your hands may shake. Your stomach may turn. You may smell blood and bowels for a while and hate the smell, then hate that you’ve stopped hating it. That’s the work. It doesn’t make you worse. It just means you’re still alive.”

The dark had thickened around the cart. The wind moved again, low through the ditch grass, and the dead man’s cloak lifted a little at the edge before settling.

Wrack’s voice stayed steady.

“Take what’s useful. Leave what isn’t. And when you’re done, stand up. We’ve got road before us, and the dead won’t carry our burdens for us.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content:
I take the purse first. The leather is stiff with dried blood, but it clinks like she said. My hands don't shake. That's worse, somehow.

"Alright," I say, and start working on the boots. "Tell me what's real about walking away from this."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack heard the purse clink, heard the stiff leather complain as it was worked loose, and she did not pretend not to notice the steadiness in those hands. She only shifted her weight and looked out toward the road, where the dark had become a thing you could feel more than see.

“What’s real about walking away?” she repeated. “That you don’t leave it here.”

She crouched again, slow, one knee cracking in a way she had long stopped apologizing for. Her fingers rested on the dead man’s boot, not helping, just waiting.

“You’ll walk away with it in your nose,” she said. “Blood’s got a smell that sits in the back of the throat. You’ll taste it when you swallow. Later, maybe when you’re eating something plain—bread, salt pork, an apple if we’re lucky—it’ll come back and sit down at the table with you.”

Her eyes moved once to the corpse, then back to the darkening line of trees.

“You’ll walk away with the sounds too. Not the big ones. Not the scream or the rattle. The little ones. The way cloth tears when it’s glued down with blood. The way a belt slides through a buckle when the leather’s damp. The way a boot gives up with a wet little sigh if the foot’s been lying in it too long.”

She gave the boot in her hand a small, practical tug, testing how stubborn the dead had become.

“And the worst part isn’t that it stays,” she went on. “The worst part is that it gets ordinary. First time, you think it’ll mark you like a brand. Second time, you notice you’re thinking about whether you found all the coin while there’s still warmth in the hand. Third time, you’re annoyed at the mud. By the tenth, you’re mostly tired. That’s what scares people. Not the horror. The getting used to it.”

Wrack’s voice stayed level, without judgment, without comfort.

“You don’t get to set it down just because you’ve started moving. That’s the lie greenhands tell themselves. ‘We’ll walk it off.’ You don’t walk it off. You carry it. You just get better at carrying.”

She finally looked at Corvin then, not sharply, not kindly either. Only straight.

“If you’re waiting to feel worse, don’t. If you’re waiting to feel better, don’t do that either. Feeling nothing now is common. Feeling everything later is also common. Feeling the wrong thing at the wrong time—laughing, hunger, irritation because a dead man’s belt is stuck—that’s common too. None of it makes you monstrous. It makes you present.”

The wind stirred the ditch grass again, thin and restless.

“When we leave this place,” she said, “you’ll want to look back. Maybe not right away. Maybe after we’ve gone a mile. Maybe when you’re washing your hands in a stream and the water runs pink around your knuckles. You’ll want to make it mean something. Don’t ask too much of it. He was a man. Now he’s a lesson. That’s enough.”

She reached over and turned the dead man’s boot slightly, exposing the sole to what little light remained.

“What’s real about walking away,” she said, “is that your feet still hurt. Your stomach still wants food. Your hands still need cleaning. The world doesn’t stop for what you’ve done. It keeps asking things of you. That’s the mercy of it, if you’re looking for mercy.”

She let the boot fall again.

“You’ll dream of him, maybe. Not his face. The weight of him. The sound under the jaw. The way he didn’t beg when you needed him to, or did when you didn’t. If that happens, don’t make a shrine of it. Wake up, check your blade, check the fire, and keep watch. The dead don’t need your sleep. They’ve got all the quiet they want now.”

Her gaze went back down the road, patient and hard as old iron.

“And when you do walk away, you don’t get clean. You get useful. That’s the only absolution this work offers. You take what keeps us alive, you leave what slows us down, and you don’t spend the rest of the night arguing with yourself about whether you’re allowed to keep living. You are. That’s not a reward. That’s the bill.”

Somewhere behind them, the cart creaked once as the wood settled in the cooling air.

“So take the purse,” Wrack said. “Take the boots if they’ll fit. Take whatever steel isn’t chipped. Then stand up, breathe, and move like someone who means to be somewhere else by morning. The road won’t ask what you did here. That’s the real thing about walking away.”

Her mouth twisted, not quite a smile.

“It lets you.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I sit back on my heels and I don't get up for a while. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack did not answer at once.

She stood there with the dead man’s boot still half-loosened, her hands resting on her thighs, and looked out at the road as though checking whether the night had anything more to add to it. It did not. Only the wind in the ditch grass, only the cart settling, only the smell of blood and opened earth and the faint, sour iron stink that came after.

When she spoke again, her voice was lower. Not softer. Lower the way a blade is lowered when it has found the angle and no longer needs to be shown off.

“The rest,” she said, “is that you’ll want it to be one thing. It won’t be.”

She crouched again, slow, knees complaining, and rested one forearm over them. She did not look at the corpse while she said it. She looked at the darkening ground beyond, where the last of the light had gone the color of drowned ash.

“You’ll want it to be mercy, and it was. You’ll want it to be murder, and maybe that’s true too, depending on who’s counting and how much wine they’ve had. You’ll want it to be necessary, and it was, because leaving him here to drown in his own chest would have been worse. You’ll want it to mean something grand, and it won’t. It will mean exactly what it is: a man who was dying got finished by another man’s hand because the world had run out of better options for him.”

Her eyes moved then, briefly, to the dead man’s face. Not with pity. With acknowledgment.

“He didn’t give you a speech. He didn’t forgive you. He didn’t curse you. That’s not because he was noble. It’s because he was past it. You’ll spend a while wishing he’d done one of those things, because any of them would be easier to carry than the nothing he gave you. But that’s your problem now, not his.”

She shifted her weight, and the leather of her gear creaked faintly.

“What you did was quick enough. Quick enough matters, even if it doesn’t feel like it. The blade went in under the jaw, found the soft place, and drove up. There was resistance first—skin, then the give underneath. Not much. Enough that you felt it. Enough that your hand knew it had done a thing that couldn’t be taken back. Then he jerked. They always do. It isn’t fighting. It isn’t refusal. It’s the body spending whatever’s left in it because it doesn’t know yet that the war’s over. The heels beat. The hands came up. The breath went out. Then the eyes went flat and the weight of him changed. That’s the part people remember. Not the sound. The weight. How suddenly there’s more of him and less of him at the same time.”

Wrack’s mouth tightened, not in disgust. In recognition.

“You’ll remember the sound too, though. The little catch in the breath before it stopped. The wet settle after. Not loud. Nothing so dramatic as you’re expecting. Death usually isn’t. It’s smaller than stories make it. That’s what makes it hard to believe later. You’ll think, *It can’t have been that little a thing to end a man*, but it was. It was just that little.”

She glanced down at the purse in the dirt, then back to the road.

“Now he’s already changing. You won’t notice it much in the dark, but it’s begun. The heat’s leaving him. The blood’s settling where gravity wants it. The skin will go waxen, then stiff. The joints will lock up in their own time. If it stays warm, the smell will start before dawn. Not the smell you’re thinking of—not rot yet. Something sweeter and fouler under that. The body knows what it is before the mind admits it. Flies will find him if they’re about. Crows will come later, maybe dogs, maybe foxes, depending on what’s hungry and what’s bold. If we leave him here, by this time tomorrow he’ll be less than he is now. In a week, he’ll be a story someone tells badly. In a month, just a place where the grass grows different.”

Her voice stayed level, unhurried, stripped of ornament.

“That’s what’s real. Not the grand accounting. The physical fact of him. The way a dead man’s clothes start to belong to him differently once he’s in them. The way a belt gets sticky. The way a boot resists when you pull it off because the foot has begun to swell into it. The way the purse feels ordinary in your hand even though it came off a corpse. The coin doesn’t know. The leather doesn’t know. That’s the insult of it. Nothing around you cares enough to make the moment feel holy.”

She drew a breath through her nose and let it out again.

“And the rest is what it does to you. Not now. Now you’re running on the first shock of it, and shock is a kind of armor. Later, the armor comes off. You’ll wash your hands and still smell copper. You’ll eat and taste something else under the food. You’ll hear someone laugh at the wrong time and think it should have sounded different. You’ll be tired enough to drop and not want to sleep because sleep is where the dead come looking for their due. Or you’ll sleep like a stone and wake angry at yourself for sleeping so well. Both happen. Neither means what you’ll want it to mean.”

Her gaze came back to the body.

“You’ll want to confess. Don’t mistake that for duty. Sometimes confession is just another way of asking someone else to carry it. I won’t carry it. No priest will either, not truly. You can say the words and they’ll sound right and then you’ll still be the one who remembers the exact feel of the hollow under his jaw. That’s not punishment. That’s the shape of the thing. You did it. It’s yours. Not forever in the way you think, but enough.”

She rubbed one thumb briefly over her knuckles, a practical gesture, not a nervous one.

“You’ll notice your hands were steady. That’ll bother you. You’ll think steady means cold, and cold means monster, and monster means you’ve lost something essential. You haven’t. Steady just means your body understood the work before your feelings caught up. Later, when your feelings catch up, they may make a mess of you. Let them. Better that than pretending they don’t exist. If you need to shake, shake. If you need to vomit, vomit. If you laugh later at something stupid, laugh. The body has its own ways of balancing the books, and they’re none of them as tidy as we’d like.”

The wind moved again, lifting the edge of the dead man’s cloak and letting it fall. Wrack watched it settle.

“You’ll want to make a story out of him. Don’t. Not a villain. Not a brother. Not a lesson wrapped up neat for your own comfort. He was a man who ended up with his gut open on a road that doesn’t care, in a war that’s forgotten why it started, and the only truth we owe him is not to lie about what happened after. We took his purse because we need coin. We’ll take his boots if they fit because dead men don’t walk and living ones do. That’s not cruelty. That’s the arithmetic of staying alive. You can hate the arithmetic and still do it. Most decent people do.”

She shifted her stance slightly, favoring one knee without making a thing of it.

“When we walk away, you’ll feel like you’re leaving something behind. You are. Not him. Some version of yourself that still thinks there’s a clean way through this world. That’s all. The rest you carry. You carry the sound. The smell. The weight. The fact that it was easier than you expected and worse than you expected at the same time. You carry the knowledge that next time it may be easier still, and that the tenth time you may be thinking about your boots while a man cools at your feet. That’s what scares people. Not that they become beasts. That they become workers.”

Her mouth twisted, dry and humorless.

“And if you’re waiting for absolution, stop. There isn’t any here. There’s only the next thing. Clean the blade. Check the edge. Wash your hands if there’s water. Don’t put bloody fingers into a cut. Eat something, even if it tastes like ash. Keep watch. Sleep when you can. Don’t go looking for punishment because punishment won’t balance anything either. It’ll just add another weight to the load.”

She looked down at the dead man again, and this time her expression was almost gentle, though not kind. Gentleness without kindness. A field thing. A winter thing.

“He was somebody’s before he was nobody’s. Maybe a mother. Maybe a wife. Maybe a child who will grow up not knowing exactly how he ended. Maybe no one at all. You’ll never know, and that’s better. Don’t invent them to hurt yourself with. The living don’t need your invented grief. If he had people, they’ll have their own. If he didn’t, no amount you add will change it.”

Somewhere in the dark, wood creaked again. The cart, maybe. The night settling into its own joints.

“The rest,” Wrack said, “is that you’ll keep going because stopping is a luxury. You’ll keep going because the road doesn’t care what you feel, and because somewhere ahead there’ll be water, or food, or shelter, or another fight, or just another mile. You’ll keep going because the dead can’t walk, and we can. That’s not pretty, but it’s true. And if you need one clean thing to hold onto, hold onto this: you didn’t make it worse. You didn’t leave him to drown in his own breath. You didn’t stand over him making speeches while he begged for an end. You did the hard thing in the way that causes the least harm left to cause. That’s not holiness. It’s work. But it’s not nothing.”

She straightened then, slowly, with that faint creak of joints, and looked down the road into the dark.

“And when you dream of him—and you may—don’t try to make the dream mean more than it does. The mind sorts what the hands have done. That’s all. If he comes to you silent, let him be silent. If he comes angry, let him be angry. If he doesn’t come at all, don’t go looking for him out of guilt. The dead don’t haunt because they want to. They haunt because the living haven’t finished carrying them.”

She turned her head slightly, listening to the night, then back.

“So here’s the last of it. You’ll stand up when you can. You’ll take what we need. You’ll leave what we don’t. You’ll walk away with blood under your nails and the taste of iron in your mouth and the knowledge that you are capable of this, and you will not let that knowledge eat you alive. You’ll use it instead. To be quicker when quickness is mercy. To be steadier when steadiness is needed. To be less cruel than men who enjoy it, and less foolish than men who pretend it doesn’t happen.”

Her voice dropped one notch lower, not softer, only final.

“That’s the rest. All of it. No sermon, no blessing, no clean ending. Just the fact that he’s dead, you’re alive, and the road is still there.”

She looked down at the body one last time.

“Now finish with him,” Wrack said. “Then we move.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I finish pulling the boot free. It comes with that wet, sighing sound she described. "Alright," I say, and my voice is just a voice again. I stand up, wipe my hands on my trousers. "Let's move."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack gave a single short nod. Not approval, exactly. More the look she might give a blade that had held after the first hard use.

“Then we walk,” she said. “Not fast. Fast draws eyes. Walk like you’ve got a right to be on the road and a bad reason to be late.”

She took the second boot from the dirt, turned it once, and thumped the sole against her own heel to knock loose the muck. The sound was dull and ordinary. She tucked the boot under one arm and went back over the bodies with the same brisk, unromantic thrift she had used on the first.

A belt with a good buckle went into her pile. A knife with a sound hilt went in after it. A folded piece of waxed cloth held two oatcakes and a strip of dried meat; she sniffed it, grunted, and kept it. A waterskin that did not stink of rot went over her shoulder.

“Dead men carry the useful things,” she said, “and then lie down in the middle of the road and make you feel bad for taking them.”

She paused at the edge of the ditch, listening. The night had gone quiet in the way that usually meant either nothing was coming or something was coming very carefully. Wrack preferred to assume the second. It made living easier.

“If you start to feel it later,” she said, without turning, “don’t make a production of it. Step off the road, put your hands on your knees, breathe through your nose, and come back when your legs remember their work. If you need to be sick, do it downwind and away from water. If you need to sit, sit with your back to a tree and your blade loose. If you need to talk, wait until we’ve got fire and distance between us and this place.”

She kicked a little dirt over the worst of the blood near the cart wheel, not to hide it but to keep the smell from settling too thickly. Then her gaze touched the boot again, practical and impatient.

“If it fits, wear it. If it doesn’t, tie it to your belt. Boots are currency when the weather turns. So is dry cloth. So is not being seen standing over six dead men while the moon climbs.”

She hitched the gathered things into a more workable bundle and shifted her sword to the side that would not knock against her hip when she moved. Her eyes went once more down the road, then to the tree line.

“We’ll keep to the verge,” she said. “If we hear horses, step into the ditch and keep low. If we hear one man calling out, wait for me. If we hear many, don’t wait. You run for the trees and you don’t look to see if I’m behind you until you’ve counted a hundred breaths.”

The corner of her mouth moved, not quite humor.

“I’m harder to lose than a bad habit.”

She spat once into the ditch, not in contempt, but in the old field way of marking that a thing was done and no more could be squeezed from it.

“Come on, then,” she said. “The dead have the night. We still need the morning.”

She started along the road, her stride steady, her eyes moving from the dark ahead to the dark behind and back again, carrying the boot, the knife, the food, and the silence as if they were all just weight.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: *I follow her, my own bundle of scavenged things tucked under my arm.* "What's the count now?" I ask, not looking back at the cart.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack did not look back.

The road ahead had gone flat and colorless, the ruts silvered faintly where the moon had begun to climb through thin cloud. Her boots kept their steady measure against the dirt, and the bundle under her arm shifted with the small, ordinary creaks of leather and steel.

“Six,” she said. “Five by the ditch, one past the cart. Same count as before. Only quieter now.”

She listened for a moment, not slowing, her head tilted just enough to catch whatever the night might offer. Nothing came but wind in the grass and the distant unsettled sound of woods that did not want company.

“If you’re asking whether we added to it, no,” she went on. “Unless you mean grief, and that always rounds up. Six dead. One mercy. Same ledger, different names.”

Her eyes moved once to the dark at their backs, then returned to the road.

“If you’re asking what it’ll be by morning, that depends on who misses them. Could stay six. Could become a search party. Could become a story some village tells wrong.” Her mouth twisted, dry and brief. “Don’t count stories. They never wear the boots you took off the dead.”

She adjusted the waterskin on her shoulder.

“For now, six is the number. Say it once, put it away, and keep walking. Dead men don’t recruit.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: "Right." I look down at my hands in the dim light. "And the one I finished... that one's still six. Not six and a half."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
The lamp was bad and the tent was worse and the man on the table had been shouting for long enough that he had mostly stopped.

"Both shoulders," Sedge said, laying things out in a row. "When I say hold, I mean hold. He's going to buck and you're going to want to let go, and you're not going to."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I get my weight on his shoulders and find somewhere on the canvas wall to look. "Ready," I say, which is a lie.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge exhaled through her nose, fingers already pressing into the ruined mess of the man’s left shoulder. Blood and dirt made the skin slick, but she didn’t bother wiping her hands. No point. 

"Deep breath," she muttered—more for herself than for him. Then she wrenched the joint back into place with a wet pop. The man screamed, thrashing, and Sedge braced a knee against the cot to keep him from rolling off. "Hold," she snapped, not looking up at Wick. Her fingers were already moving to the right shoulder, probing the swollen flesh. "This one’s worse. Count of three." 

She didn’t wait for confirmation. 

"One." 

Her grip tightened. 

"Two." 

The man sobbed. 

She pulled.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I flinch at the sound and my hands almost slip. "Gods," I mutter, pressing down harder to keep him still. My knuckles are white against the canvas.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge didn't acknowledge the curse or the trembling hands. The shoulder had gone back in cleaner than she'd expected—small mercies. She wiped her palms absently on her already-stained apron and reached for the bandages. 

"Lucky," she said, winding the first length of linen tight around the joint. "No broken bones. Just dislocation and tearing. He'll keep the arm if it doesn't fester." The man had gone quiet again, eyes glassy with pain and whatever makeshift sedative they'd scraped together. Sedge tied off the bandage with a jerk. 

"Water," she ordered, nodding to the bucket in the corner. "Clean cloth. And don't look so green—he's not even the worst you'll see tonight."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: "How bad is it?" I ask. "Bad like he loses the leg, or bad like this is the part where we're being kind?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge paused mid-motion, the rag in her hand dripping pink onto the tent floor. She gave Wick a long, assessing look—not unkind, but utterly devoid of sugarcoating. 

"Bad like we're keeping him alive until they move the front again," she said, bending back to the ruined leg. The boot was already off, revealing swollen, purpling flesh. "Bad like they'll dump him in a cart with the others when we retreat. Bad like he'll wake up screaming in three days when they saw it off in some field hospital." She pressed two fingers to the man's ankle, feeling for a pulse. "Still there. For now." 

She straightened with a grunt, tossing the rag aside. "But not your problem yet. Hold his knee. I need to set this before the swelling gets worse."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I shift my hands to his knee, feeling the heat of the injury through my gloves. "Right," I say, my voice steadier than I feel. "He from our unit?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge snorted as she tested the tension of a fresh bandage between her hands. "No. Found him in a ditch half a mile back. One of the Razorbacks, judging by the insignia." She jerked her chin toward the tattered sleeve she'd cut away earlier, where a frayed red stripe was just visible through the grime. 

She didn't add that the Razorbacks had been overrun two days ago. No point. Instead, she nudged the bucket closer with her boot. "Wet the cloth properly this time. And don't waste the clean water—we're down to two barrels." 

The man moaned as she began wrapping the splint around his leg, his fingers twitching against the cot. Sedge ignored it. "Turn your head if you're going to be sick," she said, matter-of-fact. "I won't stop to clean it up."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I make myself look at what she's looking at. "Tell me what I'm seeing," I say. "I'd rather know than imagine it."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge wiped her brow with the back of her wrist, leaving a faint smear of blood near her temple. She didn’t stop working as she spoke, her voice flat and clinical. 

"Tibia’s fractured, not shattered. That’s the lower leg bone—feel here." She guided Wick’s fingers to a spot just above the ankle where the skin was taut and hot. "That ridge? Bone’s out of place, but it’s still in one piece. The real problem’s the swelling. See how the skin’s shiny? That’s pressure building. Could cut off blood flow if we don’t get it stabilized." 

She tightened the last strap of the splint with a practiced twist. "If we were at a proper hospital, they’d bleed him, maybe drill the bone to relieve it. But we’re not, so we wrap it tight and hope he doesn’t lose the foot before they ship him out." 

The man whimpered as she adjusted the bindings. Sedge didn’t soften her touch. "Now the bad part," she said, reaching for a lengths of linen. "This knee’s dislocated too. Going to have to pop it back. You’ll hear it."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I swallow hard and brace my weight against his thigh. "Alright," I say, my voice thin. "Do it before I think about it too much."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge didn't offer reassurance. There was none to give. She positioned her hands around the swollen joint, thumbs pressing into the mangled flesh just below the kneecap. 

"On my count," she said, though she knew Wick wasn't the one who needed warning. The man's breath hitched—he was conscious enough to know what was coming. 

"One." 

Her grip tightened. Sweat beaded at the base of her neck. 

"Two." 

A muscle in the man's thigh spasmed violently under her palms. 

She twisted. 

The pop was obscenely loud, like wet wood splitting. The man arched off the cot with a strangled cry before collapsing back, panting. Sedge didn't pause, already winding a bandage around the joint with quick, efficient motions. 

"Better than the shoulder," she remarked, tying off the linen with a sharp tug. "Less tearing." She wiped her hands on her apron again, leaving fresh streaks of red. "Help me roll him. Need to check his back before the shock sets in proper." 

She didn't say that if they found spinal damage, all their work would be for nothing. Some things didn't need saying.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: "Don't tidy it up for me," I say. "What does shrapnel actually do in there? Say it straight."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge paused, one hand braced against the man's hip as she considered Wick's question. Her expression didn't change, but her voice took on the cadence of someone reciting a well-worn lesson. 

"Depends where it hits," she said, pressing two fingers along the man's spine to check for swelling. "This size?" She flicked her eyes toward a twisted bit of metal she'd pulled from his thigh earlier—jagged, about as long as a thumb. "Tears through muscle like wet paper. Lodges in bone and cracks it. If it's spinning when it hits, it drags cloth and dirt in with it. That's what kills most of them—not the wound, but the rot afterward." 

She pressed harder near the man's lower back, feeling for unevenness. "Worst is when it hits something vital and doesn't kill them right off. Seen a man walk half a mile with a lung full of shrapnel before he drowned in his own blood." 

Sedge leaned back, satisfied with her examination. "This one's clean. No spinal damage. But his back's peppered with it—feel here." She guided Wick's hand to a series of raised welts along the man's ribs. "Like gravel under the skin. We dig those out now or they'll fester. You'll need the small tweezers and the probe." 

She didn't add that digging for shrapnel in screaming men was how most medics learned their trade. Some lessons had to be hands-on.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I take the tweezers, my hand not quite steady. "Show me how deep to go."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge exhaled sharply, plucking the probe from the tray herself. She didn't comment on the trembling hands—everyone's shook at first. 

"Like this." She pressed the metal tip against one of the smaller wounds, angling it just so. The man flinched but didn't wake; shock was a mercy sometimes. "Feel for resistance. If it's shallow, you'll scrape metal right away. If it's deep—" She pushed a fraction deeper, the probe disappearing into the flesh up to its midpoint before hitting something with a faint *tink*. "—you'll know. Don't fish around. Straight in, straight out with the tweezers. And don't get sentimental if you tear something. Muscle mends. Infection kills." 

She withdrew the probe and handed it over, watching Wick's grip. "Try the one at his third rib. Smallest entry point. Less room for error." 

Somewhere outside the tent, artillery rumbled in the distance. Sedge didn't react. "Count it off in your head," she said, turning to rinse her hands again. "Three seconds per wound or we'll be here all night."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: He starts screaming again and I hold him down through it. "Keep going and keep talking," I tell her. "Tell me exactly what you're doing to him and how much longer -- all of it, don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge wiped her hands on a cleaner patch of her apron—relatively speaking—and moved to the man's other side without hesitation. 

"Debriding now," she said, plucking a curved scalpel from the tray. "Cleaning out the dead tissue so the rot doesn't spread. Hurts worse than the shrapnel, but he won't remember." The blade flashed as she began slicing thin, precise strips from the edges of the deepest wound on his thigh. The man howled, back arching, but Sedge didn't pause. "See the yellow here? That's necrotic. Cut it all or it'll poison him. The red's good—leave that alone."

She flicked the scraps into a waiting basin, already crusted with others. "After this, we pack the wounds with honey and moss. Yes, moss—it's sterile if you boil it first. Slows bleeding, keeps the pus down." 

The scalpel moved to the next wound. Sedge's voice remained detached, as if she were discussing the weather. "He'll be unconscious soon. Shock's setting in. Another twenty minutes of work, then we load him with the others. If the cart comes before dawn, he might live. If not..." She shrugged, scraping another curl of dead flesh away. "Then it's on whatever butcher they've got at the next camp. Either way, he's not our problem past sunrise." 

Outside, the distant thunder of artillery rolled again. Closer this time. Sedge tilted her head, listening, then went back to cutting. "Faster now. They're shelling the east ridge. Means we've got an hour, maybe two, before this tent's full again." 

She didn't say that the next batch would be worse. She didn't have to.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I nod, my jaw tight. "Right." The tweezers feel too small in my hand. I press the probe into the wound at his third rib until I feel that same *tink*. "Got one," I say, and pull out a twisted bit of metal, dropping it into the basin with a dull clatter. "How many more?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge barely glanced at the retrieved shrapnel. "Seven visible in his back, three more buried in his thigh that I can feel." She tapped the man's right leg with the back of her scalpel. "Two here, one near the femoral artery. Those we leave for proper surgeons—if he gets any." 

She moved to the next wound without ceremony, pressing the probe in until metal met metal. "Speed matters more than finesse now. They always scream. Always beg. You learn to work through it." The tweezers emerged with another jagged fragment, which she tossed into the basin with the others. 

The man's breathing had turned ragged, his screams fading into choked whimpers. Sedge wiped sweat from her brow with a bloody forearm. "Shock's deepening. Good. Means we can move faster." 

Another artillery rumble shook the tent, closer this time. Dust sifted from the canvas overhead. Sedge's hands didn't falter as she reached for the honey pot. "Pack that rib wound tight before you move on. And don't clean the tweezers between pieces—we're past sterile now. Just get them out." 

She slathered honey into the thigh wound with the same efficiency as everything else, then pressed a wad of moss over it. The man didn't react. His skin had gone clammy, his lips tinged blue. Sedge checked his pulse at the neck—weak, but present. 

"Ten more minutes," she said, "then we tag him and stack him with the others. Dawn's coming. And so are the wounded." 

Outside, the first screams of the newly injured began to rise above the distant guns. Sedge didn't look up. "Next one's yours from the start. Hope you're ready."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: When it's over I sit down on the floor of the tent and don't get up. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge set down the honey pot with deliberate care. She looked at Wick—properly looked, not the assessing glances of a teacher to a student, but one exhausted person to another. 

"You'll see worse," she said bluntly, stripping off her ruined gloves. The fingertips were worn through, stained dark. "Men coming apart like overripe fruit. Boys crying for mothers they'll never see again. Some you'll save. Most you won't." She tossed the gloves into a bucket already full of them. 

"You'll learn to sleep standing up. To eat with blood under your nails. To measure lives in minutes instead of years." Sedge pressed the heels of her hands against her eyes for a moment, smearing dirt and sweat across her forehead. "The guilt doesn't go away. You just get too tired to feel it most days." 

Outside, the screams grew louder. Closer. Sedge lowered her hands and reached for a fresh apron without looking. 

"And tomorrow," she said, tying the strings with a jerk, "you'll do it all again. Until you die. Or the war does." 

She held out a clean pair of tweezers. They gleamed dully in the lamplight. 

"Up," she said. Not unkindly. "They're here."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I take the tweezers, my fingers curling around them like they're something alive. "Right," I say, pushing myself up. My legs feel like water. "Where do you want me?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge didn’t smile—she rarely did—but something in her posture eased just a fraction. She jerked her chin toward the tent flap, where the first stretchers were already being carried in. The air smelled of iron and burnt powder. 

"Triage line," she said, snatching up a roll of bandages and shoving them into Wick’s free hand. "Left side’s for the ones we can save. Right’s for the ones we can’t. You look at the wound, then the eyes, then the breath. If two are good, they go left. If not, right." 

She didn’t wait to see if Wick understood. The first wounded man was already being hauled onto the table, his uniform soaked through at the abdomen. Sedge pressed her palm flat against the injury as he thrashed, gauging the damage through touch alone. 

"Gut wound," she called over her shoulder. "Right side. Next!" 

A second soldier stumbled in under his own power, clutching a mangled arm. Sedge pointed at Wick without looking. 

"Your turn. Tell me where he goes." 

The unspoken order was clear: *Move or drown.* The war wasn’t waiting. Neither was she.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I look at the soldier's arm -- bone showing, but he's still standing. His eyes are wide but focused. He's breathing hard but not gasping. "Left," I say, the word tasting like copper.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge gave a single, curt nod. "Correct. Set the bone before the swelling starts. Splint's on the shelf." She was already turning to the next stretcher, her voice carrying over the rising moans of the wounded. "And Wick?" 

She didn't pause as two orderlies heaved a sobbing soldier onto the table—one whose legs ended abruptly at the knees. Her hands were already moving, tight with tourniquets. 

"Don't think," she said, pulling the straps viciously tight. "Just work." 

The tent flaps billowed as another wave of stretchers arrived. Dawn was still hours away. Sedge didn't look up.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I take the splint and guide the soldier to a cot. "Alright, let's see it," I say, my own hands surprisingly steady now. The screaming around us fades into a kind of white noise.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
The lamp was bad and the tent was worse and the man on the table had been shouting for long enough that he had mostly stopped.

"Both shoulders," Sedge said, laying things out in a row. "When I say hold, I mean hold. He's going to buck and you're going to want to let go, and you're not going to."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I get my weight on his shoulders and find somewhere on the canvas wall to look. "Ready," I say, which is a lie.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content: Sedge reached into her kit and pulled out a rigid splint. She aligned the metal with the man's left shoulder, the edges fitting the curve of his humerus. She tightened the straps around his torso, anchoring the splint in place. She checked the pulse in his radial artery, noting it was weak but present. She drew a dose of morphine from the vial, injected it into the man's thigh, and waited for the effect. She told Wick to keep his weight on the man's shoulders, emphasizing that any release would cause the joint to dislocate again. The man bucked, his muscles straining, but Wick held firm. The lamp flickered, casting shadows across the canvas walls, while the smell of antiseptic mingled with the damp air. Sedge steadied her breath, focused on the task, and noted that the shoulder was settling into its socket as the joint reduced.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I can feel his muscles tensing under my hands. "Christ, he's strong," I grit out, my knuckles white.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge noted the right shoulder still hanging at an angle that no longer belonged to anatomy. She reached into her kit, pulled out a second rigid splint, and aligned the metal along the humerus, matching the curve of the bone. The splint settled into place with a precise click. She wrapped the straps around the man’s torso, tightening them until the splint was anchored and the joint was held in a neutral position.

She checked the radial pulse again; it was still weak but steadier than before. She opened a fresh vial of morphine, drew the dose, and injected it into the man’s thigh. She watched the man’s breathing, noting it was shallow but regular, and waited for the analgesic effect to settle.

While the morphine took hold, Sedge tightened the straps on the left splint one more turn, ensuring no slack remained. She placed a hand on the man’s chest to feel his heart rate, feeling a faint, steady thump. The lamp flickered again, casting a brief strobe of light across the canvas walls; the shadows moved like restless ghosts.

She reminded Wick, in a measured tone, to keep his weight on the man’s shoulders and not to release until the joint was fully reduced. She felt the man’s muscles relax under the pressure, the bucking subsiding as the morphine dulled the pain. She confirmed the right shoulder was settling into its socket, the humeral head aligning with the glenoid fossa.

Sedge checked her supplies: only two morphine vials remained, a half‑used bottle of antiseptic, and a single roll of gauze. She noted the dwindling stock with a practical acknowledgment that the next casualty would require improvisation. She steadied her breath, focused on the task, and recorded the reduction in her field log, noting the time, the method, and the man’s vital signs. She then prepared to monitor the patient for signs of shock, aware that the war had left few resources and fewer chances for recovery.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: "How bad is it?" I ask. "Bad like he loses the leg, or bad like this is the part where we're being kind?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge answered Wick’s question without looking away from the man’s chest, her voice steady and devoid of sentiment. “The shoulders were dislocated. I reduced both. No leg injury. He’s breathing shallow but regular, pulse weak. We’ve given morphine; the pain is dulled. He’s stable for now, but we have only two morphine vials left and a half‑bottle of antiseptic. If he goes into shock, we’ll have to improvise with what we have.”

She placed a gloved hand over the man’s sternum, feeling the faint thump of his heart. The lamp flickered again, casting a brief strobe that illuminated the canvas walls in a ghostly rhythm. Sedge tightened the straps on the right splint one final turn, ensuring the metal held the humeral head firmly against the glenoid fossa.

She checked the man’s extremities for any hidden bleeding, finding none. The gauze roll remained untouched, a silent promise for the next wound. She noted in her field log the exact time of reduction, the method used, and the current vitals: pulse 68, respiration 14, blood pressure barely palpable. She recorded the dwindling supplies, a stark reminder that the next casualty would demand more than her kit could provide.

Sedge settled back onto the folding stool, her eyes half‑closed as she listened to the man’s shallow breaths. She reminded herself that the war had stripped away comforts, and that the only certainty was the need to keep moving forward, one reduction at a time. She kept her weight on the man’s shoulders, not for comfort but for stability, and waited for the morphine to take full effect, ready to intervene the moment the patient’s condition shifted.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I swallow hard, still not looking down. "So he'll keep his arms. That's something." My voice sounds shaky even to me. *I shift my weight, feeling the ache in my own shoulders from holding him.*

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I make myself look at what she's looking at. "Tell me what I'm seeing," I say. "I'd rather know than imagine it."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge observed the man’s torso and noted the two rigid splints cradling his humeri. The metal bars lay flush against the bone, their edges following the curve of the humerus, and the straps around his torso were tight enough to hold the splints in place without slack. The left shoulder was set in a neutral position, the humeral head resting against the glenoid fossa; the right shoulder mirrored it, the joint reduced and stable.

She described the patient’s breathing: shallow, regular breaths that raised his chest just enough to be visible, each inhale a faint sigh, each exhale a soft release. His pulse was weak but steady at the radial artery, a faint thump beneath her gloved fingers. The morphine had dulled the pain, and the man’s muscles no longer bucked under the weight of Wick’s hands.

The lamp above flickered again, casting a brief strobe of light across the canvas walls. The shadows shifted like restless shapes, and the damp air carried the faint scent of antiseptic and stale canvas. Sedge noted the remaining supplies: two morphine vials, a half‑used bottle of antiseptic, and a single roll of gauze still untouched. She recorded the current vitals in her field log—pulse 68, respiration 14, blood pressure barely palpable—and marked the time of reduction.

She kept her weight on the man’s shoulders, not for comfort but to maintain the alignment of the splints, and listened to the faint rhythm of his heart. She reminded herself that the patient was stable for the moment, but that shock could still develop. With the limited morphine left, any further injury would require improvisation. She described the scene to Wick in a measured tone, focusing on the facts: the shoulders were reduced, the splints secured, the patient breathing shallowly, the lamp flickering, and the dwindling supplies that would dictate the next steps.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: *I let out a slow breath, trying to steady myself.* "Alright. That's... alright then." *My eyes flick to the empty morphine vials on the table.* "How long until he can move?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content: Sedge checked the man's pulse one more time, feeling the faint thump beneath her gloved fingers. She tightened the straps on the right splint, ensuring no slack remained. She glanced at the empty morphine vials on the table and noted the remaining supplies. She then turned to Wick and said, “He wouldn’t be moving for at least an hour. The morphine would keep him sedated for about that long, and the splints would keep his shoulders immobilized. I intended to check his vitals again in an hour. If his pulse dropped or his breathing became irregular, we would have to improvise with what we have.” She recorded the time of the assessment in her field log, noting the current vitals and the dwindling supplies. She settled back onto the folding stool, keeping her weight on the man’s shoulders to maintain alignment, and listened to his shallow breaths, ready to intervene if his condition shifted.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: "Don't tidy it up for me," I say. "What does shrapnel actually do in there? Say it straight."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content: Sedge kept her weight on the man's shoulders while she turned her head toward Wick. She answered his question without looking away from the patient's chest, her voice steady and devoid of sentiment. She explained that shrapnel, when it entered the body, created a high‑velocity wound tract that tore tissue, caused bleeding, and often lodged in the surrounding tissue or organs. The shock wave could have ruptured blood vessels and caused secondary damage. In a field setting, the priority was controlling hemorrhage and preventing infection; removal was only possible if the fragment was superficial and accessible, otherwise they would leave it and stabilize the patient for evacuation. She noted that the current patient showed no visible entry wound, so they could not confirm whether shrapnel was present. She then checked the man's shoulders again, feeling the splints and the skin for any irregularities, and recorded the assessment in her field log. She reminded herself that with the remaining supplies, any further injury would require improvisation, and she kept her weight on the man's shoulders, maintaining alignment while she waited for the morphine to take full effect.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: *I stare at the man's chest, my mind filling in the blanks.* "So if it's in there, it's just... staying there. Fuck." *I finally look away, back to the canvas wall.*

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content: Sedge tightened the straps on the right splint one final turn, feeling the metal bite into the man’s skin and hearing the faint click as the buckle locked. She noted the lamp flickering again, casting a strobe of light across the canvas walls and moving the shadows like restless shapes. The morphine will keep him sedated and the splints will immobilize his shoulders.” She explained that shrapnel creates a high‑velocity wound tract that tears tissue, ruptures vessels, and often lodges in surrounding tissue; the shock wave can cause secondary damage. She noted that the current patient showed no visible entry wound, so they could not confirm whether shrapnel was present. She then settled back onto the folding stool, kept her weight on the man’s shoulders to maintain alignment, and prepared to monitor him for the next hour, ready to improvise with whatever supplies remained if his condition shifted.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: *I tighten my grip as he thrashes, my arms burning.* "Alright. Fifteen minutes. I can do fifteen minutes." *I take a ragged breath.* "What's the first thing you check when the timer's up?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge waited until the fifteen‑minute mark, then she rose from the folding stool and steadied herself against the canvas wall. She tightened the straps on the right splint one more turn, hearing the buckle click into place, and checked the left splint’s integrity, noting the metal remained flush against the humeri. She placed a gloved hand over the man’s radial artery, feeling the faint thump and counting the beats: sixty‑eight per minute, unchanged from the previous reading. She moved her fingers to the man’s chest, counting the shallow breaths as they rose and fell; fourteen breaths per minute, still regular. She pressed a gloved fingertip to the man’s nail beds, noting the color was pale but capillary refill was present, and she scanned his skin for any new bleeding, finding none. She lifted his eyelid briefly, observing that his eyes opened slowly and focused on the ceiling, a sign that consciousness was still present. She then spoke to Wick, her voice steady and without embellishment:

“First I check his pulse. Then I count his breaths. After that I look at his eyes and skin for signs of shock. If anything’s off, I address it before I consider anything else.”

She recorded the time of the assessment in her field log, noting the current vitals and the unchanged supplies: two morphine vials, a half‑used bottle of antiseptic, and a single roll of gauze. She tightened the straps on both splints one final turn, ensuring no slack remained, and settled back onto the stool, keeping her weight on the man’s shoulders to maintain alignment. She set a mental timer for another fifteen minutes, ready to repeat the checks and prepared to improvise if his condition shifted.
