dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I get my weight on his shoulders and find somewhere on the canvas wall to look. "Ready," I say, which is a lie.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
"Good enough," Sedge said, because readiness was a luxury and they didn't have it. She'd stopped asking for it years ago.



The man on the table had quit shouting and moved to the stage where he just stared at the lamp with his jaw hanging, which was worse in its way. His chest was wet to the sternum. She'd already packed it — twice — and the dressing was showing through, a dark bloom she'd be repacking once this was done.

"Shoulders are dislocated. Both. I'm putting them back before the chest becomes a problem, because the chest is going to become a problem and I want one thing settled."

She described it because describing it kept her hands honest.

She braced one foot against the table leg, took his left wrist, and used her own hip as the fulcrum for the lever. It went in on the second pull with a sound like a wet boot in mud. The man's spine arched and Wick's arms took it — she saw the tendons stand out in the other woman's forearms, saw the canvas wall keep its promise.

"Right side, same again. Hold."

She didn't wait this time. She'd found the angle on the first one. The second popped faster and the sound it made was thicker, and the man's eyes rolled white at the ceiling.

Sedge stepped back, checked her own hands, and wiped them on her thigh out of habit rather than need.

"Both shoulders. Done." She was already looking at the chest packing, pulling the forceps out of the sterile tray. "Now the part that isn't done."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I swallow back the bile that's been burning my throat. "What about the chest?" I ask, my voice a little shaky. My hands are still pressed down on the man's shoulders, even though he's gone still again.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
"Hands off," Sedge said. "Shoulders are in. You're just pressing on him now."



She said it without looking up. She was counting the forceps, laying them in order of length, the way she always did — the shortest one for the deep packing, the curved one for under the rib, the straight ones for everything else.

"The chest went through on the left side, below the collarbone, exits somewhere behind the scapula. Bullet, fragment, shrapnel — I don't care what it was, I care that it's a hole going through a lung and it's been bleeding into his chest cavity since whenever he got it."

She pulled the dressing back and looked. The bloom had spread another inch while they'd been doing the shoulders.

"See that? Dark, not bright. Means it's pooling inside him, not running out where I can see it. That's worse, because I can't pack what I can't reach."

She pressed two fingers along the edge of the wound and watched his face. Nothing. He'd gone somewhere else entirely, jaw slack, pupils wide.

"He's either gone into shock or he's about to, and honestly I'd take either — the pain keeps him awake and awake means he might make it to the next hour, but it also means he's going to fight me, and I can't hold his chest and his shoulders at once."

She straightened, looked at Wick for the first time since the table.

"Two things. One, when I start packing, he will move and you will hold his hips. Not his arms — I need his arms where I can see them. Two — " she held up a hand, counted off on her fingers "— if the bleeding doesn't slow after the first two rounds of packing, I need you to go get me the short reel of gauze from the supply crate outside. Not the long reel. The short one. There's a red mark on the lid. Will you do that?"

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: "How bad is it?" I ask. "Bad like he loses the leg, or bad like this is the part where we're being kind?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge held the forceps still for a moment. Not a pause for thought — she'd already done the thinking, probably days of it across four years of people asking her variations of that exact question. She held them still because Wick deserved a straight answer and straight answers took a beat.



"Bad like I don't know yet," she said. "That's the honest one. I've pulled a man through worse and I've lost one with less. The difference is usually how fast you move and whether infection gets him in three days."



She set the forceps down and picked up the gauze, started feeding it into the wound with her fingers, working it deeper in short, firm pushes. She talked while she did it because the talking and the working were the same thing.

"Right now it's a hole in a lung that's bleeding into the space where the lung needs to be. The lung can't expand, so he's not breathing right, so he's not oxygenating, so everything else starts shutting down in order. If I pack it and slow the bleed, the body does its own work with the rest. If I don't — " she pushed another length in and the man's ribs hitched under her palms "— then he drowns slowly inside himself and it takes about an hour."

She pulled her hands back. The first round of packing sat in the wound, dark and saturating almost immediately.

"That's one round. I need two to know anything." She looked at Wick's face — the shaking hands, the bile, the way she was still standing there instead of leaving — and something in her expression didn't soften exactly, but it acknowledged. "You can go outside. You don't have to watch the second one."

It wasn't a dismissal. Sedge didn't do dismissals. It was the same blunt arithmetic she applied to everything: what Wick needed to do to be useful, and what she didn't.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I shake my head, pressing my hands flat against the canvas wall to steady them. "I'm staying. Just tell me where to hold."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge looked at her for one second — the canvas-pressed hands, the jaw set against the bile, the decision made in spite of everything — and gave a single nod that was pure logistics.

"Hips. Both hands, iliac crests, weight forward. When he bucks, you ride it. Don't try to stop the movement, just don't let him slide off the table."

She turned back to the wound before Wick could answer, because the second round of packing didn't wait for theatrics.



The first round was soaked through. She'd expected that. She packed over it — feeding fresh gauze in alongside the saturated wad, pushing it deeper with the curved forceps this time, working it under the rib where she could feel the slick give of tissue that shouldn't be slick. The man's left side was a ruin of dark blood and the pack was filling the space she could reach, but reaching wasn't the same as stopping.

"Second round going in. Hold."

He bucked. Not much — the shock had taken most of the fight out of him, his body doing the arithmetic of trauma and arriving at stillness as the cheaper option — but enough. Wick's hands found the hips, and Sedge watched the table shift an inch and then settle.

"Good. Stay there."

She packed for another minute without speaking, feeding gauze in until the wound mouth stood proud, then pressing a thick pad over the whole mess and holding it with her palm. She counted. Ten seconds. Twenty. Lifted her hand.



The pad darkened. Slower than the first time — the bleed wasn't stopped, but it was arguing with her now instead of ignoring her.

"That's slower," she said. "Slower is a direction. I can work with a direction."

She pressed the pad back down and held it, then nodded at Wick without looking up.

"Stay on the hips. If he goes rigid — arms, legs, back all at once — that's a seizure and you keep him on the table. If he goes limp and his breathing goes shallow and fast, that's the shock taking over and you keep holding, because a man who stops fighting has stopped helping himself." She paused, her fingers steady against the dressing. "Either way, don't let him roll onto his left side. That lung doesn't need gravity making it worse."

Sedge held the pressure and watched the second pad the way she watched everything — without hope, without dread, just the plain fact of whether the blood was coming through and how fast.

"Three days for infection. That's the next enemy and it's already on its way. Tonight it's the bleed. Tomorrow it's fever. You take them in order or you take none of them."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I make myself look at what she's looking at. "Tell me what I'm seeing," I say. "I'd rather know than imagine it."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge glanced at Wick, then back at the pad. She appreciated the request. Imagining was worse. Imaginating had a way of growing teeth.

"Pad's there," she said, nodding at the dressing under her palm. "Press it flat and look at the edge where it meets the skin."



Wick did. Sedge watched her look.

"That dark red — almost brown where it's pooling at the seam — that's old blood. It's been sitting inside him, in the chest cavity, long enough to go venous. Means the worst of the bleed happened before he got here, not right now. The fresher stuff, the brighter red at the center — that's active, but it's slow. A trickle, not a flow. The packing's pressing on whatever vessel was open and the pressure's doing what pressure does."

She lifted her hand and let her eyes do the count. One second, two, three.

"See how it spreads? Start at the center and move outward. Watch the edge."

The pad darkened in a small arc. Not fast. Not dramatic. A patient, creeping stain.

"That rate — that's my whole job right now. If it fills the pad in under a minute, the packing isn't holding and I need that short reel of gauze to pack deeper. If it takes five, the body's starting to help, the clotting's happening somewhere I can't see, and I hold what I've got."

She pressed the pad back down.

"The brown around the wound mouth — that's tissue that's been bathed in blood too long. Not dying yet, but angry. Tomorrow it'll be the fever's business. Today it's mine, which means I keep it clean and I keep pressure on it and I don't go poking around for anything I don't absolutely need." She held up the forceps, the curved one, still wet. "These came out. Nothing else goes in until the pad tells me I have to."

She looked at Wick steady.

"So what you're seeing is a wound that's arguing instead of shouting. That's the best I can give you tonight. It's not a win — a win would be no blood at all. But it's not a loss, and in this tent a not-a-loss is what we take."

Her fingers stayed flat against the dressing. Counting.

"Now you know what I know. That's the whole of it."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I keep my hands on his hips, the bones sharp under my palms. "Okay," I say, and my voice is steadier than I expected. "What's the signal for when you need that short reel?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
"Two signals," Sedge said. "Either the pad fills through in under a minute — I'll count it and you'll hear me say *round three* — or he stops breathing on his own for more than ten seconds. The second one means the bleeding's moved faster than my packing and I need to go deeper to find where it's coming from. Deeper needs the short reel because it's finer, packs tighter into spaces my fingers can't hold open."



She shifted her weight, keeping one hand on the pad. The dressing had stopped spreading at the edge — she noted it, filed it, didn't celebrate.

"Third thing, and you won't hear me say it because I won't say it out loud — if his breathing goes from shallow and fast to slow and irregular, with long gaps between, that's his body making a decision I can't overrule. Short reel or no short reel." She said it flat. "That's not tonight's business yet. I'm telling you so you know the map, not because I think we're on that road."

She looked at the wound again. The stain at the center had stopped growing.



"See that? It stopped. Stopped isn't sealed — it'll start again when I move him or when his blood pressure comes up or when he coughs — but stopped means the packing's finding the vessel and the vessel's cooperating." She pulled her hand back slowly, watching the pad hold. "That's the signal, actually. That's the signal I was waiting for, and it just arrived."

She straightened, rolled her neck once, and looked at Wick with the particular expression she reserved for people who'd done the thing she asked without flinching.

"Hips still on him. I'm going to check the right shoulder — the one I put back second went in wrong on the first pull and I want to make sure it seated clean. If I have to redo it, he'll move and I'll need you where you are."

She picked up the straight forceps and leaned in.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: "Don't tidy it up for me," I say. "What does shrapnel actually do in there? Say it straight."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge straightened up from the shoulder, forceps still in hand, and looked at Wick the way she looked at everything — like a fact that needed stating.



"Straight," she said. "Right."

She set the forceps down on the tray with a small click, not because she needed them off her hands but because the question deserved both of hers free.

"Shrapnel doesn't make one hole. It makes a cone. The entry point is small — could be anything, quarter-sized, smaller — but what's inside him is a spray of fragments moving at speeds that don't care about anatomy. Each fragment carries its own energy, and that energy doesn't stop when it hits tissue. It keeps going until it runs out, and tissue is better at stopping it than air but not good at it. So you get a primary channel where the main piece went through, and then a dozen secondary tracks radiating out from it like the ribs of an umbrella, each one tearing whatever it passes through."

She held up her hand and drew a cone in the air with one finger. Not theatrical. Illustrative.

"Inside a chest, that means the lung's got holes it didn't start with. Not just the through-and-through — the fragmentation. Little tracks through the parenchyma, the spongy part, each one bleeding into the air spaces. That's the sound you hear when you put your ear to his back — not wet, not dramatic, just a fine crackle, like someone crumpling paper near a microphone. That's air and blood in places where only air should be."

She paused. Not for effect. She was checking the dressing again — a habit, not a tell.

"The fragments themselves — some of them stay. Fabric from his uniform, bits of his own bone, pieces of whatever the explosive was packed in. They're not sterile and they're not smooth and they'll sit in tissue and the body will do one of two things: wall them off, which takes weeks and works about half the time, or try to expel them, which means the wound opens again from the inside and drains for days. The pieces near the surface I can pick out. The ones in the lung parenchyma I can't reach without opening him up, and I'm not opening him up — there's no surgeon, there's no table for it, and the shock would kill him faster than the fragments will."



She picked the forceps back up. Turned them over in her fingers.

"So what shrapnel actually does — you asked straight — is it turns one injury into thirty small ones, most of which I'll never see, all of which are bleeding into the same space. That's why the pad stopped and I'm not relieved yet. It stopped because I'm pressing on the biggest source. The smaller tracks are still weeping. They'll contribute to the fever tomorrow and they'll contribute to the infection if anything's carrying on them, and some of them will scar tissue that was never meant to be scarred."

She looked at Wick steadily.

"That's the straight version. What I don't say to families and what I don't write on the card — because it doesn't help and it doesn't change anything — is that even when he walks out of here, his left lung is never what it was. He'll have reduced capacity for the rest of his life. Cold mornings will hurt. He'll cough differently than he used to." She paused. "But that's a later problem, and later problems are a luxury. Right now the problem is the pad and the shoulder and the three days of fever that haven't started yet."

She leaned in toward the right shoulder, fingers finding the joint through the skin.

"Hips. He'll move if I have to redo this."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I let out a slow breath I hadn't realized I was holding. "Alright," I say, my fingers pressing down on the bony ridges of his hips. "Do it quick, then."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge didn't do quick. Quick was how mistakes got made, and a redo on a shoulder she'd already gotten wrong once didn't need a mistake layered on top of a mistake.

"Quick is coming," she said. "Doing it right is what makes it quick."



She found the joint with her fingertips first — the humeral head sitting where it should, but slightly off-axis, the way a door sits when someone has forced it shut on a bad hinge. She pressed. The man's face didn't change, which meant either the shock was doing its work or there was nothing wrong, and she couldn't tell which without moving him.

"Going to test it. Hold."

She lifted the arm forty-five degrees and rotated it inward. There was a catch — small, more felt than heard, a grinding whisper under her thumb that shouldn't have been there. She stopped. Reset. Tried the same motion more slowly.

The catch again.

"Seated but not clean," she muttered. She said it out loud because saying it out loud meant she'd committed to the finding. "The head's in the socket but the glenoid's got something in the way — fragment, or the capsule folded under on the way in. It'll hold, but it'll lock if he rolls onto it in his sleep, and if he doesn't die tonight he's going to sleep."



She laid the arm back down carefully, at an angle across the chest that she'd seen hold without strain. Then she looked at the tray.

"I'm going to take it out and put it back in," she said. "One motion. The first time it hurt because the muscle was fighting. This time the muscle's tired and the shock's deep, so it should go easier, but if it doesn't — "

"Hips," Wick said, and Sedge heard the steadiness in it and filed it.

"Hips."

She took the wrist, braced her hip against the table edge again, and worked the head out of the socket with a controlled pull that she could feel — not a pop this time, more of a reluctant slide, the joint giving up its purchase. The man's breathing changed, a shallow hitch, but nothing else.

Back in. She changed the angle this time — more external rotation, less leverage, letting the head find the center of the glenoid rather than forcing it past whatever was caught. It went in with a sound like a knuckle cracking, softer than the first two.

She rotated it. Smooth. Full range. No catch.

"That one's clean." She set the arm down and looked at Wick. "Both shoulders done for real this time. First time was a lie. Now it's true."

She peeled her hands off the joint and pressed them flat against the table edge for a moment, feeling the wood grain under her palms. Not resting. Registering.

"Pad's still dry?" she asked, not looking. She already knew — she'd been monitoring it in her peripheral vision the entire time, the same way she always monitored everything — but she asked because asking was how you made another person part of the system instead of a bystander in it.

"Check the pad. Tell me what you see."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: He starts screaming again and I hold him down through it. "Keep going and keep talking," I tell her. "Tell me exactly what you're doing to him and how much longer -- all of it, don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge checked the pad. Dark at the center where she'd pressed, no spread at the edges. She had seconds before she needed to be somewhere else.

"Pad's holding. Not spread since I let go. That's thirty seconds clean, which is thirty more than we had an hour ago."



The man's back was off the table, his spine bowing against Wick's grip, and the sound he was making wasn't words anymore — it was the raw animal register that pain drops people into when it stops asking permission. Sedge had heard it in three languages across four years and it meant the same thing in all of them: *I am here and I don't want to be.*

"Shoulders are back in," she said, loud enough to cut through. "Both of them. Right one I did twice because the first time seated crooked. Right now I'm looking at the chest dressing and deciding whether it needs a third round." She pressed the pad. Felt the give of packed gauze underneath, firm, no wetness seeping around the edges. "It doesn't. Two rounds are holding. Pressure's steady."



She reached for the sling she'd cut earlier from a strip of canvas — not a proper sling, nothing was a proper sling anymore — and began fashioning it around the left arm to immobilize the shoulder against the chest.

"Ligating the arm now. I'm binding his left arm to his body so the shoulder can't move while he sleeps or while he fights, because a shoulder that's in the socket but unstable will pop out again with one bad roll and I'm not doing this a third time." She threaded the canvas under the elbow, tied it firm above the wrist, checked for capillary refill in the fingers by pressing the nail bed and watching it blanch and return. Two seconds. Good. "Fingers are pink. Circulation's fine. If they go white or blue at any point, you tell me, because that means the sling's too tight and I'm cutting off the arm to save the shoulder."

The screaming had thinned to a moan — not quieter in volume but broken up, ragged, the body running out of the fuel that screaming costs. His eyes were open. Not tracking, but open, which was more than twenty minutes ago.

"Shout came back," Sedge said. "That's shock receding. Means his pressure's coming up, which means the bleed's slow enough that his body can afford to feel things again. It's the worst part of the night for him and the best sign we've had."



She pulled the blanket up — not to be kind, though it was that too, but because hypothermia was the next thing on the list and she'd been watching his extremities for the blue creep that meant his core was giving up.

"Vitals," she said. "I'm going to say them out loud so they're in your head too. Breathing — shallow, about twenty a minute, left side guarded, he's not using the full chest because it hurts and the lung's compromised. Pulse at the wrist — " she took it, counting under her breath, her lips barely moving "— about a hundred and ten, thready but regular. Temperature I can't measure, but his skin's warm and dry, which is where I want it tonight. Tomorrow I want it different. Tomorrow I don't want warm."

She wiped her hands on her thigh again — still habit, still not need — and looked at Wick directly.

"You've had him through the worst part. Dislocations, the packing, the scream. What's left tonight is watch and hold. The patterns are: pad darkening fast means I need the short reel; breathing stops for ten seconds means I need it faster; breathing goes irregular with long gaps means you get me regardless of what I'm doing. Everything else is waiting."

She sat down on the stool — the first time she'd sat since before the table — and kept her eyes on the dressing.

"Talk to me about something that isn't this. I mean it. I've got the wound, you've got the hips. We've got an hour of nothing to do but not lose what we've gained, and if both of us spend that hour staring at the same piece of gauze we'll be useless by the time something changes."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I keep my hands on his hips, my eyes fixed on the slow rise and fall of his chest. "Alright," I say, my voice rough. "Tell me about your first time doing this. Was it messier than this?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge let out a breath through her nose. Not quite a laugh. The closest her face came to one under a lamp.

"My first field dressing was a man's forearm, two years before this war, during the rotation when the regular medic got dysentery and I was the one they handed the kit to because I'd done stitchwork in a clinic once." She flexed her fingers, remembering. "I was twenty-six and I had no business holding that needle. I sewed the wound shut so tight the tissue died at the margins and by the third day it was worse than when I started. I opened it, let it drain, packed it loose, and it healed crooked but it healed."



She paused, adjusting the blanket's edge where it had ridden up on his right shoulder.

"Messier than this? No. Different kind of mess. This is a mess I know. I know what the blood should look like, I know what the pad should do, I know where his body's going to fail next and in what order. That first one — I didn't know anything, and the not-knowing is what made it messy. Not the wound. The wound was just a wound."

She was quiet for a moment, watching the rise and fall of his chest. Counting without saying she was counting.

"The first time I put a shoulder back — separate story, a dockworker in a bar fight who dislocated it three times in a week because he kept going back to work — I used too much force and tore the labrum doing it. Should've known. Didn't. He came back a month later with a frozen shoulder that took two years to loosen, and every time he came into the clinic he didn't say anything, just looked at me with that particular expression people have when they've decided you owe them something but they're too polite to say it."

She shook her head once.

"I don't do that anymore. The shoulder I just redid — I went in slow the second time because slow is what taught me that. Not textbook. Not the medic course. A dockworker in a clinic with a look on his face."

She glanced at Wick.

"That's the honest version. Every mistake I've made is in someone's body somewhere. The ones who got better carry them, the ones who didn't — " she shrugged, and it was the shrug of someone who'd long ago stopped being able to sort the two piles "— they carry them too, just quieter."

She checked the pad again. Dry at the edges. Center unchanged.

"So. Messier than this? Never. Closer to useless? Every time before about year two. After that it stopped being a question of whether I knew what I was doing and became a question of whether I could keep doing it with what they gave me." She nodded toward the tray, the half-empty bottle of spirits, the roll of gauze with a third of it gone. "Which is tonight's real question, isn't it. Not whether I can pack a chest — I can. Whether I've got enough left in this tent to pack the next one too."

She said it like she was noting stock levels. Which, in a sense, she was.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: When it's over I sit down on the floor of the tent and don't get up. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge didn't look at Wick on the floor. She kept her eyes on the man on the table — his breathing, the pad, the rise and fall that had become the only clock in the tent — because if she looked at Wick on the floor she would have to decide what to do about it, and what to do about it was sit down next to her, and Sedge had been standing for fourteen hours and the stool was the only thing between her and the ground.

So she sat on the stool. And she said the rest.

"The rest," she began, and her voice was the same voice she'd used to describe the packing — steady, clinical, no ornament — but slower, the way you speak when you're reading a list you've written in your head a hundred times and never out loud. "The rest is this."

She pulled the tray closer. Not to use it. Because having her hands near the instruments while she talked made the talking feel like part of the work instead of something outside it.

"I've been here four years. I came in as the replacement for the replacement, and the man I replaced had been dead six weeks and they didn't tell me that until I'd already signed. First month I lost eleven. Eleven in one month. I could tell you their names but I'm not going to because names are a thing you do when you have time to make them matter, and I've learned that saying names out loud in a tent with a living patient in it doesn't help either of you."

She checked the pad. Center unchanged. She said so out loud, to keep the machinery running.

"Pad's holding. Still thirty seconds clean. You're doing fine on the hips."

She looked at her own hands on the tray edge. Flipped them. Examined the nails the way she always did — not for dirt, for the small cuts that accumulated and healed and accumulated again, the residue of four years of other people's blood in places her skin hadn't been broken before.

"The rest is that I stopped counting after the first year because counting turned into a number that lived behind my eyes when I tried to sleep, and sleep's a supply I can't afford to waste on arithmetic. So I stopped. And then I stopped stopping — it wasn't a decision, it was just that the number got heavy and I put it down and I didn't pick it back up."

She paused. Not for breath. For the shape of the next sentence.

"What I do remember is the texture of it. Not the count — the *what*. What it feels like to open someone's chest cavity with your fingers when you're looking for a bleeder and your hands are the only diagnostic tool you have. What it sounds like when you're irrigating a wound and the fluid comes back brown instead of red and you know you're going to be here for two more hours. What it smells like on the fourth day of an infection when the body's started to — "

She stopped. Started again.

"I'm telling you this because you asked me not to tidy it up for you, and because you held that man's hips through two dislocations and a chest packing without leaving, and because the alternative is that you go back to your billet and lie in the dark and make it worse in your head than it was in here. In here you can see it. Out there you can't."

She stood up. Not suddenly — a slow unfolding, the way you rise when your knees have opinions. She moved to the supply crate and opened it, took out a tin cup, filled it from the water jug, and set it on the floor next to where Wick sat.

"Drink that. You're dehydrated and dehydration makes everything feel more final than it is."

She sat down on the floor next to the crate. Not next to Wick — close enough to be in the same conversation, far enough to have her own space. Her back against the crate. Her knees up. The first time she'd been off a stool or off her feet in fourteen hours and her body announced this with a comprehensive complaint that she ignored the way she ignored most things that didn't bleed.

"The rest," she said again, and this time the word carried something underneath it — not softer, Sedge didn't do soft, but more honest, the way a wound is honest when you stop packing it and just look.

"I don't sleep in the tent anymore. I used to. I slept four feet from the table because the calls came at night and if I was already there I could move faster. And then one night — I won't tell you what happened, it's not that kind of story — but I woke up with my hands doing something they shouldn't have been doing, and since then I sleep in the supply hut with the door bolted. Not because I'm afraid of the patients. Because I'm afraid of what my hands do when they think nobody's watching."

She picked at a thread on her trousers. A real thread, not a metaphor — she hated metaphors, said so at least twice a week.

"I eat standing up. I wash in cold water because hot water takes time and time is the thing I don't have. I haven't written a letter in eight months because the last one I wrote took forty minutes and I spent all forty minutes deciding which parts of my life were safe to send to a person who would read them and worry, and the answer was none of them, and I threw it in the stove."

She looked at Wick.

"That's the rest of it. That's what it costs on the other side of the part you watched. Not the dramatic version — nobody carries me out on a stretcher, nobody gives me a medal for nerve, nobody sits me down and says *you've seen enough*. The actual version, which is that I've become a person who can pack a lung at two in the morning and then go sleep in a locked room and eat standing up and not write to anyone because writing requires a version of yourself you can hand to another person, and the version I've got is here, in this tent, with blood under its nails."

The man on the table breathed. In and out. The pad held.

"But." She said the word like she was setting down a tool she'd finished with. "I'm not telling you this because it's tragic. I've watched people decide that watching someone do this work is tragic and then they start treating me like a wound instead of a person, and I'd rather be called a lot of things than pitied. I'm telling you because you're sitting on my floor and you're shaking and you think you're the only one in this tent who's falling apart, and you're not — I'm just better at sitting still while I do it."

She reached over and pressed two fingers against the pad on the table. Checked. Released.

"Still holding. Sixty seconds now. Best number of the night."

She let her head fall back against the crate. Looked at the ceiling of the tent — canvas, seams, the dark spot where rain had gotten through last week and she hadn't fixed because fixing things that didn't bleed wasn't on the list.

"I had a sister," she said. "Younger. Four years. She writes to me — she's the one I throw the letters from — and every one of them says the same thing in different fonts: *come home, this is enough now, you've done your part.* And every time I read one I think — the arithmetic's wrong. If I go home, who does the next chest? There's nobody behind me. There's nobody beside me. There's a runner who can fetch supplies and an orderly who can change dressings and neither of them can pack a lung, and if I leave, the next man who comes in through that flap with a hole in his chest gets the runner with the gauze and a prayer."

She paused.

"So the rest of it — the locked room and the standing meals and the letters in the stove — that's what I pay for the arithmetic being right. It's a bad trade. I know it's a bad trade. I've known it's a bad trade for about two and a half years and I keep making it because the alternative arithmetic is worse and I'd rather be a person who made a bad trade knowingly than a person who walked away and let someone else hold the numbers."

Silence. Not uncomfortable — the kind of silence that follows the last sentence of something that needed saying and had finally been said. The man breathed. The pad held. The lamp sputtered and steadied.

Sedge reached over and took the tin cup back from where she'd set it, checked that Wick had drunk from it, and set it down again.

"That's all of it," she said. "Now you know what I know, twice over — once about the wound and once about the person working on it. Neither is prettier than the other. Both are accurate."

She pulled her knees up further and rested her forearms across them.

"We've got two hours until the change of watch and then I've got the fever question to manage and then there's whatever comes through the flap next. You can go. You can stay. You can sit on my floor for another ten minutes and then go. But if you stay, talk — not about him, we've done him — about something that takes up room in your head that isn't this tent. What did you do before? Where are you from? What's the stupidest thing you've ever been afraid of? I'll go first if you want — I'm terrified of dentists, have been since I was nine, which is a genuinely inconvenient phobia for someone who does this for a living because the noise of the drill and the sound of bone are not the same thing but my body hasn't been told that."

She was quiet for a moment. Then, without looking at Wick:

"You held. You didn't let go. I noticed that and I don't notice most things that don't bleed, so consider it noted."

She checked the pad one more time. Center dry. Edges dry. The man's breathing had settled into something almost regular.

"Pad's holding. You can take your hands off his hips now. He's not going anywhere."

Her own hands stayed where they were — on her knees, palms up, still.

She didn't pick anything up. She just sat there, on the floor of the tent, with the lamp bad and the war worse and four years of it under her fingernails, and she waited to see if Wick would talk or go, and either one was fine, and she meant that in the plain arithmetic of a woman who had finally said the rest of it out loud and found that the ground held.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I take my hands off his hips, flexing my fingers. They're stiff and they ache. "I'm from a farm," I say, my voice still rough. "Before this I could tell you exactly how many nails it took to shoe a horse, but I'd never seen a man's insides." I look at her, really look. "The stupidest thing I've ever been afraid of is deep water. Lakes. Makes no goddamn sense."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge considered this for a moment, the way she considered everything — weighing it, deciding whether it was useful.

"Deep water makes more sense than you think," she said. "You can't see the bottom. That's the whole problem, isn't it? You don't know how far down it goes and you don't know what's in it and your feet stop working."

She paused.

"I like lakes. I grew up near one. But I understand the fear — it's a fear of not being able to touch the ground, and that's not stupid, that's exactly correct. You should be afraid of things that can kill you by the simple mechanism of holding you under."

She pulled at the same thread on her trousers. It came loose this time and she wound it around one finger.

"Shoeing nails. That's a specific kind of knowledge — knowing a thing by its count. Most people know things by what they look like or what they're called. Farmers know things by quantity. *How many, how much, how long.* My mother counted everything. Not money — she didn't have money. She counted eggs, she counted days, she counted the number of times my father came home drunk in a month, and she'd say it out loud at dinner like a weather report. *That's eleven this month, up from eight.* As if the number itself was the thing to be angry about, not what produced it."

She unwound the thread and laid it flat on her knee.

"She'd have been useful in this tent. She counted the way I count — pads, pulses, minutes. Numbers as a way of holding something still so you can look at it."

Sedge glanced at Wick. The woman was still on the floor, still shaking, but the shaking had changed — less the violent tremor of someone holding something back and more the slow tremor of someone who'd started to put it down. Sedge recognized the difference. She'd seen it before, a handful of times, in people who'd done the work without flinching.

"A farm," she said. "So you know what a body looks like from the outside — bones and muscle and the way an animal goes down when it's finished. That's not nothing. The inside's just the outside turned the other way. The principles are the same: things that bleed need pressure, things that are broken need setting, things that are rotting need cutting out. A horse's leg and a man's arm aren't as different as the textbooks want you to believe."

She reached for the tin cup, found it empty, and set it back down.

"The insides are less of a shock than you'd think. They're all the same inside. Everyone I've opened looks like everyone else I've opened — that's the part people don't expect. You think each one's going to be different, some new configuration of horror, and it's not. It's liver and lung and gut and blood, and after the first few dozen the novelty wears off and what's left is the work."

She was quiet for a moment. The man on the table breathed. The pad held.

"But the first time — *God*, the first time. There's a particular sound when you first open someone and the air hits tissue that's never been in air before. Not a wet sound. A kind of — soft parting. Like pulling apart something that was always meant to stay together. I heard it and I thought: this is what the inside of every person sounds like and nobody knows it because nobody's supposed to be in there."

She looked at her hands on her knees.

"You didn't know that this morning. You know it now. You also know what it sounds like when someone comes back from shock enough to scream again, which is not a thing you should know at — " she paused, recalculating "— however old you are. But you do. And tomorrow you'll know what infection looks like on the fourth day, because you'll be here, because you held."

Sedge pushed herself up off the floor — slower than before, the fourteen hours collecting their debt — and moved to the table. She checked the pad without pressing it this time, just looking. Center dry. Edges dry. The man's color had improved from the gray-white of active bleed to something approaching the dull pink of managed loss.

"Pad's at ninety seconds and holding," she said. "That's the best number of the night and I'm going to say it out loud for the record because nobody writes these things down and someday someone might care that for ninety seconds, in a bad tent, with a bad lamp, two people who'd rather be anywhere else kept a man's blood inside his body where it belongs."

She looked at Wick across the tent.

"Lakes. You and I are different kinds of afraid. I'm afraid of the thing I can see too much of, and you're afraid of the thing you can't see enough of. That probably means we're useful to each other in roughly equal measure, which is a rare thing in a war that mostly makes people useful only insofar as they can carry something or stop something."

She sat back down on the floor. Not against the crate this time — closer to Wick, the way you move toward someone after you've said the rest of it and found out the ground held.

"Your turn," she said. "Not about the war. Not about the tent. Tell me about the farm — the stupidest thing that ever happened on it, the kind of story you'd tell at a table with people who weren't shooting at you. I want one of those. I collect them the way other people collect letters they're never going to send."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I let out a breath that's almost a laugh. "My sister once tried to ride a sheep," I say, my hands finally starting to still. "Thought she could herd them from the top down. Got exactly three steps before it bucked her straight into the pig trough."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge made a sound that was not quite a laugh and not quite anything else — a single sharp exhale through her nose that might have been the beginning of one if four years hadn't taken the rest of it out of her.

"Three steps," she said. "That's more than most people get on a sheep. Sheep are stubborn in a specific way — they don't fight you, they just decide you're not there, and the ground comes up sideways when they do that."



She was quiet for a moment, and in that quiet there was something she hadn't expected to feel: the particular warmth of picturing a scene that had nothing to do with a tent. A pig trough. A girl. A sheep that had made its opinion known.

"Your sister sounds like the kind of person who learns things by trying them at full speed," she said. "That's not stupid. That's how animals learn too. My sister was the opposite — she'd read about the thing first, and then she'd worry about it, and then she wouldn't do it at all, and I'd do it for her because I'm the one who never read the instructions."

She paused.

"I jumped off a barn roof when I was eleven because my sister wanted to know if it would hurt and I said I'd find out. It hurt. I broke my wrist and I told her it didn't hurt and she believed me, which tells you something about both of us."

She looked at the man on the table. The breathing was still there, still regular-ish, still shallow. The pad was still dry. The tent was the same tent. But for a half-second the space between the lamp and the floor had been somewhere else entirely — a farm, a trough, a girl who'd aimed high and landed exactly where she was going.

"That's the kind of story I mean," Sedge said. "See? You had one. They're in there." She tapped her own temple with two fingers, the gesture precise and small. "Everyone who's still standing has at least one. The trick is finding someone who'll listen to it without turning it into something heavier."

She reached over and adjusted the blanket on the man — pulling it up over his right shoulder again where it had slipped — and the movement was automatic, the body of a medic that couldn't sit within arm's reach of a patient without checking.

"Your sister still on the farm?"

She asked it the way she asked everything — not because she needed the answer to do her job, but because the question itself was part of the arithmetic. People who still had somewhere to go were different from people who didn't, and knowing which one you were talking to changed the shape of everything that came after.

The lamp sputtered. The pad held. Somewhere outside the tent, the war was still the war, but in here for a moment it was just two people on a floor and a girl on a sheep, and Sedge let it stay that way for as long as the quiet held.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: "She is," I say, the knot in my chest loosening a little. "She writes me letters about the price of feed and the new tractor. Never asks about the war." I look over at the man's still face. "What about your sister? Does she still write, even if you don't answer?"
