dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
The lamp was bad and the tent was worse and the man on the table had been shouting for long enough that he had mostly stopped.

"Both shoulders," Sedge said, laying things out in a row. "When I say hold, I mean hold. He's going to buck and you're going to want to let go, and you're not going to."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I get my weight on his shoulders and find somewhere on the canvas wall to look. "Ready," I say, which is a lie.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
"Good," Sedge said. "Lie's fine. Half of holding is pretending."

She folded a strap of leather between the man's teeth and waited until his jaw clamped down on it. Then she took up the probe and talked, because talking was part of the work.

"Fragment went in through the boot-top and traveled. It's sitting against the big vessel in his left thigh now. If I leave it, it wears through inside a week and he bleeds out in his sleep, somewhere quiet, without me. If I go in after it, he hurts tonight. Those are the two choices, and there's no third one, so nobody's to blame. Including him." She set the blade low, just above the entry wound. "And before you wonder — I don't enjoy this. Anyone who enjoys it shouldn't be allowed near a table."

She cut.

The man came up off the table like the wood was electrified, a sound tearing out around the leather strap, and Sedge didn't flinch and didn't hurry. She kept the blade where she'd put it.

"Hold," she said, level, not looking up from the wound. "That's the first one. There'll be three more. He's not fighting you, he's fighting the table. Count them with me if it helps."

She widened the track, working by feel as much as by the bad light, narrating because narration kept her hands honest. "I'm following the channel. There. I can feel his pulse against my fingertip, which is how I know I'm exactly where I shouldn't be. Don't let him twist left. If he twists left, I cut the vessel, and then this stops being a surgery."

The man bucked again. Slighter this time — the body only had so much.

"Two," she said. Her voice hadn't changed at all. "You're doing fine, Wick. He's doing fine. Nobody here is doing fine, but the wound doesn't know that."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: My grip tightens on his shoulders, knuckles white against the canvas. I keep my eyes fixed on the tent wall, counting the water stains like prayer beads. "Three," I mutter under my breath before she can say it, bracing for the next jerk.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
"Three," Sedge agreed, a half-second after the man proved him right. The buck was weaker again, more shudder than fight, and she noted it the way she noted everything — out loud, flat, for the record. "You called it. Good instincts. Wrong profession."

Her fingers closed on the fragment at last. She described it because describing it was part of doing it properly. "There it is. Jagged, about the size of my thumbnail, sitting in the scar tissue like it pays rent. His pulse is on one side of my finger and this thing is on the other, and that's the whole surgery. That's the last four years of war in one inch."

She turned the fragment, slow, the way a man might turn a key in a lock he wasn't sure was his. The man on the table made a thin sound around the leather, high and animal, and his heels drummed once against the wood.

"Four," Sedge said. "That's the last one, I promise him, not you." And it was — she drew the metal out in one smooth pull, trailing a ribbon of dark, and immediately her palm was there, pressing hard enough to make her arm shake. "Vessel's intact. I felt it jump when the fragment cleared, which means it's still got its nerve, and so do I."

She held the pressure and counted under her breath — not for the man's sake, for her own — and when she lifted her hand the bleeding came slow and obedient. She packed the track, stitched the incision closed with quick, ugly, serviceable work, the kind that held and didn't win prizes.

Then she took the leather strap from between the man's teeth. He'd gone quiet somewhere in the middle of the last stitch, unconscious at last, the body's one remaining kindness.

"You can let go," Sedge said, without looking up. She was already wrapping the fragment in a scrap of cloth, because she wrapped all of them, every one. "Slowly. Your hands are going to cramp when the work goes out of them, and it'll hurt worse than the holding did. That's normal."

She straightened, rolled her neck until it cracked, and looked at the man's slack face for a moment — checking the color of his lips, the lift of his chest.

"He'll sleep till morning and hate me at breakfast," she said. "That's the good outcome. Take the water stains off the wall and look at him if you want. You earned it."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: "How bad is it?" I ask. "Bad like he loses the leg, or bad like this is the part where we're being kind?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
"Neither, tonight," Sedge said. She said it plainly, because a question asked that plainly deserved an answer without decoration. "The vessel held. The channel's clean, the pack's in, the leg stays where it is. He'll walk with a hitch and a story. That's the honest ceiling of what I can promise."

She wiped the blade and set it with the others, talking the way she always talked after — because silence after a table was where the wrong thoughts got in.

"But you asked the second question like it's a different question, so I'll answer that too. The kind part is when I stop cutting and start holding his hand. You'll know it when you see it, because I'll sit down to do it. I don't sit during surgery. I've never once sat." She pulled the stool out with her boot and didn't sit on it. "Tonight I stood. Tonight was arithmetic, not kindness. Fragment plus vessel equaled a leg. I did the sum and it came out in his favor. That's all kindness is out here, Wick — a sum that lands on your side of the line. The word's for people who need the word."

She looked at the man's face again, the slack mouth, the color coming back into his lips like weather.

"The leg's the easy fight. The next three days are the real one. Fever, rot, the track going hot — that kills more men than fragments ever did, and it doesn't do it quickly, which is the part I mind." She said it flatly, for the record. "If the leg goes bad, I'll take it off in the morning, sober, with light, and he'll have a chance. I don't do midnight amputations unless the midnight is doing it for me. That's not kindness either. That's just not being lazy about the timing."

She folded the wrapped fragment and put it in the tin with the others — she never said why and nobody had ever asked twice.

"So. He keeps the leg if the leg cooperates, and I'm kind only when I sit down. Any more questions, ask them now while my hands still want something to do."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I look at the man's face, finally, and his eyes are closed but his jaw is still clenched. "I'll sit with him," I say, surprising myself. "First watch, anyway."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
"Then he's got better company than most," Sedge said. She didn't make anything of the surprise in Wick's voice, because she'd learned long ago that pointing at a person's better instincts only made them retract like a tick. "Surprising yourself is how half of us ended up here. Don't examine it too hard. It doesn't hold up to examination."

She gave him the watch the way she gave everything — plainly, out loud, because a thing said was a thing done.

"Here's what you're watching for. His breathing first — if it goes fast and shallow, like a dog in summer, you wake me. His skin next — if the leg goes hot around the stitches, hotter than the rest of him, you wake me. If the pack soaks through, you don't change it, you press it and you wake me. And if the smell turns sweet—" she paused, and for the first time all night her mouth did something that wasn't quite flat. "You'll know it when you smell it. Nothing else smells like that. You wake me fast."

She pulled a blanket from the stack and laid it over the man, tucking it under the good leg and leaving the wounded one bare to the air.

"Don't hold his hand unless he asks. He won't ask. But if he comes to and doesn't know where he is, tell him the fragment's out. They always want to know that first. Not the leg, not the war — the thing's-out-of-me. Say it plain and say it twice."

She gathered her tin, then stopped at the tent flap with her back to him.

"I'm three tents down. I sleep light, so don't be polite about it. Politeness kills more men than fragments too." She pushed the flap aside, and the bad lamp behind her threw her shadow long across the canvas. "Wake me at four whether anything's wrong or not. Everyone should get relieved on time. That's not kindness either. That's just how a watch works."

Then she was gone, and the lamp hissed, and the man on the table breathed slow and even, doing his arithmetic in the dark.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I make myself look at what she's looking at. "Tell me what I'm seeing," I say. "I'd rather know than imagine it."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
The flap hadn't fallen all the way shut behind her. Sedge held it a moment, one boot already in the cold, and then she let it close and came back to the foot of the table, because that was the right kind of question and she'd learned not to walk away from those.

"Then look properly," she said. "Not the way civilians look, which is at the whole thing all at once. One thing at a time. Start with his face."

She pointed without touching.

"Jaw's still set. That's not pain — he's gone past pain. That's the body keeping the argument going after the man's left the room. Bodies do that. They're stubborn on behalf of people who aren't awake to be stubborn themselves. Lips are the real tell — see the color coming back in them? Gray means the blood's sulking. Pink means it's behaving. He's behaving. That's the first right thing you're seeing."

She moved her hand down, not quite to the blanket.

"Breathing. Count it. In and out is one. Fifteen, sixteen in a minute, that's where a sleeping man lives. If he climbs past twenty-five you come get me, and don't stand there recounting to be sure. Now the leg — look at the stitch line. Yes, it looks like a drunk did it. A tired woman did. Even and ugly holds better than pretty and loose, and it'll hold. There's a spot of dark on the pack the size of a coin. That's expected — a packed track always seeps a little, like a wall after rain. A coin is fine. A spreading handprint is not."

She pulled the blanket back an inch from the wounded leg, enough to show the thigh above the incision, where the skin had gone dark in a long uneven streak.

"That's the bruise, and here's the part worth knowing: by morning it'll be yellow and green and twice this size, and it'll look like the leg is losing. It isn't. Bruises are receipts. Proof of payment, not proof of debt. The bruise getting uglier is the body doing its bookkeeping. The things that kill don't get uglier — they get hot, and they get sweet, and they get fast. Ugly and quiet is the healthy direction. Remember that, because at four in the morning ugly and quiet will try to convince you otherwise."

She put the blanket back the way she'd had it, bare leg to the air.

"So. That's what you're seeing. A man whose blood is behaving, whose stitches will hold, whose bruise is going to lie to you in about six hours." She picked up her tin again. "Imagining's always worse than knowing, you're right about that. The body's honest. It's the mind that makes up the bad stories. You've got the honest version now — hold onto it when the lamp starts playing tricks."

She went to the flap a second time, and this time she meant it.

"Four o'clock," she said, and the night took her.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I pull the stool closer and sit, elbows on my knees. The man's breathing is steady, but I count anyway. "Fifteen," I say out loud, because the tent feels too quiet now.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
The flap stirred — not opening, just shifting, pressed from the outside by a shoulder that had stopped two steps into the dark.

"Good," Sedge's voice came through the canvas, flat and unhurried, as if she were still standing at the table. "Out loud is the right way to do it. It keeps your count honest, and he can hear it under. Men come to on my table asking who was talking before they ask where they are. You're giving him a voice to come back to. That's free, and nothing else in this tent is."

A pause — the kind she took when there was one more thing worth saying and she was deciding whether it was worth the saying.

"Fifteen's where a sleeping man lives, so that's right. But count it again in five minutes, and again five after. First counts flatter — it's the third and fourth that tell the truth. A man holding fifteen across an hour is a man whose blood's still behaving. And don't count every minute, either. You'll grind yourself down to nothing by two and be no use to him or me at four. A watch is a long arithmetic problem. Pace yourself, because the end is the part that matters."

Then one more, because she'd never once left a lamp unaccounted for.

"The lamp will gutter around two. That's the wick, not him. Trim it or don't. But don't let a bad flame tell you stories about a man's breathing. The flame lies. The count doesn't."

Her boots moved off through the frozen mud — unhurried, even, the walk of a woman who'd decided years ago that running was something she did only for other people's emergencies. Three tents down, canvas shifted, and did not settle again. She slept the way she did everything: light, and ready to be done with it.

Inside, the lamp hissed. The man breathed — fifteen, and fifteen again — doing his quiet arithmetic under the blanket, and somewhere under that, maybe, hearing the count kept over him in the dark.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: "Don't tidy it up for me," I say. "What does shrapnel actually do in there? Say it straight."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
The boots stopped in the frozen mud. Then came back — three steps, unhurried — and the flap opened and Sedge came in again, tin under her arm, a woman who had known the question was coming and had only pretended to leave.

"Fair," she said. "You watched me pull it. You've earned the whole of it."

She didn't go to the table. She stood just inside the flap, and she talked the way she worked — one thing at a time, for the record.

"Shrapnel isn't a bullet. A bullet's honest. It goes fast, it goes straight, it makes a round hole, and it's hot enough from travel to cook a little of what it touches — which sounds like a horror, but it means the entry's cleaner than you'd think. Shrapnel is slow and filthy and never the same shape twice."

She held up her thumb, the size of the fragment still in her memory.

"A bullet cuts. Shrapnel tears. Jagged edges don't part tissue, they rip it and crush it along the whole track. That's why his thigh looks the way it does. And it doesn't travel alone — it went in through a boot-top, so it carried the boot in with it. Leather. Wax. Whatever muck he'd walked through that week. Here's the part nobody says straight: the metal is the least of it. The body doesn't much care about metal. It cares about the dirt. Dirt is what kills."

She shifted the tin under her arm.

"It doesn't go straight, either. It tumbles. It hits bone and deflects. It follows the seams between the muscles the way water follows a crack — the body's own roads. That's how it traveled from his boot to his thigh. And because it's slow, it usually doesn't have the legs to come out the other side. So it stays, and one of two things happens. Either the body walls it off — scar around it, a little shell, and the man carries it to old age and sets off detectors. Or it sits against something that moves. A vessel. A joint. And every heartbeat works it like a file. That's what his was doing. Another week and it wears through, and he dies in his sleep with no wound to show for it."

She glanced at the man's slack face, then back.

"Last thing. While it's in there, the crushing starves the muscle around the track. Kills a little of it. Dead tissue is food, and the dirt it carried came with a mouth already in it. The fragment's a delivery, the wound's a pantry, and the fever is the dinner. That's the sweet smell. That's the thing I told you to wake me for."

She said it all flat, no relish in any of it, because there was none to have.

"So — the straight of it: the tearing does the damage, the dirt does the killing, and the wearing does it quietly. Tonight I took out the passenger and cleaned the pantry as best the light allowed. Now we wait to see how good a job I did." She tapped the tin once, softly, and didn't explain it. "Keep counting."

This time she left and the flap stayed shut, and her boots went the full three tents and were gone.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I listen to her footsteps fade into the night. My eyes drift back to the stitches, the ugly, even work. "A pantry," I mutter to the sleeping man. "You're not a pantry. You're a stubborn bastard." I start counting again.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
The lamp guttered at two, just as promised — the wick, not the man. It hissed and steadied and hissed again, and the man on the table breathed through all of it, fifteen and fifteen and fifteen, holding his arithmetic like a man holding a card he liked.

At four, the flap opened without a knock. Sedge came in with the cold still on her coat, because she'd decided years ago that relief was a thing a person shouldn't have to go fetch.

"You were supposed to wake me," she said, which wasn't a complaint, just the record. "I don't wait to be asked. Nobody asks the right questions at four in the morning, so I stopped listening for them."

She went to the table and worked through it, one thing at a time, out loud, because saying it kept it honest. Lips — pink, behaving. Breathing — she counted it herself, mouthing the numbers, and got fifteen on the first try. Pack — she peeled the blanket back and looked at the dark spot. Still a coin. Not a handprint. The thigh — she laid the back of her hand against the good leg first, then the wounded one, and held each for a slow three.

"Same heat, both sides," she said. "That's the whole game. Hot on one side is the fever sitting down to dinner. Even is even." She leaned close to the stitch line and breathed in through her nose, deliberate, unhurried, then straightened. "And no sweetness. Nothing else smells like that, so there's no mistaking it for anything else. It's absent. Good."

Then the man stirred. Not the bucking kind — the surfacing kind, the sort a body does when it wants to check whether anyone kept the light on. His eyes came half-open, unfocused, and his jaw worked once, and what came out was small and cracked and had clearly been waiting hours for its turn:

"Is it —"

"It's out," Sedge said. Plain. Then again, because she always said it twice: "It's out. All of it. You did the hard part and I did the rest. Sleep."

He went down like a lamp being trimmed, and the slack finally reached his jaw — the argument over, the man back in the room at last.

Sedge looked at the bruise while she was there. Yellow at the edges now, spread wide, exactly as ugly as promised. "Receipts," she said. "Not debts. His bookkeeping's coming along fine."

Then she turned, and stayed standing, and made a point of it.

"You'll notice I'm standing," she said. "That's the arithmetic talking. Now give me your numbers. Third count, fourth count, the pack, the smell — anything the lamp told you that wasn't true. Your eyes were here all night and mine weren't, and the record isn't complete until I have them."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: He starts screaming again and I hold him down through it. "Keep going and keep talking," I tell her. "Tell me exactly what you're doing to him and how much longer -- all of it, don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge was moving before the scream finished, because she'd seen the stitch line go dark while her hand was still on his forehead, and the scream was just the body confirming what her eyes already had.

"There it is," she said, peeling the blanket back. The pack had gone from a coin to a handprint in under a minute. "The vessel lied to me. Held all night, earned my confidence, let go when I stopped looking. They do that. It's not betrayal, it's tissue. But I'm going to talk to it anyway."

She cut her own stitches — quick, she knew where every one was — and opened the incision with two fingers, and the blood came up to meet her like something that had been waiting under the door.

"All of it, then, since you asked. A branch tore off the big vessel. Small one, the size of a wheat stalk, but arteries don't care about size, they care about pressure, and his is excellent, which right now is his enemy." Cloth in her free hand, wiping, wiping. "I can't see the end of it through the blood, so you're the tourniquet. Right hand off his shoulder — here—" she took his wrist and set his fingers high against the groin crease. "Press down against the bone. That's the artery's front door and you just closed it. Don't ease off for anything. He screams, you press. He bucks, you press. Your arm dies, you press. The only thing that lets you stop is my voice saying so."

The man was screaming around shapes that weren't words. She got the strap between his teeth without ceremony — "Bite" — and he did, and the sound became something the tent could survive.

"How long: five minutes to find and tie it, five to clean and close. Ten. I'll give you the road as we walk it." The probe went in, following the blood backward, narrating because her mouth kept her hands honest. "Wiping. Wiping again. There — I see the end of it, jumping like a fish on a line. It's a branch, not the trunk. The trunk I never tie; tying the trunk is taking the leg by the slow route. A branch I tie, and the leg complains but lives."

She laid the thread. Loop, twice around, and she said so as she did it. Then the knot, pulled down slow, and the blood that had been a fountain became a trickle, and the trickle became nothing.

"There. Feel that under your fingers? The pulse just dropped. That's mine — that's the pressure coming off the house. Ease up now. Over five seconds, slow, because if I'm wrong I want to find out gently." She watched the wound, counting silently, and nothing came back. "Good. It held. You can let go. Your arm's going to shake for a while; that's the rent it charged, and it was worth it."

The man had gone from screaming to a low animal moaning, and she noted it for the record.

"So you have all of it, as asked: I put a thread around a vessel inside his leg and pulled it shut, and he screamed because that's what a body does when a stranger ties off its plumbing. Nothing about it is pleasant, and I'd be a horror if I pretended otherwise. But hear the useful part — screaming means the blood's still moving. Men who are bleeding out go quiet. The screaming is on our side of the ledger."

She cleaned the track again, thoroughly this time, packed it, and closed it with the same quick ugly stitches.

"Blood loss — a pint, maybe a little over. A man his size carries eight or ten. That's a rent payment, not the house. But it's why he'll be pale at breakfast and weak as a kitten, and why the arithmetic changed. Yesterday he was a leg that keeps. Today he's a leg that keeps if the remaining roads can carry the closed road's traffic. They usually widen to do it. Usually. And he won't remember any of this — the body doesn't store the middle parts. He'll wake up remembering the first surgery and hating me for it, and tonight will be blank. That's the one mercy in a bleeder. The mind's already out the door."

She straightened. Rolled her neck. Didn't sit.

"You held. Second time tonight. That's twice you were the difference between a surgery and a funeral, and I'm not saying it to make you feel anything. It's in the record." She pulled the blanket back over him, wounded leg bare to the air, same as before. "I'm staying till light now. Not kindness — arithmetic. A vessel that's lied once gets watched, and I don't farm out watching to someone who's never seen one lie. You've done a full watch. Go wake the next pair of hands and teach them the count. That's how a watch works."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I nod, my hands still trembling from the pressure. "You want me to wake the next hands, or just stand here looking like I've seen a ghost?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
"Neither," Sedge said. "You look like a man who closed an artery with his hand for ten minutes, which is what you are. Ghosts don't have hands that shake. Ghosts don't have hands."

But she took one of his wrists anyway — pure reflex, the way another woman might have patted a shoulder — and counted against her own pulse. "Yours is fast. That's the rent, not the house. It'll come down on the walk over. Shaking hands carry worse than steady ones right now, which is the only reason you're not staying."

She let go and gave him the errand the way she gave everything: out loud, once, completely.

"Wake Brill. Second tent at the end of the row, the one who sleeps in his boots. Steady hands, weak stomach, and I need the first more than I mind the second. Bring him back with you and one more if you can dig them out — I want two sets of eyes on this vessel till light, and one of them can be yours if you eat something first."

She was already turning back to the table as she talked, checking the pack — still a coin, the new stitches sitting down flat and ugly in the old ones — but the instructions kept coming over her shoulder.

"The orders changed, so tell them the new ones whole. I'm here till light, so the waking rule is off — nobody fetches me, I'm already standing in the room. They watch breathing and pack with me. Teach them the count — out loud, fifteen to the minute, and why it matters, because a number without a reason is just noise at four in the morning. Teach them the smell. Don't describe it, you can't. Tell them to ask me and I'll let them smell the cloth from the last man who waited too long. That's what the tin is partly for." She said it flat, and did not elaborate on the other part.

She pulled the blanket up another inch and stood over the man a moment — lips pink, breath even, the argument gone out of his jaw at last.

"And eat, Wick. Bread, water, whatever the kitchen's got. The body spends real coin on a night like this and it wants paying back before it lends to you again. That's not advice. It's the arithmetic."

She didn't look up for the last of it, but her voice carried anyway, unhurried, for the record.

"One more thing, since you brought up ghosts. Ghosts are the ones who don't come back from the table. You've come back twice tonight, and you'll do it again, because you're going to walk out of here, eat, and come back with Brill. Whatever that makes you — and I'm not naming it, because naming things is how you scare them off — it isn't a ghost. Go on. I'll keep the count while you're gone."

And she did — out loud, alone, fifteen, and fifteen again, the lamp hissing and the man breathing and the tin sitting closed on the shelf with all its unexplained weight.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: When it's over I sit down on the floor of the tent and don't get up. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge looked at him on the floor for a long moment. She didn't tell him to get up. Floors were where the body put people when it ran out of arguments, and she'd stopped arguing with the body on anyone's behalf years ago.

"Fair," she said instead. "You've earned the rest. Most people earn half of it and get a third. You closed an artery with your hand tonight, so you get all of it."

She went to the table first — the watch didn't stop for conversation, it never had — and did the round: lips pink, pack a coin, breath at fifteen on her first count, no sweetness anywhere in the air. She pulled the blanket up an inch, and then she took the tin down from the shelf, and instead of the stool she came and sat on the floor across from him, her back against the table leg, the tin balanced on her knees.

"You've now seen me refuse a stool twice," she said. "So I'll give you the distinction before you have to ask for it. There are three kinds of sitting in this tent. The first is during surgery — I don't, ever, because sitting is what you do when the cutting's over, and I have never once operated on a man I'd already given up on. The second is the kindness, the one I told you about — when the arithmetic lands on the other side of the line and you stay in the room anyway. The third is this. Two people, a night survived, the work holding steady on the table above them. Nobody teaches the third kind because nobody plans for it. It's the rarest one. I'm doing it now. Make a note."

She opened the tin.

Inside: small bundles in waxed cloth, each tied off with thread, packed tight as seeds. And apart from the rest, a single rolled strip of linen, darker than the others.

"The roll is the school one," she said. "The man who waited too long. You'll smell it when you're ready to learn it. Not tonight — tonight your nose is full of this man and your own adrenaline, and I need it accurate tomorrow, not raw. The bundles are what you already think they are. Every fragment I've pulled since my first table." She turned the tin slightly, not offering it, just letting it be seen. "There are eleven at the bottom that weren't mine."

She let that sit the way she let a pack sit before she judged it.

"Her name was March. She had this tent before me and the habit before me and the count before me. Everything I said to you tonight that sounded like it had weight — the talking while you work, the counting out loud, the relief at four whether anything's wrong or not — that was hers. I stole it the way you steal anything worth keeping. She said it to me once and I kept it, and now I say it to you, and if you keep it, that's three of us carrying the same load, which is how loads survive."

She picked up one bundle, the smallest, and held it in her palm without unwrapping it.

"My first table. A boy, shoulder, easy pull — I found the fragment in a minute and thought I was a natural. The dirt had been in him four days before he reached us. Fever took him on the second morning. March caught the smell at the end of the first day and knew, and she sat with him through the second night, and she told me afterward: watch the ones you save, because the pulling is the easy half. Then she held out this tin and said, put it in. I asked why. She said — receipts. That was her word. I stole that too."

She put it back. Her hands went on doing the work of the tin — settling, aligning — the way hands do when the mouth is carrying something heavier.

"Now the part I left out on purpose. I told you the kind part is when I stop cutting and start holding his hand, and that I'd never once sat during surgery. Both true. What I didn't give you was the number of times I've sat after. It's not small. The first was a gut-shot man my second month. Nothing to cut that would help — you learn that fast with a gut, there's no third choice there either — and I stood over him doing sums, and March put a hand on my shoulder and pushed me down onto the stool and said: sit, watch, this is also the work. So I sat. He took forty minutes. I counted out loud the whole way down, because she'd taught me hearing is the last thing to go, and a man should go down to a voice and not to silence. Fifteen, twelve, nine, six, four, two. Then I stopped saying numbers, because there wasn't a throat to hear them, and I sat a while longer anyway, because the sitting isn't for him at the end. It's for the one still upright. That's the part nobody says."

She looked at the table above them, at the blanket, the bare leg, the even lift of the chest. Checked nothing. Just looked.

"The hand rule — don't hold it unless he asks, he won't ask. That was hers too. She never asked either, all the years I knew her. People who spend their lives watching never ask, because asking is a kind of being watched, and they can't bear the reversal." Her voice didn't change at all, which was how he would know what was coming. "Except at the end. She asked at the end."

Sedge was quiet for exactly as long as the record required.

"Scratch on the back of her hand. Off a bone fragment, third year, a bad week — you know the kind, when the tables don't stop and neither does the mud. She didn't report it. She wrapped it herself and kept working, because that's what the last medic in a row does, and she was the last one in hers the same way I'm the last one in mine now. The rot got in. And here's the joke the war tells, the one I'd laugh at if I still did: you can't smell yourself. The one smell I've taught every pair of hands since to wake me for, and she couldn't smell it on her own arm, and I didn't check her, because she was the one who checked me. I was twenty-two and she told me to sleep and I was polite about it."

She said it flat, for the record, because describing was part of doing it properly, even this.

"I woke at dawn. She'd counted herself down sometime in the small hours — out loud, I'm certain of it, because that's what she taught and she was professional to the last number. Nobody heard it. Fifteen, twelve, nine. Into an empty tent." She looked at the tin in her hands. "So. Now you have the rest of the sentences I gave you tonight. Sleep light — that's not discipline, that's debt. Everyone gets relieved on time — because she never was. Politeness kills more men than fragments — I was the politeness. And don't hold his hand unless he asks — he won't ask, until he does, and you had better be in the room when it happens."

She closed the tin. Didn't put it back on the shelf. Set it on the floor between them instead, which she had not done in front of another living person in over a year.

"Last thing, and then you can be quiet as long as you want, I'm done needing your half of the conversation. I've done the sum on that morning a thousand times. My arithmetic says nobody's to blame — she hid it, the hour was cruel, I was young, there's no third choice, nobody's to blame. I built that arithmetic myself and I stand behind every piece of it, and it has never once come out balanced. That's how I know the arithmetic is a tool and not a truth. It works on tables and vessels and fever. It doesn't work on her. I keep doing the sums anyway, because the sums are the job, and the job is the only grief I've ever been able to afford. Grief with a job. That's the tin. That's all of it."

Above them, the man breathed — fifteen, and fifteen again — and the lamp hissed, and Sedge stayed where she was, on the floor, the third kind of sitting, keeping nobody's count for once, and finding she didn't mind it.

"He'll hate me at breakfast," she said. "That part's still true. Some things hold."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I look at the tin on the floor between us. "My brother," I say, my voice rough. "He went quiet. I thought he was just...tired."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge didn't answer right away. She let the quiet Wick had just described exist in the tent for a full minute — she was good at that, had practiced it over the dying for four years — because rushing in behind a confession was a kind of tidying, and he'd asked her not to tidy.

"I told you I was done needing your half of the conversation," she said finally. "I'm never done receiving it. Different thing."

She turned the tin a quarter-turn on the floor between them, her hands doing their small work while her mouth carried the load, same as always.

"Here's what I can give you, and it isn't comfort, I don't stock it. Tired is what dying looks like from the outside. That's not a failure of yours — it's the failure the quiet is built out of. I read bodies for a living. Four years, thousands of them. I can count a man's breath from across a tent and tell you what his blood's doing by the color of his lips. And the best reader of bodies I ever met missed it on herself, and I missed it on her, sharing her washbasin, sleeping three feet away. So 'I thought he was just tired' isn't a lapse, Wick. It's the design. The body's last kindness is to stop fighting, and it does a perfect impression of a man resting. Nobody tells them apart from the outside. Not you. Not me. That's the whole of it."

She said it flat, for the record, because describing was part of doing it properly, even this.

"Now the piece that's actually going to keep you up, because you said it and I heard it: 'I thought.' That's the fragment in you, and it traveled, same as his did. So hear what I know about the matching one. You'll do the sum on that a thousand times. It'll have the same shape mine does — he didn't say, or you were far, or young, or tired yourself, or you'd been taught that brothers don't need watching. Every piece of it will be true. And the total will never come out, and that's not your arithmetic failing. It's the limit of the tool. I told you an hour ago the sums work on vessels and not on people, and I said it about her, and now I say it about him: nobody's to blame. Including you. I built that sentence myself and it sounded like nothing for years. Keep it anyway. The alternative is doing the sum without it, and that sum's worse. I've run both. I'd know."

She paused, and for the first time all night the pause wasn't for the record. It was just a pause.

"And if the version you're carrying says he'd have asked if it mattered — hear the hand rule again, because it cuts both ways. The quiet ones don't ask. Not because they don't want the hand. Because by the time a man's that tired, asking has stopped being something he can do — same as a man bleeding out can't shout. Telling is for the well. So no amount of watching closer buys you a different sentence out of him. You'd have gotten the same quiet, and done the same sum, and it would have come out just as crooked. I'm sorry." She said it the way she said everything, and then noted the rest. "First time I've said that word in this tent. It goes in the record too."

She looked at him then the way she looked at a wound before cutting — steady, unhurried, intending to do it properly.

"I wondered about you tonight. You'd never held a table, and you counted out loud like you'd been taught. You asked me not to tidy it up. You made yourself look at the leg when the wall was working fine. That's not curiosity. That's a man who already knows the price of not looking. You've been keeping his count since before you walked in here — every number you said tonight over a stranger, you said over him. And here's the thing worth marking: you just did what the quiet ones never do. You said it out loud, in a room, to someone counting. I'm not naming what that makes you. Naming things is how you scare them off. But it's the opposite of quiet."

She left the tin where it was.

"So give me his name. Say it once where I can hear it, and he goes in the record. March stays in mine because I say her out loud in rooms where someone's counting — that's all a record is, names said where they can be heard. It's the one thing I've got that I know holds. It's not much. It's carried me twenty-two years, so it's not nothing either."

Above them the man breathed — fifteen, and fifteen again — and outside, far off, the sky had started its slow gray work toward morning. Sedge stayed on the floor. The tin stayed between them, off the shelf for the first time in a year.

"It's got company now," she said. "The count can wait."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: "Kael," I say. The name tastes like rust. "He was twenty. I wasn't there."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge let the name sit in the tent the way she let a pack sit — untouched, until she knew what it was going to do.

Then she said it back. "Kael." Plain, the way she said everything. And then a second time, because the important things got said twice in this tent, and the second time was for the record. She turned toward the tin where it sat open between them and spoke the entry the way she'd speak it over a table: "Kael. Twenty. Brother of Wick, who counts out loud, who held the table twice in one night, who asked not to have it tidied." She nodded once, the nod she gave a pack that had held. "There. It's in. The tin's heard it, and the tin is the paper I've got."

She looked at him then, steady, unhurried.

"The rust is right. Don't fight the taste. Iron is what's left when the blood stops moving — it's what the names are made of now, his and March's and every one in that tin. A name that tasted sweet would be the wrong name."

Then the harder part, and she took it the way she took a bleeder — straight in.

"Now the piece you saved for last. 'I wasn't there.' I won't pretend it's the same sum I did an hour ago, because it isn't. An hour ago I told you watching closer wouldn't buy a different sentence, and that's true of a man who goes quiet in front of you. But you weren't in front of him. So the sum you'll run a thousand times is 'if I'd been there,' and here's the only thing I know that touches it: I was there. Three feet. Sleeping light, the way I still do. And it bought nothing toward the outcome. Not one thing. I've watched men go down with six pairs of hands on them and every pair wanting the opposite. Being in the room doesn't buy the outcome. It never has." She let that stand a moment, then gave him the rest flat, for the record. "It buys the witness. That's the real rent your absence charged, and I'll name it because you asked me not to tidy. Not that he died — twenties die at a rate the arithmetic can't argue with, and the war places men where it places them, and being elsewhere is a posting, not a choice. The rent is that he went down to silence. No voice. No count. March did too, in the end — into an empty tent. So I won't tell you being there would have changed his dying. I'll tell you what it would have changed: someone would have been counting. Witnessed is not nothing, Wick. Witnessed is the whole of what I do. I can't save most of them. I can be in the room."

She turned the tin a quarter-turn, hands doing their small work while the mouth carried the load.

"So here's the payment I'll take, and you can decide later whether it's a habit. The record is names said where they can be heard — that's the entire technology. No paper, no ink. It's carried by whoever's counting. March's name is carried by me and, as of tonight, by you — you heard it, you hold it. Kael's is carried by you and, as of tonight, by me. That's how loads get lighter without getting smaller. I can't explain the mechanism. I only know it's the one thing I've never seen fail." She paused, and noted the first: "And mark it — that's the first name in this record that never touched either of our tables. A record that doesn't grow is just a scar. This one grew tonight."

Outside the flap, the gray had gotten serious about its work. She tipped her head toward it.

"He'll wake inside the hour and hate me, and you'll eat something if I have to stand over you while you do it, and the count will go on, because that's what counts do — they don't stop for the good stories or the bad ones. That's not dismissal. That's the other thing that holds. Mornings come. They're the one supply this war's never run short of."

She stayed on the floor. The tin stayed between them, off the shelf, in company, till light.

"And Wick — if some night you want to say his name where someone's counting, this tent is three doors down from wherever they post you." Her voice didn't change at all, which was how he'd know it mattered. "I sleep light. Don't be polite about it."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I lean my head back against the table leg and close my eyes. The exhaustion hits like a wall. "He'd have liked you," I say, the words slurring a little. "Hated the tent, though. Hated being still."
