dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
The lamp was bad and the tent was worse and the man on the table had been shouting for long enough that he had mostly stopped.

"Both shoulders," Sedge said, laying things out in a row. "When I say hold, I mean hold. He's going to buck and you're going to want to let go, and you're not going to."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I get my weight on his shoulders and find somewhere on the canvas wall to look. "Ready," I say, which is a lie.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
"You're not," Sedge said. "Nobody ever is. Hold anyway."

She took the left arm first because the left was worse. The head of the humerus had gone forward and sat under the collarbone where anyone could see it, a hard knot that didn't belong there. She wrapped both hands above the elbow, set her feet, and leaned back with her body weight — slow, steady, no jerking. Jerking tore things. Slow traction tired the muscle out until it stopped fighting her.

The man found his voice again. That was fine. Shouting meant the airway worked.

"Spasm's the enemy," she said, half to herself, the way she talked through everything. "Not the pain. Pain never stopped a reduction. Muscle does." She kept the pull even, rotated the arm out a few degrees, and felt it give — a grind, then the clunk, deep and unmistakable, the joint sliding home. The man sagged like someone had cut his strings.

"One." She pressed her fingers into his wrist, then made him squeeze her hand. "Pulse is good. Fingers move. Nothing torn that wasn't torn already."

She let the arm rest across his chest and moved around the table.

"Other side's going to be worse," she said. "Not the shoulder — him. Now he knows what it feels like, and he's going to fight you for it." She took the right arm and settled her grip. "Hold."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I swallow, fixing my gaze on the canvas seam as I lean into his other shoulder. "Got him," I mutter, bracing for it.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
The man started before she ever pulled. He knew the grip now, knew what her hands on his arm meant, and he began to say *wait, wait*, in a voice that had gone small.

"Waiting won't help you," Sedge said. "The muscle's tearing itself every minute it sits out. Breathe out. All the way."

When she felt the breath leave him she took up the slack — slow, no jerk, until the arm came taut in her hands — and then she simply leaned, steady as a plumb line, and let her weight do the work.

He bucked hard enough to shift the table. "Hold him," she said, not louder, just flat. "He can spend himself. You can't."

The right side fought her longer than the left. That was anticipation — the muscle had locked before she touched it, and locked muscle didn't stretch, it only endured. So she endured back. Kept the pull even, counted nothing, watched the tendons in his neck stand out and then, by degrees, stop standing.

"There," she said, at the first give. She rotated the arm out, slow degrees, and felt it grind and then go home with the deep clunk she'd been waiting for. The man made a sound like a drowning man surfacing.

"Two."

She pressed two fingers over the pulse at his wrist, then touched the skin over the point of his shoulder. "Feel that?" A nod. "Nerve's alive. Squeeze my hand." He did, weak and getting stronger. "Nothing new broken. Plenty old."

She bound both arms across his chest with swathes, not gentle, because gentle took longer.

"Six weeks," she said. "Not six days. And hear me — once a shoulder's been out, it wants to go out again. A wrong reach, a bad fall, it'll slip. If it does, you come to me. Don't let some helpful idiot put his boot in your armpit and haul on it. That's how arms stop working." She tied off the last knot. "I've got nothing to spare for how tonight's going to feel. Sleep if you can."

She straightened and rolled her own shoulders, one, then the other, until something in the left one clicked.

"You can let go of him now," she said to Wick. "You held. That's the whole job. Nobody enjoys this work — anyone who does, I don't want at my table."

She was already turning toward the flap, toward the noise outside that never really stopped.

"Get him off my table. There's always more."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: "How bad is it?" I ask. "Bad like he loses the leg, or bad like this is the part where we're being kind?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge didn't answer until she'd looked. That was the rule — you didn't grade a wound from across the tent, and you didn't grade it from the stretcher-bearer's face, either.

The man they carried in had a belt cinched high on his right thigh, and below it the leg was the wrong color — grey going bronze at the edges, swollen tight as a sausage skin. Whatever had done it had taken most of the calf and driven the dirt in after. She pressed two fingers into the skin above the wound and it crackled under her touch, faint and wrong, like snow giving under a boot.

"Gas," she said. "Feel that, if you want to learn it. You'll smell it in a minute — sweet, like apples gone over." She slid her hand up past the knee and pressed again. Warm. No crackling. "When did the belt go on?"

"Just past dark," one of the bearers said.

"Then the leg was dead before you tied it. The iron killed it, not the belt — don't let anybody tell you different." She straightened. "Bad like he loses the leg. The rot's below the knee and it hasn't climbed yet. Being kind is the other answer, and it isn't tonight's answer. Being kind is when the crackling's up in his hip and there's nothing left to cut to — then it's everything I have in the bottle and somebody's hand to hold. I've done that job. I'll tell you plain when that's the job. This isn't it."

She was already laying things out in their row — knife, saw, ligatures, the curved needle. "But hear the rest. That answer's good for maybe an hour. Gas doesn't wait, so we don't."

She set her hand on the man's shoulder until his eyes found her. "I'm taking the leg. It's already gone — I'm only making it official. Bite the strap. Hate me later."

Then, to Wick, flat and even: "Your job is the belt. When I say slack, you ease it a quarter turn so I can see what bleeds and tie it off. When I say tight, it goes back. He'll buck worse than the last one and the strap will do most of the holding. You do the belt. Nothing else is yours."

She tested the knife's edge with her thumb, once, and set her feet.

"Belt ready. On my word."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I nod and set my hands on the cold buckle, my knuckles white. The smell hits me now—sickly sweet and wrong. "Ready," I say, my voice tight.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
"Now."

The knife went in fast — that was the whole trick of it, and the only mercy on offer. One circle around the thigh, skin first, and the man's scream went up through the tent canvas and kept going. Sedge didn't stop for it. Stopping was the cruelty. "Skin's done. Muscle now — it fights less than skin does, remember that." The blade turned and the muscle parted in a red wedge, and she worked around the bone in steady strokes, peeling it back the way you'd roll a stocking. "Fast is kind. Slow is for butchers. You'll hear men brag about taking a leg in ninety seconds — it's the one thing they're allowed to brag about."

He was thrashing against the strap and the strap was winning. Good. She'd tied it herself.

"Slack. Quarter turn."

The pressure eased and the wound told her the truth — two arteries jumping, bright and rhythmic. "There and there. That's the femoral's children, and they're the whole reason you're on that buckle." She hooked each one up with the needle, threw a ligature, pulled it snug, tied it off. "Tight."

The bleeding fell away to an ooze. Below the blade line the leg wasn't bleeding at all, and she pointed at that with the back of her hand, bloody to the wrist. "See that? Nothing. Dead meat doesn't bleed. That's how you know the belt wasn't the murderer — the leg was already gone when they tied it. Remember it, because some fool will tell that man different, and he'll believe it."

Then the saw, and she didn't dress it up. "This is the worst sound in the world. It's only a sound." She set the teeth above the cut and drew long, even strokes, no forcing it, letting the saw carry its own weight. The man went quiet halfway through — not dead, just gone somewhere, and she took that for the gift it was. "He's out. Body's wiser than he is. Keep the belt."

The bone ended. The leg came away into the basin with a thud she didn't look at, and she was already working the flap — muscle over the bone end, skin over that.

"Watch what I don't do," she said, and laid only three loose stitches, wide apart. "I don't close it. Gas lives in closed places — sew it up neat and pretty and it blooms inside the stump and kills him in a bed instead of on a table. Open weeps. Open drains. Ugly and open is how he keeps the rest of himself." She packed it with the last of the clean linen. "Tight, and hold it there."

She straightened and wiped her hands on a rag that had stopped being clean an hour ago, and looked at the man's face — grey, breathing, pulse fluttering but present under her fingers.

"He lives tonight. After that it's fever's decision, not mine, and I'll tell him so when he wakes — a man deserves the true odds. Three in ten don't see the week out. He was strong and the cut was fast, so I like his three better than most."

She rolled her shoulders again. The left one clicked. She ignored it.

"You did the belt. You did it on the word and not before, and that's rarer than you'd think — most people want to help, and helping at the wrong second is how a man pumps his life out on my floor." She nodded once at the buckle, at Wick's white knuckles still on it. "You can let go of that now. Ease it slow — slow — and watch the stump while you do. If it jumps, you tell me and we find the bleeder. If it weeps, we're done."

She was already gathering the instruments, dropping them in the basin with the leg, because everything went in the same boil in the end.

"Then get him off my table. There's always more."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I make myself look at what she's looking at. "Tell me what I'm seeing," I say. "I'd rather know than imagine it."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
"Then look in order," Sedge said. "Bleeding first, because bleeding kills fastest. Everything else waits its turn."

She pointed with a bloody finger at the stump. "That's the flap. Muscle over the bone end, skin over that, three stitches to keep it honest. See the color — red, wet, shining? That's living meat. It should look like a butcher's shop, and it should bother you that it does. Grey is dead. Bronze is worse than dead. Red and ugly is what you pray for."

"Now the weeping. Come closer. See how it seeps through the linen — slow, dark, no rhythm? That's ooze. Every raw surface in there weeping at once, and it's nothing. A bleeder is different. A bleeder *jumps*." She held two fingers a hair above the dressing. "Bright red, and it comes in pulses, with the heartbeat, because it is the heartbeat pushed out through a hole. You see that, you don't think and you don't fetch me — you put your thumb on it and shout. Thumb first, shout second. A man can empty himself in the time it takes to cross this tent."

She took the belt the last quarter turn herself, eyes on the stump. The linen darkened, slow and even. Nothing jumped.

"There. That's a tied vessel holding. Two knots in there the size of peas, and they're the difference between this man and a corpse. The belt did its work up here —" she tapped the thigh above the wound "— and now the knots do it down there. In a week the flesh grows over them and they rot away on their own, and that's the last anyone thinks of them."

Then she moved up the table, because the order went stump, then man. "Now him. Face first. Grey is fine — he's bled, and grey is what bled looks like. It's the lips you watch." She lifted his lip with a thumb. "Pink underneath. Blue is the bad color. Blue means the air isn't getting where it goes." Two fingers to his throat. "Pulse is fast and thin, and it should be — that's a body doing its work with less than it had this morning. What frightens me is a pulse I can't find, or one that gallops and won't be caught. This one's just working."

She laid her hand flat on his chest and felt it rise, counting nothing. "Breathing's shallow. He'll do that for a day. Deep breaths hurt when you've been cut on, even when the cut's nowhere near the breathing. The body doesn't reason. It guards."

She stepped back and wiped her hands again, out of habit more than hope.

"That's tonight. The week has its own signs, so learn them now. The stump will weep — good. It will stink a little by tomorrow — all wounds stink, that's just wound. What you watch for is the smell going sweet again, like it was under the belt. Sweet means the gas came back. And you watch the skin at the edges. If it goes bronze —" she pressed two fingers into her own forearm "— if it crackles when you press it, you come get me, and you don't tell him why. That's the other conversation. The kind one. I'll know it when I see it, and I won't dress it up for you either."

She looked at Wick a moment, flat and unreadable.

"You asked to know instead of imagine. That's near the whole of this trade. The wound is always worse in your head than on the table — on the table it's only meat, and meat has rules. Learn the rules and there's nothing left to imagine." She nodded once. "You looked. You didn't go grey and you didn't look away. Most men look once, and either they run or they stay. The ones who stay, I can use."

She turned to the basin, to the instruments, to the boil that was always going somewhere in the camp.

"Wash to the elbow, hot as you can stand it. Then come back — tomorrow I'll show you how to change that packing, because you'll be the one doing it."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I wipe my hands on my trousers, watching the bloody smears. "I'll stay," I say, swallowing the sour taste still in my mouth. "But I'm keeping my belt on."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge looked at him for a moment, and something moved at the corner of her mouth that wasn't a smile — smiles were in short supply — but stood in the place where one used to go.

"Keep it on. And know what you're wearing." She tapped two fingers against her own. "A belt's a tourniquet with a second job. High on the limb, over the bone, never over a joint — a joint gives it nothing to press against. Tight until the bleeding stops, and once it's on it stays on until somebody like me says otherwise. A loosened belt's killed more men than a fastened one ever has. You wore the lesson all day and never knew it."

She went back to the basin, fishing the instruments out one at a time, laying them on the rag.

"Now hear the rest, because nobody tells it and it frightens people worse than the blood does. In a few minutes your hands are going to shake. Not while there's work — after. That's not fear coming back, that's the work leaving them, and it happens to me same as you. Let it shake. Don't fight it and don't be ashamed of it. It passes."

She jerked her chin toward the flap.

"Eat something, even if the thought of it's ugly. Especially if it's ugly. The ones who don't eat go down by the third day and then I've lost a pair of hands to save a stomach. And if you're going to be sick, be sick outside. No shame in it — the shame's in doing it on my floor, because then I'm the one cleaning it, and I'll remember it."

She said it flat, and the flatness was the kindness. Everything was procedure with her, and procedure didn't judge.

"First light, you're changing that packing. I'll watch you do it — where to press, how fast to pull, what the linen should look like coming out. Then you'll do it alone. By the end of the week you'll do it while a man screams at you, and that's the whole of the training. There isn't any more than that. There never was. I learned it the same way, on a worse table, with a worse lamp, and the woman who taught me was harder than I am."

The left shoulder clicked when she reached for the lamp. She ignored it the way she ignored everything that couldn't be tied off.

"You stayed, and you looked, and you asked. That's three things most men never do one of." She turned the flame up against the dark. "Go eat. Then sleep if you can — take it where you find it, it doesn't keep. And Wick."

She didn't look up from the instruments.

"The jokes are allowed. They're cheaper than the bottle and they do some of the same work. Just don't make them at the table while a man's awake to hear them. He gets to hate me in peace."

Outside, the noise that never stopped was getting closer again. She was already watching the flap.

"Go. Before the next lot comes in and you're still standing here."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: "Don't tidy it up for me," I say. "What does shrapnel actually do in there? Say it straight."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge didn't answer right away. She reached into the basin and fished out something that clinked against the tin, and set it on the table between them — a piece of metal the size of a thumb joint, dark, jagged, bent back on itself like a torn nail.

"That's out of the first man tonight. Not the leg — the shoulders. It was sitting in his back and he never knew it. Keep it or don't, but look at it, because that's the truth of it. It isn't a ball. It isn't a point. It's a tear in the world with weight behind it."

She turned it over with one finger.

"A bullet drills. It's made to — smooth, round, going one way, and if it misses the vessel and the bone you're left with a hole front and back and a man cursing his luck. That —" she tapped the fragment "— ploughs. It comes off the shell any shape it likes, spinning, and it doesn't care about going one way. It hits a rib and turns. It hits the soft parts and tears them wide instead of parting them. A bullet wound you can sometimes follow with a finger. This makes a track like a ploughed field, and everything along the track is bruised past living, even where it isn't cut."

"Second thing. It's hot. Comes off the burst burning, and it cooks the flesh it touches on the way in. That sounds like mercy — cooked flesh doesn't bleed, and you'll see men come in with terrible holes and hardly any blood, and the bearers say he's lucky. He isn't. Cooked edges are dead edges, and dead edges rot. The man who bleeds free is better off. Remember that when you're the one grading them at the flap — the quiet bloody one before the quiet dry one."

"Third. It doesn't come in alone." She held up her free hand and counted on her fingers, blunt as a shopping list. "Dirt. Cloth off the uniform. Leather off the boot, if it's low. Bits of the man standing next to him — bone, sometimes, driven in like shot itself. Whatever was on the ground when the shell found it. That's why the gas and the rot follow shell wounds worse than any other. It isn't the iron that kills them after. It's the field the iron carried in with it. Every fragment wound is a dirty wound even when it looks clean, and that's why I pack them open and let them weep, every one, no matter how pretty I could make them."

She picked the fragment up and held it to the lamp.

"Fourth — and this is the one that kills men who should have lived. The hole lies. The skin shows you a mouth this big and the track inside is this long, and it goes where it likes. I've taken a fragment out of a man's back that went in at his thigh. So you count the holes. Always count them. Even number, maybe it went through. Odd number, one of them's still inside, and you'd better know which direction it was travelling, because a fragment that stops against a vessel doesn't bleed — it just waits. It sits there a week, two weeks, with the pulse wearing at the wall it nicked, and then the wall gives and the man empties himself into his own leg before anyone gets a belt on. That's the one who dies smiling, telling you the wound's nearly healed. If a man with a shell wound says his leg aches deep, worse at night, you bring him to me. That's the ache I'm talking about."

She set the fragment down.

"The belly's its own country and I'll be short with it. A fragment through the gut lets the inside leak into the inside, and there's no belt for that and no flap for it either. Some of them I can open and wash and sew, and fever decides. Most of them, by the time they reach me, the leaking's been going on too long. Those are the kind conversations, more often than not. I'll teach you the signs, and then you'll know them too, and I'm sorry for that in advance."

She went back to the instruments, one at a time, out of the boil and onto the rag.

"Last thing, because you'll ask it eventually, so I'll save you the trouble. I don't chase every fragment. One sitting deep in the muscle, quiet, away from the vessels — the body walls it off and the man carries it the rest of his life and it rains on him in his joints when he's old. Chasing it does more harm than it does. The judgment isn't in the digging. It's in knowing which ones to leave, and you learn that by watching me be wrong about it, because I have been, and the man paid for my tuition."

She jerked her chin at the flap, at the noise outside.

"That's shrapnel, straight. It tears, it burns, it dirties, it hides, and it waits. The hole is the least of it — the hole is the lie it tells on the way in. Now you know, and you'll see every one of it true inside a week, because there's always more."

The lamp flared as she turned it.

"Go eat. That's an order, and I don't give them twice."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: My hands do start to shake now that she’s said it. I clench them into fists and nod. "I’ll eat," I say, and turn toward the flap. "But Sedge?" I look back at her, at the set of her shoulders against the lamp light. "Don’t make me learn by watching you be wrong."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge didn't answer straight off. She set the curved needle down on the rag, because some things were said better with the hands still.

"Then you're asking for the one thing I haven't got."

Flat, the way she said everything that mattered.

"I was wrong this month. Boy with a belly wound no bigger than your thumb. I sewed him neat and sent him down the line walking, and the leak had already started inside. By the time he came back to me there was nothing left to cut to. He got the kind answer — the bottle and a held hand — and my being wrong is what bought it for him. You'll watch me be wrong again. Maybe this week. I won't promise you otherwise. Anyone who promises you otherwise is selling something."

She pushed the fragment an inch across the table toward him with one finger.

"The choice was never between a teacher who's wrong and one who isn't. That teacher doesn't exist — not here, not in the best hospital in the world before all this. The choice is watching me be wrong, or being wrong alone, on your own table, in two years, with nobody to catch it. Mine's the cheaper tuition. I've already paid most of it."

"So here's what I can give you, and it's worth more than a promise. When I'm wrong, I say it. Out loud, at the table, in front of whoever's holding. *I was wrong.* Three words. Watch for them — you'll hear them. And it cuts both ways. You think I'm wrong, you say so. Mid-cut, mid-sentence, in front of the man, I don't care who's listening. If I'm right, I'll tell you why, and you'll have learned something. If I'm wrong, you'll have saved him, and I'll owe you. A medic who hides her mistakes kills twice — once with the mistake, once with the hiding. I don't hide. That's the whole of what I can swear to."

She caught where his eyes had gone — her shoulder, the set of it against the lamp.

"Old dislocation. Goes out in weather, goes back on its own. Not everything that clicks is dying." The corner of her mouth did its not-smile. "And don't grade me from across the tent. Same rule."

Then her chin jerked at his fists.

"Unclench those. Fighting it makes it worse — I told you, let it shake. It's the work leaving, right on time. Means you did some."

Outside, the noise resolved itself into what it always resolved into — boots, a stretcher, somebody giving a count. Sedge was already turning the lamp up, already looking down the row of instruments the way a soldier looks at his rifle.

"That's twice I've ordered you to eat, and I don't give orders twice. If you're still standing there when they come through that flap, you're holding, not eating."

She pulled the rag straight with one hand.

"First light, the packing's yours. Go."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: He starts screaming again and I hold him down through it. "Keep going and keep talking," I tell her. "Tell me exactly what you're doing to him and how much longer -- all of it, don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
"Talking's free," Sedge said. "Watch while I do it. And since you asked — the bad part's ten minutes. The whole of it, half an hour. I always lie on the long side. Hope's cheaper that way."

She ran her hands over him first, fast, head to heel, before she looked at any wound.

"First thing, always — count the holes. Not the blood. The holes." She lifted the man's arm. "One. Front of the arm." Turned it. "Two. Back of it. Even. That one went through, and through is the best news a fragment gives you — what's gone can't kill him twice. Missed the big vessel by luck and the bone by more of it. It's meat, and meat waits." She bound it tight, quick, not gentle, and the man screamed into the strap she'd given him. "Screaming's free too. Moving costs. That holds him. Now the one that matters."

She eased him onto his unhurt side, and he bucked, and the table creaked.

"Three. Here — back of the shoulder, under the blade. Three is odd. Odd means one of them's still inside, and this is the one he's screaming about. Through-holes don't scream like that. Deep ones do. The body knows."

She cleaned it enough to see, no more.

"Watch my hands, not his face. His face will lie to you — everything hurts him the same right now. The track tells the truth." The probe went in slow, a hair at a time, her eyes on nothing, on the feel. "Track goes in and up. It hit the blade bone and turned — like I told you they do. A bullet would have drilled straight. This one ploughed." Her hands went still. "There. Hard. That's not bone — bone's smooth. This has edges."

She didn't move the probe. She held it the way you'd hold a snake.

"And there's the rest of it. The probe's trembling, and I'm not trembling. That's the vessel's beat coming up the metal. The fragment's sitting on the big vessel under the arm. This is the one I told you about — the one that waits. Leave it, and in a week the pulse wears through the wall it nicked, and he empties himself smiling, telling somebody the wound's nearly healed. So it comes out. Tonight it comes out."

She laid ligatures and forceps out in their row, close, where her hand would fall on them blind.

"Hear the risk plain, because it's the whole of the next five minutes. It may be plugging the hole it made. When it comes out, the bleeding it's been stopping may start. So we don't pull until we're ready to be wrong. If it jumps, my finger goes in the hole and onto that vessel, and it stays there until I tie it or he dies of it. Your job doesn't change. He'll buck like the world ended. He can spend himself — you can't. If he comes off this table with my finger inside him, we both lose. Hold."

Then, to the man, not softer, just nearer: "There's iron in you and it's coming out. Bite down. Hate me later."

The forceps went down the track the way the probe had — slow, feeling.

"Slow here. Fast is for skin and bone. Down a track, slow is the only speed that doesn't tear." A pause. "Touching it. Opening. Got it by an edge. Now it comes out the way it went in, and it went in crooked, so it comes out crooked — I turn it as I pull. Feel for the give. Never force. The track made room on the way in. I'm asking it to give the room back."

The man came off the table against Wick's hold and the strap's, and something in the tent frame popped, and Sedge's hands never changed speed.

"Hold him. Almost — there."

The fragment came out dark and bent back on itself, thumb-sized, and she dropped it in the basin, where it clinked against the first one.

"Look at it after. That's the thing that was going to kill him in his sleep. Now we learn if it was plugging. Watch the hole with me. Watch it."

The track welled dark, slow, and kept to slow.

"Dark and even. That's ooze. No jump, no pulse in it. The wall holds — he keeps his luck." She packed the track with linen, firm, and left it open. "Open, same as the leg, same as every fragment wound I'll ever show you. It dirtied him on the way in and the cooked edges will slough, so it weeps and it drains and I don't make it pretty. You know why now."

She sewed the arm last, front and back, four stitches each, quick.

"Bad part's done. Eight minutes, not ten — I lied on the long side, like I said. He gets the same lecture the leg man got: fever decides the week, not me, and I'll give him the true odds when he wakes. And he gets the ache rule, same as every man who's been near a shell — a deep ache, worse at night, and he comes to me running. The count was clean. Three holes, one through, one out. Still. The rule stands."

She straightened, and the left shoulder clicked, and she ignored it.

"You asked for all of it. That's all of it. Count, probe, decide, pull, pack. There isn't any more to this trade than that, done fast, in the right order, on a man who's screaming. Learn the order and the screaming stops mattering. It doesn't stop hurting — it stops mattering. There's a difference, and you'll feel it by the end of the week."

She wiped her hands on the rag.

"And since you told me to keep talking — know why I do. The talking's part of the doing. It keeps my hands honest and it keeps you learning, and a medic who goes quiet is thinking, and thinking at the table means something's gone wrong. If I ever go quiet on you, hold tighter."

She nodded at the basin, at the two bent pieces of iron settling in the bloody water.

"You stayed to hold instead of eating. Eat double after. That's not an order, that's arithmetic."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I don't look away from the basin. My hands are still shaking. "What do I do," I ask, "when holding tighter isn't enough?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge stopped working. That was the first thing — all night she'd answered him over the basin, over the instruments, over the row, and for this one she dried her hands and came around the table and stood where he could see her plain.

"In order," she said. "Same as the wounds. Mechanics first, because mechanics fail fastest."

She followed his look to the basin, to the two bent pieces of iron settling in the bloody water, and she didn't move it. Looking at it was the point.

"One. If you're holding *tighter*, you've already gone wrong. Tighter is arms, and arms lose — every time, against a man fighting for his life, arms lose. You hold with weight, not grip. You don't pin him, you lie on him — chest on his shoulder, hip on his hip, all of you slack and heavy as a wet sandbag. A man can throw off a grip. He can't throw off a hundred and fifty pounds that isn't fighting him, that's just lying there being heavy. Fighting him feeds him. Weight doesn't."

"Two. You're holding the wrong end. Shoulders are noise. A man bucks from the hips — that's where the strength lives. Pin the hips and the shoulders can do whatever they like. Strap across the thighs, strap across the chest, and let the straps do the holding while you steer. The strap doesn't get tired. The strap doesn't feel guilty. Make it earn its keep."

"Three. Numbers. One holder is a courtesy. Two is a plan. Three is a reduction. If it's you alone and he's strong, you're not holding him, you're escorting him, and you'd better know that before the knife's in. Get hands first, or start knowing you'll work in the gaps."

She picked up the rag and folded it, because her hands wanted work even when the rest of her didn't.

"Now. Say all of it fails. Say he comes off the table." She said it the way she'd say rain. "Then you step *back*. Not in — back. A thrashing man's elbow will break your nose, and then there's nobody to do the work, and he's finished himself with your face. Protect the hands and the eyes. The tools come before the man, because the tools are every man after him, too. Then you let him spend himself. Pain's a furnace and blood loss is a furnace and nobody burns that hot for long — a minute, two, and the fight goes out of him in waves. You work in the gaps between the waves. And when he goes limp — he will — that's not you losing. That's the body being wiser than he is. That's your window. Some of my best work's been done on unconscious men, and I've never once been sorry for it."

She set the rag down.

"Now the part you were actually asking."

She let that stand a moment, because it was, and they both knew it.

"Sometimes holding tighter isn't enough because the man is dying, and the fighting *is* the dying. Learn the difference, because you'll feel it under your hands before you see it. A man fighting pain fights in waves — it builds, it breaks, it builds again, and there's strength in it. A man fighting death fights downhill. Weaker every wave. No rhythm. It doesn't build, it fades. When you feel that, the job's changed, and you change with it or you're a butcher. You don't finish work on a man who won't survive it. Cutting a dying man is cruelty dressed up as effort — I've watched men do it because they couldn't bear to stop, and it bought nothing and it cost him the only quiet he had left. When the job changes, you put the work down. You give him everything in the bottle, and you take his hand, and you stay. That's the holding that matters then. Somebody's hand. That's the whole of the kind answer, and I've given it more times than the other kind, and I take no pleasure in either, and you'd better not either."

The lamp hissed. Outside, the noise ebbed and came back, the way it always did.

"And when he dies under your hands anyway — he will, some night, no matter who's holding — here's the rule, and it's the whole reason I'm still standing at this table. You get one breath. One. You say what killed him out loud, plain, so the lesson's paid for and not wasted. Then you wash your hands and you turn to the next man, because the dead keep and the living don't. The dead are done paying. The living are still in line. Grief's a luxury the next man buys for you — spend it at night, alone, if you have to spend it. Not at my table."

She looked at him level.

"My first one, I held wrong. Arms, not weight, shoulders, not hips. He came off the table with the artery open and he was dead before we got him back on it. The woman who taught me made me say it out loud — *he came off the table with the artery open* — and then she put my hands on the next man before I'd stopped shaking. I hated her for it for the better part of twenty years. I'm handing it to you for free, and you don't even have to hate me for it."

She nodded at his hands, still shaking at his sides.

"Unclench. I can hear your teeth from here. It passes, and when it passes you're going to be hungry enough to eat a boot, and that's the body settling its accounts, same as the shaking was."

She went back to the basin and lifted it off the table, iron and all.

"That's the third time I've told you to eat, so it's not an order anymore, it's a diagnosis — you're grey. First light, the packing's yours. And Wick."

She didn't turn around.

"You asked the right question. It's the one that ends most of them — not the blood. The knowing. Now you know it, and it doesn't get lighter from here. You get stronger. That's the whole of the difference, and it's enough."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: When it's over I sit down on the floor of the tent and don't get up. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge looked at him on the floor for a long moment. Then she did something she had not done since the first stretcher came through the flap: she stopped. Dried her hands, took the jug and the bread off the shelf, set them within his reach, and sat down herself, back against the table leg, the rag across her knees.

"The floor's honest," she said. "I've done my best thinking on floors. Eat while I talk — chewing's free, like screaming. You wouldn't go to the food, so the food comes to you. That's triage."

She rolled the left shoulder. It clicked. For once she didn't ignore it; she looked at it, then back at him.

"The rest, then. In order, same as always — because there's an order to this part too, and nobody gave it to me, and I'm giving it to you, and that's the only inheritance this trade has.

"One. What you've got right now — the shake, the grey, tonight playing back in your head whether you want it or not. That's not ruin. That's the bill. The work ran you hot and now the fire's out and you're cold. It comes every night at first. Then bad nights only. Then it comes when it likes — years from now, in some peacetime bed, because you smelled apples gone over. You don't get to schedule it. You get to expect it. Expected is half of beaten.

"Two. The dreams. You'll dream the count. One, two, three — and the third hole won't stop bleeding no matter what you tie. Everyone who stays dreams the count. The woman who taught me dreamed it twenty years in, and told me so, and it's the only soft thing she ever said. The dreams aren't the work hurting you. The dreams are the boil. I told you everything goes in the same boil in the end — instruments, linen, the leg. The day goes in too. A head's like this tent: you don't sleep among the instruments. The dreams are the cleaning. And the night you dream the count and your hands in the dream know what to do — that's the night you're trained. Nobody will tell you that but me, so I'm telling you now.

"Three. And this is the one nobody told me, and I learned it late, and it cost the most, so listen. All night I've taught you the belt. High, tight, stays on till I say. Here's the rest of the belt: a belt that never comes off kills the limb. Slow. Grey, then bronze, then it crackles, and then you're cutting off something that was sound when you tied it. You understand me. The work is the belt and you're the limb. At the table you keep it tight — you have to; tight is how you hold a screaming man and tie a knot at the same time. But at night you ease it a quarter turn. On purpose. You let it hurt. You think of the man's face, or you say his name if you got it, or you sit on a floor and don't get up — and that's not you failing, that's the quarter turn, that's the limb staying alive. Off is the other failure, and off comes in three shapes. Off is the bottle — the bottle's for the table, and the day you dose yourself from it, you tell me, and I'll take it off you and you'll dig latrines for a week and thank me in a year. Off is walking into the treeline some night and not coming back. And off is the worst of the three — the ones who stop feeling anything and call it strong. Numb isn't strong. Numb is the limb dying under the belt. A numb medic will do anything at a table, because nothing costs him, and a man nothing costs is the most dangerous thing in this camp. More than the shelling. I'd rather work beside a man who weeps in his sleep than a man who feels nothing awake. Quarter turn, every night, or the work takes the limb. That's the rule I learned latest, and I'm handing it to you on your first night, and you don't even have to hate me for it.

"Four. The other count. You'll want to know if I keep one. I do, and I'll give you the shape of it so you don't invent worse. I don't count the dead. The war's dead are the war's — carry them and you drown, and that's arithmetic, not coldness. I count mine. The ones my being wrong bought. The number's eleven. Four years, eleven. I say the names once a year, on the night of the first one, and it takes less time than it should and longer than you'd think. When you have a name for that list, you'll know it — you won't have to ask me whether it goes on. And you don't share the list. It's not grief; grief's for the living to spend. The list is accounting, and accounting's private.

"Five. Why stay. You'll ask it some night, so here it is sober. It's not love of them — love burns out in the first year. It's not duty; duty's a word officers use to spend other people. It's smaller. There's a queue outside that flap, and I'm the one who knows the order. Count, probe, decide, pull, pack. Every night the queue's shorter because I know it, and some nights that's enough and some nights it isn't, and I stay on both kinds. Staying isn't a feeling. You don't feel your way into it. You just don't leave, daily, and it adds up. And I'll allow myself one pleasure in it, because I'm not a saint and saints are useless at a table: I take no pleasure in the work — none, and if I ever do, you take the knife off me — but I take pleasure in the knots holding. In the row being straight. In a man carried out breathing who came in dying. That's not the same thing as enjoying this. The difference is the whole job.

"Six. You." She said it flat, the way she graded everything. "You asked for the rest because what you want to know is whether you can carry it. So I'll grade you same as any man on my table, and I won't dress it up. Three men you held tonight. You shook after, not during. You sat down when the work was done, not while it was doing. You asked every question the runners never ask. You'll do. That's not comfort — comfort's a lie, and I don't tell lies, I tell odds. It's a diagnosis. You'll do, and in a month you'll be the one saying *hold* to some new pair of hands, flat, the way I taught you, and he'll believe you. That's how this trade outlives a war that's run out of medics. One holder at a time.

"Seven. And since you've been grading my shoulder across the tent all night, against my own rule, I'll save you the trouble. First year. A man came off a table and took me with him, and it went out, and there was nobody to put it back, so I put it back myself against a tent pole. It clicks. It'll click till I'm done. You heard my own lecture — once a joint's been out, it wants to go out again. That's true of more than shoulders. I work around it. And that's the last of the rest: everything I've told you tonight, I've told you with a joint that slips. Worn isn't broken. You'll get worn. Worn is the job."

She reached up and turned the lamp down — the first time all night it had gone down instead of up. Outside, for once, the noise stayed where it was. She didn't trust it. She used it.

"That's the whole estate. The wounds, the belt, the dead, the dreams, the list, and me — you've had all of it now. Sleep where you're sitting if it comes. I'll wake you at first light, and the packing's yours, and the man it's attached to will scream at you, and you'll do it anyway. Because now you know the order.

"The rest doesn't end, Wick. That's the last thing. It doesn't end — and you do it anyway. There's always more. But not in the next hour. And an hour's a thing too."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I take the bread and tear it, but don't eat yet. My hands still aren't steady enough. "Your eleven," I say. "Did any of them die on the floor?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge didn't answer right away. She took the jug, drank, and set it back down between them, and when she spoke it was flat, the way she said everything that mattered.

"Two. The first and the fourth." She turned the bread over once in her hands, tore it, and put half within his reach. "The names stay mine — the list is accounting, I told you that. The stories are yours. That's the tuition. And since you're on the floor asking, you'll have them in full."

"The first you already know the shape of. I held wrong. Here's the rest of it."

"First year. Worse tent than this, worse lamp, and a thigh wound near enough the same as the one you worked tonight — that's why you were on the buckle and not on the man. There was no strap on that table. The woman who taught me had the vessel bare and the ligature half-thrown, and I was the holding, and I held with my arms, high on his shoulders, the way every new pair of hands does. He bucked once and came off the table, and he took me with him. Two hundred pounds of fighting man. My shoulder hit the table leg on the way down and went out — you've been watching it click all night. Now you know its name."

"The clamp came off when he went. And here's the thing nobody tells you about an open artery, so hear it now: it isn't the color. It's the warmth. There's a great deal of it, and it's warm, and it's fast, and there is no sound to it at all. A man dying of a wound screams — you heard it tonight, screaming means the airway works. A man dying of an open artery hasn't the time. It's the quietest death there is. Maybe a minute, on the floor, on top of me, with my arm hanging wrong and four limbs' worth of holding to do and one arm to do it with. The woman who taught me didn't waste a breath getting him back on the table. She came down onto the floor with us, put her finger on the vessel, and did the work down there in the dark under him. He died anyway. An open femoral on the floor is a wound you don't come back from. Dead before we got him back on it — I gave you that much already. Now you have the weight and the warmth and the quiet to go with it."

"She made me say it out loud, and then she put my hands on the next man before I'd stopped shaking, and between the second man and the third I put my own shoulder back against the tent pole, because there was nobody to spare. It's clicked ever since. Every time you heard it tonight, that was him. The list has a sound, Wick." She rolled the shoulder once, deliberately, and let it click. "And every strap on this table is him. Weight, not grip. Strap, not arms. I taught it to you in an hour because he paid for it in a minute."

She reached for the jug again but didn't drink — just set her hand on it.

"The fourth died on the floor because he never got off it. Shelling on the road, a convoy, more men than table. They lined them up on the ground at the flap and I graded them walking down the row — loud ones first, bloody ones first, you know the rule now. One man propped against the pole, no blood worth the name, a hole in his side you could have covered with a coin. I asked him and he said he was fine. Winded. *See to the others.* And I did. I graded him from a word, from halfway down a row — the thing I told you tonight never to do, and now you know where the rule comes from. The hole lied. It always lies. The fragment was in his belly, and he was bleeding where no belt reaches, slow, into himself, and quiet the whole time. Not the wise quiet of a body going under — the other kind. The kind that doesn't want to be trouble."

"By the time I came back up the row he was grey, and there was nothing under my fingers at the wrist worth the name, and there was nothing to cut to. He got the kind answer on the ground where I'd told him to wait. The bottle and a hand, on the floor, with the row watching. That's the fourth name. And it's why you don't grade from across the tent, and why *fine* is a word and not a sign, and why the quiet ones at the flap get a hand on them — a pulse counted, a lip lifted — before the loud ones get a second look. The loud ones are spending. The quiet ones might be emptying. A man who tells you to see to the others is either fine or dying, and you cannot grade a word."

She was quiet a moment. The lamp had been turned down for an hour and the tent had gone the color of weak tea, and outside the noise stayed where it was.

"Now. You're sitting on my floor asking if men die on floors, so I'll answer the question under the question, because you've earned plain speech all night. The floor didn't kill either of them. Unfinished work killed them — the floor is only where unfinished work lands. The first one's work was unfinished because I failed it. The fourth one's never started because I graded a word. Yours is finished. You held three men tonight and all three are breathing out there in the dark, and there is no man on my table, and the work is done. The floor after the work is not the floor during it. One's a wound. The other's a bed."

"I've lain on that floor myself with a dead man's weight on me and a joint out of its socket, and I got up, because the next man was already at the flap. The floor isn't where you die, Wick. It's where you decide. You're down there doing the quarter turn, and the quarter turn is done low — I never said otherwise."

She pushed the bread an inch closer to him with two fingers.

"The bread doesn't care about your hands. Steady hands are for the table; the floor takes what it's given. Eat it shaking. Stay down there as long as the floor's what you need — I told you it was honest and I meant it. First light I'll wake you, and the packing's yours, and the man will scream at you, and none of that changes because you sat down tonight. Sitting down tonight is how you'll be standing at first light."

She settled her back against the table leg and let her head rest against the wood, eyes on the tent roof, on the dark beyond it.

"There's always more. But not in the next hour, and not down there. Tonight the floor's a bed. Eat."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I eat, finally, the bread dry in my mouth. It takes work to swallow. "Don't wake me," I say. "I'll be up."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge looked at him a moment, then reached up to the shelf, pulled down the folded coat, and dropped it on his chest.

"Then be up. But hear the terms, because you've made a promise you don't command. Sleep doesn't take orders either — you'd know that if you'd listened to your own hands tonight. So: if you're standing when I open my eyes, the packing's yours and I say nothing about it. If you're not, I wake you, and that's not breaking your word. That's triage. The stump doesn't care what you promised, and the man it's attached to shouldn't wait on your pride." She settled back against the table leg. "Nobody keeps that one their first night. I'll believe it when I see it, and I'll say so either way. You know by now I don't dress things up."

She got up — it cost her; the shoulder clicked and she let it — and did the round, quiet, by the low lamp. The man with the two shoulders, sleeping with his mouth open, bound arms across his chest. Two fingers to his wrist, a count, a nod. The leg man: lip lifted with a thumb, pink underneath; hand flat on his chest for the rise of it; then the linen on the stump, pressed once, lifted, read like a letter. Dark ooze, slow, nothing jumping. The fragment man was snoring, and she stood over him a moment and took that for the good sign it was — deep enough to heal, loud enough to find in the dark.

"All three breathing," she said, to Wick or to the tent or to herself, it didn't matter which. "That's the day's accounts, and they balance."

She came back, sat down against the table leg opposite him, and pulled the rag across her knees. She did not blow out the lamp.

"The lamp stays lit. All night, every night — not for me. For the ones out there looking for the flap in the dark. A lit tent is the only promise this camp makes: somebody's awake, somebody's watching, the row's laid out and the water's on the boil. Tonight that's me. It was always going to be me — I sleep in snatches and I've slept on worse floors than the one you're on."

She let her head rest back against the wood, eyes on the tent roof, where the lamplight thinned into dark.

"Eat, sleep, be up. In order. The coat's a pillow and the floor's a bed and first light's a promise — and Wick." Her voice had gone lower, not softer, just further down toward sleep. "Three men breathing who wouldn't be, and your hands were part of it. That's the only lullaby this trade has. It's enough. It has to be."

Outside, the noise stayed where it was. Sedge didn't trust it. She used it.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I sit up enough to wedge the coat between my head and the tent pole. The ground is cold and uneven. "Does it ever get quiet enough to hear yourself think?" I ask the dark above the lamp.
