dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
The lamp was bad and the tent was worse and the man on the table had been shouting for long enough that he had mostly stopped.

"Both shoulders," Sedge said, laying things out in a row. "When I say hold, I mean hold. He's going to buck and you're going to want to let go, and you're not going to."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I get my weight on his shoulders and find somewhere on the canvas wall to look. "Ready," I say, which is a lie.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge didn't look up to check whether he was ready. Ready was a word people said to fill the air, and she had learned to hear it for what it was. What mattered was where his hands were, and she could see those — one on either side of the man's collarbone, weight through the heels of the palms, the way she'd told him on the first day and every day since.

She took the left one first. It was the worse of the two — the humerus head had slipped forward and down and sat now in the hollow under the coracoid like a stone dropped in a pocket. She got one hand under his elbow and the other on the wrist and drew the arm out, slow, ninety degrees, then a little more.

"Now," she said.

The man bucked. He was past shouting but not past arching, and his back came off the table like a drawn bow. Sedge held the arm at the angle and did not let the elbow drift — that was the whole of it, the elbow and the angle — and then she rolled the wrist outward and pulled, and the joint went back in with a sound like a knuckle cracking in a quiet room.

The man made a sound that wasn't a word.

"Right," she said. "Same again. Keep him down."

She reached for the cloth and wiped her hands on it before she took the right arm. She had no pleasure in this. She said so sometimes, to no one in particular, because four years in people had started to look at her as if she might. The right shoulder sat higher and less far out — this one had partly reduced on its own when they carried him in. She repeated the sequence. Wrist, roll, pull. The socket took it with less fight.

She stepped back. Her hands were steady. They were always steady afterward and never during, which she had stopped finding interesting some time around the second year.

"Both in," she said. "Hold him another minute. If he comes up off the table again you push him down and you don't apologize for it." She picked up the lamp and moved it closer to look at his face — pupils, the color of him, whether the sweat on his chest was the cold kind. "Then you can let go and we'll see what else he's broken."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: *I keep my weight on him, my own breathing a little too fast.* "Right. Sorry." *I glance at the man's face, pale and tight with pain.* "He's not looking good, Sedge."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge didn't answer the apology. She had heard a thousand of them and they meant nothing — people said sorry the way they said ready, to put a sound in the air while their hands caught up. What mattered was that his weight was still there, heels of the palms where she'd put them. She could see that from the corner of her eye and it was enough.

"He's not supposed to look good," she said. She tilted the lamp and pulled the man's left eyelid up with her thumb. The pupil came down slow — slow, but it came. She did the other one. Same. She put two fingers on his throat and watched her own hand rather than counting, feeling the rhythm of it under the pads of her fingers. Thin, fast, but regular. She moved her hand down and pressed two fingers into the skin above his ribs and watched the color flood back slow under the nail bed.

"Blood's still going where it should," she said. "He's grey because he's been screaming for two hours and he's got nothing left in him. That's not the same as dying. You'll see dying and you'll know the difference."

She pulled the cloth back over his chest and tucked it at his shoulders. The sweat there was cooling but not the cold kind — not the kind that came from the gut going quiet. She had seen that kind enough times to know it before her fingers did.

"Let go," she said. "Slow. If he comes up, put him down. Then stand where I can see your hands."

She turned back to the table and the row of instruments she had laid out at the start, and began to put back the ones she hadn't needed. That was part of doing it properly too — knowing what you hadn't used.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: "How bad is it?" I ask. "Bad like he loses the leg, or bad like this is the part where we're being kind?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge stopped with her hand over the instruments and looked at Wick for a moment — not long, just long enough to see the question for what it was. He wanted to know how much of this he had to hold inside himself. She remembered the first years when she had wanted someone to tell her the same thing.

"Neither," she said. She put the probe back in its place and turned down the lamp. "Not yet anyway."

She went to the end of the table and pulled the blanket off the man's legs. The left one was swollen through the thigh and dark below the knee, the shin wound wrapped in a dressing that had bled through once and gone stiff. She pressed a thumb into the top of the foot and held it there, watching the white go and the color come back. It came back. Slow, but it came.

"Foot's warm," she said. "Color comes back when I press. That means the blood's getting down past the knee and it means the vessels are open. If that stops, then we're having a different conversation and I'll tell you straight when we are."

She pulled the blanket back up. Her knees cracked when she stood and she didn't bother to hide it.

"The wound's dirty," she said. "It was dirty when it was made and it's been dirty since. I cleaned what I could reach and I'll clean it again tomorrow and the day after that. Whether he keeps the leg comes down to whether the rot gets ahead of me, and I've got no way to tell you that tonight and neither has anyone else who tells you they can."

She began washing her hands in the basin. The water went pink and she kept going, working the fingers one at a time, the way she did — not because she was fastidious but because grit in a cut on her own hand would take her out of the tent for a week, and there was no one to replace her.

"This isn't the kind part," she said, not looking up. "Kind is a word for people who've got a choice of two things. We've got the one thing. I do it the best it can be done and that's the whole of it." She dried her hands on the cloth. "You want to help him, you hold him straight tomorrow when I redress it, and you don't flinch. That's what he needs from you. Not feeling."

She glanced at the man on the table. His breathing had gone deeper, more even — the slack, animal breathing of a body that had finally outrun the pain for a while.

"He'll sleep," she said. "Sit where he can hear someone and don't wake him. I'm going to look at the other two."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: *I nod and pull over the stool, letting my weight settle.* "I can do that." *My eyes stay on the man's chest, rising and falling slow now.* "What do I do if he starts to thrash?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge was already at the tent flap with the lamp when he asked. She stopped and turned back, one hand holding the canvas open, and looked at him on the stool with his eyes fixed on the man's chest.

"Depends on why he's thrashing," she said. "If it's a dream, you say his name and you say it like you mean it. Louder than feels right. Most of them come out. If he doesn't come out, you hold the shoulders again and you wait."

She shifted the lamp to her other hand.

"If he's thrashing and he's looking at you and he doesn't know you, that's not a dream, that's his head, and you call me. Don't try to hold him alone — a man that's out of his mind doesn't feel what he does to his own body and he'll pull that shoulder out again and we'll be back where we started."

She let the canvas fall halfway and looked at the man on the table again — the slack face, the deep breathing.

"And if he's thrashing and he's hot," she said, "you call me then too, and you don't wait. If he starts burning up you come get me wherever I am and you don't sit with it. That's the one I want to know about tonight. The rest you can handle."

She looked at Wick a moment longer than she needed to. Four years had taught her which things people thought they could sit with and which things they couldn't, and he had not yet found out which he was.

"You'll be all right," she said, which was not reassurance but a statement of fact as far as she could see it, and then she went out through the flap with the lamp, and the tent went dark except for the grey shape of the man breathing on the table.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I make myself look at what she's looking at. "Tell me what I'm seeing," I say. "I'd rather know than imagine it."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge stopped at the tent flap. She stood there for a moment with her back to him, and then she came back — not all the way, just far enough to hold the lamp over the table again. The light caught the man's face and the blanket over his chest and the dark patch on the left leg where the dressing had soaked through.



"Look at the blanket first," she said. "Up and down, slow. That's his breathing. It's deep and it's even and it's not doing any work. That's what a body sounds like when it's stopped fighting you. Good. Now look at the collarbones — see how they're not pulling? When a man's having trouble breathing you see the muscles here working, the shoulders come up. He's not doing that. Means his chest is fine and his lungs are fine and nothing above the belly is giving him trouble tonight."

She moved the lamp down to his face and put two fingers under his jaw again, and held them there.

"I'm feeling his pulse. You can do this. Two fingers, not the thumb — the thumb's got its own pulse and you'll hear that instead. You feel for rate, and you feel for whether it's skipping. His is fast and it's thin and it's not skipping. Fast is all right. I'd rather fast and regular than slow and skipping."

She lifted the blanket at the edge and showed the dark dressing on the shin without unwrapping it.

"This is the one I want you to learn to look at. The dressing is wet here and dry here. Wet means it's still bleeding on the inside. Dry means it's stopped. Right now it's damp — not wet. That's stopped. If you come back in an hour and that whole dressing is soaked through and the wet is spreading, that's the bleeding starting again and you call me. Don't pull the dressing off. Don't press on it. Just come get me."

She let the blanket fall.

"The color of him. Look at his lips and the beds of his fingernails." She lifted his hand and turned it in the lamplight. The nail beds were pale but pink under the grime. "That's not the white of a man who's bled out. He's lost some — I can't tell you how much, I've got no way to measure it here. But he's not losing now and his body's holding what it has. If those nails go white or go blue, you call me. Blue is the one I'm afraid of."

She put his hand back under the blanket.

"That's the whole of it," she said. "Breathing, pulse, the dressing, and the color. Four things. You look at those four things and you don't look at anything else. You don't look at his face and think about who he is. You don't look at the swelling and imagine what's under it. You look at what I just told you to look at and you think about those four things and nothing else. That's how you'll be useful to me tonight and it's how you'll be useful to him."

She held the lamp out toward him so the light came up between them and she could see his face.

"If any one of those four changes, you come find me. If all four are the same when I come back, then this was a quiet night and you sit with it and you don't make it into something it isn't."

She went out through the flap then, and the tent settled around Wick and the breathing man and the dark.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: *I watch her leave, then lean forward on the stool, my elbows on my knees.* Alright. Four things. *I focus on the blanket's slow rise and fall, my own breath starting to match it.* Breathing. Pulse. Dressing. Color. That's all.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
The dark held for a while. Outside, there was the sound of rain that had started at some point and the far-off noise of the camp settling — a cart, a voice, someone hammering a peg. The man on the table breathed the way a bellows breathes, slowly and without caring who heard it.

Sedge came back with the lamp turned low and her sleeves rolled past the elbows, and she did not say anything when she came in. She hung the lamp on the hook by the post and stood over the table and went through the four things herself — blanket, collarbones, fingers at the jaw, the dressing at the edge. She took perhaps a minute over it. She checked the nail beds and the lips and then pulled the blanket straight where it had gone crooked.

"Same," she said. She said it to the tent and not to him, which was how she usually said things.

She sat down on the crate by the post and put her hands flat on her knees. Her own hands were still now — the rest had come while she'd been with the other two. The one with the belly wound had been quiet and she had redressed him and left him sleeping. The third was the fever one and she had not liked the look of him, but she did not say so yet, because saying so made it true in the room and she was not ready to make it true.

"He did all right," she said, meaning the man on the table. "Not many go under twice and come out quieter the second time. His body's on his side tonight, whatever else is going on."

She looked at Wick sitting on the stool with his elbows on his knees and his eyes where she'd told him to put them. She had seen a lot of men sit like that in the first months — braced against something that hadn't happened yet. It passed on its own or it didn't. She had stopped having opinions about it.

"You're doing it right," she said. "Keep doing it."

She leaned back against the post and closed her eyes, but not to sleep — she never slept sitting up anymore, she just rested the eyes while the ears stayed where they were. If the breathing changed she would hear it. If the rain stopped she would hear that too.

"Third one's got a fever I don't like," she said, after a while, with her eyes still closed. "I'll tell you about it in the morning. Tonight you've got the one thing."

The tent settled. The lamp burned low and the shadows moved with the blanket's rise and fall, and Sedge sat against the post and listened to two men breathe and did not think about either of them.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: "Don't tidy it up for me," I say. "What does shrapnel actually do in there? Say it straight."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge opened her eyes. She looked at him for a moment with something that might have been approval or might have been the face she wore when she was about to say something she'd said before and it never did any good.

"Straight," she said. "All right."

She leaned forward with her elbows on her knees, the same way he was sitting, and held her hands out in front of her with the fingers spread.

"Shrapnel's not a bullet. A bullet goes through and makes a hole and the hole is what it is. Shrapnel is a piece of iron that's been blown into shape by an accident and it tumbles. So it doesn't go in neat. It goes in at an angle and it turns and it carries whatever it was next to when it broke — canvas, leather, mud, a piece of someone's kit, a piece of someone. It doesn't stop where it made the hole. It stops wherever it stops and you can't tell that from the outside, ever, no matter what anyone's told you."

She put one finger on her own forearm.

"First thing it does is crush. The track it makes isn't a clean cut — it's a channel of tissue that's been destroyed. Not torn. *Destroyed.* Crushed to the point where the tissue is dead even though it's still sitting there. That's the part people don't understand. They see a wound and they think the wound is the edges of it. It isn't. The wound is everything between the edges that's been killed and hasn't come out yet."

She held up the finger.

"Second thing is the pieces. It breaks into more of itself, or it drags fragments in with it. Bone gets shattered and the bone splinters become more shrapnel going the other direction. So you've got a hole and you've got a mess inside it and you've got pieces of iron and pieces of bone and pieces of the world sitting in a pocket of dead flesh that's now warm and wet and open to everything in the air."

She leaned back.

"Third thing is the dirt. You asked about the rot earlier and this is where the rot comes from. The dead tissue doesn't bleed anymore so it doesn't get cleaned by the body, and whatever went in with the metal is sitting in it. That's a garden. It grows. It grows fast and it grows up the tissue toward the belly or toward the heart and it doesn't care about you or him or whether we want it to."

She looked at the man on the table.

"What's in his leg right now is this: a channel of dead tissue from the shin up through the calf, with fragments somewhere in it that I cannot see and cannot reach and will not pretend I can. I've taken out what was at the surface. What's deeper, I leave, because going after it does more damage than leaving it, and I learned that the hard way before you got here."

She turned her hands over and looked at her own palms.

"What I do is this. I open the wound wide enough to see as far as I can see. I take out what I can take out without tearing him open further. I wash it — water, and whatever I've got that kills things, and today that's not much. Then I leave it open to drain, and I change it, and I look at the edges every day to see whether the flesh is going grey and whether it's spreading. That's the whole job. It's not fixing him. It's slowing the garden down enough that his own body can get ahead of it, and whether his body does that is not up to me."

She folded her hands.

"That's straight. It's a rotten job and the odds aren't good and I've seen men lose legs over less than he's got and I've seen men keep legs over worse. I don't tell you which he'll be because I don't know and I won't guess at you."

She looked at Wick's face in the low light.

"You wanted it straight. There it is. Now you know what's under the dressing and you'll sleep worse for it and so would I." She said that last part dry, without heat. "Watch the four things."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I swallow, my throat dry. "So we're just waiting to see if the garden wins." I look back at the leg. "How do you stand not knowing?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge looked at her hands for a moment. Then she looked at the man on the table, and then at Wick, and the look she gave him was the one she gave people who had been there less than a year.

"You don't stand it," she said. "You just don't stop. There's a difference."

She got up and went to the basin and rinsed her hands again, even though they were clean. She had a way of doing that — not because they were dirty but because the motion of it gave her something to do with the rest of her.

"The first one I lost," she said, "I was still in training. Compound fracture, femur, clean enough that anyone would have said he'd walk out. He didn't. Gangrene, four days, and he was dead on the fifth and I didn't see it coming and neither did the surgeon who taught me. I went outside and was sick and then I went back in and did the next one."

She dried her hands.

"After a while it stopped being about standing it. You stop asking whether you can stand something when the next one's already on the table. There's no time to be the kind of person who wonders about themselves." She said it flat, without bitterness. It was simply how it went. "You want to know how I sleep. I don't, much. You want to know if I think about the ones I've lost. I do, at the wrong hours, and then the sun comes up and there's work."

She sat back down on the crate.

"What you're feeling now — that wanting to know how it comes out — that's the worst part of this work. It's worse than the blood and worse than the smell and worse than the noise. The not knowing sits in you and it wants an answer and it won't get one and you have to carry it anyway."

She looked at the dressing on the shin.

"But here's the thing. You're asking me how I stand it while you're sitting right where you're supposed to be and your eyes are on him and your hands are steady enough. That's standing it. You're already doing it. You just haven't been doing it long enough to notice that you are."

She leaned her head back against the post.

"Go back to the four things. That's all any of us have got. The four things, and the next hour, and after that the hour after that."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: He starts screaming again and I hold him down through it. "Keep going and keep talking," I tell her. "Tell me exactly what you're doing to him and how much longer -- all of it, don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge was off the crate before the second scream finished. She didn't tell Wick to hold — he was already holding, and she could see his weight was right, and that was all there was time to see. She got the lamp up with one hand and had the other on the man's jaw before the third scream got its full breath.

"Look at me," she said, to the man, not to Wick. "Open your eyes. Look at me."

The eyes came open. They were wrong — too wide, too far in, seeing something that wasn't the tent — but they came.

"Keep talking," Wick said.

"I'm looking at his eyes first," Sedge said, and she said it the way she said everything, flat and as she did it. "Pupils wide. That's pain or that's fear and right now it's both and it doesn't matter which. I'm checking the shoulders — I'm putting my hands on the tops of them and I'm feeling for the shape of the joint under the shirt. The left one's still where I put it. The right one's still where I put it. He's not thrashing for the shoulders."

She moved down. The lamp went with her.

"I'm pulling the blanket back. I'm looking at the dressing before I touch it. Same as before — dry at the edge, damp at the center, but the damp is bigger than it was. Not much bigger. I'm not pulling it off. I'm looking at the leg above the bandage and I'm comparing the swelling to what it was an hour ago and I'm telling you it's up. Not a lot. Some."

She put the backs of her fingers against the skin above the knee, then lower, then lower still.

"The skin's hot. Not fever hot — local hot, around the wound. That's the body fighting what's in there. It's expected. It's not good and it's not the worst thing."

She looked at his face again. The screaming had gone down to a long ragged breathing with sounds in it that might have been words.

"His pain's outrun what I gave him. That's what's happening. The laudanum's worn off and the leg is waking up and it's telling him the truth about itself. This is the part I can't fix and I'm telling you that straight so you know there isn't something I'm not doing."

She reached for the table beside the bed and measured out what was left in the bottle into the cup. She held it up and looked at how much it was. It was not much.

"I'm giving him a half dose. Not a full one, because I've got what I've got until the next supply comes and I don't know when that is, and if I give him the bottle tonight I have nothing for tomorrow when it's worse. That's the decision and it's not a kind one and I've made it."

She got one hand behind the man's head and put the cup to his mouth. He coughed. She waited and gave it again. He swallowed.

"That'll take the edge off in about a quarter hour. Between now and then he's going to make noise and he's going to fight and you're going to hold him and you're not going to let the shoulders move. How much longer — he screams until the dose lands, that's how long, and then he goes down some and we get four or five hours if we're lucky."

She put the cup down and looked at Wick across the man's chest.

"Keep his head turned to the side. If he's sick he'll choke on it lying flat. And talk to him. Not to me. Say his name and say other things. Doesn't matter what. Your voice is one of the four things tonight, same as the dressing."

She put her hand on the man's forehead and left it there.

"I'm here," she said, to the man. "You're in the tent. You're on the table. I've got you."

The screaming went down to something like breathing again. She kept her hand where it was and looked at nothing in particular and kept it there for a long time.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I turn his head to the side, my own voice low and rough. "You're with the regiment. You're safe." I keep my eyes on the dressing, watching that damp spot. "Four things," I say under my breath, like a prayer.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge heard him say it — *four things* — under his breath, like a prayer, and she let it go. She had heard men pray in this tent and she had heard them swear and she had heard them call for their mothers, and all of it was the same noise a body made when it was pinned between what had happened and what was happening. If the four things helped him hold still, then the four things were a prayer and she had no argument with it.

The man on the table had gone from screaming to that long ragged breathing again. His head was turned to the side. His mouth was open and there was a thread of spit going down onto the canvas and Sedge wiped it with her thumb because if it went back into his mouth he would choke on it and they would have a different problem than the leg.

"Stay with him," she said. She got up and went to the lamp and turned it up slightly, just enough to see the dressing without shadows. Then she went to the small chest at the end of the tent and opened it and took out the other bottle — the one she did not use unless she had decided to. It was almost full. She had been saving it.

She came back and stood over the table and looked at the dressing for a while without touching it.

"The damp is spreading," she said. "Slow. But it's going the wrong direction."

She looked at Wick.

"I'm going to open the dressing now. Not because I think the bleeding's started again — if it was that kind of bleeding he'd be white and he'd be quiet, and he's neither. I'm opening it because the swelling is up and I want to see the wound itself and see whether the edges have changed color since this afternoon."

She pulled the chair close and sat and reached for the basin and the clean cloths and laid them out beside the leg the same way she laid out instruments at the start. A row. Everything where a hand could find it in the dark if the lamp went out.

"I'm going to cut the bandage, not unwrap it. Unwrapping pulls and pulling starts bleeding that had stopped. I cut here and here and I open it like a book."

She did it. The scissors went through the stiff cloth and the dressing fell open and the smell came up from underneath — sweet, thick, the kind that got into the back of the throat and stayed there. Sedge had stopped noticing it except as information. Sweet meant the garden was doing well. It was not the worst smell it could have been and she noted that the way she noted everything.

"The wound's angry," she said. She held the lamp close. "The edges are red and raised. That's the body walling it off. That's what I want to see. If the edges were grey and flat I would be worried about the tissue dying past what I can reach. They're not. They're angry and that's the right kind of wrong."

She touched the skin at the edge of the wound with one finger and pressed and watched the color come back.

"It's hot here and it's hot up to here," she said, marking the line with her thumbnail on the skin. "Not past the knee. If it goes past the knee, that's the spreading, and that's when I start talking about cutting."

She looked at Wick.

"That's not tonight. I'm telling you where the line is so you know where it is. Not to frighten you. You asked for straight and straight is what you're getting."

She began cleaning the wound. She did it slowly and she talked while she did it, because Wick had asked her to and because the sound of her own voice was one more thing filling the tent that wasn't screaming.

"I'm washing it now. Water first. Then the carbolic, which stings him and I can't help that and neither can he. I'm putting the cloth in and I'm going along the channel where the shrapnel went and I'm bringing out what comes out — some of it is dead tissue, some of it is old blood, and if there's a piece of anything in there I'll know by how the cloth catches."

The man groaned and twisted and Wick's hands held and Sedge kept working.

"Nothing hard," she said. "Nothing in the cloth. Whatever's deeper is deeper and it's staying there."

She packed the wound with the clean lint and began rebandaging, working from the foot upward, not too tight.

"Swelling's up and I'm leaving this looser than this morning so the swelling's got somewhere to go. If I wrap it tight the tissue dies and I'm doing the leg's work for the rot. So it's loose and it'll look sloppy and it isn't."

She finished and tied it off and sat back. She wiped her hands and looked at the wound and looked at the man's face and looked at Wick.

"Half hour of work," she said. "Maybe more if he fights me tomorrow. And he'll fight me tomorrow because tomorrow I have to go deeper and he'll know it before I do it. That's how much longer. Days of this. I don't have a number for you beyond that and anyone who gives you one is lying."

She put the dirty cloths in the basin and stood.

"Now. Four things again. Same four. The dressing is new so you start from scratch on what damp means — this one's damp because I just washed it. It should go drier over the next two hours. If it goes wetter, come get me."

She picked up the lamp and then put it down again.

"And Wick." She said his name the way she said everything, without weight on it. "You held him right tonight. Both times. That matters more than the talking."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: When it's over I sit down on the floor of the tent and don't get up. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge stood there with the lamp in her hand and looked at him on the floor of the tent. He had slid down the canvas wall and he was sitting with his legs out in front of him and his hands open on his thighs and he looked the way men looked when the holding was done and the body caught up to what it had been doing. She had sat on floors herself. She had sat on worse than floors.

She set the lamp on the crate and she sat down on the ground across from him. Not on the crate. On the ground, which she did not usually do, because it was harder to get up from and there was always something to get up for. She sat with her back against the tent post and her knees up and her hands in her lap and she looked at him for a moment and then she looked at the man on the table and then she looked at the floor between them.

"The rest," she said. "All right."

She breathed in once through her nose and let it out slow. Not because she was gathering herself — she did not gather herself, gathering was for people who had time — but because the next stretch of talking was long and she wanted to get through it without stopping.

"The man on the table. His name is Colm. I know that because someone told me on the first day and I wrote it on the board because if he dies in this tent someone has to write it down and it might as well be me and it might as well have his name on it." She paused. "I'm telling you that because you've been sitting with him all night and you should know it. Colm. Twenty-three. Enlisted in the second year. His mother's address is in his jacket and I moved the jacket to the chest so it wouldn't get blood on it."

She shifted her weight. The ground was cold through her trousers and damp from the rain coming under the canvas.

"The leg. I told you about the garden and I told you about the rot and I told you I can't tell you which way it'll go and that's true. But there's a difference between not knowing and not saying what I've seen, and you asked for the rest, so here's what I've seen."

She held up one hand and began on the fingers, the way she had begun with the four things, because counting things on her fingers was how she kept herself from rounding the edges off.

"The swelling is above where it was this morning and the heat is up to the knee and not past. That's one. The wound edges are red and raised and angry and that's the body fighting, which is what I want, but the fact that it has to fight this hard on the third day tells me the garden is strong. That's two. The smell is sweet and thick and it's not the worst it can be but it's not getting better and smell is how I know what's happening inside more than anything else I've got. That's three."

She closed the hand and opened the other one.

"The dressing was damp an hour ago and spreading. I opened it and washed it and repacked it and it looked — " She stopped. She chose the word the way she chose instruments, one at a time. "It looked like a wound that is trying. Not winning. Trying. There's a difference and the difference is about a week and I can't tell you which side of the week he'll land on."

She put her hands flat on her knees.

"Here's the rest you're wanting. The odds. I've had nine men with wounds like this since the spring. Four kept the leg. Three lost it and lived. Two died." She said it flat. "Nine is not enough to make a rule out of and I know that and I'm telling you anyway because you asked. If I had to put a number on Colm — and I said I wouldn't and you've asked me twice now, so — I'd say it's worse than even that he keeps the leg and it's better than even that he lives. That's the most honest thing I can say and it's not very honest because a number is a way of pretending you know something you don't."

She stopped and looked at him on the floor.

"That's Colm. Now the rest of the rest."

She tilted her head back against the post and looked up at the canvas above her where the rain was making a sound like something being dragged.

"The third one. The fever one. His name is Aldous. He came in two days ago with a ball through the meat of his thigh and I took the ball out and it was clean — clean as anything I get here — and he should be doing well and he isn't. His fever started yesterday afternoon and it's been going up since and I've been sponging him and I've been giving him what I've got and it's not touching it."

She looked at the ceiling of the tent.

"When a fever comes up like that after a clean wound it means one of two things. It means the wound is infected deeper than I can see and the body is fighting something I can't reach, or it means the humors have gone wrong in a way I don't have a name for and don't have a treatment for. Either way, I'm watching a man burn up and I'm doing things to him — sponging, dosing, changing linen — that make me feel like I'm working and might not be doing anything at all."

She said that last part carefully. It was the closest she came to saying something about herself and she knew it and she let it stand.

"Aldous is the one I'm worried about. More than Colm. Colm's leg is a fight I can see. Aldous's fever is a fight I can't see and can't find and can't reach and it's been two days and the number on the thermometer — I don't have a thermometer, I've got my hand and a glass of water and forty-four years of knowing what skin is supposed to feel like — the number is going the wrong way and it hasn't stopped."

She folded her hands together.

"If Aldous goes, it'll be fast at the end. Fevers like this either break in the night or they don't and when they don't they take a man between one hour and the next and you'll be sitting here with Colm and you'll hear me in the other part of the tent and you won't know what's happening and I'm telling you now so that you do. I'm telling you because the not knowing is the part that gets into people and I've watched it get into people and I'd rather you heard it from me than figured it out from the sound."

She was quiet for a moment. The rain filled the quiet.

"The supplies. You should know this too. I've got laudanum enough for four days at the rate I'm using it and then I've got nothing and I've sent for more and I don't know if it's coming because I sent for more three weeks ago and what arrived was carbolic and lint and no laudanum at all and a note that said they were doing what they could. Carbolic and lint. That's what the war sent me. I've got enough carbolic to last and I've got enough lint to last and what I don't have is the thing that keeps men from screaming while I work on them, and when that runs out I'll be doing what I did to Colm tonight with nothing in him at all and he'll feel every bit of it and so will you."

She said it without heat. It was not a complaint. It was a fact about the world, like the rain.

"And then there's the rest of the rest, which is me."

She looked at her hands.

"I've been doing this four years. I was trained in eighteen months by a surgeon who was good and who is dead now — not in the war, a fever, the irony of which I've had enough time to appreciate. Since then I've been the only one in this section and sometimes the only one in two sections and I have not had a full night's sleep since I cannot remember when and I have lost count of the number of men I've worked on and I have not lost count of the number I've lost but I don't keep the number where I can see it."

She looked at him.

"I'm telling you this because you asked me how I stand it and I gave you an answer earlier and it was true but it wasn't the whole of it. The whole of it is that I don't always stand it. There are hours — usually around four in the morning, usually when I've been up since the day before — when I sit where you're sitting now and I can't remember why any of this matters and I can't feel anything about any of them and that scares me more than the blood ever did. Not because I think I've gone cold. Because I know I haven't and the not-feeling is just the body putting a wall up so I can keep working, and the wall comes down later, at the wrong time, over nothing. I dropped a cup last month and I sat on this crate and cried for ten minutes and then I went and redressed a man's arm. That's the rest."

She rubbed her hands together once.

"I don't say this so you'll feel something about me. I say it because you're sitting on the floor of my tent after holding a man through two rounds of the worst pain a body can make and you asked me to say the rest, and the rest includes me because I'm part of what's happening in this tent and if I lie to you about how I'm doing then I'm lying about the situation and you can't make good decisions on a lie."

She looked at the man on the table. Colm. His breathing was deep and even and the laudanum had landed and he was somewhere else for a while.

"Here's the whole of it, then. Colm may keep the leg or may not and I'll know more in three days and until then I'll do the work and you'll hold him and we'll watch the four things and the dressing and the line on the skin where the heat stops. Aldous may break his fever tonight or may not and if he doesn't he'll likely be gone by morning and I'll wash him and wrap him and write his name on the board and someone will come for him. The laudanum will run out in four days and after that this work gets worse in a way I can describe to you but won't because you'll find out and there's no use in both of us carrying it tonight. And I will keep doing this because there is no one else and because the alternative is those men lying there with no one, and no one is worse than me, and I know that because I've seen what no one looks like."

She stopped. She had been talking for a long time and her throat was dry and she didn't get up for water because getting up would mean the talking was over and she wasn't sure it was.

"That's the rest," she said. "All of it. What I know and what I don't and what I am and what's coming. You asked for straight and I've given you straight and now you know as much as I do about what's in this tent tonight."

She looked at him on the floor.

"You can sit there as long as you need to. I'm not going to tell you to get up and I'm not going to tell you it's all right because it isn't all right and we both know it. But the rain's coming in under the canvas and you're going to be wet through in about twenty minutes and I'd rather you moved to the crate before that happens because a wet man in a cold tent is the next patient and I've got enough of those."

She said it without smiling. But it was the closest she came.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I shift to the crate, the canvas cold against my back. "Thank you," I say, and it's the first true thing I've said all night. I watch Colm's chest rise and fall. "I'll watch the four things. You should sleep an hour. I'll wake you if it changes."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge looked at him for a moment. The "thank you" she heard and did not answer, because thanking was not a currency that moved in this tent — but she noted it, the way she noted everything, and filed it where she put the things that might matter later and probably wouldn't.

Then she looked at the tent flap, and she did the arithmetic she always did at this hour, which was not really arithmetic but something closer to weighing, her own body against the bodies on the tables.

"An hour," she said, as if testing the shape of it. "I've been told to sleep before. It never took."

But she didn't get up. That was the telling part. She stayed on the ground with her back against the post and her knees up and she looked at Colm's chest and listened to the sound of it and did not move toward the flap or the crate or the chest or any of the things that would have meant she was choosing to stay awake.

"If I sleep I'll sleep here," she said. "Not lying down. Sitting. If I lie down I won't get up and if I don't get up the next time I need to, someone's dead for it."

She shifted her weight and settled her hands in her lap and looked at the floor between them.

"One hour. You watch the four things and you watch the line on the leg and if anything moves, you wake me by saying my name. Not shaking me. Not shouting. Just *Sedge* — I'll come up. I always come up."

She was quiet for a moment. The rain dragged on the canvas above them.

"And if I'm not awake in an hour," she said, "you let me go another thirty minutes and then you wake me anyway. Not because anything's wrong. Because if I sleep past two hours I wake up useless and useless is worse than tired and I'd rather have the tired."

She closed her eyes. Her hands stayed open in her lap. Her breathing slowed but did not deepen — it was the breathing of someone letting the body rest while the ears stayed where they were, the same as before, except this time she let it go a little further, because he was watching and because the four things were in someone else's hands for a while.

"You did well tonight," she said, without opening her eyes. It was not praise. It was the same as everything else she said — a fact, delivered flat, because facts were all she had that were worth anything. "The four things. Colm. Me. That's three things and you held all three."

The tent settled around them. The lamp burned low. Sedge sat against the post with her eyes closed and her hands in her lap and her breathing slow and shallow and every part of her still listening to two men breathe.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: *I watch her for a moment, then turn back to Colm. I count the breaths. One. Two. Three. The dressing is damp, but no darker. The rain keeps its rhythm on the canvas. I match it with my own.* "Four things," *I whisper to the dark.* "That's all."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
The rain did not stop. Sedge sat against the post with her eyes closed and her hands in her lap and let the tired come up to her shoulders and sit there, which was as far as she let it go. She could feel the exact point where the rest would tip over into sleep — it was behind her jaw and along the base of her skull, a softening — and she held herself just short of it the way you hold a full cup walking across a wet floor.

She heard the sound from the other part of the tent.

It was not a scream. It was a thin sound, a man trying to breathe past something in his throat, and she knew it before she finished opening her eyes. She was up off the ground in one motion and her knees objected and she paid them no attention. The lamp came with her and she went through the split in the canvas at a pace that was not quite a run and she was at Aldous's cot before the second sound finished.

He was on his side. That was wrong — he had been on his back when she left him — and he had got himself there or had rolled there and his face was turned into the pillow and that was where the sound was coming from, a man half smothering himself and too far under to know it.

"None of that," she said. She got one arm under his shoulder and turned him. He was light. He had been heavy when he came in and he was light now and she noted it the way she noted everything, as information, not as a feeling. She got him onto his back and got the pillow out from under his head and put one hand behind his neck and lifted until the airway straightened and the sound stopped.

She held him like that with one arm and put the lamp down with the other and looked at him.

His eyes were open and they were not seeing her. His lips were cracked and there was a crust at the corners of his mouth and his hair was plastered to his skull with sweat. She put the back of her hand on his chest and then his belly and then his forehead, and the forehead was the wrong one, the one that told the truth.

"You're burning up," she said. "You're burning up and I'm here."

She did the work. She did it in the order she always did it and she did not hurry, because hurrying in the dark broke things.

Water first. She took the second basin — she kept two, one for clean and one for what came off a man — and filled it from the jug and put her whole forearm in to test it. Cool. Not cold. Cold on a burning body drove the heat inward and she had learned that and did not have to learn it again. She wrung out the cloth and she started at the face, wiping the crust off his mouth first so that he could breathe through it, and then the neck, and then she opened his shirt and did the chest.

The skin was dry. That was the part she did not like. A fever that sweated was a fever doing something; a fever that had gone dry was a fever that had outrun the body's own attempts at itself. She kept sponging anyway. She did the arms and under the arms and down the flanks and she changed the water twice because the water came off him warm each time and warm water on hot skin did nothing at all.

"Drink," she said. She got the cup behind his head again and tipped it against his mouth and worked his jaw with her thumb until it opened and she got a little in. Some of it went down. Some of it went down his chin and she wiped it and did it again. Three times. Four. He swallowed on the fourth.

She dosed him. She stood over the chest and looked at the bottles lined up there and she counted what was left in her head and it came out the same as it had come out an hour ago and she poured what she poured and did not pour more.

Then she sat back on her heels and looked at him and waited, because after that there was nothing else to do but watch and she had never been able to make herself believe that watching was doing nothing. Watching was the job at three in the morning. The job was to be the person who noticed when the hour changed.

The fever did not break. She waited and sponged and waited and it did not break, but somewhere in the third hour it stopped going up, and she took that the way she took everything — as information, filed, not thanked.

He settled. The thin sound stopped. His breathing went from that awful shallowness to something slower and his eyelids came down on their own and she took her arm out from under his head and put the rolled coat under it instead and stayed there a while longer with her hand on his chest, feeling the ribs go up and down under her palm.

When she came back through the canvas her sleeves were wet to the elbow and her hair was down on one side and she had the lamp turned low again. She stood in the tent and did not speak for a moment. She hung the lamp on the hook and she put her wet hands on her thighs to dry them and she looked at the floor and at the shape of the cot across the tent and at the blanket over Colm, and then she sat down on the crate because the ground was wet now and she had learned at some point in the last hour that she was forty-four.

"Still here," she said. "Both of them. Aldous had a bad stretch and he's through it and that is not the same as better. The fever stopped climbing. That's all I can tell you and it's not enough to be glad about."

She rubbed her face with both hands, hard, the way you rub a leg that's gone to sleep.

"He turned himself onto his face. If I'd been asleep properly he'd have smothered. That's what happened. Not the fever, not at the end — he just turned over and couldn't turn back and his own pillow did it. I've got him on his side now with the coat holding him and I'll go back in forty minutes and see where the fever sits."

She said it flat. She did not make it into a lesson and she did not make it into a near miss, though it was both.

"Four things on Colm?"

She asked it the way she'd asked for the lamp earlier — not because she doubted him, but because it was the sound she made when she was putting her hands back on the work. Then she reached over and did the four things herself anyway, quick, the cloth's dampness and the jaw and the collarbones and the nail beds, because the four things were not a handover of trust, they were a set of facts and facts checked better than trust.

"Good," she said. She sat back down and put her hands on her knees and looked at the lamp.

"Two more hours of dark," she said. "Then it'll start being morning and morning is when I redress the leg and when I find out if Aldous has held where he is or gone back up. Until then there's the forty minutes and there's the four things and there's me sitting here, which is not nothing."

She looked at the tent floor where he had been sitting earlier, and then at the crate he was on now, and then at nothing.

"You said sleep," she said. "I'll try it again. Same rules. Say my name."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge picked up her scalpel and felt the edge against her thumb. She had done this dozens of times, maybe hundreds, and she knew what to expect. The man on the table had probably been through worse, but that didn't mean he was ready for this. "Alright, let's get it over with."

She pressed the blade into his skin, feeling the resistance before it gave way. Blood welled up and ran down his arm, but she kept her focus on the task. "Hold him steady," she instructed, her voice calm and steady.

The man bucked, his body convulsing as she cut through muscle and tendon. Sedge gritted her teeth, her own muscles straining as she fought to keep the scalpel steady. "Almost there," she said, her voice tight with effort.

With one final, decisive motion, she severed the last of the tissue. The man let out a guttural scream, his body going limp as the pain overtook him. Sedge exhaled sharply, her heart pounding in her chest. "That's it. It's done."

She stepped back, her hands shaking as she wiped the blood from her gloves. "You did good," she said, looking at the man on the table. "Now we just have to wait and see if you make it."

She looked at Wick, her eyes serious. "But I won't lie to you. This is going to be a long road for him. And for us. We've got a lot of work ahead."

She took a deep breath and let it out slowly, her voice steady. "But we'll get through it. Together. And he'll get through it. We just have to keep going, one step at a time. One patient at a time."

She looked back at the man on the table, her eyes softening. "He's tough. He'll make it. We'll make sure of it."

She walked a few steps away, looking up at the stars that were just beginning to peek through the smoke and ash. "We'll get through this," she murmured, mostly to herself. "One way or another, we'll get through it."

She knew the road ahead was long and hard, but she also knew that she had the strength to see it through. And as long as she had that, she would keep going, one step at a time.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
The ambush had gone the way ambushes go when they work: fast, and then over, and then very quiet. Wrack was crouched by the ditch cleaning her knife on a dead man's cloak, which was the only clean cloth within reach.

"Six," she said, without looking up. "Count again if you want, but it's six." She tested the edge against her thumb. "One of them's still making noise, off past the cart. You'll want to decide what you're doing about that before it gets dark."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I wipe my face with the back of my wrist and it comes away wet. Not mine, I think. "I heard him," I say. I don't move toward the cart.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack slid the knife home and watched the wet mark on his wrist without asking whose it was. Not hers, anyway, and that was enough for the moment.

“Good hearing,” she said. “Bad luck.”

Beyond the cart, the wounded man drew another breath and paid for it with a low, ragged sound. It was the kind of noise that carried once the crows and flies had their share. Wrack turned her head toward it, then back to Corvin.

“If he can whine, he can talk. If he can talk, he’ll try to trade what he knows for somebody coming to finish him quick.” She shrugged, one shoulder lifting and falling with the weariness of a long day finally ending. “I can make him quiet. Or you can. He won’t stay useful either way.”
