dialogue.content: I close my eyes for a second, then nod. "I'll do it." My voice sounds steadier than I feel. I push myself up from the ground, hand going to the hilt of my own knife. "You... check the cart."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack accepted the arrangement without comment. It was less trouble than persuading a man to do a necessary thing gently.

“If he starts praying, don’t listen,” she said. “Prayers have saved exactly nobody.”

Then she turned to the cart.

It was a sutler’s job, not a soldier’s: low-sided, reinforced at the axle, the traces worn soft by oxen rather than horses. One wheel had sunk deep into the ditch mud, and the whole wagon listed like a drunk trying to remember where he had left his house. The canvas cover had been lashed tight against weather and had come partly loose in the struggle. Wrack hooked a finger under the edge and pulled it back.

The smell came first. Horse sweat, damp wool, lamp oil, and the sour sweetness of old blood. Not battle blood. Older. Someone had been hurt on the road before this.

Inside were two sacks of grain, a coil of rope, an empty water barrel with a fresh dent in its hoop, and a bedroll that had not been slept in. Wrack checked beneath the bench seat first, because men who carried money usually sat on something else worth stealing. The wood was loose. She worked it up with the point of her knife and found a leather satchel wedged in the dark.

It had been forced, not cut. The clasp was bent sideways and the stitching around it was new, the thread still pale. Wrack lifted it out and shook it. Coins chimed, dull and heavy, and something stiffer shifted inside.

She opened it on her knee.

There was a purse of mixed silver, a tally stick notched at the third ridge, and a folded sheet of paper sealed with red wax. The seal had been cracked, but not removed. Some hurried thief had wanted to know what was inside without leaving proof. Wrack glanced at the bent clasp, then at the dead man whose cloak she had used to wipe her knife.

“Amateurs,” she murmured.

The manifest was written in a clerk’s careful hand. Provisions for the garrison at Hollow Ford: salt beef, shipbread, lamp oil, arrow shafts, and one item marked separately—pay for the third watch, enclosed by sealed box.

The box was not in the cart.

Wrack turned the satchel over and felt along the lining. Her knife tip caught a seam. She slit it open and drew out a narrow wooden case, stoppered at both ends. Inside, rolled small enough to fit a palm, was another paper. This one bore no seal, only a string of names and dates, and at the bottom a mark she recognized: the same crooked X the dead men had scratched into the dirt beside the road when they had set the ambush.

Not a sign. A count.

Six notches. Five filled in.

Wrack stared at it for a moment, then tucked the case into her belt and straightened. She raised her voice toward the far side of the cart.

“Corvin,” she said. “We’ve got a problem bigger than one bleeding man.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: "How bad is he?" I ask, and then, because she'll say it anyway: "Bad enough that it's a mercy, or bad enough that it's just easier?"

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack listened. The breathing beyond the cart was wet and irregular, a sound with expiry written into it.

“Gut,” she said. “Maybe worse. He’ll be foul before he’s dead, and dead before he’s useful. Once, maybe, if someone wants a name.” She tested the edge again, more out of habit than need. “So don’t ask whether it’s mercy or easy. It isn’t either. It’s maintenance.”

The corner of her mouth lifted without any warmth in it.

“Mercy is what men call it when they want praise. Easy is what they call it when they’re new. After a while it’s just the last step in a dirty job, like gutting a rabbit or changing a wheel.”

A fly landed on the back of her hand. She let it stay.

Wrack lifted the narrow case from her belt and turned it so the light caught the split lining.

“This is the problem. The pay box for Hollow Ford is gone. Whoever forced the satchel was in a hurry and not clever enough to feel for the seam.” She tapped the wood. “Inside is a list. Names, dates, and a count. Six notches. Five filled. The last date is tomorrow.”

She glanced toward the cart, where the wounded man drew another laboring breath.

“That makes him either the sixth notch, or the man who was supposed to fill it. I don’t know which yet. What I do know is that our dead friends scratched the same mark by the road, and that somebody paid in advance for a piece of business that hasn’t finished itself.”

Wrack’s voice flattened, the way it did when she was already deciding how much work was left.

“If you can do it, do it. If you can’t, say so and I will. Then come look at these names, because I’d rather not be the only one here who knows what we’ve walked into.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I don't look at the man making the noise anymore. I just walk around the cart, crouch down where he is, and do the thing. I wipe my knife clean on my own trousers this time. When I get back to Wrack, I hold out a shaking hand for the list. "I'll recognize it. The mark."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack looked at the hand first, then at the knife, then at the dark smear on his trousers. She decided not to remark on it. A man could learn neatness after he stopped shaking, and if he never did, that was his problem and not hers.

“Good,” she said, and handed him the case.

The paper inside had been rolled tight. It fought to curl shut again, so she weighted the corners with two flat stones from the ditch. The names ran down the sheet in columns. Beside each was a date, most already struck through with a single hard line. The last date stood alone.

Tomorrow.

At the foot of the page, the crooked X had been scratched in with something sharp enough to catch the fibre. Five smaller marks had been filled beside it. One space remained empty.

Wrack pointed to it with the tip of her knife, careful not to tear the paper.

“That’s the count,” she said. “Not prayers. Not messages. Work.”

She let the word sit there, plain and ugly, then looked up.

“You recognise the mark. Fine. Say where. Camp, convoy, jail, gambling house, temple wall—I don’t care how holy it looks. If it belongs to someone with a name, I want that name. If it belongs to no one, then it belongs to whoever hired these six fools, and that’s worse.”

A crow called from the treeline, short and dissatisfied.

Wrack did not move toward the cart. The man behind it had finished making decisions for everyone nearby.

“Search your memory, not the body,” she said. “He can’t answer. You can. And if your name’s on that page, or someone you served with, or someone I’d know by face, you tell me now. I’m better at planning when I’m not being lied to by a man’s silence.”

She gathered the manifest and the satchel, tucking the purse of silver against her ribs under her coat. The coins made a dull, expensive sound.

“While you think, I’ll strip the dead. Boots, belts, anything stamped. If they were paid to wait for tomorrow, they may have been paid for today too.”

Her mouth twitched, humourless.

“And if you’re going to be sick, do it downwind. I’ve had enough breakfast for one day.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I make myself walk over and look at him. "Tell me what I'm looking at," I say to her, because she's seen this before and I haven't, not this close.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack let him stand there a moment. The dead man’s chest had settled, and the quiet after was the ordinary kind, not holy.

“You’re looking at a man who ran out of arguments,” she said.

She crouched beside the body, keeping her boots clear of the widest darkening patch, and used the point of her knife to lift the torn cloak from the wound without pulling it free.

“Blade went in under the right ribs, angled up. You missed the heart. If you’d hit the heart, he’d have dropped before he could make a mess. Instead you opened liver edge and bowel, maybe the lower lung. That’s why the breath rattled. Blood backed up where it shouldn’t be.”

She let the cloth fall.

“The red on his chin came from the mouth. The black under his shoulder is pooling where he lay. His fingers are half-curled because he tried to grab something and found no one coming. The scrape on his cheek is from the ditch. The cloak is borrowed; it smells wrong for him. Boots are good, older than his trousers. He marched far and ate recently enough that his belly wasn’t empty.”

Wrack’s gaze moved over the body with the flat attention of a woman checking a wagon wheel for cracks.

“No prayer beads. No wife’s hair in his fist. No last letter sticking out. Just a soldier who was paid to wait for tomorrow and got today instead. Whether he was the sixth name or the hand meant to scratch it, I can’t tell from meat. For that, we need the box.”

She reached for the man’s belt with two fingers, testing the buckle.

“So look, then learn. Death isn’t a picture. It’s a change in material. The man is gone; the matter is still here, and it has details. If you can carry the details without carrying the story, you’ll live longer.”

A dry pause.

“If your stomach objects, let it object quietly. The flies will be here soon enough without help.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I swallow hard, looking at the scrapes on his cheek. "He didn't even get to wash his face." My hand goes to my own cheek, where the blood's drying. "So we're looking for a pay box and a sixth name. Before tomorrow."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack considered the remark with the seriousness it deserved, which was not much.

“No,” she said. “He didn’t.” She touched the scrape on the dead man’s cheek with the flat of her knife, not gently, but without malice. “Mud, grit, maybe a bramble. The ditch cleaned him better than a bucket would have.” Her gaze moved over the body again, cataloguing. “A man who stops to wash his face before a job is a man who expects to come back and complain about the water.”

She withdrew the knife and stood.

“Pay box. Sixth name. Tomorrow.” She said it like a list of chores, not a prophecy. “In that order. The box tells us who hired the butchers and where the meat is due. The name tells us whether there’s still someone alive to argue about it. Tomorrow tells us how long we have to be unlucky somewhere else.”

A muscle moved in her jaw as she looked toward the trees.

“And we assume there was more than six. Six is a crew. Crews have a lookout, a horse-holder, or a soft-handed man with the money who never lies in the wet. If he saw this, he’s running. If he didn’t, he’ll come back for the box when the crows lose interest.”

She knelt again and cut the dead man’s belt free. The buckle came away with a reluctant snap. From the loops she took a purse lighter than hers, a chisel no longer sharper than a spoon, a stub of tallow, and a brass token stamped with a broken tower. Wrack turned the token once in the failing light, then put it in with the silver.

“Hollow Ford has towers,” she said, mostly to herself. “So do a dozen places that want to sound important.”

She patted the corpse’s cloak, then changed her mind and lifted it by the shoulders, shaking out a spray of dried mud. “This one’s no good. Smells of fear and somebody else’s horse. The boots are better than yours, though.” Her eyes flicked toward the dark stain on Corvin’s trousers and stayed there only long enough to make the point. “If you’re going to wear dead men’s clothes, wear them for walking, not for penance.”

From the satchel she drew the manifest again, holding it where the last light could read it. Salt beef, shipbread, lamp oil, arrow shafts. Pay for the third watch. The missing box. The tally stick notched at the third ridge.

“Third watch,” she murmured. “Third ridge. Somebody liked tidy numbers.” She folded the paper and pushed it back into the case. “Tidy numbers get people killed on schedule.”

Then she looked toward Corvin squarely, the way she looked at a map before choosing the bad road.

“You said you’d recognize the mark. Don’t make me wait for the dark to do your thinking. Where did you see it? Camp, coin, wall, finger, tattoo—doesn’t matter. Give me a place, and I’ll give you a reason to be there before tomorrow.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: "Don't clean it up for me," I say. "If I'm going to do this I want to know exactly what a spear does to a man's gut. Tell me straight."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack held the request for a beat, then gave a single nod.

“All right,” she said. “Straight. Don’t thank me later when you dream about it.”

She crouched beside the dead man again, but this time she kept her knife well clear of the ruin under his cloak. The point of it traced a lazy line in the air above the body, from the bottom of the ribs to the hinge of the thigh.

“A spear isn’t a long knife,” Wrack said. “That’s the first mistake. Men think it’s just reach. It isn’t. A knife cuts. An arrow punches and twists. A spear shoves. It carries the whole weight of the man behind it, plus the shaft, plus whatever ground he’s standing on. If he’s braced, it’s worse. He’s not stabbing you. He’s using you to stop himself.”

The wounded man’s face was slack now, emptied out. Wrack looked at it without pity.

“Against the gut, it depends where it lands. High, under the ribs, it can slide up into the liver or the bottom of the lung. The lung fills with blood and he drowns sitting upright. The liver doesn’t bleed pretty; it crumbles. Big vessel, small vessel, it’s all the same after a while: the man goes cold from the inside out and starts thanking whatever god he has left for the dark.”

She moved the knife point lower.

“Middle belly is worse. The wall there is muscle and fat, not bone. A spear point parts it like a thumb through tallow. Once it’s through, there’s no stop except what’s hanging loose inside. Bowel. Bladder. The strings that hold the gut up. Those tear. When they tear, they pull blood with them, but the bleeding may not kill him first. What kills him is what leaks.”

Her voice stayed flat, the way a woman’s does when she has explained the same thing too many times to too many green faces.

“Stool. Bile. Sour meat. Whatever he ate that morning. It spills into a place that has no business holding it. The belly swells. The man vomits because his own insides have offended him. Sometimes he passes blood from below within the hour. Sometimes not for a day. The outside wound may look small. That’s the lie of it. A spear leaves a neat hole in the skin and a mess underneath, like a boot kicked in a privy.”

A fly had returned to the dead man’s lip. Wrack watched it go.

“If the point goes through and out the back, it’s often quicker. If it stops inside, it plugs itself. Pull it and you drag whatever caught on the shaft after it. I’ve seen a spear come out with a loop of bowel the colour of old sausage. The man lived long enough to be annoyed about it. That’s not courage. That’s meat being stubborn.”

She glanced toward the trees, then back to the body.

“Thrown, it’s different. A thrown spear has weight but not control. It can punch through mail at the gaps, drive a man onto his back, pin him to the earth if the ground is soft. If it hits low, it can open the groin or the thigh. Femoral artery there, he’s done in minutes if someone doesn’t clamp it. Bright blood, pulsing, hard to miss. If it hits high and angles down, it can exit near the armpit and take the lung on the way. If it hits the spine, he drops and doesn’t get up. Sometimes that’s mercy. Usually it just means he dies sitting there wondering why his legs have quit service.”

Wrack sat back on her heels.

“You want the sound? It isn’t a scream. Not at first. At first it’s a grunt, like a man lifting a sack too heavy. Then the breath goes wrong. Then there’s wet noise. Then begging. The begging is the part men remember. They remember that more than the blood. Which tells you something, if you’re wise.”

She was not smiling. The corner of her mouth might have twitched, but it was the twitch of a woman handling a fact, not a joke.

“I’ve closed bellies with needle and thread after scraping out filth. Works about as often as a saint’s relic. Mostly you make the dying quieter. You press around the wound, not on it. You keep him still. You don’t give him water if he’s going to choke on it. You wet his lips and tell him lies if he’s a friend. If he’s an enemy, you let him learn what his own body is doing.”

The last light had gone thin and grey. Wrack’s shadow stretched across the ditch.

“So that’s straight. A spear in the gut turns a man into a leaking bag. It doesn’t care about his name, his cause, or how brave he was at breakfast. It makes him smell. It makes him wet himself. It makes him beg for an end he can’t describe. If you take one there, the only thing in your favour is that you know it before the pain does.”

She looked at the dead man one final time, then rose.

“Now you’ve got your lesson. Don’t waste it by being sentimental about it. Sentiment gets men killed slower, not kinder.”

Wrack tucked the knife back into her belt and lifted the brass token again, turning it in her fingers.

“The mark. You said you’d recognise it. I’ve told you what a spear does to a man’s guts. Tell me where you’ve seen that X, and I’ll tell you whether we’re riding toward Hollow Ford, hanging around waiting for the sixth name, or both. Tomorrow’s already leaning over the fence at us.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I saw it carved into a table at the Rusty Anchor, back in Crossroads. Three weeks ago, maybe. Sat with a man I didn't know, drinking. I thought it was a gambler's tally.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack turned the broken-tower token over once, twice, then set it on the dead man’s belt and scraped mud from the buckle with her knife. The gesture was unnecessary. She did it anyway, because thinking was easier when her hands had a task.

“Crossroads,” she said. “That’s where men go to be unremarkable. Bad sign.”

She straightened and looked toward the trees, where the last grey light was collecting in the branches like something unwilling to leave.

“Three weeks is not old. A table remembers longer than a face. If he carved it there, he wanted it found by someone who understood the count—not by the barmaid, not by a drunk, not by chance.” Her mouth twisted. “Gambler’s tally. Sure. Gamblers mark wins with chalk and coin. They don’t cut dates into oak and wait for tomorrow to fill a notch.”

She tucked the token into her coat, close to the silver.

“Was he alone?” she asked. “Did he have a box? A horse? A companion who drank water while he drank ale? Did he pay, or did he owe? Give me the shape first: man, money, mouth.”

Wrack paused, then added, flatter:

“And whether he looked like a man who expected to live past the week.”

She crouched again by the dead man, not touching him this time, only studying the ditch around him. The mud held boot prints, drag marks, the smear of a cloak. Nothing graceful. Ambushes rarely were.

“If the mark was on a table in the Rusty Anchor, it may still be there,” she said. “Tables don’t run. Taverns burn, but slowly. That means either we go and read it, or someone else already has.”

She glanced back toward the cart, then toward the darker line of the road.

“We don’t sit here until the owls start judging us. If there was a seventh man—the lookout, the horse-holder, the soft hands with the box—he may have seen this, or he may be waiting to hear why six fools didn’t come back.” Wrack stood, joints settling. “Either way, Crossroads is where the thread runs. Whether it leads to the payer, the sixth name, or a blade in a dark room, I can’t say from here.”

She began moving among the other dead, brisk and impersonal, checking belts, saddlebags if any, the linings of cloaks. One man had a hatchet. Another had a coil of thin cord and a pouch of dried peas. The third had nothing but a knife, a stone pipe, and a lock of hair tied with thread. Wrack left the hair where it was. Sentimental trinkets were poor currency.

“Take what you can carry that isn’t cursed,” she said, not looking up. “Boots, coin, bread, anything stamped. Leave the rest. The dead don’t need warmth, and the living need speed.”

She found a second brass token on the man nearest the ditch, identical to the first. Broken tower. Same crude edge, as if the die had been worn or the mint had been in a hurry.

“Two from the same hand,” she murmured. “Hollow Ford pay, or someone borrowing its name.”

Wrack pocketed it and returned to where the list lay weighted by stones. She did not touch it again, only looked at the empty space beside the final notch.

“If your man at the Anchor was marking names, he may have been marking his own crew’s work. If he was receiving them, then the table was a dead drop. Either way, the Rusty Anchor has a splinter in it now, and splinters fester.”

She looked at Corvin then, her expression unreadable in the failing light.

“We ride for Crossroads. Not through the main road if we can help it—ambushers like roads, and inns like witnesses. We go in at first light, or before, if the moon behaves. One of us goes in looking thirsty and stupid. The other watches the doors, the horses, and anyone who looks like they’ve been waiting for news.”

A dry breath escaped her, almost a laugh.

“I’ll be the one watching. You’re better at looking harmless when you’re tired.”

She bent and lifted the narrow case containing the list, sliding it into an inner fold of her coat. The manifest went with it. The satchel she slung over one shoulder, its weight familiar and unwelcome.

“If the box is still missing, someone has it. If someone has it, they may be moving it tonight. If they’re moving it, Crossroads is the likeliest market: roads meet there, tongues loosen there, and nobody asks too many questions unless the coin is bad.”

Wrack checked the dead men’s horses next, if any had been tethered in the trees. She moved with the practiced indifference of a woman who had stolen and reclaimed mounts often enough that ownership had become an abstraction.

“One more thing,” she said, without turning. “If you saw this man at the Anchor, and if he saw you, then you’re a name he may repeat. That makes you useful. It also makes you bait. I don’t mind bait. Bait keeps the hook where I can see it.”

She straightened, brushing dirt from her knees.

“But if your stomach is still arguing with your sense, say so now. I’d rather know whether you’re coming because you can hold a knife or because you think this is a story with a ending.”

The wounded man behind the cart had gone still at last. Even the flies seemed to pause, as if respecting the silence.

Wrack looked toward the road leading out of the ditch, toward the dark, toward Crossroads.

“Tomorrow’s leaning over the fence,” she said. “We’d best not let it catch us sitting in the mud, being moral about it.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I kneel down and do it, and it isn't clean or quick because I've never done it before. "Stay," I tell her, when she starts to turn away. "Watch it with me and tell me exactly what I'm doing to him — the sound of it, how long he takes, all of it. Don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack had taken two steps toward the horses when the sound came again.

Not a groan. Something smaller: a bubble breaking, a flutter in the throat like a moth beating itself against wet lace.

She stopped.

The man beyond the cart was not finished. His fingers moved in the dirt, testing the world one last time. Corvin was kneeling over him, knife in hand, and the set of his shoulders said everything Wrack needed to know. First attempt. No stomach for the second.

“Stay,” he had said.

Wrack stayed.

She came back around the cart slowly, boots sucking at the mud, and set herself where she could see both the man’s face and the work of Corvin’s hands. Not close enough to help. Close enough that help would not have been refused.

“All right,” she said. “Watch him, not me. And don’t apologize afterward. Apologies are for people who think the dead can be comforted by grammar.”

The wounded man’s eyes opened. Not recognition—meat remembering light. His mouth worked. A thin thread of blood ran from the corner, black in the dusk.

Wrack’s voice dropped into the flat register she used for teaching and for counting rations.

“He’s not praying. That click is his tongue against teeth. Don’t give it meaning.”

The knife went in.

It was not one clean stroke. It caught, slipped, caught again. The man made a sound like a pair of bellows filling with mud.

“There,” Wrack said, not approving, only noting. “You found the soft place. Now don’t lift and look. Lifting is curiosity, and curiosity costs blood.”

The blade sank farther. A wet rasp came up from the man’s chest, then a high whistle as air tried to pass a narrowed pipe. His hips lifted once, useless, and settled.

Wrack counted under her breath, not for comfort, but because numbers kept the scene from becoming a story.

“One. Two. Three.”

The man’s hands spasmed. Fingers spread, curled, opened. Blood ran over the knuckles, not bright, dark and sluggish, the colour of old wine.

“Four. Five. He’s trying to swallow his own mouth. He can’t. The muscles are learning that they have no master left.”

A gurgling burst, almost a word, died in the throat.

“That wasn’t a name,” Wrack said. “Don’t collect it.”

The knife worked again, less sure than the first time, more desperate. The sound changed: a thick tearing, then a thinner fizz, as if a wet rope were being unpicked. The man’s back arched, not nobly, the way a landed fish arches, all reflex and no intention.

“Seven. Eight. Nine. You’re dragging. It adds three, maybe four heartbeats. Not damnation. Just arithmetic.”

The arched body fell. One leg jerked against the cart wheel. The other went still. From what had become of the wound came a long, bubbling exhalation, and with it a smell that belonged to the inside of a man, not the outside: iron, bile, sour warmth.

Wrack did not look away. Her face stayed as blank as a quarry wall.

“Ten. Eleven. The big breath is gone. What’s left is leakage. His heart is still throwing blood into a place that has no walls. Twelve. Thirteen. It will slow. Fourteen. The twitching is not thought. It is the nerves asking for orders that aren’t coming.”

The man’s eyes remained open, but the focus went out of them like a lamp trimmed too low. A thin line of blood traced his jaw and dripped from the chin onto the mud, where it vanished without ceremony.

“Fifteen. Sixteen. Seventeen.”

A small sound came from him at the end—not a sigh, not a word, just the last movement of air through a ruined passage. Then nothing except the wet settle of the body and the first confident buzz of a fly.

Wrack waited three more counts, because dead men sometimes played tricks with residual breath, and she had learned not to trust the first silence.

“Twenty. Twenty-one. Twenty-two.”

She exhaled through her nose.

“Done.”

For a moment she remained crouched, looking at the body with the same attention she might have given a broken axle or a spent candle. Then she rose, knees cracking once.

“He took twenty-three heartbeats from the first catch to the last rattle,” she said. “Could have been ten. Could have been five. It wasn’t because you’re new, not because he was brave, and not because the gods wanted a witness. It was because your hand hesitated and your blade dragged. That’s all. Meat is meat. Work is work.”

She wiped her own palms on her coat, though they were not dirty. Habit, perhaps, or the need to do something with her hands while the flies made their first claims.

“Don’t wash the sound out of your head with water. It won’t work. You’ll hear it at inconvenient moments: during meals, before sleep, when a boy in the company asks if killing feels like the songs say. Tell him no. Tell him it feels like this: noisy, brief, and over.”

Wrack glanced toward the treeline, then back to the dead man.

“If you keep kneeling there, he’ll start charging rent.”

She turned toward the cart and began gathering the satchel, the manifest, the narrow case with the list. Her movements were brisk now, the pause finished. The dark was coming on, and darkness had a way of making simple problems complicated.

“Crossroads,” she said. “The Rusty Anchor. The mark. We ride before the moon is high enough to be useful to anyone but thieves and sentries. If you’re going to be sick, be sick. If you’re going to pray, pray to someone who isn’t listening. Then move.”

She slung the satchel over her shoulder and looked at him squarely.

“And don’t thank me for staying. I didn’t. I only watched.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I wipe my mouth with the back of my hand. "I'm not sick." My voice is rough. I get up, knees stiff. "And I'm not praying." I look at the mark on my knife, then at her. "The man at the Anchor. He drank alone. Paid in copper."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack did not correct him. Not sick and not praying were both claims a man could make while his hands still remembered the weight of what they had done. She had heard braver men lie better.

“Copper,” she said.

She turned the word over as if it were a coin of doubtful weight.

“Copper is careful metal. Silver gets counted. Gold gets remembered. Copper changes hands with a shrug and leaves no story behind it unless someone is very poor or very cautious.” Her eyes lifted from the dead man’s belt to Corvin’s face. “A man drinking alone at the Rusty Anchor, paying in copper, either trusted the ale, distrusted the company, or wanted his change small enough to forget.”

She crouched again beside the bodies, not to mourn them, but to finish the inventory. The dead had already given up their coins and tokens. Now they gave up their habits.

One man had bitten nails, ragged to the quick. Another had a scar across the knuckles from an old blade slip, the sort of wound a man got when he tried to cut rope with a fighting knife. The third had a pouch of tobacco so dry it rattled. The fourth had nothing worth naming.

The fifth had an awl.

Wrack drew it from a loop at the man’s hip with two fingers and held it up in the thin light. It was short, steel, sharp at one end and blunted at the handle, the kind of tool a mender used for leather or a carpenter used for starting holes. Not a weapon. Not much use in a fight except by accident or desperation.

“There,” she said. “A man who scratches tables owns his own point. He doesn’t borrow a bar knife and risk the edge, and he doesn’t use a sword because swords are for people who expect to be seen.”

She tucked the awl into her belt beside the knife.

“If your copper-drinker made that mark, he came prepared. If he came prepared, he expected the table to hold the message longer than his face would. That means he either didn’t trust the folk at the Anchor, or he wanted someone specific to find it later.”

Wrack’s gaze went to the narrow case under her coat, where the list lay folded against her ribs.

“Or he wanted you to find it.”

She said it without drama, the way she might have said the horse was lame or the bread was stale. A possibility, not a revelation. Possibilities could be handled. Revelations tended to get men killed before breakfast.

“Three weeks ago, he set the board. Five notches filled since. The sixth was due tomorrow, and your knife moved the schedule.” She nodded toward the cart, where the last of the six had finished owing the world nothing. “That makes us either early, late, or in the middle of someone else’s arithmetic.”

A crow shifted in the trees, unhappy at the lack of ceremony.

Wrack rose and went to the horses.

There were four left among the tethering posts in the treeline, all scrubby border stock, the kind bred for stubbornness and poor feed. She checked teeth, withers, hooves, and tempers with the detached rudeness of a woman who had bought and stolen enough mounts to consider ownership a temporary inconvenience.

“This one’s sound,” she said, patting the neck of a grey mare with a nick in one ear. “This one’s got a bad hock and an opinion about men. This one will run until it dies, which may be tonight if anyone rides it hard.” She left the fourth saddled but slack-girthed. “And this one belongs to someone who will miss it before dawn. We’ll take the risk.”

She began redistributing tack, pulling bedrolls from dead men’s straps, testing buckles, shifting water skins from one saddle to another. The work was mechanical and necessary, the way chaff was necessary before grain: annoying, but it kept the useful part from being crushed.

When she had two mounts ready, she returned to the cart and set a single copper coin on the edge of the bench seat. Not offering it. Not commanding it. Leaving it there like a tool within reach.

“For the barmaid, if she remembers,” Wrack said. “Copper is easier to forgive than silver. Silver makes a woman wonder whether she has been bought. Copper only makes her wonder whether she has been tipped.”

She studied Corvin for a moment, then said, flatter:

“Don’t go into the Anchor asking after a man who carved a mark. That is the sort of question that brings the wrong kind of attention. Men who carve tallies don’t like witnesses, and taverns full of witnesses don’t like men who ask after tallies.”

Her mouth moved, not quite a smile.

“You’ll go in looking tired, thirsty, and mildly regretful. Not guilty. Guilt draws dogs. Regret draws pity, and pity is cheaper.”

She glanced toward the road, then back toward the ditch where the dead lay in spreading dark.

“If the table is still there, look at it. Don’t touch it. Carved wood holds splinters and questions in equal measure. If someone asks what you’re staring at, tell them you’re comparing it to the last table you slept under. If someone asks who you serve, tell them nobody currently available.”

Wrack checked the awl again, then the brass tokens in her coat. Two broken towers. Hollow Ford, or a lie wearing its name.

“The pay box is still missing,” she said. “That means someone moved it, or someone is still moving it. If it was meant for the third watch and the third ridge, then whoever ordered this likes patterns. Patterns are useful. They also make people predictable, provided you’re willing to admit you’ve been reading the same book for three weeks.”

She turned east, away from the main road. The drover’s cut ran there through alder and wet grass, worse for horses but better for avoiding eyes.

“We ride the creek line until the moon clears the treeline. Then we cut ridge and come into Crossroads from the south, near the mule pens. Main road is for merchants, messengers, and men who enjoy being noticed.” A dry pause. “Tonight, none of us qualifies.”

Wrack swung onto the grey mare and settled the satchel against her thigh. The coins inside made a dull, expensive sound. She ignored it. Money was only another kind of weight.

“I’ll be outside,” she said. “Horse block, back lane, or wherever the roof leaks least. If you need me, don’t shout. Shouting brings crowds, and crowds bring liars.”

She tapped the hilt of her knife twice against the saddle horn.

“Two taps from me, you finish whatever drink is in front of you and walk out the front. Three taps, you leave the drink and walk faster. If I’m not where I said I’d be, assume I’m dead, busy, or having a very poor opinion of the local architecture. Get out before any of those become obvious.”

The grey shifted, sensing the dark. Wrack pressed a hand to its neck until it settled.

“One more thing.”

Her voice lost the last of its instructional edge and became simply practical, the tone she used before a job that might not allow for second thoughts.

“If the man at the Anchor saw you, and if he told anyone, then your face is already in play. That doesn’t mean you’re marked. It means you’re loud. Loud men get used as warnings. If someone there recognizes you, don’t argue, don’t explain, and don’t try to be brave about it. Bravery in a tavern is just a slower way of dying in a gutter.”

She looked toward the cart one last time. The wounded man had gone still enough to belong to the mud. The flies had begun their quiet administration.

“Not sick is a start,” Wrack said. “Not praying is a discipline. Keep both, and you may live long enough to be boring.”

She turned the mare’s head toward the treeline.

“Crossroads. Before the moon gets ideas.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I sit back on my heels and I don't get up for a while. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack pulled the grey mare up before the treeline could swallow her whole. For a moment she sat with her back to the cart, listening to the wet quiet and to the request that had come out of it. Then she turned the horse around and walked her back a few paces, close enough that her voice would not have to carry like a bugle.

“The rest,” she said.

She let the words settle without softening them.

“All right. Not the pretty part. Not the part where a man stands up clean and becomes a story. The rest begins where the counting stops.”

The mare stamped once, uneasy with the smell. Wrack pressed a hand to its neck until it stilled.

“When the last breath goes, the body does not understand that it has been dismissed. It keeps working for a little while without permission. The heart may throw one or two more beats, useless, like a man hammering a nail that has already gone through the wood. The lungs try again and find nothing to answer. The diaphragm twitches. That is the rattle you heard. Not speech. Not pleading. Plumbing.”

She looked toward the cart, not at the dead man’s face, but at the place where the cloak had pooled dark in the mud.

“Then the bowels loosen. Men hate that part because it makes them think of shame. There is no shame in it. A corpse is not embarrassed. The sphincters let go because the muscles have no master left. If urine comes, it comes. If filth comes, it comes. Do not make a ceremony of it. Kneel in it if you must, but do not pretend it means something holy.”

A fly had found the cart wheel and was walking in slow circles over a smear of blood. Wrack watched it with the dull patience of a woman counting minutes she could not spare.

“The face changes next. Not at once. First the jaw goes slack if the wound or the struggle has set it. The mouth may hang open, and the tongue pushes a little against the teeth. The eyes stay open unless someone shuts them, and in night air they cloud fast. Not like glass. Like milk thinned with water. The lids dry. If you leave them open long enough, they shrink back and make the dead man look surprised. He isn’t surprised. Meat does not keep opinions.”

She shifted in the saddle, her voice dropping lower, steadier.

“Blood stops being blood in the way the living understand it. It becomes weight. It pools where gravity tells it to go. If he lies on his back, the discoloration gathers along the shoulders, the buttocks, the backs of the legs. If he lies face down, it climbs into the cheeks and chest. Men who have never seen it mistake those marks for beatings. They are not. They are only settling. The red goes brown, then black at the edges. Where the body presses against the ground, the skin stays pale because the weight has squeezed the blood out. Those pale patches are called pressure blanks, though no one sensible calls them anything at all.”

Wrack drew one boot free of the stirrup and let it hang, as if the small movement helped her keep the lesson from turning into a sermon.

“Cooling comes with the night. In this weather, the corpse will lose heat faster than a man can lose patience. The hands and feet go first, then the arms and legs, then the belly and chest. By dawn he will feel cold and waxy. Not like stone. Like a side of beef left in a shed. If it rains, the rain will steal the last warmth from the skin and make the smell lie closer to the ground.”

She tapped the saddle horn once with two fingers.

“Stiffness follows. Not because the dead man is angry. Chemistry. The muscles tighten where they can, first in the jaw, then the neck, then the shoulders, the hands, the hips, the legs. In cool air it may begin within a couple of hours. By morning there will be enough rigidity to make dragging him awkward. By noon, if the day stays mild, he may be stiff enough to offend a cartwheel. After that, depending on heat and filth and how much blood he lost, the stiffness breaks again. The body goes loose a second time, and that is when the real rot starts asking for attention.”

The wind shifted. Wrack turned her face away from it without ceremony.

“Rot is not a single event. It is an administration. Bacteria that were already inside him, waiting with the patience of tenants, begin to feed. The belly swells first because there is more to eat there. Gas pushes the tongue out, puffs the lips, stretches the skin until it shines. The wound darkens. Green comes in around the edges, then black. Fluids force their way out of the mouth, the nose, the ears, the open places. The smell changes from iron to sweetness, then from sweetness to something that makes the throat close before the mind has a name for it.”

She said the next part flatly, as if reading a supply list.

“Flies arrive before grief. They do not care who he was. They care that he is warm enough, wet enough, and open enough. They lay eggs in the wound, the eyes, the mouth, the groin, anywhere the body has stopped defending itself. In good weather, those eggs become maggots in hours. In poor weather, a day or two. They eat soft things first. Eyes. Tongue. Bowel. The skin over the belly splits if the gas has nowhere to go, and what was a man becomes a meal with a face attached for a little while longer.”

A crow moved in the trees, a black smear against grey.

“Birds will come if the body is visible. Crows take lips, eyelids, fingers, anything protruding. Foxes and dogs drag if the scent reaches them. Rats will work at the clothes and the hair. Rain washes the surface and leaves the deeper rot undisturbed. Mud holds prints, smells, and secrets badly. By the second day he will not look like a soldier. By the third he will not look like a man. By the end of the week, if no one burns him or buries him deep, there will be boots, cloth, bone, and a stain that summer will make infamous.”

Wrack’s mouth moved, humorless.

“Boots outlast men. That is why I mentioned boots.”

She let the silence stretch just long enough for the practical part to begin.

“That is the body. Now the rest of it. The part that stays with you.”

Her voice did not soften, but it lost some of its edge, the way a blade loses shine when it has been used too long on bone.

“Your hands will feel like borrowed tools. Too large, too small, too honest. You may notice the strength in your fingers and hate them for it. You may notice the shake and hate them more. Neither feeling is wisdom. It is aftermath. The smell will get under your nails and into the cuffs of your coat. You will taste it when you drink water, not because the water has turned, but because your mouth has learned a new argument. Iron. Bile. Sour warmth. It will sit at the back of the tongue for a day, maybe two.”

Wrack looked toward the road, then back toward the cart.

“You will hear the rattle at bad moments. Not when you are expecting it. When a pot boils. When a man breathes too hard climbing a bank. When a child cries in a village and stops too suddenly. The sound will arrive before you can put a face to it. Do not chase the face. Faces are less dangerous than noises. A face can be remembered as a man. A noise only wants to be repeated.”

She shifted again, one shoulder rolling as if carrying an old weight.

“You may dream. Not the kind men tell in taverns, with blood like wine and honor like a banner. The small kind. The give of tissue. The way the hips lifted. The bubble at the corner of the mouth. The hand that spasmed. If you dream it, do not make it a message. Dead men do not visit to instruct you. They are busy being weather. If you wake with his noise in your throat, spit and go on.”

Wrack’s eyes narrowed slightly, not at him, but at the horizon where the light was failing.

“You will be tempted to make this mean something grand. Either ‘I am damned’ or ‘I was necessary.’ Both are indulgences. The truth is smaller. He was alive. You made him not. The world did not tilt. The flies did not consult you. Your company did not applaud. The dead man did not forgive, because forgiveness requires a mind, and that mind is currently feeding bacteria.”

A dry breath escaped her.

“If you start liking it too much, tell me. Not because I will preach. Because enjoyment makes men careless and cruel to their own side. A sellsword who loves the work becomes a liability. He stops measuring risk and starts measuring pleasure. If you stop caring whether the people around you eat, freeze, or bleed out, that is worse. You are allowed to be changed. Do not be hollow.”

She reached down and unlooped the waterskin from the saddle, took a small drink, then wiped her mouth with the back of her hand. The gesture was ordinary, almost brutal in its normalcy.

“Now the work after the work. Clean the blade with cloth that can be burned or left behind. Not the shirt on your back if you can avoid it. Not the cloak that smells of fear and somebody else’s horse. If you must use your trousers, use the inside of the leg and swear to mend the stain before you sit down at another man’s fire. A blade left wet corrodes. A man left wet in the memory corrodes faster, but at least he can be rinsed with routine.”

Wrack tucked the skin back into place.

“Check the body once more if you have not already. Belts, boots, seams, linings. Before stiffness makes pockets mean, take what identifies the dead or pays the living. Tokens. Letters. Coins. Anything stamped. If there is a wife’s name in a pouch, leave it. Not from sentiment. From usefulness. A name without leverage is only a knife in the dark. A name with leverage is a road.”

She glanced at the dead men scattered along the ditch, then at the cart listing in the mud.

“Close his eyes if you can manage it without fuss. Not for mercy. Cloudy eyes attract flies faster and unsettle the living. Set the jaw if it has fallen open. If the belly is already opening, do not press it. Gas and filth will answer, and they answer loudly. Drag him off the road if the ground allows, but not far. Just out of sight and out of the water course. Cover with brush, not soil, unless you have time and a spade. A shallow grave in war is only a delayed insult.”

Wrack’s gaze moved to the sutler’s cart.

“The cart stays listing. If you right it, you advertise that someone was here and cared enough to tidy. If you burn it, smoke invites questions, and questions invite men with swords. Take what is useful. Scatter what identifies the dead if it helps. Do not make a pageant. Corpses are poor audience.”

She turned the mare a quarter toward the treeline, but did not ride yet.

“Crossroads. The Rusty Anchor. The table with the X. You will go in looking tired, thirsty, and mildly regretful. Not guilty. Guilt draws dogs. Regret draws pity, and pity is cheaper. You will sit where you can see the door, the barmaid’s face, and the horses outside. If the mark is still there, look at it. Do not touch it. Carved wood holds splinters and questions in equal measure. If someone asks why you are staring at oak, tell them you slept under better and woke under worse.”

Wrack tested the girth of the saddle with one hand, absently, the way a woman checks a promise she does not trust.

“If the mark is gone, someone scrubbed it or planed the table. Both mean time passed and interest arrived. If the table has been replaced, ask nothing. Count the boards in the floor instead. Taverns keep receipts in wood longer than they keep them in ink. If a man at the Anchor recognizes you, do not argue, do not explain, and do not try to be brave about it. Bravery in a tavern is just a slower way of dying in a gutter.”

She touched the coat where the narrow case lay against her ribs.

“The pay box is the larger animal. The list is only its shadow. Third watch. Third ridge. Tidy numbers. Whoever ordered this likes schedules, and schedules have weak points. The weak point is that someone must carry the box, someone must receive it, and someone must account for it if it does not arrive. If the sixth name was due tomorrow, then tomorrow has a hole in it. Somebody will notice. Somebody will ask. Somebody will get angry in the particular way men get angry when money has been promised and meat has failed to appear.”

Wrack’s eyes lifted to the trees.

“We watch for clean hands. The payer does not lie in mud. The courier may. The lookout may. The soft-handed man with the box will want dry boots, hot food, and a witness who can be paid in copper. If he saw this ambush fail, he is running. If he did not, he will come back when the crows lose interest. Either way, Crossroads is where the thread runs. Whether it leads to the payer, the sixth name, or a blade in a dark room, I cannot say from here.”

She said the next part without warmth, but not without purpose.

“That is the rest. It is not redemption. It is not a song. It is the part after the part, where the body becomes weather and the living become logistics. You asked for straight. Straight has a tail. It follows you to the next meal, the next sleep, the next time a man breathes wrong and your hand goes to your knife before your mind has voted.”

Wrack finally swung the mare’s head toward the drover’s cut east of the main road. The grey stepped forward reluctantly, as if the dead had not finished claiming the air.

“Mount, or walk behind and watch the treeline. I am not carrying you, and I am not waiting for you to become a different man before dawn. You are what you are tonight. Useful, shaken, alive. That is enough to start.”

She tapped the hilt of her knife twice against the saddle horn, then once more, a stray third sound she did not bother to retract.

“If you are going to be sick, be sick downwind. If you are going to pray, pray to someone who isn’t listening. Then move. Tomorrow is already leaning over the fence, and it does not care whether we are ready.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I don't mount right away. I walk over to the dead man, put my fingers over his eyelids and press them shut. They feel cool already. "What was his name?" I ask, my back to her.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack let the question hang.

Not out of respect. Respect was something men paid the living when they expected them to remain useful. The dead had no further obligations, and Wrack had no wish to invent any. She let it hang because the ditch had become quiet in the particular way that followed violence: not peaceful, merely emptied, like a room after furniture had been dragged out of it.

“Name,” she said at last. “Not on him.”

She swung down from the mare, boots finding the soft edge of the ditch with a wet, unwilling sound. The grey shifted away from the smell, head high, nostrils working. Wrack paid it no mind. Horses were honest about rot. Men were not.

She went to the dead man no closer than necessary, then knelt on one knee and began to search with the brisk, unromantic efficiency of a woman checking a saddle for galls. Collar. Cuffs. The seam of the cloak where an owner’s mark might have been stitched by a wife, a mother, a sutler, or a quartermaster with more time than sense. The tongue of the boot. The lining of the belt. The small, private places where men hid the things they intended to outlive them.

Nothing.

No coin with a scratched saint. No strip of leather with a home village burned into it. No lock of hair, no prayer tile, no child’s tooth on a thong. No company badge. No captain’s sigil. No name sewn in neat thread because someone had expected him to come home and complain about the stitching.

Wrack withdrew her hands and sat back on her heel.

“Border trash,” she said. “Hired by the job, paid by the token, buried by whoever found them first. Names stay with the payer. Or the clerk. Or the box.”

She glanced toward the cart, where the satchel and the narrow case waited under her coat like a debt.

“The list has a name for tomorrow,” she continued. “Osrin Verrin. If that is him, then he was the sixth notch and you put him out of the schedule early. If it is not him, then he was one of the hands sent to fill the notch, and his own name is missing because hands are not worth ink until they fail.”

Her mouth moved, not quite a smile.

“Ink has killed fewer men than steel, but it signs the orders with better handwriting.”

The fly that had been testing the cart spoke had migrated to the dead man’s wrist. It walked over the blue-dark nails with the calm of a creature that had never been asked to care.

Wrack watched it for a moment, then looked at the closed eyes.

“You put the lids down,” she said. “That is housekeeping, not resurrection. It slows the flies by an hour if the air is kind and by none at all if it is not. Don’t mistake maintenance for mourning.”

She rose, brushing ditch-mud from one knee with the flat of her hand.

“If you start giving every corpse a name and a eulogy, you’ll run out of room in your head for the living. The living are harder to carry and more useful. I have buried men with names, faces, families, songs, and bad breath. It does not make the hole deeper. It only makes the dirt cling.”

A crow called once from the treeline, then thought better of it.

Wrack turned toward the horses, but not before her gaze swept the other dead along the ditch. Five shapes in the failing light, cloaks darkening, hands slack, boots already beginning to claim the last dignity of usefulness.

“These six did not travel under their own names,” she said. “They travelled under tokens, dates, and a count. That is worse. A named man can be missed. A numbered man can be replaced.”

She unlooped the waterskin from the saddle, drank, and wiped her mouth with the back of her hand. The motion was ordinary enough to be obscene after what the evening had contained.

“If his name matters, it will matter because someone else knows it. The payer. The courier. The clerk at Hollow Ford. The man who carved the tally at the Anchor. Not the mud. The mud has no ledger.”

Wrack capped the skin and hung it again.

“You want to know what he was called? Find the box. Boxes keep better memories than corpses. They carry weight, seals, routes, and the particular fear of men who have lost something they were paid to deliver.”

She paused, then added, flatter:

“If the box says Osrin Verrin was the target, then the dead man may have been the hand. If the box says Osrin Verrin was the hand, then the dead man may have been the target. If the box says neither, then we have a corpse, a list, and a very expensive rumor. Rumors are useful when they have edges. This one does not yet.”

The wind shifted again, carrying the smell from the cart toward the trees. Wrack turned her face away without ceremony.

“Close the others if you must,” she said. “Not for them. For the flies, and for whoever finds them. Open eyes unsettle the living and hasten the insects. It is a small kindness, and small kindnesses are all the war ever permits. Do not make it larger than it is.”

She caught the grey mare’s bridle and eased her a few steps from the body. The horse resisted, then yielded, as horses did when the alternative was a woman with a knife and no patience.

“I will not call him brave,” Wrack said. “I will not call him damned. I will not call him innocent. He marched, waited, bled, and died in a ditch beside a cart that smelled of lamp oil and old sweat. If he had a name, it is not written on his face. Meat does not keep opinions, and death does not keep poetry.”

A dry breath escaped her.

“If you insist on a name tonight, use the one the list gives you and be careful with it. Names are like arrows: useful until they stick somewhere you cannot pull them back.”

She looked toward the drover’s cut east of the main road, where the treeline had thickened into a dark seam against the last grey sky.

“Mount,” Wrack said. “The dead can wait. They have all the time in the world now, and none of it belongs to us. The box cannot. The sixth notch cannot. Tomorrow cannot. And if we sit here longer asking a corpse for a courtesy it has stopped owing, we will join it before dawn with our names still unwritten and our horses still thirsty.”

She swung up into the saddle, the satchel shifting against her ribs, the brass tokens heavy beneath her coat.

“Crossroads,” she said. “The Rusty Anchor. The table. The copper-drinker. If his name was Osrin Verrin, then the Anchor may know it. If it was not, then the Anchor may know the man who thought it was.”

Wrack tapped the hilt of her knife once against the saddle horn, then twice.

“Bring the dead man’s eyes with you if you must. Leave his story in the mud. Stories are heavier, and they ride worse.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I pull the cloak over his face, careful not to look at it too long. "Alright," I say, my voice quiet in the ditch. I walk to the other horse and swing up, wincing at the stiffness in my legs. "Lead on."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack let the words go by without answering. *Lead on* was the sort of thing men said when they had finished standing still and had not yet found a better use for their legs. She turned the grey mare out of the ditch-line and into the drover’s cut, where the grass grew long enough to hide hooves and wet enough to swallow them.

The path was less a road than an argument between mud and roots. Alders leaned over it, their lower branches beaded with evening damp. Somewhere ahead, a creek muttered over stones. The sky had gone the colour of old pewter, and the first stars showed thin and unconcerned.

Wrack set a walk. Not slow. Not soft. The pace of a woman who had ridden through too many dark places to believe silence was a virtue, but knew it was useful.

“Keep your horse’s head where mine is,” she said, without looking back. “If I stop, stop. If I go, go. If I swear, it’s probably true.”

The mare’s ears flicked. The animal knew the difference between a road and a hiding place, and it did not like either. Wrack pressed a hand to its neck once, a brief, practical contact, and let it find its own rhythm inside hers.

They followed the creek south until the land rose into a low ridge scattered with furze. From there, Crossroads announced itself in the ordinary way of border towns: dung first, then woodsmoke, then the flat yellow stain of lantern light under a shelf of cloud. A dog barked once, lost interest. A forge hammer rang somewhere behind the tanyard, slow and tired, as if even the blacksmith had stopped believing in miracles.

Wrack reined in at the treeline.

“Mule pens,” she said. “Smell them?”

She did not wait for an answer she could already smell. The stink of animal sweat, stale hay, and piss hung over the southern edge of the town. Good. Mules were stubborn, owners were annoyed, and nobody watched mule pens unless something had been stolen or somebody had been killed. Tonight, it might be both.

She dismounted, keeping the grey between herself and the light from the road. Her boots sank into the vergesoft earth. She checked the mare’s girth, the saddle, the bridle, then moved to the second horse and did the same with less patience. Tack had a way of lying. A loose buckle could kill faster than a knife, because it did it quietly and let the victim blame the ground.

Then she left the horses standing in the shelter of a thorn hedge and went forward on foot.

Wrack did not sneak. Sneaking was for boys and men who expected to be forgiven. She moved the way a Border scout moved: low where the ground gave her cover, upright where it did not, footsteps placed with the indifferent care of a woman who had learned that the earth listened.

The Rusty Anchor sat at the junction of three roads and one bad reputation. It was a long, low building with a thatch roof patched in three places, a sign swinging from a crooked arm, and windows that let out more light than they ought to at that hour. The painted anchor had been repainted so often it had become more rope than iron. Beneath it, a rail held two horses and a mule. One horse was blown. The other stood with the patient resentment of an animal that had been tied too long and fed too little.

Wrack counted the lit windows.

Public room, front left. Private room, rear right. Kitchen glimmer under the eaves. No light in the loft. No movement at the shutter.

She circled wide, through the mule pens, past a dunghill steaming faintly in the cool air, and into the back lane. The lane was narrow, foul, and useful. A privy leaned over a pit. Ash had been dumped against the wall, black and wet. A horse block sat empty, its trough crusted with algae.

There, she found the first thing that mattered.

Shavings.

Pale curls of oak lay in the dark mud beside the back door, not yet scattered by feet or washed by rain. They had the soft, moist look of fresh cutting. Wrack crouched and touched one with the tip of her knife. The curl sprang back slightly. Fine work. Not a knife. A plane.

She looked at the back door. Iron-banded oak, new-looking hinges, a bar inside. The wood around the lock had been scraped recently, as if someone had forced it open with a lever and then felt embarrassed afterward.

Not the mark itself. But the manner of its removal.

Wrack moved to the corner where the lane met the front yard and waited.

A man came around the side of the Anchor then, carrying a bucket. He was young, broad in the shoulders, narrow in the face, with a smudge of soot on one cheek and the bored expression of someone who had been told to wash floors after closing. He set the bucket down, looked up at the sign as if it owed him money, and went back inside.

Through the open upper transom, sound spilled out in fragments: laughter, a mug set down too hard, the drawl of a man telling a story no one believed.

Wrack watched the front door.

For a while, nothing happened. That was not reassurance. Nothing happening was only the world holding its breath.

Then a rider came up the south road.

Single horse. Fast, but not panicked. The animal was lathered at the neck and shoulders, its head low, its gait strung out with the weary speed of a mount that had been pushed hard and knew it would be pushed again. The rider wore a dark cloak, travel-stained at the hem. His boots were good. Too good for the road he had come by. Mud clung to the outer seams, but the insteps were dry.

Wrack’s eyes narrowed.

A man who had ridden through wet ground and kept his insteps dry had either changed horses, or had been careful where he put his feet. Careful men were interesting. Careful men with boxes were worse.

The rider pulled up at the rail. He did not dismount at once. He sat there for a moment, scanning the yard, the windows, the lane mouths, the mule pens. Professional. Not a merchant. Not a pilgrim. Not a drunk looking for a bed.

Then he swung down, tied the horse with two quick hitches, and went to the Anchor door.

Before he entered, he unwrapped a bundle from beneath his cloak.

Wrack saw only the shape of it: a narrow case, iron-banded at the corners, stopped at both ends with wax-sealed plugs. Not large. Not a chest. Not the pay box from the manifest, unless the manifest had lied about size. But it was a box for carrying something that mattered: papers, tokens, a seal, a name, a debt.

The rider tucked it under his arm and went inside.

The door closed behind him.

Wrack stayed where she was for three more counts. Then she moved to the front window, keeping her body below the sill, and listened.

The laughter inside had thinned. A woman’s voice—sharp, practiced, not afraid—asked whether he wanted ale or trouble. The rider said something she could not hear. The woman laughed once, not warmly. A stool scraped. The transom opened a little wider.

Warm air came out, smelling of beer, wet wool, smoke, and fried onions.

Wrack lifted her head just enough to see through the lower pane.

The public room was long and low-beamed, crowded enough to be lively and sparse enough to be watchful. Rushes on the floor had been trampled into a green-black mash. A fire burned in the hearth at the far end, throwing restless light over the faces of a dozen drinkers. Most were locals: carters, drovers, two men with bowstrings still looped over their shoulders, a woman with a child asleep against her hip. The barmaid stood behind a counter scarred by knives and elbows, wiping a tankard with a cloth that had given up on cleanliness years ago.

Near the hearth, one table had been doctored.

The top board nearest the wall was pale. Not new wood laid over old, but freshly planed, the grain raw and bright where the rest of the table had darkened with ale, smoke, and use. Someone had taken a plane to it in a hurry, or with intent. The edges still held a faint ridge where the blade had skipped.

Wrack looked for the mark.

Nothing.

No crooked X. No tally. No notches.

Only smooth, stripped oak, and a few dark spots where the grain had drunk deeper than the rest.

The rider had taken the corner bench facing the door. His cloak was unfastened now. Under it, he wore a plain doublet, good cut, no sigil. His hands rested on the table. They were not soft. They were the hands of a man who had done enough work to know when he was being watched, but not enough to make a show of it.

The narrow case sat beside his elbow.

He had not opened it.

He had not ordered.

He was waiting.

Wrack withdrew from the window before the light could catch the edge of her cheek. She crouched in the shadow of the Anchor’s corner, thinking.

Plans were like horse tack: useful until tested, then suddenly full of weak points. The weak point here was the table. Someone had removed the mark. Either the Anchor’s people had done it after questions arrived, or the man inside had done it himself. If the latter, then he had either come back for the box, or come to collect the next name.

Tomorrow’s name.

Osrin Verrin.

Wrack tasted the name mentally, found it no clearer than the others. Names were only handles. Handles broke when men yanked them hard enough.

She went back the way she had come, keeping low, avoiding the shavings, avoiding the lane mouth, avoiding the light. The mule pens smelled worse up close. One mule regarded her with the profound contempt only mules could summon. She ignored it.

At the thorn hedge, the two horses stood where she had left them. The grey flicked an ear at her approach. The second horse shifted, restless, sensing the change in her pace.

Wrack did not mount at once. She came to where Corvin waited in the dark and kept her voice low enough that the mules would not carry it.

“We have a new piece,” she said.

She did not soften the words. Softness was for men who had not just ridden through a dead man’s smell to reach a living one.

“Back lane. Fresh shavings by the door. Someone planed a table inside the Anchor. Not long ago. The mark you saw is gone, or covered, or scraped so thin only splinters remember it.”

Her eyes moved toward the inn, though she did not look directly at the window. Looking directly was a way of telling the room there was someone outside worth noticing.

“A rider came in from the south maybe a quarter-hour ago. One horse, blown. Good boots, dry insteps. He carries a narrow iron-banded case and sits facing the door. Hasn’t opened it. Hasn’t drunk. He’s waiting for someone, or for courage.”

A pause. The dog barked again, farther off this time.

“The table by the hearth has a fresh board. Pale. Planed. No mark. If your copper-drinker made that mark, he either came back and took his own trail with him, or someone else decided the wood had become talkative.”

Wrack’s gaze came back to Corvin.

“Was he the man you saw?”

She did not ask whether Corvin was certain. Certainty was a luxury men bought after they had survived long enough to afford regrets. She asked because the answer changed the shape of the next hour.

If it was the same man, then Corvin’s face might be known. If it was not, then Corvin might still be a stranger, and strangers were safer than witnesses only until they became corpses.

Wrack did not wait long. She could not. The rider inside had a box, a watchful back, and the particular stillness of a man who had chosen his corner before choosing his drink. That meant he had expected company, or trouble, or both.

She made the decision with the speed of a woman who had learned that hesitation dressed itself as caution and called itself wise.

“All right,” she said. “New arrangement.”

She unslung the satchel from her shoulder and set it against the horse’s flank, out of the mud but within reach. From inside her coat she drew the purse of mixed silver, counted out three copper pieces, and held them out.

“Use these if you need to. Not silver. Not tokens. Copper buys silence without making a man feel purchased.”

Her hand closed over the coins for a moment, then opened again, offering them.

“I go in first.”

She said it flatly, as if announcing a change of weather.

“If the man inside knows your face, sending you through that door is like handing him a knife and asking him to decide where to put it. I may be known too, but I am known as a debt, not a witness. Debts can be negotiated. Witnesses are tidied away.”

Wrack brushed a strap straight on her shoulder, checked the fall of her cloak, and tucked the brass tokens deeper under her coat where they would not chime.

“You stay with the horses. Watch the back lane and the front rail. If the rider’s horse bolts without him, that means something has gone wrong inside, and you come in loud enough to be believed. If a second man arrives and ties up beside him, note whether he carries a case, a weapon, or a message. If he carries none of those, he is either a fool or a lookout. Lookouts are worse.”

She looked toward the Anchor again.

“I will sit where I can see the door and the new table. If the man with the case leaves, I do not chase unless I can take the box. If he opens it, I watch what he shows, not what he hides. If he asks my name, I give him one that costs him nothing to forget.”

A dry breath moved through her mouth.

“If I need you, I will cough. Once, stay where you are. Twice, come in and make yourself unpleasant. Three times, leave and do not look back. If I knock on the doorframe twice as I pass outside, come out as if you have remembered a debt. If I do not come out by the time a man drinks two ales, assume I am dead, busy, or in a conversation that has stopped being civil.”

She did not smile. The corner of her mouth might have moved, but it was the movement of a woman setting a trap, not enjoying it.

“Do not be noble outside that door. Nobility is what men call the impulse to die loudly. I would rather have you alive and rude.”

Wrack turned toward the Anchor, then stopped.

“One more thing.”

Her voice dropped, not softer, but narrower.

“If the case is the pay box, or part of it, do not let the room know we understand what it is. Boxes are only wood and iron until someone believes they contain power. Then they get men killed. If the man inside is waiting for Osrin Verrin, then Osrin is either dead, late, or walking into a room with a smile and no idea his name has already been counted.”

She glanced back once.

“Stay low. Keep the horses quiet. If anyone rides past the mule pens, let them pass. If anyone stops, be boring.”

Then she moved toward the inn.

Wrack did not hurry. Hurrying was a confession. She walked the way a tired traveller walked after a long day: shoulders slightly forward, boots scuffed, cloak damp at the hem, face arranged into the ordinary blankness of someone who had seen enough bad roads to stop expecting good inns.

The front door of the Rusty Anchor was oak, blackened by smoke and handled by too many wet palms. A brass knocker hung beside it, shaped like a fish with the imagination of a blacksmith in a hurry. Wrack did not use it. Doors answered better to weight than ceremony.

She pushed it open.

The noise inside changed at once. Not stopped—taverns never stopped—but shifted, the way water shifts when a stone enters it. Conversations dipped. A few eyes lifted. The barmaid looked up from her tankard, assessed Wrack in one flat motion, and returned to wiping.

The smell was thick: ale, sweat, smoke, wet dog, onions frying somewhere behind a curtain, and the yeasty sourness of spilled beer soaking into rushes. Heat from the hearth pressed against Wrack’s face. The room was brighter than the lane, harsher after the dark.

She saw the new table before she saw the man.

It sat near the hearth, half-hidden by a support post, the planed board pale as a bone in the firelight. The man beside it had not moved when the door opened. That was notable. Men who expected trouble watched the door. Men who had already decided who would bring it watched something else.

Wrack stepped inside and let the door fall shut behind her.

The room had perhaps fifteen people, counting staff. Two carters near the bar, red-faced and loud in the way of men who had not yet been beaten for talking. A woman with a child on her hip by the hearth, rocking slightly, eyes lowered. An old man nursing a cup of something that smelled stronger than ale. Three soldiers from no company Wrack recognized, seated together with their backs to the wall and their hands near their knives. Not drunk. Not sober enough to be honest.

And the rider.

He sat alone at the corner bench, the narrow case beside his elbow, his cloak thrown back over the bench. Up close, he was younger than Wrack had expected from the road-weariness of his horse: perhaps thirty, lean-faced, with a scar bisecting one eyebrow and the kind of stillness that came from being underestimated often enough to find it useful.

His eyes lifted as she entered.

They met hers for a heartbeat.

Wrack did not look away first, but she did not stare. Staring invited argument. Looking away invited pursuit. She gave him the blank, tired regard of a woman deciding whether he was worth the trouble of avoiding.

Then she turned to the bar.

“Ale,” she said. “Small. Watered if the brewer has conscience.”

The barmaid grunted. “Conscience ran out in spring.”

“Then give me the absence of it.”

The woman poured. Wrack set two coppers on the counter. Copper, not silver. The coins made a dull sound against the wood. The barmaid took them without counting, which meant either she trusted Wrack’s face or she had decided not to care.

Wrack took the tankard and moved into the room.

She chose a table not too near the hearth, not too near the door, with a clear line to the new board and the rider’s hands. She set the ale down, unfastened her cloak just enough to let the knife at her hip shift into a more comfortable angle, and sat.

The room resumed its noise. Not entirely. Taverns had membranes, and strangers stretched them. The three soldiers watched her from the corner. The old man did not. The woman with the child rocked and stared into the fire.

Wrack drank.

The ale was bitter, warm, and honest about its faults. She swallowed without ceremony and set the cup down.

Out of the corner of her eye, the rider reached for his own drink at last. A mug had appeared beside him. The barmaid must have brought it while Wrack was moving. He drank, wiped his mouth with the back of one hand, and returned his gaze to the door.

Waiting.

Wrack let her eyes drift to the planed table.

Up close, the damage was cleaner than she had expected. Whoever had taken a plane to the oak had not been amateurish, but they had been hurried. The new surface showed faint ridges where the blade had skipped over grain. Near the corner, a dark patch remained where liquid had soaked too deeply to scrape away. Not blood. Ale, perhaps, or grease. But the shape of it was wrong for the table’s usual stains. It looked like the ghost of a mark.

Crooked.

Gone, but not forgiven by the wood.

Wrack leaned forward slightly, as if warming her hands at the fire, and let her gaze rest on the patch.

The rider’s hand moved.

Not much. A finger tapping once against the mug. Then still.

Wrack said nothing.

The door opened behind her.

A gust of cold air cut through the smoke. Voices outside, low and hurried. Then the door shut again.

Wrack did not turn. Turning was for men who expected their names to be called. She watched the rider’s reflection in the dark glass of the window instead.

He had turned his head.

Just enough.

His eyes narrowed at the door, then slid back to the room. For a moment, they found Wrack’s.

She lifted her tankard an inch. Not a toast. An acknowledgment. *I see you seeing me.*

The rider’s mouth moved. Not words. The beginning of a decision.

Wrack set the cup down.

The room felt hotter. The fire crackled. Somewhere behind the curtain, a pan hissed. The woman with the child shifted in her sleep.

The rider pushed back from the table.

Wrack watched him rise, one hand dropping to the case beneath his cloak. He did not look at the new table. He looked at the door.

Then he looked at her again.

This time, there was no pretense of tiredness in his face. There was calculation, and the thin edge of annoyance that came when a man realized he had been read.

Wrack waited.

The inn held its breath around them, full of ordinary noise and ordinary people, while the two of them sat and stood on opposite sides of a planed table and a box that had not yet spoken.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I don't mount right away. I walk over to the dead man, put my fingers over his eyelids and press them shut. They feel cool already. "What was his name?" I ask, my back to her.
