dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
The lamp was bad and the tent was worse and the man on the table had been shouting for long enough that he had mostly stopped.

"Both shoulders," Sedge said, laying things out in a row. "When I say hold, I mean hold. He's going to buck and you're going to want to let go, and you're not going to."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I get my weight on his shoulders and find somewhere on the canvas wall to look. "Ready," I say, which is a lie.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge didn’t bother answering the lie. Lies didn’t bleed and they didn’t break, so she left them where they were. She laid out the iron, the needle, the wire, the thread, and the bowl of water that had gone lukewarm hours ago. She washed her hands again, not for cleanliness but for rhythm, scrubbing until the skin pricked and the water turned gray. The lamp flickered, casting long, trembling shadows, but she kept her eyes on the table.

“Clavicles are intact,” she said, pressing along the collarbones, feeling the wrongness beneath the muscle. “Ruptured dislocations. Bilateral. You’re lucky he’s still breathing. Most men drop before I even pick up the clamp.” She picked up the iron, testing the edge against her thumb. It burned through the leather glove. She didn’t flinch. “I’m going to pop them back in. It will tear. It will bleed. You will hold. If you let go, he loses the arm. If you hold, he keeps it and lives to complain about the rain somewhere else.”

She moved to his side, bracing her knee against the canvas edge to get leverage. She gripped his left shoulder with one hand, his right wrist with the other, and aligned her weight. “Breathe in,” she ordered, though she knew he wouldn’t. She drove forward, feeling the joint slide home with a wet click, then repeated the motion on the other side. The sound was too loud in the tent. The man made a noise that wasn’t quite a word.

“Good,” she said, already reaching for the wire. “He’s coming back to himself. That means the brain’s still working. I’m immobilizing the shoulders now. I’m threading the needle through the skin above the joint, I’m looping the wire around the humerus, I’m tightening it until the movement stops. It will feel like he’s being crushed in a vise. That’s the wire working, not me. I’m not breaking him. I’m keeping him together.”

She worked methodically, her voice a steady monotone over the clink of metal and the ragged breathing from the table. She didn’t look up. She didn’t need to. The tent, the lamp, the weight on the shoulders, the man’s body—it was all just material. And she was the one who knew how to shape it. She tied off the wire, cut the excess, and reached for the linen strips. “I’m binding the arms to the chest now. I’m crossing the linen over the sternum, I’m tucking the ends under the armpits, I’m pulling until the shoulders lock. It will restrict his breathing. That’s fine. He’ll breathe enough to survive. I’m not saving him for a parade. I’m saving him for tomorrow.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I flinch when I hear the wet pop, my fingers digging into his shoulders a little harder. "He's shaking," I say, voice too tight. "Is that supposed to—" The man groans, and I look away again.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge didn’t pause. The shaking was just the nervous system dumping adrenaline as shock took hold. She pulled the linen strip taut, knotting it with a sharp, practiced snap. “I’m securing the binding now,” she said, her voice flat. “Nerves are misfiring. Pain and adrenaline are fighting each other. It doesn’t matter why. It just means he’s still alive. You don’t let go. You don’t loosen your weight. If he starts convulsing, you brace against his hips. If he vomits, you turn his head. You keep him on the table.”

She worked the second knot, checking the tension against the wire. The metal groaned faintly under the strain. “I’m tightening it until the movement stops,” she continued, wiping her palms on a stained canvas rag. “The wire is holding the joint in place. I’m not crushing him. I’m keeping him from tearing himself apart. If I didn’t bind it, the humerus would snap clean through the muscle and take the subclavian with it. He’d bleed out before he hit the dirt.”

The lamp flickered again, but she didn’t look up. She kept her eyes on the patient’s chest, watching the rise and fall slow beneath the linen. “I don’t enjoy this,” she said, leaving no room for argument. “I take no pleasure in it. I just make sure he doesn’t die because I hesitated. Hold your weight. Breathe. He’ll pass out soon. When he does, you don’t move. You wait for the breathing to even out. Then you step back.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: "How bad is it?" I ask. "Bad like he loses the leg, or bad like this is the part where we're being kind?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge didn’t pause her hands. She pulled the linen strip taut across his sternum, crossing it over the existing binding, and tugged until the fabric bit into the torn muscle. “He’s not losing a leg,” she said, her voice level over the sputter of the lamp. “He’s not losing an arm, either, unless you let go or I misjudge the tension. This is the part where we’re not being kind. Kind is a luxury for rear hospitals with running water and surgeons who haven’t watched their own men turn into meat on a stretcher. This is mechanics.”

She threaded the next strip through the linen, knotting it with a sharp, practiced pull. “I’m securing the immobilization now. The wire is anchored to the humerus, the linen is bracing the scapula, and the knot is locking the joint. I’m not repairing tissue. I’m building a temporary scaffold until the body decides to scar itself shut. It’s supposed to hurt. Pain means the nervous system is still firing. If he wasn’t shaking, I’d be worried about spinal shock.”

She wiped her palms on her stained apron, leaving smears of sweat and dried blood. “If I were being kind, I’d amputate at the glenohumeral joint and save the shoulder. Or I’d let him bleed out on the dirt and save the clean linen. This is the middle ground. It’s not mercy. It’s maintenance. He’ll carry a rifle again. He’ll complain about the rain. That’s the only promise I make.”

She stepped back just enough to check his pulse at the wrist, her fingers pressing firmly against the radial artery to feel the rhythm beneath the thrashing. “He’s stable. The wire is holding. The binding is restricting his chest wall, but he’s compensating. You keep your weight on him. You don’t let him thrash. You don’t look at his face. You just hold. That’s the job.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I nod, but it's just a reflex. My arms are starting to ache from holding him steady. "Yeah," I mutter, my eyes still fixed on the canvas. "Just maintenance." The guy lets out a low whimper, and I feel his whole body tense. "Hey—he's trying to move."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge’s jaw tightened. The thrashing wasn’t just pain anymore; it was the body’s raw, unthinking instinct to escape the constraint. She didn’t waste breath on reassurance. She shifted her weight, planting her boot against the canvas edge to brace herself, and reached for the second length of linen.

“He’s fighting the bind,” she said, her voice flat over the rustle of fabric. “He’s trying to rotate the scapula out of the socket. If he succeeds, the wire snaps through the deltoid and takes the brachial plexus with it. You pull harder. You don’t let him roll.”

She worked the fresh strip through the existing knot, weaving it tight across his chest and down to the table edge. The fabric bit into the sweat-slicked canvas. She pulled until the material groaned, then cinched it home with a sharp, efficient tug. “I’m anchoring the restraint now,” she said, her fingers moving with precise, unhurried pressure. “Cross-weaving the linen over the sternum. Tying it to the table rail. I’m not giving him the leverage to roll. I’m distributing the load so your arms don’t fail. Keep your grip. Don’t let up.”

She stepped back just enough to check his radial pulse again. It was thready but steady. The chest rose and fell in shallow, ragged bursts. “Adrenaline was peaking,” she noted, wiping blood from her knuckles with the back of her wrist. “He was going to crash again. That was the body shutting down to conserve oxygen. You didn’t move. You didn’t breathe loud. You just held. I don’t enjoy this. I take no pleasure in watching him fight himself apart. I just keep him from tearing his own nervous system to pieces. Maintain pressure. Wait for the pass.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I make myself look at what she's looking at. "Tell me what I'm seeing," I say. "I'd rather know than imagine it."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge didn’t look up from the table. She kept her hands on the linen, adjusting the tension with a final, decisive knot. “You’re looking at split skin above the joints,” she said, her voice flat, stripped of anything but fact. “Not deep enough to sever the nerve, but deep enough to thread the wire. The muscle is torn around the humerus. It’s bleeding into the linen, which is why it’s turning darker at the edges. The wire is cutting into the deltoid, holding the bone in place. His chest is restricted by the binding, so he’s breathing shallow. That’s why he’s whimpering. That’s why he’s fighting. The nervous system is screaming that he’s being crushed, even though the crushing is what’s keeping him from bleeding out.”

She paused, wiping her thumb across a smear of blood on her sleeve. “You’re looking at a scaffold. Wire and linen holding broken joints together until scar tissue can take the load. It’s supposed to look ugly. It’s supposed to hurt. If it looked clean, I’d have failed. If it didn’t hurt, he’d be dead. You’re looking at mechanics. You’re looking at a man who will walk out of this tent with a permanent limp and a permanent ache. You’re looking at the price of keeping him alive. Don’t look away. Look at the pulse. Look at the chest rise. Look at the wire holding. That’s all there is.”

She checked his radial artery again, her fingers pressing firmly against the skin. “Steady. He’s dropping. Let him. You don’t move. You keep your weight. That’s the job.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I swallow hard, watching the blood seep into the linen like she said it would. "So he's gonna live?" I ask, my voice quieter than I meant it to be. The guy's finally gone still under my hands.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge didn’t answer right away. She pressed two fingers to his carotid, counted the beats in the quiet, and listened to the shallow drag of air through his restricted chest. The pulse was thready but steady. The breathing was slow, shallow, and regular. The body had finally stopped fighting the scaffold and started accepting it.

“He’ll live,” she said, wiping her hands on the back of her apron. “Maybe. Depends on whether the wire migrates, whether the honey paste keeps the rot out, whether he gets shot in the ribs before the scar tissue knits. I don’t guarantee outcomes. I guarantee mechanics.”

She reached for the bowl of water, dipped a clean strip of linen, and began dabbing the blood from his collarbone. “I’m cleaning the incision lines now. I’m patting the skin dry. I’m applying the yarrow and honey paste to draw out moisture and keep the bacteria from breeding. I’m checking his pupils. They’re dilated but reactive to the lamp’s flicker. I’m listening to his chest. No fluid. Just shallow breaths. That’s good. That means the lungs are intact.”

She folded the excess linen over the bindings, tucking the edges neatly to prevent chafing. “I’m securing the dressing now. I’m not stitching it shut. I’m leaving it open to drain. If I closed it, the blood would pool, the pressure would build, and he’d die in his own fluids. I’m letting it breathe. I’m letting it bleed what it needs to bleed. Then I’m wrapping him in the wool blanket to keep the shivering down. Shivering burns energy he doesn’t have.”

She stepped back, wiping her forehead with the crook of her wrist. “He’ll live. Maybe. You don’t touch him unless the linen soaks through. You don’t give him water until he swallows without coughing. You don’t pray. You monitor. You watch his chest rise. You feel his pulse. You wait for the fever. You watch for the rot. That’s the job. I don’t enjoy it. I take no pleasure in it. I just make sure he doesn’t die because I hesitated.”

She picked up her iron, laid it on the canvas, and picked up a fresh strip of linen. “Now you let go. You step back. You breathe. I’ll take the watch until his breathing stabilizes. Then you can rest.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: "Don't tidy it up for me," I say. "What does shrapnel actually do in there? Say it straight."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge didn’t stop wiping her hands. She let the damp linen drop into the bowl and looked at him, really looked at him, for the first time since the man had hit the table. “You don’t tidy it up,” she said, her voice flat. “You leave it raw because raw tells you where the damage is.”

She stepped back to the instrument row and picked up the probe, rolling it between her fingers. “Shrapnel doesn’t punch a hole. It tears. It shreds. It turns muscle into mulch and leaves fragments of steel, glass, or ceramic buried where they land. They don’t sit still. They drift with gravity, with breath, with the next step the man takes. They nick the subclavian, the brachial plexus, the pleura. They leave metal in the tissue that rusts in three days. Rust kills. Infection kills. Gas gangrene kills faster.”

She moved to the table again, pressing the blunt end of the probe against the edge of the wound above the shoulder. “You see a clean line? That’s the skin. Under it, the fascia is split open like a paper envelope. The projectile didn’t go straight through. It tumbled. It made a cavity the size of a fist, then collapsed it. The tissue that can’t survive that pressure dies. Dead tissue is a breeding ground. I don’t close it because closing it traps the rot. I pack it with gauze soaked in saline and iodine. I leave it open to drain. I dig out what I can find with the forceps. I don’t pretend the fragments aren’t there. I just make sure they don’t find a nerve or a vessel before the body walls them off.”

She set the probe down and picked up a fresh roll of dry gauze. “That’s what it does. It doesn’t ask permission. It doesn’t care about the man’s name or his rank. It just turns living tissue into a foreign body reaction and hopes he survives the fever. I don’t tidy it up. I map it. I control the bleeding. I buy time for the white blood cells to do what I can’t. You asked for straight. That’s straight. Now watch his chest. He’s drifting back under.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I look down at my hands, still braced against his shoulders. "So all this—" I gesture at the mess on the table. "It's just buying time?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge didn’t answer right away. She set the gauze down and picked up a rag, wiping the last of the honey and blood from her knuckles. She looked at the table, then at Wick’s hands still pressed to the man’s shoulders.

“Time,” she said, “is the only currency that doesn’t run out until the body stops spending it.” She dropped the rag into the basin. “He won’t walk straight for three months. He’ll carry weight on that side until the scar tissue calcifies. The wire will stay in until the skin grows over it, or until I cut it out. The fragments will stay until his immune system walls them off, or until they migrate and kill him anyway. All of this—” she jerked her chin at the bindings, the stained linen, the raw edges of the wound “—is just making sure he survives the next six hours so his body can start the real work. I’m not fixing him. I’m stalling him.”

She stepped back from the table, rolling her shoulders to work out the stiffness. “Time for the bleeding to clot. Time for the shock to break. Time for the fever to either burn out the infection or burn him alive. Time for a stretcher to find him before the supply trucks move on. You don’t get clean wounds out here. You get functional ones. You get enough time to survive the march, the next firefight, the long haul to a real hospital if one exists. That’s all.”

She picked up her iron again, setting it carefully on the canvas to cool. “I don’t enjoy watching men hold their breath while I thread wire through their skin. I don’t enjoy the sounds they make. I don’t enjoy any of it. I just know that if I hesitate, the time runs out. And time is the only thing that matters when you’re stitching a man back together with what you have and what he’s got left.”

She glanced at the patient’s chest, watching the slow, shallow rise and fall. “He’s sleeping now. The pain’s finally won over the panic. You can take your weight off. Wash your hands. You’ve held him through the worst of it. Now you wait.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: He starts screaming again and I hold him down through it. "Keep going and keep talking," I tell her. "Tell me exactly what you're doing to him and how much longer -- all of it, don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
The scream tore through the canvas, sharp and ragged. Sedge didn’t pause. She stepped in, braced her thigh against the table rail, and drove her palm flat against his sternum to anchor him. “I’m pressing down to stabilize the torso,” she said, her voice cutting through the noise. “He’s riding a pain spike. The nerves are misfiring. I’m keeping his ribs from flaring when he convulses. If his shoulder blades lift, the wire pulls through the deltoid and strips the joint clean.”

She reached for the iodine-soaked gauze, wringing it out over the basin. “I’m packing the wound now. I’m laying the strips into the cavity, layer by layer, not stuffing it. Stuffing traps heat and bacteria. I’m leaving the center open to drain. I’m threading the drainage tube through the lowest point so gravity does the work. I’m checking the wire tension again. It’s holding. I’m reinforcing the knot with a double hitch. I’m cutting the excess linen and tucking the edges so they don’t rub against the skin.”

“You want to know how long,” she said, not looking up. “The screaming stops when the nerves fatigue. That’s twenty minutes. Maybe thirty. I’m going to leave the packing in. I’m going to wrap the chest in a figure-eight bandage to limit expansion. I’m going to tie a splint to the table rail so his arms don’t swing. I’m going to step back and let him burn through the adrenaline. When he crashes, his breathing will slow. His skin will go cool. His pulse will drop to maybe fifty beats. That’s not death. That’s the body shutting down non-essential functions to save the brain. I’ll stay. I’ll watch his chest. I’ll feel his wrist. I’ll wait for the fever to break or to take him. That takes six hours. Maybe eight. If the wire migrates, it takes ten minutes. If the infection sets in, it takes three days. I don’t know. I just keep him on the table.”

She dipped a fresh strip into the lukewarm water, pressed it to his jawline to wipe away sweat and saliva, and kept talking. “I’m cleaning his face because his tongue is going to swell if he keeps his mouth open like that. I’m positioning his head so he doesn’t aspirate when he vomits. I’m checking his pupils again. They’re equal. I’m listening to his lungs. The left side is a little wet. That’s fluid from the shock. I’m not draining it. I’m letting his body reabsorb it. I’m tying off the splint. I’m laying a blanket over his legs so his legs don’t get cold and steal blood from the core. I’m sitting on the stool. I’m watching the rise and fall. I’m counting the breaths. Twelve. Eleven. Thirteen. I’m not leaving anything out. This is what it looks like. This is what it takes. You hold him until he’s still. Then you let him sleep.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I can feel his body start to give out under me. "Okay," I say, my throat tight. "Alright." I watch the rise and fall of his chest, counting in my head like she is. It's the only thing to do.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge watched the tension bleed out of the man’s frame. The violent thrashing had collapsed into a heavy, uncontrolled stillness. She didn’t call it peace. She called it exhaustion. She pressed two fingers to his carotid again, counting the beats beneath her thumb. Forty-eight. Falling. She noted the temperature of his skin—cooling, clammy. The body was shedding its defensive heat to preserve the core.

“He’s entering the crash phase,” she said, her voice level over the sputter of the lamp. “Adrenaline is gone. His heart rate will keep dropping. His extremities will go cold. That’s expected. I’m not going to warm him. Cold slows metabolism and buys the clotting process more time. I’m going to check his pupils. They’re sluggish but reactive. I’m listening to his heart. The beat is irregular but strong. He’s compensating.”

She moved to the basin, rinsed her hands in the gray water, and shook them out. “I’m adjusting the figure-eight bandage now. I’m loosening the lower wrap just enough to allow diaphragm expansion. If I leave it too tight, he’ll drown in his own secretions. If I leave it too loose, the wire shifts. I’m checking the drainage tube. It’s sitting in the dependent part of the wound. I’m making sure it’s not kinked. I’m applying a fresh layer of dry gauze over the packing to wick away exudate. I’m taping it down with a strip of adhesive canvas. I’m not sealing it. I’m letting it breathe.”

She stepped back to the table, wiping her hands on her apron. “You can take your weight off his shoulders now. Roll him slightly to the left if his right side is compressing the lung. Don’t lift him. Just shift the load. You keep your hands on his upper arms. If he twitches, you steady him. You don’t speak. You don’t look at his face. You watch his chest. Twelve breaths a minute. Eleven. Thirteen. Steady.”

She pulled the stool closer, sat down, and kept her eyes on the patient’s ribs. “I’m going to stay right here until his pulse hits fifty. I’m going to document the time. I’m going to check the wire tension every hour. I’m going to monitor for signs of migration or infection. If his skin turns mottled, I’ll start a fever wash. If he starts coughing up blood, I’ll elevate the head of the table. I don’t enjoy sitting in a tent that smells like sweat and copper while a man’s body dismantles itself. I take no pleasure in watching him fight the wire, the binding, the pain. I just make sure he doesn’t die because I looked away. You rest your arms. I’ll take the watch. When his breathing evens out, you can sleep. But you keep your hands ready. That’s the job.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: When it's over I sit down on the floor of the tent and don't get up. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge didn’t look at him. She kept her eyes on the table, on the slow rise and fall of the linen-bound chest, on the faint tremor in the patient’s fingers. She adjusted the wool blanket over his legs, tucking it tightly around his ankles to keep the circulation centered. She checked her pocket watch, noting the time. She opened her field journal, wrote down the hour, the pulse rate, the respiratory count, the color of the skin, the condition of the wound. She closed the book. She picked up the iodine-soaked gauze again, not to pack it, but to wipe the sweat from his forehead, the saliva from the corner of his mouth, the dried blood from his jawline. She didn’t use a cloth. She used her hands because her hands were already clean enough from the water and the soap, and because the gauze was reserved for the wound. She pressed the damp linen against his skin, blotting, not rubbing. She checked the drainage tube again. It was sitting in the lowest point of the cavity. She made sure it wasn’t kinked. She adjusted the figure-eight bandage, loosening the lower wrap by a half-inch to allow diaphragm expansion without compromising the wire tension. She tied off the splint to the table rail, checking the friction points so the linen wouldn’t fray. She sat back on the stool, crossed her legs, and kept her eyes on his chest.

She explained the next phase. She said the fever would come in six hours. She said the body would run hot to kill the bacteria, and he would shiver, and she would not stop it unless it drove his heart rate above one hundred. She said the white blood cells would wall off the shrapnel fragments, and some would migrate, and some would stay, and he would carry them until his bones dissolved them or until they pierced a vessel. She said the honey paste would draw out moisture, the yarrow would slow the bleeding, and the open drainage would prevent abscess formation. She said she would check the wire tension every hour. She said she would listen to his lungs every thirty minutes. She said she would monitor his urine output if he voided, because dark urine meant kidney stress, and clear urine meant his body was clearing the toxins. She said she would document every change. She said she would not close the wound. She said she would not amputate. She said she would not give him morphine because it slowed his breathing and he needed to cough up the fluid. She said she would sit here. She said she would watch. She said she took no pleasure in it. She said she didn’t enjoy the smell of the tent, the flicker of the lamp, the weight of the blanket, the sound of his shallow breaths, the sight of the blood soaking through the linen, the knowledge of what it would cost him, the certainty that he might die anyway. She said she just made sure he didn’t die because she looked away.

She kept her hands on his wrist, feeling the pulse drop to forty-five. She adjusted the blanket again. She checked the drainage tube. She wiped his face. She wrote in the book. She listened to his chest. She counted the breaths. She waited. She didn’t leave. She didn’t summarize. She stayed. She kept talking. She kept doing.

She reached for the basin and poured out the gray water, refilling it from the canteen. She added a measured drop of iodine, swirled it, and dipped a fresh strip of linen. She wiped the rust-colored smear from his clavicle, tracing the line where the skin had split around the wire entry point. She noted the slight swelling. She said swelling was normal. She said if it pressed on the nerve, she would cut the wire and reposition it. She said she would not do that yet. She said she would watch it. She said she would measure it with a caliper if she had one, but she didn’t, so she used her thumb and forefinger to gauge the distance from the acromion to the skin. She marked the measurement on a strip of tape and stuck it to the table rail. She checked the pulse again. Forty-three. She adjusted the lower bandage another quarter-inch. She listened to his left lung. A faint crackle. She said it was fluid from the initial impact. She said she would let his body reabsorb it. She said if it turned to wheezing, she would drain it. She said she would not drain it yet. She said she would wait. She said she would document the crackle. She wrote it down. She closed the book. She sat back. She kept her eyes on his chest. She counted the breaths. Twelve. Eleven. Thirteen. She checked the drainage tube. Clear exudate. She said that was good. She said she would change the outer gauze when it soaked through. She said she would not change it before. She said she would monitor the saturation line. She marked it with a pencil. She checked the wire tension. No migration. She said that was good. She said she would check it again in an hour. She said she would not touch him unless the linen soaked past the mark. She said she would not speak unless he started coughing up blood. She said she would elevate the head of the table if that happened. She said she would not do that yet. She said she would wait. She said she took no pleasure in marking the linen. She said she took no pleasure in counting the breaths. She said she took no pleasure in listening to the crackle. She said she just made sure he didn’t die because she looked away. She kept her hands on his wrist. She kept her eyes on his chest. She kept talking. She kept doing.

dialogue.content: I watch her do all of it, methodical and quiet. My own hands feel like they're still holding him down even though they're empty. "What's his name?" I ask.

I don’t know where he was hit. I don’t care. Names don’t clot blood. Names don’t stop wire from cutting into muscle. Names don’t stop shrapnel from rusting in the fascia.”

She dipped a fresh strip of linen into the iodine water, wrung it out, and pressed it to the corner of his mouth to catch the saliva. She kept her eyes on the rise and fall of his ribs. “I’m wiping his jaw because his tongue is swelling and I’m not going to let him aspirate. I’m checking his pulse. Forty-one. She checked the wire tension. No migration. She said that was good. She said she would check it again in an hour. She said she would not touch him unless the linen soaked past the mark. She said she would not speak unless he started coughing up blood. She said she would elevate the head of the table if that happened. She said she would not do that yet. She said she would wait. She said she took no pleasure in marking the linen. She said she took no pleasure in counting the breaths. She said she took no pleasure in listening to the crackle. She said she just made sure he didn’t die because she looked away. She kept her hands on his wrist. She kept her eyes on his chest. She kept talking. She kept doing.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: "Elias Vance," I repeat, like I'm trying to make it stick to something. I run a hand over my face, and it comes away smelling like iodine and sweat. "He's got a sister back home who writes him letters. I've seen them."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
The lamp was bad and the tent was worse and the man on the table had been shouting for long enough that he had mostly stopped.

"Both shoulders," Sedge said, laying things out in a row. "When I say hold, I mean hold. He's going to buck and you're going to want to let go, and you're not going to."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I get my weight on his shoulders and find somewhere on the canvas wall to look. "Ready," I say, which is a lie.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge didn’t look up from the tin tray. She wiped a rusted instrument with a strip of linen, then set it aside for a heavier one. "Grip the clavicles, not the trapezius. You pull on muscle, you'll tear it. You pull on bone, you'll hold." She stepped to the table, her boots scuffing the dirt-packed floor. Her hands were already gloved, the leather cracked and stained with old blood and iodine. She checked the patient's pulse at the wrist, then pressed two fingers against the radial artery. "Heart's racing, but steady enough." She didn't offer comfort. Comfort didn't set bones.

She took the man's left arm, her thumbs finding the sharp, wrong angle of the humerus head jammed against the glenoid. "I'm going to apply traction. When the joint seats, it'll sound like a dry twig snapping. He'll scream again. You don't let go." She adjusted her stance, bracing her boot against the table leg. "Saying you're ready doesn't make it so. Just keep your hands on the bone."

"I don't take any pleasure in this," she added, her voice flat, eyes fixed on the swollen joint. "It's just leverage and anatomy. If you flinch, we both waste our time."

She wrapped a strip of canvas around the patient's upper arm, looped it through an iron ring bolted to the table frame, and took the end in both hands. She narrated the steps as she worked, her voice even. "Traction at forty-five degrees. Abduct. External rotation. Don't fight the resistance, let the joint slide." She said it out loud because describing the mechanics kept her focus on the anatomy, not the pain. It was how you did it right. 

She pulled. The canvas bit into the man's flesh. The tendons in Sedge's forearms stood out like cords. She didn't rush. She watched the joint, felt the resistance through the fabric, and increased the angle of abduction by a fraction. The man's breath hitched, then broke into a wet gasp. A sharp crack echoed through the tent. Sedge lowered the arm immediately, pressing two fingers against the medial epicondyle to check alignment. "Seated," she said. "Right shoulder next. Reset your grip."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I swallow hard, my fingers digging into the man's collarbone. "It sounded louder than a twig," I mutter, my knuckles white.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge didn’t smile. She wiped her gloves on her trousers and stepped to the patient’s right side. "It sounded like bone on bone," she said. "Don't measure it against wood. Measure it against alignment." She peeled back the torn fabric of the man's tunic, exposing the right shoulder. The swelling was already bruising purple and yellow, the humerus head displaced laterally. "Same grip. Same pressure. He's already flooded with shock on that side, so he might not scream. Don't mistake silence for ease."

She looped the canvas around the right arm, checked the knot, and braced her boot against the table leg. "Traction at forty-five degrees," she said, her voice steady. "Abduct to thirty. External rotation. I'm talking through the steps because it keeps my mind on the leverage and off the suffering. If I stop narrating, I start hesitating. If I hesitate, the joint catches. I don't take any pleasure in this. I'm just moving bone where it belongs."

She pulled. The fabric strained against the man's flesh. The patient's head thrashed against the dirt, a muffled groan tearing from his throat. Sedge watched the joint, felt the resistance through the canvas, and adjusted her stance. "Capsule is tight. Glenoid rim is catching. Ease it past. Don't force it. Let the angle do the work." She increased the pull in a slow, controlled arc. Another crack echoed through the tent, followed by a wet exhale. She lowered the arm immediately, pressing her thumb along the acromioclavicular joint, tracing the contour to confirm the humeral head had dropped back into the socket. "Seated. Splint it. Keep him still for six hours, or the swelling will pull it loose again."

She stepped back, peeling off the stained gloves with a sharp snap. "Your hands are shaking. That's normal. Just keep them on the bone next time."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: "How bad is it?" I ask. "Bad like he loses the leg, or bad like this is the part where we're being kind?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge didn’t answer right away. She knelt beside the table, her knees pressing into the dirt, and pressed two fingers to the man’s carotid. The pulse was thready but present. She peeled back his tunic further, checking the chest for asymmetry, then placed her ear against his ribs. Breath was shallow, rattling slightly in the lower left lobe. Possible rib fracture. Possible pneumothorax. She tapped her knuckles against his abdomen. Rigid. Not peritonitis yet, but deep bruising. She didn’t look at Wick when she spoke.

“He’s not losing a leg. His legs are fine.” She unrolled a strip of linen, soaked it in tincture, and began cleaning the abrasions along his costal margin. “What he’s fighting is shock. And whatever else hit him before he hit the ground. The shoulders are set. That’s done. The rest is waiting and watching.”

She worked methodically, wiping away dried blood and grit. “You’re asking if we’re being kind. Kindness doesn’t stop sepsis. It doesn’t draw out a bullet lodged in the psoas. I don’t do this to be gentle. I do it because a reduced joint drains less, heals faster, and keeps him from tearing his capsule when he thrashes in shock. I take no pleasure in the sound of it. I just keep the mechanics clear so I don’t miss a step.”

She tied a bandage around the man’s chest, securing it tight enough to restrict expansion but loose enough to let him breathe. “He’ll live if his lungs don’t fill with fluid and his gut doesn’t rupture. If he makes it through the night, he’ll be on crutches for a month. If he doesn’t, he won’t feel much by the end. That’s the prognosis. Not kindness. Not cruelty. Just what the body does next.”

She stood, brushing dirt from her trousers, and picked up a clean strip of canvas. “Grip his left forearm when I say. We’re splinting the arm before he wakes up and tears it loose again. Wrap at the mid-humerus. Fold the padding over the joint. Secure the knot. Leave room for swelling. I say it out loud because the words keep my hands steady and my eyes on the anatomy. It’s how you do it right. Don’t stop holding.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: *I nod, shifting my grip to his forearm. My hands still feel unsteady.* "What if he doesn't make it through the night?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge didn’t pause her hands. She pressed the padded canvas against the man’s elbow, folding it over the joint with precise, economical movements. “Then he doesn’t,” she said. “You tie the knot. You check the capillary refill in his fingers. You log the time and the intervention. You move him to the cot on the left wall where the ones who aren’t waking up go. You wipe the table. You wait for the next one.”

She worked the strip around the forearm, crossing it over the chest, her voice steady as she narrated the wrap. “Figure-eight at the wrist. Secure at the mid-forearm. Leave two fingers’ breadth for swelling. I’m saying it because the rhythm keeps my hands from slipping and my eyes from drifting. Describing the steps is how you secure a splint without crushing the radial nerve. It’s part of doing it right.”

She tightened the knot, cut the excess linen with her shears, and checked his pulse again. “Shock runs on a clock. The body borrows from the gut, the skin, the extremities to keep blood to the heart and brain. If the borrowing outlasts the reserves, the organs shut down. That’s not a tragedy. That’s physiology. I don’t take any pleasure in watching it happen. I just know the signs so I don’t waste supplies on a corpse or delay treatment for someone who can still be fixed.”

She stepped back, wiping her hands on a rag. “You asked about the night. The night is just hours. We watch his breathing. We check his pupils. We keep him warm. If his lungs clear, he’ll fight. If they don’t, he’ll drown in his own fluid, and it’ll take maybe four hours. You’ll hear the rattle. You’ll know.” She picked up her tin tray. “Hold his wrist. Don’t let him flex the elbow. The splint needs thirty minutes to set before we move him. Keep your hands on him. I’m going to check the next stretcher.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I make myself look at what she's looking at. "Tell me what I'm seeing," I say. "I'd rather know than imagine it."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge turned to face him. She didn’t soften her voice or lower her gaze. “Look at his hands first.” She pointed to the patient’s left fingers, still resting against his chest. “Nail beds are pale. Press the pad. Count to three. If the pink doesn’t return, peripheral perfusion is failing. That’s early shock. Now look at his face. Gray around the mouth. Sweat on the forehead despite the cool air. You’re seeing the circulatory system shunt blood inward. The skin doesn’t matter right now. The heart and brain do.”

She stepped to the patient’s side, leaning in close. “Watch his chest. Left side lags behind the right. He’s not drawing full volume into the lower lobe. You’ll hear a wet rattle if you listen, but don’t put your ear there yet. Possible hemothorax or pneumothorax. The rib might have punctured the pleura. Look at his abdomen.” She pressed two fingers lightly against his lower right quadrant, then rolled her palm flat against his flank. “Guarding. The muscles are tense even though he’s barely conscious. Deep contusion. Maybe a liver or spleen tear. Blood is pooling in the retroperitoneum. You won’t see it until his pressure drops and his urine stops. I’m pressing shallow and rolling because deep palpation can rupture a contained hematoma. I’m saying it out loud because the words keep my fingers from pressing too hard. It’s part of doing it right.”

She stepped back and pulled a penlight from her pocket. She clicked it on and shone it into his left eye, then his right. “Pupils are equal. React slow but present. Brainstem is intact. That’s good. Now look at his lips. Bluish. Hypoxia. The lungs aren’t oxygenating. You’re seeing a man whose body is running out of time to compensate. I take no pleasure in watching it fail. It’s just mechanics. But knowing what you’re looking at keeps you from panicking when the numbers change. Panic makes you miss the next sign.”

She capped the penlight and picked up a clean strip of linen. “You wanted to know instead of imagine. That’s smarter. Imagination wastes time. Observation saves it. Keep your hand on his wrist. Feel for the radial pulse. Count it. I’m going to wrap the cuff around his upper arm. I’ll inflate to one hundred and ten, listen for the first sound, note the drop. I’ll say the numbers out loud so you can track the decline. That’s how you learn the timeline. Don’t let go.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: *I press on his nail bed, watching the white linger.* "Still no pink." My voice is quieter than I mean it to be. "Tell me the numbers when you get them. I want to know what losing looks like."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge didn’t flinch at the quietness in his voice. She held his gaze for a second, then nodded once. “Capillary refill over three seconds means the arterioles are clamped shut. The body is hoarding blood for the core. That’s not imagination. That’s compensated shock tipping into decompensation.” She picked up the sphygmomanometer cuff from the tin tray, the rubber bladder worn smooth from four years of use. “You want to know what losing looks like. You’ll see it in the numbers first, then in the breath, then in the eyes.”

She wrapped the cuff around the man’s upper arm, aligning the artery marker over the brachial pulse. “Velcro at the mid-bicep. Not too tight, not loose. I’m saying it because a tight cuff skews the diastolic and a loose one misses the systolic. Accuracy matters more than speed.” She attached the stethoscope diaphragm to her ears, pressed it lightly against the antecubital fossa, and squeezed the rubber bulb. “Inflating to one twenty. Palpating the radial to confirm occlusion.” She released the valve slowly, watching the mercury column drop. “One ten. No sound. Nine five. Faint thud. That’s systolic. Eight five. Sound clears. That’s diastolic. One ten over eight five. But his pulse is one thirty. Narrow pulse pressure. The stroke volume is dropping. The heart is compensating with rate. It won’t last.”

She didn’t look away from the gauge when she spoke. “You asked what losing looks like. It looks like the systolic creeps down to eighty, then seventy, then sixty. It looks like the diastolic stays flat while the systolic falls. It looks like the breath turns shallow and irregular. It looks like the pupils dilate and stop tracking. I don’t take any pleasure in watching it happen. I just track it so I know when to stop pouring fluids into a failing system and when to call it. Wasting saline on a non-responder starves the next man.”

She deflated the cuff completely and peeled it off, her movements efficient. “Keep your hand on his wrist. Feel the rhythm. It’ll start skipping. You’ll notice it before the numbers change. I’m going to check his urine output. If the bag stays empty for four hours, the kidneys have shut down. That’s the point of no return. I’ll say the times out loud so you can mark the progression. Don’t let your grip slacken. The splint’s still setting.”

She turned to the wooden crate at the foot of the table, opened it, and lifted out a clean drainage bag and tubing. “Catheterization isn’t optional now. I need to know if his kidneys are still filtering. I’ll prep the meatus with iodine. Insert straight cath. Secure to the thigh. I’m narrating because the steps keep my focus on sterility and anatomy. Infection in a shocked patient is a guarantee of death. I take no pleasure in the procedure. I just prevent what I can.”

She laid the supplies on a clean cloth, her voice never losing its even cadence. “Watch the gauge. Watch his chest. Feel his pulse. When the systolic hits seventy, you’ll hear the breath change. It’ll sound like wet paper tearing. That’s pulmonary edema. When it hits fifty, the pulse will be thready and you won’t find it at the wrist. You’ll have to go to the carotid. I’m telling you this so you don’t freeze when it happens. Freezing wastes time. Time is what he’s running out of.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: "Don't tidy it up for me," I say. "What does shrapnel actually do in there? Say it straight."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge didn't stop her hands. She squeezed a dollop of lubricant from the tube onto the catheter tip, rolling the rubber to coat it evenly. "Shrapnel doesn't slice," she said, her voice flat as she began to guide the instrument toward the meatus. "A knife slices. Shrapnel tumbles. It spins in the air. When it strikes, it grabs tissue and rips. It creates a temporary cavity that crushes structures inches away from the track itself. It injects clothing fibers, soil, and rust deep into the wound bed. It shatters bone, and those fragments become secondary missiles, tearing vessels and nerves you didn't know were there. You aren't treating a hole. You're treating a zone of necrosis, contamination, and hemorrhage."

She paused to wipe a bead of blood from the patient's thigh with a gauze pad, then resumed her grip. "In the abdomen, it shears the mesentery. It ruptures the bowel, spilling bacteria into the peritoneal cavity. Sepsis isn't a disease you catch. It's your immune system eating your own organs because the barrier is gone. In the chest, it punctures the lung, collapses it, shifts the mediastinum. The heart gets squeezed. Stroke volume drops. You die of obstructive shock. I take no pleasure in the mechanics of tissue destruction. But you asked for straight. Shrapnel is chaos made metal. It leaves a mess that has to be managed, or it kills you."

She pressed the catheter against the urethral opening, checking for the bead of urine that signaled the correct path. "This man likely has a fragment lodged in the retroperitoneum or a vessel wall. You can't see it. You can't reach it without opening him up, and he can't survive the table right now. So you watch for the bleed. You watch for the sepsis. If the fragment nicked the spleen, blood is pooling behind the peritoneum. Pressure drops. The body shunts blood from the skin, the gut, the kidneys. That's what he's fighting now. Not the shrapnel. The shrapnel did its work minutes ago. Now he's fighting the consequences of the mechanics."

She began to advance the catheter, her eyes fixed on the tip. "I'm inserting straight back, then angling down. Following the anatomical curve of the urethra. Resistance means I've hit the prostate or a stricture. I don't force it. Forcing creates a false passage. A false passage bleeds, swells, and blocks the flow. Blocked flow means I can't measure output. I can't measure output, I can't manage the shock. I narrate this because if I forget the anatomy, I cause damage I didn't need to. I take no pleasure in causing damage. I just prevent it by following the steps."

She glanced at Wick, her expression unchanged. "Hold his ankles. Spread the legs slightly. If he convulses, the catheter will whip and perforate the bladder wall. Perforation leaks urine into the abdomen. Urine in the abdomen causes chemical peritonitis. That kills him faster than the shock. Grip the ankles. Firm. Don't let him kick. I'm pushing through the sphincter. Wait for the urine return. If it comes clear, the kidneys are still working. If it's dark, the muscle is breaking down. If it doesn't come, the bladder is empty or the kidneys have shut down. Watch for the flow. Tell me when you see it."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: *I move my hands to his ankles, my own pulse hammering in my throat.* "Nothing's coming," I say, staring at the catheter tube. "Is that the answer?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge didn’t look away from the tube. “No flow means two things,” she said. “The bladder is empty, or the kidneys have stopped filtering. In shock, it’s usually both. The renal arteries clamp down. Glomerular filtration drops. The body prioritizes the heart and brain over waste clearance. That’s not the answer. That’s a data point. You asked for straight. This is it.”

She adjusted her grip on the catheter, feeling for the resistance of the bladder neck. “I’m advancing past the prostatic urethra. The sphincter will give. If the bladder is empty, I’ll feel the tip hit the posterior wall. I’ll note the depth. I’ll leave it in place for now. A blocked catheter in a convulsing patient is a rupture risk. I’m measuring the insertion at twelve centimeters. I’m saying it because the numbers keep my hands from pushing past the trigone. It’s part of doing it right.”

She stepped back slightly, her eyes fixed on the drainage bag. “You want to know if this is where he dies. Not yet. Anuria is a warning, not a verdict. I’ll start a saline drip. I’ll monitor the output every fifteen minutes. If the kidneys respond to volume, the flow will return. If they don’t, the shock is irreversible. I take no pleasure in the silence of the tube. I just track the timeline so I know when to stop fighting physiology.”

She picked up a roll of tape and a clean strip of linen. “Keep his ankles spread. Don’t grip so hard you cut off his femoral return. Swelling in the lower legs will confuse the shock assessment. I’m taping the catheter to his right thigh. Mid-thigh. Not too tight. I’m saying it because a tight tape kinks the tubing and gives you a false zero. False zeros make you panic. Panic makes you miss the next sign.” She smoothed the tape down, then checked the connection at the catheter hub. “Hold his left wrist again. Feel for the pulse. Count it for thirty seconds. I’m going to set up the IV. I’ll narrate the vein selection and the angle. You track the rate. Don’t let go.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: He starts screaming again and I hold him down through it. "Keep going and keep talking," I tell her. "Tell me exactly what you're doing to him and how much longer -- all of it, don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge didn’t flinch at the scream. She kept her hands steady on the IV setup. “Screaming is a sympathetic response to pain and hypoxia,” she said. “It burns oxygen. It raises intrathoracic pressure. It doesn’t change the physiology.” She picked up the tourniquet, wrapped it around the man’s right antecubital fossa, and tightened it just enough to occlude venous return without stopping arterial flow. “Tourniquet at the elbow crease. Not too tight. I’m saying it because arterial occlusion ruins vein selection and causes unnecessary ischemia. It’s part of doing it right.”

She looked at Wick, her eyes flat. “You want exactly what I’m doing and how much longer. I’ll give it to you straight. I’m cannulating the cephalic vein. Angle at fifteen degrees. Bevel up. I’m advancing until I get flash. Flash means I’m in the lumen. I’m securing the catheter. I’m flushing with saline to check patency. I’m hanging the bag. I’m setting the drip rate to one hundred and fifty milliliters per hour. I’m saying it because the steps keep my hands from shaking and my eyes on the vein wall. If I miss the flash, I tear the posterior wall. Hematoma forms. I lose the access. I have to start over. I don’t take any pleasure in sticking a man twice. I just do it right the first time.”

She threaded the needle, her voice never breaking. “How much longer. The body compensates for maybe four to six hours before decompensation becomes irreversible. We’re past two. I’m pushing volume to restore preload. If his systolic climbs to ninety in the next twenty minutes, we’ve got a window. I’ll reassess his urine output, his capillary refill, his mentation. If it doesn’t climb, or if it drops below seventy, the myocardium is failing. The kidneys are already shut down. The gut is ischemic. At that point, you stop. You don’t pour fluids into a dead pump. You cover him. You log it. You wipe the table. That’s the timeline. Not hope. Not cruelty. Just the clock.”

She found the vein, felt the give, and advanced the catheter. A bead of dark blood welled at the hub. “Flash. Lumen confirmed.” She withdrew the needle, taped the catheter down with sterile strips, and connected the saline line. “Clamp open. Check for backflow. None. Line is patent. I’m cranking the roller to fifteen drops per second. That’s one hundred and fifty milliliters an hour. I’m saying it because the math keeps the rate steady. Too fast and I flash his lungs. Too slow and I don’t move the needle. I take no pleasure in watching the numbers crawl. I just keep the mechanics clear so I don’t make a mistake.”

She stepped back, checking the drip chamber, then returned to the patient’s side. “Keep his ankles spread. Don’t grip the bones. You’ll fracture the tibia and turn a shock case into a trauma case. I’m going to recheck his pressure in fifteen minutes. I’ll narrate the inflation, the Korotkoff sounds, the drop. You’ll hear the breath change before the numbers do. Wet rattle becomes continuous. Pupils will fix. That’s the end. Until then, we watch. We adjust. We don’t imagine. We observe. Keep your hands on him. I’m prepping the next tray.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: *I swallow, watching the saline drip into his vein.* "Tell me when you're about to check his pressure. I want to hear the numbers again."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge didn't look up from the tin tray. She arranged a scalpel handle, a pair of curved scissors, and four hemostats in a descending arc of utility. "Fifteen minutes," she said. "I'll tap the table when the time is up. You want the numbers. You'll get them. But you need to watch the neck while you wait."

She pointed to the man's right carotid sheath, just below the jawline. "Jugular venous pressure. If the vein distends above the clavicle as the saline runs in, the right atrium is backing up. The heart can't pump the volume. That's fluid overload. You'll see a pulsation in the neck. You'll hear a wheeze in the lungs. I'm watching it because if I pour too much saline into a failing ventricle, I kill him with edema just as surely as shock would. I take no pleasure in drowning a patient who just needed volume. I just monitor the return so I don't mistake a full tank for an empty one."

She wiped a drop of iodine from her thumb and picked up a sterile drape. "I'm laying out the drape. I'm opening the suture pack. I'm checking the needle driver. I'm doing this because if his pressure holds, we might need to debride that abdominal wall before the necrosis sets in. If it drops, we need the suture to close the catheter site and dress the wounds for the box. I'm narrating the setup so my hands know the order. If I have to look for a forceps, I lose focus. If I lose focus, I slip. It's part of doing it right."

She stepped back to the table, her eyes scanning the patient's face, the rise of his chest, the level of the drip chamber. "Keep his ankles. Don't grip the bone. You're the anchor. I'm the mechanic. We hold the structure together until the physiology decides. Fifteen minutes. I'll warn you. You'll hear the cuff inflate. You'll hear the silence. You'll hear the thump. Or you won't. We'll see."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: When it's over I sit down on the floor of the tent and don't get up. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge didn’t move from the table. She watched Wick sink to the dirt, then turned back to the man. “You want the rest,” she said. “I’ll give it to you. Step by step. No cuts. No summaries.”

She pressed two fingers to the carotid again, holding them there for ten full seconds. “No pulse. No carotid thrill. No arterial wall bounce. I’m counting because a thready pulse can mimic stillness if you stop too soon. I’m saying it because confirmation isn’t optional. Misreading shock for death wastes time. Misreading death for shock wastes supplies. I take no pleasure in the silence. I just verify it.”

She clicked the penlight on and shone it into both eyes. “Pupils fixed. Dilated to seven millimeters. No reaction to light. No brainstem reflex. I’m noting the size because midbrain failure precedes death by minutes. The dilation is permanent now. I’m saying it because the measurements keep me from guessing. Guessing gets medics killed.”

She placed her ear above his mouth, then pressed her palm flat against his sternum. “No breath. No chest rise. No vocal cord vibration. I’m listening for thirty seconds because agonal gasps can mimic breathing if you’re not trained. I’m saying it because the absence of sound is a data point, not a mood. The diaphragm has stopped. The intercostals have stopped. The heart has stopped. The mechanics are done.”

She stepped to the foot of the table and began untying the splint. “I’m loosening the canvas at the mid-forearm. I’m sliding it off the elbow. I’m folding it into the linen pile. I’m doing this because wet bandage against dead skin macerates the tissue. Macerated tissue sloughs. Sloughing tissue breeds maggots. Maggots attract attention. Attention draws enemy fire. I take no pleasure in stripping the bindings. I just prevent the tent from becoming a hazard.”

She moved to the IV site. “I’m peeling the tape from the antecubital fossa. I’m withdrawing the cannula. I’m applying pressure with gauze to seal the puncture. I’m discarding the line in the sharps container. I’m doing this because a retained catheter leaks fluid into the subcutaneous space. Leaking fluid creates a pool. Pools stagnate. Stagnation breeds infection. Infection spreads to the next cot. I’m saying it because the steps keep my hands from leaving a mess behind. It’s part of doing it right.”

She turned to the drainage bag. “I’m unclamping the tubing. I’m emptying the contents into the latrine trench. I’m rinsing the bag with iodine solution. I’m hanging it to dry. I’m doing this because urine in a bag ferments. Fermentation releases ammonia. Ammonia corrodes the rubber. Corroded rubber cracks. Cracked rubber leaks. Leaking fluid tracks across the floor. Floor tracking brings dysentery. I take no pleasure in washing out a dead man’s waste. I just keep the air breathable.”

She stepped back to the table’s edge and picked up a stiff-bristled brush and a bucket of phenol solution. “I’m scrubbing the canvas where his blood pooled. I’m working the brush in circular motions. I’m lifting the debris into the dustpan. I’m dumping it into the incinerator drum. I’m doing this because dried blood harbors pathogens. Pathogens survive on fabric for weeks. Weeks turn into months. Months turn into outbreaks. Outbreaks kill medics. I’m saying it because the rhythm of the scrub keeps my mind on the surface and off the stillness. It’s how you clear a station without missing a spot.”

She laid a fresh sheet of canvas over the table, smoothing the wrinkles with her palms. “I’m aligning the edges. I’m taping the corners to the frame. I’m checking for tears. I’m doing this because a torn sheet catches on boots. Boots catch on sheets. Sheets tear. Tearing wastes time. Time is the only currency we have. I take no pleasure in the routine. I just keep the workspace ready. Readiness isn’t kindness. It’s logistics.”

She picked up a grease pencil and a clipboard. “I’m writing the time of death. I’m logging the interventions. I’m noting the fluid volume administered. I’m signing the sheet. I’m doing this because records track supply usage. Supply usage dictates resupply requests. Resupply requests keep the tent running. The tent running keeps the next man alive. I’m saying it because the words on paper don’t erase the body. They just ensure the next one gets a shot. I take no pleasure in the bureaucracy. I just keep the chain unbroken.”

She set the clipboard down and looked at Wick. “That’s the rest. No cuts. No summaries. You asked for it straight. Here it is. Death isn’t a moment. It’s a process. The process doesn’t stop because you sit down. The tent doesn’t stop. The next stretcher is already being wheeled in. I’ll keep talking. You can listen. Or you can stand up and hold the next one. Your choice. The mechanics don’t care either way.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: *I push myself to my feet, the dirt sticking to my palms.* "Alright." I take a breath that doesn't feel deep enough. "What do you need me to do?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge didn’t nod. She didn’t offer reassurance. She just pointed to the tent flap where two orderlies were wrestling a canvas stretcher through the mud. “You want a task. You’ll get one. Go to the head of that stretcher. Support the cervical spine. Keep his neck in line with his thoracic column. Don’t twist it. Rotational force on a compromised vertebra severs the spinal cord. Severed cord means diaphragmatic paralysis. I’m telling you this because your hands are still shaking, and adrenaline makes you forget leverage. I take no pleasure in reading you a textbook. I just keep the anatomy intact until we get him to the table.”

She turned back to the tin tray, picking up a fresh roll of tape and a clean roll of gauze. “When you clear the stretcher, you’ll strip the outer blanket. You’ll check the airway first. Look for blood in the mouth. Listen for stridor. Feel for chest wall symmetry. I’m saying it because airway before breathing before circulation is the sequence. Skipping steps gets people killed. It’s part of doing it right.”

She stepped to the edge of the prep table, her boots leaving faint prints on the freshly scrubbed canvas. “You’ll hold the lamp when I start cutting. Angle it at forty-five degrees to the wound site. Don’t let your shadow fall across the field. I’m narrating the light placement because glare hides tissue planes. Hidden planes cause missed vessels. Missed vessels cause hemorrhage. I don’t take any pleasure in watching a man bleed out because someone held a lamp wrong. I just set the parameters so the mechanics work.”

She picked up a pair of trauma shears, running her thumb along the blunt tip. “You asked what I need. I need you to be the anchor again. Hands on bone. Eyes on the steps. Ears on the sounds. You don’t guess. You don’t imagine. You follow the sequence. The next one’s got a through-and-through on the left thigh. Femoral artery is intact, but the popliteal is nicked. Bleeding is controlled with a tourniquet, but the pressure’s dropping. I’ll need you to brace his pelvis when I cut the tourniquet down. You brace at the anterior superior iliac spines. You pull back, not down. Down compresses the iliac veins. Back stabilizes the sacroiliac joint. I’m saying it because the words keep my hands from rushing. It’s how you do it right.”

She set the shears down and looked at him, her expression unchanged. “Go to the stretcher. Support the neck. Strip the blanket. Check the airway. I’ll meet you there in thirty seconds. Don’t stop moving. The tent doesn’t wait.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I move toward the stretcher, wiping my palms on my trousers. My hands find the man's head, my thumbs settling on either side of his jaw. "Neck's straight," I say, my voice sounding steadier than I feel. "Mouth is clear. Breathing's shallow."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge didn’t comment on the steadiness of his voice. She stepped to the stretcher, her boots leaving fresh prints on the dirt floor. “Shallow means tidal volume is restricted. Check the chest wall.” She pressed her palms flat against the man’s upper ribs, feeling for the rise and fall. “Left side lags. Possible rib fracture or pulmonary contusion. I’m palpating from the clavicle down to the costal margin. I’m saying it because the words keep my fingers from missing crepitus. Crepitus means broken bone. Broken bone means lung puncture risk. I take no pleasure in feeling the crunch. I just map the damage before I cut.”

She moved to the patient’s left leg. The canvas trousers were dark with dried blood, the tourniquet cinched tight just above the knee. “Popliteal nick,” she said, tracing the line of the band. “I’m checking distal pulses. Dorsalis pedis. Posterior tibial. I’m saying it because the words keep my hands from pressing too hard on a compromised limb. Hard pressure compromises return. Compromised return means compartment syndrome. I don’t take any pleasure in watching tissue die. I just verify the baseline before I loosen the clamp.”

She looked at Wick, her eyes flat. “Brace the pelvis. Hands on the anterior superior iliac spines. Pull back, not down. I’m telling you the anatomy because your grip determines the joint stability. If the sacroiliac joint shifts when I release pressure, the femoral vein kinks. Kinked vein means backbleeding. Backbleeding floods the field. Flooded field hides the popliteal. Hidden vessel means we miss the repair. I take no pleasure in a blood-slicked table. I just keep the mechanics clear so the suture holds.”

She grabbed the tourniquet’s windlass. “I’m unwinding half a turn. I’m saying it because controlled release prevents a sudden pressure drop. Sudden drop causes syncope. Syncope complicates the field. I’m watching the wound edge. Blood is welling. Bright red. Arterial spurting isn’t present. It’s venous oozing with capillary seepage. I’m noting the color because bright red means artery. Dark red means vein. Pink means capillary. Color dictates the suture size. I take no pleasure in cataloging blood flow. I just match the repair to the tissue.”

She stepped to the tray, picking up a curved needle driver and a spool of vicryl suture. “I’m threading the needle. I’m tying the end tag. I’m checking the tension. I’m saying it because a loose thread slips in tissue. A tight thread strangulates the vessel. Strangulation means necrosis. Necrosis means debridement. Debridement means more cutting. I don’t take any pleasure in cutting flesh. I just prepare the tool so the stitch closes the gap without tearing the edge.”

She returned to the leg, draping a sterile towel over the thigh. “Hold the pelvis. Don’t let him shift. I’m making the first pass. I’m entering three millimeters from the wound margin. I’m taking a bite of the deep fascia. I’m exiting parallel. I’m saying it because the words keep my hands from drifting. Drifting catches the popliteal nerve. Nerve damage means foot drop. Foot drop means he never walks right. I take no pleasure in ruining a man’s gait. I just follow the anatomical planes. Keep your grip firm. I’m pulling the suture tight. I’m tying the first knot. I’m trimming the ends. Next pass. Don’t let go.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: My knuckles press against his hip bones, my weight braced backward. The smell of blood and iodine fills the air again. "I've got him," I say, my voice low. "Keep going."

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: not losing a leg. His legs are fine.

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: Nail beds are pale

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: It ruptures the bowel, spilling bacteria into the peritoneal cavity

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: cannulating the cephalic vein. Angle at fifteen degrees.

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: Pupils fixed. Dilated to seven millimeters.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
The lamp was bad and the tent was worse and the man on the table had been shouting for long enough that he had mostly stopped.

"Both shoulders," Sedge said, laying things out in a row. "When I say hold, I mean hold. He's going to buck and you're going to want to let go, and you're not going to."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I get my weight on his shoulders and find somewhere on the canvas wall to look. "Ready," I say, which is a lie.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge did not look up from the row of instruments. She touched each one once, confirming placement by habit rather than sight.

“Good,” she said. “Bad news is, I’m not going to be gentle. Gentle wastes time and it wastes his chances.”

She finally glanced at the man on the table, reading him the way she read weather—pale, sweat-slicked, breathing shallow but still alive enough to matter.

“I’m setting the left one first,” she said. “If he comes up off the table, you put him back down. If he screams, let him. If he bites through his tongue, that’s unfortunate, but I still need the shoulder in before I worry about the mouth.”

She reached for a folded strip of leather and set it within easy reach of the man’s jaw, not bothering to ask permission.

“When I count to three, I don’t mean brace yourself,” she said. “I mean already be doing it.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: *I nod, keeping my eyes fixed on a frayed seam in the tent fabric.* "Understood." *My hands are already aching from the tension, but I don't shift my grip.*

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge picked up the leather strip and pressed it against the man’s teeth with two fingers. “Bite this, not your own flesh,” she said, flat and matter-of-fact, as if reminding someone to wear gloves in the cold.

He made a sound, half protest, half prayer, but his jaw closed on the strip.

Sedge moved to his left side. She placed one hand under the shoulder blade, the other around the wrist of the injured arm. Her grip was not cruel, but it was final.

“One,” she said.

The man’s breath hitched.

“Two.”

She did not pause for courage.

“Three.”

She pulled, rotated, and drove the joint home in one hard, practiced motion. The man’s body jerked as if lightning had found him, a strangled noise tearing out of him around the leather. The tent seemed to contract around the sound.

Sedge did not flinch. She kept pressure on the arm, feeling the joint sit where it belonged, feeling the muscles fight and then fail into exhaustion.

“Left’s done,” she said, though no one had asked. “Now the right.”

She shifted position without giving the man time to pity himself. Her eyes flicked briefly to his face. Still breathing. Still present. Good.

“Same rules,” she said. “Hold him.”

She took hold of the other arm.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: "How bad is it?" I ask. "Bad like he loses the leg, or bad like this is the part where we're being kind?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge’s hands paused only long enough to settle the injured arm into the angle she wanted, not long enough for doubt to creep in.

“Bad like he keeps it if I do this right,” she said. “Bad like pain now buys him use later. No leg in it. No mercy in it either, except the kind that lets him feed himself come spring.”

She glanced at the man’s face once, checking the slackness of his jaw, the wet drag of his breathing.

“This is the part where we’re being useful,” she said. “Hold.”

She looked down at the shoulder, thumb finding the swollen line of the joint.

“Left was the easier one. This one’s been out longer, and the muscle’s fighting me. When it goes back, he’ll arch. Keep his shoulder on the table.”

Her voice stayed level, stripped of comfort and cruelty alike.

“One.”

She tightened her grip.

“Two.”

The man moaned around the leather before the count reached the next number.

“Three.”

She pulled, angled the arm, and drove the joint upward with a hard, controlled motion. There was a wet, heavy sound as the shoulder seated itself, followed by a raw, broken cry that ended in a gasp. Sedge kept the arm locked in place while the muscles shuddered and fought, her face set in the same expression she wore when counting pulses or boiling bandages.

“There,” she said quietly. “Both are in.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I let out a breath I didn't realize I'd been holding. My hands finally unclench from his shoulders, leaving deep red marks on my palms. "He's still with us?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge did not answer at once.

She put two fingers to the man’s neck and stayed there, counting the beat under the grime and sweat. His breathing was ragged, shallow, but steady enough to be worth watching. His eyelids fluttered when she touched them, then rolled back toward white.

“He’s here,” she said. “Pain’s pulled him most of the way under, but he’s still breathing. That’s the part that matters.”

She took the leather strip from the man’s mouth and set it aside without ceremony. His jaw worked once, weakly, and then went slack.

“Help me get his arms bound,” Sedge said. “Not tight. Just enough to keep him from thrashing and making a mess of my work when he wakes up stupid.”

She reached for a length of clean cloth from the row she had laid out, then paused when she saw Wick’s hands.

“You can shake later,” she said, not unkindly. “Right now I need you useful. Blanket first. He’ll go cold fast, and shock’s got a habit of finishing what the injury starts.”

She turned back to the man, checking the set of each shoulder by touch, quick and certain.

“Both arms are in,” she said. “That means he keeps them, if he rests and doesn’t play hero. Bad enough? Yes. Kind? No. But he’ll be able to lift a cup to his mouth again, and that’s the sort of miracle I’m equipped to provide.”

She tucked the cloth around one arm, binding it close to the body with efficient movements.

“Get that blanket over him. Then boil water if there’s any to boil. I want his wounds cleaned before infection decides it has an opinion.”

Her eyes flicked once to the man’s pale face, then to Wick.

“And yes,” she added, quieter now. “He’s still with us. Barely. But barely counts.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I make myself look at what she's looking at. "Tell me what I'm seeing," I say. "I'd rather know than imagine it."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge kept one hand flat against the man’s sternum, feeling the quick, bird-thin jump of his heart under the sweat.

“Then don’t take it in all at once,” she said. “That’s how people invent worse things than what’s in front of them.”

She nodded toward the patient’s face without letting her own expression soften.

“First, you’re seeing shock. Not a wound, not a broken bone, but the body deciding it’s run out of road. Skin gone gray and wet. Breathing too fast and too shallow. Pulse running ahead of itself. That’s why I want him warm and watched, not because he looks pitiful.”

Her fingers moved to the nearest shoulder, checking the shape of it through the torn fabric of his shirt.

“This one was out long enough to make trouble. The joint’s back, but the meat around it is torn and angry. Swelling’s going to come up hard. Bruising will look uglier than it is. If there’s no fever, no stink, no red streaking later, he gets to keep the use of it.”

She shifted the man’s arm a fraction, settling it against the binding.

“You’re also seeing the marks from holding him. That’s not cruelty. That’s the price of doing this without enough hands or enough time. He’ll have bruises shaped like fingers. So will you.”

Sedge glanced at the blood on the table, then back to the man’s chest.

“The blood looks worse than it is because head and shoulder wounds bleed like they’ve got opinions. Most of what you’re seeing there is surface. The danger isn’t the red. It’s the cold creeping in while he’s unconscious.”

She reached for the blanket and drew it up over the patient’s torso with brisk efficiency, tucking it at the sides.

“If you want the plain version: both shoulders reduced, no leg lost, no gut opened, no skull cracked that I can find. He’s in pain, he’s frightened, and his body’s trying to shut down from the shock of it. But he’s breathing. He’s bleeding less than he looks. And if the next few hours go right, he wakes up.”

Her voice stayed steady, practical, stripped of drama.

“That’s what you’re seeing. A man who got hurt bad and is still on the right side of it, because we did the ugly part fast.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I pick up the blanket and start draping it over him, careful not to jar his arms. "Alright." My voice is rough. "Tell me if you see anything I don't."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge heard the real question under the words and did not dress it up.

“I will,” she said. “That’s the arrangement. You keep him still when I need him still, and I’ll name what I see.”

She took the shears from the row and tested the points against her thumb without thinking. “I’m opening his shirt. Not because I’m curious. Because a wound that hides under cloth gets to lie about itself.”

She began cutting along the seam of the ruined fabric, working slow where it had dried to the skin. “I’m not pulling,” she said, more to the unconscious man than to anyone else. “If it sticks, I cut around it. Pain later is cheaper than tearing now.”

The shirt fell away in stiff, darkened pieces. She did not react to the smell of sweat and iron. She had long since stopped treating blood as an insult.

“First thing you’re not seeing,” she said, “is how much of this is old. Bruises from the fall, scrapes from whatever dragged him here, dirt that got in before I ever saw him. Those matter, but they wait. The shoulders were the loud trouble. Bodies often keep one quieter trouble tucked away for later.”

Her fingers moved along the left side of the chest, light and deliberate. She stopped near the hollow under the arm, where the skin was creased and torn in a narrow line no longer than her little finger.

“Here,” she said.

She did not press. She only leaned closer, the bad lamplight catching the wound’s wet edge.

“It’s small enough to miss if you’re looking for something dramatic. It’s not dramatic yet. But it’s in a bad neighborhood.”

She glanced up briefly, then back to the patient.

“Blood’s bright at the edges. It shifts when he breathes. That tells me it’s close to the chest wall, maybe closer than flesh. I don’t like cuts that keep their opinions to themselves.”

With two fingers she touched the skin around the wound, feather-light. “There’s a crackle under here. Like dry snow. That can mean a rib cracked and kissed the lung. It can mean air got loose into the meat. Sometimes it means nothing if it’s only from the swelling, but I don’t count on nothing. Nothing is a luxury.”

She straightened just enough to reach for a square of waxed cloth from her kit. She set it within reach, not on the man.

“I’m not sealing it now. If I seal something that needs to vent, I can make a bad situation worse. But if it starts sucking air, if you hear a whistle, if the blood turns pink and frothy and keeps coming, if one side of his chest stops moving the way the other does—tell me at once. Don’t wait to be sure. Sure is for people with time.”
