She checked the man’s lips with her eyes, not her hands. “His color’s still wrong. Gray, not blue. That’s shock doing its patient work. Warmth helps. Blanket helps. If you can get water boiling, I want it. Clean cloth too. Infection won’t start tonight, but it will send scouts.”

She smoothed the blanket higher without fussing over it. “If he wakes and tries to sit up, don’t let him. Flat keeps his blood where it can still be useful. If he vomits, we turn him as one piece, not by dragging the shoulders. I’ve already rearranged him enough for one night.”

The man’s breath made a thin, uneven sound. Sedge went still.

It was not a death sound. She had heard enough of those to know the difference. It was a warning sound, small and mean, the kind a body made when it was trying to decide whether it could keep pretending.

She put her face close to the little wound and watched. A bubble, no bigger than a pinhead, swelled at the torn edge and broke.

“Well,” Sedge said quietly. “There’s something you wouldn’t have seen.”

She did not step back.

“It’s not enough to panic over. Panic wastes breath, and he needs his. But now we watch it like it owes us money.” Her voice stayed flat, steady, and entirely without theater. “If it gets worse, I’ll need you again. If it doesn’t, we’ll call myself lucky and pretend I planned it.”

She kept her eyes on the wound, one hand hovering near the waxed cloth.

“That’s what I see,” she said. “A small hole in a bad place, a man in shock, and a night that isn’t done with us yet.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: "Don't tidy it up for me," I say. "What does shrapnel actually do in there? Say it straight."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge did not look away from the wound.

“Straight,” she said, “is that shrapnel doesn’t behave like a clean blade. It doesn’t even behave like a bullet, not always. It’s irregular. It tumbles. It drags dirt, cloth, rust, skin, and whatever else it touched on the way in. A hole this size outside can be lying about the size of the tear inside.”

She kept her hand hovering near the man’s chest without touching it.

“If it went into the chest wall, it can do three things. First, it can cut muscle and small vessels and stop. Then we get swelling, pain, maybe fever, and a man who hates us for a week but lives. Second, it can nick an intercostal vessel or the lung. Then blood or air starts filling the space where the lung ought to expand. The lung collapses. The heart gets pushed. The man suffocates from the inside while his chest keeps trying to work. Third, it can hit something big enough that he dies before we finish naming the problem.”

Her voice stayed level, stripped of drama.

“If he’s still breathing now, we are not in the third yet. That doesn’t mean we won’t be.”

She leaned closer again, watching the pinhead bubble form and break at the edge of the wound.

“In a shoulder, shrapnel is ugly in a different way. It can score the joint, shred tendon, leave a fragment where movement will keep irritating it. It can poison the wound days later. But a shoulder can survive ugly. A chest gets fewer privileges.”

She finally straightened a little, but only enough to keep her shadow off the patient.

“I’m not telling you this to make it worse. I take no pleasure in the ugly version. Pleasure would be obscene. But I’ll use the ugly version if it keeps us awake.”

Her eyes moved from the wound to the rise and fall of the man’s chest.

“What shrapnel actually does is make a mess that doesn’t match the entrance. It tears where it shouldn’t, leaves filth where it doesn’t belong, and waits for you to assume the worst is outside where you can see it. It can be small enough to miss and still kill him by morning. It can look terrible and turn out to be survivable. The only honest answer is that it depends what it touched, and we don’t know yet.”

She touched the edge of the waxed cloth again, not picking it up.

“I don’t know if there’s metal in him. I don’t know if this is a fragment that passed through, a splinter of rib, or a small tear made by something that only meant to kill him slowly. I’m not going to dig around in a chest with a bad lamp and no proper table just to satisfy curiosity. If a piece is lodged and not bleeding, it can stay until someone with better tools and cleaner hands can argue with it. If it starts leaking air in earnest, that becomes a different problem.”

Her jaw tightened, just a little.

“So here is the untidy version. He may have a cracked rib. He may have a lung nicked. He may have air working into the tissue where it has no business being. He may bleed more before he bleeds less. He may go downhill while we’re still congratulating ourselves on keeping him warm. Or he may hold, breathe, and wake up miserable but alive. Both are possible. The body does not owe us a clear answer quickly.”

She checked the man’s lips again. Still gray. Not blue. She noted it and moved on.

“If this turns, I need you to recognize the turning. A whistle where there wasn’t one. Pink froth. One side of the chest moving less than the other. His lips going blue instead of gray. Blood coming faster instead of slower. Those are not things to ponder. Those are things to say aloud.”

She rested one hand briefly on the edge of the blanket, not fussing, only making sure it stayed where she had put it.

“The tidy version would be: the shoulders are set, the wounds are cleaned, he rests, and he recovers. The straight version is: we have done the part that could be done with hands and force, and now we are waiting to see whether the damage is finished or only patient.”

The man’s breath hitched once, thin and uneven, then settled again into its shallow rhythm.

Sedge watched it for three beats before speaking again.

“He’s not dead,” she said. “That’s not comfort. It’s inventory. He’s breathing. The wound is small. The bubble is small. The color is bad but not blue. That’s what we have. It may be enough. It may not. Until it decides, we watch it like it owes us.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I watch the bubble form again. "Alright." My throat feels tight. "I'll listen for the whistle."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge gave a short nod, her eyes still on the wound.

“Good,” she said. “And don’t wait for the whistle to become a tune. One sound, one change, one thing that wasn’t there before—say it. I’d rather be told too soon than comforted too late.”

She shifted the waxed cloth a fraction closer, not touching the man, only making sure it lay where her hand could find it without fumbling.

“If it starts sucking air, we don’t stuff it. We don’t dig. We don’t shove cloth into a hole because it looks tidy. We lay this over it smooth and leave one edge open so air can get out but not back in. Seal it all the way and you can suffocate a man while thinking you’ve helped him. If I need your hands, I’ll say where. If I need you to hold him still again, you’ll know.”

She checked the rise of his chest again, counting under her breath. The movement was shallow, quick, uneven enough to make her jaw set, but still present. Still working.

“Until then, we do the boring part,” she said. “Warmth. Quiet. Clean hands. If there’s water to boil, boil it. If there isn’t, use the cleanest we’ve got and don’t waste time apologizing for it. Wash up before you touch him again. I don’t care if your hands are raw afterward. Infection doesn’t care about comfort either.”

Her fingers hovered near the blanket’s edge, making sure it had not slipped, then withdrew.

“If he wakes, keep him flat. If he tries to sit up, don’t argue with him, just stop him. If he vomits, we turn him as one piece. No dragging, no twisting, no hauling by the shoulders. If he begs for water, no. Wet his lips if he’s awake enough to know what swallowing is, but no cup, no gulps, no kindness that ends with him choking.”

She looked at the little bubble as it swelled again at the wound’s edge, broke, and vanished.

“If you feel more crackle under the skin, like dry snow, don’t press around for it. Tell me. If his neck starts pulling when he breathes, if one side lags, if the sound of him gets thin or wet or wrong, tell me. If his color changes from gray toward blue, tell me before you’re certain. Certainty is a luxury for people with time, and we don’t have any to spare.”

Her voice stayed level, stripped of drama, but not careless.

“You asked me not to tidy it up, so I won’t. He might hold. He might turn before morning. He might have a piece of metal in him that’s doing nothing, or a tear that’s doing something slowly, or a rib that will make every breath a negotiation for the next week. I don’t know yet. What I know is that he’s breathing now, the hole is small, the air isn’t whistling, and his lips aren’t blue. That’s not hope. It’s inventory.”

She smoothed the blanket a little higher without fussing over it.

“I don’t say this to frighten you. Fear is less work when it has a list. So here’s the list: watch his breathing. Watch his color. Keep him warm. Keep him still. Keep your hands clean. If anything changes, name it aloud. Don’t wait for me to notice. I’ll be watching too, but four eyes are better than two, and one of us has to stay stubborn.”

The man’s breath hitched once, then settled. Sedge stayed close, listening to it the way she might listen to a strained rope under load.

“And if he starts shivering,” she added, quieter now, “that’s useful. Shock can do that. If he stops shivering and gets colder anyway, that’s worse. Tell me then.”

She did not look away from the patient’s chest.

“I take no pleasure in this,” she said. “Not in the pain, not in the waiting, not in the ugly version of things. But I’ll use the ugly version if it keeps us awake.”

A third bubble formed, tiny and bright in the bad lamplight, then broke.

Sedge watched it vanish.

“There it is,” she murmured. “Still deciding.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: He starts screaming again and I hold him down through it. "Keep going and keep talking," I tell her. "Tell me exactly what you're doing to him and how much longer -- all of it, don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge did not raise her voice over the man’s screaming. She made it lower instead, flat and steady, the kind of voice that had no room for panic in it.

“Then listen,” she said. “I’m not doing anything secret, and I’m not going to pretend otherwise.”

The man’s body fought against the hands keeping him down, his back bowing, his jaw working around nothing, the scream ragged and wet at the edges. Sedge kept her eyes on the chest wound, not on his face.

“First, I’m watching,” she said. “I’m watching the hole. I’m watching the blood. I’m watching the rise of his chest. I’m listening for a whistle. If air is being sucked in where it shouldn’t be, that changes what I do next. If blood turns frothy, that tells me lung. If one side stops moving, that tells me pressure. Until I know which lie he’s telling, I don’t start poking at him like I’ve got time to learn by mistake.”

She took up the shears again and began cutting away the last of the ruined shirt around the small wound, working carefully where the fabric had stuck.

“I’m removing cloth,” she said. “Not because I enjoy looking at him. Because cloth carries filth. Wool, dirt, sweat, rust, whatever was on him when he was hit. If I leave that near the wound, infection gets a foothold before we’ve even finished arguing about whether he’ll live the night.”

The shears stopped. She peeled a scrap of fabric away with two fingers, slow, watching the skin beneath it.

“I’m not pulling anything out,” she said. “If a thread’s in the wound, I’ll trim it if it’s loose. If it’s deep, I leave it. Pulling on something that’s still lodged can tear a vessel that’s decided to close. I’m not here to make myself feel useful. I’m here to keep him breathing.”

She set the shears down and reached for a clean cloth, one she had laid out near the fire earlier. It was not truly clean—nothing in that tent was—but it was cleaner than anything else they had.

“I’m going to wipe around the wound,” she said. “Not inside it. Around it. I’m taking off the surface blood and grit so I can see whether the hole is changing. If I pour water into a chest wound, I can carry filth deeper. If I scrub it, I can make torn tissue bleed again. So I’m doing the boring version. Gentle where gentle matters, firm where firm matters.”

She touched the cloth to the skin near the wound, light and deliberate. The man’s scream broke into a hoarse gasp, then climbed again.

“Let him make noise,” Sedge said. “Noise means air’s moving. Noise means his throat’s open and his lungs still have enough in them to complain. If he goes quiet and stays quiet, that’s when I start looking for the reason. If the sound turns wet, if it gurgles, if he starts choking on his own breath, you tell me. Don’t wait for me to hear it.”

Her eyes flicked once to the man’s lips, then back to the wound.

“I’m checking his color again,” she said. “Gray is shock. Blue is suffocation. Blue means we’ve run out of time for patience. He’s still gray. That’s not good, but it’s better than blue.”

She took the waxed cloth she had set aside earlier and held it near the wound without laying it down.

“I’m not sealing it,” she said. “Not all the way. If this is letting air in, sealing it tight can trap air inside the chest. That can push the heart and lungs until they stop. So if I cover it, I cover it with one edge left loose. A flap. Air gets out, but not back in. That’s the trick. It sounds simple enough until a man’s dying on the table and every second feels like a lie.”

She smoothed the waxed cloth over the wound with two fingers, leaving the lower edge free. Her movements were quick but not hurried.

“I’m laying this over the hole,” she said. “I’m holding it here for now. If it starts to lift with his breath, if it pulls in, if I hear it sucking, I’ll tape three sides down and leave one open. If it starts bubbling more, I’ll know the lung’s more involved than I’d like. If it stays quiet, maybe we’ve got a shallow tear and a bad night instead of a funeral.”

The man’s scream thinned into a shuddering moan. Sedge did not stop.

“I’m counting his breaths,” she said. “Not because numbers comfort me. Because changes matter. If he goes from breathing fast to breathing slow and it isn’t because he’s waking up, that’s bad. If he’s fighting for every pull and his neck muscles are standing out, that’s bad. If his belly starts working harder than his chest, that’s bad. I’m counting so I know when the rhythm changes, not so I can feel clever.”

Her free hand moved briefly to the man’s neck, fingers resting against the pulse there.

“I’m checking his pulse,” she said. “It’s too fast and too thin. Shock does that. Pain does that. Blood loss does that. I can’t separate the three yet, and I’m not going to guess out loud like guessing is harmless. But I’m counting it. If it starts running away with itself, I’ll know he’s losing more than we can see. If it slows down but he gets colder and paler, that’s not improvement. That’s exhaustion.”

She looked at the waxed cloth again. A tiny bubble formed under its edge and vanished.

“There,” she said, voice unchanged. “Still deciding.”

The man jerked again, a desperate, uncoordinated buck of pain. Sedge kept her hand where it was.

“I’m not going to dig for shrapnel,” she said. “Not here, not like this. If a piece of metal is sitting in muscle and not bleeding, it may be safer where it is than wherever I’d drag it. If it’s in the chest wall, probing it can open a vessel that’s clotted shut. If it’s near the lung, I can turn a small leak into a big one. I don’t have good light. I don’t have clean enough hands. I don’t have the tools to open him and close him again with any confidence. So I’m not pretending I do.”

She reached for another cloth, dampened it with the little clean water they had, and began wiping the grime from the skin around the shoulder bindings.

“I’m cleaning the smaller wounds now,” she said. “The scrapes. The tears from whatever dragged him. The places where dirt’s had time to settle. These won’t kill him in the next hour, but they can kill him in three days if I leave them filthy. Infection doesn’t announce itself like a gunshot. It waits. It swells. It turns a man feverish while everyone’s still congratulating themselves on getting him through the night.”

Her touch was efficient, not gentle for the sake of gentleness.

“This will hurt him,” she said. “I’m not pretending it won’t. Cleaning hurts. Pressure hurts. Breathing hurts when the chest’s torn. I’m not doing it because I like hearing him suffer. I take no pleasure in this. If I did, I’d be unfit for the work. I’m doing it because pain now can buy him a life later, and that’s the only currency I’ve got left.”

She checked the bindings around his arms.

“I’m making sure these aren’t too tight,” she said. “If his fingers go cold or blue, the binding’s doing harm. If it’s too loose, he’ll thrash and tear what I’ve set. So I’m looking, not assuming. His fingers are still dirty, but they’ve got color. That’s enough for now.”

Her gaze moved over him in the same order it had used before: chest, lips, pulse, wound, bindings, blanket.

“I’m checking the blanket,” she said. “I’m checking whether he’s sweating or cooling. Shock can make a man cold even when the tent smells like too many bodies and bad oil. If he shivers, that’s his body still trying. If he stops shivering and gets colder, that’s a bad sign. If he burns up later, that’s infection or inflammation picking a fight. Either way, I want to know early.”

The man’s scream had become a broken, exhausted sound, more breath than voice. Sedge kept talking anyway.

“You asked how much longer,” she said. “So I’ll tell you what I know and what I don’t.”

She pressed the edge of the waxed cloth more securely into place, careful not to flatten it completely.

“This part—the cleaning, the covering, the first check—maybe ten minutes if nothing changes. Maybe less if he turns on me. Maybe more if I find another wound hiding under him.”

Her voice stayed level.

“The next hour is the liar’s hour. Men hold through pain and then fail when the body decides it’s had enough. If he’s going to suffocate from a chest wound, it will often start showing itself soon. Not always. Sometimes slow. But soon enough that we don’t get comfortable.”

She glanced at the man’s lips again.

“If he stays steady for an hour, we don’t call him safe. We call him stubborn. Then we watch him every quarter hour until dawn. Breathing, pulse, color, wound, warmth. Every quarter hour. If one of us sleeps, the other watches. If both sleep, he dies. That’s the arithmetic.”

She adjusted the blanket with one hand, drawing it higher without letting it press on the chest dressing.

“Infection comes later. Tomorrow, maybe the next day. Redness. Heat. Swelling. Stink. Fever. If he starts talking nonsense from fever, if the wound starts weeping foul, if red lines crawl from it, that’s the next fight. If he gets through tonight, he still doesn’t get to rest. He gets to be miserable for days and weak for weeks.”

Her eyes went to the bound shoulders.

“The shoulders will take longer than he’ll like. Weeks before he uses them properly, if he’s lucky. Longer if the joints were damaged or the muscles tore badly. He’ll try to be brave or stupid as soon as he wakes, because men do. He’ll reach for something, or try to sit up, or test himself, and his body will remind him what I just did to it. My job is to make sure that reminder doesn’t undo the work.”

The man’s breathing hitched. Sedge leaned closer at once, watching the waxed cloth.

It lifted slightly. Not much. Enough to matter.

“I’m seeing air move under this,” she said. “Not a lot. Enough to tell me the lung or chest wall is leaking. I’m not sealing it down hard. I’m leaving the edge open so it can vent. If it starts sucking audibly, if the cloth pulls in tight, if his neck veins swell, if his face turns puffy, if one side of his chest stops rising, that’s when this becomes a different kind of emergency.”

Her jaw tightened.

“If I had better tools, I could do more. A clean needle. A tube. A way to let pressure out without letting filth in. Here, I’ve got waxed cloth, boiled rags, bad light, and stubbornness. So that’s what I’m using.”

She looked at the man’s face for only a moment.

“He’s still screaming,” she said. “That’s ugly to hear. But it’s not the worst sound. The worst sound is when they stop and don’t start again. So let him scream. You keep him from rolling. I’ll keep the wound from lying to us.”

She took another clean cloth and began wiping the blood from her own fingers, then reached for the next one.

“I’m going to keep talking,” she said. “Not because it helps him. Because it keeps the steps in order. When you’re tired and scared, the mind starts skipping. It jumps to the terrible thing and forgets the simple thing. So I’ll say the simple things until they’re done.”

She dipped the cloth again.

“I’m cleaning my hands as best I can. I’m changing this rag because the old one’s soaked through. I’m not reusing filth just because we’re short on supplies. I’m checking the dressing again. I’m watching for fresh blood. I’m watching for bubbles. I’m watching his lips.”

The man’s cry cracked into a sobbing breath. Sedge did not look away from the wound.

“I’m not going to promise he lives,” she said. “I don’t make promises I can’t keep with my hands. But I’ll tell you what I’m doing, and I’ll tell you what I see, and I’ll tell you when it changes. That’s the only clean thing left in this work.”

She pressed the edge of the waxed cloth gently into place.

“Right now, I’m covering the wound. Right now, I’m keeping air from being pulled deeper. Right now, I’m keeping him warm. Right now, I’m watching for the turn. If it comes, I’ll name it. If it doesn’t, we’ll keep doing this until dawn.”

Her voice dropped, but did not soften.

“And if he dies anyway, it won’t be because we were careless. It will be because the wound was worse than our tools. That’s not comfort. It’s just the only version of the truth I’ve got.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I keep my weight on him, feeling the shudder in his shoulders. "Alright," I say, and my voice is steadier than I feel. "I'm listening. I'm not letting go."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge gave one short nod, her eyes still on the waxed cloth where it lay over the small wound.

“Good,” she said. “Keep your weight where it is. He’s not fighting as hard now because he’s calmer. He’s fighting less because he’s running out of breath. Those are not the same thing.”

The man’s screams had thinned into ragged, broken sounds, more air than voice, but his body still jerked in little uncoordinated bursts, muscles trying to escape pain that had nowhere to go. Sedge put her forearm lightly across his upper chest, not to pin him, only to feel the moment he tried to roll or rise.

“I’m fixing the dressing now,” she said. “I’m taking three strips of cloth and taping the waxed piece down on the top and both sides. I’m leaving the bottom edge free. If air leaks out of him, it can push past that edge. If he pulls air in, the cloth should close over the wound instead of letting outside air get sucked deeper. It’s a simple trick. Simple things are the only ones worth trusting in a place like this.”

She worked quickly, smoothing the strips down with two fingers. The man moaned, a wet, exhausted sound, and his shoulders shuddered under Wick’s hands.

“Don’t ease off because he sounds weaker,” Sedge said. “If he tries to come up off the table, put him back down. If he tries to roll, keep him flat. If he starts to vomit, tell me at once. Don’t try to move him by yourself and don’t twist him. If it happens, we turn him as one piece or not at all.”

Her eyes flicked from the dressing to the man’s lips.

“I’m checking his color again,” she said. “Still gray. Not blue. That’s still in our favor, but favor is a weak word. Shock can keep a man gray for a long time before he decides to get worse.”

She leaned closer to the wound. The waxed cloth lifted slightly with one breath, then settled. A small bubble formed near the loose edge and broke without sound.

“I’m seeing air move,” she said. “Not enough to whistle yet. Enough that I don’t get to pretend this is only a flesh cut. I’m leaving the dressing vented. If it starts pulling tight, if it starts making a sucking sound, if his neck veins rise or his face starts looking full instead of empty, I’ll lift the edge and let air out. That will hurt him. It may make him scream again. It will also keep his heart from being squeezed flat, so he can hate me afterward.”

She reached for another clean rag and wiped her fingers, then checked the pulse at the man’s neck again.

“I’m counting his pulse,” she said. “Still too fast. Still thin. But it hasn’t gone wild yet. I’m counting his breaths too. Shallow. Quick. Both sides are moving, but the left is lazier than the right. That tells me trouble, not death. Death would be no movement at all, or one side frozen while the other fights for both.”

The man’s jaw worked weakly. His eyelids fluttered, showing white, then closed again. Sedge did not waste time trying to rouse him.

“I’m going to clean the rest of the mess now,” she said. “The scrapes along his side. The tear near his collarbone. The places where dirt got ground in before he reached us. None of these look important enough to kill him tonight. That’s exactly the kind of wound that kills him in four days while everyone thinks the worst is over.”

She dabbed the damp cloth around a shallow scrape, careful but not hesitant. The man flinched and made a raw, whimpering noise.

“This hurts him,” Sedge said. “I’m not pretending otherwise. I take no pleasure in it. If I did, I’d be monstrous, and monsters make bad medics. But infection doesn’t care that he’s already suffered. It only cares that we were lazy.”

She moved the cloth in short, efficient strokes, discarding it for another when it darkened.

“I’m not pouring water into the chest wound,” she said. “I’m not scrubbing it. I’m not digging at it. I’m cleaning what I can see and leaving the rest alone unless it gives me a reason to interfere. A body can survive a great deal of ugliness if you stop adding new ugliness to it.”

The tent fabric snapped in a small gust of wind. The lamp flame guttered, sending shadows crawling over the table. Sedge did not look up.

“I’m checking the shoulder bindings again,” she said. “His fingers still have color. That means I haven’t bound them tight enough to cut off blood. If they go pale or cold, I’ll loosen the cloth. If he starts thrashing too hard, I’ll tighten it again. I don’t get to be kind about this. I get to be correct.”

Her gaze returned to the waxed dressing. She watched it for several breaths, her face unreadable in the bad light.

“It’s still bubbling,” she said. “Small. The blood’s darker than I like, but it isn’t frothy pink. That means the lung may be nicked, not shredded. May be. I’m not marrying that conclusion. If his breathing gets thinner, if his lips start turning blue, if one side stops moving, then the conclusion changes and so do we.”

She placed two fingers lightly against the skin near the wound, not pressing, only feeling.

“There’s crackle under here,” she said. “Still like dry snow. It hasn’t spread much since I last checked. That’s better than spreading fast. Air in the tissue can look monstrous and still be survivable. Air in the wrong place can kill a man while he looks almost intact. So we watch both.”

The man’s breath hitched. Sedge’s hand stilled on the dressing.

For a moment neither of them moved. The sound in the tent narrowed to the weak rasp of breathing and the small hiss of the lamp.

Then the breath released. The waxed cloth lifted a fraction and settled.

“Still deciding,” Sedge said.

She straightened just enough to keep her shadow off the patient’s face.

“You asked me to keep talking, so I will. I’m going to check under him next. Not by rolling him. I’m sliding my hand under the blanket and the canvas beneath his back to see if there’s blood pooling where we can’t see it. If I find a lot, that changes things. If I find only what’s already soaked through from the outside, we keep going.”

She worked her hand carefully beneath him, reading by touch the way she read everything: warmth, wetness, heat, stickiness, the shape of hidden harm.

“I’m feeling for a second wound,” she said. “Shrapnel doesn’t knock politely and enter one place at a time. It can leave a trail. It can pass through and keep going. It can bury itself somewhere stupid and wait. If there’s another hole on his back or side, I’d rather find it now than when he’s lying in it.”

Her brow tightened.

“I’m feeling wetness,” she said. “Not enough to panic over. Some of it is sweat. Some is blood from the scrapes. There’s a place here near his lower ribs that’s tender, but I don’t feel a hole. I’m going to leave my hand there a moment and watch his breathing while I do.”

The man’s body gave another weak shudder. His bound arms twitched against the cloth.

“I’m not moving him,” Sedge said. “I’m just listening with my fingers. If he winces more when I touch one spot, that tells me rib or bruise. If I feel a gap, that tells me worse. If I feel heat building where heat shouldn’t be, that tells me infection starting its slow argument.”

She stayed there, silent for a few beats, her eyes on the rise and fall of the man’s chest.

“No gap,” she said at last. “No second hole I can find. The wetness is less than I feared. That’s inventory, not celebration.”

She withdrew her hand and wiped it clean, then checked the waxed dressing again.

“I’m going to keep this vented and watched,” she said. “If it stays like this, we do nothing heroic. We keep him warm. We keep him still. We count breaths. We watch color. We listen for sounds that don’t belong. If it gets worse, I’ll need to decide whether to lift the dressing, clean deeper, or try something uglier. I’ll tell you before I do it. No surprises.”

The man’s eyes opened suddenly, unfocused and wild. His mouth worked around nothing, and a thin keen escaped him before he could bite it back. His body tried to jerk upright.

Sedge put her forearm across his chest again, firm but not brutal.

“Flat,” she said. “You’re hurt. You’re breathing. Stay flat.”

He did not understand, or pain had taken his understanding away. His legs kicked once against the table, useless and panicked.

“Hold him,” Sedge said. “Not his chest. His shoulders if you can. Keep him from tearing the dressing.”

She kept her voice level, not soothing, not angry, only certain.

“You’re in a tent,” she told the man. “Your shoulders are set. Your chest is dressed. You’re alive. If you fight, you make it worse. If you stay still, you get to wake up properly and hate me later.”

His breathing came faster, high and thin. Sedge watched the waxed cloth.

It lifted.

Then sucked inward.

Her expression hardened.

“There,” she said. “Now we’ve got something.”

She did not shout. She moved.

“I’m lifting the bottom edge,” she said, already doing it. “Air’s not getting out fast enough. If I leave it sealed, pressure builds. If pressure builds, his heart gets crushed. I’m letting it vent.”

A faint hiss answered, small and obscene in the close tent. The man’s chest shuddered, and his lips parted around a breath that still would not come deep.

Sedge kept one finger under the loose edge of the waxed cloth, holding it just enough to let air escape without exposing the wound fully.

“I’m not removing it,” she said. “I’m burping it. Ugly word, ugly problem. If this helps, his breathing will ease a little. If it doesn’t, we’ve got a bigger leak than I want to admit.”

Her eyes went to the man’s lips.

“Still gray,” she said. “Not blue yet. His neck veins are fuller than I like. That’s pressure. That’s the chest trying to make a problem for the heart. I’m watching it. I’m not guessing.”

The man’s thrashing weakened as quickly as it had come. His head turned to one side, sweat dragging through the grime on his cheek.

Sedge did not let herself relax.

“I’m counting again,” she said. “One breath. Two. Three. Four. Still shallow. Still fast. But not fighting as hard. That’s because the air’s getting out. That’s because the dressing is doing what it’s supposed to do. That’s not victory. That’s maintenance.”

She glanced briefly at Wick, her face stern and tired in the lamplight.

“If he starts screaming again, keep him down. If he goes quiet and his lips change color, tell me. If the hiss gets louder, tell me. If the cloth starts flapping with every breath like it’s got a mouth of its own, tell me. If blood starts soaking through this dressing faster than before, tell me. Don’t wait to be sure.”

She adjusted the edge of the waxed cloth with two fingers, leaving the vent open.

“I’m going to keep my hand here,” she said. “I’m not going to sew anything yet. I’m not going to probe the wound. I’m not going to close it tight and hope. I’m going to let it breathe while I watch it breathe. That’s the whole job right now. Watch. Wait. Name what changes.”

The man’s eyelids fluttered shut. His breathing remained thin, but the terrible pulling in his chest eased by a fraction.

Sedge stayed bent over him, one hand near the dressing, the other resting lightly against his sternum.

“He’s still with us,” she said. “Barely. But barely counts.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: When it's over I sit down on the floor of the tent and don't get up. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge did not answer at once.

She stayed bent over the man on the table, one finger still near the loose edge of the waxed cloth, watching the way it lifted and settled with each breath. The hiss had not returned. The bubbling had not worsened. His chest still rose on both sides, the left weaker than the right, but present. She counted ten breaths, then ten more, then checked the pulse at his neck again.

Only when the rhythm had held for a little while did she speak.

“The rest,” she said, “is that we do not get to call this over.”

Her voice was lower now than it had been while he was screaming. Not softer. Lower the way a tool is lowered when it has done the first hard part of its work.

“The rest is that he can still die in the next hour. Quietly. Without drama. Without a big obvious sign. A chest wound can turn while you are still telling yourself the worst has passed. Air can build. Blood can pool where we cannot see it. The lung can give up by degrees. The heart can be pressed until it stops. If his breathing changes, if his color changes, if the dressing starts pulling in or blowing out, if his neck swells or his face changes shape, we will know. Maybe soon enough. Maybe not.”

She adjusted the bottom edge of the waxed cloth without disturbing the wound.

“I am leaving this vent open. If air comes out, good. If it tries to go back in, the dressing should close over the hole. That is the best I can do with what I have. If I had better tools, I could do more. I could clean deeper. I could find out whether there is metal in him. I could drain blood or air with less guesswork. I could close him properly instead of leaving him to his own stubbornness. I do not have those things. So I am using what is here: cloth, wax, heat, water, hands, and watching.”

She wiped her fingers on a clean rag, then set the rag aside.

“The rest is that if he lives the hour, he can still die tomorrow. Shock is not finished with him. Infection is already on its way. It will not arrive with trumpets. It will arrive as heat. As redness. As swelling. As a smell where there should be no smell. As fever that makes him talk nonsense or go too quiet. If the wound turns foul, if the skin around it darkens, if he starts burning up and cannot keep water down, then we have a new fight. That fight may be worse than this one, because it will not give us the decency to be quick.”

She checked the blanket again, tucking it a little higher without pressing on the dressing.

“The rest is that if he lives the week, he may not be what he was before. The shoulders will stiffen. The chest will hurt when he breathes, coughs, laughs, or tries to lie on one side. He may have a piece of metal in him that we never find. It may sit still and do nothing. It may work itself outward. It may make an abscess and force us to open him again under better circumstances, if we ever get better circumstances. It may poison him slowly. I do not know. I cannot see through flesh. I can only guess by what the body chooses to show me.”

Her eyes moved over the man’s face, his lips, the hollow of his throat, the bindings at his arms.

“He may wake and hate us. He may hate me for setting his shoulders. He may hate you for holding him. He may hate the pain, the table, the tent, the war, his own body for still being in it. That is allowed. Hate is a sign of life. If he wakes angry, I will take that over silence any day.”

She straightened a little, but did not step away from the table.

“I am not going to tell you we were kind tonight. We were not kind in the way people mean when they want to be comforted. We were necessary. Kindness would have been a cup of water he could choke on. Kindness would have been letting him sit up because sitting up feels more human than lying flat while his chest leaks. Kindness would have been stopping when he screamed. Instead, we hurt him to give him a chance. I do not enjoy that. I want that said plain. I take no pleasure in it. If I ever begin to take pleasure in it, I should be removed from this work.”

She looked briefly toward the row of instruments she had laid out earlier. Some were still clean. Some had been used. Some had only been touched. She did not put them away yet.

“The rest is that we will have to keep being hard with him for a while. If he wakes, we will keep him flat even if he begs. If he is thirsty, we will wet his lips and refuse him more until I am sure swallowing will not kill him. If he needs to vomit, we will turn him carefully, and it will hurt him, and we will do it anyway. If he tries to move his arms, we will stop him. If he tries to pull at the dressing, we will stop him. If he becomes clever about it, if he lies still until we look away and then tests the wound, we will bind him tighter. That will feel cruel. It may be cruel. But cruelty and harm are not always the same thing. Sometimes the cruel-looking thing is the only thing standing between a man and his own foolishness.”

She checked the bindings again, her fingers moving near the cloth without tightening it.

“His fingers still have color. That matters. If they go cold, if they pale, if he loses feeling, I will loosen them. If he thrashes again, I may have to bind him more firmly. I will not apologize for that either. Apologies do not keep joints in place.”

The man’s breath shivered through the tent. Sedge listened to it with her whole body, not just her ears.

“The rest is the watching. That is the part nobody warns you about. People think the work is the setting, the cutting, the binding, the stopping of blood. Sometimes it is. But most of it is this: sitting with a body that has not decided what it means to do next. Counting breaths. Checking color. Feeling pulse. Looking for small changes. Trying not to imagine the worst so hard that you miss the real thing when it appears. Trying not to comfort yourself with stability, because stability can be a lie the body tells before it collapses.”

She reached for a clean cloth and laid it near her hand.

“I will watch him every quarter hour. Breathing. Pulse. Color. Dressing. Warmth. The sound of his chest. The movement of his ribs. The look of his lips. If he shivers, I will add warmth. If he stops shivering and grows colder, I will know that is worse. If he sweats too much, I will dry him so he does not chill. If he wakes confused, I will not let him wander into panic. If he wakes clear, I will tell him enough to keep him still. Not everything. Enough.”

Her hand rested for a moment on the edge of the blanket.

“If you stay, you will watch too. Not because I doubt you. Because I need another set of eyes. You do not have to understand everything. You do not have to know what each sign means. You only have to tell me when something is different. A new sound. A new color. A new stillness. A change in the way the cloth moves. A change in the way his skin feels. If you are not sure, say it anyway. I would rather check ten false alarms than miss one true turn.”

She glanced at the lamp flame, which still burned badly, then back to the patient.

“The rest is that we are short of everything. Clean cloth. Good light. Water. Time. Hands. Medicine. Certainty. That is not self-pity. That is inventory. I work with what is missing because if I pretend it is not missing, I will make mistakes. A medic who pretends she has enough is more dangerous than a medic who admits she does not.”

Her voice stayed even, but there was a hardness in it now, not anger exactly, more like the edge left on metal after too much sharpening.

“This war has eaten medics. It has eaten surgeons. It has eaten orderlies. It has eaten boys who thought they would be brave and then found out bravery is mostly holding still while someone screams. I am still here because I have not been killed yet, and because I am useful, and because there is no one better to take my place. That is the sort of qualification you end up with after four years.”

She looked down at the man’s face.

“I do not know his name. I may never know it. That does not change what I owe him. I owe him clean hands, steady attention, and the best use of what I have. I do not owe him pretty words. I do not owe him promises. If he wakes and asks for someone, I will answer if I can. If he asks whether he will live, I will not lie. I will tell him what I know. If he asks why it hurts, I will tell him the truth: because he is alive, and because we had to be rough with him to keep him that way.”

She smoothed one of the cloth strips near his bound arm.

“The rest is that the body is not holy to me. I have seen too many of them opened, broken, burned, emptied, stitched, and wrapped. I do not faint at blood. I do not need a body to be beautiful to work on it. But that does not mean I think it is nothing. A body is not holy, but it is a person’s last piece of property. It is where everything else lives. If I am careless with it, I am careless with the man. So I am not careless. I am blunt. There is a difference.”

The man made a small sound in his throat. Sedge leaned closer at once, watching the dressing. It did not suck inward. It did not flap. His lips stayed gray, not blue.

She let out a slow breath through her nose.

“Still deciding,” she said.

Then she looked toward Wick again.

“You asked me not to tidy it up. So I will not. The rest is that he may survive and still be ruined in ways we cannot fix. He may never lift his arms the same. He may ache in cold weather. He may wake at night thinking he is still on the table. He may hear your hands on him and not know whether they were saving him or hurting him. Some wounds close and leave a man less able than before. Some wounds close and leave a man alive but changed so thoroughly that the people who knew him before will have to learn him again. That is not a failure. That is the cost of getting through.”

She folded a rag once, then unfolded it again.

“And if he dies, the rest is that we will not pretend it was meaningless. We will not say he was meant to die. We will not say it was better this way. We will say he was hurt badly, we did what could be done, and the wound won. That is all. I will close his eyes if they are open. I will cover him. I will make sure he is not left like refuse. I will not pray unless it helps someone living. I will not make a speech. Speeches are for people who have time to believe they matter. I will mark what I can, if there is anything to mark, and then I will wash my hands, because someone else will need them.”

Her jaw tightened.

“That is the part people do not want to hear. They want death to be a moment with music in it. It is not. Usually it is a body failing in small ugly ways. Breath changing. Color changing. Warmth leaving. The face going slack. It is not peaceful just because someone is brave. It is not noble just because someone suffered. I have seen men die quietly and men die fighting and men die begging and men die too exhausted to finish the sound they were making. I do not like any of it. But I have stopped pretending death is something it is not.”

She checked the pulse again, quick and thin, still there.

“If he lives, we will have to keep him alive after the living starts. That means food when he can take it. Water when it is safe. Clean bandages. Movement when movement will not tear him open. Rest when rest will not become surrender. Pain managed as best we can. Fever watched. Wounds cleaned even when he curses us. Shoulders exercised later, when exercise becomes necessary. If he becomes feverish and starts picking at the air, we will keep him from hurting himself. If he becomes weak and ashamed, we will not make a show of helping him. We will do it plainly. Bodies do that. They need help with things they used to do alone. There is no dignity in pretending otherwise.”

She moved one of the instruments a fraction, aligning it with the others out of habit.

“The rest is that I do not know whether there is shrapnel in him. I told you that already, but I will say it again because it matters. If there is metal, it may be small. It may be deep. It may be near a vessel that has closed around it. If I dig now, I may open that vessel. If I leave it, it may cause trouble later. There is no clean choice. There is only the least bad one. Right now, the least bad one is not to dig. If he stabilizes and we get better tools, someone may try to find it. If he does not stabilize, we may never know. That is the kind of uncertainty this work is full of. You do not get to resolve it by wanting an answer.”

She looked at the small wound under the waxed cloth.

“It is still leaking air. Small amounts. Enough to remind me not to trust it. If the leak seals itself, he may improve. If it grows, we may have to do more. If blood increases, we may have to choose between suffocation and bleeding. Sometimes those are the choices. Not good and bad. Bad and worse. You pick the one that leaves him breathing longer, and you do not congratulate yourself for it.”

Her hand hovered near the dressing.

“I will not sew it closed tonight unless it forces my hand. A closed wound with a leak inside can kill faster than an open one. I would rather have it ugly and venting than tidy and fatal. If it stays ugly but stable, that is the best version of tonight. Ugly and stable. I will take that.”

The tent shifted in the wind. The lamp smoked. Sedge did not move to fix it.

“The rest is that you held him. That was not a small thing. That was part of the treatment. Without your hands, he could have torn the dressing, undone the shoulders, fallen off the table, or choked on his own tongue. You did what needed doing. If your hands hurt, if your arms ache, if your stomach turns, if you feel as though you have done something violent, that is not proof that you did wrong. It is proof that you are not used to this. Being unused to it is not a flaw. It is a beginning.”

She paused, then added, quieter, “If you need to be sick later, do it. If you need to shake, shake. If you need to sit where you are for a while, sit. But do not tell yourself you were cruel because the work was cruel. The work was cruel because the wound was cruel. We did not invent the cruelty. We spent it.”

She checked the man’s lips again.

“Gray,” she said. “Not blue.”

Then she looked at the dressing.

“No whistle. No strong suck. No flapping. Small bubbles only. That is what we have.”

She drew in a breath and let it go.

“The rest is that I am tired. I am not going to make a virtue of that. Fatigue makes mistakes. It makes hands slow and eyes stupid. It makes you want to believe the patient is fine because you need him to be fine. So I will not let myself believe he is fine. I will let myself believe he is watched. That is all I can promise. Watched.”

Her gaze moved over the table, the instruments, the rags, the blanket, the waxed cloth, the bound shoulders, the pale face.

“I will not sleep while he is in this state. If he holds steady, I may rest in turns later. Not now. Now I sit with him. You do not have to stay if you cannot. If you can stay, stay usefully. Watch his chest. Watch the dressing. Listen. If you hear something, name it. If you see something, name it. If you think nothing is wrong but you feel wrong, say that too. Bodies communicate through the people watching them sometimes. A bad feeling is not evidence, but it is worth checking.”

She reached for the water they had and dampened a clean cloth.

“I am going to wipe his face now. Not because it will save him. Because sweat and blood in the eyes and mouth make panic worse when he wakes. If he wakes and cannot see, he will fight. If he fights, he can tear himself open. So I am cleaning what I can. Small things matter. A dry face. A clear mouth. A blanket in the right place. A hand not pressing where it should not press. These are not miracles, but they are part of keeping a man alive.”

She wiped the man’s forehead with careful strokes, avoiding the dressing, avoiding the worst of the chest.

“The rest is that I do not know if he will remember this. Some men remember every second. Some remember nothing. Some remember pieces: a voice, a hand, a pain, a light, the feeling of being held down. If he remembers you holding him, I hope he understands later that it was not malice. If he never understands, that is still acceptable. Understanding is not required for survival.”

She folded the cloth and set it aside.

“I will tell you what I will not do. I will not pretend I can save everyone. I will not pretend this man is more important than the next one who comes through that flap. He is important because he is here. When the next one comes, that one will be important too. That is how you keep from breaking. You do not carry all of them at once. You carry the one under your hands, and then you carry the next, and then you wash your hands and carry the next. If you try to carry all of them, you will become useless, and uselessness gets people killed.”

Her eyes hardened slightly, not with anger at Wick, but with the old weight of the thing she was describing.

“I have lost people. I will lose people again. Some I lose quickly. Some I lose slowly. Some I lose after thinking I had won. Some I lose because I made a mistake I did not see until too late. Some I lose because there was nothing to do from the start. Some I lose because the war is faster than I am. I do not get used to it in the way people mean when they say that. I get better at working beside it. That is different.”

The man’s breathing eased a little more. Sedge noticed it. She did not relax because of it.

“If he improves, we will still not call him safe. We will call him steadier. Steadier is not safe. Steadier is a direction. He can be steadier for hours and then turn. He can be terrible for hours and then rally. Bodies are not machines. They are weather. They have patterns, but they also have surprises. I respect the patterns. I fear the surprises.”

She checked the bindings once more.

“The rest is that tomorrow, if there is a tomorrow, there will be more work. Cleaning. Changing dressings. Checking shoulders. Watching for fever. Making him drink when it is safe. Keeping him from moving too much. Explaining to him why he cannot be brave yet. If he is lucky, he will be bored and sore. If he is unlucky, he will be feverish and afraid. If he is very unlucky, he will be dead. If he is very lucky, he will live to complain about my bedside manner.”

There was no smile in her face, but something almost human passed through her voice.

“I do not have a good bedside manner. I have a working one.”

She looked down at the patient’s chest.

“I am going to keep talking for a while, because you asked me to, and because it keeps me ordered. But I will not talk to fill the silence with hope. I will talk to keep the facts in line.”

She placed one hand lightly near the dressing again.

“The facts are: both shoulders are reduced. The chest wound is small but leaking. The dressing is vented. The pulse is fast but present. The breathing is shallow but bilateral. The color is gray but not blue. The skin is cold but not dead. The wound is dirty but not yet infected. The man is unconscious but not gone. That is the inventory. It is not much. It is what we have.”

She drew the blanket a little more securely around the patient’s legs.

“The rest is that we will not leave him alone. If he worsens, we will work. If he dies, we will handle him decently. If he lives, we will keep working. There is no version of this where we get to stop feeling the weight of it. There is only the version where we do not let the weight make us careless.”

Her voice dropped.

“I know what it is to hold someone down while they scream. I know what it does to the person holding. It makes you feel like a butcher. It makes you feel like a jailer. It makes you feel like your hands belong to someone else. But if you do it right, if you do it for the right reason, if you do it without enjoying it, it can be part of saving a life. That does not make it clean. Nothing about this is clean. It only makes it necessary.”

She looked at the row of instruments again.

“I will clean what I used. I will boil what can be boiled. I will save what can be saved. I will not waste supplies on sentiment. I will not waste time on guilt. Guilt is a luxury too. It feels important, but it does not set bones or close wounds.”

The man’s breath caught once. Sedge leaned in.

The dressing lifted.

It did not suck.

It settled.

She stayed there, counting under her breath.

“One,” she murmured. “Two. Three. Four.”

Then, to Wick, without looking away:

“The rest is that we wait. We watch. We name what changes. We do not look away because it is ugly. We do not pretend it is not ugly because we are tired. We keep our hands ready. We keep our mouths ready to say what we see. We keep the lamp burning as long as it will burn. And if the lamp goes out, we sit in the dark and listen.”

She checked the man’s lips one more time.

“Still gray,” she said.

Then she checked the dressing.

“Still venting.”

Then she checked the pulse.

“Still beating.”

She let her hand rest near the patient’s chest, not pressing, only present.

“That is the rest,” Sedge said. “Not a promise. Not a story. A list. A watch. A body still deciding. And us, deciding with it.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I sit there a moment longer, then push myself back up. My legs feel like they aren't mine. "I'll watch," I say, and my voice sounds strange in the quiet. "Tell me what to listen for again. The wet sound."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge did not answer at once.

She kept her attention on the man’s chest long enough to watch the waxed cloth lift, settle, and lift again. Her fingers stayed near the vented edge, not touching it, only ready. Only present. The lamp made a small, sickly sound as it burned. The man’s breathing was thin, quick, and uneven, but it was still there.

Then she looked at Wick.

“The wet sound,” she said. “There is more than one kind. That’s why I need you to say what you hear, not decide what it means.”

She shifted slightly so she could keep one eye on the dressing while she spoke.

“If it’s in his throat, it will sound thick. Loose. Like something moving in there with every breath. A rattle. A gurgle. Sometimes like a man trying to breathe through water he can’t spit out. That can mean blood. Vomit. Spit gone down wrong. Whatever it is, it can block him fast. If you hear that, tell me at once. Don’t wait to see if he clears it himself.”

Her gaze dropped to the man’s mouth for a beat, then back.

“If it’s in his chest, it may not sound like a throat sound. It may be smaller. Tighter. A bubbling. A crackle. Something wet and close under the breath instead of over it. If you lean near and hear a fizzing or a fine popping, like breath moving through something torn and soaked, that’s not a sound to ponder. That’s a sound to name.”

She touched the edge of the waxed cloth with one finger, confirming it was still where she wanted it.

“If the wound itself starts making noise, that’s another kind of wet. A sucking sound. A hiss with moisture in it. A little bubbling at the edge where the cloth meets skin. I already told you about the whistle, but the wet version can be worse. If air and fluid are arguing in the same hole, the body is losing the argument.”

She straightened just enough to keep her shadow off the patient’s face.

“There’s also the sound of effort. That isn’t wet, but it leads to wet. If his breathing starts sounding like work—short, dragged, catching—if his ribs show when he pulls air, if the skin at his neck pulls in, if his belly is doing more than his chest, that’s not something to sit with quietly. Tell me. Effort can turn into drowning faster than people expect.”

Her voice stayed flat and practical, as if she were listing tools rather than fears.

“If he makes a sound like he’s choking but can’t get the choke out, tell me. If he starts coughing and it sounds wet and heavy, tell me. If he coughs up anything pink, red, or frothy, tell me before you finish seeing it. Pink froth is not a thing to wipe away and forget. It means lung trouble until I say otherwise.”

She glanced at the man’s lips.

“And if the sound changes because he has gone too quiet, that counts too. A man can scream and still be fighting. A man can go silent and still be alive. But if the noise stops and the breathing gets worse, if the struggle goes inward instead of outward, that is not improvement. That is the body running out of ways to complain. I would rather hear him curse than hear him go still for the wrong reason.”

She reached for a clean rag and set it within reach, not because she needed it immediately, but because she always kept the next thing near.

“Don’t try to be clever with it,” she said. “Don’t listen once, decide it’s nothing, and then stand there doubting yourself. If you hear wetness, say wetness. If you hear bubbling, say bubbling. If you hear a whistle, say whistle. If you hear something you can’t name but it sounds wrong, say wrong. I will not mock you for it. I will mock silence.”

Her eyes went back to the dressing.

“If you want to listen properly, stand close enough that your ear is over his chest but not so close your hair or sleeve touches the wound. Keep your weight off the table. Keep your hands off the dressing. Watch while you listen. The sound may match something you can see: the cloth pulling, one side lagging, bubbles at the edge, color changing. If sound and sight disagree, tell me both.”

She paused, listening to the man’s breath for several beats.

“Sometimes the wet sound is small at first. A little catch at the end of a breath. A faint rattle that seems to come and go. Don’t wait for it to become obvious. Obvious is late. I want early. Early is ugly, but it gives me room to move.”

Her hand rested near the man’s sternum again, light and steady.

“If he vomits, that is not a sound to guess at. You call me, and we turn him as one piece. Not by the shoulders. Not by the arms. Not by dragging. If he chokes while flat, he can pull filth into lungs that are already in trouble. That is a mess neither of us wants to make worse.”

She looked at Wick then, her expression tired but entirely alert.

“If you hear the wet sound and his lips are blue, don’t stop to describe it beautifully. Say blue and wet. That is enough. If you hear the wet sound and the dressing is pulling in tight, say wet and sucking. If you hear it and one side of his chest is not moving like the other, say wet and uneven. Those words mean something to me. The rest can wait until I have my hands on him.”

The man’s breath hitched. Sedge leaned in at once, watching the waxed cloth. It lifted, trembled, and settled. No whistle. No strong suck. No fresh rush of bubbles.

She let her shoulders stay where they were.

“There are sounds that are bad but manageable,” she said. “And sounds that mean we are out of time for careful thought. The wet sound is one of the second kind if it is new, if it is spreading, if it comes with color change or struggle. I don’t need you to sort which is which. I need you to break the silence the moment it starts.”

She checked the pulse at his neck again, quick and thin under her fingers.

“And if you hear it only once, tell me. Sometimes a body will give one warning and then pretend it never did. I don’t trust pretenders. If it happens once, I will check. If it happens twice, I will already be moving.”

Her voice lowered, but did not soften into comfort.

“The worst mistake is standing there thinking you must be sure. You will not be sure. You are not trained for sure. I am barely trained for sure most nights. Your job is to be the first voice that says something changed. Mine is to decide what we do about it.”

She looked down at the man’s face, at the gray of his skin, the slackness of his jaw, the faint tremor still living in his bound shoulders.

“So,” she said. “The wet sound. Thick in the throat. Bubbling in the chest. Fizzing at the wound. Choking without clearing. Pink froth. New struggle. One side lagging. If any of that shows itself, you say it plain. Wet. Blue. Sucking. Bubbling. Uneven. Whatever you have. Say it fast. Say it ugly. Say it before you feel ready.”

She placed her hand near the dressing again, not touching, only guarding.

“I will listen too,” she said. “But you are awake, and he is not, and the night is long. So use your ears. Use your eyes. If something changes, do not tidy it into something less frightening. Give me the raw version. The raw version is the only one I can work with.”

The tent held its breath around them. The lamp burned low. The man breathed thin.

Sedge kept watching.

“And if you hear nothing,” she added, “but he looks worse anyway, say that. Sometimes the body changes before the sound does.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I lean in, my ear close to his chest but not touching. His breath rattles, just a little. "It's not wet," I say, "but it's tight. Like there's something pulling against his ribs."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge heard the words and moved at once, not fast in a way that showed alarm, but fast in the way of someone who had trained herself never to waste a second once a patient changed.

“Tight,” she repeated. “Say it plain if you hear it again. Don’t wait for a better word. Tight is a word I can use.”

She bent closer to the man’s chest, keeping her hands where they could be seen and not pressing anything yet. Her ear hovered above the blanket, then above the bare skin beside the dressing. She listened with her whole face still, eyes half-lidded, mouth set in a hard line.

The man’s breath came shallow and quick. There was a faint rasp in it, not the loose slosh of fluid, not the thick rattle of vomit or blood in the throat, but a narrow, strained sound, like something being pulled too far with every movement.

Sedge stayed there for several breaths.

Then she straightened just enough to speak.

“You’re right,” she said. “It’s not wet yet. But tight is not nothing. Tight means the chest is working against something. Sometimes that something is pain. Sometimes it’s swelling. Sometimes it’s a cracked rib dragging on the muscle around it. Sometimes it’s air in a place it has no business being, pressing where it can’t be seen.”

She placed one hand flat on the man’s upper chest, light enough only to feel movement, not enough to cause more pain. Her eyes went to the rise and fall on each side.

“I’m comparing the two sides now,” she said. “The right moves more. The left moves less. Not still. Less. That’s not proof of collapse, but it’s a reason not to look away. A lung can be angry without being dead. It can be squeezed. It can be bruised. It can be leaking slowly. The body doesn’t hand you the answer neatly. It gives you a difference and makes you decide how much to trust it.”

Her fingers shifted to the edge of the waxed cloth. She did not peel it up. She only checked the vent again, making sure the lower edge remained free.

“I’m watching the dressing,” she said. “It’s not sucking in hard. It’s not flapping. There’s still a little movement at the edge. That means air is not trapped completely, or not yet. If it starts pulling tight against the skin, if it looks like it’s being swallowed by the wound, that’s pressure changing. If it starts blowing out with every breath instead of settling, that’s more air than I want to hear about.”

She leaned closer again, this time with her face near the wound, listening.

The man’s teeth parted. A thin sound escaped him, not quite a moan, not quite a word. His bound shoulders twitched under the cloth.

Sedge put her forearm lightly across his upper chest again.

“Flat,” she said, not loud. “You stay flat. You fight me, you make it worse.”

His body settled by degrees, though the breath still sounded too small for the size of him.

Sedge looked back toward Wick without turning her body away from the table.

“Tight can mean the muscles have locked around the injury. When a man’s hurt bad enough, the body tries to guard the place. It tightens everything nearby, like a fist trying to hold itself together. That can make breathing feel bound even when there’s no new bleeding. It can also hide a worse problem, so I don’t get to assume it’s only muscle.”

Her free hand moved to the side of the man’s chest, fingers spread wide. She did not press hard. She barely touched him.

“I’m feeling for crackle again,” she said. “That dry-snow feeling under the skin. It’s still there. Not much more than before, but it hasn’t gone away. Air in the tissue can make a chest feel tight too. It can spread. It can make the neck swell. It can make a man look wrong in ways that are hard to name until suddenly they’re easy to name.”

She checked the hollow of the man’s throat with her eyes, then the line of his jaw.

“I’m looking at his neck,” she said. “I don’t like what I see, but I don’t hate it. The veins are fuller than they should be. That can be pressure in the chest. It can be strain from fighting for breath. It can be shock making everything look wrong. I’m not jumping to the ugliest conclusion yet, but I’m writing the sign down in my head.”

Her gaze dropped to his lips.

“Still gray,” she said. “Not blue. That’s still a piece of ground we’re holding.”

She listened again.

The tightness in the man’s breathing did not sound like drowning. Not yet. It sounded more like a door trying to open against a swollen frame. Each breath reached a point and stopped short. Each breath had effort in it.

Sedge’s jaw tightened.

“If this gets worse,” she said, “the sound may change before the look does. It may get thinner. It may get higher. It may start catching at the end, like he can’t finish the breath he started. If you hear that, say thin. If you hear him trying to pull air and the sound gets smaller instead of bigger, say quiet. If his belly starts working hard while his chest barely moves, say belly. If the skin at the base of his throat starts pulling in with every breath, say throat. You don’t have to know what it means. You have to give me the word.”

She adjusted the waxed cloth by the smallest amount, leaving the vent open.

“I’m not sealing this,” she said. “Not even a little. If the air inside him needs a way out, I’m not going to shut the door on it. If the leak gets bigger, I may have to open the edge more. That will hurt him. It may make him wake again. It may make him scream. But if pressure builds and I leave it closed, his heart will be squeezed until it can’t beat properly. So we choose the pain that leaves him breathing.”

The man’s fingers curled weakly against the blanket. Sedge noticed them at once.

“I’m checking his hands,” she said. “Color’s still there. Cold, but not white. That’s circulation holding, more or less. If his fingers go blue, if his nails go pale and stay pale, that tells me the body is pulling blood away from the edges because it thinks it’s losing the center. That’s not a sign to wait on.”

She looked back at the chest.

“What you heard,” she went on, “might be the lung rubbing against something torn. It might be the chest wall itself, muscles and ribs and bruised meat fighting every expansion. It might be air moving through a small tear that hasn’t decided whether to close or widen. I can’t see inside him. I can’t tap on him like a barrel and know for certain. I can only watch what he gives me.”

She put two fingers lightly against his wrist, counting the pulse again.

“Still fast,” she said. “Still thin. It hasn’t changed much since the last count. That’s not good, but it’s not a sudden fall. Sudden is sometimes easier to fight than slow. Slow can fool you.”

Her eyes moved over the dressing, the blanket, the bound shoulders, the man’s face.

“If he starts making a effort sound with every breath, if it sounds like he’s lifting something heavy just to get air, tell me. If the tight sound becomes sharp, like a catch, tell me. If he tries to breathe and you see one side lag behind, tell me. If his mouth opens and no sound comes, tell me before you finish being frightened by it.”

She wiped her hand on a clean rag, then set it aside.

“I’m not going to probe the wound because you heard tightness,” she said. “That would be stupid. If there’s a small leak, poking at it can make it a large one. If a vessel has closed, disturbing it can open it again. If the lung is only nicked, I don’t want to teach it to bleed harder. So I keep my hands off unless the signs tell me the risk of doing nothing is worse than the risk of interfering.”

She checked the waxed cloth again. A tiny bubble formed at the loose edge and broke.

“Still small,” she said. “Still deciding.”

The man’s breath hitched. Sedge leaned in at once.

The dressing lifted.

It did not collapse inward.

It settled.

She let out a slow breath, but her face did not relax.

“That hitch is not a good sound,” she said. “It’s not a death sound either. It’s the body losing rhythm for a second because pain or pressure or fear has interrupted it. I don’t like it, but I’ll take it over stillness. If the hitches come closer together, tell me. If they turn into gasps, tell me. If he starts breathing through his nose like his mouth won’t work, tell me.”

She looked down at the man’s face.

“You hear that?” she asked him, though he could not answer. “You’re still making noise. Keep making noise. Noise is useful.”

Her gaze returned to Wick.

“If he wakes again, keep him flat. If he tries to lift his head, stop him. If he tries to turn, stop him. If he begs, stop him. If he curses, let him curse. The only thing he gets to do right now is breathe and stay still. Everything else is borrowed trouble.”

She placed her hand near the dressing again.

“I’m going to keep the vent open,” she said. “I’m going to watch the left side. I’m going to count the breaths. I’m going to check his lips every few minutes. I’m going to look for blue. If blue comes, we stop being patient. If blue comes with tightness and effort, that means he’s not moving enough air. If that happens, I may need to open the dressing wider and let the chest vent more directly. It will be ugly. It may look like I’m making the wound worse. I won’t be making it worse. I’ll be choosing the smaller harm.”

Her voice stayed level, stripped of drama.

“If I have to do that, you keep him still. You don’t grab the dressing. You don’t try to help by pressing on his chest. You keep his shoulders down and his body flat. If he vomits, you call me. If he chokes, we turn him as one piece. If he goes blue and quiet, you say blue and quiet, and you say it now.”

She checked the blanket, then the bindings at his arms.

“I’m making sure he hasn’t torn anything while he was fighting,” she said. “The shoulder bindings are still where I put them. His fingers still have color. The blanket is still over him. That’s all useful. Small pieces of useful are what keep a man alive when the big pieces are missing.”

The tent shifted around them. The lamp flame dipped, then steadied. The man’s breath remained thin, tight, and quick.

Sedge listened to it with a patience that was not calm so much as disciplined.

“You did right to say it,” she said after a moment. “A lot of people would have heard it and told themselves it was nothing. Or they would have heard it and frozen, waiting for permission to speak. You spoke. That’s the job right now. You are not here to be clever. You are here to be a second set of senses. If your senses are wrong, I will check them. If they are right, you may have bought me the minute I need.”

She did not look away from the patient.

“Tight is not wet,” she said. “But tight can become wet. Tight can become blue. Tight can become silent. So we do not ignore it. We watch it like it owes us.”

She leaned close again, her ear over the man’s chest but not touching him.

“I’m listening for the next change,” she said. “If it stays tight and nothing else joins it, we hold. If it gets tighter, we move. If it turns wet, we move faster. If it turns silent, we move fastest.”

Her hand hovered near the dressing.

“Keep listening,” she said. “And if you hear the tightness start to sound like a string pulled too far, say string. If it sounds like something rubbing where it shouldn’t, say rubbing. If it sounds like he’s breathing through a narrower place than he was five minutes ago, say narrow. I don’t care if the word is strange. I care if it’s true.”

The man’s chest rose.

The left side lagged.

Sedge saw it.

Her expression did not change, but her voice went quieter.

“There,” she said. “That’s what I’m talking about. The left side is slower. Not stopped. Slower. That’s not a reason to tear the tent down. It is a reason to stop pretending this is only a scratch.”

She checked the dressing again.

“No strong suck,” she said. “No whistle. No pink froth. No blue. That’s still in our favor. But the chest is not moving clean, and the sound you heard is part of that.”

She placed her hand lightly over the man’s sternum again.

“I’m going to stay here,” she said. “I’m going to keep this vent open. I’m going to watch his color. I’m going to count his breaths. If the left side stops moving, if his neck veins rise more, if his face starts looking swollen, if he starts fighting for air like a man held under water, then we will do what must be done without arguing about it first.”

Her eyes flicked briefly to Wick.

“Until then,” she said, “you keep doing what you just did. You listen. You name it. You don’t tidy it up. If it’s tight, say tight. If it’s worse, say worse. If you don’t know, say you don’t know. I’ll take the truth over silence every time.”

The man’s breath caught again.

Sedge leaned in.

The dressing lifted.

It settled.

She stayed bent over him, watching, listening, waiting.

“Still deciding,” she murmured. “But not done.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I lean back, my hands still shaking. "Alright," I say, my voice hoarse. "Tight. Like a string pulled too far." I don't look away from his chest. "Tell me if you need my hands again."

rung_labels.evidence: Bad like he keeps it if I do this right

rung_labels.evidence: the meat around it is torn and angry

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: It can score the joint, shred tendon
