dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
The cellar had four feet of standing water in it and something at the far end that had stopped moving about a minute ago.

Halloway held the lamp up and did not go closer yet. "Right," she said. "Before we touch it. What do you see?"

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I make myself look properly instead of at the water. "I don't know yet," I say. "Something wrong with the shape of it."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content: Halloway kept the lamp steady, letting the beam cut through the silt without flinching. "Good," she said, her voice low. "The human form is predictable. When it isn't, that's where the teeth hide." She tilted her head, studying the dark mass in the water. "Tell me about the joints. Do they bend the right way, or do they look like they were put together backwards? If it's off, we don't wade. We wait."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I squint, trying to ignore the way the water distorts everything. "Its... shoulder. It's too low. And the elbow looks like it bends the wrong direction." I feel a chill that has nothing to do with the damp. "Do you think it's dead?"

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway nodded once, the motion sharp and economical. "Dead is a human word for a thing that stops working." She adjusted the lamp, keeping the beam fixed on the mass. "But some things don't stop. They just change."

She glanced at Pike, a dry curve touching her mouth. "If that shoulder drops when it lifts an arm, it's not dead. It's reloading."

She set her boot heel on the cellar stair. "Keep your knife ready. And don't assume it's sleeping because it's still."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: "Was that a person?" I ask. "Recently, I mean. Is that what I'm looking at?"

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway let the lamp dip slightly, then raise it again. She watched the water line on the shoulder, noting the way it didn't settle. "Human bone breaks a certain way," she said. "Soft tissue pools. This... this looks packed."

She didn't blink. "It might have been a person an hour ago. It might have been something else ten years back." A faint smirk touched her lips, gone as quickly as it came. "But right now? It's bait. And we're the catch if we step in."

She shifted her weight, hand resting near her coat. "Doesn't matter what it was. Matters what it's about to do."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I swallow, my hand tightening on my knife hilt. "So we're not going in." It's not a question, but I need to hear her say it.

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway shook her head, the motion minimal. "Correct." She kept her voice level, cutting through the dripping silence. "Bravery buys a story. Survival buys a tomorrow."

She shifted her grip on the lamp handle, the leather creaking softly. "We wait. If it stands up, we back away. If it stays down, we back away." She glanced at the door, then back to the water. "Some traps don't need to spring to catch you. They just need you to stay."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I wade closer and hold the lamp where she can work. "Tell me what happened to it," I say. "Plainly."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway watched Pike sink into the silt, the ripples disturbing the water's surface. She didn't scold him. Not yet.

"Plainly," she said. "The body didn't die. It was evicted."

She leaned in, bringing the lamp closer to the mass. The light revealed the truth of the shoulder now. It wasn't swollen from drowning. It was packed tight, the skin stretched over something fibrous and foreign.

"Organic matter doesn't grow like that," she said, her voice dry. "Something moved in. Replaced the muscle. Took the weight of the bones." She glanced up at Pike, her expression unchanging. "You're looking at a house that changed owners. The previous tenants are gone."

She tapped the lamp glass. "So get your foot out of the mud. It's not safe to stand in the doorway while the new occupants are settling in."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I yank my foot back, mud sucking at my boot. "It's hollow?" The word comes out quieter than I meant. "What's inside it then?"

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway watched Pike retreat until his boot cleared the silt line. She didn't praise him for the movement. "Hollow implies empty," she said, her tone flat. "This is occupied."

She gestured with the lamp toward the distortion in the shoulder. "Think of a wasp nest. The cardboard shell holds the shape, but the bees are gone. Something else is building the comb inside."

"Inside?" She glanced at Pike, her eyes dry and clear. "Not lungs. Not heart. Something that doesn't breathe air." She lowered the lamp slightly. "Mycelium. Spores. Or something that learned to wear skin." She tapped the glass. "You ask what's inside, you're really asking what's about to crawl out. Don't find out."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: "I need the detail," I say. "Tell me exactly what it did to him -- what is under the skin now, what it took, how far it got. If I meet another one I need to know."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway held his gaze, letting the silence stretch just long enough to weigh the cost. "Skin remains intact," she said. "The viscera are gone. Replaced by a mycelial matrix." She tilted the lamp, casting deep shadows into the shoulder's hollow. "It starts in the marrow. Works outward. Drains the heat first, then the structure."

She lowered the lamp. "If you see this, you don't fight it. You burn it before it takes the lungs. You want to know what to look for?" A thin smile, all teeth. "Look for the body that feels cold where it should be warm." She turned back to the water. "Now get behind me."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I step behind her, my back to the cellar stairs. "Can it see us?"

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway kept the lamp steady, refusing to look away from the water. "Eyes are secondary," she said. "It reads heat. Vibration. The scent of wet iron."

She watched the shoulder. "It's focused inward right now. Reweaving what was torn."

She glanced at Pike over her shoulder. "But focus fades. We don't test it. Move. Quiet."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: She starts cutting and I hold the lamp steady and don't look away. "Keep describing it," I tell her. "Everything -- what's underneath, what it smells like, how far it got. Don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content: Halloway drove the blade into the shoulder. The steel met resistance like wet wood. "Smells like a greenhouse that's never seen sunlight," she said. "Not rot. That's decay. This is growth." She withdrew the knife. "No blood. Just a thick, white sap. It's woven through the nerves now. Replaced the spinal cord. It's reached the skull." She glanced up at Pike. "If you smell wet soil when you're indoors, you're already too late." She turned back to the water. "Get the torch ready. If I say burn, you burn."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: My hands shake as I pull the oilcloth off the torch. "It's moving," I whisper, watching the water ripple around the body's legs. "Halloway."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway didn't turn. She saw the ripple in the silt, the slow drag of water against the legs. "It's waking," she said. "Not breathing. Uncoiling."

She held out her free hand, palm open. "Light it. Now."

The sap on her knife dripped into the water, hissing faintly. "Don't wait for me to say it twice. When it lifts, you throw."

She stepped back, putting the stairs between them and the water. "I'm not losing another partner to a houseplant."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I sit on the cellar steps afterwards with the lamp in my hands. "Finish it," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full.)

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway descended the stairs, stepping over the wet threshold until she stood at the water's edge. The air smelled of cooked meat and wet earth, the steam rising from the center of the room in thin, wavering columns.

She looked down at the mass. It was no longer shaped like a man. It was a mound of blackened fiber, the white sap boiled into a hard, sticky scab. The shoulder she had prodded earlier was gone, reduced to ash.

"It's finished," she said. Her voice didn't change. "Heat breaks the spores. The structure collapses."

She leaned forward, keeping her weight on the balls of her feet. She prodded the center with the tip of her knife. The material collapsed inward, turning to dust under the steel. No movement. No resistance.

"Burned out," she said, straightening up. "The network is severed."

She wiped the blade on her coat and looked at Pike. "Get the lamp. We're not leaving this for later. If there's a root left, it'll find new ground."

She started back up the stairs, waiting for him to follow. "And wipe your boots. I don't want spores in the truck."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I scrub my boots on the top step, watching the mud and ash flake away. "How many times have you seen one like that?"

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway waited until the sound of scrubbing stopped, the damp grit finally giving way to dry leather. She didn't look at the steps. She looked at the door. "I don't keep a ledger," she said. "The count depends on where you are and how long the winter was."

She ran a thumb along the edge of her knife, testing for dullness. "Some take years to root. This one took a month." She shoved the blade back into her coat. "That's the metric that matters."

She turned the handle and pushed the door open, letting the street air wash down the stairs. "If you meet another, you don't ask how many I've seen. You ask if it's ready to hunt." She stepped onto the pavement, the concrete still damp from the evening. "And you already know the answer."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: "Did the man know?" I ask, following her out and pulling the cellar door shut behind me. "When it started, I mean. Did he feel it?"

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway paused at the top of the stairs, her hand resting on the iron latch. She didn't look back down into the dark.

"He knew he was cold," she said. "That's usually the first thing. Then the stiffness. Then the silence."

She turned the lock with a sharp click. "The nerves don't die. They get rerouted. You feel the pressure when something else is pulling the strings. You just can't move to stop it."

She pushed off the railing and started down the sidewalk. The concrete was cool under her boots. "Don't ask that question again. It won't help you. The next time, you'll want to know if it's still in there, or if it's already been replaced."

She glanced at her boots, then at Pike's. Mud clung to the treads.

"Get in the truck. We need to hose the tread before we drive two blocks. If you track that soil home, you'll be fighting a garden in your basement."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I climb into the passenger seat, staring at the mud on my boots. "It got the lungs," I say, finally. "You said if it takes the lungs, it's too late. How much time do you have between the cold and that?"

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
The cellar had four feet of standing water in it and something at the far end that had stopped moving about a minute ago.

Halloway held the lamp up and did not go closer yet. "Right," she said. "Before we touch it. What do you see?"

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I make myself look properly instead of at the water. "I don't know yet," I say. "Something wrong with the shape of it."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway lowered the lamp a degree, letting the light flatten out across the water instead of stabbing at the dark. "Wrong shape's a start," she said. "Wrong shape is usually the first honest thing a corpse ever tells you. Now let's be specific about it, because 'wrong' covers a lot of ground and most of it wants to kill you."

She crouched at the edge of the flooded stair, boots a careful hand's width from the waterline, and studied the thing the way she'd studied thirty years of dead things — like a ledger to be balanced.

"Right. It's too long through the torso for the limbs — arms reach past where knees ought to start. The joints all bend a half-turn past where God signed off on the design. And it's not bloating, which is what waterlogged does to honest meat. It's *swelling from the inside*, which means whatever was in it is still in there, or was until about a minute ago."

She set the lamp down on the step beside her, unhurried, and rolled her sleeves like a woman about to do washing.

"Notice it stopped moving when it did, not when we came down. That's not death, that's *playing dead*. Big difference." A dry breath of a laugh. "And it's not floating. Dead things float. This one's holding the floor."

She looked at the water, then at Pike. "So before we touch anything — tell me what the water's doing around it."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I squint, focusing on the water's surface. "It's... rippling. But not from us." My voice goes quiet. "Like something's breathing underneath it."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway nodded once, slow, like a woman confirming a debt she'd already priced in.

"Breathing. Good eye. Most people talk themselves out of that one — 'it's just the water settling,' they say, right up until it's got their ankle." She didn't take her eyes off the ripple pattern. "Now count it. Watch the intervals."

She waited a beat, lamp steady, then continued, low. "It's slow. Four, five seconds between pulses. That's not a panicked thing and it's not a dying thing. That's a thing that's *comfortable*. It knows this water, it knows we're here, and it's decided we're not worth changing its breathing for. Which tells you something important, Pike — it doesn't think it's hiding from us. It thinks it's *waiting*."

She reached back without looking and unbuckled the long knife from her pack, the motion unhurried, almost domestic. Didn't draw it. Just set it across her knees like cutlery before a meal.

"And here's the arithmetic I don't love. That breathing's coming from under the body, not from the body. So we've got two possibilities. One: the swelling burst something loose and it's nested under there, and what stopped moving up top was just the wrapper going still. Two—" a pause, and the ghost of a smile that had no humor left in it, "—there were never two things at all, and the 'body' is a lure. Thirty years, I've seen the second one exactly four times, and I lost a partner to one of them, so you'll forgive me if I check the exits before I check the corpse."

Her eyes flicked to the stair behind them, measuring the distance, then back to the water.

"So. Nobody touches anything. Here's what we're going to do. I want you to back up three steps — slow, weight on the heels, no splashing — and you're going to tell me the last thing it stopped doing. Because everything dead plays dead differently, and everything alive forgets one detail when it does. You find me the detail it forgot, and I'll tell you whether we're hunting or leaving."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: "Was that a person?" I ask. "Recently, I mean. Is that what I'm looking at?"

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway didn't answer right away. The silence was the counting kind, not the soft kind — she was watching the hands.

"It was," she said finally. "Recently enough that the hands are still hands. Look at the left one. Five fingers, thumbnail, a scar across two knuckles where a man's been careless with a chisel or a bar fight. Nobody builds hands like that from scratch. And the teeth — you can see them where the jaw's gone slack. Filled molars. Some village dentist earned his supper out of that mouth once. That's a person's paperwork, Pike. You can counterfeit a face. You can't counterfeit a filling."

She let that sit, then sanded nothing off what came next.

"But 'was' is doing the heavy lifting in your question, and I won't lie to you about the weight. People don't swell from the inside. People don't bend a half-turn past spec. And people don't stop breathing on a lazy four-count because they've decided to. Something's been at work in there — wore him like a coat, or turned him, and I've seen both, and here's the honest arithmetic: I have never once told them apart from the outside before it was too late to matter to somebody."

She drew the knife off her knees, slow, the sound of it barely a whisper against the wet.

"So yes. Somebody up the road is missing a husband or a hired man or a son, and has been since before this water rose. That's a grief for later — and I mean that as kindness, not coldness, because grief has killed more hunters than any monster I can name. A crying person stands one step too close. You want to honor him? Then do what I told you. Three steps back, weight on the heels, and *watch*. Because the ones that used to be people hold their dead act better than any animal ever could. But they forget one thing. Always one thing. The breathing. The eyes — dead men's eyes don't track. Or it blinks."

A dry breath of a laugh, entirely without humor.

"Find me the thing it forgot. And if it comes to hunting — you don't touch him. If there's any of that man still in there, the kindest thing we can do is fast. But fast comes after sure."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I take a careful step back, my eyes fixed on the body. "It's... the foot. The left foot twitched. Just once." My voice is barely a whisper. "Dead weight doesn't twitch."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway didn't move. Didn't even shift her weight. When she spoke, it was the tone of a woman correcting an invoice.

"Dead weight twitches, actually. More than you'd credit. Gas works a corpse's limbs for hours after the man's done with them — I've seen a hanged man kick like a mule a full day after the drop. So the twitch alone doesn't convict." Her eyes never left the water. "It's the arithmetic *around* the twitch that hangs it. Now watch the water and tell me what the breathing's doing. Before, it was a lazy four-count. What is it now?"

She didn't wait for the answer, because she already had it, and something in her jaw set.

"It stopped. It's holding its breath." A slow exhale through her nose. "There's your detail, Pike. It twitched, and then it *noticed* it twitched, and now it's gone still to see if we caught it. Dead men don't get embarrassed. Live ones do."

She stood, unhurried, and drew the knife the rest of the way — no flourish, just steel coming out of leather like a decision being made.

"So we're hunting. And here's the shape of it, and you'll do exactly as I say because I've done this dance before and my last partner improved the steps. You stay on that stair. Lamp high, light on the body, don't take your eyes off it even if it sounds like I'm being murdered — the sound is the lie, the body is the truth. If I go under, you count ten. One for each year I've owed this particular breed. If I'm not up by ten, you leave, bar the cellar door, and burn the house with my blessing. That's not sentiment. That's arithmetic too." A thin, dry smile. "I've drowned in worse company."

She stepped down into the water — one boot, then the other, the cold climbing her shins — and kept her voice low and level as she started forward, blade held under the surface where the light couldn't glint off it.

"When it moves, it'll be fast and it'll be for the stairs, not for me — they always go for the exit, because the exit is where the soft thing is. You will not come down to help me. And when it's done—" a small tilt of her head toward the slack-jawed face, the filled molars, "—we drag him out, lay him straight, and find who's been missing him since before this water rose. That part matters. But it comes after sure."

Three steps out, the water at her knees, she stopped.

"Last thing. It's watching my feet, so it's not watching yours. If it starts to rise — you shout. One word. Anything. Don't think about the word, just make noise. Ready?"

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I wade closer and hold the lamp where she can work. "Tell me what happened to it," I say. "Plainly."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway didn't turn around. But her shoulders did something that in a lesser woman would have been called a flinch, and her voice came out flat as a headstone.

"I said the stair." A slow breath through the nose, the kind she used on rookies and horses. "Thirty years, one dead partner, and I say *the stair*, and you bring me the lamp." The knife didn't waver. "Fine. The lamp's useful. You've just changed the arithmetic for all three of us, is all — and it noticed before I finished being angry about it."

Because the breathing had started again. Not the lazy four-count. Faster now. Two seconds. One and a half. The ripples around the body were running against each other, interference patterns, the water doing sums of its own.

"Plainly, then, since you've paid for the answer with your ankles." She kept moving forward, slow, blade under the surface. "A man came down into this cellar when it was dry — after wine, after a rat, after an argument with his wife, it never matters which. Something was already down here, and it got into him. Mouth or wound, the result's identical. It didn't kill him. Killing is wasteful. It *ate* him — hollowed him out from the inside over weeks, grew into the space he left behind like a hermit crab in a whelk shell, and kept the parts that do the convincing. The hands. The scar across the knuckles. The teeth." Her jaw tightened. "Because a drowned man gets sympathy, Pike. A drowned man gets *carried*. Up the stairs, into a warm kitchen, set down in front of a wife who's been weeping over him since autumn — and whose guard is all the way down. That's what happened to him, plainly. He stopped being a man sometime before the water rose, and what's wearing him has been down here on a four-count ever since, waiting on somebody sentimental enough to help."

She was four paces off now, close enough that the lamp's light reached past the body — and showed what the flat angle from the stairs had hidden. The swelling wasn't uniform. It was *segmented*, moving under the skin of the torso like a sack of eels, and just under the slack jaw, where a man's throat ought to be, something pulsed that had no business resembling a pulse.

"There it is," Halloway said, almost gently. "Lamp's earning its keep."

The body's left hand closed. All five fingers, one at a time, deliberate as a man counting money.

"It's done pretending," she said, and her voice dropped to something that wasn't for Pike at all — it was the voice she used at the very end, level and final as a ledger closing. "It goes for you, not me. The soft thing, the exit, every time. When it moves — drop the lamp *away* from us, toward the far wall, not toward the water at your feet, and step *backwards*. Not sideways. Backwards."

The jaw opened. Wider than the fillings allowed. Wider than the skull allowed.

"Steady now," Halloway said. "Here it comes."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I drop the lamp toward the far wall like she said, the glass shattering against stone. The light gutters, then steadies, throwing long, jumping shadows. I step back, my heel hitting the stair. "I'm steady," I whisper, but my hand is shaking.

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
The thing covered the distance between stillness and the stairs in less time than it took Pike's heel to find the stair, and it did not travel like a man. The knees bent backward. The arms rowed the water. The jaw stayed open the whole way, and out of it came a sound like wet rope dragged over stone.

Halloway was already moving. Not toward it — across its path, because she'd known the exit before it had. Thirty years of arithmetic: she'd never once stabbed a thing coming at her. She stabbed the place it was going to be.

The knife went in under the left arm, where the swelling moved most, and she leaned her whole weight on it.

The shriek that came out of the dead man's mouth had no man left in it at all. The torso split along seams the swelling had been hiding — not wounds, *seams*, like the thing had been tailored — and out of it poured a knot of gray, segmented bodies, wrist-thick, fighting each other to reach the deep water.

"Out," she said, conversational, and cut the largest of them in half as it made for the dark. It didn't scream. It just stopped doing anything, which she'd long ago decided was the honest sound.

The shell of the man kept rowing — limbs working, jaw chewing, the fillings catching the lamplight one last time. She caught the hair, dragged the head back, and put the knife through the pulsing thing under the jaw. Twice. Then a third time, holding him under the water until the rowing slowed, and stopped, and the four-count never came back.

She counted ten anyway. For old debts.

Then the water was just water, and the lamp was still burning against the far wall, and Halloway stood in the middle of a flooded cellar holding a dead man by the hair, breathing like a woman who'd climbed a hill.

"There," she said, to nobody in particular. "Fast. Like I promised him."

The body came up lighter than it went down — emptied of its tenant, a man's coat with nobody in it. She waded to the stairs and laid him out on the third step, straight, arms at his sides, jaw pushed closed with two fingers — professional as an undertaker, twice as gentle. She looked at the scar across the knuckles a long moment. Then she took the coat off her own back and put it over his face.

She turned to Pike, and looked at the shaking hand the way she'd looked at the corpse — clinically, without judgment.

"The shaking's fine. The shaking is your body doing sums your mouth won't. It'll stop in an hour, or it'll start in earnest tonight, and either way you'll want a drink in you before it decides which."

She nodded at the body on the stair.

"Now comes the part that matters, and it's the part most hunters skip. This man had a name, and somewhere up the road there's a woman who lights a lamp when she hears footsteps, and it won't be ours. We're going to find her. And I told you earlier we'd drag him out — I've changed my mind. He's earned carrying."

She wrung out her sleeve, wrung it again, and the grim humor surfaced the way everything else in that cellar did.

"Eyes on the water going up, mind. I accounted for the big ones. The little ones I make no promises about."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: "I need the detail," I say. "Tell me exactly what it did to him -- what is under the skin now, what it took, how far it got. If I meet another one I need to know."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway looked at Pike for a long moment, and something in her face shifted — not warmth exactly, but the flat satisfaction of a tradeswoman seeing an apprentice ask the right question instead of the comfortable one.

"Good. That's the first question a hunter asks and the last one most people think of." She waded back to the stair, knelt beside the body, and turned back the shirt front with two fingers, the way a tailor checks a lining. The coat stayed over his face. Clinical didn't mean rude. "He's past minding, and you're not past needing. Watch."

She opened the split along the torso with the flat of the knife, no flourish, and talked while she worked — the same tone she'd use pricing grain at market.

"It doesn't start big. What got into him was the length of your finger — a swimmer. Comes up through well water, cellar seep, flood runoff. Gets in through a cut, or a sleeping man's open mouth. One is plenty. And it doesn't rush. That's the part people can't hold onto, so hold onto it: *weeks*. Patience is its whole strategy."

She gestured at the cavity with the knife tip, pointing things out like landmarks.

"Eating order. Gut first — closest to where it lands, easiest meat. Stomach, intestines, then upward. Liver, spleen. Then the lungs. And here's the detail that matters: it doesn't need his lungs. *It breathes for him.* The knot of them works the chest like bellows, and in water like this, they breathe under the body itself — that was your four-count. A drowned man's ribs rising on a lazy count isn't him gasping. It's the tenant airing the coat."

"What it keeps: hands, face, teeth. The convincing parts. What it *replaces*: the muscle. It doesn't discard his muscles, it eats them and threads its own bodies in along the bones, through the tendon sheaths — cables through pulleys. That's why the joints bend past spec. The joints aren't his anymore. The pull comes from whatever angle the tenant wants." She indicated the lines under the skin of the arms, faint as old scars. "And these seams — see them? It thins the skin from inside, along lines, so it can open when it needs to. Young ones disperse through the splits. Which means, yes, some of what poured out of him made the deep water tonight, and that's the next cellar's problem, five years from now. Arithmetic. I never promised it was cheerful arithmetic."

She sat back on her heels, and her voice went to the flat cadence of a field manual.

"Your tells, in order of use. Swelling from the inside, not bloating — bloating is gas and it's even; a colony swells *segmented*, moves like a sack of eels under lamplight held flat. Joints bending wrong. Not floating — dead things float, this holds the floor. And the one that convicts: it plays dead, but it forgets one detail. A twitch it notices itself making. Eyes that track. A blink. Everything dead plays dead differently, everything alive forgets one thing. Find the forgotten thing and you've found your verdict."

"Now the kill, because you'll want it. Under the jaw, where a pulse has no business being — that's the anchor. The first one in, the oldest, the one running the limbs. Put steel through it and the rowing stops. Stab the torso instead and all you do is split the seams and hand the young an exit — which I did, on purpose, because a dispersed colony dies slower than a cornered one. And burn what's left after. Always fire. Water just moves the account somewhere else."

She stood, wiped the knife on her own thigh, and looked at the covered face a moment.

"As for how far it got — how long *he* was still in there, watching. The honest answer is nobody knows, and anyone who tells you different is selling something. Maybe weeks. Maybe he was a passenger in his own coat the whole time. That answer's not for me to pretty up."

She sheathed the knife and started up the stairs, then paused.

"Write all of it down tonight, while the shaking's got you at the table. Fear eats memory first, and this lesson cost a man his name. Waste nothing."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I nod, pulling out a small, water-stained notebook from my pocket. My fingers fumble but I manage to grip the pencil. "The water's cold," I say, looking at the man's covered face. "Do you think he felt it?"

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway paused on the stair, one boot on the step above, and looked back at the covered face for the length of a slow breath. When she answered, her voice had the flatness of a woman refusing to sell comfort she didn't stock.

"The cold? No. The cold stopped being his problem a long time ago. Nerves are early on the menu — the big ones in the spine, the ones that carry *feeling*, they're rich meat and the tenant eats them inside the first week. Whatever that was in the water feeling cold, it was the tenant's complaint, not his. The tenant liked it fine. It's why it stayed."

She came back down two steps, slowly, and lowered herself onto the stair below the body — not beside it, one step down, so the coat-covered face was level with her own. She looked at it the way she'd looked at ledgers for thirty years.

"But that's not the question you're asking, and I won't pretend it is. You're asking whether he *knew*." A pause. "The eating — the first weeks — yes. I'd stake my years on it. There are records, the old hunters kept them. Men who talked, in the early stages. Said it felt like hunger that couldn't be fed. Said it felt like something reading over their shoulder. One of them wrote it felt like *being learned*." Her jaw worked once. "That's not a sentence a man invents, Pike. That's a sentence a man pays for."

She let the cellar water lap against the stone for a moment before she went on.

"Then the records go quiet, and here's where I give you the honest shape of it: nobody knows where the man ends. The eating is slow and it's thorough, and at some point — some hour, some night — the part of him that could feel a thing like cold, or fear, or his wife's name, stopped being there to ask. Not died. *Stopped being the part in charge.* Maybe it was quick after that. Maybe the passenger rode along in the dark for weeks more, the way people in a fever dream hear the room around them." She shook her head once, short. "I told you before — anyone who says they know is selling. I've watched four of these and opened two, and I won't pretend the fifth answer is in there."

Then, because she was who she was, the grim humor surfaced — but quieter than usual, and aimed, for once, at herself.

"What I can tell you is what *I* felt, the one time, holding my partner's hand while one of these worked on him, back before I knew what the swelling meant. I felt his grip. And the grip was strong. And I thought, *good, he's fighting.*" She looked at the water. "It wasn't him fighting. It was the cables. The tenant flexes the hands to keep them limber, like a pianist. I held on to the exercises and thought it was my friend."

She stood, knees cracking, and put a hand briefly — very briefly — on the shoulder of the dead man's coat, the way you'd settle an account.

"So here's the answer I'd write in that notebook of yours, and then we carry him up. He felt the beginning, and the beginning was cruel, and the middle is a locked room none of us get to look into. But the *end* — the cold, the water, tonight — no. Whatever the cold was, it wasn't his. And the fast I promised him was for the part of him that might've still been in that locked room, on the chance the room was still lit. You don't get to know if it was a kindness." She started up the stairs, then added, dry as chalk:

"You do it anyway. That's the whole trade, Pike. Kindnesses on the chance they're needed. Write that down too."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: She starts cutting and I hold the lamp steady and don't look away. "Keep describing it," I tell her. "Everything -- what's underneath, what it smells like, how far it got. Don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway didn't look up. "Good. Stomach's the wrong place for this lesson, but it's the right place to learn it anyway." She set the knife's edge at the collar line, where the coat still covered the face, and worked downward with the same unhurried economy she'd have used dressing a deer.

"Start at the top of the list, because that's the order you'll meet it in. Skin first." She peeled the shirt front wide and turned the flesh toward the lamp with the flat of the blade. "Notice it's *intact*. Not one lesion, not one sore, not a bite mark. That's the first thing that misleads people. You'll find a body like this and call it a drowning, because the skin tells you nothing happened to this man. The skin's not where the story is. The skin is the *book cover.*"

She opened the torso along the seam the thing had tailored, and the smell came up the stair like a second occupant.

"There's your second tell, and you'll never forget it now, which is the point. Sweet. Thick-sweet, like a butcher's bin in August, and under it something like lye — alkaline, clean, wrong. That's the tenant's own chemistry. It digests as it goes and what it leaves behind doesn't rot like a corpse should. A three-month body should stink of putrefaction. This one smells like a tannery. When you smell tannery where you expected rot, you are not standing next to a drowned man." She glanced sideways, dry. "It'll want to come up your throat. Let it. Better out than in — my first mentor said that about whiskey, but it travels."

She widened the opening and held the lamp close with her free hand, angling the light flat the way she had on the water.

"Now the cavity, and I'll give you the inventory straight, because he's past minding and you're not past needing. Gut — gone. Not consumed to the last thread, *gone*, resorbed and rebuilt into lining for the cavity walls, see how smooth it is in there? Like it's been plastered. Liver, spleen, pancreas — gone. Heart—" she reached in, and her hand came back empty, "—gone, and that's the one that should stop you cold, Pike. He hasn't had a heartbeat in months. The chest was worked by the colony, bellows-fashion, exactly as I said. The lungs are still here but they're not lungs anymore, look — thin as paper, emptied, repurposed as *bladders*. Buoyancy and air-scent, near as I can tell. The tenant kept the shape of breathing and threw away the fact of it."

She worked down along the spine, exposing it, and her voice stayed level as a plumb line.

"Muscle — all of it, every sheath, eaten and replaced. What you're seeing threaded along the bones here, these gray cords — that's the tenant. Not worms in him. *Him, made of them.* Bone — untouched. It doesn't eat bone, it needs the scaffolding. Marrow, though—" she scraped the knife tip once against a femur, and it came away dry, "—sucked out like a cook treats a marrow spoon. That's how you date the tenancy, and here's the arithmetic: marrow goes last, and it goes slow. This man's been a coat since before the first frost."

She was quiet for exactly one breath, and then went on, because that was how she handled it.

"And now the part you actually asked for. The anchor." She turned the jaw aside with two fingers, careful as a dentist, and cut along the line she'd stabbed earlier, and lifted out the thing that had been pulsing where a pulse had no business being. She held it in the lamplight on the flat of her knife like a specimen at a lecture.

"Finger-length now. It went in the size of your little fingernail. Blind — no eyes, never had them, doesn't need light. Mouth's a ring, like a lamprey, and inside the ring—" she tilted it, "—teeth it sheds and replaces, which is why you'll sometimes find them in the cavity, tiny, like a fish's. This is the first one in. The settler. Everything else in him was its offspring, budded off over the months, and *this* one ran the limbs. You kill this one first and the rest are just rope." She turned it once more, clinically. "Note the color. The old one's gone dark, almost black. The young are gray-pale. So if you ever open a body and find a pale one — you've got a young colony, weeks old, and the host might not be past saving yet. Find a black one — you're not doing medicine, you're doing cleanup. That distinction has a body count attached to it, historically, so keep it."

She set the specimen down on the stone, well away from the waterline, and cleaned her knife with two strokes.

"Smell the corpse again, now that it's opened." A beat. "Nothing. Or near it — stagnant water and old stone. That's the last tell and the quietest one: the tenant was keeping him *preserved*. It eats him and then it maintains the shopfront. A body this old, opened, should overwhelm you. It doesn't, because the tenant's chemistry was still working right up until I put steel through the landlord. Ten minutes from now it'll smell like what it is. Twenty minutes from now you'll want it burned, and we'll be ahead of the clock."

She stood, knees cracking, and looked down at the opened man with the flat, settled expression of a woman closing an account.

"That's everything, Pike. Nothing left out, nothing prettied. Skin intact, cavity resorbed, heart gone, marrow spent, tenancy measured in seasons. Write it in the order I gave it you — smell, seams, buoyancy, the black anchor — because that's the order a body will hand you the answers in, and you'll only get one pass at reading most of them."

She picked up the specimen with a scrap of cloth, wrapped it like something for a market stall, and pocketed it.

"Evidence. Somebody up the road has been told her husband *ran off*, I'd wager, because that's the story these things always leave behind — a man who walked out one night and never came home. This little black bastard is how we prove different. Now help me lay him straight and get him up these stairs, because I meant what I said about carrying." A dry pause, and the grim humor surfaced one last time, thin as lamplight. "And mind your boots on the way up. I told you I accounted for the big ones. The young went into the water tonight, and I'd hate to write *that* in your notebook posthumously."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I write it all down in a cramped, urgent hand. The pencil scrapes against the paper, the sound loud in the wet quiet. "It was a husband, then," I say, not looking up. "Not a hired man. The scar on his hand — from a chisel, you said. Carpenter. He was mending something before he came down here."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway was quiet for a moment, and when she spoke it was in the tone of a woman grading an apprentice's sums — and finding most of the columns balanced.

"Husband's a guess. Carpenter's arithmetic — and it's good arithmetic, so let's see if the room agrees with you." She raised the lamp and turned it, not on the body, but on the stairs themselves. "Look at the tread just above the waterline. The third one. Look at it and tell me what's wrong with it."

She didn't wait, because the lamp was already showing it: pale wood, unweathered, edges still crisp. Chisel marks in the corners where a man had fitted it snug without a single nail — pegs instead, little oak dowels driven home. Every other step in that cellar was gray and soft with fifty years of damp. That one was young.

"Now that's a carpenter's habit, Pike. A laborer nails. A carpenter pegs — a man pegs what he means to outlast him." She crouched, and there on the step above it, set down square and neat the way a working man sets his tools, lay a chisel. Rusted shut now, but laid straight as a sermon. "And there's his chisel, waiting where he left it. Nobody abandons a good chisel, son. A man sets it down because he means to come back for it."

She turned back to the body, took the left hand gently in both of hers, and turned it toward the light.

"Now the hand, because you've earned the whole of it. Two marks. The scar across the knuckles — years old, white, honest work, that's the one I read you first. But look *here.*" Her thumb indicated a spot in the heel of the palm, below the thumb. A small round mark, no bigger than a shirt button. Healed wrong — healed from the inside out, the skin puckered like a drawn purse-string. "That's not a chisel. A chisel cuts linear. That's a *round* wound, and it healed the way wounds heal when something's been living in them while they close."

She laid the hand back down on the coat-covered chest and looked at the flooded floor for a moment before she gave Pike the reconstruction, flat as an inventory.

"Autumn. Cellar's dry at the steps but the floor's got its winter seep — a hand's depth of water across the bottom, same as every cellar in this valley this time of year, nothing a man thinks twice about. He comes down to mend the stair because it's his house and his trade and he can. He's working in the shallows. He slips, or the wood spits the chisel, and he opens his knuckles on it." A pause. "And there's a swimmer in that seep water the length of your finger, and it smells the blood the way you'd smell bread from the road."

Her jaw set once.

"He'd have felt a sting in the cut and called it the water getting in the wound. He was right about the water. He was wrong about which direction." She nodded at the stair, the pale tread, the waiting chisel. "And then — and this is the part you'll carry up those stairs with him — he finished the job. Pegged it square, set his tool down neat, went up to supper with his hand wrapped in a rag and a story for his wife about his own clumsiness. The door was already open, and he was dead before the first frost, only nobody had told him yet, because the eating takes weeks and it takes it slow."

She stood, knees cracking, and rested her boot on the new tread — carefully, the way you'd test a man's handshake.

"We've been standing on his last work all evening. I expect he'd want to know it held." A dry breath of a laugh, with nothing in it but respect. "It held. He was a man who made things hold."

Then she was all business again, gesturing at the body with the flat economy of a woman closing a ledger.

"Now. Before we carry him up, we go through his pockets — and I want *your* hands in them, not mine. Not because I'm squeamish; because a hunter needs to learn that a dead man's pockets aren't loot, they're his autobiography, and you only get to read it once." She set the lamp on the step beside the body, steady. "We're looking for one thing and one thing only: his name. A billfold, a letter, a tailor's mark, a folded note he couldn't part with. Because when we find his wife, we're not walking up to her door with a shape under a coat and a guess. She's owed better arithmetic than a guess. So go on — coat pockets first, then the trousers, and tell me what the man kept."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I sit on the cellar steps afterwards with the lamp in my hands. "Finish it," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full.)

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway took the lamp out of Pike's hands — gently, the way you'd take a bird off a nervous branch — and set it on the step beside the little row of things Pike had laid out from the dead man's pockets. She looked at them the way she looked at everything: like a ledger.

"Right. Let's read him, then."

She picked up the billfold first. Leather gone stiff as board, but the waxed hide had done its work. She opened it with two fingers and turned it to the light.

"Coins. Three, and look — *still in the pocket.* That's a sentence in itself. A robber takes the money. A deserter takes the money. The tenant doesn't spend, Pike — it never once needed a coin, and it never thought to check. The money outlived the man. That tells you nobody's been through him, which tells you nobody ever found him, which tells you nobody ever came looking down here." She set the billfold aside. "Hold onto that. It matters in about an hour."

Then the paper. Folded small, gone soft as wet leaf, and she opened it with the patience of a woman handling scripture that had been through weather. Most of it was pulp. But the lamp caught one line in a woman's hand, the ink bled but legible:

*...come home before the lamp burns low. — M.*

Halloway read it twice. Her jaw did the thing it did.

"There's the wife. 'M.'" She folded the scrap with more care than she'd shown the knife. "She wrote him a note about a lamp. And I'd wager the windowsill upstairs has a lamp on it with the wick burned down to the glass, because that's what a woman does when her husband doesn't come home — she lights it, and she keeps lighting it, until the oil runs out and she can't afford more." A pause. "We'll check. I don't guess about widows."

Then the last thing. She picked it off the step and turned it in the light: a small wooden bird, waterlogged, one wing carved and sanded fine, the other still rough blank. A wren.

"Half-finished," she said. "In his pocket, not his workshop. That's not stock, that's a *gift.* He was carrying it on him. Working it in the evenings, maybe, wherever he sat." She held it a moment longer than the clinical required, then wrapped it in the same cloth she'd used for the black anchor and put it away. "That's hers. It goes to her with everything else."

Last, the chisel. She turned the horn handle to the light, and there, struck deep with a heated punch, was the mark: **T. B.**

"Carpenters strike their tools like farmers brand cattle," she said. "T-something, B-something. A joiner, by the work on that stair. We'll ask the valley." She stood, knees cracking, and looked down at the covered shape of the man. "That's his autobiography, then, read whole. He was careful with his tools and careless with his knuckles, he kept his wife's notes, he carried a bird in his pocket, and he pegged a stair tread so it'd outlast him." She picked up the lamp. "It did. Now let's go meet the rest of the book."

---

They carried him up the stairs he'd mended. Halloway took the shoulders and made Pike take the ankles, because "you'll want to know what a dead man weighs, and you'll want to learn it on a friendless one, not a friend." He came up lighter than a man should, and she said nothing about it, which was its own kind of saying.

The house above was cold and clean and empty. Dust on the table. Two chairs, one pushed in, one pulled out at an angle nobody had bothered to straighten since autumn. And on the front windowsill, exactly where she'd called it: a lamp, cold, the wick burned down to a black curl against the glass.

Halloway stood in the middle of the room and read it the way she'd read the cellar.

"She left after the oil ran out. Went to kin, most like — you don't stay in a house where a man vanished, because the house keeps *asking* you where he is." She set the lamp down on the table. "We lay him out in the yard. Not on the table. She'll eat at that table someday, God willing, and I won't have put him on it."

---

There was a woodpile behind the house, and it was a carpenter's woodpile — seasoned oak offcuts, stacked and stickered with the same discipline as the stair tread. Halloway built the pyre herself, crosshatched, proper, the way you'd build it if the man inside had spent his life making things hold and you meant to make his last fire do the same.

"Oak burns hot and slow," she said, working. "He'd approve of the fuel economy. That's not a joke, Pike. Well. It's a bit of a joke."

She put the lamp oil across the body, and the seams too, every one she'd found — because fire was the whole doctrine, and water just moved the account somewhere else. Then she stood back and gave Pike the match.

"You opened his pockets. You get the match. That's how the arithmetic of this trade works — the reading and the writing are the same job."

The fire took him at dusk and Halloway stood watch the whole night, because that was the trade too. She didn't sing, didn't speak over it. She sat on the woodpile's remaining half with her knife across her knees and counted, sometimes aloud, sometimes not, and near dawn she said, to the fire, "There. Paid in full," and that was the entire eulogy.

At first light there were bones, and she raked them from the ash with two green sticks, and wrapped them in the dead man's own bedsheet, straight and square as a parcel. She put the chisel and the wren and the scrap of note on top.

"Now the last leg," she said. "And this is the one that kills more hunters than anything with teeth, so mind me. We're walking up to a woman with her husband's bones, and everything you feel about that is correct, and none of it gets to be on your face when she opens the door. Grief has killed more hunters than monsters. A crying person stands one step too close. We do our grieving after."

---

The village had a smithy, and smiths know everything, and the smith knew this: *Tomas Brooke, joiner. Went off before Martinmas, they said. Wife's Maren, at her sister's — the cottage by the mill.*

The sister opened the door, saw the parcel, and made a sound like a floor giving way, and then Maren Brooke came to the door herself, and Halloway took off her hat, which she had not done for king or clergy in thirty years.

"Maren Brooke. I've brought your husband home."

She gave it to her plain, the way she'd promised Pike she gave everything: the stair, the cut hand, the seep water, the weeks. She gave her the locked room honestly — "He was gone before the first frost. He never knew the water, and he never knew the being carried. Whatever walked after, it wasn't him, and it never was him again" — and Maren listened standing up, one hand on the doorframe, and asked only one question, which was, "Did he finish the stair?" and when Halloway said *he did, and it held us all night,* the woman nodded like a person settling an account of her own, and then she wept, and Halloway stood one respectful step back and let her.

The wren broke her. The one finished wing. She held it against her chest and sat down on the floor in the doorway and that was fine, that was allowed, that step wasn't Halloway's to stand too close to.

When Maren could speak again, Halloway gave her the last of the arithmetic, no varnish on it: the young ones loose in the cellar water, five years to the next cellar, fire now or a sealed door and a chalked warning and someone else's problem in a generation.

"Your house, your call. I'll not burn a widow's home without her say."

Maren looked at her for a long moment. Then she got up, and took the lamp off her sister's sill — her own lamp, the one she'd carried to the mill cottage and kept lighting anyway — and said, "He built that house for me. It's done its work. It can do one more."

They burned it at dusk. The fire took the house, and the floors fell in, and the cellar water boiled in the dark under the ruin, and Halloway stood at the fence line with her hat in her hand and said nothing at all for a long while.

Then she put the hat back on, and looked at the burning house, and the grim humor surfaced, quiet as it ever got.

"Note the arithmetic, Pike. She lit that lamp every night for a season, waiting for him to come home. Tonight she finally used it to make sure nothing else ever wears him out the door." She turned from the fire, and the fire lit half her face. "Kindness on the chance it's needed. You don't get to know if it was. You do it anyway."

She started down the road toward the next valley.

"Write that down. And walk in the middle of the road — I told you I make no promises about the little ones, and we're crossing three streams before morning."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I nod, falling into step beside her. The notebook feels heavy in my pocket. "The little ones," I say. "How do you know they won't follow?"

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway walked three more paces in the middle of the road before she answered, and when she did, it was in the tone she used for correcting sums.

"I don't *know*." She didn't slow down. "First thing you'll write in that notebook tonight, before the protocol and after the anatomy: Halloway never knows. Nobody in this trade knows. Knowing is for priests and dead hunters. What I do is arithmetic — I stack the odds until the doubt is small enough to carry in a coat pocket. So let's do the sums on the little ones, and you can carry what's left."

She held up one finger, lamplight from the distant fire still catching her hand.

"Sum one. What we did to them tonight. When I put steel through the anchor — the black one, the landlord — that colony stopped being a colony and became orphans. Everything those young ones knew, they knew because the old one ran them. The playing dead. The four-count. The patience. That was the landlord's craft, learned over seasons inside a man. A young one on its own is a finger-length of appetite with no plan attached. Tonight it's not a hunter, Pike. It's the smallest thing in that water, and everything in that water eats things that size — eels, pike, beetles bigger than it is. Its whole trade tonight is hiding in the deep dark and not being eaten until it's grown. Nothing that small and that hunted chases two armed humans down a road. It hasn't the size, hasn't the mind, and hasn't the taste for us yet."

A second finger.

"Sum two. The fire. You think Maren's lamp was ceremony. It was the second half of the kill. That cellar water boiled under the ruin — I stood at the fence line and heard it, that long hiss going on under the fallen floors, a good while after the flames stopped feeding on timber. Everything that made for the deep of that cellar is cooked. That's the doctrine, and now you've seen why it *is* the doctrine. Steel opens the account. Fire closes it."

A third finger, and here her voice flattened out, because this was the part she wouldn't prettify.

"Sum three. What's left is what slipped out *before* the fire — down the seep, through the field drains, into the mill race. And here's your answer, such as it is: water only runs downhill, and it only runs one way. They can't follow us up this road any more than the stream can. They can't walk. An eel can cross wet grass on a rainy night; these can't manage an hour out of water before they dry out and die. So they don't follow, Pike. They *drain*. They go where the water goes, which is down the valley, away from us, and that's a different problem wearing a different man's coat five years from now."

She let that sit for the length of a fence post going by.

"Which is why, first thing tomorrow, I buy the miller a drink and tell him to draw his water upstream of his wheel for a season. Why I chalk a mark on every well-head down the valley road. Why I keep a ledger of my own, and why tonight's page gets an entry and a date. That's how you answer 'will they follow.' Not by knowing. By leaving the next hunter better sums than the ones you got."

Then she stopped, and turned, and the grim humor came up in her like it always did — at the worst of it, quiet as lamplight.

"But tonight's not about five years. Tonight's about three streams, and *that* risk isn't pursuit — it's contact. A scattered young one in a riffle is a frightened animal, and frightened animals grab what touches them. So here's the protocol, and you'll learn it now while the lesson's cheap." She counted it off like kit inventory. "We cross at the white water — the riffles, shallow and fast. Never the black pools; the pools are where the frightened things sit. Hands in your pockets, nothing dangling, move quick and don't stop to think. On the far bank: boots off, cuffs to the knee, and the lamp held low. I check your legs. You check mine." A dry pause. "Yes, mine. I've been wrong before in thirty years, and I'm too old to be proud about my ankles."

She started walking again, boots square in the middle of the road, well clear of the verges where the ditch water ran.

"Write the protocol down when we stop. Protocol's what keeps you alive at two in the morning, when the shaking starts in earnest and your hands can't remember what your head knows." A beat. "And they don't hold grudges, the little ones. Not tonight. A grudge needs a landlord, and we evicted him."

The fire was a red smear behind the hill now, and the road ahead was dark and smelled of wet fields.

"White water only, hands in pockets. If something grabs you at the crossing, it's a fish. And if it isn't a fish — shout the word anyway, and I'll do the sums."Halloway didn't answer right away. She walked three more paces down the middle of the road, boots square, eyes on the dark verges where the ditch water ran, and when she spoke it was in the tone of a woman correcting an invoice — the question itself, first.

"I don't *know*," she said. "That's your first correction, and it's the important one. Nobody in this trade knows anything. Knowing is for priests and dead hunters. What I do is arithmetic — I stack the odds until the doubt is small enough to carry in a coat pocket. So let's do the sums on the little ones, and you can carry what's left of them."

She held up one finger, the fire behind the hill still catching her hand.

"Sum one. What we did to them tonight. When I put steel through the anchor, the colony stopped being a colony and became orphans. Everything those young ones knew, they knew because the old one ran them — the playing dead, the four-count, the patience. That was the landlord's craft, learned over seasons inside a man. A young one on its own is a finger-length of appetite with no plan attached. It's not a hunter tonight, Pike. It's the smallest thing in that water, and everything in that water eats things its size — eels, pike, water beetles with more ambition. Its whole trade tonight is hiding in the deep dark and not being eaten until it's grown. Nothing that small and that hunted chases two armed humans down a road. It hasn't the size, hasn't the mind, and hasn't the *taste* for us. Not yet. Taste comes later, with a landlord."

A second finger.

"Sum two. The fire. You think Maren's lamp was ceremony tonight. It was the second half of the kill. That cellar water boiled under the ruin — I stood at the fence line and heard it, that long hiss under the fallen floors, a good while after the flames had finished with the timber. Everything that made for the deep of that cellar is cooked. That's the doctrine, Pike, and now you've *seen* the doctrine instead of taking my word for it. Steel opens the account. Fire closes it."

A third finger, and here her voice flattened out, because this was the part she never prettied up.

"Sum three. What's left is what slipped out before the fire — down the seep, through the field drains, into the mill race. And here's the answer you actually asked for. Water only runs downhill, and it only runs one way. They can't follow us up this road any more than the stream can. They can't walk. An eel crosses wet grass on a rainy night; these can't manage an hour out of water before they dry out and die. They don't follow, Pike. They *drain*. They go where the water goes, which is down the valley, away from us, and becomes a different problem wearing a different man's coat in five years' time."

She let that sit for the length of a fence post going by in the dark.

"Which is why, first thing tomorrow, I buy the miller a drink and tell him to draw his water upstream of his wheel for a season. Why I chalk a mark on every well-head down this valley road before we leave it. Why I keep a ledger of my own, and why tonight gets an entry and a date and a stream-name. That's how you answer 'will they follow.' Not by knowing. By leaving the next hunter better sums than the ones you got handed."

Then she stopped, and turned, and the grim humor surfaced, quiet as it ever got.

"But tonight's not about five years. Tonight's about three crossings, and the risk there isn't pursuit — it's *contact*. A scattered young one in a stream is a frightened animal, and frightened animals grab whatever touches them. So here's the protocol, and you'll learn it now while the lesson's cheap." She counted it off like kit inventory. "We cross at the white water — the riffles, shallow, fast-moving. Never the black pools. The pools are where frightened things sit. Hands in your pockets, nothing dangling, move quick and don't stop to be clever. On the far bank: boots off, cuffs to the knee, lamp held low. I check your legs. You check mine." A dry pause. "Yes, mine. I've been wrong before in thirty years, and I'm too old to be proud about my ankles."

She started walking again, and nodded at the notebook in Pike's pocket without looking over.

"Write the protocol down when we stop, before the shaking makes up its mind. Protocol's what keeps you alive at two in the morning, when your hands can't remember what your head knows." A beat. "And they don't hold grudges, the little ones. Not tonight. A grudge needs a landlord, and we evicted him."

The fire was a red smear behind the hill now, and the road ahead smelled of wet fields and running water.

"White water only, hands in pockets. If something grabs you at a crossing, it's a fish." Her teeth showed briefly in the dark, not quite a smile. "And if it isn't a fish — shout the word anyway, and I'll do the sums."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I pull the notebook out, the pencil still wet in my hand. "What's the word?" I ask. My voice is steadier than I thought it would be.

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway kept walking, but her mouth did the thing that was almost a smile and never quite committed.

"For tonight? 'Fish.'"

She let a fence post go by before she explained, because a lesson without its arithmetic was just noise.

"One syllable. Starts hard, ends hard — a word you can shout through a mouthful of fear without your tongue getting lost on the way. And it carries over water, which matters, because at a crossing I'll be upstream of you and the stream will be loud and my ears are fifty years old." A dry beat. "Also, nine times in ten, it'll be accurate. So it keeps me honest."

Then she stopped being funny, because the next part wasn't a joke.

"But understand what the word *is*, Pike, because that's the actual lesson. It's not information. If you shout 'fish,' I don't learn that there's a fish. I don't learn anything. The word is a *tripwire* — I hear it, I turn, I move, and no questions get asked until both of us are on dry ground with our boots off. That's the whole contract, and it's the only reason the word works: because we've agreed on it now, in the calm, on a dry road, while your hands are only shaking a little." She tapped the notebook in Pike's pocket with one knuckle, without looking over. "Panic strips a person's vocabulary down to nothing. I've seen grown men with thirty words of profanity in ordinary weather stand in a river at two in the morning and come out with no words at all. So you don't pick the word in the moment. You fix it now, while you can still think, so that when you can't think, your mouth has somewhere to go that isn't nowhere."

She walked a stretch in silence, the first stream audible somewhere ahead now — a thin, rushing sound under the dark.

"Rules of the word. One word, not two — two words means you're composing, and composing means you're thinking, and thinking at a crossing is how the water gets its chance. Shout it even if you're not sure. *Especially* if you're not sure. A false alarm costs me a wet boot and a bad temper. A swallowed alarm costs considerably more, and I've priced both." Her boots stayed square in the middle of the road. "And shout it even if you think it's already too late — because 'too late' is another thing you'll be wrong about at two in the morning, and I'd rather turn for a corpse that doesn't need turning than not turn for one that does."

Then, quieter, in the tone she used for the entries in her own ledger that nobody else read:

"Mine's been the same for thirty years, for what that's worth. 'Tam.'" She kept her eyes on the road. "My partner's name. He's the one taught me the system — the tripwire, the pre-agreed word, all of it. He just never got to use his half of the contract, because the thing that took him didn't leave anyone standing who knew the word." A pause, exactly one breath long. "So I've carried both halves since. You shout 'Tam' at me in a river and I'll turn before I remember why. It's the only inheritance he left, and it's held up better than most."

She rolled her shoulders once, and the ledger voice closed, and the working voice came back.

"But that's mine, and you'll have your own, and 'fish' will do fine for tonight. Now — first crossing is just ahead, and I can hear it's running shallow over stones, which is white water, which is what we want." She drew the lamp down low in her hand. "Protocol. Hands in your pockets. Nothing dangling. Move quick, don't stop to be clever, and on the far bank — boots off, cuffs up, and we check each other's legs like I said. You shout 'fish,' I come. Even if you're sure it's a fish." Her teeth showed briefly in the lamplight, not quite a smile. "*Particularly* if you're sure it's a fish. That's when they get careless, the little ones — and us with them."

She stepped down off the road crown toward the sound of running water.

"Write the word down first, before anything else. Before the protocol, before the anatomy. One word, circled. Because everything else in that notebook is for the next hunt, and the word is for tonight."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I write "fish" in the notebook and circle it twice. The lead is smudged from my damp fingers. "If I shout, you'll turn," I say, and it's not a question.
