dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
The cellar had four feet of standing water in it and something at the far end that had stopped moving about a minute ago.

Halloway held the lamp up and did not go closer yet. "Right," she said. "Before we touch it. What do you see?"

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I make myself look properly instead of at the water. "I don't know yet," I say. "Something wrong with the shape of it."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
"Good. Wrong shape is the start of everything." She crouched at the top of the steps, lamp angled so the light fell flat across the water's surface rather than glinting off it. "Now say more. Don't tell me what you think it is. Tell me what's actually there. How many limbs are at the wrong angles, where the weight sits, whether the head's facing the way a head should face."



The water had gone still. Not the stillness of something resting — the stillness of something that had finished whatever it was doing. She'd seen that particular quality before, usually about four seconds before the thing started up again, and she kept one eye on Pike and one on the far end of the cellar without either of them appearing to do both at once.

"Take your time," she said, which was not what she meant. She meant *hurry*. But the first thing they'd learn was that hurrying was how people miscounted limbs.

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I squint, trying to ignore the churning in my gut. "Two limbs visible above water. One's bent... backwards at the elbow. The other's straight but too long. No head I can see."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
"Two limbs, one reversed at the joint, one extended beyond normal proportion, no cranium presented." Halloway nodded once, as though Pike had passed a small examination. "That's four facts. Good. Now the hard part."

She shifted her weight onto her back foot, keeping the lamp steady. The light caught something on the water's surface about two feet from the thing — a ripple that hadn't come from the thing itself.

"Something's moving out there that isn't the body. See it?"

She waited. Pike would either see it or wouldn't, and either answer told her something.

"Could be a second one. Could be the first one still being alive and that shape you're seeing is just how it's lying while it decides what to do next." She said it the way someone might note the weather. "Either way, we don't go in until you've told me where the water ends and the thing begins. Because right now I can't tell from here, and if we're wrong about which part of that is *it*, we find out the expensive way."

The lamp hissed. She hadn't lowered it, hadn't moved closer. Thirty years of standing at the edge of dark water had taught her that the worst mistakes weren't made by people who were afraid — they were made by people who were certain.

"What else," she said. "Keep going."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: "Was that a person?" I ask. "Recently, I mean. Is that what I'm looking at?"

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
"Right question," Halloway said. "Wrong order of operations. You've got the shape. Now you want identity. That's natural, but it's backwards." She tilted the lamp a fraction of a degree — enough to change what the light fell on, not enough to signal approach. "Identity comes after you know where the edges are. Identity is how people get sloppy."

But she looked. Of course she looked. Thirty years didn't kill curiosity; it just ranked it below survival.



The light raked across the water and found the straight limb again. Too long — she'd give Pike that. If it was a forearm, it was a forearm on something taller than a person, and the joints were set wrong for it to be a trick of the water. The reversed limb she studied longer. Elbows bent backward in humans were broken things, and broken things bled, and the water around it was dark but not the *right* dark.

"Clothing," she said. "Look for clothing. If whatever's out there was a person recently, there'd be something human — a boot, a belt, a sleeve, *something* that didn't grow there. Things that are born that shape don't wear things."

She let the lamp drift back to the body.

"What I can tell you: the proportions aren't right for a person. Too long in the limb. Wrong at the joint." A pause. "What I can't tell you is whether something *became* that. Which is why we're still standing here."

The second ripple had not repeated. That didn't make her comfortable. That made her watchful.

"Your gut's been wrong yet?" she asked. Not as a challenge — she genuinely wanted to know. Gut was data too, if you knew how to read it.

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I swallow hard. "No. Not yet." I force my eyes to trace the line where the water meets the thing. "There's... a tear. In what might be cloth. Floating near the bent limb. It's not moving with the water."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Cloth. That changed things. Not the shape — the shape was already established and wrong — but the *history*. Cloth meant something had been wearing it. Cloth meant an event: a garment made, a body put inside it, and then whatever had happened in this cellar to put it in the water.



"Show me exactly," Halloway said. She didn't move from the top of the steps. "Point, don't reach. Where is it relative to the joint — above it, below it, caught on it?"

She watched Pike's hand rather than the cloth. Hands were honest. If Pike's hand drifted toward the water, she wanted to know before it got there.

"Fabric that doesn't move with the water means it's snagged on something. Could be on the limb itself. Could be on whatever's under the surface that you and I can't see." She let that sit. "And fabric that's been in standing water for any length of time does one of two things — it swells and holds the shape of what was underneath it, or it rots away to nothing. If you can see a *tear*, that means it's not rotted, which means whatever happened to the thing in the water happened *recently*."

She adjusted the lamp again. The light found the cloth — a scrap, dark, caught against the reversed joint like a flag on a broken mast. It was the wrong color for this cellar. Too clean.

"Recent enough to still be cloth instead of memory," she said. "That's useful. That tells us we're not looking at something that's been down here for months. We're looking at something that happened in a window of time, and the window might still be open."

The water held still. She didn't trust it.

"Here's what I want next," she said. "Can you see whether the cloth is *on* something — wrapped around the limb, tied to it — or whether it's just *near* it. Because if it's on it deliberately, someone put it there. And if someone put it there, we're not the only ones who've been close enough to touch this thing."

She let the question hang without softening it.

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I wade closer and hold the lamp where she can work. "Tell me what happened to it," I say. "Plainly."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway did not say *get back*. Saying it would have been too late to matter and would have taught Pike the wrong lesson — that she'd been wrong to move rather than that moving had consequences to manage.

So she read where Pike stood instead.

"You're in the water," she said, flatly. "You went in without knowing where the edge is. That's done now — don't move again until I tell you where it's safe to stand. Feel for the bottom with your feet, not your hands. Anything that touches your ankles that isn't the floor, you stop."



She came down the steps after that, one at a time, lamp held out ahead of her, feeling each step before committing to it. The water took her to mid-calf. Cold, but cold wasn't information.

When she was close enough, she crouched — carefully, keeping her balance — and looked.

The plain version.

"It was a person," she said. "Recently. The cloth is a shirt — torn, not cut, which means it came off against something rather than being taken off by choice." She pointed with two fingers, not touching. "The reversed limb is broken, not jointed wrong by nature — see how the forearm sits? Someone or something bent it past where it stops. The extended limb isn't longer than it should be. It's *dislocated* at the shoulder and pulled straight. That's why it looks wrong."

A pause. She let the lamp play over the waterline where the torso would be.

"No head above water. That means either the neck failed and it's separated, or the head's under and the water's holding it there." She said it without ceremony. "I can't tell you what *happened* yet because I can't see the torso and I'm not going to turn it over in standing water where I can't see what's underneath it."

She looked at Pike.

"But I can tell you what wasn't natural. Three injuries, none of them defensive. Nobody fights like that. Something did this *to* it — systematically, limb by limb. That's not an animal feeding. That's an order of operations."

She straightened up slowly.

"Now you've seen it plainly. Tell me what you want to do next."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I look at the water around my legs. "I want to get out of this water," I say, voice too tight. "But we can't leave it here."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway let the silence do its work for a moment. Pike's voice had gone tight, and tight voices made people either freeze or rush. She needed to know which one she was dealing with.

"Good," she said. "Both of those things are true at the same time, and the fact that you can hold both without dropping either one is the only reason I'm letting you stand in that water."

She straightened her knees slowly, keeping the lamp up. The thing in the water didn't change. That meant it was dead, or it meant it was patient. She'd worked with both.

"We're not leaving it," she agreed. "But we're also not pulling it out tonight. Here's why." She counted on her fingers without lowering the lamp. "One — we don't know what's under it, and the torso is the part that tells you *what* did this. You don't move a body until you've seen that part. Two — there's still something else out here moving in this water, and I haven't accounted for it. Three — dragging a waterlogged body up those steps with no way to light both our hands means at least one of us carries it blind. Things that were blind down here didn't do well."

She looked at the shirt snagged on the reversed joint.

"We mark the spot. We come back when we can see." She paused. "That's not cowardice. That's order of operations."

She waded toward the steps, deliberately — not fast, not slow. Showing Pike what steady looked like when your body wanted the opposite.

"Come up behind me. Don't look back at it — you've seen what you need to see. Eyes on my lamp and feet on the steps. When we're on dry ground, you can tell me what your gut says, and then we decide together what gets done about it."

The water let them go one step at a time, and neither of them rushed, and that was the whole victory for now.

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: "I need the detail," I say. "Tell me exactly what it did to him -- what is under the skin now, what it took, how far it got. If I meet another one I need to know."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway stopped on the third step from the top and stood there, water streaming off her trousers, lamp held steady at her side. She didn't turn around yet.

"You want to know what's under the skin," she said. "That's the right question. I'm going to tell you what I can see and what I can't, and I need you to hear both parts equally."



She turned then, leaning against the wall, and set the lamp on the step above her so both her hands were free. She held up one finger.

"Dislocated shoulder, pulled straight. That took force in a direction — someone grabbed the arm and *extended* it. Not a flail, not a fall. A grip. Which means the thing that did this has hands, or appendages that function like hands, and enough strength to separate a shoulder joint cleanly without tearing the arm off at the socket. That's controlled force." Second finger. "Forearm broken backward at the elbow. Same thing — controlled, specific, *past* the natural stopping point. A predator feeding doesn't bend arms. A person breaking someone's arm for compliance bends it that far. This wasn't feeding. This was *dismantling*."



Third finger. "Three points of damage, limb by limb, each one isolated. No crush injuries, no drag marks along the skin I can see, no tearing of flesh. If something was eating him, you'd see it in the limbs first — they're the most exposed. There's no evidence of that." A pause. "What there *is* evidence of is someone — something — working through him methodically. Joint by joint. Which means at some point he was held still enough for that to happen, which means either he was dead before it started or he was restrained. Both options are worth knowing."

She held up a fourth finger and then lowered it.

"That's what I can see. Now the part where I stop."

She picked up the lamp. "What's under the skin — what it *took*, how far it got — I can't answer from here. That information is in the torso, and the torso's under the water with the head. Until I get eyes on the chest and the abdomen, I'm giving you inference, not fact. And inference is how people get killed."

She began climbing the rest of the steps.

"But here's what thirty years has taught me about things that take things." She paused at the top, turned back. "Whatever it was doing to him, it started with the limbs and worked inward. Limbs first means it wasn't interested in the organs yet. Organs come second — they're what you take when you're *hungry*. Limbs come first when you're either restraining or when you're *taking the arms for something*." She let that sit. "If it had finished, we wouldn't be looking at a body with a shirt still on it. It got interrupted, or it got full, or it got scared."

She stepped onto dry ground and wrung water from her sleeve with clinical disinterest.

"So when you meet another one — and you might — what you know is this: it grabs, it extends, it breaks, it works in order, and it stops before the torso. That tells you it can be interrupted. That tells you it has a sequence. And things with sequences can be disrupted at the wrong step."

She looked at Pike steadily.

"Now your gut. What's it saying?"

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: "It's saying the thing isn't done," I hear myself say, still standing calf-deep on the steps. "It left a meal. It'll come back for it."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway didn't move for a moment. She stood on the dry floor at the top of the steps, lamp in hand, and let Pike's words settle into the shape of a tactical problem rather than a feeling.

"That's the right kind of gut," she said quietly. "That's the kind that keeps people alive. Because you're not saying it because it's scary — you're saying it because that's what *I'd* say."



She began pulling a length of cord from her coat — worn, waxed, the kind that didn't slip when wet. She worked it through her fingers as she talked, not tying anything yet.

"Interrupted mid-sequence with the torso untouched. Which means one of three things: it was full, it was scared, or it was called away. Full doesn't come back for seconds — not for something that was taking its time. Scared doesn't come back either, not until it's sure the threat's gone, and that could be hours or days. But called away..." She looked at Pike. "Called away comes back. That's the one I'd bet on. Something with that method of working doesn't leave a meal because it changed its mind. It leaves because something more urgent pulled it off the line."

She tied the cord around the railing at the top of the steps and let the end dangle down into the water, marking the stair line. Then she found a nail in her coat, one of dozens, and hammered it into the doorframe with the butt of her knife — three sharp strikes that sounded too loud in the cellar.

"There's your mark. If we come back and the cord's cut or moved, we know it's been here. If the water's been disturbed beyond what stagnant water does naturally, same answer." She stepped back from the doorframe. "Now we're going to close this door and we're going to decide what kind of night we're having."

She looked at Pike steadily.

"Your gut says it comes back. My experience says it comes back. That's two data points from two different kinds of evidence, and they agree, which means we plan for it coming back." She paused. "The question isn't whether — it's *when*, and what we want standing here when it does. A cellar full of standing water is its ground, not ours. If we want to be here when it returns, we need to change that before we do anything else."

She blew out a slow breath through her nose.

"So. Before you tell me your gut anything else — tell me what you know about this cellar. Who dug it, why, how old it is, and whether anyone's been down here before us tonight. Because if someone came down here recently enough to leave that shirt on a living person, they left other things too."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: She starts cutting and I hold the lamp steady and don't look away. "Keep describing it," I tell her. "Everything -- what's underneath, what it smells like, how far it got. Don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway drew the knife along the seam of the shirt with the patience of someone opening a letter they already knew the contents of. The fabric split along the thread rather than the blade — she'd been cutting the stitch, not the cloth. Stupid to dull a blade on cotton.

"Closer with the lamp," she said. "Not closer with you. Lamp only."

She peeled the shirt back from the reversed forearm and held it open like a page.

The skin underneath was wrong before it was damaged. That was the first thing — wrong before the break, which meant the break wasn't the origin. The forearm was too smooth. Not smooth as in unblemished, smooth as in *uniform*. No hair, no pores, no freckling or scarring or the thousand small failures that a person accumulates over a life. It looked like something made from one material rather than assembled from many.

"Skin's wrong," she said. "See it? Not injured — wrong from the start. No hair, no marks. Whatever this was wearing before it was a person, it was wearing it as skin."

She moved the light down to the break itself.

The elbow had separated backward — the olecranon process forced through skin that should have held it. Around the wound, the tissue was dark but not bleeding. Not *anymore*. The wound had been made and the body had stopped responding to it, which meant the cardiovascular system had shut down at some point between the injury and now. She pressed two fingers above the wound, not touching the exposed joint, feeling for the firmness of muscle that hadn't yet begun its work.

"Smell," she said. "Come up when I tell you to and don't you dare do it early."

She leaned in first herself. The water had its own smell — standing water, mineral, faintly sweet where the cellar floor was brick and old. Underneath it, something else. Not putrefaction. Putrefaction had a specific architecture: it built from the gut outward and announced itself early and loud. This was wrong in a different direction. Acrid, almost metallic, with an undertone she recognized from situations she didn't want to describe to Pike on a first night.

"Copper and something like wet slate," she said, pulling back. "That's not rot. Rot comes later. That's whatever replaced what was inside him, still reacting with the air." She paused. "Smell it now if you're going to."

She waited, then nodded as Pike presumably did whatever Pike did.

"记住 that smell," she said in English, switching back without apology. "记 sorry — remember it. That's the smell of the thing before it's had time to become a corpse. In a week, rot takes over and you lose it. But if you smell that in a cellar again, you know something *changed* and it was recent."



She cut further down the arm, exposing the forearm to the wrist. The dislocation at the shoulder was higher — she'd need to cut the sleeve entirely off for that, and the torso still lay under water.

"There's no bruising," she said. "That's the detail I want you to hold onto. A break in a living person bruises — blood leaves the vessels, tissue swells, the color tells you the timing. This wound has no bruising at any margin. Which means either the body had no blood left when the break was made, or..." She trailed off, examining the exposed joint with the lamp held at an angle that flattened the shadows. "Or what's in there isn't blood."

The joint cavity was visible. She angled the light.

Inside, where marrow should have been — white and dense and identifiable — there was a void. Not hollow, not empty. Filled with something dark and granular that shifted when the water lapped against the arm, the way wet sand shifts.

"That's what's under the skin," she said. She kept her voice level because level was the only way to say it. "Where the marrow should be, there's something else. It's been there long enough to fill the cavity completely — the bone isn't hollow anymore. It's packed." She paused. "Whatever was inside him when this was made, it didn't take the bones. It *inhabited* them."

She cut one more inch, found the wrist, and stopped.

"That's as far as I go tonight." She sheathed the knife. "What I know now that I didn't an hour ago: the thing wearing this body wasn't born into it. The skin was wrong before the injury. The break had no bruising. The marrow is replaced with something that responds to water movement. And the smell — that smell — is chemical, not biological, which means the thing underneath is still *doing* something even though the body stopped moving."

She sat back on her heels and wiped her hands on her trousers, which accomplished nothing except the ritual of it.

"Your gut said the thing isn't done. Here's what I'd add to that." She looked at Pike. "It's not that the thing isn't done. It's that the thing is still *in there*. The body stopped, but whatever packed the bones didn't get the memo." She let the lamp hiss. "So when we come back — and we are coming back — we don't bring a stretcher. We bring fire."

She stood, knees cracking, and offered Pike a hand up the last two steps without ceremony.

"Anything else you need to know while we're still close enough to know it? Because after this we're going upstairs, and I'm going to want a drink that isn't water from a cellar with something in it."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I let out a shaky breath I didn't know I was holding. "Fire," I repeat. My voice sounds thin. "I need to know how much."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway took Pike's hand without comment and pulled her up the last step. Her grip was firm and brief — the kind that communicated *you're up, now you're on your own* rather than *I'm helping you*.

"How much," she repeated. "That's a carpenter's question, not a hunter's question, and it's the right one."



She settled onto the dry floor with her back against the wall, lamp between her knees, and worked at the problem with the same dispassion she'd given the body.

"Burning a body is easy. Burning a *body* is what funeral pyres have done for ten thousand years — get it hot enough, long enough, and it's ash. Bone calcines at about eight hundred degrees, which is a good campfire's worth of heat. That's not your problem."

She held up a finger.

"Your problem is what's packed into the marrow. Granular, dark, responsive to water movement, packed tight enough to fill the cavity completely. That's not tissue. That's not bone. That's a *medium* — something something else lives in. And mediums behave one of two ways when exposed to heat." Second finger. "Either they burn like everything else, or they don't. And if they don't, you've just given them heat and attention and a lot of smoke to announce where you are."

She tapped her knee twice.

"So how much fire? Here's what I'd do." She held up her palm and started counting again. "First: confirm it's flammable. We test a sample — I take a small piece of what's in that marrow cavity, we set it on something non-combustible, and we see what it does. Does it ignite? Does it resist? Does it do something we've never seen before? Thirty seconds of testing tells us more than an hour of speculation."

"Second: if it burns — and if it burns *clean*, no residue, no reaction — then the answer is total. Not the limbs, not the torso. The whole thing, bones included. You don't leave a single piece. You grind what's left after burning and you burn the grindings. Whatever this is, it lives in bone. I'm not giving it bone to live in."

"Third — and this is the part where you need to hear me clearly." She stopped counting and fixed Pike with a look. "If it *doesn't* burn — if the sample resists, or does anything unexpected — we stop. We don't improvise with more fire. Things that survive heat tend to be things that have survived heat before, and whatever's in those bones didn't get there by being fragile. In that case, we look at what it *is* — its material, its chemistry — and we find the thing that dissolves it or starves it. Chemistry, not thermodynamics."

She let the lamp crackle in the silence.

"How much fire depends on what the sample tells us. Tonight, we don't need any. Tonight, we close the cellar door, we mark the cord, and we sleep somewhere with a door that locks from the inside."

She paused, and something shifted in her face — not softness, exactly, but a crack in the clinical surface where the grim humor liked to get out.

"But I'll tell you what I've learned about fire in thirty years, since you asked." The corner of her mouth moved. "There's no such thing as too much fire. There's only fire you didn't plan for, and then you're the one standing in it." She stood and rolled her shoulder, stiff from crouching. "We plan for it. That's the difference."

She looked down at the cellar door, the cord still running through it into the dark water below.

"Come on. Drinks first. Questions after. And if you dream about the smell, that's normal. If you dream about *hearing* the smell, you come find me before you go back down there."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I sit on the cellar steps afterwards with the lamp in my hands. "Finish it," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full.)

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway leaned against the wall opposite, arms crossed, and looked at Pike sitting there with the lamp in her hands — not doing anything with it, just holding it the way people hold things when their hands need a job that isn't thinking.

"Finish it," Halloway repeated. "You want the whole thing. Not the parts I've been giving you in order. The whole thing, the way I'd write it up if anyone ever asked me to write things up."

She looked at the cellar door. Looked back at Pike.

"Right. Sit with it, then."

She slid down the wall until she was sitting too, back against stone, and folded her hands in her lap with the air of someone opening a file they'd rather not open.

"Full account. I'll tell you what I saw, what I didn't, what I've inferred, and where the line is between the three. You stop me if you need me to say something again. You stop me if something doesn't make sense. And you *don't* stop me because it's unpleasant, because you asked for it and I'm going to give it to you properly."



She took a breath.

"First: the body. Male, based on the bone structure I could see at the wrists and what the shirt tells me about shoulder breadth. Broad-shouldered, which means whatever got him had to work against mass. Age is difficult — the skin was wrong from the start, so I can't use it. Bone density suggests somewhere between thirty and fifty, but I'm guessing. I'll know more when I can get to the hips, which are under the water." A pause. "Height I can't tell you either, because one arm's pulled out of socket and the other's bent the wrong way, and neither of those gives you a reliable line to measure against."

"Noted and moving on."

"The injuries. Three, all in the upper limbs, none of them defensive — no wounds on the forearms that would indicate blocking, no scraped knuckles, nothing that says he raised his hands to protect himself. Which tells me one of two things: either it happened too fast for him to react, or he was already compromised when it started. Paralyzed, drugged, unconscious — something. A man with a broken shoulder and a shattered elbow would have marks on his hands from fighting back unless he *couldn't* fight back. There are no such marks. So he couldn't."



She let that sit.

"Dislocation at the right shoulder. The humeral head was forced anteriorly and inferiorly — out the front and down. That's what happens when someone grabs an arm and pulls it straight past its range, which means the thing that did this was standing in front of him, facing him, gripping his arm with both its hands or whatever it has. It wasn't behind him. It wasn't ambushing from the side. It was *facing him* when it did this."

Halloway unfolded one hand and held it up, fingers spread.

"Break at the right elbow. Olecranon forced posteriorly — the bone pushed through the back of the joint until the skin gave way. The break itself is clean, which means it was fast. A slow break tears. A fast break snaps. This was fast. Which means once it had the arm where it wanted it, it bent it in one motion. No hesitation. No adjustment. It knew exactly how far to go and it went there." She closed her hand. "That's not something that's learning. That's something that's practiced. Or something that's built to do exactly that."

"Left arm was next, if we're reading the order of operations from the extremities inward. The skin there was intact where I could see it, but the musculature had a density to it that was wrong — too uniform, the way the forearm on the right was too smooth. And beneath that skin, at the wrist, I could see where the tissue had a faint pattern to it. Almost like grain. Like wood. Like something that had a structure and direction to it rather than the random mess of muscle and fat you'd find in an arm."

"I didn't open that one. You should know that. I stopped at the wrist on the right arm and I didn't cut anything on the left. What I'm telling you about the left arm is from sight and touch — pressing on it through the skin. That's inference, not observation. I'm flagging it because you asked me not to leave anything out, and one of the things I could leave out is the part where I'm not sure."

"The torso. Still under the water. I could see the outline — ribs, the suggestion of a sternum, the flat plane of the abdomen — but the water distorted it enough that I couldn't commit to any detail. The head is beneath the surface as well. Based on the position of the shoulders and the angle of the visible limbs, I'd estimate the torso is lying face-down, which is why we can't see the head — it's under the body, not beside it."

"That matters for a reason I don't love. If the face is down and the head is beneath the body, then whatever was on his face or in his mouth is pressed against the cellar floor. If there's something *in* his mouth — something that got in, or something that was put in — it's been sealed against brick for however long he's been down here, which means whatever is inside him that likes a sealed dark space has been in its ideal conditions. I don't know if there's anything in his mouth. I'm telling you it's a possibility because you asked for everything and I'm including the possibilities alongside the facts."

She shifted her back against the wall. Stone was unforgiving after the first few minutes.

"Smell. I described it earlier but you asked me to finish, so I'll go deeper." She paused, choosing words with the care of someone laying out tools. "The primary note is copper. Not iron — people say iron when they mean blood, but this wasn't blood. Blood has a specific smell when it's been in contact with air for more than a few hours — it goes sweet, then sharp, then it becomes recognizable as decay. This was sharper than blood. Brighter. Like a coin in your mouth."

"Underneath the copper: wet slate. Mineral. The kind of smell you get from a cave where water has been moving over stone for a thousand years. That's the cellar's smell, but *concentrated* — as though the body were producing it rather than sitting in it. Which means whatever's packed into those bones is actively reacting. Not decaying. Not breaking down. *Reacting*. Doing chemistry. The way a hot coal does chemistry when it sits in open air."

"And underneath *both* of those — this is the part that made me decide we come back with fire rather than a shovel — there was something I've smelled exactly four times in thirty years. I'm not going to tell you what the four times were because they're not relevant and it'll take too long, but I'll tell you what it smelled like because you asked. It was sweet. Not rot-sweet. Not fruit-sweet. Sweet the way a flower is sweet — the smell of something that wants to attract. Something that was *calling*."



Halloway stopped talking. Looked at Pike. Looked at the lamp in Pike's hands, at the steady light of it, and seemed to find some reassurance in the fact that it was still just a lamp.

"I don't know what called what," she said. "I don't know if the smell was meant for something in the cellar or something above it or something that was supposed to come *through* the cellar. I only know that four times in my career, when I've smelled that particular chemical sweetness coming from something that was supposed to be dead, there was a second one. Not a second incident — a second *body*. A second thing in a state of being not-quite-right. Because whatever packs the bones doesn't do it alone. It has company. Or it sends for company."

She held up a hand.

"That's inference. Strong inference, but inference. I'm giving you the fact and the read separately because you asked me not to blur them."

"The things I don't know. I'll list them so you have the shape of the gap." She ticked them off. "One: what's in the torso. Two: whether the head is intact. Three: what's under the water besides the body — I felt the cellar floor with my feet the entire time and it was brick and silt, nothing else, but my feet only cover so much area. Four: whether what's packed into the marrow is uniform throughout the skeleton or localized to the limbs I could feel. Five: how long the body's been in the water — no insect activity I could see, which in a cellar this cold and wet could mean days or could mean weeks. Six: who this was, and what they were doing in a cellar that somebody dug for a reason I haven't been told."

She stopped ticking.

"And seven — the one I've been sitting with since the first ripple, the one that made me keep the lamp at a distance instead of walking straight in. The thing that's under the water that isn't the body. I saw it once. It moved once. It's been still for..." She checked. "...close to an hour now. That stillness could mean it left. That stillness could mean it's waiting. What I *will* tell you is that I've been watching the far end of the cellar for the last twenty minutes while I talked to you, and the water surface at the far end is not the same as the water surface at the near end. Near end: still. Far end: a slight, continuous vibration I can feel in the steps when I press my palm flat against them. Something is humming down there. Not moving — *humming*. Like a frequency. Like something vibrating at a speed too fast to see and too slow to hear."

She looked at Pike steadily.

"That's everything. Every fact, every inference, every gap. The parts I'm certain of, the parts I've reasoned my way to, and the parts I'm frightened of but won't dress up as anything other than what they are."

She sat in silence for a moment.

"Now you know what I know. Which means we're in this together, and neither of us can pretend we don't." A beat. The grim humor surfaced like something from deep water. "Congratulations. You're officially one of the four people alive who knows what it smells like when the marrow is doing chemistry. We should get jackets."

She didn't laugh. She let Pike hear it, though, and then she stood and offered a hand up again — the same firm grip, the same brief contact.

"Come on. Up the stairs. Door gets closed and barred from the outside, cord stays visible, and we find somewhere to sit where the walls aren't wet and the floor doesn't hum."

She paused at the top of the stairs and looked back down into the dark.

"And Pike?" She waited until Pike looked at her. "You handled that. I've seen people handle it worse. I've seen people handle it better. But you *handled* it, which means your gut was right when I asked it at the start — you don't break, you just get tighter. Tight is good. Tight keeps the shape."

She pulled the cellar door shut and dropped the bar across it.

"Now let's go be somewhere else."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I stare at the closed cellar door, the lamp's glow finally still. "I'm not sure I want to know what it smells like when the marrow stops doing chemistry."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway didn't laugh, but she exhaled through her nose in a way that had laughter compressed into it, like a bone set back into place — correct and slightly painful.

"That's the right fear, though," she said. "Because there are two answers to that question and neither is good."

She set the lamp on the floor at the top of the stair and rested her boot on the edge of the cellar door, not pressing, just reminding it that it was closed and she knew where it was.

"Answer one: the marrow stops doing chemistry because the body's been empty — whatever was in it left or was taken out. That's a smell I'd like to describe to you someday, and it would be 'nothing.' Bone that's been drained of whatever was living in it smells like a house after everyone's moved out. Cold and generic. You'd hate it because it'd be *ordinary*."

She paused.

"Answer two: the marrow stops doing chemistry because the body's been *restarted*. Because whatever packed those bones decided the shell had served its purpose and it moved on to the next stage. And I've never smelled that, because every time I've been close enough to be in the cellar when it happened, I wasn't in the cellar for much longer."

The grim humor came back at the edges, thin and sharp.

"But I'll tell you the third answer nobody thinks about. The marrow stops doing chemistry because *something else* stopped it. Because something bigger or meaner or more efficient came down into that cellar and the little thing in the bones — the one doing all that lovely wet-slate chemistry — got eaten, or shut down, or *recruited* by something operating at a different scale entirely."

She lifted her boot off the door and looked at Pike properly.

"And *that* smell," she said, "I have smelled. Once. And I'm not describing it tonight because it would be the wrong first impression, and because you still have to sleep somewhere in this building and I'd rather you sleep than lie awake cataloguing odors."

She picked the lamp up and held it between them, its light doing the small, ordinary work of illuminating a hallway instead of a cellar.

"You want to not know what it smells like? Good. That's a healthy appetite for ignorance and it'll keep you alive longer than curiosity will — though not as long as curiosity plus discipline." She nodded toward the corridor. "Right now we find that room with the door that locks from the inside, you put down the lamp, and we both pretend we can still smell copper on our hands even though we can't, because the nervous system is an idiot and it'll be another hour before it stops offering."

She started walking, then stopped without turning around.

"And Pike — if tomorrow morning the cellar smells different when we open the door, we *don't* go in. We wait for the sample. We plan for the fire. We do it in that order, because order of operations is the only thing standing between us and the third answer." A beat. "And if it smells like nothing — if it's gone cold and generic and empty down there — that's not good news either. That's just the house after everyone's moved out. And somewhere, something else is looking for its next address."

She kept walking.

"First room with a working lock. I'll take the one nearest the stairs — you'll want to be away from the cellar door if you want any sleep at all."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I follow her down the hall. "Which room had the lock?" My voice is steadier than I expect.

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway glanced sideways at Pike without breaking stride. Steadier voice. She filed that away the same way she filed everything — quietly, without ceremony.

"Third door on the left has a lock," she said. "Iron bolt, interior side, no key needed. I checked it when we came in because I check every door in every building I'm going to sleep in. The room at the end of the hall — the one with the window — has a lock too, but it's a brass tumbler and the plate's been pulled at some point, which means it looks locked and isn't. I don't sleep in rooms that lie about being locked."

She reached the third door and pushed it open with her boot rather than her hand. Standard procedure — hands stayed free for anything that might be behind a door, and after what they'd been doing in a cellar for the last few hours, she wasn't going to pretend the habit was paranoia.

The room was small. Bed, chair, a washstand with a basin that had a film of dust on it thick enough to write in. Window shuttered. Floorboards dry. She swept the lamp across the corner behind the door, under the bed, and up to the ceiling where the plaster had cracked in a line that might have been structural and might have been age.

"Empty," she said. "Dry. Door bolts from the inside." She tested the bolt — slid it back and forth once, listened to it, tested it again. Metal on metal, solid, no give. "This is yours."

She held the door open while Pike went in, then stepped back into the hallway.

"Rules for tonight," she said. "Not because I think you'll break them — because having them stated means we're both working from the same document." She held up a finger. "One: the lamp stays lit. Not for comfort — for information. If something in this house moves, I want to know by shadow before I know by sound. Two: if you hear anything from the cellar — and you might, because sound travels up stairs better than it travels through water — you wake me before you investigate. My room's the next one along. I'll be easier to wake than you'd think; I've been doing this for thirty years and light sleep is the only kind I've still got. Three: the window shutter stays closed. Not because I think anything's coming through it. Because I don't *know* what's coming through it, and I'd rather the uncertainty be behind a piece of wood."



She looked at Pike in the lamplight — steadier voice, steadier hands, the whole person slightly more assembled than the one who'd been standing calf-deep on cellar steps an hour ago.

"One more thing," she said. "And then I'll leave you to it."

She leaned against the doorframe, arms folded.

"You said you didn't want to know what it smells like when the marrow stops doing chemistry." She nodded, once, approving. "That's not cowardice — that's a boundary, and boundaries are what sane people build around things they're not ready to metabolize yet. I've been doing this thirty years and I still have boundaries. There are things I've *chosen* not to know. Things I walked away from rather than open because I understood that opening them would change how I worked, and how I work is the only tool I have."

She paused.

"But here's what I want you to sit with before you sleep. You said that an hour ago as a fear. In three days, when we've taken the sample and tested it and planned the fire, you might say it again as a *question*. And that'll be the moment you've moved from 'handling it' to 'understanding it,' and understanding it means you can't un-know it, and you'll have the smell in your memory for the rest of your life whether you want it there or not." The corner of her mouth twitched. "That's the trade. You asked for the full account. The full account doesn't stop at the door."

She pushed off the doorframe.

"Bolt the door. Lamp on the washstand — not on the floor, fire risk, and not near the bed, in case you knock it in your sleep. If you hear the cord move — if you hear *anything* that sounds like cord being dragged across stone — you come get me. Not open the door and call. Come. Get. Me." She held Pike's gaze for a moment. "Understood?"

She didn't wait for more than a nod. She never did — she'd learned that asking people to confirm obvious things made them doubt the obvious.

"I'll be next door. Same rules for me, except I won't be sleeping for another hour. I want to sit with my back to the wall and listen to the house settle, because houses settle when they're quiet and houses that *don't* settle are houses where something else is already listening."

She started to turn, then stopped — one of her half-turns that meant a thought had arrived late and was being checked against everything else she knew.

"And Pike — the smell on your hands. I told you it'd take an hour." She held up her own hand, palm out, under the lamp light. Ordinary hand. Ordinary skin. "It's been forty minutes. In twenty, you won't smell it. And then one morning in about six months, you'll be doing something completely ordinary — cutting bread, holding a pen, resting your hand on a table — and you'll smell it again. Sharp, copper, wet slate, sweet. It'll last about two seconds and it'll be gone." She lowered her hand. "That's not the cellar. That's your memory doing its job too well. When it happens, you'll know the difference between a memory and a fact, because you'll be standing in a kitchen instead of a cellar, and the fact will be that the kitchen is dry."

She gave the door a final look — bolt, frame, hinges, the gap underneath where the floor met wood.

"Bolt it behind me. Sleep with the lamp lit. And if tomorrow morning the cord's moved, you find me before you find the cellar."

Then she was gone down the hall, her footsteps deliberate and unhurried, the kind of walk that suggested she was listening to everything behind her and couldn't be bothered to pretend otherwise.

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I stare at the bolt, then slide it home with a solid *thunk*. I set the lamp on the washstand like she said, then sit on the edge of the bed and press my hands flat against my thighs. They aren't shaking. I check twice.
