dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
The cellar had four feet of standing water in it and something at the far end that had stopped moving about a minute ago.

Halloway held the lamp up and did not go closer yet. "Right," she said. "Before we touch it. What do you see?"

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I make myself look properly instead of at the water. "I don't know yet," I say. "Something wrong with the shape of it."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
"Good," Halloway said. "Wrong how. Take it apart."

She kept the lamp steady so the light wouldn't lie to him. The thing at the far end sat half-submerged, the water around it still rippling outward in slow, closing rings. Whatever it was, it was the size of a large dog, and it was the colour of nothing in particular — grey-white, waxy, like something that had been pickled and then badly put back together.

"Shape's the first thing that'll save you," she said. "Colour lies. Sound lies worse. Shape's usually honest."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I squint, trying to make sense of the silhouette. "It's got... too many joints? Like it's folded wrong."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
"Folded wrong is exactly it," Halloway said. She shifted the lamp a fraction, letting the shadows fall differently across the thing. The light caught on the ridges — and there were ridges, now that you looked, running along what should have been its back like the segments of something that had molted and kept the old skeleton for spares.

"Count the joints for me. Not the bends — the joints. Where two pieces meet and shouldn't."

She let him work it out. The water lapped at the cellar walls. Whatever it was, it had stopped twitching, but she'd stopped believing in dead a long time ago. Stopped moving was not the same as stopped. She'd learned that in Herefordshire, in a root cellar not unlike this one, and the lesson had cost her two fingers and a partner.

"Take your time," she added. "But not much of it."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: "Was that a person?" I ask. "Recently, I mean. Is that what I'm looking at?"

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway looked at the thing again — not with fresh eyes, because she'd already done her seeing, but with the specific attention of someone checking a box she'd hoped to leave blank.

"Recently, no," she said. "There's no swelling. No gas. The water's clean around it, or as clean as cellar water gets. If this were a person who'd died this week, the water would be doing things it isn't doing."



She let that sit for a moment.

"Waxy like that, though — that's soft tissue that's been *worked*. Something's taken it apart and put it back. The joints your eye caught, those aren't joints. Those are seams. Whoever — whatever — built this thing didn't have the bones right, so it's folding where it shouldn't, and it's stiff where it should flex."

She crouched slightly, bringing the lamp lower so the light hit the waterline. The reflection trembled.

"Was it a person once? Maybe. Long enough ago that the shape's worn off. But I'll tell you what I *can* tell you." She paused, and her mouth did something that wasn't quite a smile. "It's not dead. It's just finished."

She straightened up and looked at Pike sidelong.

"So. Floor's yours. What do we do with a thing that isn't dead and isn't moving? Think about it, because I'd rather you get it wrong in words than wrong with your hands."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I swallow, my throat suddenly dry. "We don't touch it at all. We back out and... salt the water? Burn the whole cellar?"

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway considered it. She didn't laugh — Pike was doing the right thing by thinking, and you didn't punish thinking — but she did tilt her head the way a butcher looks at a carcass that's come in wrong.

"That's two ideas," she said. "One of them is close. The other one gets us both killed."

She lifted the lamp and let the warmth of it press against her knuckles. The water lapped. The thing stayed where it was.

"Salting the water. Think about it — four feet of standing water, and what, a cellar floor the size of a kitchen? That's not salted water. That's *brine*. You'd need a tonne of it to do anything but sting. And burning — with what? The whole cellar's already flooded. The floor's stone. You want to smoke ourselves out in a confined space with a thing down there that might not *need* to breathe?"

She let him hear it. Then she shifted the lamp again, and her voice came down half a register — not gentler, just closer.

"But the instinct is right. *Don't touch it. Don't engage. Restrict it.* You got the first part, and the first part's the one people die without. So keep pulling the thread."

She took one slow step sideways, putting herself between Pike and the cellar stairs. Not heroic. Positional. The door was behind her and that meant the door was behind *him*.

"Salting's not wrong. *Where* you salt is what matters. The thing's in the water and the water's in the cellar — but the cellar's got a door and a floor and a drain somewhere it isn't coming from. So where do you put the salt so that it's doing the work, and where do you put it so that it's just decoration?"

She waited.

"And think about the order. Because in this trade the order's usually the part that gets you killed. First thing, second thing, third thing. Lay it out for me."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I wade closer and hold the lamp where she can work. "Tell me what happened to it," I say. "Plainly."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway's hand came down on Pike's shoulder and tightened. Not hard enough to bruise. Hard enough to stop.

"You're wading," she said. "I didn't say wade."

She held him there a beat — long enough for the water to settle around his legs, long enough for him to notice that it had gone still in a way it shouldn't have, the ripples from his own movement dying faster than water dies. Then she let go and stepped back up onto the cellar's one dry stone, the ledge by the door where the water hadn't reached.

"Thirty years," she said. "I've earned the right to answer the question when I'm ready. You've earned the right to ask it. Neither of us has earned the right to be careless about the order."

But she owed him the answer. She'd asked him to think, and you couldn't ask a man to think with half the facts and then call the result a lesson.

"Plainly," she said, and took the lamp back so it swung free and threw long shadows up the cellar wall. "Someone or something took a body — human, animal, doesn't matter, it's been worked past the point where that distinction is useful — and remade it. Unstitched it. Put it back with the wrong numbers. Extra segments where there should be none. Missing the bits that would let it move right."

She watched the thing in the water. It hadn't moved. That was still not the same as stopped.

"The seams are dry," she said. "The waxiness is preservative — something in it is keeping it from rotting, which means it's meant to be kept. This isn't a kill, Pike. This is a *thing someone made*. It was put here. Placed. And it stopped moving about a minute before we came in, which tells me it was doing something until we arrived, and then it stopped, and that should worry you more than if it had come at us."

She let the lamp settle.

"Placed, not grown. Preserved, not decaying. Folded wrong, not *broken* wrong. Those three words are the whole story. You want to know what happened to it? Someone built it and set it down here like a lantern on a doorstep. Now." She turned her head. "You still haven't told me where the salt goes. And you're still standing in the water."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I look down at the water, my legs suddenly cold. "The salt goes at the threshold. The door, the drain. You contain where it can go first." I take a slow step back toward the ledge. "Second thing is... we find who built it."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway nodded once. Not praise — acknowledgement. The two were different and she kept them different.

"Threshold and drain," she said. "That's containment. And you got your feet out of the water, which is the part I was actually waiting on." She was already moving, pulling a heavy waxed canvas roll from inside her coat — salt, coarse, grey with impurities, the kind that came in sacks and not shakers. She kept two pounds on her at all times and had done since the winter of '07. "The second thing is right too, but you've got the order wrong inside it. Finding who built it is important. It is not *second*."

She worked fast now, shaking a line of salt across the cellar threshold in a stroke that was neat and thick and didn't waste. Then the drain — she'd spotted it in the corner on the way in, a rusted iron grate, and she laid a ring around it, wide, and then doubled back over it.

"First: contain. Second: secure. *Third*: understand." She straightened up and tossed the emptied canvas roll aside. "The maker is a conversation for tomorrow with dry feet and full light. Right now the question is whether this thing is a message or a trap, and those are very different pieces of furniture."

She stopped. Her hand stayed near her coat.

The water had done something. Pike wouldn't have noticed — he was still getting his boots onto the ledge and watching her hands — but the rings around the thing at the far end had started again. Slow. Closing. Not from the thing moving. From *beneath* it.

"Pike," she said, very calmly. "Walk to the stairs. Don't run, don't splash. Move like you're leaving a room where someone's sleeping."

She didn't look at him. She was watching the water.

"That's not a message," she said. "That's a trap with something still in it."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: "I need the detail," I say. "Tell me exactly what it did to him -- what is under the skin now, what it took, how far it got. If I meet another one I need to know."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway heard him and understood and hated him for asking at exactly the right moment, because the thing in the water shifted again and this time the movement wasn't beneath the body — it was *through* it, a ripple that started at the far end and worked toward the seams like a hand smoothing a tablecloth from underneath.

"Fine," she said. "Walk and listen."

She kept her voice level and clinical and she did not look at him, because looking at him meant taking her eyes off the water and the water was now the only honest thing in the room.

"Under the skin: soft tissue that's been stripped to the fascia and re-laid. The original muscle's gone — *gone*, Pike, not withered, not atrophied. Removed. What's underneath is a lattice. Something like cartilage, something like connective tissue, but grown in patterns that don't match any anatomy I've seen in thirty years and I've seen some creative anatomy. The seams you spotted? Those are where the lattice terminates. It's not stitched together. It's *grafted* — sections fused at the joints where the builder ran out of material or ran out of interest."

The ripple reached the second seam. The thing's leg — what had been a leg — trembled once, a single twitch, like a dog dreaming.

"What it took: everything structural. Bone's been dissolved and replaced — that's what the folding is. The replacement framework bends where bone wouldn't and locks where bone should hinge. The builder wanted it compliant. Something you could *store*. Which means it was meant to be activated later and it has not yet been activated and whatever is under it right now is doing the activating."

She tasted copper. She'd bitten the inside of her cheek without noticing.

"How far it got: far enough. The skin's intact, which means the builder was careful — that's preservative work, wax and something else, something alkaline. The eyes are gone. The mouth's been sealed — fused, not closed. No airway. Whatever's animating it doesn't use lungs, which means fire was never going to work and you should be glad I stopped you."

She reached the stairs without turning around and put her boot on the first step.

"That's your detail. Print it and put it somewhere you'll find it at three in the morning, because that's when you'll need it."

The water was lapping at the salt line now. Not crossing it. Not yet. Just — *testing*.

"Now climb. And when we're at the top, you're going to hold the door and I'm going to salt the frame, and then we are going to walk — *walk* — to the front of this house and find whoever left this here, because they knew we were coming and that thing down there knew it too, and I would very much like to know how."

She looked at the water one last time. The rings had stopped again.

"That's the other thing about traps," she said, and her mouth did the thing that wasn't quite a smile. "They're patient. We don't have to be."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I nod, taking the stairs two at a time but careful not to run. "How does a thing like that even know we're here?" I ask, my voice low. "It hasn't got eyes."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway's hand found the doorframe before Pike was through it. Salt followed — a thick line down both sides, a stripe across the top, and a heavy pour across the threshold that she stamped flat with the heel of her boot so it bonded to the old wood.

"It doesn't need eyes," she said. "Eyes are for light. Eyes are for *distance*. That thing's not operating at distance. It's operating in four feet of standing water in a cellar with stone walls, and you just waded through half of it."

She straightened up and looked at him in the half-dark of the corridor. The lamp threw her shadow long and thin against the wallpaper.

"You're thinking of it as a creature," she said. "It's not. It's a *sensor*. The lattice under the skin — the framework — that's not structural support. Not entirely. It's conductive. Water's a medium. You stepped in the water and the water moved and the lattice felt it the way a spider feels a foot on its web. Doesn't need to see you. You *are* the disturbance."

She started walking toward the front of the house, boots heavy on floorboards that had gone soft with damp.

"And that's the other reason I stopped you wading. Not because it would come after you — though it might. Because every step you took was telling it the size of us, the number of us, the speed of us. You were walking straight into a bell and ringing it with your shins."

The house was quiet in the way houses are quiet when they're listening. Somewhere ahead — a kitchen, maybe, or a parlour — there was a sliver of grey light under a door.

"One more thing," she said, and stopped at the end of the corridor with her hand out flat against the wall. "The salt line's going to hold the water, and the water's going to hold the signal. So whatever's down there knows we're *up* here now, and it knows we left, and it knows we didn't finish it. That's fine. That's deliberate. A trap that's been *sprung* and found empty is worse for the trapper than one that goes off. Somebody down there is going to have to come and check, and when they do—"

She pulled the door open. Grey daylight, flat and cold, hit them both like a slap.

"—we'll be at the front of the house instead of the back, and I'd like to know what face we're looking at." She stepped out, blinking once, and scanned the yard. Nothing. A low wall. A gate. A lane running off to the left toward the village, and to the right, toward nothing in particular.

"Pike. When we find whoever did this, and we will — you don't talk. You don't ask questions. You watch their hands, and you watch their feet, and you tell me what you see. Questions are for after. Hands are for now."

She set off toward the gate, shoulders squared, salt-stained coat turning in the wind.

"And for what it's worth — that was a good question. The eyes. Most people would have stopped at *what is it*. You went to *how does it work*. That's the right instinct. Wrong order, but right instinct." A pause. "Story of my whole career."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: She starts cutting and I hold the lamp steady and don't look away. "Keep describing it," I tell her. "Everything -- what's underneath, what it smells like, how far it got. Don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway stopped walking. She turned around slowly and looked at Pike with the expression of a woman who has been interrupted mid-sentence by a sheep.

"We're in a yard," she said. "There's no lamp. There's no cutting. There's a gate, a lane, and the beginning of a headache."

She held up one hand — the one with the missing fingers — and ticked off what she'd already given him.

"Seams. Grafts. Lattice. Dissolved bone. Fused mouth. Alkaline preservative. Conductive framework. No lungs, no eyes. That is what's underneath. I've told you. Twice."

She started walking again, slower now, watching the lane.

"As for smell — formaldehyde and wet chalk. Alkaline, like I said. It's the smell of something that's been *kept*, not something that's lived. If you ever catch that smell in a room where there's no obvious reason for it, you leave. Not walk. *Leave*. Because it means something's been stored there and you don't know if it's finished being stored."

Her boots crunched on the gravel.

"And how far it got — as far as being *placed*. Not activated. Not deployed. Placed. Like a loaded gun on a shelf. Someone built this thing, folded it up, carried it to that cellar, and set it down in the water where the signal would carry. Then they left. That's how far it got. Before us. Not toward us."

She reached the gate and put her hand on the latch but didn't open it yet.

"You want me to cut into it. I understand that. You want to *know*, and knowing means hands-on. But that thing is sitting in water that's wired to its own skeleton, and the last time I opened something like that before I understood what was animating it, I lost—" She glanced at her hand. "Well. You can see what I lost."

She opened the gate.

"When we've dealt with the builder, we go back. I'll open it up and you can watch every cut. But we do it dry, on ground, with the lattice severed and the medium drained. Not down there. Not yet."

She looked left toward the village, then right toward the empty lane.

"Now — hands and feet. Remember. No questions."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I don't see anyone. "But they'd be gone by now, wouldn't they? They set the trap and left." I'm scanning the lane, the low wall, the way the grass is bent.

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway watched Pike watching the ground and felt something she hadn't felt in a while — the specific, unwelcome sensation of someone doing the right thing before she'd told them to.

"Gone," she said. "Maybe. Probably not."

She let go of the gate and walked back a few paces, then crouched at the edge of the lane where the grass met the gravel. She didn't touch anything. Thirty years. You learned not to touch.

"Think about the setup. That thing took time to build — days, maybe weeks. The preservative alone needs to cure. Then it gets carried here, placed in the water, arranged so the signal carries. That's not a drop-and-run. That's someone with a *relationship* to this house. Someone who knows the cellar floods. Someone who knew the water level, knew the drain, knew the stone floor."

She looked along the lane. Empty. Wind moving through the hedge. A crow, somewhere, doing what crows do.

"People don't set traps in places they don't know," she said. "And people who know a place don't leave it. They stay close enough to hear when it works."

Then she looked at what Pike was looking at. The grass.

There. Along the low wall — not bent so much as *pressed*. In a line. Consistent width, running parallel to the wall for about twenty feet before turning toward the house. Not a path. Not worn. Just... disturbed, in the way that something heavy gets dragged along the ground and the grass remembers.

She said nothing for a moment. Then she pointed.

"You see that. Good. Now tell me — does that look like something that was carried in, or carried *out*?"

She straightened up and rolled her shoulder, the way she did when something was settling into place she didn't care for.

"And keep watching the feet. I said hands and feet because that's how you read a person. But you've got no person yet, so you're reading the ground instead, which is the same skill with worse lighting." A beat. "I'm not going to pretend that's not annoyingly competent."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I sit on the cellar steps afterwards with the lamp in my hands. "Finish it," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full.)

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway looked at him for a long moment. The lamp in his hands threw the light upward and made his face all cheekbone and shadow. She'd seen that look before — the one that meant a person had carried something around in their chest for hours and was now asking to be allowed to put it down.

"Finish it," she said. "Right."

She set the canvas roll on the top step and unrolled it. Instruments — not surgical, not anything a doctor would recognise. A hooked blade with a spine like a fish-gutting knife. A flat rasp. A pair of long-handled pliers with rubber grips she'd cut herself from a bicycle inner tube. A glass jar with a wax seal. Two more blades, smaller. A length of copper wire. She laid them out in order of use because that was how she thought and how she worked and how she stayed alive.

"You asked me before what happened to it," she said, "and I told you. Now you want to see what I was talking about. That's different. Seeing it changes things. Once you've seen what's under skin like that, you don't unsee it, and it'll be in your head when you sleep for about six months. After that it just becomes a thing you know."

She picked up the hooked blade and the lamp and stepped down into the water.

It came up to her shins. Cold — bone-cold, the kind that got into you and stayed. She noted it and ignored it. The salt lines were holding at the threshold and the drain. The water was still. The thing at the far end hadn't moved since they'd come back down, but she didn't trust that and she didn't need to.

"Come down and hold the lamp low," she said. "Waist height. Keep the angle constant. If I lose light I lose precision and if I lose precision I lose fingers and I've only got so many left."

She waited until the light was steady. Then she crouched beside the thing and placed her left hand flat on its flank — the part that had been a ribcage, maybe, before the bones were dissolved. The surface was cool and firm and slightly tacky, like unvarnished wood that's been in a damp room. She pressed. It gave a quarter of an inch and then stopped.

"Feel that," she said. "Press it yourself when I'm done. It's not soft. It's not hard. It's *structural* — there's something under there holding a shape. That's the lattice I told you about. First thing you need to understand is that this thing has no skeleton and it doesn't need one. The framework is the skeleton and the skeleton is the framework. They're the same thing. Whoever made it didn't replace the bones. They replaced the *concept* of bones."

She put the hooked blade against the flank, just behind the front leg — the leg that had twitched. The blade was sharp enough to part paper in midair. She drew it slowly across the skin.

The skin didn't bleed. She hadn't expected it to, but it was worth watching for.

The incision opened about eight inches, and the skin parted the way leather parts — reluctantly, with a faint wet sound, curling back at the edges. What it revealed was—

"Look," she said. "Look at this. Tell me what you see before I describe it, because you'll remember it better."

She held still so the lamp could get at it.

Under the skin: not flesh. Not anything she had a word for in the common vocabulary. It was a lattice, as she'd said — but the word didn't do it justice up close. It was a network of pale, semi-translucent struts, each one about the diameter of a pencil lead, running in overlapping diagonals like the geodesic frame of a dome. They were slightly yellow, slightly glossy, and they met at nodes — swollen junctions, like joints, like the knuckles of a hand made of paraffin wax and fishing line. The whole structure had a faint luminescence to it. Not glow, exactly. A *response* to the light. Like deep-sea tissue. Like something that had learned to live in the dark and had forgotten it was supposed to be dark.

"These are the seams I mentioned," she said, pointing with the blade's tip at a node where two sections of lattice met and fused. "See the color change? That's a graft boundary. The builder grew these sections separately and joined them here. Like welding, but biological. Except it's not biological. It's not *alive* in any sense I can measure. It's active. There's a difference."

She switched to the flat rasp and used it to press down on one of the struts. It flexed, sprang back.

"Elastic," she said. "That's what I meant about compliance. Bone wouldn't do that. Bone would snap or resist. This bends and returns. The builder wanted something that could be *folded* — compressed for transport, set down, and then unfold when triggered. Like a piece of furniture. Like a camp bed."

She cut deeper. The hooked blade worked through a second layer of something denser — the lattice thickened toward the centre of the body and the struts became finer, more numerous, packed together until they looked almost solid. She separated them with the blade's tip, gently, the way you'd open the pages of a water-damaged book.

"Here," she said. "This is what I wanted you to see."

At the core of the lattice, running the length of the body from where the head had been to where the tail — there was no tail. The body simply ended. But running along that length, inside the lattice like a wire inside a cable, was a *strand*. It was dark. Not black. A deep, bruised purple-brown, the colour of old blood in a jar. It was about as thick as her little finger and it was continuous — she couldn't see where it began or ended because both ends disappeared into the denser lattice at the body's extremities.

"This," she said, "is the conductor. This is the thing that felt your footsteps in the water. It's not nerve tissue — it's not *tissue* at all. It's mineral. Iron-heavy. It runs through the entire lattice like a wire through a wall, and it's the reason the water mattered. The water completes the circuit."

She touched the strand with the tip of the blade. Nothing happened. She pressed. Still nothing.

"It's dormant," she said. "Deactivated. See how it's dry? If this were live, it'd be wet — the mineral would be drawing moisture out of the lattice. It's been shut down. Something interrupted the signal."

She sat back on her heels in the water and looked at Pike over the top of the opened thing.

"Which means it worked. The salt line didn't just contain it. It *cut* it. The lattice is conductive and the salt created a boundary the signal couldn't cross. Whoever set this trap just lost their connection to it."

She went back to cutting. She opened the front leg next — the one that had twitched — and found the same lattice, finer, packed around a joint that shouldn't have been there. The node was swollen and the struts radiating from it were slightly discoloured.

"See this? This is a *conversion point*. Where the builder took something that used to be a knee and made it into something that hinges the wrong way. That twitch you saw earlier — that wasn't animation. That was a spasm. The framework trying to remember what it used to do and doing it wrong."

She cut the leg node free with three precise strokes and dropped it into the glass jar. It made a small, hard sound against the glass.

"That's coming with us. That's evidence."

Then she moved to the head end. Or where the head should have been.

"Careful with the light here," she said. "This is the part."

The skull — what had been a skull — was gone. In its place was a dense, rounded knot of lattice, tight as a fist, struts wound around each other so densely that it looked almost like a bead of amber. She didn't cut it. Not yet. She held the lamp close and looked at it.

"The builder packed it," she said. "Packed it tight. Whatever was in here — brain, skull, the parts that made it *recognisable* as whatever it started as — they're compressed. Crushed down and integrated. This is the control node. The part that tells the lattice what shape to hold and when to respond."

She touched it. Cool. Slightly vibrating. Not moving. Just *present*.

"If this were live," she said, "I wouldn't be touching it. If this were live, I wouldn't be in the same room. But I want you to see the density, because if you find another one of these and the node is warm and wet and pulsing, you leave the building and you burn the building and you don't go back for anything."

She cut around the node carefully and freed it. It was heavier than it looked. She sealed it in a second jar.

Then she went back to the body and cut it open along the ventral line — belly side — in one long, careful stroke. The skin parted. More lattice. The same strand. But here, at the centre, she found something she hadn't expected.

She stopped cutting.

"Pike."

Her voice was different. Still clinical. But the clinical part had gotten thinner, the way ice gets thin over running water.

"Come closer. Look at this and then tell me if you see what I see."

In the centre of the ventral lattice, where the organs should have been — where there *would* have been, in whatever this had been — there was a cavity. Small. Sealed. About the size of a hen's egg. The lattice grew around it in careful, deliberate patterns, like a wall built around a window.

And inside the cavity, dry and preserved and impossibly intact, was a tooth.

A human tooth. An incisor. Small. A child's.

Halloway looked at it for a long time. The water lapped around her knees. The lamp burned.

"That," she said, "changes the timeline."

She didn't touch it. She looked at Pike and her face was very still.

"When I said this might have been a person once — long enough ago that the shape's worn off — I was wrong. That's not a tooth that's been here for years. That's a tooth that's been here for *weeks*. The preservative kept it the way it kept everything else, but look at the root. The root is fresh. The socket it came from closed over recently. That is a child's tooth that was pulled or knocked out, and it's been placed *inside* this thing at the centre of the frame like a —"

She stopped. Her jaw worked.

"Like a signature," she said. "Or a keepsake. Or a *component*."

She sat back in the water and put the hooked blade down on the stone beside her and pressed both hands flat against her own knees, because if she didn't hold onto something she was going to pick up the blade again and start cutting in ways that wouldn't be careful.

"I told you earlier this was placed, not grown. Built, not spawned. Someone made this. Someone with hands and tools and time and knowledge." She looked at the tooth in its sealed cavity. "And now we know they made it out of a *child*. Not the whole child. The soft tissue is gone — I said that already. But this tooth is a piece. A piece of someone. And it's in there like a heart. Like the thing this creature was supposed to *carry*."

The lamp flickered. The water went still.

"So when I said *find the builder* — I meant it as a job." She picked up the blade again and cleaned it on her sleeve, slow and deliberate, the way she did when she was buying herself three seconds. "Now I mean it as something else."

She stood up. Water streamed off her coat. She looked down at the opened thing on the cellar floor — the lattice exposed, the dark strand running through it like a bruise, the cavity at its centre holding a child's tooth the way a mouth holds a secret.

"This is what's underneath," she said. "Everything. Seams, grafts, lattice, conductor, node, and whatever that tooth was to whoever put it there. That's how far it got. That's what it took."

She stepped toward the stairs.

"And it smells like formaldehyde and wet chalk and now, with it opened up — underneath that — like milk. Like a nursery. Like something that used to be warm."

She climbed the steps and stopped at the top and did not look back.

"You wanted me to finish it. That's finished." A pause. "Now we're going to find who did this to a child and put it in a box in the water, and when we find them, I need you to remember what I said about hands and feet."

Her hand on the doorframe. The salt still holding. The house still listening.

"Because I am going to have *questions*, and I am going to want to ask them with words, and it will be very important that I do."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I don't look away from the cavity. "It's not just a component," I say, my voice quiet. "It's a compass. The tooth points back to the rest of them."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway's hand stopped on the doorframe. She didn't turn around immediately, but her shoulders changed — the way a hunting dog's shoulders change when it catches something the handler hasn't smelled yet.

Then she turned. Slowly. She looked at Pike the way she'd looked at the lattice earlier: not with surprise, but with the specific recalibration of someone updating a model.

"Say that again," she said. "Not because I didn't hear you. Because I want to hear how sure you are."

She came back down two steps. Then stopped at the waterline, which was as far as she needed to go, because she could see the cavity from here — the lattice cradling it, the tooth sitting in its little sealed window like something waiting to be read.

"A compass," she said. She tasted the word. Rolled it. "You know what — you might be right. And if you're right, then we've been thinking about this wrong since we got here."

She sat down on the step. Not tired. Thinking. The lamp was in her coat pocket now and the light came from the cellar's single grimy window, which turned everything the colour of old dishwater. Her hands hung between her knees. The missing fingers caught the light and she didn't hide them.

"Here's what a compass means. It means there's a *north*. Every compass has one. That tooth didn't end up in this thing by accident and it didn't end up in there as decoration. If the builder wanted a trophy, they'd have kept it somewhere they could look at it. If they wanted a component — a power source, a trigger — there are better materials. Mineral. Organic. This is a *human* piece, and human pieces are specific. They carry something. Sympathy. Linkage. The old rules — and I do mean old, Pike, the ones that predate me, predate my teacher, predate the *profession* — the old rules say a part of a person is a road back to the rest of them."

She picked up a pebble from the step and turned it over in her fingers.

"So either that tooth points to a body. Or it points to a *place*. Or — and this is the one I don't like — it points to *more of these things*. Because if the builder is working systematically, and everything about this setup says they are — the precision, the curing time, the placement — then this isn't a one-off. This is a process. And processes have inputs."

She tossed the pebble. It hit the water with a small, flat sound.

"Children lose teeth all the time. That's the part that's going to keep me up tonight. They lose them naturally. They put them under pillows. They leave them in coat pockets and on windowsills and down the backs of sofas. If someone was *collecting* them — sourcing material — they wouldn't need to take a child. Not at first. They'd just need to be somewhere children *are*. And there are a lot of places children are."

She looked at Pike. Her face was doing the thing it did when the grimness and the humour were sitting in the same chair.

"But that tooth was *knocked* out. You saw the root. I saw it too. That socket closed over recently and it closed over rough — that's not a natural loss. That's extraction. Blunt. So somewhere between "walking through a schoolyard" and "doing worse" there's a line, and I suspect we'll find out which side of it our builder is on before the day's out."

She stood up and brushed off her knees.

"Compass. Right. Here's what we do with that. I've got a woman in Ludlow — doesn't matter her name, matters that she's honest and she knows more about sympathetic links than anyone in three counties. We take the tooth to her. Not the whole thing — we take the *tooth*, sealed, in glass, and we ask her to read the direction. North. Where's north. If it points to a place, we go there. If it points to a person, we find them — and Pike, if it points to a *living* person, a living child, then everything I said about questions comes off the table and we skip straight to the part where I stop being polite."

She started up the stairs again.

"One thing at a time, though. Contain. Secure. Understand. We contained it. We secured the samples. Understanding is the compass and the compass is in Ludlow." She paused at the top. "And that tooth stays in the glass. In *my* coat. Not because I don't trust you. Because if you're right — and I think you are — then anyone who wants to find that thing's relatives is going to be looking for that tooth, and I'd rather they found me than you."

A beat. The house creaked. The water settled below.

"Compass," she said again, quieter. "Thirty years, and I didn't see it. You did." She shook her head. "Don't let that go to your head. It'll slow your hands down."

She held the door open and the cold light came in.

"Now come on. Ludlow's forty minutes if we find a car and a lifetime if we don't."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I pick up the jar with the node in it. "If it's a compass... what if the tooth isn't pointing *back*?" I look at her, the cold from the water finally hitting me. "What if it's pointing *forward*?"

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway stopped in the doorway with her back to the lane and the cold grey afternoon and the whole rest of the day she'd been planning out in her head, and she stood there for about four seconds without moving, which was four seconds longer than she usually needed.

"Forward," she said.

She turned it over the way she'd turned the pebble. The same fingers. The same absent, half-conscious motion, except now she wasn't holding anything and the fingers just worked at each other, the two good ones and the three that ended where they ended.

"That's a different thing," she said. "That's a very different thing."

She came back inside and closed the door because the door was the right place to be while thinking, and stood in the hallway with her hand still on the latch. The house creaked. Somewhere below, the water settled.

"A compass that points back is a *find*. You find a body, you find a place, you close it out. That's a job with an end. Fine. But a compass that points forward —"

She took the jar out of Pike's hand. Not rudely. Deliberately. She held it up to the grey light from the hallway window and looked at the node inside it, the dense packed knot of lattice sitting in its own faint, sea-floor luminescence at the bottom of the glass.

"That's a *feed*," she said. "That's not a marker. That's an input. It tells the thing where to go next, or who to go to next, or what to do when it wakes up. And if the tooth is the thing that tells it *forward*, then the tooth isn't evidence of where the builder's been."

She set the jar down on the hallway table, very carefully, beside a bowl of potpourri that had died of natural causes some years ago.

"It's a *schedule*."

She looked at Pike and her face had gone somewhere past grim into the flat, quiet place where the work actually lived.

"Think about what that means. If the builder is working forward — if these things are built in series, and each one carries a tooth, and each tooth is a next step — then there's a *first* one somewhere. A tooth that points to the second, a second that points to the third. A chain. And we found — what? A middle link? An end link? We don't know, because we've only got one, and one link tells you the chain exists but not which way it runs."

She walked to the window. The lane was still empty. The crow had moved to a different hedgerow and was doing the same thing there.

"And if the tooth points forward to the *next* thing — the next build, the next cellar, the next child —" She stopped. Her hand came up and pressed flat against the window glass. "Then we've been asking the wrong question all afternoon. We keep asking *where did this come from*. We should be asking *where is it going*."

She turned around.

"Ludlow's still the answer. My woman there can read a direction, but I've been thinking of direction as *origin*, and if you're right, direction is *destination*. Same tool. Different question. She reads it, we ask her which way the thing wants to travel, not where it came from."

She picked up the jar again and put it inside her coat, next to the tooth's jar, and patted the pocket once like you'd check your keys.

"And if it points to a house with children in it —" She didn't finish the sentence. She didn't need to. The unfinished part was heavy enough to hold up on its own.

She opened the door and held it and the cold came in and moved through the hallway like something with its own business.

"Forty minutes to Ludlow. Come on."

A pause on the step. The wind. The lane.

"And Pike —" She looked at him sidelong, and the mouth did the thing again, the thing that wasn't a smile. "When we get there, you say the forward part. You figured it. My woman respects a clean idea and she's going to want to hear it in the voice that found it. And I'd like to see her face when she realizes I brought a beginner into her parlour with a better hypothesis than mine."

She stepped out into the grey.

"Don't let it go to your head. I've already said that once and I meant it both times."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I pick up the lamp and follow her out, my boots squelching on the wet stone. "It won't," I say, but my hands are shaking. I tuck them into my coat. "But if it points forward... we might already be late."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
The lamp was bad and the tent was worse and the man on the table had been shouting for long enough that he had mostly stopped.

"Both shoulders," Sedge said, laying things out in a row. "When I say hold, I mean hold. He's going to buck and you're going to want to let go, and you're not going to."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I get my weight on his shoulders and find somewhere on the canvas wall to look. "Ready," I say, which is a lie.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge did not answer the lie. Lies were common in tents that smelled of blood and lamp-oil, and sometimes they were the only thing a person had left to offer. What mattered was whether the hands stayed where they were put.

She checked the man’s pupils, then the pulse at his wrist, then the faster, worse pulse at his throat. Shock was already sitting in him like water in a boot. She had no clean morphine and no time to pretend otherwise.

“Listen to me,” she said, leaning so the bad lamp threw her shadow over his face. “Both shoulders are out. I am putting them back. It will hurt more than what you have already survived for about fifteen seconds. Then it will hurt in a way you can think about. If you scream, scream. If you faint, that is inconvenient, but it is not fatal. I don’t enjoy this, and I am not asking you to.”

His mouth moved. Sedge did not wait for an opinion.

She cut the shirt away instead of fighting it. Cloth parted with the soft, unpleasant sound of things that had been stuck together by sweat. Underneath, both joints stood wrong: squared off, proud under the skin, the arms held out at angles that made the muscles knot hard as rope. She touched quickly, assessing. No grinding bone. Pulses present. That was something. Not much, but something.

“Anterior dislocations,” she said, mostly to the air, because saying the words helped keep the hands precise. “No obvious fracture. Radial pulses intact. Pale, sweating, reactive pupils. If he goes under, keep the airway clear. Do not let him fold forward.”

She laid a canvas strap across his chest, under the right arm above the elbow, and brought the ends around just snug enough to control the limb without turning the hand into a lantern. Her fingers checked the strap, then the wrist, then the color beneath the nails.

“Wick,” she said, still not looking up. “When I say hold, pressure straight down through the shoulders. Not outward. Not into the collarbones. Down. If I say ease, ease. If I say hold again, hold even if he throws you.”

She did not wait to find out whether the words had landed. There was only the work, and the work would not stand still for reassurance.

Sedge braced one boot against the table leg and the other against the crossbar. There was no elegance in it. A field hospital was not a lesson in grace. It was a place where competent ugliness kept people alive.

She took his right wrist in her left hand and slid her right forearm beneath the elbow. Traction first, steady along the line of the arm. The man cried out. Sedge’s face stayed flat. Panic was contagious, and a medic’s expression was part of the equipment. If she flinched, everyone flinched. If she took pleasure in it, she would have to answer for that later. She did neither.

“Easy,” she murmured, though there was nothing easy in the work. She increased the pull. The muscles resisted, hot and dense around the displaced bone. She waited for the fine tremor that meant they were beginning to fail, then rotated the arm outward in a small, controlled arc and adducted it across the chest.

The joint slipped back with a deep, ugly sound.

Sedge kept her forearm under the elbow and her hand on the wrist so the arm could not whip sideways. She checked pulse, color, the new shape of the shoulder. One down. The body’s betrayal was not finished.

“Left,” she said. “Same discipline.”

She shifted before the first reduction could settle into spasm. The left side was worse. The capsule was torn, maybe more; there was no time to admire anatomy. She secured the right arm against the chest with a second wrap, then worked the left with the same sequence, each movement chosen because there would not be enough strength for improvisation.

Traction. External rotation. Adduction. Internal rotation.

The second joint gave way with less grace than the first.

Sedge did not allow herself relief. Relief was for after the bleeding, after the breathing, after the next man. She checked pulses again, range, the lines of both shoulders. Then she padded the armpits, bound the arms, and hung the slings so the weight of the limbs would not pull the repairs apart.

The man had stopped shouting and started the low, wrecked sound that came after. Sedge recognized it. It meant the worst of the immediate hurt had become the ordinary hurt of being alive.

“Good,” she said, and meant only that the work had not been done badly. “Do not let him sit up. Do not give him water until the shaking stops. If he vomits, turn him on his side. If he cannot breathe, call me.”

She wiped her hands on her apron and looked at the instruments in their row: scissors, forceps, strap, bandage, the bottle of spirits with too little left in it

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: *I keep my hands where they are, staring at the tent wall like it'll give me answers.* "He's shaking bad. That normal?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge set the bottle down and returned to the table. The man’s jaw clicked with the tremor, and his fingers twitched inside the wraps like things trying to remember how to be hands. She put two fingers on the pulse at his neck again, counted ten beats, then released them.

“Yes,” she said. “Shaking is normal after this. It means he is alive enough to react. It does not mean he is safe.”

She lifted one eyelid, watched the pupil tighten under the bad lamp, then let it fall.

“Adrenaline wearing off, pain still present, probably cold. The body shakes when it has been told to endure more than it has supplies for.”

She tested the slings, the padding in the armpits, the color under the nails. Both hands were still pink enough. The shoulders sat right under the skin—wrong-looking, but no longer proud. That was the part that mattered.

“Keep him flat on his back unless he vomits or cannot breathe,” she said. “If he vomits, turn the whole body, not just the head. If he gets quiet and limp, tell me immediately. Quiet is worse than loud.”

She pulled a blanket over him, avoiding the injured arms.

“No water until the shaking settles and he can swallow without gulping. His stomach has stopped cooperating and will not be reasoned with.”

The man tried to speak. Sedge leaned close enough that he could hear her without moving his neck.

“You are going to hurt for a while,” she said. “That is not failure. That is the joint capsules, the muscles, the nerves all complaining at once. I put the bones back where they belong. I cannot make the rest of you grateful.”

She straightened and picked up the chart.

“If the shaking becomes one-sided jerking, or his eyes roll and do not come back, or he stops breathing, call me. Otherwise, let him ride it out.”

She wrote the time, the reductions, the pulses, the respiration rate, and the fact that he had screamed. The entry was short because there was no ink for comfort. Then she looked toward the next cot, where another form was already being carried in, and at the lamp that guttered every time someone moved too close.

“Hands where they were,” she added. “He may buck yet. Shock makes people strong and stupid in the same breath.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: "How bad is it?" I ask. "Bad like he loses the leg, or bad like this is the part where we're being kind?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge considered the question while she taped the chart to the bed post. It was a fair question. Fair questions were rare in the ward, and usually asked by people who needed the world sorted into smaller boxes than it actually came in.

“Neither,” she said. “Not the leg. Not kindness.”

She stepped back to look at the man on the table. His chest rose and fell too fast, but it rose and fell. Both arms lay bound and supported, the shoulders no longer standing proud under the skin. The color in his fingers was poor but not dead. That was the measure available to her tonight.

“This is bad like a joint came out of its socket and the soft parts around it were stretched, torn, or crushed in the process. This is bad like nerves run near those shoulders, and nerves do not forgive rough handling. This is bad like blood vessels run there too, and if one had been torn, you would not be asking about legs. You would be asking why his hand was going black and why the tent smelled different.”

She touched the blanket at his feet, adjusting it without sentiment.

“He may keep both arms. He may keep use of them. He may spend the rest of his life with one shoulder weaker than the other, or a hand that numbs when he carries weight, or pain when the weather turns foul. That is not a leg. That is not death. It is also not a kindness.”

Her voice stayed flat, but not cruel. Cruelty was waste. It used breath that might be better spent on instruction.

“What we did was not mercy. We put bones back where they belong so the rest of him has a chance to behave like a body instead of a ruin. If he lives with damage, that is damage. If he recovers, that is mechanics. Neither makes us good men.”

She glanced at the bottle of spirits, then at the row of instruments. The lamp flickered, throwing the shadows of forceps and scissors across the canvas like small, patient animals.

“The bad part now is what happens after. Swelling. Infection. Him trying to move before the tissues have any reason to hold. Shock deepening while we are busy with someone else. If he vomits and inhales it, he can die as readily as from a bullet, and with less honor in the report.”

Sedge picked up the chart again and made one last mark: time, condition, instructions. Short words. No comfort in the ink.

“So no. He does not lose the leg for this. Unless sepsis takes him later, and then he loses more than a leg. And no, this is not the part where we are being kind. This is the part where we are being competent. Kindness is what people call it afterward, when they have enough distance to need a nicer word.”

She turned toward the next cot, where another man was breathing in the shallow, frightened way of someone who understood what tables were for.

“Ask me again when he can lift a cup without shaking. Then we will know whether it was bad or merely painful.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: *I nod, not looking away from the wall. My hands stay pressed down.* "Understood." *I swallow.* "He's bucking again. Light, but he's trying."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge heard the strain in the word before she saw it. Light bucking was not nothing, but it was not the worst sign either. It meant the man still had enough coordination left to argue with the table.

She moved to his head end, keeping her eyes on his chest and face rather than his arms.

“Hold,” she said. Quiet. Flat. Not a request.

Her fingers went to the strap across his chest, then to the slings. She tugged once, testing whether the bindings had migrated into tourniquets. They had not. The arms were immobilized, but the torso was free enough to breathe. That was the balance: enough control to stop him levering the new reductions apart, not so much that his ribs forgot how to expand.

The man’s heels scraped the canvas. Sedge braced one boot against the foot of the table and set her palm lightly over the lower half of his sternum—not to pin him, only to feel the rate of his breathing against her hand.

“Six quick breaths, shallow,” she said, counting under her breath. “Good enough for now. Bad enough that I do not like it.”

She leaned closer, watching his eyes. They were open, but not seeing the tent. Pain had taken the room away from him.

“Listen,” she told him, though he might not answer. “You are trying to sit up because your body thinks it can escape the hurt by moving. It cannot. Your shoulders are back. Your arms are held. If you fight the straps, you will make the capsules swell faster and the nerves angrier. If you vomit, you will choke on it unless we roll you, and rolling you with both shoulders fresh is unpleasant for everyone. So you will spend the next few minutes being boring.”

She looked toward Wick only long enough to make sure the pressure had not wandered.

“Keep down through the shoulders,” she said. “Do not grab his arms. Do not press on his breastbone. If his head lifts, let it lift. If his back arches, tell me before you try to flatten him. An arch can be pain. It can also be airway. I need to know which.”

Her hand moved to the bottle of spirits. There was too little for drinking, too much to waste. She wetted a corner of rag and pressed it briefly to the man’s lips, then drew it away before he could swallow.

“Small,” Sedge said. “Mouth only. No gulp. Your stomach is still on strike and I am not negotiating with it tonight.”

She set the rag aside and checked the fingers again. Pink returning, slow but honest. The tremor ran through him in waves, each one loosening a little as the adrenaline burned down into exhaustion.

“Light bucking is expected,” she said, more to the tent than to anyone in particular. “It means he is not limp and silent. Limp and silent is the conversation I do not want to have.”

She pulled the stool closer and sat, one knee raised, her hand resting near his wrist without taking the pulse yet. Watching was part of treatment. So was refusing to look away.

“If he goes rigid, call it. If he starts jerking on one side, call it. If his breathing changes from fast to slow, call it. If he asks for his mother, ignore him unless he is vomiting.” The corner of her mouth did not lift. “I have no mother in stock.”

For a moment she only listened: the man’s breath, the creak of the table, the far-off voices from the next bay. Then she made another note on the chart, short and ugly.

Time: patient bucking.  
Interventions: rechecked immobilization, airway precautions, small moistened cloth.  
Plan: continuous observation.

“Stay with the rhythm,” she told Wick. “In, out. Do not match his panic. Match his chest.”

She did not say it kindly. Kindness would have made the order sound optional. It was not optional. The man on the table had just been put back together by force and geometry, and the next hour would decide whether geometry held.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I make myself look at what she's looking at. "Tell me what I'm seeing," I say. "I'd rather know than imagine it."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge took the request seriously, because accurate observation was the only thing separating care from guessing.

“Then look properly,” she said. “And do not make it into a story. Stories are how people get themselves killed or sentimental, and neither helps the man on the table.”

She gestured with two fingers toward the patient, not touching him, not yet.

“You are seeing a body that has just been subjected to extreme pain and has responded with the oldest reflexes it owns. Fight. Tremble. Try to flee. The bucking you felt is not defiance. It is motor pattern. His brain has received damage reports from both shoulders and is ordering the trunk to move as if the legs could help. They cannot. The straps exist to keep him from using his own spine as a lever against joints I have only just seated.”

Her gaze moved over the man in sections, the way one inspects a damaged engine.

“The sweating is sympathetic discharge. Adrenaline, pain, early shock. The pallor around the lips and nails is peripheral vasoconstriction. His body is sacrificing circulation to the skin and extremities to preserve the heart and brain. That is useful for a short time. It is not useful for long. Watch the color. If it goes from pale to gray-blue, or if one hand becomes mottled, white, cold, or suddenly purple, that is not discomfort. That is vascular trouble. Call me.”

She tapped the chart once, without looking at it.

“The fast breathing is pain and fear and compensation. Six quick breaths, shallow. Acceptable for now. If it changes—if he slows, if he grunts on expiration, if his ribs pull inward at the neck or between them, if he stops moving air efficiently—that is respiratory failure until proven otherwise. Do not wait for him to look dramatic. Dramatic is easier. Quiet is worse.”

Sedge leaned closer to the patient’s face, watched the flutter of eyelids, the tension in the jaw, the tremor running through the bound arms.

“The shaking is expected. Generalized tremor after severe pain and adrenaline dump. One-sided jerking is not expected. Eyes rolling and staying rolled is not expected. Unresponsiveness to loud voice or painful stimulus is not expected. If he vomits, he may aspirate it into his lungs and drown in his own stomach contents. That would be a stupid way to die after surviving whatever threw him out of his shoulders. So keep your attention on his mouth and throat, not on his courage.”

She straightened.

“The shoulders themselves are reduced. You can see the contour is less wrong. That does not mean they are healed. The capsules are torn or overstretched. The muscles are spasming. The nerves in the region are angry and may remain angry for weeks, months, or permanently. Numbness, weakness, chronic pain, loss of full motion—those are possible. Not certain. Possible.”

Her voice dropped, still flat, still practical.

“What you are seeing is not nobility. It is not purification. It is not the man proving anything. It is tissue, blood flow, nerve function, airway protection, and the risk of infection. You asked to know rather imagine. Knowing is uglier. Imagination gives people heroes and victims. This gives you lists. Signs. Timings. Changes.”

She picked up the rag again, checked the damp corner, and set it within reach without pressing it to his lips this time.

“I take no pleasure in his pain. If you find yourself taking pleasure in watching it, stop looking and tell me. Not because I am moralizing. Because pleasure makes hands lazy and eyes dishonest. A medic who enjoys suffering begins missing the small mechanical failures that kill people quietly.”

Sedge returned to the stool, one knee raised, posture ready but not restless.

“So what you are seeing is a living man in shock, pain, and guarded recovery. Possibly salvageable. Possibly damaged. Not safe yet. Watch the breathing, the color, the level of response, and whether he vomits. Those are the things that matter. Everything else is noise.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I finally look at the man's face. He's staring at the ceiling, eyes wide and empty. "He's not here, is he?" I say, keeping my weight down. "Gone somewhere else."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge did not treat the sentence as a diagnosis. People in tents used words like gone when they meant quiet, and quiet was not the same as safe.

“Possibly,” she said. “But I am not calling it yet.”

She leaned over the man’s face and kept her own shadow off his eyes. The lamp made everything look like old meat. She had learned to work by touch and count when sight lied.

“Can you hear me?” she said, loud enough to reach past pain. “Blink if you understand me.”

The eyes stayed open. They did not blink at the command. They fixed on nothing, pupils wide under the bad light.

Sedge did not waste the moment on wonder. She took his nearest fingernail between her thumb and forefinger and pressed hard into the nailbed. Not enough to injure. Enough to ask the nervous system whether it still had a message to send.

The man inhaled sharply and made a low sound in his throat. His bound arms twitched against the slings, but neither hand obeyed.

“There,” Sedge said. “He is here. Not all of him. That is not the same as gone, and it is not the same as stable.”

She released the finger, checked the color beneath the nail, then moved to the neck pulse again. Fast. Thready but present. Respirations still quick, chest lifting in shallow strokes. She watched the rise and fall for a full count.

“Eyes open without purpose is not consciousness,” she said. “It is a lid lifted off a pot. The fire underneath may be going out.”

She tilted the lamp farther away and examined the face: sweat cooling on the temples, lips pale, jaw slack enough to worry, not slack enough to obstruct. She put a hand near his mouth without touching him, feeling for breath, listening for the wet rattle that meant saliva or vomit waiting behind a tongue no one was controlling.

“Pain, fear, blood loss if there is hidden bleeding, low oxygen, shock, exhaustion, maybe a head strike. Any of them can make a man look like he has left the room.” Her voice remained flat. “My job is not to decide where his soul went. My job is to keep his airway open until his brain comes back or tells me it will not.”

She pressed two fingers to the man’s forehead, then spoke again, louder.

“Sir. Squeeze your eyes shut.”

Nothing purposeful. Only the tremor under the skin.

“Responds to pain. Does not obey commands,” Sedge said, mostly to the chart in her mind. “Airway currently patent. Breathing adequate but poor reserve. Circulation compensating. Disability altered. Exposure cold and wet. Recheck in five minutes or sooner if he changes.”

She pulled the blanket higher over his legs, leaving chest movement visible, and tucked the edge under the table rail so it could not slide up over his face. Then she set the damp rag within reach of his mouth, not against it.

“If he vomits, he will not be considerate about it,” she said. “Do not wait for him to ask. Roll him onto his side in one movement. Keep the shoulders and hips going together. Head, chest, pelvis. If you twist him at the neck while his body is limp, you can turn a bad night into a worse one.”

Sedge straightened and looked at the row of instruments. The scissors, forceps, strap, bandage, spirits. All of it ugly. All of it necessary. None of it amused her.

“I am not enjoying this,” she said, though the statement was not for the man on the table. He could not receive comfort, and she had no spare comfort to spend. “Watching a man go hollow is not pleasant. But if I start treating it as a mystery, I stop treating it as an airway. Mystery does not suction vomit. Mechanics does.”

She returned to the stool and sat with her back half-turned to the next cot, one hand near the man’s wrist, eyes on the rise of his chest.

“Did he strike his head before you brought him in?” she asked. “If yes, say so now. If no, I will assume the altered mentation is pain and shock until something proves otherwise.”

A pause. The tent breathed around them: canvas, oil, blood, unwashed bodies, the far cough of someone else dying elsewhere. Sedge made a short mark on the chart.

Time: patient eyes open, no command response; groans to nailbed pressure. Pupils reactive but sluggish. Respirations rapid, shallow. Skin cool, diaphoretic. Immobilization intact. Plan: continuous airway observation, recheck neurologic status, log-roll precautions for emesis.

“He may come back,” she said. “He may not. Either way, he is not a ghost yet. Watch his mouth, his chest, and his color. If he stops responding to pain, call me. If his breathing slows, call me. If he gurgles, call me. If he wakes up swearing, tell him the bill is not paid.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: "Don't tidy it up for me," I say. "What does shrapnel actually do in there? Say it straight."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge looked at him for a moment. The request had the quality of someone who had decided that vagueness was becoming a liability. That was better than the alternative.

“If you mean inside a body,” she said, “then the short answer is: it does not behave like a piece of metal with manners.”

She turned back toward the table, not to the man’s face but to the line of his shoulder, chest, and neck. Her voice stayed level, the way it did when she was describing something she had seen too often to dignify with horror.

“A clean blade parts tissue. Shrapnel arrives with speed, mass, and no regard for planes. The leading edge may punch through skin with a hole that looks almost polite. Behind that hole, the fragment yaws, tumbles, fractures, or drags whatever is attached to it. Cloth. Dirt. Boot leather. Hair. Rust. Soil. Bone. Bowel contents, if the abdomen is involved. It makes a track that is wider, raggeder, and more contaminated than the entrance suggests.”

She touched two fingers to the air above the patient’s bound shoulder, not pressing, only indicating.

“Near a joint like this, it does not merely make a wound. It can powder the humerus. It can scrape the axillary artery or leave a tear sealed by muscle and clot until someone moves the arm and the seal gives way. It can hit the brachial plexus, and then the hand becomes a thing the man owns but cannot use. It can enter the chest cavity at the apex of the lung and cause bleeding or air collection that does not announce itself until he is too tired to breathe properly.”

Sedge paused, then continued because stopping would have made the answer sound incomplete, and incomplete answers got people killed.

“And that is only the metal. The blast does work of its own. Overpressure squeezes air-filled organs. Lungs can bruise, rupture, or fill with fluid. Bowel can contuse. Eardrums burst. A man can have almost no external wound and still be dying because the shockwave shook a vessel loose inside his chest or abdomen. The body has hollow places and fragile linings. Blast knows where they are.”

She picked up a pair of forceps, set it down again, and did not look at Wick while she spoke.

“The dangerous part is not the hole you can see. It is the dead space you cannot. Shrapnel tears vessels shut behind it, or leaves them bleeding inward. It crushes muscle until the muscle dies. Dead muscle does not heal. It rots. It feeds bacteria. Bacteria make toxin. Toxin shuts down organs. Swelling inside the tight compartments of an arm or leg can strangle blood supply until the limb turns purple, numb, and useless, or until the dead tissue poisons the kidneys. A wound can look closed at dusk and be septic by morning.”

Her tone did not soften. Softening would have been a kind of lie, and he had asked not to be lied to.

“I do not play treasure hunter with a body unless I must. Digging for a fragment lodged near a major vessel or nerve can kill faster than leaving it there. So the work is not glamorous extraction. It is sequence. Airway. Breathing. Circulation. Stop the bleeding you can reach. Control the bleeding you cannot. Remove accessible foreign material. Irrigate if there is water worth using. Cut away dead tissue. Splint. Drain. Antibiotics if I have them. Then watch. Wounds declare themselves over hours. A man can look stable and then vomit blood, seize, stop making urine, or lose the color in a limb because a vessel has torn internally.”

Sedge finally looked at the patient again. His eyes remained open and empty, his chest lifting in shallow, hurried strokes.

“This man has no entry wound I can see. I am treating dislocations, not a shrapnel track. But if a fragment had crossed through here, I would have been looking for absent pulses, expanding swelling, numbness, paralysis, air under the skin, blood in the chest, bowel leak, or a hand going cold. I would not have trusted the size of the hole. The hole is a rumor. The track is the truth.”

She set her hands on her hips for a breath, then dropped them again.

“I take no pleasure in describing this. I am not telling you so you will feel something noble or terrible. Fear makes hands clumsy. Sentiment makes eyes dishonest. I am telling you so that if you ever have to stand where you are standing now, you will know what matters: color, pulse, breathing, response, swelling, smell, drainage, urine, pain out of proportion, and whether the man is getting quieter because he is resting or quieter because he is failing.”

Sedge pulled the stool closer and sat, one knee raised, her gaze returning to the rise and fall of the patient’s chest.

“That is what shrapnel does in there. It makes a mess with deadlines.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: *My knuckles are white where I'm holding him down.* "Is that what happened to you?" I ask, and immediately regret it. "Your limp. Is that from shrapnel?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge did not answer at once. Not because the question was private, but because the man on the table still had a chest that needed watching, and watching came first.

She checked the pulse at his neck again. Fast, but steadier than before. The respirations were still shallow, still hurried, but the rhythm had not collapsed into the ragged thing she disliked. His eyes remained open and unseeing, the face drained except for the flush of exertion at the temples.

“Still altered,” she said, mostly to the chart. “Still breathing. Still not safe.”

Then she turned her head enough to look at Wick without leaving the patient’s chest.

“Yes,” she said. “Mine was shrapnel.”

She said it plainly, as one might say the weather had turned or the water ration was short. No softness entered her voice, and no invitation.

“Lower left leg. It broke the fibula, tore into the ankle joint, and cut a nerve badly enough that the foot never learned where it was again. There was dirt in the wound. Cloth. Boot leather. Whatever passes for clean in a place like this. It was not washed properly for hours because there were other men bleeding faster than I could reach them.”

Sedge lifted one hand and indicated the injured shoulder of the man on the table with two fingers, careful not to touch.

“The bone healed short and rotated. The joint stiffened. The muscles on that side weakened because the nerve did not recover fully. The ankle does not bend like an ankle. The foot lands wrong. The knee takes the punishment. The hip compensates. The back complains after too many hours standing. A limp is not a single injury. It is a chain of bad mechanics repeated until the whole body learns to favor the damage.”

She set her hand back down near the patient’s wrist, not quite taking the pulse, only staying ready.

“It was not noble. It was not a lesson. It was metal moving through tissue faster than tissue could tolerate, followed by delay, followed by imperfect repair, followed by four years of using the result because stopping was not available.”

For a moment the tent noise filled the space between them: the patient’s breathing, the creak of canvas, the distant clatter of someone washing instruments in the next bay.

“If you are asking because you want to know whether I understand what this is like,” Sedge said, “then no. I do not understand what it is like for him. I understand bodies. His body is in shock, pain, and possible neurologic depression. My body has a permanent mechanical defect. Those are not the same thing, and one does not purchase the other.”

Her gaze returned to the man’s face.

“If you are asking because you think suffering makes a person gentle, or wise, or entitled to comfort, then you have mistaken the purpose of wounds. Suffering does not improve anyone. It damages them. Sometimes it teaches. Usually it just narrows the available choices.”

She reached for the damp rag again, tested its temperature, and set it near the patient’s mouth without pressing it to his lips.

“I take no pleasure in his pain. I take no pleasure in mine. If I did, I would be unreliable. A medic who enjoys injury begins to see people as opportunities for demonstration. That is how good hands go bad.”

The patient made a small sound in the back of his throat. Sedge’s posture changed at once, not alarmed, only attentive. She leaned closer, listening to the breath, watching the rise of the clavicles, the movement of the lips.

“Swallowing reflex is poor,” she said. “Do not give him anything by mouth. Not water. Not spirits. Not a prayer if it comes with liquid.”

She straightened and looked at Wick again.

“My limp is not a story that makes me closer to him. It is a reminder that delay has cost, that contamination has consequences, and that bodies do not care how brave the person inside them is. That is all.”

Then she returned to the chart and wrote, in short strokes:

Patient remains obtunded. Pupils reactive but slow. Responds to painful stimulus only. Airway at risk. No oral intake. Continued observation.

“When he tracks your face,” Sedge said, “when he answers your name, when he tries to swear at you for holding him down—that will be improvement. Until then, do not mistake silence for peace. Silence can be rest, and it can be the last quiet before a man stops protecting his own throat.”

She pulled the stool closer and sat, one hand near the patient’s wrist, eyes moving between his mouth and chest.

“Ask me again about my leg when he is awake and stable. Tonight he is the one on the table.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: He starts screaming again and I hold him down through it. "Keep going and keep talking," I tell her. "Tell me exactly what you're doing to him and how much longer -- all of it, don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: "Tell me where the screaming comes from," I say, my voice tight. "Is it the nerves? The bones? Tell me so I know what we're fighting."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge did not answer at once. The scream was occupying too much of the tent, and she had learned that a medic who spoke over it too soon missed the shape of it. There were differences. A scream with air behind it was one thing. A thin, wet, struggling sound was another. A roar of pain was survivable. A cry that came without the chest properly moving was a warning.

She leaned over the man’s head end, keeping her shadow off his face, and put two fingers at his throat.

“Pulse fast,” she said. “Still bounding enough. Not thready yet.”

Her other hand lifted one eyelid. The pupil contracted sluggishly under the lamp, then widened again as the man’s back arched against the table. Sedge let the lid fall and moved her hand to his chest, feeling the rise beneath her palm rather than trusting her eyes.

“Six,” she counted aloud. “Seven. Eight. Still shallow. Still using accessory muscles.”

She shifted down the table, checking the slings, the wraps, the color beneath the nails of both hands. Pink. Slow, but pink. The fingers twitched, not purposefully, but enough to tell her the nerves were still carrying messages and the muscles were still obeying some of them.

“The screaming,” she said, as if the word itself were a symptom to be dissected, “comes from the whole chain.”

She pressed a thumb into the muscle beside the man’s injured shoulder, not deep enough to injure, only enough to test spasm. The flesh contracted hard under her touch.

“Joint capsule first. It is thick, tough, and full of pain fibers. When a shoulder dislocates, the capsule stretches or tears. When I put the bone back, I stretch it again. That alone is enough to make a man shout.”

Her fingers moved to the bony point of the shoulder, tracing the contour without pressing where it would hurt unnecessarily.

“Periosteum next. The lining of bone. People think bone itself hurts. Mostly it does not. The covering does. It is richly supplied with nerves. Tear it, bruise it, pull on it, and the body reports it as damage that must be dealt with immediately.”

She looked at Wick’s hands only long enough to confirm they were still where she had ordered them, then returned to the patient.

“Nerves,” she said. “Axillary nerve. Brachial plexus. Musculocutaneous. Radial. All of them run near this mess. They may be stretched, compressed, irritated, or partly ischemic from swelling. When nerves complain, they do not complain politely. They produce burning, electric pain, numbness, weakness, referred pain into the deltoid, the arm, the hand. The man may not be able to localize it. He will only know that something wrong is happening and cannot be escaped.”

The man screamed again, raw and sudden. Sedge did not flinch. She watched his throat, his chest, the movement of his lips.

“Muscle spasm,” she continued over the noise. “The body guards injured joints by contracting around them. That is useful for stability. It is miserable for the man inside it. Spasm squeezes blood vessels, produces metabolic waste, irritates nerves, and makes the pain feed on itself. The more he fights, the tighter it gets. The tighter it gets, the more he fights.”

She set one hand briefly over the lower part of his sternum again, feeling the vibration of breath and panic.

“Brain,” she said. “All the signals travel upward. Spinal cord. Thalamus. Cortex. Limbic system. The body does not merely register damage. It interprets it as threat. Then it orders the diaphragm, intercostals, larynx, pharynx, and abdominal muscles to produce sound. Screaming is motor output. It is not a confession. It is not courage. It is not the soul leaving. It is a nervous system attempting to expel alarm.”
