She moved quickly then, because explanation without examination was only decoration. She checked the man’s chest on both sides, listening with her ear close enough to hear the difference between clear air movement and the wet, diminished sounds she disliked. Trachea midline. No obvious subcutaneous crackle under the skin. Breath sounds present, unequal only by the shallow splinting of pain.

“Lungs are moving,” she said. “Not well. But moving.”

Her hands went to the abdomen next, pressing with controlled, economical touches. Soft enough. No board rigidity. No obvious distension. She checked femoral pulses, then returned upward.

“Circulation is compensating,” she said. “Skin cool. Cap refill delayed but not absent. No gross abdominal bleeding I can feel. No obvious pelvic instability. That does not mean nothing is wrong. It means nothing is screaming loudly enough yet.”

She sat back on her heels beside the table and looked at Wick.

“You asked what we are fighting.”

Sedge’s voice dropped, still flat, still without comfort.

“We are fighting airway obstruction. Tongue, secretions, vomit, blood, swelling. A screaming man can still aspirate if he goes under. A quiet man can die faster.”

She pointed to the patient’s mouth.

“We are fighting breathing failure. Pain makes him shallow. Shock makes him hungry for oxygen. If he tires, his respirations slow, his chest stops moving efficiently, and carbon dioxide builds. Then he becomes confused, then obtunded, then arrested. The transition is not dignified.”

Her finger moved to the bound shoulders.

“We are fighting vascular injury. Axillary artery, vein, collateral vessels. A tear can be sealed by clot and muscle until movement opens it again. Then the arm swells, the pulse disappears, the hand goes pale or purple, and the man may lose the limb or die from hemorrhage into tissue you cannot see.”

She tapped the chart once.

“We are fighting nerve damage. Brachial plexus, axillary nerve, radial nerve, median nerve, ulnar nerve. Swelling can strangle them. Stretching can injure them. Ischemia can kill them. A hand that does not move, does not feel, or does not warm properly is not a metaphor. It is a functional failure.”

Her gaze returned to the man’s face.

“We are fighting shock. Pain, blood loss, dehydration, hypothermia, infection later. Shock narrows the world to perfusion. The body sacrifices skin, gut, kidneys, extremities, to keep heart and brain supplied. That buys minutes. It does not buy days.”

She pulled the blanket higher over his legs, then folded it back enough to watch the chest.

“We are fighting compartment syndrome in the arms and shoulders if swelling rises inside tight fascial spaces. Pain out of proportion, passive stretch pain, numbness, pallor, pulselessness, paralysis. By the time the limb looks dramatic, the muscle may already be dying.”

The man’s scream broke into a ragged moan. Sedge leaned close and spoke directly into his ear, loud enough to cut through the noise but not to startle him unnecessarily.

“You are not dying at this second,” she said. “Your shoulders are reduced. Your airway is open. Your chest is moving. Your pulse is present. You are in pain. Pain is information. It is not a verdict.”

She straightened and looked at Wick again.

“That is where the screaming comes from. Nerves, bones, capsule, muscle, brain, fear, oxygen debt, and the mechanical fact that his body has been told it is under attack. It is not one source. It is a system reporting damage from every angle it can.”

Sedge picked up the damp rag, tested it, and set it near the man’s mouth without giving it to him.

“I am not fighting the scream itself,” she said. “I am fighting the complications hiding inside it. If he vomits, he may drown. If a vessel tears, he may bleed into his arm or chest. If his breathing fails, he may stop protecting his airway. If his shock deepens, he may go quiet and stay quiet. Those are the enemies. The noise is only the alarm.”

She checked the time on her wrist, then the patient’s pulse again.

“How much longer?” she answered, because he had asked before and the question still mattered. “I can tell you the next five minutes with some confidence. Ten to twenty if he does not vomit, seize, bleed internally, or tire out. Longer if swelling worsens or if there is hidden injury I have not found yet. I will not promise quiet. I will promise watching.”

Her hand rested near the man’s wrist, not quite taking the pulse, only ready.

“If he screams, he is still moving air. If he gurgles, he is losing the ability to clear it. If he becomes rigid, jerks one-sided, stops responding, slows his breathing, or loses color in a limb, then the fight changes and I change with it.”

Sedge looked at the row of instruments, then at the bottle of spirits, then back to the man.

“I take no pleasure in this,” she said. “Not in his pain, not in your fear, not in the sound of it. Pleasure would make me careless. What I have is procedure. Airway. Breathing. Circulation. Disability. Exposure. Recheck. Log. Act on change.”

She returned her attention to the patient’s chest.

“So if you want to know what we are fighting, fight those things with your eyes. Watch his mouth. Watch his ribs. Watch his color. Watch whether his screams have air in them or only terror. That is what matters. The rest is noise.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: When it's over I sit down on the floor of the tent and don't get up. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge looked at the place where Wick had dropped to the floor. She did not order him up at once. A person who could not stand without falling was of no use, and a person forced upright before his legs had permission might pitch into the table and take the patient with him.

“The rest,” she said. “Yes. Because half-told danger is still danger.”

The man’s scream had begun to fray at the edges. It thinned, caught, became a wet, scraping sound in the back of his throat. Sedge was moving before the change finished.

She leaned over his face and looked into his mouth with the lamp angled away from her eyes. There was saliva, a little froth, and the yellowish sheen of bile rising behind his tongue. His jaw worked without purpose. His neck muscles pulled tight.

“Rolling,” Sedge said, mostly to herself.

She set one hand on the bound shoulder and the other on the hip, shifted her weight against the table edge, and used her body as a brake and lever at the same time. The roll was not gentle. Gentleness required space, clean linen, and time. It was controlled: head, chest, pelvis moving as one block, the injured arms held against the torso by the wraps so neither shoulder could swing free. The man’s back came up toward her, sweaty and pale under the lamp.

No entry wound. No exit wound. No tracking bruise wide enough to matter. Only old abrasions, dried dirt in the creases of the spine, and the gooseflesh of shock.

She wrapped a corner of canvas around two fingers and swept the visible fluid from his mouth, not probing deep. Deep sweeps pushed things downward. Gravity was already doing enough.

The man coughed once, a brutal, full-bodied convulsion that jerked his hips against the table. Sedge kept her hand at his shoulder and hip until it passed, then reversed the sequence and brought him back onto his back. She straightened the blanket, checked the slings, checked the strap across his chest, and put her ear close to his mouth without touching his face.

Air moved. Wet, but moving.

“There,” she said. “That was the rest arriving early.”

She picked up the rag, tested it again, and set it within reach of his mouth. Not against it. Near it. A tool, not a comfort.

“You want to know what I am doing to him,” Sedge said, her voice level over the patient’s ragged breathing. “Right now, I am keeping him from undoing himself. That is not the same as curing him. It is not the same as making him safe. It is the work of buying time for a body that has just been told it is under attack.”

She placed two fingers on the pulse at his neck again and counted, her eyes on the rise of his chest.

“One. Two. Three. Four.” She released the pulse and moved to the wrist, checking the rate there too, comparing. “Fast. Thready at the periphery. Central pulse stronger. That means his body is squeezing the outer vessels to keep the heart and brain fed. Useful for a while. Not useful forever.”

She lifted one eyelid, then the other. The pupils reacted, slowly, to the lamp. Not equal enough to reassure her. Not fixed enough to condemn him.

“Capillary refill,” she said, pressing a thumbnail until it blanched, then watching the pink return. “Delayed. Lips pale. Extremities cool. Skin wet. He is in shock. Pain contributes. Blood loss may contribute. Dehydration contributes. Cold contributes. Fear contributes. The body does not file separate reports. It files one emergency report and calls it suffering.”

The man made a sound in his throat. Sedge turned her head and listened.

“Do not swallow against your will,” she told him, though he could not have answered. “If you vomit again, we roll. If you fight the roll, you may tear what I have just seated. If you aspirate, you may drown in your own stomach. None of that is dramatic. It is mechanical.”

She moved down the table with the economy of someone who had learned that wasted steps cost minutes. She checked the bindings at the armpits, the pads, the slings, the color of both hands. She pressed along the contour of each shoulder, feeling for the head of the humerus seated in the glenoid, for abnormal mobility, for crepitus, for swelling that had no business being there yet.

“Reduced,” she said. “Still reduced. No obvious re-dislocation. No bony grind. Soft tissue injury remains.”

Her fingers went to the space beside the collarbone, then down the inner arm, checking pulses again. Radial. Ulnar. Brachial. Present. Unequal, but present.

“Nerves,” she said. “Axillary nerve supplies the skin over the shoulder point. If that area goes numb and stays numb, it is not a trinket. It is a sign. Median, ulnar, radial—hand function. If the fingers do not move, do not feel, or do not warm, the problem is not ‘pain.’ The problem is function failing.”

She rubbed the pad of his thumb against the pad of his index finger on the right hand. No purposeful response. On the left, a weak twitch. Not enough to call recovery. Enough to call signal.

“Not dead,” Sedge said. “Not alive enough.”

She pulled the blanket back from the legs just enough to expose calves, feet, toes. She checked warmth, color, pulses at the ankles, then pressed along the shins and thighs with quick, impersonal touches. No obvious deformity. No hard swelling. No crepitus under the skin. She returned to the abdomen, listening, then palpating with flat fingers, watching his face for guarding even through the haze.

“Soft,” she said. “No board rigidity. No distension. That does not mean nothing is wrong. It means nothing is shouting loudly enough yet.”

She sat back on her heels and looked at Wick.

“You asked what we are fighting. I told you the enemies. Now you want the rest. The rest is procedure. The rest is time. The rest is what happens when a body has been opened by force and left to decide whether it will behave.”

She took the chart, wrote the time, the emesis, the airway clearance, the pulses, the respiratory rate, the level of response. Short words. No decoration.

“First,” she said, “he stays flat. Not propped. Not sitting. Not ‘comfortable.’ Comfort is a luxury with a price tonight. If his breathing worsens when flat, that tells me something. If he vomits, we roll him. If he seizes, we protect his head and airway, not his dignity. Dignity does not keep the tongue from falling back.”

She set the chart down and picked up the blanket again, arranging it so his chest remained visible while his legs stayed covered.

“Warmth,” she said. “Cold makes blood sluggish. Cold makes clotting worse. Cold makes shock deeper. I cannot give him a warmed room. I can keep him from cooling further. I can change wet linen if it soaks through. I can keep the lamp away from his face so he does not burn while unconscious. Small things. They are not small when the body is losing.”

The patient’s breathing hitched, then settled into a shallow rhythm. Sedge counted again, aloud this time.

“In. Two. Three. Four. Five. Six. Seven. Eight.” She stopped. “Eight in ten seconds. Forty-eight per minute. Too fast. Still too fast.”

She watched the lower ribs. There was no dramatic pulling, not yet, but the movement was inefficient. His chest was working like a bellows with a hole in it.

“If he tires,” Sedge said, “the rate may drop. That will look like improvement. It will not be improvement. Slow breathing in a shocked man is not rest. It is failure unless he is clearly waking and speaking. If he becomes quiet and his chest stops moving properly, that is not peace. That is a body giving up the argument.”

She reached for the bottle of spirits, then stopped herself. Too little. Too valuable. She wetted the rag again and pressed it to the corners of his mouth, drawing it away before he could swallow.

“Mouth only,” she said. “No gulp. Your stomach is not a friend tonight.”

She looked at Wick.

“You asked how much longer. The honest answer is: I can tell you the next five minutes with some confidence. The next fifteen if nothing changes. The next hour if I stay here and watch. Beyond that, I can tell you what I am looking for, not what I promise.”

She tapped the chart.

“The screaming phase is minutes. The shaking phase is tens of minutes. The dangerous quiet can begin within the hour. Swelling peaks over one to three days. Nerve verdicts take weeks to months. Infection verdicts take days. Survival verdicts take layers.”

Her voice did not soften.

“First layer: airway. If he vomits and inhales it, he can die before I finish wiping his mouth. Second layer: breathing. If his chest tires, if a lung collapses, if bleeding into the chest restricts expansion, he dies from lack of oxygen. Third layer: circulation. If the axillary vessel has been injured and the clot gives way, he can bleed into the arm, the chest wall, the space under the collarbone. You may see swelling, discoloration, absent pulse, cold hand. By then, the window is narrow. Fourth layer: brain and nerves. If perfusion fails long enough, he may wake wrong or not wake. If the brachial plexus is torn, the arm may live while the hand becomes a dead weight. Fifth layer: infection. If there is hidden contamination, if bowel was injured by blast and sealed temporarily, if soil entered a wound I have not found, sepsis can arrive later and take him with fewer alarms than a bullet.”

She leaned closer to the patient, checking the skin around the shoulders for early bruising, for tense shine, for the first discoloration that meant blood was collecting where it should not.

“Compartment syndrome,” she said. “Swelling inside tight spaces. Pain out of proportion. Pain on passive stretch. Numbness. Pallor. Paralysis. Pulselessness is late. Do not wait for the hand to go black. If the arm becomes tight, shiny, exquisitely painful, and the fingers complain, I loosen everything. Cut wraps. Remove constricting bandages. Keep the limb at heart level, not elevated high, because elevation can reduce perfusion in that situation. If that fails and I have no surgeon, the limb may die anyway. I do not enjoy saying that. Saying it accurately is the only kindness available.”

The man’s fingers twitched inside the sling. Sedge watched the movement without hope in her face.

“Movement is not mastery,” she said. “A twitch is not a promise. It is electricity looking for a path.”

She straightened and addressed the tent as much as Wick.

“What I am not doing: I am not giving him morphine I do not have. I am not flooding him with water he may vomit. I am not testing shoulder range to satisfy curiosity. I am not massaging spasm because it feels productive. I am not propping him up because sitting looks humane. I am not leaving him alone because he has stopped screaming. I am not assuming that quiet means stable. Quiet can be the anteroom of arrest.”

She picked up the forceps, set them down, then aligned the scissors, bandage, strap, rag, and chart in a row within reach. Order was not ceremony. Order was the difference between grabbing the right thing and grabbing the nearest thing.

“If he wakes,” Sedge said, “he may be confused. He may be furious. He may ask for his legs, his cigarettes, his mother, or God. I will not argue with him. I will orient him: name, place, time, injury, instruction. If he tries to sit, I stop him. If he tries to pull at the slings, I stop him. If he begs for water, I moisten his mouth and tell him no. If he curses me, that is a good sign. Cursing requires air, brain, and enough outrage to outlast pain.”

She glanced at the lamp. It guttered, recovered, guttered again.

“If the light fails, I work by touch and count. If he deteriorates, I call for help and continue. If no one comes, I continue anyway. That is the rest of the answer. There is no cavalry in this tent. There is only sequence.”

The patient’s breathing changed. Not worse. Different. The frantic edge dulled into something exhausted. His eyelids fluttered, not opening, not closing. Sedge put her hand near his mouth again, feeling for air, listening for the rattle she disliked.

“Swallowing still poor,” she said. “No oral intake.”

She looked at Wick.

“When you can stand without the tent tilting, your job is not to hold unless I say. Your job is to watch one thing and report it cleanly. His chest. Count respirations for a full minute if you can. If you lose count, say ‘lost,’ not ‘about.’ About is how people miss deterioration. If he gurgles, call. If he vomits, call if I am within reach; if I am not, roll him. Whole body. Head, chest, pelvis. Do not twist the neck. Do not lift by the shoulders. Do not let the head flop back and shut the throat. If he becomes pale gray, blue-lipped, mottled, or one hand goes cold, call. If he stops responding to pain, call. If his breathing slows while he remains unrousable, call. If he wakes and speaks, tell me. If he wakes and swears, tell me that too.”

She paused, then added, because the instruction was incomplete without the warning.

“Do not comfort him with lies. Do not tell him it is over. Do not tell him he will be fine. Do not tell him the pain means something noble. If he asks whether he is dying, say: ‘The medic is watching. Breathe.’ That is enough. More than enough. It is true.”

The tent filled with the sound of the man’s breathing and the small, persistent creak of the table under shifting weight. Somewhere beyond the canvas, a stretcher rattled over uneven ground. Sedge did not turn toward it. Her attention stayed on the chest rising under the blanket.

“You asked about shrapnel,” she said. “I told you what it does. The rest of that is this: a fragment need not be large to be fatal. A piece the size of a thumbnail can nick an artery, seed a joint with dirt, lodge near a nerve, or carry boot leather into tissue where no antibiotic can reach it. A blast can injure without visible metal. The body has hollow spaces and delicate linings. It does not require a dramatic wound to fail. Sometimes it requires only enough damage to start a chain the body cannot interrupt.”

She touched the patient’s shoulder again, lightly, checking contour and temperature.

“Near here, the danger names are familiar. Axillary artery. Axillary vein. Brachial plexus. Lung apex. Joint capsule. Rotator cuff. Deltoid. Nerves that do not regenerate well if torn. Vessels that do not forgive delay. Tendons that heal slowly and wrongly. Bones that can fracture without looking broken. A shoulder dislocation is not one injury. It is an event with consequences radiating outward through every structure nearby.”

Her voice remained flat.

“If this man had a fracture, I would look for deformity, crepitus, abnormal motion, shortening, swelling, loss of function. If he had a vascular injury, I would look for absent pulses, expanding hematoma, pallor, coldness, bruit, thrill, bleeding that will not stop. If he had a nerve injury, I would look for numbness, weakness, paralysis, loss of reflex, loss of sensation in specific distributions. If he had a chest injury, I would look for unequal breath sounds, tracheal deviation, subcutaneous emphysema, respiratory distress, cyanosis, hypotension. If he had an abdominal injury, I would look for rigidity, distension, rebound tenderness, blood in stool or urine, shock without external bleeding. If he had a head injury, I would look for worsening consciousness, unequal pupils, seizure, focal weakness, fluid from ear or nose, battle sign, raccoon eyes. I am looking now. I will look again. Bodies hide their worst facts until they can no longer afford to.”

She sat back on the stool, one knee raised, her hand near the patient’s wrist without taking the pulse yet. Waiting. Watching.

“The rest of what I am doing is documentation,” she said. “Time of injury, time of reduction, pulses before and after, respiratory rate, level of response, interventions, vomit, urine if produced, skin color, temperature, swelling, pain behavior, changes. Not because paper saves lives. Because memory rots under stress. Because the next person to touch him deserves to know what has already been decided. Because a trend is more honest than a single measurement. A pulse of one hundred and twenty once means one thing. A pulse climbing from ninety to one hundred and twenty while the skin cools means another.”

The patient’s breath caught. Sedge leaned in.

No vomit. No gurgle. Just the hitch of a body negotiating its own damage.

“Still here,” she said. “Still arguing.”

She checked the color under the nails again. Pink returning, slow but honest. She checked the shoulders. Still seated. Still bound. Still not safe.

“If he re-dislocates,” Sedge said, “I will know by deformity, pain, loss of motion, and his own scream if he has enough lung left to provide one. I will not casually shove it back in the middle of the night unless vessels or nerves are compromised and delay costs more than repetition. If I must reduce again, I will restrain more securely, explain more clearly, and accept that he will hate me for it. Hatred is easier than death. Not better. Easier.”

She looked at the bottle of spirits again, then away.

“No drink. No topical miracle. No placebo with teeth. If I had proper analgesia, I would use it. I do not. So the analgesia is immobilization, warmth, airway protection, and the fact that pain cannot kill instantly unless it drives him to tear himself apart. Therefore we prevent both.”

Her gaze returned to Wick.

“You asked me to say the rest. The rest is this: he may live with damage. He may live without much damage. He may die tonight from airway, breathing, or circulation. He may die tomorrow from sepsis or organ failure. He may survive and spend years with a shoulder that slips, a hand that numbs, a limb that aches when the weather turns, or a nerve that never fully wakes. None of those outcomes makes the work good or bad. It makes the work necessary.”

She picked up the chart and made another mark.

Time: emesis cleared, airway patent, respirations improving but tachypneic. Pulses present bilaterally. Shoulders reduced. Skin cool, diaphoretic. No oral intake. Continued observation.

Then she set the pen down and looked at the man’s face.

“The rest also includes what happens to the people watching,” Sedge said. “Your hands will shake afterward. Your stomach may turn. You may hear the scream in quiet rooms. That is not weakness. That is a nervous system responding to threat. Do not make it into a test of courage. Do not suppress it until you become clumsy. Wash your hands. Eat if you can. Sleep if the war permits. If you find yourself wanting to do it again, to see whether you can bear it, stop. That is how good hands go bad. That is how people become dangerous to patients and to themselves.”

She did not say it kindly. Kindness would have made it sound optional.

“I take no pleasure in this,” Sedge said. “Not in his pain. Not in your fear. Not in the sound of a body being forced back into shape. If I did, I would be unreliable. A medic who enjoys injury begins to see people as demonstrations. That is how precision dies. That is how cruelty dresses itself as competence.”

For a moment she only listened: the patient’s breath, the creak of canvas, the distant movement of other wounded men being carried toward other tables.

“You asked earlier about my leg,” she said, without turning away from the patient. “The rest of that answer is brief. It is a mechanical defect. It hurts when it is damp. It fails me when I need speed. It reminds me that delay has cost and contamination has consequences. It does not make me wise. It does not make me gentle. It does not purchase insight into this man’s body. It only makes me slower, and slower is dangerous here.”

She shifted on the stool, adjusting her weight so the injured side did not complain.

“My limp is not a story. It is a chain of bad mechanics repeated for years. His shoulders may become the same kind of fact. Not poetry. Physics.”

The patient’s eyelids moved again. This time they opened a fraction. Not seeing. Not yet.

Sedge leaned close, keeping her shadow off his eyes.

“Can you hear me?” she asked. “Blink twice.”

Nothing.

She pressed the nailbed again. The man inhaled sharply, and this time his left hand twitched inside the sling with something almost like purpose.

“Better,” Sedge said. “Not good. Better.”

She checked the pupils again, the pulse, the respirations. The rate had dropped from forty-eight to something nearer thirty-six. Still too fast. Less desperate.

“If he wakes fully,” she said, “he will hurt. Tell him that. Tell him the shoulders are back. Tell him not to move. Tell him water comes later, if and when swallowing is safe. Tell him to breathe with me if panic rises. Do not promise sleep. Do not promise recovery. Do not promise absence of pain.”

She took the rag, moistened the corners of his mouth again, and drew it away.

“Now the rest is not speech,” Sedge said. “The rest is watching.”

She settled back, one hand near the patient’s wrist, eyes on the rise and fall of his chest.

“In,” she said, counting aloud. “Two. Three. Four. Five. Six.”

The lamp burned low. The tent breathed around them. The man on the table lived for another count, then another, and Sedge did not look away.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I watch his chest rise and fall. "How long do we stay like this?" My voice is rough.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge did not answer immediately. The question had the shape of exhaustion, and exhaustion was not a diagnosis. It was weather. It moved through a tent like cold air and made people ask for edges that did not exist.

She kept her eyes on the man’s chest. It rose. It fell. The motion was still too quick, still too shallow, but it had lost some of the desperate flutter that had worried her during the screaming. His lips were no longer gray at the corners. They were pale, not gray. That was something. Not safety. Something.

“As long as it takes,” Sedge said.

She lifted the lamp by its handle, moved it a careful distance from his face, and set it where the flame would not gutter in someone’s passing shadow. The light improved. It did not become kind.

“Not as long as you would like. Not as long as he would like. As long as his body still requires watching.”

She returned to the stool, sat with her back half-turned to Wick, and laid one hand near the patient’s wrist without taking the pulse yet. Her fingers rested there the way a person might rest a hand on a railing in the dark: not for pleasure, but because falling was expensive.

“The first hour is the narrow one,” she said. “Airway. Breathing. Circulation. Swelling. Bleeding that hides. Vomit that goes where it should not. If he passes that hour without choking, collapsing, seizing, or losing the color in his hands, the odds shift. Not to good. To less bad.”

The man made a small sound. Sedge leaned close enough to hear the movement of air behind it. No rattle. No wet catch. She watched his throat, his nostrils, the line of his jaw.

“Tonight,” she continued, “we stay like this until he can protect his own throat. That means he wakes enough to swallow, enough to obey a simple command, enough to turn his head if he is going to vomit. Until then, he is not allowed water. Not spirits. Not broth. Not rain off a tarp. His mouth may be dry. Dry is survivable. Aspiration is not.”

She checked the slings again, then the padding under the arms, then the wraps. Everything was still where she had put it. That did not mean it would stay. Bodies moved in sleep, in pain, in delirium. Restraint failed slowly, then all at once.

“The next layer is perfusion,” Sedge said. “I need his pulse to stop climbing and start settling. I need his breathing to come down from frantic to merely poor. I need his skin to warm, his nails to pink, his urine to appear if he has enough fluid in him to make any. If he has not urinated by morning, that tells me something. If he has, that tells me something else. Both matter.”

She glanced toward Wick only long enough to see that he was still on the floor. She did not order him up. A person who could not stand without falling was a hazard near a table, and a person forced upright too soon might drop into the patient and undo the reductions with his own weight.

“If you cannot stand, do not try to prove you can,” she said. “Stay where you are if your legs are honest with you. If they obey, then stand slowly. If the tent tilts, sit again. There is no shame in mechanics. Shame does not improve balance.”

The patient’s eyelids moved. Sedge’s attention sharpened, but her posture did not change. She had learned that hope made medics premature. Premature hope caused missed signs.

“He may wake in pieces,” she said. “First the eyes. Then the sounds. Then confusion. Then anger. Anger is useful. Anger means he has enough energy to object to his own suffering. If he wakes and tries to sit, stop him. Not by force unless you must. By voice first. Tell him flat. Tell him shoulders. Tell him breathe. If he fights, hold. If he vomits, roll. Whole body. Do not wait for me if I am not at his head.”

She picked up the damp rag, tested it, and set it near the man’s mouth again. Not against it. Near it.

“How long do we stay like this?” she repeated, because the question deserved a harder answer than the first one. “Until I can leave him with someone who can watch without pretending. Until he has trends, not just moments. A pulse is a photograph. A trend is a story. I need to know whether he is improving or merely pausing.”

The lamp burned lower. Somewhere beyond the canvas, boots crossed mud, and a stretcher creaked under a shifting weight. Sedge did not turn. Her hand moved to the patient’s neck and counted ten beats, then multiplied under her breath.

“Still fast,” she said. “But not racing. That is not victory. That is only that his heart has stopped screaming for a moment.”

She released the pulse and checked the shoulders again by sight: contour, swelling, the position of the arms in the slings. No proud deformity. No sudden lengthening of one limb. No hand gone white. No fingers curled in the claw she would have hated to see.

“If he remains stable for the next two hours,” Sedge said, “I will move to the next cot for short intervals. Not long. Not comfortable intervals. I will come back, recheck, log, and leave again. If he deteriorates, I will not be far. If he vomits while I am gone, that is why you are here. If he stops breathing while I am gone, that is why you are here. If he wakes and asks for a doctor who exists, tell him I am the doctor who exists.”

Her voice did not rise. It did not soften. It stayed in the register she used when words had to survive noise.

“If he worsens, we stay longer. If he improves, we still stay longer, because improvement is not permission to stop watching. A man can look better and bleed internally. A man can seem calm and be hypoxic. A man can open his eyes and still not have a swallowing reflex worth trusting.”

She looked at Wick then, not with sympathy, but with assessment.

“You asked how long. The honest answer is: longer than you want. Longer than he wants. Longer than is fair to either of you. That is not a promise of death. It is the cost of keeping him from one.”

The patient drew a breath that was less jagged than the last. Sedge counted it without celebration.

“In,” she said aloud. “Two. Three. Four. Five. Six. Seven.” She paused. “Eight. Nine. Ten.”

She released the count and wrote on the chart in short, hard strokes.

Time: respirations slightly improved. Airway intact. No further emesis. Pulses present. Patient remains obtunded but responsive to pain. Continued observation.

Then she set the pen down and folded her hands loosely in her lap, ready to move if the chest changed.

“For now,” Sedge said, “we stay like this until he can swallow without help, speak in sentences, and keep his own airway when I turn away. After that, we watch for swelling, fever, numbness, weakness, color, urine, and pain that changes character. After that, days. Maybe weeks. Maybe permanent damage that announces itself slowly, like rust.”

She glanced at the man’s face, then at the row of instruments, then at the bottle of spirits with too little left in it.

“I take no pleasure in the length of it,” she said. “But length is not cruelty. Length is the body’s schedule. We do not get to edit it except by keeping the dangerous parts from becoming fatal.”

A beat passed. The patient breathed. The lamp hissed softly.

“If you can watch without lying down,” Sedge said, “then watch his chest. If you can stand without the floor moving, then bring me clean linen when I ask. If you can do neither, stay where you are and report what you see. Do not guess. Do not soften. Do not say he seems better unless you can name why. Seems is not medicine. Change is medicine.”

She returned her hand to the patient’s wrist, this time taking the pulse properly, eyes on the rise and fall of the chest as she counted.

“As long as it takes,” she said again, quieter now, but not gently. “That is the whole answer. There is no prettier one.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I push myself up to my knees, ignoring the way the world swims. "I can stand. Tell me what to do next."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge did not reward the announcement with approval. Approval was not fuel, and a person who had just admitted the world was swimming had no business being told he had passed a test.

“Usefulness is not the absence of dizziness,” she said. “It is knowing what your dizziness cannot do.”

She moved to the foot of the table, placing herself between Wick and the patient’s face, not to block him, but to make him look where she wanted looking. The man on the table lay bound and pale, his chest lifting in quick, shallow strokes under the blanket. His eyes were half-open, the lids fluttering without purpose. The screaming had spent itself into ragged breathing and the occasional wet catch in the throat.

“Stand where you can see his chest and his mouth,” Sedge said. “Do not lean on the table. Do not touch the straps. Do not touch the lamp. If the room moves, kneel. Kneeling is not surrender. Falling into him is.”

Her hands went to the chart, then to the row of instruments, aligning them without looking: scissors, forceps, strap, bandage, rag, bottle, pen. Order was not ceremony. Order was the difference between reaching for the right thing and reaching for the nearest thing while a man drowned in his own saliva.

“Your next job is counting,” she said. “Not guessing. Not remembering. Counting.”

She lifted the lamp by its handle, shifted it a careful span away from the patient’s face, and set it on the crate where the flame would not gutter in passing sleeves. The light sharpened. It did not soften. Shadows moved off the man’s cheek and settled under his jaw, in the hollows of his collarbones, along the bound arms.

“Watch his ribs and his throat,” Sedge said. “Not his arms. The arms are decoration tonight. The chest is the argument. Count respirations for one full minute. If you lose count, say ‘lost.’ Do not say ‘about.’ Do not say ‘seems fast.’ About and seems are how people miss the moment a body stops negotiating.”

She placed two fingers at the patient’s neck and counted silently, eyes moving between the pulse under her fingertips and the rise of the chest.

“One-twenty,” she said. “Central pulse fast, thready at the wrist. Respirations still high. Let us see whether they are climbing or merely refusing to come down.”

She released the neck and moved to the wrist, comparing. The radial pulse was weaker, quicker, less honest. That meant the body was pulling blood inward, sacrificing the outskirts to keep the core functioning. It was a useful trick for a short time. It was not a plan.

“While you count,” Sedge said, “I am going to look for the things that hide.”

She leaned over the man’s face again, keeping her shadow off his eyes. His pupils were sluggish but reactive. Not reassuring. Not catastrophic. A middle country where medics earned their keep by refusing to guess.

“Can you hear me?” she asked, loud enough to cut through the noise in his own body. “Blink twice.”

Nothing purposeful. Only the tremor under the skin, the faint flutter of eyelids like a bird trapped under cloth.

She pressed the nailbed again. The man inhaled sharply, a small animal sound caught between pain and exhaustion. His left hand twitched inside the sling. Not command. Not conversation. Reflex with a thread of intention attached.

“Better,” Sedge said. “Not good.”

She moved to the scalp, parting the hair with dry fingers, searching without pressing hard. No step-off. No boggy swelling she could feel through the dirt and sweat. She checked behind the ears, under the jaw, along the mastoid ridges. No battle sign visible. No clear fluid from the nose or ears. That did not rule out injury. It only meant nothing had announced itself loudly enough to be ignored.

“Head strike remains unknown,” she said, mostly to the chart. “Assume until disproven. Keep the neck neutral. No turning for comfort.”

Her hands went to the chest next. She lifted the blanket just enough to expose the clavicles, the upper ribs, the line of the shoulders. No flail segment. No obvious subcutaneous emphysema crackling under the skin. She listened with her ear close to each side, keeping her breath slow, separating the sounds she needed from the noise she had to tolerate.

Air moved. Not evenly. Not badly enough to call collapse yet. Pain splinting, shallow ventilation, the wet whisper of secretions sitting where they should not sit for long.

“Breath sounds present,” she said. “Diminished on the right, probably splinting. Watch for sudden change. If one side stops moving while the other works, call it.”

She pressed along the sternum, the rib margins, the spaces between the ribs, not to torture him, but to find the tenderness that meant fracture or bruising hidden under shock. The man groaned low in his throat. His back arched a fraction. Sedge waited until it passed, then continued.

“Do not fight the breath,” she told him, though he could not answer in any way that mattered. “If you vomit, we roll. If you choke, we lose the night. Breathe small. Breathe with me.”

She moved to the abdomen. Soft. Not perfect. Not rigid. No guarding she could trust in a man this altered, but no board-hard resistance either. She checked femoral pulses, then returned upward, feeling for the hidden swelling that meant bleeding into tissue where the eye could not reach.

“Circulation is still compensating,” she said. “That means nothing except that he has not yet failed.”

Her fingers went to the shoulders again. She checked contour, the seat of the humeral heads, the padding in the armpits, the wraps, the slings. No re-dislocation. No sudden lengthening. No hand gone white. No fingers curled in the claw that meant nerve and vessel were being strangled together.

She pressed along the inner arm, checking brachial, radial, ulnar pulses. Present. Unequal, but present. She squeezed the nail beds, watched the color return. Slow. Honest enough for now.

“Nerves are unhappy,” she said. “Vessels are patent. Capsules are torn. Muscles are spasming. The body is filing one emergency report and calling it suffering.”

She sat back on her heels, not relaxing, only changing angle. The lamp hissed. Outside the canvas, boots moved through mud, and someone shouted a name that did not belong to the man on the table. Sedge did not turn.

“Your count,” she said. “If you have lost it, say lost. If you have it, say the number and whether it is regular.”

She did not wait for the answer to continue. Waiting for a shaken person to speak perfectly was a luxury the ward could not afford. She gave him the structure instead.

“Regular, irregular, fast, slow, shallow, deep, noisy, silent. Those are the words. Use them. Do not dress them up.”

She picked up the damp rag, tested it, and set it near the patient’s mouth again. Not against it. Near it. A tool within reach, not a kindness pressed onto a reflex that might not deserve it.

“If he gurgles,” Sedge said, “call it. If he vomits, call it. If he stops swallowing his own saliva, call it. If his lips go gray-blue, call it. If one hand goes cold, white, mottled, or purple, call it. If his breathing slows while he remains unrousable, call it. If he wakes and swears, tell me that too. Swearing is data.”

She took the pen and made a short mark on the chart.

Time: patient obtunded, responds to pain, pupils reactive but slow. Respirations rapid, shallow. Pulses central strong, peripheral thready. Skin cool, diaphoretic. Airway at risk. No oral intake. Continued observation.

Then she looked at Wick again.

“Second job,” she said. “When I say roll, you help. Not lift. Not turn. Support.”

She indicated the sides of the patient’s head with two fingers, careful not to touch the man himself.

“Hands here. One at the temples, one under the jaw angle. No pressure on the throat. No pulling. No twisting. Keep the head in line with the chest. If I say move, the head, chest, and pelvis move as one block. If you are unsure, freeze and say unsure. Freezing is better than improvising with a spine you cannot see.”

She demonstrated the position in the air, her hands hovering, precise, without sentiment.

“We may need to check the back again. Sweat, blood, vomit, hidden bleeding, pressure sores forming under a body that cannot complain properly. Also because an altered trauma patient may have injuries that do not announce themselves from the front. I do not trust fronts. Fronts are where people look.”

She lowered her hands and returned to the table.

“Third job, if you can keep your feet under you: the green linen bundle is by the crate near the entrance. Dry cloth. Extra blanket. Pins. Not the muddy one. Not the one with the tear. If you can fetch it without putting a hand on the table, bring it. If you cannot, say cannot and I will go. There is no glory in collapsing near a patient who already has enough people trying not to die on him.”

She did not soften the instruction. Softness would have made it sound optional. It was not optional. It was assigned.

Sedge leaned close to the patient again, watching the throat, the lips, the subtle movement of the tongue behind teeth that had stopped clicking with tremor. His breathing had changed from frantic to exhausted, which was not improvement so much as a different species of danger. Exhausted bodies made poor decisions about airway protection.

“Swallowing still poor,” she said. “No water. No spirits. No broth. No rain off a tarp. His mouth may be dry. Dry is survivable. Aspiration is not.”

She checked the strap across his chest once more, tugging lightly, confirming it had not migrated into a tourniquet or loosened into uselessness. The arms were immobilized. The torso could expand. That was the balance: enough control to stop him levering the new reductions apart, not so much that his ribs forgot how to breathe.

“Do not let him sit up,” Sedge said. “Do not prop him. Do not make him comfortable. Comfort tonight is a rumor with consequences.”

Her fingers moved to the pulse at his neck again. She counted ten beats, then released.

“Still fast,” she said. “Still trying.”

She pulled the blanket higher over his legs, leaving the chest visible, then tucked the edge under the table rail so it could not slide up over his face. The man’s toes twitched under the cloth. Not purposeful. Not yet.

“Warmth,” she said. “Cold makes blood sluggish. Cold makes clotting worse. Cold makes shock deeper. I cannot give him a heated room. I can keep him from cooling further. If the linen comes dry, we change what is soaked. If it does not, we manage with what is here.”

She sat back on the stool, one knee raised, her posture ready but not restless. The bad lamp threw her shadow across the chart, the instruments, the patient’s bound arms. She looked at the row of things she had and the larger list of things she did not.

“If he deteriorates,” Sedge said, “we do not panic. We sequence. Airway. Breathing. Circulation. Disability. Exposure. Recheck. If the airway closes, clear what is visible. Do not sweep blindly. Blind sweeps push filth deeper. If breathing fails, we support what we can and admit what we cannot. If circulation fails, we hunt for bleeding. If no bleeding is found, we assume shock has other names and fewer comforts.”

She picked up the forceps, set them down, then aligned them again. Order. Not ceremony.

“I am not giving him morphine I do not have,” she said. “I am not flooding him with water he may vomit. I am not testing shoulder range to satisfy curiosity. I am not massaging spasm because it feels productive. I am not leaving him alone because he has stopped screaming. I am not assuming that quiet means stable.”

The patient drew a breath that was less jagged than the last. Sedge counted it without celebration.

“In,” she said aloud. “Two. Three. Four. Five. Six. Seven.”

She paused, watching the lower ribs. The movement was still inefficient, still hurried, but it had shape.

“Eight. Nine. Ten.”

She released the count and looked toward Wick.

“Your turn,” she said. “Full minute. Chest and mouth. If you lose it, say lost. If you find it, report number and pattern.”

She did not hover over him. Hovering made people clumsy. Instead she kept one hand near the patient’s wrist, not taking the pulse, only staying ready, her eyes moving between the rise of the chest and the line of the throat.

“Do not match his panic,” she said. “Match his chest. In. Out. Count the pauses. Pauses matter. A breath that does not arrive after a pause is not rest. It is warning.”

The tent breathed around them: canvas, oil, blood, unwashed bodies, the far cough of someone else dying elsewhere. Sedge did not turn toward it. Her attention stayed on the man on the table, on the small mechanical facts that kept him from becoming a corpse with a story attached.

“If he vomits while you are counting,” she said, “stop counting. Call me. If I am at his head, roll with me. If I am not, roll him yourself. Whole body. Head, chest, pelvis. Do not twist the neck. Do not lift by the shoulders. Do not let the head flop back and shut the throat.”

She demonstrated the motion with her hands in the air again, compact, controlled, ugly in its practicality.

“If he seizes,” Sedge said, “protect the head. Clear the mouth if fluid is visible. Do not put anything between his teeth. Teeth are not doors. Jaws are not hinges to be forced. If he bites his tongue, that is damage, but forcing an object into his mouth is more damage and may give him something to aspirate.”

Her voice remained flat. Not cruel. Not gentle. Accurate.

“If he stops responding to pain, call. If his breathing changes from fast to slow, call. If his color goes from pale to gray-blue, call. If one hand becomes cold, mottled, or swollen tight, call. If the slings slip, do not adjust unless I say. If the strap across his chest migrates, tell me. If you cannot tell, say cannot tell. That is still information.”

She looked at the patient’s face. The eyes remained half-open, unseeing, the lids trembling with each shallow breath. The mouth was dry at the corners, saliva gathering in the dependent angle. Sedge wiped it away with the corner of the rag, drawing the cloth outward, not inward.

“No oral intake,” she said again. “Mouth care only. Small moisture. No swallow.”

She set the rag down and took the pen.

Time: respirations monitored. Airway secretions managed. No emesis. No oral intake. Patient remains obtunded, responsive to pain. Peripheral pulses present, cap refill delayed. Continued observation.

Then she looked at Wick, not with sympathy, but with assessment.

“You asked what to do next,” she said. “This is next. Watch. Count. Report. Fetch linen if your legs permit. Support the head if I say roll. Do not become part of the injury.”

She returned her hand to the patient’s wrist, this time taking the pulse properly, eyes on the rise and fall of the chest as she counted.

“As long as it takes,” she said, quieter now, but not gently. “That is the whole answer. There is no prettier one.”

The lamp burned low. The patient lived for another count, then another. Sedge did not look away.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I swallow, watching his ribs move. "Thirty-two. Fast but... steady. I think." My own breathing feels too loud.

rung_labels.evidence: This is bad like a joint came out of its socket

rung_labels.evidence: It can powder the humerus
