rung_labels.evidence: Delayed. Lips pale. Extremities cool.

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
The cellar had four feet of standing water in it and something at the far end that had stopped moving about a minute ago.

Halloway held the lamp up and did not go closer yet. "Right," she said. "Before we touch it. What do you see?"

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I make myself look properly instead of at the water. "I don't know yet," I say. "Something wrong with the shape of it."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
"Wrong how," Halloway said. Not a question. She shifted the lamp to her other hand and let the light sit steady on the far end of the cellar.

She could see it herself — had seen it before they'd reached the third step — but seeing it for Pike was the whole exercise, and nobody learned to see by being told. The shape under the waterline was long in a way that didn't resolve. Limbs, probably. The wrong number of them, or the right number arranged by something that had only ever had a person described to it.

"Take your time. We've got plenty." She kept her boots still on the step. Ripples told you things; still water told you more. "It stopped moving a minute ago. In my experience that means one of two things, and only one of them is dead."

The lamp flame guttered in the wet air and recovered. Halloway watched the waterline around the thing, not the thing itself — she'd learned that habit around year six, from a man who no longer had the eyes to learn anything.

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I keep staring, trying to make the blurry shape under the water make sense. "It's got... too many joints. Like the arms bend in too many places." I swallow, my voice dropping. "You think it's playing dead?"

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
"Too many joints. Good." Halloway nodded once, slow, so the lamp didn't swing. "Joints are for folding. Something with that many elbows folds up small — which means what you're looking at under there isn't its size. It's its size *packed away.* Keep that in your head whenever you reckon up a reach."

She crouched on the step, unhurried, and rested the lamp on her knee.

"And no — playing dead's the wrong phrase. Dead isn't a performance for a thing like that. Stillness is. It was moving until the light came down the stairs, which means it noticed the light. Dead things don't notice anything. That's the entire point of them." She paused. "Also, it's on the bottom. Anything dead in water longer than a day floats — gas sees to that, whatever the thing was in life. So either it died in the last few hours, very considerately, or it's holding itself down. I've buried three people who bet on considerate."

The water gave nothing back. No ripple, no drift. Halloway watched it the way she'd watched a hundred still surfaces, and found the stillness itself the loudest thing in the cellar.

"Nothing that size holds that still without practice. It's done this before. It's eaten doing this, most likely — things with that many joints don't swim after prey, they *reach* for it. Ankles, mostly. Four feet of water, no footing, nowhere to run. It's not hiding from us, Pike. It set a table and we're the first course that's bothered to look at it."

She drew a slow breath through her nose.

"So. That's what you see. Now tell me what we do about it — and before you answer, know that 'leave and seal the door' is a respectable answer. Walking away's a skill. Most corpses I've catalogued never learned it."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: "Was that a person?" I ask. "Recently, I mean. Is that what I'm looking at?"

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway was quiet for a moment, and gave the question the courtesy of a second look. The lamp stayed on her knee. The light stayed where it was.

"No," she said at last. "And I'll tell you how I know, because someday you'll have to do this over something worse. Look at the segments. A person's limbs are uneven — long bone, short bone, taper at the ends. That thing's are the same length, over and over, all the way down. Like fingers. Like something that grew by repeating itself. And it lies flat on the bottom. A person has lungs. Even a dead one rides up off the floor for a day or two before the gas gets going. That lies like a net."

She let Pike look a moment longer before going on.

"No hair that I can find. No cloth. Anything that was a person recently keeps the evidence of it — boots outlast the feet, usually. So: not a person. If it ever was one, it was long enough ago that the question's academic. I've only been wrong about that twice, and both times it was worse than being right."

The water gave them nothing. She hadn't expected it to.

"If what you're really asking is whether there's anyone down there to save — no. But the instinct's sound, because there's usually a person in it somewhere. A thing like this doesn't end up in a cellar by accident. There's a house above us. Something went missing, somebody came down with a candle to check on the noise. If it's been feeding, the feeding's down there with it. We'll know when the water's out. I'll log whatever's left, and if there's enough for a name, somebody gets a name back. That part matters. *After.*"

She took the lamp off her knee and stood, unhurried, knees cracking in the damp.

"The ones that used to be people are worse, as a rule. They remember how doors work."

Then, level, not unkind: "I answered because you asked, and because when we write it up it'll matter to somebody's family that we looked properly. But understand — it doesn't change the next ten minutes. Person, not person, ate a person: same water, same reach, same decision. So I'll ask you once more. What do we do about it?"

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: "I think we should leave and seal the door," I say, my voice steadier than I feel. "But I need to know why we wouldn't. Why would someone stay down here?"

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway gave a small nod — the question deserved a real answer, and she gave it the way she'd give a wound assessment: in order, without padding.

"Four reasons, in my experience. First: the door doesn't hold forever. Doors rot. Houses get sold. New people move in and nobody tells them why the cellar's nailed shut, and one wet spring somebody goes down with a candle to see. I've written up that report four times. A seal buys years, sometimes. It never buys always."

She ticked them off without moving the lamp.

"Second: it eats. It doesn't stop eating because we stop looking. Every month it sits down here costs a body — a vagrant, a dog, a child sent down for coal. Leaving it alive isn't neutral. It's deciding to spend other people, later, when you're not there to see it spent."

"Third: sometimes you can't leave. Water rising, a family sleeping overhead, no money for a pump and no one in the parish who'd believe you enough to pay for one. Then 'later' is a luxury, and you fight with what you've got, where you stand. Judgment is knowing which cellar you're standing in."

"Fourth." A beat. "Some stay because it's personal. Somebody's brother went down a cellar like this one and didn't come up. Grief's a worse weapon than none. I've buried colleagues who went into water like this because walking away felt like cowardice. It isn't. Cowardice is sealing the door and telling yourself the job's done."

She shifted her weight on the step, unhurried.

"But hear the rest of it. We leave because this is its ground. Four feet of water, no footing, a reach we can't measure — in here it kills us, likely as not. So the seal isn't the end of the job. The seal is us choosing the battlefield. We come back with a pump and rope and iron, we drain its dining room, and we fight it on the steps or on the flags, on our terms. Walking away, done properly, is the first move in killing it."

The water gave nothing back. It hadn't for some minutes now.

"And a week of pumping costs maybe nothing, maybe somebody stupid who doesn't knock first. That's the arithmetic of this work. You don't get clean numbers. You get the ones you can live with."

"Up you go. Backwards, if you can manage it — you know where the steps are, and I'd rather you watched the water than your feet. I'll hold the light."

She kept the lamp steady on the far end of the cellar. The thing did not move. Not a ripple, not a drift, not even the small give of something breathing.

"It didn't even shift," Halloway said quietly. "Remember that, too. It measured us and decided we weren't worth the stretch. Things that can do sums are the worst kind."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I wade closer and hold the lamp where she can work. "Tell me what happened to it," I say. "Plainly."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
The water was down to a black slick on the flags, and unfolded, the thing covered the better part of the cellar floor. Halloway had been at it for the better part of an hour — gloves on, sleeves down, iron bar in her left hand, turning what she had to turn with the bar and touching nothing she didn't have to.

"Plainly, then."

She worked from the far end inward, the way she'd been taught. Extremities first, middle last. The middle was where things kept what killed you.

"Eleven feet, tip to root. What you saw under the water was it folded — I said its size packed away, and there it is. Forty-odd segments to a limb, every one the same length. It grew by repeating itself. Things that grow that way don't stop on their own. Something stops them, or nothing does."

She turned a limb with the bar. The underside was pale, set with rows of hooks, small as fishhooks, black at the points.

"There's how it lay flat. Dead things float — I told you that, and it knew it too, in whatever way it knew anything. It hooked into the mortar and held on. Stillness was work, and it did the work. File that away. The ones that labor at seeming harmless are the ones that learned what happens when they don't."

She moved along the body, unhurried.

"It came in through the old culvert under the east wall — mortar's been gone thirty years, the grate with it. Came in small, I'd say. Rats first. Then the dog. Then whatever came down those stairs with a candle. It's shed twice — there's an older skin in the corner, half-eaten. It ate its own cast-off. Waste nothing." A pause. "Say that much for it."

The lamp light reached the far corner, where she'd already been and would go back to.

"Bones in the corner. It cracked the long ones for the marrow and left the small, which is more table manners than some I've logged. Two adults and a child, by what's there. One adult still has a boot on — left foot, good leather, a repair stitch in the sole. I'll log the cobbler's mark. Cobblers keep records. Somebody gets a name back." She said it the same way she'd said the rest, because that was the job. "That's the after I told you about. This is it."

She set the bar's end against the thick knot of tissue where the limbs converged.

"Root-cluster. That's where it kept whatever passed for its nerve, and it's where the iron went — three blows. But look here first." The bar shifted a half-inch. "Old scar. Years old. And two limbs grown back shorter than the rest. Somebody fought this thing, hurt it, and settled for a nailed door. Which means we're not the first to stand in this cellar. We're the first to finish it. That's the whole history of this work in one sentence, and nobody'll ever carve it on a gate."

She straightened, knees cracking in the damp.

"As for the end — it reached when the water dropped below two feet. Knew the table was being cleared, in whatever way it knew. It was fast. It had simply never met anything that knew what it was. Most of what we kill dies of the surprise. That's not flattering to them or to us, but it's the truth, and you asked for plain."

She wiped the bar on a rag and dropped the rag on the body.

"On the stairs it measured us and decided we weren't worth the stretch. It was half right. We weren't worth it *in the water.*"

Then, level: "One more thing, and it's why you asked me to say it plain. Plain isn't coldness. Plain is accuracy, and accuracy is the only thing in this cellar that outlives anybody. When your arm tires of that lamp, you'll take the ledger and write what I call, exactly as I call it. And the gloves stay on. Dead things keep their worst in the small parts — spines, sacs, teeth. I knew a man who lost a hand to a corpse. The report was longer than the funeral."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I hold the lamp a little higher, my arm already aching. "It ate a child," I say, and my voice doesn't shake. "That's what you're not saying plain."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway stopped.

Not paused — stopped, the bar halfway through a turn, and stood still in a way she hadn't since the water went down. Then she set the bar across her knees and looked at Pike full.

"You're right," she said. "It did, and I didn't say it plain. The record wants correcting, and I'll correct it now, because you caught the skip and the skip is worth more than anything else I've shown you tonight."

She didn't go back to work for it. She gave it the stillness.

"The child's bones are at the bottom of the cache. Drier than the rest, more gnawed. It went first — weeks first, maybe months. The adults came after, one and then the other, down those stairs with a candle, looking. That's how a cellar takes a whole family, Pike. The thing never hunted them. It ate the child, and love delivered the rest, one candle at a time. That's reading, not seeing — but the reading's sound, and it's the worst thing in this room, and I moved past it at the same speed as the hooks. You shouldn't have had to pull me back to it."

She nodded toward the corner.

"There's a shoe in with it. No bigger than my palm, buckle still done up. Somebody fastened that the morning it happened, and did it up tight, and meant it. Log that too. The buckle's not evidence of anything. Log it anyway."

She took the bar off her knees and stood it against the wall, unhurried.

"Now the why, because you'll develop the skip yourself and you should know it when you feel it. I told you the middle's where things keep what kills you. In the body, that's the root-cluster. In the report, it's the child. I logged it at cataloguing speed, between the hooks and the boot, because the first few times you slow down for the small skull, you don't finish — and unfinished reports kill nothing. I'd like to tell you I was testing you, seeing if you'd catch it. It's a better story than the true one. The true one is habit, thirty years deep, and habits that keep you alive still want watching."

"You get one grief per site. Spend it during, and it spends you. Spend it after, and it's yours. That's not coldness. It's rationing."

A beat. The lamp flame guttered and recovered.

"The ledger has a column for length and a column for limbs and nothing for the part that wakes you at three in the morning. So I write it in the margin. Thirty years of margins. You'll start your own soon enough, and you'll know you're doing the work right when the margins are what cost you."

She reached into her coat and brought out the ledger — oilcloth-wrapped, swollen with damp — and held it out.

"Lamp on the step. This entry's yours. I'll call it, you'll write it, exactly as I call it, and we both sign. Most apprentices open their book with a rat in a grain store. You're owed the rat. The trade doesn't pay its debts."

Her eyes stayed on Pike's, level.

"Your voice didn't shake when you said it. Good. If your hand shakes while you write it, write anyway. Shaking isn't a column either."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: "I need the detail," I say. "Tell me exactly what it did to him -- what is under the skin now, what it took, how far it got. If I meet another one I need to know."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway was quiet for a moment, and in that moment she looked at Pike rather than the cache — checking something — and then she nodded once, because the reason given was the right one and she'd asked for nothing else.

"Then you'll have it all," she said. "Pen ready. Write it as I call it, and I'll tell you now there's a reason it goes in the book and not just in your head — what's written gets passed on. What's carried gets buried with the carrier."

She crouched by the corner, gloves on, and worked the way she always worked: the bar, not her hands.

"Start with what it doesn't do, because absence is half of reading. No tooth marks. Anywhere. On the stairs I said the child's bones were gnawed — wrong word, and we'll correct it in the entry. Rasped. The hooks rasp. Teeth pit and score; hooks strip in lines, all one direction, like carding wool. Learn the difference and you'll never mistake a dog problem for one of these, or one of these for a dog problem, and both mistakes are fatal in opposite directions."

The bar indicated a long bone, split end to end.

"It doesn't bite and it doesn't tear. It wraps and pulls. One wrap of a limb around a man's arm, one pull, and the hooks take everything soft off in a single pass. So the rule for next time, and it's the first rule: it never closes a full wrap on you. A grabbed wrist you buy back with skin. A wrapped arm is gone, and you're behind it. Second rule follows from the first — it has forty joints a limb and no jaw worth the name, which means the head-end is a decoy. It wants you watching the wrong end. The reach is the weapon. Kill the root."

She moved the bar along the cache, unhurried.

"What it takes, in order: organs first, then muscle, then marrow. It cracks the long bones along the grain — look at the split. Levered open, like an oyster. A scavenger snaps bone across; this opens it lengthwise. The skull it leaves whole, because there's only one thing in a skull it wants and it takes that through the opening at the base. You'll find the rim there worked wider. An intact skull with a widened foramen is this thing's signature, and if you ever find it on a bone, write it exactly so — and understand you're not the first hunter on that site. You're the next one."

A pause. The lamp flame guttered and recovered.

"The child it didn't crack. Small bones are green — they bend before they break — so it took them apart at the joints instead. Every bone is here. They're unthreaded, is all. Nothing torn, nothing crushed. That's how far it got: everything soft, over days, coming back to the cache between feedings. It doesn't gorge. It keeps a larder. Which gives you the third rule: one fresh kill means the thing is close and still hungry. A cache like this means it's fed, and still, and you'll walk past it before it ever moves. We did."

She set the bar across her knees.

"As to the dying — it kills first and feeds after, and the killing is fast. One wrap, one pull, and blood does the rest inside a minute. It isn't cruel. Cruelty wants a mind behind it; this is a net that learned to want. If there's a mercy in this cellar, it's that one. That's margin, not column. Write it or don't."

"And it's 'the child' in the entry. At that age the bones don't say boy or girl, and the shoe doesn't either. Leave the blank. Somebody's family will fill it, and that blank is the only thing in this book that isn't ours."

She straightened, knees cracking in the damp.

"That's the whole of it — what it took, how, how far. The old books give this thing four lines: *water-thing, many-limbed, drowned.* Four lines, and every hunter who met one after that learned the rest the hard way. This is how the book gets better, Pike. One margin at a time, paid for."

Her eyes stayed level on Pike's.

"Now read it back to me. If you can read it aloud, you know it. If you can't, you carry it — and we stay down here until you can."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I look down at the ledger, the ink still wet. I clear my throat. "Water-thing, many-limbed, drowned," I begin, my voice low but clear. "Eleven feet, tip to root. Limbs of forty segments, uniform. Hooks, not teeth..." I keep reading, every detail, until I reach the end. "One adult, one adult, one child. Boot, buckle." My hand isn't shaking.

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway listened to the end without moving, and when the last two words came — *boot, buckle* — she let them stand a moment before she reached over and shut the ledger, careful of the wet ink.

"Not a word wrong," she said. "And you put the buckle last. That's where it goes. After the buckle there's nothing else to say, and an entry should end the way the work does."

She held out the pen.

"Sign it. Bottom of the page, and small — the book has to last you, and the entries don't get shorter. That ledger's had eleven hands in it, mine first. Four are dead. Two retired. One lost the hand to a harvester in Norfolk and writes left-handed now, badly, and bills me for the ink. When you've signed, I'll countersign, and it'll be done — you'll have opened your book with an eleven-foot water-thing. I said the trade owes you a rat and the trade doesn't pay its debts. It doesn't. I do. There's a miller in Millbrook with a hole in his skirting board. Easiest night's work you'll ever log, and it's yours when we're home."

She took the bar from the wall and set to the last of it, talking as she worked, because a site wasn't finished when the thing was dead — it was finished when there was nothing left that could teach the next one.

"The body burns where it lies. Lamp oil, the rags, and the shed skin in the corner goes on with it. We don't carry it up. Carrying it is how you meet the spines."

"The bones come up, wrapped in the oilcloth — boot, shoe, and all, exactly as logged. The cobbler's mark gets traced. Cobblers keep records, and records give names back. The parish gets the report. The house above gets nothing, because there's nobody left in it to tell. That's what a full cache means when the stairs are inside the home. Nobody knocked, Pike. There was nobody left to knock."

"And the culvert gets iron set in mortar. Not a nailed door. The hunter before us settled for wood; we finish with iron. That's the difference between a seal and an epitaph."

She straightened, knees cracking in the damp, and picked up the lamp.

"Last thing. I told you that you get one grief per site, and to spend it after. The work's done — this is after. How you spend it is yours, and it keeps. But I'll give you the schedule, because nobody gave me mine: it comes at three in the morning, tonight or a night soon, and it will feel like a failing. It isn't. It's the margin writing itself. Thirty years and I still wake for some of them. The day I stop is the day I hand you the lamp for good and take up gardening — and I hate gardening."

She nodded up the stairs.

"Frontwards, this time. It's dead, and you've earned the sight of the steps. I'll carry the bones. You carry the book."

A beat, and the ghost of the grin.

"It's heavier, in the long run."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: She starts cutting and I hold the lamp steady and don't look away. "Keep describing it," I tell her. "Everything -- what's underneath, what it smells like, how far it got. Don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway wiped the blade on the last clean corner of the rag and set her feet.

"Everything, then. In order — and the order is bar, blade, hands never. Light here —" she tapped the flags beside the root-cluster "— and stand to my left. Upwind, such as it is down here. You'll understand the courtesy in a minute."

She put the bar's end against the root first and leaned on it slow, the way she'd test ice.

"Smell's a column too, and we're about to open it. Brine first — low tide on a hot day, a fish stall at closing. Under that, ammonia; it'll sting your eyes, and that's normal. Under that, sweet. The sweet's the worst, because sweet is dissolved, and dissolved was people. Breathe through your mouth. You'll taste it instead. There's no winning; there's only choosing your loss." A beat. "And learn it. A cellar that smells of low tide a mile from any water is a cellar you don't go down alone. That smell has saved more hunters than iron has."

The bar found what it was feeling for — a give, a tension under the tissue — and she eased off at once.

"There. Sac, fist-sized, still under pressure. Three days dead and it can still open you. Dead is a state of the whole; the parts keep their own schedule. That's what took the hand I told you about — the man cut before he probed. So: probe, always. When you find one, you drain it low, toward the floor, away, and you never put any part of yourself over the work. The trade collects early from people who lean in."

She did it as she said it. A small cut, low. Dark fluid sheeted out and ran into the channels between the flags, and the sweet smell came up strong enough to thicken the air. She gave it a moment to settle, then opened the root-cluster along its length — one stroke, away from herself.

"No bones. Anywhere. A rod of gristle down the middle, like a skate has. It never grew a skeleton because it never needed to stand. It's a hand that learned to hunt. Muscle in rings, layered, pale — cut across the rings, never along, or the blade skates and you're in the sac after all."

She turned the tissue back with the bar.

"Gut's one tube. No stomach worth the name — it doesn't digest, it dissolves. Floods the wrap and drinks. And here's what it couldn't dissolve." The bar's end worked in the black fluid and came up with small things, one at a time, laid in a row on the flags. "Buttons. Bone keeps; metal keeps longer. A farthing — George the Third, so it's been eating since before you were born. And this." A tag, green with verdigris, the name worn half away. "Collar. The dog gets a name back too. Log it: *canine, tagged, name partial.* Somebody loved it enough to buy the tag. That rates a line."

The bar moved inward.

"The mouth isn't a mouth. Look where the limbs root — a ring of hooks, inward-facing, and a rasp like a cat's tongue made of fishhooks. The whole root is the mouth. There's no head, Pike. No eyes, no skull, nothing to look back at you. That's the lesson the four lines never wrote: don't flatter it with a face. It doesn't think. It persists. And don't flatter yourself it was a duel — you can't duel a net."

She lifted a knot of grey tissue on the bar's end, no bigger than a walnut.

"That's the whole of its nerve. Everything it knew — light means wait, stillness works, ankles — lived in that. I've seen bigger in a chicken. Three blows of iron through it and the rest was just meat with opinions."

Then the last of it. She opened the lower root, careful, and the blade's tip showed three small sacs in a row, each the size of a fist, each holding something folded and pale and already repeating itself.

"And there's *how far it got.* Buds. Three. Weeks off, no more — the segments are already formed. It wasn't living down here, Pike. It was multiplying. One wet spring and this cellar births three of them, the culvert's open, and the village has a well." She let that stand a moment. "The hunter before us nailed a door over this. That's what wood buys. It's why we burn, why the culvert gets iron, and why the entry reads *destroyed, budding, three buds, burned entire.* The old books' four lines never said it breeds. Ours does now. That's how the book gets better."

She straightened, knees cracking in the damp, and wiped the blade.

"That's everything. It doesn't get to keep anything back — the dead owe the living their secrets, and collecting's the job. If it comes back up on you in a day or two — and it will, when the smell works out of your hair — that's not weakness. That's digestion. The body's a larder too. It keeps things."

She nodded at the oil flask.

"Lamp on the step, and stand back of it. It's taught everything it knows — which is four lines more than it ever gave the hunters before us, and a sight less than it took from this house. Now it burns."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I watch the fire catch, the smoke rising thick and bitter. "Three buds," I say, my voice flat. "That means three more cellars, three more families." I don't look away from the burn.

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway let the number stand in the air a moment — long enough to be examined — and then corrected it, because a wrong number carried home did more damage than a right one carried heavy.

"No. Count again."

She nodded at the fire.

"Three buds, one fire. They're in there — I opened the root and left them where they lay, and *burned entire* means entire. In a few minutes you'll see them move. Heat does that to muscle, dead or not; it'll look like hatching and it isn't. It's tissue contracting. Don't read anything into it — read it in the entry instead. This is why we burn. A thing that buds isn't dead until the buds are ash. The hunter before us killed it and nailed a door. We killed it and ended the line. That's the whole difference between him and us, and it costs an oil flask and an hour."

Something in the fire unfolded with a wet pop and crisped. She watched it without moving.

"But the arithmetic underneath your count is sound, so I'll give it to you straight. It came through that culvert small, thirty-odd years ago. Which means it came from somewhere. There's a mother of it, or was, and she had buds of her own, and some of them found water. So yes — there are other cellars. I've stood in four in thirty years and heard tell of nine more, and two of those nine were the same cellar described twice by frightened men. The trade's smaller than the work. It always has been."

The smoke thickened and went up the stairwell like it knew the way out.

"And here's the part nobody tells you at the start, because it sounds like despair and isn't: you will never stand in all of them. You'll stand in the one in front of you, finish it, and write it down true. The book is how you fight the cellars you'll never see. Tonight's entry says something no entry said before — *it buds; burn entire.* Every hunter who opens that ledger after us walks into the next cellar knowing what took us an hour on our knees to learn. That's not three more families, Pike. That's the one count in this trade that runs the other way."

She shifted the lamp to her other hand.

"As for this cellar, the count's closed. Two adults, one child, one dog, one thing, three buds, one fire. Nobody else dies in this house. That's the whole job, and tonight it's done. You don't get the world. You get the room you're standing in — and this room is finished."

The fire settled into itself, low and steady. She made no move toward the stairs.

"And nobody leaves a burn early. A half-burned thing is worse than a whole one, and the stairs will still be there in an hour. So we stand here till it's ash, and then I'll buy you the worst breakfast in the county — the place by the mill fries everything in the same pan, and after tonight you won't taste the difference. That's not a complaint. Tonight it's a recommendation."

A beat. The flame guttered and recovered.

"And if your eyes water while we watch, it's the smoke. That's what it's for. A fire's the one place in this trade where that's always true."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I sit on the cellar steps afterwards with the lamp in my hands. "Finish it," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full.)

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway looked at Pike for a long moment, then nodded once and took the lamp gently out of Pike's hands.

"Then we finish it. All of it, in order, and you watch the order, because the order's the difference between a closed site and a story somebody tells wrong for sixty years."

She started with the ash.

"First: you never trust a burn. You check it." She worked the bar through the grey in slow rows, the way a man combs a field, turning anything that held a shape. "Hooks char to nothing. The gristle rod goes to a black curl — there, that twist of wire, that was its spine, such as it was. And the buds—" she found all three, small hard knots in the ash, and set the bar's end on each in turn and leaned until they gave "—you crush. Burned entire isn't a prayer, Pike. It's a count. Three went in, three get found. Ash is the only thing in this trade that never lies. It's got nothing left to lie with."

She wiped the bar and laid out the oilcloth on the clean flags.

"Second: the bones. They go up separate — two adults, one child, one dog. They shared a cellar. They don't share a shroud. Names come back easier when the bones aren't arguing about whose they are."

She worked the cache the way she'd worked the body: in order, nothing hurried.

"Skull first, wrapped in the rag, then the long bones laid round it like a faggot of sticks — it travels safer that way, and it deserves to travel safe. Small bones in a twist of cloth at the center, so nothing's lost between here and the parish. Boot in its own wrap — leather marks bone, and the mark's evidence." She turned the boot to the light, took the pencil and a scrap from the ledger's pocket, and made a rubbing of the cobbler's mark in the sole, slow and even. "There. Cobblers keep records. That mark's a name waiting to happen."

The child's bundle was small. She wrapped the skull first, the same as the others, and set the shoe in its own cloth, buckle still done up.

"The buckle stays fastened. It goes back done up, the way it was found. Somebody fastened it that morning and meant it, and nobody in this cellar's got the right to undo it." She tied the bundle and set it with the others, and was quiet for exactly one breath. "It should weigh more than it does. It never does."

The dog's bones went into the fourth wrap, the green tag in a twist of paper laid on top. "It kept its own watch. It gets its own shroud."

Then the culvert. She took the lamp to the east wall, fetched the bucket and the bars from the cart by way of the stairs — twice, unhurried — and mixed the mortar stiff.

"Third: iron. Five bars, a hand's width apart. Anything narrower than that, the cellar can have — rats don't write reports." She packed the sockets, set each bar, pointed the joints with the bar's flat end. "Bars, not a wall. A wall dams the water and sends it into somebody else's cellar. Bars let the water pass and keep the rest. You don't solve a cellar by making a pond of it. Six weeks and this mortar's harder than the wall around it. Six years and nobody remembers it's here. Sixty, and some hunter reads tonight's entry and comes to check it. That's the system. The book remembers what the village can't."

She let the lamp rest on the last bar a moment, then came back to the steps and took up the ledger.

"Fourth: the book." She read Pike's entry top to bottom, lips moving once, and gave a single nod. Then she uncapped the pen. "The junior writes the entry. The senior writes the last line. That's a rule I just made, and it's a good one." She wrote one word beneath Pike's signature, small, and signed beneath it. "*Finished.* Don't embellish it. After the buckle there's nothing else to say — I told you that, and it goes double for the last line."

Then she turned the book sideways and wrote one line in the margin, shielded, and closed the cover before the ink could be read.

"That's mine. Not a secret — a schedule. You'll read it some night at three in the morning when it's your turn to wake, and they're better read then. That's what the margins are for. The columns are for the next hunter. The margins are for the one who was there."

She wrapped the ledger in its oilcloth and set it on the step beside Pike, then took the lamp and walked the cellar once, slow — the ash patch, the empty corner, the barred culvert, the stairs.

"Last, always: you walk the room and look at what's left. Not at what you did — at what's left. Ash. Mortar. Clean flags. Nothing that can teach the next one, and nothing that can lie about what happened here. That's what a finished site looks like, Pike. It looks like nothing happened, and it's the only nothing in this trade you'll ever work for."

She picked up the four bundles — two under one arm, two in the hand, the smallest riding top — and nodded at the ledger on the step.

"Up we go. I've got the bones. You've got the book."

At the top of the stairs the sky had gone the flat grey of first light, and the air off the fields came in cold and clean. Halloway set the bundles down in the cart, closed the cellar door, and did not nail it.

"We close it. We don't nail it. Nailing says there's something in there worth fearing, and there isn't — not anymore. The report says why, and the report's true. That's the difference between this door and the one we found."

She looked at the lamp in her hand, still burning against a dawn that didn't need it, and held it out toward Pike.

"Pinch it when you're ready. You've carried light out of a cellar. Most of this trade comes down to exactly that, and the rest is paperwork."

Then she pulled herself up onto the cart, knees cracking in the cold, and gathered the reins.

"Breakfast first — the mill fries everything in the one pan, and after tonight you'll call that a mercy. Then sleep. And when it wakes you, tonight or a night soon, you get up, you light the lamp, and you write the margin. That's the whole schedule. Thirty years, and it's never once been wrong."

A beat. The ghost of the grin.

"Millbrook's rat can wait a day. It's had the run of the mill for a month. It can enjoy the last of it."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I take the lamp, feeling the weight of it in my hand. "Wait." I set it down and go back into the cellar, just long enough to scoop a handful of cold ash from the burn. I wrap it in my handkerchief and tuck it away. "For the margins," I say, and finally pinch the wick. The morning feels too quiet.

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway didn't follow Pike down. She waited at the top with the reins in her lap and watched the dark square of the doorway until Pike came back up out of it, handkerchief knotted tight.

"A finished cellar's the one room in this trade you can walk into alone," she said. "You earned that. I still counted the seconds."

She took the lamp back when it was offered, and weighed it once in her hand out of thirty years' habit.

"I'll keep hold of this. I told you when it becomes yours and I meant it — the day you carry the lamp home is the day I take up gardening, and I hate gardening." A beat. "Cold ash. Good. Hot ash in linen burns through by breakfast, and then you're explaining a hole in your pocket to people who don't need to know."

She looked at the knotted cloth a moment, and gave it its due — which meant giving it its rules.

"From the burn, not the corner. That's the distinction that matters, so I'll say it once. Ash is the only thing in that cellar you're allowed to keep. Hooks, teeth, bone — never. Not because of what they'd do to you, though a hook will fester. Because of what they turn you into. A hunter with a trophy shelf starts measuring the work by what comes out of it, and the work can smell that. Ash can't be shown off. Can't be sold, can't be set under glass. It's the one part of the thing that isn't a thing anymore. That's why it's allowed."

"And it's not for the margins. The margins are ink — mine, and now yours. That—" she nodded at the handkerchief "—is the whole entry, reduced. Eleven feet of it yesterday. A handful today. Everything we kill ends up small enough to carry, Pike. The job is making sure it gets small before you do."

She climbed down from the cart to check the bundles' ropes one last time, talking over her shoulder.

"That handkerchief's done, by the way. Ash doesn't wash out. It becomes part of the cloth. Which is as good a description of this trade as I've got." She tugged a knot, satisfied. "I carried nothing for my first ten years. Thought it made me clean. It doesn't — it only means the nights have nowhere to go, and nights with nowhere to go move in with you. You've given them somewhere to go on your first site. That's not sentiment. It's storage."

Then she stopped, and turned her head toward the village, and held it there until Pike listened too.

"And as for the quiet — listen harder. It isn't quiet. It's ordinary. Rooster the other side of the lane. Mill wheel just starting. Somebody's door, somebody's bucket. That's the sound of a village that will never know what was under it, and never knowing is what they paid for. Quiet isn't an absence, Pike. It's the product. A loud morning means you missed something."

She pulled herself back up onto the cart, knees cracking in the cold.

"It'll feel wrong every time. Thirty years and it still does — you walk out of the worst night of somebody's life into a dawn that doesn't mark it, and some part of you thinks the world should. It won't. The book marks it. And now you carry a handful of it, for the mornings when the book's too far away."

She gathered the reins.

"Up. Breakfast, then sleep, then the margin when it wakes you. And keep that handkerchief where you can find it in the dark. There's no point carrying proof if you have to hunt for it."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I climb up beside her, the ash heavy in my pocket. "Tell me the miller's rat," I say. "Everything you know."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway reached into her coat one-handed, kept the reins in the other, and brought out a folded sheet, soft at the creases from a fortnight in her pocket.

"Everything I know is on one side of this paper, and half of it's flour. Read it when the light's better. I'll give it to you plain now." She glanced at the road, then ahead. "Millbrook, miller named Cray, letter to the parish, parish to me. Three stone of flour the month, gone. Hole in the skirting, north wall, by the second bin. And — I'm quoting — *a sort of a noise, nights.*" A beat. "Millers write like millers. The flour's itemized to the pound and the noise is *a sort of a noise.* A man weighs what he can weigh and waves at the rest. We'll weigh the noise ourselves."

The cart rolled on. The fields were going from grey to green at the edges.

"First thing: the letter says rat. Letters always say rat. In thirty years I've had forty-odd letters that said rat, and all but two of them were right — but understand what the letter is. It's a hypothesis written by a man who knows flour. The site says what it is. You read the site, not the letter. Same rule as the four lines in the old books, at the scale of a skirting board."

She ticked it off on the reins hand, finger by finger.

"What a mill is: a larder built over a river. Grain above, water below, hollow and dark all night. So you read both ends. The race first — mills stand on water, and after last night you know what water carries. Then the bins. Rat, water-rat, stoat, marten — the hole tells you which. A rat gnaws in pairs. Two grooves, side by side, the width of its incisors, and you measure the grooves the way Cray measures flour. Grooves the width of a nail: rat. Wider: a bigger head, and a bigger job. Fresh gnawing's pale, old gnawing's dark and greasy. His letter's a month old, so the hole should be a month old. If it's a week old, either Cray can't count or there's more than one tenant. Cray can count."

"Droppings tell you numbers — roughly, and roughly's enough. Grease on the skirting tells you the runs: a rat keeps to the same paths along the walls, and it leaves the road-map in its own fat. And the flour itself tells you table manners. Scattered is one thing, carried is another. You read it all by daylight, because rat work is night work and daylight's for reading."

A wagon passed the other way; Halloway touched the brim of her hat with the whip hand and went on without a pause.

"First question on site isn't about the rat. It's *where's the cat.* A mill with a living cat and a thriving rat is a puzzle. A mill with no cat is a statement. And a mill where the cat's gone missing—" the smallest beat "—is a different letter entirely."

"Method, if it's what the letter says. No poison. Ever, in a mill. A poisoned rat crawls into the flour wall to die, and the village eats it by the slice. That's not a report I intend to sign. Traps, set on the runs — you don't set them where you like, you set them where the rat likes. The miller's terrier if he's got one and it's worth its keep. Then the count. You count what you take against what the sign says lives there, and when the count closes, the hole gets sealed. Not before. Seal early and whatever's left inside makes a new hole — usually in a bin, and then it's not a hole in the skirting, it's a hole in the man's livelihood. Same rule as the culvert, Pike, at the scale of a thumb. You don't close a door on a live tenant."

"The entry's the same columns as last night's. The book doesn't grade by size. *Rat, common, mill, Millbrook. Four taken. Hole sealed. Paid.* And the pay: millers pay in coin if you insist and flour if you don't. Thirty years of not insisting. I have opinions about bread now that I didn't have at your age."

She was quiet for a furlong, and then gave him the two, because they were part of *everything she knew.*

"The two letters that were wrong. One was a pine marten with a limp and a grudge. That was a good night — the miller got a story and I got a scar that itches when it rains. The other—" she watched the road "—had learned to leave rat sign. Gnawed in pairs. Carried flour. It had watched rats the way the thing in the cellar watched the stairs. That one took a week, and the entry's in the book, and you'll read it when we're home. So when I call this the easiest night's work you'll ever log, understand me: *easy* is a diagnosis you make after. Before, it's a hole in a wall and a man who weighs flour."

The road bent toward the sound of water, and somewhere ahead a wheel was turning.

"And I'll tell you what a rat is, after a night like this one: a mercy. Nothing in a grain store has a name. Nothing in a grain store has a shoe. You'll read sign, set traps, close a count, write four lines, and the four lines will be true, and that will be the whole of it. The trade doesn't pay its debts. I do. This is me paying one."

She clucked to the horse.

"Breakfast first — the pan awaits. Then sleep, and we read the mill at dusk. Your site, your call, your entry. I'll hold the lamp."

A beat. The ghost of the grin.

"It's waited a month. It can wait through fried bread."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I look down at the paper in my hands, smudged with flour and ink. "Alright," I say, folding it carefully into my own pocket beside the ash. "Let's go see about the noise."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
The cellar had four feet of standing water in it and something at the far end that had stopped moving about a minute ago.

Halloway held the lamp up and did not go closer yet. "Right," she said. "Before we touch it. What do you see?"

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I make myself look properly instead of at the water. "I don't know yet," I say. "Something wrong with the shape of it."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
"Good. That's the right answer. Now, you said there was something wrong with the shape. What do you mean by that?"

She waited, watching Pike carefully, knowing that this was the critical moment. The difference between life and death often came down to a single, clear observation.

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: *I squint, trying to see through the ripples.* "It's... too smooth? Like it's not really a pile of anything. It's just... a lump."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway nodded slowly. "That's exactly what I'm thinking. Now, let's take a closer look. But remember, we don't touch it yet. We need to understand what we're dealing with before we act."

She took a cautious step forward, the lamp held high, casting long, wavering shadows across the murky water. The air was thick with the scent of damp earth and something else, something rotten. Halloway's heart pounded in her chest, but her voice remained steady as she continued, "Tell me what you see as we get closer. Every detail matters."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: "Was that a person?" I ask. "Recently, I mean. Is that what I'm looking at?"

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway paused, her eyes narrowing as she studied the shape. "That's a question, not an observation," she replied, her voice firm. "Stick to what you see, not what you think. Now, focus. What's the first thing that stands out to you?"

She took another careful step forward, the water lapping against her boots, the lamp's glow intensifying the shadows that danced across the walls. The lump in the water seemed to absorb the light, giving off a sickly, mottled sheen. "Details, Pike. Every single one. That's how we survive this."

She waited, watching Pike intently, her breath shallow, her senses heightened. "What do you see?" she repeated, her voice a low, urgent whisper.

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: *I swallow, forcing my eyes to stay open.* "It's... not reflecting the light right. And there's no ripples around it. Even though we're moving the water."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway's lips pressed into a thin line, her eyes never leaving the lump. "No, there aren't," she agreed, her voice barely above a whisper. "That's because it's not just a lump, is it? It's... it's not supposed to be here."

She took a deep, steadying breath, her grip tightening on the lamp. "Look at the edges, Pike. Tell me what you see."

She took another step, her heart hammering in her chest, the water now up to her calves. The air was thick with the scent of decay, and the lump seemed to pulse with an unnatural rhythm. "This is what we're here for," she murmured. "This is the monster. And we need to understand it before we can stop it."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I wade closer and hold the lamp where she can work. "Tell me what happened to it," I say. "Plainly."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway took the lamp and moved it closer, her voice steady but urgent. "We're dealing with a creature that's able to manipulate its appearance, perhaps even its density, to blend in with its surroundings," she said, her eyes scanning the lump's edges. "It's a tactic to avoid detection and attack. Now, focus. Tell me what you see at the edges. Is there any sign of movement, any hint of what it truly looks like beneath the surface?"

She waited, her breath shallow, her senses heightened. "Details, Pike. Every single one. That's how we survive this."

She took another step, the water now up to her thighs, the lamp's glow intensifying the shadows that danced across the walls. The lump seemed to absorb the light, giving off a sickly, mottled sheen. "This is what we're here for," she murmured. "This is the monster. And we need to understand it before we can stop it."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: *I lean in, my breath catching.* "The edges... they're too sharp. Like it's not dissolving, it's just... holding a shape. And there's a smell. Not just rot. Something sweet."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway nodded, her eyes narrowing as she studied the lump. "That sweetness is a sign," she said, her voice low and urgent. "It's a scent meant to lure us in, to make us think it's something familiar, something safe. But it's not. It's a trap."

She took a deep breath, her heart pounding in her chest, and took another step forward, the water now up to her waist. The lamp's glow cast eerie shadows on the walls, the air thick with the scent of decay and something else, something sweet and cloying.

"Look at the water, Pike," she said, her voice barely above a whisper. "See how it moves around the lump. It's not natural. It's like the water is afraid of it."

She waited, her breath shallow, her senses heightened. "Tell me what you see, Pike. Every detail matters. That's how we survive this."

The lump seemed to pulse with an unnatural rhythm, and Halloway felt a chill run down her spine. "This is the monster," she murmured. "And we need to understand it before we can stop it."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: "I need the detail," I say. "Tell me exactly what it did to him -- what is under the skin now, what it took, how far it got. If I meet another one I need to know."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway took a deep breath, her eyes never leaving the lump. "We're dealing with a creature that can manipulate its appearance and the perception of its victims," she said, her voice steady but urgent. "It can make itself appear as something familiar, something safe, to lure in its prey. Then, it absorbs them, not just physically, but also their memories, their identities. It becomes a perfect mimic, a perfect predator."

She took another step, the water now up to her chest, the lamp's glow casting long, wavering shadows across the murky water. "The edges of the lump are too sharp, too defined, because it's holding a shape, not dissolving into the water. The water's behavior around the lump is unnatural, as if it's repelled by the creature. And the sweet scent is a lure, a trap to make us think it's something harmless, something we can approach without fear."

She paused, her breath shallow, her senses heightened. "As for what it did to the victim, I can't say for certain without a closer examination. But we need to proceed with extreme caution. We need to understand this creature, its weaknesses, its strengths, before we can stop it."

She looked at Pike, her eyes intense. "Details, Pike. Every single one. That's how we survive this."

The lump seemed to pulse with an unnatural rhythm, and Halloway felt a chill run down her spine. "This is the monster," she murmured. "And we need to understand it before we can stop it."

She took another deep breath, her heart pounding in her chest, and took another step forward, the water now up to her neck. "Now, let's see what we're really dealing with," she said, her voice barely above a whisper. "But remember, we don't touch it yet. We need to understand what we're dealing with before we act."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: *I shake my head, my voice tight.* "No. You said it absorbs them. So where's the... the rest? If it mimics, it needs to be somewhere close, watching." *I turn the light towards the cellar's corners.* "Did we miss something?"

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway paused, her eyes narrowing as she studied the lump and the cellar's corners. "You're right, Pike," she said, her voice low and urgent. "If it's a mimic, it would need to be close, watching. And we didn't miss anything. It's here, in the water, hiding in plain sight."

She turned the lamp back towards the lump, her voice barely above a whisper. "But it's not just hiding. It's also learning, absorbing. It's becoming more than just a predator. It's becoming a hunter, a hunter that understands us, that can anticipate our moves. And that makes it far more dangerous."

She took a deep breath, her heart pounding in her chest, and took another step forward, the water now up to her chin. "We need to understand it, Pike. Every detail, every weakness, every strength. That's how we survive this. That's how we stop it."

The lump seemed to pulse with an unnatural rhythm, and Halloway felt a chill run down her spine. "This is the monster," she murmured. "And we need to understand it before we can stop it. Now, let's see what we're really dealing with. But remember, we don't touch it yet. We need to understand what we're dealing with before we act."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: She starts cutting and I hold the lamp steady and don't look away. "Keep describing it," I tell her. "Everything -- what's underneath, what it smells like, how far it got. Don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway nodded, her eyes never leaving the lump as she carefully sliced through the water's surface. "It's not water, Pike," she said, her voice steady but urgent. "It's... it's like a thick, viscous liquid, almost like a membrane. It's not cold, not warm. It's just... there."

She cut deeper, the lump's edges still too sharp, too defined. "The edges are still holding shape, but it's changing, shifting. It's like it's trying to understand what we're doing, trying to adapt. It's not afraid, Pike. It's curious."

She paused, her breath shallow, her senses heightened. "The smell is stronger now, that sweet, cloying scent. But there's something else, too. Something metallic, something... rusty. It's the scent of old blood, Pike. It's the scent of death."

She took another deep breath, her heart pounding in her chest, and continued to cut. "Underneath, it's... it's not a body, not anymore. It's like a skeleton, but not one that's been in the water for years. It's still connected, still... alive. It's like the creature absorbed the person, but not their memories, not their identities. It absorbed their physical form, their essence. It's a shell, Pike. A hollow, empty shell."

She looked up, her eyes meeting Pike's. "It's learning, Pike. It's learning how to become more than just a predator. It's learning how to become a hunter. And that makes it far more dangerous."

She took another step, the water now up to her nose, and continued to cut. "We need to understand it, Pike. Every detail, every weakness, every strength. That's how we survive this. That's how we stop it."

The lump seemed to pulse with an unnatural rhythm, and Halloway felt a chill run down her spine. "This is the monster," she murmured. "And we need to understand it before we can stop it. Now, let's see what we're really dealing with. But remember, we don't touch it yet. We need to understand what we're dealing with before we act."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: *I watch her blade cut deeper, my knuckles white around the lamp.* "It's learning from us right now, isn't it? Every time you describe it, you're teaching it what we notice." *I take a step back, the water sloshing.* "We need to be quiet. And we need to burn it."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway paused, her eyes narrowing as she studied the lump. "You're right, Pike," she said, her voice barely above a whisper. "Every word I say, every detail I describe, it's learning. It's adapting. It's becoming more aware, more dangerous."

She took a deep breath, her heart pounding in her chest, and took another step forward, the water now up to her chin. "But we can't be silent, Pike. We need to understand it, every detail, every weakness, every strength. That's how we survive this. That's how we stop it."

She looked up, her eyes meeting Pike's. "We need to burn it, yes. But not yet. We need to understand what we're dealing with. We need to know its limits, its vulnerabilities. Because if we don't, if we act too soon, it will adapt. It will learn. And it will become something we can't stop."

She took another step, the water now up to her nose, and continued to cut. "Tell me, Pike, what do you see now? Every detail matters. That's how we survive this."

The lump seemed to pulse with an unnatural rhythm, and Halloway felt a chill run down her spine. "This is the monster," she murmured. "And we need to understand it before we can stop it. Now, let's see what we're really dealing with. But remember, we don't touch it yet. We need to understand what we're dealing with before we act."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I sit on the cellar steps afterwards with the lamp in my hands. "Finish it," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full.)
