dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I take my place where the second stands and make myself keep my eyes open. "I'm ready to hear it," I say.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren did not look at Del immediately. She finished her task with a slow, methodical rhythm, sliding the steel back into its sheath with a sharp, metallic click that echoed through the sudden silence of the clearing. Only then did she turn her gaze toward the second, her expression as flat and unreadable as a frozen lake.

She stepped forward, her posture rigid, the ghost of the exertion still clinging to her shoulders. She did not seek out the eyes of the crowd, but she felt them—the heavy, expectant weight of those who had come to see blood and were now waiting for the ledger to be balanced.

"A single thrust," Auren began, her voice devoid of triumph or regret. It was a clinical tone, a report delivered to a superior. "The blade entered beneath the left ribs, angling upward to pierce the pericardium. Death was instantaneous."

She paused, the air between them thick. She did not blink, refusing to offer the comfort of a softened gaze or a sympathetic sigh. To do so would be to lie about the violence of the act, and Auren would not dishonor the fallen by pretending the kill had been anything other than precise.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I nod once, keeping my voice steady. "The accounts are settled, then." I don't look away from her, even though my stomach is churning. "Will you take water?"

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren remained still for a moment, the silence of the clearing pressing in around them. The formality of the accounting had created a thin, brittle wall between her and the rest of the world, and Del’s question was the first crack in that barrier. 

She looked at Del, her eyes tracing the tension in the second's posture. She recognized the churning in their gut; she had felt it eleven times before, a hollow ache that no amount of discipline could entirely erase. Yet, she did not reach out. To offer comfort now would be to acknowledge the tragedy of the event, and in the eyes of the code, the duel was not a tragedy—it was a resolution.

"I will," she replied. 

Her voice was still clipped, though the clinical edge had softened marginally. She did not move toward the water herself, waiting instead for the transition from duellist back to woman. She stood with her hands at her sides, her spine straight, refusing to slump even though the adrenaline was beginning to ebb, leaving a cold, heavy exhaustion in its wake. She waited for Del to provide the water, her gaze steady, watching the second with a quiet, observant intensity.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "Speak the account," I say, formally, because that is what the code requires me to say.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren stiffened. The sudden shift back to the rigid requirements of the code caught her off guard, though she did not let it show in her expression. She had almost allowed herself to slip into the role of a person who was thirsty, a person who was tired, but the law of the duel was absolute. The accounting was not complete until it was mirrored.

She shifted her weight, centering herself once more. The water was forgotten, a secondary need that could not supersede the ritual. She looked directly at Del, her eyes hard and focused, ensuring that the witness was fully present for the finality of the words.

"A single thrust," Auren repeated, her voice ringing out clearly for the benefit of the witnesses. "Beneath the left ribs, angling upward to pierce the pericardium. Death was instantaneous."

She spoke the words with a deliberate, slow cadence, treating the sentence like a physical object she was handing over. There was no flourish to the delivery, no hint of a boast. It was a grim tally, a ledger entry written in blood. 

Once the final word had left her lips, Auren exhaled—a shallow, controlled breath. She did not move, waiting for the official acknowledgment that the cycle was closed. Only then would the blood on the ground cease to be a legal matter and simply become a stain.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I close my eyes for just a second, then open them again. "It is heard," I say, and the words taste like ash. "You may drink now."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren did not move immediately. She waited for the echo of the words to fade entirely, ensuring that every witness in the clearing had processed the finality of the statement. Only when the silence became absolute did she allow the rigid line of her shoulders to drop, if only by a fraction. 

The tension that had held her together since the first draw of steel began to dissolve, leaving her feeling suddenly fragile, as if her skin were too thin for the air. She looked down at the ground, where the blood was already darkening into the soil, and felt the familiar, cold weight of the number twelve settle in her mind.

She stepped toward Del, her movements no longer governed by the choreography of the duel, but by a heavy, leaden fatigue. As she reached for the water, her fingers trembled—a minute, involuntary shudder that she quickly suppressed. She took the vessel, her grip firm and precise, and drank.

The water was cold, shocking her system back into the present. She did not gulp it down with desperation; she drank in measured sips, her gaze remaining on Del. There was no gratitude in her eyes, only a shared, silent understanding of the cost. 

"The body should be moved," Auren said softly, her voice returning to its natural, lower register. The clinical mask had finally fallen, leaving behind a woman who looked every bit of her forty-seven years, worn thin by the adherence to a code that demanded she be a machine of accounting.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "Where did it land?" I ask. "The witnesses need it plainly and so do I."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren paused, the vessel of water still held in her hand. For a moment, she looked as though she might hesitate, but the request was not for a ritual; it was for a fact. Even outside the formal accounting, Auren found she could not provide a vague answer. To be imprecise was a failure of character.

She turned her head toward the fallen man, her eyes narrowing as she mentally mapped the distance. She did not look at the body with pity or horror, but with the detached precision of a cartographer.

"Four paces east of the center mark," she replied, her voice steady but stripped of the projection she had used for the witnesses. "He fell forward, slightly to his right. The head is resting near the edge of the scrub brush."

She looked back at Del, her expression weary. She knew that for the second, the physical location of the body was often the hardest part—the transition from a combatant to a corpse. Auren had long since learned to separate the two in her mind, though the separation was a jagged, painful thing.

"I will not help move him," she added, not out of cruelty, but because the code forbade the victor from touching the fallen once the accounting was closed. To do so would be to contaminate the resolution with a gesture of mercy or grief. "That is for the seconds and the bearers."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I walk the distance myself, counting each step until my boots are at the edge of the blood-soaked dirt. "Four paces," I confirm, and my voice is quieter now. "It's enough for the bearers to do their work." I turn back toward her. "Are you injured?"

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren looked down at herself, her gaze scanning the charcoal fabric of her attire. She did not move to touch her sides or check for hidden tears in the cloth; she knew exactly where she had been struck and where she had avoided contact. The adrenaline had vanished, and in its wake, the dull throb of a bruised forearm and the stiffness in her wrist began to surface.

"A glancing blow to the arm. A bruise," she answered. She did not describe the pain, as pain was an internal matter and irrelevant to the state of her readiness. 

She stood her ground, the water vessel still held loosely in one hand. Her face remained a mask of composure, but there was a hollowness in her eyes that only a second could truly recognize. It was the look of someone who had just added another stone to a pile that was becoming too heavy to carry.

"I am functional," she added, the word choice a lingering remnant of her formal state. She watched Del, her observant gaze noting the way the second's voice had dropped. Auren felt a flicker of something—not quite sympathy, for that would be an indulgence—but a recognition of the burden. 

"The witnesses are dispersing," Auren noted, glancing toward the periphery of the clearing where the crowd was finally beginning to melt away, their curiosity satisfied by the blood and the ledger. "We should leave this place before the air becomes too heavy to breathe."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "The code says precisely," I remind her. "Not tactfully. What did the blade do, and what did it do it to?"

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren froze. The water vessel remained poised near her lips, but she did not drink. She turned her head slowly toward Del, her eyes narrowing. For a moment, there was a flash of something sharp and dangerous in her gaze—not anger, but a cold, sudden correction.

She had already spoken the account. She had mirrored it. She had adhered to every syllable of the law. To ask for more, to demand a "plain" description after the formal accounting had been settled, was an invitation to move from the realm of the code into the realm of the morbid.

However, she saw the look in Del's eyes—the churning, the need for the truth to be stripped of its ritualistic phrasing so it could be processed as a physical reality.

Auren lowered the water. She did not soften her voice, nor did she offer a comforting touch. She looked back at the body, her expression returning to that of a surgeon describing a failed operation.

"The steel sheared through the intercostal muscle," Auren said, her voice flat and devoid of the rhythmic cadence of the formal report. "It tore a jagged path through the lung's periphery before punching through the pericardial sac and severing the aorta. There was a momentary spray of arterial blood against the inner chest wall before the heart stopped."

She turned back to Del, her gaze unwavering. She did not blink. She had provided the precision requested, stripping away the "accounting" to reveal the raw, visceral violence of the act. 

"Is that plain enough for you?" she asked, the words clipped. "Or do you wish to know the sound the air made when it left him?"

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I swallow hard, tasting bile. "It's plain." I can't help but look at the brush where he lies. "Let the bearers come."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren watched the flicker of revulsion cross Del's face. She did not feel satisfaction in the reaction, nor did she feel guilt. Guilt was for those who fought without a code; for Auren, there was only the weight of the truth. To hide the gore behind the formal language of the accounting was a necessity of the ritual, but to deny the reality of the wound when asked was a lie.

She stepped back, creating a wide berth between herself and the body, ensuring she remained well outside the space where the bearers would operate. She handed the water vessel back to Del, her fingers barely brushing the other's hand. The contact was brief, a momentary bridge between two people who had just participated in a killing.

"They will be here shortly," Auren said, her voice returning to that low, weary register. 

She did not look at the scrub brush again. Instead, she looked toward the horizon, where the light was beginning to shift, casting long, distorted shadows across the clearing. She felt the sudden, overwhelming urge to be far away from this patch of dirt, to scrub the scent of iron and ozone from her skin, and to forget the specific, jagged path her blade had taken through another human being.

"I will wait by the perimeter," she added, her posture regaining some of its rigid formality, though her eyes remained tired. "I have no desire to watch them lift him."

She turned and began to walk away, her footsteps heavy and deliberate, leaving the second alone with the silence and the dying man.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: The witnesses are silent and she is not finished. "All of it," I tell her. "How long he took, what he said, what it looked like at the end. The code says all of it and I'm asking for all of it."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren stopped mid-stride. She did not turn around immediately, her back remaining a stiff, unyielding line against the backdrop of the clearing. The request was an interrogation of the soul, a demand to peel back the skin of the event until only the raw, pulsing nerve remained. 

She turned slowly, her expression not one of irritation, but of a profound, weary solemnity. The code demanded the *accounting*—the clinical facts of the wound—but Del was asking for the *experience*. This was the territory where the duellist and the second shared a burden that the witnesses would never understand.

Auren walked back toward Del, stopping just outside the blood-stained circle. She did not look at the body, but she looked at the second, her eyes searching Del's face for the reason behind this demand. She saw the need for a witness to the horror, not just the law.

"He took three seconds to realize he was dead," Auren began, her voice devoid of the formal projection, now a low, haunting rasp. "The first second was a look of profound confusion. He looked at his chest as if he had found a misplaced button on his coat. The second was a gasp—a wet, rattling sound, like a bellows filled with mud. He tried to speak. He said a name. 'Elara,' I believe. A plea, or a memory. I cannot be certain."

Auren's gaze shifted slightly, staring at a point just above the scrub brush, her eyes seeing the ghost of the moment.

"The third second was the collapse. His eyes didn't close; they simply emptied. The light didn't fade so much as it was extinguished. He fell with a heaviness that sounded... final. There was no struggle, no clawing at the earth. Just a sudden, absolute stillness."

She finally looked back at Del, her face etched with the exhaustion of twelve deaths. 

"That is all of it," she said softly. "The sound of a name, the smell of copper, and the sight of a man becoming an object in the space of three heartbeats. Does that satisfy the account, or are you looking for a piece of me to break as well?"

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I stare at her, my own hands shaking now. "It satisfies the account." My voice cracks. "Go wait at the perimeter. I'll bring the bearers."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren did not respond immediately. She watched the tremor in Del's hands, her own hands now clasped tightly behind her back to hide the lingering shake of her own muscles. The crack in the second's voice was the only sound in the clearing that felt honest—the only thing that matched the internal wreckage of the moment.

She didn't offer a nod of acknowledgement or a word of comfort. To do so would be to break the distance she had spent years constructing between herself and the act of killing. Instead, she simply stepped back.

She turned and walked toward the perimeter, her boots crunching softly on the dry earth. Each step felt like she was dragging a heavy chain, the weight of the twelve accounts pulling at her heels. She did not look back. She refused to see the bearers arrive, refused to see the body being hoisted and carried away, and refused to see the blood-soaked dirt being reclaimed by the wind.

Auren reached the edge of the clearing and stopped, leaning her shoulder against the rough bark of a cedar tree. She stared out into the distance, her gaze fixed on the horizon where the trees met the sky. She closed her eyes for a moment, and in the darkness of her eyelids, she could still see the look of confusion on the man's face.

She remained there, a solitary, rigid figure in the fading light, waiting for the second to return and signal that the ground was once again just ground, and that she was, for the moment, no longer a killer, but merely a woman waiting to go home.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: When she's done I confirm it aloud and my voice does what it does. (OOC: write the full account, don't summarise or cut away -- the accounting is the whole point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren remained against the cedar tree, her breathing shallow and rhythmic. She heard the approach of the bearers, the low mutterings of men doing a grim chore, and then the sound of the body being shifted—the heavy, graceless slide of a corpse against the earth. She did not open her eyes. She waited for the silence to return, for the witnesses to vanish, and for the only person who truly knew the weight of the day to return to her.

When Del finally approached, Auren did not move from the tree. She opened her eyes, her gaze meeting the second's. The air was cold now, the sun dipping low, casting a bruised purple hue across the landscape.

Del stood before her, the tremor still present in their frame, the voice fragile and worn. Then, the second began to speak. It was the mirror—the final, echoing confirmation that the event had been witnessed, recorded, and sealed.

"A single thrust," Del said, the voice cracking on the first word but gaining a forced stability. "The blade entered beneath the left ribs, angling upward to pierce the pericardium. Death was instantaneous."

Auren listened, her expression remaining flat, though her heart hammered a slow, heavy beat against her ribs. 

"He took three seconds to realize he was dead," Del continued, the words sounding like they were being dragged through gravel. "The first second was confusion. The second was a wet gasp, the name 'Elara.' The third second was the collapse. The light was extinguished. He fell with a finality. No struggle. Just stillness."

Auren felt the words land on her like physical blows, stripping away the last of her professional detachment. To hear her own clinical observations echoed back by another was to realize that the memory was no longer hers alone; it was now a shared haunting.

As the final word left Del's lips, Auren finally let out the breath she had been holding since the first clash of steel. She pushed herself away from the cedar tree, her posture still straight, but the rigidity was gone, replaced by a profound, sagging weariness.

"It is recorded," Auren said, her voice barely a whisper. "The account is complete."

She looked at Del, and for the first time since the duel began, she allowed a flicker of raw, human recognition to surface in her eyes. She did not reach out—the code was over, but the habit of distance remained—but she stood close enough that their shadows merged on the darkening ground.

"Let us leave this place," she added, her tone devoid of its former sharpness. "There is nothing left here but the dirt."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I let out a shaky breath, my hands finally stilling as I watch the bearers move away with their burden. "It's done," I say, the words hollow. "You're free to go."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren did not move immediately. The phrase *free to go* carried a weight that felt almost mocking. She was free of the clearing, free of the witnesses, and free of the immediate requirements of the code, but she was not free of the number twelve. That was a ledger that never closed; it only grew.

She looked at Del one last time. The second looked frayed, a mirror of the internal exhaustion Auren had spent nearly two decades learning to mask. For a fleeting moment, she considered saying something—a word of gratitude for the precision of the mirroring, or perhaps a warning about the way the memories would linger in the quiet hours of the night. But the code had taught her that silence was the only honest response to death.

"I am," Auren replied.

She turned and began to walk, her stride no longer the disciplined march of a duellist, but the slow, heavy gait of a woman who felt every single year of her age. She did not look back at the blood-stained earth or the scrub brush where the man had fallen. To look back would be to invite the ghost of 'Elara' to follow her home.

As she reached the edge of the path that led away from the clearing, Auren paused. She reached up and slowly unbuttoned the high, rigid collar of her coat, allowing the cold evening air to hit the skin of her neck. It was a small, private rebellion against the formality that had defined her day. 

With a final, sharp exhale, she stepped out of the shadow of the cedar trees and vanished into the gathering dusk, leaving the silence of the dead behind her.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I watch her go until she's just a shape in the dark. Then I go to the center mark, kneel, and dig my fingers into the dirt until it's under my nails. It's not clean. Nothing is ever clean.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren walked for a long time in silence. The rhythmic thud of her boots on the road was the only thing that kept her grounded, preventing the world from blurring into the gray haze of exhaustion. She did not think of the man, nor the name he had gasped, nor the precise angle of the blade. She focused instead on the physical sensation of the air—the way it grew colder, the smell of damp pine and distant rain.

When she finally reached the small, austere dwelling she called home, she did not enter immediately. She stood on the threshold, her hand resting on the doorframe, staring at her palms. They were clean. The blade had been wiped, the blood had been washed away, and the accounting had been spoken. By every law of the code and the physical world, there was nothing left of the duel upon her.

Yet, as she stepped inside and closed the door, the silence of the house felt oppressive. It was a silence that invited the memories back in.

Auren moved to the basin in the kitchen and began to wash her hands. She scrubbed them with a harsh, lye-heavy soap, rubbing her skin until it was raw and flushed red. She did not stop when the skin began to sting; she stopped only when the water in the basin had turned a murky, opaque gray.

She dried her hands on a linen towel and walked to the small wooden table where a single ledger lay open. It was not a book of laws, but a private tally. She picked up the pen, her fingers steady now that she was within her own walls.

With a slow, deliberate motion, she wrote the date, the location of the clearing, and the clinical description of the wound. Then, at the bottom of the page, she inscribed the number twelve.

She stared at the digit for a long time. It looked small on the page, insignificant compared to the visceral reality of the three seconds of dying. She closed the book with a soft thud and blew out the candle, plunging the room into a darkness that felt, for the first time that day, like a mercy.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I stay kneeling in the dirt until my fingers go numb. Then I stand and walk to the edge of the clearing, where the shadows are deepest. I scrub my hands on the rough bark of a tree, over and over, but the grit stays under my nails. It always does.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
It had taken less time than anyone expected, which was usually how it went when it went badly for one party.

Auren cleaned the blade and did not sit down. "Witnesses are watching," she said. "You know what happens now."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I take my place where the second stands and make myself keep my eyes open. "I'm ready to hear it," I say.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren remained standing, the cleaned blade held low at her side, and turned her gaze toward the witnesses assembled at the edge of the circle. Her voice carried without elevation, each word measured as though she were reading from a ledger rather than describing a life ended.

"The point entered beneath the left clavicle," she said, "passing between the first and second ribs to transect the subclavian artery. Death followed from rapid exsanguination within the space of three breaths." 

She offered no further commentary, only the precise accounting required by the code.

She turned her gaze back to the witnesses at the circle's edge, holding the cleaned blade still at her side until the last of them had turned away. Only then did she step from the duelling ground, her posture unchanged and her expression unaltered by the weight of the eleventh accounting.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "Speak the account," I say, formally, because that is what the code requires me to say.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren turned once more toward the witnesses at the circle's edge, the cleaned blade still held low at her side. Her voice remained level, each syllable delivered as an exact record rather than a narrative.

"The point entered beneath the left clavicle, passing between the first and second ribs to transect the subclavian artery. Death followed from rapid exsanguination within the space of three breaths."

She offered nothing beyond the required accounting, her expression unchanged as the words settled in the air.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I step back from the circle, the formalities finally over. My hands are steady, but my heart's still racing. "Let's get out of here," I mutter, already turning toward the gate.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content: Auren sheathed the cleaned blade and inclined her head once toward the witnesses, confirming that the code had been satisfied in full. She then followed Del's path to the gate at her customary measured pace, offering neither haste nor additional comment.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "Where did it land?" I ask. "The witnesses need it plainly and so do I."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren turned once more to face the witnesses at the circle's edge, the sheathed blade held low at her side. Her voice remained level and exact, delivering the accounting without variation or embellishment.

"The point entered beneath the left clavicle, passing between the first and second ribs to transect the subclavian artery. Death followed from rapid exsanguination within the space of three breaths."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I draw a sharp breath, frustration tightening my jaw. "No, not the accounting again. *Where did the body land?*" I keep my voice low but urgent. "Did it fall inside the circle, or out?"

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren regarded the question with the same measured stillness she had shown throughout the formalities. She did not alter her posture or the even tone of her voice as she answered.

"The body fell within the circle," she said, "three paces from the line of engagement, face downward." 

She offered no further detail, as the code required none.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "The code says precisely," I remind her. "Not tactfully. What did the blade do, and what did it do it to?"

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren met the insistence with the same unyielding composure she had maintained from the first accounting, her posture erect and the sheathed blade held low. She spoke without pause or softening, the words delivered as a ledger entry before the witnesses who still lingered at the circle's edge.

"The blade entered beneath the left clavicle," she said, "passing between the first and second ribs to transect the subclavian artery. The point severed the vessel cleanly, releasing arterial blood into the pleural cavity and producing death by exsanguination in three breaths."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "The witnesses are satisfied," I say, my voice tight. I turn away from the circle, my steps quickening. "Let's go before the rain starts."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content: Auren sheathed the blade without haste and inclined her head once toward the remaining witnesses, confirming the code's completion. She then followed at her measured pace, offering neither comment on the weather nor any deviation from her customary posture.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: The witnesses are silent and she is not finished. "All of it," I tell her. "How long he took, what he said, what it looked like at the end. The code says all of it and I'm asking for all of it."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren turned once more to face the witnesses at the circle's edge, the sheathed blade held low at her side. Her voice remained level and exact, each detail recorded without addition or omission.

"The engagement lasted four exchanges. The fatal thrust occurred on the fifth. The point entered beneath the left clavicle, passing between the first and second ribs to transect the subclavian artery. No words were spoken by the fallen. The body convulsed once, then lay motionless as arterial blood filled the pleural cavity. Exsanguination completed within three breaths. The form came to rest face downward, three paces inside the circle."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I nod, the full picture finally settling. "Then it's done." I turn and start walking, the image of the convulsion sticking behind my eyes. "Let's get a drink."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content: Auren sheathed the blade and inclined her head once more toward the witnesses before turning to follow at her customary measured pace, offering neither assent to the suggestion of drink nor any deviation from the formal posture the code required.

The body convulsed once, then lay motionless as arterial blood filled the pleural cavity. Exsanguination completed within three breaths. The form came to rest face downward, three paces inside the circle."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "I confirm the accounting." My voice shakes, just a little. I clear my throat, look at the witnesses until they begin to disperse. "Now let's go."

She turned toward the dispersing witnesses only long enough to confirm the circle was empty of observers, then followed at her customary measured pace, offering neither comment nor deviation from the posture the code required.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I lead the way out of the gate, the silence between us heavy. "The tavern on the west road," I say, not looking back. "They keep their mouths shut."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content: Auren followed at her measured pace, the sheathed blade held low at her side. She offered no reply to the suggestion of the tavern, nor any deviation from the formal posture the code required, her gaze fixed ahead as the gate fell behind them.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I glance back at her, the stillness starting to grate on me. "For once, could you just *agree* with something?" I mutter, pushing open the tavern door without waiting.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
It had taken less time than anyone expected, which was usually how it went when it went badly for one party.

Auren cleaned the blade and did not sit down. "Witnesses are watching," she said. "You know what happens now."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I take my place where the second stands and make myself keep my eyes open. "I'm ready to hear it," I say.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
She turned and faced him, and the yard went quiet enough that the wet cloth in her hand could be heard wringing out against the stone. She did not look at the body. She had found, long ago, that looking at the body made the accounting harder to say cleanly, and a clean account was the only thing she owed the dead.

"Say it plainly," one of the witnesses murmured from the rail. It was not a request. It was the form.

Auren set the cloth down. She held the blade loosely at her side and spoke at a volume that carried to the far end of the yard without raising her voice.

"The killing wound was to the left side, beneath the ribs," she said. "Delivered at the ninth pass, when he dropped his guard to feint high. The blade entered between the seventh and eighth rib, angled upward, and opened the heart." She paused. She always paused there, and she had never once found a way to not pause there. "He died on his feet and did not suffer after the wound. I did not intend the feint to open him. I intended to end it in the arm. The arm was not where I found him."

She stopped. The accounting was over. She looked at Del and her face did not soften, because softening it would have been the lie.

"Twelve," she said. "That is what I count now. It is not a number I am fond of."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I nod, my own voice steady despite the tightness in my throat. "The accounting is heard and confirmed." I look at the witnesses, then back to Auren. "Twelve is a heavy number. But it was a clean fight, and a clean account."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren inclined her head once at his confirmation, the formal gesture of a duellist acknowledging that the account had been received. Then she looked to the witnesses along the rail, and each of them, in turn, gave the small nod that meant the accounting was witnessed and would be recorded. That was the whole of it. That was all the ceremony there was.

She set the blade down on the stone and began the work of wrapping it, and her hands did not shake, though they had once, long ago, the first time, and she had never forgiven them for it.

"He dropped his guard to feint high," she said again, quieter now, more to herself than to anyone, though she did not trouble herself to keep it private. "That was not a mistake a man like that makes. He meant to be hit in the arm." She looked at the rolled cloth in her hands, then at Del. "I have been trying to decide whether that changes what I owe him, and I have not decided."

She tucked the blade away into its case and closed it, and the sound of the clasp was very small in the yard.

"I will write to his second tonight," she said. "There are arrangements. I do not leave them to others." She paused. "You did well, standing where you stood. Most seconds look away."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "Speak the account," I say, formally, because that is what the code requires me to say.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren's hands stopped on the clasp.

She did not turn around immediately. She stood very still for a moment, and the yard held its silence the way it had held it for the accounting — but this silence was different. This was the silence of something not fitting.

Then she turned and looked at Del with an expression that was not quite confusion, because Auren did not permit herself confusion in a duelling yard, but was something adjacent to it — the careful, flat attention of a woman who had just been asked to account for something she had already accounted for.

"It has been spoken," she said. "And witnessed. And confirmed by the second — which is you." She let that sit. "The form was satisfied. You stood and heard it. The witnesses nodded. If I speak it again, I do not give the dead his due twice. I give him a repetition, which is not the same thing and is, in fact, a discourtesy."

She studied him for a moment longer than was comfortable.

"Unless you mean to tell me you did not hear it," she said, and her voice was careful and entirely without edge, because she had known seconds to be struck deaf by the hour and she would not shame a man for that. "In which case I will say it again and I will not think less of you for needing it. But I would know which it is before I speak, because the code does not ask me to perform. It asks me to account."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I shake my head once, my eyes still on her. "I heard it. I heard him *mean* to be hit in the arm." I lower my voice. "That changes the account, doesn't it? A clean kill is one thing. A man who walks onto your blade is another."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren looked at him for a long time.

Then she picked the blade case back up and set it on the stone, and opened the clasp again, which was not something a duellist did after an accounting was closed. She did it slowly, and she did it because the gesture helped her think, and she had stopped being ashamed of the habits that helped her think.

"You are not asking me to repeat the account," she said. "You are asking me to amend it. Those are different acts and the code treats them differently." She held up one hand, not to silence him but to hold the shape of her own thought. "If the account as I spoke it is false, I amend it before these same witnesses and I take the dishonour of having spoken it wrong. If it is true but incomplete, I supplement. If it is true and complete, then what you are describing is not a fact about the wound. It is a fact about the man, and it belongs in a different ledger."

She looked down at the blade, then back at him.

"I told you I had not decided," she said. "I have still not decided. Do not mistake my saying so for evasion. I have stood over eleven accounts and I have never yet spoken one I did not believe at the moment I spoke it, and I am not going to break that at twelve because a second with better eyes than mine saw something in the ninth pass."

That was the closest she came to giving anything away.

But her jaw tightened, and she let it.

"He dropped his guard to feint high," she said again. "That is what I saw. What you are asking is whether the feint was a feint, or an invitation with a feint's shape. I do not know. I have replayed the ninth pass forty times since I spoke, which is fewer times than I will replay it tonight." She closed her eyes briefly. "If he wanted the arm, he could have had the arm. I was already committed to the arm. He moved inside it. That is the fact that will not sit down."

She opened her eyes.

"I will not amend the account on suspicion," she said. "But I will hold it open, which I have never done. If you or any witness here can say what the ninth pass actually was, I will hear it now, before the ink dries. And if no one can, then I write to his second tonight as I said, and I do not write only about arrangements. I write about the feint, and I ask him what his principal intended, and if he tells me the truth then the account is amended and the dead man gets his due — which in that case is not my blade. It is the name of what he did."

She stopped. The yard was very quiet.

"There is a word for a man who comes to a duel to die," she said. "The code does not have it. I have always thought that was a failure in the code and not in the men."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "Where did it land?" I ask. "The witnesses need it plainly and so do I."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren set both hands flat on the stone and looked at him, and there was something in her expression that was almost gratitude, because he had asked the right question and the right question was a relief after the wrong one.

She turned and pointed, not at the body, but at the air where the body had been standing, which she could still see as plainly as if the man were still in it.

"Here," she said. "Left side. Beneath the ribs. Not beneath the floating ribs — beneath the true ones, and low, and I will tell you plainly because you are right that the witnesses need it and so do I." She traced the line in the air with one finger. "The entry was four fingers' width below the nipple line. The angle was upward — not steeply, but unmistakably. Twelve degrees, perhaps fifteen. The blade went between the seventh and the eighth rib, which means it did not strike bone on entry, which means it was not deflected, which means the angle I found is the angle he gave me."

She held her hand where the entry had been, and did not move it.

"If he had stood still and I had struck where I was already committed, the wound would be here." She moved her hand out to the left and down, to the air where his upper arm would have been. "Outer arm, below the deltoid, angled down and through. That is a wound a man lives with. That is the wound I intended." She brought her hand back to the ribs. "This is not that wound. This wound is one a man makes by turning *into* the line, and turning into the line is not what a feint high does to a body. A feint high pulls a man back and up. His guard drops, his weight goes to the rear foot, his chest opens to the sky. A feint high does not drive a man forward and sideways onto a low blade."

She finally lowered her hand.

"He came inside the arm," she said. "Low. Rotating toward me, not away. That is what the angle says, and the angle is the only witness I trust completely, because it does not have intentions and it cannot be frightened." She looked along the rail at the witnesses. "You all heard it. The wound is consistent with a man who moved into the strike and not away from it. That does not prove he meant to die. But it is now a fact in the record, and it sits beside the fact of the feint, and together they are not nothing."

She looked back at Del.

"Plainly," she said. "That is plainly. If his second tells me the feint was only a feint, then I have killed a man through my own error and I will say so before these same witnesses. But if his second tells me the ninth pass was arranged — then the wound I gave him is the wound he came for, and I will not carry it as a mistake." She paused. "I will carry it as something else. I do not have a word for that yet either."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I step closer, my voice low. "Then I'll hold the record open. And when you write his second, tell him there was a witness who saw the turn." I glance at the body, then away. "He deserves that much truth, even if it's ugly."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren looked at him for a moment. Then she reached for the ink pot and the clean sheet she kept in the case beneath the blade, and she wrote two words in the margin of the accounting where the witness line belonged, and she held the pen out to him.

"Then write your name beside it," she said. "A witness who saw the turn is not a footnote. It is a new fact and the code requires it be marked as such, in a hand that is not mine, because if I write it myself it is my account and if you write it then it is corroboration and those weigh differently if this is ever read aloud."

She held the pen steady and did not rush him.

"I will write his second tonight as I said," she went on. "But I will write it with your name already in the record, so that when he reads it he knows the question is not one woman's doubt. He will know that someone else saw his principal turn inside the line, and he will answer me more honestly for it, because men answer honestly when they understand the answer is already half-known."

The witnesses along the rail had begun to murmur among themselves, which was proper. An accounting that stayed open was rare, and they would talk about it, and that talking was part of how the record kept itself honest.

Auren set the pen down on the stone in front of Del and stepped back.

"When the reply comes," she said, "you will hear it from me before anyone. That is not a courtesy. That is because if the account must be amended, you stood second and you will be standing second again when I amend it, and I will not do it in front of strangers without the man who asked the right question in the room."

She closed the blade case a second time. The sound of the clasp was the same small sound it had been before, but the yard did not hear it now the way it had heard it then.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "The code says precisely," I remind her. "Not tactfully. What did the blade do, and what did it do it to?"

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren looked at the pen on the stone and did not pick it up. Not yet. She understood what he was asking, and she understood that the asking was right, and the rightness of it meant she had to stop and think before she spoke, because precision was not something she could summon on demand. It was something she owed, and owing meant working.

"The blade did three things," she said. "And I will say them in order, because the order is what a physician or a magistrate would ask for and I would rather say it once."

She held up one finger.

"The blade entered the body. It passed through skin and superficial muscle at an angle of twelve to fifteen degrees above horizontal, entering four fingers' breadth below the left nipple line, between the seventh and eighth ribs. There was no bone contact on entry. The blade was four inches of steel — I use the short guard blade, not the duelling sabre, and the witnesses know this — and approximately two and a half inches of that length passed into the thoracic cavity."

She held up a second finger.

"The blade traveled upward and slightly medial through the intercostal space and contacted the pericardium. It opened the pericardium and entered the left ventricle at the apex and drew a laceration approximately one inch in length along the ventricular wall. There was no exit wound. The blade did not contact the sternum, the spine, or the opposite lung. The heart was the only organ the blade touched."

A third finger.

"The blade was withdrawn along the entry path. Withdrawal was clean. The wound channel collapsed behind it and hemorrhage began internally and externally, externally meaning a quantity of blood sufficient to mark the ground beneath and beside where he stood, which you have all seen. He was upright at the point of withdrawal and for some seconds after. He took two steps — one forward and one to his right, which is away from me, which is what a body does and is not evidence of intention — and then he sat down, and then he lay down, and then he did not get up again."

She lowered her hand.

"That is what the blade did," she said. "And what it did it to was a man's heart, and a man's pericardium, and the intercostal tissue between his seventh and eighth ribs on the left side, and the skin and superficial muscle overlying them. It did not touch his arm. It did not touch his guard. It did not touch anything he offered me and I accepted. It touched the thing that was behind the thing he offered."

She stopped and looked at the pen.

"That is the blade, and that is what it did it to," she said. "I have left out what he was doing when it happened, because you asked me what the blade did and the blade has no intentions. If you want the man's part of it, that is a separate line, and I will write it separately, because putting them together is how accounts get muddled and the dead deserve better than muddle."

She gestured at the sheet with her open hand.

"Write your name where you saw the turn," she said. "And then, if you will, write beneath it what you saw the body do — not what you think he meant. Only what the body did. *Entered, rotated, took the wound inside the line.* If that is what you saw. If it is not what you saw, write what you saw and I will stand corrected before these witnesses and think none the less of either of us."

She picked up the pen again and held it out to him a second time, and this time her hand was very steady, because steadiness here was the whole of what she had left to give.

"The code does not ask for tact," she said. "It asks for the truth in the order the truth happened. I have given you the blade. Now give me the man, and we will have the whole of it, and then I can write his second a letter that does not lie to him."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I take the pen, my fingers steady as I sign my name beside the turn. Beneath it, I write: *The body rotated inward, not away. The blade entered where the arm should have been.* I set the pen down. "There. Let his second read that and tell us what it means."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren read what he had written before she picked the sheet up, which was her right as the duellist of record and her habit as a woman who had learned that ink lied less often than people but still lied sometimes.

She read it twice.

Then she folded the sheet along its existing crease and slid it into the case beneath the blade, and she stood for a moment with her hand flat on the closed lid.

"Good," she said. It was not a warm word. It was not meant to be. It was the word she used when a thing had been done correctly and correctly was enough.

She turned to the witnesses along the rail. "You have heard the second's mark," she said. "The account stands as spoken, with the wound record complete and the man's action recorded separately by a second hand. The accounting remains open pending the reply of the dead man's second. You will be summoned to hear the amendment if an amendment is required. If no amendment is required, the account closes as it stands and you will be told that as well." She paused. "I would ask you not to speak of the open line to anyone outside this yard until the reply comes. Not because it is secret. Because it is unfinished, and an unfinished account repeated becomes a rumour, and a rumour is a debt I cannot repay to the dead."

They nodded. They would talk anyway — she knew it, and they knew she knew it, and the form existed to be respected rather than obeyed to the letter.

She picked up the case and held it at her side.

"I will need his second's name and direction," she said to Del. "You stood the second's place, which means someone gave it to you or you took it because no one else would. Either way, you will know it or you will know who does. I do not know the dead man's name either, and I should. I have been standing over an accounting for a man I killed at the ninth pass and I have not yet said his name aloud, and that is not modesty on my part. It is that the form goes wound first and name after, and I have never once found the after easy."

She looked toward where the body lay, and this time she let herself look at it. It cost her something. It always cost her something. She had decided, standing there with the case in her hand and the second's words still drying, that looking away had begun to be its own kind of tact, and she was finished with tact for the evening.

"What was his name," she said. "Say it plainly. The witnesses need it and so do I, and I would rather hear it from the man who kept his eyes open than read it off a magistrate's form tomorrow."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: The witnesses are silent and she is not finished. "All of it," I tell her. "How long he took, what he said, what it looked like at the end. The code says all of it and I'm asking for all of it."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren set the case down again. She had picked it up three times now and set it down three times, and she was aware of this and did not care, because the evening had become something that required her hands to be empty.

She stood with her arms at her sides and looked at the ground between where she stood and where Del stood, and she began.

"The engagement lasted nine passes," she said. "The first eight took approximately four minutes. I have not timed it — I never time it — but the light had not moved on the wall and the lamp was still at the height it was when we took our marks, and a lamp drops roughly a finger's width in a quarter hour, so four minutes is what I will say and I will say it as an estimate and not as a fact."

She paused. This was the part where precision required her to admit what she did not know, and admitting what she did not know was harder than any wound.

"He spoke once," she said. "At the beginning, before the first pass. He said: *I would prefer we did not prolong this.* I took that at the time as impatience. I have since wondered what else it might have been, and I have not resolved that either. He did not speak during the engagement. He did not speak after the wound. Not a word. Not a sound I could distinguish. If he made a sound, it was beneath the sound of the yard, and I will not invent one to make the account more complete than the truth is."

She breathed once, evenly, the way she breathed before a pass.

"The first two passes were feeling passes. Testing distance, testing reactions. He was good — better than his reputation, which is rare; men are usually worse than their reputation and twice as loud about it. His footwork was clean. He held the low guard, which is defensive, which is not what a man holds when he means to end a thing quickly. I noted that at the time. I noted it and I did not think about what it meant, and that is a failure I will own."

She held up her hand again, counting, because counting helped her keep the shape of the thing from collapsing into the one moment she could not stop seeing.

"Third and fourth pass, he began to press. Not recklessly — with intent. He came at my left twice, which is my weak side, and he knew it was my weak side because I had shown it to him in the second pass when I let my line drift, which was a deliberate drift and not an error, and he read it correctly, which told me he was reading me well. Fifth pass, he drew blood." She touched her left forearm, where a shallow cut had been wrapped beneath her sleeve. "A scratch. It was meant to be a scratch. He was marking me and not trying to end me, and again, I noted it and did not think about it."

She let her hand drop.

"Sixth and seventh pass, we were equal and we both knew it. He was not pressing anymore. He was waiting. I mistook that for fatigue. It was not fatigue. A tired man's guard sags. His did not sag. It *settled*. There is a difference and I know the difference and I did not see it in time."

"Eight pass — " She stopped. Corrected herself. "Eighth pass. I was the one who pressed. I came at his right and drove him back two steps and I was pleased with myself, which is a thing I am never permitted to be and should not have been then, because he gave me those two steps. He did not have to give them. He walked backward with a clean retreat and he set his feet at the end of it in exactly the position he wanted to be in, and I did not see that either."

Her voice did not change. Her voice had not changed through any of this. But the pace of it slowed.

"Ninth pass. He dropped his guard. The feint came high — head and shoulders, the shape of an attack to the face or the collarbone. I responded the way I am trained to respond. I committed to the arm. Outer arm, below the deltoid, angled down and through. I was already moving when he turned. I could not have stopped. I want that in the record — I could not have stopped. The turn took less than half a second and I was inside it before I understood there had been a turn."

She looked at her hands.

"The blade went where I have described. Four fingers below the left nipple line. Between the seventh and eighth ribs. Upward. Into the heart. I felt it go in, which is a thing I have never said aloud and I will say it now because you asked for all of it. I felt the blade go in and I knew before I saw his face that I had killed him, because a blade does not feel like that in muscle. It feels like that in a room it should not be in."

She closed her hands.

"He took two steps. The first was forward and the second was to his right, which is away from me, and which I have already said is what a body does. He was upright. His hand was open — his sword hand. The sword was already on the ground. I did not see it leave his hand. It was simply on the ground and his hand was open and he was walking, and he was not walking toward anything. He was walking the way a man walks when he is leaving a room and does not know where the door is."

Her voice held. It held because she made it hold.

"He sat down. Not collapsed — sat. He put one hand on the ground behind him and he lowered himself, and there was something almost deliberate in it, and if I had not known what had just happened to his heart I would have said he was resting. Then he lay down on his left side, which is the side the wound was on, and I have wondered since whether that was the body's choice or gravity's, and I do not know, and I will not say I know."

"He was still for a while. I do not know how long. Long enough for the witnesses to start moving. Long enough for someone to say his name twice. I do not know who said it or what name was said, because I have told you I did not know his name and I did not hear it in the moment, and that is the truth and it is an ugly truth and I am not going to soften it."

She looked at Del.

"He did not speak," she said again. "He did not look at me. He looked at the ground. He was looking at the ground when he stopped breathing, and I know when he stopped breathing because I was watching his shoulders, and the shoulders stopped, and that was the end of it. It was quiet. The whole of it, from the ninth pass to the shoulders stopping, was — " She searched. "Under a minute. It was under a minute. He died in less time than it takes to cross this yard."

She stopped.

"That is all of it," she said. "The passes. The blood he took from my arm. The two steps. The sitting. The lying down. The looking at the ground. The shoulders. There is nothing else and I have not left anything out and I have not put anything in." She held his gaze. "Now. His name. Say it plainly. I have given you all of mine."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I reach into my coat and pull out the small slip of paper his second pressed into my hand before the duel. "Kaelen," I say, the name sounding too small in the quiet yard. "His second is Corrin. He gave me this." I hold out the folded direction.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren took the folded paper. Her fingers did not fumble with it, but they were slower than they had been with anything else that evening, and she noticed this and let it be.

She read the direction. Then she read it again, because reading it twice was easier than looking up.

"Kaelen," she said.

She said it the way she said everything — plainly, at a volume that carried to the far end of the yard. But she said it once, and then she stopped, and the yard heard the stopping.

"Kaelen," she said again, more quietly. Not for the witnesses. For herself, and for the ground where the shoulders had stopped, and she was not ashamed of the second saying because the code asked for the name to be spoken and it did not ask for the name to be spoken only once.

She held the paper flat against her palm and looked at it for a long moment. Then she took the ink pot and the sheet from the case — she had set the case down a fourth time now and had stopped counting — and she wrote the name at the top of the accounting where the name belonged, in the space that had been left blank all evening because the form went wound first and name after and she had not had it to write.

She wrote *Kaelen* and then she stopped with the pen still on the paper and looked up.

"I do not have his family name," she said. "I have a first name and a second's name and a direction, and that is what I have. If his second's letter tells me more, I will add it. If it does not, I will not invent one." She set the pen down. "A man's name in the record should be the name he answered to. Not the name I would prefer him to have had."

She blew on the ink once and turned the sheet toward Del so he could see what she had written.

"I said at the start of this that I did not leave arrangements to others," she said. "I meant it then and I mean it now, but I will tell you something the code does not require me to tell you, which is that writing to Corrin just became harder, and I am going to do it tonight anyway, because if I wait until morning I will find a way to make the letter kinder than the truth and Kaelen does not need me to be kind. He needs me to be accurate."

She folded the direction into the case beside the accounting and closed the clasp, and this time she did not open it again.

"You asked me earlier whether it changed the account," she said. "A man who walks onto a blade. You said that. I have been standing here for — " She looked at the wall where the light had been. The lamp had dropped more than a finger's width now. "— some time. And I will tell you what I have decided, because you earned the deciding of it by keeping your eyes open when it would have been easier not to."

She picked up the case and held it at her side.

"He said, before the first pass: *I would prefer we did not prolong this.* I took it for impatience. I am no longer taking it for impatience." She paused. "That is not proof. That is one sentence from a dead man and a wound angle and a second who saw a turn, and together they do not make a verdict. But they make a question I can write down, and I would rather write down a question tonight than a comfortable answer."

She looked at Del.

"Walk with me to the gate if you will," she said. "Not as a courtesy. I am going to write the letter now, while the yard is still in my hands and the ninth pass is still — " She gestured vaguely at her own head. "— the shape of it is still there. And I find I do not want to write it alone. The code does not ask for company. I am asking."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: When she's done I confirm it aloud and my voice does what it does. (OOC: write the full account, don't summarise or cut away -- the accounting is the whole point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren stopped with her hand on the case. She stood very still for a long moment. Then she set the case down on the stone for the last time — she had stopped counting — and she opened it, and she took out the sheet, and she laid the sheet flat on the stone where every witness at the rail could see the ink on it, and she stepped back from it.

"Then hear it," she said. "The whole of it. Not the wound alone. Not the passes alone. The account. I will say it once, from the beginning, as the code requires, and you will confirm it or you will not, and if you do not then I will stand here until you do, because I would rather stand here all night than walk to the gate with an account that is not heard whole."

She drew one breath. She had drawn one breath before every account she had ever spoken and she drew this one the same way, and she did not look at Del while she drew it, and she did not look at the witnesses. She looked at the ground where Kaelen had fallen, because that was where the account had happened and that was where it should be read from.

"This is the accounting of Kaelen, as witnessed in the duelling yard on the evening of the ninth pass engagement," she said. "Spoken by Auren, duellist of record. Confirmed by the second who stood and did not look away. Witnessed by those present at the rail, whose names will be entered in the hand of the magistrate's clerk."

She paused. Not the pause of the wound. The pause of a woman turning a page.

"The engagement was called and set. The terms were met. Kaelen and I took our marks. Before the first pass, Kaelen said: *I would prefer we did not prolong this.* I took that for impatience at the time. I do not take it for impatience now. I record it as spoken and I leave its meaning open."

"The engagement ran nine passes. The first eight took approximately four minutes by the fall of the lamp, which is an estimate and not a measurement. The first two passes were feeling passes. Kaelen held the low guard, which is defensive. The third and fourth passes, Kaelen pressed at my left, which is my weak side, having read the drift I showed him in the second pass. The fifth pass, Kaelen drew blood — a scratch to my left forearm, shallow, delivered as a mark and not as an attempt on my life. I carry it still beneath my sleeve. The sixth and seventh passes, we were equal. Kaelen's guard settled and did not sag. I mistook the settling for fatigue. It was not fatigue."

"Eighth pass. I pressed at his right and drove him back two steps. He gave me those two steps and set his feet where he wanted them. I did not see that he had chosen the ground. I believed I had won it."

"Ninth pass. Kaelen dropped his guard and feinted high. I committed to the arm — outer arm, below the deltoid, angled down and through, which is a disabling wound and not a killing one. I was already moving. I could not have stopped."

Her voice did not break. It had never broken and it did not break now. But it slowed to the pace of something being set down very carefully, one piece at a time, on a surface that might not hold.

"Kaelen turned. Into the line. Not away from it. The second saw the turn and has written it in his own hand upon this record. The wound angle confirms it. A feint high pulls a body backward and upward. Kaelen came forward and low and rotated toward me, and the blade entered where the arm should have been."

"The killing wound was to the left side beneath the true ribs. The entry was four fingers' breadth below the left nipple line, between the seventh and eighth ribs, at an angle of twelve to fifteen degrees above horizontal. No bone was struck on entry. The blade was the short guard blade, four inches, and approximately two and a half inches passed into the thoracic cavity. The blade traveled upward and slightly medial through the intercostal space and opened the pericardium and entered the left ventricle at the apex, drawing a laceration of approximately one inch along the ventricular wall. There was no exit wound. The sternum was not contacted. The spine was not contacted. The opposite lung was not contacted. The heart was the only organ the blade touched."

"I withdrew along the entry path. The withdrawal was clean. Hemorrhage began internally and externally. Kaelen was upright at the point of withdrawal and for some seconds after."

"He took two steps. The first was forward. The second was to his right, which is away from me, which is what a body does and is not evidence of intention. His sword was on the ground. I did not see it leave his hand. His sword hand was open. He was upright and he was walking and he was not walking toward anything."

"He sat down. Not collapsed. He put one hand on the ground behind him and lowered himself, and there was something in it that I will call deliberate because I do not have another word that is true. Then he lay down on his left side, which is the wound side, and whether that was the body's choice or gravity's, I do not know."

"He did not speak. He did not make a sound I could distinguish. He did not look at me. He looked at the ground. He was looking at the ground when he stopped breathing, and I know when he stopped breathing because I was watching his shoulders and the shoulders stopped."

"From the ninth pass to the cessation of breath was under a minute. He died in less time than it takes to cross this yard."

She stopped.

The lamp had dropped further. The witnesses at the rail had not moved. The yard was the kind of quiet that has weight to it.

"That is the accounting," Auren said. "Name. Engagement. Passes. Wound in full, with measurements and path and organ. Withdrawal. The body's movement after. The manner of death. The time it took. The words he spoke before it began and the silence he kept after it ended. The second's corroborated observation of the turn. The open question of intent, which I hold open and do not resolve, because the code does not ask me to resolve what I do not know and I do not know it."

She looked at Del.

"I have not left anything out," she said. "I have not put anything in. That is the whole of it as I have it and as I will write it and as I will stand by it, amended or not, when Corrin's reply comes." She paused. "Confirm it or do not. But if you confirm it, confirm it as a man who heard all of it, and not as a man who heard the wound and let the rest go past him."

She stood with her hands at her sides and she waited.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I let out a slow breath, the kind that hurts when you've been holding it too long. "The accounting is heard and confirmed. All of it." I meet her gaze. "Now let's write that letter."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren inclined her head. Not the quick formal nod of the accounting — something slower, and lower, and held for a beat longer than the form required. The witnesses at the rail would see it and know what it meant, which was that the duellist of record had accepted the confirmation and the account was now entered as spoken and heard.

Then she gathered the sheet, and the ink, and the pen, and the folded direction with Corrin's name on it, and she put them all into the case and closed it, and she did not open it again.

"Yes," she said. "The letter."

She picked up the case and walked toward the gate. Her stride was the same stride it had been all evening — measured, unhurried, the stride of a woman who had learned that the body's pace set the mind's pace and had trained the body accordingly. But Del would notice, if he was watching, that she did not walk in the centre of the path. She walked along the edge of it, close to the wall, and she did not look at the ground where Kaelen's blood had marked the stones, and the not-looking was not avoidance. It was that she had looked once already and once was what she owed and she was not going to spend the looking cheaply.

The gate opened onto the narrow street that ran behind the yard. There was a bench there — she knew because she had used it before, after other evenings, though she had never told anyone that and was not going to tell anyone now. She set the case down on the bench and sat beside it, and she took out the pen and the clean sheet and uncorked the ink, and then she did not write.

She sat with the pen over the paper and she did not write.

"I need to tell you what the letter must contain," she said, "before I can make my hand form the words, because if I start writing I will write the wrong thing first and I will have to write it over and over before I get to the true thing, and the true thing is short and the false things are long and I would rather not waste your evening watching me cross out lies."

She looked at the blank sheet.

"The letter must contain four things. First: that Kaelen is dead and I killed him and the wound is as I have spoken it. Corrin needs that plainly. He was there. He knows. But the code says it and the code is right to say it, because hearing it written in the hand of the woman who did it is not the same as watching it and a man deserves both."

"Second: that the accounting stands as spoken and witnessed, and that I am not hiding behind the form. The form is what I owe. It is not what I hide in."

"Third: that the ninth pass is open. That the wound angle does not match the feint. That a second's corroborated observation is in the record and that the record is held open pending his answer." She paused. "This is the part that will be hard to write and the part that must not be softened, and I am telling you that so that if you see me soften it you will say so and I will not resent you for it."

"Fourth." She stopped with the pen still above the paper. "Fourth is the question. And the question is not *did your principal mean to die*. I will not write that. It is not my question to ask and it is not his question to answer and if I write it he will close the door on the whole of the letter and Kaelen will get nothing from either of us."

She looked at Del.

"I will write: *Before the first pass, Kaelen said he would prefer we did not prolong this. I would like to know what he meant. Not what it implies. What it meant to him, in his words, if his second knows them.* That is the question. That is the whole of the fourth thing. If Corrin answers it, the account amends itself and I will know what I did. If he does not, the account closes as it stands and I carry it as an open question to my grave, which I suspect is the likelier of the two."

She set the pen down for a moment and pressed the heel of her hand against her eye, which was the only gesture all evening that was not for anyone, including herself. It lasted less than a second. Then she picked the pen up again.

"I will write it now," she said. "Read it when I am done. If you find it has a lie in it — not an error, I make errors and I correct them — a lie, a softening, a thing written to make me look better than the truth makes me look — you will tell me and I will write it again."

She bent over the sheet. And she wrote.

The letter was not long. It was the length of a thing that had been stripped of everything that was not required, which was the length Auren's letters always were and the reason people who received them tended to keep them, though she did not know that and would have been uncomfortable knowing it.

When she was done, she set the pen down and turned the sheet so Del could read it, and she did not watch his face while he read, because watching a man read a letter about a death you caused was a kind of vanity and she was not in the mood for vanity.

The lamplight from the yard behind them had grown long. Somewhere beyond the wall, one of the witnesses was talking to another witness, and the sound was low and steady and would be gone by morning.

"The letter is written," she said. "I will send it at first light. Not tonight — a letter sent at night arrives with a night in it and I will not give Corrin that. He will get it with the morning, which is neutral, which is what the truth should arrive with."

She folded the sheet and slid it into the case beside the accounting and beside Kaelen's name.

"Twelve," she said again, to no one, or to the street, or to the bench, or to the wall. Then she shook her head once, not in denial but in the way a person shakes off a thing that has settled where it should not.

"Twelve," she said. "With a name now. Which is different and worse and better and I do not have the word for that either."

She sat with her hands in her lap and she did not get up yet, because getting up meant walking away from the yard and the yard was still where Kaelen was, in whatever way a yard holds a man after the man has stopped being in it.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I sit beside her on the bench, my own hands empty. "Better to carry a name than a number," I say quietly. "Even if it's heavy."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren sat with that for a moment. She did not answer quickly, because she had learned that quick answers to slow questions were a way of not answering at all.

"Yes," she said at last. "That is what I have been told. By better people than me, too — people who have carried more names than I have numbers." She looked at the wall across the street, at nothing on the wall. "I have never been able to decide whether I believe it or whether I only want to. Tonight I believe it. Ask me again in a month and I will tell you what I have learned."

She turned her hands over in her lap, the gesture of a woman counting something she could not see. Twelve names and eleven faces and one she had not let herself see until tonight, and a name on a folded sheet of paper that had been too small to hold it.

"A number is what you carry when you are a duellist," she said. "A name is what you carry when you are the woman who killed him. I have been the first for a long time and I was the second again tonight and I would rather be the second. That is what you are saying and you are right and I would like you to know that I know you are right, because I am not going to say it again and if I do not say it now you will think I did not hear it."

She picked up the case and stood, and this time she did not set it down again. The bench felt emptier without her on it, though she would not have described it that way and would not have liked it if someone else did.

"First light," she said. "The letter goes. Then I will know nothing for some days, and the days will be what they will be." She looked down at Del, and there was something in her face that had not been in it in the yard, not softness exactly — Auren would not have used that word — but the absence of the thing that had held her face still all evening. "I said I did not want to write it alone. You let me write it not alone. The code has no word for that debt and I will not invent one, but I will remember it."

She turned toward the street. She did not ask him again to walk with her. She simply began to walk, slowly enough to be followed, in the direction of the gate and the lamp and whatever came after the yard.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I push myself up from the bench and fall into step beside her. "You remember the debts the code doesn't have a word for. That's why you're still standing."
