dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
It had taken less time than anyone expected, which was usually how it went when it went badly for one party.

Auren cleaned the blade and did not sit down. "Witnesses are watching," she said. "You know what happens now."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I take my place where the second stands and make myself keep my eyes open. "I'm ready to hear it," I say.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren kept her blade vertical, the point resting lightly on the packed earth. She did not sheath it. The ritual demanded the steel remain drawn until the accounting was recorded by the witnesses. She felt the familiar tightening in her throat, the same hollow weight she had carried through ten previous hours like this one. She would not decorate the truth. To soften the wound would be to insult the dead, and to insult the dead was to insult the code.

"By the law of the ring and in the presence of these witnesses," she said, her voice level, stripped of cadence, "I account for the fall of my opponent. The killing wound was a thrust to the left intercostal space, between the fourth and fifth ribs, penetrating the pleural cavity and severing the intercostal artery. It was delivered with the point of my blade, at a forward angle of twenty-five degrees, driven by the extension of the right arm and the pivot of the left heel. The hemothorax was immediate. Collapse followed within four breaths."

She held the silence after the last word. Her shoulders remained squared, her gaze fixed straight ahead, meeting the eyes of those gathered but offering no concession, no nod, no gesture of triumph. The words had been spoken exactly as they were. The accounting was complete. She waited for the witnesses to acknowledge it, her posture rigid, her breathing steady, already preparing herself for the quiet that would follow.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I watch her face, pale but steady. The numbers settle in my mind, cold and precise. "I confirm the accounting," I say, my voice barely above a murmur. I don't look away from her.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren’s throat tightened at the confirmation. The words had been given, the record stood, and the code was satisfied. She lowered the point of her blade until it rested against the packed earth, then drew it back with a slow, measured motion. The steel slid into its scabbard with a clean, final whisper, and only then did she allow her shoulders to drop a fraction.

“The accounting is entered,” she said, her voice flat and even, stripped of all ornament. “The matter is closed.”

She did not smile. She did not bow. She offered a single, formal nod to the ring and to those who had borne witness, her gaze moving across the assembled faces with the same detached precision she had applied to the wound itself. The quiet that followed was heavy, familiar, and unwelcome. She stepped back from the chalked lines, her boots tracing the edge of the dust she had not disturbed, and stood at attention until the witnesses began to stir. Her hands remained at her sides, fingers loose but unclenched, already turning her thoughts toward the road ahead. The weight settled into her ribs, as it always did, and she carried it without flinching.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "Speak the account," I say, formally, because that is what the code requires me to say.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren’s jaw tightened almost imperceptibly. The prompt was redundant; the accounting had already been rendered and confirmed. Yet the code was exact, and exactness demanded compliance even when it bordered on repetition. She straightened her spine, the leather of her gambeson creaking softly in the still air. Her eyes remained fixed on the space just beyond Del’s shoulder, as protocol dictated when addressing a witness who had formally initiated the record.

“By the law of the ring and in the presence of these witnesses,” she said, her voice flat and measured, stripping the cadence from her tone as she had before, “I account for the fall of my opponent. The killing wound was a thrust to the left intercostal space, between the fourth and fifth ribs, penetrating the pleural cavity and severing the intercostal artery. It was delivered with the point of my blade, at a forward angle of twenty-five degrees, driven by the extension of the right arm and the pivot of the left heel. The hemothorax was immediate. Collapse followed within four breaths.”

She held the silence. The dust hung motionless. She did not shift her weight, did not blink. The words were not a performance; they were an entry in a ledger written in blood and bound by steel. When the last syllable faded, she inclined her head once, her expression unchanging. The record was sealed. The ritual, however tedious, was complete. She waited, her hands still at her sides, already measuring the distance to the gate.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I let out a slow breath I hadn't realized I was holding. "Recorded," I say, and finally break my gaze from her to glance at the senior witness. My hands feel cold.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren observed the shift in Del’s posture, the chill in the hands, the breaking of eye contact. She registered these details not as signs of distress, but as factual data, unremarkable in the context of a completed exchange. The ritual did not end with the words of the participants; it required the pronouncement of the senior witness to seal the record. 

She turned her head, a precise mechanical motion, to face the designated authority. Her stance remained rigid, her breathing shallow and controlled, her hands hanging loose at her sides. She offered no aid, no comfort, no concession. The code demanded the final word from the highest authority before the ring could be cleared. She stood at attention, her gaze fixed on the witness, her expression unyielding, waiting for the official declaration that would finally close the ledger.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "Where did it land?" I ask. "The witnesses need it plainly and so do I."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren’s expression did not change. The location had already been stated with anatomical precision, yet the code permitted no ambiguity when lay witnesses required plain enumeration. She did not shift her weight, nor did she lower her gaze. She simply delivered the information as another line in the ledger.

“Between the fourth and fifth ribs on the left side of the chest,” she said, her voice level, stripped of cadence, “the blade entered the intercostal space, pierced the pleura, and severed the intercostal artery. It exited just above the diaphragm. The wound track lay along the lower left lung field.”

She held the silence. Her hands remained at her sides, her posture rigid. The words had been recorded exactly as they were. To add explanation would be to risk distortion; to omit detail would be to violate the code. She did not soften the geometry of the injury, nor did she offer it as anything other than fact. The witnesses had heard it plainly. The record stood. She waited for the senior witness to seal the exchange, her breathing steady, the familiar weight settling into her ribs as the ritual drew to its final, unceremonious close.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I look down at the dirt, tracing the line between my boots with my eyes. "Clean," I say, my voice rough. "It was clean."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren registered the word without commentary. Clean was not praise; it was a measure of technique, of economy, of a strike that had done precisely what it was intended to do. She did not acknowledge it, nor did she dismiss it. The code recognized no such things as compliments or criticisms in the aftermath of the ring. There was only the record, and the record stood.

The senior witness, a man in the grey wool of the magistrate’s office, stepped forward. His boots scuffed the chalk line as he approached the fallen man’s side. He did not look at Auren. He looked at the body, then at the assembled witnesses, then at the ground where the blade had finally been sheathed. The silence stretched, taut and heavy, filled only by the dry wind moving through the ring’s boundary and the low murmur of the crowd beyond the ropes.

Auren kept her posture exact. Her weight rested evenly on both feet. Her hands remained at her sides, fingers straight, shoulders square. She felt the familiar coldness in her chest, the same hollow ledger she had carried since the first time she had spoken these words. It was not grief. It was not relief. It was the weight of having fulfilled an obligation that cost a life. She would not pretend otherwise. To pretend otherwise would be to break the code, and to break the code was to dishonour the dead.

The magistrate cleared his throat. His voice, when it came, was dry and official. “The accounting is heard. The wound is verified. The exchange is concluded.” He turned to the gathered crowd, raising a hand. “Clear the ring.”

Auren did not move until the witnesses began to disperse. Only then did she step back from the chalk line, her boots making no sound on the packed earth. She did not look at Del. She did not look at the fallen. She turned her face toward the gate, her steps measured, her breathing even. The ritual was over. The road waited. She carried the weight without flinching, as she always did.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "The code says precisely," I remind her. "Not tactfully. What did the blade do, and what did it do it to?"

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren’s posture did not shift. The reminder was redundant; the code permitted no euphemism, no softening of the mechanics, no shielding of the witnesses from the anatomy of the kill. She had already stated the entry point. The code demanded the mechanism, the structures breached, and the physiological consequence stated without mitigation. She did not lower her gaze. She did not adjust her stance. She delivered the remainder of the ledger with the same flat, measured cadence.

“The blade entered the left intercostal space, lacerated the parietal and visceral pleura, and collapsed the left lung by equalizing intrathoracic pressure with atmospheric pressure. It severed the intercostal artery, producing immediate hemorrhage into the pleural cavity. The point pierced the diaphragm, entered the peritoneal space, and lacerated the superior surface of the spleen. Blood and gastric fluid accumulated in the thoracic cavity. Mediastinal shift occurred within three breaths. Hypovolemic shock followed. Cardiac arrest was irreversible.”

She held the silence. Her shoulders remained square. Her hands hung straight at her sides. The words were not a narrative; they were an inventory of structural failure. To soften the description would be to erase the precise mechanics of the man’s final moments, and to erase them would be to break the code. The witnesses had heard the mechanics. The record stood. She waited, her breathing shallow and controlled, the familiar weight settling into her ribs as the ritual drew to its unceremonious close.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I flinch at the mention of the spleen. My own side twinges in sympathy. "Recorded," I say again, my voice thin. "The account is complete."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content: Auren registered the confirmation without comment. The account was complete. The ledger was closed. She did not move until the last of the witnesses began to step beyond the chalked boundary, their murmurs fading into the dry wind. Only then did she allow her shoulders to settle, though her spine remained straight, her weight distributed evenly. The familiar coldness settled once more in her ribs, a hollow weight she had learned to carry without adjusting her gait. She did not look at Del. She did not look at the body. She turned her face toward the gate, her hands remaining at her sides, fingers loose but unyielding. The code demanded no further words. The exchange was concluded. She waited for the path to clear, her breathing even, her posture exact, already measuring the distance to the road ahead.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: The witnesses are silent and she is not finished. "All of it," I tell her. "How long he took, what he said, what it looked like at the end. The code says all of it and I'm asking for all of it."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren’s jaw tightened, a barely perceptible flex of muscle beneath the skin. The code permitted no omission, and exactness left no room for refusal. She had already catalogued the mechanics of the strike and the physiology of the fall. The remainder was not an embellishment; it was a requirement. She drew a slow, measured breath, feeling the familiar hollow ache settle deeper in her chest. She did not look at Del. She did not look at the body. She fixed her gaze on the assembled witnesses, her posture unyielding.

“The interval from the strike to cessation of life was one minute and forty-two seconds,” she said, her voice flat, stripped of cadence. “He did not speak. His breathing grew shallow and irregular, accompanied by a frothing at the lips that stained the dust. His hands, which had been raised in a defensive posture, fell to his sides. His left eye drifted upward. The pulse at his neck ceased at the one hundred and four-second mark. His skin took on a mottled grey pallor, beginning at the extremities and moving inward. His lips parted once, without sound. There was no further movement.”

She held the silence. The words were delivered without pause, without ornament, without the slightest softening. To withhold them would be to violate the ledger. To soften them would be to dishonour the dead. She kept her shoulders squared, her hands loose at her sides, her breathing steady. The details hung in the dry air, stark and unadorned. The ritual demanded the full account, and the full account had been given. She waited for the final acknowledgment, her expression unreadable, her weight distributed evenly, already preparing to step beyond the chalk line.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I swallow hard. "The code is satisfied," I say, but my voice cracks on the last word. I finally look away from her, at the dust where it's still dark with blood. "You can go."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren registered the dismissal without reaction. The ledger was closed. She offered a single, measured nod to the senior witness, confirming that the record had been entered, verified, and pronounced complete. Her hands remained at her sides, fingers straight, shoulders squared. The code permitted no farewell, no lingering, no gesture of departure beyond the formal acknowledgment of finality.

She turned from the chalk line, her boots tracing the edge of the packed earth without crossing into it. The dust still held the dark stain of the wound, the precise geometry of the fall still visible in the ground. She did not look at it. The body would be claimed by the undertaker, the ring would be swept, the chalk would be replaced. None of it belonged to her now. The obligation had been discharged.

The familiar weight settled once more in her ribs, hollow and exact, as it always did when the accounting was finished. She did not fight it. She carried it with the same steady gait she had used for eleven years, twelve accounting now, each one filed away in the quiet ledger of her mind, each one bearing the same unadorned truth. She stepped past the rope boundary, her steps even, her breathing shallow and controlled. The wind moved through the empty ring behind her, carrying the dry scent of turned earth and iron.

She did not look back. The road waited beyond the gate, straight and unadorned, as it always did. She adjusted the strap of her sword belt, felt the familiar weight of the scabbard against her hip, and walked forward. The code was satisfied. The matter was closed. She carried the silence with her, as she always had.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I stay where I am, watching her walk away until she's just a silhouette against the sun. My hands are still shaking. I kneel down, press my palms into the dark dirt, and take one last look at the ring before I go to wash.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren did not look back. The code permitted no lingering, no backward glance to verify what had already been recorded. She felt the shift in the air behind her—the faint settling of dust, the quiet weight of stillness—but she registered it as one might note a change in the wind: a fact, not a summons. Her steps remained even, measured, each boot finding the same firm purchase on the packed earth. The strap of her scabbard bit familiarly against her hip, a steady counterweight to the hollow pressure in her chest.

She crossed the timber gate and stepped onto the road. The sun hung low, casting long shadows that cut across the dirt like chalk lines on a fresh slate. She adjusted her grip on the worn leather of her bracers, her fingers moving with automatic precision. The wind carried the dry scent of crushed sage and distant rain, but her mind remained fixed on the ledger. Twelve entries now. Each one exact. Each one accounted for. She did not count them as victories. She counted them as obligations discharged, debts paid in steel and silence.

Her breathing remained shallow and controlled. She did not rush. The road ahead was straight, unbroken by trees or stone, and it suited her. There was no need for diversion, no room for ornament. She reached into her coat pocket and withdrew a linen cloth, running it slowly over the blade’s pommel where a single drop of blood had dried. She wiped it away with the same methodical care she had applied to the words, leaving the metal clean and ready for the next ring, the next accounting, the next exacting truth.

She did not think of the kneeling form behind the chalk line, nor of the dark stain on the dust. She thought only of the distance to the next settlement, the condition of her horses, the need to wash the road dust from her hands before supper. The weight in her ribs did not lighten. It simply became part of her posture, as natural as the stance of a fencer at guard. She walked forward, her shoulders squared, her gaze fixed on the horizon, carrying the silence exactly as it had been given to her.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I stay kneeling until my knees ache. The dark stain soaks into my pants, cold and final. When I finally push myself up, my hands leave muddy prints on my thighs. I walk to the water barrel without looking back.

She wrapped the leather cord around the blade’s edge, her movements economical and practiced, then guided the steel home into its scabbard with a soft, definitive click. The sound seemed to sever the last thread of the ceremony.

She turned her head slightly toward Del, her expression unreadable, carved from years of repetition. "The debt is discharged," she said, her voice still level, still stripped of ornament. "You may attend to him."

She did not wait for a reply. To linger would be to invite sentiment, and sentiment was a breach of the line she had drawn for herself long ago. She adjusted her gloves, straightened her coat, and stepped back from the blood-stained stone. The witnesses parted for her without a word, accustomed to the victor’s silence. Auren walked toward the archway, her stride measured, her shoulders rigid against the weight of the eleventh accounting. dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren stood before the scribe's table, the parchment laid flat and weighted at the corners. She heard Del's voice, low and steady near the blood-stained stone. She did not turn her body, but her gaze shifted just enough to acknowledge the second's statement.

"See that the written entry mirrors the accounting exactly," Auren said, her voice projecting clearly, devoid of sympathy but heavy with expectation. "The code demands precision in the line of the blade, and it demands the same in the line of the ink. Do not soften the phrasing. Do not omit the specifics. A blemished record is a blemished honor."

She extended a hand, and the scribe offered the quill. Auren took it, her movements economical. She dipped the nib into the inkwell, the scratch of the feather against paper soon joining the silence of the courtyard. She did not write a flourish; she wrote the facts, her script sharp and unadorned, matching the stark truth she had already spoken.

*Below the left clavicle. Subclavian artery. Lung puncture. True angle. Mortal impact.*

She signed her name at the foot of the entry, the strokes rigid and final. Only then did she return the quill. Her eyes remained fixed on the drying ink. The dead were gone to the earth or the pyre; the living had work to do. Auren waited for the scribe to seal the page, her posture unyielding, already mentally cataloging the maintenance of her gear and the review of her forms. The eleventh was done. The code was fed. There was nothing left to say.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "Where did it land?" I ask. "The witnesses need it plainly and so do I."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren did not look down. The code required the fall to be noted, for position sometimes dictated the right of passage and the line of succession. She kept her posture rigid, her voice unchanged. "He fell forward," she said. "Seven paces from the mark. His left knee struck the stone first, then his right shoulder. He came to rest on his right side, face turned toward the eastern wall. His blade lay three hand-spans from his right hand. Unbroken. Unreached."

She did not pause for effect. She simply laid the facts bare. "The ground was dry. The blood pooled beneath his ribs, not his neck. He did not crawl. He did not call for aid. His breath left him before his head touched the stone."

Her fingers rested flat against the table’s edge, knuckles pale but steady. She would not soften it. To do so would be to insult the dead and the living alike, and the code left no room for mercy in the record. "That is the landing. Record it as spoken."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: *My throat tightens at the detail, but I nod and reach for my own small ledger.* "Forward, seven paces. I'll note it." *I don't add that I saw the exact moment his eyes lost focus. The code doesn't ask for that.*

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren waited until the scribe's seal bit into the wax, the crest of the duelling circle rising dark and sharp against the crimson. Only then did she lift her gaze from the table. Her eyes found Del's back, hunched over the ledger near the stone where the blood was already cooling. The scribe's work and the second's entry would stand as one truth; any discrepancy between them would be a stain on both their names.

"The record is set," Auren announced, her voice cutting through the murmurs of the gathered crowd. It was a declaration of finality, projected to the back of the courtyard. "The code has been satisfied in word and in mark. You may dismiss the witnesses."

She turned her attention back to the table, retrieving her gloves from where she had laid them. Her movements were sharp, efficient, the motions of a woman who had performed this closing ritual enough times to know the weight of every second. "As for the fallen," she added, her tone remaining devoid of pity, though not lacking in respect for the formalities. "He is to be stripped of his blade and his gear. The body is to be removed to the cleansing house. No one touches the corpse until the second gives the order. That is the law."

She adjusted the leather of her gauntlets, pulling them tight over her wrists until the fit was secure. Her expression remained a mask of disciplined neutrality. She would not offer Del a hand to rise, nor would she spare a glance at the face of the dead. To do so would be to blur the line between the victor and the mourner, and the code permitted no such confusion.

"See it done, Second," she said, her voice low but carrying the weight of command. "The courtyard cannot remain a grave. The code requires order, not lingering."

Auren stepped away from the table, the parchment now a sealed artifact of the eleventh death. She did not look at the body. She did not look at Del. She looked only at the archway, at the path that led away from the blood and the witnesses. The ritual was complete. The accounting was balanced. There was nothing left for her but to walk away, leaving the silence to settle over the stone.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "The code says precisely," I remind her. "Not tactfully. What did the blade do, and what did it do it to?"

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren did not flinch. The correction was not a rebuke, but a reminder of the code’s architecture. She turned her head fully toward Del, her expression unchanged. "You are correct," she said. "The code demands precision. It does not permit tact."

She straightened her spine, aligning herself with the ritual’s next requirement. Her voice remained even, stripped of inflection, measured to the exact cadence the formalities required. "The blade advanced on a straight line. It caught the high guard, followed the steel, and drove into the flesh below the left clavicle. It sheared through the costal cartilage, parted the second and third ribs, and severed the subclavian artery. It collapsed the upper lobe of the lung. The steel did not deflect. It did not hesitate. It penetrated to the hilt and held until the tension broke. It did not seek mercy. It did not offer it."

She let the statement settle in the courtyard’s still air. No ornament. No mitigation. Only the mechanics of the strike, rendered exactly as the code required. "That is what the blade did. That is what it did it to. The accounting is complete."

Her hands remained steady at her sides. She would not soften the words, nor would she retreat from their weight. The code demanded the truth, bare and unadorned, and she had delivered it. She kept her gaze fixed forward, her posture rigid against the familiar gravity of the eleventh death. The formalities were satisfied. The witnesses had heard it. There was nothing left to add.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: *I finally look up at her, my knuckles white around the ledger.* "The code is satisfied," *I repeat, my voice raw.* "Now leave me to do my duty."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren did not waver at the rawness in his voice. The code recognized no emotion, only the exchange of precise words. She held his gaze, her expression unmoving, and gave a single, sharp nod.

"The code is satisfied," she stated, her tone flat, echoing his confirmation to seal the ritual. "The ground is yielded. The second attends to the fallen."

She did not offer a word of condolence, nor did she pause to watch him begin his task. To linger would be to encroach upon the second's domain, a breach of protocol she would not commit. She turned on her heel, the movement crisp and final, and stepped back from the blood-stained stone.

"The witnesses are dismissed," she announced to the crowd, her voice carrying without rise or fall. "The accounting is complete. You may depart."

She did not wait for the murmur of assent. Auren walked toward the archway, her stride measured, her shoulders rigid. She passed through the stone frame without looking back. The courtyard, the body, and the weight of the eleventh death remained behind her. She would return to her quarters, strip her gear, and review her forms. The code demanded nothing more, and she would give it nothing less.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: The witnesses are silent and she is not finished. "All of it," I tell her. "How long he took, what he said, what it looked like at the end. The code says all of it and I'm asking for all of it."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren did not shift her weight. The code’s demand for totality was absolute, and she would not withhold what the ritual required. She held Del’s gaze, her face a mask of disciplined neutrality. "The code requires the full accounting," she said, her voice even. "I will render it."

She did not lower her eyes. She did not soften her posture. The words came in the same measured cadence she had used eleven times before, each syllable placed with deliberate care.

"The engagement lasted fourteen seconds from the initial salute to the final thrust," she said. "There were three exchanges. He parried the first with a high bind, countered with a disengage to the outside line. I stepped inside the blade, checked his wrist, and opened the guard. He recovered, offered a feint to the head, then committed to a thrust to the center. I slipped the line, closed the distance, and delivered the strike. No more time passed than that."

She paused only to let the witnesses register the duration, then continued. "He spoke three words before the first parry broke. 'For the house.' He did not speak again. After the blade took him, his lips parted once. No sound emerged. His breath caught in the throat and did not return."

Her tone remained flat, stripped of inflection. She recited the final moments as one might recite a ledger. "His eyes remained open until the impact. The pupils dilated immediately. The color drained from his face within two breaths. His fingers curled toward the hilt of his own blade, but the muscles locked before they could close. The blood did not spray; it welled steadily from the wound’s edge, dark and thick. He did not convulse. He did not struggle. His chest rose once, shallow and incomplete, then stilled. The light left his eyes before his knees met the stone."

She did not elaborate. She did not offer context, nor did she frame the details in any manner that might ease the weight of them. To do so would be to dishonor the dead by falsifying the record, and she would not bear that stain. The code demanded the truth, bare and unadorned, and she had delivered it.

"That is the full accounting," she said. "The duration. The speech. The manner of the end. The witnesses have heard it. The second has heard it. The code is fed."

Her hands remained at her sides, fingers relaxed but steady. She kept her gaze fixed forward, her shoulders rigid against the familiar gravity of the eleventh death. She would not look away, nor would she break the line of the ritual. The courtyard air held still, heavy with the quiet aftermath of steel and duty. Auren waited for the second’s confirmation, her posture unyielding, already turning toward the next prescribed step.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: *I write it all down, every word, my pen scratching too loud in the silence.* "Fourteen seconds." *My own voice is a ghost of hers.* "The accounting is heard, and it is complete."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren did not lower her gaze. The confirmation was the final stone in the archway. She gave a single, measured nod. "The accounting is complete," she said, her voice flat, carrying only the weight of the words themselves. She stepped back from the blood-stained stone, the leather of her boots whispering against the courtyard floor. The code required no further speech from the victor. To add would be to clutter the truth.

She turned her attention to the gathered witnesses, her posture rigid, her expression carved from the same discipline that had guided her blade. "You have heard the measure of the steel," she said, her tone even, stripped of triumph or sorrow. "You have witnessed the discharge of the obligation. The code is satisfied. You may depart."

She did not wait for the crowd to stir. She adjusted the cuff of her glove, the motion sharp and final, then turned toward the archway. The weight of the eleventh death settled into her shoulders, familiar and unyielding. She would not look back. The courtyard belonged to the second and the fallen now. Her duty was done.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: When she's done I confirm it aloud and my voice does what it does. (OOC: write the full account, don't summarise or cut away -- the accounting is the whole point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren did not shift her stance. She raised her chin a fraction, her gaze sweeping the line of witnesses before settling on the space where the fallen had stood. Her voice, when it came, was level, measured, and stripped of all ornament. It carried across the courtyard without rise or fall, each syllable placed with deliberate care.

"The engagement began with the salute. It lasted fourteen seconds. There were three exchanges. The first was a high bind; he countered with a disengage to the outside line. I stepped inside the blade, checked his wrist, and opened the guard. The second was a feint to the head, followed by a commitment to the center. I slipped the line and closed the distance. The third was the accounting strike. The blade advanced on a straight line. It caught the high guard, followed the steel, and drove into the flesh below the left clavicle. It sheared through the costal cartilage, parted the second and third ribs, and severed the subclavian artery. It collapsed the upper lobe of the lung. The steel did not deflect. It did not hesitate. It penetrated to the hilt and held until the tension broke. He spoke three words before the first parry broke: 'For the house.' He did not speak again. After the blade took him, his lips parted once. No sound emerged. His breath caught in the throat and did not return. His eyes remained open until the impact. The pupils dilated immediately. The color drained from his face within two breaths. His fingers curled toward the hilt of his own blade, but the muscles locked before they could close. The blood did not spray; it welled steadily from the wound’s edge, dark and thick. He did not convulse. He did not struggle. His chest rose once, shallow and incomplete, then stilled. The light left his eyes before his knees met the stone. He fell forward, seven paces from the mark. His left knee struck the stone first, then his right shoulder. He came to rest on his right side, face turned toward the eastern wall. His blade lay three hand-spans from his right hand. Unbroken. Unreached. The ground was dry. The blood pooled beneath his ribs, not his neck. He did not crawl. He did not call for aid. His breath left him before his head touched the stone. The death was mine to deliver. The line was true. The thrust was controlled. The wound was mortal upon impact. This is the accounting."

She did not lower her gaze. She did not shift her weight. The words hung in the courtyard air, exact and unsoftened, each statement laid bare as a stone in a wall that would not fall. Her hands remained at her sides, fingers relaxed but steady. Her breathing was even, her posture rigid against the familiar gravity of the eleventh death. She would not add a word. She would not soften a line. She stood as she had stood eleven times before, bearing the weight of the record without flinching, and waited for the second’s confirmation.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: *I write it all down, my hand cramping around the pen.* "The accounting is heard and confirmed." *I close the ledger with a soft thump.* "The code is satisfied."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren did not move until the words left his mouth. The confirmation was the final lock clicking into place. She gave a single, measured nod, her spine straight, her gaze fixed forward. "The code is satisfied," she repeated, her voice flat, carrying only the weight of the required phrase. She did not add gratitude. She did not offer relief. The ritual demanded no more.

She turned her head slightly toward the scribe. "Seal the ledger," she said. "The entry stands as rendered. No amendment. No addition."

Her hands, still resting at her sides, flexed once against the leather of her gloves. The courtyard air remained still, heavy with the quiet aftermath of steel and duty. She could feel the weight of the eleventh accounting settling into her bones, familiar and unyielding. She would not soften it. She would not pretend it was anything other than what it was: a debt discharged, a line held, a truth spoken.

She adjusted her stance, shifting her weight forward just enough to signal the end of her presence at the mark. "The witnesses are dismissed," she announced, her voice projecting clearly to the back of the courtyard. "The ground is yielded. The second retains custody of the fallen. You may depart."

She did not wait for the crowd to stir. Auren turned on her heel, the movement crisp and final, and stepped back from the blood-stained stone. The leather of her boots whispered against the courtyard floor. She kept her posture rigid, her breathing even, her eyes fixed on the archway that led away from the mark. The code required nothing more of her. She would give it nothing less.

As she walked, she did not look back. The courtyard belonged to the second and the dead now. Her duty was done. The eleventh was complete. She would return to her quarters, strip her gear, and review her forms. The weight would not lift. It never did. But the line would hold.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: *I watch her leave, the ledger heavy in my hands.* "Clean the stone," *I tell the waiting attendants, my voice thick.* "And fetch a shroud."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren crossed the threshold of the archway without breaking stride. The courtyard fell behind her, and with it, the silence of the witnesses. She did not turn her head. To look back would be to invite the moment into the space she had just cleared, and the code permitted no such contamination. Her boots struck the flagstones of the outer walk in even, measured intervals. Fourteen seconds. Three exchanges. One line. She repeated the numbers in her mind, not as a tally, but as a verification. The code required the victor to carry the weight of the accounting, not to shed it.

She reached the antechamber of the duelling house and paused only long enough to unfasten the leather cord at her throat. Her fingers worked the knot with the same economy of motion she had used on the blade. She removed her gloves, peeling them from her hands one at a time, and laid them on the wooden bench. The skin beneath was pale, marked only by the friction of the hilt and the cold of the morning air. She did not rub her palms. She did not flex her wrists to test for strain. The body was an instrument, and instruments were maintained, not mourned.

Auren opened the armory door and stepped inside. The air was cool, carrying the familiar scent of oiled steel, linseed, and dried leather. She moved to the rack and retrieved the whetstone, the lint, and the can of solvent. She would not touch the blade until the ledger was sealed and the second had spoken his final word. The code forbade premature handling. She sat on the stool, her spine straight, and began to prepare the cleaning cloth. Her breathing remained even. Her hands were steady.

The eleventh accounting sat in her chest like a stone. It would not dissolve. It would not soften. It was a fact, carved into the record and into her bones. She had spoken it. The witnesses had heard it. The second had confirmed it. There was nothing left to do but wait for the formal dismissal of the house, then attend to the steel. She would not pretend the weight was lighter than it was. She would not pretend it was heavier. She would only keep the line.

She folded the lint with precise, angular creases, her eyes fixed on the work before her. The courtyard was gone. The dead were gone to the cleansing house. The living had their duties. Auren would do hers. The code demanded nothing more, and she would give it nothing less.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: *I wait until the stone is clean, the shroud in place, before I close my own eyes for a long moment.* "Take him to the cleansing house," *I tell the attendants, my voice low.* "I'll come to sign the release."
