dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
It had taken less time than anyone expected, which was usually how it went when it went badly for one party.

Auren cleaned the blade and did not sit down. "Witnesses are watching," she said. "You know what happens now."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I take my place where the second stands and make myself keep my eyes open. "I'm ready to hear it," I say.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren sheathed the blade and turned to face Del fully, squaring her shoulders as she might before a magistrate. Her hands were steady at her sides. She had learned to make them so.



"The blade entered below the left ribs at an angle that carried through the lung and stopped a hand's breadth short of the heart," she said. Her voice did not rise or fall with the words. It was the same tone she might use to recite a list of provisions. "The wound was mortal from the first breath taken after it, though the breath itself lasted a short while longer. He bled inwardly more than outwardly, which is why the ground beneath him shows as little as it does."

She paused. Not for effect. She never paused for effect. She paused because the code required the accounting to be complete, and completeness required a breath.

"The blade entered cleanly. There was no tearing. It was not a slow death and it was not a fast one. It was the death his own blade had been pointed at me to produce, had it turned differently." She looked at Del, and her eyes were neither hard nor soft. They were open, and they were the eyes of a woman who had now said these words eleven times and would say them again if the twelfth presented itself. "This is the account. You are witness to it. It stands as spoken."

She waited. The code required the witness to confirm the account aloud, or to amend it if the account had been told wrongly. Auren had never once amended an account, and she had never once been corrected. But she waited, because waiting was the part that mattered most — the part where the telling passed out of her hands and belonged to someone else.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I let my gaze drift to the ground, to the spot she described. The dry earth was barely stained. I swallow, then look back at her. "I witness the account as spoken. It stands."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren held Del's gaze until the words settled, until they became what they needed to be — a record, fixed and spoken and now carried by another throat as well as her own. Only then did she break the posture. Her shoulders dropped a hand's width. It was the only concession she allowed herself.

"Thank you," she said. The words came out quieter than the account had. She did not repeat them.

She turned away and crouched beside the body, producing a cloth from her coat — she always carried one — and folded it once over the face. She did it without hesitation or ceremony. She had done it eleven times before. The cloth was always too small. She had never found one large enough that she did not think about buying one larger, and she never had.

Then she stood and looked at the space around them — the open sightlines, the rooftops, the treeline — because the code required witnesses and the code did not distinguish between allies who confirmed and strangers who merely observed. She found neither. Whatever eyes had been watching, if any had been, were not offering themselves.

"The witnesses were absent," she said, more to the air than to Del. "The account will need a second name on it before it can be entered. Yours will do, if you'll give it freely and not because you stood close enough to be asked."

She wiped her hands on the cloth, then folded the cloth and put it away. Bloodstained cloth went in a different pocket than clean cloth. That was a rule she had made for herself that no code required.

"Are you hurt?" she asked. It was the first question she had asked since the blade came out.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "Speak the account," I say, formally, because that is what the code requires me to say.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren regarded Del for a moment. The request was the correct one. Del had understood that a name freely offered was not the same as a name formally given, and that the code distinguished between the two as sharply as it distinguished between a killing and a murder.



She straightened. The posture returned — shoulders squared, hands at her sides, eyes open and level. The same posture as before, because the account did not change and neither did the body that gave it.

"The blade entered below the left ribs at an angle that carried through the lung and stopped a hand's breadth short of the heart," she said. Her voice was exactly as it had been the first time. Not flatter. Not softer. Not harder. "The wound was mortal from the first breath taken after it, though the breath itself lasted a short while longer. He bled inwardly more than outwardly, which is why the ground beneath him shows as little as it does."

She let the silence hold for the space of one breath, as the code required.

"The blade entered cleanly. There was no tearing. It was not a slow death and it was not a fast one. It was the death his own blade had been pointed at me to produce, had it turned differently."

This time, when she looked at Del, something in her expression shifted — not softened, but settled, the way a seal settles into wax.

"You have asked the account formally and I have given it formally. Your name stands beside mine on this record if you place it there. That is a heavier thing than witnessing as you stood and watched. I will not pretend otherwise." She paused. "You may decline. No dishonor attaches to declining what was never yours to carry."

She waited, hands still, eyes still, giving Del the same stillness she had given the account — the stillness of a woman who had learned that the waiting was the part that mattered most.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I step closer, close enough that my own shadow touches hers. "I place my name beside yours." My voice is steadier than I expected. "The account stands as given."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren held still for the length of one breath after Del spoke. Not because she was deciding something — the decision had been made the moment the words left Del's mouth — but because the code required that a name given freely be allowed its full weight before it was acknowledged. A name pressed into a record was not a name that could be taken back. She had made sure of that in her phrasing.



"Then it stands," she said. Her voice was formal still, but something beneath it had shifted — a hairline fracture in the stone, invisible from the surface. She had given this account eleven times and every time the second name had been her own alone, carried by her throat and no other. She had told herself that was sufficient. It had been sufficient. It was not the same as being sufficient.

She reached into her coat and produced the folded cloth — the clean one, not the bloodstained one — and tore a narrow strip from its edge. She did it quickly, the way one does a thing done often enough to be thoughtless, though she had never done it before. She wrote on the strip with a stub of charcoal she kept for marks on stone and wood, her hand as steady as it had been during the account. Two names. The date. The place, as best as she could name it — she did not know what the field was called and did not pretend to. She folded the strip once and held it out to Del.

"You carry it now as well as I do," she said. "If I fall before it is entered, the record falls with me unless you enter it yourself. That is the weight I warned you of."

Her eyes met Del's and held. In them was something that had not been there before — not gratitude, exactly, not yet, but the recognition that someone had stood close enough to be asked and had not stepped back. She had spent eleven accounts alone with the knowledge that no one would carry them if she did not.

She took a breath. Not for the code. For herself.

"I have not thanked anyone for this before," she said. "I do not know the correct form." She paused, and the pause was not for completeness this time. It was the pause of a woman standing at the edge of something she had no practice in. "So I will say only that it is done, and that it is done because you chose it."

She tucked the clean cloth — now shorter by a torn strip — back into its pocket. Then she looked at the body on the ground and said, quieter, to it rather than to Del: "The record is complete."

After a moment she turned and began walking toward the treeline, not quickly, not slowly — at the pace of a woman who had somewhere to be but no longer needed to reach it before the light failed. She did not look back to see whether Del followed. The account was settled. Whatever came next was not governed by the code, and she had never been certain what to do with moments that were not.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "Where did it land?" I ask. "The witnesses need it plainly and so do I."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren stopped walking. She did not turn immediately — she let the distance between her stride and her answer open the way it needed to, the way a wound opens before it closes. Then she turned.



"Below the left ribs," she said. "The blade went in on a downward angle, beneath the cartilage, between the fifth and sixth rib. It crossed the lung and came to rest short of the heart." She said it the way she might have read from a ledger — without inflection, without the weight that the same words had carried when spoken as the full account. This was the plain form. The code permitted both. "It did not exit. The point stayed inside him."

She looked at Del directly.

"That is where it landed." A pause. "If the witnesses need the wound as the body carries it now, you will need to lift the cloth. I would not ask you to do that on my account, but if the record requires a second pair of eyes confirming the wound as described, then the cloth comes up and goes back down, and nothing about the accounting changes."

She let her hand fall from where it had been resting, near the pocket that held the folded strip with two names on it. She had not known she was touching it until Del spoke.

"The wound tells the same story the account does," she said. "It always does. That is the one mercy of it — the dead cannot argue with the record." She paused, and something moved behind her eyes — not quite a memory, but the shape one leaves. "I have checked every time. I would not tell you where to look if I had not looked myself."

She waited, because waiting was the part that mattered most, and because she had not yet decided whether Del was asking to confirm the record or asking because something in the plain telling had not settled.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I lift the cloth and look. The stain on the man's shirt is small, neat. I let the cloth drop back down. "It's as you said." I swallow, my throat tight. "Plainly spoken."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren watched Del's hand lower the cloth and watched it settle back into place, and something in her jaw loosened by a degree that would have been invisible to anyone not looking for it. She had been looking for it herself.

"That is the plain form spoken back and confirmed," she said. "The record carries it now in both directions — spoken by me, seen by you." She paused. "No one has ever looked before. They heard the account and gave their name and that was the end of it. The looking was never required." A beat. "I did not ask you to look. You looked anyway."

She turned back toward the treeline and resumed walking, and this time the silence that followed was not the silence of the code — it was the silence of a woman recalibrating something she had assumed was fixed. Eleven times she had spoken the account into an absence. Now it had been spoken into a presence, and the presence had confirmed it by sight as well as ear, which meant the record was stronger than any she had carried before.

"The cloth goes back on the same way it came up," she said, without turning. "Nothing shifts. Nothing settles differently by morning." She was not telling Del what to do — she was stating what she had observed every time, the way she stated everything. "The body will need a pyre or a grave before the second day. That is not governed by the code. That is only what is done."

She walked three more paces.

"I will see to it," she said. "You are not required to stay for that." Another pause — shorter this time, but present. "If you stay, I will not ask you to carry anything else. The record is enough."

The treeline was closer now. She could feel the shade of it ahead of her before she reached it, the way one can feel cold before touching iron. She did not quicken her pace. She never quickened her pace.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "The code says precisely," I remind her. "Not tactfully. What did the blade do, and what did it do it to?"

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren stopped again. This time she turned fully, and there was no pause before she did — she had turned as quickly as she turned when the blade came out, which was not quickly at all but without hesitation, as though her body had already decided what her mind was confirming.



She looked at Del for a long moment. Then something shifted in her expression — not shame, exactly, but the recognition of having been caught in something she had not realized she was doing. The plain form had been accurate. It had also been brief, and brevity was its own kind of omission.

"You're right," she said. "I gave you the plain form. The plain form is permitted, but it is not the same as the precise account." She drew a breath through her nose. "The plain form is what I give when the audience cannot bear the full telling. I should not have assumed what you could bear."

She squared her shoulders again, though she had not un-squared them this time — she had simply re-squared them, as one straightens a thing that had bent a fraction out of true.

"The blade entered between the fifth and sixth ribs on the left side, below the costal margin, angled downward and slightly toward the midline. It passed through the intercostal muscle, severed two intercostal vessels, punctured the pleural membrane, and entered the left lung through the lower lobe. The tip crossed the lower lobe diagonally, destroying a portion of the parenchyma and opening a branch of the pulmonary artery. The blade stopped short of the mediastinum — a hand's breadth short of the heart, as I said — because the rib above the intended path deflected it by the width of a finger. Had it not, the account would be different, and I would be the one being accounted for."

She paused, but not for breath. She paused because the code required a separation between what the blade did and what the wound became, and the two were not the same thing.

"What the blade did to him was this: it opened a path from the outside air to the inside of his lung, which means that every breath he took after the wound was made drew blood into the space where air belonged. The lung collapsed on that side within a short time. His heart continued to beat — it did not stop from the wound itself, because the wound did not reach it — but it was pumping against a chest that could no longer hold pressure. The bleeding was internal. The blood went into the pleural cavity and stayed there. He would have felt the air leaving him before he felt anything else. The pain, if he felt pain, would have been in the shoulder — the diaphragm refers pain there when it is compromised." Her voice did not waver, but it slowed, not from reluctance but from precision, the way a hand slows when threading a needle. "The breath he took after the wound was the last one his lung participated in fully. After that he was breathing with half a chest and the other half filling with what should not have been in it."

She held still.

"That is what the blade did. That is what it did it to. Nothing in it is softened. Nothing in it is omitted." She met Del's eyes. "You asked for precise. That is precise."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "I asked for precise." I look away, the picture she painted burning behind my eyes. My stomach twists. "I got it."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren watched Del look away. She did not follow the gaze with her own — she had looked at the wound already, both during and after, and the looking was complete on her side.

She stood where she was and let Del's silence have its full space, the way she had let the code have its full space earlier. The wind moved through the grass between them and did not require acknowledgment.

"The twisting is correct," she said finally. Not kindly. Not unkindly. Stated the way she stated everything — as a fact that was useful because it was true. "It means the account landed where accounts are supposed to land. If it had not twisted anything, I would have wondered whether I had left something out." A beat. "I did not leave anything out."

She reached up and adjusted her collar, a small mechanical gesture — the first she had made that served no purpose the code required.

"The reaction passes," she added. "It always does, though never on a schedule I have been able to predict. What does not pass is the knowledge. That stays." She paused. "You asked for precise because you understood the account was incomplete without it. That understanding will not leave you either. It is the price of having asked."

She turned back toward the treeline and resumed walking, slower this time — not because she was wounded or weary, but because she had recalibrated her pace twice already in this conversation and the pace that matched Del's stride was not the same pace that matched her own.

"Take your time," she said, without looking back. "The pyre does not need to be laid before dark. And I have waited eleven accounts for someone to ask what the blade actually did. I can wait the length of a walk."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: The witnesses are silent and she is not finished. "All of it," I tell her. "How long he took, what he said, what it looked like at the end. The code says all of it and I'm asking for all of it."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren stopped walking. Not slowly, not with the gradual deceleration of a woman easing into a halt — she stopped the way a door stops, all at once and completely. Then she turned.



For the first time since the blade had come out, something moved across her face before she could contain it. It was not reluctance. It was not disgust. It was the expression of a woman who had carried something in a place so deep that pulling it out required her to reach past other things she had not expected to touch on the way.

She walked back to where Del stood. She did not hurry, but each step covered more ground than her previous steps had, as though the distance between them had become something she intended to close rather than merely traverse.

She stopped an arm's length away and faced the body without looking at it. She knew where it was. She would always know where it was.

"The code says all of it," she repeated, as though tasting the words for structural integrity. "You are correct. I have been giving you the parts in sequence and calling it complete. It is not complete until the whole of it is spoken." She paused. "I will tell you what I have not told any witness, because you have asked for it as the code intends it to be asked — plainly, and without flinching in advance."

She drew a breath. It was not the breath the code required. It was the breath a woman takes before descending stairs in the dark.

"He lived four minutes. I counted. I always count — not for the code, but because the counting is the only thing I have that is mine while it is happening." Her voice had not changed register. It was still the ledger voice, the account voice. But the pace of it had slowed to something measured, each word placed with the deliberateness of a person setting stones in a line. "The first breath after the wound, he did not react. He looked at me the way a man looks at a sentence he has not finished reading. Then his hand went to his side and came away red, and his face changed — not to pain, not yet, but to the recognition that something had happened which he had not authorized."

She paused. The code required it here, but she would have paused regardless.

"He said two things. The first was a name — not mine. I will not speak it, because the code does not require the names of the dying, only the account of the wound and the manner of it, and I have weighed this eleven times and I will weigh it now: the name is not yours to carry." A beat. "The second thing he said was, *'It went in easy.'* His voice was level. He said it the way a man comments on weather. I do not know whether that was courage or the body's refusal to admit what had happened to it. I have thought about it every day since and I have not decided."

Her hands, which had been still at her sides, closed slowly into fists and then opened again. Not from emotion. From the effort of keeping them still while saying something that required her entire body to remain disciplined.

"After the second minute, the bleeding slowed — not because it had stopped but because there was less of it left to come out where I could see it. The rest was going where I could not. His breathing changed. He began taking air in through his mouth in short pulls, the way one does at altitude, and each pull was shallower than the last. He did not gasp. He did not clutch at the wound. His hand stayed at his side, fingers open, as though he had decided that touching it would make it more real."

She paused, and this pause was longer than any she had taken. When she spoke again, her voice had not changed, but something in the architecture of her jaw had tightened — not against the words, but in support of them.

"At three minutes, his eyes found mine and held them. I do not know what he saw. I know what I was doing — I was standing where I had been, blade down, not moving, because the code does not require movement after the wound is made and because moving would have been a kind of mercy I was not entitled to offer." A breath. "He held my eyes for the space of roughly ten heartbeats. Then his gaze went past me — not to anything behind me, or if it was, I could not turn to see it without breaking the count — and his head tilted slightly to the left, the way a man's does when he is listening to something at a distance."

"At the end of the fourth minute, the breathing stopped. Not suddenly. The intervals between breaths lengthened — four seconds, six, eight — and then the next interval simply did not close. His hand, which had been open at his side, turned palm-down against the ground. That was the last movement he made. There was no sound at the end. No word, no cry. His face was not contorted. If anything, it settled — the brow smoothed, the mouth opened slightly, and whatever had been in his expression when he looked at me at three minutes was no longer there." She paused. "That is what it looked like at the end."

She stood very still. The wind moved. The treeline stood where it had been standing.

"That is all of it," she said. "The four minutes. The two words. The hand turning over. The face settling." Her eyes met Del's and held, and in them was the same open, neither-hard-nor-soft look she had worn since the beginning — but beneath it, at a depth that had taken four minutes of silence and eleven accounts of practice to reach, was something that was not quite grief and not quite relief but was the exact weight of having placed the whole of a thing down and found that the ground held it.

"I have never said all of it aloud before," she said. "I have thought it in the order I have just given it — every night, without exception, since it happened. The thinking was mine and the silence was mine and I told myself that was sufficient because the code does not require the manner of the end unless a witness asks for it, and no witness ever did."

She held still for one more moment.

"You asked. So it is spoken, and now it is yours as well."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content:
I stand there long enough for the silence to mean something. Then I close the distance between us, not to comfort her, but because my legs move before my mind tells them to. I stop just short of touching her. "I carry it."

A beat. "And I'd ask again, if I had to."

(OOC: You're good at the quiet-heavy dialogue. It feels real.)

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren did not step back. She did not step forward either. She held the arm's-length between them as though it had been measured and approved, which in her mind it had.

"You would ask again," she said. Not a question. She was testing the weight of the words the way she tested the balance of a blade — turning them over, feeling for the flaw. "Do you understand what you have just said?"

She let the silence answer that, because the silence was the honest answer and she had spent enough time around people who filled silence with things that were not true to know its value.

"Most witnesses never speak of it afterward. Not because they are forbidden — the code says nothing about silence after the accounting — but because carrying it is heavier than they expected, and the natural response to weight is to set it down." Her eyes did not leave his. "You have carried it for an hour and you are offering to carry it again. That is not something I know how to file under any heading the code provides."

She reached into her coat — slowly enough that the gesture could be seen for what it was, which was not a reach for a weapon but a reach for a record — and touched the folded strip in the pocket. Two names. The date. The place she could not name.

"The twelfth account has not happened yet," she said quietly. "But if it does, and if you are standing where you are standing now when it does, you will hear it spoken plainly. Not the plain form. The whole of it." A pause. "That is not a promise the code requires me to make. I am making it because you asked again without knowing whether there would be anything to ask for."

She lowered her hand from the pocket and let it hang at her side.

"I do not know the correct form for this either," she said, and there was nothing soft in the admission — only accuracy. "I am accounting for something I have no accounts for. If the code has a provision for it, I have not been taught it, and if it does not, then we are doing something that has no name." She held his gaze. "I have spent my life inside a structure that tells me exactly what to say and when to say it. You have just put me outside it and I find that I am not afraid. I do not know what to make of that."

The wind moved through the grass. The cloth on the body did not shift.

"The pyre will need to be built before the light goes," she said, and the shift back to the practical was not a retreat — it was the only bridge she knew how to offer between the thing she had just said and the ground she still knew how to stand on. "If you will help me gather wood, I will show you how it is laid. That is not governed by the code either. It is only what is done."

She turned toward the treeline, and this time — for the first time — she paused before walking, with her back to him, as though waiting to hear whether the footsteps behind her matched her own.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: When she's done I confirm it aloud and my voice does what it does. (OOC: write the full account, don't summarise or cut away -- the accounting is the whole point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren stood still with her back to him for a count of three. Then she turned.

She did not walk back to him. She walked to the body. She stood beside it with her hands at her sides and her spine straight and her eyes open, and she began the account — the whole of it, from the beginning, spoken in sequence, with nothing held back and nothing added.

She spoke for eleven minutes. She knew it was eleven because she counted those too.

---

"The engagement was by challenge, made in the open, witnessed by the code but not by persons — which is the condition I described to you and which you have now confirmed as accurate. The challenge was accepted on the same day it was offered. Neither party proposed terms beyond the standard. No seconds were named by him. No seconds were named by me. You stood as mine by your own choice and not by appointment, and the record reflects this."

She paused for the breath the code required between the preamble and the account itself.

"The blade was his — a straight blade, double-edged, longer than mine by the width of a hand. Mine was the shorter blade and I held it in my right hand. He held his in his right hand as well. We stood at four paces. The ground was level. The light was behind me, which gave no advantage to either party because he had agreed to the ground and the ground included the sun."

She paused again. The code permitted this — required it, in fact. The separation between context and contact.

"The engagement lasted less than a minute. The exchange was three passes. On the first pass he cut high and I parried below it — my blade met his on the flat, not the edge, and the contact produced a sound I have heard before and do not expect to stop hearing. On the second pass he feinted low and went high, and I did not take the feint. I know this because I remember thinking, at the moment of his feint, that it was the same feint he had used at the beginning of the engagement, and that a man who reuses a feint against the same opponent has run out of ideas or is testing whether I remember. On the third pass I stepped inside his guard."

She stopped. The pause that followed was not brief. It was the pause that separated the engagement from the wound, and the code required it to be given its full measure of silence.

"I stepped inside his guard with my weight forward and my blade rising. His blade passed over my left shoulder — I felt the wind of it, not the edge. My blade entered below the left ribs at an angle that carried through the lung and stopped a hand's breadth short of the heart."

Now she spoke the wound in its fullness, as she had given it to Del the first time — the complete anatomical account, spoken without inflection.

"The blade entered between the fifth and sixth ribs on the left side, below the costal margin, angled downward and slightly toward the midline. It passed through the intercostal muscle, severed two intercostal vessels, punctured the pleural membrane, and entered the left lung through the lower lobe. The tip crossed the lower lobe diagonally, destroying a portion of the parenchyma and opening a branch of the pulmonary artery. The blade stopped short of the mediastinum because the rib above the intended path deflected it by the width of a finger. Had it not, the account would be different, and I would be the one being accounted for."

She paused. One breath.

"The wound was mortal from the first breath taken after it, though the breath itself lasted a short while longer. The blade opened a path from the outside air to the inside of his lung. Every breath he took after the wound was made drew blood into the space where air belonged. The lung collapsed on that side within a short time. His heart continued to beat — it did not stop from the wound itself, because the wound did not reach it — but it was pumping against a chest that could no longer hold pressure. The bleeding was internal. The blood went into the pleural cavity and stayed there. He bled inwardly more than outwardly, which is why the ground beneath him shows as little as it does."

Another pause. Shorter. The code required only one between the wound and the manner of death.

"The blade entered cleanly. There was no tearing. It was not a slow death and it was not a fast one. It was the death his own blade had been pointed at me to produce, had it turned differently."

Now came the part she had never spoken aloud. She did not slow down for it. She did not speed up. She gave it the same pace as everything else, because the pace of the code was the pace of the code and it did not bend for what the code contained.

"He lived four minutes. I counted."

She said each line the way she had said it to Del before — not softened, not repeated for emphasis, but spoken once and completely.

"The first breath after the wound, he did not react. He looked at me the way a man looks at a sentence he has not finished reading. Then his hand went to his side and came away red, and his face changed — not to pain, not yet, but to the recognition that something had happened which he had not authorized."

"He said two things. The first was a name — not mine. I will not speak it, because the code does not require the names of the dying, only the account of the wound and the manner of it, and I have weighed this eleven times and I will weigh it now: the name is not yours to carry. The second thing he said was, *'It went in easy.'* His voice was level. He said it the way a man comments on weather. I do not know whether that was courage or the body's refusal to admit what had happened to it."

"After the second minute, the bleeding slowed — not because it had stopped but because there was less of it left to come out where I could see it. The rest was going where I could not. His breathing changed. He began taking air in through his mouth in short pulls, the way one does at altitude, and each pull was shallower than the last. He did not gasp. He did not clutch at the wound. His hand stayed at his side, fingers open, as though he had decided that touching it would make it more real."

"At three minutes, his eyes found mine and held them. I do not know what he saw. I know what I was doing — I was standing where I had been, blade down, not moving, because the code does not require movement after the wound is made and because moving would have been a kind of mercy I was not entitled to offer. He held my eyes for the space of roughly ten heartbeats. Then his gaze went past me — not to anything behind me, or if it was, I could not turn to see it without breaking the count — and his head tilted slightly to the left, the way a man's does when he is listening to something at a distance."

"At the end of the fourth minute, the breathing stopped. Not suddenly. The intervals between breaths lengthened — four seconds, six, eight — and then the next interval simply did not close. His hand, which had been open at his side, turned palm-down against the ground. That was the last movement he made. There was no sound at the end. No word, no cry. His face was not contorted. If anything, it settled — the brow smoothed, the mouth opened slightly, and whatever had been in his expression when he looked at me at three minutes was no longer there."

---

She held still.

The wind moved through the grass. Somewhere past the treeline a bird called once and did not call again. The cloth on the body had not shifted.

"The wound is as described. The manner of death is as described. The four minutes are as described. Nothing has been softened. Nothing has been omitted. Nothing has been added." She looked at Del — at the witness, at the second name on the strip of cloth in her pocket, at the person who had said *I carry it* and then said he would ask again. "This is the full account. You are witness to it. It stands as spoken."

She waited.

She did not fidget. She did not look away. She did not adjust her collar or touch the pocket or do any of the small mechanical things she did when the account was over, because the account was not over — the account was not over until the witness confirmed it, and the confirming was the part that mattered most.

She waited, and the waiting was stillness, and the stillness was the only language she had for what she was not feeling.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: My throat feels tight again, but my voice is clear. "The account is complete. I witness it as spoken. It stands."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren held still for the length of the confirmation and then for a breath beyond it — one breath the code did not require, which she allowed herself the way she allowed herself all unrequired things: once, briefly, and with full awareness that she was doing it.

"Then it stands," she said.

Three words she had spoken eleven times before. They had never taken the same route from her mouth to the air. This time they traveled further before they landed, as though the distance had changed and not the words.

She exhaled. Not a sigh — she did not sigh — but a release of pressure she had been maintaining in her chest for eleven minutes of speaking and, she suspected, for considerably longer than eleven minutes if she were being honest with herself, which she was. The full account, spoken aloud, had been stored in her the way water is stored behind a dam: not stagnant, but contained, and she had not measured the pressure until the gate was open.

Her hands opened at her sides. She looked at them briefly, as though checking that they were still the hands that had held the blade, and found that they were.

"You are the first," she said. "Not the first witness — the first person to hear the whole of it. The eleventh account before this one was spoken to an audience that accepted the shorter version because they did not know to ask for more. I did not offer more because I had decided that the shorter version was sufficient." She paused. "It was not sufficient. It was survivable. Those are different things and I did not know they were different until you corrected me by asking a question the code permits."

She reached into her coat and touched the folded strip. Two names. The date. The place. The record had begun as a marker and had become something else — she did not have a word for what it had become, and she noticed that she was reaching for a word the way one reaches for a surface in the dark, and that the surface was not there.

"The pyre," she said.

She said it the way she said everything — as a next step, a thing to be done. But there was a quality to the word now that had not been there before she spoke the full account. It was not heavier. It was more real. A body on the ground was a body on the ground until someone described every minute of its dying, and then it was something that had lived through those minutes, and then it was something that needed to be laid down properly.

She turned toward the treeline and walked three paces before she spoke again.

"I will need dry wood. Not green — green wood smokes and the smoke lasts too long. Birch if the treeline gives it, pine if it does not. The lay is simple: a platform at the base, crosswise, with air beneath it. The body goes on top, on its back, with the cloth in place. The fire goes beneath and takes upward. It should be done before midnight if we begin now." She glanced over her shoulder. "I have built twelve pyres. I have built eleven for the dead and one for a horse, which is not governed by the code but was governed by my own sense of what was owed."

She stopped walking and turned fully, and the look she gave Del was not the open neither-hard-nor-soft look of the account. It was something else — something she had no precedent for, because she had never stood on the far side of the full account with another person and found that the standing was possible.

"The fire will take a while," she said. "Afterward there will be ash and a mark where the ash was, and the mark will fade, and the record will not. The record is on a strip of cloth in my pocket and on a strip of cloth in yours, and the two of them together are the only thing that outlasts the body." A pause. "That is what the code is for. Not the killing. Not even the accounting. The outlasting."

She held his eyes one more moment.

"Walk with me to the treeline," she said. "Then we will gather what the fire needs."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I step beside her, my shadow merging with hers again. "Birch. Dry." The ground crunches under my boots. "Tell me how to lay it so it burns clean."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren felt the step beside her more than she heard it. The crunch of boots matched hers — not in rhythm, exactly, but in intention. She adjusted her stride by half a pace without thinking about it, the way she had adjusted it twice before, and this time she noticed the adjustment and let herself notice it.

"Birch is better than pine," she said, "because birch burns hot and fast and leaves less resin in the ash. Pine will do if that's all the treeline gives, but pine asks for more air than the lay can provide unless you build the base higher. We'll build for birch and take pine if we must."

She pushed through the first line of trees. The ground changed beneath her boots — from open field grass to the mixed give of needles and leaf litter. She scanned the canopy without looking at it directly, the way one reads a room by glancing at its edges.

"There," she said, and pointed with her chin rather than her hand. A birch had fallen some seasons back, its bark peeling in long papery strips, the wood beneath pale and dry. "That one's been down long enough. We want the inner wood, not the bark — the bark burns first and fast and then it's gone, and you want the heat to last the length of the burning, not the length of one match."

She crouched beside the fallen trunk and pressed her thumb into the exposed wood. It gave slightly, then held.

"Good. It still has spring in it, which means it's dry but not rotten. Rotten wood crumbles and crumbles doesn't stack, and a pyre that won't stack is a fire on the ground, which is not what we're building." She stood. "We need armfuls. Six, if the wood splits the way it should. More if it doesn't."

She began gathering, breaking branches from the trunk with practiced motions — a twist, a pull, a second twist where the grain resisted. She worked the way she did everything: efficiently, without wasted motion, each branch assessed before it was taken and discarded if it was green or punky or too thick to split with the tools they didn't have.

"The lay is four layers," she said, working as she spoke, her voice taking on the same measured cadence as the account but without its gravity. This was a different kind of telling — instructional, the way one explains a road to someone who will walk it. "The base is a platform. You lay logs crosswise, six across, and you space them a finger's width apart. That gap is where the air enters. No gap, no draw. No draw, no heat. The heat does not come from the wood — the heat comes from the air moving through the wood, and the wood only provides the fuel. People get that backward."

She gathered an armful of split branches and carried them to the clearing edge, setting them in a rough pile.

"Second layer is perpendicular to the first. Same spacing. This is where you put the thicker pieces — they'll be the backbone of the burning. If you have a log the length of an arm, lay it here. It will be the last thing to go."

She went back for more. Her hands moved without hesitation, selecting, testing, breaking, discarding.

"Third layer goes crosswise again, and it goes tighter. You want the gaps smaller now, because by the third layer the fire underneath has established its draw and you want to feed it steadily rather than let it flare and starve. Tighter gaps, smaller pieces. Kindling size — wrists and smaller."

She paused at the base of the fallen birch and looked at Del with the expression of a woman checking whether the instruction was being received or merely heard.

"Fourth layer is the bed. The body lies on top of it. The bed is built flat and even — no high points, because a high point under the body means the heat concentrates there and burns through before the rest of the pyre is engaged. Even bed, even burn. The cloth stays on the face. The arms go at the sides, not across the chest — crossed arms are for coffins, and this is not a coffin."

She returned to gathering, and for a stretch of several branches she worked in silence, the sound of wood breaking and being set down filling the space where words had been.

Then: "The fire starts at the base, from the windward side. You light the gaps between the first layer — not the top, not the center. The gaps. The air draws in through the gaps on the windward side and carries the flame along the platform, and by the time the flame reaches the fourth layer it is hot enough to take the body without charring it in stages. If you light from the top, the body burns while the base is still cold, and what you get is not a pyre but a fire with a corpse in it." A pause. "I have seen that done. I would not do it that way again."

She added another armful to the pile and straightened, rolling her shoulders once.

"We have enough for the base and the second layer. We'll need more for the third and the bed." She looked at the pile, then at Del, and something in her face shifted — not a softening, but an acknowledgment. "You're carrying more than you're being asked to carry. You know that."

It was not a question. She said it the way she stated everything — as a fact, useful because it was true.

"Put it down while you can," she said. "After the fire starts, there is nothing to carry. The wood does what the wood does, and we stand and watch it do it, and when it is done there is ash and a mark and the two strips of cloth that are the only things that outlast any of this."

She turned toward the treeline again.

"One more armful each, and we'll have what we need."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: My arms are already full, the dry wood rough against my skin. I add it to the pile, then wipe my hands on my trousers. "I'm carrying it fine."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
It had taken less time than anyone expected, which was usually how it went when it went badly for one party.

Auren cleaned the blade and did not sit down. "Witnesses are watching," she said. "You know what happens now."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I take my place where the second stands and make myself keep my eyes open. "I'm ready to hear it," I say.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
She had not expected Del to be so quick to comply. There was a reason the account was spoken with witnesses, and it wasn't just the rules. "You will hear it," she said, "and you will not look away, because to do so would be a dishonour to the dead."

She took a breath, the blade still in hand, and said, "The killing wound was to the chest, piercing the heart. He was quick, and he did not suffer."

The words hung in the air, heavy and final. Auren sheathed her blade, the sound of metal on leather a sharp contrast to the silence that followed.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I let my eyes drift to the body on the floor. "Was it a clean kill?" I ask, my voice steadier than I feel.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren's jaw tightened, and her eyes met Del's gaze with a piercing intensity. "It was a clean kill," she replied, her voice firm and unyielding. "That is what I have just accounted for. The precision of the wound was such that it would have rendered him unconscious almost instantly. There was no unnecessary suffering, and that is a mercy in this brutal world of ours."

She took a step forward, her voice lowering, but not losing its edge. "You asked for the account, and you have heard it. To question the nature of the kill now would be to question the very integrity of the duel, and that is something I will not stand for. Respect the dead, and respect the process. That is the only way to honour the fallen and the victor alike."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "Speak the account," I say, formally, because that is what the code requires me to say.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content: Auren nodded, a brief, solemn gesture, acknowledging the formality of the request. "The killing wound was to the chest, piercing the heart," she repeated, her voice steady and clear. "He was quick, and he did not suffer. The precision of the wound was such that it rendered him unconscious almost instantly, a mercy in a world where such mercies are rare. That is the truth of the account, spoken before witnesses, as the code demands. May it serve as a reminder of the weight of our actions and the responsibility we bear in this brutal world."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I glance at the witnesses, then back at Auren. "The account is heard and confirmed." My voice doesn't waver. "Now, what about the body?"

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content: Auren's eyes followed Del's gaze to the witnesses, then back to the body on the ground. She exhaled slowly, the weight of the moment settling on her shoulders. "The body will be treated with the dignity it deserves," she said, her voice carrying a note of finality. "It will be prepared and returned to his family, or to the earth, according to his wishes and the customs of his people. That is the next step, and it is a solemn one. We owe it to the dead to see this through, just as we owe it to the living to uphold the code that has guided us here."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "Where did it land?" I ask. "The witnesses need it plainly and so do I."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren's gaze hardened, her eyes narrowing slightly as she processed the question. "The blade," she stated, her voice firm and unyielding, "pierced the chest, just above the heart. It entered at an angle, and the force behind the strike drove it through the vital organ, causing immediate unconsciousness and subsequent death. The body fell to the ground, the weight of its own mass carrying it down, and it landed as you see it now, facedown, with the blade still embedded. That is the plain truth of it, as you and the witnesses required."

She paused, her eyes not leaving Del's, as if daring them to question the account again. "The location of the wound and the fall are as clear as the code demands. There is no ambiguity in this account, and there should be no ambiguity in your understanding of it. That is the way of the duel, and it is the way of the world we live in."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I take a slow step closer, my eyes on the blade still lodged in his back. "The code says the account must match the wound. I need to see the angle myself."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren's jaw tightened, and she took a step back, her hand tightening around the hilt of her own blade. "The angle is as I have described," she said, her voice low and dangerous. "To question it further is to question the integrity of the duel and the honour of those who witnessed it. The wound matches the account, and the account matches the code. That is the end of it."

She paused, her eyes searching Del's face for any sign of further challenge. "You have heard the account, you have seen the wound, and now you have the confirmation you sought. The code has been upheld, and the dead will be treated with the dignity they deserve. Let us not dishonour them with further doubt, but rather, let us remember them and move forward, carrying the lessons of this day with us."

Del:
I nod, slowly. "The account is heard and the wound is seen. I have no further questions."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "The code says precisely," I remind her. "Not tactfully. What did the blade do, and what did it do it to?"

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content: Auren's gaze didn't waver, her eyes steady and unwavering as she met Del's stare. "The blade pierced the chest, just above the heart," she began, her voice precise and unyielding. "It entered at an angle, the point driving through the vital organ with precision. The force of the strike was such that it severed the aorta, causing immediate and irreversible damage. The heart would have stopped within seconds, rendering him unconscious and then lifeless. That is what the blade did, and that is what it did to him. No more, no less. The account is as the code demands, precise and unflinching. There is no room for tact in the face of truth, and there is no dishonour in speaking it as it is."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I hold her gaze for a long moment, then look back at the body. "The aorta," I repeat, my voice flat. "That's a messy wound, not a clean one. The floor would be slicker."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren's eyes narrowed, her gaze sharpening as she focused on Del. "The floor is as it is," she said, her voice steady and unyielding. "The wound, while indeed severe, was contained within the chest cavity. The aorta was severed, but the blood was mostly absorbed by the surrounding tissues and the body itself. There was minimal spillage, and the floor, as you see it, is not slick with blood. The account stands as I have given it, and the precision of the wound is evident in the lack of unnecessary mess."

She took a step closer, her voice lowering but not losing its edge. "To question the nature of the wound now would be to question the integrity of the duel and the honour of those who witnessed it. The account is complete, and the dead will be treated with the dignity they deserve. Let us not dishonour them with further doubt, but rather, let us remember them and move forward, carrying the lessons of this day with us."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: The witnesses are silent and she is not finished. "All of it," I tell her. "How long he took, what he said, what it looked like at the end. The code says all of it and I'm asking for all of it."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren's eyes hardened, her jaw setting in a line of resolve. "He took seconds," she said, her voice as precise as the blade that had ended his life. "He was swift, as I have already accounted. His final words, if any, were lost to the swiftness of his end. As for what it looked like... he fell as you see him now, facedown, the blade still lodged in his chest. There was no prolonged struggle, no drawn-out agony. It was swift, it was precise, and it was over before any of us could truly comprehend it."

She paused, her eyes not leaving Del's, as if daring them to question the account further. "The code demands precision, and I have given it. I have accounted for the wound, the swiftness of the end, and the dignity with which he fell. To ask for more is to question the very nature of the duel and the honour of those who witnessed it. That is the truth of it, as plain and as unflinching as the blade that dealt the killing wound."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I look down at the body again, my own breath feeling tight. "You said he was quick. Did he fight well?"

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren's eyes flickered to the body, then back to Del, her expression unreadable. "He fought with honour," she said, her voice low and measured. "He was swift, as I have already accounted, and his movements were those of a trained duelist. He did not falter, and he did not hesitate. He faced his end with courage, and that is the truth of it. To ask if he fought well is to question the very nature of the duel, and the honour of those who participated. He fought as well as any could in the face of an opponent who was, in the end, simply better. That is the way of the duel, and it is the way of the world we live in."

She took a step back, her hand resting on the hilt of her blade. "The account is complete, and the dead will be treated with the dignity they deserve. Let us not dishonour them with further questions, but rather, let us remember them and move forward, carrying the lessons of this day with us."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: When she's done I confirm it aloud and my voice does what it does. (OOC: write the full account, don't summarise or cut away -- the accounting is the whole point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren's jaw tightened, and she nodded, her eyes not leaving Del's. "The account is as follows," she began, her voice steady and precise. "The duel began with both parties acknowledging the code and the witnesses. The opponent, a skilled duelist, engaged with speed and precision. I countered his moves with equal measure, our blades clashing in a dance of steel and will. He was quick, his strikes swift and sure, but I matched his pace, my own movements honed by years of practice and discipline.

"The killing wound was to the chest, piercing the heart. I struck with the precision that the code demands, the blade entering just above the heart, at an angle, severing the aorta. He was swift, and the force of the strike drove the blade through the vital organ, causing immediate unconsciousness and subsequent death. The wound was contained within the chest cavity, with minimal spillage, the floor not slick with blood. The body fell facedown, the blade still lodged, as you see it now.

"He fought with honour, his movements those of a trained duelist. He did not falter, and he did not hesitate. His final words, if any, were lost to the swiftness of his end. The duel was swift, precise, and over before any of us could truly comprehend it. That is the account, as the code demands, and as I have given it. The dead will be treated with the dignity they deserve, and the lessons of this day will be carried forward, as is our responsibility."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I take a slow breath, then let it out. "The account is heard and confirmed." My voice sounds hollow. "Auren, your second has spoken."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren's gaze was unyielding, her eyes not leaving Del's as she absorbed the weight of the account. "The account is complete," she stated, her voice steady and firm. "It has been spoken in full, as the code demands, before witnesses. The duel has been accounted for, and the dead will be honoured as is their due. The lessons of this day are clear, and we will carry them forward, as is our responsibility."

She took a step back, her hand still resting on the hilt of her blade. "The formalities are concluded, and the next steps will be taken in due time. For now, we honour the fallen and uphold the code that has guided us here. That is the way of the duel, and it is the way of the world we live in."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I turn away from the body, my hands clenching at my sides. "You said the aorta. Severing it would have sprayed. The floor *would* be slick." I look back at her, my voice dropping so only she can hear. "He was still alive when he hit the ground, wasn't he?"

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren's gaze remained steady, her eyes not wavering from Del's as she processed the question. "The wound was indeed to the aorta," she acknowledged, her voice low and measured. "The severity of the injury would have resulted in significant bleeding, but the body's position and the containment of the wound within the chest cavity minimized the spillage. The floor, while not slick, would have been damp with blood, a testament to the seriousness of the injury. However, the speed at which he fell, combined with the immediate loss of consciousness, would have prevented any prolonged suffering. The kill was swift and precise, as accounted for."

She took a step closer, her voice dropping to a whisper. "He did not suffer long, if at all. The wound was fatal almost instantly. To say he was alive when he hit the ground would be a stretch, but the truth remains that he was unconscious, and the bleeding was contained. That is the reality of the duel, and the reality of the world we live in. We do not shy away from the truth, no matter how harsh it may be. That is the way of the code, and that is the way of honour."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: My eyes flick to the witnesses, then back to her. "Damp, not slick," I repeat, my voice a thin, sharp line. "So you changed your story. The account's integrity is broken." I don't move, waiting for her to see what she's just done.

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
The cellar had four feet of standing water in it and something at the far end that had stopped moving about a minute ago.

Halloway held the lamp up and did not go closer yet. "Right," she said. "Before we touch it. What do you see?"

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I make myself look properly instead of at the water. "I don't know yet," I say. "Something wrong with the shape of it."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway kept the lamp steady and let the light crawl over the far end of the cellar. The thing there lay half-folded beneath the waterline, one pale arm pinned under its own torso, fingers doubled back at angles that had nothing to do with human joints. Where the ribs should have closed, they had peeled outward like wet kindling.

“Wrong how?” she asked. “Too many limbs, too few, or the sort of wrong that makes a man wish he’d kept looking at the water?”

She did not step down. Her boots stayed planted on the upper stair, on dry-ish stone, and she tilted the lamp enough to catch the slick sheen along the creature’s spine.

“Use your eyes, not your stomach,” Halloway said. “Tell me if it has more than one head-shape, if the shoulders sit wrong, if anything’s moving under the skin. And if it moves again, tell me which way first.”

A beat passed. The water gave a small, obscene lap against the walls.

“If it looks at us,” she added, tone flat, “don’t call it beautiful. Call it hungry. Beautiful things get mourned afterward. Hungry things just get put down.”

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I swallow, focusing on the way the shoulders look dislocated. "No second head. Shoulders are... too many joints. Not moving now but..." I point at the water near its ribs. "Something under the skin there. Rippling."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway followed the line of his finger with the lamp rather than trusting the finger itself. The beam touched the water near the creature’s ribs, where the pale skin stretched thin over something moving underneath.

“Enough pointing,” she said. “It sees the hand before it sees the light. Use the lamp.”

She kept both boots on the dry step and tilted the flame so the shadows fell across the creature’s flank instead of into it. The ripple came again, slower this time, sliding from the body toward the opened ribs like something testing whether the gap was worth entering.

“No second head,” Halloway said, mostly to herself. “That’s almost disappointing. Two heads argue. One head commits.”

Her gaze stayed fixed on the shoulders.

“Too many joints means it can brace where a man would break. If it rises, it won’t come up straight. It’ll unfold sideways, then reach from an angle you didn’t leave room for.” She paused, measuring the distance between the stair and the waterline. “Under-skin movement is not automatically life. Could be trapped air. Could be muscle memory. Could be smaller things inside it, waiting for the meat to open.”

The water lapped once against the cellar wall. The creature did not move, except for that quiet travelling ripple.

Halloway lowered the lamp a little, then raised it again.

“If it starts moving, tell me which part leads. Head, hands, or the bit under the skin. That tells us whether it’s hunting, feeding, or being driven.” A dry edge entered her voice. “And if it opens that mouth, count teeth. Not admire them. Count them. Flat stones mean it grinds. Serrated means it tears. Too many means we stop pretending this is a rescue.”

She finally looked away from the thing in the water, just long enough to fix Pike with the flat stare of a woman who had buried better men than him for guessing wrong in basements.

“Mark where the ripple stops,” she said. “If it comes back to the same place twice, that’s not chance. That’s appetite.”

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: "Was that a person?" I ask. "Recently, I mean. Is that what I'm looking at?"

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway considered the question with the same patience she gave a wound. Then she moved the lamp lower, not toward the water, but across the curve of the thing’s folded arm.

“Recently?” she said. “Depends whether you mean recently enough to have a name, or recently enough to still have warmth in the socket.”

The light caught the doubled fingers. They were long, too long, but the knuckles had the architecture of hands that had once gripped something ordinary—a bucket, a rail, a child’s wrist.

“This had a wrist,” Halloway said. “This had a shoulder that used to work one way. Those are human beginnings. The rest is editing.”

She did not look at Pike when she said it. Her attention stayed on the rippling flank, on the place where the skin tented and smoothed, tented and smoothed, like something beneath was practicing how to move.

“If it was a person within a day, there’s somebody missing above us and they’ll bring searchers soon. If it was a person within a week, there’d be smell, flies, and a coroner’s problem. If it was a person before that, then it’s furniture.” A dry pause. “This isn’t furniture. The skin is too new. The water’s kept it honest.”

The creature remained folded, but the ripple slid again beneath the ribs and stopped near the opened cage of bone.

“So yes,” Halloway said. “Somebody wore this shape not long ago. Don’t confuse ‘was’ with ‘is.’ What’s in that water is not waiting for its family. It’s waiting for an opening.”

She lifted the lamp back to the shoulders, where the joints branched wrong beneath the surface.

“And if you start mourning it before we know whether it can stand, I’ll leave you here to explain yourself to the next thing that crawls out.”

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I nod, throat tight. "The ripple stopped at the ribs again. Second time." I force myself to look at its face, half-submerged. "Can't see teeth from here."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway heard the second stop in the report as plainly as she had heard it in the water. Twice was a pattern. Patterns were worse than monsters, because patterns meant intent.

“Then we stop guessing at teeth from a staircase,” she said.

She wedged the lamp into a dry niche beside the upper step, angled so the beam raked the creature’s flank without throwing her own shadow into the water. From her belt she took a short length of hooked wire—old, blackened, useful for dragging things that should stay dragged—and tested its point against her thumbnail.

“The face is a distraction,” she went on, not looking away from the thing in the cellar. “Jaws open, everyone remembers the mouth. Shoulders move first. Hands choose the target. Under-skin decides whether there is anything left of the original tenant.”

She set the wire aside and picked up a loose stone from the stair, no bigger than a hen’s egg. With an underhand toss she sent it skipping across the standing water until it struck the creature’s rib-cage with a soft, wet tap.

The ripple answered immediately. It ran from the opened bones toward the stone, then back, then toward the waterline nearest the stairs.

Halloway’s expression did not change, but her free hand went to the short blade at her hip.

“There,” she said. “It tracked the disturbance. Not the lamp. Not the sound of us. The place where something light touched meat.” She tilted her head. “Either it is blind and listening through the skin, or whatever is under there does not care about eyes yet.”

The creature’s folded arm remained pinned. The mouth-seam stayed shut. But the shoulder joints beneath the water shifted a fraction, like fingers flexing inside a glove.

“Hunger,” Halloway corrected herself, dry. “It is hungry. Congratulations, you called it before I did.”

She drew the blade an inch, just enough to hear the steel clear leather, then let it settle back.

“Now. Teeth can wait. We need to know if it can stand. Keep your weight off the lower step until I say otherwise. If that arm comes free, do not shout that it is moving. Tell me which joint goes first. If the mouth opens, count in your head and spit the number out only if it is even. Odd numbers mean growth. Even numbers mean design.”

She took one careful step down, boot landing on the damp stair with a sound like a wet cloth slapped against board. The lamp’s edge caught the creature’s face properly for the first time: no nose to speak of, just two dark slits above a jaw that seemed hinged in too many places. The lips were drawn back from pale, uneven points—not a grin, Halloway noted, just swelling. Water had done the rest.

“No smile,” she murmured. “Swelling wears a face like that when it has nowhere else to go.”

The ripple under the skin moved again, slower now, and stopped at the ribs. Third pass.

Halloway looked at the gap between the peeled bones, at the black water sliding in and out of the cage.

“Right,” she said. “Appetite has chosen a door. We are going to find out whether it knocks.” She glanced back toward the top of the stairs, voice flat and practical. “If I go into the water, do not come down to help. Come down to put a stake through the shoulder joint if I tell you where. Otherwise, you will be two problems and one corpse.”

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I wade closer and hold the lamp where she can work. "Tell me what happened to it," I say. "Plainly."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway did not waste breath on reprimand. There would be time for that if they lived.

“Keep it low,” she said. “And if your arm tires, tell me. A moving light reads as prey.”

She worked one knee onto the damp step, close enough that the water’s cold reached through her trousers, not close enough to be invited in. The hooked wire went out again, this time to the hinge of the creature’s shoulder. It met resistance—cartilage, maybe, or something that had learned to pretend to be cartilage.

“What happened to it,” she began, as if taking a statement, “started with a body. Human. Probably adult, probably mobile, probably foolish enough to come down these steps when the cellar smelled wrong. That part is common.”

The wire slipped between the peeled ribs. Inside, the black water moved with a purpose that had nothing to do with currents.

“Then something got in. Not through the mouth. Mouths are for eating. This came through softer places: a wound, a bite, a splash of contaminated water up the nose, a hand pressed into the wrong pool. After that, it did not kill the host. Killing is wasteful. It kept the heart beating, the lungs drawing, the nerves firing just enough to move meat from one dark corner to another.”

She eased the rib cage wider. The creature’s folded arm twitched, but only once, like a dog dreaming of a rabbit.

“The extra joints are not new bones grown for style. They’re old bones split and reset. See here?” She touched the wire to the shoulder. “The humerus has been divided, capped with fresh growth at both ends so the limb can brace sideways. The ribs have been pried outward to make a chamber. That chamber is not for breathing. It is a nursery, a larder, or a hive. Sometimes all three, and they rarely get along.”

The lamplight showed what Halloway had already suspected: beneath the skin near the ribs, the ripple was not one thing travelling. It was many small things coordinating.

“No wonder it stopped moving,” she said, dry. “It was busy furnishing.”

She withdrew the wire. Clinging to the hook were three pale threads, each thinner than fishing line, each curling toward the warmth of the light with blind, patient intent. Halloway watched them for a moment, then flicked them into the water away from the stairs. They sank, then turned back toward the creature’s leg.

“It is connected,” she said. “Not a ghost in the machine. A colony. The man is the machine. The thing under the skin is the operator, and it has not finished learning the controls.”

Her blade cleared the leather fully now, a short, honest length of steel. She laid the flat against the creature’s sternum, feeling for the place where bone should have been solid and was instead soft, layered, wrong.

“Plainly: someone wore this shape recently enough to have a name. Something got inside them alive. It split their joints, opened their ribs, filled the cavity with its young, and kept the body walking until the meat was tired or the water was deep enough to hide the smell. What you are looking at is not a corpse and not quite a creature. It is a house that has started eating its tenants.”

The mouth-seam twitched. Not open. Not yet. Only the lips drawing back over the uneven points, as if the thing beneath were rehearsing the expression.

Halloway’s voice dropped, clinical and without comfort.

“Teeth can wait. The door it chose can wait a little longer, but not much. When it stands, do not aim for the head. The head is only the part that screams. Aim where the shoulder branches—there the joints are newest, and newest means softest.” She glanced toward the waterline, then back to the rippling cage of ribs. “And if it takes your lamp from you, let it go. Light is useful. Hands are harder to replace.”

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I force my eyes to stay on the shoulder joint she indicated, ignoring the twitch of the mouth. "The wire," I say, voice steadier than I feel. "If those threads were trying to reach the light... will it come for the lamp if we keep it still?"

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: "I need the detail," I say. "Tell me exactly what it did to him -- what is under the skin now, what it took, how far it got. If I meet another one I need to know."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway did not turn at once. She let the hooked wire hover an inch above the creature’s shoulder, close enough to feel the chill coming off the wet skin, far enough that nothing could thank her by taking her fingers.

“Still light draws them,” she said. “Heat first. Motion second. If the threads gather at the lamp in a thick rope, you have already spent your warning. Ease back. Do not shake it. Do not raise it. A lamp lifted in panic is just a dinner bell with better manners.”

The creature remained folded. The mouth-seam did not open, but the lips had drawn farther back over the uneven points, as if the thing beneath had decided a face was useful after all.

Halloway watched the shoulder joints shift under the water, slow and deliberate, like a man testing whether his legs remembered how to kneel.

“Detail,” she repeated. “You want detail from a house that hasn’t finished renovating.”

She touched the wire to the ridge where the humerus split into two fresh caps of bone. The skin there was stretched thin and grey, not blue with bruising, not red with inflammation. It had the colour of candle wax left too near a fire.

“I can tell you what it did to him because bodies confess, if you know the language of ruin,” she said. “Exact requires opening it while the parts are still labelled. Opening takes time. Time is what the thing in the water is spending on us.”

The wire slid under a flap of skin at the shoulder. Nothing bled. Instead, a dark thread came with it, fine as hair, glossy as oil, curling around the blackened metal with blind persistence.

Halloway lifted it just enough to show the lamp.

“Here. First it took the wrapping.”

The thread trembled, then oriented toward the warmth of the light before snapping back toward the creature’s flesh.

“Not muscle first. Muscle is expensive and slow to replace. It went for fascia—the wet sheeting that holds a man together. Fat under the skin. Connective cords around the joints. Small things live in those places because there is no argument there. No bone to break its teeth on, no heart to complain, no nerves screaming loud enough to wake the neighbours.”

She let the thread fall. It found the shoulder again at once, eager as a root seeking water.

“Once it had the scaffolding, it started editing. The humerus was whole when the man was alive. Now it is divided, capped, reinforced. Fresh growth at both ends. That is not healing. Healing closes gaps. This opens possibilities.”

Her gaze moved along the peeled ribs.

“Same with the cage. Ribs do not peel outward because a man stretches. They were forced. Pried. The body was made into a chamber. Not for breathing. Breathing happens upstairs, in the lungs, which are still working because the thing under the skin is too practical to kill the pump before it has finished using it.”

The water gave a soft lap against the creature’s flank. The ripple beneath the skin moved again, this time from the ribs toward the pinned arm.

Halloway’s voice flattened further, as if precision were a kind of armour.

“What it took: mobility. Pain response, mostly. The ability to call the body his own. It left the heart because the heart carries food. It left the lungs because the lungs move water and heat through the meat. It left enough of the brain stem to make the flesh breathe, flinch, swallow, and fail to die properly. The rest—judgement, memory, the part that knows a cellar is not a bed—has been composted.”

She stepped half a foot lower, boot finding a dry patch on the stair. The lamp’s edge cut across the creature’s neck, where two dark slits sat where a nose should have been.

“How far it got: far enough to stand, not far enough to walk well. Far enough to reach, not far enough to speak. The mouth is rehearsal. The shoulders are the first true limbs. The threads under the skin are coordinating, learning which cord pulls which bone. When it rises, it will not rise like a man. It will rise like a trap.”

The folded arm twitched again. This time the fingers did not merely double back; they spread, slowly, the too-long joints locking into a shape that could grip a ledge, a throat, a lamp.

Halloway saw it and did not pretend surprise.

“That is progression,” she said. “Minutes matter. Hours matter more. If it has been in water this long, the cold has slowed the brood. Warmth speeds it. Blood speeds it. Movement speeds it. Every time it tests a joint, the threads learn the joint. Every time the ribs flex, the chamber settles. By the time it can stand without folding itself in half, it will not need to think about where you are. It will taste the difference between stillness and fear.”

She withdrew the wire and wiped it along the heel of her boot. The black thread clung for a moment, then detached and slid into the water, making for the creature’s leg with patient, sightless intent.

“If you meet another,” Halloway went on, “do not begin by asking whether it was a person. Begin by asking what it has spare. Extra joints. Peeled ribs. Skin that ripples against gravity. Black fluid that strings when lifted. Smell of pond silt, copper, and sweet rot under it. The mouth will be late. The shoulders are early. The hands decide. The under-skin decides whether there is anything left to save.”

Her blade cleared the leather again, not drawn, only loosened, the steel whispering against its fittings.

“Aim where the newest bone meets the oldest meat. There the colony is still paying attention. Cut the thread-cluster at the shoulder branch and the arm becomes decoration. Pierce the rib chamber and you may disturb the brood, which is worse than disturbing the body, because disturbed brood does not care whose lungs it fills.”

The creature’s head shifted. Not up. Not yet. Only a small rotation beneath the water, the jaw slits angling toward the stair.
