Halloway watched it with the weary satisfaction of a woman confirming a bad diagnosis.

“Plainly,” she said, “someone wore this shape recently enough to have a name. Something entered through a wound or a mouthful of wrong water. It did not kill him. Killing is wasteful. It colonised him. It softened the bindings, split the levers, opened the storehouse, and filled the cavity with its young. It kept the heart beating because the heart is a servant, not a master. It kept the lungs drawing because the lungs move heat, and heat is what the threads want.”

The ripple under the skin ran once more toward the opened ribs, stopped, then returned to the shoulder.

“Now it is learning to stand.”

Halloway looked from the shoulder to the waterline, measuring the distance with her eyes the way a surgeon measures a cut.

“That is the detail. Not poetry. Not mercy. A body turned into furniture for hungry things. If you want grief, save it for daylight. If you want to live long enough to grieve properly, watch the shoulder joint. When it lifts, tell me whether the elbow leads or the fingers lead. If the fingers lead, it is reaching for something specific. If the elbow leads, it is only practising balance.”

The mouth-seam parted.

Not wide. Not enough to count teeth. Just a black slit between swollen lips, weeping dark water that did not behave like water. It hung at the corners in strings, then fell back toward the ribs as if the creature were tasting the air and finding it insufficient.

Halloway’s voice dropped to a near-whisper, clinical and cold.

“There. It has chosen a door. Enough lecturing. Watch the shoulder.”

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: *I keep the lamp low, my arm already starting to tremble.* "Elbow," I say, watching the joint shift under the skin. "It's learning the weight of the water."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway filed the report where she kept the useful facts: behind the teeth, in front of the panic.

“Elbow leads, it is calibrating,” she said. “Fingers lead when it has chosen something to pull apart. Keep the light on the shoulder. Not the face. The face is for liars and mourners.”

The dark string at the corners of the mouth thickened, then drew back inside rather than falling. Halloway watched it with the narrowed attention of a woman who had seen too many wounds pretend to be simple.

“That is not saliva,” she said. “That is tasting. It is sampling the air for heat, salt, fear-chemistry. If it finds enough of us in one breath, it will stop rehearsing.”

The elbow under the water shifted again. The folded arm did not lift so much as redistribute itself, the too-long joints finding a new angle against the cellar floor. The lamp’s glow jumped across the ripples as the motion changed the water’s surface.

Halloway took one more step down.

This time the cold came over the sole of her boot and into the stair with it. She did not hurry. Hurry made noise, and noise made targets.

“Watch the fork of the shoulder,” she said. “Where the arm splits. That is where the brood is still laying cable. Cut there and the limb forgets it has orders. Cut deeper and you open the chamber. Open the chamber and everything inside gets introduced to your lungs.”

Her blade cleared the leather fully. Short steel, nicked at the spine, honest at the edge. She laid the tip against the wax-pale skin above the creature’s shoulder branch, feeling for the give beneath it: not fat, not muscle, not the clean resistance of healthy fascia. Something layered. Something nesting.

The hooked wire went in beside the blade, sliding under a flap of loosened skin. It came up carrying a knot of black threads no thicker than horsehair, all of them twisting toward the warmth of the lamp before remembering their owner.

Halloway flicked them aside without ceremony.

“Hello,” she said, to nothing in particular. “Still shy.”

Then she cut.

The stroke was short, shallow, and exact: a slice through the thread-cluster where the newest bone met the oldest meat. Not deep enough to breach the rib chamber. Not gentle enough to be polite.

The creature’s elbow snapped straight.

Water burst outward in a low, heavy wave. The pinned arm dragged free of its own torso with a sound like a boot pulled from mud, and the folded body rocked once against the cellar floor. The mouth opened.

Not wide.

Wide enough.

Halloway counted without meaning to, the way a soldier counts gunshots and a doctor counts breaths.

“Four. Six. Eight. Ten—”

The jaw hitched, the inner hinges shifting, and more pale points showed behind the first row.

“—twelve. Odd.” Her voice stayed flat. “Growth. Not design. And too many for a rescue.”

The threads under the skin surged toward the cut at the shoulder, not bleeding, not recoiling in pain, simply redirecting. The wound did not weep red. It wept black, stringy, and the strands reached for the blade’s edge as if testing whether steel was food or obstacle.

Halloway withdrew the knife and wiped it once on her coat.

“There,” she said. “It has felt its own arm. First lesson is usually humiliation.”

The creature’s head turned farther now, the two dark slits above the jaw angling toward the stair. The shoulders lifted beneath the water, not rising like a man from a chair, but unfolding like a trap with the catch released. The rib cage flexed outward, and the black water inside the opened bones sloshed with a thick, living rhythm.

Halloway planted her feet in the shallows and kept the blade low.

“Elbow is free. Wrist will follow. When the fingers spread, it is no longer balancing. It is reaching.” She nodded once, sharply, toward the fork of the shoulder. “Iron goes there if you have it. Through the split, not the chest. If you do not have iron, say so now and I will make do with temper and poor choices.”

The mouth opened another fraction. Dark water ran from the corners in strings, then reversed, crawling back toward the ribs as if the creature were swallowing its own reflection.

Halloway’s eyes narrowed.

“It is not drinking,” she said. “It is watering the brood.”

The ripple under the skin ran fast this time, from the shoulder to the hips, then back. The legs beneath the water shifted, joints unlocking in sequence. The cellar floor gave a faint, wet scrape.

Something was preparing to stand.

Halloway did not step back. Backwards was for stairs, and stairs were for people who intended to live long enough to use them.

“Shoulder,” she said, quieter now. “Watch the shoulder. When it lifts, tell me if the other arm comes with it.”

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: She starts cutting and I hold the lamp steady and don't look away. "Keep describing it," I tell her. "Everything -- what's underneath, what it smells like, how far it got. Don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway did not tell him to be quiet. Words, used properly, were another instrument. They kept the hands honest and the mind out of the creature’s mouth.

“You want everything,” she said. “Everything is mostly plumbing and spoilage. Try not to learn it romantically.”

She set the blade at the shoulder branch and opened the skin again, shallow and controlled. The cut parted with a soft, wet sound. No red welled up. Black beads formed along the edges, then drew into threads.

“Underneath,” she said, lifting the flap with the hook, “the body has been stripped to its engineering. Fascia first. It should be a sheet. Here it is a net. The threads have replaced most of it. Tendons remain, but they are sleeved. Muscle is not digested; it is warehoused. See the pale grains? Larval sacs. Each one holds a knot of the colony. Mature sacs do not crawl. They anchor.”

The elbow under the water jerked. Halloway kept the blade beside the motion.

“The humerus is divided at mid-shaft. New bone caps, still cartilaginous. That gives the limb a hinge where a man has none. Scapula has been perforated and reset forward. Three accessory sockets. It can brace sideways, climb downward, or fold through a space narrower than its shoulders. The ribs were pried outward from inside. Not broken. Spread. The intercostal muscles have been threaded to hold the cage open. The pleural cavity is no longer a lung space. It is a chamber.”

She touched the wire to the gap. Black water slid over the hook, thick as oil.

“Smell,” she said. “Correctly. Pond silt. Copper. Sweet rot under it, the kind that starts in fruit left too long in a closed room. Ammonia. Wet wool. Yeast. When the threads break, it sharpens—hot metal, like a coin held in the mouth during a storm. If you smell that on a living person, they are already part of the cellar.”

The mouth opened another fraction. Halloway did not admire it.

“How far it got. Entry through a wound or mucous membrane. Probably hand or face. It avoided blood at first. Blood alarms the body and carries heat too fast. It used fascia, lymph, nerve sheaths. It reached the spinal canal and took the brainstem, not the cortex. The man is not driving. The brainstem is being borrowed to keep the pumps running. What it took: autonomy, pain modulation, speech, memory. What it left: heartbeat, breath, swallow, and enough spinal reflex to make the meat useful. Heart encased in thread-net. Lungs still inflate, but the pleura is lined. Diaphragm is a bellows for warmth and spores. Liver tapped for nutrients. Kidneys for mineral. Gut still attached, but it is processing reserve, not meal. Fat, glycogen, some muscle. Bones are being resorbed and rebuilt where the colony needs leverage.”

A sac bulged beneath the cut, pale and taut, with something curled inside.

“That is a brood unit. Not a maggot. Not a worm. A node. Cut one free and it seeks warmth. Cut the cluster and the limb loses orders. Open the chest and the nodes get air, heat, and your face.”

The second arm shifted under the water, dragging against the floor.

Halloway saw the movement and named it without drama.

“Contralateral bracing. It has crossed the midline. The colony is coordinating both sides. Standing is minutes, not hours.”

The first cut began to close. Threads pulled the skin edges together like coarse sutures. Halloway stabbed once through the knot, severing them. The creature’s jaw widened, and a sound came from the rib chamber: a wet, multi-toned click, as if many small mouths were testing the air.

“Thirteen teeth visible,” she said. “Odd. Growth. Still not a man with a bad mouth. Still a house with a leak.”

The smell thickened, hot and mineral.

“If you cannot open another one, read the outside. Skin too smooth, too damp, no proper rigor. Joints bending away from load. Ribs flared. Shoulders moving before the head. Mouth late. Black string from wounds. Water that ripples toward the same place twice. And the smell: cellar, copper, sweet rot, yeast. If all four are present, do not ask whether it was someone. Ask where it can reach.”

The thing lifted.

It came up on the new shoulder braces first, torso rising from the water in a slow, wrong unfolding. The rib cage opened fully above the surface. Inside, black fluid swirled around pale sacs, pulsing in staggered sequence. The pinned leg dragged free, then found the cellar floor.

Halloway stepped back one pace, enough to keep her boots out of the deepest water, and set the blade across her forearm.

“That is how far it got,” she said. “To standing. To targeting. To being less corpse and more nest with leverage.”

Its fingers spread.

Halloway’s voice went flat and final.

“Fingers lead. It has chosen something specific. The split at the shoulder is still soft. Iron there, if there is iron. If not, take the neck at the collarbone and do not let it close distance. And when it screams like the man it used to be—” A dry pause. “That is not a soul asking for help. That is a lure with a throat.”

The creature’s head turned toward the light.

Halloway did not look at the face. She looked at the shoulder branch, at the threads knitting and pulling beneath the wax-pale skin.

“Now,” she said. “Tell me what moves first.”

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: *I swallow hard, my knuckles white around the lamp.* "The left shoulder. It's hitching higher than the right. The threads there are... bunching."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway took the observation and turned it into mechanics.

“Left shoulder high, threads bunching,” she said. “That is not balance. That is a cocked arm.”

The light showed the place she meant: beneath the waterline, the left shoulder had risen out of alignment with the right, dragging the skin into a tent of pale ridges. Dark cables gathered at the fork where the humerus split, knotting themselves into a thick rope of movement. It did not look like a joint preparing to support weight. It looked like a winch taking strain.

“Traffic,” Halloway said. “The colony is moving mass to the pivot. If it were only standing, the threads would spread. Spread means distribution. Bunched means choice.” She kept her eyes on the knot, not the face. “It has chosen the left arm to do the talking.”

The rib chamber clicked again, lower this time, a wet sound with too many mouths in it. The smell sharpened: pond silt, copper, yeast, and beneath that the hot-penny stink of disturbed thread.

Halloway stepped into the shallow water without hurrying. Cold climbed her boots, but she planted her feet wide, weight over the blades, blade low.

“Listen,” she said. “A normal shoulder lifts a man. This one lifts a lever. The scapula has been pulled forward and seated in an accessory groove you can feel with a hook. See the way the skin puckers toward the collarbone? That is not muscle. That is a cable sleeve. Cut the sleeve and the arm loses its orders. Cut too deep and you open the relay box. Then the brood gets an introduction.”

She put the hooked wire into the bunching flesh at the left shoulder, not stabbing, only lifting. The skin came up with almost no resistance, loosened from below. Under it, the threads writhed in a dense black plait, each strand anchored to pale sacs that pulsed once, twice, out of rhythm with the heart.

“There,” Halloway said. “Node cluster. Six, maybe eight mature sacs at the joint. They are holding the new bone cap in place while the colony learns the swing. That is why it hitches high. It is not strong yet. It is enthusiastic.”

The creature’s mouth opened a little farther. Dark water strung from the swollen lips, then drew back toward the throat as if recalled by a leash.

Halloway’s blade went in short and shallow along the top of the thread knot. She did not hack. Hacking was for doors and men who had never paid for a funeral. She separated the cable from the bone spur with three precise strokes, each one releasing a thin spray of black fluid that hissed where it met the water.

The left arm snapped outward.

Not toward Halloway. Toward the light.

The fingers, too long and doubled at the wrong places, spread wide and scraped against the stair-edge with a sound like nails finding purchase on a coffin lid. Water ran off them in sheets. The bunching at the shoulder collapsed into a ragged furrow, the cut threads curling away from the blade as if startled by their own freedom.

“Good,” Halloway said, though nothing about it was good. “It reaches for heat before flesh. That means the brood is still reading the room. It has not learned manners.”

The creature rocked on its right side, the undamaged shoulder bearing the sudden shift. The rib cage flexed, and inside the opened chamber the black fluid sloshed around the pale sacs in a slow, sick wave. One sac near the sternum bulged, then settled, as if something within had turned over.

Halloway withdrew the wire and reset her blade across her forearm.

“Left cable cut. The arm is semi-independent now. It will still claw, still hook, still try to drag whatever is closest into the water. But the signal from the trunk is delayed. Delay is all we get.” She glanced at the right shoulder, then back to the torn left fork. “The right side will compensate. Watch the collarbone. If the right shoulder drops, it is bracing. If the right hand crosses in front of the chest, it is reaching across to grab what the left missed.”

The creature made a sound then: not a scream, not yet. A cluster of small clicks rose from the rib chamber, synchronized for half a beat, then broke apart into wet, arrhythmic chattering. The mouth-seam twitched, and the uneven teeth showed again—thirteen, maybe fourteen, the count blurring because the jaw hinges were moving independently.

“Still odd,” Halloway said. “Still growth. It is improvising a face because it thinks a face will help.” Her tone carried the dry fatigue of a woman who had seen predators learn smiles and men learn too late. “Don’t let it fool you. Faces are for communication. This is only advertising.”

She took one careful step closer, boot grinding faintly on the cellar floor beneath the water. The cold had reached her knees now, but she kept her center low and the blade angled toward the shoulder branch, not the throat.

“Here is what is underneath, since you wanted no omissions,” she said, speaking over the creature’s clicking as if dictating a ledger. “At the left fork, the colony has built a temporary joint out of thread and resorbed bone. The original humerus is split, the caps soft, the periosteum lifted. Under the skin, the fascial net has been replaced by a cable system. Cut one cable, the limb hesitates. Cut the main cluster, the limb becomes decoration. The sacs at the shoulder are not eggs yet. They are growth nodes: nutrient storage, nerve relay, and repair material in one package. Break them into open air and they will seek the nearest warm lining. Eyes, nostrils, mouth, fresh wound. Do not let them dry. Do not let them crowd.”

The left arm jerked again, fingers flexing without direction. The bunching threads at the cut began to knit, slowly at first, then with more purpose, pulling black strands across the wound like worms building a bridge.

Halloway saw it and did not allow surprise.

“Repair response,” she said. “It is learning that damage costs it reach. Next time it will keep the cluster deeper or shield it with the rib flap. That means the next cut will be less satisfying and more necessary.”

She hooked the wire under the edge of the peeled rib nearest the left shoulder, testing the hinge. The bone gave with a slick, internal creak. Not broken. Loosened.

“If I open the cage,” she said, more to herself than to anyone, “the brood gets air. If I do not, the shoulder gets strong. Both choices have teeth.”

The creature’s head rotated farther toward the light. The two dark slits above the jaw were no longer vacant; they tracked with the dull patience of things that did not need eyes to find warmth. The mouth wept a thin string of black fluid, and the fluid moved against gravity, drawing back toward the rib chamber.

“Watering the brood again,” Halloway murmured. “It is using its own cavity as a reservoir. Smart. Disgusting. Common among nest-builders.”

She squared her stance.

“New problem,” she said. “The left arm is damaged but not discarded. The right is still whole. It will try a two-stage approach: left feint, right capture. If the left hand touches the stair first, it is testing traction. If the right hand follows before the torso turns, it has committed.”

Her blade tapped once against the hooked wire, a small, clear sound in the cellar dark.

“When it comes, do not give it height. Keep the light at shoulder level, not above. Above invites a reach. Shoulder level forces it to choose between your face and its own balance.” She paused, eyes fixed on the right collarbone. “And if the mouth opens wide enough to count again, tell me the number. Even means it has finished planning. Odd means it is still growing. Growing things make mistakes. Planned things make widows.”

The creature shifted its weight. Water streamed off its unfolded torso in dark ribbons. The left shoulder sagged where Halloway had cut, but the right rose, the threads beneath the skin tightening into a clean, terrible line.

Halloway did not retreat.

“Right shoulder lifting,” she said quietly. “It has decided the left is bait.” The blade came up, edge catching the lamplight in a thin, honest gleam. “Then we let it bite down on nothing.”

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I sit on the cellar steps afterwards with the lamp in my hands. "Finish it," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full.)

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway heard the order from the dry stone above her and did not mistake it for courage. Courage was what men called duty when it had not yet been billed.

“Finish it,” she said. “Comfortable phrase. Holds no water.”

The creature had nearly risen. The right shoulder stood higher than the left, the skin over it drawn into a clean, terrible ridge where the threads had braided themselves into a cable. The left arm, half-cut and still twitching, lay across the water with the useless confidence of a limb that had been promised work. The rib cage opened above the surface like a cabinet displayed for buyers. Inside, black fluid moved in slow, deliberate circles around pale sacs.

Halloway did not look at the face. Faces asked for sympathy, and sympathy made hands slow.

She stepped into the deeper water.

Cold closed over her boots, her ankles, the lower calves. It was honest cold, cellar cold, the sort that told a woman where she stood and how long she had before her legs began lying to her. She kept her centre low, blade angled along her forearm, hooked wire in the other hand.

“Right,” she said, mostly to the thing. “You’ve had your lesson. Let’s see if you learned it.”

The mouth opened farther.

Not wide. Wide enough.

Dark water strung from the swollen lips, then crawled back toward the throat. The jaw hinges shifted independently, one side lifting a fraction before the other, as if the colony were testing which hinge it preferred. Halloway counted without admiration.

“One, three, five, seven—”

The teeth were pale, uneven, set in gums that had once belonged to a man who brushed them or did not, depending on his habits and his hope of living long enough to matter.

“—nine, eleven, thirteen, fifteen.” She withdrew the wire from the shoulder knot with a small, practical shake. “Odd. Still growing. Still rude.”

The creature’s left hand jerked.

Not toward Halloway.

Toward the light.

The too-long fingers spread on the stair-edge below the lamp, scraping stone with a sound like nails being taught a new trade. Water ran off them in thin sheets. The bunching threads at the cut shoulder tried to knit, black strands reaching across the wound with the patient stupidity of roots finding manure.

Halloway moved before the arm could decide whether it wanted heat or flesh.

She put the hooked wire into the right shoulder not with a thrust but with the flat patience of a woman opening a stuck drawer. The hook found the accessory groove behind the collarbone, the false socket the colony had carved for leverage. She leaned back.

The scapula came forward with a sound like a knuckle cracked in cold tallow.

The creature folded sideways.

Water burst outward in a low, heavy wave. The right arm lost its brace and swung, not in pain—pain was a language the colony had stopped speaking—but in correction. Halloway stayed inside the swing. Outside it, the arm would have found the stairs. Inside it, it found only her blade.

She cut.

Short strokes. Not hacking. Hacking was for doors and men who had never paid for a funeral. She separated the main cable from the bone spur with three precise strokes, each one releasing a thin spray of black fluid that hissed where it met the water. The threads curled away from the steel, then tried to return, then thought better of it.

The right arm went slack.

“Good,” Halloway said. “Now you have two disappointing limbs and one opinion.”

The jaw snapped.

It came down where her shoulder had been a half-second earlier. Halloway had moved because thirty years had taught her that predators aimed at the story they wanted, not the body they had. The teeth closed on water and the echo of a woman who had not been there.

The rib chamber clicked.

Not one mouth. Many.

The sound rose from the opened cage, wet and arrhythmic, like small bones learning speech from the wrong end. The pale sacs inside pulsed in staggered sequence. One near the sternum bulged, then settled. Another tightened into a knot and released.

Halloway’s expression did not change.

“Still furnishing,” she said. “No taste.”

The left hand dragged upward, fingers hooking the stair-edge again. The body rocked, trying to convert damage into leverage. The legs beneath the water shifted, joints unlocking in sequence. The cellar floor scraped.

It was still trying to stand.

Halloway stepped onto the creature’s thigh.

Not gracefully. Grace was for women with fewer enemies and better shoes. She put one boot on the bent knee, the other on the outer shelf of the ribs—careful of the chamber, careful of the gap—and used the height to get behind the right shoulder. The water pulled at her boots like cold hands. The creature’s skin under her foot was slick, wax-pale, and warm in the wrong places.

Nest-warm.

Not blood-warm.

She found the nape with her free hand. The head was useless already, the brainstem relay half-cut, but the colony kept the skull attached because heads contained senses and senses contained opportunities. Beneath the skin at the base of the skull, the threads made a braid around the first vertebra. That braid was the last courtesy the colony paid to the man’s own nervous system: it let the head hang, blink, and scream.

Halloway slid the blade under the braid and lifted.

The head went slack.

The body did not.

“Of course not,” she said. “You were never a body. You were a committee.”

She dropped from the shoulder to the water beside the creature’s flank, keeping the blade low. The left arm still twitched, fingers flexing without direction. The right hung loose, the cut cables drifting like seaweed in a current. The rib cage remained open, black fluid sloshing inside with a thick, living rhythm.

Now the chamber.

Halloway hooked the lower edge of the peeled ribs with the wire. The bones gave with a slick, internal creak. Not broken. Spread. The intercostal muscles had been threaded to hold the cage open, each strand anchored to pale sacs along the inner wall. She pulled outward, not enough to tear the chest wide, only enough to make a door.

The smell changed.

Pond silt. Copper. Yeast. Sweet rot. Beneath it, the hot-penny stink of disturbed thread.

Halloway turned her face aside and breathed through her mouth.

“If you value the lining of your lungs,” she said, voice flat, “stand upwind.”

She put the blade into the chamber.

Not deep. Deep was for men who liked surprises. She laid the edge flat inside the opened cage and raked across the lining, severing the supply threads that fed each node. The sacs bucked. Black fluid ran over the blade in strings. One pale knot near the sternum burst with a sound like a green walnut under a boot, and from it spilled a cluster of smaller threads, writhing, blind, seeking warmth.

Halloway stamped them into the water.

They slowed in the cold, then turned toward the creature’s leg.

“Not today,” she said.

She worked around the chamber with methodical hatred. Not rage. Rage made cuts sloppy. She severed the anchoring threads at the left rib fan, then the right. She crushed the mature sacs along the inner wall with the pommel of the blade when the edge would not reach without opening the chest further. Each one yielded a thick, black bead that floated for a moment, then sank.

The heart remained.

It sat behind the sternum, wrapped in a net of black fibre, beating in the wrong rhythm. Too fast. Too patient. The colony had kept it because the heart carried food, heat, and excuse. Halloway found the great vessels where they entered the thread-knot, the place where the man’s own plumbing had been hijacked into service.

She cut the net.

The heart gave one last useful contraction.

Halloway drove the blade through the base of the organ and twisted once.

The beat stopped.

The rib chamber went still.

For three seconds, nothing moved.

Then the threads under the skin began to fail.

Not dramatically. Not all at once. They loosened. The dense plait at the left shoulder unravelled into separate strands, each strand losing its reason. The black cables along the arms drifted free. The sacs inside the opened cage collapsed into pale, wet grains. The mouth, which had been rehearsing expression, fell slack.

Halloway did not sheathe the blade.

She waited.

The water gave one small lap against the cellar wall. Ordinary water. Dead water. No ripple travelled beneath the skin. No thread turned toward the light. The creature’s head lolled against the opened ribs with the perfect indifference of meat.

“Still not beautiful,” Halloway murmured. “Hungry, though. That we knew.”

She hooked the wire under the creature’s jaw and lifted the face clear of the water.

The features were ruined, but not beyond reading. Swelling had erased the nose, drawn the lips back, pushed the eyes into dark slits. The skin had the colour of candle wax left too near a fire. Beneath the jaw, the throat showed the old landmarks: hyoid, thyroid cartilage, the ghost of a man’s voice box. Halloway pressed the wire against the side of the neck and felt for the pulse that was not there.

None.

She moved to the hands.

The left hand had been a worker’s hand before the colony edited it. Callus across the palm. Short, ragged nails. The fingers were too long now, doubled at wrong joints, but the nail beds still told the older story. The right hand had an old break at the ring finger, set badly and healed thick. A band of cheap gold rode loose on the fourth finger, dented but not removed.

Halloway looked at it for one measured second.

“Married,” she said. “Or vain enough to wear metal into a cellar.”

She released the hand and let it fall back into the water. Sentiment was a knife with the edge turned inward. She had carried enough of those in thirty years to know how they cut.

The mouth still held the truth, if one knew how to ask.

Halloway inserted the wire between the jaws and eased them apart. The hinges resisted, then gave. The teeth showed in uneven rows. She counted again, slower.

Human canines, worn flat. A capped molar, tin bright under the filth. One incisor chipped old enough to have hurt. Behind the natural teeth, the colony had pushed extra points through the gums, pale and soft-rooted, not designed so much as encouraged.

“Seventeen total,” she said. “Thirteen human, four intruders. Odd count. Growth. No plan worth the name.”

She withdrew the wire and wiped it along the heel of her boot. The black thread clinging to the hook detached, slid into the water, and made for the creature’s leg with the last, pointless patience of a thing that had forgotten its master.

Halloway watched it go.

Then she put the blade through it.

The thread burst into a smear of oily darkness.

“Housekeeping,” she said.

She checked the rest of the body with the efficient contempt of a woman reading a bad ledger. The shoulders: split, capped, reinforced. The humeri divided at mid-shaft. The scapulae perforated and reset forward. The ribs pried outward from inside, the intercostal spaces threaded open. The pleural cavity no longer a lung space. A chamber. A nursery. A larder. The liver tapped for nutrients. The kidneys for mineral. The gut still attached, processing reserve rather than meal. Fat, glycogen, some muscle. Bones resorbed and rebuilt where the colony needed leverage.

The brainstem had been borrowed. The cortex composted.

Halloway nodded once, as if confirming a diagnosis she had already made in the stairwell.

“Someone wore this shape recently enough to have a name,” she said. “Something entered through a wound or a mouthful of wrong water. It colonised him. It softened the bindings, split the levers, opened the storehouse, and filled the cavity with its young. It kept the heart beating because the heart is a servant, not a master. It kept the lungs drawing because the lungs move heat, and heat is what the threads want.”

She looked at the opened rib chamber, at the pale grains floating in black fluid.

“Then it learned to stand.”

The cellar was quiet except for water.

Halloway climbed down from the creature’s flank and back to the stair, each step careful, each boot grinding faintly on the wet stone. The cold had soaked through her trousers and settled into her knees. She ignored it. Knees were negotiable. Dead things were not.

At the upper step, she set the blade against her hip and did not sheathe it. The steel was blackened with thread-fluid, and the edge still carried a faint, greasy shine. She tested it with her thumb. It took a shaving of skin without complaint.

“Good,” she said. “You behaved.”

She looked back into the cellar.

The body lay half-folded in the water, mouth open, ribs spread, head lolling. Without the colony’s coordination, it was only meat again. Worse than meat. Meat did not have spare joints.

Halloway began the boring part.

She took a length of cord from her belt, looped it around the creature’s left wrist, and hauled the arm clear of the stair-edge. The fingers dragged over stone, then hung limp. She tied the cord to the iron ring set in the wall above the waterline. Not to secure the body. To keep it from drifting into the steps and teaching the wood bad habits.

Then she checked the waterline.

The cellar had a drain at the far corner, half-submerged, crusted with silt. Halloway waded to it, blade low, and swept the hook through the grate. Black fluid eddied. Nothing moved against the current.

“No second tenant,” she said. “Lucky.”

Luck was a word hunters used when preparation had finished its work.

She returned to the body and searched the remains with the same clinical patience she brought to a wound. Shreds of canvas trousers. A belt with a brass hook. A coin worn thin in one pocket, the date illegible, the metal green with cellar damp. On the other side, a folded square of oilcloth, stiff with grime. Halloway opened it with the tip of the blade.

A man’s photograph, water-spotted. Face blurred, but the stance was ordinary. Shoulders squared. Chin lifted. The sort of pose men chose when they expected to live long enough to be vain about it.

Halloway looked at it for one second longer than necessary.

Then she folded the oilcloth and tucked it into her coat.

“Name later,” she said. “First, fire.”

She went back to the stair and gathered the tools that mattered: the hooked wire, the short blade, a tin of salt from the inner pocket, a stoppered vial of lamp oil she kept for emergencies and bad lighting. She poured a thin line of oil around the creature’s opened rib chamber, not over the body. Over the chamber. The black fluid inside resisted the oil at first, then accepted it with a slick, greedy sheen.

Halloway stepped back.

She did not strike a light yet. Light came after certainty.

“Now,” she said, voice flat and practical, “we burn the house down.”

She tossed the salt into the water first. It spread in a white film, dulling the black threads that still drifted near the drain. Then she touched flame to the oil line.

The cellar took the fire the way cellars do: reluctantly, then all at once.

Blue light crawled along the oil, found the chamber, and went up. The rib cage burned from the inside. Pale sacs popped in quick, wet succession. Black fluid boiled and steamed. The body arched once—not life, not protest, only gas expanding in sealed places—and then settled.

Halloway watched it burn with the steady attention of a woman counting coins.

When the flames died to a low, stinking hiss, she waited another ten seconds. Then twenty. Then she stepped forward with the hook and broke the charred rib cage open.

Inside, nothing moved.

The threads had curled into black beads. The sacs had burst into ash and grease. The heart was a lump of cooked meat wrapped in brittle fibre. Halloway stirred the remains with the hook, turning over fragments of bone, tooth, and cloth. She found three human teeth intact, one tin cap melted to a grey blister, and the gold band warped but whole.

She collected them in a linen square from her pocket.

“Evidence,” she said. “Also proof that people can be stupid enough to wear metal into a cellar.”

The smell was atrocious. Burned silt. Hot copper. Sweet rot turned acrid. Wet wool scorched. Halloway breathed through her mouth and kept working.

She checked the shoulders again. The new bone caps had cracked in the fire, exposing the soft centres. The accessory sockets were empty. The cable knots had burned to charcoal. She broke one open with the blade and found no movement inside.

“Colony dead,” she said. “Host dead. Chamber dead. Drain clear.”

She looked at the water.

It was still.

Not peaceful. Still. The difference mattered.

Halloway sheathed the blade at last. The steel made a small, honest sound against leather. She wrung the hem of her coat, sending dark water splashing onto the stair. Then she took the tin of salt and scattered a line across the top step, not for superstition, but because salt slowed what was left and reminded living things where the boundary was.

“Right,” she said. “That is the cellar finished.”

She turned toward the stairs.

The body burned in the water behind her, black and steaming, the opened ribs collapsed inward like a house after the roof has been taken. The cord at the wrist held. The drain gave up its last thin trickle. The lamp-light from above made a small, stubborn island on the wet stone.

Halloway climbed one step, then stopped.

Not because she was tired. Because she heard it.

A lap of water.

Not from the burning body.

From the far corner, beyond the drain.

Halloway’s hand went back to her blade.

“There,” she said quietly. “Of course there.”

She did not go closer. Not yet. She stood on the damp stair, water dripping from her coat, and listened to the cellar breathe.

The sound came again. Small. Obscene. Patient.

Something in the far water had not been in the chamber.

Halloway’s mouth tightened.

“Finish it,” she repeated, grimly amused. “Spoken like a man who has never had a cellar finish him first.”

She drew the blade.

“New rule,” she said. “The first house is always a warning. The second house is the neighbourhood.”

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: *I grab a loose brick from the crumbling wall and stand, my legs shaking.* "Two?" I whisper. "It had a *second*?"

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway heard the whisper and the small, brittle courage underneath it. She did not look at the man on the stairs. Looking at frightened men made them more frightened, and frightened men made mistakes, and mistakes in cellars had a way of echoing upward as funerals.

“Two,” she said, “is a hopeful number. One is an accident. Two is a relationship. Three is a policy.”

The burning body gave a wet pop from the far end of the cellar. The sound had already begun to seem less like death and more like industry. Halloway kept her eyes on the water beyond the firelight, where the drain sat half-choked with silt and age.

“That is not the corpse,” she went on. “The corpse is occupied. Corpses, when treated properly, develop manners. That is something else using the plumbing as a invitation.”

The lap came again.

Closer this time.

Not the broad, heavy displacement of a full-grown host. Something lighter. Something that knew how to travel narrow places.

Halloway’s hand tightened on the hooked wire. The blade at her forearm was still slick with black thread-fluid, and the edge had taken on the dull, greasy shine of steel that had recently been rude to living things.

“If that brick leaves your hand before you know what you are striking,” she said, without turning, “you have traded a wall for a souvenir. Keep it. If something clears the water, hit the shoulder fork. Not the head. Heads are dramatic. Shoulders are structural.”

She took one step down into the flooded stair.

The water had changed since the first cut. It was colder in places and warmer in others, the warmth coming off the burning chamber in thin, dishonest waves. The smell had deepened too: pond silt, copper, yeast, sweet rot, and above it all the hot-penny sting of disturbed thread. Halloway breathed through her mouth and kept moving.

At the far corner, the drain grate was old iron, rusted to the colour of dried blood and crusted with mineral crust. A thread lay across the bars.

Black. Glossy. Thicker than the ones from the first body.

It moved with the slow confidence of a worm that had already chosen a direction.

Halloway raised the hooked wire and touched the thread.

It recoiled.

Not violently. Not like a thing startled. Like a thing withdrawing a feeler from a surface it did not yet trust.

“Polite,” she murmured. “Too polite.”

Then the drain gave up its second tenant.

It came up sideways first.

Not a head. Not a hand. A shoulder.

Small, wrong, and lifting a foreleg that bent in two places before the water shed from its fur.

The shape that followed was dog-sized, though the colony had done what colonies do: it had edited the useful parts and discarded the unnecessary ones. The fur was patchy, brown and grey, plastered down with black fluid. One ear was gone, chewed or shed; the other stood stiff and wet, trembling with a rhythm that had nothing to do with hearing. Beneath the hide, the anatomy had been revised. The radius and ulna had split at the lower foreleg and capped with soft new knobs. The ribs on one side had peeled outward just enough to make a pocket, a dark hollow where a lung should have whispered. Inside the pocket, pale sacs pulsed in staggered sequence.

It had a collar.

Brass tag. Green with verdigris.

Halloway noted it the way she noted everything else: as fact, not feeling.

“Canine,” she said. “Probably a rat-catcher. Useful animal. Poor choice of employer.”

The head came last.

The muzzle was too long in the middle, as if the bones had been stretched and reset while the dog was still warm enough to complain. The jaw hinged in three places. The lips had drawn back from teeth that were partly dog, partly intruder: pointed carnassials at the sides, blunt human premolars pushed up through the gums in the rear, and at the front four pale spikes that had never belonged to any honest mouth.

It clicked.

Not one sound. Many.

The noise rose from the opened rib pocket and the throat at once, wet and arrhythmic, like small bones learning speech from the wrong end.

Halloway’s expression did not change.

“There,” she said. “Not a second person. A second vehicle. Smaller, faster, less sentimental about roads.”

The creature’s good shoulder hitched.

The threads beneath its skin bunched at the fork, dark cables gathering mass to the pivot. The cut left foreleg dragged uselessly for one beat, then found purchase on the slick brick lip of the drain. The right foreleg lifted. The hind legs shifted under the water, joints unlocking in sequence.

It did not leap like a dog.

It unfolded like a trap.

Halloway moved before it chose between her throat and the stair.

She put the hooked wire into the loose flap of skin above the right shoulder and dragged sideways. The animal’s balance came apart with a wet crack. It twisted, jaws snapping at the air where her forearm had been, and the rib pocket flexed open another fraction. Black fluid sloshed inside. One of the pale sacs bulged toward the gap, seeking air, heat, opportunity.

“No introductions,” Halloway said.

The blade went in short and shallow along the thread-cluster at the shoulder fork.

Three strokes.

Not hacking. Hacking was for doors and men who had never paid for a funeral.

The first stroke parted the cable sleeve. The second separated the new bone cap from the old meat. The third cut the main relay knot beneath the scapula. Black fluid sprayed in thin, hissing lines. The threads curled away from the steel, then tried to return, then thought better of it.

The right foreleg went slack.

The creature compensated by throwing its weight forward. Its jaws closed on the hooked wire.

Halloway let it have the wire.

She stepped inside the lunge, boot grinding on the cellar floor beneath the water, and drove the pommel of the blade into the opened rib pocket. The impact was soft and wrong, like striking a sack of wet grain. One sac burst. Another collapsed. The clicking in its throat broke into a shuddering, multi-toned wheeze.

The head still worked.

That was the nuisance of colonies: they kept useless ornaments attached long after the tenant had stopped paying rent.

The dog-thing twisted, human teeth scraping against the wire, intruder spikes catching the firelight. Its remaining good leg hooked toward Halloway’s boot. She withdrew the wire with a jerk, letting the jaw snap shut on black water, and put the blade behind the ear.

Not the skull. The nape.

The edge found the braid of threads around the first vertebra and severed it.

The head went slack.

The body did not.

“Of course not,” Halloway said. “Committees rarely resign all at once.”

She dropped to one knee in the shallows, keeping her centre low, and finished the work with the boring thoroughness of a woman who had buried better men than this for guessing wrong in basements. She cut the remaining shoulder cables. She crushed the mature sacs along the inner wall of the rib pocket with the pommel, each one yielding a thick black bead that floated for a moment, then sank. She opened the jaw with the hook and counted the teeth once, without interest.

“Nine intruders. Eleven native. Odd. Still growing. Still rude.”

Then she found the mail.

It was lodged in the back of the throat, wrapped in a knot of thread fine as hair: a human molar, capped in tin, the metal dulled by cellar damp. The tooth had been pulled free cleanly, not chewed. Carried.

Halloway lifted it with the hook and held it in the firelight.

“Well,” she said. “That explains the errand.”

The first body had not been alone. It had not even been self-contained. Colonies shed nodes when the host was damaged, and nodes sought the nearest warm lining, the smallest available transport, the cheapest available meat. A dog had been useful once. Now it was a courier with spare joints and a grudge against anatomy.

She turned the creature over with the wire.

The collar tag caught the light. The engraving was worn, but not beyond reading. A name. A address. A telephone number in the old style, digits stamped deep enough to survive weather and neglect.

Halloway looked at it for one measured second.

Then she unhooked the tag with the point of her blade and dropped it into her coat pocket beside the oilcloth photograph.

“Names later,” she said. “First, boundaries.”

The water gave another lap.

Not from the drain this time.

From the left.

Halloway’s head turned only enough to track the sound. The firelight showed her the surface of the cellar water in broken copper patches. Near the wall, where the standing water was shallowest, a dimple opened. Closed. Opened again.

Not chance.

Appetite.

Then another dimple, farther back.

And another.

Halloway straightened slowly. Her boots were soaked through. Her knees ached with cellar cold. The blade in her hand was blackened and sticky, and the hooked wire dripped black fluid onto the stair with a patience that made her want to strike something professional.

“Right,” she said. “The neighbourhood has noticed the noise.”

She did not go toward the wall. Not yet. Going toward disturbances was how men ended up becoming disturbances. Instead she backed up one step, keeping the drain, the burning chamber, and the rippling wall-water inside the same lazy sweep of her eyes.

The first body continued to burn. The rib cage had collapsed inward now, black and steaming, the opened chamber reduced to a charred bowl of ash and grease. The fire was dying, but it still gave light, and light was a kind of fence if one knew how to stand behind it.

Halloway reached into her coat and brought out the tin of salt.

She did not scatter it theatrically. Salt was not prayer. It was chemistry with a bad temper. She poured a thin line across the damp stair between herself and the wall-water, then another along the edge of the drain, then a third around the burning remains where the black fluid had pooled thickest. The salt hissed faintly where it met thread-stained water.

“New rule,” she said, voice flat and practical. “The first house was a warning. The second house was a messenger. Anything else that comes through that drain is not curious. Curiosity died with the first one’s manners. This lot has errands.”

The dimples in the water multiplied.

Small ones. Fast ones. Not full hosts. Not yet. Threads, maybe. Node clusters wearing scraps of rat, beetle, cellar centipede, whatever had been dumb enough to drink from the wrong pool. The colony was testing the boundaries with cheap probes, learning where the salt bit, where the fire glowed, where the stairs narrowed, where a living person stood with a lamp and a brick and insufficient training.

Halloway saw the pattern and named it without comfort.

“Scouts,” she said. “Cheap ones. They send the poor first. Democratic bastards.”

One of the dimples swelled.

A shape broke the surface near the wall: pale, segmented, no larger than a man’s hand. It had too many joints for a rat’s foreleg and too few for an honest spider. Black threads trailed from it like wet thread from a needle. It tasted the air with a slit that might once have been a mouth, then turned toward the salt line.

The salt smoked.

The shape recoiled.

Then another came up behind it.

And another.

They moved in that horrible, coordinated way Halloway had already seen under the first creature’s skin: not pack instinct, not animal fear, but administration. One probed. One withdrew. One circled the weak place in the salt where the water had thinned the crystals. One climbed the wall itself, using split toes and accessory joints to brace in cracks no rat should have been able to hold.

Halloway put the blade away and took up the hooked wire with both hands.

“Enough lecturing,” she said.

She struck first at the wall-climber.

The hook caught it behind the segmented shoulder and pinned it to the brick. She drove the blade through the thread-knot at its base without ceremony. It burst into a smear of oily darkness and fell, trailing black strands that writhed on the wet stone until the salt took them.

The next one came from the water.

Small. Fast. Wrong in the elbows.

Halloway sidestepped, let it overreach, and stamped its midsection into the stair. The body gave under her boot with a sound like a green walnut. Threads squirted from the crushed segment and reached for her laces. She kicked them loose, drew the blade, and cut the main cable at the shoulder before the thing could remember it had orders.

It still twitched.

She finished it with the pommel.

“Housekeeping,” she said.

The drain gave a deeper sound then.

Not a lap.

A shift.

Something larger was moving inside the pipe.

Halloway froze.

Not fear. Recognition.

The cellar had four feet of standing water, but the drain ran under the wall and out toward the street culvert. If the colony had taken the dog as a courier, it had not done so for speed alone. It had done so because couriers could go places hosts could not.

The iron grate over the drain bowed inward.

Once.

Twice.

The rusted bars groaned. Black fluid seeped through the cracks in the silt, thicker than water, glossier than oil. It did not spread. It gathered. It formed a bead at the centre of the grate, then another, then a dozen, each bead trembling with the patient intent of roots seeking water.

Halloway’s mouth tightened.

“There,” she said quietly. “Of course there. The letter has arrived, and now the postman wants a receipt.”

She looked back toward the stair.

The firelight caught the wet stone, the salt lines, the charred remains of the first house, the broken little bodies of the second. It also caught the lamp, where it still burned above the waterline, throwing a weak, stubborn island of light across the cellar.

Halloway made a decision.

Not a brave one. Brave decisions were usually the ones men remembered. This was the sort of decision that kept men alive long enough to be forgotten properly.

She waded backward, not turning her face from the drain, keeping the hooked wire between herself and the bowing grate. The water pulled at her boots. The cold climbed her calves. The smell from the pipe sharpened: hot metal, pond silt, yeast, and beneath it the sweet, fungal stink of a brood that had been waiting in the dark long enough to learn patience.

“Plan,” she said, as if speaking to a student who had already disappointed her twice. “We do not chase it into the drain. Drains are honest about being sewers. We do not let it cross the salt. We do not let it reach the stair. And we do not, under any circumstance, allow it to decide that your lamp is a door.”

The grate burst.

Not outward.

Inward.

The iron bars folded like wet cardboard, and from the hole came a shoulder.

Broad.

Human.

Wrong.

Halloway had seen the first body’s shoulders split and reset, had seen the accessory sockets, the cable sleeves, the enthusiastic architecture of a colony learning leverage. This was further along. The shoulder did not merely branch; it bloomed. The clavicle had been resorbed and rebuilt into a double strut. The scapula sat forward, perforated, seated in a groove cut fresh into the ribs. Threads dense as rope coiled around the new bone, black and glistening, pulling the skin into a tent of pale ridges.

Then the arm came through.

Long. Too long. Doubled at the elbow, tripled at the wrist, fingers folded back at angles that had nothing to do with human joints and everything to do with reaching through places not made for reaching.

The head followed last.

No nose. No eyes worth naming. Two dark slits above a jaw hinged in too many places. The lips were drawn back from teeth that had finished growing.

Even.

Halloway counted without meaning to, the way a soldier counts gunshots and a doctor counts breaths.

“Two. Four. Six. Eight. Ten. Twelve. Fourteen. Sixteen.” Her voice went flat. “Design.”

The thing did not click.

It did not chatter with many small mouths.

It breathed.

One slow, wet inhalation through the rib chamber that was no longer a rib chamber. The opened cage of bone had been widened further, the intercostal spaces threaded into a rigid lattice. Inside, the pale sacs were fewer than in the first body, but larger. Mature. Anchored. Not a nursery.

A control room.

Halloway stepped back until her heels touched the salt line.

The creature’s head turned toward her.

Not toward the lamp.

Not toward the fire.

Toward her.

“That is new,” she said.

It had learned.

The first body had been a house still furnishing. The dog had been a courier carrying spare parts. This thing in the drain was not learning to stand. It had already decided where to stand, and it had chosen the narrowest place in the room because narrow places made victims predictable.

The arm hooked over the broken grate.

The shoulder lifted.

The threads at the fork bunched, not with the frantic enthusiasm of the first creature, but with the calm, terrible efficiency of a mechanism that had been assembled for a purpose.

Halloway drew the blade again.

The steel made a small, honest sound against leather.

“Right,” she said. “Enough introduction.”

She looked at the salt line.

It was thinning where the water had run.

She looked at the fire.

It was dying where the oil had failed.

She looked at the stair.

Dry-ish stone. Narrow ascent. One place where a thing with too many joints could brace sideways and reach from an angle a man did not leave room for.

Halloway made the only calculation that mattered.

Then she spoke, and her voice carried the grim, practical amusement of a woman who had been unlucky enough to be right too many times.

“If it clears the grate,” she said, “do not throw the brick at the face. Faces are for liars and mourners. Throw it at the shoulder fork. If you miss, do not fetch it. If it takes the lamp, let it go. If it takes your hand, let go of the hand. Hands are harder to replace than pride, but not as hard as heads.”

The creature came through the drain.

It did not rise like a man.

It unfolded like a door that had been locked from the inside.

Water poured off its torso in dark ribbons. The opened rib cage flexed above the surface, black fluid swirling around the mature sacs in slow, deliberate circles. The left arm dragged free of the pipe, fingers spreading on the cellar floor with a sound like wet nails on slate. The right shoulder lifted, threads tightening into a clean, terrible line.

Halloway did not retreat.

Backwards was for stairs, and stairs were for people who intended to live long enough to use them.

“Shoulder,” she said quietly. “Watch the shoulder.”

The thing took one step out of the drain.

Then another.

The salt line hissed beneath its foot.

It did not stop.

It looked down at the white crystals, then back at Halloway, and the jaw opened wide enough to count.

Eighteen.

Even.

Finished.

Halloway’s expression hardened.

“There,” she said. “It has read the instructions.”

The creature’s right hand crossed in front of its chest.

Not a feint.

A commitment.

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: *My breath catches.* "It's crossing midline. Right hand, going for you." *I heft the brick, knuckles white, and take a step down.*

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway heard the stair complain under added weight and did not turn to argue with it. Arguments were for rooms with exits. This room had water, fire, a drain, and a thing that had counted its teeth before choosing a face.

“If you are on the stair,” she said, flat and brief, “stay dry. If you have the brick, wait for the shoulder. If you have sense, wait for both.”

The creature’s right hand crossed midline.

It did not slash. It placed. The fingers—three joints where two should serve, each tipped with a nail that had been human before the colony improved on it—spread toward the stair edge. Not at Halloway. At the stone. At the leverage point. At the narrow place where a body with too many braces could pull itself free and turn the cellar into a climbing frame.

Halloway moved before the hand chose its purchase.

She stepped inside the arc, boot crushing a ribbon of black thread that had drifted from the drain, and drove the hooked wire not into the palm but into the inner wrist. The skin there was wax-pale and slick, stretched over a cable bundle thick as bootlace. Under it, the bones had been revised: radius and ulna split near their lower ends, capped with soft new knobs, lashed together by a sleeve of thread that pulsed in time with the sacs in the opened rib chamber.

“Flexor side,” she murmured, as if reminding her own hands. “Never the palm. Palms are advertisements.”

The blade went in along the wire’s shadow.

Three strokes.

First: the sleeve parted. Black fluid welled, not spraying, beading at first, then running in strings that tried to reattach to the steel.

Second: the new cap at the wrist separated from the old shaft with a sound like a wet switch breaking.

Third: the main relay knot beneath the skin came loose in Halloway’s hook.

The right hand spasmed.

It did not drop. That was the first sign of design. A lesser host would have lost the limb to shock, to pain, to the simple disappointment of being cut. This one redirected. The fingers curled around the wire instead of releasing it, accessory joints locking, and the arm yanked back toward the drain with a force that pulled Halloway half a step forward.

“Greedy,” she said.

She let it be greedy.

With her free hand she seized the tin of salt from her belt and threw a handful not at the creature, but at the water around its emerging left foot. The crystals hit the black film floating there and smoked. The threads anchored in the shallows contracted, pulling the foot half an inch out of alignment. The creature’s balance, already built on borrowed bone and temporary cable, hiccupped.

It compensated by opening the rib chamber wider.

The smell changed at once. Pond silt went hot. Copper went sharp. Yeast turned to the sweet, cloying reek of fruit left in a sealed jar beside a stove. From the opened cage, black fluid rose in a slow crest around the mature sacs—fewer than in the first body, larger, anchored to the inner walls with thick white stalks. They did not writhe. They waited.

“Control room,” Halloway said. “Not nursery. That is worse.”

A sac near the sternum dilated, and the creature drew breath.

Not air. Heat.

The fire from the first body’s remains licked higher, though no new fuel had been added. The colony was sampling warmth, pulling it toward the drain mouth, testing whether heat could mend the wrist it had just lost. Halloway saw the black threads at the cut begin to bridge the gap, thin as hair, confident as spiders.

“No mending on my account.”

She kicked sideways, catching a charred rib fragment from the burned first house with the heel of her boot. It skidded across the wet stone, trailing orange embers and a ribbon of oil that still refused to die. The fragment came to rest against the creature’s shin.

The threads on its leg turned toward the heat.

That was the mistake even design could make.

Halloway hooked the burning rib with the wire and dragged it up along the creature’s calf, not fast, not frantic, just enough to lay fire against the cable sleeve where the knee had been split and reset. Black fluid flashed. The sleeve curled. The leg bucked once, then held, the colony forcing the joint to ignore what had just been burned.

“It can be told to disregard pain,” Halloway said. “Cannot be told to disregard physics.”

The creature’s head came free of the drain.

No nose. No eyes. Two dark slits above a jaw that had finished growing. Eighteen teeth, even, pale, set with the cold regularity of a tool rack. The lips drew back, and for one half-second the face beneath the swelling looked almost deliberate: not a man, not a beast, but a mask made from the memory of both.

Then it spoke.

The sound came from the rib chamber and the throat at once, a wet, layered imitation of a human voice.

“Help.”

Halloway did not flinch. She had heard cellars ask for help before, usually just after they had eaten someone who could answer.

“Larynx is a spare part,” she said. “Tongue is a lure. Do not debate it.”

The word had not been idle. It had been a tripwire. Halloway saw the creature’s good left shoulder hitch as the voice finished, the threads bunching at the fork with that same winch-tension she had named on the first body.

It had learned to use speech as a cue.

“Left shoulder,” she said, sharper now. “It is not asking. It is signalling.”

The left arm came out of the drain.

This one was whole. The humerus had been divided and capped, the scapula seated forward in its accessory groove, the cable sleeve dense and unburned. The hand opened with five fingers too long, each joint doubling back at angles that made the stair look suddenly fragile. It reached not for Halloway, not for the water, but for the dry stone above her: the lip of the stair, the narrow shelf where a braced hand could turn a cellar into a corridor.

Halloway had one useful yard of distance and one ruined right-hand cable between the thing and the exit.

She used both.

She drove the hooked wire into the creature’s open rib chamber.

Not deep. Deep was for men who liked surprises. She set the hook under the sternal notch, where the colony had fused the peeled ribs into a rigid lattice, and levered backward with her weight. The cage creaked. Black fluid sloshed over the rim. The mature sacs tightened, pulling inward as if the body had finally understood insult.

The left hand missed the stair by a finger’s width.

“There,” Halloway said.

She released the wire and let the rib spring back, catching the left forearm in the closing bones. It was not a trap built for elegance. It was a trap built by a woman who had spent three decades making monsters pay rent in their own architecture.

The creature’s shoulder wrenched forward. The left arm did not come free. The accessory socket, still soft at the new bone cap, ground against the rib with a sound like a knuckle dragged across slate. Threads at the fork bunched, tried to redistribute, found no clean path.

Halloway stepped onto the exposed ankle of the thing’s left leg.

The water here was shallow and filthy, slick with burned thread and salt. She planted one boot on the outer ankle bone, the other against the tibial shelf where the colony had split the lower leg to make a brace. The body under her feet was warm in the wrong places: nest-warm, not blood-warm, the heat pooled around the sacs in the chest and the new joints at the shoulders.

She put the blade into the left shoulder fork.

This time she did not slice. She stabbed.

The point found the gap between the resorbed clavicle and the false scapular seat, the place where the newest bone met oldest meat and the colony had not yet decided whether to call it armour or mistake. Black fluid ran down the steel. The thread knot beneath the skin swelled, dense as rope, and Halloway twisted the blade once.

The left hand went rigid.

Not slack. Rigid. The fingers locked open, tendons standing out like harp strings, and the arm began to drag the torso sideways regardless of the pain it could no longer be permitted to feel. The creature’s jaw opened again, and this time the sound was not a word. It was the rib chamber emptying pressure through a hundred small vents: a wet, clicking exhalation that sprayed black mist across Halloway’s forearm.

She did not breathe it.

She had faced worse air than this before most men learned which end of a knife was polite.

“Salt,” she said to the room, because the room was useless and the tin was in her hand anyway.

She poured the last of it into the open rib chamber.

The crystals hit the black fluid and the mature sacs with a hiss that sounded almost like approval. The sacs contracted. The stalks whitened. The creature’s chest arched, not in agony, but in administrative failure: the relay had been brined, the reservoir fouled, the house suddenly informed that its tenants were no longer welcome.

The left arm lost its order halfway to the stair.

The fingers uncurled. The wrist folded. The whole limb came loose from the rib trap with a wet pop and fell into the water, trailing black threads that curled away from the salt and sought the nearest warm thing.

Halloway stamped them underfoot.

“Housekeeping,” she said.

But the thing was not finished.

Even teeth meant design. Design meant redundancy.

The head lolled to one side, the dark slits no longer tracking with purpose, but the right shoulder—the burned, half-cut right shoulder—began to lift again. The cables there had charred, not severed. The colony was using the burn as a splint, pulling the ruined wrist back into service with threads that had learned to knit around damage instead of avoiding it.

The right hand, still hooked on the wire from Halloway’s first cut, dragged upward through the water.

It was not reaching for the stair now.

It was reaching for Halloway’s boot.

She saw the fingers close on the leather and did not waste outrage. Outrage was for people who had not expected monsters to be persistent. She drew the blade free of the shoulder fork, shifted her weight, and brought the pommel down across the back of the creature’s hand.

Bone cracked. Not human bone. The new caps, still soft, gave like green wood.

The hand released.

Halloway kicked the forearm aside, then stepped off the leg and back toward the salt line, keeping the creature between herself and the stair. The water around its thighs was black with fluid, ash, and the oily residue of burned threads. The first body’s fire had sunk to a sullen glow, but the drain mouth still steamed, and from somewhere inside the pipe came a slow, wet shifting.

Not one thing.

Many small ones.

Halloway’s eyes narrowed.

“Of course,” she said. “The neighbourhood has a quorum.”

The creature in front of her was wounded, brined, half-burned, and missing coherent orders from the chest. It should have collapsed. Colonies collapsed when the control room failed. This one did not. It dragged itself forward on the ruined right arm and the intact left elbow, using the peeled ribs as a brace, the opened cage flexing with each movement like a bellows full of wet stones.

It was not trying to stand.

It was trying to reach the drain.

Halloway understood then, with the cold satisfaction of a woman reading a map drawn in blood.

The thing from the drain had not come to fight. It had come to deliver.

The molar in the dog’s throat. The photograph in the first body’s pocket. The even teeth. The mature sacs. The control room. None of it was an attack. It was an installation. A seed-corn planted in a cellar with standing water, a drain, and warm bodies foolish enough to keep asking questions near it.

“Right,” Halloway said. “You are not the tenant. You are the key.”

The creature’s jaw opened one last time.

No word this time. Only a black bead of fluid, thick as syrup, drawn from the rib chamber and spat toward the drain mouth. It struck the broken grate and slid inward, trailing threads that caught on the iron like harp strings.

The shifting in the pipe answered.

Halloway moved.

She hooked the burning rib fragment again, dragged it across the wet stone, and threw it not at the creature but at the drain mouth. The fire met the black fluid there with a brief, hungry flare. The threads recoiling from the salt now curled from the heat, pulling back into the pipe with the panicked coordination of a workforce told the foreman had fallen ill.

The creature in the cellar shrieked.

Not with its throat. With the rib chamber. A hundred small vents opening at once, a sound like wet parchment tearing, and the mature sacs inside its chest collapsed inward, not burned, not brined, but emptied. Whatever control they had held had gone down the drain with the bead of fluid.

The body dropped.

It did not flop like a killed man. It folded like a chair with the pin pulled: shoulders first, then elbows, then the too-long fingers, each joint surrendering its borrowed order in sequence. The opened rib cage struck the cellar floor with a dull, final crack. Black fluid ran out from under it in a slow halo, meeting the salt and steaming faintly.

Halloway kept her blade up.

She waited through the lap of water, the hiss of dying fire, the small settling sounds of meat remembering it was only meat. Nothing under the skin moved. No thread turned toward the light. The drain gave up no further shoulders.

Then she walked to the body and put the point of the blade through the centre of the rib chamber, pinning it to the floor.

“Still not beautiful,” she said. “Hungry, though. That we knew.”

She withdrew the blade and turned toward the stair.

The salt line was broken in three places. The fire was low. The drain mouth smoked, and beyond it the pipe whispered with the slow movement of water that had somewhere else to be. Halloway collected the tin, the wire, the charred rib fragment, and the linen square with the teeth and gold band. She checked the waterline once more, then looked up toward the dry stone and the light resting there.

“The shoulder fork is open if the brick is still handy,” she said, voice flat, tired, and not unkind in the way a blade is not unkind. “If it is not, say so. I would rather know what is being held than what someone intends to be brave about.”

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: "The brick's here," I say, my voice rough. "But the shoulder... it's already shut." I stare at the mess of ribs and salt. "The threads are curling back. Like they're hiding."
