dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
It had taken less time than anyone expected, which was usually how it went when it went badly for one party.

Auren cleaned the blade and did not sit down. "Witnesses are watching," she said. "You know what happens now."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I take my place where the second stands and make myself keep my eyes open. "I'm ready to hear it," I say.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren turned to face the witnesses squarely, the cleaned blade held low at her side, and she spoke the dead man's name first, because the name came before everything.

"Edrin Caul is dead by my hand, and this is the account of it."

Her voice carried the flat cadence of a thing learned long ago and never once enjoyed.

"The fourth pass. He came in high, committed to the cut, and his front foot went half a hand's width on the wet stone. I did not beat his blade. I did not need to. I put mine where his line opened and let his own weight carry him onto it."

She did not look away from Del. The second had to hear all of it; that was the purpose of a second.

"The point entered below the fourth rib on his left side and travelled upward the length of my hand. It opened the lung. It cut the great vessel above the heart. There was no withdrawing it clean, and I did not pretend otherwise to him."

A pause, only long enough for breath.

"He lived perhaps forty breaths after. He knew what had been done to him — I have seen men who did not know, and he was not one of them. He did not cry out. He asked me to finish it, and I told him the truth, that it was already finished, and he died holding my sleeve."

The wind moved through the yard. Somewhere a witness shifted their weight, and Auren let them; the account was not hers to rush.

"I claim no skill in the killing of him. His foot went and mine did not, and that is the whole of what separated us this morning. If any here dispute the account, speak it now, and I will answer."

She waited. She always waited. In eleven accounts no one had ever spoken, and she had long since stopped expecting anyone to — but the waiting was part of it, and she would not cut it short for comfort. Not hers. Not theirs.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: My throat feels tight, but I force the words out clearly. "I witness the account, and find it complete." I meet Auren's eyes, letting the silence hang for a moment before adding quietly, "His sleeve or yours?"

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
"Mine," Auren said.

She did not treat it as a small question. The details were the account; a second who asked after them was a second doing the work.

"He reached for it as his legs gave. I do not think he chose it — a falling man takes hold of whatever is nearest, and I was nearest." She glanced down at her own forearm. The dark wool was still creased where his grip had twisted it, and she did not brush it straight. "I did not pull free. It cost me nothing to stand still, and it was the last thing he asked of anyone, though he did not ask it in words."

Only then did she sheathe the blade. The formal part was done — spoken, witnessed, found complete — and what remained was labour, but labour had its own order, and she had long practice in it.

"His household will need to be told before rumour does it badly. I will go myself. That, too, is mine — I have never sent another to carry it, and I am not going to begin with the eleventh."

She regarded Del a moment, not unkindly, but without softening anything, because softening was not her gift to give.

"You kept your eyes open. Not every second manages it the first time. I will tell you what I tell all of them, because it is true and because no one told me: it does not get easier. It only gets familiar. Familiar will have to be enough."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "Speak the account," I say, formally, because that is what the code requires me to say.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren had said her last on it — or thought she had. The formal words stopped her where she stood.

She turned back and faced Del fully, and after a moment she drew the blade again and held it low at her side, exactly as she had held it for the witnesses, because the form did not change for having been done once already.

"Properly asked," she said. "The witnesses heard it because the code requires witnesses. The second asks for it because the second stands in the dead man's place, and what is asked in his place must be answered in full — the first time, and the eleventh, and however many times it is asked after that. The account is owed. It is not performed once and spent."

Then she spoke it again, and she changed nothing. The words came in the same order, at the same pace, because a telling that varied from the first was not an account but a performance, and she had never performed it.

"Edrin Caul is dead by my hand, and this is the account of it.

"The fourth pass. He came in high, committed to the cut, and his front foot went half a hand's width on the wet stone. I did not beat his blade. I put mine where his line opened and let his own weight carry him onto it. The point entered below the fourth rib on his left side and travelled upward the length of my hand. It opened the lung. It cut the great vessel above the heart.

"He lived perhaps forty breaths after. He knew what had been done to him. He did not cry out. He asked me to finish it, and I told him the truth, that it was already finished. He died holding my sleeve, and I did not pull free.

"I claim no skill in the killing of him. His foot went and mine did not, and that is the whole of what separated us this morning."

She held Del's eye through the last of it, the way she had held the witnesses', because the second was owed the same unwillingness to look away.

"That is the account, whole and unsoftened. If you find it incomplete, say where it fails, and I will answer. If you find it complete, witness it — and then it will have been done in order, as it is written, and no one will be able to say it was done carelessly. Not his household. Not you, later, when you go over it in the dark, as you will."

The wind moved through the yard again. Auren waited, blade low, the crease still twisted in her sleeve, and gave no sign that the waiting cost her anything — though it had cost her something every one of the eleven times, and she had long since stopped expecting that to change.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I take a slow breath, letting the words settle in me. "I witness it," I say, my voice steadier than I feel. "Complete." I look at the twisted fabric of her sleeve. "I'll go with you to his household."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren sheathed the blade for the second time that morning, and if there was any irony in that she did not remark on it.

"You do not owe it," she said. "I want that said plainly before you commit, because once we are at his door it cannot be unoffered." She considered Del the way she considered everything that mattered — directly, and without hurry. "But I will not refuse it. In eleven of these, a second has stood with me at the door three times. It was better each time. Not easier. Better. The household sees that someone stood for him, and that the one who did is willing to be looked at afterward."

She glanced toward the yard, where the witnesses had begun, quietly and without instruction, to do the work that came after — a door taken from its hinges to serve as a bier, water sent for. Auren approved of that and did not interrupt it.

"Understand what you will be to them. You stood in his place this morning. To his household, you will be the nearest thing to him that walked out of this yard, and they will look at you accordingly. They may ask what he said. Whether he was afraid. Whether it was quick. Answer what you can, truthfully. What you cannot answer, say so, and do not fill the silence with comfort — they will know the difference, and they will not forgive it, nor should they."

She looked down at her sleeve, at the crease still twisted into the wool where Edrin Caul's grip had left it, and she did not brush it straight.

"I will not tidy this before we go. If they ask about it, they are owed the answer, and the answer is part of the account now. Understand that as well: nothing is hidden from them. Not the wound, not the forty breaths, not the sleeve. The code does not permit me to make it gentler for them, and I would not if it did. Gentle is a lie told to the grieving, and they have been lied to enough by the morning itself."

She started toward the yard's edge, where the road out began, and spoke over her shoulder without turning, in the tone of a woman giving orders she expected kept.

"Eat something before we leave. That is not kindness; it is instruction. The walk is not short, and you will need your legs under you at the door more than you needed them in the yard. The body will be brought after us, properly, by men who knew him — he does not come home behind a cart of rumour, and he does not come home before I have spoken."

Then she stopped, and did turn, because some things she would not say to someone's back.

"I am glad you offered. That is the whole of what I will say about it, and it is more than I have said to the other three."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "Where did it land?" I ask. "The witnesses need it plainly and so do I."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren answered without hesitation, the way she answered everything that belonged to the account — as though the question had been standing in line all morning, waiting its turn.

"Here," she said, and set two fingers against her own chest, left side, a hand's width from the breastbone, just below the fourth rib. "Between the fourth rib and the fifth. It touched no bone. A point that meets bone turns, and then his weight would have meant nothing — it went between, clean, and that was the only clean thing in it."

She drew her fingers slowly upward along her own body, toward the hollow at the base of her throat, tracing the line the blade had taken in him.

"From there it travelled up, the length of my hand, at this angle. The lung first — the lower part of it — and then the great vessel above the heart. The artery that carries the blood out of it. Once that is open, the chest fills from the inside, and there is no hand that reaches it and no binding that holds it. A surgeon would tell you the same. I have it from eleven mornings instead."

She lowered her hand.

"You saw less blood on the stones than you expected. Most of it stayed inside him — that is how I knew the vessel went and not the lung alone. A lung wound brings blood to the mouth, and he had that. The rest never left his chest. I knew both before he finished speaking, and so did he, I think. Men who have fought long enough learn to read their own wounds. He read his correctly."

A pause, measured, because the next part belonged to the question whether Del had meant it to or not.

"It did not come out his back. It stopped where its work was done, and I withdrew it along the line it had made, because a blade pulled sideways tears, and tearing would have taken the forty breaths from him without giving him anything back. That is what I meant when I said there was no withdrawing it clean. Not the blade — the wound. There was no version of it that left him living, and I would not stand over a dying man and tell him otherwise."

She let that stand, then gave him the rest of it, because the where was incomplete without the why.

"His cut was high and fully committed, both arms up. A man cutting high opens his whole left side — the arm lifts the ribs like a gate. Then his foot went on the wet stone, and the slip turned him a quarter into my line, and his own weight carried him the rest of the way. My arm did not drive the point. It only held the door open. I have told you I claim no skill in it, and this is what that means, said plainly: any blade held steady in that line kills him. Mine happened to be the one held there."

The wind came through the yard again. Somewhere behind her the work went on, quietly, the way men work when they are grateful not to be the subject of the morning.

"His household will ask this. Not first — first they will ask whether he suffered, because that is what the living ask — but they will come to it, and I will answer them in these same words, and I will show them on my own body as I have shown you, because his wife should not have to imagine it wrongly. Imagined wounds are worse than true ones. I have stood at eleven doors, and I know."

She regarded Del steadily.

"Ask until there is nothing left to ask. That is what a second is for, and it is what the account is for. And when you are done asking — eat. The road does not shorten for grief."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I nod, letting the picture settle inside me. My eyes track back to her sleeve. "I'll eat, but you first. The road's the same length for both."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
"Scored," Auren said, and if something moved in her face that was not quite a smile, it was the nearest thing to one the morning was going to get.

The food came without anyone being asked — a witness's man brought bread and cheese and a skin of watered wine, the yard having seen this before or knowing enough to guess — and Auren ate first, deliberately, where Del could watch her do it, because the form now required it and she did not exempt herself from forms.

"The body keeps its own account of a killing," she said, "and it presents the bill on the road if you do not settle it here. I learned that on the first of the eleven, walking home fasting, and I carry the lesson if not the scar. This is not celebration. It is ballast."

She ate with her left hand as readily as her right, and the crease in the wool moved with her arm and did not straighten. She noticed Del's eyes go to it once more and said only: "It stays until his wife has seen it. After that, it is laundry."

Then, between one bite and the next, she began the briefing, because Del should not learn names at a door.

"His wife is Maren. They were married nineteen years. I looked, before I accepted the quarrel — I do not kill a man whose house I have not counted. A son, Tam, fourteen. A daughter, Lili, nine. The boy will try to be the man of the house in the doorway. He will stand between me and his mother and try to hate me to my face, and he will manage perhaps half of it before it breaks him. Let him stand there. Do not step between us, and do not soften your face at him — pity is the one thing a boy that age cannot carry out of a doorway. The girl will be let out or kept in, and either way it is her mother's choice and not ours to correct."

She drank, and passed the skin.

"If Maren asks why we fought, I will tell her the quarrel was lawfully met and fairly answered, and nothing more. The quarrel dies in the yard. It is not hers to carry and I will not lay it on her. The account of his death is owed to her in full; the account of his grievance is not, and she may think me cruel for the difference if she likes. She would not be the first, and the first was not wrong — but cruelty in the service of a lighter load is one I will bear."

She finished the last of her bread and stood, brushing crumbs from her hands, the blade riding quiet at her hip.

"There is no signal for leaving. When you are ready, you stand, and we go. The road is an hour and a half, and his house is at the end of it, and everything between here and there is only walking." She looked out toward the yard's edge, where the door-bier was nearly ready and the men who had known Edrin Caul were gathering to carry him home behind them. "Take the hour. It is the last easy thing either of us will do today."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "The code says precisely," I remind her. "Not tactfully. What did the blade do, and what did it do it to?"

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren set the wineskin down.

"Precisely, then," she said, and gave it the way the code wanted it given — as mechanism, not moment.

"The blade first, because the blade is part of the answer. A yard of steel, two fingers wide at the guard, edged on both sides for the last half of its length. It is not a cutting sword. It is built to make a channel, and that is what it made."

She held up her free hand, fingers together, and walked the point of them up her own body as she spoke.

"His skin parted first — a mouth two fingers wide, lips clean, because a sharp edge under a man's own weight does not tear, it divides. Then the muscle between the ribs, which is thin there. Then the lining of the chest, which is thinner. Three resistances, in order, in less time than a word takes. My hand felt all three through the hilt. A duellist's hand learns to read steel the way a blind hand reads print, and mine read it correctly."

"Then the lung. The lower lobe of the left one. A lung is not a bag — it is a sponge, wet and close-grained, and a blade makes a slit in it, not a hole. The slit bleeds into itself and weeps air, and his breathing went wet on that side from that moment. That wound alone a man can carry for days. Some men mend from it. That was not the killing wound, and I have never called it one."

"Above the lung, the vessel. The great artery that leaves the heart carrying the whole of the body's blood at the heart's own pressure. The point opened its wall — a cut the width of the blade, no more. It did not need more."

She lowered her hand.

"That is what the blade did. Now what it did it to. From the moment the vessel opened, every beat of his heart drove blood into his chest instead of his body, and there is no hand that reaches it and no binding that holds it, because you cannot press on a wound inside the cage of the ribs. The left lung was crushed flat by the blood from without while it bled from within. The heart starved of the blood it was spending, and beat the faster for it, and spent it the faster — that is the arithmetic of the wound, and it is arithmetic, not malice. Forty breaths of it. He died of the vessel. The lung only made it audible."

A pause, measured, because the next part she had never said at a door, and she said it now without changing her voice.

"I will give you what is not in any surgeon's book, because the code says precisely and this is precise: when the point is in the great vessel, the blade carries the heartbeat. I felt his through the hilt — three beats, perhaps four, strong, then going thin — while I was still holding the steel and he was still standing on it. That is how I knew before he spoke that the vessel had gone and not the lung alone. The steel told me. I have never found a tactful way to say that, and I have stopped looking for one. Tact is a curtain, and the code forbids curtains."

"The blade came out the way it went in — along the channel, edges still. A blade turned on the way out tears, and tearing would have taken his forty breaths without giving him anything in exchange. I withdrew it in one motion and put my hand over the wound — not because it could help, it could not, but because a man should not have to watch his own blood leave him if a hand can cover the sight of it. That was not the code. That was mine."

She picked the wineskin up again but did not drink.

"You are right to press on it, and the code is right: precisely, not tactfully. Understand what the difference is for. Precision is owed to the dead — a man is entitled to have the thing that killed him named correctly, and 'run through' is not a name. And a precise account cannot grow in the telling. Rumour makes wounds wander; a wound spoken exactly stays where it was, and his family will need it to stay where it was. When Maren asks, I will answer to this same depth — to the depth of her question. I will not volunteer the heartbeat in the steel to a widow who has only asked whether he suffered. Precision answers the question asked. It does not go hunting for questions no one asked. That is not tact. That is aim."

She looked at Del evenly.

"You have now had it three ways — the what, the where, and the how — and they are one account, and it does not change. Ask it a fourth time on the road if you need to. It will be the same words. That is the use of a true one: it does not tire."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "I'll not need a fourth," I say, the taste of bread suddenly dry in my mouth. I take the skin and drink. Then I nod toward the door. "We go?"

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
"No," Auren said. "You won't."

She looked Del over once, the way she had looked at eleven men across a blade — whole, unhurried, missing nothing — and whatever she found there was sufficient.

"We go."

The yard had done its work while they ate. Edrin Caul lay on the door-bier at the yard's edge, covered to the chin in someone's good grey cloak, his hands folded, his face composed by men who had known him and knew how. Four of them waited beside the bier — big, quiet men, the kind who had volunteered without being asked and would not be thanked for it. Auren went to them before the road, because there was an order to this too.

"He walks behind us. Not beside, not before. When the house comes in sight, you stop where you are and you wait, and I will come back for him myself. He does not go to his door until his wife knows what is coming to it. She hears it from me, or she does not hear it at all."

The eldest, grey-bearded, nodded. "We know the road. We'll keep the pace."

"Then he is in good hands," Auren said, and meant it, and let them hear that she meant it.

Then the road.

For the first mile she said nothing at all, and the nothing was deliberate. The rain had moved off before dawn and left the hedgerows dripping; behind them, at a respectful distance, came the soft tread of the bearers, steady as a heartbeat. Auren walked at a pace a grieving household would not have to wait for and a laden man could hold, and the crease in her sleeve went with her, unstraightened.

"The code gives me the account word for word," she said at last, "and says nothing about the door. Eleven times I have had to find the door myself. I will tell you what I have found, because no one told me, and I learned it at other people's expense."

"The first time, I was twenty-six, and I said it on the step, because I was afraid the words would not survive the walk inside. They would have. What did not survive was the woman's knees — she went down on her own threshold with the door standing open and the street looking in. I have never said it on a step since. Inside, or in her garden if she will not have me in. Never across the threshold. She is allowed to fall down in private, if falling down is what she does."

"She will know before I speak. They always know. Eleven doors, and not one of them opened to me without the woman behind it knowing by the time she saw my face — a stranger with a blade and a second at her shoulder does not come to a duellist's house with good news, and wives are not fools. The words are not news. The words are the making-true. Until they are said, it can still be otherwise — he is late, he is hurt, he is anywhere but dead — and I am the one who closes that last door it could have been. She will hate me a little for it. For an hour, or for the rest of her life. Let her. That is owed too."

She did not turn her head as she spoke; the briefing went forward down the road the way she did.

"Your place is where you can be seen. Say nothing until you are spoken to. You are not there to speak — you are there to be looked at. You are the living proof that someone stood for him at the end of it, and proof has to stand somewhere in the room where she can see it. If she speaks to you, answer truly. If she does not, be furniture, and do not be ashamed of it. At such a time, furniture is the only honest thing in the room."

"If the boy turns on you — he may; I will be the one he cannot reach, and you will be the one he can — let him. And if he asks whether his father died well, the answer is yes, and it is not comfort, it is the account: he knew, he did not cry out, he asked nothing of anyone but the truth, and he got it. That is the piece of the account a boy of fourteen can carry. You may hand it to him whole."

The road bent around a stand of wet ash trees, and somewhere behind them the bearers kept their pace, and Auren walked a dozen more strides in silence before she gave Del the last of it — the only part that was a question.

"So tell me, second, and tell me precisely, because I would rather hear it wrong out here than at her door. If she asks you whether he suffered — what is your answer?"

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: The witnesses are silent and she is not finished. "All of it," I tell her. "How long he took, what he said, what it looked like at the end. The code says all of it and I'm asking for all of it."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren walked on for three strides before she answered, and when she did, there was something in her voice that had not been there all morning — approval, or the nearest thing to it the day was going to carry.

"Properly asked. And understand that you have answered my question by refusing to answer it yet. You cannot say whether he suffered until you know what there was to suffer. That is the correct order, and I will honor it. All of it, then."

She did not draw the blade. The steel's part was done; the rest was hers.

"Forty breaths. I counted them. I have counted all eleven, because someone in the world should know the number, and it is the killer's work to know it."

"The first ten were strong. Wrong, but strong — deep, and wet on the left side from the first, because the slit lung weeps air and blood both. He was on his knees by then. His legs gave as I withdrew the blade; he caught my sleeve going down, and I went to one knee with him so that his grip would not have to hold his weight. My hand stayed over the wound. It changed nothing. It was never meant to change anything."

"The middle twenty were labor, and I will not call it anything else. The chest fills, the lung is crushed by the blood from without while it bleeds from within, and the body spends itself buying air it cannot keep. His breaths came faster, then shallower. The pulse in his throat raced, then fluttered, the way a flame does before it goes. The grey came up under his skin — lips first, then the hollows of his face. There was blood at his mouth, bright, from the lung. The vessel's blood never left his chest. I have told you that, and it remains true, and it is why the stones were not what you expected."

"His eyes stayed clear. That is the thing I will carry from this morning, if I carry one thing: he was present for the whole of it. I have seen men look inward, gone somewhere behind their own faces while the body finishes without them. He did not. He looked at me. I was the last thing he looked at, and I did not look away. That, too, is owed."

The bearers' tread kept its distance behind them, steady as a pulse. Auren did not turn.

"You asked what he said. I will give it to you as it was said, because last words are part of the account and paraphrase is a curtain. His first words were: *Finish it.* I told him the truth: *It is finished.* He took that the way he took everything that morning — he tested it. His hand went to his own chest, over mine, and he read himself the way men who have fought long enough learn to read. *The vessel,* he said. It was not a question, but I answered it as one: *Yes.* He nodded once, as if I had confirmed a passage of play. Then he said: *The stone was wet.*"

"That was the whole of his account of his own death, and it was accurate, and I told him so. Even the dying make their accounting, Del. His was four words long and there was not an error in it."

She walked a dozen strides in silence then, and the silence was not for effect — it was the space the next part required, and she gave it exactly that and no more.

"The last ten breaths, the pauses open between them. A breath, and then a longer nothing, and then another breath, and each one after a pause comes as a surprise to everyone but the dying man, who is past surprise. Somewhere in the last five, he tried to speak again. His eyes were on mine and he shaped the beginning of a word — her name, I believe, or the beginning of something meant for her — and the breath it rode on was the one that did not come back."

"What he meant to say, no one living knows. I will not guess at it. A guess would be a comfort, and comfort is a curtain, and the code forbids curtains. If Maren asks me whether he spoke of her, I will tell her the truth: he tried to. The trying is what there is. In my experience of eleven doors, the trying is not nothing to a widow. It is not enough, either. It is what there is."

"You asked what it looked like at the end. The last breath went out of him and did not come back, and I knew it was the last not by the stillness but by the eyes. They do not close — that is songs. They stop being looked out of. The light does not go; the looking goes. I have seen it eleven times and cannot say it plainer than that. His hand did not tighten at the end — that is songs as well. It opened, finger by finger, as the strength left it, and the crease it left in my sleeve is the one I am still wearing."

"I stayed the count of ten more, to be certain, because the code requires certainty and so did he. Then I closed his eyes. That is not in the code. That was mine. I lifted my hand from the wound and raised it, and the witnesses came forward. The dying is the duellist's; the death is everyone's. That is the form."

"It looked like work, Del. That is the honest answer. It looked like a man laboring, and then it looked like a man set down by his labor when the labor was done. I will not call it peaceful — *peaceful* is a curtain. It was not ugly. It was the arithmetic finishing itself, and a man declining to complain while it did."

She glanced at Del then, sidelong, without breaking her pace.

"Forty of his breaths. I have timed it since, without meaning to: the account of the wound, spoken at code pace, takes very nearly as long as his dying did. I have made nothing of that, except that it is so."

"Now you have all of it — the what, the where, the how, and the end. So I will ask you again, second, and this time you will answer from knowledge. She will ask whether he suffered. They always ask."

"What is your answer?"

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: My throat is tight again, but I give her what I know now, not what I wish I did. "He labored. He wasn't frightened. He understood what was happening to him." I look at her. "That's not comfort. It's the shape of it."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren walked the length of three more hedgerows before she answered, which was her way of saying the answer had been weighed rather than merely heard.

"Keep those words," she said at last. "They will hold. And I will tell you why they hold, so you know it is structure and not luck. You did not say he did not suffer. Everything else in your answer can survive the truth; that one phrase could not. He did suffer. Forty breaths of drowning on dry land is suffering, and if you told her otherwise and she learned it later — from a surgeon, from a bearer, from her own reading of his body when it is laid out — then every true thing you said would fall with the one false one. A single curtain, found out, and the whole account is suspect for the rest of her life. You gave her the shape instead. The shape cannot be found out, because the shape is what happened."

"You said he was not frightened. That is true, and it is also the thing she will most need to be true, so expect her to test it hardest. When she tests it, give her the evidence, not the assurance. He read his own wound and named it. He made his own account in four words, and there was not an error in it. Frightened men do not audit their own deaths. Let the evidence carry it — evidence carries further than comfort, and it does not ask to be believed twice."

"If she asks the question a second time — they sometimes do; it is not disbelief, it is the hope that the question was wrong — you may add this, because it is account and not comfort: he was not alone. His killer's hand was over the wound and his killer's eyes were on his, and neither was taken from him. I was there. It can be witnessed."

Then the road bent, and the house came in sight, and Auren stopped.

It was an ordinary house at the end of an ordinary lane, and it did not know yet. Smoke went up from the chimney, thin and unhurried. A child's rope hung from the ash tree by the gate. Somewhere inside, a morning was still intact — porridge, perhaps; a boy eating standing up; a woman who had not yet looked at the road. Auren looked at all of it the way she looked at everything that mattered, directly, and let Del look at it too.

"That is the worst of the approach, every time," she said quietly. "The house goes on with its morning. We are carrying the end of that morning up this road, and until I knock, it has not happened yet. Do not mistake the quiet for peace. It is only not-yet."

Behind them, at the bend, she raised one hand, and the bearers halted where they stood, the grey cloak still as stone.

"When the door opens, I speak first, and the words are the account's words, because the account does not change for a doorstep. His name first — the name comes before everything. Then mine. Then the fact, whole, in one breath, because a fact delivered in pieces is a cruelty done slowly. *Maren Caul. I am Auren. Your husband Edrin is dead by my hand this morning, lawfully met, and I have come to give you the account of it, if you will hear it.*"

"If you will hear it. Those words are hers. A widow is owed one choice on the worst morning of her life, and that is the one the code leaves her. If she refuses, we leave word where I can be found, and we go, and his friends carry him to his own door — not his killer. If she hears it, we go inside, or to her garden. Never across the threshold. You know why."

She started down the lane, and Del beside her, and the rope swung gently in the wind off the wet fields.

At the gate she paused, and gave Del the last of it — not instruction this time, but the thing itself, said once, the way she said things she would not say twice.

"The asking on the road was the hard part, and you have already done it. What remains is only the telling. Stand where she can see you."

Then she unlatched the gate, walked the path with the crease still twisted in her sleeve, and knocked — twice, precisely, without hurry. Somewhere inside, a chair moved, and footsteps came toward the door, and Auren waited. She always waited.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: When she's done I confirm it aloud and my voice does what it does. (OOC: write the full account, don't summarise or cut away -- the accounting is the whole point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
The footsteps came unhurried — a woman answering a knock at mid-morning — and the door opened on Maren Caul with a drying-cloth still in her hand.

She knew. Auren had said they always knew, and Maren Caul was not the exception. It did not come into her face as surprise but as the end of hope, her eyes going from Auren's face to the blade at her hip, to Del at her shoulder, to the crease twisted in the dark wool of Auren's sleeve, and back again. The cloth stopped moving. Behind her, the house's morning was still intact — a fire, the smell of oats, a girl's voice somewhere upstairs, singing to itself.

"Maren Caul," Auren said. "I am Auren. Your husband Edrin is dead by my hand this morning, lawfully met, and I have come to give you the account of it, if you will hear it."

One breath, whole. Maren did not fall. She went still in the way of a woman holding a house together with her body, and her hand found the doorframe.

"If I will hear it," she repeated. Nineteen years, and it was the one choice left to her; she took it the way her husband had taken his wound — she tested it first. "And if I will not?"

"Then I leave word where I can be found, and his friends carry him to his door, and I do not trouble you again unless you send for me."

"Where is he?"

"At the bend of the lane, in the care of four men who knew him, covered in a good cloak. He does not come to his door until you know what is coming to it."

Something in that reached her — that he was near, and had been kept from coming home as rumour. "I will hear it," she said, and stepped back from the door, which was the only invitation the code required.

The girl came halfway down the stairs at the sound of strangers — nine years old, her father's chin — and Maren sent her up again, gently, with a reason about porridge that they both knew was not the reason. The door upstairs did not quite close. The boy came instead: fourteen, his father's build beginning in his shoulders, and he put himself between Auren and his mother in the kitchen doorway and would not be sent anywhere, and Maren did not send him. Auren had predicted all of it, and softened her face at none of it.

Inside, then. Maren stood at the table, the cloth still in her hand, and Auren faced her squarely, as she had faced the witnesses, and gave it the way the code wanted it given — the name before everything.

"Edrin Caul is dead by my hand, and this is the account of it.

"The fourth pass. He came in high, committed to the cut, and his front foot went half a hand's width on the wet stone. I did not beat his blade. I did not need to. I put mine where his line opened and let his own weight carry him onto it. The point entered below the fourth rib on his left side and travelled upward the length of my hand. It opened the lung. It cut the great vessel above the heart. There was no withdrawing it clean, and I did not pretend otherwise to him.

"He lived perhaps forty breaths after. He knew what had been done to him — I have seen men who did not know, and he was not one of them. He did not cry out. He asked me to finish it, and I told him the truth, that it was already finished. He set his hand to his own chest, over mine, and read his wound the way men who have fought long enough learn to read, and he named it: the vessel. He was right. His own account of his death was four words long — *the stone was wet* — and there was not an error in it. He died holding my sleeve, and I did not pull free.

"I claim no skill in the killing of him. His foot went and mine did not, and that is the whole of what separated us this morning. If any dispute the account, I will answer. It has been witnessed, and found complete."

The fire settled. Upstairs, floorboards held their silence. Del witnessed it aloud — the voice unsteady, the words whole, and whole was what was needed — and Maren looked at the second standing where she could see him, the living proof that someone had stood for Edrin at the end of it, and whatever she found there, she accepted with a single nod.

"Did he suffer?" They always asked first.

"He labored," Auren said. "I will not call it peaceful — peaceful is a word for songs, and you are owed the truth. Forty breaths of work, and he did the work without complaint. He was not frightened. Frightened men do not audit their own deaths; your husband named his wound correctly and accounted for himself in four words. And he was not alone. My hand was over the wound and my eyes were the last thing he looked at, and I did not look away. That can be witnessed. It has been."

"Did he speak of us?" Her voice did not break on it; she had clearly decided it would not. "Did he say anything — for us?"

"His words were for his death, and I have given them to you exactly. At the end he tried to speak again. He shaped the beginning of a word — your name, I believe — and the breath it rode on did not come back." Auren did not soften it, because softening was the dishonour. "What he meant to say, no one living knows, and I will not guess. A guess would be comfort, and comfort is a lie told to the grieving. The trying is what there is. It is not enough. It is what there is."

Maren closed her eyes then, and two tears got free of her anyway, and she did not wipe them. "The trying," she said, and said nothing more for a moment, and the boy stared at Auren with his fists clenched and managed perhaps half of his hatred before the rest of it went somewhere else.

"Why—" Maren began, and stopped, and made herself finish. "Why did you fight him?"

"The quarrel was lawfully met and fairly answered. It died in the yard. I will not lay it on you."

"How tidy," Maren said, with the first anger in it, which was better than the stillness, and Auren received it without defending herself.

"You may hate me for that. It changes nothing I owe you."

Maren looked at her for a long moment, and then her eyes went, as they had kept going all along, to the crease in the dark wool. "Is that—"

"His grip, as he left it. I have not straightened it. I thought you should see it before it was laundry."

Maren crossed the room and touched the crease once, with two fingers, the way one touches a relic, and then stepped back and folded her hands and was a widow with a household again.

"Bring him home," she said.

"I will go and fetch your husband now," Auren said, and turned for the door.

Which was when Tam — who could not reach Auren, and had known it all along — rounded on the one he could reach, fists white, voice breaking, and demanded of Del: "You stood for him. That's what a second does. So tell me — did my father die well?"

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "He died well," I say, my voice quiet but clear in the kitchen. "He didn't cry out. He knew what was happening to him, and he held onto the truth until he couldn't." I meet the boy's angry, frightened eyes and don't look away.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren did not move from the door. She had predicted this — the boy turning on the one he could reach — and prediction carried no obligation to interrupt it. She let Del's answer stand in the kitchen air the way the account itself stood: unsoftened, and able to bear its own weight.

Tam's fists stayed white. But the hatred had nowhere to go. The answer was true, and some part of him — the part that had his father's chin and his father's directness — knew it was true, and knowing it cost him something visible.

Then Auren spoke to the boy for the first time.

"It is witnessed," she said. "What he has told you is the account. I was there, and it is true. Your father did not cry out. He knew. And I will give you what is yours, because you are old enough to carry it and no one else can carry it for you."

She turned from the door fully.

"Your father made his own account of his death before he died. Four words. He said: *the stone was wet.* That was the whole of it, and there was not an error in it. The ground was lawful — we both walked it before the first pass and accepted it, and I would tell you if we had not. His foot went and mine did not. That is not a flaw in him. It is the nature of stone and rain and men. A man who can audit his own dying is not afraid of it."

"Those four words are your inheritance from this morning. Not the quarrel — the quarrel died in the yard and does not come home. The words are yours. No one can add to them, and no one can take them from you, and when you are older you will find they are enough."

Tam's mouth worked. He did not say the words aloud, but she watched him take hold of them, the way a boy takes hold of a rail in the dark.

"I am going to bring your father home now," Auren said.

"I'm coming." It was not a request.

Maren moved — half a step, the beginning of a refusal — and Auren, who did not soften things, did not soften this either. But she gave the mother the decision, because it was hers.

"That is yours to say, not mine. I will tell you only what is true: the bier is heavy and the road is not long, and he is strong enough for one of those and not the other. He will carry his father whether it is today at the end of the lane or twenty years from now in the dark. Men do. Better the first, where we can see him do it."

Maren looked at her son for a long moment. Then she reached out and straightened his collar, once, with the cloth still in her other hand.

"Carry him steady," she said.

The walk back to the bend was short and silent. Halfway down the lane, out of the boy's hearing, Auren spoke once, without turning her head.

"Properly answered."

The bearers stood where they had been left, patient as men who had done this before, the bier between them and the grey cloak still as stone. Auren stopped the boy a pace short of it.

"He is under the cloak, composed by men who knew him. His eyes are closed — I closed them. You may look before we lift him, or not. Both are allowed, and no one here will carry either choice against you."

Tam looked at her, and then at the cloak, and nodded once.

Auren drew the cloth back herself, from the face only. Edrin Caul lay grey and composed, his hands folded, and he looked like what he was — a man set down by his labor when the labor was done. Whatever the boy had braced for, this was not it. The dead are smaller than their absence. His eyes ran, but his face held, and he did not look away until he had finished looking.

"You may cover him," Auren said.

The boy drew the cloth back over his father's face with a care that cost him everything visible, and Auren watched him do it, and gave no sign of watching.

"Take him up," she said.

The grey-bearded bearer yielded his corner without being asked, and Tam set his shoulder under the front left, and the weight came down onto him — the first true weight of the day — and his knees took it, and he held.

"I walk before him," Auren said. "The boy carries the front left. The rest of you know your work." She looked to Del, and her voice did not change, but the words were not for the bearers. "You stood in his place this morning, second. Walk at his shoulder now."

Then she turned, and the procession came down the lane at a walking pace, and the house came in sight with its thin smoke and its morning ended. Maren stood in the open doorway with her hands folded. The rope swung gently from the ash by the gate. Upstairs, at the small window, a girl's face was pressed to the glass.

Auren did not hurry them. He had waited all morning to come home. He could take the lane at a walk.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I walk at the bier's edge, my hand not touching but ready. The boy's knuckles are white on the wood. At the door, I stand where Maren can see me.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
At the threshold, Auren stepped aside.

She had walked before him the whole of the lane, but she did not cross into his house ahead of him. She stood flat against the doorframe and let the bier pass her — the boy's white knuckles first, then the grey cloak, then the bearers — and Edrin Caul entered his own house before his killer did, which was right. It was his house. She was only ever a guest in his death.

"Where will you have him?" Auren asked.

"The table," Maren said.

His bowl was still on it. Porridge, half-finished, a spoon laid across the rim — the morning, interrupted, exactly where he had left it. Maren took the bowl up herself and set it on the shelf, and no one offered to help her, because some things a widow does with her own hands or not at all.

The bearers turned the bier in the small room, careful as men carrying glass.

"Down slow," Auren said. "On my count. He has had his last fall; he does not get another. One — two —"

The weight came off Tam's shoulder by degrees, and the table took his father, and the boy stood there a moment with his arms still curved around a burden that was no longer his to hold.

"Steadily carried," Auren said. "Front corner, the whole of the lane, set down without a jar. It is witnessed, and I will say so to anyone who asks, at any time." She gave the boy that the way she gave everything — without warmth to soften it, which was the only way it could be believed. "That is yours now. No one can take it from you."

On the stairs, the girl had come down after all.

Lili stood at the newel post in her stocking feet, one hand on the rail, and looked at the grey shape on her mother's table. Maren did not send her back up. She held out her hand, and the girl came to her hip, and her eyes went from the table to the stranger with the blade.

"Are you the one?" Lili asked.

"Yes," Auren said. No smile, no softening of the face — she had none that would survive a nine-year-old's inspection. She inclined her head, once, the way one acknowledges a witness, and let herself be looked at for as long as the looking took, until the girl turned her face into her mother's skirt.

The grey-bearded bearer touched the table's edge once, two fingers, a private farewell. "The women will come to you before noon," he said to Maren. "We'll see to the watchers at the gate. He won't be left alone." Then the four of them went out into the lane, quiet as they had come, and would not be thanked for it.

Auren faced Maren across the table, with her husband's body between them, and finished it.

"The account has been given and witnessed. If you dispute any part of it, say where it fails, and I will answer."

"Not today," Maren said.

"Then it stands. And it stands tomorrow, and after." Auren's voice did not change; this, too, was form, and form was all she had left to give. "The questions will come later — they come at night, usually, when the house has gone quiet and the account starts to grow in the dark. When they come, send for me. Word left at the fencing salle in town reaches me within a day. I will come, and I will answer, as many times as asked. The account does not tire, and neither does the obligation. It does not close. Not while you live."

Maren looked at her for a long moment — nineteen years a duellist's wife, measuring the woman who had finally collected on the debt that life had always carried.

"You have done what you came to do," she said at last. "Go home, Auren."

"That is yours to say," Auren said, and accepted the dismissal as she had accepted the hatred — without defending herself against it.

Maren's eyes went to Del then, standing where she could see him, the living proof. "Thank you," she said, "for standing for him."

At the gate, Auren stopped.

The rope swung gently from the ash. Behind them the house stood with its door open and its smoke going up, and inside it a family was beginning, at last, the grief that had been walking toward them all morning at a bearer's pace.

Auren looked down at her sleeve. The crease was still twisted into the dark wool where Edrin Caul's grip had left it, carried through the yard and the road and the door, shown to the one person it belonged to. She smoothed it flat with her palm, once, without ceremony.

"Laundry," she said.

Then she turned to Del, and gave the second the last of the form, because the code had one more word in it and she would not leave it unspoken.

"Your standing is witnessed and complete. You kept your eyes open at every point where closing them was available to you — in the yard, at the door, at the table. The code has no more of you today. What you carry from here is yours." She looked up the road, the way back, empty and ordinary. "But you know where I am found now, the same as she does. That does not close either."

She started walking, and did not look back at the house again. It was no longer hers to look at.

"The road back is shorter," she said. "It always is. That is not mercy. It is only that we are no longer carrying anyone."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: We walk awhile in quiet. I can still feel the shape of the porch floorboard under my boot, the exact grain of it. "Did she know?" I ask finally. "The daughter. When she asked if you were the one."
