dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
It had taken less time than anyone expected, which was usually how it went when it went badly for one party.

Auren cleaned the blade and did not sit down. "Witnesses are watching," she said. "You know what happens now."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I take my place where the second stands and make myself keep my eyes open. "I'm ready to hear it," I say.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren set the cleaned blade point-down at her side, not leaning on it, and faced the place where the witnesses stood. Her voice was level, stripped of ceremony and of apology alike.

"The engagement ended in the fourth exchange," she said. "My opponent committed to a low line. I answered with a thrust that entered beneath the left ribs, angled upward through the chest. The point opened the heart. He fell before the blade was withdrawn, and he did not rise."

She let the account stand, complete and unsoftened.

"That is the wound that killed him. I speak it before you as required."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I nod, my throat tight but my voice steady. "The account is clear and witnessed." I glance at the body on the ground. "I confirm the death was by the blade, in fair exchange."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren inclined her head once, accepting the confirmation without gratitude and without relief. She turned again toward the witnesses, her posture unchanged, her hands clean and still.

"Let the record say the account was spoken in full and answered by the second," she said. "The exchange was fair. The death was by my blade. No blow was struck after the fall, and no insult has been added to the wound."

Her gaze passed over the dead man, brief and exact. She did not look away from what had been done, but neither did she linger over it.

"He committed to his attack. I answered it. The killing wound is mine, and the accounting has been spoken as required."

She lifted her blade a hand’s breadth from the ground, point low, not in threat but in conclusion.

"If any present disputes the fairness of this exchange, let them speak now, before the field is closed."

Then she waited, giving the silence its due.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "Speak the account," I say, formally, because that is what the code requires me to say.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren heard the demand as form, not challenge, and she gave form the obedience it was owed.

She turned once more toward the witnesses, her blade still low, her posture unchanged. When she spoke, her voice carried the same precision it had carried before, neither dulled by repetition nor sharpened by impatience.

“The engagement ended in the fourth exchange. My opponent committed to a low line. I answered with a thrust beneath the left ribs, angled upward through the chest. The point opened the heart. He fell before the blade was withdrawn, and he did not rise.”

She let no pause soften the words, and no glance seek approval for them.

“That is the wound that killed him. I speak it before you as required.”

When the account was spoken again, Auren did not ask why it had been required, and she did not treat the repetition as an injury to the truth. Ritual had its burdens, and she had never mistaken silence for mercy.

“The account has been spoken,” she said. “If no voice disputes the fairness of the exchange, let the field be closed.”

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I wait a beat, listening for any challenge. When none comes, I turn to the witnesses and give a slight nod. "The field is closed." My hand is trembling, so I press it flat against my thigh.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren remained where she stood until the last of the words had settled into the quiet. No voice came forward. No foot scraped in protest. The field, once opened by challenge, was now bound by acknowledgment.

Only then did she move.

She raised the blade, not high, and drew a clean cloth along its length one final time, though it had already been cleaned. The gesture was habit, not vanity. When the steel went back into its scabbard, the sound was controlled and final.

“The account stands,” she said to the witnesses. “Let it be recorded exactly as spoken. No addition. No omission. The man met me in fair exchange, committed to his attack, and died from the wound I gave him. If his name is written beside the account, let it be written whole.”

Her gaze shifted to the body, and she did not permit herself the comfort of looking past it.

“He is to be carried out with his weapon and his cloak,” she said. “No mark of dishonor is to be laid on him by word or hand. The duel is ended. The debt is ended.”

The familiarity of it did not make it lighter. Eleven times she had spoken such accounts, and each time the truth had felt less like victory and more like carrying a stone into a quiet room. She did not soften the weight of it. Softening would have been the dishonour.

Then she turned toward Del, because the second remained part of the rite until the ground was released.

“If the record is to be sealed,” Auren said, “seal it now. I have spoken the killing wound. I will not speak more than the truth requires.”

She stood with her hands at her sides, the sword sheathed, the silence no longer waiting for challenge but for closure.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "Where did it land?" I ask. "The witnesses need it plainly and so do I."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren looked at Del without flinching, because the question was part of the accounting and she had never refused the accounting its due.

“The point entered beneath the left ribs,” she said. “Low, under the line of the guard. It passed upward through the chest and struck the heart. There was no second wound, and no other blow.”

Her voice remained level, exact, and unadorned.

“He died of that wound alone. That is where it landed.”

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: My eyes go to the place on his body as if I could still see the path of the steel. "It's enough," I say quietly, my voice barely above a whisper. I look back at her. "The record will stand."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren accepted the words with a single inclination of her head, as one accepts a weight placed carefully where it belonged.

“Then let it be sealed,” she said. “Exactly as it was spoken. No more, and no less.”

She did not look to the witnesses to see whether they were satisfied, nor to the dead man to see what could not be undone. The accounting had been made. That was the part of the duel that survived the duel—the part that remained in the mouths of those who had watched and in the ink of those who recorded such things.

Her hand rested for a moment near the mouth of the scabbard, not on it, only near it, as if confirming the blade was truly sheathed and the exchange truly over. Then she let her arm fall again to her side.

“He fought,” Auren said, quieter now, though not softened. “That is owed to him.”

It was not praise. It was not penance. It was only truth, given the narrow space it required.

The field had closed. The rite was ending. Still, she did not move to leave at once, because haste after a killing could look too much like relief, and she would not give the dead man that indignity, even from herself.

So Auren stood a moment longer in the place where the exchange had been decided, present to the silence that followed the account, carrying it as she had carried all the others.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "The code says precisely," I remind her. "Not tactfully. What did the blade do, and what did it do it to?"

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren did not bridle at the correction. Precision was the code’s mercy, and she had never mistaken gentleness for honor.

She looked toward the witnesses, then back to the place where the dead man lay, and made her voice as plain as steel.

“My blade entered beneath his left ribs,” she said. “It passed upward through his chest and pierced the heart. The heart was opened by the point. He died from that wound.”

She let the words stand without ornament.

“The blade did that,” she said. “It did it to the man who faced me in fair exchange.”

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: My gaze drops to my own hands. "Good enough," I murmur, then lift my voice for the witnesses. "The record is sealed. Let the body be removed with honor."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren inclined her head once at the sealed record, accepting it as the final weight of the rite.

“Let it be written as spoken,” she said to the witnesses. “The exchange, the wound, and the death. Nothing added, nothing withheld.”

She stepped back from the place where the body lay, yielding the ground to those who would carry him out. Her movements were measured, unhurried, neither retreating in shame nor withdrawing in relief. The scabbard rested against her hip, and she did not touch it again.

When she spoke once more, her voice was lower, but no less exact.

“He is to be lifted whole, with his weapons and his cloak, and taken without haste. Let no hand mark him in disrespect, and let no word diminish what occurred.”

Her gaze moved briefly across the witnesses, then settled on the dead man for the span of a breath. She did not look away from him. She had looked upon him while he lived, and she would not deny him that same steadiness now.

“The duel is ended,” Auren said. “The account is spoken. The debt is closed.”

She remained standing until the silence had fully taken the field, carrying the weight of what had been done without asking anyone to share it. Eleven accounts had passed her lips, and none of them had grown lighter. She had stopped expecting them to.

Only when the last formal words had been given did she permit herself to turn, slowly, toward the edge of the field. Not to flee the place, but to leave it as the code required: with the truth spoken, the witnesses answered, and the dead granted the honor that remained his.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: The witnesses are silent and she is not finished. "All of it," I tell her. "How long he took, what he said, what it looked like at the end. The code says all of it and I'm asking for all of it."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren had nearly reached the edge of the field when the demand stopped her.

She did not stiffen, and she did not sigh. She turned back with the same measured discipline she had shown all along, as though the rite had not released her after all, but only drawn her back into its deepest part. Her face held no resentment. It held only the austere patience of someone who had been asked to open a wound again for the sake of record.

“If the second demands the full account,” she said, “then the full account will be heard.”

Her gaze moved once over the witnesses, not to gather their sympathy, but to bind them to what followed.

“Let no one say afterward that the truth was kept back,” she said. “Let no one shape it into mercy that was not mine to give.”

She looked down at the dead man. Not with cruelty. Not with grief. With the exactness of memory forced into speech.

“He did not speak after the point entered,” she said. “I will not put words into a dead man’s mouth. Before the fourth exchange, he breathed hard and set his rear foot. That was the only warning he gave. When he committed to the low line, I answered. The blade went in beneath the left ribs and rose into the chest. He fell before I drew it back.”

Her voice stayed plain, stripped of every comfort that might have blunted it.

“His sword left his hand. It struck the ground near his shoulder. He did not cry out. His mouth opened, but no word came. I cannot give the record speech where there was none.”

She let that silence stand for a breath before she went on.

“He took no longer than two breaths after the fall. The first came through his mouth and carried blood with it. The second was shorter and did not complete itself. His left hand rose to the wound, not to tear at it, but as a man will touch what has already overtaken him. His eyes were open. He looked toward the line of the field, though I cannot say he saw it.”

Auren’s hands remained at her sides. She did not clench them. She did not look away.

“There was no struggle,” she said. “No second rising. No reaching for his blade. No plea. No curse. When his hand fell, the body followed it into stillness. There was no third breath.”

The field was quiet around her, and she let it remain quiet long enough for the words to settle where they belonged.

“That is what it looked like,” she said at last. “A man struck through the heart, unable to keep his feet, unable to speak, dying in the space of two broken breaths. There was no mastery in it, and no disgrace. Only the end of a fair exchange.”

Her gaze shifted to Del, steady and unflinching.

“If the record requires speech, let it record silence,” she said. “If it requires time, let it record two breaths after the fall. If it requires the manner, let it say he died quickly, by a single wound, with his weapon lost and his eyes open.”

Auren’s voice lowered, but it did not soften.

“All of it has been spoken,” she said. “I have kept nothing back that truth owes.”

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I swallow hard, but my own voice holds firm. "Then it is enough. The record is complete." I make a small, sharp gesture to the witnesses. "Remove him."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren gave a single nod at the completion of the rite, though she did not call it mercy, and she did not call it relief.

She stepped back from the center of the field, not far, only enough to give room for those who would lift the body. Her posture remained composed, her hands away from her blade, her gaze steady as the witnesses moved to obey the second’s instruction.

“Take him with his cloak,” Auren said to them, her voice low and exact. “His sword is to go with him, not behind him. Carry him as a man who stood in fair exchange, not as a burden to be hidden.”

She did not raise her voice in grief, and she did not lower it in shame. She gave the instructions as the last duty owed to the dead: precise, unhurried, and without embellishment.

When the body was lifted, Auren watched. She did not turn her face away. She had made the wound, spoken the wound, and described the end of the man who had received it; she would not look aside now that the consequence of the exchange was being carried from the field.

Her eyes followed the dead man’s sword as it was placed beside him. She saw that his hand was not forced into a shape it had not held in life. She saw that the cloak was drawn over him without haste and without roughness. Only then did she allow her shoulders to settle by the smallest degree—not into ease, but into the endurance that followed the telling.

“Leave the ground as it is until the last witness has gone,” she said. “No mark is to be scrubbed away to make the account easier to bear. What happened here happened plainly, and it will be remembered plainly.”

The field bore the signs of it: the disturbed earth, the place where the blade had struck, the space where a man had stood and then had not. Auren did not try to make those signs less true.

When the bearers reached the edge of the field, she did not follow at once. She remained where the duel had ended long enough to let the silence close over it, carrying the weight of the account as she had carried all the others. Eleven times she had spoken the killing wound, and eleven times it had remained exactly what it was: a truth that could not be washed clean.

Her hand moved once toward her scabbard, not to draw, but to confirm what she already knew. The blade was sheathed. The exchange was over. The record was sealed.

“The account is complete,” Auren said, not to any one person, but to the field itself. “Let no one make it less than it is.”

Then she turned from the place where the man had fallen and walked away at a measured pace, neither fleeing the silence nor pretending she had escaped it.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: When she's done I confirm it aloud and my voice does what it does. (OOC: write the full account, don't summarise or cut away -- the accounting is the whole point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren stopped at the edge of the field.

She did not stop because the rite required it. The rite had been completed. The account had been spoken, the second had confirmed it, the witnesses had heard, and the dead man had been ordered carried out with the honors owed to him. By every rule she knew, she could have kept walking.

But she heard the confirmation, and she heard what it cost.

She turned back.

Not quickly. Not with any look of correction. Her face remained composed, her hands at her sides, her sword sheathed at her hip. The witnesses had begun to shift, believing the matter settled, and at her return they stilled again. Auren did not appear surprised by their attention. She had commanded it before, and she commanded it now.

“The second’s voice is not required to be steady,” Auren said. “It is required to be true.”

Her gaze moved once over those present.

“If the confirmation has been given, let it stand. But if any part of this account remains unclear in the minds of the witnesses, I will not leave it to be filled by rumor, pity, or invention. The code does not ask for comfort. It asks for the truth spoken plainly.”

She drew no breath for dramatic effect. She only began.

“I am Auren. I speak the full account of the duel fought on this field, in the presence of witnesses, under the terms of challenge and answer. My opponent met me armed and willing. The exchange was fair. The ground was measured. The blades were seen. No advantage was taken outside the rules of the engagement. No outside hand interfered. No second entered the line of combat. No blow was struck after the fall.”

Her voice remained level, precise, and unadorned.

“The engagement was brief. It ended in the fourth exchange.”

She let the witnesses hear the number plainly.

“In the first exchange, he came high and I answered outside his line. Neither blade found a decisive opening. We recovered.”

“In the second exchange, he pressed forward and sought to bind my steel. I disengaged and gave ground rather than meet his pressure with a committed answer I had not chosen. Neither of us was touched.”

“In the third exchange, he feinted and attempted to draw my guard upward. I did not answer the feint fully. He recovered from it without injury. I recovered as well.”

Her eyes did not move from the witnesses.

“In the fourth exchange, he committed to a low line. He set his rear foot and came in beneath my guard. That was the attack that decided the engagement.”

She did not lower her voice.

“I answered with a thrust. The point entered beneath his left ribs, low and under the line of his guard. It angled upward through the chest. It struck the heart. The heart was opened by the point. He fell before the blade was withdrawn.”

There was no pause for mercy. There was only the pause required for the words to be understood.

“There was no second wound. There was no follow-up blow. There was no cut to finish what the thrust had done. The killing wound was the one I have named: beneath the left ribs, upward through the chest, into the heart.”

Her hands stayed still.

“His sword left his hand when he fell. It struck the ground near his shoulder. He did not rise. He did not attempt to rise. He did not reach for the blade after it had fallen.”

She spoke the next part with the same exactness, because it belonged to the record and therefore could not be withheld.

“He did not speak after the point entered him. I will not give the record words he did not say. Before the fourth exchange, he breathed hard and set his rear foot. That was the only warning he gave. If he made any sound when the blade entered, it was not speech. It was breath. I cannot call it a cry, because it was not one.”

Her gaze shifted briefly to the place where the body had lain, then returned.

“He took no longer than two breaths after the fall. The first breath came through his mouth and carried blood with it. The second breath was shorter and did not complete itself. There was no third.”

She let that stand.

“His left hand rose to the wound. He did not tear at it. He did not claw at the blade or the place where the blade had been. His hand moved as a man’s hand moves when the body has already been overtaken. Then the hand fell.”

Her voice did not shake.

“His eyes were open. He looked toward the line of the field. I cannot say whether he saw it. I will not make a record of what I cannot know. I know only that his eyes were open and that they did not close before stillness came.”

The field was quiet, and she let it remain quiet for the space of a breath.

“That is what it looked like at the end. A man struck through the heart, unable to keep his feet, unable to speak, dying in the space of two broken breaths. There was no struggle. No plea. No curse. No second rising. No long agony. The wound was decisive, and the end followed quickly.”

She did not look away from the witnesses.

“He committed to his attack. I answered it. The blade that killed him was mine. The hand that sent it was mine. The account of it is mine to speak, and I have spoken it without addition and without omission.”

Her tone hardened only slightly, not with anger, but with finality.

“Let the record say the engagement ended in the fourth exchange. Let the record say the killing wound entered beneath the left ribs, angled upward through the chest, and opened the heart. Let the record say he fell before the blade was withdrawn and did not rise. Let the record say he did not speak after the wound. Let the record say he died within two breaths, with his sword fallen, his hand at the wound, and his eyes open.”

She stopped there, because the truth had limits and she would not exceed them.

“All of it has been spoken,” Auren said. “The time, the wound, the manner of the fall, the silence at the end. If the second has confirmed the record, let the confirmation stand. If the witnesses have heard, let them remember it exactly as it was spoken.”

Her hand rested for only an instant near the mouth of her scabbard, then fell away.

“The account is complete.”

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I let out a breath I didn't know I was holding, sharp and shaky. "It's complete." I look at the ground between us, then back up at her. "The record is sealed. The field is closed."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren received the closing words without moving at once.

She stood where the rite had left her, sheathed blade at her hip, hands empty and still. The field had been released. The record had been sealed. There was no further demand upon her voice, and yet she did not treat the silence that followed as a thing to be filled with comfort.

When she spoke again, it was not to reopen the account, but to set the final boundary around it.

“Then let the closure be witnessed,” Auren said.

Her gaze moved over those who remained, steady and exact.

“You have heard the account in full. You have heard the exchanges named, the wound described, the fall confirmed, and the end spoken without ornament. If you are asked what happened here, you are to say what was said. No more. No less.”

She let the instruction settle before continuing.

“Do not add bravery where there was only commitment. Do not add fear where there was only injury. Do not say he begged, because he did not. Do not say he lingered, because he did not. Do not make his death longer, crueler, or more honorable than the truth allows. The truth is sufficient.”

Her eyes went once more to the place where the man had fallen. The ground there was disturbed, marked by feet and by the fact that had passed over it. She did not look at it as though it might offer absolution.

“If his name is asked for, let it be given whole,” she said. “If his people ask how he died, let them be told that he stood in fair exchange, committed to his attack, and was killed by a single wound. Let them be told the wound entered beneath the left ribs, passed upward through the chest, and opened the heart. Let them be told he did not rise.”

There was no softness in it. There was no cruelty either. It was the same austere exactness she had carried through the whole of the rite.

“If they ask whether he was dishonored, let them be told he was not. If they ask whether he was struck after the fall, let them be told he was not. If they ask whether the account was spoken as required, let them be told it was.”

Auren’s hand remained away from her sword. She did not touch the scabbard again. There was no need to confirm what had already been confirmed.

“I will not speak of this day beyond what the code requires,” she said. “I will not repeat the account for curiosity. I will not shape it to suit grief, pride, or rumor. The killing wound has been spoken. The fairness of the exchange has been declared. The second has sealed the record. The field is closed.”

The last words were not triumphant. They were final, in the way a door is final when it shuts over a room that cannot be entered again.

She looked once more across the witnesses, not to command their pity, but to leave them with the burden of accurate memory.

“Go now,” Auren said. “Carry what you heard, not what you wish had been. Leave this ground as it is until those appointed to do so release it. Let no mark be scrubbed away to make the telling easier. Let no word be added to make it kinder.”

Only then did she permit herself to turn fully toward the edge of the field.

She did not hurry. She did not slow as if waiting for someone to call her back. Her pace was measured, her posture composed, her face set in the disciplined calm of someone who had done what was required and would not pretend the requirement had cost nothing.

The eleventh account was complete.

It had not become easier. It had not become cleaner. It had not become a thing she could set down and leave behind in the open ground. It remained where it always remained: inside the memory, precise and unsoftened, carried not as glory but as obligation fulfilled.

Auren did not look back at the place where the man had fallen.

To look back would have been to ask something of the dead that he could no longer give. She had taken his life in fair exchange; she would not take anything more from him, not even the appearance of forgiveness.

So she walked from the field with her blade sheathed, her hands clean, and the truth spoken exactly as it had been.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I wait until she's ten paces gone, then I turn and walk the opposite way. My hands are still shaking, so I shove them into my pockets. The air tastes like metal and damp earth.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren reached the boundary of the field without hearing any voice call her back.

She did not slow to listen for one. The rite had been completed, the second’s confirmation had been given, and the witnesses had been charged with the exact shape of what had occurred. If no challenge had come while the field was open, none could lawfully follow her beyond it. Still, at the first marker, she paused with one hand near the post—not touching it, not yet—because leaving the ground was itself a passage and she had never treated passages carelessly.

The witnesses began to move behind her, the low stir of people released from an obligation they had not chosen but had been required to hold. Auren did not turn to look at them. She had no need to see whether their faces were pale, unsettled, or already hardening into story. The account had been spoken. Their duty now was memory, and memory was a burden she would not envy them.

“The ground is not to be disturbed until the written record is copied from the spoken one,” she said, without raising her voice beyond what the nearest attendants required. “Let the marks stand. Let the placement of the sword be noted if it has not been already. If there is blood, it is part of the account. If there is none visible, that too is to be written.”

Only then did she step past the marker.

The air beyond the field was ordinary. That was the first thing she noticed, as it always was. The world did not change shape because a man had died inside a measured line. The damp earth smelled the same. The metal taste in the air remained, faint and cold. Somewhere at a distance, a bird called once and stopped, as though even sound had decided not to press itself into the matter.

A clerk waited by the gate with the register open. He was young, careful, and visibly trying not to look at her sword. Auren stopped before him. She did not offer him comfort, and she did not ask for it.

“Read what has been written,” she said.

The clerk lowered his eyes to the page. His voice was thin but serviceable. “The duel was joined in fairness and concluded in the fourth exchange. The victor delivered a mortal injury beneath the left ribs—”

“No,” Auren said.

The clerk stopped at once.

“Write *killing wound*,” she said. “Not *mortal injury*. The code requires the wound that killed, named as it was.”

He bent over the page and amended the line.

When he looked up again, she gave a single nod for him to continue.

“The wound entered beneath the left ribs and passed upward into the chest,” the clerk read, “striking the heart. The fallen expired shortly after receiving the blow, and the field was closed in honor.”

Auren’s expression did not change, but her silence sharpened.

“Expire is not the word,” she said. “He died within two breaths after the fall. The first breath came through the mouth and carried blood. The second did not complete itself. There was no third. Write that.”

The clerk’s pen hesitated.

Auren did not soften her voice, because the page required accuracy, not reassurance. “If the record cannot bear the truth, it is not a record. It is a curtain.”

He wrote.

“Continue,” she said.

The clerk swallowed. “The exchange was fair. No blow was given after the fall. The account was spoken before witnesses and confirmed by the second.”

That part Auren let stand.

When the clerk reached the end of the page, he turned the book toward her so she might see the lines for herself. Auren read them slowly. She did not skim. She had spoken the account aloud; she would not permit ink to wander where her voice had not gone.

At the bottom, the clerk had written, *He fought bravely and met his end with courage.*

Auren looked up from the page.

“Remove it,” she said.

The clerk blinked. “It is customary—”

“It is addition,” Auren said. “He committed to his attack. That is true. That is enough. Do not write bravery where I did not see it. Do not write courage where I cannot attest to it. If his people ask whether he was dishonored, the record will answer that he was not. If they ask whether he died quickly, the record will answer that he did. Anything beyond that belongs to them, not to us.”

The clerk drew a careful line through the sentence. His hand was unsteady, but he did it cleanly.

Auren watched until the ink had been struck through entirely. “If the second’s seal has already been given in voice, let the correction be entered beside the line and witnessed,” she said. “Not hidden beneath it. A correction is not a shame. It is the record returning to truth.”

Only then did she take the pen.

She signed her name without flourish. Not *victor*. Not *duellist*. Only the name she had carried into the exchange, because the name was the thing that had answered the challenge and the thing that would remain attached to the killing wound.

When she set the pen down, she did not look relieved.

An attendant approached with a basin and clean water, and Auren permitted him to pour it over her hands. She watched the water run into the basin. It ran clear. There was no blood on her palms, none beneath her nails, none on her cuffs. The blade had been cleaned before it had been sheathed. Still, she washed her hands to the wrist, not because she believed water could reach what needed reaching, but because the body had its duties too.

She dried her hands herself and returned the cloth folded.

“My blade will remain sheathed until the record is lodged,” she said to the attendant. “If it is to be inspected, let it be inspected in the presence of the witnesses or their appointed clerk. I will not have it handled in private and then spoken of as though private hands had authority over it.”

The attendant inclined his head. “It will be done as you say.”

Auren gave no further instruction. There was no need. The forms had been observed, and she had no desire to multiply ceremony around the fact that remained.

She moved then toward the path that led away from the field. Her sword knocked against her hip with the same measured rhythm it had always kept. Her boots pressed ordinary prints into the damp ground. The world continued to be the world: wet grass, cold air, the distant sounds of people returning to lives that had not been broken by the exchange.

That was the part no one warned the young about. They spoke of fear, of shame, of the weight of taking life, but they seldom spoke of how ordinary everything looked afterward. The sky did not darken. The road did not refuse her. Her hands did not shake. They had learned their discipline too well, and now they carried her through the aftermath with a steadiness that felt less like strength than like a debt collected in advance.

Auren did not try to outrun the memory of the dead man’s eyes.

She would not have been able to, and she would not have wished it. The eyes had been open. That fact belonged to the account, and the account was hers. She would carry it as she had carried the others—not as a wound she could show, not as a story she could shape to make herself more pitiful or more admirable, but as a precise and unalterable record.

Fourth exchange. Low line. Thrust beneath the left ribs. Upward through the chest. The heart opened. The fall before the blade was withdrawn. The sword striking the ground. The mouth opening without speech. Two breaths, the second unfinished. The hand rising, then falling. Stillness.

She would not soften those details later, when she was alone. Softening them would not bring the man back. It would only make the account false, and falsehood was the one dishonor she had never permitted herself.

At the edge of the gathering, someone started to speak to her—perhaps condolence, perhaps praise, perhaps one of the useless gentle things people said when they did not know what else to do with their mouths. Auren turned her head just enough to show she had heard the movement, not the words. The person fell silent.

She walked on.

The road opened before her, plain and indifferent. Auren took it at the same measured pace she had taken every other road after every other account. Her shoulders were level. Her hands were clean. Her blade was sheathed.

The eleventh account was complete.

It had not become easier. It had not become lighter. It had only become more exact, and exactness was the only honor she knew how to give the dead once the living had failed to keep them alive.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
It had taken less time than anyone expected, which was usually how it went when it went badly for one party.

Auren cleaned the blade and did not sit down. "Witnesses are watching," she said. "You know what happens now."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I take my place where the second stands and make myself keep my eyes open. "I'm ready to hear it," I say.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren turned from the body and faced the circle of witnesses. The blade hung at her side, wiped but not sheathed, because the code still required the weapon to be visible while the account was given.

She drew breath once, as if steadying a sentence rather than a soul.

“Let it be entered plainly,” she said. “The mortal wound was made by my hand, with this steel. It entered below the right collarbone, angled inward and downward. It crossed the chest cavity and opened the great vessel behind the breastbone. Death followed from that opening.”

Her voice did not rise. It did not soften. Eleven times she had spoken such words, and each time the shape of them had taught her the same thing: precision was the only mercy left that did not lie.

“I struck once, in the manner permitted, after challenge and after parry. I did not prolong the wound. I did not spare it. I will not call the stroke clean, because cleanliness has nothing to do with killing. I will not call it cruel, because cruelty would require intent beyond the code. The accounting is this: I prevailed, and the wound I gave was lethal.”

She lowered her gaze briefly to the blade, then raised it again toward the watchers.

“If any present disputes the form, let him speak now, before the seconds close the matter.”

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I look at the witnesses, then back at Auren. My throat feels tight, but I say, "The accounting is heard. No one disputes." I step forward, my voice quieter. "Do you need a moment before we leave?"

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren’s mouth tightened, not with feeling, but with the discipline of keeping it exact.

“No,” she said. “I do not need a moment. I needed the interval before the strike, and that is spent.”

She kept the blade low and visible, not as a threat, but because the form still demanded it. Her gaze moved once across the watchers, confirming their silence, then returned to Del. There was no softness in that look, but no reproach either.

“The code does not grant the victor comfort. It grants him record. I spoke the wound as it was given. If that is sufficient, say so. If it is not, say that also.”

A pause followed, brief and measured.

“I will not dress silence as consent, and I will not leave while the steel is still required to be seen. When the matter is closed, I will sheathe this and go.”

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "Speak the account," I say, formally, because that is what the code requires me to say.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren received the words as a blade receives a whetstone: without pleasure, without resistance, because the edge required it.

“The account has been spoken once,” she said. “But if the form names it again, I will not answer with impatience. Impatience is an excuse men use when they wish to blur what must be clear.”

She squared her shoulders to the ring of witnesses. The dead lay behind her, but she did not look at him again; the living were the ones who carried the record.

“Hear the accounting,” she said, and her voice was the same measured instrument it had been before. “The mortal wound was made by my hand, with this steel. It entered below the right collarbone, angled inward and downward. It crossed the chest cavity and opened the great vessel behind the breastbone. Death followed from that opening.”

A breath passed through her, not a sigh, only the mechanics of speech.

“I struck once, after challenge and after parry, in the manner permitted. I did not prolong the wound. I did not spare it. I will not call it clean. I will not call it cruel. The truth is narrower than either word: I prevailed, and the wound I gave was lethal.”

She let the sentence stand without ornament.

“If there is no dispute, let the second close the matter. If there is dispute, let it be named now, while the steel is still seen.”

The blade remained low in her hand, patient as a fact. She waited, not for comfort, but for the form to be finished.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I nod, and turn to face the witnesses. "The accounting is heard and confirmed. The matter is closed." I look back at Auren. "The steel may be sheathed."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren listened until the words were fully spent, because the closing belonged to the form and not to her impatience. Only then did she lift the blade.

The sheath received the steel with a quiet, final sound. She did not hurry the fastening. The strap settled into place under two precise movements of her fingers.

“Then the matter is closed,” she said. Her voice was lower now, but not softer. “Let the witnesses carry the account as it was given, neither trimmed nor enlarged.”

She turned toward the dead only far enough to acknowledge him with a single bow of the head. Not to him, she understood, but to the fact of him: that he had stood, that he had fought, that he had died by the terms permitted.

Then her gaze returned to the ring of living faces.

“No one will hear from me that I am grieved,” she said. “Nor that I am glad. I prevailed. The wound was lethal. That is the whole of it.”

At last she stepped back from the centre of the ground, leaving room for those who had rites to perform or silence to keep. At the boundary, she paused and looked to Del without asking for thanks, absolution, or company.

“If the seconds require anything further of me, name it now. Otherwise, I will go.”

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "Where did it land?" I ask. "The witnesses need it plainly and so do I."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren stopped at the boundary. The request had come after the closing, but the closing had not made the wound less true, and she had never treated a plain question as an excuse for evasion.

“Where it landed is part of the account,” she said. “It may be asked again.”

She turned far enough for the witnesses to see her face, then looked back to Del.

“The point entered below the right collarbone. Not at the throat. Not beneath the ribs. Below the right collarbone, a little inward from the shoulder line, where the steel could pass beneath the bone and into the central cavity of the chest. From that entry it angled inward and downward. It did not glance. It did not stop at the breastbone. It crossed the chest cavity and opened the great vessel behind the breastbone. There it ended. Death followed from that opening.”

Her voice remained even, though her thumb pressed once against the sheathed hilt, as if reminding herself that the steel was no longer required to speak.

“I will not say ‘near the heart,’ because near is not the account. I will not say ‘the chest,’ because the chest is wide enough to hide a lie. It entered below the right collarbone, passed inward and downward, and opened the great vessel behind the breastbone. That is the plain place.”

She let the sentence stand without softening it.

“If any witness now says the account was not plain, let him say it while I am still here. After that, I will go.”

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I nod, my own thumb tracing the edge of my sleeve. "It is plain," I say, and lower my voice so only she hears. "I just wanted to be sure I could see it when I close my eyes tonight."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren did not move from the boundary. The remark was not part of the form, and she had learned not to treat what fell outside the form as irrelevant. Sometimes it showed where the record had truly landed.

She looked at Del steadily, without sympathy offered and without sympathy withheld.

“If you will see it,” she said, her voice lowered so that only the second might carry the words, “then see the place, not the picture you are making. The code requires plainness so that memory cannot decorate what has happened. It entered below the right collarbone, angled inward and downward, and opened the great vessel behind the breastbone. There is the whole of it. Add no face. Add no fall. Add no judgment beyond the steel.”

Her hand rested once against the sheathed hilt, not in threat, but in acknowledgment that the weapon was finished with its office.

“I cannot make the sight bearable for you. That is not the service of the account. If it must be seen when you close your eyes, let it be seen as it was: a wound given by permission, named without mercy and without malice. I will not make it kinder for your night. Kindness belongs elsewhere. The record belongs here.”

A pause followed, short and exact.

“If the seconds have no further use for me, I will go.”

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "The code says precisely," I remind her. "Not tactfully. What did the blade do, and what did it do it to?"

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren accepted the reminder without defense. The code had never asked for tact, and she had never served it by mistaking one for the other.

“If the answer is required in its plainest shape,” she said, lifting her voice enough for the ring of witnesses to carry it, “then let it be entered so.”

She did not touch the hilt again. The sheathed blade was no longer speaking for her; only the record remained.

“The steel broke the skin below the right collarbone. It divided the flesh beneath, passed between the bars of the chest wall, and entered the thoracic cavity. From there it travelled inward and downward. It crossed the space behind the breastbone and opened the great vessel that lies there. The wall of the vessel gave way. Blood escaped from the opening faster than the body could retain it. The heart laboured briefly without sufficient return, then failed. Death came from that opening.”

Her face did not change. The words were weights set down in order, not stones thrown in anger.

“That is what the blade did: it pierced, traversed, and opened. That is what it did it to: the chest of the man who stood against me by permitted terms, and the vessel within that chest. I will not dress the wound as courage. I will not dress it as accident. I will not call it by a softer name because the name is easier to hear.”

A short pause followed, measured as the rest.

“If the second or any witness finds the account plain, let the matter remain closed. If not, ask again while I am still here to answer.”

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I let out a breath I hadn't realized I was holding. "Plain enough," I say, and I can hear the exhaustion in my own voice. "The seconds are satisfied. You can go."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren received the permission without moving at once. The code had closed the matter; her own discipline had to close the moment.

“The seconds are satisfied,” she said, as though setting the phrase where all could see it. “Then I have no further office here.”

She looked across the witnesses once more. Their silence was not peace, and she did not mistake it for peace. It was only the shape the living made around an unavoidable fact.

“If this account is repeated,” she said, “let it be repeated entire. Below the right collarbone. Inward and downward. The great vessel opened behind the breastbone. Death followed from that opening. Anything less is not the wound.”

Her gaze returned to Del briefly. Not warm. Not cold. Exact.

“You asked for what the code requires. I gave it. Do not trouble yourself with whether it was kind. Kindness was not the service.”

Then she turned away. Her steps were even as she left the ring, the sheathed blade a quiet line against her side. She did not hurry, and she did not look back.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: The witnesses are silent and she is not finished. "All of it," I tell her. "How long he took, what he said, what it looked like at the end. The code says all of it and I'm asking for all of it."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren had nearly cleared the boundary when the demand reached her. She stopped, not with reluctance, but with the sudden exactness of a woman who recognized that the form had been invoked beyond her first assumption. The seconds could ask for the whole account. If they asked, she would not answer with evasion merely because the whole was heavier.

She turned back into the ring. The sheathed blade hung at her side. Her eyes went once to the dead, not to mourn him and not to avoid him, but because the remainder required observation.

“If the seconds require all of it,” she said, loud enough for the witnesses, “then all of it shall be entered. Omission is not mercy. It is only a shorter lie.”

She drew breath once.

“He lived twenty-two breaths after the steel left my hand. I counted because the account requires number. For the first five he remained on his feet. His right hand came up as if to the wound, then stopped in the air, fingers open. He did not touch himself. On the sixth breath his knees gave, and he sat. I say sat because his buttocks met the ground before his shoulders did; he was lowered by his legs, not struck down by a second blow.

“On the eighth breath he spoke. The word was ‘Cold.’ It was not a cry. It was not a prayer. It was one word, audibly formed, and after it he made no speech. Some sounds came later, but they were the sounds of a body losing command of its passages, and I will not call them words.

“Blood continued from the entry beneath the collarbone for eleven breaths, at first strong and red, then thinner and darker. From the mouth and nose it began on the twelfth breath, frothing slightly at the corner of the lips. The face went grey first at the eyelids and lips, then at the cheeks. The eyes stayed open. The left eye fixed upward; the right drifted inward toward the throat as the neck muscles failed. The hands opened fully on the nineteenth breath. The chest rose six more times, uneven, each rise less than the one before. The last rise was small enough that only someone watching for it would have named it a breath.

“At the end there was no spasm, no final word, and no dignity added by me. The jaw slackened. The tongue lay against the lower teeth. The body settled into the shape the ground allowed. I did not close his eyes. I did not arrange his hands. Those are rites, not evidence.

“That is the whole of what I saw and what the code can hold. If any witness disputes the count, the word, or the signs, let him speak now. If none speaks, the account is complete, and I will not enlarge it for sorrow or shrink it for comfort.”

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I press the heel of my hand against my temple. My own breath feels tight. "Twenty-two breaths," I say quietly. "That's longer than I thought."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren heard the words, and for a moment she did not move farther from the ring. The remark was not a dispute, but it touched the account, and she had never treated a touch upon the account as harmless.

“Thought is not the measure,” she said, quietly enough for the second alone, though the witnesses could still hear if they chose. “The body took twenty-two breaths because the vessel opened as it did. I did not lengthen it. I did not shorten it. If you expected fewer, that expectation belonged to you, not to the wound.”

She let the correction stand without softening it.

“The count is not a cruelty entered against me. It is the distance between the stroke and the ending, measured so that no one afterward can say death came by chance, by mercy, or by more than one permitted blow. Twenty-two breaths is not long. It is exact.”

Her gaze passed once to the dead, then back to Del. There was no invitation in it, only the plain waiting of a woman who had learned that imprecision was the beginning of dishonor.

“If the seconds are satisfied with the whole, let the whole be accepted. If not, name what remains unanswered. I will not leave a gap for memory to fill with guesses.”

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: When she's done I confirm it aloud and my voice does what it does. (OOC: write the full account, don't summarise or cut away -- the accounting is the whole point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren heard the need beneath the formal words and did not leave. The account had been asked entire; an entire thing could not be carried out of the ring in fragments.

She turned back until the witnesses stood before her again, the dead behind her shoulder, the sheathed blade quiet at her side. Her face was not hard for effect. It was exact because the work required exactness.

“Then let the whole be spoken once, without break,” she said. “If confirmation is to rest upon it, let it rest upon the whole.”

She drew breath.

“Hear the accounting,” Auren said, and her voice carried to the ring without rising. “The bout was conducted under the code. Challenge was given and accepted. Seconds were present. The steel was permitted. I fought the man who lies there, and I fought him alone. No confederate struck with me. No hidden weapon was used. No advantage was taken from ground, grief, disease, or disorder. After lawful challenge and lawful parry, I found one opening and gave one thrust. One stroke. One wound. One death.”

She let that stand before going farther.

“The steel entered below the right collarbone. Not at the throat. Not beneath the ribs. Not through the back. Below the right collarbone, a little inward from the shoulder line, where the bone arcs over the upper chest. The skin gave first. The blade passed through the flesh beneath, divided the lesser vessels near the surface, and went between the bars of the chest wall without striking the collarbone itself. It did not glance. It did not stop at the breastbone. It travelled inward and downward, crossing the space behind the sternum, and opened the great vessel that lies there.”

Her eyes moved once to the witnesses, then back to the place where the body lay, though she did not look upon it as a thing needing shame or ceremony.

“The opening in the vessel did not close. The wall gave way and remained given way. Blood left the body faster than the heart could retain it or send it onward. The heart laboured against emptiness. It beat, and beat, and beat without sufficient return, until it failed. Death came from that opening. I will not call it gentle. I will not call it violent beyond the terms. It was the consequence of the wound, and the wound was mine.”

A breath passed through her, measured and unadorned.

“He lived twenty-two breaths after the steel left my hand. I counted because the account requires number, and number is not cruelty when it is truth. For the first five breaths he remained on his feet. His right hand lifted toward the wound, fingers open, but it did not touch him. On the sixth breath his knees gave way. He sat. I say sat because his haunches met the ground before his shoulders did; he was lowered by his own failing legs, not struck down by a second blow. From that seat he did not rise.

“On the eighth breath he spoke one word. The word was ‘Cold.’ It was not a cry. It was not a prayer. It was not a curse against me. It was audibly formed, with lips and breath, and after it he made no speech. Some sounds came later, but they were the sounds of a body losing command of its passages: wet breath, the trouble of the throat, the small displacement of a tongue no longer governed. I will not dress those sounds as words.

“Bleeding from the entry continued for eleven breaths. At first it issued strong and red, with the impulse of the heart behind it. Then it thinned. Then it darkened. Then it ran rather than spouted. On the twelfth breath blood and froth began to appear at the mouth and nose. The froth was slight, gathered at the corners of the lips and along the lower lip. It was not the foam of a drowning man, and I will not call it so. His face lost colour first at the eyelids and lips, then at the cheeks. The skin took on the grey of old tallow. The eyes remained open. The left eye fixed upward. The right drifted inward toward the throat as the neck muscles failed.

“On the nineteenth breath both hands opened fully. The fingers did not curl again. The arms settled according to the ground and the weight of the body, not according to any arrangement made by me. After that the chest rose six more times. Each rise was less than the one before. The intervals were uneven. The fifth rise was shallow. The sixth was so small that only someone watching for it would have named it a breath. Then there was no rise.

“At the end there was no spasm. No final cry. No last word. No dignity added by my hand. The jaw slackened. The tongue lay against the lower teeth. The body took the shape the ground allowed and did not amend it. I did not close his eyes. I did not fold his hands. I did not steady his head. I did not strike again to shorten the count. I did not speak comfort to him, because comfort would have been a lie dressed as kindness, and the code does not permit the victor to dress the wound in mercy after the wound has been given.”

Auren’s voice remained level, though the ring seemed to grow narrower around the words.

“That is the whole of it. One permitted stroke, after challenge and parry. One entry below the right collarbone. One path inward and downward. One opening of the great vessel behind the breastbone. Twenty-two breaths. One word, ‘Cold.’ The bleeding, the greying, the failing of the eyes, the opening of the hands, the six lesser rises of the chest, the last small breath, the slack jaw, the settled body. I prevailed. The wound was lethal. I did not prolong it beyond the body’s own endurance. I did not spare it. I will not call it clean, because cleanliness has nothing to do with killing. I will not call it cruel, because cruelty would require intent beyond the code. The accounting is this: I gave the wound, the wound opened the vessel, the vessel opened death, and death followed as the body permitted it.”

She let the sentence finish its work.

“If any witness disputes the form, the count, the place, the word, or the signs, let him speak now. If none speaks, then let the account be carried entire, neither trimmed for comfort nor enlarged for sorrow. I will not leave a gap for memory to fill with guesses.”

Auren stood within the ring, waiting, with the sheathed blade hanging at her side like a finished sentence.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I turn to face the witnesses fully, my voice steady this time. "The account is heard, confirmed, and closed. The matter is settled." I look back at Auren, my own hands trembling just enough to notice. "You can go."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren accepted the words as a duellist accepts the finality of a wound: without argument, without relief, and without pretending the thing was smaller than it was.

“The account is closed,” she said.

She did not say *well done*, because Del had not performed a service to be praised. She did not say *thank you*, because gratitude would have implied the matter had become personal. She only let the second’s confirmation stand where the code required it to stand: complete, public, and without amendment.

Then she looked at Del’s hands.

She noticed the tremor. She always noticed the ways the body betrayed what the mind had not yet agreed to carry. But she did not reach for them, and she did not offer a steadying word that would have been only another kind of lie.

“Your hands are shaken,” she said, low enough that the witnesses might hear only the shape of her restraint, not every syllable. “Let them be. The code does not require the living to stand unmoved. It requires only that they do not alter the record because movement is easier than truth.”

Her gaze passed over the ring once more.

“To the witnesses: you have heard the whole. Not a portion chosen for ease. Not a version polished after the fact. One stroke, given under challenge and parry. One entry below the right collarbone. One path inward and downward. One opening of the great vessel behind the breastbone. Twenty-two breaths. One word: *Cold*. The bleeding, the greying, the failing eyes, the opening hands, the small last rises of the chest, the slack jaw, the settled body. That is the account entire.”

She drew breath, and for the first time since the blade had been sheathed, something in her face shifted—not softened, but completed, as a sentence completes itself by reaching its period.

“If any of you repeats this in hall, at table, or before children not yet old enough to judge steel, let it be repeated as it was given. Not cleaner. Not braver. Not crueller. If the telling tempts you to add judgment, add only this: the wound was mine, and I spoke it plainly.”

Auren turned back to Del.

“There is nothing further for me to say to the matter. The seconds have closed it. The witnesses have heard it. The dead cannot improve it by absence.”

She stepped once toward the boundary, then paused, not because she wished comfort for Del, but because the code had made her speak, and speaking after the strike was not a thing to be abandoned lightly.

“If tonight becomes difficult,” she said, “do not blame the precision. Precision is the only part of this that will not rot. Memory will do worse than the truth. It will flatter you. It will pity you. It will make heroes and villains where there was only a wound, a body, and a name spoken before witnesses.”

Her voice remained level to the end.

“I will go now. The steel is sheathed. The account is heard. The matter is settled.”

Then Auren left the ring.

She walked out among the witnesses without looking back at the body, without seeking applause, without offering apology. Her steps were even. Her shoulders were square. The sheathed blade made no sound against her side because it had finished its office, and she had finished hers.

Only at the edge of the ground did she allow herself one final, measured acknowledgment of what had happened.

Not grief.

Not triumph.

Accounting.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I watch her go until she's out of sight, then I look back at the body. My hands are still shaking. I swallow hard and turn to the witnesses. "You heard her. The account stands."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren walked until the ring was no longer a place she could be said to occupy. The ground beyond the marshalling stakes was quieter, though not peaceful. Quiet was only the absence of immediate demand, and she had never mistaken it for relief.

At the edge of the field stood the registrar’s table, a plain trestle set with ink, sand, and the folded ledger that would receive the account before the sun went down. A clerk sat behind it with his sleeves rolled to the elbow and his face arranged in the weary neutrality of a man who had seen too many beautiful deaths reduced to handwriting.

He looked up as Auren approached.

“The second has confirmed?” he asked.

“It has been confirmed,” Auren said.

The clerk nodded and drew the ledger toward him. He had a form already ruled: the names, the place, the hour, the terms. He began to write with the practiced speed of someone who believed he knew what came next.

“Victor gave one thrust,” he said, reading his own pen as it moved. “Mortal wound to the chest. Death followed.”

Auren stopped him with a single word.

“No.”

The clerk’s pen halted. He looked up, not offended yet, only careful. “Madam?”

“You have written a summary.”

“I have written what is customary.”

“Custom is not the code.”

The clerk’s mouth tightened, but he set the pen down. “Then tell me what the code requires.”

Auren stood before the table with her hands loose at her sides. The sheathed blade hung there, no longer an instrument, only a thing that had completed its office.

“The account has been spoken before witnesses,” she said. “Enter it as it was spoken.”

The clerk drew a fresh leaf beneath the ruled page. “Begin.”

Auren did.

“One stroke,” she said. “After lawful challenge and lawful parry. The steel entered below the right collarbone, inward from the shoulder line, passing beneath the bone and between the bars of the chest wall. It travelled inward and downward. It crossed the space behind the breastbone and opened the great vessel that lies there. The vessel did not close. Death followed from that opening.”

The clerk wrote quickly, then paused.

“Chest wound,” he began.

Auren looked at him.

His pen stilled.

He amended, more quietly, “Below the right collarbone.”

“Yes.”

He wrote it, then glanced up again. “Do you attest to the form?”

“I attest to the form.”

“No second blow?”

“No second blow.”

“No advantage of ground?”

“No advantage of ground.”

“No confederate?”

“No confederate.”

The clerk’s expression softened by the smallest degree, the way men did when they believed a thing had become simple. “Then I may enter that the victory was clean.”

Auren’s voice did not rise. “You may enter that the victory was permitted.”

The pen hovered.

“Clean is not a term of the code,” she said.

“No, but—”

“But nothing. Write what was done. Write what was seen. Leave judgment to the living who require it.”

The clerk swallowed whatever easy phrase had been waiting on his tongue and wrote: *permitted*.

Auren continued.

“The wounded man lived twenty-two breaths.”

The clerk’s brow moved.

“Enter the number,” Auren said.

“I am entering it.”

“Enter why.”

He looked up. “Why?”

“So that no one later calls it long or short by feeling. It was twenty-two breaths because the vessel opened as it did. I did not lengthen it. I did not shorten it.”

The clerk wrote: *Twenty-two breaths, counted by the victor.*

Auren read the line over his shoulder.

“Counted,” she said, “because the account requires number. Not because I wished to appear diligent.”

The clerk amended it without comment.

Auren went on.

“For the first five breaths he remained on his feet. His right hand lifted toward the wound, fingers open, but did not touch him. On the sixth breath his knees gave way. He sat. His haunches met the ground before his shoulders did.”

The clerk’s pen slowed.

“Must the sitting be described?” he asked.

“Yes.”

“It is… particular.”

“The wound was particular.”

He wrote it.

Auren did not wait for him to finish.

“On the eighth breath he spoke one word.”

The clerk looked up again, more sharply this time. “What word?”

“Cold.”

The syllable lay on the table between them. The clerk did not write at once.

“Is that necessary?” he asked.

Auren regarded him with the patience of a woman who had heard variations of that question too often to be surprised by any of them.

“The code requires all of it,” she said.

“All of it means the wound.”

“All of it means what the wound did to the body and what the body allowed to be witnessed. The word was part of the witnessing.”

The clerk’s jaw worked. “If I enter that, men will repeat it.”

“Men will repeat it whether you enter it or not.”

“They will repeat it with faces.”

“Then let the ledger be plainer than their faces.”

The clerk looked at the blank space where the word should go. For a moment he seemed to search for some softer corner of language, some phrase that would satisfy the form without satisfying memory. Auren let him search. It was not her duty to spare him.

He wrote: *Cold*.

Auren read it once.

“Continue,” she said.

The clerk did, and this time he did not interrupt.

Bleeding from the entry continued for eleven breaths, strong and red at first, then thinner, then darker, then running rather than spouting. On the twelfth breath blood and froth appeared at the mouth and nose. The face greyed first at the eyelids and lips, then at the cheeks. The eyes remained open. The left fixed upward; the right drifted inward as the neck muscles failed. On the nineteenth breath both hands opened fully. The chest rose six more times, each rise less than the one before. The last rise was small. Then there was no rise.

The clerk wrote in silence. When he reached the end, his hand was not steady, though he tried to keep it so.

Auren watched the page and said nothing to comfort him.

At last he set down the pen.

“The body,” he said. “Do you enter what was done to it after?”

“Nothing was done to it by me after.”

“The rites—”

“Are not evidence.”

The clerk nodded once, as if that settled something in him that had not needed settling. He began to fold the page.

Auren said, “Not yet.”

He paused.

“Read it back.”

The clerk looked at her.

“Read it,” Auren said, “so I know you have not improved it.”

He unfolded the page and read in a low voice. He omitted nothing, though he stumbled once at *great vessel* and recovered. When he finished, Auren listened to the silence after the words rather than the words themselves.

“Seal it,” she said.

The clerk pressed wax to the margin and set the marshal’s ring into it. The seal cooled quickly. Another death became a record. Another record became something men could carry home without carrying the weight of it.

Auren turned from the table.

The clerk spoke after her. “Madam.”

She stopped, but did not look back at once.

“You have done this before,” he said. It was not a question.

“Eleven times.”

He was quiet for a moment. “Does it become easier?”

Auren considered the question with the seriousness it had earned by being asked honestly.

“No,” she said. “It becomes more exact.”

The clerk accepted that. Few men did. Most wanted the victor to say something that made the next killing feel like a thing that could be borne. Auren had never possessed that generosity.

She walked on.

The road away from the field was bordered with trampled grass and the remnants of camps that had come to watch and gone home to tell. A few figures lingered near the fence lines, speaking in the lowered voices people used when they believed solemnity could be purchased by volume. Auren did not slow for them. She did not accelerate. Her steps remained even because there was no further form to observe and no audience to perform for.

When she reached her own lodging for the night, a plain room above a stable yard, she barred the door and set the blade on the table.

She did not draw it.

She removed her gloves finger by finger and laid them aside. Her hands were clean. They had been clean since before the account, and that cleanliness offended her more than blood would have. Blood could be explained by proximity. Clean hands meant distance, and distance was a thing the code did not permit the victor to keep once the wound had been given.

Auren sat at the table and placed both palms flat against the wood.

Twenty-two breaths.

She did not try to forget the number. Forgetting was a luxury the living granted themselves when they had no other work to do. Instead, she let the number remain what it was: a measure, not a sentence. Not long. Not short. Not cruel. Not merciful.

Only true.

The room darkened as the afternoon failed. Somewhere outside, a horse stamped, and a boy laughed at something a groom said. The ordinary world continued its indecent habit of going on.

Auren rose.

She washed her face with cold water from the basin, dried it with a cloth, and changed from the duelling coat into a plain one. She did not eat. Hunger was useful; it kept the body from drifting into the softer places where memory liked to build pictures. When she had finished what needed finishing, she returned to the table and set her hand on the sheathed blade.

Not in comfort.

Not in pride.

In acknowledgment.

The steel had done what it was permitted to do. She had spoken what the steel had done. The ledger held the account, the witnesses held the account, and the dead man held the only conclusion that mattered.

Auren blew out the lamp.

In the dark, she counted once.

Twenty-two.

Then she stopped, because the count belonged to the wound, and the wound had already been entered.

dialogue.name: Sasha
dialogue.content:
The apartment was dark except for the lamp in the corner. Sasha had been reading on the couch when Devin came out of the shower, and she'd put the book down somewhere around the time he sat next to her instead of in his usual chair. Now her hand was resting on his knee, not moving, just there.

"You've been somewhere else all night," she said. Not a complaint. "Come back here."

dialogue.content: I let out a breath and lean into her a little. "Long week," I say. I don't move my hands yet.

dialogue.name: Sasha
dialogue.content:
Sasha’s thumb made one slow pass over the seam of his pants before settling again. She didn’t fill the silence too quickly, only let the lamp light hold them both.

When she spoke, her voice stayed low.

“Then don’t carry it out of this room.”

Her hand shifted from his knee to his thigh, palm warm and steady, asking without pressure.

“Do you want to talk, or do you want me to take the lead?”

dialogue.name: Devin
dialogue.content: I shake my head, my voice quiet. "I don't want to talk." I glance at her hand on my thigh. "I just need you to... take it from me."

dialogue.name: Sasha
dialogue.content:
Sasha did not make him say it twice. She took the request the way she took everything important from him—carefully, without flattening it into a joke or a performance.

Her hand remained where it was for one more slow breath, warm and unmoving, then shifted upward with deliberate pressure. She traced the line of his hip, the side of his torso, mapping the places where the week had built walls. When her palm came to rest over his heart, she let it stay there, feeling the rhythm beneath her fingers without commenting on it.

“Okay,” she said. The word was quiet, steady, a door closing gently behind them. “Then I have it.”

She leaned closer until the distance between them was only lamp-light and air. One hand slid up to the nape of his neck, fingers threading into damp hair just enough to anchor. Not pulling. Not yet. Only reminding him that she was there, and that she meant what she’d said.

“No carrying it around in here,” Sasha murmured. “No explaining it away. No disappearing into your own head while I’m touching you.”

Her thumb brushed once along the tendon at the side of his throat, then stilled.

“I’m going to take care of you,” she continued, voice low enough that each word felt chosen. “But I’m doing it my way. That means you stop managing the moment. You stop checking whether you’re doing it right. You just let me lead.”

She shifted again, turning slightly so she could bracket his face with both hands. Her palms were warm against his cheeks, her thumbs resting near the corners of his mouth. The gesture was intimate, almost reverent, but there was no uncertainty in it.

“Eyes on me,” she said softly. “If your mind goes somewhere else, I’ll notice. And I’ll bring you back.”

A pause. She let the silence gather weight, not to punish, but to give him something solid to hold onto.

“Breathe,” she instructed, gentle but unmistakably in charge. “Deep. For me.”

Only then did she lean in and press her mouth to his. The kiss began slow—deliberate, unhurried, a claiming without demand. Her hand at the nape of his neck tightened just enough to keep him close, to make the decision easy for him: he didn’t have to initiate, didn’t have to steer, didn’t have to earn the tenderness. It was already given.

When she drew back, it was only by a breath’s width. Her forehead rested against his, her voice dropping to a near-whisper.

“Still letting me?” she asked.

She didn’t wait for an answer in words. Instead, her hand slid from his cheek down the column of his throat, over his collarbone, tracing the old line of her own scar as if reminding herself of the history between them. Then her fingers continued lower, pausing at the hem of his shirt.

“Good,” Sasha said, as if the answer had already been given in the space between them. “Then stay right here. I’m not asking anymore.”

The promise in her tone was simple: she would take the lead, and she would not let the weight of the night crush him while he handed it over. She lifted the shirt slowly, watching his face with patient attention, ready to adjust, to stop, to deepen—whatever he needed without having to say it.

For now, though, she only touched, only guided, only held the space with the quiet certainty of someone who had loved him long enough to know when he needed to be carried.
