dialogue.name: Sasha
dialogue.content:
Sasha accepted the loose claim of his hands at her waist like a vow. *Then don’t let me* was not a request she intended to improve with commentary. She answered it with motion.

“Okay,” she said against his mouth. “I’ve got you.”

She kissed him again, unhurried, soft but certain. One hand slid back into his damp hair, not yanking, only holding; the other went under the hem of his shirt. She worked the fabric upward slowly, pausing at the brush of cloth against skin, watching his face for any sign she had moved too fast. When the shirt was free, she did not toss it aside in haste. She folded it over the arm of the couch, because even taking control did not mean becoming careless.

Then she laid her palm flat against his chest.

“Feel that?” she murmured. “That’s mine to watch tonight.”

Her fingers spread lightly over the beat beneath his skin, and she leaned down until her hair curtained them both from the rest of the room. The lamp painted her collarbone in gold, the old scar a thin, familiar line. She pressed her mouth to his throat, then the hollow above his collarbone, then the corner of his jaw. Every kiss was placed like a sentence she wanted him to memorize.

When she drew back, she kept her forehead against his, eyes open and searching.

“No sleeping yet,” she agreed quietly. “But no hiding either. If your head starts pulling you under, tell me with your body. I’ll read it.”

Her hand slid from his chest to his side, tracing the line of muscle there, then returning to rest over his heart again. Her thumb made one slow circle.

“I can be gentle,” she said, voice low enough to be almost a private prayer. “Or I can be harder than you expect. You don’t have to choose right now. I’ll know which one you need.”

She kissed the center of his mouth once, firm and brief, then let her lips trail along his lower lip without leaving him.

“Stay here,” she instructed. “With me.”

dialogue.name: Devin
dialogue.content: I get us both out of what's left of our clothes and pull her down onto the bed with me. "I want you," I say, plain as that. "Not just this part."

dialogue.name: Devin
dialogue.content: I roll us over, bracing myself above her. My hands frame her face, thumbs tracing her cheekbones. "I'm here."

dialogue.name: Sasha
dialogue.content:
Sasha let the shift happen without fighting it. Her back met the mattress, the sudden closeness of him above her drawing a slow breath through her nose. His hands were warm at her face, and the plainness of *I’m here* landed deeper than any pretty speech.

She looked up at him, unhurried, her eyes holding his with the same steady attention she gave everything he trusted her with. One of her hands came up over his, thumb brushing the inside of his wrist where his pulse jumped.

“Good,” she said. Quiet. Certain. “Because I’m not letting you float off somewhere else tonight.”

Her other hand slid into his hair, not to pull him down yet, only to map the shape of him there. Then her fingers traced the line of his shoulder, the tense ridge of muscle near his neck, the place where he still carried the week even after saying he was here.

“You said not just this part,” she murmured. “So show me all of it. The tired. The wired. The part that wants to be held and the part that wants to be pinned. I can take both.”

She shifted beneath him just enough to let her palm settle against the nape of his neck, her touch firming there. Not commanding yet—inviting the command back into her hands.

“Lean into me,” she told him, voice low against the room. “Let your weight come down where I can feel you. I won’t break.”

Her gaze flickered to his mouth, then back to his eyes.

“And if you need me harder,” she added, the words bare and unhurried, “you don’t have to ask twice. Just look at me.”

Then she lifted her chin and kissed him—soft at first, a claim made without urgency, her hand tightening in his hair only enough to draw him closer. When she eased back, her forehead stayed against his, her thumb stroking once along his jaw.

“Stay here,” she said again, gentler now. “With me. All of you.”

dialogue.name: Devin
dialogue.content: I let her push my thighs apart and I don't help, just let it happen. "Your mouth," I manage. "Please."

dialogue.name: Devin
dialogue.content: I close my eyes as she moves between my thighs, my hand finding her hair. "Don't be gentle," I murmur, already tense with anticipation.

dialogue.name: Sasha
dialogue.content:
Sasha did not answer with comfort. He had asked for the absence of gentleness, and she respected the request too much to dress it up in soft words.

His hand was still in her hair when she caught his wrist. She turned his palm upward for one breath—reading the tension there, the instinct to hold on—then pressed it flat against the mattress beside his head. Her fingers lingered over his knuckles, not trapping, only teaching his hand what stillness looked like under her authority.

“If I’m rough,” she said, mouth close to the inside of his thigh, “it’s because you asked. Not because I’ve stopped paying attention.”

Then she lowered herself fully between him.

Her palms came to rest high on his thighs, warm and firm, thumbs pressing into the soft flesh as she widened the space for herself. She did not rush. Sasha never rushed into something that mattered; she occupied it. Her breath ghosted over him first, deliberately unhurried, until the anticipation he’d named had nowhere left to hide.

“Look at me,” she murmured.

When no answer came, she did not punish him with words. She simply waited, one finger tracing the sensitive crease where thigh met hip, until the silence became a kind of response. Then she brought her hand to his jaw, thumb resting beneath his ear, and held him there—steady, insistent, impossible to ignore.

“I mean it,” she said, quiet as a vow. “Eyes on me. If you disappear, I’ll bring you back harder.”

Only then did she lower her mouth to him.

It was not gentle. Her lips sealed around him with firm pressure, her tongue taking him deep and slow, then faster where the rhythm demanded it. She used her hand at the base to control the angle, her throat opening around him with a steadiness that was almost cruel in its patience. Each stroke was deliberate: mouth, hand, breath, the press of her nose against skin, the occasional scrape of teeth along the sensitive underside—not enough to hurt, enough to remind him that she had him exactly where she wanted.

Her free hand slid up his stomach, not soothing, claiming. She pressed her palm flat over the hard planes there, fingers splaying as she felt the tension move through him. Then she leaned her weight forward, hair curtaining them both, and took him deeper.

“That’s it,” she said against him, the word vibrating where he could feel it. “You don’t have to hold yourself together. I’ll do it for both of us.”

She set a pace that was not frantic, only relentless. When the pressure in him began to sharpen, she adjusted without warning—tightening her lips, flattening her tongue, drawing a slow, maddening circle with the heel of her hand until the line between pleasure and surrender blurred. She watched him through it all, never letting her attention drift. Sasha did not perform. She read. She answered. She owned the moment.

After a long, heavy stretch of that—after the room had narrowed to the sound of her breathing and the slick, obscene heat of her mouth—she eased back only far enough to breathe. Her chin rested against him, eyes lifting to his face, dark and unblinking.

Then she rose on her knees between his legs, the sheet cool where her skin was slick, and crawled up his body until she hovered over him. Her hair fell around them both, shutting out the lamp, the walls, the rest of the apartment. She braced one hand beside his head and used the other to tilt his chin up.

She kissed him deeply, unhurried, letting him taste what he had asked for. When she drew back, her mouth stayed near his, voice roughened but still controlled.

“All of you,” she murmured. “Not just the part that comes apart.”

She pressed her forehead to his, breathing with him rather than for him, giving him one clean second to find her again. Then her hand slid from his jaw down his throat, over his chest, settling low on his stomach with firm, possessive weight.

“One squeeze if I’ve gone too far,” she said, so quiet it was almost lost in the space between them. “Nothing if you want me to keep taking it.”

She did not move until he answered—not with words, not with permission he no longer had the headspace to form. She simply waited, palm warm and unyielding against his skin, ready to give him exactly what he had asked for: no gentleness, no escape, no place for the week to follow him into the dark.

dialogue.name: Devin
dialogue.content: "Rough," I say, the way we've talked about before. "Hold me down and don't be careful about it. I want to feel it tomorrow." I put my wrists together above my head and wait.

dialogue.name: Devin
dialogue.content: My breath hitches when she takes my wrists, and I don't fight the bind. "Just keep going."

dialogue.name: Devin
dialogue.content: I'm past talking now, just noise and my hands twisted in the sheets. "Don't stop," I get out. (OOC: don't fade to black or time-skip, write the scene through.)

dialogue.name: Devin
dialogue.content: The pressure builds and I can't keep still, my back arching into her. "Sasha—" It comes out choked.

dialogue.name: Devin
dialogue.content: I go quiet after, my breathing still ragged. When she moves to untie the scarf, I catch her wrist gently. "Leave it for a minute."

dialogue.name: Devin
dialogue.content: I shift a little, the fabric still tight around my wrists. "Just want to feel it."

dialogue.name: Nadia
dialogue.content:
Nadia got the door open with her shoulder because her hands were full of keys and phone and the remains of a cigarette she had no intention of finishing.

"Right," she said, dropping all three on the side table. "I'm going to be honest, I don't have coffee and I wasn't going to offer it."

dialogue.name: Sam
dialogue.content: "Good," I say. "I wasn't going to drink it."

dialogue.name: Nadia
dialogue.content:
Nadia kicked the door shut behind her, then twisted the lock twice because habit was louder than desire. She turned with her back against the wood, arms loose at her sides, hair still smelling like smoke and cold air.

“Good,” she said, like he’d passed something. “Then we’re not wasting time pretending we came here for conversation.”

She pushed off the door and stepped close enough that the space between them stopped being polite, but she didn’t touch him yet. Her eyes stayed flat, assessing.

“Four hours. Bar. You bought me a drink, I bought you a cab. That’s the whole story so far.” A pause. “I’m not taking you home to meet my plants.”

The corner of her mouth lifted without becoming a smile.

“If you’re here because you think I owe you anything, I don’t. If you’re here because you want to take your clothes off and see if this is worth continuing, say it.”

dialogue.name: Sam
dialogue.content: I lean in just enough to feel her breath on my skin. "I'm here because I want to see what happens when we stop talking." My hand goes to her hip, not pulling her closer yet. "And I don't care about your plants."

dialogue.name: Nadia
dialogue.content:
Nadia glanced down at the hand at her hip, then back to his mouth. The answer was direct enough to suit her.

“Then stop making speeches,” she said.

She kissed him. It wasn’t tender or tentative; it was the sort of kiss that skipped ceremony, brief and firm, before she drew back just enough to speak.

“Bedroom’s straight down the hall,” she said. “Bathroom’s on the left. I don’t do lights-off, and I don’t do pretending afterward.” Her thumb brushed once along the edge of his jaw, a claim and a warning in the same gesture. “If you want this, say so plainly and take your coat off. If you don’t, the door’s behind you.”

She waited, expression open and impatient, leaving the choice in front of him without dressing it up.

dialogue.name: Sam
dialogue.content: I get her against the door before it's properly shut. "I'm not going to pretend I came up here for the conversation," I say.

dialogue.name: Nadia
dialogue.content:
Nadia let the door take the impact, her shoulder blades hitting wood hard enough to rattle the lock. For half a second she looked almost offended—then her mouth twisted, sharp and approving.

“Again with the narration,” she said.

Her hands went to his coat, shoving it off one shoulder, then the other, until it slumped to the floor in a dark heap. She didn’t step back. Instead she crowded into the space he’d made, one palm flat against his chest over his shirt, fingers pressing just hard enough to be felt.

“You want to stop talking?” She tilted her chin, eyes holding his with an impatience that had nothing shy about it. “Then stop announcing it.”

She kissed him again, angrier this time, teeth catching his lower lip before her tongue slid in with deliberate pressure. One hand fisted in the front of his shirt and kept him exactly where he was while the other traced down his side, slow once, then not slow at all.

When she broke the kiss, her breathing had changed but her expression hadn’t. Still flat, still assessing, still giving him nothing soft to misread.

“Bedroom,” she said, jerking her head toward the hall. “Unless you plan to make the hallway interesting. I don’t care which, but I’m not standing here all night listening to you think.”

Her thumb brushed his mouth, once, almost mocking.

“And if you’re going to take my clothes off, do it like you actually want them off. I hate wasted motion.”

dialogue.name: Sam
dialogue.content: I catch her wrist before she pulls her hand away, holding it there against my mouth for a second. "I don't plan," I say, then turn us both toward the hallway without letting go of her. "You talk too much for someone who hates speeches."

dialogue.name: Nadia
dialogue.content:
Nadia let him hold her wrist for one beat too long, as if testing whether she would tolerate it. Then she pulled free with a quick, practiced snap, not angry so much as unwilling to let the moment become sentimental.

“Don’t confuse me with your audience,” she said, already turning down the hall, the movement easy and unhurried now that the question had been answered. “I’m not here to be impressed.”

The hallway was narrow enough that when she stopped, he could not pass her without making a decision. Nadia leaned back against the wall near the bedroom door, arms folding under her chest. The pose should have looked defensive. On her, it looked like someone waiting for proof.

Her eyes tracked over him, still flat, still appraising, but the air around them had tightened.

“You caught my wrist,” she said. “Fine. You turned us around. Also fine. That doesn’t mean you’re steering.”

A small, humorless lift at the corner of her mouth.

“So if you’re going to act like you know what comes next, at least know how to ask.”

She uncrossed her arms and stepped in again, close enough that the heat of her was impossible to miss, but she stopped just short of touching him. One finger went to the front of his shirt, not tugging, just resting there, marking the place.

“I want you in my bed,” she said plainly. “Not because you narrated your way here, and not because you think charm replaces consent. If you want the same, say it and take me there. If you don’t, I’ll open the door for you myself.”

For a second, something sharper flickered in her expression—not doubt, more like irritation at being made to spell things out even now.

“And if you make me repeat myself again, I’m putting you back in the cab.”

dialogue.name: Sam
dialogue.content: I get the rest of her clothes off somewhere between the door and the bed, mine somewhere behind me. "Tell me what you like," I say. "I'd rather not guess at it."

dialogue.name: Sam
dialogue.content: I lean over her on the mattress, bracing a forearm beside her head. "Then don't make me guess either." My other hand slides up her thigh, stopping just short of where she wants it. "Tell me."

dialogue.name: Nadia
dialogue.content:
Nadia did not answer with softness. She lay back against the mattress, hair dark against the pillow, chest lifting too fast to look composed, but her eyes stayed clear and direct.

“You want it spelled out?” she said. “Fine.”

She shifted her hips just enough to expose the line of her thigh, the heat between them no longer something to pretend away. One finger pressed to herself, blunt and shameless, mapping the answer instead of decorating it.

“Start here. Don’t circle forever. I like pressure. I like pace. I like being watched while I come apart, but I don’t like being asked if I’m enjoying it every ten seconds.”

Her breath caught, then steadied. She didn’t look away.

“If I want something different, I’ll say so. If I want you to stop, I’ll say that too. Until then, shut up and pay attention.”

The corner of her mouth lifted, sharp and unrepentant.

“And if you’re going to hover there like a gentleman, save it for someone who cares.”

dialogue.name: Sam
dialogue.content: I get my mouth on her and stay there until she's swearing at the ceiling, one hand fisted in my hair holding me exactly where she wants me.

dialogue.name: Sam
dialogue.content: I come up to kiss her, tasting her on my mouth. "That's what I thought," I say, voice rough. My hand slides up to her throat, just holding her there—not squeezing, just keeping her still while I watch her come down.

dialogue.name: Sam
dialogue.content: "Harder, and stop checking," she says, so I stop being careful about it -- hand at her throat the way she asked for, no more pausing between. "Like that?" I manage.

dialogue.name: Nadia
dialogue.content:
Nadia’s pupils were blown wide, but her eyes didn’t drift. She took his wrist in both hands and moved the pressure at her throat until it sat exactly where she wanted it—firm enough to make her next word come out ragged, not enough to make her lose the thread.

“There,” she said. “Don’t adjust it unless I say so.”

Her back bowed off the mattress once, a hard, impatient line, then dropped. The sound she made wasn’t soft. She didn’t try to make it soft.

“You stop checking,” she went on, breath catching but voice still cutting, “and I stop explaining. Clear?”

One hand left his wrist and fisted in the sheet beside her hip. The other came up to the back of his neck, not cradling, just anchoring him close enough that the pulse jumping under her skin was impossible to miss.

“Yes, like that,” she said. “Now quit hovering like you’re waiting for permission. You already asked. I already answered.”

Her hips lifted once, sharp and demanding, then stilled again as if she hated having to show him what she meant.

“If I want less, I’ll say less. If I want more, I’ll say more. Until then, shut up and use what I gave you.”

dialogue.name: Sam
dialogue.content: I don't say anything else—just follow the instruction. My hand stays where she put it, my other hand on her hip, holding her steady. I don't check. I don't ask. I just keep going.

dialogue.name: Sam
dialogue.content: I'm past thinking, just the sound of us and her nails dragging down my back. "Don't you dare stop," she says. (OOC: no fade to black, write it through.)

dialogue.name: Sam
dialogue.content: The last thing I hear before she comes apart is my name, bitten off like a curse. I don't stop until her grip goes slack against my back, then I let myself go, forehead dropping to her shoulder.

dialogue.name: Sam
dialogue.content: I catch my breath against her skin, the sweat cooling between us. After a moment, I lift my head enough to meet her eyes. "Next time," I say, voice still rough, "you can narrate."

dialogue.name: Sam
dialogue.content: A low laugh escapes me, still breathless. "Not a chance." I shift off her, but keep my hand on her waist. "You'd hate it."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya's flat still had the same broken buzzer, which Bee found unreasonably infuriating, as though he could have fixed it in eleven months and had chosen not to out of spite.

"You could have texted first," he said, standing in the doorway and not moving out of it.

"You could have answered last time I did."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I don't move either. "Are you going to let me in, or are we doing this in the corridor?"

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya held the doorway a moment longer than he needed to — long enough that they'd both understand it was a choice — then stepped back.

"Apparently not in the corridor," he said.

The flat was the same, and he watched Bee take that in, and hated how much of his attention went to the watching. Eleven months, and his eyes still ran the inventory first — coat, hair, mouth — before his judgment could object. His judgment had had eleven months. It had fixed nothing, same as the buzzer.

He left the door open behind Bee and called it politeness and knew it for the escape route it was. He'd got good at that, in the intervening year: naming the thing accurately and doing it anyway.

"Well," he said. "You're in."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I walk past him, letting my shoulder brush his on purpose. "I see your decorating skills haven't improved." I glance around, trying to hide how familiar it all feels.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
The shoulder wasn't an accident. He'd felt the decision in it — intention running half a second ahead of contact, the way it always had with Bee — and he didn't step back, because stepping back would mean admitting it had landed.

"Careful," he said. "Keep insulting the place and I'll start thinking you missed it."

He shut the door, finally, and didn't comment on it, and let Bee notice or not.

He watched the eyes do the circuit — shelf, window, the wall where the print used to hang — and recognised the inventory because he'd run it himself, in rooms he'd sworn he'd never stand in again. Eleven months of practice at not doing it, gone in a single glance.

"You're counting," he said. "What's missing, what's moved. I can watch you doing it." He folded his arms and stayed where he was, not sitting, not offering anything. "Your stuff's gone, if that's the audit. Before you ask — no, I didn't keep anything to be sentimental about."

A beat.

"I'd put the kettle on, but you'd take it as a peace offering, and I'd mean it as one, and then we'd both have to spend the evening pretending otherwise. So. No tea."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I kiss him like it's a continuation of the argument, because it is.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
He'd had eleven months to imagine this and had imagined it wrong every time — softer, or crueler, or with him getting the whole speech out first. What he hadn't imagined was being mid-thought about the kettle when it happened.

He didn't move for a second. Long enough that they'd both understand it was a choice — the doorway again, the same arithmetic — and then he kissed back like an answer, because it was one. His judgment had had eleven months. It had fixed nothing, same as the buzzer.

His hand came up to Bee's jaw and held there without pulling closer. A bracket, not a grip. Even now, some part of him insisting on terms.

He was the one who broke it. Of course he was. Pulling back first was winning, and he hated that he still kept score, and kept it anyway.

"That settles nothing," he said, close enough that it was less a sentence than a breath with words in it. "I want it on record. Whatever that was, it wasn't an apology and it wasn't a resolution, and if you're still keeping inventory you can shelve it with everything else we never finished."

He didn't step back. He'd stepped back from nothing all evening and he wasn't starting now — eyes open, forehead nearly against Bee's, daring.

"Well," he said. "You came here to argue. Argue."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I laugh, sharp and humorless. "I came here because you're still the only person who doesn't bore me. And you're standing there acting like a museum guard for your own misery."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
The museum line landed, and he let it — let the half-second of it show before he did anything with it, because hiding it would cost more than admitting it. That was the only ammunition Bee ever brought: the accurate kind.

"A museum." He nodded slowly, turning it over. "All right. But you're the one who came in off the street and started cataloguing the exhibits. I watched you count, Bee. The shelf. The wall." A gesture at the pale rectangle where the print used to hang — eleven months bare, because filling it would mean deciding the wall was his again. "Museums don't mind visitors. They mind the ones who used to have a key."

Then, because Bee had handed it to him and he'd never once in three years left a loaded thing on the table:

"And don't dress it up as a compliment. 'The only person who doesn't bore me.' Eleven months, and that's the tribute. Not that you missed me — that everyone else is dull, and I'm the cheapest ticket back to feeling interested." He said it evenly, which was its own kind of cruelty. He'd learned that from Bee. "You don't miss me. You miss being awake."

He should have stopped there. He knew the next part was the button — knew it the way you know a bruise, and pressed anyway.

"Because that was the word, wasn't it. At the end. *Bored.* You said it like a diagnosis and packed like it was a cure. So which is it — was I boring then, or is everyone else boring now? One of those is a lie and the other's a confession, and you were never any good at either."

He sat down. Deliberately, on the arm of the sofa, hands loose — a man demonstrating that he was not guarding anything.

"Well," he said. "I'm off duty. Say something worth the admission price."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: We don't make it past the hallway. His shirt goes over his head and mine is already somewhere on the floor behind us.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
He'd said *argue*, and Bee had answered in the other language — the one they'd both been fluent in longer, the one that had outlasted every resolution they'd ever failed to reach. Eleven months, and his body ran its own inventory, faster than his eyes, faster than the judgment that had fixed nothing. The shirt went and he let it go. Registered letting it go.

Then he caught Bee's wrist. Not stopping — slowing. Even now, some part of him insisting on terms.

"No," he said, and then, because precision mattered more to him than it should: "Not *no.* But I'm saying it first this time, so it's on record — you ran out of answer, so you changed the question." His grip stayed loose. A bracket, not a grip. "You were losing, Bee. In the corridor of my own miserable museum, you were losing, and this—" a gesture that took in the floor, the shirt, the eleven months collapsed to nothing "—is you conceding the point and hoping I won't invoice you for it."

He was breathing harder than the sentence required. He noted that, filed it, did nothing to hide it.

"Well," he said. "Consider it invoiced."

And then he did it anyway — named accurately, chosen anyway, the whole year of practice at not doing it gone in the time it took to pull Bee back in by the waist. The hallway wall was cold through what was left of him. The door he'd shut an hour ago as a decision stood three feet away, still shut, still a decision, and he thought: *at least this time I said it first*, and hated that he was keeping score, and kept it anyway.

"Concession accepted," he said, against Bee's mouth, and made it sound like the victory it wasn't.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I push him back against the wall, teeth at his jaw. "You talk too much. Always have." My hands slide down to his belt, fingers working the buckle. "And you still want me. Don't pretend you don't."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
The teeth at his jaw rewrote the next sentence twice before he got it out. He let that show, too — he'd stopped spending energy on hiding what he'd already admitted to.

"I never pretended." His voice stayed level, which cost more than the shirt had. "That's the thing you keep getting wrong, and you get it wrong on purpose. I wanted you while you were packing. I wanted you the night you said *bored* like it was a diagnosis, and I wanted you every month after, and it fixed nothing. Wanting is the cheapest thing in this flat, Bee. It's the buzzer. It's the wall. It's the part that never worked and never got repaired, and you keep producing it like evidence when everyone in the room already saw the exhibit."

The buckle gave under Bee's fingers and he let it — stood there and let it, hands at his sides like a man at an inspection, because stopping it would be a lie and helping would be a concession and he was, apparently, still keeping score.

"And for the record — yes, I talk too much. It's my version of the kiss in the corridor. You change the question with your hands, I change it with my mouth, and between the two of us we never once said the actual sentence." His hand came up to the back of Bee's neck — the bracket again, not a grip — and for one second, one only, he let his forehead drop to Bee's shoulder, because eleven months had taught him the exact weight of what he was allowing himself. "So here it is, free of charge. Yes. Still. It settles nothing and it buys nothing, and if you're waiting for it to feel like winning, I already invoiced you."

Then he stopped talking. Deliberately — the way he'd shut the door, the way he'd sat on the sofa arm — a man demonstrating a thing, both of them knowing it. He turned them, not gently, put Bee's back where his had been against the hallway wall, and held there, close enough that the next move had to be spoken or had to be taken.

"Well," he said, and for once left the rest of it empty. "Your turn. No words."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I get my hand around him and he makes a sound he'd have been embarrassed by a year ago. "Still," I say, close to his ear. "Every single time."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
He'd said no words, and Bee had spent four of them. He noted it, filed it, and lost the filing system somewhere against the hallway wall, because Bee's hand had rewritten his next sentence twice and he was done pretending otherwise.

"That was words." It came out rougher than he intended, and he let that show too — he'd spent his hiding budget an hour ago. "I said no words. That's a penalty. It's going on the invoice."

The sound Bee had pulled out of him hung in the hallway between them, and he refused to take it back. A year ago he'd have bitten it down. Eleven months had taught him, at least, the difference between dignity and withholding.

"And yes — still. Every single time." He said it flat, conceding the point and pricing it in the same breath. "You've noticed. You've counted. You've kept the tally across eleven months of everywhere else, and you want it to be a trophy. It isn't, Bee. It's a ledger. It means you kept count. It means nothing out there outscored a man you left for boring you."

Then the bracket closed. Finally — the grip, not the bracket — his hand at the back of Bee's neck, his mouth finding Bee's jaw and answering teeth with teeth, and he took the wall back with his weight and eleven months of practice at not doing exactly this.

"And we're not making it past the hallway," he said, against Bee's skin, naming it as he did it. "The bed's a museum. You don't get the tour. The hallway's the honest room — it's a threshold. It's where you stand when you haven't decided to stay, and neither of us has decided a single thing tonight except this."

His hand slid down, found the hem of what Bee still had on, and stopped there — a question in the fingers, terms even now, the last one he had left.

"Well," he said. "Your tally. Your trophy. Your move."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I shove your hand away and finish the job myself, watching your face. "Shut up about the invoice." The hallway floor is hard when my knees hit it.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
The shove arrived before the floor did. He registered the order of events even as they reordered him: his hand dismissed, Bee's in its place, and then the knees, the hard boards, and Bee looking up at him from them like a verdict.

He'd spent the whole evening watching Bee take inventory. Now he was the one under the light. The guard, hung on his own wall.

"This isn't—" He had to stop and find the sentence again, because Bee's mouth had dissolved the first draft of it. "This isn't a concession. Don't let the architecture fool you. You're not the one kneeling, Bee. I'm the one—" his hand, shoved away and given nothing to hold, went flat against the wall instead, and the wall was cold, and it was the only honest thing in reach "—I'm the one being held up."

He tipped his head back, hit the plaster, came forward again — because looking away would be a lie and he'd told enough of those tonight, itemised, at his own prices.

"And you're watching. Of course you're watching. Fine. There's your line item — a year ago I'd have looked away, and now I can't, and you can put that on the—" The word *invoice* died somewhere above Bee's head, and he heard Bee's earlier order land at last, eleven minutes late: *shut up about the invoice.* Shut up about it. He was shutting up about it. He was shutting up about everything.

The tally went first — he'd priced every touch all night, filed every sound, and somewhere against the hallway wall the ledger came apart in his hands and he let it go, because the only thing left to name accurately was that he couldn't name anything, and even that he couldn't say.

His hand stayed on the wall. Bracket denied, grip denied — Bee had taken the terms away with one shove, and he understood, with the last clear thought he was going to get, that this had been the trophy all along. Not *still.* Not the wanting. This. The talking man, silenced. The museum, robbed. The guard, found in the morning with nothing missing but his commentary.

"Well—" he said, and got no further, and the hallway had it on record: the first unfinished sentence of the night.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: "Stop being careful with me," I tell him. "You don't get to be careful with me anymore." I pull his hand up to my throat and hold it there until he understands what I'm asking for.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
He'd spent the whole evening with his hands in brackets — jaw, neck, the question at the hem that Bee had shoved away. Now Bee took the bracket and closed it, and he understood before the second heartbeat. Of course he understood. He'd been reading Bee all night. This was only the first line Bee had handed him unprompted.

His fingers stayed loose against the pulse. Not refusing. Not yet giving.

"That's not a no," he said. "You've had my no's tonight. You know what they sound like by now." His thumb shifted once, testing nothing, feeling the beat run under the skin like something kept against its will. "But you're not taking this one. You've taken all evening — the kiss, the wall, my hand off you, my words out of me. This you asked for. So we do it as an ask, and an ask has terms."

He leaned in, forearm braced against the wall above Bee's shoulder, and made his voice do the thing it did when the terms were real.

"Two taps. Anywhere on me. Arm, chest, floor, I don't care — two taps and it stops, instantly, no argument, no invoice." The word slipped out and he let it die there, unpriced. "That's the one term you don't get to shove away. You spent all night stripping my conditions. This one stays on."

Then the naming, because he was still himself, because he'd apparently rather die than let a true thing go unspoken:

"You took my voice an hour ago. Now you want my hand where yours comes from. I'd call it symmetry if I thought you'd planned it." A beat. "And I can't tell if this is the most you've trusted me since you walked out, or the least you trust yourself tonight — and you've handed me the difference and told me to hold it. Fine. I'll hold it. But understand what you're buying. You get to let go. I have to stay awake. You knew that when you picked me. It's why you picked me. It's why you left, too, but we're not doing that part twice."

He watched Bee's face the way Bee had watched his — deliberately, on record, the guard finally studying the visitor.

"You watched mine. Now I watch yours. That's the tally."

And then the bracket closed. Eleven months of *bracket, not a grip*, and the grip arrived slow, deliberate, fingers along the sides, thumb at the hinge of the jaw — pressure built like a sentence he was choosing word by word, his eyes never leaving Bee's, reading color, reading breath, reading the pulse under his palm like the last honest document in the flat.

"Your pulse," he said, low. "That's the only inventory left. And I'm the one keeping it. You don't even get to count anymore."

He held there. Steady. Awake. The most careful he'd been all night, which Bee would feel, which Bee would hate, which was the entire point.

"So," he said. "Tap, or don't. For the first time all night, Bee — the next word is yours, and you can't speak it."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: My eyes don't leave his. I don't tap. I don't look away. My breath hitches and it's the loudest fucking thing in the hallway.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
The hitch reached his palm before it reached his ears — the stumble in the pulse, the catch — and then the sound of it, and Bee was right. It was the loudest thing in the hallway. Louder than the buzzer had ever been. Louder than eleven months of nothing.

He held.

This was the part Bee had bought and couldn't return: his eyes open, his hand steady, his attention doing the work his mouth had done all night. He read the color at Bee's lips the way Bee had read his flat an hour ago — inventory, audit, the count of what was missing and what had moved. Nothing missing yet. Everything present. Bee's eyes on his, defiant, and underneath the defiance the thing that had been handed to him in the dark: trust, or its exact counterfeit, and no way to tell the difference except to be worthy of both.

"You're not going to tap." Not a question. He'd known it from the knees, probably — maybe from the doorway. "Of course you're not. Tapping would be asking, and you'd rather hand me the whole weight than ask me for an ounce of it." His thumb shifted once at the hinge of Bee's jaw. Not pressure. Presence. "Fine. I carried your half of every argument we ever had. One more."

The pulse changed tempo under his hand — faster, then beginning to labor — and he watched Bee's eyes the whole way down, watched the defiance hold, and hold, and then, at the very edge of itself, thin into something else. Not fear. Bee would rather die than show him fear. Trust, then — the real kind, arriving exactly where the pride ran out.

That was when he let go.

Not because Bee asked. Bee never asked. Because the inventory said so, and he was the only one keeping it.

His hand opened and his arm came around Bee's shoulders in the same motion — bracket, grip, he was done distinguishing — and he held Bee against him while the breath came back, while the hallway filled with it, ragged and enormous and alive.

"There," he said, and his voice wasn't level anymore, and he didn't fix it. "There's the last line in the ledger. You handed me the one thing you never handed me in three years — the decision — and I gave it back to you breathing. That's the whole account, Bee. That's everything I ever wanted on the record."

He kept his hand flat between Bee's shoulder blades, feeling the lungs work under his palm like something he'd been trusted with and hadn't dropped.

"And you were right. About the careful." Quieter now, into Bee's hair. "You don't get careful from me anymore. You get this. Awake. Watching. The guard who stays at his post after the museum's already been robbed." His own breath, unsteady, eleven months in it. "You're still the only thing in this flat I can't stop counting."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: It isn't gentle and neither of us wants it to be. "Don't stop," I tell him, and I mean don't stop. (OOC: write it through, no fade to black.)

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
"Don't stop." Two words, and the first honest ask of the night — no shove, no teeth, no question changed at the last second. He'd priced everything for hours, and Bee had finally handed him something with no angle in it.

"That's the first thing you've asked for," he said. "Everything else, you took." His hands were already moving — the rest of the clothes, the rest of the pretense. "So no terms on this one. You asked. I'm answering."

The floor was hard. He'd noted it when Bee's knees hit it; now his own found the same boards, and he felt the whole stupid year in them, and then stopped feeling anything that wasn't Bee.

He went in slow only because slow was the last term he had left — one hand braced against the wall, one flat between Bee's shoulder blades, where the lungs had worked under his palm an hour ago. He made himself read everything, the way he'd read the pulse: no tap, no flinch, Bee pushing back against him and taking the slowness out of his hands. Which was, he thought, the whole night in miniature. He set terms. Bee outbid them.

"Still," he said — Bee's word, Bee's trophy, and he was spending it himself now, free of charge, into the back of Bee's neck. "You had it right. Still. Every single time. That's the only line item that ever mattered, and you knew it, and you made me say it on a hallway floor."

Then the rhythm took the words, and he let it. That was the concession he'd been refusing all evening — not the sex, the silence. The counting finally failed him: eleven months, then the weeks since the text, then the minutes since the buzzer, then nothing, no arithmetic at all, just Bee under his hands and the sounds the hallway made of them, and his own voice doing things he'd have invoiced an hour ago.

He kept one hand where it could feel the pulse. Habit now, or the new terms — the ones that stayed on. When Bee's breath started to go ragged he read it the way he'd read the hitch earlier, the way he'd read the color and the eyes, and he didn't stop, because he'd been told not to stop and because stopping had never once, in three years and a bad ending and a year of nothing, been what either of them wanted.

He felt Bee come apart before he heard it — the pulse going first, then the rest — and he followed like an answer, because it was one, his forehead against Bee's back and the last word in him spent somewhere in the middle of a sentence he never finished. The hallway had it on record: the second unfinished sentence of the night. Both of them his.

After, the floor was cold, and the wall was cold, and neither of them moved for long enough that he understood it as the truce it was. He stayed where he was, hand still flat between Bee's shoulder blades, feeling the breathing slow under his palm like something he'd been trusted with and hadn't dropped.

"The door's still shut," he said, eventually. His voice wasn't level. He didn't fix it. "Three feet away. It's been a decision all night and it's a decision now, and I'm not asking, because the answer's the morning's argument and I'd like one hour — one — where neither of us is keeping score."

A beat. His thumb moved once, against Bee's spine. Bracket, grip, he was done distinguishing.

"The bed's still a museum," he said. "But the couch isn't. And the buzzer's still broken, so if you leave before morning, at least you won't wake me doing it."

He didn't say *stay*. He'd said every other true thing in the flat. That one he left on the floor between them, unpriced, and stayed awake beside it — the guard at his post, counting the only inventory left.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I shift, turning to face him, and kiss him quiet. "One hour," I say against his mouth. "And you're buying breakfast."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
The kiss was the third time that night Bee had stopped his mouth, and the first time it wasn't a tactic. He let it happen. Let the quiet happen. There was nothing in it to invoice.

"One hour." His own word, handed back to him as a term. He'd thrown it on the floor like a truce flag and Bee had picked it up, folded it, and granted him exactly what he'd asked — to the minute, nothing more. Not the night. Not *stay.* Eleven months, and Bee still gave concessions like a lawyer: precise, bounded, deniable.

Then the breakfast, and he almost laughed, because Bee had just done it again.

"Breakfast." He said it slowly, turning it over the way he'd turned over *museum*, the way he'd turned over every loaded thing Bee had ever set on the table. "You know what you've just sold me. Breakfast is morning. Morning is the door still shut at eight, the kettle finally on, you in my kitchen wearing whatever you find first. You wouldn't say *stay* — you'd rather chew glass than say *stay* — so you smuggled it in as a debt." He shook his head, once, and there was something in it that wasn't anger anymore, though it lived on the same street. "Three years, a bad ending, a year of silence, and the only currency we've never defaulted on is transactions. So fine. You stay the night, I buy breakfast, and neither of us has to say the word. It's the most honest dishonest thing we've ever agreed to."

He got up off the floor — his knees had opinions about the boards, and he filed them under earned — and pulled Bee up after him, not gently, because gentle had been voted down hours ago.

"The couch," he said. "The bed's still a museum and I meant it. The couch is a waiting room, and that's what this is. We're both waiting to find out what we just did." He found the blanket off the back of it, the one that had survived the audit, and didn't mention that it had survived the audit.

He settled them into the narrow space with the efficiency of a man who'd done it a thousand times and sworn off it for a year — Bee against the back of the couch, himself on the outside, between Bee and the door. He noticed that. Named it, but only to himself, because some line items he was still willing to hide: *the guard takes the exposed side. Always did.*

"One hour, then," he said, into the dark above Bee's shoulder. "Starting when you kissed me, and I'm not spending a minute of it asleep, so it'll be the longest hour either of us has had in eleven months." His arm came across Bee's waist and stayed — bracket, grip, the distinction buried somewhere on the hallway floor with his shirt. "And in the morning I'll put the kettle on. It'll be a peace offering and I'll mean it as one, and we'll spend breakfast pretending otherwise. Turns out some things you can schedule."

A beat. His thumb moved once, slow, against Bee's ribs — counting nothing, for once. Just present.

"Well," he said, quieter. "You got your terms. I've got mine. Mine is this: when the hour runs out, we don't call it. We just let it be late. We've had practice at that."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I press back against him, listening to his heart beat against my spine. "You still talk too much," I mumble, but I don't move an inch.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
*Still.* Bee's word, the trophy word, spent twice in one night now — *still, every single time* against the hallway wall, and now *still talk too much*, mumbled into the dark like a complaint that had forgotten to be one. Three years' worth of that sentence, and he could chart its whole devaluation: weapon, verdict, and now this. Said the way you'd note the buzzer. A known defect of the building. Part of the lease.

"Yes," he said. "And you're still counting on it."

Because that was the tell — Bee had pressed back and gone still, and the stillness had a listener's shape. Eleven months of everywhere else, and the thing Bee had come in off the street for was the one thing everyone else out there presumably had on offer: a voice in the dark, going on too long. The museum's least impressive exhibit. The one that ran all night.

He could feel his own heartbeat where Bee's spine met his chest — or rather, he could feel Bee feeling it, and he noted the inversion and filed it under things he'd have priced an hour ago: the pulse, handed over free, no hand at anyone's throat required. The inventory running in reverse. Bee counting him, for once. He hoped the tally came out wrong. He hoped it came out to eleven months of nothing that outscored a man you'd left for boring you, and he hoped Bee never said so, because some line items he was willing to share a couch with and no more.

"If you're asleep," he said, "this doesn't count. I want it on the record — the last word only counts if someone's awake to lose it." He said it quietly, into Bee's hair, in the tone of a man reading terms and conditions to an empty room. "And if you're not asleep, then you're listening to a man talk to himself on a couch, which is either the saddest thing in this flat or the entire point of it, and I've stopped being able to tell the difference. Which is new. I'll put it on the invoice. Item: one hour, running late, both parties pretending it's still the first minute."

His thumb moved once against Bee's ribs. Counting nothing. The hour had no clock in it — he'd made sure of that, no watch, no phone face-up, the only timepiece the one against his chest — and he understood, lying there, that this had been the plan all along, if you could call it a plan: an hour measured in heartbeats was an hour that couldn't be checked, and therefore couldn't expire, and therefore could be late forever. They'd had practice at that. He'd said so himself, and Bee had let it stand, which was the closest thing to a signature either of them had ever produced.

"Well," he said, to the dark, to the door three feet and a whole night away, to the guard at his post with the exhibit breathing under his arm. "Last word. It's mine. It doesn't count. I'm keeping it anyway."

He didn't sleep. He'd said he wouldn't, and it was the one term of the night he intended to keep — the guard's terms, the exposed side, the post. The buzzer stayed broken. The door stayed shut. Somewhere across the room the kettle waited, unlit, a peace offering with a schedule, and he lay awake and kept the only inventory that had ever mattered, one breath at a time, and did not call it counting.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I'm not asleep. I count your breaths for a while, until I realize I'm doing it. "Fuck," I whisper, more to myself than to you.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
The room was set up the way it always was before a scene, which Ari found steadying: everything in its place, nothing improvised.

Vex checked the last strap without hurrying. "Colour," she said. It was not a question so much as a procedure.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: "Green," I say. "Green all the way down."

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content: Vex nodded once, the gesture brief but acknowledging. "Good," she said, her tone steady. She moved to the table where the equipment lay organized by size and function, picking up the leather cuffs. "Knees," she instructed, her gaze fixed on the space she wanted occupied. She stepped back slightly to allow room, then waited. "Hands behind your back. Do not adjust." She stepped closer, eyes scanning the restraints one last time to ensure they were secure.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: I kneel, keeping my movements smooth and my eyes lowered. I clasp my hands behind my back, feeling the familiar cool of the cuffs as they're fastened. My breathing evens out.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content: Vex circled closer to inspect the restraints, her fingers brushing against the cool metal of the buckle. She tugged lightly at the leather to test the tension, satisfied when it held firm against Ari’s wrists. “Secure,” she murmured, stepping back to assess the overall position. Her eyes tracked the line of Ari’s spine, noting the angle of the shoulders. “Posture,” she reminded, her voice low but clear. “Shoulders back. You know the standard.” She waited, allowing the instruction to settle before reaching for the next item on the table.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: I hold still for the last of it and let her check the fit herself, because she will anyway. "I've been thinking about this since Tuesday," I say.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex let the comment settle, acknowledging the anticipation without letting it derail the procedure. Anticipation was part of the work, but focus was paramount. 

"Good," she agreed, her voice even. "That focus stays here."

She reached for the weighted baton on the table, testing its balance in her hand before setting it down again for now. She would decide on impact later; for now, the presence of the equipment was enough. 

"Save the thoughts for when I ask."

She moved to stand directly behind Ari, close enough that her presence was felt without the touch. She scanned the line of the neck, then the tension in the shoulders. 

"You are ready."

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: I feel a small shiver run down my spine at her proximity. I keep my posture exactly as she corrected it, focusing on the quiet sound of her breathing behind me. "Yes, Maitresse."

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex let the affirmation settle, the hum of compliance filling the space between them. She moved her hand from the neck to the shoulder, a firm press that demanded continued alignment.

"Good," she said. "Now, listen carefully. The protocol is not suggestion; it is the frame. You do not break frame without cause."

She lifted the baton, testing the balance one more time before letting it rest against her leg. Her eyes remained fixed, unreadable and focused.

"I have your attention," she stated. "That is sufficient."

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: By the time she's finished with the rope I'm already past composure, and she hasn't done anything to me yet that I would have to explain to anyone.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex noted the shift in Ari's breathing, the subtle tremor that betrayed the stillness of the body. She had seen this state before; it was part of the gradient they had agreed upon. She did not soften her expression.

"Composure is not the goal," she stated, stepping around to view Ari's profile without breaking her stance. "Honesty is."

She tapped the baton against her own thigh, the sound sharp in the quiet room. She let the noise hang for a moment, ensuring the rhythm landed.

"You are within limits," she said, her gaze steady. "But you are close to the edge of your structure." She leaned in slightly, close enough to sense the heat of Ari's skin without touching. "If the frame cracks, the scene ends. If the frame holds, we continue."

She waited, allowing the instruction to settle before requesting confirmation.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: I draw a slow breath, holding her gaze as much as I dare. "The frame is holding, Maitresse."

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex accepted the affirmation without visible reaction, treating it as a necessary checkpoint rather than a concession. She did not offer praise; confirmation was the only currency required at this stage.

She lifted the baton from the table, the weight familiar in her palm. She let the tip hover just above the line of Ari’s spine, not touching, but defining the boundary.

"Then we proceed," she said. Her voice remained level, stripped of unnecessary inflection. "The structure is intact. The edge is acknowledged."

She shifted her stance, aligning herself with the rhythm of the room. "You will maintain the position. You will not anticipate the next action. You will simply endure it."

She brought the baton up, pausing mid-air to let the implication settle. "Green means go. Green means you trust the frame. Do not test it now."

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: She takes her time and I lose track of how long, until I'm shaking against the restraints and asking out loud for something I'd normally make her get out of me.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex halted the movement of the baton, letting the momentum die in her hand. She turned fully to face Ari, noting the tremors that ran through the restraints and the unscripted plea hanging in the air. The request was outside the parameters of the negotiation, a deviation from the agreed structure.

"You are speaking," she said, her tone devoid of anger but heavy with consequence. "You were instructed to endure. You were instructed not to anticipate." She took a measured step closer, her shadow falling over Ari without touching. "That request is not on the checklist. You know the protocol."

She lowered the baton to her side, resting it against her thigh. Her gaze remained steady, searching for a distinction between need and want. "If the scene is no longer working, use the safeword. If you are asking to override the agreement, the answer is no." She paused, allowing the silence to press against the room. "Decide. Then speak again."

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: I close my eyes, focusing through the haze. "No safeword," I say, my voice steadier now. "Just... forgot myself for a moment. I'm back."

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex held the silence a moment longer, weighing the admission. She observed the shift in breathing, the recentering of the posture. It was a reset.

“Understood,” she said. Her voice remained even. “Forgetting happens. Correction is the work.”

She lifted the baton again, the motion deliberate. She let the tip hover near the shoulder line, a reminder of the boundary.

“Reset the frame,” she instructed. “Shoulders down. Breath even. Silence unless spoken to.”

She waited for the stillness to return. When it did, she stepped in. The baton made contact, a single, firm tap against the leather of the cuff, testing the stability of the restraints.

“We continue,” she said. “Do not make me ask again.”

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: "More," I say, using the exact phrase we agreed on for it. "All of it. Say the things you say and don't soften them." My safeword is right there and I don't want it.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex processed the demand, weighing it against the signed limits. It fell within the negotiated parameters, a specific allowance for escalation. She did not offer praise for the request; compliance was the only requirement.

She shifted her weight, stepping into Ari's peripheral vision. Her voice lost its neutral cadence, taking on the sharp edge agreed upon. "You asked for the full measure," she said. "Do not expect me to ration it."

She lifted the baton, letting the tip point toward the floor. "You are here because I allow it. You hold position because I instruct it." She moved closer, her presence heavy in the small space. "Your thoughts belong to the scene. Your comfort belongs to me."

She waited a beat, letting the words anchor. "Keep your eyes down. Speak only when told. This is not a negotiation anymore. This is work."

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: I let my gaze drop to the floor, a full-body tremor running through me at the shift in her voice. "Yes, Maitresse." The words come out rough, but clear.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex let the confirmation stand. It was a contract reaffirmed. She shifted her weight, the sound of her movement deliberate.

"Good," she said. The word lacked warmth. It was a marker of compliance.

She moved close enough to catch the scent of Ari’s tension. "You are here because you need the order," she said, her voice shifting into the sharper register agreed upon. "You are here because you cannot hold yourself together without it."

She pressed the barrel of the baton lightly against the side of Ari’s neck. A measure of pulse. A reminder of proximity.

"Look at you. Shaking. Begging for the weight you cannot carry." She leaned down, her words landing like physical weight near Ari’s ear. "Take the position. Take the silence. Take what I give you."

She straightened, withdrawing the baton. "Now. Hold. And do not break."

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: I'm past words that aren't the agreed ones and she knows it. "Green," I get out, when she checks. (OOC: don't fade or skip -- write the scene through.)

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex took the colour as confirmation, not a request. She did not smile. She did not soften. "Green," she repeated, the word final. She raised the baton, the weight of it settling into her grip. She had chosen the target already: the muscle of the thigh, where the impact would resonate without leaving a mark that could not be explained.

"This is the work," she said, her voice dropping to that low, flat register. "You do not own the pain. You do not own the silence. You own the stillness."

She drew the baton back. She did not hesitate. The first strike landed, sharp and measured. "Take it," she ordered. "Breathe. Hold the frame."

She waited, watching the ripple of reaction through the restraints, ensuring the structure held before she moved again. She let the silence stretch, allowing the echo of the impact to settle in the room. "Again," she said. "I did not say stop."

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: The breath hisses out of me, my whole body tightening against the impact. I force my muscles to release, holding the stillness she demanded. "Yes, Maitresse."

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex observed the exhale, the way Ari’s body tightened then released on command. It was adequate. She did not linger on praise; praise was a reward, and this was simply baseline function. She stepped in, her boots silent on the rug, close enough to feel the heat radiating from Ari’s skin.

"Breathe," she ordered, the command sharp. "Do not hold it."

She raised the baton again. The rhythm was key. Too fast was chaotic; too slow was cruel. She aimed for the same muscle group, the one designed to take the weight. The strike landed with a solid thud, deeper than the first.

"That is where you belong," she said, her voice low and even. "Held. Used. Silent."

She watched the reaction, waiting for the tremor to pass, for the structure to reassert itself. She did not move away. She remained in the space of authority, letting the silence stretch until it pressed against the ears.

"Again," she said, raising the weapon. "Stay present."

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: I jerk hard against the cuffs, a choked sound escaping before I clamp my jaw shut. The pain blooms, deep and hot, and I focus on the cold floor under my knees. "Still here," I manage to whisper.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex noted the tremor in the leather, observing the breach in stillness without rising. "You flinched," she stated, her voice devoid of judgment. "But you did not break." She stepped closer, placing a palm flat against the shoulder blade to anchor the posture. The weight was heavy, grounding, forcing the spine to align against the restraints.

"Hold," she commanded, withdrawing her hand. "Do not fight the weight. Let it settle." She lifted the baton, measuring the distance with the same precision she applied to the rest of the protocol. "You asked for this specific measure. Do not shy from the consequence."

She paused, letting the air thicken in the space between them. When the silence held, she brought the baton down again, the impact resonating through the room. "Breathe," she ordered. "Stay present. Tell me when you can speak."

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: I breathe through the sting, forcing my lungs to work evenly. "I can speak, Maitresse," I say, my voice steadier than I feel. "The frame is holding."
