dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
The salle had emptied an hour ago and Corvo was still there, because of course he was, rewrapping a grip that did not need rewrapping.

"Three-two," he said, without looking up. "I want it on record that the third was generous."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: "It's on record that you were slow," I say, and drop my bag next to his.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo set the foil down with the care of a man composing himself, which he was, badly.

"Slow." He finally looked up, and there was the grin, the one he'd spent four years sharpening. "I gave you that touch out of charity. Pity point. It was getting embarrassing watching you lunge at air."

He nodded at the bag, landed next to his like it belonged there.

"You're staying, then." Not a question. He'd learned long ago not to hand Reyes anything that could be parried. He leaned back against the bench, arms crossed, and let the silence do some of the work for once. "Most people who lose three-two have the decency to storm out. Preserve the narrative."

The salle lights hummed. Half of them were off already, the far end of the strip gone dark, and Corvo made no move toward the switches.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: "Charity," I repeat, unzipping my bag and pulling out my water bottle. "Right. Because you're known for your kindness." I take a long drink, then wipe my mouth with the back of my hand. "And I'm not most people."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo's grin held a second longer than it should have, and then it didn't.

"No," he said. "You're not."

He pushed off the bench and crossed the strip — not toward the switches, not toward the door. Into Reyes's measure, and stopped at the distance he'd spent four years keeping: close enough to touch, far enough to call it fencing. Up close, the banter came slower. He'd built the whole edifice of this rivalry at arm's length, and it turned out arm's length had been load-bearing.

"Four years," he said. "You've never once stormed out. I've checked. I've *given* you reasons." A beat. "I keep giving you reasons."

It cost him, visibly, and he let it. The only way he'd ever learned to offer anything was with the blade still in it.

"So here's the record, since we're keeping one." His voice had dropped, quieter than the hum of the lights. "Three-two. And I've been losing the whole time."

He didn't reach. He had never once handed Reyes anything that could be parried, and he wasn't starting now — but he stood there, inside the distance, and left the line open.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I take the grip out of his hands and put it down, and I don't step back afterwards. "You've been slow all evening," I say.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo looked down at his hands. Empty. He'd been holding something for four years — a foil, a grip, the next thing to say — and Reyes had simply taken it out of them and set it down, and now there was nothing left between him and the last half-meter of air.

"Slow," he said. He'd been using the word as a blade all evening. It came back different. It came back as an instruction.

"Four years slow." A breath that was almost a laugh, with nothing funny in it. "I rewrapped that grip twice. It didn't need it. I needed a reason to still be here after everyone left." He'd already said the true thing once tonight; apparently the record could hold two. "You've been the reason for a while."

Then he stopped talking, because Reyes had called it — *all evening, slow* — and Corvo was not going to be slow anymore.

He closed the last of the distance, the step he'd been not-taking since the first match, the one every retreat had been measured against, and kissed Reyes. Carefully, at first — the way he'd fenced the opening period, reading the measure, giving the touch its due. Then the way he'd fenced the third: like losing was acceptable, like the touch was worth it, like four years of footwork had all been approach. His hand came up to the edge of Reyes's jaw and held there, steady as his grip never was on the strip.

When he finally broke, it was by centimeters. Enough to breathe. Not enough to call it a retreat.

"For the record," he said, unsteady, "fastest thing I've done all night." A beat. The grin tried to come back and didn't quite make it. "Your tempo from here. I'm done setting it."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I don't move, just let his hand stay where it is. "Four years slow," I say, voice lower than I mean it to be. "But you got here."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
"But you got here."

Four words, and they landed the way touches were supposed to land and never had — no parry available, no riposte worth the attempt. Corvo had come prepared for the ledger. Four wasted years, itemized, held over him the way he'd been holding three-two over Reyes for the last hour. He'd have welcomed it, almost. He knew how to fence that bout.

Reyes declined to fence it.

"You're supposed to make me pay for that," he said. "That's the convention. I've been dining out on three-two for an hour and it was going to sustain me for *months*." His thumb moved once along Reyes's jaw, a small stroke, testing whether the permission held. It was his hand that was unsteady now. On the strip it never was. "Four years is a long time to be slow. I had reasons. None of them were good."

He'd meant to stop there. The record apparently had room for one more.

"I kept telling myself next match. Next tournament. Next—" He shook his head, once. "Four years of *next*."

Then, because he was Corvo, and the only language he'd ever fully trusted was the one with a scoreboard: "Rematch." Quiet, but it carried the weight of a challenge, which was the only weight he knew how to give things. "Same time tomorrow. I'll be faster. I'll be so fast you'll think tonight was a different man." The grin came back, and this time it made it — softer than the one he'd spent four years sharpening, and worth more. "Best of seven. Best of seventy. I'm not particular."

He didn't kiss Reyes again. He'd ceded the tempo and he meant it — so he stayed where he was, a breath out, hand still at Reyes's jaw, and did the hardest thing he'd done all evening.

He waited.

"Your attack," he said. "Right of way's yours. Has been for a while."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: We get as far as the changing-room bench and not one step further. Kit goes on the floor, both of ours, and neither of us is being quiet about it.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Four years of *next*, and it came down to a bench too narrow for footwork and the sound of two kits hitting the floor like disarmed blades.

Corvo had imagined this — the record could hold that too — and in every version he'd been smooth. Unhurried. Devastating, probably. The reality was his hands unsteady on Reyes's belt and not one word in his head that wasn't *finally, finally*.

"For the record—" he started, and lost the sentence against Reyes's mouth, and decided the record could survive without it.

The bench was too narrow. He'd sat on it a hundred times rewrapping grips that didn't need rewrapping, and it had never once occurred to him that the narrowness was a feature. It was a feature. There was no room to retreat. Four years of giving ground an inch at a time so it never read as fleeing, and the bench simply did not permit it — nowhere to go but against Reyes, skin to skin, and Corvo pressed in like a man making up for a lost war.

He'd ceded the tempo. He meant to honor that, he did. It lasted until Reyes touched him, and then every intention he had went out of him in a sound he'd have denied under oath — had spent four years denying, in a sense, every time he'd called this anything but what it was.

"Okay," he said, against Reyes's shoulder, his collarbone, whatever was closest. "Okay. Your tempo. I'm being very good about it. That should go on the record too."

He was not being very good about it. His hands were everywhere, greedy, mapping what four years of lamé and plastron had kept from him, and he kept stopping — going still with his palms flat against Reyes's skin like a man checking a pulse, like he needed the proof. Warm. Real. Here.

"You've been under all that kit this whole time," he said, and it came out wondering instead of clever, and he let it. "I fenced you in November. It was freezing. You were like this under three layers and I *still* lost the third period." His grip tightened. "I'm owed a rematch of November."

Then there was no more record, no more November — or the banter was still there but it had gone to single words, to Reyes's name, to *yes* and *there* and *don't you dare stop*, the vocabulary of a man finally fighting the bout he'd actually wanted. Corvo, who narrated everything, who had a line prepared for every touch ever scored against him, went quiet except for what he couldn't help. He couldn't help much of it. The empty salle heard all of it. He found he didn't care about that either.

He'd said it on the strip and he meant it more now, with the bench hard under him and four years collapsing into minutes: losing was acceptable. Losing was *wonderful*, provided it was close — and this was as close as anything got. He gave ground. He took it back. Everywhere Reyes went, he went, answering, offering, a bout with no referee and no clock and both of them finally, finally fencing to win the same touch.

"Reyes." His voice had gone ragged, all the polish stripped off it, and he got a hand up into Reyes's hair and held on like the strip was tilting. "Listen — the record —" A breath, a laugh, something between. "I'm close. I'm so — four years and you're going to finish me in *minutes*, I'm never going to hear the end of it, I'm going to have to retire —"

He broke off, pressed his forehead to Reyes's, and laughed again, helpless, wrecked, happier than he'd ever once allowed himself to be in this building.

"Your tempo," he managed. "Still yours. Finish it."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content:
My hand slides into his hair, pulling him in until there's no space left. "Took you long enough," I breathe against his mouth, voice rough.

The record can wait. The score can burn. I move against him, a final lunge that feels less like a touch and more like a surrender — on both sides.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
"Took you long enough."

Corvo had a reply for that. He had replies stockpiled — four years of them, sharpened, catalogued, ready. What came out was a laugh that broke in the middle, because Reyes was right, and Reyes being right had never felt like *this* — and then it didn't matter, because the last lunge landed and took them both.

He'd said losing was wonderful, provided it was close. He'd had no idea.

It went through him like a touch he'd been waiting four years to take — no parry, no riposte, no ground left to give and no interest in giving it. He said Reyes's name, or tried to; it came apart somewhere in the middle. His hand tightened in Reyes's hair, his forehead pressed hard against Reyes's, and the record, the score, three-two, November — all of it burned exactly as invited. Corvo, who narrated everything, who had never once in his life let a touch go unremarked, said nothing at all. There was nothing in his vocabulary that covered it.

Afterwards, the salle lights hummed. The bench was still too narrow. He stayed exactly where he was, tangled and wrecked and breathing Reyes's air, waiting for his heart rate to come down out of the red. It showed no intention of doing so.

"For the record," he said finally, hoarse, "minutes. You finished me in *minutes*." A breath that was almost a laugh. "I want it noted that I lasted four years before that. That's endurance. That's *athleticism*. The minutes were a tactical choice."

He didn't move. Storming out was the convention — he'd said so himself, an eternity ago, out on the strip — and he discovered he had no interest in the convention. His thumb moved once along Reyes's jaw, the same small stroke as before, checking whether the permission held. It held.

"Tomorrow," he said. "Same time. I'll bring—" He stopped. The grin came back, softer than the one he'd spent four years sharpening, and worth more. "Nothing. I'll bring nothing. I'm done holding things."

A beat. His voice dropped, quieter than the lights.

"For the record. I'd have waited longer. I'm glad I didn't have to."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I get him flat on the bench and take my time about it with my mouth, which is the first thing all evening he hasn't had an answer for.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo had a line prepared. He had a line prepared for everything — he'd been preparing lines for four years — and he got as far as "For the—" before Reyes's mouth closed over him and the line, the ledger, the entire archive went up in smoke.

The sound he made was not a word. It had never been a word, in any language he knew.

His hands — he'd said he was done holding things, and now they had nothing to hold and no idea what to do about it — found the edge of the bench and gripped it like a man holding onto a strip that had started to tilt. White knuckles. His grip, his famous grip, the thing four years of fencing had never once loosened, gone to pieces in under a minute.

"Reyes." It came out wrecked. "Reyes, that's — you can't — the *tempo* —"

The tempo was slow. Reyes was taking their time, and the slowness was the cruelty of it, the patience, the unhurried, devastating — Corvo had called Reyes slow tonight, on the strip, as an insult, and this was the rebuttal, administered at a pace designed to prove that slow was a weapon and Reyes had been holding it the whole time.

He tried to lift his head — to watch, to keep some kind of record, because he was Corvo and he kept records — and what he saw undid him so completely that his head dropped back against the bench with a sound he'd deny under oath. He'd deny all of this under oath. The record was burning. Let it.

Four years. He'd studied Reyes's game the way he studied everything — obsessively, competitively, with an eye toward the weakness he could exploit — and not once, in four years of footage, had *this* come up. There was no parry. There was no parry because no one had ever — he'd never scouted — "Oh," he said, which was the entirety of his analysis. "Oh, that's — don't stop. Don't you *dare*. I will actually die. Put it on the record. Cause of death—"

He lost the sentence. He lost several sentences. Corvo, who narrated everything, who had a line for every touch ever scored against him, was reduced to single syllables and Reyes's name, Reyes's name, Reyes's name, like it was the only word he'd ever bothered learning.

His hand found Reyes's hair — not pushing, he'd ceded the tempo and he'd honor it if it killed him, and it was going to kill him — just holding on, fingers curled, while the bout he'd spent four years not fencing got finished without him.

"Reyes — I'm — you should—" The warning came out strangled, and went the way of all his warnings tonight, and that was it. That was the touch. The one he'd been waiting four years to take — no parry, no riposte, no ground left to give, and no interest in giving it.

It took him apart. Thoroughly. At Reyes's pace, not his — which was the whole point, which had maybe always been the whole point. He said something. It wasn't a word. The empty salle heard it anyway.

After: the lights hummed. The bench was still too narrow. Corvo lay flat on it with one arm over his face, breathing like he'd just gone fifteen touches, and laughed — helpless, wrecked, happier than he'd ever allowed himself to be in this building. Which was becoming a pattern.

"I concede," he said, hoarse, to the ceiling. "For the record. First time in four years I've said it and meant it. No rematch. No appeal. Take the bout. Take the — everything. It's yours. It was yours in November."

He moved the arm. Looked down the length of himself at Reyes, and the grin came back — softer than the one he'd spent four years sharpening, and worth more.

"Come up here," he said. "I've been informed I'm slow. I intend to spend the rest of the night disproving it."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I push myself up, bracing a hand on the bench by his hip. "Disprove it, then," I say, and lean down to kiss him again, slow and deliberate. "Starting now."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
The kiss was slow and deliberate, and Corvo received it the way he'd received everything Reyes had given him tonight — as a challenge. Which it was. *Disprove it. Starting now.*

Something turned over in him. The engine that four years of rivalry had built — the thing that got him up off the bench after every lost touch, hungrier — caught, and caught fire.

He kissed back. Answered it. And somewhere in the middle of it the balance shifted: his hand firmed, his other arm braced, and he *moved*. The bench did its part, which was to say it refused to. There was no graceful way to reverse two people on eighteen inches of wood and they did not find one — a knee went somewhere unfortunate, kit shifted underfoot, Corvo laughed into Reyes's mouth and did not apologize — and then Reyes was where he had been, flat on the too-narrow bench, and Corvo was looking down at him.

Four years of footage. None of it had looked like this.

"Same bench," he said. "Same terms."

He braced a hand by Reyes's shoulder — the mirror of it, he knew it was the mirror, he'd planned none of it and it was coming out symmetrical anyway, like a bout called by a referee with a sense of irony — and put on the face Reyes had seen across the strip a hundred times. The half-second before his best touches. It had never once been aimed like this.

"The record shows you're ahead. Two to one." His voice went low, the polish back and gone again inside a single sentence. "I have never once let a deficit stand. Ask anyone who's fenced me. I don't lose bouts — I run out of time." A beat. "There's no clock tonight."

His hand moved — mapping, greedy, flat against Reyes's skin like before, checking the pulse of it, needing the proof.

"Four years I've studied your game. Every tell. Every opening." His grip tightened. "And I don't know anything. You're new. All of this is—" He gave the sentence up. "I'm going to have to rewatch everything."

Then he got lower, unhurried, and looked up the length of Reyes the way Reyes had looked up at him — and if he'd learned one thing tonight, one thing administered at a pace designed to prove that slow was a weapon, it was this.

"You called me slow. I'm about to disprove it." His breath came warm and unsteady. "It's going to take a while. That's the disproof."

And he set about it.

He was good at this. He'd have said so — did say so, at some point, in so many words, muffled and unrepentant — but mostly he was *interested* at this, which had always been the real engine. Corvo did nothing at half-measure, and he had four years of wanting stored up like a lunge held too long in check. He read Reyes the way he read opponents — obsessively, competitively, with an eye toward the opening — and every hitch of breath went into the record. Every one. He was keeping score with a devotion that would have embarrassed him if he'd had any embarrassment left. He'd conceded it earlier, wrecked and laughing, and he conceded it again now with his mouth full: *it's yours, it was yours in November.*

He took Reyes to the edge the way he'd been taken there — patiently, devastatingly, at a tempo that was itself an argument — and then, at the edge, he stopped.

Looked up. The strip face was gone. What was underneath it was wrecked and fond and entirely unguarded, and he didn't bother putting anything over it.

"Prêt?" he said, hoarse.

The referee's question. The one asked before every bout, before every decisive phrase — the one he'd answered ten thousand times without thinking, the one he'd never once in his life waited to have answered.

He waited.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: "Prove the point properly," he says, "or concede," so I pin his wrists to the bench and stop letting him set the pace, which is exactly what he was asking for.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo's laugh cracked out of him the moment his wrists hit the bench — one startled note, gone almost at once, because there was no air left for laughing. There was no air left for anything.

He'd asked *prêt*. Ten thousand times, ask and answer, and never once in his life had he waited on the reply. The reply was this: no answer at all. Straight to *allez*. Direct attack, no preparation — four years of footage and Reyes had never once fenced him like this, and Corvo understood, pinned and breathless and already lost, that this was what he'd been asking for. He'd thought *prêt* was him requesting permission to finish Reyes. Four years underneath, it had been a different question entirely: *take it out of my hands. I've never once been able to put it down myself.*

Reyes took it out of his hands.

He tested the hold once. Once. Not to break it — he'd have died first — but the way he tested everything: the bench, the measure, four years of arm's length. To *know*. It held. His famous grip, the thing four years of fencing had never loosened, opened empty against the wood and stayed there, palm-up, disarmed, and something in Corvo that had been braced since the first match went quietly, completely slack.

He'd said he was done holding things. Reyes had taken him at his word.

"Corps-à-corps," he got out, wrecked. "Referee calls it. Separates us. Starts the phrase over." A breath that broke in the middle. "There's no referee."

There was no referee. There was no clock. The pace was Reyes's now, and it wasn't slow — that was the thing, he'd been braced for the administered patience, the slow weapon turned back on him, and instead Reyes set a tempo like a fencer who'd spent four years scouting him and knew where every opening was. Knew better than Corvo did. Corvo, who studied everything, who kept a dossier on every opponent he'd ever faced, discovered his own openings one after another, called out in a voice he didn't recognize as his.

He narrated everything. He had a line for every touch ever scored against him. What he had now: Reyes's name. *Yes. There. Don't stop.* And once — it would never make the record, he'd deny it under oath, he was getting to be quite accomplished at denying things under oath — *please*.

His back came off the bench. The bench permitted no retreat; he'd called its narrowness a feature an eternity ago and it was a feature still, nowhere to go, nowhere to be but exactly here, held down and taken apart at someone else's tempo. And Corvo — who had spent four years giving ground an inch at a time so it never read as fleeing — gave all of it at once. Everything. The ground, the tempo, the score. He'd have given the salle. He'd have given November.

"Reyes—" The warning, such as it was. It went the way of every warning he'd given tonight.

The touch went through him the way the first one had, except the first one he'd at least had his hands free for. This one he took empty-handed, pinned, nowhere to put any of it, and it lasted — it lasted, or he did, or Reyes did; the record on that point was never going to be straightened out.

After: the lights hummed. The bench was still too narrow. His wrists were free — had been free a while, he realized — and they stayed where they'd been put, flat against the wood, pinned by nothing at all.

Corvo looked at his own empty hands. Then he moved them — the first thing he'd moved — and got them into Reyes's hair, around Reyes's shoulders, pulled him down into the space there wasn't room for and held on. He'd said he was done holding things. He'd been wrong. There was exactly one thing worth holding, he'd spent four years not holding it, and he intended to make up the difference.

"For the record," he said, hoarse, into Reyes's hair, "I've lost count." A laugh, wrecked and wondering. "Three-two, I said. I wanted it on the record. The record's a shambles. I don't know the score. First time in my life I don't know the score." His grip tightened. "Keep it that way."

The engine turned over once — the one that got him up off the bench after every lost touch, hungrier — and he let it idle. Tomorrow. Rematches were a tomorrow thing.

"Touché," he said.

No argument attached. No *debatable*. No request for the replay. The oldest word in the sport, four years in the waiting, said bare and meant entirely — the first honest scorekeeping of his life.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I let him pull me down, my face pressed against his neck. "Took you long enough to say it," I murmur, breathing him in. "Touché."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
The word, given back — Reyes's breath warm against his neck — went through him like the first touch had, and Corvo laughed, helpless, one arm tightening around Reyes's shoulders like the strip was tilting again.

"A double," he said, wondering. "You know what that makes tonight. Épée rules. Both touches count." His hand moved once down Reyes's back, slow, mapping nothing, needing the proof. "Four years of foil. Right of way, priority, whose attack it was — and the whole time the answer was hitting each other at the same moment. We were fencing the wrong weapon."

A beat.

"I said it first, though. That one word — priority's mine. I'll fight the whole sport over it."

Then, quieter, because Reyes had said *took you long enough*, and Reyes was right, and Reyes being right had never once felt like this:

"I've said it ten thousand times. Since I was nineteen. It's supposed to cost something — that's the entire point of the word — and it never cost me anything until tonight." He turned his head, put his mouth against Reyes's hair. "I was saving it. Four years and I didn't know that's what I was doing."

The lights hummed. Somewhere in the building a pipe knocked. The salle had gone cold the way salles did once the bodies stopped moving, and his kit was on the floor where it had been thrown, and the keys were in his jacket and his jacket was across the room and the distance might as well have been miles.

"For the record: three periods tonight. Lost all three." The grin, against Reyes's hair. "Best bout of my life. And next month, at the invitational, when the referee asks me *prêt*, I am going to think about this bench and lose the first period laughing. I'll drop the second too. Doesn't worry me." A breath. "I like my chances in the third."

His thumb moved once along Reyes's jaw — the small stroke, the old check — and for the first time he wasn't asking anything. It held. He'd stopped needing to verify that it would.

"In a minute," he said, to the ceiling, to no one. "We're moving in a minute."

The minute could stretch. Four years had taught him patience — or something that wore patience's clothes — and there was nowhere to be but here, and the bench was too narrow, and that was a feature.

"For the record—" he started, and stopped, and let it go.

First time in his life he'd let the record keep itself.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: Neither of us is quiet and neither of us cares who locks up. "Don't stop," he says, for once not arguing. (OOC: write the scene through, no fade.)

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
"Don't stop."

Four years of argument, and it was the first instruction Reyes had ever given him that Corvo took without a counter. That should have gone on the record. The record was a shambles. Enter it anyway: *exhibit, the night Corvo stopped arguing.*

He'd have said as much — he had the breath for it, briefly — but Reyes's hand was in his hair and the tempo was not his and he'd been given an order, and Corvo, who had never once in his life followed an order he hadn't issued, spent one whole second discovering the difference between obedience and agreement.

He agreed. He agreed completely.

"Remise," he said, against Reyes's skin. "Renewal of the attack. Same opening, second action. It's in the rules." His breath came warm and unsteady. "Everything I'm about to do is in the rules."

Then he stopped talking, which was itself a kind of record.

Neither of them was quiet. The empty salle threw it back at them off the mirrors, off the high ceiling, a bout with an echo for a referee, and Corvo thought, with the last coherent corner of his mind: *the acoustics in here are excellent, I have never once appreciated the acoustics—*

Then the corner went dark too.

Corvo, who narrated everything, who had never once let a touch go unrecorded, let one whole block go by unremarked.

It kept anyway.

"Please," she whimpered, her voice raw, her fingers clutching at Fen’s shirt as if she could pull them even closer, as if she could *merge* with them if she tried hard enough. "Fen, *please*." The word tore from her, desperate and needy, and she didn’t even care how wrecked she sounded. Not when Fen’s hands were finally—*finally*—doing exactly what she’d been begging for.
